# NICCOLÒ MASSA’S
# MEDICAL
## EPISTLES
## VOLUME ONE,

IN WHICH ARE TREATED THOSE MATTERS WHICH
seem to pertain both to medical Theory and Practice, and which also contain questions concerning the immortality of Souls, the creation of the World, and the faculty of Logic. <note>Niccolò Massa (1485–1569) was a prominent Venetian physician. This volume reflects the Renaissance ideal of the "physician-philosopher," combining practical medical advice with deep philosophical inquiries into the nature of the soul and the universe.</note>

TO THIS SECOND EDITION HAVE BEEN ADDED SEVERAL EPISTLES, OR CONSULTATIONS, WHICH had not been published before; especially a short work on the plague that troubled the city of VENICE in the year 1556. <note>Medical "consultations" were formal letters written by doctors to colleagues or patients regarding specific cases, serving as a primary way medical knowledge was shared before the era of modern journals.</note>

->With grace and privilege.<- <note>original: "Cum gratia & priuilegio." This indicates that the printer had been granted exclusive rights to publish this work by the Venetian Senate, a precursor to modern copyright.</note>

# NICOLAUS RANTANA
## *The Brazilian, to the reader.* <note>original: "Brasiliehensis." This is a fascinating geographical designation for 1558. While it literally translates as "of Brazil," it is exceptionally early for a literary credit to a Brazilian; it may alternatively be a rare variant spelling for a European city like Basel (usually Basiliensis) or Bratislava (Bratislaviensis).</note>

<margin>E. N. 3. 2.</margin> <note>This alphanumeric code is likely a library shelf mark or an old inventory number from a historical collection.</note>
> *Whoever desires to learn the hidden secrets of sacred medicine,*
> *let him take up this present, useful work.*
> *The Goddess's arrows and the threats of the heavens are now in vain,* <note>original: "Irrita tela Deæ sunt iam, cœliq́;, minæq́;". The "arrows of the Goddess" (likely referring to Diana) and "threats of the sky" (astrological omens) were common metaphors for the sudden and seemingly random strike of diseases like the plague.</note>
> *since here is the wisdom that may relieve every ill.*

->[A faded heraldic emblem is centered on the page. It features a decorative shield, though the specific details are obscured by time and the transparency of the paper. A star or sun motif is faintly visible at the center of the shield.]<-

<note>The text is written in elegiac couplets, a classical form of Latin poetry consisting of alternating lines of dactylic hexameter and pentameter. This style was frequently used by Renaissance humanists to lend an air of authority and elegance to scientific works. The "q́;" symbols seen in the original are standard scribal abbreviations for "que" (meaning "and").</note>

<summary>This page contains a short, four-line Latin poem by Nicolaus Rantana praising the medical wisdom of Niccolò Massa. The verse frames the book as a vital tool for overcoming the "divine" or "heavenly" threats of disease and plague.</summary>
<keywords>Nicolaus Rantana, Brazil, medical poetry, elegiac couplets, Renaissance medicine, disease metaphors, 16th-century printing</keywords>

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST SERENE,
## Sacred Queen of Poland, Lady Bona Sforza of Aragon, 
## Grace and Ornament of the World, Nicolaus Massa 
## sends his greatest greetings and wishes her a 
## Nestor-like life and happiness.
<note>original: "nestoreamq́; vitam." A reference to Nestor, the legendary Greek hero of the Iliad known for his great wisdom and for living through three generations of men; thus, Massa is wishing the Queen an exceptionally long life.</note>

<note>The following paragraph begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a scholar at a desk with a globe.</note>

MOST ILLUSTRIOUS QUEEN, our ancestors were accustomed—as they handed their work down to posterity—to greatly commend it to the patronage of some prince of their own times. This practice (which in my opinion is worthy of nothing but praise) has continued down to our own age. They did this especially for the reason that they believed their labors and sleepless nights, if fortified by some favor, would live for an everlasting (so to speak) time, and bring utility and benefit. 

For this reason, since I have decided—on account of the excessive pleas of certain scholars—to bring to light several letters which I had written at various times to absent friends, regarding medicine as well as philosophy and logic <term>dialectica<span>the art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions</span></term>, it seemed right to me to commend them to you, most illustrious Queen, so that they might not lack a patron and protector. 

For when I enumerate the greatest and most sacred kings of our times, I truly find no one to whom I might more safely entrust the defense of this work of mine than to you. Indeed, you far excel all others, both in blood and lineage, as well as in the gifts of mind and body. 

For who does not know the Sforza family? Who does not know your father, Gian Galeazzo Maria Sforza <note>original: "Ioannem Mariam Sfortiam"</note>? Who is ignorant of your ancestors Galeazzo and that Francesco, the "pupil of Mars" <note>Francesco Sforza (1401–1466) was a famous mercenary commander and the first Sforza Duke of Milan; "pupil of Mars" refers to his military brilliance.</note> and the glory of all Italy? They achieved almost every kind of virtue. I omit their vigorous deeds, which were nearly innumerable, for this is not the place for such speech. 

I have also deliberately set aside the long and well-known lineage <note>original: "analogiam"</note> of the illustrious kings and dukes of Aragon, and by what forces of arms, virtue, and talent they overcame so many powerful peoples. Furthermore, I have omitted by what right and order they ruled in the Kingdom of Naples and in the Duchy of Milan, and almost throughout all Italy. For many have written of this, and histories everywhere are full of it. But why do I [speak] of your [ancestors' deeds...]

<summary>In this dedication, the Venetian physician Niccolò Massa presents his collection of medical and philosophical letters to Queen Bona Sforza of Poland, praising her illustrious Sforza and Aragon ancestry to secure her royal patronage.</summary>
<keywords>Niccolò Massa, Bona Sforza, Queen of Poland, Sforza family, Francesco Sforza, Medical Letters, Renaissance patronage, Duchy of Milan, Kingdom of Naples</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Queen Bona Sforza. The OCR notes bleed-through from the reverse side and a modern digital watermark, which are ignored in the translation of the historical text.</meta>

...the virtues and deeds of your ancestors: are you not alone sufficient for me? For even if no memory or famous recollection of their own virtue and highest dignity existed—though indeed innumerable examples do exist—certainly in you alone they could all most happily rise again. You are a Queen. You are the wife of a King. You are also the mother of a King. For you have brought forth a son from King Sigismund Jagiello <note>Sigismund I the Old (1467–1548), King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania.</note>, a son who is incomparable whether in his most holy character, his wisdom, or his vigorous pursuit of arms; like a shining Sun, he outshines other illustrious princes (and let this be said without offense to them) in both glory and splendor. 

Truly, in your greatness of soul and sincerity—than which nothing is better—you far surpass all others. Why should I mention your almost divine intellect? For you are exceptionally well-educated in both the <term>humanities<span>the study of classical literature, rhetoric, history, and moral philosophy</span></term> and in heavenly and Christian philosophy. You truly live in such a way that you seem to understand the precepts of Christ perfectly, and you show these things most clearly through your good works. For faith, charity, and divine hope itself flourish abundantly in you and shine most brightly. What shall I say of your most holy character? What of your supreme prudence and your vigilance in difficult matters? I pass over your generosity, which makes princes like God. I pass over your justice and mercy, seen in all things but especially in the pronouncing of civil and—as they say—criminal judgments. 

Good gods! <note>original: "Dii boni"</note> How many things I pass over in my desire for brevity, though they are proclaimed by everyone—especially by the Reverend Lord Francesco Lismanino <note>Francesco Lismanino (c. 1500–1566) was an Italian-born Franciscan and diplomat who became a leading figure in the Polish Reformation.</note>, Master of Sacred Theology and Minister of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note> for all of Poland, whom I wished to name here for the sake of honor. Now, what more should I mention? For if I wished to follow every detail point by point, this speech would be prolonged too far. 

Therefore, all these things have led me, most illustrious Queen, to appoint you as both the patroness and the protectress of this work of mine. I do not doubt that, on account of your supreme kindness and great benevolence toward all those dedicated to learning, you will defend it. If you do this, I hope it will be most pleasing to everyone. Farewell, most splendid Queen, and as is your custom, look with favor upon those who cultivate good literature. 

->**Venice, 1550.**<-
->**The Ides of November.**<- <note>November 13th.</note>

<summary>In this concluding part of the dedication, Niccolò Massa praises Queen Bona Sforza’s family, her education in the humanities, and her Christian virtues, officially naming her the patroness of his medical work.</summary>
<keywords>Bona Sforza, Sigismund Jagiello, Francesco Lismanino, Venice, Poland, Franciscans, medical patronage, Renaissance humanities</keywords>

# TO APOLLONIUS
## MASSA, THE FIRST EPISTLE,

->which is a certain method for curing<-
->specific diseases, and for organizing<-
->all intentions in consultations,<-
->embracing all parts<-
->of medicine.<-

ALTHOUGH I know that you have now for a year been a student of <note>original: "audientem," literally "hearing," commonly used to describe a student attending a master's lectures</note> Auerbach <note>Heinrich Auerbach (1482–1542) was a prominent physician and professor at the University of Leipzig, famously associated with Auerbach's Cellar.</note>, a most learned man and one who provides outstanding healing to the sick in Leipzig: who, since he is a man of learning and most fond of me, will instruct you at all times in civil manners and the precepts of medicine, so that you can desire nothing beyond your own diligence and study: especially since there you are able to learn appropriately, along with philosophical and medical instructions, also those things which relate to the elegance of the Latin language: especially because you have the most learned Philipp Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a leading German reformer and scholar, known for his vast influence on the educational systems of the time.</note>, who is fond of you: nevertheless, so that you may emerge even more learned through my own studies and labors, I shall write to you—in order to comply with your request—those things concerning the method of healing which you sought in your letters regarding this particular work. 

<margin>Method of proceeding</margin>
Furthermore, these things you must learn will be like a sort of artificial memory <term>artificial memory: a system of mnemonic techniques or structured frameworks used by Renaissance scholars to organize and recall vast amounts of information</term>: since they contain a concise method, first for recognizing illnesses, causes, and symptoms <note>original: "accidentia," refers to clinical signs or "accidents" of a disease that happen to the patient</note>, and soon after for predicting the outcome of the disease: and for correctly providing help to the sick through contraries <note>The Galenic principle of "contraries," where a "hot" disease is treated with "cold" remedies, and vice versa.</note>, and for teaching how to care for the removal of the cause. Indeed, true cure is the removal of the cause, according to the opinion of Galen in the 22nd commentary on the second section of the Aphorisms <note>This refers to Galen’s influential commentary on the "Aphorisms" of Hippocrates, which served as a primary medical textbook for centuries.</note>. Truly, these things will not only serve for illnesses, causes, symptoms, prediction, and the method of correct healing, but they will also be of the greatest help in organizing intentions <note>In Renaissance medicine, "intentions" are the specific clinical goals a physician sets to restore a patient's health.</note>—both speculative and those pertaining to treatment—within the colleges or discussions which [take place] between Me- <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword "Me-", likely continuing with "Medicos" (physicians) on the following page.</note>

<summary>This opening letter to the student Apollonius Massa establishes the work's purpose: to provide a systematic method for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment based on Galenic principles. The author notes the student's prestigious education in Leipzig under figures like Heinrich Auerbach and Philipp Melanchthon.</summary>
<keywords>Apollonius Massa, Heinrich Auerbach, Leipzig, Philipp Melanchthon, Galen, medical method, diagnosis, prognosis, therapeutics, artificial memory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "First Epistle" to Apollonius. The opening word "dicos" completes "medicos" (physicians/medical) from the previous page's transition.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE

medical <note>original: "medicos," continuing from the previous page</note> treatments are usually held, in arduous and difficult diseases, since they contain all the necessary primary medical **intentions** <term>intentions: "intentiones" in Renaissance medicine refers to the specific therapeutic goals or plans a physician forms to treat a patient</term> in order, according to the intention of the most learned Princes of Medicine, and especially **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and **Avicenna**: I would therefore have you commit these to your memory by reading them very frequently: when you are free from public lectures and desire to reason with me (as you write). Nor would I wish for these words to be thought of as spoken arrogantly by you—namely, that in this one Epistle you can speak fearlessly, aptly, distinctly, ornately, and learnedly about all medical intentions among the most learned physicians, if you are ever called to speak to those illustrious Princes and Nobles, especially if you wish to apply to them those things which you learn in daily studies and readings of both Galen and also Avicenna. I want you to be urged never to set aside these two most eminent authors. And, so that you may have that which you write you desire with all your mind, [I provide it] through a way, or **Method** shown with brevity, by which you may recognize affections contrary to nature <term>affections contrary to nature: "affectus praeter naturam," a standard term for diseases or pathological states</term>, and restore men so affected to a natural habit <note>i.e., a state of health</note>, where the thing is possible: but if they cannot be restored to health at all, at least you should know how to predict future outcomes from these, so they may know you lack no part of the medical art, which can perform things not repugnant to nature. Now receive the summary of the proposed matter, divided into two parts: for

<margin>Introduction</margin> one of the parts looks toward the knowledge and prediction of the disease, while the other teaches the rational cure. You must understand the first part through the diligent knowledge of **ten things**. 

The **first** of these is the disease and its essence: The **second** is the cause: The **third** is the accidents, or Symptoms: The **fourth** is the temperament: The **fifth** is the Power, or Powers <note>original: "Virtus," referring to the vital, natural, or animal faculties of the body</note>: The **sixth** is age: The **seventh** is sex: The **eighth** is custom <note>or habit/lifestyle</note>: The **ninth** is the air: The **tenth** is the time of year. 

Furthermore, the knowledge of these ten stated things necessarily requires the knowledge of all the parts of the body, which we have through dissection, 
<margin>Anatomy</margin> (which is called **Anatomy**). Since I know you are exceptionally well-versed in this knowledge of anatomy, and hear that you exercise yourself daily in anatomical matters, I have mentioned it not so that you might learn it now for the first time, but so that you may demonstrate it as something most exactly known to your fellow students and listeners, since from the science of dissection we most perfectly grasp the causes of the powers and operations. For healthy actions proceed if the members are unharmed. They will indeed be unharmed if [they maintain their] substance, temperament, quantity, number, position, [and] figure,

<summary>Massa outlines a medical "Method" based on classical authorities, listing ten essential factors—such as cause, temperament, and age—needed to diagnose and predict the course of a disease. He emphasizes that a deep knowledge of anatomy through dissection is the fundamental requirement for understanding bodily functions and health.</summary>
<keywords>medical methodology, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, diagnosis, prognosis, anatomy, dissection, symptoms, medical education</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "First Epistle" to Apollonius, picking up from the previous page's final incomplete word ("pertain..."). It transitions into a discussion on the necessity of diagnosis before treatment.</meta>

->A FIRST<-

<margin>Recognizing the disease</margin> ...and proximity, according to natural justice. By what means the Physician can first recognize the disease and its essence, you have seen in *Galen* in his booklet *On the Differences of Diseases*, and *On Affected Places*, and also in *Avicenna*, the first and second sections of the first Canon, as well as in others of their books. <margin>Cure</margin> That the knowledge of the essence of the disease is necessary, *Galen* testifies in many places in the second and fourth books of his *Method of Healing* against the *Empirics* <note>The Empirics were an ancient school of medicine that relied on experience rather than underlying causes</note>; for he says that the curative indication must be taken from the essence of the sickness, since the knowledge of the disease and the beginning of the curative intention are in the same place. Furthermore, when one wishes to apply remedies correctly to a disease, knowledge of the disease is undoubtedly necessary. Regarding this same opinion, he wrote in the third commentary of the first book of *The Regimen of Acute Diseases*, when he says: it is worthwhile, first of all, that we recognize the nature <note>original: "esse," literally "to be"</note> of the disease, and then turn our mind toward its cure. The most learned *Avicenna* declared this opinion in the fourth section of his first Canon, saying: knowledge of medicines is not possessed except through knowledge of the species and quality of the disease, since contrary medicine must be applied after the knowledge of the disease's quality has been certified; and in the first section of the fourth book concerning the cure of putrid fevers in general, when he says that a fever cannot be cured unless we first recognize it. Therefore, since reason dictates and all wise men confirm that knowledge of the disease is necessary, the first worthwhile thing is to know in which of the three types the disease itself belongs: namely, whether it is in the **temperament**, or in the **composition**, or in the **dissolution of continuity**. <margin>In which disease</margin> If the disease is a **bad temperament** <term>bad temperament: "mala temperies," an imbalance of the four bodily qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</term>, it must be seen whether it is hot, cold, moist, or dry; simple or composite; and whether it is with or without matter <note>i.e., whether there is a physical buildup of humors or just a change in quality</note>; and whether it is a fever or some other disease that indicates a malice of the **complexion** <term>complexion: "complexio," the specific physiological balance of an individual</term>; and if it is a fever, whether it is ephemeral, or putrid, or habitual; and you shall proceed thus in other complexional diseases. But if the disease is a **bad composition** <note>an anatomical or structural abnormality in the way organs are formed</note>, it must be seen whether it arises from the formation <note>or "plasmation"</note>, or the figure, or the quantity, or the number, or the position. Likewise, if the disease is a **dissolved continuity** <term>dissolved continuity: "soluta continuitas," a physical break in bodily tissues, such as a wound or fracture</term>, take notice whether it arises from a wound, dislocation, fracture, convulsion, abscess, or any other mode of ulceration; about all of which *Galen* wrote more in his book *On the Constitution of the Medical Art*, and *Avicenna* in the second section of the first Canon. Furthermore, pay attention in your mind to whether the disease is one or several, and whether they are simple or composite, and whether they are primary, or through con...

# EPISTOLA

<margin>Timing of the disease</margin>
...sense, and whether it is in the process of becoming (as they say), or already established <note>original: "in fieri... uel iam facti"</note>, and also whether these stages are universal or particular. Furthermore, the knowledge of the stages of the disease is extremely necessary if anyone wishes to administer a correct cure: about which Galen has written most learnedly in three books *On Crises*, and Avicenna in the second book of the *Canon*, and in other places; it is necessary to observe this same process in all types of disease, so that nothing necessary for the cure is omitted.

<margin>Causes of the disease</margin>
And so that you may know everything perfectly, the causes must be investigated in the second place. Since to know is to understand through the cause, you will therefore study the knowledge of causes second in order. To confirm this, there is the opinion of Galen in the seventh book of *On the Causes of Symptoms*, where he says that it is not enough for the Physician to know only the impaired functions, but also all the efficient causes; and in the third book of the *Art of Medicine* <note>original: "Artis paruae," referring to the "Microtegni," a foundational textbook of the era</note>, he states that the cause must first be removed, then the disease that proceeded from that cause must be cured. He followed this same opinion in the third book of the *Method of Healing*, when he warns that one must focus on the removal of the cause, since no disease can be healed if the cause is unknown. Similarly, there are opinions of Avicenna in the first book of the *Canon*: when he says it is worthwhile in medicine to know the causes of sickness and of health; and similarly in the third book concerning the cure of cold colic.

<margin>Three grades of causes</margin>
Indeed, the causes which Physicians are accustomed to recognize beforehand for the understanding of a disease are of three types: namely, primitive or evident causes, which the Greeks call <term>procatarctic</term> <note>External triggering factors, such as heat, cold, or diet, that set a disease in motion</note>, and these are external; next are the antecedent causes, and third the conjunct <note>immediate or internal</note> causes, which must be investigated most excellently and diligently. However, I do not want you to believe that this three-fold positioning of causes opposes the sayings of Galen in the second book of *On the Causes of Diseases*, and the first of the *Method of Healing*, and in many other places, where he identifies only two types of causes—namely one external and the other internal. If you divide that internal cause into two parts, as the most learned Avicenna, a faithful interpreter, divided it along with many other most eminent physicians, you will not contradict the doctrine of Galen, despite what the modern Galenists believed, persuaded by their own crude wit <note>original: "crassa minerva," a Latin idiom referring to a lack of refinement or simple-mindedness</note>. For those things which are consistent with reason do not conflict with Galen's truth, if one correctly weighs what Avicenna intended through the two internal causes, and if one wishes to observe the process of nature in causation from every side. And so that you may understand the truth in this matter, let there be for the sake of example someone who, from movement and the eating and drinking of hot things, falls into an abundance of humors and thin...

-># FIRST [PART]<-

...and [if a patient] should fall into a state of refinement <note>original: "subtilitatem," referring here to the thinning or "subtlety" of bodily fluids</note>, and soon, through such abundance and refinement, obstructions are created by any cause, and he is seized by a <term>tertian fever</term> <note>a fever that recurs every third day, historically attributed to an excess of yellow bile</note>; in this case, are there not two internal causes for the fever? Namely, one is the abundance of thin <term>humors</term> <note>the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health</note>, and the other is a putrid smokiness in the heart arising from those rotting humors, which actually produces the fever. The former cause <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook for centuries</note> most learnedly named the "antecedent" cause, and the latter the "conjoined" cause. But, lest I delay you with these matters, I shall proceed to my primary instruction.

Those primitive or evident causes must be considered, from which some curative intention can be drawn according to the essence or magnitude of the disease, or pertaining to the prognosis <note>the forecast of the likely course and outcome of the disease</note>. You shall also observe internal causes most diligently, distinguishing the antecedent from the conjoined where it is worthwhile. It is also necessary to know whether the cause is a bad "material" or "immaterial" <term>complexion</term> <note>the unique balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an individual</note>, or an unnatural composition, or a "dissolution of unity" <note>original: "unitatis dissolutio," a medical term for a physical break like a wound or fracture</note>. You will also strive to recognize other differences, namely, which causes are "instrumental" and which are "fostering." All these things are understood through the senses and are better known to us, forming the principles of art and science according to the testimony of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>the Greek philosopher whose logical works provided the framework for medieval and Renaissance science</note>. For <term>Galen</term> <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> says in the second book of the *Small Art* <note>original: "Artis Paruae," a nickname for his "Ars Medica"</note> that it is beneficial to judge all things by the senses and not merely by the nature of things; otherwise, there is a danger that the patient may suffer permanent illness, which Avicenna also testifies to in the second [book] of the first [part of the *Canon*].

The signs known and sensed by us are those which either belong to the substance itself—which are recognized through touch and the pulse, or by quantity and number—or through "effects," such as impaired bodily functions and altered quality, or through those things called "causals," such as bowel excrement, urine, spit, sweat, and other superfluities. <term>Galen</term> speaks of all these in the second book of the *Small Art*, as does <term>Avicenna</term> in the second of the first. <margin>symptoms</margin> Furthermore, in the third place, one must recognize the "accidents" <note>secondary symptoms or complications that result from a primary disease</note> which follow a disease just as a shadow follows a body. Thus, when the disease is removed, the accidents also vanish, as is written by <term>Galen</term> in the eleventh book of his *Method [of Healing]*. <term>Avicenna</term> established this necessity in the first [book] of the first when he said it is necessary in medicine to know the accidents that occur in health and in sickness. For these accidents follow the disease and are removed along with it upon the disease's departure. However, sometimes by their own strength and malice, they either produce a worse disease or prostrate the patient's strength, even if this does not happen primarily or of its own accord. # E P I S T L E

...deviate, so much so that it becomes necessary to leave the primary disease aside and heal the <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentibus"; in Galenic medicine, these are the secondary symptoms or complications that arise from a disease</note> by administering contrary remedies. The Physician must take care that, by neglecting these symptoms, he does not lead the patient into the greatest risk to life and total ruin. For this reason, symptoms are not to be overlooked; <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> alludes to this same opinion in the twelfth book of his *Method of Healing*, saying that powerful symptoms can overthrow the <term>vitality</term> <note>original: "uirtutem" (virtus); the innate power or "life force" of the body to heal itself and maintain function</note>. He taught how to assist them in the eighth commentary on the first part of the *Aphorisms*, ordering that food be offered immediately if the vitality should fail. <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, whose work formed the backbone of medieval university medicine</note>, moved by similar reasoning, stated in the fourth [chapter] of the first [book]: "it is proper to focus on the matter that is most suspect," and that is the vitality. For if you do not oppose the symptoms that overthrow the vitality—for example, extreme <term>insomnia</term> <note>original: "uigiliis"</note> and headaches during a fever—there is a danger that these may increase the fever or produce a worse disease, such as <term>phrenitis</term> <note>a condition of delirium or brain inflammation believed to be caused by yellow bile</note> arising from excessive wakefulness and headache.

And, because we can hardly recognize abnormal conditions except by knowing the natural disposition of the same kind (by way of contrast), therefore, in the fourth place,
<margin>Temperament.</margin> it is necessary to understand the <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperaturam"; the specific balance of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—unique to an individual</note>, so that through it you may recognize the disease of that kind. Once this is perceived and compared with the natural balance, you will be able to know whether the illness is greater or lesser, as you find throughout the volumes of Galen, and especially at the beginning of the first book of the *Art of Healing, dedicated to Glaucon*, where he says: "to the extent we see someone has distanced themselves from their natural state, to that extent we shall judge the magnitude of their disease." Avicenna also mentions this in the fourth [chapter] of the first [book]. Therefore, you shall investigate the temperament of the sick so that you may know whether they have contracted an equal temperament according to "justice" <note>original: "secundum iustitiam"; referring to a state of perfect humoral equilibrium</note>, or whether heat, cold, moisture, or dryness predominates. For thus (as I said a little before), you will recognize the magnitude of the disease by its distance from the patient’s own temperament.

<margin>Vitality.</margin> To this record, you shall fifthly add the knowledge of Vitality; for vitality and temperament agree in some ways, even if they differ in others. According to the opinion of <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian philosopher and physician known for his commentaries on Aristotle and Galen</note> in the ninth chapter of the first [book], you will gather that they act as the primary and the instrumental forces. You shall investigate with the greatest diligence what kind of vitality the patient possesses. For as Galen said in the eleventh book of his *Method*, vitality is the opponent of disease, like a strong warrior; and in another place he said that the Physician ought to direct his right eye toward the vitality and his left eye toward the sickness. And Avicenna, in the first [chapter] of the fourth [book] on the cure of fevers in general, said it is necessary in all things to [evaluate] the vitality...

<header>F I R S T [ P A R T ]</header>
<sig>A 4</sig>

# F I R S T [ P A R T ]

...to observe the disposition. And to teach you about this in a single word, this is the opinion of all illustrious wise men: namely, to guard the **vitality** <note>original: "uirtutem" (virtus); in early medicine, this refers to the body's innate "life force" or power to function and heal</note> and to expel the **disease**. Therefore, one must attend to whether the vitality is strong or weak; and if it is weak, whether it is burdened, or dissolved, or oppressed by the malice of the disease, as happens in pestilential fevers. From this knowledge, you will also gather the reasoning for feeding and **evacuating** <note>the medical practice of purging harmful fluids or "humors" through bloodletting, laxatives, or other means</note>; namely, whether the **offending matter** <note>original: "materia peccans"; the excess or corrupt humor believed to be causing the illness</note> can be drawn out in one go, or gradually over several times. I would more highly praise this [gradual] method of evacuation when the matter is not **swelling up** <note>original: "turgens"; an acute state where humors are in motion and ready to be expelled</note>. Thus also you will know whether the patient can tolerate a light diet, and whether food should be offered twice, three times, or more often in a day, and similarly according to the [food's] qualities.

Furthermore, the vitality itself reminds us of the strengthening of the **principal organs**. If the "vital power" <note>centered in the heart</note> has been weakened, aids for the heart must be administered; if the "animal power" <note>centered in the brain, governing sensation and movement</note>, the brain must be succored; but if the "natural power" <note>governing nutrition and growth</note>, then the liver, the stomach, and the other organs serving the liver must be aided.

<margin>Age.</margin> Sixth in order, I have placed **age** to be considered. For the strengths and functions are stronger or weaker according to age, and diseases also arise with different appearances in their severity and lightness, so that some diseases happen often in one age but rarely in another—just as **smallpox** <note>original: "uariolæ"</note> occurs in children. Therefore one must see whether the disease is proportional to the **temperament** <note>the individual's unique balance of the four humors</note>, the age, the season, and the rest. For those that have proportion are less dangerous than those that are disproportionate, by the testimony of <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note> in the second part of the *Aphorisms*, Aphorism 34, and <term>Galen's</term> 14th commentary on the first part of the *Aphorisms*. But the opposite is true if it is not proportionate, as when he said: *if an acute fever occurs in an old man, it will without doubt be a sign of destruction, because that fire is strong which is not extinguished by water.* <note>original: "ſi in ſene acuta fuerit febris, proculdubio perditionis ſignum erit, quoniam fortis eſt ille ignis, qui nõ extinguitur aqua"</note> Similarly you will see that <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The influential Persian physician and philosopher</note> feels the same in the first [part] of the fourth [book], in the chapter on rigor, saying that the fevers of the elderly are **buried** <note>meaning the fever remains internal and does not manifest with the same outward heat as in youth, making it harder to treat</note>. Indeed, through all ages the powers change, and the digestive power first, as Galen said in the 20th commentary of the second part of the *Aphorisms*.

Following age, <margin>Sex.</margin> in the seventh place I have listed **sex**, because women and men do not have the same degree of strength, resistance, and other powers. This clearly appears in women, as they are **colder** than men <note>In the Galenic system, women were considered to have a "cold and moist" temperament compared to the "hot and dry" temperament of men</note>, and are liable to many ailments of the stomach and the **womb**, such as the monthly evacuations <note>menstruation</note> and pregnancies; which conditions, although they are natural, nevertheless very often hinder medical oper[ations]...

->E P I S T L E<-

...reasons. There are also not a few **preternatural** affections <note>original: "affectus... præternaturales"; conditions that fall outside the normal course of nature, often referring to illnesses or symptoms</note> in these matters, such as the **wandering of the womb** <note>original: "cursus matricis"; a historical medical belief that the uterus could move within the body, causing various physical and emotional symptoms</note>, suffocations, prolapses, softening, and many other things which it is necessary to investigate through them.

<margin>Habit</margin>
I said that the eighth thing to be considered is that, according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>an ancient Greek physician regarded as the "Father of Medicine"</note> in the second book on the *Regimen in Acute Diseases*: it is not entirely safe to immediately change a sick person from their accustomed foods and other things familiar to them, but a habit changed **gradually** is most often beneficial and frees one from future evil—especially if the habit was a bad one. For that reason, you will consider habit more closely so that, through it and the other things mentioned, you may be able to prescribe a diet and regulate the rest according to the tolerance of particular habits in men. **Hippocrates** desired this consideration in the second part of his *Aphorisms*, in **Aphorism fifty**, when he said: "Those accustomed to labors bear them more easily, even if they are old and weak, than those who are robust but unaccustomed." Therefore, one must use such prudence that a bad habit is removed entirely; for even if it seems to do very little harm in the present, it will nonetheless be harmful in the future when a bad habit persists for a long time.

<margin>Air</margin>
I said the ninth thing to be observed is the **air**, which observation all the ancients placed as highly necessary. Indeed, we live in the air itself, which touches our body both externally and internally without any intermediary, as you can see by your senses. Regarding this necessity of the air, **Galen** <note>a prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> spoke in his first commentary on the first book of *Predictions*, in the ninth book of his *Method of Healing*, and also in the third book of the *Art of Medicine* <note>original: "artis paruæ"; also known as the *Tegni*, a standard medical textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>: it is necessary to reach a natural temperament from the intemperance of the air by altering it through an equal contrary. For indeed, the air changes the body in every mode of change, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> said in the fourth part of his first book, chapter one, when he says that air is more worthy than all other things which must be preserved, because by changing the body, it can sometimes do more than the other things which physicians call **non-naturals** <note>original: "non naturales"; in Galenic medicine, these are six external factors—such as air, diet, sleep, and exercise—that affect health but are not part of the body's innate makeup</note>. Therefore, if the air is contrary to the disease according to its qualities, it will be no small protection for the sick person. From this, I want you to know that changes and alterations of the air very often lead to long-lasting and destructive diseases, if (as I said) it is of a contrary quality. You will see this opinion in **Avicenna**, in the first part of his fourth book, chapter one.

<margin>Season of the year</margin>
The tenth and final consideration is the knowledge of the season of the year—namely, whether it is **Spring**, **Summer**, **Autumn**, or **Winter**. For these seasons are both healthy and unhealthy by their very nature, and they either prolong or shorten diseases.

->F I R S T [P A R T]<-

...as **Hippocrates** <note>an ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> testifies through almost the entire third section of his *Aphorisms*. For Spring and Summer, if they proceed according to their nature, are friends to our nature; but Autumn and Winter are contrary. Therefore, you will very easily be able to not only recognize diseases but also provide the correct remedy for them through the knowledge of the seasons of the year, according to their qualities—both natural and accidental. Indeed, the season of the year often prevents us from being able to apply the correct cure according to the nature of the disease. For **Hippocrates** used to say that under the **Dog Star** <note>original: "sub cane"; referring to the "Dog Days" of summer associated with the star Sirius</note> and before the **Dog Star**, **evacuations** <note>medical procedures to remove humors, such as bloodletting or purging</note> are troublesome. Furthermore, **Galen** <note>a prominent Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> in the first book of *The Art of Healing to Glaucon*, concerning the cure of continuous fevers, warns physicians to observe the "canicular days" <note>the hottest days of summer</note> regarding **bloodletting** <note>original: "venae sectione"; the surgical opening of a vein</note>, if they are very hot; because all those from whom physicians drew blood without thinking of the season of the year perished. Moreover, evacuations are dangerous not only in a hot constitution, but also in a very cold one, because the seasonal conditions are like certain accidents following the diseases, by which the physician is hindered—lest by that contrariety and malice, he performs what is [actually] appropriate for the disease. From these sayings, you will indeed not only recognize diseases, but you will also be able to judge whether they are short, long, healthy, or deadly. <margin>Toward prognosis</margin> One must surely take this method of predicting from the essence and magnitude of the disease, and from the stability or weakness of the **vital faculty** <note>original: "virtutis"; the body's natural power or strength to fight illness</note>. **Galen** expressed this in the second book of *The Art of Healing to Glaucon*, and **Avicenna** <note>a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> in the second part of his fourth book. For if the faculty is strong and the disease is weak, the patient will undoubtedly be healed in a short time. For example, if a **classic tertian fever** <note>original: "tertiana exquisita"; a fever that peaks every third day, typically associated with malaria</note> occurs in a robust youth, he will escape before the seventh attack; or if, in a **burning fever** <note>original: "Causonide"; from the Greek "kausos," a high inflammatory fever</note>, sweat appears on the fourth day, the disease will completely recede on the seventh. But if an old man falls into a known tertian fever, so that the onset and the chill hold the man for a longer space of time, and the heat also plagues him for the whole day and more, it will undoubtedly be a fearsome or long-lasting disease. For according to the opinion of the **Prince** <note>original: "Principis"; referring to Avicenna, known as the "Prince of Physicians"</note> in the first part of the fourth book, the fevers of old men are deep-seated and destructive. Similarly, if someone falls into a severe **apoplexy** <note>original: "Apoplexiam"; a sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis, similar to a stroke</note>, it will be a lethal disease, since it admits very little cure, by the testimony of **Hippocrates** in the second section of the *Aphorisms*, number 42. If you also add the season of the year to the things mentioned above, it will be most helpful in **prognosticating** <note>predicting the likely course and outcome of a disease</note>; for as **Hippocrates** says, Spring is the healthiest season and the least fatal.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of medical prognosis and the timing of diseases, specifically focusing on how the physician must time treatments and food intake based on the "climax" or "vigor" of an illness, as established by Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

->E P I S T O L A<-
<note>original: "E P I S T O L A"; meaning "A Letter" or "Epistle," likely the heading of this section of the book.</note>

# EPISTLE

...and shortening <term>and shortening</term> <note>original: "abreuianstq;"; the "q;" is a common Latin shorthand for "-que," meaning "and"</note> all diseases; conversely, Autumn is disease-bearing and destructive, prolonging illnesses. It will also be of no small help <margin>⨁</margin> to have a material knowledge <note>knowledge of the physical substance or "humors" causing the illness</note> of the cause, by the testimony of **Galen** <note>the influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> in *On the Differences of Fevers*, and **Avicenna** <note>a Persian polymath and author of the "Canon of Medicine," the standard medical textbook for centuries</note> in the first [part] of the fourth [book], concerning **quotidian fever** <note>a fever that returns every day</note>. In such a fever, because of the thickness of the matter, the period of increase is very long, so that before the disease has reached its **vigor** <term>vigor</term> <note>the peak or turning point of an illness</note>, the patient's strength is often rendered so weak that it is least able to overcome the disease or the cause of the disease, and thus the patient must be in danger.

Nor should you neglect this part of the timing of the disease for predicting the outcome and providing care: since the method of healing, of prognosis, of the quantity of food, and of treatment must be taken from the knowledge of the "times" of the illness, especially the peak of the sickness. This is according to the opinion of **Galen** in his booklet *On the Times of Disease*, and in his booklet *On Crises*, and of **Avicenna**, in the second [part] of the fourth, and also the first of the fourth, in the chapter on the knowledge of the times of disease and its peak. There he said that in the true **decline** <note>the stage where symptoms begin to subside</note> of the disease, the patient is least likely to die from the disease itself.

However, it is a worthwhile effort to observe the constancy or inconstancy of strength in making a prognosis, so that you are not deceived by it, which happens very often. Regarding these errors—both in judging strength and in the patient's confidence or fear—**Avicenna** spoke in the first [part] of the fourth, in the chapter on the knowledge of the patient's state. Often <margin>☜</margin> a condition occurs near death which makes it seem as if the patient has escaped the illness; however, one must not believe this. For it will be your task to recognize the condition of the **pulse** <term>pulse</term>, and to notice whether it increases, or becomes strong, or rather fails. Similarly, he urged us to attend to the opposite regarding fear in the second [part] of the fourth, chapter two, when he exclaimed: "Oh, how many fearful signs have we seen in the depth of sleep, in the falling of the pulse, and in the stopping of sweat, which nevertheless led to a good **crisis**!" <note>a "crisis" was a sudden change in a disease, leading either to recovery or death</note>.

Nor do I wish to pass over the fact that crises are not to be expected in all diseases, but only in those in which nature preserves the matter for a single "judicial" expulsion <note>a sudden, decisive purging of the diseased humors</note>. Such are continuous acute fevers and in certain **abscesses** <note>original: "apostematibus"</note>. In other diseases, however, which expel the matter gradually—such as intermittent fevers and **pleurisy** <note>original: "laterali morbo"; an inflammation of the lungs and chest</note>—crises are rarely expected, unless the matter is acute or the strength of the body is robust enough to cause this expulsion. <margin>—</margin> Furthermore, you shall count the **critical days** <note>days thought to be decisive for the patient's recovery, usually based on a seven-day cycle</note> or the days of judgment according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, which **Galen** explained in the first commentary of the third [book] of *On Prognosis*. You will count them thus: the first two weeks are **disjunct** <note>separated into distinct units</note>, but the third is **adjunct** <note>joined together</note>. For example: the first week takes up the entire seventh day, so that the eighth is the beginning...

But lest I delay you with a longer speech, I shall write down the method of healing for the things already listed. <margin>Method of healing</margin> This method of healing must certainly be drawn primarily from the nature of the disease itself. It will then be necessary to correct and regulate this method based on those indicators taken from the patient's **strength**, **age**, the **time of year**, and other signs.

However, I wish to warn you first: never promise to cure diseases that are congenital <note>diseases one is born with, literally "from the seed"</note> or those that are resistant for some other reason, whether they be continuously afflicting—such as <term>satyriasis</term> <note>a term used historically for various conditions; here, as the author notes, Avicenna identifies it with a form of leprosy</note> (which **Avicenna** calls **Leprosy**), or **cancer**, or **ulcers of the lung**, or that "habitual" third species of fever—or whether they be intermittent, such as **Gout** and **Kidney ailments**. Since these can rarely be restored to health, you should—before proposing any treatment—warn the patient or those standing by of the powerlessness of both Nature and the Medical Art.

Under this honest prediction, you may then administer aids which, although they cannot cure the disease, may nevertheless make it lighter and less troublesome, so that you may prolong the patient's life. For it is humane and in accordance with the **Gospel of Christ** to take action so that a disease becomes less burdensome, even where there is no hope of a total recovery, rather than to abandon the patient without hope.

This is enough regarding the ten considerations and the method of prognosis before you proceed to the cure. Therefore, for curable diseases, you shall follow this Method: First, succor the disease immediately, before its violence renders the patient's **vital strength** <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtus"; in this context, it refers to the patient's innate life force or internal power to recover</note> weak. This is a precept of **Galen** in the first part of his *Aphorisms* (Aphorism 23) and **Avicenna** in the fourth part of the first book (Chapter 1).

You will truly provide aid if you apply **contrary remedies**, as **Hippocrates** taught in the second part of the *Aphorisms* (Aphorism 22): *"Whosoever diseases arise from repletion..."* <note>original: "Quicunque morbi ex repletione fiunt"; a reference to the idea that diseases caused by "fullness" or an excess of humors are cured by "emptying" or depletion</note>. **Galen** also teaches this in his commentary and in the third book of the *Art of Medicine*, as does **Avicenna** in the first part of the fourth book, where he says that a disease must be removed by its **contrary**, while health must be maintained by its **like**.

And lest you be deceived regarding these contraries, take note that there are two types. First, the **internal**; second, the **external**. The internal contrary is the **vital strength**, which is always opposed to the disease and—as I said above by the testimony of **Galen**—fights like a brave warrior. The external contrary is twofold; the first...

...instrumental, and the other disposing. The instrumental part is the rule of the **six necessary things**, which they call "non-natural" <term>six non-natural things</term> <note>In medieval medicine, these were the six external factors that a person could control to maintain health: air, food and drink, sleep and waking, movement and rest, excretion and retention, and the passions of the mind.</note>; but the disposing part is the **Physician**, who above all, by regulating those things that are contrary to the sickness or its cause—whether through things administered externally or internally, such as potions and the work of the hands—offers himself as an opponent to the disease. Indeed, you would not be wrong to say that these aids provided by the Physician are "contrary" to the patient's evils.

On the reasoning by which diseases are regulated and with what aids, **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose writings dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> wrote learnedly in the eleventh book of his *Method of Healing*, where he enumerated the six non-natural things and said: if we are able to heal by the regulation of these things, that will undoubtedly be the best method. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, known as Avicenna (c. 980–1037), was a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard medical textbook.</note> also said in the first chapter of the fourth part of his first book that it is often enough to use the goodness of the regimen; for this part regarding <term>dieting</term> <note>In this historical context, "dieting" (diætandi) refers to the entire regulated lifestyle and regimen of the patient, not just calorie restriction.</note> is the greatest part of care, because it is the primary instrument of healing, without which all other instruments are in vain. Therefore, when a situation does not force you toward strong medicines, you must first attempt to restore the patient to health through regimen and food without drugs; by acting in this way, you will achieve health more safely and successfully.

First, let the **Air** be regulated so that it is contrary to the disease. Next, let **food and drink** be moderated in quality, quantity, and timing. Regarding this moderation of food, you have much from **Galen** in the third book of his *Art of Medicine* <note>original: "artis parvae"; also known as the "Microtegni" or "Tegni," a concise summary of Galen's medical system.</note> and in the second section of the *Aphorisms*, commentary nineteen; and from **Avicenna** in the first part of the fourth book, regarding the feeding of those suffering from fever.

For it hinders the **virtue** <note>The "virtue" or "power" (uirtus) refers to the patient's internal vital strength or life force.</note> so that it is less able to resist the disease; it also harms the stomach at that time, causes distress, and the food becomes "corrupted." This is in addition to the hindrance of the **concocting power** <term>concocting power</term> <note>The body's internal ability to "cook" or process food and disease-causing humors; essentially what we now call digestion and metabolism.</note>, which is prevented from governing the material cause of the disease or any other matter. From this comes the prolonging of the disease and the increase of symptoms.

However, in terms of the general stages of the illness, it is different: the patient should be fed more generously in the beginning than when the disease is increasing; but at the **vigor** <note>The "vigor" (uigor) is the peak or most intense point of the illness.</note> of the disease, one should give very little food or none at all. And because men are accustomed to taking food twice a day: therefore, so that the night may be more restful, it is better to take little or nothing at supper—not only when the disease is in its peak, but also at other times. For in the evening hours, the vital power is more occupied with digesting, and also the "accidents" <note>Secondary symptoms or complications.</note> of the disease, and often the diseases themselves, are accustomed to be more troublesome; as the sun sets and the day declines, the power of the spirits becomes weaker. # A P R I M A I

...modern Galenists <note>original: "Galenistæ"; physicians who followed the medical system of Galen, though the author here critiques contemporary interpretations.</note> explaining whatever they please regarding a passage in the first book of the *Method*, which interpretation, since it agrees neither with reason nor with that most faithful interpreter Avicenna, must be rejected. Nor should they be listened to when they say that the text of Avicenna is corrupted, since for a long time most learned men—both Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous Italian physician and commentator on Avicenna.</note> and Peter of Abano <note>Petrus Aponensis (1250–1316), known as "The Conciliator" for his influential work reconciling Greek and Arabic medical traditions.</note>, the Conciliator, and others—have affirmed it by explaining it most eloquently and elegantly. 

But I return to my first purpose. <insert>You shall therefore moderate food, for example, by giving a barley broth</insert> <note>original: "iusculum hordeaceum"; a thin, strained soup made from barley, considered the standard light diet for patients with fever.</note> at dinner; for where the **vital power** <term>vital power</term> <note>original: "uirtus"; the body's internal strength or life force responsible for healing and maintaining functions.</note> is steady, it is enough to preserve it as it is. Nothing is so contrary to **digestion** <note>original: "concoctioni"; in pre-modern medicine, digestion was viewed as a process of "cooking" or ripening food within the heat of the stomach.</note> as the quantity and variety of foods, since they hinder the vital power and fight amongst themselves, as gathered from the sayings of Galen in the second [book] of *On the Causes of Diseases*, chapter 3. For he says that most diseases have their origin in both the abundance and the variety of foods. Avicenna says the same in the third [part] of the first [book], in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk, where after he condemned an excessive quantity of food, he said nothing is worse than eating diverse foodstuffs at a single table.

Similarly, you shall moderate sleep and waking, since during the onset of a **paroxysm** <term>paroxysm</term> <note>A sudden attack or increase of symptoms, such as a sharp spike in fever or a fit of shivering.</note> sleep is harmful, as it concentrates the matter <note>Refers to the "humors" or fluids in the body that were thought to cause disease when out of balance.</note> more, and thus prolongs the shivering, or cold, or **goosebumps** <note>original: "horripilationem"; the bristling of hair or skin often associated with the onset of a feverish chill.</note>. Consequently, from the presence of the matter and the retention of heat, the vital power is hindered from being able to thin the matter for an easier exit, since it is for the most part scattered throughout the entire body. 

We also forbid sleep after eating, except where the vital power is weak and we seek to recall the heat to the interior, and especially to the **stomach** <note>original: "uentriculum".</note>, so that the digestion of the taken nourishment might be improved; in this case, it is appropriate to sleep a little after food, but only while lying on one's back. But while sleeping at night, one should first lie on the right side, so that the descent of the consumed food to the base of the stomach is easier; then one should place oneself on the left side, so that from the greater "embrace" of the **liver** <note>original: "hepatis"; medieval medicine taught that the liver wrapped around the stomach like a warm hand to assist in the "cooking" of food.</note> around the stomach, the power of digestion is made stronger. 

You shall proceed with the same reasoning in regulating waking hours: namely, so they do not become excessive. For **Hippocrates** <note>The Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC).</note> said in the second part of his *Aphorisms* that when sleep and waking exceed their limit, it is bad; Galen most beautifully interpreted this Aphorism in the third [book] of *On the Affected Parts*. Therefore, when too much sleep or waking causes distress, the sick must be awakened if they sleep too much; likewise, when waking is excessive, it will be necessary to induce sleep. # E P I S T L E

...offering food so that **vital power** <term>vital power</term> <note>original: "uirtus"; the body's internal strength or life force responsible for healing and maintaining functions.</note> is guarded, not increased, as Galen says in the ninth commentary of the first section of the *Aphorisms*. And Hippocrates also said in the second section of the *Aphorisms* that **impure bodies** <note>In the humoral system, a body "filled with humors" or toxins that have not been properly digested or expelled.</note> are harmed the more you nourish them; and Avicenna says in the first part of the fourth book, chapter one: nourishment is forbidden when the power is hindered in the preparation of the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which must remain balanced for health.</note>, if they overwhelm the body either by their quantity or their quality. And in the fourth part of the first book, he said that food is an enemy to nature and a friend to disease; therefore, **repletion** <note>original: "repletio"; the state of being overfull or having an excess of bodily fluids/food.</note> must be avoided.

This is especially true in material illnesses, since abstinence from food purges the whole body equally; thus, abstinence from food is a certain species of **evacuation** <note>The medical process of removing harmful substances from the body, usually through purging, bloodletting, or sweating.</note>, as Galen said in the second commentary of the fourth section of the *Aphorisms*. Labor and movement should also be forbidden for the weak and those with fevers; instead of exercise, **massages** <note>original: "fricationes"; therapeutic rubbing of the skin to stimulate the body without exhausting the patient's strength.</note> should be performed, which nevertheless must not dissolve the strength. 

Nor should one neglect those things which can remove the **passions of the soul** <note>original: "animi passiones"; emotions or mental states which were believed to have a direct physical impact on health.</note> or perturbations of the mind. These are achieved through pleasant words and other things in which the sick person may delight: first by promising health, and then it is fitting to praise the man and extol his virtues. Thus, relying on the benevolence, authority, and learning of the Physician, the **vital power**—which opposes the disease—is made stronger and can more easily expel it. For Galen himself testified how much confidence can achieve when he said that the physician in whom the most people have confidence heals the most. 

And Hippocrates, in the second section of the *Aphorisms*, said it is good that in any disease the mind should be delighted, and also if the patient shows himself cooperative toward what is offered; for through these two things, you will know that both the **natural and animal power** <note>Medieval medicine divided the soul's functions into "natural" (nutrition/growth), "animal" (sensation/movement), and "vital" (heart/spirit).</note> have strength, which is rarely seen without the fortitude of the vital power, unless the matter has taken on the form of a poison, as happens in **pestilential diseases** <note>original: "Pestilentibus morbis"; contagious diseases like the plague.</note>. 

And Galen, in the third book of the *Small Art*, said that if the perturbations of the mind are bad, they destroy the power and change the body from its natural constitution. Avicenna, in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk, said it thus: if the "accidents of the soul" <note>Refers to sudden emotional shifts or mental events.</note> are horrible, they prevent **digestion** <note>original: "coctionem"; literally "cooking," the process by which the body processes food and humors.</note>; from which it happens that very many diseases are prolonged and increased. 

Having touched upon these things for you, Apollonius, regarding the **regime of the six non-natural things** <term>six non-natural things</term> <note>original: "regimine sex rerum non naturalium"; the six external factors that govern health: air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and the passions of the soul.</note>, I shall now set down the rules which you must observe in curing diseases. These concern the part of the "offending matter," if it be a material disease, and the part of "alteration," if it be an immaterial disease; which things are to be considered and administered in the second place...

-># FIRST<-

...come. For since healing is accomplished by one of three instruments—namely, by **regimen** <term>regimen</term> <note>A controlled lifestyle, specifically focusing on diet, exercise, and environment.</note> in one’s diet, or by the use of medicines, or by the work of hands <note>surgery or manual manipulation</note>—where the physician cannot induce health by regimen, he will procure it by the other two instruments, namely by medicines or potions, and by the work of hands. Regarding these, **Galen** wrote in the first book of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases*, and **Avicenna** in the fourth part of the first book, and **Hippocrates** gave warning in the second section of his *Aphorisms* when he said: "At the beginning of diseases, if something seems to you to need moving, move it." In the peak of the illness, he ordered no such thing to be done. And **Galen**, in his commentary, said that no **evacuation** <term>evacuation</term> <note>The medical removal of harmful fluids, usually through purging, sweating, or bloodletting.</note> is appropriate if the disease is fatal, no matter the timing, neither by drawing out other **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which must be balanced for health.</note> nor by **bloodletting** <note>original: "sanguinis missionem"; the surgical removal of blood.</note>. 

<margin>The text here is marked with red brackets to emphasize the rules of timing for treatment.</margin>

But if the disease is survivable and at its extreme, the extreme remedy is to open a vein and let blood, and sometimes to give a purging potion. Neither are loosening or strong medicines helpful in the early stages of mild diseases, but rather those which, as they say, are able to reduce the matter by soothing it. These are, primarily, soothing **enemas** <term>enemas</term> <note>original: "clysteria"; liquids injected into the rectum to clear the bowels or deliver medicine.</note>, or cassia <note>a mild laxative derived from pods</note>, or manna <note>a sugary sap used as a gentle laxative</note>, or a laxative rose syrup made from a multiple infusion of roses. Similarly, where there is a need for the reduction of blood, one must draw out the blood by opening a vein according to the requirements of the disease. Thus, you will observe this first rule by operating in this way after the diet.

The **second** rule immediately follows: the alteration or the **ripening** <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctio"; the process where the body’s heat 'cooks' or processes raw, diseased fluids so they can be safely expelled.</note> of the offending matter. Whether you call this administration, ripening, digestion, or preparation does not matter. This second intention is truly most necessary, as **Hippocrates** says: "Treat and move things that are ripened, not those that are raw." **Galen** praised this opinion in the third book of the *Small Art*, saying that this ripening very often removes putrefaction while the matter still remains—specifically by opening the passages and by either thinning the matter or by cooling the feverish heat. Similarly, **Avicenna**, in the first section of the fourth book on the cure of putrid fevers in general, lists syrups, decoctions, and other devices for this purpose, which act toward ripening, or extinguishing <note>cooling the excess heat of a fever</note>, or another mode of preparation and alteration. Such remedies in a putrid fever include simple vinegar syrup and water of bugloss <note>the oxtongue plant, often used to cool the blood and heart</note>, and for opening obstructions, the syrups of the "three roots" and of the "five roots" <note>standard herbal formulas containing roots like fennel, celery, and parsley</note>, and Byzantine syrup, and waters of fennel, celery, and endive.

or decoctions of those things: and by altering—for instance, in a habitual fever—with moistening potions, and we shall apply ourselves to cooling treatments, and even to washings with fresh waters after the alteration or the **concoction** <note>original: "coctionem"; the process where the body "ripens" or prepares "bad humors" for removal.</note> of the matter. The third rule will be the legitimate method for **evacuation** <term>evacuation</term> <note>The medical removal of excess or corrupt fluids from the body.</note> where the illness is caused by physical matter; it is that you cure by the opposite and by the removal of the cause, as **Galen** <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> taught in the third book of the *Small Art*, and **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> in the fourth part of the first book, chapter one. This evacuation must be carried out through the appropriate region, as **Hippocrates** <note>Often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> said: it is necessary to lead it out where nature pushes, through the appropriate part. For example, if in a fever there is a desire to vomit, you shall help nature so that the bad matter is expelled through vomiting. Similarly, if a movement of the matter toward the intestines appears, you will give medicine that purges the appropriate matter from below. Indeed, medicines must be listed according to the requirements of the matter—whether it is pure, or impure, or affected by any other alteration or quality. But if possible, the milder ones should be chosen, such as **Cassia** <note>A mild herbal laxative.</note>, **Manna**, **Rhubarb**, **Agaric** <note>A medicinal fungus.</note>, the **mild cathartic electuary** <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>A universal laxative paste made from various plants.</note>, of dates, **hiera** <note>A traditional bitter purgative powder or syrup.</note>, and other medicines that do not destroy the patient's strength nor loosen the bowels violently. And be mindful of **Rhubarb** where it is appropriate, because, as **Averroes** <note>An influential Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> says in the fifth book of the *Colliget*, it is a wonderful medicine for purging that excels almost all others, since it partakes very little in toxicity, but rather acts as an **amulet** <note>original: "amuletum"; here meaning a protective remedy or stabilizer.</note> against the toxicity of other medicines. Similarly **Manna**, which they call Syrian dew, is a medicine that is accustomed both to correct and to bless other medicines. I would also have you remember to mix into the evacuating medicines those things that can strengthen the principal organs, such as the heart, liver, brain, and especially the stomach. These are the things that are pleasing by their scent and fragrance; for example, pure juice of roses, rose syrup from multiple infusions of roses (which they call "solutive"), **sandalwood**, and similar things, for these benefit both the stomach and the heart by their odor and substance. Fourthly, after the evacuation of the matter, you will administer things that strengthen the principal organs so that, with the organs strengthened and the forces increased, nature may be able to correct the residue of the matter in a material disease (or the quality in a non-material one), lest perhaps the disease should return from the remaining causes of the ailments. For as **Hippocrates** said in the second part of the *Aphorisms*, commentary thirteen: "Those things left behind in diseases are prone to cause a relapse," which residue **Avicenna** called "wicked" in the first part of the fourth book,

...of the fourth book, the last chapter. **Galen** <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> affirms this opinion in the second part of the *Aphorisms* <note>original: "Aphorismorum"; a reference to Galen’s commentary on the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates.</note>, comment thirty-one; and **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> in the second tractate of the fourth book concerning the judgments of a disease's relapse. The fifth thing, which you must investigate altogether with the points already mentioned, is that you should strive to assist with appropriate, timely, and ready remedies for the **symptoms** <note>original: "accidentibus"; in this period, "accidents" referred to symptoms or secondary conditions arising from a disease.</note>. And since very often disturbances of the mind, in addition to the physical symptoms, can lay low one's strength and bring about ruin when they are strong and long-lasting, you should therefore strive for the removal of both. We provide relief for these—as I said above regarding the treatment of diseases—with contrary aids; for example, if they have a "hot" cause, they require "cold" remedies.

Indeed, Galen taught how to treat disturbances of the mind in the little book he wrote on curing the diseases of the mind <note>Likely referring to *On the Passions and Errors of the Soul*.</note>, using wit, jokes, games, harmony, joy, and similar things. The last rule in treating, which I would always wish you to observe, is that you do not treat a specific local disease or any symptom with medicines when there is a **fullness of the body** <term>fullness</term> <note>original: "plenitudine"; also known as "plethora," a medical condition where there is an excess of bodily fluids or "humors," believed to cause disease.</note>, unless you first remove that fullness, whether it be of blood or of other humors. For it is a fearful thing to administer local remedies for a local disease or symptoms when the body is "full," but once you have cleansed the body, you shall fearlessly and boldly apply specific and individual aids.

These are the things which I could write to you as briefly as possible concerning the manner of proceeding in the knowledge and cure of diseases—and also in consultations, or discussions and disputes—so that I might satisfy you despite the lack of time. But as for the rest, which are missing from this method of healing, you will be able to find them in all the books of Galen, and especially from two: namely, from the *Method of Healing* <note>original: "methodo curandi"; Galen’s major work on the principles of therapy.</note>, from which you will draw all universal intentions, and from the *Therapeutic Art to Glaucon*.

But if you desire to have everything both clearer and more distinct, I command, persuade, and urge you to read **Avicenna**; for he, the most learned of all, both gathered and organized the wisdom of the ancient masters of medicine. Thus, as you see, he placed at the ready the essence, causes, symptoms, signs, and remedies of each and every disease, so that he did not rashly say in the first chapter of the first book that there is nothing more anyone could add to his writings. Farewell, and devote yourself to the study of good literature, and greet in my name the excellent **Hendericus Haurbach** and the most learned **Philip Melanchthon** <note>A primary leader of the Protestant Reformation and a renowned scholar, known as the "Teacher of Germany."</note>.

->Venice. 1541. On the Kalends of December.<- <note>December 1st, 1541.</note>
