# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT LORD
## Paolo Magnolo from Eburo <note>original: "e burno"; likely referring to the Porta Eburnea district of Brescia.</note> of Brescia. Letter II.
### On the hour for taking **purgative medicines**, and the time for eating after their administration.

I have read your letters, most learned Paul, who are likewise most dear to me, which delighted me in no small measure. To remain silent about the other parts of them, I read one part in particular and have repeated it quite often: that in which you ask that I might wish to write my opinion on the hour for taking **purgative medicines** <term>purgative: a substance used to induce the evacuation of the bowels, believed to remove harmful humors</term>, and the time for eating after they have been administered. 

Indeed, I—who am always accustomed and obliged to love the learned and to serve my friends to the best of my ability—will take care to satisfy you fully, even though you ask a difficult matter and one not worked out in every part by the ancients. For if **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, **Avicenna**, and other most eminent physicians wrote anything on this matter, they dispatched it with a few and mutilated words. Thus, the matter itself requires a most learned and practiced physician for its explanation—one who knows how to elicit meanings and form conclusions from the writings and non-explicit sentiments of the ancients. You will soon see me do this in this matter, so that I may satisfy both you and the subject as much as I am able; since (as I said) the will of old friends, and especially learned ones, has great power with me. 

Therefore, I shall begin the explanation of this matter from my own judgment and the corroboration of the ancients. In doing so, it has pleased me to state beforehand that I shall clarify the sayings of these authors with reasoning, where the evidence lacks sufficiently suitable witnesses. However, so that you may have my clear opinion on all the rest, beyond even those things which you signify you desire with your whole heart, I shall write on everything that must be considered in this matter—both what precedes and what follows—for more abundant instruction. I shall proceed in order, so that if possible, no doubt may occur in any part afterward. 

The first thing, therefore, which is useful to notice before **purgation** <note>original: "purgatione"</note> is the subject who comes to be evacuated: namely, whether they be young or old; strong or weak; of a hot, cold, or another **temperature** <term>temperature: in Galenic medicine, this refers to the "complexion" or the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in a person</term>; healthy, sick, or neutral (as the physicians say); of a strong or feeble stomach and other members; and even in what season of the year. Similarly, we must consider whether we wish to purge in a **minorative** <term>minorative: a gentle, gradual method of clearing the bowels</term> and gradual way, or in a **thorough and eradicative** <term>eradicative: a more intensive cleansing intended to "root out" the humors</term> manner (as they say), and other factors that could lead in different directions regarding evacuation...

# SECOND [LETTER]

Just as is the custom for purging, and when some urgent cause arises: such as a pestilential atmosphere <note>original: "constitutio pestilentialis"; a period where the environment is believed to be disposed toward spreading disease</note>, accidents, strikes, dislocations, fractures, wounds, and finally the form and strength of the medicines themselves. All of these things—once any diseased disposition in the remaining parts has been removed—demand a specific approach, not only for evacuation but also for the general medical regimen. **Hippocrates** appears to have mentioned these matters in various books, as is clear to those reading especially the treatises *On Ancient Medicine*, *On the Nature of Man*, *On Humors*, and the rest. Even the words of **Galen** in his book *On the Method of Curing by Bloodletting* <note>original: "de curandi ratione per sanguinis missionem"</note> near the beginning seem to support this prior knowledge, as does **Avicenna** in the fourth part of his first book, chapter iii. Furthermore, this prior knowledge easily clears the way toward the proposed question regarding the giving of evacuating medicines, so that the physician may not err in the things to be administered before and after: such as food and drink, movement and rest, sound and wakefulness, and other necessary things, and especially the preparation of the stomach. For it is worthwhile to observe all these things in the administration of **purgative medicine** <term>purgative: a treatment used to expel excess or "corrupt" humors from the body</term>.

But that which you seek must be especially noticed: the time for eating after the medicine. For the sake of clearer teaching, let us imagine a young man who is, first of all, **plethoric** <term>plethora: a state of "fullness" where the body has an excess of blood or other humors</term> from excessive eating of diverse things, near the prime of his age. His temperament <note>The "temperament" was the unique balance of Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry in an individual</note> inclines toward **hot and dry** from a balanced state; he is healthy, but in this stage of life he is accustomed to suffering from **tertian fever** <term>tertian fever: a fever that spikes every third day, traditionally associated with "yellow bile"</term> caused by a boiling of the blood that multiplies the bile, which then putrefies after obstructions are formed. This man is not accustomed to taking a purgation unless he is actually sick. 

In the springtime, he consults a physician because he wishes to be protected so that he does not fall into his usual tertian fever in the summer. I say, therefore, that the physician, having knowledge of the aforementioned things, must strive to remove the **plethora**. However, because **Hippocrates** taught in the first part of his *Aphorisms*, section 22, to "medicate things that are mature, and do not move things that are crude" <note>This refers to the "cooking" or digestion of humors; one should not try to purge humors until they are "ripe" or ready to be moved</note>, and **Galen** affirms this in his commentary (but more clearly in the first book of *On Crises*, chapter ix, and in other volumes such as the eighth book of *On Medicines According to Localities*), a sentiment which **Avicenna** repeats very often, especially in the fourth fen of the first book, chapter v, and the first of the third, chapter vii. Therefore, a preparation must precede. For example, if the body abounds with a mixture of bile and phlegm, one must give a purgative medicine according to the nature of the overflowing humors, which can lead out both materials that are mixed and ready for putrefaction—such as **purging cassia** <note>original: "cassia fistularis"; the pulp of the Golden Shower tree, used as a mild, safe laxative</note>.

# LETTER

...which they also call the **Egyptian pod** <note>original: "siliquam ægyptiacam"; another name for the purging cassia fruit</note>, or if compound medicines are more pleasing, such as **rose syrup** made from multiple infusions of roses, which they call "laxative rose syrup," or lozenges or pills made of **violets**. But if we desire a stronger medicine: the best is **agaric** <note>original: "agaricus"; a type of fungus used since antiquity as a powerful laxative</note>, which is able to purge both types of matter <note>likely referring to the "thick" and "thin" humors discussed in humorism</note>; there are also **electuaries** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term> which can evacuate thick matter, such as the electuary of **dates**, of **sebesten** <note>a fruit of the genus *Cordia*, often used as a demulcent or mild laxative</note> and others. 

Even though I believe these are known to you, nevertheless—so that we may handle the matter as if with our own hands, and because this passage demands it, and so that all things may be known, clear, and before our eyes—let us take for example the case where a physician has decided to administer **cassia fistula** <term>cassia fistula: the "purging cassia" or "golden shower tree," prized for its mild laxative pulp</term> as a purging medicine. 

In the first place, it is doubtful at what hour the medicine should be taken; next, it is also doubted how much time it is beneficial to wait after taking the cassia before the patient takes food. We know, of course, that cassia is the lightest among the evacuating medicines, so much so that physicians frequently call it a **food-like medicine** <note>original: "medicinam cibalem"</note>. This is because it is often overcome by the strength and heat of the stomach, so that it sometimes transforms into nutrition <note>i.e., it is digested as food rather than acting as a medicine</note>, unless the physician prevents this by some skill, either of the order of administration or by mixing it with other things. 

If one decides to give this cassia, it is beneficial to give it in the **morning hours**. Similarly, other stronger evacuating medicines should also be given in the morning hours, unless some singular cause prevents giving it at this hour (of which I will inform you immediately). That the morning hour is more suitable is clear from the explanation of the words of **Hippocrates** in the fourth part of the *Aphorisms*, discourse five and six, and in the forty-seventh [aphorism] of the same discourse <note>original: "Aphorismorum, sermone quinto, & sexto... xxxxvii"</note>. 

In these passages, he said that we will purge better when it is necessary to purge during **moderate seasons** rather than in those that are hotter or colder—such as in **spring and autumn**. This is evident by both reason and experience. For in the time of greatest heat, such as during the **dog days** <note>original: "dierum canicularium"; the hottest weeks of summer associated with the star Sirius</note>, and similarly in the winter time during the colder days, the body’s strength <note>original: "uirtus"; the vital force or "virtue" of the body</note> is weaker. 

First, this is because in the summer time the strength is dispersed and dissipated by the heat, as **Galen** said in his commentary on the first of the *Aphorisms*, [number] 15. Therefore, since the strength is diminished in no small way, it cannot direct the medicine toward evacuation. Second, the humors—which are not so close to the paths of the ducts because they are scattered through the outer parts of the body, attracted by external heat—can only be evacuated with difficulty. Also, in the time of greatest cold, the strength is weaker...

->S E C V N D A<-
<margin>SECOND [PART]</margin>

B 3

For as to what **Hippocrates** said—that in winter and spring the bellies are warmer—this must be understood to refer to that part of winter which is close to spring. For where there are both ice and snow, and northern winds also blow, the whole body is chilled and the **natural heat** <term>natural heat: in ancient medicine, the internal fire or energy that drives digestion and metabolism</term> is dulled, and thus does not function properly. Furthermore, the **humors** <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health</term> are thicker and less fluid, and consequently not as fit for evacuation. This can also be very clearly deduced from the progression of **Galen’s** fifteenth commentary on the first of the *Aphorisms* <note>original: "Galeni primi Aphorismorum"; referring to Galen's famous commentary on Hippocrates' medical maxims</note>, since even at that time the bowels are constricted, as is evident in the seventeenth aphorism of the third part. This happens because the cold constricts the passages, and the protective power of the body—acting as a guardian—excludes the attacks of the cold.

Indeed, experience itself also proves that medicines are harmful in the hottest and coldest times. Therefore, it remains for us to say—comparing the parts of the day to the seasons of the year—that the most suitable hours are the morning and the evening, as appears from the authorities of the ancients and the reasons confirming them. This is because it is not safe to evacuate the body on the coldest or hottest days, but rather in the middle times, namely in spring and autumn, since these are the intermediate seasons in which all the **virtues** <note>original: "uirtutes"; the innate biological powers or "faculties" of the body, such as the power to digest or expel</note> are stronger and the humors are also readier. In these times, the humors are not so scattered toward the outer parts of the body, and in their substance, they are more fit for the movement of evacuation. 

Nevertheless, the time of spring is still more opportune for evacuation than the time of autumn; for besides the fact that the air is more temperate in spring, the sun is also approaching us, which clearly favors the operations of living creatures. You will see that **Galen** affirmed these reasons in his commentary on that aphorism regarding the time "under the Dog Star" and "before the Dog Star" <note>original: "sub cane, & ante canem"; the Dog Star (Sirius) marks the "Dog Days" of mid-to-late summer, which ancient physicians considered too hot for safe purging</note>, and **Avicenna** in the fourth [fen] of the first [book], chapter five, where he said the time least suitable for taking purging medicines is during the days of greatest heat and cold. 

These foundations having been laid, allow me to apply these reasons to the particular hours of the day, so that by reasoning in this way, I may afterward draw a conclusion from what has been said. That hour of the day is the most suitable for taking purging medicine which is more temperate—just like the season of the year which is spring or autumn. But that is the morning hour at sunrise (which is likened to spring), or the evening hour at sunset (which is likened to autumn); for these two parts of the day are more temperate than the remaining two parts, and the bodily virtues are also stronger, although in those nocturnal hours... <note>the text breaks off mid-sentence</note>

<summary>This page argues that purgative medicines should only be administered during temperate seasons (spring and autumn) and hours (sunrise and sunset), as extreme heat or cold thickens the humors and weakens the body's internal heat.</summary>

->E P I S T O L E<-

...labor and wakefulness, the natural powers are weaker than in the morning. Therefore, medicines should be administered during the morning and evening hours, unless there is some impediment. Morning hours, however, are better; and even though morning hours in winter may not be so temperate, if you look toward the time of the rising of the morning star <note>original: "luciferi"; the "light-bringer," referring to the planet Venus as it appears before sunrise</note>, they are indeed less cold. Furthermore, as I said, because of the sun’s arrival toward us, those hours are better and more suitable than the rest, since that first **concoction** <term>concoction: the "cooking" or digestion of food in the stomach to turn it into chyle</term> of ingested food which takes place in the stomach has already been completed, and the **expulsive power** <term>expulsive power: the body's natural faculty for driving out waste or harmful substances</term> rises up for the expulsion of excrement more at that hour than at others.

Nor would I wish anyone to be troubled in mind or to raise an eyebrow because I said the evening hours are also appropriate, even though medicine is rarely or minimally given by physicians at this hour. For I have very often given, I do give, and I shall give drinkable medicines in the evening hours before dinner, especially where necessity demands and reason dictates. I believe you have also read **Avicenna** and the divine **Mesue** <note>original: "Mensuem"; likely referring to Masawaih al-Mardini, known as Mesue the Younger, a famous medieval authority on pharmacy</note> giving pills and syrups after dinner, and even teaching that they should be given for certain illnesses. But since the use of pills has now prevailed, I will leave this with you as a firm and constant point, if I first add this from the words of **John of Damascus** <note>original: "Ioannis Damasceni"; the author refers to the Mesue/Damascene medical aphorisms widely used in the Middle Ages</note> in Aphorisms 22 and 66, where the most learned Damascus clearly seems to advise physicians to give pills in the evening hours after dinner for afflictions of the head and the organs of the senses.

However, there is still a difficulty as to whether the ancient physicians administered drinkable medicines in the evening hours and even after dinner. But whatever the ancients said or did not say, did or did not do, I would wish you to believe that I have almost no doubt of this: namely, that purging medicines can be administered at any hour of the day, and even at any time of year, if necessity so demands. But where a delay is permitted, and nothing else is required by the nature of the illness or the circumstances, the more convenient hour is the morning hour before sunrise. For at that hour, the stomach is free from labor, since it has already completed the digestion of the previous food; also, the natural power—restored by sleep and not yet scattered outward but unified within—is more fit and can better bring the medicine to its intended action. And lest the divisions of the day according to various customs deceive us, it is necessary to divide the day in this place as follows: The first part of the day, which is the morning...

->S E C V N D A<-
<margin>The Second Part</margin>

<note>original: "dicitur incipit..."; the sentence begins mid-thought from the previous page</note> ...is said to begin at the rising of the morning star, or the dawn, and lasts for six hours, after which follows the second part of the day, which comes after the aforementioned six hours and lasts for another six hours, or until the midday hours. The third part, which is after midday, is called the evening part, and it also contains six hours. The fourth and last is the nocturnal part, which also has six hours that terminate the night itself, after which is the rising of the morning star; this part is colder than the rest. And even though there is some controversy regarding **winter days** <note>original: "brunalibus"; referring to the shortest days around the winter solstice</note> from sunrise to sunset, and also regarding the longest days of summer, lest I be troublesome to you by describing too many difficulties, I dismiss them for the present, dividing the twenty-four hours as I have said. 

But although I have said that medicine can be administered at any hour where the nature of the disease or its symptoms compels it, one must remember those hours I said are more suitable, which resemble Spring or Autumn. Truly, as to why the morning or evening hours are superior to the others: these are the reasons—since just as the seasons of the year are healthy for us for these two principal reasons (namely, from the moderate temperature of the air and from the arrival of the sun toward us), so also these parts of the day are more beneficial. For in the morning hours, besides what I said about the **restored strength** <term>restored strength: the "instaurata virtus," or the renewal of the body's vital forces after sleep</term> resulting from the now-completed **concoction** <term>concoction: the "cooking" or digestion of food in the stomach to turn it into nutrients</term> of the stomach, the sun also, arriving toward us at 그 hour, begins to temper the coldness of the air. 

Similarly, the evening hour has a sufficiently temperate sky, even though the sun begins to recede, though for this reason it is not quite as suitable as the morning. You see, therefore, how the day, which is a space of twenty-four hours, has a proportion to the whole year, such that our body is both stronger and weaker according to the different parts of the day. This occurs because of the different movement of the sun and also from the different **regimen** <term>regimen: a prescribed way of life, including diet and activity, to maintain health</term> which men use, both in food and drink and in other necessary things, and especially in certain customary businesses and abuses. 

But regarding the hour for taking medicine, these reasons could be enough for you; however, so that this part may be more detailed, I shall add some not unwelcome things from the ancients. Indeed, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon" was the standard medical text in Europe for centuries</note> in the first book of the third part, chapter 29, and in the fifth book of the **Canon** concerning **Albaromaki pills** <note>original: "pilulis Albaromaki"; a specific historical compound of pills named after the Barmakids, a prominent family in the Abbasid Caliphate</note>, orders pills and potions to be given after food is taken, or after dinner. He even instructed that one should sleep after taking them in certain conditions, so that those taking them might have a more successful effect—as in the case of a headache, two hours after dinner, more or less.

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>L E T T E R</header>

# L E T T E R

...ness, or according to the patient's need and the strength of the **stomach** <term>ventriculus</term> <note>While literally 'little belly,' in this period it refers to the stomach as the primary site of digestion</note> in preparing [the medicine]. For indeed, various medicines often acquire different substances—namely soft or hard—according to their composition and preparation. According to the different nature of the disease, they are even given after dinner; for sometimes (as I have said) they are taken with food so that they may linger longer in the stomach. Doctors also command the patient to sleep afterward, lest through wakefulness and movement the medicine's power be destroyed by the heat of the stomach if it has not been unified. Furthermore, where the heat and strength of the stomach are not robust, it frequently happens that the medicine is dissipated and fails to reach its intended effect. 

Moreover, beyond the fact that by a longer stay in the stomach, medicines are accustomed to draw from the more distant parts of the body the matter causing either pain or another **unnatural condition** <note>original: "affectum præternaturam"; a medical state that deviates from the healthy, "natural" state of the body</note>, it can, by evaporating through both its quantity and quality, refresh the brain and other members, or impress some quality contrary to the unnatural condition. This is true whether that condition be manifest—such as heat, cold, and the rest—or hidden (as they say, arising from a **specific form** <note>original: "forma specifica"; the essential nature of a substance that gives it unique powers beyond just being hot or cold</note> or its **humoral balance** <term>complexional</term> <note>The unique mix of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual</note>). 

For this reason, the ancients gave not only hard medicines, such as pills and other **lozenges** <term>pastilli</term>, but even drinkable medicines in the evening hours after dinner, ordering the patient to sleep after their administration (if they were strong in composition or efficacy). I said "strong in composition" because even if medicines are not strong in their own substance and power, they are nonetheless called strong because of the manner of their composition, such as the **pills of Hiera** <term>pilulae assahieret</term> <note>original: "assahieret"; a Latinized Arabic term for Hiera Picra, a famous ancient purgative "holy" bitter medicine</note>, which **Avicenna** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in Europe for centuries</note> described in the first part of the third book. 

For although these are light in their ingredients, they nonetheless become strong from the manner of their composition, since they are hard and dry substances. Therefore, so that their power may be able to take effect, they require strong heat, which occurs most beautifully during sleep, when heat is recalled to the internal organs during those hours. Similarly, I would like you to consider that even with drinkable medicines, it is more convenient for them to work in certain conditions, for the reasons stated, if they are taken after food—for instance, when we need greater evaporation or some other effect. Indeed, when they remain longer in the stomach, vapors also ascend more easily and in greater abundance to the head—why say more? Very often, medicines move the bowels with less discomfort if they are taken after food, especially if the one taking them sleeps afterward. You will see this lesser discomfort if the person who took them [is] among...

<header>S A E  I C  O V  T N 2 D  A</header>

...[inte]stines are weak, along with other natural virtues. For through sleep, by the unifying of the body's internal heat, medicine is more easily brought to its intended action and works with less discomfort. Nor indeed does the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC)</note> stand in the way, as found in the fourth part of his *Aphorisms*, section 14, regarding "less sleep," etc. This is because here we are speaking of a brief sleep at the beginning of treatment, whereas the words of Hippocrates are understood to refer to a long sleep during the actual process of evacuation <note>The physical expulsion of humors or waste from the body</note>.

However, from what was said before, one can see that certain ancients—and not without reason—gave **purgative medicines** <term>purgatorias</term> <note>Medicines intended to cleanse the body of excess humors</note> in the evening hours and after food, even ordering the patient to sleep so that the medicines might work more conveniently. I indicated a little while ago how movement and wakefulness are an impediment to medicines, because both excessive movement and wakefulness move the internal heat toward the external parts of the body. For that reason, the **stomach** <term>ventriculus</term> is not able to direct the medicines toward their action.

Therefore, in fevers and even where the patient's strength is not robust, it is beneficial to sleep a little after the administration of medicine, even if the medicine itself is mild. Such is the case with **purging cassia** <term>cassia fistularis</term> <note>A mild laxative derived from the golden shower tree</note> and **manna** <term>manna</term> <note>A sweet, dried sap from the flowering ash tree, used as a gentle purgative</note>. For this same reason, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> ordered sleep after taking a potion of **tamarinds** <term>tamarindorum</term> for the cure of **burning fever** <term>causonis</term> <note>original: "causonis"; an acute, inflammatory fever characterized by extreme thirst and heat</note>. If they do this for the weak (as I have said), they should do it much more when the medicines are strong in their substance, power, and composition. In support of this stands the opinion of Hippocrates in the booklet *On External Diseases*—a booklet which **Galen** <note>A Greek physician and philosopher (129 – c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium</note> believed was actually written by **Polybus** <note>A pupil and son-in-law of Hippocrates</note>—whose words are these:

> Medicines which are provided for diseases and wounds should be given after dinner or after food.

Lest I be too long, I will return to the case I proposed above. I will say that since cassia is a weak medicine which can easily be overcome by the body's heat and converted into nourishment according to its nature (which would not be beneficial in every respect), it could cause much harm. As Galen beautifully taught in his booklet on *When and with Which Medicines One Ought to Purge*, in this specific case it is beneficial to give food two hours or less after administering the cassia. This prevents the strong heat from converting the medicine into "bad nourishment" and ensures the food does not mix with it entirely. By that time, the cassia should have reached the bottom of the stomach within the hour, especially since the other factors examined above agree. Furthermore, the patient is a young and strong man with the aforementioned **bilious temperament** <note>A physical constitution associated with "yellow bile," characterized by being hot and dry; such people were thought to tolerate hunger poorly</note>, which cannot tolerate an empty stomach without harm, and also because of the current time of year in which...

The author cites Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna to justify providing food or rest alongside mild purgatives like cassia and manna, particularly for patients with "bilious" constitutions.</summary>

the strength of the stomach is robust. The matters to be evacuated are near the channels of the ducts, so that they can be purged without delay and gradually through **bowel movements** <note>original: "secessum"; refers to the physical expulsion of waste</note>. The medicine is also weak, and the person who took it is very little accustomed to medicines. But where the strength of the stomach is not so robust, a longer time should be expected after its administration, so that the body's **natural power** <term>uirtus</term> <note>The internal faculty or "virtue" that governs bodily functions</note>, unhindered by food, can better lead the medicine to its act of operation.

But if the medicine were moderate, then indeed it is proper to wait a longer time to provide food—say, five or six hours. In that time, we may believe the medicine has completed its work. However, this timeframe is not to be followed in all cases; rather, there should be an estimated interval between the medicine and the food, since a fixed quantity of time can hardly be assigned, given that some bodies are affected by medicine more quickly and some more slowly. We see this even in the medicines administered and in the timings, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note> testifies in the first chapter of the first part of his fourth book.

Furthermore, more recent physicians seem to agree with these sayings: namely, that after taking a moderate medicine, food should be delayed for five or six hours, more or less according to the strength of the patient and the manner of the operation. Although these physicians observe this rule, some of them do not act entirely correctly or according to the precepts of the ancients. Indeed, they err in this part of medicine as in many others, because it is not always proper to give food five or six hours after taking medicine, as they do. Rather, in many cases, one must wait for a **complete evacuation** <note>The full purging of the targeted humors or waste from the body</note>, taking a sign from the thirst and the tolerance of the patient. This is gathered from **Hippocrates** <note>The Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC)</note> in the nineteenth discourse of the fourth part of his *Aphorisms*, and from **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) in the Roman Empire</note> in the commentary on the same, and also from the often-cited passages of the first part of the fourth book of Avicenna.

Thus, it would sometimes not be inappropriate if even ten or more hours passed, provided the person taking it can tolerate it. This (as I said) will be known from the thirst and the remaining signs. When these appear, it is necessary to give food. For this reason, a firm rule for the quantity of time cannot be given from what has been said; rather, we determine it based on the reasons mentioned and by estimated judgment. Therefore, those who feed the patient in this way after the administration of medicine are following the principles that both Hippocrates and Galen set forth in the second book of *On the Method of Diet in Acute Diseases* <note>original: "de ratione uictus in morbis acutis"</note>, as well as what Avicenna said in the fourth chapter of the first book. ->### SECOND ###<-

<meta>The header "SECUNDA" refers to the second part or section of the treatise. The original page notes significant bleed-through from the reverse side, making the header difficult to read in the original manuscript.</meta>

...it will be worthwhile not to wait, however, according to different intentions. For we wait when we desire an **exquisite and eradicative evacuation** <note>original: "exquisitam, & eradicatiuam euacuationem"; a medical term for a complete and deep cleansing of the body's humors</note> (as they say), provided the medicine is neither weak nor as strong as **hellebore** <note>original: "eleborus"; a potent and toxic plant used as a violent purgative in antiquity, requiring great caution</note>, but moderate—one which, neither by its substance nor its quality, can harm the stomach. This is as **Hippocrates** <note>The 5th-century BCE Greek physician considered the "Father of Medicine"</note> and **Galen** <note>The Roman-era physician whose theories on the four humors dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> have left written in many places, and especially in the location cited a little earlier, in the twelfth word and toward the end of the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>original: "de morbis uulgaribus"; referring to Hippocrates’ observations on common or seasonal diseases</note>. 

**Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard text in European universities</note> follows this opinion in the fifth chapter of the fourth book of the first part, when he says that one who has taken medicine ought not to eat, nor drink, nor even sleep, unless they wish to diminish its operation. In such a case, it is appropriate to give food sooner, such as **barley water** <term>ptisana</term> <note>A thin medicinal porridge or drink made from boiled barley</note>, or barley broth, or chicken broth—which is what more recent physicians are accustomed to do. But when we desire not a complete, but a **minorative evacuation** <note>A gentler treatment meant to slightly reduce the volume of harmful humors rather than fully purge them</note>, one should by no means wait for the medicine to complete its operation. Thus you see that food has various roles. These depend not only on the person taking it, but also on the strength, moderateness, or weakness of the medicine itself, both in terms of the power operating from its own substance and its composition. 

But in those who come to be evacuated during a **pestilential constitution** <note>A state of the atmosphere or environment believed to cause outbreaks of plague or epidemic disease</note>, or in cases of blows, wounds, and other such causes, light medicines are to be given. In these instances, food should be provided before the full evacuation is complete. For I do not believe you doubt whether it is appropriate to evacuate the body during a pestilential constitution, since I know you have seen that **Galen**, in his book *On the Differences of Fevers*, and **Avicenna** in the fourth book of the first part, prescribed evacuation to prevent a future plague. Similarly, in the case of blows and other causes arising from external factors, both **Galen** in the fourth book of *The Method of Medicine* and **Avicenna**, regarding a **headache** <term>soda</term> resulting from a blow, ordered the administration of purging medicines to prevent a future **abscess** <term>apostema</term> <note>A swelling or collection of pus (an inflammatory tumor)</note> and pain. 

But so that those things which are scattered through this long discourse may be more easily gathered, I shall place all the aforementioned points—which primarily serve the prescribed teaching—in a **table or figure**. Indeed, this will ensure that the teaching of these matters is clearer, and also that they may be better committed to memory.

**If the person taking it and the medicine are both strong**, let it be administered in the morning, and let the patient eat after the operation is complete. But if it is feared that the medicine, by its substance or quality, might leave harm in the stomach, food should be given soon—such as barley water <term>ptisana: the juice of boiled and pressed barley</term>, or chicken broth as the modern physicians <note>original: "recentiores"; referring to contemporary practitioners as opposed to the "ancients" like Galen</note> do. To help the medicine work more comfortably, the patient may sleep if necessary.

**If the person taking it is strong and the medicine is weak**, let it be administered in the morning and let the patient eat soon after—for instance, one or two hours later.

**If the person taking it is strong and the medicine is moderate**, let it be administered in the morning and let them take food after the medicine has finished its work. Among "strong" takers are counted the young, those who have an excellent temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, "temperament" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in an individual</note>, and those with strength of the stomach and other organs.

**If the person taking it is weak and the medicine is strong**, one must completely abstain from this kind of medicine at any hour.

# SECOND PART

<margin>If the person taking it is weak and the medicine is weak</margin> Let it be administered in the morning, not without caution: and let food be delayed or hastened according to the tenor of the patient's strength <note>original: "uirtutis"; in this context, the patient's vital force or innate energy</note> based on the judgment of a prudent physician, so that the medicine can be brought to its work, and so that strength may be preserved.

<margin>If the person taking it is weak and the medicine is moderate</margin> Let it be administered in the morning with even greater caution, and let food be delayed or hastened by the judgment of a wise physician, so that the medicine may operate and strength be guarded. However, among the weak are numbered the elderly, those having a feeble temperament, and **melancholics** <note>Those believed to have an excess of "black bile," often associated with a cold, dry, and fragile constitution</note>, those convalescing from a long illness, and also those who have a weak stomach and other weak limbs, and those who are not accustomed to medicine.

<margin>If the person taking it is strong and healthy</margin> Let him forgo medicines, unless he wishes to take them to prevent a future illness; then, however, let the medicine be mild or moderate. The time for taking both the medicine and food should be as stated above.

<margin>If the person taking it has a neutral body, which is "neutral" either in falling into sickness or in convalescence</margin> If it is the neutral state of falling into sickness <note>Galenic medicine recognized a "neutral" state between health and disease; "decidentiae" refers to the state of beginning to "fall" into illness</note>, let the medicine be administered in the morning, and let it be weak or moderate to prevent the future disease; and let food be given (in the case of a weak medicine) one or two hours afterward. For those in convalescence, medicine should not be administered, except those which physicians call **food-like** <term>cibale: medicinal substances that have nutritional properties, such as medicinal broths</term>.

<margin>If the person taking it is sick.</margin> Let the medicine be given according to the demands of the disease—strong, moderate, or weak—and at the hour that is expedient. For example, in the morning, if there is nothing that forbids it, such as an onset or the beginning of a fever, a peak of the disease, and similar things, or other accidents <note>In early medicine, "accidents" referred to symptoms or complications that arise during a disease</note>. And so let it be given at any hour of the day; for in acute diseases, it is expedient to administer medicine at that very hour. Likewise, let food also be given as both the patient's strength and the disease require.

<margin>If the person taking it is strong and healthy during times of extreme heat or cold</margin> Medicine is not to be administered.

# EPISTLE

<margin>If the person taking the medicine is strong and healthy in spring and autumn</margin> To prevent future illness, weak medicines should not be administered <note>The author suggests that for a strong person in a healthy season, a weak dose is unnecessary or ineffective for preventative care</note>. Let him eat light foods before the medicine's action <note>original: "operatio"; the period when the drug is working through the body</note>, and moderate foods once the action is complete. But during a pestilential constitution <note>A period when the environmental conditions were thought to favor the spread of plague or infectious fevers</note>, it is beneficial at any time to purge with light medicines to prevent a bad fever.

<margin>If the person taking it has been struck or has fallen</margin> Let a light medicine be administered to prevent a future abscess <term>apostema: an internal swelling or collection of pus, often used here to mean any inflammatory buildup</term> or pain.

<margin>If the person taking it is strong and the medicine is soft or drinkable</margin> Let it be administered in the morning, and let him eat once the action is complete, unless there is an impediment caused by the timing of the disease's onset or its "accidents" <note>In Galenic medicine, "accidents" refers to the specific symptoms or side effects that accompany a primary disease</note>, or on account of a particular limb, such as the head, chest, and similar areas. In such cases, let it be given at [other] hours, specifically in the evening before and after dinner, and let him sleep if the necessity of the situation requires it.

<margin>☛ If the person taking it is weak, and the medicine is soft or drinkable</margin> First, let only a light medicine be administered in the morning, unless there is some hindrance; if there is, let it be given at the most beneficial hour, whether before or after food, and in the evening before and after dinner, and this according to the judgment of a wise physician.

<margin>If the person taking it is strong and sick, and the medicine is light and minorative</margin> <note>minorative: a gentle purgative intended to gradually reduce or "diminish" harmful humors rather than causing a violent evacuation</note> Let it be administered in the morning unless something on account of the disease or the symptoms prevents it, and let him be fed one or two hours after taking the medicine.

<margin>If the person taking it is strong and sick</margin> Let the medicine be given once the matter is "digested" <note>The "coction" or ripening of the humors; doctors believed medicine worked best once the body had processed the "raw" fluids of the disease into a state where they could be expelled</note> so that it purges thoroughly; let this be in the morning, unless there is a hindrance by reason of the disease or symptoms, in which case let it be given at other suitable hours; and let him eat when the purging is complete.

<margin>If the person taking it is strong or weak and the medicine is hard, such as pills and other similar compositions</margin> Let them be administered according to the nature of the diseases, or the limbs in which the disease resides, or according to the matter that it is appropriate to purge. For example, if the illness is in the stomach and neighboring passages, or the chest and lungs, let it be given in the morning; or in the evening, before food, and let him eat sooner or later according to the strength of his vital force. But if it is on account of remote limbs <note>Areas of the body far from the digestive tract, such as the extremities</note>, let them be administered after both the morning and evening meals, and if need be, let him sleep afterward, especially if the medicine is strong.

<meta>This page continues the technical medical advice from the previous section, moving from the timing of doses to the classification of drugs by their "degrees" of intensity—a cornerstone of Renaissance pharmacology. It concludes the letter with a personal address to the recipient, "Magnolo," and a date from Venice in 1544.</meta>

# SECOND SECTION

I will state certain final things that should be observed, as they contribute significantly to a clearer understanding of the aforementioned teachings. To avoid tediousness by listing every single detail, I will explain the matter in these few words. In particular, there are many who can hardly endure the hunger of the stomach; if the medicine has not yet begun to work, it is necessary to provide them with food so that they do not fall into a **fainting spell** <note>original: "animi deliquium"; a sudden loss of strength or consciousness often attributed to a "sinking of the spirits"</note> or similar states. These patients are usually those of a **bilious temperament** <note>In the humoral system, bilious or "choleric" individuals were thought to be hot and dry, making them prone to irritability and physical exhaustion if they did not eat</note> and those accustomed to eating frequently and in large quantities.

It is also useful at times to consider the hours of the day in which the natural force of the humors is most active. For when humors are resistant to being purged—such as the **melancholic humor** <term>melancholy: the "black bile," considered cold, dry, and the most difficult humor to move or clear from the body</term>—it is drawn out more successfully and with less distress if it is moved during its own proper hour.

Nor should I omit what I had previously touched upon only briefly regarding weak, moderate, and strong medicines, as these are relevant to our present business. Physicians call those medicines **weak purgatives** which are of the **first or second degree** <note>The Galenic system ranked medicines from 1 to 4 based on their perceived intensity of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</note>. These include:
*   Violets
*   Tamarinds
*   **Cassia fistula** <term>cassia fistularis: also known as "purging cassia" or "pipe cassia," a tropical legume used as a mild laxative</term>
*   **Manna** <term>manna or Syrian dew: a sweet, solidified sap from trees like the flowering ash, used as a gentle purgative</term> and similar substances.

**Moderate medicines** are those which do not exceed the second degree, such as **senna**, **rhubarb**, **agaric** <note>a type of medicinal fungus found on larch trees</note>, and the like.

**Strong medicines** are those which, after the second degree, even ascend to the third, such as **scammony** <note>a harsh resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia</note>, **colocynth** <term>colocyntis: the "bitter apple," a powerful and potentially irritating purgative</term>, **hellebore** <note>original: "veratrum"; a plant used for drastic purging</note>, and similar things.

One must not resort to those medicines which fully possess the **fourth degree** in the administration of treatments, as they are categorized among **lethal poisons** rather than medicines.

And since a single "simple" <note>A "simple" is a medicine made of only one ingredient, usually a plant</note> purgative medicine can rarely have all the necessary virtues precisely so that nothing is lacking or excessive, it is very often necessary to add another of the same or a different degree. This is done either to increase its strength, to correct some defect within it, or to fulfill the intention of other parts of the formula. This is well known to experienced physicians, among whom I judge you to be, most learned **Magnolo**, and most dear to me. Thus, they not only achieve what we have said through the mixing of medicines but also very often change them from one degree to another. Because of this, they also change and choose both the time for taking the medicines and the time for eating. For a fixed time for taking both medicine and food cannot be assigned, as can be gathered from what was written above.

For this reason, most of this business—once the foundations have been laid—has been left by the illustrious ancient physicians to be managed by the **rational judgment** of the experienced doctor.

->Farewell. Venice, the Kalends of August <note>August 1st</note>, 1544.<-

# TO THE MAGNIFICENT AND ILLUSTRIOUS
## Senator Lord Sebastian Foscarini
### Most Eminent Philosopher. Letter
#### III. On the preservation of health and the prolongation of old age.

**P**lato, who undoubtedly discussed natural matters with the greatest precision, O most illustrious and learned senator—the glory of the Venetian Republic—considered man to be a certain **divine miracle** <note>original: "miraculum quoddam diuinum"; a central theme of Renaissance Humanism, emphasizing man's unique place in the universe</note> in the second book of *The Laws*. I, too, have always been persuaded that a wise man is the greatest miracle; for he is not only intent on living well and happily for himself, but brings utility and fruit to his homeland and (if I may say so) to the world. For a wise man, like a **celestial body** <note>Referring to the stars and planets, which in Aristotelian thought were unchanging and moved in perfect, eternal circles</note>, exists above the reach of fortune, eternal, undisturbed, and untiring. Furthermore, if we believe the most learned commentator **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Spanish-Arabic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to university education in the Renaissance</note> in his preface to the *Physics* <note>original: "phisica auscultatione"</note>, the wise man, joined with God, strives for happiness. 

Nature itself has revealed this greatest miracle of nature in you to this very day. Therefore, so that this miracle and divine gift—which the mother of all things has bestowed upon us—may continue to shine and be of service among you for a long time, I decided to write these things to you concerning the protection of health, the delaying of old age, and the prolongation of life. I do this not because I think you are ignorant of these matters (since, as is proper, nothing more can be desired in you regarding the knowledge of things), but because I see you neglecting your private concerns to study the administration of the Republic with such tireless devotion to your homeland. For that reason, I thought you should be reminded that whenever you are free from public business (which happens rarely), you should look to your health, lest the world lose this miracle of nature. 

I shall therefore begin the work itself. First, since all the wise have divided medicine into **theory and practice** <note>original: "theoricam & praxim"</note>, and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known as the "Prince of Physicians," whose 'Canon' was the primary medical text of the era</note>, easily the prince of physicians, has placed both parts under the speculative side—affirming that when one possesses them, he has achieved both speculative and practical knowledge at once, even if he has never actually performed a medical operation—I will therefore complete this instruction by mixing both parts. For, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), the most influential physician of antiquity whose humoral system dominated medicine for 1,500 years</note> witnesses in the first book of *On Medicines According to Location*, two things were given to us by nature—namely, **reason and experience** <note>original: "ratio & experientia"</note>—by which we judge the actions of life.

<header>THE THIRD</header>

## THE THIRD

These two <note>Referring to the principles mentioned on the previous page regarding the preservation of the body</note> teach how to rule a healthy body so that it does not fall into disease from unknown causes. A body will surely fall into a type of imbalance of diseases if it leans toward corruption; indeed, as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> said in the first book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: "de tuenda sanitate"</note>, this corruption happens in two ways according to nature, and no one can escape them. Of these, one is the drying out of the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the innate, vital fluid that Renaissance physicians believed we are born with; it acts like the "oil" in a lamp that sustains the flame of life</term>, which is followed by old age; the other is the continuous dissolution of our body by the action of **innate heat** <term>innate heat: the natural internal warmth produced by the heart that powers digestion and life, but which also slowly "burns" the body's moisture</term>, because of which a living being requires nourishment so that he may, in effect, restore the parts that have been dissolved. For food and drink restore the substance of the dry and the moist, while breathing preserves the moderated heat. Moreover, these operations are implanted in us by nature, as we do not have to learn how to eat, nor how to drink, nor how to breathe.

I would not want anyone to believe, most illustrious senator, that I think a man can be liberated from death by a regimen for preserving health, or be defended entirely from external harms so that he might reach the absolute extreme of old age and life; rather, [this science] provides two benefits to men: first, it prohibits the inflammation of the **moistures** <note>The humors or fluids of the body</note>; and second, it prevents the **radical moisture** from being consumed too quickly. For an inflammation of the humors occurs and they waste away if they are seized by a non-natural heat, whether from without or within—though not in the same manner as usually happens in fevers—for a man is indeed inflamed by labor and other external causes, as well as by anger and other internal heating factors. Furthermore, they are dried out by the passage of time <note>original: "æratiuum decursum"; likely referring to the transformative passage of the years</note>, and thus by this double path we tend toward our end.

Therefore, lest the **radical moisture** be consumed by nature's own work before its time, or rendered foreign [to the body],

# THE EPISTLE

->The first chapter teaches us to recognize the causes<-
->which tend to move the body away from health.<-

**S**ince the causes of disease are said to be numerous, there are just as many causes of optimal health. But the causes of diseases are of three general types; therefore, it is necessary to list an equal number of causes for diseases. **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> wrote this opinion in the first book of *On Diseases* <note>original: "de morbis"</note>, and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook</note> in the second chapter of his first book. Indeed, the first type is that of a **bad temperament** <term>bad temperament: an imbalance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which were thought to govern health</term>, the second is improper composition, and the third is the **dissolution of unity** <term>dissolution of unity: a medical term for injuries that break the physical continuity of the body, such as wounds, fractures, or ulcers</term>. Therefore, the preservation of optimal health will be achieved if we maintain the causes of optimal temperament, composition, and unity. For if anyone observes these dictates, they will undoubtedly lead a man to the final limit of his natural life. Furthermore, as **Plato** said in the *Philebus*, life and health consist in a certain proportion of hot, cold, moist, and dry, just as diseases occur in their disproportion, from which untimely death hastens. He took this same opinion from the most ancient and divine **Hippocrates** in his booklet *On the Nature of Man*. One must observe this same proportion in composition and unity, as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> learnedly wrote in his booklet *On the Length and Shortness of Life*. All the most serious physicians have established that the causes of all these disproportions lie in the improper management of the **six necessary things** <term>six necessary things: also known as the "non-naturals," these are environmental and lifestyle factors—air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, evacuation and retention, and the passions of the mind—which humans must manage to remain healthy</term>. To these, they even add other causes which easily coincide with the former, such as a fall, a blow, and similar things which are outside of nature, and which we can avoid just as we do the six other necessary things. But since the regimen for protecting health is not merely one single way but is manifold—varying according to age, temperament, region, custom, and the seasons of the year, as **Galen** testifies in *On Preserving Health*—I will certainly not list them all. Instead, I will note those which are beneficial from the age of vigor <note>The period of full adulthood or maturity</note> until final old age. Nor will I entirely omit the regimen for youth and other ages, since through them I will often demonstrate, with clearer teaching, what is necessary for the remaining stages. However, concerning the specific traits of the individual, where general discussion is least possible, it is worthwhile to trust in practical experience. All of these things—though they require long examination to reach perfection—I will nonetheless strive to provide as much as I possibly can...

# THIRD [EPISTLE]

I will do this briefly, and so clearly that not even a word shall require interpretation. First, however, I pray to God—as **Plato** <note>Plato (c. 427–348 BC), the Greek philosopher</note> advised in the fourth book of the *Laws* <note>original: "de legibus"</note>—who, hearing me, may come to my aid, propitious and kind, and direct my mind so that I may provide precepts everywhere. I will not say that these can correct "natural" causes, since this is least possible for a physician, but rather those factors which, by accident, lead to dissolution, suffocation, and withering <term>withering: "marcor," the gradual drying out of the body's vital fluids associated with aging</term>. For **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> wrote in his small book *On the Causes of the Length and Shortness of Life* <note>original: "de causis longitudinis et breuitatis uitae"</note> that those bodies possess a longer life which have more and more of the principles of life. These principles of life, for our present purpose, are two: namely, **innate heat** <term>innate heat: the vital warmth believed to be present in the heart from birth, fueling all biological processes</term> and **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the fundamental fluid of the body that acts as fuel for the innate heat; its exhaustion was thought to cause old age and death</term>. And this is—as **Aristotle** said in the same book—because we live by heat and are nourished by moisture. The whole logic of this business, therefore, will be to protect these two from both external and internal things that dry them out, or dissolve and suffocate the heat. Those things that perform such actions are the **necessary things**, also called the **non-natural things** <term>non-natural things: in Galenic medicine, these are environmental and lifestyle factors like air, food, exercise, and sleep that are not part of the body but affect health</term>. And although many of the ancients taught the method of exercise first, I shall begin with the air.

### Chapter two teaches how to correct the air.

**A**ll wise men have established that the greatest precept in the preservation of health is that the air be corrected. For the air continually changes our body through many variations across the four seasons of the year and their accompanying events—such as rains, or if it does not rain at all, sweltering heat, freezing or deadly colds, foul evaporations, or pestilential corruptions. There is also a certain mode of alteration through which multiple and evil diseases are produced, the causes of which are often unknown. Astronomers, however, strive to provide these causes. But since they are for the most part liars, we can by no means safely trust them; but we undoubtedly trust physicians, since they derive everything only through the external senses and reason, as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), whose medical system dominated European medicine for centuries</note> testifies throughout all the books of his *Method* <note>likely referring to Galen's "Method of Medicine"</note>. For animals that breathe, such as man, require a continuous cooling of the heart which occurs through the inspiration of external air; as **Hali Abbas** <note>‘Ali ibn al-‘Abbas al-Majusi (died c. 994), a famous Persian physician</note> learnedly said in the fifth book of the *Theory*, chapter two: no one can escape it, whether he wishes to or not, for it is necessary to live within it. Let the air, therefore, be primarily clear, open, pleasant, and temperate. For

# EPISTLE

This air is beneficial for all ages, complexions <term>complexions: the "temperament" or balance of the four humors in an individual</term>, sexes, and times, as **Hippocrates** <note>Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC), the ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> taught in his little book *On the Nature of Man* <note>original: "de natura humana"</note>. Indeed, temperate air is recognized if it is cooled shortly after sunset, and is also warmed as soon as the sun rises, and its fragrance is pleasant. On the other hand, air that exceeds its bounds, whether in its primary or secondary qualities, must be shunned—such as air that is too hot, cold, dry, moist, thin, or thick, and the like. This is especially true if vapors rising from marshes and putrid places are mixed with it, such as from latrines, sewers, and cemeteries of the dead, as well as foul-smelling trees like boxwoods, walnuts, and similar plants. For, says **Paulus Aegineta** <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), an influential Byzantine physician whose works summarized ancient medical knowledge</note>, in every age and time, bad air is disease-bearing; therefore, it requires correction, varying according to its distance from a temperate state and its specific malice, and also according to the seasons of the year and other differences.

For if the air proceeds in its natural course, it should by no means be altered by art. But if it should decline toward some exceeding quality—either primary, secondary, or (as they say) hidden—it should be met with its contrary or a remedy <note>original: "amuleto"</note>. For example, in an excess of heat, one should use the irrigation of the house and bedroom and the sprinkling of water alone, or water with roses, violets, apples, citrus, and similar things. Let these also be boiled, so that the air of the house may be rectified <note>original: "rectificetur"</note> <note>Dot above 't' likely denotes 'rectificetur'</note> through its evaporation. Let rose water also be sprinkled <note>original: "Spargatur"</note> <note>Abbreviation mark above 't' likely denotes 'Spargatur'</note>, and let them smell it alone or mixed with some other sweet-smelling substance; with this and similar things, let them also wash their hands and face.

Likewise, if the air exceeds in other qualities, it must be corrected by its contraries, such as moist air by dry things, and similarly in other cases. In summer, indeed, when heat and dryness overcome the temperate state, let the house be sprinkled <note>original: "aspergatur"</note> <note>Abbreviation mark above 't' likely denotes 'aspergatur'</note> with the aforementioned decoction or another similar one. There are also sweet-smelling, cold leaves and flowers which may be scattered throughout the house, such as roses, violets, and **water lilies** <note>original: "nympheæ"</note>; or let the said flowers and herbs—sweet-smelling and cold, with a portion of **sandalwood** <note>original: "sandalorum"</note>—be boiled, and the house and bedroom be sprinkled with it. 

Northern winds also cool the air; therefore, let the windows facing those directions be opened, nevertheless taking care lest the winds perhaps be raised from marshy places, or pass through places where putrid vapors are lifted. Let sweet-smelling fruits also be present, such as apples, pears, peaches, quinces, citrus, lemons, and others. Nor do men safely expose themselves to Southern winds in the greatest heat of summer; for they relax the body and render the nerves weak...

...they disturb the <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern human health and temperament</term>, dull all the senses, and fill the brain with <term>superfluities: excess waste products or fluids that the body fails to process, thought to cause sluggishness</term>, nourish laziness, weaken the digestion and the power of appetite, and finally harm the entire body. But because **autumn** is rarely or never consistently the same—being sometimes rainy and hot in its parts, and sometimes windy from the north and cold—there is no single rule for correcting its air. Instead, it should be moderated in different ways according to its variation. For example, if it is hot, use the cooling methods mentioned before; if it is cold or moist, use warming and drying agents so that the air may be reduced to a healthy balance. 

This is done, for instance, by adding warmer flowers and herbs to the previously mentioned leaves and flowers, and to the sprinklings of waters and decoctions. These include citrus flowers, leaves of rosemary, sage, marjoram, and the like, as well as branches of laurel and cypress. The house should be fumigated with the aforementioned decoctions or with incenses in which there is also a portion of cloves, cinnamon, mace, and **macalef** <note>original: "macalef," likely referring to the Mahaleb cherry seed (*Prunus mahaleb*), valued for its fragrance</note>, which is a quite fragrant and sweet seed growing in the region of Damascus. One should also boil **storax calamita** <note>a fragrant resin obtained from the bark of the *Styrax officinalis* tree</note> and **benzoin** <note>original: "belzuim"</note>, which I believe is closer to true myrrh than the kind we commonly use, and it better fits the ancient descriptions of myrrh itself. 

To these are also added waters and ointments which the nobility use in their luxuries, such as water from citrus flowers mixed with a portion of musk and ambergris, with which both the hands and face may be washed. However, it is worth knowing one thing: that **fire** destroys every bad, accidental, and putrefying quality of the air. Similarly, the evaporation of **vinegar** is useful, because by its coldness and dryness it corrects the vapors of bad air and prevents rot within them.

But in **winter**, when the air first declines from a balanced state through cold, it must be corrected with fire. If it is rainy or changed toward some other quality, it should be moderated by its contraries, such as the aforementioned decoctions of hot herbs and other refined and sweet-smelling things. These include leaves of laurel, rosemary, sage, mint, pennyroyal, hyssop, and the like. Fumigation should also be performed by placing **labdanum** <note>a sticky resin obtained from the *Cistus* (rockrose) plant</note>, storax, benzoin, and similar things upon glowing coals. Alternatively, one might use mixtures of these or common fragrances favored by the wealthy, such as **musk-gallia** <note>original: "gallia muscata," a complex aromatic compound used in medieval and Renaissance perfumery</note> and **musk-alipta** <note>original: "alipta muscata," a perfumed ointment or medicinal paste</note>, or pastilles of aloe wood. Or, one may boil cloves, cinnamon, mace, and aloe wood to create a vaporizer, especially in the bedroom; or a paste may be made of the aforementioned aromatic simples, kneaded in a mortar with fragrant wine, and placed upon the coals...

If the fire is made from fragrant woods—such as laurel, juniper, cypress, pine, and the like—you can improve the air through fire much more effectively. Furthermore, so that everything which might change the air into some bad quality may be removed, let the latrines, nearby sewers, and canals—especially in **Venice**—be cleaned, lest they offend the houses and streets with their foul vapors. 

In this way, with all diligence and in every season of the year, one must strive for the improvement of the air, so that it may be as close to a temperate balance as possible. Indeed, air that is moderate in its qualities and purged of foreign matter clarifies all the <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that govern health</term> and <term>spirits: subtle vapors in the body believed to facilitate life and thought</term>; it strengthens digestion and all natural virtues and operations, increases both internal and external natural strengths, preserves health, prolongs life, and delays old age. 

But if by chance the air has changed, becoming putrid in itself or through some other cause, such that it acquires a quality called **pestilential**, it produces foul and deadly illnesses in everyone. This is recognized when a great number of people, without distinction, perish from one and the same sickness. In such a case, the most healthful remedy is to flee far away from that place. But if some necessity forces one to remain in that location, let there be a perpetual fire in the home, and a continuous sprinkling of water mixed with vinegar, along with the other measures I have written about more extensively in my book on the pestilential fever.

## Chapter three teaches the manner of exercise and rest.

**E**xercise and motion greatly preserve bodies, while idleness corrupts them, as **Plato** said in the *Theaetetus*. This sentiment he applied not only to the health of the body, but also to the acquisition and preservation of the soul's teachings. **Hippocrates** also wrote wisely and healthfully on this opinion in his book on the <term>regimen: the systematic management of diet and lifestyle for health</term>; he commanded that labors be measured according to age, the constitution of the body, the season of the year, the change of weather, the places in which people live, and even the quantity of food. For he said that food and labor have a contrary relationship to one another...

...to be. Yet both of these contribute to health when moderate labors remove superfluities, and thus provide the best health. Therefore, exercise is beneficial, provided it tires a person very little so as not to make the limbs sluggish. Furthermore, nothing contributes more to health than exercise; if it is temperate, it rouses the <term>innate heat: the vital warmth believed to be the source of life and digestion</term> in all limbs. Consequently, the best preparation, <term>digestion: original "coctio," meaning "cooking" or processing of food by internal heat</term>, distribution, and assimilation into the limbs of foods and other <term>humors: the body's vital fluids</term> follows, as well as the expulsion of <term>excrements: waste products, including sweat and phlegm as well as feces</term>. 

For even if every rule is followed in both food and drink, waste products are nevertheless necessarily produced; modest exercise consumes these and helps to expel them through the appropriate channels <note>original: "meatus," referring to pores and passages in the body</note>, and thus it renders the body clean of superfluous waste. And since exercises are diverse—some being forceful and laborious, others moderate and gentle—the first kind should be forbidden because they primarily destroy all the body’s virtues and hinder the digestion of food and other natural operations. Therefore, let exercises be moderate, as they strengthen the innate heat and the bodily forces. By this reasoning, all operations—natural as well as vital and even <term>animal: referring to the "animal spirits" that governed movement and sensation</term>—are made most strong. 

Among other things, moderate exercises make not only the body but also the mind cheerful. These include hunting, fishing, and others which induce joy along with temperate movement or walking. Indeed many (as **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> said) are freed from bad illnesses by light exercises. And although for the robust and young—as he himself said in his little book *On Exercise with the Small Ball*—greater exercises are praised, I will recount those which are useful for the elderly, which also benefit the young. 

Therefore, a healthful exercise will be if, every day in the morning before leaving bed, all parts of the body are lightly rubbed with one's undershirt or some linen cloth—especially the chest, under the arms, the belly, and the groin. Soon after, the stockings and other garments and ornaments of the body should be put on with one's own hands. For in this way the body is modestly exercised, and the heat and <term>spirits: the subtle vapors that carry life and thought through the body</term> are roused. While these things are being done, it is useful to cough, to stir up spit and other wastes. Then, one should attend to untangling the hair and beard with a comb while using a mirror, lightly scratching the skin for some time. For during such a delay, by rubbing, the channels of the skin of the head are opened, and superfluities are drawn outward, whereby all the interior virtues—namely the imaginative, the meditative...

If it happens that you must deliver a speech in the senate or before a private magistrate, you should begin primarily with a low voice and ascend by degrees, so that the speech is completed comfortably and without damage to your strength. If a long speech must be held, let the talk be tempered in the middle, then the voice may be raised again gradually. Indeed, if the exercise of speaking is moderate, it rouses the <term>natural heat: the internal warmth believed to drive life and digestion</term>, produces a good color in the body, cleanses the chest, and by dilating the passages and veins of the lung, renders it more open to breathing in and out—especially if the breath is held somewhat while speaking. 

For the retention of breath recreates the body by gathering the heat and the <term>vital spirit: the subtle substance in the blood responsible for life and movement</term>, and it strengthens all the powers. On the other hand, it is very harmful if one shouts loudly and for a long time, since from this comes a great expulsion of internal air, a dissolving of the spirits, and even a shaking of the brain, from which follows a <term>catarrhal descent: the flow of excess phlegm or mucus from the brain to the lower body</term>. This is evidenced by the hoarseness found in those who shout loudly. And to sum up, one must know that just as a moderate voice contributes much to health, so an immoderate, impetuous, high, and long voice is very harmful. Therefore, when the speech is finished, one should descend and walk gradually, afterwards resting; and one should withdraw to a place where wind or cold air can least enter. If a fire is also lit, it will be beneficial.
