<header>THE THIRD SECTION</header>

## THE THIRD SECTION

If one should be tired and weary, let him go to bed and rest until his strength is regained. For indeed, through rest, once the heat has been called forth, the powers are restored. However, it must be observed that custom is a second nature, as **Aristotle** wrote in the book *On Memory and Reminiscence*, and **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the first book of the *Lectures on Physics*. For this reason, in exercise as in other things, one ought to take the measure from custom in some part, and (as **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> said in the first part of the *Aphorisms*), one must give something to custom, time, and age; and those who are accustomed to labors bear them more easily even if they are old and weak. In the second part of the *Aphorisms*, he wrote that after labors—for instance, if they occurred in the morning—after a period of rest, they should take themselves to lunch. But if it is evening, care must be taken that he does not engage in them <note>Referring to strenuous activities</note>, whether it be for speaking or for anything else, unless food has first been in the stomach for some hours—namely, for four hours at least. But any kind of exercise is always detestable if a significant amount of time has not passed since taking food; and those who do not take care often fall into bad illnesses and fevers, and this results from the penetration of <term>raw matters: undigested food or "humors" that have not been properly processed by the body’s heat</term> into the veins and the other passages of the body.

There are also other types of light exercises, such as moving the hands and the extension of the arms, which is done by twisting, rubbing, and striking them against each other and also squeezing them. We also extend the arms if we lift them to the head, or draw a bow, or perform similar exercises. But the most healthful among the rest is the exercise of walking; especially after a long rest, and when many raw matters are in the stomach. For when the heat cannot consume them, **Avicenna** <note>A Persian physician and polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> advised using exercise to stir up the <term>innate heat: the vital internal warmth that ancient doctors believed powered digestion and life</term>, which is nature’s instrument. If sometimes for the sake of the spirit it happens that one seeks the <note>original: "Rhus," likely a misspelling of "Rus," meaning the countryside</note> or open fields, a moderate run and light dancing is the best exercise, which is more suitable for the young and robust. 

But riding on horseback, being carried in a carriage, and playing with a lance or a small ball are those noble exercises which **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years.</note> among others praised; however, they are not suitable for the elderly. Finally, it is useful to wash the head and beard before lunch with <term>lye: a cleaning solution made from wood ashes and water</term> in which they have boiled fragrant herbs, at least once a week; and similarly wash the feet. But whether it be this or that exercise, it ought to be moderate: for immoderate labor (as I said) dries out the body; therefore, let the one who [brings] the body to a sweat...

For **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath (Ibn Sina) and one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> used to say that the prohibition of exercise makes all the <term>faculties: the functional powers of the body and mind</term> weak. 

For immoderate rest produces many <term>superfluities: excess waste or harmful fluids (humors) in the body</term>, from which not a few physical diseases arise; indeed, when the body is completely at rest, <term>raw matters: undigested or unprocessed substances</term> increase and obstructions follow, and subsequently, impediments to the distribution of nourishment. On the other hand, exercises prevent <term>repletion: an unhealthy state of being overfull or having an excess of bodily fluids</term>, increase natural heat, keep the passages open, provide agility to the body, prepare daily superfluities for evacuation, and strengthen the whole body—the nerves, the joints, and finally all the faculties. But if by some chance weariness and languor should occur from some labor, to rest soon (according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** in the *Aphorisms*, and **Galen** in the *Art of Medicine*) is the remedy.

### Chapter four examines sexual embraces.

**Q**uoniam <note>The large initial letter 'Q' begins the word 'Since'</note> Since sexual embraces <note>original: "venerei complexus"; referring to sexual intercourse</note> do not happen without movement and exercise, for that reason the discussion of sexual matters follows the instructions on exercise. And although there are many who think this topic should be placed among the "passions of the mind" <note>Emotions or psychological states</note>, I nevertheless will write of it here following the section on exercise. Furthermore, as **Galen** said in his small book *On Affected Places*: when semen is in excess, it is among those things that require evacuation, just like other <term>excrements: in this context, any waste or substance the body needs to discharge</term>, such as urine, the waste of the bowels, and the rest. For if it is retained so that it becomes spoiled, it acquires the nature of poison, and thus it produces bad and fearful conditions. Bad illnesses also occur if anyone engages in too much sexual embrace, since it both dries out the body and accelerates old age. Indeed, **Plato** prescribed in the fifth book of the *Republic* the time for sexual use for the procreation of men up to the fifty-fifth year. He surely believed this limit to be the time of the final vigor of life. Even in the robust, it often weakens the stomach, severely harms the brain and all the <term>animal faculties: the powers of the soul, divided into internal (like memory) and external (the senses)</term> both internal and external, and leads to <term>hectic: a persistent fever associated with wasting</term> and <term>marasmus: a state of extreme physical wasting</term>. For that reason, **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> said in his small book on the medical art that sexual matters, according to **Epicurus**, can be of very little benefit. Therefore, at any age and time, one must abstain from immoderate sexual activity as if from a poisonous snake, but especially in old age.

## Chapter five: on regulating sleep and wakefulness.

**A**ll living creatures have need of a regeneration of that <term>radical moisture</term> which is consumed through labor and wakefulness, and a restoration of the spent spirit; nature conveniently accomplishes and completes this through moderate sleep. For indeed, sleep aids <term>concoction: the "cooking" or digestion of food by natural heat</term>, removes labor and weariness, and by recalling the internal heat, warms the natural parts and the other limbs. Thus it increases and strengthens all the faculties, and especially the internal animal ones, as if by their opposite; for since wakefulness is likened to labor and sleep to rest—and what labor consumes, rest restores—for that reason, after the two modes of exercise already mentioned, let us speak consequently of sleep and wakefulness, so that this discourse might continue in some rational part...

...not lack reason. Therefore, sleep should be at night and moderate, starting two hours after dinner has been taken, so that the food has already descended to the bottom of the stomach and the period of wakefulness has now ended. I said **moderate sleep** because when it is superfluous and prolonged (if we believe the most learned **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rha."; referring to the Persian physician Al-Razi</note> in the fourth book *To Almansor*), it cools and dries the body and generates a phlegmatic humor; when this humor is multiplied, it renders the body lazy, sluggish, and torpid. However, sleep should not be less than a space of six hours, even in the robust and the young; yet longer sleeps are beneficial for the elderly, seeing as they require a greater restoration of <term>radical moisture: the innate vital fluid believed to sustain life and bodily heat, similar to oil in a lamp</term> and the <term>concoction: the "cooking" or ripening of food and humors by internal heat; essentially digestion</term> of raw materials in the stomach. For this reason, it is beneficial for them to sleep for a longer time—namely, for a space of eight and up to ten hours at the most.

Nor should one sleep during the midday hours after taking lunch if it can be avoided, since from this arises a great deal of evaporation to the head and an accumulation of <term>catarrhal: related to "catarrh," an excess of bodily fluids or phlegm believed to flow from the brain</term> materials therein. These, descending to the lower members, cause many bad conditions contrary to nature: for instance, if they go to the chest, they cause coughs and asthma; and if to the stomach, they impede **concoction**, dull the appetitive power <note>the natural desire for food</note>, and cause poisonous obstructions. Nonetheless, sleep is sometimes to be granted to those accustomed to sleeping during the day, and also to those who did not sleep at night for some reason, and also to those who have a weak stomach, such that they can only digest food with difficulty. 

Whatever the case may be, daytime sleep is always bad if we wish to compare it to nighttime sleep, especially on the hottest summer days. If, as I said, some necessity forces one to sleep during the day, let it be done while sitting. At night, however, it should be in a bed, covered with cloths, lying upon the side and not the back, and with some elevation of the head—the limbs not extended, but with some slight contraction. For the rest of the limbs, as **Galen** said in *On the Movement of Muscles*, consists in a certain moderate contraction of the limbs. In this way, we are also accustomed to sleep more comfortably and to see truer and more pleasant dreams, as **Plato** said in his book *On the Republic*. 

Therefore, we must strive to sleep moderately in all things; for indeed, wakefulness harms the elderly, and even more so if it is excessive, since superfluous wakefulness dries out the body, ruins its form, and prepares the body to receive fevers. On the contrary, moderate wakefulness (as **Aristotle** said in his book *On Sleep and Waking*), since it is that which is first intended in a living being, is of great benefit to those who live; sleep, however...

### Chapter six teaches the taking of suitable foods and drink.

**H**itherto I have treated the use of air, exercise, rest, sexual matters, sleep, and wakefulness—seeing as these are things that empty the body and take up superfluities, and also excite the appetite for food if administered moderately; therefore, with the best right, I have now resolved to speak about those things which are eaten and drunk. For indeed (as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years</note> said in the first book of *On Foods* <note>original: "de alimentis"</note>), without moderate nourishment, humans—whether they be healthy or sick—can live very poorly indeed. 

Therefore it is worthwhile that foods be chosen which first might restore the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the innate vital fluid believed to be the source of life and heat, which depletes as one ages</term> with a praiseworthy juice, and which are least thick and excrementitious; for a weak heat, such as the heat of the elderly, cannot transform a thick substance of nourishment. Let them also be from those things that are easily digested in the stomach and descend from the stomach in a short time. Wherefore, first of all, let the bread be from the best wheat, not old, but clean of foreign matter, and in short, without any foreign quality in its substance, smell, taste, or otherwise; and let it be well-leavened, salted, and moderately baked,

# E P I S T L E

...small chicks should be eaten before larger chicks, and soft-boiled eggs should precede other kinds. Likewise, other things that are of a light substance and generate good nourishment, such as milk and similar items, should come first. However, one must beware of liquid dishes <note>original: "ferculis sorbilibus"; literally "sipping dishes," such as thin broths or gruels</note> that descend quickly from the stomach and leave it too moist, lest they be taken before heavier foods. This is because they render the stomach unable to retain food, so that the remaining food descends to the intestines before **complete digestion** <term>complete digestion: "complectam concoctionem"; the Renaissance view of digestion as a process of "cooking" or ripening food within the body</term> is achieved. From this, obstructions of the **mesaraic veins** <term>mesaraic veins: the mesenteric veins, which carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</term> are formed, which are the nursery of many evil conditions. It also frequently causes harm if something that is easy to digest is taken after heavier foods; since the later items are digested before the earlier ones, they "float" atop the undigested earlier foods and either turn them rotten or prepare them for rot. For this reason, fruits should be eaten before heavier foods, unless perhaps they are taken after other foods to suppress vapors so they do not rise to the head. In that case, the quantity should not be great—for instance, taking a few pieces of pear or roasted quince with sugar after lunch or dinner, or similar things such as **quince preserve** <term>quince preserve: "diacydonite," a medicinal confection made of quince, often used as a digestive aid</term>. 

The time of taking food is also of great benefit in a prescribed regimen; for **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in Europe for centuries</note> said in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk:

> He who intends to preserve health should eat nothing 
> at all unless there is a natural appetite,

and he said "natural" to distinguish it from a "corrupt appetite" <note>a craving caused by illness or humors rather than true hunger</note>. Indeed, a natural appetite is when the stomach is empty of previous food. This happens at the very least in the elderly within a space of ten or twelve hours; it also happens in those who are not accustomed to vigorous exercise, but are weak and delicate nobles. In the thirteenth [chapter] of the third [book], Avicenna himself orders a delay of twenty-four hours. And there is that which he said in the chapter on those things which are eaten and drunk, namely: if anyone has been burdened by too much food, let him eat three times in two days—that is, let him take food once one day, and twice the next. 

Nevertheless, in all things, something must be granted to habit, age, and the season of the year; for we cannot abandon habit without danger, as **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BCE)</note> testifies in the second [book] of *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*, and also in his booklet *On Human Nature*. This same thing must be observed regarding ages. For children and decrepit old men need frequent administration of food, though not for the same reason. Furthermore, we give children very much and frequent food because they have a great deal of **innate heat** <term>innate heat: "calorem nativum," the vital warmth believed to be present in all living things, which was highest in youth and faded with age</term> and the power of growth, which in them...

# THIRD [PART]

[Youth] is most vigorous, having much moisture; then, being in a relaxed state, it also requires [food] for the growth of the limbs. But for the elderly, [food should be given] in smaller quantity and frequently, since they possess a weak heat which is not at all capable of digesting a very large quantity. By this reasoning, the foods of the elderly are frequently served in small amounts, generating much and excellent **juice** <note>original: "succum"; in this context, it refers to "chyle," the nutritious fluid produced by the first stage of digestion</note>; this rule must be observed at almost all times, but especially in summer.

It is also necessary to observe, according to the opinion of <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician in Roman and Medieval medicine</note>, in the third book of *On the Natural Faculties*, namely, that enduring hunger fills the stomach with bad and putrid humors. And this happens because when the stomach is empty of food, the **attractive faculty** <term>attractive faculty: "uirtus attractiua"; the biological force believed to allow organs to draw in necessary nutrients</term> draws in neighboring waste products since it has no other nourishment. And when this happens, it harms the elderly especially, whom (even if <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>Known as the father of Western medicine, his aphorisms were foundational to dietary theory</note> said it) bear fasting most easily; he did not say this because they should abstain from food entirely, but he believes they sustain hunger with less harm than youths (as has been said), who have the greatest amount of **innate heat** <term>innate heat: "natiui caloris"; the vital heat believed to be the source of life and the "fire" that cooks food in the stomach</term>.

Nevertheless, the seasons of the year must be observed, and in summer, food should be given in smaller quantities and more frequently. Since they are also somewhat reduced in hot qualities and are easier in substance to digest, such as small chickens, pigeons, and also the meat of kids and the like. And on the most burning days, they should be seasoned or sprinkled with **verjuice** <note>original: "succo uuæ acerbæ"; the tart juice of unripened grapes, used to cool the body</note>, rose water, and similar things. The most convenient hour for taking food is in the morning, two hours after sunrise and before the air grows hot, and in the evening, after the heat of the air has lessened. One must abstain during the midday hours.

Furthermore, in summer, some cooling fruits may be eaten in moderation, such as plums, muscat pears, sweet apples, and sour or mild cherries, which they call *amarascas* and *amarenas*. Also figs and ripe grapes. 

But in winter, a time which is the opposite of summer, a more abundant quantity and a thicker substance of food is appropriate, such as veal, two-year-old **wethers** <note>original: "castrati bimi"; castrated rams</note>, and also young beef may sometimes be eaten. Also most highly praised at this time are capons, hens, pheasants, partridges, quails, pigeons, thrushes, blackbirds, and the like, which can be seasoned with some spices so that they are more pleasing to the taste and easier to digest. The spices should be such as cinnamon, nutmeg, mace, cloves, and of this kind, or seeds of fennel, anise, and such things, concerning all of which...

-># EPISTLE<-

I shall speak extensively about foods in the course of this work. <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>original: "Hippocrates"; the ancient Greek physician whose theories on the seasons and the "four humors" dominated medical thought for centuries</note> says that in the spring and winter, our stomachs are warmer, and for that reason, better digestions occur during those times; but in the middle periods, namely in autumn, one must observe a middle ground in the things we eat. Indeed, because the body has been made weak in autumn by the dissipation of the heat from the preceding summer, food should be taken in smaller quantities and should be easier to digest. In the spring, however, one may eat slightly more fully, since the bodily virtues are now beginning to grow strong. 

One thing must be strictly observed: nothing can be worse for maintaining health at any age than eating many different dishes at a single table. Many troubles usually follow from this. First, because of the variety of foods, we tend to eat more than is appropriate. Second, because the things we have consumed are diverse, a certain conflict in digestion must necessarily occur. For that reason, undigested food becomes mixed with that which is already digested. Thus, the **juice** <note>original: "succus"; referring here to the chyle, the nutrient-rich fluid produced by the stomach that is later refined into blood</note> which ought to be converted into blood becomes tainted and corrupted. 

Finally, because the stomach labors more when digesting a wide variety of consumed foods, <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "Auicēna"; the Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook in Europe</note> praised the ancients because they satisfied themselves with only a single kind of food and practiced exercise. Therefore, simple foods are the ones that are most conducive to preserving health. For example, in the morning at lunch, let there be a dish made of egg mixed in broth, or of **spelt** <note>original: "farre"; an ancient species of wheat, often used in porridges</note>. The meat should be boiled or even roasted, provided it is from a young animal. However, nourishment from boiled meats is more praiseworthy and easier to digest. 

In the evening one should dine, but eat in a smaller quantity—for instance, bread cooked in broth, or another light dish along with lighter meats. This should be adjusted according to the season: in summer one should eat young chickens, young partridges, or goat meat and similar things; at other times, one should increase or decrease the amount as the season requires. At dinner, always take a smaller amount, especially if one had a very hearty lunch in the morning. During the evening hours, due to the day's activities, the body's heat is not as strong as it is in the morning, nor is the morning food ever entirely digested in all its parts by the evening. Therefore, I judge that one must be careful not to add a great quantity of food in the evening to a stomach still struggling with its previous digestion. Let the quantity be such that it neither hinders nightly rest nor interferes with the recovery of the **spirits** <term>spirits: "spirituum"; in medieval physiology, these were subtle, invisible substances that circulated through the body to maintain life, movement, and thought</term>. And since wine, among those things which...

Therefore, one must attend to the rules concerning wine with no less diligence than those concerning food. Thus, let the drink for the elderly be, above all, the best wine, in that quantity and strength that ought to be taken, and also according to the season—as in winter, stronger wines are better. And since in all things some consideration must be given to habit, he who is accustomed by habit to drink strong wines and in large quantities may use them more liberally both in quantity and quality. 

And although <term>Plato</term> <note>the famous Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC)</note>, in the second book of the *Laws*, allowed the elderly a great deal of wine for drinking, he nevertheless said that wine is not useful for all ages. For he says: "In the first place, we shall decree by law that boys until their twenty-second year <note>original: "uigeſimum ſecundum annum"</note> should not dare to drink wine at all." For we shall warn them that one must not add fire to fire <note>original: "ignem, igni"; a classical metaphor warning against adding the "heat" of wine to the natural "heat" and passion of youth</note> in the body and soul before they have reached manhood and begun the labors of that age. 

Youth also should flee from draining raging wine; soon, let them begin to drink it moderately until their thirtieth year, and let them abstain entirely from being full of wine and from drunkenness. And when they reach forty, then reclining at banquets, let them invoke both others and especially <term>Dionysus</term> <note>original: "Dionysium"; the Greek god of wine, also known as Bacchus</note> to the sacred rites and games of the elderly—the god who granted wine to men as a remedy against the harshness of old age. These are the words of Plato. 

A little later, he added that the minds of the elderly who drink—just as iron becomes soft in a fire—become more tender and youthful by glowing with wine, so that it acts as a remedy and medicine; namely, so that the soul gains modesty, and the body gains health and strength. It is worthwhile to understand that all these things in Plato refer to the moderate drinking of wine, since he also wrote of many evils and inconveniences resulting from immoderate drinking in that same second book of the *Laws*. 

Indeed, if the drinking of wine is excessive, it extinguishes the senses, the intellect, and the memory, and reduces men to the ignorance of children, since a person who drinks immoderately is least of all master of himself. Thus, not only will the old man be "a child twice over" <note>original: "senex, bis puer"; a common proverb suggesting that old age brings a return to a child-like state</note>, but so too will the drunkard <note>original: "remulentus", likely a variation of "temulentus"</note>, from excessive wine-drinking. There are other harms besides those mentioned from immoderate wine-drinking; for beyond the fact that it harms the brain, it also brings a bad temperament to the nerves, and causes <term>apoplexy</term> <note>original: "apoplexiam"; a sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis, similar to a stroke</note> and the "resolution" of the nerves <note>original: "neruorum reſolutionem"; a term for paralysis or loss of motor function</note>. For this reason, at any time and in any month, strong wine must be drunk moderately and according to one's tolerance. However, if in the morning...

# E P I S T O L A

After a soft-boiled egg, a morsel of bread dipped in aromatic wine—such as **Malmsey** <note>original: "maluaticum"; a sweet, high-alcohol wine originally from Greece, prized in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>—should be taken. This benefits the stomach, excites the appetite, and aids digestion. Therefore, the wine served at the table should be moderate; neither new nor old, but in between the two. This is because new wine harms the liver and intestines, while all the ancients believed old wine to be more a medicine than a food, though it does still provide nourishment.

Let the wine be clear and tending toward red, not of a thick substance, and a medium between sweet and acidic. It should not be watery, but rather possess a certain sweet **astringency** <note>original: "stipticum"; a dry, mouth-puckering quality similar to tannins in modern red wine</note>. It should be potent, with a good aroma and a pleasant flavor. For wine that is too sweet causes inflammation, creates obstructions, and fills the head. Conversely, sour wine harms the stomach and the nerves and generates **raw humors** <note>original: "cruditates"; undigested matter that was thought to cause illness in the humoral system of medicine</note>, especially in the elderly.

Similarly, wine that has turned to vinegar is bad; for besides harming the stomach with its coldness, its sharp quality <note>original: "inciſione"; literally a 'cutting' or penetrating action</note> directs raw matter toward the nerves and causes it to penetrate their substance. However, because it is often necessary to drink potent wines even in summer for some greater reason—for example, if the stomach is suffering from raw humors or a similar condition—in such a case it should be diluted with water boiled with coriander seeds, a portion of cinnamon, or something else that can temper its harmful heat by cooling it. For drinking potent wine causes **yellow bile** <note>original: "cholera"; one of the four humors, associated with heat and fire</note> to run wild; for that reason, in summer, it is safer to drink it mixed with a portion of spring water.

In winter, however (as the nature of the season requires), many benefits usually follow from a moderate drink of wine: specifically, an abundance of **spirits** <note>original: "spirituum"; the "vital spirits" believed to circulate through the body to provide energy and life</note>, bodily strength, good sleep, excellent preparation of food in the stomach, and the proper distribution of its nourishment.

Nevertheless, one must abstain from excessive wine drinking, especially when the stomach is empty of food. Furthermore, wine taken before a meal, being quick to penetrate, moves the stomach so that the food eaten afterward descends to the intestines before its time. Conversely, wine taken after a meal does the same thing by its sheer volume, as it carries the food to the intestines before **digestion** <note>original: "coctionem"; literally 'cooking,' the metabolic process where the stomach was thought to 'cook' food into nutrients</note> is complete. From this, diseases arise due to obstruction and decay.

Therefore, let the drink taken during the meal be small and frequent, so that the preparation of food for nourishment may be handled conveniently, and let it be (so to speak) a light tasting by sipping. Nor should one entirely abstain from a draught of wine after food, as it is sometimes permitted for those accustomed to it, or for the strength of the stomach, to take some wine after eating. ->THIRD [PART]<-

...[if it is] less, it causes no trouble to the head. And since there are some who are so accustomed, or for some other reason gladly drink water, one must generally abstain from drinking water, especially if they are elderly or weak, since it chills and debilitates the stomach, intestines, nerves, and other limbs; furthermore, by its penetration and humidity, it leads humors toward distant limbs. However, the moisture of water may be corrected by boiling. 

And since a **false thirst** <note>original: "sitis mendosa"; a sensation of thirst not caused by a genuine lack of fluids, often attributed in historical medicine to saltiness or heat in the stomach</note> is often known to occur by day and night, you shall correct this first by enduring it and by sleeping. But if a powerful thirst should distress you, as often happens in the summer time, rinsing the mouth with cold water or some other moistening and cooling thing is a ready remedy. 

But if it is a "true thirst," which arises from a lack of moisture, it will be best to drink something that can moisten the stomach according to the opportunity of the season: such as in summer, spring water with **rose syrup**, and in winter, with wine. However, let the drink be moderate; indeed, at whatever time or hour the necessity of drinking arises, whether it be water, wine, or another thing taken as a drink, let it be clear, light, pleasant to the taste, and free from all bad odor. Thus far, I have wished to briefly touch upon the general rules of those things which are eaten and drunk. Now, we must deal with each thing individually, beginning first with **meats**.

All meats are generally hot and moist. For this reason, they generate the most blood and nourish the body best. Yet there are some among them which excel in other virtues and effects: for the meat of four-footed animals <note>quadrupeds</note> nourishes more than others, as they are moister. Both <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his theories on the four humors shaped medicine for over a thousand years.</note> and the other most eminent ancient physicians praised **pork**, for the reason that its qualities have an affinity with the human temperament. Indeed, pork is hot and moist, and very nourishing.

But because its moisture is excessive, very many **phlegmatic humors** <note>original: "pituitosi humores"; thick, cold, and moist fluids which, in the humoral system, were thought to cause sluggishness or respiratory issues if they became excessive</note> are generated from its substance; this moisture is corrected with salt or some other dry spice, such as <term>pepper</term>, <term>clove</term> <note>original: "garyophyllum"</note>, <term>fennel</term>, <term>anise</term>, <term>cumin</term>, <term>savory</term>, <term>oregano</term>, and the like. It is common practice, however, for pork to be prepared with salt, especially the thighs <note>hams</note> and shoulders. These parts, when so salted, are pleasant to the taste and provide worthy nourishment. But if they are too salty, it is the opposite, because they provide poor nourishment, being inflammatory and drying, and should not be eaten. Therefore, let them be eaten...

->T H I R D<-

...those which adhere to the bones, and produce more praiseworthy nourishment. These should be minimally sinewy; furthermore, the right side is more excellent than the left. Similarly, the meat of the male is better than the female, and the meat of darker animals is more excellent. Beef is commonly eaten boiled, and it provides the best and most praiseworthy nourishment (as I said), especially if it comes from animals that are young and fat. Yet some parts are most flavorful if they are eaten roasted, such as the parts located around the vertebrae of the back, and the two large internal muscles along the spine proceeding to the **sacrum** <note>original: "os sacrum"; the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note>, which they call the **loins** <note>original: "lombos"</note>. These are better and are eaten more during the height of winter. But the internal organs, such as the heart, liver, spleen, intestines, head, feet, and the rest, provide little nourishment, are difficult to digest, and produce **bad humors** <note>original: "mali succi"; literally "bad juices," referring to poor-quality bodily fluids produced during digestion</note>. For this reason, they are suited neither for the elderly nor for others. Similarly, other parts that have been salted are not entirely beneficial, as they are drier and generate **melancholic blood** <term>melancholic blood: one of the four humors, associated with black bile, believed to be cold, dry, and prone to causing sadness or sluggishness</term>. But the best parts prepared with salt are the tongue and the **udders** <note>original: "mamillæ"</note>, which are very pleasing to the taste. Cow udders are prepared or preserved with salt in this manner: after they are cut from the body, they are sliced here and there, especially following the path of the veins so that any milk within them may flow out. Then, one must rub them all over with salt that has been reduced to a very fine powder. Once prepared with salt in this way, let them hang for three days; then place them between two boards with a weight added on top so that all moisture is pressed out, and let them remain for nine days. Afterward, hang them for a month in the **smoke-room** <note>original: "vaporarium"; a chamber for drying or curing meat by the heat and smoke of a fire</note> by the fire. They should be eaten boiled in the first course, and this is a most pleasing food to the taste.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The meat of suckling **calves** <note>original: "Vitulorum"; veal</note> is far superior to beef, for it is pleasing to the taste, has the best juices, provides much nourishment, and is easy to digest. Furthermore, a most temperate nourishment is generated from them. Because of the goodness of both their substance and **temperament** <term>temperament: the balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) within a substance</term>, these may be eaten at any time of year without distinction; they can be boiled, roasted, or otherwise cooked and prepared, for instance in a frying pan with fat and spices. This is a middle way of cooking between boiling and roasting; and so that it may be made softer and more flavorful, it should be frequently sprinkled while cooking with **rose water** <note>original: "aqua rosacea"</note> mixed with meat broth and **Malmsey wine** <note>original: "uino maluatico"; a strong, sweet wine popular in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>, or with the juice of unripe grapes <note>original: "succu uuæ immaturæ"; verjuice</note>, or of oranges and similar fruits.

->E P I S T O L A<-

# E P I S T O L A

...of the **castrated ram** <note>original: "castrati arietis"</note>, especially those two years old. Indeed, these are pleasing to the taste and provide praiseworthy nourishment. However, those that are too fat usually loosen the stomach and intestines with their excessive moisture; on the other hand, the lean ones are said to be less suitable for nourishment. The meat of **lambs** <note>original: "agnorum"</note> is exceptionally moist; while it does nourish, it produces a great deal of **superfluity** <note>original: "superfluitatis"; the metabolic waste or excess fluids that the body cannot process</note> and is resistant to digestion, so much so that it very often spoils in the stomach before it can be digested. From this spoilage, foul and wicked belching follows. Similarly, **mutton** <note>original: "ovila caro"; sheep meat</note> provides poor nourishment and is difficult to digest; for this reason, I do not recommend it, not only for the elderly but for other ages as well. The meat of a **suckling kid** <note>original: "lactentis hœdi"</note> is superior to all others; indeed, for every age, but especially for old age, it generates the most and best nourishment. Nor is there any notable excess of moisture in them; they are easy to digest and pleasing to the taste. They are eaten boiled or roasted in the spring and summer, and at other times if they can be found. But the meat of **he-goats** <term>Hyrcorum: male goats, noted in ancient medicine for their rank smell and tough, indigestible flesh</term> and of goats—as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his works on the properties of foods remained authoritative for over a millennium</note> wrote in the second book of *On Foodstuffs*—is detestable.

The meat of wild animals is drier than that of domestic animals. For this reason, it provides less nourishment, especially those animals that live in the mountains and exhaust themselves. But those that graze in damper places are also moister and provide better nourishment. Let us begin, therefore, with those that are more commonly used. First, the **rabbit** <term>cuniculus: the European rabbit, often distinguished from the larger hare in dietary manuals</term>, which is also called a small hare, provides excellent nourishment; those raised at home are better and more pleasing to the taste. They are roasted or prepared in a frying pan with fat and other ingredients.

The meat of **hares** <note>original: "leporinæ"</note>—when young, fat, and caught in the hunt—is intermediate between beef and veal. For that reason, it generates moderate nourishment, and the better parts of them are the hindquarters and the loins; however, frequent use generates **melancholic blood** <term>melancholic blood: a thick, dark blood associated with the humor of black bile, believed to cause heaviness of spirit or "melancholy" if it became excessive</term>. They are cooked in various ways according to the diverse luxuries of the palate, but they are most often seasoned with pepper and other spices, a method that is not entirely praiseworthy. It would be better, after roasting, to eat them moistened with broth, rose water, cinnamon, and **cloves** <note>original: "garyophyllo"</note>. For in this way, more praiseworthy nourishment is generated from them.

Yet **young chickens** <note>original: "pulli gallinacei"</note> are very easily digested. They generate much and excellent nourishment if they are fat, nor does any notable waste remain from them; they are beneficial at all times and for all ages, and their use strengthens the stomach and appetite, and balances the humors, especially in summer. They are prepared by boiling, and also by roasting, and in a pan in various ways—for example, in summer with grains of sour grapes and **orange juice** <note>original: "arāciarum succo"</note>. In this way, it extinguishes the sharpness of the bilious humor; in other bodies, cinnamon and other spices should be added. Let the chickens be fat (if they are male), from those that have not yet begun to crow; the females, however, should be larger, and those raised at home are far better.

# L E T T E R

...restores me to walk with power, even though I was almost deprived of sense and motion. And finally, it refills depleted bodies with the best nourishment. I have said all these things concerning young birds <note>specifically squabs or young pigeons</note>. For the flesh of old pigeons is both drier and colder, and is of difficult digestion. Its nourishment is not as good. Young ones are sometimes prepared by boiling, but for the most part, they are eaten roasted or cooked in a frying pan.

The flesh of turtledoves, if we believe the most eminent and wisest physicians, is the food of wise old men; for besides the fact that it generates an excellent and praiseworthy humor <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health</note>, its use strengthens all the senses and also sharpens the faculty of thought and preserves the memory. However, these turtledove meats should be young and fat, for indeed the old ones, being drier, are not so suitable for the elderly. Let them be prepared just like young chickens, according to the requirements and manner of the season, with spices and other things.

Among domestic meats that are eaten, geese and ducks are very much in use, since they differ little from each other in substance, complexion <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, or dry qualities in a substance</note>, and virtue. Therefore, they shall be discussed together. For indeed they are very moist, moderately hot, hard to digest, of bad juice <note>original: "mali succi"; meaning they produce poor quality blood or fluids</note>, full of many superfluities, and they even generate humors prone to corruption, which physicians say are the matter of putrid fevers. Let those be chosen which are middle-aged, between youth and old age; however, domestic ones are better than those from the water or marshes. But in my opinion, it is better to leave them aside. They are prepared in various ways for eating, namely by roasting with salt and **fennel**, **anise**, and also some other spices, such as **cinnamon**, **mace**, and the like. There are also those who prepare them by boiling—namely, first cutting them into pieces and seasoning them together with spices in water with vinegar and salt until they are perfectly cooked in a pan; they eat them thus prepared at the first course, and only in winter.

All the flesh of wild birds is drier than that of domestic ones, among which there are certainly some that are more temperate and less moist, and for that reason, they produce a more praiseworthy juice for nourishment. There are also some that are less approved, especially those which are difficult to digest and generate bad juice. But those which are held to be the very best are **pheasants**; for they nourish the most, and no superfluous moisture is generated from them. Likewise, the young ones are more praiseworthy...

They have a small body of an ashen color, whereas the others have red and black colors here and there. Therefore, let those who hunt these birds to break stones take care lest, deceived by the similarity, they labor in vain; it is enough to have given this warning. # L E T T E R

[those birds] which are predatory <note>original: "rapaces"; birds of prey like hawks or eagles</note> are said to be worse than others, for they are tough and difficult to digest, generating a meager and dry nourishment; for that reason, they are least suitable for the elderly and those recovering from illness. One thing, however, must be observed in every kind of meat: that meats which have been exposed to the air for some time tend to be more pleasing and flavorful to eat, and are also more easily cooked <note>original: "coquuntur"; refers here to both culinary preparation and the metabolic "cooking" of digestion</note>. Likewise, those animals that are still growing produce a more moist nourishment. Furthermore, among the parts of animals, some are seen to be better and some less good; for all the extremities—such as the head, neck, feet, and tail—are considered unpraiseworthy if you compare them to the remaining parts. Moreover, they are difficult to digest and provide little and coarse nutrition. But among the parts of birds, those that are found around the wings, the breast, the neck, and the back are better and more flavorful. 

Indeed, among the internal organs, the livers are praised, especially those of geese and chickens, for among the other organs they generate a better juice <note>original: "succum"; the nutritional essence or humor extracted from food</note>. Truly, the testicles of roosters are extolled with the highest praise by everyone for the elderly and those recovering from illness, on account of their praiseworthy quality and the abundance and goodness of the nourishment they provide.

Similarly, certain parts of four-legged animals are better and others worse for nourishing. As an example, the meat that is close to the bone is more praiseworthy and more pleasing to the taste. Similarly, that of the right side is better than that of the left, and that of the front part better than the back. And that which is closer to the heart is better than that which is further away; as it is better regulated by the heat of the heart, it becomes more fit for nourishing <note>In Galenic medicine, the heart was the source of "vital heat" that refined the blood and nutrients; proximity to this heat meant the meat was "better processed"</note>. Furthermore, the meats near the back, especially the internal loins, are more easily digested and also exist as better-tasting. After these, the parts of the hips follow in goodness. Indeed, the remaining parts in the area of the belly are not so approved. For due to the mixture of many sinewy <note>original: "neruosarum"; referring to connective tissue or tendons</note> parts, they are neither easily digested nor do they generate a praiseworthy juice. Finally, the intestines—such as the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and other internal members—generate a worse juice. Nevertheless, the liver of pigs and kids, and even of suckling animals, is considered better; for this reason, it is eaten as a delicacy among spices, either boiled along with broth and raisins, or fried with some fat. It is also a custom in certain cities to eat boiled intestines sprinkled with spices, which is not greatly praised by physicians. Furthermore...

### THE THIRD LETTER

They make a jelly <note>original: "gelatinam"</note> from feet and heads boiled together, with the addition of vinegar and spices (such as ginger, mace, cinnamon, and cloves). Since this food is heavy and provides poor nutrition, it is in no way suitable for the elderly. Finally, it should be known that the blood of animals, of whatever kind it may be, is minimally suitable or useful for nourishment; the worst is that which is drawn from older and more earthy animals, such as beef. But among birds, the blood of a duck is the least bad; and among four-legged animals, the blood of pigs and kids <note>young goats</note> is preferable. Nor should the brain be omitted, for if it is eaten, it may harm the stomach and produce a bad juice <note>original: "succum"; refers to the nutritional humor or essence extracted during digestion</note>. However, the brain of chickens was a very famous medicine among the ancients for strengthening the human brain. For this reason, they order the eating of them for weakness of the brain, and they praise hare brains for strengthening the nerves <note>original: "nervos"; in this period, this could refer to nerves, tendons, or sinews</note>. But lest I be tedious with a long discourse, let what has been said about meats for eating suffice, and I shall move on to other edible things.

And since people are accustomed to eating not only meat, but also milk and many other things made from milk, there will now be a discussion concerning milk and dairy products <note>original: "lacticinis"</note> that are beneficial for the elderly. Furthermore, milk stands out above other nutrients, so much so that in restoring those who are exhausted and renewing the radical moisture <note>original: "humidum radicale"; in medieval medicine, this was the vital fluid or "lamp oil" of life that diminished with age</note>, nothing can be more convenient or apt (provided the stomach can tolerate and regulate it). There is no lack of opinions regarding the diversity of its substance, varying according to the genus of the animal, its age, the time since birth, its pasture, and the seasons of the year. These difficulties will become clear as we proceed. The first thing worth knowing, which is a matter of dispute among the most serious physicians, is its temperament <note>original: "temperamentum"; the balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. However, since it is generated from blood, and its origins testify to its principles (according to the opinion of Aristotle), one must believe its temperament to be close to that of blood. This is further demonstrated by its light substance and the pleasant sweetness within it. Of all types, they first praise the milk of women as the most temperate and fit for nourishment; they require that the woman be young, close in temperament to the patient, not too far removed from the time of childbirth, and eating the best foods. But among the animals <note>original: "brutis"</note>, they first praise goat's milk, then sheep's milk, and finally cow's milk. That milk is better which is milked in the morning and drunk while still warm. The animal from which it is milked should be young, healthy, and plump, one that has not long since given birth and is grazing on praisew-

# THE LETTER

...praiseworthy pastures; and although many doctors have praised donkey's milk for those whose radical members <note>The "radical members" refer to the vital organs believed to contain the "radical moisture" or life force of a person</note> have not been consumed by habitual heat, since it cools more and is less likely to curdle in the stomach. However, it is not beneficial in every respect for the elderly and the decrepit. Whatever the case may be, milk should be taken in the morning before other foods.

Since it is not safe to mix milk with other foods, nor is its frequent use secure, for frequent use causes obstructions in the mesenteric veins <note>original: "meseraicis"; the veins that transport nutrients from the digestive system to the liver</note> and generates small stones in the kidneys. Therefore, it should only be administered with caution; and to ensure it does not primarily curdle <note>original: "casceetur"; literally "turn into cheese"</note> or spoil in the stomach, and may also pass down more quickly, doctors order a portion of salt or honey to be mixed with it for eating.

We, however, very often use sugar <note>original: "saccarum"</note> in place of honey; but when an unnatural flow of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> occurs from the use of milk, it would be best to extinguish a piece of glowing steel or stones in it many times, so that its watery, whey-like parts, and even the buttery parts, might be somewhat dried out. 

The most convenient time for taking milk and those things made from milk is spring, since at that time the pastures are best, and the animals are also in the best health, so that they produce the best milk. If the milk is fresh and curdled, it is a heavy food and difficult to digest; and although it may be pleasing to the taste, it is not very beneficial. Similarly, cheese <note>original: "caseus"</note> is a very heavy food, which is suitable only for the robust and those who labor, as it is most difficult to cook <note>In Galenic medicine, "cooking" (concoction) refers to the process of digestion</note>; and salted cheese is better for digestion than unsalted.

Furthermore, sour milk <note>original: "lac acetosum"; this likely refers to buttermilk or a naturally fermented yogurt-like product</note> is not as harmful to the stomach as other dairy products, which is why it is more beneficial for the elderly, especially if a portion of sugar is mixed with it. 

After sour milk, in terms of quality, is cream <note>original: "cremor lactis"</note>, which among us is commonly called "the head of the milk." Not too much of it should be eaten, as it relaxes the stomach, fills the head, and softens the nerves; however, its moderate use with sugar and rose water as a first course is very nourishing. Butter <note>original: "butirum"</note> is of nearly the same quality, since it is itself a kind of cream. 

Finally, that part of the milk is praised which they collect from the watery portion after the curdling of cheese by means of a light boiling; they commonly call it "twice-cooked milk" or "recooked" <note>original: "recocta"; this is the origin of modern ricotta</note>. This is also eaten as a first course with sugar, yet it does not nourish as much as milk and cream, for it is difficult to digest. Other types of cheeses are hard to digest and weigh down the stomach; they generate a bad juice...

# THIRD

...since they also cause many obstructions, especially if they have been dried out by age; for besides what has been said, they bind the bowels, harm the kidneys, and prepare the way for the generation of small stones <note>kidney stones</note>. Therefore, if they are to be eaten, let it be those that are between fresh and old, and somewhat salted, having neither too much stickiness nor toughness.

Eggs are most highly praised among all other nutrients, for they nourish through all their parts—especially their yolks <note>original: "uitella"</note>—so that almost no part of them is waste. Furthermore, they are well-balanced and easy to digest. Even though their parts, such as the yolk and the white <note>original: "albumen"</note>, are of different substance, color, and temperament, a most balanced nourishment is produced from their mixture. One should not believe (as many wise men assert) that the white is naturally hotter than the yolk because the chick's limbs are generated from it while they are nourished by the yolk. It is not because the white is hotter that the chick's limbs are made from it, but because the rooster’s seed is mixed with the white; this seed warms that white so that the chick's limbs can be generated from the white substance itself. Nevertheless, the whole substance of the egg (as I have said) is quite close to a balanced temperament.

The best method and use for them is soft-boiling <note>original: "coctio ad sorbendum apta"; literally "cooking fit for sipping"</note>. To make them tastier and so they pass more quickly from the stomach, a little salt should be added, and they should be taken before other foods. They are also cooked whole, without shells, in water or meat broth; these are tasty and excellent, especially if seasoned with sugar and cinnamon. There are also those who first lightly cook eggs in a frying pan with simple water and a little sugar or rose water; I do not disparage this. A most praiseworthy dish is also made from them if they are eaten mixed into meat broth, with which it is beneficial to add a little vinegar or verjuice <note>original: "succi uuæ acerbæ"; the tart juice of unripened grapes used as a culinary acid</note>. For the elderly and those recovering from illness, however, I most gladly provide a portion of aromatic wine or excellent Malvasia wine with sugar and cinnamon. 

But fried, hard-boiled, and hardened eggs—and especially those cooked with oil or butter—are bad; for they are difficult to digest, generate bad humors <note>original: "malum succum"; refers to poor quality bodily fluids in the Galenic system</note>, harm the stomach, and pass from it slowly. Whatever the preparation, one should always add a portion of salt, as they are thus more easily digested and descend from the stomach. And since, besides chicken eggs, there are also others that are eaten, such as those of ducks...

# E P I S T O L A

of geese and other birds, both domestic and wild. For this reason, chicken eggs are the best among them, followed by those fresh eggs laid by birds that have an affinity with chickens, such as **pheasants** <note>original: "fasciani"</note> and similar species. Eggs are truly an excellent food for the elderly and those recovering from illness, as they serve to restore the radical moisture <note>In Renaissance medicine, "radical moisture" was the vital fluid thought to be the fuel for the body's life-force, much like oil in a lamp.</note>. For this reason, I praise eggs most highly.

There are also, besides the things mentioned, other animals that humans are accustomed to eating. Some of these have been highly praised for their goodness and the way they provide nourishment, though physicians have no shortage of questions regarding their substance. This is especially true since they were not entirely categorized by the ancients among either the quadrupeds or the birds, nor even among the types of fish; rather, they possess a certain middle nature between the two. These are, namely, **turtles**, **snails**, **frogs**, and their kind. Because they have a nature that falls neither strictly among meats nor fishes, I have decided to say something about them before the discussion turns to fish. 

For indeed, as the genus of turtles is twofold—namely, land-dwelling and sea-dwelling—and the land-dwelling kind is further divided into those of the woods and those of the water, first and foremost the most praiseworthy food comes from the forest-dwelling land turtles. Immediately after these in quality are the aquatic ones. Among the aquatic turtles, the marsh-dwellers that live in stagnant pools are the worst. Their entire temperament leans toward the cold and moist. Their substance is nourishing because it possesses a great deal of stickiness <note>original: "lentoris"; a viscous or gummy quality believed to have soothing medicinal properties.</note> combined with moisture. For this reason, they are given to those suffering from wasting diseases <note>original: "tabidis"; typically referring to consumption or tuberculosis.</note> as nourishment, if they have been consumed by a heat that has become habitual in their limbs. For by its own moisture, the turtle's substance blunts the heat, and by its stickiness, it resists sharpness <note>original: "acredini"; referring to the "acrid" or "sharp" humors like yellow bile that irritate the body.</note>. It is not a useful food for the elderly; however, if it must be given, it should be seasoned with cinnamon, mace, and other spices which increase its heat and assist its distribution through the body. 

**Sea turtles**, however, produce poor juices and are difficult to digest; therefore, they should be avoided. **Snails**, or slugs <note>original: "limaciae"</note>, also nourish through their moisture and stickiness, and they work by resisting the sharpness of the heat that has settled in the limbs. They are eaten boiled, sprinkled with sugar and cinnamon (though rarely), since they are difficult to cook. **Frogs** (even though they are eaten by many) produce a bad and unpraiseworthy nourishment. For they are born from rot and dwell in putrid waters; they cause pains and other evil ailments of the intestines. For this reason, their consumption should be forbidden at any age or time.

-># THIRD PART<-

->E<-

**Fish** are by no means praised for the elderly as a primary or simple means of restoration <note>original: "instauratio," referring to the recovery of strength and vital fluids</note>. For a cold and humid nourishment is generated from them, and since the elderly are already of such a temperament, fish are generally unsuitable. However, among them, some are not quite so humid—especially those from the sea and those that live among rocks (if you wish to compare them to river fish). Truly, among the marine fish, some are more praiseworthy, such as those with scales and those that dwell near rocks. Those from the marshes, however, are indisputably bad, as they feed upon mud. 

It is useful to note this same distinction in those fish that live in fresh waters: for those that live and feed in stagnant or non-flowing waters are bad. Better are those that swim in rivers and clear waters. Furthermore, because certain marine fish often live and feed in fresh waters—and vice versa, such as river fish in marine waters—one must be careful. **Sturgeon**, **trout**, and **eels** are always problematic, yet marine fish are even worse if they remain in fresh waters, such as **grey mullets** <note>original: "cephali"</note> and **plaice** <note>original: "pascere," likely "passeres," a term for flatfish like plaice or flounder</note>. Conversely, if river fish enter salt water—as happens to **tench** <note>original: "tinchis"</note> and others—they improve. This is because the saltiness of the seawater, possessing a hot and dry power, partially reduces their superfluous coldness and humidity. Therefore, sturgeon and trout generate more praiseworthy nourishment if they are caught in marine waters. 

The worst of all are those that smell foul and have a poor substance to their flesh, such as **rays** <note>original: "ragiae"</note>, **dogfish** <note>original: "canes," literally "dogs," referring to small sharks or dogfish</note>, and the like. Indeed, from eating these, dangerous diseases often arise; they benefit no one and are always bad. Therefore, I in no way praise eating them. 

And even though certain fish may be pleasing to the taste, very little nourishment is actually generated from eating them; furthermore, it is a type of nourishment that tends to dull the internal heat of the convalescent and the elderly rather than increase it. For that reason, if fish are to be eaten, they should be seasoned with a condiment that is able to dry out their humidity and resist their coldness. In no other way can the elderly eat them safely, even if they are the best of their kind. 

The best method of preparation and cooking, if they are fresh, is first of all roasting on a **grill** <note>original: "craticula"</note> (for those that can withstand roasting), and then boiling <note>original: "elixatio"</note>, so that they simmer together in water, wine, and salt. After cooking, spices should be added, such as **pepper**, **ginger**, **cinnamon**, **mace**, and **cloves** <note>original: "gariophali"</note>. Frying <note>original: "friscio"</note>, however, is a worse method of cooking, as it makes them harder to digest, especially for those with a weak stomach, such as the elderly. Nor shall I pass over the fact that after...

# E P I S T O L A

...their cooking, while they are still hot; if they are covered, they acquire a putrid and bad quality. However that may be, salted fish are less harmful than fresh ones, since through salt, their substance is rendered hotter and drier. Yet those that remain salted for a long time, or are over-salted, provide little nourishment, and such nutrition seems least suitable for the elderly. Salted fish should be boiled in water or sweet wine, and after they are removed from the cauldron <note>original: "læbete"</note> onto a platter, add vinegar in which raisins <note>original: "passulæ"</note> have been boiled and some cinnamon. The vinegar is added so that the heat of the salt may be tempered, while the raisins resist the dryness. And lest I dwell too long on these matters which must be repeated elsewhere, I shall turn my discourse to the specific methods of preparation.

First, concerning sea-creatures, among which the **sturgeon** has obtained the primary glory at banquets. The sturgeon is thus savory, and among fish (in which there is some measure of excellent nourishment), it is the most highly nourishing. For this reason, in all parts of the earth where sturgeons are caught, they are held in the greatest esteem, especially by princes and those who indulge the palate. They are born in the sea; nevertheless, because they delight in fresh waters, they very often dwell in rivers and their mouths. 

Sturgeon is prepared by boiling in water and salt, and after cooking they add spices <term>aromata: aromatic seasonings used to balance the "cold" or "moist" nature of the fish</term> such as pepper, ginger, cloves, and nutmeg in winter. In summer, however, they add cinnamon, mace, and the like. There are some, however, who first boil it in wine and then add spices, a method which is pleasing in winter and spring. For in this way, it is better digested <note>original: "concoquitur," referring to the internal "cooking" or digestion of food by the stomach</note> by the stomach, and its viscosity <note>referring to the thick, sticky quality of the humors</note> is corrected, and the nourishment generated from it is more easily distributed to the limbs. Furthermore, unless you remove its excessive humidity, it generates cold and sluggish phlegmatic humors. 

They also very often eat it roasted upon a grill, namely with salt and fennel. This method of cooking (as I have said) is more highly praised, for through roasting, much of the moisture (which is resistant to the stomach's digestion) is consumed. But if it is sometimes fried in oil and sprinkled with the juice of oranges or citrons <note>original: "mali medici," literally "Median apples," known to us as the citron</note>, or with verjuice <note>original: "succus uuæ acerbæ," the tart juice of unripened grapes</note> and cinnamon, it will not be a dish ungrateful to the palate, even if it is rarely served fried at banquets. Furthermore, in whatever way it is cooked fresh, it is less harmful in summer, for a cold nourishment is produced from it. Wherefore it is of very little use to the elderly, since they require the best restoration of their radical moisture <term>radical moisture: the vital fluid believed to be the essential fuel for life and heat in the body</term>. There are also fish which are commonly called *porceletas*... <note>likely referring to a "little pig" fish, perhaps a small sturgeon or a species of gurnard</note>

Therefore, they are of a different species.

Although they are very pleasing to the palate, they nonetheless produce "bad blood" and are digested slowly by the stomach. However, those mullets caught in the open sea are not so poor. # THIRD [PART]

...they are eaten, whether boiled or roasted on a grill with spices. 

There is also the **tuna** <note>original: "tomus" or "thimus"</note>, a fish of great and remarkable size, which is given different names according to its various ages; for some call it **palamida** <note>often referring to the Atlantic bonito or young tuna</note> or **parmula** when it is still small and in its first year of life, but it is called a **tuna** <note>original: "tomus"</note> if it is large and several years old. It is customary to cook tuna on a grill with salt and fennel seeds. It is a heavy food, difficult to digest, and harmful to the stomach and the head; nor is there anything in it that can favor health or the restoration of the body. 

Furthermore, there are certain fish called **salema porgies** <note>original: "salpas"</note>; these produce poor nourishment because they spoil very easily in the stomach, and their substance is not very pleasing to the taste. 

There are also **turbot** <note>original: "rumbi"</note>, elegant fish among the noble varieties, which are cooked by boiling in water, and also with wine and salt, with spices added at the end of the cooking process. There are also those who praise this fish when cooked in a frying pan with oil. 

There are also **flounder** <note>original: "passarae," likely European flounder or plaice</note>, fish which are at their best in the spring and the beginning of summer, cooked in the same way as turbot. **Sole** <note>original: "soliae"</note> are also prepared for eating in that manner, especially in a frying pan with oil, and afterwards sprinkled with orange juice or **verjuice** <term>uuæ immaturæ: the acidic juice of unripe grapes, used as a souring agent before lemons were widely available</term>. Similarly, the **John Dory** <note>original: "citula," which he notes is called "St. Peter’s fish"</note> is prepared both by boiling and by frying. 

And although **conger eels** <note>original: "grongi"</note> and **moray eels** <note>original: "murene"</note> are rare in our region, they are very common among the Sicilians and in that part of the sea; they are highly praised, especially if they are prepared by boiling with spices. 

However, **common eels** <note>original: "anguillæ"</note> are not praised, even though they are in such frequent use among us; while they are very pleasing to the taste, they produce poor nourishment and are most difficult for the stomach to digest. They harm all the internal organs, especially the head. They are prepared by roasting on a spit, having been sprinkled with plenty of salt before roasting. There are also those who eat them boiled with spices, but they are more harmful that way. Truly, those that are salted are less offensive, especially if they are eaten along with salt and fennel seeds, or certain spices such as pepper, cloves, cinnamon, and the like. 

Besides the fish already mentioned, there are also some people who eat many other fish of poor substance that produce bad nourishment, which I would least approve of in a regimen for maintaining health. These are **dogfish** <note>small sharks</note>, **rays**, **stingrays** <note>original: "columbus," likely the eagle ray</note>, **angelsharks** <note>original: "squatina"</note>, **cuttlefish**, **octopus**, and **squid** (which is commonly called *caramale* <note>the Italian "calamare"</note>). All these fish are bad, as they [harm] both the head and the stomach...

<note>Epistle or Letter</note>

...and are most harmful. I could have listed many other sea-dwelling fish that people are accustomed to eating, but those already mentioned shall suffice as examples, and I now turn my discussion to those creatures that dwell in fresh waters. There are indeed many of them, just as there are in the sea, yet they are generally less praised. However, among these, some are better—even the best—and are praised by all. I shall list them accordingly.

First, **trout** <note>original: "trota"</note> and **carp** <note>original: "carpio," specifically the *carpione* or Lake Garda trout</note> are praised as being the most flavorful and superior; although they are pleasing to the taste, they are nevertheless difficult to digest. They are boiled down in wine with **cloves** <note>original: "garyophilis"</note>, **mace**, **cinnamon**, and similar spices. Because there is no lack of those who argue over which of these two fish is superior, some claim that the *carpioni* are nobler because they are nourished near "golden sand" <note>A poetic reference to the clean, mineral-rich lakebeds believed to improve the flavor of the fish</note> and because they can be preserved from rot for a longer time. These carp are caught only in **Lake Benaco** <note>The Roman name for Lake Garda</note>; if they are found in another place, it is a rare sight. Whatever the case may be, both are excellent when fresh, and they are prepared by boiling with spices, and also by frying in oil. Indeed, they have been such a pleasing food to men that they are even transported to very distant places and regions, specifically when salted and fried in oil.

**Lake shad** <note>original: "sardæ," likely referring to the *agone* or freshwater sardine common in Italian lakes</note> are also most highly praised and caught in that same lake; when fresh, they are eaten roasted on a grill, and also fried. Furthermore, after these, **grayling** <note>original: "themuli"</note> are most praised; these are caught near **Treviso** <note>original: "tarvisium"</note> and also near **Bologna**, and they are prepared by boiling with spices or by frying. **Barbel** <note>original: "barbi"</note> are prepared similarly: by roasting, frying, or boiling with spices.

**Pike** <note>original: "lucii"</note> are also very common among us. Because they lack a "slimy moisture" <note>A reference to the Galenic humoral theory; "slimy" or "phlegmatic" foods were thought to cause imbalances in the body</note>, they are numbered among the less harmful foods in the **diet for the elderly** <note>original: "regimine senum"</note>. They are very often prepared by boiling with wine or water and spices (as I have said). Sometimes they are roasted on a spit in this manner: after they have been warmed for a little while on the spit over the fire so that the scaly skin can be easily separated from the meat, the skin is removed; then, they sprinkle a mixture of flour, sugar, and cinnamon over it to create a kind of crust. They proceed in this way until the fish is perfectly roasted; prepared thus, they are excellent and flavorful.

Others that are in frequent use among us—such as **frogs** <note>original: "rainæ," likely the edible frog common in Lombardy and the Veneto</note>, **tench** <note>original: "tinchæ"</note>, and **rudd** <note>original: "scardæ"</note>—should all, in my opinion, be forbidden, as they provide poor nourishment. However, **lampreys** <note>original: "lampredæ"</note>, since they have almost no sliminess in them, can sometimes be eaten. Nor should the diversity resulting from a change of location...

### PART THREE
<page-num>36</page-num>
<meta>Catchword: ad (to)</meta>

...the consideration of fish should not be overlooked, since there are some who, although they are born in the sea, nevertheless delight in fresh waters and live and are nourished within them. Conversely, there are others who are born in fresh waters and yet delight in the sea and are nourished there, such as **sea-needles** <note>original: "varioli"</note>, **sea bass** <note>original: "lupi"</note>, **eels**, **mullet**, **flounder**, **tench**, and others (as I said a little while ago) who are accustomed to changing locations. 

From this change of location, those who move from fresh waters to the sea are made better, while those who move from the sea to fresh waters are made worse. For **sea-needles** or **little spines**, **sea bass**, **eels**, **tench**, and similar types—among which is the **sturgeon** <note>original: "sturio"</note>, which, even though it is a sea fish, nonetheless enjoys fresh waters—become fattier and worse when they stay in fresh waters. On the contrary, if **tench** or **pike** <note>original: "lucii"</note> grow in maritime waters, they are made better. 

Human use also includes **shellfish** <note>original: "ostrocoderma"</note> and **crustaceans** for eating; all of these (according to **Galen** <note>A highly influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years</note>) provide poor nourishment. Indeed, they irritate the stomach and provide little nutrition. However, the **oyster** <note>original: "ostrea"</note> is beneficial for those in whom food is corrupted in the stomach, and they even increase both the digestive and **expulsive powers** <note>the body's ability to move food and waste through the digestive tract</note> when a very large quantity of meat has been consumed. This is especially true if they are eaten after meat, for by their saltiness they increase heat and stimulate the expulsive power. 

There is no shortage of those who believe that eating oysters increases **sexual desire** <note>original: "venerem," referencing the goddess Venus</note> and multiplies the seed, but they are deceived, since from their consumption only a small amount of poor nourishment is generated. It does not stimulate desire because it increases the seed, but because its subtle heat excites **wind** <note>original: "ventum," referring to the medical belief that certain foods caused "gases" or "spirits" to move through the body</note> and drives it toward the genital paths; thus it happens that those who eat oysters are stimulated and experience erections and titillation. 

Among oysters, the best and least harmful are those caught in places that are not muddy, but where the waters are flowing, which are also pleasing to the taste and have a good smell; however, if they smell bad and have grown in putrid marshes, they are bad. 

The method of preparation for eating is varied: some pour boiling water over them and eat them that way; there are also those who cook them on a **grill** <note>original: "craticulam"</note>; and there are those who open them raw, add oil and pepper, and cook them on the grill. Furthermore, there are those who eat them raw, but this can in no way be praised in a **health regimen** <note>original: "regimine sanitatis"</note>, for it is a heavy food. Nor should they be eaten except after other foods, so that by warming with their saltiness and stimulating the expulsive power, they may aid the digestion and expulsion of the stomach...
