# E P I S T O L A

...might help, nor should the quantity be great, since they are poor and offer little nourishment. Besides oysters, people eat various kinds of **shellfish** <note>original: "conchiliis"</note>, which, since almost all are of the same substance and property—generating bad and sharp blood—the author therefore forbids their use. Among those believed to be better are the ones that grow in sandy rather than marshy places; the better method of preparation for the smaller ones is boiling with wine and spices until they open slightly. But **fan mussels** <note>original: "lasturæ", likely referring to large bivalves like the Pinna nobilis</note>, which are a kind of shellfish of quite a large size, are boiled first in water; then, once the inner parts are removed and cut into pieces, they are prepared with oil and spices. Whatever the case may be regarding their preparation, all kinds of shellfish—whether they are large or small, long or round—are considered detestable. There are also **crustaceans** <note>original: "crustacei pisces"</note>, such as the sea-mussel, freshwater crabs, **crayfish** <note>original: "camari"</note>, and the like, which, whether large or small, all provide little nourishment. Nevertheless, the **medical school** <note>original: "medicorum scola"</note>, in a **restorative regimen** <note>original: "regimine resumptiuo"; a diet intended to rebuild strength after illness</note> (for example, for those suffering from a habitual fever), has praised freshwater crabs. This is not because they nourish greatly, but because their moisture and the "sluggishness" of their nutrient blunt the heat fixed in the limbs—which physicians call "habitual" and "fixed"—and they resist the **wasting away** <note>original: "coliquationi"</note> of the solid parts of the body. For this reason, since the elderly, through the course of age, have become cold and dry and require warm and moderately moist nourishment, these are least suitable for them—unless perhaps they sometimes require **medicinal food** <note>original: "cibo medicinali"</note> to provoke urine. Otherwise, they are of no use, as they are hard to digest, harmful to the head and stomach, and disturb the bowels. The freshwater varieties are better. Even if (as I said) all are heavy and provide little nourishment, since they are eaten by many, the better ones should be chosen: namely the soft ones, captured when they have been stripped of their hard shell (which are commonly called **soft-shell crabs** <note>original: "molechas"</note>), and these are pleasing to the taste when fried in oil; this should be understood to apply to both sea and freshwater types. The others that are hard, whether from the river or the sea, small or large, are prepared by boiling with water and salt. There are also those who, after boiling the large ones, open them and add vinegar and some spices, and thus they become more pleasing to the taste. And although all salted foods are of very little use in the restoration of bodily moisture, nonetheless, since men frequently eat salted things...

<header>THIRD [PART]</header>
<meta>Digitized by Google</meta>

Concerning these, it will not be unpleasant to list their varieties and preparations, provided I first state the reason why they are not conducive to **restoration** <note>original: "instaurationi"; the process of rebuilding the body's strength and moisture after illness</note>. Therefore, <term>salted foods</term> [salita] are altogether of very little use for restoring lost moisture. First, this is because they dry the body out and violently inflame it, exciting a wicked thirst and harming the liver and kidneys; furthermore, very little moisture suitable for nutrition can be separated from them, as the greater part of them becomes excrement.

Nevertheless, if they are eaten in a modest quantity by those who have a great deal of **phlegmatic matter** <note>original: "materiam pituitosam"; according to the theory of the four humors, phlegm was cold and damp, often associated with sluggishness</note> in their stomach, they are of no small benefit. They act by heating and thinning that cold, damp phlegm and by stimulating the appetite; for this reason, they can be useful for the elderly. 

Salted foods are therefore prepared in this manner: First, the <term>carp</term> [carpio], among other salted things, is fried in a pan with oil—not just once, but several times—and then stored. Prepared through several fryings, it can be preserved for a long time and transported to diverse regions; when it is time to eat it, it is fried once more in fresh oil or heated over a grill.

There are also certain foreign salted fish which are held in the highest (so to speak) reverence, such as the <term>salmon</term> [salmon], which is prepared by boiling in wine with spices. There is also the <term>cod</term> [Morona] <note>likely referring to dried or salted cod, such as baccalà</note>, which is prepared by boiling in water and eaten sprinkled with vinegar. Similarly, there are the dorsal parts of <term>sturgeon</term> [sturionum], which they call <term>moronellas</term> [moronellas]; these are cooked on a grill and eaten with vinegar sprinkled over them, though all of these are considered bad for the health.

Furthermore, people eat many other salted fish and their parts, such as <term>grey mullet</term> [cæphali], <term>barbel</term> [barbi], or <term>red mullet</term> [triglæ], <term>mackerel</term> [sgombri], and both large and small <term>sardines</term> [sardæ] (which the Genoese call <term>anchovies</term> [inchio]), as well as <term>eels</term> [anguilæ] and others. Although these may be pleasing to the taste and the palate, they must be forbidden because they neither generate proper nourishment nor are they easy to digest. 

But <term>bottarga</term> [ouataricha or botargas]—a name slightly corrupted from the Greek—since they are not unpleasant to the taste and even strengthen the stomach, dry out the phlegmatic matter within it, and stimulate the appetite, I praise them when served as a first course. Similarly, salted <term>sturgeon eggs</term> [ova sturionum], which they call <term>caviar</term> [cauiarum], can sometimes be eaten (though in smaller quantities) to dry out the <term>phlegm</term> [pituita] in the stomach. 

I wanted to say this same thing regarding other salted foods: they should only be used by the elderly for some medicinal purpose—namely, when we intend to dry out certain parts of the body or to move the bowels through stimulation.

But if we desire to extinguish the sharpness of the salt, it is conveniently done with the juice of unripe grapes; or of a middle-apple <note>original: "pomi medii"; likely a generic term for a pome fruit like an apple or quince of moderate ripeness</note>, or orange, or lemons, or citrons, and similar things. And this is enough concerning the preparation of fish.

Various <term>dishes</term> [fercula] made from different foodstuffs, both simple and mixed, are approved by common human usage. Therefore, I will enumerate their compositions and differences in part, especially those that seem suited to our purpose—namely, that health may be protected and life prolonged. For well-tempered and flavorful dishes do much to restore the <term>innate moisture</term> [humidum congenitum] and the vital spirit, if they are eaten moderately, at their proper times, and are conveniently prepared; for they acquire and admit various virtues through different boilings and mixings.

Furthermore, those things which are cooked with meats receive the "virtue" or nutritional quality of those meats and provide nourishment along with that natural quality. The same reasoning must also be applied to fish; for if dishes are composed with them, or if something is boiled with them, those ingredients will undoubtedly receive some part of those fish and nourish, alter, and change the body with that virtue. 

So that no error occurs in these matters, I will first note those which are beneficial. Indeed, the most praised dish is bread softened in meat broth, especially in the broth of the carp. But it will be even more praiseworthy if the bread is boiled with the broth so that what is called a <term>panatella</term> <note>A traditional bread soup or porridge made by boiling breadcrumbs in broth until smooth</note> is created. Furthermore, this is beneficial not only to the elderly but also to children and other ages, since it nourishes properly and is quickly transformed and descends from the stomach. In fact, it becomes the best nourishment because it nourishes quickly and even greatly restores the natural moisture in the elderly, and it softens the roughened and dry parts of the chest. For this reason, it is of no small benefit to those suffering from a cough.

Furthermore, a most praised and noble dish is made from boiled meats, almonds, and breadcrumbs, worked together in a mortar and mixed with the best broth, rose water, and sugar. This dish restores and refreshes the elderly and those convalescing wonderfully; in it there exists almost no <term>excremental part</term> <note>original: "excrementosa pars"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to the waste products of digestion that the body cannot turn into blood or tissue</note>. Instead, almost all of it is converted into nourishment, and, so to speak, with very little or no "labor of heat" <note>This means the body's "digestive fire" does not have to work hard to process the food</note>. Therefore, its use is very beneficial for the elderly. 

After this is <term>alica</term> <note>A grain porridge highly valued by the Romans for its medicinal qualities</note>, a dish made from grains of <term>spelt</term> [zeae] (our people call it *spelta*), and it is made from grains of this kind cleaned of their hulls, with the meat broth of the food...

### THE THIRD PART

[It is] most pleasing: because it nourishes <note>original: "impinguat"; literally "fattens" or "makes plump," which was a sign of health for the frail</note> the elderly and others who have a weak <term>innate heat</term> [imbecillem calorem], such as women and those recovering from illness, provided it is prepared in the best way. Although barley and <term>ptisan</term> [ptisana] <note>A medicinal porridge or decoction made from pearled barley, highly praised in ancient Greek medicine</note> made from it are lauded with wonderful praise by Hippocrates and Galen, they are nevertheless not useful for all ages and times for the purpose of achieving the best health. But a dish made from <term>spelt</term> [far] with meat broth, or cooked in water with the addition of ground almonds and sugar, nourishes excellently and is easily digested by the stomach. Similarly, a dish is made from rice <note>original: "oriza, sive rizio"</note> with meat broth, or with almonds, sugar, and a little saffron, which indeed tastes good and nourishes; except that it stirs up and generates <term>wind</term> [flatum] <note>gas or flatulence</note> in the intestines, which cinnamon and almonds remove. Furthermore, they make many foodstuffs from wheat flour, and all of them are heavy and produce <term>obstructions</term> [obstructiones] <note>blockages in the vessels or organs, thought to cause disease in humoral medicine</note>; although they may nourish, they are not praised in every respect, whether they be broths, flatbreads, or any other kind of dish made from wheat flour, such as those called pastries <note>original: "pastilia"</note> and the rest. For this reason, they should not be eaten except with temperate spices, such as cinnamon, and then only rarely. Similarly, all legumes are heavy, among which the black and red chickpea is not entirely bad, since it nourishes quite conveniently and assists the chest and lungs, especially if they are burdened by thicker <term>humors</term> [humoribus]. For it thins the blood, provokes urine, and clears out sluggish humors and small stones <note>original: "arenulas"; literally "little sands"</note> from the kidneys. It also excites wind in the stomach and intestines, and for that reason, it stimulates <term>sexual desire</term> [ad venerem]. This is not because it increases the genital seed; to correct this [the wind], one should boil rosemary, or the roots of fennel or parsley, with the chickpeas themselves. Common folk and peasants, however, cook garlic with these chickpeas, which is praised not without reason. For garlic puts to flight all wind, both in the stomach and also in the intestines. Truly, the other legumes—such as beans, peas, kidney beans, lentils, and vetch—are bad and provide little nourishment. Indeed, beans, besides the fact that they nourish little, generate a great deal of wind, and their vapors harm the head in no small measure. Peas also produce a thick nourishment and nourish only slightly. But kidney beans are worse, as they are easily corrupted in the stomach, generate bad blood, and excite bad fevers. Lentils also nourish little and bind the bowels; but besides the fact that their nourishment is bad and they are difficult to digest, frequent use of them excites the "bad itch" <note>original: "scabiem malam"; likely referring to skin irritations or scabies</note>, and the decoction of lentils, as the physicians say, is...

# E P I S T O L A

It now stimulates, and a decoction of lentils (as the doctors say) drives **bad blood** to the skin; for this reason it is given when **smallpox**, **measles**, **pimples**, or <term>petechiae</term> [pestichiæ] <note>Small red or purple spots on the skin caused by broken capillaries, often seen in "pestilential" or highly infectious fevers</note> break out during pestilential fevers. Lastly, <term>chickling vetches</term> [cicerculæ] <note>A type of pea (Lathyrus sativus) often used as a famine food, known today to cause paralysis if eaten in excess</note> are bad, and exist as food more for peasants and those who labor heavily than for refined men. And in short, in all these things, of whatever kind they may be, their preparations or the dishes made from them are not at all beneficial to the elderly, nor to those who have a **weak stomach**.

Vegetables likewise are not at all conducive to nourishment for the elderly, for they offer little nutrition and produce <term>bad juice</term> [mali succi] <note>In Galenic medicine, "juice" or "succus" refers to the fluid produced by digestion which becomes the four humors; "bad juice" leads to illness</note>. Truly, among the vegetables, certain ones are said to be more praiseworthy, such as **borage**, **bugloss**, **lemon balm** [mellifsa], and **lettuce**, which **Galen** praised very much; nevertheless, it harms the sight, dulls all the senses, and makes a man sleepy. 

The vegetables which are in frequent use, besides those mentioned, are **cabbage**, **blites** <note>A leafy green similar to spinach or amaranth</note>, and **spinach**; but since all herbs (as I have said) provide little nourishment, they should only be cooked in **meat broth** so that they may nourish better; thus, besides softening [the bowels], they will also have something they can use to nourish. 

And although stalks or cabbages are in frequent use during the winter time, and the ancients praised cabbage very much, I for my part can by no means praise it in every respect. First, it generates a **bad juice** which infests the head and darkens the eyes; the white ones are even worse, which the Arabs call <gloss>canabit</gloss> <note>original: "canabit"; likely a Latinization of the Arabic "kanabit" for cauliflower or cabbage</note>, but are commonly called <gloss>capuzi</gloss> <note>original: "capuzi"; likely referring to "capitata" or headed cabbage</note>. For they are digested with difficulty by the stomach and nourish little, and for that reason, they are cooked together with **fennel seeds**. 

Dishes are also prepared from certain seasonal fruits, such as **cucumbers**, <term>watermelons</term> [citruli], and **white and green gourds**, which they call "marines"; these are of very little benefit to the elderly, since they are excessively **cold and moist**, provide little nourishment, and are difficult to digest. Dishes made from them will be better if they are boiled in meat broth with **cinnamon** or **saffron** during the summer. Similarly, watermelons and cucumbers are worse [on their own], but they will be better for digestion and more pleasing to the taste if, after cooking, an **egg** is mixed with them along with a portion of saffron or cinnamon; for this method of preparation generates more praiseworthy nourishment. 

The **turnip** is a root from which a dish is made in winter with meat broth, which provides little nourishment and is heavy on the stomach. However, a better preparation of it will be if the turnips are first **roasted on coals** and cleaned of their peels, and then, cut into small pieces in meat broth with **fennel seeds**...

...of fennel, or cooked with **cinnamon**, since in this way their <term>windiness</term> [uentositas] <note>Refers to intestinal gas or flatulence, which humoral medicine sought to "disperse" or "resolve" through warming spices</note> is removed, and they are more flavorful to the taste. I would say the same of **turnips**, if they are eaten occasionally, as I did of **rapes**, namely, that they should be cooked with **fennel** and **meat broth**, and well salted, because they will descend more quickly from the stomach. There are certain other fruits which are of very little use, such as **eggplants** [melengana] and the like. For their substance is bad, which weighs down the stomach and corrupts the blood. There are also bad **mushrooms**, and certain tubers (which the common people call <term>little sponges</term> [spongiolas] <note>likely referring to morels or perhaps truffles, given the "tuber" description</note>), for besides causing distress to the stomach, their moisture has the nature of poison, which the heat of the stomach can by no means regulate. Indeed, I have seen many perish from eating mushrooms, as **Galen** also testified. 

Besides the things mentioned, there are many other things growing from the earth, such as the **parsnip**, both wild and cultivated—the latter is commonly called a **carrot** [cariota]—and **radishes**, **onions**, **leeks**, **bulbs**, **garlic**, and similar things, which should by no means be eaten as food, since they are harmful to the stomach and the head, and they infect the **good humors**. Nevertheless, they can sometimes be eaten as medicinal food; for example, **radish** after other foods, to invigorate the digestive power of the stomach. And **parsnips**, or boiled **carrots**, seasoned with vinegar, with sugar and cinnamon added as a first course to excite the appetite. 

Similarly, so that the stomach may better digest thick and cold foods, **onions**, **leeks**, **bulbs**, and **garlic** are eaten; for this reason, many are accustomed to eat **garlic** mixed with **nuts** or **almonds** and vinegar, along with fish and fatty meats. Whatever the case may be regarding these, one should always abstain from them, as they are the food of peasants and not of refined men. Yet I will not pass over the utility of **garlic** in silence, for if one eats it moderately at times, it strengthens the stomach's digestion, dissolves windiness in the intestines, and draws out <term>phlegm</term> [pituitam] <note>One of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture; an excess was thought to cause sluggishness and respiratory issues</note> from the intestines through bowel movements. 

Furthermore, **onions** roasted in ashes and seasoned with vinegar, oil, and salt are not an unpleasant food; although they provide poor nourishment, they nevertheless have something that can sometimes be very beneficial, especially for those in whom much thick, sluggish, or sticky matter is stuffed in the stomach and chest—among whom are the elderly and the fat. Similarly, **leeks** can also do this, but not as strongly. If perhaps we desire this effect from eating **leeks** in the elderly for the cleansing of the chest, they should be cooked and with...

...eaten mixed with honey, yet their quantity should not be very great, since they produce **bad blood**. <note>In the Galenic system of medicine used at this time, "bad blood" refers to blood that is too thick, too hot, or contaminated by improper humors, leading to various illnesses.</note> And to bring this part to an end, and to equip myself briefly for the rest, there are many things growing from the earth that are eaten at the first course, both raw and cooked, seasoned with oil, vinegar, and salt; these are called **salads** <note>original: "acetarria, siue salaticia"</note>, which are eaten to whet the appetite and not for nourishment. Among these herbs, **lettuce** is in most frequent use, along with **borage**, **bugloss** and their flowers, as well as **endive**, **chicory**, **lemon balm**, **marigold**, **mint**, **pennyroyal**, **pimpernel**, and the like. All of these are not only of no use to the elderly, but indeed are not for nourishment at any age. For this reason, only a small quantity of them ought to be eaten. However, **rocket** <note>original: "eruca," known today as arugula</note>, **watercress**, and similar herbs are entirely forbidden, for from their consumption **bad blood** is generated, which corrupts the entire <term>mass of humors</term> <note>The "mass of humors" refers to the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Renaissance doctors believed had to stay in balance for health.</note>.

There are, however, besides those mentioned, certain herbs which are most highly praised, such as **asparagus**, which provides much nourishment, provokes urine, and cleanses the blood from wateriness, which is of great benefit to everyone, but especially to the elderly. After asparagus in goodness is **hops** <note>original: "lupulus"</note> that has not yet expanded its leaf; for it strengthens the stomach, thins the <term>phlegm</term> [pituitam] within it, and cleanses the blood; these are eaten cooked. Similarly, **capers** are also excellent, since they strengthen the stomach, thin the thick humors within it, and open obstructions of the **spleen** and other internal organs.

Different **sauces** <note>original: "salsamenta"</note> and seasonings are also placed upon meats and fish so that they may be made better and more pleasing to the taste. Such are those placed upon roasted fish, made from vinegar, salt, and oil, with spices added such as **ginger**, **pepper**, **cinnamon**, and the like. There are those who boil **rosemary** in vinegar with salt and place it thus over fish, which is both pleasing and useful; for it corrects the "moistness" and "coldness" of the fish and makes for a delightful meal. <note>Renaissance dietaries classified fish as "cold and moist." Rosemary, being "hot and dry," was used to balance these qualities to prevent digestive upset.</note>

Similarly, the sauces eaten with meat are excellent, such as those made from **parsley**, **mint**, and **almonds**, with **ginger** and **sugar** ground in a mortar and dissolved with vinegar and **rose water**; this composition can be in use at all times. In winter, however, they eat <term>must</term> [defrutum] made from grapes; it is made from the juice of sweet grapes, boiled down in a cauldron to the thickness of honey, in which they also boil **quinces** cut into pieces; and at the end, some add **cinnamon**...

# ## THIRD [PART]

...cloves, mace, and nutmeg; this provides a most pleasing flavor, suitable for the wealthy. In frequent use during the winter, however, is mustard; and in the summer, a composition made from squeezed sour cherries—which they call *amarascas* and *amarenas* <note>original: "amarascas" and "amarenas"; these refer to varieties of tart or bitter cherries often used in preserves.</note>—boiled with sugar to the thickness of honey. There is also a flavor prepared from quinces in the same way, which people eat with meat. But where we might fear a weakness of the stomach (as is common in the elderly), a portion of cinnamon and cloves should be added. Regardless, these [heavy sauces] are not useful for the elderly; those flavors are better which are made from almonds with sugar, cinnamon, vinegar, and rose water.

There are, furthermore, sauces made from the livers of chickens or capons, prepared with almonds, egg yolks, raisins, cinnamon, and sugar; these are very pleasing and wonderfully beneficial for the elderly. Olives are also eaten to stimulate the stomach’s <term>appetitive faculty</term> <note>The "appetitive faculty" was the biological force Renaissance doctors believed was responsible for the desire to eat.</note>. I do not praise them—even if they strengthen the stomach in some way—because they are not properly digested, and the nourishment they provide is meager and poor. Furthermore, those that are salted harm the liver and "sharpen" the blood <note>In Galenic medicine, "sharpening" the blood meant making it too thin, acidic, or prone to causing inflammation.</note>.

I would have finished here with the edible things that spring from the earth, were I not drawn to discuss the many fruits eaten by humans. Indeed, just as all fruits differ in their substance, so too do they possess different qualities. Those are considered better which approach a warm and moist <term>temperament</term> <note>A "temperament" or "complexion" refers to the balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> and are less prone to rot.

I will begin, therefore, with the "hourly" fruits <note>original: "horariis," referring to highly perishable seasonal fruits that must be eaten quickly after harvest.</note>, so called because they cannot be kept for long. These are melons, pumpkins, watermelons, cucumbers, citruls, and gourds, of which I have said something above. If these are eaten, they are easily converted into whatever humor they find in the stomach; therefore, they are not beneficial for the elderly, as they already abound in <term>phlegmatic humor</term> <note>Phlegm was the cold and moist humor; doctors believed the elderly were naturally "cold," so eating cold/moist foods like melons would cause an unhealthy excess.</note>. Add also that their excessive moisture cannot be overcome by the stomach heat of the elderly; instead, it dulls that heat, and thus they are harmful not only to the stomach but to all the internal organs. Indeed, the juice generated from them usually causes nausea, flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, and bloating, no matter how they are prepared.

Melons and pumpkins have a primary cooling power, and for that reason, they are not as harmful if eaten in summer. They are beneficial to those who are overheated or exhausted from labor, especially the white ones called *pepones* <note>original: "pepones"; large, ripe melons.</note>. They ought to be eaten before other foods. But should wine be drunk after eating them...

->LETTER<-

...neat wine, or whether it is better to drink water, is a question not only among the common people but also among doctors. I will settle this question as follows: namely, that after eating those things which are considered cold and moist—specifically those which have little or no sweetness—drinking neat wine <note>original: "vinum meracum"; this refers to wine that has not been diluted with water, which was the standard way to drink in the ancient and Renaissance worlds.</note> is extremely beneficial, provided the quantity is not excessive but moderate. However, after eating those which are very sweet, it is not safe to take neat wine, because from such a mixture the matter of burning fevers is often generated. For that reason, it is safer to drink water with pomegranate wine <note>original: "vino granatorum"; a tart liquid made from pomegranate juice, used here to temper the heat or sweetness of the fruit.</note> afterward. But, however the case may be, the consumption of melons stimulates urine and often causes a looseness of the intestines; the best precaution against this harm is if they are eaten together with cheese. 

As for the watermelon <note>original: "patecha"; likely referring to the watermelons common in Italy.</note>, or the cucumber, the citron-gourd, and the pumpkin, enough has been said previously, as they are very rarely used as food for the elderly. It remains for me to write about those fruits which grow on trees, beginning with the fig. Indeed, the fig is among the fruits of the best and most laudable nourishment, and is pleasing to the taste. Doctors affirm that its <term>temperament</term> <note>The "temperament" in Galenic medicine refers to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> is hot and moist, though those that are dried are less moist. 

One should choose white figs that have already partially dried on the tree, and they should be eaten before other foods. Even though they provide excellent nourishment, they inflame everyone and produce "sharp" blood <note>original: "acutum sanguinem"; in this context, blood that is overly thin, hot, or acidic, which was thought to cause skin irritations.</note>, which excites scabies and itching; likewise, they stimulate the bowels to move. Dried figs do the same, but they sharpen the blood even more.

Furthermore, grapes are themselves of laudable nourishment, being hot and moist. Among grapes, the white ones are considered superior, especially those grown in mountainous places. But whether they be white, red, or black, it is worthwhile that they be mature, and either left for several days after picking or allowed to partially dry on the vine. They should be eaten before other foods along with bread, or even with meat, for in this way they generate the best nourishment and are less gas-inducing. Sour grapes <note>original: "omphatiæ"; referring to the juice of unripe grapes used as a tart condiment.</note> and those which are immature or harsh harm the stomach and bind the bowels. However, dried grapes that are kept hanging during the winter do not nourish as well. 

But raisins <note>original: "uuæ siccæ"; literally "dry grapes."</note>, which are imported to us in great quantities from other places, vary in quality. The best and most praised are considered to be the small black ones without seeds <note>These are likely what we now call currants or Zante currants.</note>, for they provide the most nourishment and are suitable for the stomach, chest, lungs, and kidneys; they are a singular medicine for ailments of the liver and for its weakness. As for the remaining dried grapes...

->### THIRD SECTION<-

...although [figs] are said to be good, they are not praised in every respect, such as those which are imported from Damascus, Crete, and Smyrna; for they are all <term>flatulent</term> <note>original: "inflatiue"; meaning they cause gas or bloating.</note>, more or less in proportion to their fatness. Indeed, those which are less fatty cause less flatulence but also provide less nourishment; yet all of them are very nourishing. However, their immoderate use causes a looseness of the intestines, which is corrected if they are eaten with cheese.

Dates <note>original: "dactili"</note>, if they are ripe, are useful for the elderly. For their substance is hot and moist, which provides much nourishment; but if they are eaten in too great a quantity, they are not easily digested by the stomach and generate a <term>thick humor</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "thick humors" were sluggish bodily fluids thought to cause blockages.</note>. Thus, a great consumption of dates causes obstructions of the liver and spleen, yet they are beneficial to those who have a weakness of the kidneys.

All apples <note>original: "poma"</note> are cold and moist, and for this reason, they are very harmful to the elderly. And since there are many different types of apples, if they are eaten, those which are sweet, of good substance, and pleasant-smelling should be chosen; for those which are tasteless, odorless, and soft are worse. But whatever kind they may be, their immoderate use eventually prepares the way for pains in the joints <note>likely referring to gout</note> and for the rupture of the veins of the chest. When cooked, however, they are less harmful, and those which are fragrant help with <term>hot passions of the heart</term> <note>In the medical theory of the time, the heart could suffer from an excess of heat, which fragrant, cooling fruits were thought to temper.</note>.

Similarly, pears <note>original: "pira"</note> are bad for the elderly. Those which have a more brittle substance and are sweet and fragrant with the scent of spices, with a rose or red color, are said to be better. For this reason, Muscat pears are the best, and after those, the ones which most closely match these descriptions; they benefit hot ailments of the heart by their scent and coldness.

Quinces <note>original: "poma cotonia"</note> are cold and dry, and harder to digest than pears because of their tough substance. They are beneficial for a "heated" stomach; they stop vomiting and flux of the belly <note>i.e., diarrhea</note>, and they stimulate the appetite. It is not true, as many believe, that eating them after a meal loosens the belly by relaxing it; rather, that effect occurs by reason of compression <note>The author suggests quinces might physically push food through the digestive tract rather than acting as a chemical laxative.</note>. Those which are ripe, sweeter, and more fragrant are said to be better; they benefit the heart and, if eaten after a meal, prevent vapors from ascending to the brain. Nevertheless, they are not suitable for the elderly. Nor will I pass over service-apples <note>original: "sorbas"</note>, medlars <note>original: "Mefpilas"</note>, and jujubes <note>original: "Iuiubas"</note>, although...

...should be eaten rarely, since they are more of a medicinal food than bodily nourishment. First, both **serviceberries** <note>original: "sorbæ"; the fruit of the Sorbus domestica tree, known for its astringency.</note> and **medlars** <note>original: "mespilæ"; a fruit that must "blet" (soften) before being edible.</note> strengthen the stomach with their <term>astringency</term> <note>original: "stipticitate"; a drying, mouth-puckering quality believed to "bind" the digestive system.</note>, and they stop vomiting and intestinal flux. Similarly, **jujubes** <note>original: "iuiubæ"</note> are useless, as they are colder and provide little or no nourishment and harm the stomach; they are beneficial to the chest, however, and help with hot discharges <note>original: "destilationibus calidis"; refers to catarrh or runny mucus caused by an excess of "heat."</note>, making it easier to spit up such matter.

There are also many species of **cherries**, which differ in substance, flavor, and color. For some are soft and fragile, and some hard; some white, some reddish or rosy, some red, and some black. Similarly in flavor, some are almost tasteless, some sweet, some mild, and some acidic; all, however, are cold and moist. But the sweet ones are not as cold [as the others], just as the acidic ones are not as moist. All cherries are bad for the stomach and prone to <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrescendū"; in Galenic medicine, this meant the fruit quickly "rotted" into bad humors rather than digesting properly.</note>. The acidic ones, however, do not rot; the tasteless ones are detestable to eat; the sweet ones less so. The best ones are the acidic kind, which they call *amarasias* or *amarascas* <note>sour cherries or amarena</note>; nevertheless, they are not suitable for the elderly.

There are also what the Greeks call *crissomilia*, the Latins call "golden apples," and the common people call **apricots** <note>original: "armelini"</note>, because these fruits were brought to us from Armenia. They are cold and moist, and their substance is prone to rotting, and thus it prepares the way for "bad fevers"; for this reason, they should be forbidden entirely. Similarly, **peaches** are cold and moist, and their substance is easily corrupted; nevertheless, according to the common opinion of all illustrious physicians, they strengthen an overheated stomach. They are flavorful and have a good smell, but when dried they are better and less harmful. The harm caused by eating them fresh is corrected by drinking aromatic wine after eating them.

There are also many other kinds of fruits which are not at all suitable for the elderly, such as **pomegranates** (whether you call them *granata* or *punica* does not matter), **oranges** (or "Median apples"), **citrons**, **lemons**, and that sort. I will begin, however, with pomegranates, which come in three varieties: namely sweet, mild, and acidic. All are cold, but the sweet ones have a certain slight (so to speak) heat; indeed, they are said to be both beneficial and harmful to the stomach in different ways. They are certainly beneficial because they prevent "hot corruption" in the stomach, as they extinguish the <term>choler</term> <note>original: "cholera"; yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors, associated with heat and bitterness.</note> within it, and [strengthen] its mouth [opening]...

...[they might] strengthen <note>original: "roborant"; the first word "borent" is the completion of "roborant" from the previous page.</note>, but nevertheless they cause harm if they encounter too much phlegmatic matter in the stomach, or if the stomach is weak. However, sweet cherries soothe the chest, make spitting easy, and soften the lower belly.

**Oranges** <note>original: "Arantiæ"</note> are also cold in nature, especially those that are acidic. The sweet ones are less cold than the acidic ones; they extinguish <term>bile</term> <note>original: "coleram"; in this context, yellow bile, which was thought to cause heat and irritability.</note> and can be eaten in the summer with salted foods, yet they are not suitable for the elderly.

Similarly, **citrons** <note>original: "citria poma"</note> are cold if you look at their inner substance. However, because their rind is also eaten—which differs in both substance and flavor from the inner parts—it also has a different <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperaturam"; the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. Indeed, its outermost part is hot and dry, while the middle part possesses both moisture and heat. All parts, however, provide little nourishment and are difficult to digest. For this reason, they are considered more of a medicine than a food. They are beneficial against "hot" poisonous qualities acquired within the <term>humoral mass</term> <note>original: "massa humorali"; the total collection of fluids—blood, phlegm, bile—in the body.</note>, and for that reason, they are given during pestilential fevers. Furthermore, by their scent, they benefit the "principal members," namely the heart, the liver, and the brain. Similarly, citron seeds are very beneficial for afflictions of the heart; they strengthen the stomach and correct a corrupted appetite.

**Lemons** themselves also have a cold temperament, though the rind is hot. They are very contrary to the stomach and for that reason are unsuitable for the elderly, yet they are beneficial in malignant and pestilential fevers, just like citrons. Those that are salted and preserved in seawater, however, are hot.

## Concerning fruits having a hard shell; first there will be discourse on almonds.

**Almonds** <note>original: "Amigdalæ"</note> are moderate in temperament but hard to digest. They do provide nourishment, and their nourishment is of a praiseworthy sort. The fresh ones, and those that are green, are better and easier to digest. If eaten after a meal, they fill the head and produce a heavy sleep; furthermore, they soothe the chest, facilitate spitting, and open obstructions of the liver and the spleen.

**Hazelnuts** <note>original: "Auelanæ"</note> are also hot and do not contain much moisture. They are difficult to digest, but when the stomach can tolerate them, they provide much nourishment; if the stomach cannot, they cause significant harm and cannot nourish. The green ones are better. If eaten to excess, they fill the head and provoke sleep.

# E P I S T L E

...furthermore, if they are eaten with figs and rue, they resist poison, just as I will now say concerning nuts.

**Nuts** <note>original: "Nuces"; in this context, usually referring to walnuts.</note> themselves are also hot and moist, yet they do not lack a certain dryness that is harmful to the chest. They are bad for the stomach and cause nausea; therefore, they are not suitable for the elderly. However, they are less harmful if eaten with figs or honey. On their own, they generate bad <term>juice</term> <note>original: "succum"; referring to the humors produced during digestion.</note> and harm the head and the nerves. For this reason, they should not be eaten for nourishment; nevertheless, a medicine against poison may be made from nuts, rue, and figs mixed together with honey.

There are also **pine nuts** <note>original: "pineæ"</note>, which are quite hot and moist, even if the ancients believed otherwise. For this reason, they provide excellent nourishment, though they are digested by the stomach only with effort. They benefit the chest, head, nerves, and intestines. They clear the voice and make the spitting <note>of phlegm</note> easy. They are better when fresh or soaked in lukewarm water, for when prepared this way, their heat is reduced.

**Pistachios** <note>original: "Fistici siue pistachia"</note> are hot, but in other respects quite balanced. They do not provide much nourishment but are easy to digest. They benefit the stomach and open obstructions of the liver and spleen. They promote urine and help the chest and lungs; therefore, they are very suitable for the elderly.

**Chestnuts** <note>original: "Castaneæ"</note> are also hot and dry and difficult to digest. They do provide nourishment, but it is a thick and gas-inducing kind. They bind the bowels and calm the flow of blood from hemorrhoids and the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "matrice"</note>, as well as stopping <term>involuntary discharge</term> <note>original: "gonoreum fluxum"; a general historical term for various bodily discharges.</note>. The flatulence in them is corrected if they are roasted in an oven or by some other method, or if they are dried out.

Besides these, there are also certain **foreign fruits** which are very noble and wonderfully praised by the most excellent physicians for protecting health. These include preserved <term>myrobalans</term> <note>original: "mirabalani"; dried astringent fruits used in Ayurvedic and medieval medicine.</note>, both the Chebulic and Emblic varieties. All of these strengthen the stomach and all the internal organs. However, they should not be taken as food, but as a noble and light medicine, and this should be done in the morning a few hours before eating. Indeed, taken this way, they benefit the heart, liver, and spleen, and provide strength to the entire body. They even make the elderly feel young again, especially the Emblic variety.

The rinds of **citrons** are also preserved in sugar, as are small **lemons** and **bitter oranges** <note>original: "aranciolæ"</note> in the same manner. Noble and wealthy people use these as a final course at the table <note>original: "in ultima mensa"; referring to the dessert course.</note>. If these are eaten moderately,
plenty <note>original: "pluri"; catchword for the following page's first word, "plurimum" (very much).</note>

they are very beneficial, especially for the elderly. For besides the fact that they nourish in a praiseworthy manner, they also benefit the heart and strengthen its power. Furthermore, preserved ginger roots (which they call **green ginger** <note>original: "uiridem zinzibere"</note>) are useful for the elderly if they are taken in the morning before food; for by their heat they strengthen the stomach and its appetitive power, and they thin and dissolve the **phlegm** <term>phlegm: one of the four bodily humors, believed to be cold and moist and often found in excess in older people</term> which the elderly have in abundance, drive wind from the intestines, and even stimulate the bowels. They are beneficial in winter, but in summer they should be avoided.

Wealthy and noble people also use, in addition to what has been said, fruits and seeds at the **final course** <note>original: "ultima mensa"; the dessert or "banquet" course</note>, as well as many other things preserved in sugar, such as almonds, pine nuts, pistachios, anise, coriander, cinnamon, orange peels, and similar confections. They also temper the vapors ascending to the head, dissolve wind in the stomach, and leave a good scent in the mouth. Other foodstuffs are also made with sugar and rose water, such as those called **marzipan** <note>original: "marzapani"</note> and **canisones** <note>original: "canisones"; likely a type of wafer, biscuit, or sugar-crusted confection</note>, and various pastilles of that kind, which are prepared in the same way from pistachios and pine nuts; these are certainly pleasing and very nourishing, yet they are not easily digested.

I could have added many other things that are eaten and drunk, but since I see they do not entirely fit our purpose, and also so that the discourse is not drawn out too long, I have decided to omit them. I will, however, add this at the end: although I have written many things in order, the advice of all illustrious physicians (which many reasons prove true) is that there should not be a great variety in foods, nor a vast quantity; and this is not only for the elderly, but indeed for all ages.

### emptiness.

From this food, many **superfluities** <note>waste products or excess humors</note> are gathered, besides the excrement of the bowels; these, although through exercise...

# E P I S T O L A

...[diges]tion most of these are consumed, but not entirely and always removed; since frequently, because the body's power is hindered or made weak, or for some other cause, remnants of **waste** <note>original: "excrementorum"</note> are retained. Therefore, it will be worth the effort to draw out these **superfluities** <term>superfluities: excess substances or waste products that the body fails to expel, thought in Galenic medicine to cause disease if they accumulate</term> from the body by some skillful means. Since these are not of one kind but diverse (as can be seen in all things), different wastes are purged, such as spittle, nasal mucus, sweat, urine, bowel waste, and other bodily filth. If these are not precisely expelled from the body, they produce various conditions contrary to nature, such as obstructions in the limbs—both internal and external—fevers, pains, various abscesses, and other unnatural conditions.

Therefore, one must strive for their evacuation in this way: First, when rising from bed in the morning, spittle should be provoked first, then urine and bowel waste are to be moved. This should be done moderately, so that everything corresponds to the food and drink taken. But if by chance one lacks the evacuation of the lower belly—which is very common for the elderly—let it be provoked by art, namely by a **clyster** <term>clyster: a liquid injected into the rectum; an enema</term> or by a **suppository** <note>original: "glande supposita"; literally "a placed acorn," referring to the shape of the medicinal plug</note>.

If he does not wish to use these, an easy movement of the bowels should be procured by taking fatty meat broth in the morning, into which sugar is added; or let him take a broth of vegetables, namely **mallow** <note>original: "malvae"</note>, **blites** <note>original: "blitis"; a leafy green similar to spinach or amaranth</note>, spinach, cabbage, and the like. Or let him eat two or three ounces of raisins with sugar before a meal; fat figs eaten in the morning several hours before lunch are also very effective for this.

If after doing these things the belly does not flow moderately, he should use some light medicine, such as one made from raisins, the pulp of fat figs, and also the marrow of **safflower** <note>original: "cartami"</note> seeds in equal parts. These, mixed together with rose honey, he should take in the quantity of two ounces in the morning before food. Or let him take half an ounce of **turpentine** <note>original: "terbentinae"; often used historically in small doses for its supposed cleansing properties</note> with sugar, because it moderately softens the belly in the elderly and wonderfully benefits the liver, spleen, stomach, and all the intestines. Or let the bowels be moved by taking a decoction of half an ounce of **polypody root** <note>original: "radicis polipodii"; a type of fern used as a laxative</note> and two ounces of raisins in meat broth in the morning.

There are also other methods for moving the common superfluities of the belly, such as pills of washed aloe, mastic, **hiera** <term>hiera: "Hiera Picra" or "Holy Bitter," a traditional purgative powder made of aloes and other herbs</term>, and similar things. I cannot praise these in every respect, since **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD) was a Greek physician whose theories formed the basis of European medical science for 1,500 years</note> condemned the use of aloe for the elderly, and this because it dries the body too much. But if other things cannot be administered, then together with...

->T E R T I A<-

...with pills, he should take some broth in which either **borage** <note>original: "borago"</note> or **bugloss** <note>original: "buglossum"; both are herbs traditionally used to treat "melancholy" and provide moisture to the body's humors</note> has been boiled, so that it may remove the dryness which can in no way benefit the elderly; for which reason, it is better to use softening agents. But if there should be an extreme **fullness** <note>original: "repletio"</note> from an abundance of ingested food, that can be removed through abstinence from quantity; for indeed abstinence from food (as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for over 1,000 years</note> says) purges the whole body equally. 

Nor should one abstain from foods for a long time in old age, since extreme old age requires frequent and not excessive restoration, on account of the weakness of the **innate heat** <term>innate heat: in ancient medicine, the natural warmth vital to life, thought to reside in the heart and diminish with age</term>. Therefore, let him eat moderately and drink; for indeed excessive abstinence is detestable not only for the elderly but also for the young, since it often leads to senile wasting or **marasmus** <term>marasmus: a state of extreme malnutrition and physical wasting away</term>. 

But since often, not only in the elderly but also in the young, the belly is accustomed to flow more than is due <note>referring to chronic diarrhea or loose stools</note>, so that an excessive emptying of the body follows, from which follow not a few conditions contrary to nature, such as weakness of the stomach, liver, spleen, and intestines, as well as many other inconveniences. 

Therefore, in this case, it will be useful to use light **astringents** <term>astringents: substances that contract bodily tissues, used here to stop excessive bowel movements</term>, such as a mixture of thickening and **styptic** <note>original: "stipticarum"; referring to substances that contract tissues or stop flows</note> things which are able to strengthen the stomach, such as dishes made of rice, or of spelt, or of millet, cooked in the broth of the legs or heads of animals. Or let roasted meats be eaten, especially of birds, such as turtledoves, partridges, and the like, since in these there is the power and property of strengthening the stomach and intestines, and of stopping the flow of the bowels. Furthermore, cheese is excellent in such cases, and likewise certain fruits, such as chestnuts, **service berries** <note>original: "sorbe"</note>, **medlars** <note>original: "mespile"</note>, and **quinces** <note>original: "cotonea"</note>, which ought to be eaten before food, especially roasted. And let this rule, regarding both fullness and emptiness, be administered moderately according to the diversity of the season and the strength of the body.

## Chapter eight: Teaches how to moderate the accidents of the mind.

**F**ittingly, we shall next say in this part how the mind can be conciliated, so that it might live properly composed and undisturbed for a long time. For since the body is primarily ruled by the mind as by the nobler part of the composite being, and especially by that part or virtue which is called the governing power of the body. We shall easily keep the mind undisturbed if that which is harmful to the **animal virtue** <term>animal virtue: (from Latin 'anima', meaning soul/life force) the vital power responsible for sensation and movement according to Galenic physiology</term> is removed, and what is pleasant and brings joy...

<meta>This page continues the medical and philosophical advice for the elderly, moving from physical treatments to the "passions of the soul." It connects to the previous page's discussion on avoiding physical weakness by emphasizing the psychological foundations of health.</meta>

->E P I S T O L A<-
<meta>catchword: lationses (translations/relations)</meta>

# E P I S T O L A

...be given and preferred. Therefore, I first advise that one should be far removed from all distress, since joy <note>original: "leticia"</note> frees men from many bodily discomforts, just as anxiety and sorrow produce many unnatural conditions. What more? Indeed, **Galen** <note>a famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose ideas shaped medicine for centuries</note> wrote that disturbances of the soul undoubtedly change bodies from their natural state of health. Furthermore, the unnatural passions of the soul <note>original: "animi affectus præter naturam"</note> are impulse, anger, fear, sorrow, envy, vehement desire, hatred, and excessive longing for anything. Moreover, the soul itself and its composure are disturbed by darkness, horrific sights, impetuous movements, noise, weeping, the telling and the sight of miserable things, stench, care, and anxiety. Therefore, those who desire to live long and happily should flee all these things, as well as anger, sorrow, envy, hatred, desires, and excessive passion for any of them.

Truly, if the soul shrinks from these things, it will undoubtedly preserve health, delay old age, and prolong life. This will be achieved even better if one lives in places that are pleasant, bright, and delightful, and which lack all impurity. Furthermore, let all knowledge of miserable things, weeping, and all other things disturbing to the soul be far away; thus one should strive for joy by staying in decorated chambers and pleasant places (such as gardens), and also by spending time with those who delight in music and this kind of thing—such as those playing the **cithara** <note>a stringed instrument like a lyre</note>, or the **lute** <note>original: "testudine," literally "tortoise shell," referring to the lute's rounded body</note>, and singers. For (as **Plato** said in the ***Timaeus*** <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the world and the nature of the human soul</note>), harmonic proportion makes the soul cheerful. Likewise, the company of friends who love one another contributes greatly to living a happy life. Similarly, it is beneficial to wear precious clothing dyed with colors pleasing to the eyes, and also to wear rings and glittering gems. Likewise, let there be bright vessels of silver or gold on the table, and similarly for the rest of the furnishings of the chamber and house, since things of this sort render the soul cheerful when they are looked upon.

And in short, since the senses—such as sight and others—also serve the soul, if the soul is directed toward what is pleasant for each individual sense, it will lead greatly to the goal at hand. And first, one is to look upon (as I have said) gold, silver, glittering gems, and "middle" colors which share much light, such as purple, green, rose, yellow <note>original: "citrinus"</note>, sky blue, and the like; for all these provide no small delight. Likewise, the sight of most beautiful women greatly delights the soul. The same is done by conversations...

They also place these in a pot over the fire in the bedchamber, so that through a light evaporation the chamber is filled with a fragrant vapor; from the inhalation of this, the brain, heart, and the remaining principal members are greatly restored.

->E P I S T L E<-

...is not possible, unless they keep the principal members strong and in vigor. To strengthen these, I will add what follows, beginning with the restoration of the stomach <note>original: "uentriculi recreatione"</note>. Although the stomach is not among the primary organs from which the vital powers <term>primariæ uirtutes</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, these were the natural, vital, and animal powers seated in the liver, heart, and brain respectively</note> proceed—as do the heart, liver, and brain—it is nevertheless a servant providing a common duty to all the principal organs by preparing their nourishment. Therefore, so that the stomach (if it should be weak, as often happens to the elderly) may properly supply this preparation to the liver first of all, it will be worthwhile to recognize its weakness through certain signs.

You will recognize this weakness if a heaviness is felt in the stomach, or if the food consumed is digested with difficulty, and if tasteless or sour burps frequently bother the person. In such a case, I say it will be best if, in the morning before food, he eats preserved ginger root <note>original: "radicem zinziberis conditi"</note>, or a piece of cinnamon, or something else that strengthens the stomach, such as sweet flag <term>acorus</term> preserved with honey—not the tasteless kind, but the fragrant sort that has a sharp taste. I have often seen this root among the roots which modern people call galangal <term>galanga</term> in the merchants' shops.

There are also many compound medicines that strengthen the stomach. If one uses these in the morning before food, they properly fortify the stomach; these include "aromatic of roses," *diagalanga*, *pliris archonticon* <note>A restorative powder used in medieval medicine for the heart and stomach</note>, *diamusk*, *diambra*, the "electuary of gems," Rhazes' "Joy-giver" dedicated to Al-Mansur <note>original: "laetificans Rasis ad Almansorem"; Rhazes was a famous 9th-century Persian physician</note>, the Mithridatic confection <term>metridatica</term>, and Theriac <term>theriaca</term> <note>An ancient herbal "panacea" or universal antidote containing dozens of ingredients</note>. These are called the "greater confections," and they all warm and dry the body.

But some of these do so more intensely, such as the Mithridatic confection and Theriac, once they have reached their "vigor." I say "vigor" because ages are assigned to Theriac just as they are to humans: there is infancy, adolescence, youth (or its peak state), and finally old age. For when it is new, it undoubtedly produces the effects of "cold" medicines—if it is taken then—because it induces sleep and a state of stupor, according to the testimony of Galen in the fifth book of his *Method of Healing* <note>original: "Galeni quinto methodi"</note>. Therefore, it is in no way useful for the elderly for strengthening the principal internal organs before it has aged twelve years. Nor is that which is too old—having passed its fortieth or fiftieth year—praised by the ancients in this case, since it excessively dries out the moist substance in bodies, especially if its use is frequent. Therefore, we must always use it sparingly and mixed with something that can moderate its dryness—for instance, with the flowers of bugloss or borage mixed with sugar as a preserve of bugloss, and...

Therefore, let the stomach be strengthened with those things that can aid digestion <note>original: "concoctionem"</note> and are able to refresh the other members—such as the heart, liver, and brain—with moderate heat and a pleasant scent.

Indeed, all the prescribed confections not only restore and increase the power of the stomach, but they also clarify the blood and the spirit, and guide them toward a *judicial temperament* <term>temperamentum iusticiale</term> <note>A medical term referring to the ideal balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—necessary for health</note> (as doctors say). Furthermore, the most excellent physicians praise preserved **myrobalans** <term>mirabulanos</term> <note>The astringent fruit of several species of the Terminalia tree, prized in both Arabic and Ayurvedic medicine</note>, such as the *emblic* and *chebulic* varieties, which (as the divine Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century physician influential in the Latin West</note> wrote) make men grow young again. I, however, do not praise their use in those who are very old and consumed by decrepitude. In the elderly who possess only a small amount of heat, these fruits neither warm the stomach nor are they able to regulate the phlegmatic <note>original: "pituito/fos"</note> humor within it; although they may dry out external moistures, they cannot increase the weak heat which the elderly require.

For this reason, it is worthwhile to eat **preserved ginger** <term>zinziber</term> along with the aforementioned myrobalans, so that through such an addition they may increase heat and be able to strengthen the stomach, heart, liver, and brain; thus, they will be stronger for all their functions. Nor did it seem right to me to pass over in silence any consideration of **vinegar of squill** <term>aceto scilitico</term> <note>A medicinal vinegar infused with the sea onion (squill), used to clear phlegm</note>, since it is able to cut through and thin the thick, sluggish, and phlegmatic humors in which the elderly abound; it also increases the heat of the stomach so that it may more easily drive these humors toward the intestines. Therefore, Galen and other most excellent ancients highly praised its use. Furthermore, besides the fact that it [cuts through] sluggish [humors]...

This is because it greatly restores the **innate moisture** <note>A vital fluid thought to be born with a person and slowly "consumed" by life’s heat; its preservation was the key to longevity.</note> and the powers of the stomach and liver in the elderly and the weak—such as those recovering from illness, or even those gripped by some pestilential disease <note>Referring to the plague or other highly infectious and "spirit-dissolving" epidemics.</note> that greatly dissolves one’s strength. It is indeed beneficial if a quantity of one or two ounces is mixed with other dishes.

I omit many things which strengthen the primary organs by their scent. Since I have already partially spoken of these above—such as compounds made from spices—but **musk** and **ambergris** are most highly praised if they are smelled. Nor should one omit fumigations <note>Incense or medicinal smoke produced by burning resins.</note> made from **aloeswood**, **storax**, and **benzoin** <note>A balsamic resin from the bark of Styrax trees.</note>, which not a few learned men of great experience believe to be true myrrh, because they wonderfully refresh the principal organs by their fragrant inhalation. ## TO THE MOST EXCELLENT LORD
## Paulus Magnolus, of the house of Eburo, of Brescia, 
## Letter IV. On lunch and dinner, regarding the noble 
## truth, in which many things concerning the 
## method of eating are handed down.

When I had enjoined upon the most illustrious Lord Vladislaus <note>Likely a member of the Polish or Hungarian nobility visiting Venice.</note> in my medical advice that he should take a smaller quantity of food in the evening hours than in the morning, you modestly objected during our conversation, most learned Paul, that certain others have both written and affirmed by word of mouth that the opposite should be done, claiming this was also the opinion of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (c. 129–216 AD), the most influential Greek physician of antiquity, whose theories on the four humors formed the basis of medicine until the 19th century.</note>. Since we were by no means able to finish that discussion on that day, I promised to write to you my reasoned opinion on **lunch and dinner** <note>original: "prandio & cœna." In the 16th century, *prandium* was the midday meal and *coena* was the evening meal.</note>, which we experience daily; namely, what the reason is why wise physicians believed that dinner should sometimes (though rarely) be larger, but for the most part smaller than lunch. 

It is not, however, as some of those who profess to be "Galenists" believe—that it must be held as a constant rule that eating copiously at dinner is more healthful. That this is neither a constant rule nor rational (as they claim) will be established from Galen's own opinions and from reason itself. Regarding this matter, so that I do not detain you with a longer preface, I shall begin to open the subject itself. First, however, those who have gone so mad in this opinion—so much so that they seem to fight for their own reputation rather than speak for the truth—say that for men, without any distinction of circumstances, whether...

# L E T T E R

...or sick, to dine most sumptuously and to eat little or nothing for lunch. They attempt to prove this opinion of theirs with strained interpretations and the authorities not only of **Galen**, but also of **Hippocrates**, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a primary textbook in European universities for centuries.</note>, and other illustrious ancients. I have judged that the recording of all these authorities would offend the mind of anyone with boredom and confusion; however, for a clearer understanding, I shall review only certain points that have some likeness to the truth, while omitting the rest. Moreover, it would seem that I have accomplished nothing in my pursuit of brevity if I do not respond with evident reasons and explain the authorities according to the truth—rather than using forced logic or poorly understood authority as they do.

First, however, no wise physician denies this primary principle: namely, that **custom is a second nature** <note>A famous philosophical proverb suggesting that habits, once established, are as difficult to change as biological nature itself.</note>. **Aristotle** very often proved this, as did his faithful interpreter **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher famous for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> especially, in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle’s foundational work on the study of nature.</note>, in the seventy-first commentary. He mentions it also in the preface of the third book of the same work, and in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, as well as in not a few other places. Therefore, this first foundation they have laid down collapses—namely, that a larger dinner is suitable for everyone. For many who are accustomed either not to dine in the evening, or to eat more heavily at lunch and very little at dinner, a larger dinner is not appropriate.

Furthermore, there is another principle granted by all wise men: namely, that **experience is the teacher of things**, since (as **Aristotle** said) experience produces art <note>The Greek "techne," meaning a systematic skill or craft.</note>. Wherefore, since many people find through experience that they are better off if they eat little or nothing for dinner—even if they have taken little food at lunch—than if they had done the opposite. Therefore, that position <note>The idea that dinner must always be the largest meal.</note> is not true without exception. Indeed, there are the private and specific circumstances of men: their natures, ages, temperaments, the seasons, regions, habits, exercises, the occurrences of life, and many other such things, in which that opinion will not be plainly true without any exception.

To respond to certain things they say: they praise a larger dinner over lunch even in afflictions of the head and eyes, asserting that a larger dinner is beneficial. What, then, I ask you, most learned Paul, can physicians say to these things? For the primary intention of the method of healing is to remove the cause of the disease, or that which could increase the cause of the disease and the disease itself. But to dine copiously, in diseases of both the head and the eyes, increases the disease and the cause of the disease, since from a very large dinner comes a very great **evaporation** <note>In the medical theory of the time, it was believed that food "cooking" in the stomach released vapors or fumes that rose to the head, potentially causing illness if excessive.</note> toward the head, which [weakens] the strength...

->FOURTH<-

...it disturbs the [stomach] and increases the disease. Nor do I see how they can defend their assertion by claiming that the benefit in digesting is greater than the harm in evaporating <note>Refers to the medical theory that digestion produces "vapors" which, if not properly managed, can rise to the brain and cause harm.</note>. If they take this statement in an absolute sense, it is undoubtedly false; but if they wish to apply it to some specific physical disposition, they will find it to be true at times. For that same heat, while sleeping, can more easily digest a smaller quantity of food than a larger one—if we are likewise considering natural heat <note>The innate warmth of the body believed to drive all physiological processes.</note> in an absolute sense.

Please observe what kind of position this is, which is consistent with neither sense nor reason. Is it not true that, all other things being equal, the vital power will digest a smaller quantity of food better while sleeping than a larger one? Therefore, they misinterpret **Galen** in the fifth book of *On Simple Medicines* <note>Original: *De simplicium medicamentorum*; a major work by Galen on the properties of various medicinal substances.</note> by comparing vapors to the spirit, which is the instrument of the soul.

They would have spoken better, however, if they had understood how nature is assisted, as in the example given by **Galen** in the same book—namely, regarding those who embrace children or puppies at night so that the heat of the stomach, increased by the heat of the child, can better digest the ingested food. For there is nothing that can better increase the heat of the stomach than heat meeting the stomach in that way; and certainly not that evening hour which they prioritize above all things for digestion <note>Original: *concoctio*; the physiological process of "cooking" or breaking down food via internal heat.</note>.

Nor do I see why we should not praise the reapers, who are accustomed to taking a larger lunch, especially since they have been used to this from the cradle, such that their tireless labors even seem to require it. Furthermore, a very great dissipation of moisture <note>Original: *humidi reſolutio*; refers to the loss of the body's essential fluids or "radical moisture" through sweat and exertion.</note> occurs in those whose labor is both continuous and extreme, as happens with farmers. Therefore, lest the body be dried out by the great dissipation resulting from labor and heat during the day, it is necessary to take note of that dissipation and to lunch copiously.

But at dinner, this is not so necessary, since strength is restored—as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician.</note> said—not from food alone, but from sleep. For when the body rests, no further movement dissolves the heat, which has already been made weak by continuous labor toward the end of the day. Furthermore, the heat having been rendered weak in the evening hours, it could not regulate a great quantity of food; but in the morning and at lunch, having been made fresh, strong, and more potent by the night’s rest, it can best digest what is offered. Nor does the labor that follows lunch stand in the way of the food being processed, since these people have been accustomed from their tender years to both eating and working a great deal. Nor can anyone cite **Galen** to the contrary, in the second book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>Original: *De tuenda ualetudine* (or *De sanitate tuenda*).</note>...

# L E T T E R

...to bring forward [an authority] saying that the protection of health must begin with labor <note>In this context, "labor" refers to physical exercise or bodily exertion intended to maintain health.</note>, which food ought to follow, even though **Galen's** opinion is far removed from that foreign speculation. **Galen** neither intended to say what they claim in that passage, nor would he have ever believed it even in his sleep. You can confirm this from the opinion of the most eminent **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was the primary medical textbook in Europe for centuries.</note>, who, in the third tractate of the first book, second doctrine, third chapter—not only as many moderns do, who merely receive words and write what they have received, but through his own sharp judgment and never-sufficiently-praised doctrine—moderated what he received from **Galen**. 

Nor should it be believed that those accustomed to strong labor abound in many humidities <note>Original: "humiditatibus"; referring to the "moist" humors or fluids in the body. Excessive moisture was thought to cause sluggishness and disease.</note>, even if they eat much during the day according to their custom, since labor consumes those [moistures]. Instead, those who enjoy leisure are the ones who abound in them. This is what the divine **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> hinted at in his booklet *On the Manner of Living* <note>Original: "de victus ratione"; also known by the title "Regimen."</note>, when he said that those who eat cannot be healthy if they lack labor. **Galen** also says this in the sixteenth aphorism of the second part of the *Aphorisms*, stating that labor is not suitable for workers unless they have eaten first—and this ought to be done all the more where they are so accustomed. Supporting this opinion are the things **Hippocrates** felt in the second book of *On the Manner of Living* regarding the changing of habits.

I ask you, most learned Magnolus, because of your love for me, that for my sake you do not find it tedious to read again the series of the divine **Hippocrates** (which I believe you have often read). I want you to understand how certain moderns do not only tear (so to speak) the royal robes of medicine itself, but also of other sciences; they seem to pluck out the principal members, like the heart itself, in the manner of thieves. They do this while they deny these truths, even claiming that the arrival of the sun to us does not benefit all powers <note>Original: "virtutibus"; in Galenic medicine, "virtues" or "powers" are the biological faculties (natural, vital, and animal) that govern the body.</note>, especially the natural power. Yet this is untrue, not only regarding the daily arrival of the sun, but also its annual return, since both spring and summer themselves increase one's strength. This is testified by the wise **Aristotle** together with his most faithful interpreter, and also **Hippocrates** and **Galen**. Since their works are so well known, I have decided not to write them here, lest this speech be stretched out too long.

You remember that saying of **Hippocrates**: *Stomachs are warmer in winter and spring* <note>A fundamental principle in ancient medicine: "antiperistasis." It was believed that when the outside air is cold, the body's internal heat retreats to the core, making the stomach hotter and digestion stronger.</note>, not only from the concentration of heat but also from the arrival of the sun to us, which strengthens the heat of the living being. Thus, by "winter," the final part is understood, which is near spring; for if the cold from above has forced the heat to the innermost parts, the approaching sun contributes even more, just as it does to warm things externally...

Indeed, this seems to be the effect of external heat or cold upon our own internal heat: moderate levels help, but excessive levels hinder.

Moderate external cold unites and strengthens [our internal heat], while too much cold extinguishes it. Likewise, external heat that is not too powerful increases our heat; but the opposite [excessive heat] dissolves it. In the evening, however, having been dissolved by the day's heat and not yet refreshed either by the night’s moderate cold or the renewal of the <term>spirits</term> <note>The "vital spirits" were thought to be refined substances in the blood that fueled bodily functions; they were believed to be replenished during rest and sleep.</note> (which happens much later), the heat will be weaker.

Truly, I am ashamed to answer all their points, since the things said by them are frivolous and possess almost no wisdom. Those who are unable to respond with logic very often attack the dead with insults. Would that modern physicians were as learned and experienced as those who came before us, who clarified the questions and doubts of the ancients and left them in writing! Good gods, how great was the diligence, the labor, and—if I may say so—the charity of the ancients? And yet some are so witless that they dare to say the ancients were poorly educated.

But I return to where the speech began. They say—those who affirm that <term>dinner</term> <note>Original: "cœnam." They claim that heat is stronger in those evening hours because it is turned inward by sleep and the cooling of the surrounding air. Therefore, they argue, it is appropriate to give a larger quantity of food in the evening hours, which are the hours of dinner. They attempt to prove this reasoning by the authority of **Galen** in the fourth book of *On the Causes of Symptoms*. See, I ask you, how easy it is to be deceived by a plausible reason, as we are sometimes accustomed to say among ourselves by the authority of **Plato** in the *Phaedo* <note>A famous Socratic dialogue by Plato; the author likely refers to the warnings therein about being misled by "misology" or false arguments.</note>. For their apparent reason seems to affirm something entirely in their favor, since even the words of the most learned **Galen** affirm the same thing.
