### E P I S T L E

But let us distinguish, as wise men do, between the beginning—which is the path to increasing the living creature’s heat, occurring through sleep via the cooling of the surrounding environment—and the time in which the heat has already been increased, the restoration of the <term>spirits</term> <note>The "vital spirits" were thought to be a subtle substance produced from blood and air that fueled life and movement.</note> having been accomplished, which is when a person has already slept enough. For in the evening hours, the heat is dissolved and weak from the day’s labor and its expansion to the exterior limbs; this is attested by everyone's own senses, as well as by **Aristotle** and **Averroes** in the book *On Sleep and Waking*. And for this reason, nature has provided them restoration through sleep, which is a form of rest, by multiplying the spirits at night, when the cooling of the air also seems to assist. 

But the works of nature do not happen except over time; therefore, that restoration of spirits and that stronger heat will not exist until after the heat has been entirely recalled to the interior and has changed the matter of the blood into the substance of the spirits. This operation of nature, however, takes place over time. For **Hippocrates** said in the fourth book he wrote *On Diseases*—although **Galen**, in his commentaries on the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>original: "de morbis vulgaribus"</note>, doubted whether it was his—that whatever the case may be, that book was written by none other than a learned man; for he says that the food taken in is retained by the stomach and does not nourish on the same day, but three days later, so that the body is not nourished immediately. This is apparent, for if the consumed food left the stomach quickly, men would become thin and not robust (and so he spoke concerning food), so that the excrement of the food is evacuated three days later: it is then that men become strong and powerful. 

In those evening hours, however, in which we are accustomed to dine, even if the heat begins to be recalled a little later, it is not yet entirely on the inside. This is indicated by those whose heat increases late at night, with the exterior flesh being inflamed; these, just like <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>A "cupping glass" (cucurbitula) was a medical instrument used to draw blood or heat to the surface of the skin through suction.</note>, draw [the heat] out, and since they are so inflamed, they neither allow the natural heat to yield to the interior, nor are the spirits yet restored in the first part of the night so that they might then, being stronger, <term>concoct</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "concoction" refers to the process of digestion, viewed as a literal "cooking" of food by internal heat.</note> better. For even if the heat were suddenly recalled, a great space of time must pass before it restores the lost spirit, as you saw **Hippocrates** saying, so that it labors through that time. Therefore, the heat will not be powerful for digesting in the evening. But according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, those first hours are principally and especially for the restoration of the spirits. For although the food is cooked first, the ultimate goal is the restoration of the spirits; wherefore, first in the digestion of the food currently taken in, the power of the stomach...

Once this restoration of the spirits has been completed, all parts of the body and all its <term>powers</term> <note>The Latin "virtutes" refers to the specific functional capacities of the body, such as the ability to digest or move.</note> become more robust. This, however, does not occur until after the living beings have slept for a notable amount of time; and these are the morning hours, unless someone were to change their schedule, staying awake at night and exerting themselves by day. This we all experience within ourselves, as all powers—the vital, the <term>animal</term> <note>Refers to the "animal virtue" or psychic power, which governed the nervous system and thought.</note>, and also the <term>natural</term> <note>Refers to the "natural virtue," which governed growth, nutrition, and digestion.</note>—are stronger. This is easily proven regarding the natural powers, since all excrements—whether from the bowels, the urine, the phlegm, and the like—are more easily evacuated in the morning hours. 

This evacuation is the work of the final natural power, following all others. Without it, nutrition would not be perfectly completed so that a healthy individual might thrive—that is, unless the superfluities were expelled. This was the view of **Galen** in his book *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: "de tuenda valetudine"</note>, when he said that it is beneficial for bodies to be awakened at that time when they are cleansed of excrements. However, he did not say this because labor hinders <term>concoction</term> <note>The historical term for digestion, viewed as a "cooking" process by the body's internal heat.</note>, especially in those who are accustomed to it (as we were saying). 

This same thing is apparent in living creatures, both in their internal and external aspects; even the operations of the soul and the perfections of reasoning occur in the morning hours, as all students and those who deal with difficult matters through discourse can testify. Those who perform physical labor to earn their living experience the same, as do many animals, such as horses and oxen. The vital power also seems to be far stronger in these hours, as physicians find the pulse to be significantly better then. 

Therefore, whether we like it or not, based on the reasons brought forward (by those who argue that a larger supper is appropriate, though they misunderstand the time when the body's power is strongest), we must say that a larger quantity of food is more suitable for the morning hours, since the body’s power is stronger in the morning than in the evening. But when they claim that **Galen**, in the passage cited, said the natural power is stronger while a person is sleeping, this is true in the sense that it becomes stronger gradually, so that it reaches its peak by morning. This is especially true through its final operation, which is <term>sanguification</term> <note>The physiological process of turning digested food into blood.</note>, the distribution of nourishment to the limbs, and the separation of waste. This occurs when the blood, prepared from the digestion of the previous foods, is drawn in by all the limbs and (especially in the way of physicians) by the heart, to be converted into spirit for the preservation of life...

This allows them to be converted into blood and spirit through successive digestion by other organs, such as the liver <note>original: "æpar" (hepar)</note> and the heart. This entire operation of nature does not happen except over a longer period of time. For instance, the first digestion in the stomach is not completed in most people except in the space of eight hours, by which only that <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid produced from digested food in the stomach before it is transformed into blood by the liver.</note> is produced, which is not yet far removed from the substance of the food itself. Furthermore, the chyle is not changed into blood except over a greater amount of time; likewise, the change of blood into spirit does not occur until after the [natural] power has labored in the aforementioned preparations. Therefore, we should not say that all natural powers are stronger during sleep. Instead, that which contributes most to the powers—since it comes not from the first digestion but from the later ones—will occur in those morning hours (as was said), in which we have said it is better to take the larger meal. # TO THE MOST EXCELLENT LORD,
## ANTONIO FRACANZANO, Professor of
### Public Medicine at Padua, Concerning
#### Anatomy. Epistle V.

**I** know not by what act or cause, most learned **Fracanzano** <note>Antonio Fracanzano (d. 1567) was a prominent professor of medicine at the University of Padua.</note>, some are urging me to record in writing the errors of modern anatomists for the benefit of students, affirming that you also know I intend to do so. I have replied to them that this is by no means fitting for me, an old man—and one who was the first after **Galen** to teach learned men the true discipline of dissecting bodies (and showing all the parts) and understanding their uses. Especially so since no rational cause impels me to do it. Nevertheless, they insist that I should do this not only for the utility of students, but also in your honor, as you not only desire this work, but have always treated **Massa** <note>The author, Niccolò Massa, refers to himself here in the third person.</note> with love and benevolence...

### FIFTH EPISTLE
->G 4<-

I would wish, therefore, that I do not appear unrefined, but at least seem to show equal gratitude to you, to whom I am indebted, and also satisfy the students in some part. If not exactly what they seek, I wanted at least to write to you what was said in a discussion with them regarding **anatomical** <term>anatomicis</term> <note>The study of bodily structure through dissection, which was undergoing a revolution during this period.</note> matters. 

And to proceed in order: while they were requesting these things, and seeing me resisting because of many other tasks, they first began to ask what I thought of the **huge volume** <note>This likely refers to Vesalius’s massive and groundbreaking anatomical work, which was famous for its size and its critique of Galen.</note>. I responded to them thus: I, who am detained by so many affairs in visiting the sick, can hardly read huge volumes—or to speak more truly, not even taste them—however, I have heard many who praise the work with great applause. Indeed, I also cannot help but praise it. Good gods! It was certainly a monumental labor in compiling it, which could not have been perfected except by vigils, studies, and practice. 

"Fair words," they said, "but we desire to know from you whether they say everything from themselves, or report things received from others; and also whether those things which they show to be errors (in their contempt for the ancients) are truly so. For they very often reproach, refute, rebuke, and pursue with calumnies **Galen**, **Aristotle**, and the moderns." 

To these students I kindly responded thus, in honor of the most eminent ancients—and especially **Aristotle** and **Galen**—citing the testimony of **Averroes** <note>original: "Auerroi"; the 12th-century philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> from the course of his 36th commentary on the third book of **On the Soul** <note>original: "de anima"</note>: that no one can perfectly complete the practical or theoretical arts by themselves, except through prior knowledge, to which those seeking perfection add their own findings. 

In this way, **Aristotle** completed his work by adding to what he received from the ancients; and **Galen** similarly strengthened medicine—received first from **Hippocrates**, and then from other ancients, both the "rationalists" and "empirics"—with wonderful and incomparable teaching and eloquence. This medicine was then completed by **Avicenna** the Arab, his most faithful interpreter; though he lacked elegance of language, he left nothing untouched in his summary with his order and wonderful erudition. 

Similarly, the modern anatomists of our own time have done the same. For when they had received and imitated many things from **Aristotle**, **Galen**, and other more recent authors—and even from my own writings on anatomy printed many years ago—they usurped them as their own (giving no credit to those authors, nor to me). But what is worse, they pursue with calumnies and insults (as you say) **Aristotle**, **Galen**, and others from whom they received these gifts for free. Yet, to these stolen things they have added many others which, I testify before God, are worthy of all praise, as they could only have been acquired through the greatest study...

# E P I S T L E

[...the students] were. But those things which were said in contempt, insultingly, and with mocking laughter against the most eminent ancients and the **lights of the world** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for the great Greek and Roman philosophers and physicians whose works were seen as the foundation of knowledge.</note>, I could never praise; since, in order to exalt their own findings, they misinterpret the wise ancients. Very often, too, as I hear, they are lying, since they have added many things which neither **Aristotle** nor **Galen** ever dreamed of, let alone wrote. I dismissed these things from them, saying (as **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator and philosopher.</note> used to say) that **truth** possesses this quality: that by its own power alone it protects itself from slanderers. When I first explained this to them, they said, "You believe most rightly, and so it seemed to us as well; but we pray you to respond to the remaining points." I, who (as I said) could neither hear these men nor read their writings, replied: "I cannot satisfy your requests." They said: "If it pleases you to hear it from us, we will gladly explain those things to you, but we always desire your opinion in all matters."

"Speak, learned young men," I responded, "since I have leisure at present to speak with you." They said: "We desire to know whether these are errors or truths, but we will narrate them to you individually. First, did Galen ever dissect human **cadavers** <term>cadavera</term> <note>Bodies used for anatomical study. In the Renaissance, there was a heated debate over whether Galen’s anatomical descriptions were based on humans or only on apes and other animals.</note> at any time, and did he write his anatomy faithfully? Or did he, through a wrong understanding of other ancients, describe things poorly to us in his writing? Into this error, according to their opinion, even **Aristotle** seems to have fallen."

To these things I responded to them that it is manifest that **Galen** and **Aristotle** indeed dissected very many bodies of **brute animals** <note>Non-human animals. Ancient Greek law generally prohibited human dissection, leading Galen to rely heavily on animals that resembled humans, like Barbary macaques.</note> (as seen from their writings), and also human cadavers, and wrote faithfully about their knowledge of them. I easily persuaded them of this truth by reciting the words of Galen and his opinions written in very many books. For in the first book of **Anatomical Procedures** <term>De anatomicis aggressionibus</term> <note>Galen's major manual on dissection technique. Its "rediscovery" in the 1530s was a catalyst for the anatomical revolution.</note>, near the beginning, he wrote thus: "First, one must know the bones of apes, so that afterward you can more easily recognize them in a human cadaver; for you will not be able to have knowledge of anatomical matters from reading alone, nor from the inspection of apes, but also from humans." 

That he saw both human bones and other members is also testified by those things he wrote in the little book *On Bones*. And in the first book of *Anatomical Procedures*, he affirms he saw them in **Alexandria** <note>A major center of Hellenistic learning where human dissection had been practiced in earlier centuries (notably by Herophilus and Erasistratus), providing Galen with human skeletal evidence.</note>, and also by those words which follow shortly after in this vein: "Apes are very similar to humans, yet they differ in many things; for the head of the femur is in a certain way more oblique where it joins the socket of the hip, as are also certain muscles which descend into the hip." He also advised in the third book of the same work to first practice by dissecting apes...

### FIFTH

...so that he might afterwards more boldly approach the **corpses** <term>cadavera</term> of humans. Finally, in the fourth [book] of the same work on anatomical procedures, he said that the ape does not have a hand exactly like a human’s, since it has a small, stunted thumb <note>original: "mutilum magnum... digitum"; Galen observed that the primate thumb was shorter and less developed than the human one, a detail the author uses to prove Galen knew the difference between species.</note>. Therefore, he advises one to look at the anatomy of the hands in humans alone. You see, therefore, from these sayings that Galen wrote his anatomy not only from the inspection of **brute animals** <note>In this period, "brutes" refers to any non-human animals.</note>, but also from the inspection of human limbs; he wanted not only to see the parts of animals and humans, but even to compare them with one another. Indeed, in the second book of the same work, while reprimanding those who wanted to learn about limbs not from humans but from animals by dissecting oxen, he says that the tongue of an ox is most unlike the human tongue. How, I ask, could Galen—otherwise a diligent man, learned and of incomparable judgment—have described the differences between the limbs of humans and animals unless he had seen both?

But they will say: Galen puts these things forward as examples received from others, not because he himself had dissected the corpses of humans. But please, listen to Galen himself in the sixth book of **On the Use of the Parts** <note>original: "de usu partium"; one of Galen's most influential works, arguing that every part of the body was perfectly designed for its function.</note>, shortly after the beginning, who writes thus: "Furthermore, it is not my purpose to define the number of lobes of the lungs of every other animal, nor do we touch upon the construction of their instruments, unless perhaps we were compelled to do so while explaining the human body; for if we are not prevented by death, we shall at some time explain their construction limb by limb, just as we are now dissecting that of humans." These are Galen's words, from which you see that he himself dissected human bodies when he spoke about human limbs, even promising that he would describe the limbs of animals if he survived. This you can confirm from the words of the eleventh book of the same *On the Use of the Parts* near the end, where he gives the reason why humans walk upright while many other animals walk prone. There, giving the reason, he said it was because the human has a different formation of both the spine and its muscles than the spine and muscles of animals. Similarly, in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, he compares the human stomach, both in shape and substance, to the stomachs of other animals.

"You teach correctly," they said, "and you illuminate the truth; we also believed this, although we had not noticed these passages in Galen. But what do you believe," they added, "concerning those things which **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose biological works remained authoritative for nearly two millennia.</note> wrote in the book **On the Parts of Animals** <note>original: "de partibus animalium"</note>?"

I respond: This is a superstitious inquiry for those who [have read] those things which Aristotle...

[Ari]stotle <note>The Latin text "stotiles" is missing the initial "Ari-", likely due to a decorative initial that was never completed.</note> wrote on **animals** <note>original: "de animalibus"; referring to Aristotle's biological works, particularly *History of Animals*.</note> copiously, distinctly, learnedly, and subtly: they may have read him sometimes. For indeed, he wished to commit nothing to writing except what was seen and agreeable to reason. Therefore, let those men stop presuming against the most eminent men; and I exhort and implore you, young men, that if the desire holds you to emerge in the number of both philosophers and physicians, you should be willing to read Aristotle's book *On Animals* and Theophrastus's *On Plants* <note>original: "Theophrasti de plantis"</note> attentively, diligently, and often. For they contain those things which, without doubt, are generally necessary for proceeding learnedly in both theory and practice. 

"The warning is pleasing, and it will be observed," they say, "but come, and explain the rest to us." 

I ask, "What are those things?" 

They say, "Many indeed." 

But I [say], "This matter will be explained to you by me neither off-hand nor even from premeditation; for indeed, the parts of a living body are innumerable. If you should wish to run through all things individually, and I should wish to answer you, a year would not suffice." 

Those who are both learned and most modest respond: "We do not desire to know all things at present, but certain things as introductory to the remaining difficulties. We shall begin from the head, and we wish to know whether the brain has its own and native shape tending toward roundness from the <term>informative virtue</term> <note>original: "uirtute informatiua"; in Renaissance biology, this was the internal power or "blueprint" that guided the physical development of an embryo.</note> operating in such a way so that it might better perform animal operations, or rather if it follows the shape of the bone covering it, which they call the **cranium** <note>original: "craneum"</note>."

To this I [say] to them: "This question seems childish to me, if someone were to treat it with philosophers. For indeed, who is so unrefined, though well-versed in the works of nature, that he would be ignorant of this (so to speak) first principle: namely, that from the human seed and that of many other 'perfect' animals <note>In this context, "perfect animals" refers to higher mammals that produce live young.</note>, after it is retained in the womb, those three principal members are generated: specifically, the heart, the liver <note>original: "æpar"; a Latinization of the Greek word for liver, *hepar*.</note>, and the brain. In that first formation, nature first conforms them to a certain round shape, as can be seen in **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Hyppocrate"</note> regarding the woman who had conceived and afterwards, when she was leaping, had a miscarriage <note>This refers to a famous passage in the Hippocratic work *On the Nature of the Child*, where the author describes observing an early-stage embryo after a patient followed his instructions to leap vigorously to induce an abortion.</note>. This is also seen in adults, in whom, even if these three members are not seen to be perfectly spherical in their entirety, they nevertheless tend toward roundness. As can first be seen in the heart, which has obtained a pine-cone shape, which is not without roundness. The liver also has a somewhat round shape, not however because of the containing <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septotranuerso"; the transverse septum or diaphragm.</note>, but from the informative virtue—or if you say 'from nature' it makes no difference—thus [governed] first by an intelligence that does not err...

Having established the importance of ancient authorities, the author now addresses the morphological principles of the body, arguing that nature prioritizes the "perfect" spherical shape for both the cosmos and the human organs.</meta>

<page-num>54</page-num>

->FIFTH<-

...directed, so that through its substance, quantity, temperament, and figure it might perform the necessary natural operations according to the proper proportion <note>original: "iustitiam," literally 'justice,' referring here to the biological balance or 'due' of the body</note> of its own body. And even if the stomach is placed against the convex part of the liver <note>original: "iocinoris"</note>, and the liver is made hollow in that part, it does not primarily claim this shape from the touching members, but from nature. Nature works this way first in the formation of almost all members: first introducing a round figure, and then—according to the necessity of its operation and sometimes secondary to its location—it shapes that roundness into an oblong, wide, or another suitable configuration. 

This can be seen in the kidneys, stomach, spleen, intestines, bladder, uterus, testes, bones, muscles, and other members, whether they be "similar" or "organic" <term>similar and organic parts: a traditional medical distinction where 'similar' parts are uniform (like bone or flesh) and 'organic' parts are complex organs (like the hand or liver)</term> (as doctors call them). Even if they have diverse figures, whether oblong or wide, they are nevertheless not deprived of some manifest roundness. Furthermore, the primary figure intended by nature, wherever it is possible, is circular and round, as Aristotle learnedly said in the second book of **On the Heavens** <note>original: "secundo coeli"</note>: for this reason, the heavens are by nature spherical in shape, as it is the most perfect and noble of figures. Nature intends to preserve this same design even in the microcosm <term>paruo cosmo: the 'small world,' a philosophical term for the human body as a reflection of the universe</term> as much as it can, so that through this kind of figure the members might be less vulnerable to harm and have greater capacity, as Galen also testified near the beginning of the fourth book of **On the Use of Parts**. 

But let me return to where the discussion left off. The brain, therefore, similarly received a round figure from nature, though not entirely spherical, but rather as much as was suitable for its proper operations. We observe this even in a great many animals, such as horses, oxen, dogs, and the like: even if they have an oblong head-bone, the substance of the brain itself is nonetheless seen to have a round shape, and nature fashioned the case <note>original: "thecam"</note>—that is, the bone by which it is contained—to be round in that part to match the thing placed within it. Indeed, the skull <note>original: "craneum"</note> contains the brain and is its protection and storehouse, made *after* the formation of the brain. Since a figure tending toward roundness (for the useful reasons already mentioned) first suited the brain, and since the brain is a noble and principal member that had to be safely guarded, it was rational for nature to have providently formed the citadel for the protection of this principal member according to the shape and convenience of the member itself, rather than having the member follow the shape of its covering. Because...

It specifically asserts that the skull forms its shape to accommodate the brain, rather than the brain being shaped by the skull.</summary>

# E P I S T O L A

...justice <note>original: "iustitiam," continuing from the previous page</note>, if the brain in any part follows the shape of a small portion of the skull itself—as can be seen where the nerves descend to the nostrils through two holes in the basal bone <note>likely the ethmoid bone, which sits at the base of the skull and has a sieve-like plate for olfactory nerves</note>—so that the configuration of the brain appears to mirror the shape of those holes, resembling two nipple-like processes <note>original: "papillis mamillarum"; these are the olfactory bulbs</note>, and if this is also seen in other places where certain veins pass through, this does not happen because the brain lacks its own proper shape. Rather, it is for a better purpose: namely, that by filling those openings in that specific area, it might prevent harmful vapors from rising to the brain. Likewise, the same was done regarding the veins out of necessity, so that nourishment might be more easily delivered. For indeed, nature does not overflow in superfluities, nor does it fail in necessities <note>original: "natura non abundat in superfluis, neque deficit in necessariis," a fundamental principle in Aristotelian and Galenic science</note>. For if nature can achieve many operations and benefits with a single part, it certainly completes them, yet without diminishing the primary function of the limb or altering it to the detriment of the individual. Furthermore, that part of the brain which receives the form of nipple-like breasts from the cavity of the bone is so small that it seems like nothing if you choose to look at the whole substance of the brain. Nevertheless, it contributes by warming (as I said) the brain and the thin, soft nerves descending to the nostrils—nerves which, if anyone denies their existence, shows that he has not noted them carefully in the dissection of bodies. From what has been said, you have heard how some people are misled, deceived by some apparent but false reasoning. For even if the brain is soft, so that besides its own shape—which tends toward roundness—it can also be shaped into another, one should not say for this reason that the brain has no proper shape of its own but receives it from others; because (as I told you) nature gave the bone for the protection of the brain, like a case <note>original: "thecam"</note> guarding it. These reasons are pleasing, but there is another question, namely: concerning the bone of the head, which they call the cranium, when they say it consists of three parts, is this true? And also, was the part of the bone that is thin and spongy <note>original: "spongiosa"; referring to the diploë, the porous layer between the hard inner and outer layers of the skull</note> created first, so that by its thinness it would be lighter and not weigh too heavily? To which I also replied: no one even moderately experienced in anatomy is ignorant of the threefold distinction of the skull bone. But those who assign the benefits of the different parts in the way you just mentioned do not explain it correctly. For the middle part of the skull bone was not primarily made spongy and thin simply to make the skull weigh less, but so that the nourishment drawn there by the power of the limb might be transformed, through a period of delay, by the limb's power or temperament into the substance...

<page-num>55</page-num>
<header>FIFTH [PART]</header>

...the proportion <note>original: "iustitiam"</note> of the bone. Nor can the bone, by that middle amount of space <note>referring to the diploë, the spongy layer between the hard inner and outer surfaces of the skull</note>, be too heavy; for even if it were a single solid piece without that porosity, it would not weigh more, since that part is always full of nourishment <note>marrow or blood</note>. Therefore, it seems to weigh almost the same as if it were solid, especially since the skull is supported in its entirety by the spine. Indeed, although it is of a rounded shape and flattened on both sides, it sits like a pot <note>original: "olla"</note> upon the first vertebra <note>the atlas</note> of the neck, and it cannot weigh down too much. It follows, however, that since it has a porous middle part, it is inherently lighter. Add also that the parts of the skull are held together by sutures <note>the interlocking joints of the skull bones</note> and cannot in any way sink down into the substance of the brain, but remains firm. 

"Until now, you have explained these things to us in a way that is not unwelcome. But we ask," they say, "that you might not find it troublesome to reveal certain other things to us. For they say that the hard membrane, which they call the 'hard mother' <note>original: "duram matrem," the dura mater, the outermost layer of the meninges surrounding the brain</note>, is attached to the skull only by the sutures. They also claim that the muscles of the forehead are not truly muscles, but are instead part of the fleshy membrane <note>the panniculus carnosus, a layer of muscle tissue found under the skin in many mammals, but reduced in humans</note> that surrounds the entire body beneath the skin, after the fat. Finally, we also desire to know from you about the tiny bones which are in the skull bone near the ear, at the drum <note>tympanum</note> or the membrane of the ear—acting as the 'strikers' of the drum—both regarding their nature and who discovered them." 

I respond: "I would truly wish to satisfy all of you, but since the hour now calls me elsewhere, and it is not my place to wish to respond to everything offhand in such a difficult matter, if I do not do you a disservice, I will leave the remaining matters to be explained on another day." 

"Come," they say, "we entreat you, for you have seen the things we proposed six hundred times; therefore, you will be able to satisfy us in few words." 

Softened by these words, I linger, and respond to the remaining points thus: I have always seen the hard mother <note>dura mater</note> attached to the entire skull by ligaments that are very strong for the nature of that member; however, it is bound by stronger and thicker ligaments at the sutures. If others have sometimes found otherwise, this is not a natural state, but a condition outside of nature <note>a pathology or anomaly</note>, as can be clearly seen in the little book which I wrote on the method of dissecting bodies as an introduction for young men. 

But concerning the muscles of the forehead: if there are two of them, I see no reason for a distinction as to why they should not be called muscles, since they are fleshy, possess nerves passing through to their composition, and move with voluntary motion. Nor can I say that they are membranous muscles, or part of the fleshy layer <note>the panniculus carnosus</note>, even if in this part the fleshy membrane is so integrated with the muscle, or rather the muscle...

...of the forehead <note>Completing the thought from the previous page: "the fleshy membrane that surrounds the [part] of the forehead..."</note> is so mixed together that it can by no means be separated, just as we can observe this in other parts of the body, especially in the lips where neither the skin, nor the fleshy membrane, nor the muscles that move them can be distinguished from one another. Indeed, anatomists discovered these ossicles in the time of **Alessandro Achillini** <note>1463–1512, a prominent Italian anatomist and philosopher</note>, a man most eminent in every kind of science (as can be clearly seen from his writings). Therefore, they were not first discovered or demonstrated by those [modern] men, especially since **Jacopo da Carpi** <note>Also known as Berengario da Carpi (1460–1530), who was among the first to describe the malleus and incus in print</note> teaches how to find the locations of these ossicles. I pass over those things which they claim for themselves that were actually discovered by me, giving me no credit—such as the fleshy membrane, the muscles moving the tongue from the outside, and many other parts and their uses, as can be seen in my already printed anatomical works, and as you will see, God willing, in the rest. Having said these things, I dismissed them; and wishing them a good night, I went about my usual duties. After I returned home, I decided to write to you what I had discussed with those most learned students, so they might serve as a testimony of my respect for you. Farewell, most learned sir, and do not cease to hold me in your affection. Venice, January 20, 1543.

-> ### SIXTH QUESTION <-

...[He asked] you to explain some things to us that we previously heard from you while you were explaining the anatomy of the head. And I say: what are these things? First, they say, since the discourse about the head took place four days ago <note>original: *nudius quartus*</note>, and it was not permitted to explain everything we desired (due to the shortness of time), we have approached you so that you might explain what remained; for you neither questioned us, nor did you make mention of those things we desired to know (beyond those you had already set forth) while you were speaking.

And I say: "What are those things you desire so much?" 

But they say: "We desired to know why it is that nature (according to the opinion of **Aristotle** in the second book of *On the Parts of Animals*, and of all illustrious wise men, and also from sensory knowledge) gave to man a greater quantity of brain—in respect to the size of his body—than in any other animal."

But I [responded] to them: "Because man has a larger quantity of blood, if we look at the size of his body, and also if we wish to consider the <term>final cause</term> <note>The 'final cause' refers to the purpose or goal for which a thing exists—in this case, the purpose of the brain's size is to facilitate human intelligence</note>, because man excels other animals in learning. And for that reason, nature gave him a greater mass or quantity of brain substance."

"We did not know this at all," they say, "since almost everyone who writes on the use of the parts of our body assigns no reason for this matter by which we might know in what way the quantity or mass contributes to the perfection of learning. But at another time we heard you assign a reason; since we have not entirely committed it to memory, we ask that you repeat it for us again."

I, indeed, who always strive to satisfy the learned in those matters I am able—having perceived their burning desire of mind for knowledge—began to manifest the matter more clearly in this way: 

"I say this was done because the internal <term>animal operations</term> <note>In the medical tradition of this time, 'animal operations' (from *anima*, soul) referred to the functions of the brain, including sensation, movement, and thought</note> of man, which are shared with other creatures, are observed and exist with far greater perfection and nobility in man than in any other animal. Furthermore, besides all other powers and operations which the rest of the animals possess, the rational power and its use is given to man alone, as **Aristotle** testified in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*. From this it follows that man has a similarity to the <term>intelligences</term> <note>Likely referring to the 'separate intelligences' or celestial beings in Aristotelian philosophy, which are pure intellect without bodies</note>. For reason or intellect is that one thing by which we excel other living creatures; through it we are able to conjecture, argue, refute, discuss, achieve, and conclude. Sense, however, which we share with the other animals..."

# L E T T E R

[The senses] are commonly located in the head, not only for the necessities of life—as is granted to the beasts—but also because they serve to recognize the many differences between things. This is as written by **Aristotle** in the first book of the *Divine Science* <note>original: "divinae scientiae"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>, for the senses are interpreters for the rational soul and messengers of external things. They work with the <term>imaginative power</term> <note>original: "fantastica virtute"; in the Renaissance, the "fantasy" or "imagination" was a specific faculty of the brain that processed sensory data</note> serving them, so that the soul may be able to ascend even to things that are insensible and abstract. Indeed, only human reason is able to penetrate all the way to heaven, nor is any other power more excellent than the rational power. 

To add these points to what was said shortly before: by this power, man engages with many things and ranges over them very quickly; he sees the causes of things and their consequences. He also likens many diverse things to one another, separates what is joined, and joins what is separate. He couples future things with the present, and finally strives to know all things. He does not only assign causes to those things that are in the lower world, but even dares to seek knowledge of what occurs in heaven. 

For these noble operations, glorious **God** and **Nature** (His servant) applied greater care. They gave man not only a distinguished quantity of blood and <term>spirits</term> <note>In historical medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors in the body—natural, vital, and animal—that acted as the instruments of the soul to produce movement and thought</note> to perform the aforementioned noble operations, but also a greater quantity of the "governing member" <note>the brain</note> as well as the veins and arteries within it, and the place in which the spirits are prepared to perfect those operations, than they gave to any other animals.

"These things do not satisfy us," they say. "Since they are quite obscure and far removed from what we desire to know. On other occasions, we heard you clearly when you were publicly teaching the utility of the larger mass of the brain, which utility you also promised to write about in your work on anatomical dissections."

But I [responded]: "I already intended to explain that perfectly to you, but first I will tell you why you did not find it written in my *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "de anatomicis aggressionibus"</note>. As it happens, after I had written about the dissection of the brain, and after I had read what I had written some days later, I added this part concerning the utility of the brain’s size in the margin. The printer, either not noticing it or not understanding it, omitted it. But now, in the new printing, you will find it, and many other things which before were not in it, though they are very beautiful and worthy of knowledge."

They respond: "Tell us those things, whatever the printer may have erred in or left out."

# THE SIXTH [QUESTION]

H

Human <term>animal operations</term> <note>original: "operationes animales"; in this context, these are functions of the soul (*anima*), such as logic and memory, rather than "animalistic" behaviors</note> are more perfect, such as recollection and discourse. To perform these operations, a very large quantity of **spirits** is necessary, beyond one's own ordinary <term>temperament</term> <note>the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) unique to an individual</note>. This is also the **final cause** <note>the ultimate purpose or "the why" of a thing's existence</note> for the quantity of blood, for from blood all spirits are born. 

But first, I say alongside the physicians that from a portion of the blood which is drawn by the heart, the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus uitalis"; the life-giving vapor produced in the heart and carried by the arteries</note> is created within it. This spirit then reaches the head through the arteries, where it is moderated by the brain’s power or temperament and converted into **animal spirit**. For this quantity, a greater and more comprehensive supply of arteries was primarily necessary—both in terms of number and in terms of width and extension—so that the vital spirit could be altered and changed by the power of the brain in all its parts, becoming a fit instrument for animal operations. 

Indeed, in a small quantity of brain, the power would not have been so great, nor would it have had that moderated operation required to properly refine a sufficient supply of spirit to complete the animal operations of man. For this reason, it was the work of provident Nature to provide a large mass of brain, so that there would first be greater power to balance the spirits; she also gave larger and more numerous veins and arteries so the spirits could be conveniently contained by them. 

Nor would I wish you to believe that the veins or arteries are spread through the inner substance of the brain; rather, they are on its surface, either passing through the membranes—which they call the <term>pia and dura mater</term> <note>original: "piam, & duram matrem"; the "tender mother" and "tough mother," the protective layers surrounding the brain</note>—or through its **ventricles**. 

Furthermore, the inner substance of the brain is bloodless, which some (incorrectly) call **medullary** <note>marrow-like</note>. For since the brain is one of the "principal members," it is not bone marrow; indeed, the skull has a porous middle section in which marrow, or a softer substance, is seen <note>The author is distinguishing between the brain's white matter and the actual bone marrow found in the spongy layer of the skull</note>. These are the reasons for the greater mass of the brain in man. 

**Brute animals**, however, since they deviate greatly from this balanced temperament—some being dominated by heat, others by cold, some by dryness, and many by immoderate moisture—produce a smaller quantity of good blood and spirits. For this reason, Nature did not give them such a number or size of veins and arteries, nor such a large quantity of brain. They do not possess refined and balanced animal virtues and operations, nor did they need them; therefore, they were given only as much as was necessary for their food and preservation.

# E P I S T O L A

...was necessary for the species. This occurs without any universal internal discourse <note>In this context, "discourse" refers to the process of step-by-step reasoning or logical thought</note> and even without external labor. For Nature prepared food for the **brute animals** <note>original: "brutis"; a standard term for non-rational animals</note> first and foremost; they neither sow nor cook, and they are clothed in hair, or feathers, or scales, or hide, or some other covering. This protects them from the sun and other external harms, and also allows them to defend themselves from others lying in wait for them. 

For man alone, Nature prepared none of these things which serve for life and protection. But she gave him a **rational soul**, by which he understands all things, and gave him hands—the <term>organs of organs</term> <note>original: "organa organorum"; a classical Aristotelian description of the hand as the tool that makes and uses all other tools</note>—with which he can prepare all things, both for sustenance and for the protection of the body. Thus you see that God, and Nature as God's servant, have given the intellectual animal all the instruments: both the intrinsic ones serving the intellect and the extrinsic ones serving the body for its preservation. 

Furthermore, because man is an intellectual animal, once he recognizes through reasoning and logic that he lacks many things, he uses his hands to prepare everything: he makes clothes, builds a house, sows wheat, prunes the shoots from the vines, and finally makes wine from pressed grapes. He carries out everything else—not only those things shared with the brutes for sustenance, but also those things pertaining to the logic of living well and blessedly. 

Similarly, Nature bestowed upon the intellectual soul a sufficient quantity of blood and **spirits**, as well as the mass of the brain and the multiplication and dilation of the veins and arteries. This was done so that the soul might have an abundance of spirits for its noble operations. For with fewer spirits, man would not have been able to remember, nor reason, nor exercise those other operations in which he excels over all other living beings. Nor, with a smaller brain size, could he have received the appropriate <term>temperament</term> of spirit necessary for exercising the rational operations of the soul. 

From this, you recognize that Nature gave a greater quantity of brain to humans so that the quantity of spirit, along with its proper temperament, would not fail; for **spirit** is the ultimate instrument of the rational soul. It follows from this that man has a greater and more balanced quantity of spirits—a fact you can prove for yourselves if you wish to consider the operations and limbs of other animals. 

I pass over land animals since they are very well known, but consider aquatic ones, such as fish. Although they have a very large body size due to their high moisture, they have a dominant **cold temperament**. Consequently, they have no blood (or very little relative to their body size) and no significant mass of brain; only a tiny quantity is found in their heads, even though the head itself is large in some species. Having explained these matters to them, I asked whether I had done enough for them, since I had labored through many repetitions. They replied that I had indeed satisfied them, but they added that there are other things not explained by all writers—both ancient and modern—who have written on the **fabric of the human body** <note>The author likely refers to the general study of anatomy, but specifically targets the famous work by Vesalius later in the paragraph</note> and included illustrations in their writings; these things they still desire to know.

I responded to them in this way: I did not set out to address every member, power <note>original: "uirtutes"; the innate faculties or biological abilities of an organ</note>, and operation <note>original: "operationes"; the active functions or physiological workings</note> found in the human body. Instead, I attempted only one thing: to open a path for my contemporaries and for posterity, so that they might more easily approach the **dissection** <note>original: "sectionem"; the act of cutting or anatomizing a corpse</note> of the human body. This effort has certainly succeeded according to my wishes. For after they heard and saw me dissecting—and those who did not see me in person read the introductory little book I wrote on **anatomical procedures** <note>original: "anatomicarum aggressionum"</note>—they conducted themselves so excellently in this field that they seem not only to have equaled the ancients but even to have far surpassed them. I cannot help but rejoice greatly at this.

Yet, it has always troubled me that, although they learned so much from me—and had I not shown and committed to writing things that were previously entirely unknown (such as certain members, powers, and operations), they would have been unable to write anything or demonstrate anything to observers—they still rely on common knowledge. Before my work, they could show nothing except those common things taught in all the schools <note>original: "gimnaſiis"</note>, which were taken from certain old manuscripts and poorly demonstrated or explained through the **senses** <note>i.e., through direct observation or sensory experience</note>. You have seen this for yourselves in that volume titled **On the Fabric of the Human Body** <note>A reference to Andreas Vesalius’s landmark 1543 work, *De humani corporis fabrica*. The author is critiquing Vesalius for following ancient authorities rather than his own observations in certain areas</note>.

For when he writes about the nerves originating from the brain and begins to explain the anterior <note>front</note> part, he preferred—along with **Theophilus**, **Marinus**, and **Galen** <note>These were the primary authorities of classical anatomy; Galen's word was considered law for over a millennium</note>—to leave this part undetermined rather than investigate its components through the senses and confirm its powers and operations through logical reasoning. Indeed, if anyone reads Galen correctly in the sixteenth book of **On the Use of the Parts**, they will recognize that Galen said the **soft nerves** <note>These are the olfactory nerves. Galen famously did not count them as the first pair of cranial nerves, starting his count instead with the optic nerves</note> descend from the substance of the anterior brain to the nostrils. However, when Galen enumerated the nerves originating from the brain, he did not include these first soft ones. You should not find this strange, as he did the same in other parts of his books: for instance, listing all the symptoms of a disease in one book, but in another book where he discusses the same disease, listing only some and not all. Whatever the case may be regarding the most learned and never-sufficiently-praised Galen, the **Senses**, however, in the investigation of the nerves originating from the brain...

# EPISTLE

First, in the front part, where that substance of the brain is located which they call the **mamillary caruncles** <note>original: "carunculas mamillares"; these are the olfactory bulbs, the structures at the base of the brain that process smell</note>, he discovers two soft substances. Nor is their substance so soft [as to be formless], since it is shaped in the figure of other nerves, and they undoubtedly descend to the nostrils, are fixed there, and are spread through the inner substance of the nostrils to provide the sense of smell. 

Since this is the case, why did they not rather say that these nerves provide the sense of smell? This is especially puzzling since they say they do not believe the **mamillary caruncles** themselves provide the sense of smell, but rather the processes of those nerves. Yet, he does not dare to fully approve his own affirmation because of the softness of the said substance. Nor did they wish to place those nerves absolutely first in the order [of the cranial nerves]—an order which he could not help but praise based on the flow of his own words.

They ask in response: why have the **modern anatomists** <note>original: "moderni anatomiste"</note> written so sluggishly about these nerves and their operations? But I say it is because they relied on the anatomical books of the ancients—which are either corrupted by age or incorrectly interpreted by grammarians rather than physicians—and they did not attempt the **dissection of the members** <note>original: "sectionem membrorum"; the surgical opening of the body parts</note> so that they could testify to the truth through their senses.

(Why was it done this way? they ask.) But I say it was because they did not have a book by any of the ancients teaching the method of finding the small parts of the human body; indeed, most of the ancients who wrote on the **dissection of the human body** <note>original: "dissectione corporis humani"</note> neglected this method of discovery. But at present, after I have written and taught the method of finding each and every member, they not only boldly dissect bodies and find the members, but they have even written on **anatomical procedures** <note>original: "anatomicas administrationes"; a reference to the title of Galen’s famous manual, which the author implies he has improved upon</note> and, as you have seen, have adorned them graphically with very many figures. In these illustrations, all parts of the body can be seen as if in a mirror by those who have inspected the "sensible" anatomy <note>Anatomy as perceived through the physical senses, especially sight and touch</note> of the human body. 

This is a matter worthy of all praise; yet, for all that, they have not perfected the matter in every part, as I was indicating to you a little while ago when we were speaking about that substance descending to the nostrils, which he said he believed served the sense of smell. But because of the authority of the ancient men (as you gather from his words), he did not want to affirm anything openly, either regarding the order or the operations [of the nerves]. 

To this, they say: "We have seen the book and read certain things in it, and to speak frankly, many things seem to be lacking, and some things disturb us by being abundantly unpleasant." 

"And what more can be desired in the booklet beyond what has been said, or what unpleasant things disturb you?" I ask. 

They respond: "What is missing are the **faculties** <note>original: "uirtutes"; the innate biological powers or 'virtues' of an organ</note> in some members, and the method of operations in some small parts—not in every part—and rightly..."

They themselves respond: "We have indeed read their writings (as we said a little while ago) and we have viewed the painted figures; yet our mind is not at rest because of them, since they show the difficulty of the dissection <note>original: "diſcectionis"</note> of this member, nor do they therefore reveal the cause of all the tongue's operations—as we read in your own introductory booklet on anatomical treatises <note>original: "libello introductorio ad anatomicas aggreſsiones"</note>."

But I wrote more for them in that booklet which (as I said) the ancients did not know, and I showed those things to all those standing by, along with many other things which I did not wish to add to that introductory work lest the booklet grow to an excessive size. Nevertheless, regarding very many members of the human body, I have written more distinctly than the ancients did concerning their substance, size, figure, number, position, location, functional powers, operations, and other matters.

These movements and operations, therefore, are not natural ones <note>meaning involuntary or automatic processes like the heartbeat</note> from nerves moving of their own accord naturally, but voluntary, as all the ancient and more recent wise men testify, and experience teaches. # TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS SENATOR AND
## Most Eminent Philosopher, Lord
## Girolamo Marcello, <note>Girolamo Marcello was a member of a prominent Venetian noble family; the author addresses him as both a political leader and a learned philosopher.</note> Epistle.
## VII. or an Epitome on fevers,
## and their cures.

**Q**UAT I previously promised you regarding fevers, I am now compelled to fulfill; and first, to declare what a fever is, and then by what reasoning the ancients decided to cure them. And although it would be a long method to write about both the theoretical <note>original: "speculatiuam"; the study of the causes and nature of disease rather than just the treatment.</note> and practical, or curative, aspects of fevers, I will nevertheless strive as much as I can to do so briefly. I shall approach the proposed subject thus:

The substance of a fever, therefore (as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD) was the Greek physician whose systems of anatomy and "humoral" medicine remained the standard for over a thousand years.</note> said in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*), is a heat contrary to nature <note>original: "calor præter naturam"; in Galenic medicine, this is a heat that exceeds the body's healthy "innate heat" and causes disease.</note>, located in the heart, then diffused through the whole body via the arteries and veins—unless it is hindered. However, it is not so hindered that it is not ignited in either most or some parts. Furthermore, it often happens that when the febrile heat is blocked, the entire skin shows no evident heat contrary to nature, neither to the patients themselves nor to us when we touch them. But in the innermost parts of the body, the languishing patients themselves feel and suffer it. Or we might say that a fever is an affliction by which heat contrary to nature is excited, and so forth.

<meta>This page continues Epistle VII to Girolamo Marcello, picking up from the introduction of Galen’s definitions to categorize the different types of fevers based on their physical manifestations and the biological "material" they affect.</meta>

# L E T T E R

The first and most important differences between fevers are those which touch itself recognizes; thus, we distinguish fevers according to a greater or lesser force of heat, specifically by that **heat contrary to nature** <note>original: "caliditate præter naturam"; in ancient medicine, a fever was defined as an unnatural heat that disrupts the body's healthy balance.</note> which is painful to the touch. Secondly, differences are derived from the matter in which this unnatural heat feeds. Based on these primary differences, some fevers are called "great," others "small," and others "mild," if we compare them to a heat that is particularly sharp or stinging. From this same difference, fevers are later described as either "acute" and quickly ending, or "not acute" but "long" <note>Referring to chronic or lingering fevers.</note>.

Regarding the second set of differences—those taken from the "subject" or location where the unnatural heat is grounded—there are three types. This corresponds to the three things that constitute a living body: namely, the **members**, the **humors**, and the **spirits** <note>term: spirits <gloss>original: "spiritus"; in this context, the "pneuma" or vital vapors believed to circulate through the arteries and nerves to sustain life.</gloss></note> or vapors.

To begin listing them from the last:
1. If the heat is received in the **spirits and vapors**, physicians have been accustomed to call it an **ephemeral** or **daily** fever <note>original: "ephemeram seu diariam"; a fever lasting only one day, usually caused by environmental factors like overexposure to the sun or exhaustion.</note>.
2. If the heat is received in the **humors**, they call it a **humoral** and **putrid** fever.
3. But if the heat is in the **members** and the **solid substance** of the body, they call it a **hectic** or **habitual** fever <note>original: "hecticam seu habitudinalem"; from the Greek "hektikos," meaning "habitual." A wasting fever that has taken root in the actual tissues of the body.</note>.

Thus, there are as many kinds of fevers as there are parts of the living body. To explain this, the physician Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential medical authority in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>—who can never be praised enough—provided a most beautiful example.

He says that if the substance of the heart becomes hot, it is like imagining a **cauldron** <note>original: "læbetem" (lebes); a bronze vessel or kettle.</note> that is hot and glowing with fire, into which you then pour cold water. That is a **hectic fever**, because the heat first seizes the substance of the heart (which is likened to the cauldron), and from that substance the humors within it are heated.

However, if the unnatural heat seizes the **humors** of the heart itself, and the heart becomes hot because of its proximity to that hot moisture, it is that fever which they call **humoral** and **putrid**. It is like pouring hot water into a cold cauldron, so that the body of the cauldron is heated by the water. In this case, the heat is first in the water, and the body of the cauldron only becomes hot from that water. This heat is not inherent to the cauldron, but follows continuously from the heat of the water.

Thirdly, there is the **ephemeral** or **daily fever**, for which Galen did not use the same example. Instead, he devises another most beautiful one: imagine a **bellows** <note>original: "follem"; a device used to blow air into a fire.</note> drawing very hot air into itself. In this bellows, one must imagine there is cold water and that the bellows has holes through which it draws and expels air. These holes are so narrow that they do not allow the humors <note>the liquid water</note> to pass through, yet the bellows can draw in the air...

<summary>This page classifies fevers into three categories—ephemeral, humoral, and hectic—based on whether the "unnatural heat" resides in the body's spirits, fluids, or solid tissues. The author uses Galen’s famous metaphors of the heated cauldron and the bellows to illustrate how heat transfers through the body.</summary>

# SEVENTH

...to draw in and expel: and so the water poured into the bellows will be heated by the warmth of the hot vapors, and soon even the body of the bellows itself will be heated. This heat (as you see) is not primarily in the water within the bellows, nor in the substance of the bellows itself, but in the hot vapors that were drawn in. A very similar example is found in an **ephemeral fever** <note>original: "ephemera"; a fever lasting only a single day.</note>. For if first the spirits and vapors of the heart are set on fire, they indeed heat the fluids contained in the heart, which afterwards inflame the very substance of the heart; yet the fever is not primarily in the heart’s tissue, but in the spirits and vapors.

   See, most illustrious and most learned **Jerome** <note>Addressing the recipient, Girolamo Marcello.</note>, how learnedly and how ingeniously **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> has shown the differences between the three kinds of fevers, and the manner of heat in the three substances that constitute our body—beyond which no other physical part is found. Furthermore, we can briefly gather from this that heat first ignited in the **solid parts** <note>The "members" or organs of the body.</note> is communicated to the **humors** <note>The four primary body fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> from the spirits; and also that heat ignited in the humors is communicated to the solid parts and the spirits; and similarly, heat ignited in the spirits is communicated to the humors and the solid parts.

   It is useful next to list the causes of this **heat contrary to nature** <note>original: "caloris praeter naturam"; the medical definition of fever as a heat that disrupts the body's natural balance.</note> which exist in these three substances. First, in the spirits and vapors, this "ignition" occurs in many ways: namely, from the skin being constricted either by a sunburn or by being tightened by the cold; or from anger and outbursts of temper; or from sadness, fear, anxiety of the mind, and evil thoughts; from lack of sleep, hunger, drunkenness, indigestion, physical labor, unnatural tumors, or pain. To summarize them all in a single word, these are the <term>procatarctic causes<gloss>original: "procatarcticae"; from the Greek, meaning the external or triggering causes that set a disease in motion.</gloss></term>—the evident and exterior causes of **ephemeral** or **daily** fevers—which sometimes cause heat directly and sometimes by accident. Obstructions are not counted among these causes, especially if they do not come from something external.

   But the ignition that occurs in the fluids is either with **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredine"; in humoral medicine, this refers to a process of decay or "fermentation" of the body's fluids.</note> or without it. That which occurs without putrefaction comes from both preceding and exterior causes, and is of two different types: namely, either from an abundance of blood with a blockage of the passages, or from the burning of **bile** <note>original: "cholerae"; here meaning yellow bile.</note>. However, that which occurs with putrefaction and inflammation exists in the four humors and the remaining fluids, and it happens when respiration is first prohibited...

# L E T T E R

...they putrefy <note>original: "putrescunt"; to rot or decompose. In ancient medicine, fevers were often classified by whether the body's fluids were "rotting" or merely overheated.</note>, or from contact, as in a pestilential fever. Therefore, a **humoral fever** <note>A fever originating in the body's humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> arises from the blood without putrefaction in those whose temperament is of the kind that generates a great deal of blood, and also in those who eat foods that increase the blood, so that the veins are overfilled by the sheer quantity. Because the passages are obstructed, they are barely able to "breathe" <note>original: "respirare"; this refers to the medical theory that vessels and humors need to vent excess heat and vapors to stay healthy.</note>; thus, it first grows hot in some part, then in the neighboring parts, until the fluids of the heart are set on fire. This heat is afterwards spread through the veins and arteries to the entire body without putrefaction. Nevertheless, unless they are treated correctly as the heat progresses and the obstructions remain, it turns into a continuous putrid fever, which the Greeks call <term>synocha</term> <note>A Greek medical term for a continuous, non-remitting fever often associated with an excess of blood.</note>.

A fever also occurs without putrefaction if the bile <note>original: "cholera"; specifically yellow bile.</note> is burned and heats the neighboring humors, and these ignited humors then heat the rest up to the fluids of the heart. In this type of fever, there are certain difficulties regarding whether the bilious humor can be scorched by an unnatural heat without putrefaction before its—to use the medical term—"incineration" <note>original: "incinerationem"; the process of a humor being burned down into a dry, ashy residue (black bile).</note>.

The third type of humoral fevers occurs if the remaining humors putrefy, and the vapors or putrid "soot" <note>original: "fuligo"; metabolic waste products thought to be like smoke or soot produced by the body's internal "fire."</note> heat the heart itself, after the fluids of the heart have first been heated.

Truly, the fluids and the four humors putrefy for many reasons. For if the things eaten and drunk are of poor substance, or too moist, and easily corrupted, or made of things that are not converted into the best blood, or are not properly prepared, or because they are consumed at an hour when the faculty <note>original: "uirtus"; the body's natural power or "virtue" to process food.</note> is unable to "cook" <note>original: "coquere"; ancient physicians viewed digestion as a process of "cooking" or ripening food using the body's innate heat.</note> them; or finally because the proper order of food and drink is not observed, so that some things are eaten first which should have been taken later. Indeed, the foods that are often the cause of generating humors prone to putrefaction are many fruits, vegetables, milk, and the like. There are also causes on the part of the body why humors prone to putrefaction are generated, such as a defect in temperament, resulting in obstructions from undigested humors, or because the faculty is weak and unable to digest the food. Therefore, it either corrupts the food or produces something else that nature did not intend; from this, obstructions arise, which soon lead to putrefaction since the humors are unable to "breathe." However, it must be noted that they do not always putrefy...

...the fluids of our body from hindered breathing <note>original: "respiratione"; in this context, it refers to the body's ability to vent internal heat and vapors through the pores and vessels, not just lung activity.</note>, since very often even from contact with a rotting thing, that which is not rotting rots. Furthermore, whatever is touched by something rotting must necessarily rot: and this mode of rotting occurs in pestilential air, or putrid air such as that of stagnant pools <note>original: "lacunarum"; literally pits or puddles of standing water, which were believed to release "miasma" or diseased air.</note>, and other places from which putrid vapors are raised. Air of this kind is found where they prepare skins <note>i.e., tanneries, which were notoriously foul-smelling and considered centers of disease.</note> and handle other rotting and stinking things. 

And although many causes are listed, they are not always singular, but often multiple, such as a bad temperament and even the eating of bad things. But the corruption of the surrounding air and all these causes together more easily induce rotting if the body abounds in many bad, sticky, and thick fluids, since both their quantity and thickness are naturally suited to create obstructions. 

And since there are four humors <note>The "four humors" are blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile; health was seen as a balance of these four.</note> which differ among themselves in substance and qualities—to which other non-natural fluids are also reduced by similarity—doctors therefore enumerate four kinds of humoral fevers besides the two species already mentioned which exist without rotting. 

The first of these is that which comes from the inflammation of the blood, which the Greeks call <term>synochia</term> <note>original: "synochiam"; a continuous fever caused by an excess of blood.</note> and the Latins call **continuous**, and it is halfway between the <term>ephemeral</term> <note>original: "ephemeram"; a fever lasting only one day.</note> and the putrid fever since it is humoral and inflames the heart by heating it through vapors. Similarly, that which arises from inflammation or burning of bile <note>original: "cholarae"; specifically yellow bile.</note> without rotting is of this kind, until something of it rots. For in both one and the other kind of kindling, rotting usually follows after several days. 

But of the putrid species, first is the **continuous putrid fever**, and it arises from blood seized by rotting: which, although it is a single humor rotting, is not a single mode of fever, since it has three variations: 
1. For one of these maintains the same magnitude of heat from the beginning until its decline; the Greeks call this <term>humotonon</term> <note>original: "humotonon"; a fever of "equal tone" or constant intensity.</note>, and the Latins call it "continuous of equal vigor." 
2. The second has a heat that increases until the decline; the Greeks call this <term>epacmatic</term> <note>original: "epacmaticam"; an intensifying fever.</note> and the Latins call it "strengthening." 
3. The third gradually decreases in heat; the Greeks call it <term>paracmatic</term> <note>original: "paracmaticam"; a fever that has passed its peak and is declining.</note> and the Latins call it "decreasing." 

All, as I have said, are continuous and involve rotting blood in the veins. This fever does not affect everyone, but fleshy young bodies full of excessively moist blood. As for what the cause of the three aforementioned processes...

->E P I S T O L A<-

# E P I S T O L A

In this kind of fever, doctors will disagree. However, one must understand this diversity first from the abundance and thickness of the blood, and also from the proximity and distance of the location <note>The "location" refers to where in the body the feverish "rotting" is taking place.</note>, and from the strength or weakness of the **vital force** <note>original: "uirtutis"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the body's innate power to function and heal itself.</note> from the beginning. Thus, if the resistance is equal, the inflammation proceeds until it reaches its turning point. But if it resists and overcomes the vital force by constantly increasing, it proceeds toward its turning point to see if it can end the putrid matter—or even lead to death if the rotting is extreme—unless the patient is aided by the vital force or by medical art. The opposite is true if the heat proceeds by constantly declining; in that case, the patient will escape, and there is almost no danger.

The third genus of fevers is the **hectic**, or habitual fever, which itself contains several species. This is based on the truth of the heat "feeding" and consuming the body, which they call the first, second, and third types. The first is when an abnormal heat first occupies the solid parts of the heart, so that it does not merely depend on the humors being heated (as they say). The second is when the heat has already clearly begun to dry out the moisture soaked into the solid substance <note>The "solid substance" refers to the flesh and organs, as opposed to the liquid humors like blood.</note>. This species, however, has a range: namely, a beginning, an increase, and a state of consistency in which the flesh is already evidently changed. After this is that third type, which they call the **hectic of old age**, in which—though there is no abnormal heat—an ultimate consumption of the flesh appears. The Latins call this **wasting** <note>original: "marasmum"</note> and the Greeks call it **consumption** <note>original: "phtysim"; specifically a wasting away of the body, often associated with the lungs.</note>. When this reaches its final stage, there is no medical skill that can cure it. However, one must know that this species cannot properly be called a fever.

But since fevers are conditions **contrary to nature**, from which a non-natural state follows, all wise men teach that those things which exist contrary to nature must be removed by contrary remedies. This can by no means be done unless we first understand them through their cause. In this knowledge, I have labored until now with as brief a method as I could, so that I might succinctly explain their nature and their causes. It remains, therefore, for me to write down the reasoning by which they are healed. This will be done more easily if we take care to recognize them specifically through their signs. I will therefore follow with the cure for each kind of fever, after I have declared them by their signs. These signs are of three kinds: according to substance, according to operations, and according to accidents. I shall begin first with the **ephemeral fevers** <note>original: "ephemeris"; fevers that typically last only one day, often caused by exhaustion or environmental heat rather than rotting humors.</note>.
