<header>S E V E N T H</header>

First, indeed, the **unnatural heat** <note>original: "calor præter naturam"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to a fever, which was viewed as an excess of the "heat" element rather than just a symptom of infection.</note> is not sharp, but mild: the pulse also, even if it has changed, is nonetheless neither large, nor fast, nor frequent, if you look at its natural state. It maintains this same character in its rhythm and other aspects. Similarly, the urine appears excellent in its substance, color, and the "cloud" it contains <note>Physicians of this era diagnosed illnesses by "uroscopy," examining the color, thickness, and sediment (the "cloud" or nebula) of a patient's urine.</note>. They sweat during the **decline** <note>original: "inclinatione"; the stage when a fever begins to break.</note> with a dewy and (if I may say so) vaporous sweat, with which all the unnatural heat recedes; nor does any bad symptom appear. 

There are also, besides those mentioned, signs of specific causes, which I will pass over so as not to trouble you with a long speech; for example, if the **ephemeral fever** <note>original: "ephemera"; a fever lasting only one day, usually caused by external factors like exhaustion or heat rather than internal rot.</note> came from lack of sleep, the pulse in those patients is small, and they can barely lift their eyes; the face appears slightly swollen, and its color is spoiled. Similarly, if it came from sadness and mental anxiety, besides the smallness of the pulse and the hollowed appearance of the eyes, there is also dryness and paleness of the face. 

But since the causes of these and other symptoms are by no means hidden from you, it should be enough to have written two examples, since the **regimen** <note>A patient’s total lifestyle, including diet, exercise, and environment.</note> and the method of curing are more conducive to this business, which is done through those things that are contrary to the disease. For since all the **triggering** <note>original: "procataracticæ"; from the Greek *prokatarktikos*, referring to external starting causes like over-exposure to the sun or excessive fatigue.</note> and external causes of these fevers are known, the entire intention must be toward the disease. Let the disease therefore be removed by a domestic cooling of the air, and a diet that is moderately moistening and cooling, consisting of those things that have **good juice** <note>original: "boni succi"; refers to foods that produce healthy blood (chyme) when digested.</note> and are easy to digest; nor should a little wine be denied to them. 

This regimen is certainly suitable first for all daily or ephemeral fevers. But if the fever came from a lack of sleep or mental anxiety, foods should be given which, besides being moistening and cooling, also encourage sleep and clarify the blood. Those who are exhausted should rest. And those who fall into this fever from hunger are to be fed more copiously, and thus in other cases one must give aid through those things that can inwardly relieve the necessity. 

Nevertheless, for everyone after the decline of the fever, it is beneficial to bathe, especially for those accustomed to it and for thin people. However, it is worthwhile to know and guard against one thing in this matter: namely, that this fever does not turn into one of the other two types if it is not treated correctly in the beginning. One of these types is the **putrid** fevers, and the other is the **habitual** <note>Referring to the "hectic" or wasting fevers discussed on the previous page.</note> fevers. And therefore, for this reason—even though there is no danger in the fact that it is an ephemeral fever—yet because it will not be without danger if converted into another kind, it must not be neglected. And this is enough regarding the signs and cure of the ephemeral fever.

-># LETTER<-

...are known as putrid, and I shall now descend to the **curative method** <note>original: "curatiuam methodum"; the systematic approach to treating a disease.</note>.

I have said that **humoral fevers** <note>original: "Humorales"; fevers caused by an imbalance of the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> without putrefaction arise either from an inflammation of the blood—which they call an "ephemeral" fever of several days—or from an inflammation of bile without putrefaction, which they call a "burning" fever resulting from the combustion of **cholera** <note>original: "choleræ"; here meaning yellow bile, not the modern bacterial infection.</note>. Nor does this contradict the sayings of **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> in the third book of *On Crises*, since it is not inconsistent for a drier humor to be less liable to putrefaction.

Therefore, the signs in the first instance of a **continual fever** <note>original: "febris continentis"; a fever that stays at a high temperature without returning to normal.</note> without putrefaction will be these: a heat that is generally not sharp, nor biting to the touch, nor drying out the exterior skin; a large and full pulse; difficulty breathing; and a body habit characterized by an abundance of blood, such that the color of the entire body is red, and the veins are swollen and full, especially those of the eyes; and youthful age. The urine is red and thick, but not lacking signs of **digestion** <note>original: "digestionis"; in this context, it refers to "concoction," the process where the body's internal heat "cooks" or processes the humors to restore health.</note>. These are all the signs by which we recognize this fever.

Once the fever is recognized, one must immediately institute a regimen through the **law of opposites** <note>The medical principle of "contraria contrariis curantur" (opposites are cured by opposites); for example, a "hot" disease is treated with "cold" remedies.</note>: therefore, first let the patient rest in a place where the air has been cooled. If the air is not naturally so, it must be altered, namely by the sprinkling of fresh water and other cooling things. Similarly, the diet should be moist, cold, and light. This applies not only to this fever without putrefaction, but also to that which occurs with the putrefaction of blood and bile in its refined state. Indeed, since all these fevers are of very short duration, a very thin diet is most helpful in their management. For this reason, let the foods be liquid broths, which they call **ptisan** <term>ptisana: a medicinal porridge or decoction made from boiled barley, the standard "sick-room" food of antiquity.</term>, and let the drink be spring water or barley water as much as desired, unless there is some reason to forbid it. 

And after an **enema** <note>original: "clisteri"</note> has been administered, let the **basilic vein** <note>original: "vena basilaris"; also known as the "liver vein," located on the inner side of the arm near the elbow.</note> of the right arm be opened, and let blood be evacuated as much as the patient's strength can tolerate; for by this single and unique aid, the fever will be driven away. For the letting of blood not only causes the putrefaction to cease, but also preserves the body from falling into putrefaction.

The signs and notes of a **choleric fever** <note>A fever caused by an excess of yellow bile, traditionally associated with a "hot and dry" temperament.</note> arising from inflammation without putrefaction are these: a heat that is sharp, intense, and biting throughout the body, and dryness of the outer skin; a large and frequent pulse, not without tension; a body habit with a fullness of thin blood and also an abundance of bile; the age of youth or the prime of life; a hot and dry time of year or constitution; a similar geographic region; and a vital power that is capable of multiplying bile, as well as exercise, which...

-># SEVENTH<-

This is because it first evacuates all fullness of the veins, both the pure and the mixed, and also preserves the body from putrefaction. But where bile is abundant, those things should be given which can draw out the bile, such as tamarind, cassia, manna, and laxative rose syrup. # SEVENTH

**burning fever**, and a proportional continuation; they differ from those continuous fevers arising from the **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredine"; the decay of humors within the body, thought to be the cause of many illnesses.</note> of the blood, because in **choleric** <note>original: "cholericis"; referring to patients with an excess of yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note> patients, certain exacerbations and increases appear every third day, although in the burning fever these are not so manifest, and in **sanguine** <note>Those with a dominance of the blood humor.</note> patients, they are seen the least.

I will begin with the continuous fevers, providing the signs and the cure for each, and first, the marks of the glowing or **burning fever** <term>causon</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for a highly acute, inflammatory fever characterized by intense heat and thirst.</note> are: a sharp heat throughout the entire body without any shivering, both inside and out, and like a consuming fire without any obvious apparent remission (I said "apparent" because there is always some slight remission every third day); a red and citron-colored face; eyes also red and almost sparkling; a frequent and large pulse; unquenchable thirst; dryness of the tongue with blackness and citron-coloring; difficulty breathing; restlessness; sleeplessness; and also sometimes a profound sleep, especially when there is a mixing of evaporating **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitae"; one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note>; there is also a confusion of the mind and incoherent muttering, headache, and throbbing of the temples. The urine is red and fiery, tending toward a citron-color, and there is constipation of the bowels. If shivering should come upon this fever and they sweat profusely afterward, the patient will escape healthy. But if sweat does not follow, it is converted into an intermittent **tertian** fever <note>A fever that returns every other day.</note>.

This fever is cured by a cooling regimen, such as cold air achieved through the tempering of water and the scattering of leaves of willow, lettuce, and the flowers of water-lilies, violets, roses, and the like, or by ventilation with fans. The food should also be cooling, made of barley or cooling vegetables such as endive, chicory, lettuce, sorrel, and similar plants. The drinking of cold water or a decoction of barley is also appropriate. And in this fever, finally, the drinking of plenty of cold water is a most singular medicine, unless there is something hindering it, such as a weak constitution, or an **abscess** <note>original: "apostema"; an internal swelling or collection of infected fluid.</note> in some organ, or pain in the intestines, or any other prohibiting cause. Let the patient also use cooling medicines, such as syrups of sorrel juice, pomegranate, and **oxysaccharum** <note>A medicinal syrup made from sugar and vinegar.</note> with a decoction of tamarinds and violets, in distilled waters of endive, sorrel, bugloss, borage, lettuce, and the like. And so that all things may be ready for you, practicing physicians order and arrange them thus:

Take syrup of pomegranate, 1 ounce; of sorrel juice, half an ounce; of bugloss and endive waters, 1 and a half ounces of each; or let them give other syrups, such as rose syrup or syrup of endive with waters of lettuce, chicory, and similar things.

# THE EPISTLE

->E P I S T O L A<-

These should be taken in the morning at dawn, and in the evening before dinner. In place of water, physicians often prescribe a decoction of **tamarinds** <note>original: "tamarindorum"; the fruit of the tamarind tree, used in medieval medicine for its cooling and laxative properties.</note> or other cooling substances. And since this fever stems from **putrid matter** <note>original: "materia putrida"; waste products or humors that have "decayed" within the body, causing infection or heat.</note>, there is a need for treatments that evacuate these putrid materials in addition to those that alter the body’s state. If these materials are mixed with a great deal of blood, and the patient is of a fleshy constitution, and if the season and the patient's strength allow it, the **liver vein** <term>vena iecoraria</term> <note>Also called the basilic vein of the right arm; it was traditionally bled to treat disorders of the liver and yellow bile.</note> should be opened, and blood should be drawn according to the necessity. Immediately after drinking, something should be given to extinguish the **bile** <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile, the humor associated with heat and dryness.</note>, such as a syrup of **sorrel juice** <note>original: "succus acetosae"; sorrel was prized for its acidity and cooling effect.</note> diluted with chicory water. On the second day, a gentle laxative should be given to evacuate the bile, namely **cassia** or **manna** <note>Two common mild plant-based laxatives used to "purge" the humors.</note> with a decoction of tamarinds. But if, besides the pure and thick bile, you wish to clear out mixed matter in the passages of the ducts, you must add a portion of an **electuary** <note>A medicinal paste made with honey or syrup.</note> with similar properties, such as **diaphoenicon** <note>original: "diafinicõ"; a traditional purgative preserve made primarily from dates.</note>.

Another type of fever, which is continuous, arises from bile that putrefies within the vessels; it is said to be proportional to **two tertians** <note>A "double tertian" fever where two different cycles of bile-driven heat overlap, making the fever appear constant rather than intermittent.</note>. It is recognized by the vehemence and sharpness of the heat, provided the bile is pure. However, this heat is not quite as sharp or as stinging to the hand of the person touching the patient as the heat of the glowing fever, which they call **causon** <term>causoné</term>. But when the bile is not pure, due to the admixture of **phlegm** <term>pituita</term> and other humors, it is recognized because its heat appears less sharp and the symptoms are milder. 

The signs of the pure form are these: the pulse is large, swift, and irregular compared to other fevers, and no shivering or coldness appears. Nevertheless, the worsening of the heat corresponds to every third day. For that reason, it is called proportional to two tertians. There is also difficulty breathing, restlessness, dryness of the tongue, intense thirst, headache, sleeplessness, and often pain in the stomach as well as **bilious vomiting**. The urine is red, fiery, and tending toward a deep yellow; if the matter is impure, the urine will also be thick. 

The cure is almost the same as the one mentioned above regarding air, food, and drink, except that such a large amount of cold water should not be given, especially if the matter is thick (which they call **impure bile**). In the process of evacuation, since the disease is caused by physical matter, they often begin by letting blood from the appropriate vein—namely the liver vein of the right arm. Immediately after, one must give the "extinguisher" of bile mentioned above, or something that can prevent the "boiling" of the blood, such as **rose syrup** and sorrel juice with endive water, and...

Or let a decoction be made from cooling herbs, such as **sorrel**, **endive**, **borage**, and similar plants. And when signs of **digestion** <note>In Galenic medicine, "digestion" or "concoction" refers to the process where the body "cooks" or matures the offending humor so it can be expelled.</note> appear in the urine—which are recognized by its substance and uniform color, and by a white **cloud** <note>original: "nebula"; a suspension or sediment in the urine sample used for diagnosis.</note>—an **evacuative** <term>evacuativum</term> <note>A purgative medicine intended to clear the humors out of the body.</note> must be given (especially if the matter is abundant), consisting of **cassia**, **manna**, and laxative rose syrup with a decoction of **tamarinds**. But if the urine is thick, **agaric** <note>original: "agaricum"; a type of larch fungus used as a potent purgative.</note> or some **electuary** <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note> should be added (as I mentioned above).

But that fever which arises from **bile putrefying outside the vessels** <note>Bile that has escaped the veins or gallbladder and is decaying in the body's tissues.</note>, which they call **intermittent**, exists in two different forms: the **exquisite** <note>A "textbook" or pure case.</note> and the **non-exquisite** (which they call "noted"). When it is pure bile that putrefies, the signs of this fever are as follows:

*   It begins with **shivering** <term>horripilatio</term>, such that it feels like the **pricking of needles** through the back and other parts.
*   The heat is sharp and biting, leaving the patient after twelve hours.
*   The pulse is large, frequent, and irregular.
*   There is restlessness, difficulty breathing, thirst, headache, anxiety in the stomach, and bilious vomiting.

Those who have a bilious temperament, or are in their youth or prime of life, are more likely to fall into this fever, especially in summer or the hot latter part of spring. Their urine is red, thin, fiery, and tending toward a lemon-yellow color.

This fever is cured by a cooling regimen (as I mentioned above) and by **barley gruels** and drinks of barley water, or distilled waters of bugloss, endive, sorrel, and the like. In all bilious fevers, **wine** should be forbidden until the decline of the disease, for it is extremely harmful. After the fever’s peak, a very small amount may be given, mixed with much water. Patients must be careful not to take food or drink at the start of a fever **attack** <term>accessio</term>, but it should be given five hours before. Likewise, they should not be fed at all until the fever has completely declined. Nor should they sleep at the start or during the increase of the fever; however, in the decline, sleep helps greatly, as it provokes sweat and urine. At the very height of the **paroxysm** <term>paroxysmus</term> <note>The period of highest intensity or "fit" of the fever.</note>, sleep is sometimes beneficial, especially where the patient’s strength is weakened by the magnitude of the attack. 

Once these things are ordered and administered, the medicinal regimen for the evacuation of the matter should be established as follows. If the body is "full," a **minorating evacuative** <note>original: "evacuativum leuæ, minorans"; a gentle purge that reduces the humor gradually rather than all at once.</note> should be given, for instance, of one ounce...

Then, on the following day, let syrups or decoctions be administered that open obstructions and extinguish the febrile heat, such as simple **syrup of vinegar** <note>original: "syrupus acetosus"; a mixture of vinegar and sugar/honey used to cut through thick humors.</note>, or syrups of **endive**, **sorrel juice**, or **oxysaccharum** <note>A medicinal syrup made from vinegar and sugar.</note>. | Additive | Amount |
| :--- | :--- |

This should be adjusted as seems better and more suitable for the patient’s needs in the physician's judgment. Give this potion during the most quiet hour before the onset of the fever, as much as possible. Give food five hours later.

It is necessary to know that in a **pure tertian fever** <note>original: "exquisita tertiana"; a classic malaria-like fever that recurs every third day (every 48 hours).</note>, bloodletting is not entirely praised, except where the body abounds in much blood in addition to the bile; in which case the urine appears both thick and red. 

The signs of a fever from "impure" bile—which they call a **spurious fever** <term>notha</term>—are almost all those mentioned above. For when impure bile putrefies, the fever begins with **horripilation** <note>The medical term for goosebumps or shivering.</note> and with a great shuddering, like the movement of boiling water. If the bile is more pure, there are rigors and cold, especially where raw **phlegm** <term>pituita</term> has been mixed in. You will note, however, that an impure fever differs from a pure one by its duration; the time of heat is longer. In an impure fever, the heat is acute but not as sharp and stinging as in the pure type. Similarly, the pulse and the other signs mentioned above are present, but milder—more or less according to the heat, thickness, and quantity of the matter mixed with the bile. The urine is also thicker. 

These fevers decline with sweat, but it is not copious; often they do not sweat at all if the matter is very thick or the patient's strength is weak. In these cases, the **paroxysms** <note>The sudden attacks or peaks of the fever.</note> often join together and become **overlapping** <term>subintrantes</term>, so that the patient is continually feverish, even though the matter is putrefying outside the veins. You should also know that when someone is feverish every day, accompanied by the signs of putrefying bile, they say there are **two tertians** present. But if the fever strikes twice in one day, physicians call it a **double tertian**.

<header>THE SEVENTH</header>

# THE SEVENTH

The method of treatment in these cases differs somewhat from the treatment of an **exquisite** <note>original: "exquisitæ"; refers to a "pure" or textbook version of a fever, such as a pure tertian fever, which follows a predictable and sharp pattern.</note> fever, for in all these cases the dietary regimen is not quite as thin as in the exquisite form, since the state of the illness in these is more prolonged. Therefore, after correcting the air <note>Improving the patient's immediate environment, a standard first step in humoral medicine.</note>, let **soups** be given, or **barley broths** in a broth of young chickens in which **parsley roots** have been boiled. Similarly, the drink should be barley water boiled with parsley roots, or equivalent distilled waters; and this should continue until the **vigor** <note>The peak or most intense stage of the fever.</note> of the fever. For when it has reached its peak, then a very thin diet is appropriate, which should be varied according to the greater or lesser impurity of the **putrefying matter** <note>The harmful, decaying humors believed to cause the fever.</note>.

Regarding those things which must be done to evacuate the matter, they are as follows. First, if there is **fullness** <note>original: "plenitudo"; an excess of humors (plethora) in the body.</note>, the belly must be lightened with a common **clyster** <note>An enema.</note> made from a decoction of leaves of **mallow**, **violets**, **beet**, or **blite**, and **mercurialis** <note>Herb-mercury, often used as a laxative.</note>. Of this decoction, take:

| Ingredient | Amount |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Violet oil** | 1 pound |
| **Red sugar** | 3 ounces |
| **Common salt** | 1 drachm |

Mix these, and let it be administered in the morning before food, or at a more quiet hour. We can also soften the belly by taking by mouth 1 drachm or 1 ½ drachms of **flower of cassia** <note>A mild laxative pulp from the "pudding-pipe tree."</note> one hour before food. But if the urine is thick, red, and the patient's strength is sufficient and their age permits, the **liver vein** <note>original: "vena iecoraria"; historically the basilic vein of the right arm, believed to drain the liver.</note> should be opened. After this, let the remaining matter be prepared with **oxymel** <note>A medicinal mixture of vinegar and honey.</note> and **syrup of endive** diluted with waters of **borage**, **bugloss**, and **hops**, or with a decoction of said herbs or their roots. As the fever proceeds, composite syrups may also be given, such as oxymel with **two and three roots** <note>A standard pharmaceutical preparation using the roots of smallage, asparagus, fennel, parsley, and butcher’s broom.</note> and **Byzantine syrup** <note>A complex syrup made of smallage and endive juices, sugar, and vinegar, used to treat liver and spleen obstructions.</note> mixed with waters of **wormwood**, **fennel**, and similar plants, or with decoctions of wormwood, **betony**, endive, and the like.

Later, when **concoction** <note>The stage where the body's heat has "ripened" the humors for expulsion.</note> appears, let the humors be purged with **cassia**, or **catholicon** <note>A "universal" or general laxative electuary.</note>, or **laxative rose syrup**, adding something to evacuate the thicker matter, such as the **electuary diaphenicon** <note>A date-based purgative electuary.</note>, as it is a safe medicine. Where the matter is still thicker, **agaric** <note>A fungus from the larch tree used as a powerful purge for phlegm and thick humors.</note> should not be omitted. Likewise, **rhubarb** is useful because, besides evacuating both thick and subtle **choler** <note>Yellow bile.</note>, it also opens obstructions of the natural organs. The cassia and other medicines should be dissolved with a decoction of **barley**, **raisins**, **licorice**, **plums**, **endive seeds**, **fennel**, and similar ingredients. And since all these fevers are usually followed by the aforementioned symptoms—though not always all of them, but sometimes one and sometimes several—therefore for their care...

For this reason, **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> warned us to direct our right eye toward the patient’s strength and our left eye toward the sickness; and when strength fails, let both eyes be directed toward that strength itself. This is made by first boiling a young chicken in waters of bugloss and endive, and then placing this whole material in an <term>alembic</term> <note>A chemical still used for distillation.</note> over a fire to be distilled. Give this to the patient as they please, or let meat water be made in a "double vessel"—what they call a <term>Mary’s bath</term> <note>original: "balneum Mariae"; a double boiler used for gentle heating.</note>—or by extraction with a press after the meat has first been roasted. If the shivering fits are laborious, they should be countered before their arrival by anointing the spine with oil of dill or something similar, or by washing the legs with fresh water in which dill has been boiled. I shall next follow with the signs and cure of the third species of fever, which arises from the putrefaction of <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; according to the theory of the four humors, an excess of black bile caused "melancholy" and specific types of recurring fevers.</note>, or the melancholic humor. This fever is sometimes continuous and very often intermittent; it usually occurs most frequently in autumn, especially in bodies abounding in the melancholic humor. And although I have many times seen a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day (counting the day of the fit), associated with black bile.</note> just beginning, it usually happens after other putrid fevers, and most especially after <term>tertian fevers</term> <note>A fever that recurs every third day, traditionally associated with yellow bile.</note>.

...and it gradually declines with a contraction of the muscles: after which heat begins, which is not intense, and from the start brings with it a certain slight shivering <note>original: "horripilationem"</note>, which shivering recedes at the height of this onset. After this, the entire body grows hot with a burning heat, yet not sharp, unless it is obstructed. At the beginning, the **pulse** shows no greatness, but is rare and slow; soon, as the heat increases, it becomes of some magnitude, speed, and frequency with variation. The **urines** are reddish with a certain darkness, and often not thick, and for many days without signs of <term>concoction</term> <note>In ancient medicine, this was the process where the body "cooked" or matured the humors to overcome a disease.</note>. 

The same signs are also present in a continuous or persistent fever, where the matter putrefies within the veins, except that no rigor appears, and it is more exacerbated on the fourth day. One thing, however, I should not overlook, and it is that all humors very often turn toward the nature of **melancholy** <note>Also known as "black bile," one of the four vital fluids or humors believed to regulate health and temperament.</note>, which later, by putrefying, cause a **quartan fever** <note>A fever that returns every four days (counting inclusively, so every 72 hours).</note>; for that reason, the occurrences in such fevers are both stronger and milder, namely according to the nature of the humor converted into melancholy. 

I also advise that it must be noted, since it matters not a little in the cure—namely, to recognize the nature of the humor, both in preparing it and in evacuating it. For if the putrefying humor is recognized, we can easily choose the medicine for it, and according to its nature and requirement, evacuate it by various means: for instance, if the blood has been converted to the nature of melancholy, or you recognize a melancholic humor mixed with the blood, then in that case **opening a vein** <note>referring to phlebotomy or bloodletting</note> at the start and drawing out a great deal of blood is the best remedy. 

However, one must observe the sayings of **Galen** in the first book *To Glaucon*, and of **Avicenna** in the first part of the fourth book of the *Canon*, namely: if the physicians see thin, red, and clear blood, let them close the vein, nor should they dare to let blood, but rather pursue health by other remedies. Therefore, after this, one must move to other aids, and first to the cooling regimen often mentioned above, which can in no way either obstruct or make the humors thick. 

Wherefore let the foods be of those that cool moderately, nor is an entirely thin diet appropriate at the beginning. Let there be given, therefore, a **barley broth** <note>original: "iusculum hordeaceum"</note>, or bread cooked in a broth of meats, in which are boiled the roots of **bugloss**, **endive**, **fennel**, **parsley**, and the like, or the seeds of said herbs; and this according to the diversity of the obstructing and putrefying matter...

...curing. In **quartan fever** <note>A fever that recurs every four days, historically associated with malaria.</note>, one must also always look out for obstructions of the **spleen**, or its hardness; it rarely happens that the spleen does not either ache or become swollen. When this occurs, the fever will be worse and more difficult to heal. Therefore, ingredients that assist the spleen must be mixed into both the food and the drinks used to prepare the <term>matter</term> <note>In humoral medicine, "matter" refers to the excess or corrupted fluids—like phlegm or bile—causing the disease.</note>. These include **capers** and their roots, and similarly **tamarisk** roots, leaves of **hart's-tongue fern** <note>original: "scolopendria"</note>, and the like.

Patients should therefore take syrups of **fumitory**, **bugloss**, and a compound **oxymel** <note>A traditional medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note>—though in a smaller quantity because of the vinegar—along with waters of hart's-tongue, bugloss, borage, **maidenhair fern**, and similar herbs; or with a decoction of caper roots, hart's-tongue, tamarisk, **hops**, and the like.

Furthermore, those suffering from quartan fever should not be purged with strong medicines at the beginning. However, if there is a "fullness" <note>original: "repletio"; a state where the body is overloaded with humors</note>, they may be relieved with soothing **clysters** <note>An ancient term for an enema.</note>, or a soothing medicine may be given made from a decoction of raisins, **senna**, and similar things, since these can hardly draw out any humors other than general waste and those found near the intestines.

Because the **melancholy humor** <note>Also known as "black bile," this humor was considered thick, cold, and dry, making it the most difficult to move or "evacuate" from the body.</note> is resistant to purging and cannot be "prepared" except over many days, one must abstain from harsh purgatives at the start. But once the matter has been prepared—which is recognized by the healthy quality of the heat and the **sediment** <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> in the urine—purging medicines are appropriate. These should be given gradually and according to the nature of the humor, whether it is naturally melancholic or has been converted into a melancholic state. 

At that time, it is convenient to give a soothing **electuary** <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note>, or *dia senna*, or a compound syrup of apples. These may be given together or dissolved on their own in waters of fumitory and borage, or with a decoction of **dodder of thyme** <note>original: "epithymi"</note>, senna, **polypody fern**, tamarisk, bugloss flowers, borage, and the like.

But where the melancholy has resulted from the "burning" of **choler** <note>Yellow bile; "adust" or burnt humors were thought to become particularly toxic and dark.</note>, **rhubarb** is exceptionally helpful in addition to the things already mentioned. If it has resulted from burnt **phlegm**, or a mixture of it, the **agaric mushroom** must not be overlooked; it not only purges putrid humors but also benefits the spleen, which is usually suffering in these cases. If the spleen aches or becomes swollen, after the purging it should be anointed with chicken fat, oil of sweet almonds, and caper oil, together with a little **ammoniacum** <note>A medicinal gum resin.</note> dissolved in vinegar.

One should proceed in this way, purging gradually until the decline of the illness. If the matter has been digested and prepared, then strengthening remedies for the principal organs should be given during the decline, such as **theriac** <note>A famous "universal" antidote and cure-all consisting of many ingredients.</note>, or **mithridatum**...

...[cath]artic confection or another, according to the patient’s condition.

And since the **shivering fits** <note>original: "rigores"</note> are often so violent that they require immediate assistance, in this case, one hour before the onset of the fever, the entire **spine** should be anointed with a mixture of **oils of rue**, **dill**, and **scorpion** <note>In early modern medicine, oil of scorpions was a common topical treatment for various ailments, believed to "draw out" toxins.</note>. If other strong symptoms appear, such as headache, thirst, or palpitations of the heart, they should be helped by those remedies and medicines mentioned above in the section on **acute diseases**.

The final type of **putrid fever** is that which arises from the rotting of **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitae"; one of the four vital humors, characterized as cold and moist.</note>. This phlegm is sometimes natural, and sometimes it is unnatural phlegm that is rotting. This fever occurs in "phlegmatic" bodies, such as those of women and infants, and also in those who consume a phlegmatic diet and live in cold, damp regions. Indeed, this fever occurs rarely among us. The signs are those of an **intermittent fever**: first, it begins with a certain pattern and shivering, or a kind of cold, and this happens daily, starting from the extremities. This cold is followed by a heat that is not difficult to bear, which does not show itself or proceed quickly, but gradually tends toward an increase; it is neither troublesome nor annoying to the hand of the person touching the patient. The pulse is frequent, intense, irregular, and small. These patients have no difficulty breathing, no thirst, no dryness in any part of the body, nor do they sweat. They are troubled by this rotting heat for no less than eighteen hours. The **urines** are white and thin, often even watery, and sometimes thick without color. All other excrements are phlegmatic, both from the lower and upper belly, such as **sputum** and the like. Even if all these symptoms seem mild, because the source of the rot is both cold and thick, the condition is not without danger due to its long duration.

There is another kind in which the matter rots within the veins, which is called a **continuous fever**; it is similar to the intermittent kind in all respects, except that no cold or shivering troubles the patient.

These fevers are treated by a **regimen of the air** <note>A reference to the "Six Non-Naturals," environmental factors like air and diet that doctors believed governed health.</note>; first, the air should not be cooled with strong refrigeration, as is done with other putrid fevers, but rather tempered, perhaps even with some warming. Therefore, in the bedroom, if it is winter, a fire should be lit. The foods and dishes should be boiled in the broth of the best meats, and also with roots and seeds that have the power both to **open** the vessels and to **cut** <note>original: "incidendi"; a medical term for thinning or breaking down thick, sticky humors like phlegm.</note> through the humors.

If this kind of humor rots within the veins near the heart, it causes a **causon** <note>original: "causonem"; a traditional term for a highly acute, "burning" fever.</note>. The treatment of these fevers differs according to the variety of the matter: for where the matter is colder, one must use warmer regimens and medicines; but if the humor is "salty," it requires more cooling remedies. If these fevers occur alongside **fainting** (which physicians call **syncopal** fevers), they are not without the greatest danger. Indeed, they require immediate remedies, both by strengthening the heart and by evacuating the humors, and also by restoring the "vital faculty" <note>The body's natural power or energy to sustain life.</note> with things that in no way weigh down, dissolve, or suffocate that power. In such cases, before the strength fails, it is necessary to apply remedies; for delay is dangerous.

# THE SEVENTH [PART]

certain [fevers] are called pestilential due to malignancy and extreme **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredinem"; the decomposition or "rotting" of bodily fluids, which was believed to be the root cause of infectious disease.</note> in the **humors** <note>original: "humoribus"; the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that medieval doctors believed governed health.</note>, as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> writes in his *booklet on the differences of fevers* <note>original: "libello de differentiis febrium"</note>.

The signs by which they recognize these are as follows: namely, that the body may be quiet on the outside, yet internally disturbed, so that the patients are weak, anxious, and restless, even without a notable sharpness of heat; sometimes, however, they are also disturbed internally with the most vehement heat on the outside. From the beginning, the **pulse** <note>original: "pulsus"</note>, although changed from its natural state, often does not change greatly, except in the "depressions" (the downward stroke) being larger than the "elevations" (the upward stroke). Afterward, as the fever progresses, it shows its pestilential malignancy in various ways. For the pulse becomes large when the heat increases in the heart, and it also becomes weak if the **spirits of the heart** <note>original: "spiritus cordis"; the vital life-force or "pneuma" believed to be generated in the heart and distributed via the arteries.</note> have already been infected by the pestilential malice. The **urines** <note>original: "urinae"</note> are for the most part disturbed, lead-colored, and murky; nor do they always remain the same, as they may be seen as green, red, clear, and bright, and even very often without any **cloud** <note>original: "nebula"; a suspension or sediment in the urine used by doctors to judge the "concoction" or ripening of a disease.</note>. Indeed (as the "Prince" **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university textbook.</note> said), often both the pulse appears good and the urine appears good, yet the patient dies. For this reason, these cases are considered difficult.

There are also "accidents" <note>original: "accidentia"; a medical term for symptoms or secondary complications arising from a disease.</note> showing this pestiferous malignancy, such as pustules of the throat and palate, and blackness of the tongue, and even **alchola** <term>alchola: a term derived from Arabic meaning ulcers or sores of the mouth and throat</term>, or ulcers of the throat, sleeplessness, **delirium** <note>original: "alienatio"; a wandering of the mind.</note>, and tension of the **hypochondria** <note>original: "hypochondriorum"; the upper abdominal region just below the ribs.</note>, which is never absent in such a fever. Very often, **spots** <note>original: "maculæ"; a rash or skin discoloration often associated with the plague or typhus.</note> also appear on some parts of the body, and even all over, but especially on the back and chest, which differ in both size and color. But those that appear black or lead-colored are worse; red and whitish ones are healthier. Whatever the case may be, those who suffer this fever—if extreme malignancy exists in the humors, which is recognized by great internal turmoil and the severity of the symptoms—for the most part perish.

The primary cure is based for the most part on the **purification** <note>original: "rectificatione"; the act of cleansing or correcting the quality of the air.</note> of the external air and the strengthening of the spirit of the heart. Therefore, one must first purify the pestilential air with fire (as **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> and Galen taught); then you shall administer those things which prevent putrefaction and also strengthen the heart, such as the sprinkling of the chamber where the patient remains with water mixed with vinegar, rose water, and other sweet-smelling things, such as citrons, apples, and other similar things of no great heat. But whatever these things used for purifying the air may be, such as...

must be dried out. Other necessary things should be of the same quality, so that besides providing nourishment, they also strengthen the **spirits of the heart** <note>original: "spiritus cordis"; the vital life-force believed to be generated in the heart and carried through the arteries.</note>. Therefore, foods should consist of the best meats, such as **roosters** <note>original: "pulli gallinacei"</note> and similar birds; among these should be dishes such as **ptisana** <note>original: "ptiffana"; a medicinal porridge or decoction, typically made from barley.</note> and similar items that are drying in some manner. For this reason, the juices of oranges, lemons, citrons, and sour grapes are best.

**Wine** should be forbidden in every way from the beginning until the decline [of the fever], because its ability to penetrate and the sharpness of its heat causes poisonous matter to reach the heart. The drink should be distilled water of sorrel, chicory, **bugloss** <note>original: "bugloffae"; an herb often used to "comfort the heart" and treat melancholy or fevers.</note>, borage, and the like; or let it be spring water boiled with barley in its husk, or with the seeds of sorrel, citron, and similar plants, with which is mixed sour syrup, or syrup of citron peel, or simple **oxymel** <note>original: "acetofus fimplex"; a traditional mixture of honey and vinegar.</note>. 

And in this fever, since we are especially concerned about the patient’s **vital strength** <note>original: "uirtute"; the underlying energy or "power" of the body to sustain life and fight disease.</note>, everything should be given that can maintain that strength, such as the aforementioned meats: partridge, pheasant, kid [goat], and the like. There should also be given in the morning and evening hours—to prepare the [bodily] matter and extinguish its malignancy—syrups of citron peel, sorrel juice, simple oxymels, and similar things, along with a decoction of chicory, endive, **lettuce leaf** <note>original: "cereris folii"; likely a reference to cooling greens or lettuce used to temper heat.</note>, and bugloss.

And as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the foundational Greek physician whose theories on the "humors" ruled medicine for centuries.</note> warned us in the first [book] of *On the Differences of Fevers*, we must strive for drying by using things that remove **fullness** <note>original: "repletionem"; an excess of humors in the body.</note>. Therefore, if the bowels do not move on their own, common **clysters** <note>original: "clyfteria"; enemas used to clear the digestive tract.</note> should be administered; soon, since the matter is "furious" and swollen, the rest of the body’s superfluous fluids should be evacuated. 

Because opening a vein [bloodletting] after the fourth day cannot be done without the greatest risk to life—as the diseased matter may be drawn back to the heart—whenever there is an indication that a vein should be opened, instead of bloodletting by opening a vein, **cupping glasses** <note>original: "cucurbitulae"; glass cups used to draw blood to the skin's surface to relieve internal pressure.</note> should be applied to the back, buttocks, and hips. Thus, the blood may be evacuated according to the patient's tolerance of strength and the requirements of the disease. 

It is also important to note that before the fourth day, opening a vein in **bilious bodies** <note>original: "biliofis"; individuals with a temperament dominated by yellow bile, often perceived as hot and dry.</note> is suspicious; even if they are not bilious, [it is risky] when signs of "rotting" bile appear and the urines are thin and fiery. But if the body is **sanguine** <note>original: "sanguineum"; a temperament dominated by blood, usually considered robust.</note> and abounds in much blood, the vein can be cut boldly. But besides the letting of blood, the other [humors] should also be evacuated...

Take one drachm of **cordial spices**; two drachms each of bugloss, borage, and violet flowers; four drachms of citron seeds. Let a powder be made from these and placed in a purple silk pouch, and let it be applied to the region of the heart. Since (as I have said) the greatest intention in these fevers is to support the "virtue" <note>original: "uirtuté"; the patient's innate strength or life-force.</note>, if that virtue is weak, add **meat water** <note>original: "aqua carnis"; a restorative meat essence or broth.</note> to the diet, made in a double boiler or by extraction with a press. Between meals, give distilled water made from the broth and meat of a young chicken boiled in waters of bugloss and sorrel. As for other symptoms—namely headache, thirst, delirium, and the rest—let them be relieved as was described above regarding the symptoms of putrid fevers.

Having dispatched these matters, it remains to treat the third kind of fever, in which an unnatural heat has already taken hold in the **radical members** <note>original: "membris radicalibus"; the vital, foundational organs such as the heart, liver, and brain.</note> and consumes its **radical moisture** <note>original: "humiditatem radicalem"; the vital fluid believed to be the "fuel" of life, often compared to the oil in a lamp.</note>. This habitual fever the Latins and Greeks call <term>hectic</term> <note>original: "hæcticam"; from the Greek 'hektikos', meaning habitual or relating to the constitution; a wasting fever.</note>, and it has a wide range. Physicians categorize it into three levels. For this reason, they describe the first, second, and third types of hectic fever. The first type is when, due to unnatural heat, the moisture in a member is consumed just like the **oil in a lamp**. The second is if the heat, beyond merely consuming the moisture...

The signs of the aforementioned fevers are, first of all, heat, but not so sharp as is common in many putrid fevers; rather, it appears mild to the touch at first, then as the hand remains over the artery, it impresses itself more strongly, so that the heat acts more and more upon the hand and presses more forcefully. Afterward, the heat is equal throughout the whole body without intermission or sudden onset; this heat is always increased by food, which is a characteristic and inseparable sign in <term>hectic fever</term> <note>original: "hæctica"</note>, and although this sometimes happens in putrid fevers, it is not as manifest in them. The **pulse** <note>original: "pulsus"</note> is small, weak, frequent, hard, and remains in one and the same order.

The first species is difficult to recognize but easy to cure; the second is more easily recognized and becomes clear from the signs already mentioned, and also because a certain wasting and dryness appears throughout the whole body. The **urine** <note>original: "urinæ"</note> are somewhat oily and carry a burnt smell in their odor. And this fever, although it can be healed, is not cured without the greatest difficulty. Regarding the third species of hectic fever, which is not truly a fever since it involves a wasting of the entire body and a consumption of moisture, no one is in doubt; for in this, besides the wasting of the whole body, there is a hollowing of the eyes, the temples are collapsed, and there is a festering dryness throughout, without any heat. And this can by no means be healed (as I have said).

Foods should be of the best meats, cooked with leaves of lettuce, endive, purslane, borage, and similar plants. Let the dishes be made of barley, or of...

daily fevers, and even one type of putrid fever joined with another type, such as a <term>tertian</term> <note>a fever that returns every third day</note> with a <term>quartan</term> <note>a fever that returns every fourth day</note>, and a daily fever. These do not just occur together, but often become so confused that—if the fever is continuous—one continuous fever complicates another, or one intermittent fever complicates another intermittent one. However this happens, these cases are recognized only by the most skilled and experienced physicians through a set of overlapping signs, both essential and <term>accidental</term> <note>secondary symptoms that are not part of the disease's core definition</note>.

The cure for these will be a mixture of the treatments for simple fevers. For example, if a <term>hectic</term> <note>a chronic, wasting fever</note> and a putrid fever are complicated together, the air should be altered to be moist and cold, using sprinkling and leaves as I advised above. Next, the putrid <term>humors</term> <note>the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which doctors believed had to be kept in balance</note> should be evacuated if <term>signs of concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctionis signa"; evidence that the body has successfully "cooked" or processed the diseased fluids so they can be expelled</note> appear. This should be done with mild medicines, such as <term>cassia</term> <note>a legume used as a gentle laxative</note>, <term>manna</term> <note>a sugary sap used as a purge</note>, and laxative syrup of roses. But if the putrid matter is thick, <term>agaric</term> <note>original: "agaricus"; a medicinal fungus used as a strong purgative</note> should be mixed in, or some other medicine that evacuates thick humor without leaving any heat in the limbs after the evacuation, and without drying out the body. In these cases, extreme purgings are not safe. Therefore, in both quantity and quality, physicians should proceed with a moderate approach. Nevertheless, the hectic fever must not be neglected. After the putrid fever has been cured, use the regimen for hectic fevers mentioned a little earlier, including bathing in fresh waters.

But in compound putrid fevers, everything should be compound—both the lifestyle regimen and the medicines. Furthermore, if it should be a *hemitriteus* (as the *Greeks* say), which the *Latins* call a *semi-tertian*, it is composed of a daily and a tertian fever—or rather, from <term>pituitous</term> <note>phlegm-based</note> and <term>bilious</term> matter putrefying separately. These should be treated (as I said) with a compound regimen according to which of the two appears to predominate. The physician will easily determine this from the signs. For if <term>cholera</term> <note>original: "cholera"; here referring to yellow bile, not the modern bacterial disease</note> prevails, the shivering fits are greater, and the heat also appears more "biting," along with the other signs mentioned regarding tertian fever. In this case, those things which both prepare the matter (much of which is mixed with yellow bile) and evacuate it are useful. 

On the other hand, if the pituitous matter <note>phlegm</note> predominates, there is almost no shivering, or if there is, it is very slight; the heat also seems mild, the patients do not feel thirst, and so you will see the other "accidents" familiar to daily fevers. Therefore, in these cases, both for preparing and evacuating, those things which prepare and draw out thick, phlegmatic humors are appropriate—such as <term>compound oxymel</term> <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, <term>syrup of wormwood</term> <note>original: "syrupus de absinthio"</note>, and agaric for evacuation. We recognize them in a similar way.

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT PAULUS
## Magnolus of Brescia, Epistle VIII.
## On the logic of the anticipation and 
## postponement of paroxysms in fevers.

**C**OMMONLY, as is our custom, there have been conversations between us regarding philosophy and medical matters. When our talk began to focus on the logic of the anticipation <note>when a fever attack arrives earlier than expected</note> and the postponement <note>when a fever attack arrives later than expected</note> of fever paroxysms, the great number of patients needing to be visited interrupted us. I have wished to write these things to you to complete that begun conversation, taking this opportunity to write. 

From reading these notes, you will be able to more easily recognize whether a disease is malicious or mild, and the strength or weakness of the patient. You will be able to foreknow the timing and the outcome of the fever, and also what ought to be said and ordered to the sick and those standing by. I would have gladly undertaken this study earlier, but (as I said) I rarely have a vacation from visiting the sick. Only occasionally can I provide something—if I may put it this way—to my dearest friends who ask for it...

...[that] I might write skillfully, especially to you, my dear Magnolus, the best of friends, whom I have always not only esteemed for your most modest character and rare learning, but also loved deeply, and will always love. Indeed, nothing is more precious to me than either the goodwill of friends toward me or their affection. Thus, throughout my entire life, I have considered myself most happy when I could do a favor for my friends, and especially for teachers of the liberal arts; and among them, most of all for you, for whose sake I write these things, trusting in your love for me for the common benefit of the sick. If, as a busy man, I do not perfect this in every part, your moderate virtue and well-suited learning will supply the rest. 

Moreover, this very doubt has kept not only our minds in suspense, but also those of many ancients and moderns, who undoubtedly seem to disagree among themselves on this matter. However, regardless of what others have said, and setting aside their disputes, I will personally show the truth to the best of my ability, relying on reasons and the authorities of the ancients. 

The <term>question</term> <note>In scholastic medicine, a "quaestio" was a formal debate or inquiry into a specific problem.</note> therefore concerns diseases of matter <note>Diseases caused by an excess or corruption of the bodily humors like bile or phlegm.</note> which have <term>attacks</term> <note>original: "accessiones" — the periodic spikes in fever or symptoms, often called "paroxysms."</note>, such as in intermittent fevers—for example, the <term>tertian</term> <note>a fever recurring every third day, or every 48 hours</note>, the <term>quartan</term> <note>a fever recurring every fourth day, or every 72 hours</note>, and even the <term>quotidian</term> <note>a fever that returns every day</note>—specifically, what the **anticipation** <note>when an attack starts earlier than the previous one</note> and **postponement** <note>when an attack starts later than the previous one</note> of these attacks signifies: whether it shows an increase or a decline of the illness. 

I will explain this question with less effort if I first touch upon all the ways in which attacks occur in fevers, beyond simple anticipation or postponement. It happens that sometimes fevers proceed in the same steady course with no change in the order of hours; at other times they change, but so variedly and inconsistently that they proceed toward their peak by sometimes anticipating and sometimes postponing. 

Thus, four things must be noted by us: 
1. What should be said if the fever proceeds always maintaining one order of time, neither anticipating nor postponing.
2. If it proceeds always by anticipating.
3. If the attacks proceed always by postponing. 

To make these things appear more clearly, I will take as an example a <term>bastard tertian intermittent fever</term> <note>original: "tertianam febrem intermittentem ex putredine bilis nothae" — "nothae" (bastard or false) refers to a fever that does not follow the classic symptoms of a pure tertian fever, usually because the bile is "corrupted" or mixed with other humors.</note> arising from the putrefaction of bastard bile. Suppose this fever burns through all its tertian attacks at a fixed and steady hour—let us say the fourth hour of the day—and ends on the following day at the tenth hour of the day, without any change in time at all. In this case, with the attack always occurring at the same hour, if the duration of the feverish heat also...

->### A V A<-

...if the degree of heat has been equal, with no sign of digestion <note>In Galenic medicine, "digestion" or "coction" refers to the body's process of ripening or thickening "raw" humors so they can be expelled.</note> appearing, whether in the **urine** <note>original: "lotio" — the analysis of urine was a primary diagnostic tool.</note> itself or in other signs. It shows this to be the **beginning of the illness**, for this process shows an equality between the power of the **virtue** <note>the "virtus" or natural healing power of the patient's body</note> and the matter of the disease <note>the corrupt humors causing the sickness</note>, both in quantity and in quality, so that with neither prevailing over the other, the same course is maintained. And thus, one must say it is the "beginning" for as long as the attacks remain equal without signs of digestion. 

This opinion is held by **Galen** in the first book of *On Crises*, and also by **Avicenna** in the first chapter of the fourth book, *On the knowledge of the hours of sickness*. We can affirm this all the more easily if we recognize the virtue fighting against the disease: if this virtue is strong against "thick matter" (heavy humors), the beginning will be long; if it is weak, it will signify death or a long-lasting illness. This is the opinion of Galen in his short book *On the Times of the Whole Disease*, and also in his commentary on the 30th aphorism of the fourth part of the *Aphorisms* <note>The Aphorisms of Hippocrates, a foundational medical text.</note>.

But if the attack always begins at the same hour, it is a **bad sign**, whether the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the period of highest intensity in a fever attack</note> is longer or shorter; in this, we have a bad omen, for it signifies either a long duration or death. 

On the other hand, if the attacks are equal, and the urine and other signs show **coction** <note>the process where the body 'cooks' or ripens the diseased humors to be expelled</note>, one must judge it to be the <term>vigor</term> <note>original: "vigor" — the peak or height of the disease</note> of the disease. We say this if we believe reason and Galen in the third book of *On Crises*, for when the **concocting virtue** <note>the body's power to digest or transform harmful humors</note> has prepared and overcome the matter, it then ceases and rests, awaiting the work of the **excretive virtue** <note>the body's power to expel waste or diseased matter</note>, which (just as happens with food) follows the concocting power. 

Similarly, the matter itself, now almost defeated and no longer irritating the body, is a cause for the attacks coming neither earlier nor later, and thus equality occurs. If this happens while the patient's virtue is strong, we say the illness will be short. But if it happens while the patient is weak, it will not be without danger; and if the matter is digested under such weakness, we can undoubtedly predict a long duration for the disease. 

The **peak** (vigor), therefore, will be that time when the attacks are equal—if there are several—and especially if you see signs of maturation in the urine and other excrements. This stage is clear from its name, as it remains steady and behaves in the same way through the entire period until the <term>decline</term> <note>original: "inclinationem" — the stage where the disease begins to lose its strength</note>. 

But what I seem to see you wanting to hear more about is whether the ancients recognized the time of the disease's increase or its decline by whether the attacks arrived earlier or later. In order that this might be clearer, how an equal manner of [at-]...

-># EPISTLE<-

We have spoken thus far of how the beginning of an **attack** <note>original: "accessionis" — the periodic onset or "fit" of a fever.</note> is sometimes signified, and sometimes its **peak** <note>original: "vigorem."</note>. Although this discourse is not the primary matter we were seeking, it nevertheless assists in the discovery of that first question: namely, whether the **anticipation** <note>the attack coming earlier than expected.</note> or **postponement** <note>the attack coming later than expected.</note> of an attack indicates the growth or the decline of the illness. To satisfy this doubt, I say that **anticipation** indicates **growth** <note>original: "augmentum" — the stage where the disease is getting stronger.</note> if, along with that anticipation, the duration of the heat is longer, and the heat itself is greater, together with other symptoms and discomforts—especially if manifest signs of **coction** <note>original: "coctionis" — the "ripening" or processing of harmful humors by the body's natural heat.</note> do not appear in the **urine** <note>original: "lotio."</note>. 

<margin>I.</margin> The reason for this is that the matter of the disease—either by its own quantity or quality, or by the "preparing power" of the body—is rendered thinner, but not yet "kinder" <note>meaning the humors are still toxic/malignant despite being less dense.</note>. Thus, as the body's **virtue** <note>the "virtus" or natural healing power of the patient.</note> is moved to labor and attempts to overcome the matter, that matter is moved more quickly (causing anticipation) because it is thinner; however, this is not because the virtue has yet conquered the matter. In this way, anticipation occurs during the **growth** of the disease. 

But if the attack anticipates and the duration of the **paroxysm** <note>the period of highest intensity in the fever fit.</note> is not longer, the feverish heat is milder, and the other symptoms are improved—and if signs of coction appeared previously in the urine—then it indicates a **decline**. This is because the matter has been partly thinned and partly reduced, and also because the body's virtue has become far more powerful than the disease; thus the attack comes sooner but the paroxysm is shorter.

Similarly, if the attack is **postponed**, yet the duration of the heat is extended and the feverish heat is increased, and the symptoms are severe without clear signs of digestion in the urine, it signifies the **growth** of the disease. The cause of this indicates that the matter is perhaps "thick" and not so stimulating to the body, while the virtue is weak and cannot regulate the matter to make it easier to move, or it is not sufficiently provoked; thus the attacks are delayed. 

If, however, the attack is also **postponed**, but the duration of the heat is shorter, the heat is lesser, and the symptoms are milder—accompanied by signs of coction in the urine—it undoubtedly shows the **decline** of the disease. This happens because the thick matter is no longer stimulating the sensitive members, especially if it has been dominated by the body's **natural heat**. Consequently, the onset of the attack is delayed and the matter is consumed in a shorter time. Thus, a lesser heat will appear along with fewer symptoms, and in the urine there will be a **hypostasis** <note>a sediment at the bottom of a urine sample.</note>, or a "cloud," that is smooth, white, and even. From this sign, physicians receive a proper and inseparable indication of digestion and of **health**. Where, however, there is only one type of matter causing the disease, all these things...

One will receive this from Galen, if they wish to read the first book on **Crises** <note>original: "Crisibus" — the turning point of a disease</note>, and from Avicenna, if they observe what he wrote in the first part of the fourth [book] concerning the recognition of the hours of sickness. With this truth thus explained, it must also finally be noted—as I also touched upon at the beginning—that sometimes the **accessions** <note>original: "accessiones" — the periodic onset or "fit" of a fever</note> are inconsistent, so that they keep no order; but they proceed sometimes by **anticipating** <note>coming earlier than expected</note> and sometimes by **postponing** <note>coming later than expected</note>, and sometimes they trouble the patient for a longer time, and sometimes a shorter one.

From which it happens that neither the motions nor the times are equal. Indeed, often with anticipation, the time of heat will be shorter, and sometimes longer. Similarly, both the amount of heat and the time very often appear in postponing attacks with no order preserved; and you shall attribute the cause of such diversities to the diversity of the **matter** <note>the bodily humors or fluids causing the illness</note>—in its thickness and thinness, and in its abundance and scarcity, in its **biting** <note>original: "mordicando" — refers to the caustic, stinging, or irritating quality of the humors</note> or non-biting quality—or in the **virtue** <note>original: "uirtute" — the body's natural vital force and healing power</note>, which virtue, sometimes rendered less strong by the **febrile** <note>feverish</note> heat, cannot regulate the matter in such a way—or in both. Whence the fever will move that matter more or less, in a shorter or longer time.

<margin>1</margin>
When this appears and the **virtue** is weak, one must judge the disease to be long-lasting and not without danger to life, especially in its beginning and its **increase** <note>the "augmentum" stage where the disease gains strength</note>. But in the **decline** <note>the "declinatio" stage</note>, besides a long duration, it also shows a conversion into another, worse sickness, such as into a **quartan fever** <note>a fever that recurs every fourth day</note>, into **dropsy** <note>original: "hydropem" — swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, or into **consumption** <note>original: "phthisim" — a wasting disease, usually of the lungs</note>. 

And lest there be any doubt regarding what was said above, I will further declare certain things for clearer instruction. And first, it is useful to know that "equal accessions" are those which keep an equal order both in the hour of the beginning and the hour of the end; so that they neither anticipate the beginnings nor postpone the endings, but proceed in the same manner through all their attacks, with no change made in the heat, either in quantity or quality. Therefore, if any of these should change, whatever that change might be, they shall always be called "unequal accessions." For example, if the changes were in anticipating or postponing, but the duration remained equal, this will be called an "inequality of order." But if it should keep the same hour for the beginning—for instance, if the first hour of the first attack is the same as the first hour of the second attack, and so on for the rest—and nevertheless the duration of time is either greater or less—

-># L E T T E R<-

...if it has been <note>The text begins mid-sentence; the preceding context likely referred to the "matter" or humor causing the illness</note>, the **accessions** <note>original: "accessiones" — the periodic fits or "attacks" of a fever</note> will also be unequal. And these are called **inequalities of time**. There are other inequalities which, because they primarily consist of greater or lesser heat, prevent us from calling the accessions "equal." Similarly, if a diversity appears in the **accidents** <note>original: "accidentibus" — the symptoms or outward signs of a disease</note>, they prevent equality in the accessions on their part. To see all of this proven, one should look to **Galen** in the first book of **On Crises** <note>original: "De Crisibus" — Galen's foundational text on the turning points of illnesses</note>, who not only warns us to recognize the **anticipations** <note>fits coming earlier than expected</note> and **postponements** <note>fits coming later than expected</note> of accessions, but also the length of time, and the magnitude and malice of the disease. This is because these factors often provide indications contrary to those taken from the motion <note>the timing or rhythm of the fever</note> alone; and a little further down he says, confirming these points, that **anticipation** of the fit's increase is by no means a sufficient sign on its own.

And so, from the reasons stated and from Galen’s opinion, you see that although anticipating and postponing can signify one thing or another, nonetheless, if they are considered simply on their own, they signify neither. This is because the "character" of the disease changes the aforementioned rules for the most part. For example, if the fever arises from the putrefaction of that **burnt choler** <term>choleræ adustæ — a humor (yellow bile) that has become thickened and toxic through excessive heat, often associated with severe or "malignant" illnesses</term>, which is said to be of lesser fame and bad character; since this matter is malignant and is difficult for **Nature** to regulate, it moves **symptomatically** <note>original: "symptomaticæ" — acting as a side effect of the disease's poison rather than the body's natural cycle</note> and without order. Because of its malice and sharpness, it stimulates the limbs before it is properly **prepared** <note>the process of "concoction," where the body "cooks" or ripens the humors to expel them</note>. Thus, it causes the accessions to anticipate, which shows destruction or a long-lasting illness rather than recovery. 

This happens because the matter is not moved by the body's **virtue** <note>original: "uirtute" — the natural vital force or healing power of the patient</note> of its own accord, so to speak, but is moved because it is irritated by its own bad quality. This motion is followed by those "accidents" <note>symptoms</note> which show malignancy and sharpness, such as:
*   Intense heat
*   An unequally disordered pulse
*   Restlessness
*   Headache
*   Persistent sleeplessness
*   Most intense thirst
*   Difficult eliminations <note>original: "eradications"</note>
*   along with many other bad symptoms.

When these appear, whether the accessions arrive early or late, they denote the increase of the disease. Even after the peak of the illness, they signal a long decline—if the disease reaches a decline at all—since such is the nature of this matter that, besides resisting the body's vital force, it also makes that force feeble. Even if this virtue eventually conquers, nonetheless, because it has been made weak from the battle and its aftermath, it must labor longer before it can expel the rest of the matter and restore itself. ->## TO JUSTA I<-

...in such fevers, the **peak** <note>original: "uigor" — the highest point of intensity in a disease</note> is always slow to arrive, and the **decline** <note>original: "inclinatio"</note> is long. This is a matter touched upon by **Galen** in his small book *On Crises*, and by **Avicenna** in the first part of the fourth book in the places already cited. Furthermore, certain authors writing on this subject attribute many things to the movement of the **major stars** <note>This refers to medical astrology, where doctors believed the planets influenced the "critical days" of an illness</note> and to other causes. Although these theories may be quite beautiful, I have decided not to recount them here; instead, as you see, I have chosen to base the entire matter on the consideration of two things: namely, the **quantity and quality of the matter**, and the **strength or weakness of the virtue**.

Thus, if the matter is lesser in its resistance to the virtue, the disease will be short in itself and absolute, and the **accessions** <note>the individual fits or attacks of the fever</note> will arrive early and be brief. But if the matter is more powerful than the virtue because of its quantity—as I said in the previous case where I described a fever arising from the putrefaction of **vitelline bile** <note>original: "cholerae uitellinae" — a type of yellow bile thought to look like egg yolks</note>—then without a doubt the increase of the disease will come with **postponement** <note>arriving later than expected</note> and with long-lasting accessions. This is because one and the same virtue cannot process and conquer a greater quantity of matter in the same amount of time.

And so, by considering these different factors in the matter and the virtue, you will say that one state is the anticipation of the increase, and the other is the decline. Indeed, **Galen** in the first book of *On Crises* and **Avicenna** in the first part of the fourth book said nothing else than that the **decline** of a disease is the victory of the virtue over the matter of the illness. They say this victory is followed by a "cloud," or a white, smooth, and equal **sediment** <note>original: "hypostasim" — the material that settles at the bottom of a urine sample, used by physicians to judge the progress of a disease</note>. 

It is worthwhile to understand this "equality" in every sense: namely, that the sediment be equally white and equally smooth—not more here and less there—and also consistent throughout the whole **urine** <note>original: "lotium"</note>, so that the color and substance are the same everywhere. In order that all these things might be understood more clearly and more easily committed to memory, I wished to add here at the end of the letter a figure or table, containing the principal points of the aforementioned **anticipations** and **postponements** of the **paroxysm** <note>the periodic peak of the fever</note>, arranged in the following order:

-> **EIGHTH** <-

...of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum was the Roman-era physician whose theories dominated European medicine for over 1,500 years</note>, regarding the timing of the disease. They signify that there is neither vigor nor decline if the symptoms have not lessened, nor the urine shown signs of **concoction** <term>concoction: the process where the body’s heat 'cooks' or ripens diseased humors so they can be expelled</term>; which signs of concoction are to be understood in this way: that they are far removed from severe symptoms, and then they demonstrate for certain what the final outcome will be. However, the beginning, the increase, and the decline of the illness are not proclaimed with absolute certainty by an **anticipation** <note>the early arrival of a fever attack</note> or a **postponement** <note>the delayed arrival of a fever attack</note>. Indeed, attacks often both anticipate and postpone, either because of new heat acquired in the **matter** <note>original: 'materia' — the physical substance of the disease, usually an excess of one of the four humors</note> which causes anticipations by stimulating the body, or because—due to greater heat or malice—the senses (which were previously duller) are made sharper and excite the body's **virtue** <note>original: 'uirtus' — the body’s innate vital power or natural healing force</note>. Thus, due to the greater sensitivity of the feeling members, the attacks arrive early.

On the other hand, one may hear of postponements; namely, when the matter has become colder for some reason and reduced to a greater thickness, and the senses have successively become duller, nature is delayed in its movement. Nor should one overlook the additions of heat and intensity, or the prolongations of the duration of the heat, as these always signify an increase [in the disease], while their lessening, along with other signs, shows a decline. 

You have therefore, most learned Paulus—and through you, other studious men shall have—my opinion regarding the significance of both anticipations and postponements, as well as the equalities and inequalities in the fever attacks. I decided to write all these things to you as briefly as possible, especially since I have known you to be most learned and uniquely fond of me, even though other most studious young men were present at our conversations. 

Farewell. Venice. The 25th Day of February, 1544.
