**Phlegm, Avicenna, Canon, Humors, Concoction, Blood, Bile, Melancholy**

...black. Moreover, the generation of **phlegm** <note>original: 'pituita' — one of the four bodily humors, characterized as cold and moist</note>, in the case of phlegm-producing foods, always precedes the blood; and through its middle generation, the foods pass into blood. This happens not only with poor-quality foods, but even with some of those which seem healthy, and so forth. The Prince Avicenna <note>Avicenna, or Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), was a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the primary medical text in Europe for centuries</note> established this very order (if one wishes to attend more diligently to those things which he wrote in the first book of the *Canon* regarding the generation of humors). For he says that in every **concoction** <term>concoction: the process where the body’s innate heat 'cooks' or ripens food and fluids into humors</term> of moisture, something is separated from it which is like foam, while another part is like dregs. Sometimes there is even present that which is prone to burning, if the concoction was intense; and sometimes something almost raw, if the concoction was weak.

The foam, therefore, is yellow bile itself; the dregs, however, are black bile, and both are natural. Indeed, the burnt part, which is the thinner portion, is "vicious" <note>unbalanced or diseased</note> bile, and the thick part of that same substance is "vicious" black bile, which is not natural. The raw part is phlegm itself; but that which is strained and cooked from this entire sum is indeed blood.

And a little later he says: the **efficient cause** <note>the primary source or force that brings something into being</note> of blood is moderate heat. The efficient cause of phlegm is weak heat. I could add many other things which are said scatteringly by the most learned Avicenna throughout his volumes concerning the order of generating the humors, beyond what has been said. He also wrote in the cited passages that natural phlegm is that which is ready to be converted into blood, and that it is blood not yet perfectly cooked; and also that bile has an efficient cause of excessive heat, and that **melancholy** <note>original: 'melancholia' — black bile, the humor associated with coldness, dryness, and the dregs of the blood</note> is the dregs of the blood. 

He also wrote about the manner of the humors' generation in his books *On the Nature of Animals*. For indeed in book 10, chapter 5, he says: Phlegm is the material of blood, bile is produced through the further action of heat, and the dregs of blood are melancholy. From these things it is therefore clear that phlegm is the first among the four humors to be generated by heat acting briefly upon the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid formed from digested food in the stomach before it is refined by the liver</term>. If, by some occasion, this phlegm does not preserve its own nature or is increased, it is expelled by Nature as a manifest waste, or it putrefies. The same reasoning applies to the generation of phlegmatic humor from weak heat, and also from eating cold, phlegm-producing things, such as fish and other cold items. This is because an agent does not act beyond its own inherent power, unless it happens by accident—just as it sometimes happens that something is heated by a cold cause. Similarly, from the manner of the preparation of the **matter** <note>original: 'materia' — the physical substance being acted upon by the body's heat</note>, the thing acted upon is usually changed by the agent; for anything is not made from just anything, but from specific matter, with the due and...

-> ## E P I S T L E <-

<meta>Digitized by Google watermark at bottom right corner</meta>

...with the appropriate quantity and preparation, according to the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose theories on biology and physics formed the foundation of medieval science</note>.

From what has been said, it must therefore be said that **phlegm** <note>original: 'pituita' — the humor associated with coldness and moisture</note> is the primary matter of blood, whether it is generated in the stomach or in the liver; though you would more correctly say it is produced in the liver and then converted into blood. But if a phlegmatic humor is produced in the stomach (as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose humoral system dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> preferred), it is not immediately changed into blood when it is received in the liver; instead, it requires a prior change and alteration by the heat of the organ that generates blood, so that the phlegm might achieve this. For it is not "true" phlegm but a "phlegmatic humor," which does not possess all the conditions of phlegm in its substance and qualities; nevertheless, if such a humor is received in the liver, it is converted into blood without controversy after some prior disposition. 

For a greater space of time is required in the generation of blood than in the generation of phlegm, as Galen also testified in the second book of *On Crises* <note>original: 'de Crisibus' — Galen's work on the critical days of a disease</note>. Furthermore, blood is the primary humor intended by nature for nourishment and the restoration of the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the 'innate' fluid or oil thought to be the fuel of life and vitality in every living being</term>. For this reason, nature strives as much as possible for the generation and preservation of blood; and so that she may guard it and distribute it to the limbs, she constructed the veins proceeding from the liver and passing through the whole body. 

With these things declared, it is easy to explain the order and quantity of the humors. For since blood is the first humor intended by nature (as I said), because the body needs it most, its quantity is greater than all other humors. After blood, phlegm follows in quantity, which is itself significant since it is the proximate matter from which blood is produced. Indeed, after phlegm has received the "form" or quality of blood from natural heat, if the heat operates further and for a longer space of time, it will refine the blood by heating it and convert those more refined parts into **bile** <note>yellow bile</note>; the quantity of this bile is less than the quantity of blood. 

Finally, the active heat separates out the **black bile** <note>original: 'cholera nigra' or 'atrambilis'</note> (which the Greeks call **melancholy**), which is the dregs <note>sediment or waste</note> of the blood generated from the thicker part of the blood-nourishment. In this generation (although the quantity of this humor is smaller), nature nevertheless requires much more time for its perfection. The same logic of order and time applies to the generation of those humors which physicians call "non-natural" <note>humors that are imbalanced, corrupted, or otherwise not useful for healthy nourishment</note>, which are not fit to be converted into proper nourishment. For raw humors are generated in the stomach, on account of the weakness of the heat...

-> # ANCONA <-

...[weakness], or from eating cold and viscous foods of poor quality. These humors (as I said a little earlier) are not truly **phlegm** <note>original: 'pituita'</note>, nor are they fit to be converted into blood at first. Similarly, a **bilious humor** <note>yellow bile</note> is often produced by both the stomach and the **liver** <note>original: 'iocinore'</note> due to immoderate heat and from consuming hotter foods of poor quality (if we believe **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose humoral system dominated Western medicine</note> and all other most eminent doctors). This type of bilious humor is not natural bile, which is produced from blood through further **concoction** <term>concoction: the "cooking" or ripening process of humors by natural bodily heat</term> by natural heat for the utility and necessity of life and its functions; such a humor can serve no use for nature, neither for nourishment nor any other benefit. Instead, it is always harmful and a cause of some disease or symptom.

The same must be said of non-natural **black bile** <note>original: 'cholera nigra'</note>. For that too is produced by immoderate and excessive scorching heat, or some other cause, and also from bad food matter which, by its own substance and quality, is ready to be converted into a **melancholic humor**. This humor is neither natural, nor can it serve any use or utility (as was said of non-natural yellow bile). Rather, it is the matter and cause of various long-lasting conditions contrary to nature, and of **accidents** <note>in medieval medicine, 'accidents' refer to symptoms or secondary complications</note> which are both evil and difficult.

What I have said regarding the order, timing, and diversity of the generation of the humors, I could prove with many examples and reasons. This can be seen in many fruits; when they are first unripe, they change and mature if the external heat or the power of the plant proceeds further. However, they do not ripen if the surrounding air is cold—as can be seen in figs during the autumn. Yet, when heat or power proceeds steadily, fruits that are unripe at the start mature and change into a different flavor and color. If that heat proceeds further in its action, it changes them into another, sharper quality, flavor, color, and substance, according to some of their parts; in others, it changes them into something else, such as **dryness** and **earthiness** <note>original: 'terrestritatem' — the physical quality associated with the element of earth</note>, and it changes the flavor as well. This change can easily be detected in **boiled things** <note>original: 'rebus elixatis'</note>; for we see different changes from one and the same heat in a boiled object due to the continued action of the heat. In the first part of the time of its action, the thing to be cooked undergoes an imperfect cooking, so that it is called **half-cooked** <note>original: 'semicocta'</note>; afterwards, by...

-> E P I S T O L A <-

# LETTER

By the action of that same heat, the matter is perfectly cooked and becomes the fulfillment of its "concoction" <note>the medieval term for the body's biological "cooking" or digestion of food</note> according to the substance and qualities of the thing being boiled. If it is cooked further, it changes even more, taking on a different substance and taste; that which remains after this process is thick and full of dregs. I will pass over many examples used by the **alchemists** in their sublimations and transformations performed by fire or other heat. They call that first matter which comes forth **phlegm** <term>phlegm: the humor associated with cold and moisture; here compared to the first, watery vapors of distillation</term>, as it has not yet been perfectly prepared by the heat. Then, as the action of the fire's heat proceeds, that which comes out is more perfect, possessing a certain balance in its substance and qualities. Compared to the first and the last parts, it is more suitable for its intended work; this part is likened to **blood** <term>blood: the most balanced and life-giving of the four humors</term>. 

As the action of the heat continues around the vessel containing the matter, that matter in the vessel is refined and elevated; the alchemists say this part corresponds to the substance of fire. Doctors, however, call this refined part of the humors **bile** <term>bile: or "yellow bile," the hot and dry humor compared here to the fiery products of distillation</term>. That which remains at the bottom of the alchemist’s vessel is a thicker matter and earthy dregs; this part of the humors is called **melancholy** <term>melancholy: or "black bile," the cold, dry, and heavy "dregs" of the blood</term> by doctors. In this part, the heat works longer than in the other humors to achieve its preparation, separation, and collection. This is truly the "dregs" of the humoral mass. 

I do not see how the example of **must** <note>original: 'musto'; freshly pressed grape juice</note> and other expressed juices—which settle by themselves or with help into the four humors—can be properly adapted to the generation of humors. In must, whether by internal or external alteration, there is only a separation of parts and not a change of one substance into another, such as occurs in the digestion of food and nutrition. For even if different parts are separated during the boiling of juices or must—differing in both substance and qualities—we do not say because of this that their substance is changed into another substance, as occurs in "generation." According to the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>the Greek philosopher whose theories on "generation and corruption" (change) were central to medieval science</note>, generation occurs from the "corruption" <note>the breaking down or transformation</note> of another form. If humors are truly generated, then the form in the matter of the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid produced from food in the stomach before it is turned into blood</term> is changed or "corrupted," and the form of the humors is introduced or generated—namely **phlegm** <note>original: 'pituita'</note>, **blood**, and the rest. As I said a little earlier, this is done by the successive heat of the organ. Juices, however, are not generated in this way; they are either squeezed out by art or flow out of things by themselves. 

Nor do the things I have said contradict the writings of those who state that the matter of nourishment is distributed to the smallest veins of the **liver** <term>liver: original 'iocinoris', the primary organ responsible for creating blood and humors in this medical system</term>, so that it may be worked upon from every side by the heat of the organ...

...elaborated <note>this continues from the previous page's discussion of how matter is processed</note> so that it may be converted into blood, whether nature distributes it into the smallest parts or into parts not so small. It is necessary in the process of **concoction** <term>concoction: the "cooking" or ripening of food by the body's internal heat</term> that the time of the action has a sufficient duration. In the first part of that time, while you are cooking that matter, it remains in some way raw; doctors call this semi-cooked matter **phlegm** <term>phlegm: "pituita" in Latin; the cold, moist humor that represents the first stage of digestion</term>, as I have said. But if that same heat continues to act upon the same matter, it converts it into **blood**.

If the heat acts even further, it renders certain parts of that matter more refined and others thicker and more earthy. The first part becomes **bile** <term>bile: or "yellow bile," the hot, dry humor</term>, and the second becomes **melancholy** <term>melancholy: "black bile," the cold, dry, and heavy humor</term>. Furthermore, one must consider that the matter of our nourishment is not uniform; for that reason, it cannot be changed equally in all its parts by the **heat of the liver** at the same time, even if it is located in the thinner veins. 

There is, moreover, a continuous attraction and supply of new matter from the food we eat, according to the intention of Nature. This does not allow the matter which was first received to be perfectly elaborated before new matter is supplied. Instead, it remains semi-cooked along with the blood. As I have often said, doctors call this **phlegm**, and it remains with the blood to nourish those parts of the body which are sustained by phlegmatic blood, as well as for other functions and benefits to the limbs. This is why Nature generates phlegm in such an order, before the perfection of the blood. 

Indeed, that earlier matter (as new matter arrives) gives way to the second before it is perfected in every part. This phenomenon can be seen in **gluttons**, **drunkards**, and **children**, who accumulate many **crudities** <note>original: "cruditates"; refers to undigested or poorly processed food matter that causes illness</note> due to the continuous supply of new nourishment. In this order of the generation of the natural humors, it is worth noting not only the priority and posteriority of the time of generation, but also the duration of the heat's action and the quantity of the humors produced. 

The time of the heat's action in the generation of phlegm is less than in the generation of blood, since phlegm is produced while the blood is still being generated. The duration of the generation of blood is longer than that of phlegm, yet shorter than the generation of bile. The generation of bile requires more time than that of blood, but less than the generation of melancholy. Finally, melancholy requires more time for its generation than bile. However, it must be observed that the **quantity of blood** is greater than the quantity of any of the other humors. After the quantity of blood, the quantity of phlegm is greater than that of bile or melancholy. But the quantity of bile is less than the quantity of blood...

First, a faculty that is either strong or weak; second, everything that can in some way move the matter, the limbs, or the vital faculty toward expulsion—such as a harmful **distemper** <term>distemper: an imbalance of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry)</term> existing alongside the matter of the disease, and also that which has increased and gathered anew in such quantity that it causes distress. These are easily moved later by some sharp, stimulating quality, or if they are seized by putrefaction, they obstruct the passages of the body. 

I thought it necessary to touch upon these things before I explain to you the causes of attacks in almost all **putrid fevers** <term>putrid fevers: fevers caused by the "rotting" of one of the humors, as opposed to simple fevers caused by heat alone</term>. The causes of the attacks depend on these factors in those fevers that have periodic worsenings. This is because a fever arising from the putrefaction of the blood is uniform—either increasing, decreasing, or staying at the same level until it begins to fade. I shall therefore begin to explain the attacks in each specific fever, following the order in which the humors are produced.

**Phlegm** <term>phlegm: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor</term> (as I have said) is produced first every day; once produced, it travels through the veins, either drawn along or pushed. Nature uses it for various necessities and benefits of the body, provided it maintains its proper temperament, substance, and quantity. But if it exceeds in substance, quantity, or quality, Nature expels it as something harmful. If it should putrefy, it generates a fever; and this happens daily because phlegm is generated and gathered daily. When this distressing matter is driven out—especially (as I said) if the body has been prepared for a putrid fever by obstructions, or if that humor has been corrupted by some defect—it triggers the attack. For humors corrupted by a harmful quality are not drawn to the site of putrefaction by choice, but are driven there as troublesome and burdensome surpluses or stimulants. Nor is the "expulsive faculty" always the sole cause of the movement of matter to the site of putrefaction; sometimes it is moved by some other cause, which...

<header>-> E N A N T I O S <-</header> <note>This header is a mirrored "bleed-through" of the word "ENANTIOS" from the reverse side of the page.</note>
-> L 2 <-

A fever is caused either by something containing matter, or even by some external factor separate from matter. For example, a cause "with matter" occurs if there is some bad and harmful quality, an excess in amount or quantity, or some other stimulating or burdensome factor existing alongside the matter. On the other hand, that which is external and "separate from matter" would be (for instance) the heat or coldness of the surrounding air. 

Indeed, the heat of the air greatly assists the elderly in the perfection of all natural operations, and it is beneficial even in other ages, since it can strengthen the **faculty** <note>the "virtus" or vital power of the body</note> and open the paths and passages of the body. Coldness also, if it is not excessive, makes the faculty stronger by concentrating and uniting it. But as I said a little while ago, the quantity of a **vitiated humor** <term>vitiated humor: a humor that has become corrupted, spoiled, or imbalanced</term>, whether through **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the chemical "rotting" or decay of humors, believed to be the primary cause of fevers</term> or some other sharp quality, does much to excite the **expulsive faculty** <term>expulsive faculty: the natural power of the body to drive out or "vomit up" harmful substances</term>. This quantity cannot be generated instantly, but rather over an undetermined space of time. 

Since this is so, the **quotidian fever** <term>quotidian fever: a fever that recurs every single day</term>, which arises from the putrefaction of **phlegm** <term>phlegm: the cold, moist humor; called "pituita" in the original Latin</term>, has its **attacks** <note>original: "accessiones"; the periodic episodes where fever symptoms are most intense</note>, or increases, or worsenings every day, because phlegm is generated and gathered in a span of no less than a single day. 

**Blood**, however, is continuously produced from phlegm after the phlegm itself is formed, and it is collected in the veins in greater quantity by the design of nature. In this generation, the internal heat still works after the transformation of **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid produced from digested food, which was thought to be the precursor to the humors</term> into phlegm. Nature guards this blood as a beloved treasure of life; she draws it successively through the veins to nourish the limbs and preserves it within them. Nor is it any intention of nature to expel it, but rather to preserve it for the restoration of the limbs and the spirits. 

Therefore, if the blood should putrefy or become heated in any way, it produces no periodic attack or worsening—neither a daily, nor a **tertian** <note>a fever recurring every other day</note>, nor a **quartan** <note>a fever recurring every third day</note>—but (as I said shortly before) the heat and the distress it causes are uniform. That is to say, it either always distresses by increasing, or always by decreasing, or uniformly, until a general decline. It has no intervening day of relief, nor any specific pattern of decline. For blood is always generated equally, and first from phlegm; it is not expelled from the veins, nor does it have any quality by which it ought to be distinguished from the other humors. Instead, nature distinguishes and separates all other humors from the blood to render it purer. 

**Bile** <note>Yellow bile, or "cholera"</note> is indeed known to be produced after the generation of blood, based on what was said above; and I have said its quantity is smaller because nature does not primarily intend for its creation, nor does she require it in great quantity for the preservation of the individual. And since after the generation of phlegm and blood...

# E P I S T L E

...bile, therefore, is generated and collected over a longer space of time than blood—specifically on the third day, as I demonstrated above. For the heat works from the first until the second day so that **phlegm** and **blood** may be generated and gathered from the **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid produced from digested food in the stomach</term>. On the third day, however, it converts into bile and is collected. When this bile has increased and been seized by **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the internal rotting or corruption of a humor, believed to trigger fevers</term>, or by some other harmful quality, it is expelled. From such a movement an **accession** <term>accession: a sudden "attack" or onset of fever symptoms</term> occurs, which is a **tertian** <term>tertian: a fever that recurs every third day (Day 1, Day 3, etc.)</term> one, because it is on the third day, and not before, that such a quantity is generated and gathered that it can provoke nature to expel it, should it have putrefied. 

**Melancholy** <note>also known as black bile</note> holds the last place in both generation and quantity, since it is generated last from the chyle after the generation of phlegm, blood, and bile. It is made from the thicker part of the first nourishment and is smaller than all the other parts of the three humors. Because the active heat still works upon that matter to produce melancholy after the bile is finished—and since bile was not made and collected until the third day—melancholy is perfected and gathered on the fourth day. It too is separated from the humoral mass; this happens if its quantity has increased to a bothersome level along with a putrefactive quality, or some other altering disposition that renders it sharper and more harmful, as I have said concerning the other humors. 

Indeed, since melancholy is generated and gathered on the fourth day, if it should become troublesome in its quantity and quality after its generation and gathering, it is expelled by nature to the site of the putrefaction—or at least nature attempts to expel it. This happens on the fourth day and not before, because it was neither generated nor collected earlier due to the thickness of its substance. Thus occur the **quartan** <term>quartan: a fever that recurs every fourth day (Day 1, Day 4, etc.)</term> accessions or exacerbations, as well as other longer ones from the same matter if it should be even thicker, as I shall write shortly hereafter.

You have, therefore, the reason why different and specific accessions occur: from the diversity of the generation of the humors, and also from the diversity in their substance, quantity, and qualities, as well as other assisting causes that I indicated above, along with which I noted the strength or weakness of the **faculty** <note>the "virtus" or the body's innate vital power to heal and regulate itself</note>. For the faculty is that which regulates and directs all things, since it always strives to moderate the blood and also to expel every contrary thing. If it can expel that thing outside the body, it certainly does so; if not, it thrusts it toward the less noble members. If these things should rot, they are accustomed to cause various fevers according to the diversity of the expelled humors; in this expulsion, **patterns** <note>original: "tipi", referring to the specific "type" or periodic rhythm of a fever</note>, chills, and rigors occur. 

And since melancholic humors, both natural and non-natural, are diverse in their substance and qualities due to the diversity of the matter and the active heat—so much so that they sometimes resemble the substance of a stone and possess an extreme dryness—from this diversity (in the putrefaction of the humors)...

...of the **melancholic humor** <note>original: "ris melancholici"; the text continues from the previous page's discussion of black bile</note>, various **attacks** <term>attack: "accessio" in Latin, the periodic onset of fever symptoms</term> sometimes occur which are prolonged. This happens because nature cannot prepare, collect, and then expel such thick matter by the fourth day. Instead, nature proceeds to move the matter only after it has been prepared and gathered—on the fifth day, or the sixth if it is even thicker, or the seventh, eighth, ninth, or another day if it becomes increasingly thick. This also depends on the quantity of the humor and the strength or weakness of the body’s **power** <term>power: "virtus," the internal biological force or "nature" that governs bodily functions</term>. 

Often, if this power is strong, it can lead the matter out of the body through some sensible or insensible evacuation. However, if the power does not dissolve it and push it out gradually, but allows it to aggregate, it causes attacks on the fifth day and others, according to how these humors stimulate or weigh down the body by their thickness. 

I could prove this slow expulsion—caused by the power and the matter, and by the quantity not yet weighing upon or stimulating nature—by the example of several unnatural and natural conditions that are periodic. One example is **epilepsy** <note>original: "morbus comitialis," literally "the assembly-day disease," so called because ancient Roman assemblies were dissolved if someone had a seizure</note>, which does not trigger the symptoms appearing in it unless the matter is bothersome or heavy in both quantity and quality to both nature and the affected limb. This stimulates the **expulsive power**, which rises up against the harmful and weighing humor or quality. Thus, in epilepsy, it happens because of a great mass of matter or a troubling malice <note>in this context, "malice" refers to the harmful or toxic quality of a humor</note>, which is not collected or acquired except over a space of time. 

Similarly, this occurs in natural conditions, such as the **monthly evacuations** <note>menstruation</note> in women, which are not moved until a bothersome quantity of blood has gathered in the veins. The cause is the same for the thick, altered melancholic humor: it is so resistant to nature that the body's power cannot prepare and collect it by the fourth day, but instead labors further until it is ready. Once it is prepared, gathered, and becomes bothersome, the body expels it. 

Thus occur attacks on the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth days, and others that may occur. All such fevers belong to the category of **melancholic fevers**, which are usually called **quartans** <term>quartan: a fever that typically returns every four days</term>, because most often, in the putrefaction of the melancholic humor, the attacks happen on the fourth day. But due to thickness, these attacks are postponed. I have seen such fifth-day and sixth-day attacks more than once, and I know other doctors of our time have seen them as well—regardless of what the most learned **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> might have said about this. But in non-intermittent fevers, whether they involve **phlegm**, **bile**, or **melancholy**, the reason for a daily, **tertian** <term>tertian: recurring every third day</term>, or quartan worsening is the same, since...

<page-num>88</page-num>

# THE LETTER

First, it follows the prescribed order based on the timing of the humor's generation and collection, as well as its quantity and the other factors mentioned. However, the humor is not entirely expelled from the veins if it is excessive and thick, or because of strong and severe obstructions, or because the body's **power** <term>power: "virtus," the innate vital force that governs health and bodily functions</term> is insufficient. 

When it is not pushed outside the veins, a full **attack** <term>attack: "accessio," the periodic onset of a fever's symptoms</term> does not occur. Instead, from the new buildup of decaying matter, the feverish heat simply grows more intense <note>original: "exasperatio"</note> according to the nature of the humor. For instance, **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita"</note> causes daily flare-ups because new phlegmatic matter is generated every day, distressing the body with its quantity and quality. These aforementioned attacks and flare-ups are noted in complicated and composite fevers. 

As you know, fevers can be complicated—either involving the same type or different types and species. For example, there might be two, three, or even more **quotidian** <note>original: "quotidiana," a fever that recurs every day</note> fevers. Whether you call them "double" or "triple" fevers makes no difference; I myself have observed this in a certain noble elderly woman and in others. 

The reason why multiple fevers of the same type can occur is that there are various locations in the body where "unnatural" humors can be produced. Since these are harmful and distressing to nature, they are expelled and gathered at a site of **decay** <term>decay: "putredo," the rotting or fermentation of humors believed to trigger fever</term>, where they rot and cause a fever. 

But since these humors are not generated in one single place at the same time, nature strives to expel the harmful matter at different times or hours. Consequently, several attacks or flare-ups occur in a single day at different hours for the reasons stated above. If phlegmatic matter is generated and expelled from different parts of the body (as I have said), corresponding daily attacks or flare-ups occur. 

However, if **bilious** <note>original: "biliosa," relating to yellow bile or choler</note> matter is generated in different limbs and parts, and this burdensome or harmful matter is expelled, then **tertian** <note>original: "tertiana," a fever that usually recurs every other day</note> attacks occur at different hours in one day or on individual days, depending on the number of locations where the matter is gathered or generated. If an attack occurs every day due to the movement of decaying bilious matter, more modern physicians are accustomed to calling such attacks "double tertians." If attacks occur twice in a single day from the decay of bile, they call these "double-double tertians." 

I have seen—not once, but many times—four, five, or even six tertian fevers in one patient. In these cases, there were attacks resulting from the decay of bile twice or three times every single day. This was due entirely to the variety and number of locations where the bilious matter was collected or generated, just as was said regarding phlegm. But so as not to detain you with a longer speech, you may apply these same reasons to **melancholic** <note>original: "melancholis," referring to black bile</note> humors if they should become complicated.

It clarifies how complex fever patterns, such as "double tertians," are actually overlapping cycles caused by decaying phlegm or bile.</summary>

Whether two, three, or more **quartan** <note>original: "quartane," a fever that recurs every fourth day</note> fevers are joined together, it is unnecessary to labor to prove it, since there is no one who has not very often seen such complications. There are, moreover, complications of different species of fevers which are so well known that there is no physician who has grown old in this most populous city who would not affirm he has seen them many times. This is in addition to those descriptions left to us in writing by the ancient physicians, such as the **hemitriteos** <note>original: "emitritei"</note>, which are called **semitertian** <term>semitertian: a complex fever combining a continuous daily fever with an intermittent fever that peaks every third day</term> by the Latins. These occur if an intermittent tertian fever and a continuous daily fever are combined, arising from a mixture of **decaying phlegm** <note>original: "pituitae putridae"</note> and **decaying bile** <note>original: "bilis... putridae"</note>. Thus, in such a complication, both the attacks of the tertian and the various flare-ups of the daily fever occur according to the differences mentioned regarding the humors. 

But since, if I wished to write everything to you concerning the different types of fevers, I would be writing not a letter but a massive volume, let these things be sufficient for the present. You may find the rest in the book *On the Differences of Fevers* by **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose writings formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries.</note>, and in his work *On Crises*. You will also find much regarding the manner and timing of **nutrition** <term>nutrition: in this context, the entire process of how food is transformed into the body's humors and tissues</term> which serves to prove the points made above. You might also wish to read the book *On Diseases* by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BC; the author mentions a scholarly debate about whether he or his son-in-law Polybus wrote this specific text.</note>—which Galen believed Polybus wrote—for in that book the author declared at great length that complete nutrition cannot happen before the fourth day. This is because the heat involved in the transformation of ingested food into the various substances of the humors works through a certain succession of time. 

And although **Trusianus the Monk** <note>Also known as Turisanus (Pietro Torrigiano), a famous 14th-century commentator on medical texts.</note> and **Peter of Abano** <note>Known as "The Conciliator" (1257–1315), a famous philosopher and physician who tried to resolve contradictions between different medical authorities.</note>, men most learned in every respect, along with the greater part of the medical school, believed that the generation of the humors happens simultaneously and not successively (following the intention of **Aristotle**), I would not want this rational position of mine to be displeasing to you. All physicians confirm that the humors are distinct in their species by very strong arguments. If some stubborn people argue and say that "from one thing, insofar as it is one, only one thing can come" <note>This is a reference to a classical philosophical principle (Ex Uno Non Nisi Unum) suggesting a single cause should produce a single effect.</note>, that argument is valid for material and active causes when they exist together. In our case, however, the matter is not like that; for the matter of the food, or **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid produced in the stomach and intestines during digestion before it is turned into blood</term>, is a single mixture of different substances and parts. The natural heat acting upon it is also one, but it does not act continuously or uniformly, partly because it is dissolved and restored through labor, rest, or sleep, and also from the restoration of moisture.

<summary>The author explains how different fevers can combine into "semitertian" types and argues that the body creates different humors from food over a period of days rather than all at once.</summary>

<page-num>32</page-num>

# LETTER

Since the matter is different from the prior action. For if food is changed into <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "chilum"; a milky fluid produced in the digestive system from food</note>, and chyle into <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituitam"</note>, and finally into blood and other humors, undoubtedly neither is the acting heat a single force, nor is the matter one and the same (considering all these different states). From this, it is clear that the heat acting upon the chyle-like matter, or upon the phlegm as a single underlying substance, is not always the same; furthermore, in its action, it does not first change the whole mass, but first changes the parts that are readier and which the agent first touches, while those which are not so ready resist. Therefore, the acting heat labors longer in their transformation. 

One must also observe this same order in the generation of <term>non-natural humors</term> <note>Humors that have become corrupted or are produced in an unhealthy state.</note>. Furthermore, if unnatural bile—for instance, <term>verdigris bile</term> <note>original: "eruginosa"; bile that has turned a greenish color like copper rust due to extreme heat</note>—or the <term>melancholy humor</term> <note>original: "humor melancholicus" or black bile</note> is generated in the stomach by some occasion, the heat certainly does not always act in the same way for the reasons stated; consequently, the preternatural heat will require a longer space of time in the generation of the melancholy humor than in the generation of the biliary humor. 

I could have written many other things to you concerning the causes of the <term>attacks</term> <note>original: "accesionum"; the periodic worsening or "paroxysms" of a fever</note> and exacerbations in fevers for a clearer understanding of these matters—such as the fact that even if humors are distinguished by species by physicians, they do not always decay in a pure state, since they are rarely found in any limb in a pure, precise form. Nor does it matter whether we speak of "form" or "quality" in the humors, since the <term>substantial form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "substantial form" is the essential nature of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> in most things is quite hidden from us. We therefore distinguish the humors from one another by their qualities and operations. 

From what has been said, most learned **Nicholas**, you have the manifest causes of all attacks in all kinds of fevers—causes thought of by no one before. And even if these things seem somewhat harsh (when you recount them to others), especially to those who have read the ancients repeatedly and have <term>sworn by the words of the master</term> <note>A reference to a Latin idiom (from Horace) describing students who follow their teacher's authority blindly without thinking for themselves.</note>, I nevertheless hope they will be very pleasing to them if they weigh them with a quiet mind. 

And lest you labor too much in a long discussion of speech, or in searching out and collecting the causes of fever attacks, I have written the summary of the causes of these attacks in order, as follows: First, the humors which are generated in chronological order, gathered in that quantity which is able to trouble and weigh down nature; next, that they are corrupted by some harmful quality, namely a <term>putrid</term> one or another. And this is the primary cause of the movement—along with the quantity of the matter—to expel the harmful humors; and in <term>continuous fevers</term>, since the matter cannot be expelled...

<summary>The author explains how digestion produces various humors through different intensities of heat and argues that fever attacks are caused by the body's attempt to expel a specific quantity of corrupted or "putrid" humors.</summary>

<page-num>85</page-num>

# NINTH

That new accumulation is the cause of greater exacerbation <note>a worsening or "flare-up" of symptoms</note>, and this occurs in the three humors, since blood does not have a time in which it is not generated part by part, accumulated, and preserved in the veins, as nature intends it foremost and keeps it like a beloved child. Indeed, nature always intends to sequester <note>separate or set aside</note> the remaining humors from the blood in order to make it purer, whether they be natural or non-natural; it sequesters the natural ones for bodily functions and benefits. 

But because non-natural humors are troublesome, nature is therefore more intent on their sequestration; if they become putrid <note>original: "putridi"; decayed or corrupted by heat</note>, they produce fevers, and if they do not rot but are expelled, they cause various unnatural conditions, such as pains, or <term>abscesses</term> <note>collections of pus</note>, or <term>papules</term> <note>pimple-like skin eruptions</note>, and other material unnatural conditions. For very many swellings arise from some matter gradually congested in the limbs; if this matter is not seized by putrid heat, it remains there longer, nor does nature first strive to drive it elsewhere, since it has already been gradually expelled to some <term>ignoble limb</term> <note>original: "ignobile membrum"; parts of the body considered less vital, like the extremities, where the body "dumps" excess waste to protect vital organs like the heart</note>. Therefore, even if it weighs down or troubles that limb, no <term>accession</term> <note>original: "accessio"; the sudden onset or periodic return of a fever</note> occurs, since it is a humor that is generated and collected successively from ingested food for nourishment. 

Farewell, my most learned Nicholas; if I have satisfied you as I desired, it will indeed be most pleasing to me; if not, the matter—which is most difficult and new—has its excuse. If someone in the future should imagine something better or more reasonable, let them add their own thoughts to these of ours, for they too will have deserved well of posterity and will be praised among the most learned. Finally, I would ask you to reflect sometime on such a difficult subject, and if you conceive anything good, let me know, for it is my intention to write more on this matter again. Farewell. Venice.

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT PHILOSO-
## pher and Physician, Lord Giovanni Battista
## Montano, publicly professing the ordinary practice
### of medicine at Padua. Letter 10. That pestilential
### fever can exist without the
### putrefaction of the humors.

**I** CANNOT fail, most distinguished man, to fulfill through this letter what I promised you in person: namely, the truth concerning pestilential fever occurring without the putrefaction <note>the decay or "rotting" of bodily fluids due to heat</note> of the humors, according to the opinion of Galen <note>an influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD)</note>. This was a subject which, because of the shortage of time during those evening hours of our conversation then, I was not able to pursue. Nor would I judge you to be averse to this truth, although Galen—in his book *On the Differences of Fevers*, and in his commentaries on the books *On Diseases Wandering Everywhere* <note>original: "morbis passim uagātibus"; this refers to the *Epidemics* of Hippocrates</note>, and in not a few other places—has said that in most putrid fevers, the pestilential element becomes destructive where, in addition to the putrefaction of the air, there has also been the greatest putrefaction in the humors. 

Certainly, for that reason Galen did not deny that pestilential air, by a poisonous alteration <term>alteration</term> <note>a change in the state or quality of the body's parts</note>, can also alter the other parts of the living body, beyond the putrid alteration that occurs in the humors, and beyond the manifest <note>obvious or observable</note> qualities; since he posited this poisonous quality in the air as the most powerful <term>procatarctic cause</term> <note>original: "causam... procatarcticam"; an external, triggering cause of a disease, such as the environment</note>. Although this poisonous quality does not exist without an obvious alteration of the primary qualities <note>the fundamental properties of hot, cold, wet, and dry</note> and a putrefaction of the substance of the air itself, it does not always produce a final putrid alteration in the humors (though it often does). Instead, it sometimes produces only a poisonous quality, and that indeed without the putrefaction of the humors. 

For even if the substance of the air, changed into putrefaction, works together with the body's suitability to contract pestilential illnesses, it is not a constant rule that those things which are altered by something putrid must themselves turn out putrid—as Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and influential medical philosopher (c. 980–1037 AD)</note> testified regarding the fever of the blood. For although an agent <note>the thing acting or causing a change</note> acts primarily according to its own nature, it is often unable to make the recipient <note>original: "passum"; the thing being acted upon</note> similar to itself due to the resistance of the recipient. When, however, in addition to putrefaction, there is also a "dissolving" quality arising from the <term>malice of the air</term> <note>original: "aeris malitia"; the harmful, toxic, or malignant state of the atmosphere</note> which is contrary to life, that quality alters the vapors, the <term>spirits</term> <note>the vital energies or "pneuma" believed to circulate through the body and sustain life</note>, and even the solid limbs, without putrefaction; Galen wrote this most beautifully in the third book of *On Foretelling from the Pulse*, in the following series of words: "For there are (as we have taught) pe..."

<summary>This page introduces a letter to the physician Giovanni Battista Montano arguing that pestilential fevers can be caused directly by poisonous air affecting the body's vital spirits and solid parts, rather than always requiring the corruption of bodily fluids.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the Tenth Letter to Giovanni Battista Montano. It follows the discussion from the previous page regarding how the air acts as a "procatarctic" or triggering cause of disease, even when the body's internal humors are not yet "putrid" or decayed.</meta>

# THE TENTH

<note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of the air as a triggering cause</note> of pestilential fevers, not a few of which are **hectic** <note>original: "hectice"; a type of fever believed to be seated in the solid parts of the body rather than the fluids</note> from the very beginning. These differ from all other fevers that arise from a great putrefaction <note>the "rotting" or breakdown of bodily humors due to excessive heat</note>. These are the views of Galen <note>the famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note>; for he knew that in his book *On the Differences of Fevers* he had stated that pestilential fevers can be caused even in those who do not possess a contamination <note>original: "coinquinationem"</note> arising from a fullness of humors.

Furthermore, among other causes preparing the way for maximum putrefaction, he did not deny that this could happen from the bad quality of the air alone—especially if an external cause, such as grief or anger, acted as a contributing cause along with the air. These fevers were not of the "putrid" kind, but of other types, as mentioned in the cited passage. For Galen believed that the cause of these fevers lay more in the predisposition of the person receiving the disease than in the air itself; he illustrated this using two nearly opposite physical conditions. 

The first condition was a body full of waste products prepared in every way for putrefaction. The second, on the contrary, was a body that was clean, pure, and maintained under the best lifestyle regimen. Although this second type of body is affected by the pestilential quality of the air with much greater difficulty, Galen did not say it was impossible for it to be infected, only that it happened more rarely. This is consistent with reason, since such clean bodies, which do not err in their regimen, are rarely found. 

For bodies lacking the superfluities <note>excess waste fluids</note> ready for putrefaction are not immune <note>original: "impassibilia"</note>; for the malice of the air—which is not without heat, since it is putrid—is imprinted even onto the solid members, or into the **spirits** <note>the "vital breaths" or subtle fluids thought to carry life through the nerves and arteries</note> and vapors. This is indeed the true mind of the ancients, which I myself, in pursuit of the truth, seemed to confirm in the short book I wrote on pestilential fever for the benefit of young students, based on Galen's authority and on the reasons for a clear explanation of that passage.

I pass over the questions of illustrious modern scholars, since, according to the book *On Procatarctic Causes* <note>original: "de causis procatarcticis"</note>, extrinsic causes (which they call "primitive" or primary triggers) do not always produce the same effect in everyone. As I have most elegantly stated regarding the agent of putrefaction: it is not an absolute rule that a putrid state must arise from every action of a putrid agent. 

With these words, most learned man in every respect, I wished to greet you after your departure and to fulfill what I had promised to provide. May you be happy according to your desire; I commend myself greatly to your excellence. Farewell. Venice, 1541.

->June 10th.<-

# TO THE REVEREND LORD
## John, Canon of Torcello. Letter 11. On complicated fevers—namely, putrid and habitual fever—and also on the descent of catarrh to the chest and the ulceration of the lungs.

YOU ASK, Reverend Sir, that I write to you frankly, both regarding the essence of the various unnatural conditions you suffer from, as well as the remedies beneficial for them. Therefore, to satisfy your requests most diligently and touch upon everything briefly—as our habit and long-standing goodwill demand, especially since you seek those things which physicians are bound to do by their office (as they say)—I shall begin. 

From what you have written to me, it is manifest that you are gripped by a **fever**. For fever is an unnatural heat that first occupies the heart, and then warms the entire body through the veins and arteries. Since you recognize that you are always held by a manifest unnatural heat, and that it does not affect you equally or in one way but plagues you more in the evening hours, there is no doubt that this heat depends on a **putrefaction** <note>original: "putredine"; in Renaissance medicine, this referred to the "rotting" or breakdown of bodily humors due to trapped heat</note> of the humors decaying within the veins. 

Because you say you feel neither shivering, nor cold, nor any trembling <note>original: "ororem", likely *horrorem*</note>, and because the heat is quite sharp, I would say that the humor rotting in the veins is for the most part **bilious** <note>original: "biliosum"; relating to yellow bile, one of the four humors</note>. Thus, you first suffer from a "continuous choleric fever" arising from the decay of bile in the veins. 

But besides this fever, there is another fever joined to it which is "fixed," such that it occupies not only the humors but the very substance of the organs. Physicians call this a **habitual fever** <note>original: "habitudinalem"; today known as a hectic fever, where the heat has settled into the "habit" or solid constitution of the body</note>. Because the heat has now passed into the "habit" of the body, it seems to bother the patient almost not at all, even though it actually causes great harm. It feels less bothersome because the heat has become firm and fixed in the limbs. 

I say this because I hear from your letters that you perceive a greater heat for an hour or a little more after both lunch and dinner—a fact you say you have noted for a long time—and also because of the wasting of all your limbs and the thinness of your entire body. Furthermore, you write that you are troubled by a **continuous cough**, with phlegm <note>original: "sputaminibus"</note> of varying substance, color, and even taste; you say these are sometimes lemon-yellow, sometimes white, and sometimes slightly livid <note>original: "subliuida"; a leaden or bluish-grey color</note>...

And to answer you in a single word regarding the causes of all these unnatural conditions, it must be believed and held without hesitation that all the listed conditions have arisen from that **double tertian fever** <note>original: "febre duplici tertiana"; a type of malaria-like fever where paroxysms occur daily because two separate cycles of three-day fevers overlap</note> which you suffered. This occurred because you were unwilling to permit anything, either in the <term>regimen of necessary things</term> <note>original: "regimine rerum neceſſariarum"; the "six non-naturals" of Galenic medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind</note> or in the matter of medicines.

Thus, since your lordship was already prone to **catarrhs** or **distillations** <note>the dripping of excess "cold and moist" humors from the brain down into the lower body</note> due to a fullness in the head, it was easy afterward for that matter—which used to descend to the throat and chest—to be scorched by the febrile heat or mixed with **cholera** <note>yellow bile</note>. This has ulcerated the pulmonary parts, and thus causes a perpetual cough and varied sputum. And let me not delay you with these matters; since the diseases and their causes are clear, I shall turn my discourse to those things you seek with your whole mind. These are: whether such complicated dispositions and diseases can be cured; then, by what aids you might do so if they can be cured; or, if they cannot be cured, by what remedies you might be able to prolong your life. 

I say, therefore, that if complicated diseases (even if they are small) cannot be cured without the greatest labor even in young men, how much more will great diseases in the **first stage of old age** not be able to be cured? However, lest I lead your Reverend Lordship into despair, I say that if you are willing to show yourself obedient to physicians, you can prolong your life for many, many years, and thus it will be in your hands. 

You shall do this through the **regimen of necessary things**. First, let there be a temperateness of the **air** with a certain dryness, by reason of the ulcer of the lung. Because it is winter, and there are rains, and also clouds and **vapors** moisturizing the air, a fire should be lit in the bedchamber, especially at night. The windows should be closed in the evening hours so that too many humid vapors do not enter, and they should not be opened until morning, when the sun's rays have already dried the air for a little while. 

Let the **foods** be those which restore the most in the smallest quantity, which should not lack a cooling effect entirely, along with some light **drying** <note>original: "exiccatione"</note>; therefore, in the case of **consumption**...

**Barley ptisan** <note>original: "ptisana hordeacea"; a medicinal porridge or strained decoction of barley used as a staple for the sick</note> in the broth of a chicken or a young capon, in which herbs that extinguish febrile heat have been boiled—such as **borage**, **bugloss**, and similar—will be the best food. For drink, let there be white wine with little body and diluted with water in which sugar has been boiled; it should not be drunk after a meal, as it fills the head and leads to the descent of **catarrh** <note>the downward flow of excess humors from the head to the chest</note>. Let the hours for eating be chosen when you know the febrile heat bothers you least, both in the morning and evening; and in the morning before food, care must be taken that the superfluities of the lower belly are purged. Therefore, if a bowel movement does not occur naturally, it should be prompted by a common enema or a suppository.

And although exercise contributes greatly to a **regimen of health** <note>the "six non-naturals" governing daily life: air, food, sleep, exercise, excretion, and emotion</note>, it is nonetheless harmful to those with fever and the weak; therefore it should be set aside, and in its place, very light massage should occasionally and rarely be used. Sleep, as it strengthens all the vital powers, is very appropriate; for that reason, you may sleep during the night hours, but very little during the day, as daytime sleep prepares the way for catarrhal diseases. And the position of the body should be face-up so that the materials do not descend to the chest.

Finally, what will be most beneficial is that you be of good cheer and rejoice with friends, and have everything that can return the mind to a cheerful state, such as musical instruments, singing, and pleasant conversations, and seeing and hearing things that can generate joy.

Once these things are regulated, the cure through medicinal means presents itself, which, as <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the foundational authority on Western medicine whose theories of the four humors dominated for over a thousand years</note> said, consists of the removal of the cause. But since—due to the complication of both the fevers and the catarrhal matter descending to the lungs and causing ulceration—it is very difficult to find medicines that can benefit one condition without harming the other, the primary focus must be on that which is most urgent. Therefore, the first intention must be toward the extinction of the febrile heat with those...

Let them boil in three parts water and one part white wine. Let a fomentation be made over the region of the stomach with a sponge soaked in this decoction. Then, rub the stomach area with this liniment: **Take:** oils of rose, wormwood, and mint, half an ounce of each; the medicinal powder **diarodonis abatis** <note>a classical rose-based digestive tonic</note>, one and a half drams; red coral, one dram; and a little wax. Mix these to make a liniment, and use it after the warm compress before lunch and dinner.

Similarly, let the back be rubbed with violet oil or with the **rose ointment of Mesue** <note>a famous preparation by the Persian physician Masawayh</note>. In the same way, the chest area should be rubbed with violet oil and sweet almond oil mixed together.

Furthermore, it will be excellent to take by mouth—by licking—those things which facilitate phlegm and somehow stop the descent of matter from the head. In this case, mixtures or **electuaries** <note>medicinal pastes made with honey or sugar</note> prepared thus are helpful: **Take:** sugar of roses, violets, bugloss, and borage, half an ounce of each; **penidium** <note>a pulled-sugar candy used for coughs</note>, **diadraganth** <note>a gum-based soothing powder</note>, and sugar candy, three drams of each. Mix these with syrup of licorice and compound violet syrup to make a mixture to be taken frequently at any hour. For this purpose, it is also helpful to lick compound violet syrup and a **saponea** <note>a thick, linctus-style medicine</note> made from sugar and scabious water.

Finally, since a great deal of matter descends from the head, the head must be helped so that its strength is reinforced and the descent of those fluids (if possible) is prohibited. This is very difficult, but whatever the case, let it be attempted first with a powder placed twice a day upon the **coronal suture** <note>original: "futuram capitis coronalem"; the joint between the bones at the front-top of the skull</note> of the head. This is in the anterior part of the head; you find it by placing the heel of the palm at the root of the nose between the eyebrows, and where the middle finger ends on the upper part of the head, there is the seam of the coronal bone. Therefore, in that place, after first shaving the hair, let the powder be applied.

# THIRTEENTH [COMMUNICATION]

You ask and insist that I write to you regarding what should be done about a certain impediment in moving the arm, so that the discomfort in movement might be removed, as well as the unsightly nature of its shape or composition. This ailment (as you write) seems to have its cause in the fact that the muscles <note>original: "lacerti"; literally 'lizards,' a common anatomical term for the muscles of the arm</note> and tendons which facilitate movement to the shoulder blade <note>original: "os scabulæ"</note> are relaxed, not without harm to the entire arm and the other joints of the body—namely the hip <note>original: "ischiæ"</note>, the knee, the foot, the fingers, and those of that kind. 

Indeed, since I read of no evident or external cause in your letter, it seemed worthwhile to me to consider some internal one. Since both reason and experience often teach that these causes are numerous, I will first apply myself to investigating them. No one can doubt the locations or the suffering parts, since the impaired actions, the physical shape, and the pain during movement declare them. But it is helpful to know whether the primary cause is in those external suffering members themselves, or whether it arises through the "consent" <note>A medical term meaning "sympathy," where one organ's ailment is caused by another's dysfunction</note> of other members, or from some other cause. 

To be sure, this evil of which you write is often accustomed to follow other conditions that are "contrary to nature," such as **apoplexy** <note>In the Renaissance, this referred to a sudden loss of consciousness and motion, similar to a modern-day stroke</note> or some long-lasting disease, whether it be a fever or any other specific ailment. Thus, over a stretch of time, the **natural heat** <note>The vital energy believed to fuel the body’s functions</note> is rendered weak, and many "unnatural humidities" are increased. This heat cannot reach the functions of the limb because the nerves and muscles can hardly be actuated by that heat or spirit <note>original: "spiritu"; the "animal spirits" were believed to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to create movement</note>. This is because the many aforementioned humidities, soaked into the nerves, make them moist and—by obstructing the pathways—prohibit the passage of the spirits coming to them. 

I would say, as far as I can gather from your letter, that these unnatural effects arise from both causes, as I had heard that you had already been sick with a long and lethal disease. For they said that the doctors had left you for dead <note>original: "te deploratum"; literally "deplored" or given up on</note>, saved only by the help of God, when there was no sensation or movement. This incident, above all, I cannot believe to have been anything other than **apoplexy** (according to **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose work formed the basis of Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> in *On the Affected Parts*, and the Prince **Avicenna** <note>An 11th-century Persian physician; his 'Canon of Medicine' was the standard textbook in European universities</note> in the third book of the *Canon*). This is primarily a passion of the brain, since in it all **animal operations** <note>The functions of the "anima" or soul, including movement, sensation, and thought</note>, both internal and external, are removed. This surely happens if a cold, thick, slow, or viscous and impure humor has filled the ventricles <note>cavities</note> of the brain and obstructed them. If these superfluous humidities and obstructions are not removed by art or by nature (which is always contrary to the disease and its cause), death is not far off.

->E P I S T O L A<-

# EPISTOLA

...they conclude without doubt at last from the failure of respiration. Nature is healed, truly, either by herself or aided by medical art, once obstructions are opened and the matter is expelled, or shifted to the nerves. If that matter is brought down to all the nerves of the spine, a universal resolution—or **paralysis**—occurs. But if it is only on one side, there will be a partial paralysis of one side. For you know from the science of dissection <note>original: "incisionis scientia"</note> that the <term>nuca</term> <note>From the Arabic 'nukha,' referring here to the spinal cord</note>, or as they say, the marrow passing through the spine, is bipartite, just as you have seen the brain divided into two parts. You also know that this marrow is covered by a thin veil proceeding from the brain itself, which they call the <term>pia mater</term> <note>Literally "tender mother," the innermost membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord</note>. This was done so that if some harm should happen to one part, the other would remain uninjured.

Furthermore, I seem to see that this is what happened in your case: namely, that the expelled matter moved to one side of the origin of the spinal nerves, and with the passages obstructed and a softening produced in them, the force of the <term>spirits</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "animal spirits" were subtle substances that traveled through hollow nerves to facilitate movement and sensation</note> is barely able to reach them. Even if some force does proceed, it cannot complete the actions of the limbs, since those parts have already been made sodden by the presence of humor, moisture, and cold. And it is from this that the shoulder blade is relaxed or "resolved," as is the head of the arm—indeed, the entire arm, the hand, the hips, the knee, the foot, and the fingers are all weak for movement. But since neither the neck, nor the tongue, nor any other part of the head is hindered in movement or sensation, we know that the brain remains unharmed. 

But since (as Galen wrote in the third book of *On Diseases*) the things we note in bodies that are "contrary to nature" are either Diseases, or Causes, or Accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to symptoms or secondary effects of a disease</note> of the disease, it seemed best to me to descend to this distinction and enumeration so that we might more easily find the life-giving aids for this case, and to gather them from what was said above. 

<margin>[</margin> The first Disease is the obstruction of the origins of the spinal marrow nerves, and a certain chilling and moistening of them, arising from a material cause—namely, from the humor already transmitted from the brain. From this follows the weakness in voluntary movement, which is an Accident. For since the nerves arising in one part of the spinal marrow are obstructed and proceed to the muscles <note>original: "lacertos"</note> of that side of the body, voluntary movement (which occurs by means of the spirits coming to them) is hindered. If there is also any bad configuration in the limbs, that occurs because of the relaxation of both the muscles and the ligaments. I do not think there is any dislocation <note>original: "luxationem"</note>; but if there is any "sad sensation" which we call pain, that...

->THIRTEENTH<-

...xed, it must be believed to arise from the same <term>unnatural temperament</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, health was a balance of four "humors" or qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry). An "unnatural temperament" meant these qualities had fallen into a state of disease-causing imbalance.</note>. Therefore, having touched upon these matters, let the regimen—the <term>six necessary things</term> <note>These are the "six non-naturals" of ancient medicine: environment, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, evacuation and repletion, and the passions of the mind.</note>—be organized for the proper method of care. First, therefore, since the method of healing is by opposites, and the winter time presents no small obstacle to care, one must beware as much as possible of the cold and also of excessively damp places. For this reason, the place of habitation should be warm; this will be easily achieved if a fire is kept constantly lit in the chamber. It will be more beneficial if the fire is made from juniper, laurel, or similar woods. 

Foods also should be of a kind that can neither moisten the body with external dampness nor cool it down. For this reason, bread should be made from the best wheat, not entirely purified of all its bran, salted, and very well fermented. Meats also should not be too moist, such as pork and the like, but should be dry, such as woodland and mountain birds—for instance, quails, partridges, pheasants, thrushes, blackbirds, and similar ones. Capons are also excellent. Among the four-legged animals, the meat of young <margin>+</margin> kids and hares is not entirely displeasing. Soft-boiled eggs (as they say) and those mixed into the broth of the aforementioned meats can be eaten conveniently, as can dishes made from spelt or chickpea broth. Capers are also excellent, as they both warm and dry. 

Wine, however, is suspect, because it often turns into vinegar in the stomach, and where there are many raw materials <note>referring to "undigested humors"</note>, it carries them down to the nerves. For this reason, even if there were no fear of it turning into vinegar, you should wish to drink very little of it unless it is mixed with a great deal of honey-water <note>original: "aqua mellita"</note>, and only in a small quantity; not strong, but as they say, "weak." However, if you are willing to listen to me in all things, I would set wine aside and drink <term>hydromel</term> <note>A mixture of honey and water, sometimes fermented but here likely a medicinal decoction.</note>, or water boiled with honey together with sage leaves. 

Indeed, other foods such as fish, cold fruits, and all acidic things must undoubtedly be forbidden. Nevertheless, certain fruits like pine nuts, <term>fustici</term> <note>An archaic term for pistachios.</note> or pistachios, and anise are praised, as is cinnamon before and after a meal. Preserved ginger, which they call "green," is also very beneficial, especially in the morning before food; similarly other spices, and especially pepper. Every form of over-fullness <note>original: "repletio"</note> is to be avoided, and effort should be made to soften the belly; if it does not flow of its own accord, this can be done conveniently with a <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema.</note> made from a decoction of betony and similar herbs with <term>hiera logodion</term> or <term>hiera pachi</term> <note>These were famous "holy" purgative compounds or bitter pastes used in ancient and medieval pharmacy.</note>, the description of which you will find in <term>Scribonius Largus</term> <note>A Roman physician of the 1st century AD known for his book of medical recipes.</note>. # LETTER
## M

...with honey and the varieties of the aforementioned <term>hiera</term> <note>original: "hiera"; a "holy" medicinal bitter paste or powder, usually based on aloes, used as a purgative.</note>, you will be able to accomplish this; nor should any light exercise before lunch be omitted. Sleep moistens the body and restores all the <term>virtues</term> <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the body's natural faculties or powers, such as the ability to digest or move.</note>, whereas wakefulness dries and inflames the system. For this reason, sleep should be brief, yet not so brief that it cannot suffice for <term>coction</term> <note>The Galenic belief that digestion was a process of "cooking" food in the stomach and organs.</note>—first in the stomach and then in the remaining organs—so that finally the <term>spirits</term> <note>Subtle vapors or fluids believed to travel through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note> may be restored. These spirits are the instruments of nature with which it fights against disease and the causes of disease. Furthermore, the bad "accidents of the soul" <note>This refers to distressing emotions or passions like grief or anxiety.</note> and the use of venereal acts [sex] must be avoided, since they make all the faculties weak. Anger, however, as well as shouting and laughter—since they do not occur without some inflammation of the heart and body—can in this case sometimes be beneficial. But in all things we usefully follow the comic maxim, namely, **nothing in excess** <note>original: "ne quid nimis"; a famous Roman proverb from the playwright Terence.</note>; finally, to be joyful and to rejoice is always best. And let these things said to you, the physician, about the regimen be sufficient.

But since what has been said can by no means remove every evil, I will also set down those aids and medicines which are able to take away the cause and the disease. Indeed, since the symptom follows the disease like a shadow follows the body, that symptom will recede by itself once the disease is removed. Again, since it is a "material" disease <note>A disease caused by a physical substance or humor rather than just a change in temperature.</note>, it ought to be cured by evacuation according to the opinion of **Hippocrates**. However, this should not be done through bloodletting, since it is by no means a fullness of blood alone, nor does the blood seem to abound with other humors. You need, therefore, an extraction of the cold, phlegmatic humor, not without some admixture of natural bile; this indeed can first be conveniently done by vomiting, and it will be the removal of the antecedent cause. 

But if you cannot rouse yourself to vomit without danger, or if you desire to evacuate with medicines not only that matter which is in the stomach but also that which resides in the veins and limbs, it must first be "prepared" with suitable syrups or decoctions. These include syrups of betony, of Arabian lavender <note>original: "stoechados"; Lavandula stoechas.</note>, honey of roses, and the like. And let a decoction be made from betony, ground pine <note>original: "yua"; Ajuga chamaepitys, often used for joint and nerve pain.</note>, Arabian lavender, sweet flag <note>original: "acoro"</note>, polypody fern, and similar things. By their qualities, these are among those things which can prepare the mixed phlegmatic matter for evacuation, and they also assist with obstructions and other injuries to the nerves. When the matter has been "prepared"—a state you will easily recognize from the **urine** <note>original: "locio"; physicians analyzed urine color and sediment to see if the humors were "cooked" or ready to be purged.</note>—it is beneficial to evacuate it with "blessed" drugs (such as larch fungus <note>original: "agaricus"; a medicinal mushroom used as a powerful purge for phlegm.</note>), which larch fungus I would never leave out of purgative medicines. The *hiera* are also effective, and especially the composite ones, namely the *hiera*...
