# THIRTEENTH

...of Hermes, <term>hiera logodion</term> <note>original: "hiera logodion"; a "holy" medicinal powder or paste specifically formulated for neurological issues.</note> and (as I said above) <term>hiera pachi</term> <note>original: "hiera pachi"; a "thick" or "fat" version of the hiera purgative.</note> please me greatly. There are also other electuaries <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powder with honey or syrup.</note> which, for the sake of brevity, I shall omit. Also excellent for the evacuation of the matter are <term>cochia pills</term> <note>A common purgative pill usually containing aloes, colocynth, and scammony.</note>, and those made of <term>serapinum</term> <note>A gum resin from a plant in the fennel family, used to break up thick humors.</note> and <term>opoponax</term> <note>A herb resin used in ancient medicine as an antispasmodic.</note>. However, I have very often used **pills of euphorbium** <note>The resin of the spurge plant, known for its extremely potent purging effects.</note>, which in similar cases have always been health-bringing; indeed, **Avicenna** praises them in the third book of the *Canon* regarding the cure of apoplexy and also the cure of paralysis. For he said, in both the one chapter and the other, that pills of euphorbium are better than all these others. Furthermore, they draw out <term>phlegmatic matter</term> <note>original: "materia pituitosa"; in the medical theory of the time, an excess of cold, wet "phlegm" was believed to block the nerves and cause paralysis.</note> from the nerves and other distant parts of the body. These can be administered all the more safely the more chronic the disease has become; you should not have taken them safely at the beginning, nor can they safely evacuate all the matter if administered only once now. Instead, it will be worthwhile to take them often and in smaller quantities.

While these evacuations are being administered, it is also useful to use strengthening remedies both internally and externally, such as by taking a **Mithridatic composition** <note>original: "mithridaticam compositionem"; Mithridatum, a famous semi-mystical "universal" antidote and tonic containing dozens of ingredients.</note>, or **theriac**, or the preparation **diatrion piperion** <note>A medicine made primarily of three types of pepper, used to warm the stomach.</note>, or **diamuscum** <note>A musk-based cordial used to strengthen the heart and brain.</note>, and similar things.

Externally, however, anointings of the spine—from the neck all the way to the tailbone—are beneficial, using oil of lilies, costus, juniper, or peppers; it is also appropriate to anoint the loosened limbs and affected areas with these. It is also profitable to wash the spine and the loosened limbs with a decoction of betony, stoechas <note>A type of wild lavender.</note>, ground-pine, costus, sage, rosemary, lavender, and the like; not just once, but twice a day, and to continue this over a period of time. For indeed, in long-lasting diseases, remedies do not help unless they are continued.

I wanted to say these things (deferring to your wishes). Not because I believe you are ignorant of them, but rather to satisfy my own feelings; for such is the magnitude of your virtues and my benevolence toward you that I never seem to have satisfied you enough, but wish to counsel you in all good things. For what I have written so far seemed necessary to me in order to respond fully to your letters, in which you ask whether, in addition to what has already been said, the use of a decoction of **Indian wood**—which they call "holy" <note>original: "ligni indici quod sanctum vocant"; this refers to Guaiacum, a wood from the Americas newly introduced to Europe, famously used to treat "cold" diseases like syphilis and paralysis.</note>—would be beneficial for this disease. If I believe it might be profitable in some part, and how or with what it might be better and more usefully boiled, I respond to this: **Indian wood** is a suitable medicine according to its manifest qualities, since it is hot and dry, and is able to both warm and dry our bodies. Add also that, besides the primary qualities mentioned, it has secondary qualities [suited] for this ailment...

May God, who is the best Father of all, deign to extend the hand of His omnipotence to this our counsel for your health. **Farewell.** Venice. 1545. The 15th day of December.

-># FOURTEENTH<-

I have written to you in my letters. That cure is happy and health-giving which the physician can perform through the management of the **six necessary things** <note>original: "sex rerum necessariarum"; in Renaissance medicine, these are the "Six Non-Naturals": air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, excretion and retention, and the passions of the soul. Doctors believed health was maintained by balancing these.</note>. But if, besides this management, the second instrument of medicine should be necessary—which is the administration of drugs—in this **condition of yours against nature** <note>original: "præternaturam affectu"; a medical term for a disease or state that deviates from the healthy "natural" state of the body.</note>, I have judged those things to be beneficial which are light and easy.

Wherefore, if you also cook certain meats (as you write) together with the things already mentioned in the other letter, and wash your limbs with the decoction, I see nothing that can either greatly hinder or greatly help, since if I weigh the qualities of meats in general, you have nothing that can greatly alter the body. And I would say the same regarding oil of sweet almonds.

But if by chance you seek some **specific property** <note>original: "proprietatem aliquam"; referring to "occult properties," which were medicinal effects that could not be explained by the simple qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note> (as they say) beyond the manifest qualities, **oil of earthworms** <note>original: "oleum de lumbricis"; earthworms were often steeped in oil and used topically to treat joint pain and "cold" nerve disorders like paralysis.</note>, composed with plenty of oil of bitter almonds, would please me exceedingly; nor would I wish the oil to boil in the decoction with the herbs and other **simples** <note>Medicines made of only one ingredient, usually a plant.</note>, but after the washing, I would anoint the entire body with the said oil, and especially the **relaxed limbs** <note>original: "membra resoluta"; a common term for limbs affected by paralysis.</note> and the other weaker parts.

Indeed, let the decoction with which the limbs ought to be washed be made of **betony**, **sage**, **French lavender** <note>original: "stæcados"; *Lavandula stoechas*, used for head and brain disorders.</note>, **agaric** <note>original: "agarico"; a type of tree fungus used in purgative and strengthening medicines.</note>, and a portion of roses to temper any immoderate heat they may have. And so that the virtue of the decoction may be better delivered and penetrate the innermost parts of the limbs, I would also add some portion of white aromatic wine—say, a twentieth part—and I would wash the affected limbs with the said decoction at a moderate heat.

As for what you ask regarding the powers of **whey** <note>original: "seri lactis"; the liquid remaining after milk has been curdled and strained.</note> in this condition of yours against nature, namely whether it can benefit you in any way, I have nothing certain to say. I know indeed that whey has a sufficiently moderate temperament, both in heat and in dryness, such that it can modestly warm, disperse, and thin; and also, since it is of a light substance, it is able to take on the powers of many medicines—namely of roots, herbs, flowers, fruits, or seeds—if they are infused in it for some time or boiled. And for that reason, it is called the "material for infusions and decoctions" by physicians. 

Nor would I believe, as you write, that whey is the "last resort for an extreme disease"; since **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> often said that the extreme remedies in diseases are the abstinence from food and the letting of blood. But I would wish that you would wrest and twist the said authority, or any other of **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–c. 370 BC), to whom the foundational clinical texts of Western medicine are attributed.</note> and Galen alike, toward this condition of yours, which as it persuades me...

by God’s grace, it will bring no small benefit to your health. There is a saying that what **fire does not cure, nothing can cure** <note>original: "quo'd ignis non sanat nihil fanare poteft"; a famous aphorism attributed to Hippocrates, suggesting that if extreme measures like heat or surgery fail, the condition may be incurable.</note>. This will be easily done if, twice a day, you place a **cabbage leaf** with butter over the burned areas; and also if you press a wax or silver **pill** <note>A small bead or "button" used to keep a cautery wound from closing.</note> deep into the said ulcerations with a compress pressed down on top. For the **sanies** <note><term>sanies: a thin, greenish or bloody discharge from a wound, distinct from healthy pus.</term></note> which will flow from the ulcers will cleanse the entire body of the thin and **virulent excrements** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "excrements" were any waste fluids produced by the body's processes, not just feces.</note> scattered through the limbs. Thus, you will see the remaining parts of the body become healthier day by day, as that thin and poisonous matter—which greatly distresses the nerves—is called back and drawn out. Lastly, I wonderfully praise your change of location, for I hear that the place is exposed to very cold winds. When I indicated this to our friend Lord Giovanni Maria, he greatly praised the advice. But as for the most distinguished **Nullus** <note>This may refer to a specific individual or indicate a lack of acquaintance with a certain person mentioned in previous correspondence.</note>, since I have no familiarity with that most noble and grave man, I can say nothing appropriate to him. Whatever is decided or done by you regarding the business, please do not be reluctant to notify your friends. Even if I can be of little or no use to you in this matter, I will nevertheless favor your affairs at all times. Farewell, and love me. Apollonius and your other friends salute you most dutifully and pray for your best health. From Venice. May 10, 1546.

# THE FIFTEENTH

when he was five years old, because he could not speak. It has now been six years since—owing to many hardships, both of the body (from the air and other affairs) and also from the greatest disturbances of the mind—he first fell into a heaviness of the head and a weakness of its functions, as well as a looseness of the entire body. Finally, it has now been two years that he has been in this present unnatural condition which troubles him greatly.
This unnatural condition is a resolution, or <term>Paralysis</term> <note>original: "Paraleſis"; a loss of voluntary motion in the muscles, often called "resolution" in this period.</note> of the right side, such that the entire right part—namely the arm and the leg—is deprived of voluntary motion, so that he can neither walk nor lift his arm to his head without some support, such as using his other, healthy arm. Along with this resolution of the nervous members of the half-part of the body from the head downward, there is also a very great difficulty in speaking, arising from the same and another cause, so that he can hardly speak six words continuously. There is also a notable injury to the faculty of memory, so that he recalls things with difficulty and is hardly able to remember; there is also a notable weakness and darkening of the sight and the eyes.
And although he has been worse in these past months—and for two and a half months since the beginning of this new recurrence or greater attack (which occurred at the end of the month of October)—he has felt better due to many applied remedies, both internal and external; nevertheless, the limbs remain resolved and powerless of motion, both the leg and the arm. The difficulty of speaking and the impediment to the faculty of memory remain in the same state; it has now been two months with a notable (as I said) weakness of sight, so that after proceeding through two or three lines of reading, his vision is always darkened.
These matters were reported and given to us in writing so that, if it were possible, we might wish to prescribe health-giving remedies for the stated conditions. Since these remedies cannot be chosen without first declaring both the essence of the disease and its causes, I shall therefore first begin to declare the unnatural conditions for their clarification, starting from the resolution or <term>Paralysis</term> which seems to trouble the man more.
Resolution or (as the Greeks say) Paralysis, is therefore a suffering of the nerves which arise from the spinal cord <note>original: "nuca"; a medieval anatomical term derived from Arabic, referring here to the spinal cord or the nape of the neck.</note>, as evidenced by the senses and by <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> in his book *On the Affected Parts*. And since the resolution is on the right side, and is a general suffering of that part, the injury will primarily be in the right part of the spinal cord. Nor is it a wonder among upright physicians that only the right side is weakened;

# E P I S T L E

Since the spinal cord <term>nucha</term> <note>original: "nucha"; a term used by medieval and Renaissance physicians to refer to the spinal cord, a word with Arabic origins.</note>, as well as the brain—from which the spinal cord has its beginning and origin—is divided into a right and left part by a visible membrane, and even though the "resolution" <note>In this context, "resolution" (resolutio) refers to the loosening or loss of function in the muscles, known today as paralysis.</note> appears in the external members, such as the arm, hand, leg, foot, and other limbs, the paralysis of these limbs is not the primary affliction. Rather, it is because from the head or the spinal cord, some matter, or a bad quality <note>In Galenic medicine, a "bad quality" refers to an imbalance of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>, or both together, proceed down to the lower limbs from a poor temperament of the head or spinal cord, or by some other alteration. These factors block the passage of the sensory and motor spirits <term>spiritus sensitiui, & motiui</term> <note>Medical theory held that "spirits"—weightless, fluid-like substances—traveled through the nerves to facilitate feeling and movement.</note> from the brain.

That this paralysis had its origin in the head is evidenced by the heaviness and weakness of the head from the start of its development, which has greatly troubled him for six years now. Finally, it is now the second year since he was first seized by paralysis, and most recently by a greater attack again at the end of this past October. This last attack was so severe that for two and a half months he was without speech and without movement in both the arm and the leg of the same right side. And although his internal senses <note>The "internal senses" typically included imagination, reason, and memory.</note> remained unharmed, he nevertheless could not remember.

From these damaged actions and other details, it is clear that the disease is a cold temperament with an abundance of phlegmatic matter <term>materia pituitosa</term> <note>Phlegm (pituita) was one of the four humors; an excess was thought to cause "cold" and "wet" diseases like paralysis.</note> in the brain. These cause obstructions of the spinal cord and the pathways of certain nerves proceeding from them. This is accompanied by a thickening caused by that same matter being absorbed into the area, which prevents the "spirit" from proceeding to the nerve passages and moistens the nerves. Thus, from both of these causes, the active power of the nerves is hindered.

This bad temperament, along with the matter, was able to be received even more on this right side because the passages on the right side are larger, since the right side is naturally hotter than the left. For this reason, when a great deal of matter was transmitted to this part, the "animal virtue" <term>uirtus animalis</term> <note>The faculty of the soul responsible for sensation and voluntary motion, centered in the brain.</note> was first made weak. However, all the "natural virtues" also appear weaker, such as the **attractive**, the **retentive**, the **concoctive** <note>The power of digestion or "cooking" nutrients.</note>, and the **expulsive** powers. This is because, due to the bad temperament and the presence of cold matter which prevents the proper passage of the spirit to the limb, the heat—or the healthy balance—of the affected limbs languishes. For that same reason, the "resolved" or paralyzed limbs wither away <note>The text notes that the limbs "become thin" or undergo muscle wasting (atrophy).</note>, as I have heard.

That phlegmatic matter is the material cause of this unnatural affliction can be easily proven, even in a "bilious" <note>A person of a "choleric" or hot/dry temperament.</note> body; and first, because in Germany...

->### FIFTEENTH<-

...lives in [Germa]ny, which is a cold region; and perhaps he also consumed heavier foods, as the **German nobles** do by eating fatty dishes, such as **butter** and other fatty meats which blunt the **natural heat** <note>In Galenic medicine, "natural heat" (calor naturalis) was the internal fire maintained by the heart that fueled digestion and life; excessive fat was thought to "smother" this flame.</note>. Add to this that, since he is a man most busy and of great labor, he could have rendered that natural heat weak through those many tasks. 

But that which could be the cause besides what was mentioned is that he was always prone to **Venus** <note>original: "uenerem"; here referring to sexual activity, named after the goddess of love.</note>, in which he wandered far; for immoderate Venus harms all the limbs, as well as the **brain** and the **stomach** <term>ventriculo</term> <note>While "ventriculus" can mean the ventricles of the brain, in the context of "crudities" and "after food," it here refers to the stomach.</note>. And this is because in the emission or evacuation of seed, we evacuate heat, or rather the **natural spirit**, and thus the whole body is cooled. This harm appears first in the brain and the stomach, since in those using excessive Venus, all the senses are made weak; they appear sluggish and effeminate, and so fixed that they can hardly sustain their own body, and they also age quickly. But the worst venereal embrace is that which occurs after food. 

All these things can only happen from cooling, but (as I said) the stomach and head are harmed first; thus **crudities** <note>Undigested or poorly "cooked" food matter in the stomach.</note> are created in the stomach itself, which continually evaporate toward the head and fill it. Within and from the head, all resulting operations are weakened, as can be seen in both the internal and external senses; and not only in the senses, but the inability of movement also shows this weakness of the head. 

Thus it is no wonder if he feels a looseness of the whole body from what has been said—namely, a bad temperament with matter communicated to the brain of the **spinal cord** <term>nuchæ</term>, and from the cooling of the natural heat, and from the resolution <note>Paralysis.</note> of a long-term disease. From this matter, both moist and cold, gathered in the brain and not dried out or dispersed due to the weakness of heat, there follows long sleep and damage to the faculty of **memory**, since memory is perfected by dryness <note>Physicians believed the brain needed to be relatively "dry" to retain impressions, like a wax tablet; excessive moisture made the "wax" too soft to hold a shape.</note>. That matter also descends to the nerves leading to the **tongue**, moistening them and prohibiting the proper passage of the spirit; this is the cause of his sluggish speech. From the same matter, vapors are raised seeking the nerves of the **eyes**, and when they move, on some occasion they darken the sight. 

And although the cure of confirmed **paralysis** has always been difficult, it is not yet such a difficulty that it takes away hope from every side, especially since the remaining virtues—namely the **vital** and **animal** <note>The "vital virtue" (centered in the heart) governed life and pulse, while the "animal virtue" (centered in the brain) governed thought and movement.</note>—do not entirely lack strength, and his age is also vigorous...

# LETTER

...and the time of year, since it is spring, is health-giving; and also because I hear he was doing worse previously, and at present (from the remedies already applied) he is doing better; and this is enough concerning the Diseases and their Causes.

Therefore, from what has been said, let these first be the health-giving remedies: namely, let him stay in a place where the air is of moderate warmth, yet exceeding slightly in dryness—much like the air in the first part of summer. Because such air may not occur naturally <note>The author suggests the local climate might be too damp/cold, requiring artificial intervention.</note>, but rather the opposite, let the chamber and the place of habitation be altered with fire from the best dry woods, such as **juniper**, **laurel**, **pine**, **fir**, **mastic**, **ash**, and the like, so that the air is thoroughly dried by artifice. Or let fumigations <note>The practice of burning aromatic substances to "purify" or change the quality of the air.</note> be made with rosemary, or wood of aloes, or with myrrh, or frankincense, and similar things; however, let him beware of fumigations that are too hot, since such vapors fill the head and produce heaviness and pain. Furthermore, if it is possible, before food let him engage in some light exercise, such as a light walk; but since he cannot stand on his own, let him be supported by a staff, or staves, or let there be a servant helping him. Or let him ride a horse if he can sit, or be carried in a carriage. But after food, let him rest and play pleasant games, such as **tables** <note>original: "tabulæ"; a family of board games including backgammon.</note> and **little soldiers** <note>original: "latronculi"; a Roman strategy game similar to chess or checkers.</note>, etc.

Let him also strive to have a daily evacuation of the bowels before food; if these feces are not passed spontaneously, let them be drawn out and led down by a **clyster** <term>enema</term> made from a decoction of betony, mallow, and beets, in which decoction you should add lily oil, common salt, and rose honey. Let him also beware of repletion <note>Over-eating or over-filling the stomach.</note>, both of food and of drink. The regimen of his foods should be that which is called "thinning" or "drying" <note>In Galenic medicine, "thinning" (attenuating) foods were used to break up the thick, sluggish humors thought to cause paralysis.</note>; wherefore first let him eat bread that is well-leavened and salted, in which there are seeds of fennel, anise, or cumin, and let it be very well baked. Let him use meats such as the flesh of capons and woodland birds, like partridges, quails, pheasants, thrushes, blackbirds, and the like; and for the meat of four-legged animals, let them be, for example, young kids, young hares, and similar, and sometimes veal. Let them be cooked by boiling or roasting, and let fennel roots boil with them, or some seeds—specifically fennel, anise, or cumin—or let them be seasoned with cinnamon, mace, ginger, pepper, and the like. All moist foods and those of thick substance are to be avoided, such as those from pork, lambs, and fish. Furthermore, all dairy products are to be given up, such as milk, butter, and cheese.

## FIFTEENTH

Likewise, all fruits must be given up, such as apples, pears, cucumbers, melons, pepos <note>A type of large melon or gourd.</note>, pumpkins, and the rest. Also to be avoided are citrons, lemons, oranges, and similar things; in short, all things that are cold, sour-tasting, or acidic are bad and very harmful.

<margin>A red vertical bracket or line is marked in the right margin next to the following paragraph.</margin>
For a drink, let it be water in which **sage** and **betony** have been boiled with honey and cinnamon; let the honey be one-eighth part of the water, and let them boil until a third part has been consumed. But if he cannot do without wine, let a small amount of white wine be given, diluted with the aforementioned decoction, or let it be diluted with plenty of water boiled with cinnamon and even peppercorns; let him beware, as we have said, of acidic things. But if at any time, for the sake of the palate, he wishes to season his food with things that add flavor, let this be done with cinnamon, mace, nutmeg, cloves, ginger, pepper, and similar things, adding a portion of sugar or boiled and skimmed honey. 

Furthermore, in the morning before food, let him eat preserved ginger root (which is commonly called "green ginger"), or preserved sweet flag root <note>Aromatic root of *Acorus calamus*, used for digestion.</note>, or galangal <note>A root similar to ginger, used in medieval medicine to treat "cold" stomach ailments.</note>. After lunch and dinner, let him eat anise seeds preserved with sugar, or fennel seeds, or pine nuts prepared with sugar; one should not drink after these. Let him sleep at night, and let the sleep be no longer than seven hours; nor should he begin to sleep until two hours after dinner. By no means is it helpful to sleep during the day, especially in the afternoon hours. 

Instead (as I have said), after lunch let him play pleasant games and rejoice with friends, and let there be conversations that can make the mind cheerful, or let him listen to musical instruments and sweet songs. He should also beware of the **venereal embrace** <note>Sexual intercourse.</note>; for among other things that most harm this condition is **Venus** <note>The author uses the name of the goddess of love to refer to sexual activity.</note>; indeed, she is more harmful than all others, and the damage she causes is almost impossible to correct.

And since the primary disease and the other unnatural conditions are "material"—that is, they exist together with cold "matter" <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, "matter" refers to the physical fluids or humors (like phlegm) that have become diseased.</note> for the most part, which one must reasonably believe has thickened over the passage of time—for that reason, this nobleman cannot be restored to health unless the matter, which is abundant, is first evacuated with suitable medicines; for this matter nourishes the primary disease and was also its cause. Suitable medicines for evacuation are those which can draw it out gradually and without distress through repeated use; once this matter is led out or evacuated...

# A LETTER

In that place, the bad temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, a "temperament" is the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile). A "bad temperament" signifies a chronic imbalance causing illness.</note> must be corrected as the primary disease. Thirdly, the affected parts must then be strengthened—such as the stomach, the head, and the remaining limbs, like the arm and the leg—and this should be done with appropriate medicines, both internal and external. First, therefore, it will be worthwhile to prepare the raw and thick matter <note>Referring to the "cold" or "phlegmatic" humors believed to be clogging the nerves.</note> for evacuation with these syrups:

> ℞ <note>Recipe, or "Take."</note> Syrup of betony: 1 ounce.
> Syrup of stoechas <note>A species of lavender (*Lavandula stoechas*) used to treat the brain and nerves.</note>: 1/2 ounce.

Let it be taken warm in the early morning at dawn; let him sleep for two hours afterward (if he can), then four or five hours later let him take lunch. If he also takes the same syrup three hours before dinner, it will help him greatly. Let him proceed by taking these syrups for several days until some signs of concoction <note>The "ripening" or breaking down of humors by the body's natural heat, usually assessed by observing the sediment in urine.</note> appear in the urine. > ℞ Lenitive electuary <note>A mild, honey-based medicinal paste used as a laxative.</note>: 1 ounce.
> Hiera of Galen <note>A famous "holy" bitter purgative recipe containing aloes, used since antiquity.</note>: 7 scruples <note>A scruple is a small unit of weight, roughly 1.3 grams.</note>.

Mix and let a potion be made from them.

Let it be given in the early morning at dawn; let him also sleep, if he wishes, for an hour after taking it. Then five hours later let him take lunch. On the following morning, let a cup of capon broth be given, or that of other excellent meat, with two ounces of rose honey to cleanse the stomach and intestines, and also to provide strength. For (as we have said) in a long-lasting illness, it is inevitable that the stomach is rendered weak; for that reason, I have made an effort to include in both the syrups preparing the matter and in the evacuating medicine those things which can strengthen the stomach. But since the matter is plentiful and cannot be purged in a single evacuation, it is necessary for the residue to be prepared once more. Furthermore, after these evacuations, or even while they are being completed, effort must be made toward **diversion** <note>The medical theory of drawing "bad humors" away from an affected organ to a different part of the body to be expelled.</note> from the affected sites, and the resolution <note>The breaking down and dispersal of a blockage or swelling.</note> of the matter which is in the affected limbs as the immediate material cause of the harm to those limbs. [paraly]sis has occurred, one must not for that reason desist from the things undertaken. Instead, my advice is to turn to other remedies which have healed many people in a worse condition. These are the drinking of **mineral waters** composed of sulfur and saltpeter, such as the thermal waters in the **Paduan district** in Italy. Not only will the drinking of said waters be of use, but it will also be very helpful to wash the **weakened limbs** <note>original: "membra reſſoluta"; in the medical theory of the time, paralysis was often described as a "resolution" or loosening of the nerves, where they lost their tension and ability to carry "animal spirits."</note> in them, and even to take a **shower** <note>original: "duciam"; from the Italian 'doccia,' this refers to the therapeutic pouring of a stream of water from a height onto a specific part of the body.</note> upon the head. Finally, one should place the weakened limbs in the **mud**, according to the order which I shall presently describe. 

And although, as I hear, he has himself used the baths which are in Germany, which were by no means able to restore him to health, the aforementioned Paduan baths are not for that reason to be neglected. Therefore, from the middle of the month of May, after the said **purgations** <note>referring to the internal cleansing treatments described on previous pages</note> have been performed, let him go to those baths which are in the Paduan district, to the waters of the place of **Abano** <note>original: "Aponenſis loci"; Abano Terme, famous since antiquity for its volcanic mud and hot springs.</note>. It will be worthwhile first to drink these waters for several days, and it will be necessary to wash the affected and weakened limbs in them, and especially the leg and the arm. Then the head, namely by receiving a **shower** over the **coronal suture** <note>the joint where the bones of the skull meet at the top of the head</note> of the head, where the **nape** <note>original: "nucha"; here referring to the start of the spinal cord as it exits the brain.</note> proceeds from the brain to the spine. 

But in taking the aforementioned shower, it must be noted that it is necessary to administer this shower upon the head for many days if one desires to receive notable and firm help from it. For in a long-term disease that is already **confirmed** <note>meaning the illness has become chronic and deeply rooted in the body's tissues</note>, it is not to be believed that the water itself can both dissolve the matter and reduce it to its former temperament, except through frequent and long-lasting administration; for even if it works through heat and dryness, these qualities are not excessively great. For this reason, let him receive that shower on the head for no less a time than the space of fifteen or twenty days. If he even administers it twice a day—provided his strength can tolerate it—the Lord himself <note>referring to the patient</note> will escape [this illness] better and more quickly.

After the shower has been administered for several days, if any paralysis still remains in the arm and leg, let the weakened limbs be washed again in the said waters. Also, let **mud** <note>original: "lutum"; therapeutic volcanic clay for which Abano was famous.</note> be applied to the weakened limbs morning and evening. This should be done cautiously, both on the arm and on the leg, lest perhaps from the excessive drying of the mud and the "resolution," the weak limbs be dried out too much. The caution in the application of the mud will be in the timing and the quantity, so that he does not stay in that mud for too long, nor should a huge quantity of mud be applied.

...[be done], but let all things be done with moderation. It will be well worth the effort to obtain the proper method of administering these treatments (as much for the drinking of the waters as for the bathing, the **showers**, and finally the **mud**) either from an experienced physician or at least from the local attendants. These are the people who daily experience the effects of those waters—in drinking, bathing, and applying the shower to the head—upon a great many people. I say this particularly regarding the quantity and the duration of time spent in the mud.

After the administration of all these remedies, I hope that the Magnificent Lord <note>the patient</note>, with the help of **GOD**, the Best and Greatest, may be restored to health; may **GOD** himself, in His ineffable goodness, deign to grant this to you.

However, I will not omit one thing: namely, that even after he feels well, or better, as a result of the remedies performed above, it is also worth the effort that he himself, for at least a year, should beware of all cold air and also of eating cold and moist things. Similarly, let him beware of the quantity and variety of foods, especially the drinking of various and sweet wines, because wine primarily and of itself harms the head, but harms the nerves indirectly <note>original: "per accidens"; a philosophical term meaning a secondary or non-essential effect.</note>; furthermore, a variety of foods generates many **superfluities** <note>excess humors or waste products that the body cannot process, thought to cause disease.</note>. Likewise, let him beware of excessive and laborious exercise, and also of long periods of idleness; and similarly of long sleep, and also of all disturbances of the mind, such as **fits of passion**, fear, anger, and thoughts of sad things. Let him also abstain from **Venus** <note>a common euphemism for sexual activity.</note> and from all other things which dissipate the strength and the **spirits** <note>original: "spiritus"; in medieval medicine, these were subtle vapors that carried life and sensation through the body.</note>. Finally, care must be taken for the evacuation of common superfluities from the intestines through the bowels and the urine. If the feces of the lower belly do not exit of their own accord, it will be useful and of great help to use certain **pills** that draw out the common waste of the intestines and also strengthen the stomach and the head. These include pills of **simple hiera** <note>original: "hiera simp."; Hiera Picra, or "holy bitter," was a traditional laxative made of aloes and herbs.</note>, hiera with **larch fungus** <note>original: "agarico"; used as a purgative.</note>, or **Mastic pills**, or **Alefangine pills** <note>a compound pill made of aloes, cinnamon, and other aromatics.</note>, and the like, which are effective (as we have said) in easing the belly and preventing raw matter from accumulating. And let these things suffice, given the shortness of time for me, who am most busy in visiting the sick. To the Praise of Almighty **GOD**.

# TO THE SAME MOST EXCELLENT
## Lord Paul Magnolus. Letter XVI.
### Concerning the emaciation, or wasting, of the entire body.

The reason why I have not responded until this day to your letters, which you wrote to me on the Kalends of July <note>July 1st</note>, most learned Magnolus, was partly because I labored under a fever for several days, and also because our Lord Ioannes Maria <note>John Mary</note> was away. Now, however, since I am in excellent health and he has returned, I have shown your letters to him so that he might read them, and I have heard his opinion on this matter; thus, I respond to yours. 

First, I rejoice that you have attained excellent health, and I praise the fact that you long for Venice—a place especially healthy for you, where you will lack nothing in the way of expenses so that you may live a "political" and "philosophical" life <note>A refined, scholarly, and socially engaged life</note> (if I may put it that way). I, my dear Paul, as Aristotle left written (by whom I have been taught), am very often accustomed to say: "To live is to be for the living" <note>original: "Viuere uiuentibus esse"; a philosophical concept suggesting that the essence of life is the act of living it well</note>, but to enjoy excellent and blameless health, and to be among the sons of men—especially the learned ones—is the fulfillment and perfection of those who live. 

Therefore, if this air in Venice was always safe for you, and that other air was disease-bearing, I do not know why I should not persuade you to set out for Venice, especially since you know you already have enough money from your income to suffice for the sustenance of those practicing philosophy, who are content with little. Nor do I believe (as you also know) that there are lacking here those who would gladly receive you as a teacher, both of good literature and of philosophy and medicine. 

I pass over the benefits of medical method and practice, or <term>therapeutics</term> <note>the branch of medicine concerned with the treatment of disease and the action of remedial agents</note> in healing; even if these are not so broad and generous among the youths who are newer to the city, there are nonetheless some, and they increase more and more every day, according to human industry and excellence. 

But regarding what pertains to your health, you ask whether it is beneficial to drink a decoction of <term>Indian wood</term> <note>original: "ligni Indici"; also known as Guaiacum, a resinous wood from the Americas used as a "wonder drug" in the 16th century</note>, or as they say, <term>Guaiac</term>, during these very hot times. You also ask whether it is worthwhile to sweat with covers applied and remain in bed after drinking, or whether it is more appropriate to rise and walk about so that the medicine may be better distributed throughout the whole body. # LETTER

->(since I was waiting for a milder temperature for its administration)<- it is better to rest. For although **natural heat** <note>In the medical tradition of this time, "natural heat" was the vital energy or internal fire believed to drive digestion and life</note> is excited in some way by movement, it is nonetheless also scattered and dissolved (so to speak) and becomes less powerful for its intended task; thus, for both reasons, the body is rendered weaker—namely, because of the movement and exercise itself, and because the heat is dispersed, even if the exercise was light. 

Nor is this medicine of such a kind that it lacks the power to open the passages and distribute itself, along with whatever is taken with it, throughout the entire body. Since it is primarily "hot" in nature and possesses a thinning power, it can conveniently induce both sweat and urine. Furthermore, consider that this drink is a medicine of **subtle parts** <note>This refers to a substance made of very fine particles that can easily penetrate the body's smallest channels</note>; it does not require the inflammation of our natural heat or any movement of the body to be brought into action, nor does it need movement to descend more quickly from the stomach, as is necessary for those who ingest a great deal of heavy food. 

Therefore, it will be better, after the potion has been drunk, to rest in a small bed and to cover yourself with suitable blankets according to the state of the weather and your own constitution. Nor would I wish, if you intend to drink this decoction, for it to be made perhaps from a larger quantity of wood or through excessive boiling—especially since (as you say) your entire body is already thinned, so much so that your flesh appears visibly diminished. I worry lest you fall into some irreparable wasting <note>The original term "tabem" refers to a slow consuming or wasting away of the body, often associated with atrophy or tuberculosis</note> from further drying of the tissues. Therefore, it is necessary to boil the <term>Indian wood</term> <note>original: "lignum Indicum"; refers to Guaiacum, a resinous wood from the Americas used widely in the 16th century to treat syphilis and other "phlegmatic" conditions</note> with a larger quantity of water, and it should not be drunk in such large amounts. 

Furthermore, you must beware of excessive and copious sweating. I would not wish for you to provoke it by any artificial means; rather, accept in moderation that which flows spontaneously without any external help. And although many people have become fat after drinking this decoction, it was not because this potion is inherently "fattening" in its substance. Rather, it happened because the **liver** <note>The liver was traditionally viewed as the primary organ of nutrition and blood production</note> was restored by the medicine, and the passages of the body through which nourishment travels to the limbs were opened. This made the attraction of nourishment to the limbs easy, and thus they became fat. This occurs primarily because there are two powerful virtues in this decoction that cause this task to be performed so well: the first is changing the liver to its best possible temperature, and the second is preparing the pathways for distribution so that they are not at all obstructed. 

But regarding that which you finally desire to know, and your question as to whether the anointing of the limbs with the sublimation and distillation of butter (turned into a liquid), with the addition of both musk and laven-

...marrow, and also with fragrant ointments, it can be usefully administered, so that in some way they may be able to help that wasting <note>Latin: *macies*, referring to the thinning or emaciation of the body</note> of yours through that anointing. I say that two things are primarily necessary in this emaciation <term>emaciation: the Latin *excarnatio* literally means "unfleshing," describing the loss of muscle and fat</term> of the limbs; first, the health of the natural organs, so that the best nourishment is prepared; second, the "pathways" of the limbs to be nourished, so that the preparation for them is made optimal in every way. Therefore, once you have confirmed the excellent health of the internal organs, if there is any impediment in the external limbs to their nutrition, that—or those, if there are many—must be addressed. Thus, the best nourishment will follow.

Those things which can impede the nourishment of the external limbs are, first and foremost, a **cold temperament** of the limbs, such that they cannot attract the nourishment or transform what has been attracted; also, some **obstruction of the pathways** preventing the passage of nourishment to the limbs. This happens either from some absorbed matter, or from an extremely foreign quality—whether hot, or dry, or whatever else it may be—that obstructs by condensing and thickening, or by drying them out too much. Consequently, neither a suitable quantity of nourishment is brought to the limbs, nor can what is brought be converted into the substance of the limbs. 

For this reason, in this case, I would wish first to diligently investigate these aforementioned causes, and then to apply contrary medicines and those rich in nature to the emaciated limbs as the opportunity dictates—presupposing the best substance and quantity of food and drink. Indeed, if you recognize the cause of the evil to be from the chilling of the limbs, so that the chilled limbs are not able to attract nourishment, in that case the best help will be to rub the wasted limbs in the morning after waking with hands anointed with **warm oils** that are not dry. Use not only oils, but also fats, among which are the oil of mature olives, sweet almonds, pistachios, and the fat of a hen or a wether <note>A castrated ram, often used in medieval medicine for its "temperate" fat</note>, and such things.

If you wish to add something scented, let it be something such as labdanum, amber, storax, mace, and the like. But in this case, besides what has been said, a **decoction of the heads of wethers** and their meat in water greatly pleases me, along with some portion of wine with betony, mace, and fenugreek seeds. The decoction should be boiled almost until the meat is consumed. After this boiling, all the fat floating on top should be collected, and first, by rubbing with the aforementioned broth...

# E P I S T O L A

...the limbs should be washed, then soon after they should be anointed with the aforementioned fat, remaining afterwards in bed, covered with cloths as the season permits, until the hour of lunch. It will also be best to do this before dinner, since in this way you will be able to moderately warm the chilled limbs, so that by this means they might be able to draw nourishment to themselves. This same method can contribute greatly toward overcoming the impediment caused by drying and constriction.

Nor do the many methods of illustrious ancient and modern physicians displease me, provided they are reasonable and you wish to use them moderately; among these, a decoction <note>original: *decoctio*, a concentrated liquor made by boiling medicinal substances—in this case, flesh—to extract its properties</note> of the flesh of suckling puppies is praised. From this decoction, the fat floating on the surface <note>original: *pinguedo supernatans*</note> must first be taken up, then the limbs should be washed in the said broth while rubbing them, and afterwards anointed with the said fat. This should be done in the morning before lunch, and in the evening before dinner; nor should those aids be neglected by which dry limbs can be made soft, draw nourishment moderately, and be warmed with a gentle heat. Such treatments include pitch-based liniments <term>linimenta picacea: medical ointments containing pitch or resin, used here to stimulate blood flow and provide "leui" (gentle) warmth</term> made from a large quantity of oil and a small amount of pitch, or an application with honey and other similar methods, together with a diet <note>original: *regimine cibariorum*</note> (as I said a little earlier), about which Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his works remained the gold standard for medical practice in the Renaissance</note> said much in Book 14 of *The Method of Medicine* and Book 6 of *On the Preservation of Health*.

And so let the body always be kept clean from superfluous and bad humors <term>humors: according to ancient medicine, these are the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which must stay in balance for a person to remain healthy</term> and nourished with suitable foods: which, besides providing excellent nutrition, also have the power to distribute that nourishment to the limbs. I wanted to repeat this point, because if there is an error in the diet, without a doubt the rest will be of little or no benefit; moderate exercise should always be combined with this. I would write more to you, were I not aware that I am advising a wise physician. Therefore, farewell, and strive for the best of health. Venice.

# TO LORD ULRICH STEYDLER.
# Letter XVII.
## Concerning many severe conditions: namely, the dripping of matter from the head, a cough with pus-filled and bloody phlegm, dizziness, blurred vision, pain and bulging of the eyes, apoplexy, and even the inability to move the legs.

**I** RECEIVED the letters which you wrote to me on the ninth day of November. Having read them while the messenger was waiting, I shall respond as briefly as I can to those matters which I see you most desire. You ask, first of all, that I might wish to write to you concerning what should be done regarding the unnatural conditions of a vigorous man of thirty-seven years. These are (as you write) firstly, a dripping <note>original: *destillatio*, a catarrh or downward flow of bodily humors from the head</note> from the head to the chest, caused by a certain evaporation from scorching <term>adustione: the medical concept of "adustion," where humors are "burnt" or overheated, leading to thick or toxic substances in the body</term> (since he is of a hot and dry temperament), which produces blood. Thus, a certain subtle matter descends to the lungs, which, however, is reduced to a complete suppuration <note>original: *suppurationem*, the formation of pus</note> during the night. 

By irritating him, this matter sometimes provokes vomiting before lunch and even after lunch, during which a great deal of that matter is cast out, accompanied by a powerful and difficult cough. You also write that he emits white and copious pus. Following this evacuation, these severe symptoms follow: namely dizziness, blurred vision <term>scotomia: a condition where dark spots or "dizziness with darkness" appear before the eyes</term>, pain, and a bulging of the eyes. However, this discharge of infected matter <note>original: *saniei*, a mixture of blood and pus</note> is not daily, but sometimes it happens that for two or three weeks he discharges no infected matter (which, as I hear, is white), and after the vomit has been cast out, it even associates itself with him. 

But another deadly symptom seems to arise from the retention of this kind of matter, and that is apoplexy <note>original: *apoplexia*; in this period, it referred to a sudden loss of sensation and movement, often believed to be a "stroke" or a blockage of the brain's functions</note>. During this symptom, he lacks sense and motion during the time that nature is laboring to prepare this kind of matter for expulsion. In this expulsion, besides the pus, a significant quantity of blood often comes out due to the rupture of a lung vein <note>original: *ruptura vaenae pulmonis*</note> (as you write). 

I cannot, most learned Ulrich, but praise everything you have done up to this day, both in the lifestyle regimen and in the medicinal remedies you have provided. However, I fear that things may turn out poorly, as I hear of such diverse conditions—all of which would demand a physician like Hippocrates <note>The author is emphasizing the extreme difficulty of the case by suggesting it requires the skill of the "Father of Medicine."</note>. But since you ask that I write my opinion to you on what should be done in the future, I shall write it briefly: namely, first, let the air be regulated so that in no way does the heat in it...

# L E T T E R

...should yield, but rather incline toward a certain coolness bordering on a balanced temperament, so that it is least likely to cause constipation. Instead, it should cool the blood just enough so that, once cooled, there is less evaporation rising to the head; it should also incline toward a certain dryness. For this reason, a steam room or a <term>hypocaust: an ancient Roman system of underfloor heating, here used to mean a sauna or sweat-bath</term> is by no means suitable in this case. Therefore, let the air be managed by other means, and since the man is strong, let him engage in some light exercise (specifically in the morning before lunch) and likewise in the evening before dinner. This should be light, however, and he should use massages in the morning before he rises from bed. These should be vigorous and continued for as long as he can tolerate without exhaustion, and the legs especially must be rubbed. 

But first, care must be taken that the bowels flow; if they do not flow of their own accord, use <term>clysters: enemas used to clear the bowels</term> into which "hiera" itself is introduced—specifically <note>original: *hiera logodiō*, a "holy" bitter purgative recipe traditionally containing various herbs and spices</note> *hiera logodion*, or *hiera pachii*, which Scribonius <note>Scribonius Largus, a 1st-century Roman physician to Emperor Claudius</note> wrote about, as it is of great benefit. He should sleep with his head elevated, and his sleep should not be long, nor should it occur immediately after taking food. The head must be protected from both excessive heat and cold. 

The foods, moreover, should be those which provide the most nourishment in the smallest quantity and are the least "vapory" <note>Early medicine held that certain foods produced "vapors" that rose to the head to cause dizziness or seizures</note>, nor should they be stripped of all dryness. Therefore, let well-leavened bread be given, not too heavily salted and moderately baked. Likewise, meats are better which are not too moist, such as those of certain birds—for example, partridges, quails, pheasants, and capons—and of small birds, such as blackbirds, thrushes, and the like. The meat of kids <note>young goats</note> is also praised, although the meat of adult male goats may trigger <term>epilepsiam: epilepsy or "the falling sickness"</term>. Fattier and moister meats must be avoided, such as lamb, pork, and the rest. I would also give soft-boiled eggs, for they nourish greatly and no significant waste remains from them. 

You may also give a dish of spelt, or of an egg beaten into a broth. You can also give him a barley broth—that is, with the barley first boiled in <term>chalybeate water: water in which hot iron or steel has been quenched, believed to have tonic properties</term>, with which seeds of purslane or myrtle are also mixed. All salted and sharp things must be avoided, as well as viscous things that stay too long in the stomach, such as cheese, butter, and similar items. I would also allow no wine whatsoever; if he wishes to drink beer, I would want honey to be boiled in it. But if he prefers a decoction of barley with honey, a small portion of ginger, and peony root, it will help in a wonderful way. However, let him beware of excessive drinking, and in other matters, let him be governed by the same logic. He who is thus guided by the said medical regimen...

For example, I would take one drachm of each, to which I would add rose-sugar and also flowers of borage, half a drachm of each. Thus, with myrtle syrup, I would create a mixture for him to use, both to make coughing easier and to stop the bleeding for a while.

I would also rub the exterior parts of the chest with oil of sweet almonds and fresh butter, one drachm of each, to which I would add one and a half drachms of Armenian bole. This is so that there might be less labor in coughing up phlegm. You will also give him <term>diadraganth: a medicinal powder based on gum tragacanth, used for coughs</term> with Armenian bole, or <term>diacodion: a sedative syrup made from poppy heads</term> to stop the flow of matter from the head. One must use these cautiously, however, because they make the matter thick; if that thick matter is then held back in the brain, it may block the passages of the <term>ventricles: the internal cavities of the brain</term>. From such a blockage follows that terrible and formidable <term>accident: a sudden medical event, likely referring here to an epileptic seizure or stroke</term>.

But since it appears the stomach is also not well-affected—for besides the mentioned symptoms, he is also troubled by vomiting—it will be best to rub the stomach region with a strengthening ointment. # L E T T E R

...(as has happened in these cases) should trouble a person, you must not neglect it, coming to his aid with appropriate remedies, so that you leave nothing un-foreseen and nothing without help; therefore, it will be your duty to moderate the treatment according to the current opportunity. Furthermore, many things change in the sick from day to day, which also changes the curative intentions.

Regarding the boy of thirteen years, who suffers from a lack of power in both legs preventing all movement, due to a <term>procatarctic: an immediate or external cause, such as an injury or exposure to cold, that triggers a disease</term> <note>original: "procatarticha"</note> or evident cause—specifically from washing with cold things—I would indeed first purge the boy with appropriate evacuations. Then I would wash him with baths made from a decoction of sage, rosemary, <term>stoechas: a type of wild lavender often used in medieval medicine for head and nerve ailments</term>, and similar gently warming herbs.

However, it is worthwhile to consider whether this evil has its origin from some affliction in the **spine** itself; for you know from the **knowledge of anatomy** that the nerves descend from the spine to the legs. It is also necessary to inspect whether the legs are contracted and dried out, or rather moistened and relaxed.

If the first is true, then softening and temperately warm things are appropriate, such as decoctions of meat—for instance, from sheep, wether <note>a castrated ram</note>, and the like—with certain herbs, flowers, and seeds added, such as mallows, marsh-mallow, sage, stoechas, and the seeds of **fenugreek**, bitter vetch, and similar things. From this decoction, you should collect the fat floating on top; with this, after washing the legs and stimulating them with a cloth, you should anoint the injured members, and especially the back.

If, however, the situation is of the second type—namely, if the cause was from some affliction of the **spine**—I would use a decoction of, for example, <term>ground pine: a medicinal herb (Ajuga chamaepitys) used for joint and nerve pain</term> <note>original: "yua artetica," a medieval Latinization of "Iva arthritica"</note>, sage, rosemary, costus, stoechas, chamomile, and betony in a potent white wine. ->now two considerations come to mind, of which the first is certain<-
intestinal pains from **thick matter** converted into wind.

[Let the fish] be scaly ones living in clear waters, such as trout, pike, grayling, and barbel; from the sea, let them be sea bream, barbel, sea bass, scorpion fish, dentex, moena <note>original: "menæ"; a small Mediterranean fish often pickled or salted</note>, and the like. These, however, are all "humid" <note>in Galenic medicine, fish were considered naturally cold and moist, which could cause an imbalance in the body</note>, and therefore should be eaten rarely, and preferably roasted rather than prepared in other ways, and sprinkled with spices such as cinnamon, mace, and the like. Or let there be dishes seasoned with cloves, which are praiseworthy and can be eaten, such as spelt <note>original: "far"</note> in meat broth, or eggs beaten into broth with a moderate amount of vinegar or <term>verjuice: the acidic juice of unripe grapes, used to balance "heavy" foods</term> and a little cinnamon to temper their coldness. 

**Panatella** <term>panatella: a traditional bread soup made by boiling bread crusts in broth with spices</term> is also excellent, or bread soaked in broth. Similarly, dishes are excellent which are prepared from borage, bugloss <note>an herb often used to "cheer the heart" and purify the blood</note>, fennel, and similar plants. Also excellent are hops <note>original: "lupuli"; likely refers to hop shoots, eaten like asparagus</note>, asparagus, and capers, even when preserved with vinegar and cinnamon. Sauces are also good when made from almonds, sugar, mint, ginger, cinnamon, vinegar, rose water, and similar ingredients; these are to be eaten with meats. 

After food, it will be best to chew pistachios, coriander, or anise seeds; but if before food—especially in the morning—a root of preserved ginger is eaten, I praise it most highly, for it strengthens the stomach and puts wind to flight <note>meaning it relieves gas and bloating</note>. Those true food items which are excessively humid should be abandoned, such as all fatty meats and those that are too moist, like pork, lamb, goose, duck, and the like. Similarly, all dairy products are bad, such as butter, milk (whether curdled or not), cheese, and similar things. Eggs that are fried or hard-boiled are also bad, as are vegetables like cabbage and other more "humid" plants; likewise all fruit, such as apples, pears, and other moist varieties.

That wine is praiseworthy which is neither sweet nor sour, of middle color, of good odor, not too potent nor watery, from which one should drink temperately. One should not drink before eating, nor after, but it is proper to drink often and in small amounts while eating. If the wine is too strong, let it be <unclear>diluted</unclear> with clear, sweet water—not from a swamp, nor having a bad odor or taste. 

Excessive **repletion** <term>repletion: the state of being dangerously overfull with food or drink</term> is harmful, and it is especially most harmful to eat too much at dinner. Therefore, let dinner be smaller than lunch. Care must be taken in the daily expulsion of superfluities, especially the feces and the urine. To this end, the consumption of things that make the belly easy for evacuation is helpful, such as broths taken in the morning with sugar, and dishes made of vegetables such as borage and bugloss, and also raisins eaten in the morning before food, because they make the belly soft. If evacuation is not made easy by these things, pills... <note>the text cuts off mid-sentence, likely continuing with a recipe for laxative pills on the next page</note>

# E V P A I I S T A O I L O A I G

...let those which they call "common" be taken, for they consist of two parts **aloes**, and one part **myrrh**, and also one part **saffron** with the best wine. Of these, let one be taken an hour before lunch, because besides the fact that it moves the fecal waste through the bowels, it also protects against **pestilential fever** <note>a general term for highly contagious, epidemic fevers, including the plague</note>. Before food, however, a light walk is beneficial, for it excites the **natural heat** <note>In Galenic medicine, "natural heat" was the vital energy responsible for digestion and metabolism; it was thought to "cook" the food in the stomach</note>, both for the expulsion of residual superfluities and for digesting the food to be ingested by stirring up that heat. Therefore, let no day pass without exercise, yet let it not be so much that it might dissolve your strength.

Sleeping at the customary hours also does much good and is praised. However, daytime sleep, **Reverend Father**, will always be harmful to you, for it fills the head and leads to **rheumatisms** <note>original: "rumatismos"; in this context, it refers to the "flow" of excess humors from the brain to other parts of the body</note> and to **catarrhal ailments** <note>illnesses caused by a "downflow" of mucus or cold humors, such as colds or respiratory issues</note>. But if by habit or some other cause—suppose because you did not sleep at night, or because the heat of the stomach is so weak that it digests food with difficulty—sleep is not denied altogether; but let it be brief, and at least two hours after taking lunch. At night, however, you must sleep as you please, for instance up to eight hours, but not less than seven.

Morning sleep is useful until the first hour of the day; excessive wakefulness certainly causes harm, as it renders all the powers weak. Finally, to be joyful and to be with dear friends is wonderfully beneficial; and therefore, sadness must be avoided, as well as anger, outbursts, and bad thoughts (since, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> said, they destroy the body and change it from its natural consistency).

If these things are observed, your **Reverend Lordship** may be preserved not only from the two aforementioned unnatural conditions but also from many others. If these conditions should occur (which God forbid), they may be aided according to their diversity. The first, which is pain of the intestines, if it comes from eating bad things or from eating too much, let it be treated in this way: First, one must abstain from bad and excessive foods; then, purge the belly with these pills, though first easing the belly with a common **clyster** <term>clyster: an enema, used to clear the lower intestines</term> with chamomile oil. Let the pills be taken early at dawn.

**Recipe:**
**Benedicta pills** <note>original: "pilularum de benedicta"; a "blessed" laxative compound popular in the Middle Ages</note>: 1 <term>drachma: a unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term>
**Alephangine pills** <note>original: "alephanginarum"; aromatic aloe-based pills used to purge the head and stomach</note>: 2 <term>scruples: a unit of weight, approximately 1.3 grams each</term>
Let 5 pills be made.

Lunch should be delayed for five hours afterward. After the operation of the pills, let the pained area be **fomented** <note>treated with warm, moist medicinal applications</note> with oil of chamomile or dill, or with a decoction of the flowers of chamomile, dill, fennel, wormwood, betony, and similar plants. Likewise, warmed cloths applied to the site of pain are appropriate. One must beware...

### Epistle 19. TO THE MOST EXCELLENT PHYSICIAN
### of Ancona. Concerning the painful affliction 
### in the right jaw of the Noble 
### Lady Joanna Landriana.

SINCE YOU HAVE WRITTEN to us in many and varied ways (as you say) concerning the **preternatural** <note>meaning abnormal or pathological</note> affliction of the Noble Matron, Lady **Joanna Landriana**, most learned Doctor: indeed, many things are desired for the perfection of information which can by no means be had at present; therefore, I shall reveal the matter itself from your **fragmented writings** <note>original: "mutilatis scriptis"; suggesting the case notes provided were incomplete</note> by reasoning and conjecture. You have (as you write) a Matron forty-five years of age, of an excellent **temperament** <note>the balance of the four humors</note>, which declines from a balanced state toward **heat** in its active qualities and toward **moisture** in its passive qualities (as you have from perceptible signs). At this age (for the most part), women are accustomed to cease from their **monthly purifications** <note>menstruation</note>; for this Lady, since it has already been two years since her monthly evacuations were suppressed, she has appeared to have fallen into a certain specific preternatural affliction of the right [jaw]...

->EPISTOLA<-

...namely of the inner part of the **jaw** of the mouth, and indeed a painful one, with a visible change in the color of the area toward redness but without any swelling. From this affliction, two natural functions are clearly impaired; for (as your Excellence writes) she can neither prepare food with her teeth <note>meaning she cannot chew</note>, nor can she even swallow comfortably. This evil has so far not been able to be cured by six hundred rational remedies. Indeed, most learned man, even if I have not personally inspected the patient nor even the affected part, I will nevertheless attempt to investigate the cause—or the disease from which this symptom of violent pain arises—based on your writings.

For with her menstrual evacuations failing—although I have not inspected her <term>temperament</term> <note>the specific balance of humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) unique to an individual</note> and age at the time—it is nonetheless at, or close enough to, the time in which nature is accustomed (as I said) to cease from this kind of evacuation <note>referring to the onset of menopause</note>. Truly, even if nature no longer evacuates that material as it used to, it cannot generate blood so pure that it is free from such **superfluities** <note>original: "superfluo"; waste products or excess humors that the body failed to expel</note> and useless blood. When this is retained alongside the good blood and is no longer expelled, very often many diseases and unnatural conditions arise for that reason, as **Galen** <note>the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium</note> testifies in the fifth part of his *Commentary on the Aphorisms*, [aphorism] 57, and the sixth, 28.

For when the menstrual blood is retained—partly because the power of expulsion has become weak due to the passage of age, and partly because the internal heat cannot **concoct** <note>original: "concoquere"; the process of "cooking" or refining food and humors into usable energy and blood</note> it as well as before—numerous and thicker superfluities are produced. Add also that women, since they exercise little and eat much, retain many superfluities in the blood for all these reasons. These are cold, yet mixed with some hot superfluities, first generated in the **liver** <note>original: "eptate", from the Greek "hepar"</note>, because somehow, through the <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "consensum"; the medical idea that distant organs could affect one another</note> of the obstructed passages of the womb, it does not prepare the blood for the other limbs as well as before, but produces it thicker. 

When this blood is attracted by the body parts and not properly assimilated—and especially by the head—its superfluities (which are primary, though mixed with hot ones) descend to the throat or to the jaw. They cause that violent pain, which, based on what has been said, can undoubtedly only arise from a disordered temperament. Whether the pain is localized or continuous there, I leave for you to decide. From these points, you can conclude two things: first, a bad, specifically cold, temperament of the **liver** <note>original: "iocinoris"</note>, evidenced not only by the things said above, but also by the long duration of the affliction.

->THE NINETEENTH<-

There is also a subsequent secondary cooling of the head, or rather the brain; if you were also to add the cooling of the entire body, you would not be in error. From these factors, it appears primarily that the disease lies in the <term>temperament</term> <note>the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, bile, and black bile)</note> of a corrupted liver; then, it affects the head and the whole body, from which follows the symptom of violent pain caused by a <term>distillation</term> <note>original: "distillatione"; in pre-modern medicine, this referred to a "dripping" or downward flow of excess fluids or "catarrhs" from the brain or upper body to other parts</note> of cold matter, mixed also with hot humors.

Whether the humor thus mixed and descending is salty or not, I cannot affirm at present. For a salty taste—according to the testimony of **Aristotle** <note>the Greek philosopher whose works on biology and physics were the foundation of medieval science</note> in his book *On Sense and the Sensible*, and **Averroes** <note>the influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> in his commentary—requires not only heat but also both moisture and dryness. If the Lady herself should affirm that she perceives such a taste, we would have no further question on this point. However, regarding what is visible to the senses—namely the red color of the affected area—I would say that because the place is red, there is a mixture of some hot humor, which also contributes to the intensity of the pain.

But the long duration of the affliction in that specific part, her age (at the beginning of old age), her sex, and other factors—since these are always accustomed to generating thicker **superfluities** <note>original: "superfluitates"; excess or waste fluids that the body fails to process or expel</note>—show me a dominance of cold matter. Therefore, I must necessarily conclude that the material cause of this affliction is cold matter by predominance, though mixed with some hot humors, as she possessed a hot temperament from the time of her birth.

Why nature has sent these superfluities specifically into the jaw, and the right one at that, and continues to send them daily, is not an easy solution to find. But considering the disposition or preparation of the receiving site—whether due to its inherent weakness, or because the paths and channels there are wider, or due to some other circumstance—it is easy to resolve the question. 

One thing, however, must not be overlooked: namely, whether—as is common in many painful conditions in our times—some hidden quality, beyond the manifest ones mentioned, has been contracted in such a diverse humor in the liver through some contagion. This is what they call an "epidemic" and the **French Disease** <note>original: "morbum Gallicum"; a common historical term for syphilis, which had recently spread across Europe in the late 15th century</note>. Indeed, since this disease is primarily constitutional, it does not show a manifest change in the patient (as **Galen** <note>the most famous physician of antiquity, whose theories on humors lasted for 1,500 years</note> said in the first book of *On Diseases and Symptoms*), but proceeds hiddenly. Thus, it may infect only one member while the others seem to remain unharmed. On this point, the discourse would be too long if I wished to write everything that pertains to the knowledge of this disease; but those signs which can easily lead you to the recognition of this disease, which in the earli[er]...

# E P I S T O L A

...[information] you will be able to have from the lady herself if you ask: from the past events that happened to her, and from her present symptoms, about which I wrote more extensively in my booklet on the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "morbo Gallico," a common name for syphilis in the 16th century, though here it may be cited for general pathological comparison</note>. Truly, let your excellence consider this for yourself, so that if you gain anything good from the things mentioned above toward the understanding of this unnatural and evil affliction, you will give praise to God, the Best and Greatest. Otherwise—since so many things have already been done, and done indeed according to medical rules—you have a difficult case on your hands, and one not without the risk of some future malignant tumor or even erosion of the bone in that area.

Having briefly previewed these points, one must derive the curative intentions as follows. First, having established the rule of the <term>six non-naturals</term> <note>the six factors essential to health in Galenic medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions</note> by their opposites: namely, let her beware of cold and damp air, and also of damp and cold foods, and of too little rest, and of over-filling [the stomach]; and let her strive so that the superfluities of the stomach and intestines are evacuated daily through a bowel movement. Similarly, let her beware of bad thoughts of the mind, and of all other things that can cool the body. 

Second, the <term>liver vein</term> <note>original: "uena iecoraria," the basilic vein of the right arm, which was traditionally believed to be connected to the liver's function</note> of the right arm must be opened; for although the affliction depends very little on a purely hot cause or matter, it is nevertheless not without an admixture of hot humors. Indeed, <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "uenæ sectio"</note> evacuates the abundance and malice of the blood, even in those who are cooled (according to the author <term>Galen</term> <note>the Roman-era physician whose theories dominated medicine until the 17th century</note> in his booklet *On Bloodletting* and as experience proves) and it is beneficial for extreme diseases, not only present ones but also future ones. 

Therefore, if her strength permits—since both her age and the time of year invite this, and there is a suppression of her menses—after the opening of the liver vein, I would also cut the vein of the right foot which they call the <term>saphenous vein</term> <note>a large vein in the leg; bleeding it was thought to "draw down" harmful humors from the upper body</note> as far as her strength allows. Thus I would hope, by first unburdening these members, to make them better, and to divert and diminish the matter. 

While these things are being done, let the remaining matter be prepared for evacuation with those things that can strengthen the liver, the womb, and even the head: and among other things, I recommend <term>syrup of betony</term> <note>a plant used historically to treat headaches and nervous disorders</note> and <term>syrup of maidenhair</term> <note>original: "capillis ueneris," a fern used for various "cleansing" medicinal purposes</note>, with distilled waters—for example, of <term>wormwood</term> <note>original: "absintii," known for its bitter, digestive properties</note>, chicory, and betony—or with a decoction of wormwood, betony, maidenhair, and similar things. In this way, I would wish to <term>ripen</term> <note>original: "decoquere," the process of preparing or "cooking" humors so the body can expel them</note> or prepare the matter for easy evacuation, and at the same time strengthen the members previously harmed. Thus, when the sign of <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "concoctionis," the stage where the body has successfully processed the "raw" harmful humors</note> appears in the urine, by reducing and frequently drawing it out with a light medicine, I might lead that matter out through a bowel movement. And since the matter is thick...
