(As I said) the condition itself cannot be drawn out by a single, and (as it were) eradicative evacuation <note>In Galenic medicine, "evacuation" refers to purging the body of harmful humors through means like laxatives or bloodletting.</note>: therefore I would wish to draw it out gradually, namely after some maturation <note>original: "coctionem," the process where the body "cooks" or prepares humors for elimination</note>, so that it may be lightly evacuated; and afterward, let digestive and preparatory syrups be given again, and again an evacuating medicine. The area should also be eased externally with rose oil, chamomile oil, and almond oil. Let there also be applied externally anodyne plasters, such as those made from barley flour, fenugreek, flaxseed, and chamomile flowers with sapa and waters of mallow and nightshade.

However, I will not overlook one thing: you must observe whether some tooth, poorly affected in its hidden roots, being perforated or decayed, might be the cause of this pain; or rather, whether a corrosion of the jawbone is infesting the internal membrane <note>original: "paniculum," referring to the periosteum or lining of the bone</note> covering it, which the great prince <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The famous 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina, whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook</note> calls <term>spina ventosa</term> <note>literally "windy thorn"; a historical term for a bone abscess or necrotic swelling that feels "hollow" or "windy" inside</note>. If you recognize either or both of these conditions in that place, the true local cure—once the general treatments have been completed—would be manual operation: either the extraction of the tooth, or the opening of the site of the bone corrosion and the <term>cleansing</term> <note>original: "mundificatio," the surgical cleaning or scraping of diseased tissue</note> of the bone.

Once all these things have been seen, done, and considered, if the pain remains stubborn (I frankly confess), I would wish that this lady drink a decoction of <term>Indian wood</term> <note>original: "ligni Indici," referring to Guaiacum or "Holy Wood" from the Americas, famously used to treat the "French Disease" by inducing heavy sweating</note>, with such a dietary regimen as she can tolerate. And since these things are written copiously in my short work *On the French Disease* <note>original: "de morbo Gallico"</note>, it will be your task (if it pleases you) to take the remainder from that booklet, which pertains to the perfection of the cure and, finally, to the strengthening of the previously affected limbs. These are the things, most learned sir, which I wished to write to you in this most difficult case, given the constraints of time. Farewell. 

Venice, the 9th day of April,

# TO MASTER JEROME
## Denemira of Arbe. Letter 20. On a bad condition of the stomach with its bloating.

**I**n recent days I received your letters, in which you describe having a stomach filled with much <term>phlegmatic humor</term> <note>original: "humore pituitoso," one of the four bodily fluids in Galenic medicine; phlegm was characterized as cold and moist, and its excess was thought to cause sluggishness and indigestion</note>, along with its bloating, and with frequent (though tasteless) belching, and also with much passage of wind through the lower parts, especially after taking food. For this reason, you ask that I be willing to send you healthy remedies in writing. Indeed, I—who have always followed you with paternal love—cannot fail to comply with your requests in a matter where I am able to help. But so that all things may proceed in order: first, since curative intentions for all diseases (according to the opinion of **Galen**) <note>the influential 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium</note> are drawn from the knowledge of the disease, and such knowledge is nothing other than the understanding of causes, I must first address the cause. Since wind appears continuously both through the mouth and below, I say that this occurs only from a "cooling" of the stomach, or ventricle, resulting from a decrease in its natural heat. 

As **Avicenna** <note>the 11th-century Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a core text for European doctors</note> testified in the 13th [chapter] of the third [book], saying: "when someone feels bloating and distension of the stomach after the ingestion of food, or before, and it does not subside except with belching, this proceeds from a cooling of the stomach." I can confirm this authority with several reasons. First, because the elderly, in the course of their age—even if they possessed a very hot temperament from the beginning of their generation—nevertheless decline into a cold and dry state. For to grow old is nothing other than the consumption of the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidi radicalis," the vital fluid believed to be the "fuel" of life, which slowly dries out as we age</note> and the dissipation of the heat. 

The result of this dissipation of <term>native heat</term> <note>original: "calor nativus," the internal warmth responsible for "cooking" or digesting food in the stomach</note> is that the elderly generate many raw materials, first in the stomach. Later, if these raw materials are drawn to the limbs of the elderly along with nourishment, they generate a kind of fatness. This is not true fat, however, but rather a certain fullness of that raw, phlegmatic humor. And although the natural temperament of the liver tends mostly toward the hot, it cannot, in this elderly age—in which (as I said) many phlegmatic materials are generated in the stomach—correct or entirely consume them, since at present it has become weaker, and there is also a greater quantity of material in the stomach...

<summary>In this letter, the physician diagnoses Jerome Denemira's chronic bloating and indigestion as a "cooling of the stomach" common in old age. He explains that as the body's innate heat and radical moisture diminish with age, the stomach fails to "cook" food properly, leading to an accumulation of phlegm and gas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Letter 20 to Jerome Denemira. The previous page established that the patient's bloating and gas are caused by a "cooling" of the stomach. This page explains the physiological mechanism of how "vapors" become "wind" and begins listing specific dietary and lifestyle changes (the "six non-naturals") to restore the stomach's heat.</meta>

[ventri]culo <note>The word "ventriculo" (stomach) began on the previous page; this is the concluding syllable.</note> are continuously present; indeed, the heat of the liver, by stimulating the expulsive faculty of the stomach, causes most of the windiness to be driven out through the lower part. For since the heat of the stomach (as was said) is weak, it is not regulated by the heat of the liver, but rather [the liver's heat] dissipates and dissolves it. While this [heat] acts in such a diminished state and does not resolve the matter, it converts it into vapors; these vapors, when they push themselves along, are called "flatus" or "wind," since wind is nothing other than driven vapors. That wind is produced by diminished heat is attested by **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the first book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Metheorum"; a reference to Aristotle’s work on natural phenomena, which Averroes commented upon.</note>. For in giving the reason why winds do not become strong or frequent in summer and winter as they do in other seasons, he says this is because in the excessive heat of summer, the thick vapors raised by the sun are dried out, burned up, and consumed. In winter, however, they are condensed by the coldness of the air, so that they can only be raised and driven with difficulty. Yet in other seasons, namely spring and autumn, the winds become greater and more frequent because the heat of the air is mild; thus it raises the vapors which, while they are being driven, become wind. 

This operation of heat also appears in the "lesser world" <note>original: "minori cosmo"; the concept of the "microcosm," where the human body reflects the mechanics of the "macrocosm" or universe.</note>—that is, in man. For if a man’s heat is powerful, it can consume all vapors; if it is less so, while they are being raised and driven, they cause stretching <note>bloating</note>, belching, and lower winds, as the heat is not strong enough to consume the <term>phlegmatic matter</term> <note>original: "materiam pituitosam"; thick, cold, and moist fluid that doctors believed caused blockages and sluggish digestion.</note> which is in the stomach and intestines. From what has been said, you can see that the bloating of the stomach arises from the cooling of its heat, partly from the passage of time since you are elderly, and also from the bad management of the <term>six necessary things</term> <note>original: "sex rerum necessariarum"; also known as the "non-naturals," these were the six factors physicians believed patients could control: air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, excretion, and emotions.</note>. For I hear that you eat many cold things, such as lettuce, gherkins or cucumbers, and fish, and other moist things like pork and fatty meats, and also a great quantity of butter. All of these things either diminish or blunt the heat. Furthermore, the lack of exercise, studying (especially after meals), and excessive wakefulness also fill the stomach with "crude" <note>undigested or raw</note> humors; if these are added to what was mentioned, they can all render the natural heat very weak. Having briefly touched upon these things:

->**Curative and preventative remedies**<-

I shall write these down according to the principle of contraries, since all diseases are healed by their opposite, just as health is preserved by its like <note>A fundamental rule of Galenic medicine: a "cold" disease must be treated with "hot" remedies.</note>.

The first thing that must be regulated is the air, in which it is always necessary to remain. Let the air in the home, therefore, be dry and warm, but...

-># LETTER<-

...[the heat] should not greatly exceed <note>This sentence completes a thought from the previous page regarding the balance of bodily heat.</note> [the proper measure], for coldness destroys heat, and humidity blunts and weakens it. Therefore, in winter and in colder or more humid seasons, a fire should be lit in the room, especially at night and in the morning hours; and in times of rain and foggy air, one should not leave the house, and a fire should be kept in the chamber perpetually.

The second thing to be regulated is food and drink, which require moderation in both quantity and quality. Therefore, bread should be made of the best wheat, well-leavened, salted, and very well baked in the oven, in which there should also be seeds of fennel, or anise, or cumin, or celery in a suitable but not excessive quantity. 

Meats should also be of the best quality, neither fatty nor moist, but rather leaning toward a certain dryness, such as the meat of the best birds and quadrupeds. Among these, the most praised are partridges, thrushes, blackbirds, large quails, pheasants, hens, capons, and the like; and among quadrupeds, the best are kid, hare, and young venison, since the meat of both old hare and old deer generates a melancholic humor <note>original: "humorē melancolicū"; in the theory of the four humors, black bile was associated with coldness, dryness, and depression.</note>. Veal, however, even if it is moist, is not entirely bad; it nourishes and produces excellent blood. Other meats that are moist, if they are eaten, should be seasoned with salt and fennel. Similarly, if fish are eaten, they should be prepared with salt, fennel, and other spices and seasonings; but botargo <note>original: "ouatarica"; salted and cured fish roe, valued here for its ability to "dry out" excess phlegm.</note> is excellent, as it can dry out phlegm. Furthermore, roasted meats are more suitable in this case than boiled ones. 

Cheese should also be avoided; if it is eaten occasionally, let it be old and salted, yet it is better to give it up entirely, as it generates a phlegmatic <note>original: "pituitoſum"; phlegm was considered a cold, wet humor that caused sluggishness.</note> and slow-moving humor. Soft eggs—either sipped, stirred into broth, or cooked soft and not hardened—are good with cinnamon or another spice, because they provide nourishment with little or no waste <note>original: "excrementis"; referring to the indigestible matter left over after digestion.</note>. 

All legumes <note>Beans, peas, and lentils.</note> are bad since they cause gas and also produce waste. Similarly, most greens are bad, except for certain ones such as fennel, dill, mint, rue, and celery. All fruits should be cut out of the diet except for pistachios, dried figs, olives, capers, cardoons, and similar savory items. Salads and dishes of hops, asparagus, capers, and sea samphire <note>original: "cretanomarino"; a coastal plant often pickled in brine.</note> are useful; similarly, seasonings made from parsley, mint, and almonds with cinnamon and ginger are beneficial in this case. Likewise, if after a meal one eats anise, fennel, or pieces of cinnamon preserved with sugar, they are most beneficial because they strengthen the innate heat of the stomach...

...and other spices may be mixed with the food, such as pepper, ginger, cloves, nutmeg, mace, and the like. However, care must be taken in their use so that you do not overheat the body with an excessive quantity; nevertheless, if their use is moderate, they will be beneficial by strengthening the heat of the **stomach** <term>ventriculi: the stomach was viewed as a vessel where food was "cooked" by bodily heat</term> and by dissolving windiness <note>gas or flatulence</note>, especially if they are combined and ground in this manner:

**Take:**
*   **Cinnamon**: half an ounce
*   **Cloves**: one and a half drachms
*   **Nutmeg, mace, zedoary, ginger, cardamom, galangal**: six drachms of each
*   **Spikenard**: one drachm
*   **Anise, fennel, black cumin**: five drachms of each
*   **Saffron**: two drachms

All should be ground together and kept for use with side dishes and other foods.

As for your **drink**, let it be the best wine—fragrant and clear, neither sweet nor sour, but of a middle flavor. If the wine is too strong and "winy," it should be diluted with water in which seeds of anise, fennel, or pieces of cinnamon have been boiled. The quantity should be moderate, since too much drink makes the food "swim" and also hinders its proper **digestion** <term>concoctionem: the process of transforming food into nutrients</term>.

The hour for taking the morning meal should be the **third hour of the day** <note>roughly 9:00 AM in the seasonal hour system</note>, because in the morning the stomach is better disposed toward the digestion of food, since after the night's rest the heat has been unified and is stronger for carrying out all natural operations. Supper should be lighter than lunch, because in the evening hours the heat has been scattered by the day's labor and is weaker than in the morning. A suitable time should be placed between lunch and supper, a space of no less than eight or ten hours.

You will note, however, that nothing is so contrary to good digestion as a **variety of foods** at one table, for the qualities of different foods often fight among themselves, and thus one prevents the preparation of the other. I could indeed, most learned man, write many other things about food and drink, but lest I detain you with a long speech and lead you to boredom, let these things suffice. From these instructions, you understand that the food for this condition should be that which contains much nourishment, inclines toward warmth, and does not produce much waste <note>original: "excrementi"; refers to any byproduct the body cannot use</note> or increase excessive humidity.

Furthermore, all overfilling must be avoided, as it produces thick humors, and one must strive for the **evacuation of waste**, both from the stomach and the intestines. Indeed, if the belly does not flow of its own accord, a half-drachm of **aloes** <note>a common plant-based laxative in historical medicine</note> taken an hour before food moderately loosens the belly, thins the phlegmatic matter in the stomach, and even [reduces] windiness...

# A LETTER

...it dissolves [the humors], and since the use of medicinal solvents that loosen the bowels dries out the body—especially the use of **aloe**—one may therefore use a **clyster** <term>clisteri: an enema used to clear the bowels or deliver medicine</term> in which, besides softening agents, those things which truly dissolve [the humors] are mixed. For example:

**Take:**
*   **Mallow, mercury-herb, betony, chamomile, dill**, and similar herbs; let them boil in common water.
From this decoction, **take**:
*   **Oil of chamomile**: one pound
*   **Common salt**: 3 ounces
*   **Red sugar**: 2 ounces

Let this be administered. However, one must beware of excessive **emptiness** <term>inanitione: a state of exhaustion from lack of nourishment or excessive evacuation</term> since it weakens the strength of the stomach; nevertheless, abstinence from food is safer than overfilling, because the abstinence from food is itself a form of evacuation. Thus, through abstinence, thick humors are often consumed. For this reason, it will be excellent to skip dinner once a week. Regarding **moderate exercises** to stir up the **innate heat** <note>the vital warmth believed to be fundamental to life and digestion</note> and for the expulsion of excrements, Galen is a witness in his book *On the Game of the Small Ball* <note>original: "de ludo parvae pilae"; a famous treatise by Galen advocating for exercise that engages both body and mind</note>.

For this reason, it will be best to walk for an hour or two in the morning before the midday meal, or to use some other kind of exercise, as it aids in the descent of the thick humors that are in the stomach. It also stirs the spirits and natural heat so that, through this movement, the passages of the body are opened and vapors can more easily escape; once the heat is stirred, the stomach may better **concoct** <term>conficiat: the process of "cooking" or digesting food</term> the food.

But after taking food, it is better to rest for some time (say, for two hours), so that the heat is not scattered from the center to the extremities through movement. By that reasoning, the internal power would be rendered weaker; also, exercise after eating causes undigested food to descend too quickly. Furthermore, you ought to know that although moderate exercise can be very beneficial, one should not use heavy exercise before the digestion of the food currently in the stomach is complete. Such exertion causes the ingested food to descend before it has been processed, since proper **digestion** <note>original: "concoctio"</note> is perfected through rest. 

**Sleep** must also be regulated because both sleep and wakefulness are harmful if they are excessive. Although wakefulness dries the body, it renders the [bodily] power weak, especially the digestive power; therefore, a somewhat long sleep is better than excessive wakefulness. Indeed, the heat becomes stronger when concentrated during sleep, and consequently, the processing of food and the expulsion of waste are better achieved. One must, however, beware of sleeping during the day and of that sleep which occurs immediately after taking food, because it fills the head with vapors, which afterwards unify and turn into 
-> watery <-
matter.

...turned into a watery state, they descend to the lower limbs, especially to the stomach, and render it more weak. The position of the body while sleeping also contributes greatly. Therefore, when you first lie down, it will be best to lie on your right side for two hours, because such a position allows for an easier descent of the ingested food; afterwards, it is suitable to lie on the left side, as it increases digestion by increasing the heat of the stomach, but it is far better to begin sleep upon the belly. 

Finally, the **passions of the mind** <term>accidentia animi: psychological states or emotions</term> help very much if they are good, such as joy, because it strengthens the soul and excites the **innate heat** <note>the vital warmth believed to power digestion and life</note>. For this reason, the divine **Hippocrates** said in the second part of his *Aphorisms* that in whatever disease, to be comforted in mind is of the greatest benefit, just as the opposite of this is most harmful. By the "opposite," one must understand sadness, which **Galen** said destroys the body in his book the *Little Art* <note>original: "parvae artis"; referring to the *Ars Medica*, a standard medical textbook</note>; and the prince **Avicenna** similarly said that if the passions of the mind are horrific, they hinder digestion. 

Similarly, bad imaginations and thoughts move the **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined health</note>, especially the melancholic ones. Furthermore, one should by no means read after eating, or ponder any difficult matter in the mind, since the **faculties** <term>uirtutes: the natural, vital, and psychic powers of the body</term> serve one another; while one is working, the others give way to serve it. Thus, while the **animal faculty** <note>the power governed by the brain, responsible for thought and sensation</note> is operating, the **natural faculty** <note>the power responsible for digestion and nutrition</note> does not work as strongly, since it is also serving the other. 

Let this be enough said regarding the **necessary things** <note>original: "rebus necessariis"; the 'six non-naturals' or lifestyle factors like air, diet, and sleep</note>. The regimen of necessary things having been so established, it is worthwhile to descend to medicinal remedies, since in great diseases involving matter, according to Galen's opinion, we also need the administration of purging medicines and the strengthening of the natural organs. Wherefore the body must first be purged at least twice a year—namely, in spring and autumn—and this with those things that draw out thick humors and can strengthen the stomach. Therefore, at the beginning of spring, it will be best to take this scheduled evacuation:

**Take:**
*   **Lenitive electuary** <term>electuarii lenitivi: a mild laxative paste</term>: 1 ounce
*   **Of dates**: 4 ounces
*   **Species of Hiera** <term>hiera: a traditional bitter purgative powder</term>: 2 drachms
*   **Species of Diaciminum** <term>diaciminum: a cumin-based digestive powder</term>: 1 drachm

Mix these, and with sugar let a **bolus** <term>a soft, medicinal mass intended to be swallowed</term> be made, and let it be taken four hours in the morning before food. This is a medicine that can, without violence, draw out the thick matters contained in the common passages, strengthen the stomach, and dispel gas. On the following morning, for the digestion of the remaining matter and for the strengthening of the stomach, let this syrup be given:

**Take:**
*   **Syrup of betony**
*   **Syrup of wormwood**
*   **Oxymel of rose honey** <term>oxymellis: a medicinal drink of vinegar and honey</term>
*   Equal parts: 1/2 ounce each.

Let them be dissolved with a decoction of wormwood and betony in fennel and hop waters. Let it be taken at dawn, and let him take lunch five hours later. 

In all these things, you may increase or decrease the quantity according to the responsiveness of the bowels and the tolerance of your strength. Once the evacuation is performed, as stated above, it will be best to use things that strengthen the stomach and all the intestines. 

Therefore, first, both before lunch and before dinner, let the region of the stomach be anointed, both on the right and on the left, and the entire belly up to the top with this liniment: 

**Take:** oil of wormwood, mastic oil, and oil of spikenard <note>original: "de spica"; a fragrant oil derived from the nard or lavender plant family</note>, half an ounce each; chamomile oil, 3 ounces; species of diagalanga <note>a compound powder based on galangal root, used for warming the stomach</note>, 1 ounce; species of triasandalum <note>a cooling powder made from three types of sandalwood</note>, half an ounce; a little wax. Mix and let a liniment be made, and use it as I have said. 

Furthermore, in the morning four hours before food, let one or two **lozenges** <term>rotula: a small, round medicinal disc or tablet</term> of this confection be taken: 

**Take:** species of diagalanga, 2 ounces; species of diacyminum <note>a cumin-based digestive powder</note> and species of triasandalum, half an ounce each; as much fine sugar as is sufficient. Let a confection be made into lozenges with rose water. 

And since this condition is long-lasting and cannot be removed except over a stretch of time and with the greatest effort—especially in an elderly man—it will therefore be worthwhile, in addition to the said evacuations, to use frequent strengthening and purging of the stomach. This you can do conveniently if occasionally—say once a week—you take one ounce or one and a half ounces of **alefangine pills** <note>original: "pilularum alefanginarum"; a common aromatic purgative pill containing aloe, cinnamon, and nutmeg</note> in the morning four hours before lunch. Pills of aloe, mastic, *hiera*, "blessed" pills <note>original: "de benedicta"; likely referring to *benedicta laxativa*, a standard laxative formula</note>, and all other similar medicines are also beneficial, as they draw out waste without distress and strengthen the stomach. 

And if there is a need to use stronger things, both for preparing and digesting the matter as well as for evacuating it, you may use compound **oxymel** <term>oxymel: a medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</term> with two or three roots, or even squill oxymel <note>honey and vinegar infused with sea onion, used as an expectorant or digestive aid</note> together with syrup of wormwood and a decoction of wormwood, agrimony, betony, and fennel. 

Truly stronger purging medicines are compound *hieras*, such as the *hiera pacchi* from the description by **Scribonius the physician** <note>Scribonius Largus, a Roman medical author of the 1st century AD</note>, the "Indian electuary," and other similar stronger medicines. I could have written many other medications, but since they have similar virtues, I wanted to omit them, lest by repeating the same...

### Epistle XXI. On water between the skin, 
### or dropsy.

<margin>P</margin> You write many things to me, Reverend Lord, which were done according to my opinion and have wonderfully benefited you, so that you may believe yourself to be healthy shortly, if I write to you those things which can be correctly administered in the future. Indeed, I cannot fail to satisfy your requests, but so that all things (as doctors say) proceed canonically <note>meaning "according to the rules" or established medical principles</note> and also so that you may communicate the matter itself with your most excellent physician, I will begin from those things which preceded. 

The case was presented to me thus: for when, from a long-lasting fever and also a bad <term>regimen</term> <note>a prescribed course of diet and lifestyle</note>, both dietary and medicinal, you had fallen into <term>water between the skin</term> <note>original: *aqua inter cutem*; a historical term for edema or dropsy</note>, and this from the greatest weakness of the liver <note>original: *iocinoris*</note>, so that not only the lower belly from the multitude of watery matter (with which there was also much wind) but even the entire body had swollen: namely the legs, arms, head, the face, and the chest area. 

All your limbs were raised into such a swelling that you could neither walk, nor stand on your feet, nor lie in bed, but could only remain sitting. Even that position was not without the greatest discomfort, since you were permitted neither to sleep, nor to breathe, nor to eat, or to perform other functions without the greatest distress. You had even come to that final remedy of a Christian man, so that after receiving the Eucharist you also wished to have extreme unction <note>the final anointing of the sick, performed when death is believed to be imminent</note>. Wherefore, even if many senior doctors...

...were present, I, having been summoned and seeing that everyone—both the doctors and the relatives—was without any hope of recovery, ordered first that the skin of the legs and hips be scarified <note>original: *scarificaretur*; the practice of making small incisions in the skin to drain fluid</note> with a lancet <note>original: *sagitella*; a small surgical knife, literally a "little arrow"</note>, not only on the shins and calves, but also in the parts of the hips. Once it was eaten, you wished to settle yourself down in your little bed and began to sleep. After that sleep, you were able to walk about. All these things are certainly worthy to be committed to writing, so that men may know how much medical ingenuity can achieve and prevail in diseases, even when hope is sometimes lost.

However, since being healed in this way does not remove the causes from every part—since Galen <note>original: *Gale.* (Claudius Galenus), the influential Roman physician of the 2nd century</note> said that a true cure is through the removal of causes, and this [treatment] was through the removal of the effect <note>meaning the doctor drained the fluid (the effect) but has not yet fixed the organ (the cause)</note>. Therefore, although many natural operations <gloss>operations</gloss> have returned almost unharmed, they are not yet altogether at their best or blameless, nor are they all restored. This is because that primary concoctive power <note>original: *vis concoctiva*; the liver's ability to 'cook' or transform nutrients into blood</note> of the liver <note>original: *iocinoris*</note> is still weak, so that it can produce very little good blood. This (as I said) is from the cooling of its natural heat; but that which is produced is for the most part water, or rather thin, watery blood. This cooling of the liver <note>original: *iecur*</note> has now been communicated to the whole body.

Therefore, both the liver and the other members need assistance so that they may be brought back to their proper temperament <note>the healthy balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note>. But first the liver must be treated, which cannot be done without a long duration of time and also the greatest labor, since the disease has now taken hold as a habit. Beginning with the <term>regimen of the six necessary things</term> <note>also known as the "six non-naturals," a standard medical framework of the time: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind</note>, I say that these must be the opposite of the disease. Hence, since it is winter and quite humid, one must strive to rectify the air by heating and drying it. You will do this conveniently if you keep a fire constantly burning in the room; for fire heats and dries the air more easily and better than other artificial things. Furthermore, one must beware of the night air, and the rainy or foggy air. For this reason, it is better to remain...

...stay at home, lest from the inhalation of moist and cold air the already mentioned bad temperament <term>temperament</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, the "temperament" or "complexion" was the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual's body.</note> of the body proceed to get worse. Furthermore, exercises are very beneficial, both because they stimulate natural heat and also because they dry the body; and therefore, walking in the morning before lunch leads to the warming of the body. You may also use some other kind of exercise, such as playing the game of the small ball <note>original: *ludo paruæ pilæ*; a popular Renaissance pastime and precursor to modern tennis or handball, often recommended by doctors for its aerobic benefits</note>, or something similar; and in summer, since the air is dry, you can freely leave the house and walk through sandy or rocky places until the body is tired, which will be very beneficial. Nor in any way can rest be useful for this ailment, since it moistens and cools the body and thickens all the waste products <note>original: *excrementa*; in this context, metabolic byproducts that the body has failed to "cook" or eliminate properly.</note>. 

Food and drink, if not properly administered, are very harmful, since they can cause great harm in diseases—both in terms of quantity and quality—especially when the matter <note>the morbid fluids or humors causing the illness</note> is of this kind. Therefore, first, let the bread be made from the best wheat, very well leavened, salted, and well baked in the oven; nor should the flour from which it is made be entirely clean of all bran, but it should certainly have some bran in it, into which should also be placed crushed seeds of fennel or anise, since such bread can both warm and dry moderately, and also nourish very well. 

Similarly, let the meats be those which nourish best, but are not too moist, such as pork and lamb. Therefore, drier meats should be chosen, such as partridges, thrushes, blackbirds, pheasants, capons, and hens; and of the land animals, the meats of kid <note>young goat</note>, young hare, and also veal are best. Eggs, and especially soft-boiled eggs <note>original: *sorbilia*; literally "sippable" or poached eggs</note> or those mixed in broth, are wonderfully praised. All fish are bad. Nevertheless, fish roe <note>original: *ouatarica*; likely referring to bottarga, or salted and cured roe</note> are excellent, but dairy products, vegetables, and legumes are very harmful, as they produce bad humors <note>original: *succum*; literally "juice," referring to the fluids produced during digestion</note>, contain many waste products, and are difficult to digest. 

Similarly, all fruits are bad, except for pine nuts and pistachios <note>original: *fisticos*</note> and sometimes almonds; all others, since they generate bad humors, [should not] be admitted. Capers are good, for they strengthen the stomach and open obstructions of the liver and spleen, and prepare the phlegmatic <term>phlegmatic</term><note>Related to "pituita" or phlegm, the cold and moist humor which, in excess, was thought to cause swelling and sluggishness.</note> matter for expulsion. You can also use, with the already mentioned meats, salted meats and "sauces" (as they call them) made of parsley, mint, and sage with almonds and ginger; and before food, it will be best if you take one root, or less, of preserved ginger, which they call green ginger. And after food, it is also very beneficial to eat seeds of anise, or fe[nnel]...

And since sleep does a great deal for perfect <term>concoction</term> <note>The process by which the body's internal heat "ripens" or processes the humors.</note>, it should be taken at night, two hours after dinner. It should be no less than seven hours long, nor more than ten, since excessively long sleep blunts the natural heat and cools the body. Similarly, sleeping during the day fills the head and generates <term>catarrhal</term> <note>original: *catarales*; referring to an excess of phlegm or "down-flowing" fluids that cause respiratory or joint issues.</note> illnesses. Therefore, daytime sleep should be avoided unless you did not sleep during the night.

When that appears, it will be best to take this medicine:

...let there be dissolved one ounce of Galen’s hiera <note>original: *hiera Galeni*; a "holy" bitter purgative powder used in ancient medicine to cleanse the head and digestive tract.</note>, one and a half <term>drachms</term> <note>original: *ʒ. i. He took this recipe from Galen’s eighth book *On Medicines According to the Parts of the Body*. It is the ultimate medicine for assisting both the natural organs <note>the liver and digestive system</note> and the vital organs <note>the heart and lungs</note>, and especially for a weaker liver. It is necessary to use it for many days in the morning, specifically before lunch.

I could have written many other things, Reverend Father, but I judged these to be sufficient; for if they are diligently administered, without any doubt, both the liver and the stomach will return to their former healthy balance. May God the Best and Greatest direct and keep you. Farewell.

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT LORD
## John of Ulm. Letter 22. On the weakness of the stomach, with colic pains, and ulceration of the kidneys and the neck of the bladder, with burning urine, and a very great quantity of small kidney stones, and also a stone in the bladder, with a continuous fever.

**I** HAVE RECEIVED the letters of your Excellence together with the information from the most Excellent Lord Aloysius Mondele <note>likely the patient's primary physician</note>, from which I understood the various unnatural conditions <note>original: *affectus præternaturam*; medical conditions that deviate from the body's healthy state</note> that you have suffered for a long time; the sequence of the report's words is as follows. A most excellent man, 38 years of age: of a hot and dry temperament, as clearly appears from the signs and operations of the heart and liver, even if the humidity of the brain and the coldness of the stomach—in which a great deal of phlegmatic <gloss>and</gloss> <note>original: *atq<gloss>ue</gloss>*</note> pituitous <term>matter</term> <note>original: *materia pituitosa*; thick, cold, and moist fluid or phlegm believed to cause blockages</note> is generated—work against it not a little. 

He suffers, I say, first from a fever without intermission arising from the putrefaction of bile <note>original: *coloræ*; yellow bile</note>—which they call a "notary" <note>original: *notam*; likely referring to a specific "known" or recognizable fever type</note>—putrefying within the veins, and ulceration of the neck of the bladder, along with stones of the kidneys and the most vehement pains of the colon, resulting from the pituitous matter generated in the stomach and transmitted there. Along with these there is frequent urination with most vehement pain, which for five years previously and now in the discharge of urine <note>original: *locii*</note> most often tortures him; yet this pain sometimes does not trouble your excellence at all for several days, in which urine there is seen a putrid and foul-smelling sediment of no small quantity. 

To treat these unnatural effects, a most learned man has administered many and most healthful remedies, not without the greatest relief, so that the pains have been for the greatest part removed; and although the sediment and substance of the urine at present appear praiseworthy enough, he nevertheless does not believe himself fully restored to health, so as to be safe from a relapse of the said unnatural conditions. For this reason, he asks of me whether a decoction of Indian wood <note>original: *ligni indici*; also known as Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," a resinous wood from the Americas used as a "wonder drug" for chronic conditions in the 16th century</note>, since it is a most healthful medicine for many difficult diseases, might also be able to preserve your excellence from the aforementioned things. To which petition I shall respond more easily if I first recall to memory certain things that pertain to the said unnatural conditions. I recall that I saw your no-
bility <note>This is a catchword: "bilita" completes the word "nobilitatem" (nobility/excellence) on the following page.</note>

->TWENTY-SECOND<-

...weakness (and it has been many years now) suffering from certain **hard tumors**, both in the shins and even in the lips, which arose after a long and difficult fever. When these were healed, there arose pains in the kidneys, the generation of small stones in the kidneys, pain in the neck of the intestine <note>likely the colon</note>, and even an ulcer of the neck of the bladder, with a frequent desire to urinate and most intense pain in the urinary passage. These unnatural conditions are accompanied by a **putrid fever** arising from the putrefaction of "spurious bile" <term>spurious bile</term> <note>original: *cholera notha*; a Galenic term for a fever that mimics the symptoms of a bilious fever but follows a different or irregular pattern</note> within the veins.

And since (as Galen said in his booklet *On Diseases*) those things which happen to us unnaturally are either diseases, or causes, or symptoms following upon diseases, I will first speak of the primary disease. From the events that preceded it, it is worthwhile to say that this disease is a **cold temperament** <note>original: *frigidam temperiem*; an imbalance where the body or organ lacks the necessary "innate heat" for digestion</note> combined with matter. For the conditions that occurred previously generated a significant amount of cold matter in the natural organs. Afterward, when cold abscesses <note>original: *apostemata*</note> arose from it, these matters were not generated except from the coldness of those natural organs.

Indeed, if one were to correctly examine those things which (at present) trouble your Excellency, he will recognize that the same cold matter is the cause. The pains in the kidneys are not vehement, and the small stones are not red but of an **ashen color**, which shows the presence of pituitous matter <term>pituitous matter</term> <note>original: *materia pituitosa*; a thick, cold, phlegm-like substance believed to be the raw material for stones</note>. Similarly, I say that the pains in the neck of the intestine arise only from pituitous matter generated in the stomach <note>original: *uentriculo*</note> because of its weakness. For indeed, phlegm, or pituitous matter, is first generated in the stomach due to its cooling.

Thus, it must be said that the whole explanation for these conditions is the aforementioned cold temperament combined with matter. While this temperament exists, the liver—which is **hot and dry**—is preserved in the strength of its heat. Furthermore, because of certain obstructions caused by the cold matter within the liver, its heat is increased and it does not preserve its native disposition. This results in a "diverse bad temperament," as Galen wrote extensively and most beautifully in his booklet *On the Diverse Bad Temperature*. 

This same diversity is attested to by the remaining symptoms: the whiteness and thickness found both in the urine and in its sediment, the burning during urination, and the fever arising from the putrefaction of spurious bile. For indeed, the whiteness, stickiness, and thickness in the urine <note>original: *lotio*</note> and its sediment denote a great deal of pituitous matter in the veins and the liver along with the blood. This phlegm, as I said, is generated in the stomach due to its cooling; however, the burning is caused by the overheating of the liver and kidneys...

Furthermore, all the ancient authorities affirm that phlegmatic matter is generated from the coldness of the stomach, and unnatural bile from the heat of the liver. This thick matter obstructs the passages; because this obstruction prevents "ventilation" <note>original: *euentatio*; the cooling process of the body, often associated with breathing or the release of vapors</note>, there follows a putrefaction in the humors. From this putrefaction, vapors are raised which heat the heart itself and thus cause the said fever. When this fever has lingered long in a body already wasted of flesh, it is not without danger that the heat impressed upon the soft substance of the limbs may turn into a habitual state <note>original: *habitudinalem*; likely referring to a "hectic" fever, which was believed to have settled into the solid tissues of the body, making it much harder to cure</note>, as we have often observed in similar cases.

From what has been said, it clearly appears that the primary disease is a **bad temperament** <term>bad temperament</term> <note>original: *mala temperies*; a state where the body's natural balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry is disrupted</note>, namely the cooling of the stomach and the over-heating of the liver. The causes of these conditions were both external and internal. The external causes were the improper management of the "necessary things" <note>the 'six non-naturals' of ancient medicine: air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, excretion, and passions</note>, and the internal cause was the weakness and inequality of the [vital] power due to the long duration of the disease, which generated the aforementioned unnatural matter. 

For while your Lordship is intent upon arduous and numerous affairs, and observes no rule in food, nor in drink, nor in proper hours, nor in movement, nor in the consistency of the air, all your powers are weakened. From this it happens that difficult, unnatural afflictions have arisen. And although particular pains—such as those of the kidneys, the colon, and the bladder—follow the specific ill-temperament of that organ, or a **loss of continuity** <term>loss of continuity</term> <note>original: *solutionem continuam*; a medical term for a physical break in tissue, such as an ulcer, wound, or fracture</note>, or both; since these depend on the previously mentioned diverse ill-temperament, they are in this case called **accidents** <term>accidents</term> <note>original: *accidentia*; symptoms or secondary conditions that occur as a result of a primary disease</note> of the primary disease. 

Nor does this contradict the teaching of Galen <note>the most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> in his booklet *On Diseases and Symptoms*. From these facts you may see that the pains, both in the back and in the colon, and even in the penis during urination, are "accidents" following the primary diverse bad temperament. And although Galen says that fever is a hot temperament in the heart communicated to the whole body, nevertheless, since it depends on the prior causes, it must be determined as being partly an accident and partly an essential disease.

...to be present not in the bladder but in the kidneys—and this is no small matter—for stones <term>stones</term> <note>original: *lapilli*; literally "little stones" or calculi</note> of significant size and in great number, generated in the kidneys, have been seen in the urine. For as I have heard, the stones were both large and uneven, so that they could have scraped the passage of the bladder. I would also add that the alteration caused by the sharpness of the passing urine, which changes the temperament of the area, can cause sudden pain. This is easily proven if one urinates when the area has not acquired such sharpness; for when the urine is not sharp, it exits freely without labor and without any pain. 

But since I hear of frequent urination, as well as pain and heaviness in the **lower abdomen** <term>lower abdomen</term> <note>original: *ſumine*; refers to the pubic or lower abdominal region</note>, I would believe that, in addition to the aforementioned conditions, there is a significant stone in the bladder. The reason which leads me to believe there is a stone in the bladder, besides what I have said, is this: because the primary disease is old and has generated a great deal of sluggish matter which afterwards descended to the bladder with the urinary matter; while it remained there for a long time, it was easily converted into a stone by the heat of the kidneys and the liver. Nor is it a sign that a stone is not present in the bladder if one sometimes urinates without pain, since I have seen many who urinated easily but in whom there was burning of the urine, and heaviness, and **tenesmus** <term>tenesmus</term> <note>original: *teneſmus*; a distressing and constant urge to evacuate the bladder or bowels</note>, and...

# AE P M O S E T O M L Z A D I V
<note>This header appears to be mirrored or "ghosted" text from the reverse side of the page.</note>

...since they could be healed neither by the medicines described by the ancients, nor by the waters of hot springs, the place was cut <note>original: *inciso loco*; a reference to lithotomy, the surgical procedure of "cutting for the stone."</note>, a stone was found and extracted, and thus they were restored to health. This happened last year in Venice to Lord Giovanni Peroto, who for many years passed urine with a foul sediment and a burning sensation during urination; yet very often it passed freely and without pain. Nor could he be freed from this condition by medicines taken by mouth or applied externally. 

Finally, since I judged from the heaviness and other signs that a stone was in the bladder, a surgeon <term>surgeon</term> <note>original: *opatore* (operator); in this period, "operators" or surgeons were often distinct from "physicians" and performed manual procedures like cutting for stones.</note> most expert in such operations was summoned. He cut the man in that place, and having found the stone, he extracted it; thus the man lives restored to health, and is no longer troubled by the burning of urine. Whatever the case may be, in this difficult matter one must consult men who have very often practiced this kind of cutting, so that the insertion of an instrument into the bladder might clarify the doubtful matter. Once that is clarified, learned Physicians <term>Physicians</term> <note>original: *Medici*; university-trained doctors who focused on theory and internal medicine rather than surgery.</note> may determine the remaining steps regarding the cure. 

You have, from what has been said, all these things explained: namely, first, the disease of the stomach and the various ill temperaments <term>ill temperaments</term> <note>original: *mala temperies*; an imbalance of the four primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—believed to cause disease.</note> of the liver. You have also the continuous fever, a disease in itself, even though it began from the previous causes. You have also the ulceration of the kidneys, the frequent urination with burning and pain, and the generation of many little stones within them, along with urine containing sanious <term>sanious</term> <note>original: *ſanioſum*; a discharge of thin, blood-stained pus.</note> and putrid sediment. Furthermore, there is the wasting away of the glandular caruncles <note>original: *caruncularum adenoſarum*; small fleshy or glandular structures at the neck of the bladder.</note> at the neck of the bladder, and the excoriation <note>Chafing or scraping of the tissue.</note> of the bladder neck and the urinary passage. 

These little stones are truly not red, because the matter from which they are generated is phlegmatic <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>original: *pituitoſa*; relating to "pituita" or phlegm, one of the four bodily humors, characterized as cold and moist.</note>. And although the ancients might indicate the location where stones are formed by their color, the reality is not always so; for white, lemon-yellow, and ash-colored stones have often been found in the kidneys. You also have pains of the bowel and the bladder neck arising from this phlegmatic matter. 

But as for what I said regarding a stone in the bladder—about which even a most excellent man was in doubt—the senses and the instruments of a surgeon expert in this matter will reveal the truth. All these conditions, since they are now long-standing <note>original: *inueteratæ*; chronic or deep-seated.</note>, make the cure most difficult, yet not impossible—especially if I rightly inspect the remaining factors, both external and internal, which contribute most to health in times of sickness. For, in the first place, the time of year is most healthful, as is the patient's vigorous age, the native strength of his body, and a prompt and ready will to do all things necessary to be restored to his former health, together with the most healthful remedies of the most learned and diligent Physician...

<center>### TWENTY-SECOND</center>

Through the continuous administration of remedies, all these things promise health even in the most difficult diseases, which physicians achieve through a contrary regimen <note>In Galenic medicine, a "regimen" was a controlled lifestyle plan (diet, sleep, exercise) used to balance the body's humors.</note>, involving both necessary lifestyle adjustments as well as medicines and manual operations. Therefore, after guarding the quality of the air, let the regimen consist of food and drink. First, all cold and viscous things must be avoided, as they are harmful to the stomach <term>stomach</term> <note>original: *ventriculo*; this term often referred to the entire digestive cavity.</note> and can generate phlegmatic matter <note>original: *materiam pituitosam*; according to the theory of the four humors, excess phlegm (pituita) was thought to thicken and form stones.</note>, unless the cause of a fever or some other urgent reason makes it necessary to provide cold things to extinguish an unnatural heat.

Therefore, fish and dairy products such as cheese should be forbidden, as well as dishes made from wheat flour, rice, and similar items. Likewise, sharp foods that provoke urine should be forbidden, among which are chickpeas and other legumes, or those prepared with pungent spices. Pastries made from eggs, cheese, and similar ingredients should also be set aside. 

The foods that are beneficial are, first of all, leavened bread that is moderately baked, and also excellent meats such as chicken, partridge, pheasant, thrush, as well as veal and suckling kid. Soft-boiled eggs mixed into meat broth are excellent. Furthermore, a dish made of spelt and almonds, and also of borage, bugloss <note>Bugloss and borage were common medicinal herbs thought to "cheer the heart" and temper the humors.</note>, and similar plants, is the best food. 

Wine should be moderate in color, flavor, and strength, so that its color is of the middle sort which they call "golden." Its flavor should be neither bitter nor sweet, but rather astringent <note>original: *stipticum*; an astringent quality was believed to "bind" or strengthen the tissues of the stomach.</note>, so that it can strengthen the stomach. If for any reason water must be mixed with the wine, it should be done using a decoction of cinnamon. 

Also, all overindulgence in both food and drink must be avoided, and one must strive for the daily evacuation of the belly's waste. If the belly does not flow of its own accord, use soothing enemas <term>enemas</term> <note>original: *clisteribus*; a common method for delivering medicine and clearing the bowels.</note> in which there is some power to ease pain, such as this one: 

**Recipe:** <note>original: *℞*; the traditional symbol for a medical prescription.</note> Take a handful each of mallow leaves, violets, poppy husks, and winter cherry seeds <note>original: *grana alkakengi*; the winter cherry or bladder cherry was specifically used for urinary complaints.</note>. Let them boil in common water until well-boiled. Afterward, take:
- One pound of the said decoction
- Two ounces each of fresh oil of violets and sweet almonds
- One and a half ounces of fresh butter
- Two egg yolks

Mix these and apply the mixture slightly warmer than lukewarm, so that it can be held in the belly longer. For besides the fact that it softens the belly and draws out the waste of the intestines, it wonderfully dulls the pain and the burning or sharpness of urine, especially if it is held for one or two hours. Sleep also, if it is moderate, greatly strengthens the stomach, and...

And to explain everything in a single word: it is a medicine for the whole body and a strengthener of all its powers. 

And since particular organs have many medicines that are specific and proper to them—and since different organs are affected and the specific afflictions are varied—it is necessary to consult the needs of the particular organ in addition to the general drink. It will be best for afflictions of the kidneys and bladder to provide every other day, in the morning hour along with the first drink, one dram of **winter cherry troches** <term>troches: small medicinal lozenges. Nor do I wish for Your Excellency to give up the eating of the best meats while drinking this decoction, nor the drinking of the aforementioned wine, diluted with the second decoction. This is because, as **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – 370 BC); his works remained the foundation of medical practice in the Renaissance.</note> used to say, "habit must be given its due." And also because in long-lasting diseases, a "thin" or meager diet is sometimes a grave error. 

The time for drinking the said potion should be **forty days**. When that term has passed, and after a short break of a few days has been taken and the patient's strengths restored, it will be best to seek out the **Paduan thermal springs** <note>The famous baths at Abano Terme near Padua, known since antiquity for their healing properties.</note> or baths. One should drink those waters and also wash in them, especially the parts and regions of the kidneys and bladder. Thus, from the drink of the Indian wood and the water of the Paduan baths, the stomach and the rest [of the organs] will be strengthened...

<page-num>119</page-num>
# THE TWENTY-SECOND

Having aided the [troubled] parts, safely and conveniently as your Excellence desires, on warmer days you will be able to drink the water of the **Calderian bath** <note>original: *balnei calderiani*; these are the thermal springs of Caldiero, located near Verona, famous since antiquity for their healing properties.</note>, and in those waters you can wash the poorly affected and painful limbs, and in this lies the last hope of health. But in all these things, some precautions are necessary, especially in the administration of the Calderian waters, whether drunk internally or used for washing externally. Indeed, since they are cold, the best precaution in the morning before you drink them will be to take one or two **rose-aromatic lozenges** <note>original: *rotulam... aromatici rosati*; a medicinal tablet or "troche" made with roses and spices intended to protect the stomach.</note>, and also to warm the region of the stomach externally with oils—namely **wormwood** <term>wormwood: *Artemisia absinthium*, a bitter herb used to stimulate the stomach and liver.</term> and **mastic** <term>mastic: a resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree, often used in the 16th century to strengthen the digestive tract.</term>—and with the fomentations and plasters described above.

And since you, a most learned man, also asked whether the administration of milk would be of use in this case, I respond—so that our letter does not fail in any part—that milk is in no way suitable at present. This is because, besides the fact that it is greatly harmful to those suffering from **putrid fever** <note>original: *febre putrida*; in Galenic medicine, a fever caused by the "rotting" or corruption of humors within the vessels.</note>, the use of milk also produces and increases **stones** <note>original: *lapillos*; small mineral deposits, specifically kidney or bladder stones.</note> in both the kidneys and the bladder, and it is very harmful for pains of the colon. And although milk is a most excellent remedy for ulcers of the kidneys and bladder, and for the ulceration of both organs, in this case it can in no way be beneficial, as it increases the stones which are one of the causes of the ulceration. But as I said above, it must first be investigated whether there is a stone in the bladder, as I believe there is; if one is found, only **extraction by incision** <note>original: *extratio per incisionem*; this refers to lithotomy, a hazardous and painful surgical procedure to remove stones before the age of anesthesia.</note> can cure it.

These are the things, most noble man, which I wished to signify to you in this letter for your health. Indeed, I would have written many other things, which I have deliberately omitted, because I see that your Excellence has a learned physician, both expert and most devoted to you, who in all things has conducted himself so that he has left nothing unthought of for your health. May that highest eternal God, author of all good things and giver of safety, direct all things so that you may attain your desired and original health.

->Farewell. Venice. 1546.<-
->The Third Day of April.<-

# TO APOLLONIUS MASSA.
## Letter XXIII. On the descent of the intestines into the scrotum, and on the tumor in the lowest part of the belly near the groin, and on the monstrous positioning of the testicles.

<margin>O</margin>I WAS INDEED HOPING for a much greater rest of both mind and body 
than what is currently granted to me, so that I might respond to 
your most learned **Johann Dryander** <note>original: *Ioanni Dryandro*; Johann Dryander (1500–1560) was a famous German physician and anatomist, known for his early public dissections.</note>—who is most dear to me 
on account of his uncommon learning, even though I have 
never met him face to face—to his questions, which are no less 
learned than they are excellently selected from a huge heap of problems 
and questions from the weightiest physicians, pertaining as much 
to theoretical as to practical speculation, until his mind reached 
tranquility. Since that is not granted to me at present—indeed, 
both because of the health of my body and because of medical 
business, almost no time remains for writing—nonetheless, I will 
endeavor to write in this narrowness of time those things which 
seem chiefly to regard the matter at hand. Therefore, if I do not 
adorn those desired questions and responses with the elegance of 
speech worthy of the man's dignity, and do not satisfy that most 
learned man in every part, I do not doubt that, once these things 
are known, I shall be excused by such a prudent man. I will 
therefore approach the business itself in a hurried manner: and first 
I will say what I think regarding the proposed case. Soon I will 
reply briefly to certain inquiries. The case is proposed thus: A 
certain learned and noble man suffers from various bad conditions. 
And first, from his tender years, on the left side, either from a 
rupture of the **peritoneum** <term>peritoneum: the original uses *sifaci*, a term derived from Arabic (*sifaq*) used by medieval and Renaissance anatomists to describe the lining of the abdominal cavity.</term> or a dilated **inguinal canal** <term>inguinal canal: the text uses *didymus*, a term that could refer to the groin, the testicles, or the passages through which they descend.</term>, through 
which the intestines are able to descend to the **scrotum** <term>scrotum: the original uses the term *oscheum*.</term> 
in the lowest part of the belly, he has a very troublesome **tumor** <note>In the 16th century, "tumor" referred to any swelling or growth, not necessarily a malignancy.</note>. 
And he also has, a little lower down around the groin, a tumor 
exceeding the size of a head, which previously had been the 
size of a goose egg, but soft and varying, which when touched 
feels like a **bundle of ropes** <note>original: *globi funium instar*; this likely describes the sensation of a varicocele or a complex hernia.</note>. And this is permanent. 
In addition to what has been said, he has this condition: that in the 
right side, no testicle is felt in the scrotum bound by a suspensory 
ligament, but rather on the left side, in the lowest part of the belly, 
touch detects the testicle, so that on the left side one may see both 
testicles: one, namely, which is in a bad state from disease...

[The patient] has one in the scrotum, and the touch discerns another in the lowest part of the belly on that same left side, so that two testicles are placed on one side. However, the most learned man <note>referring to Johann Dryander</note> persuades us from these writings not to believe this is a very great evil, since the patient himself is not only capable in sexual embrace, but has also procreated children of both sexes. For that most keen-eyed man writes that the former tumor has presently and gradually reached a weight of three pounds; with which there are no violent pains, though there is some pain, which is either from matter cast down to the place, or some part of the intestines descending, or from excessive drink or labor. 

This tumor, however, easily hides <note>recedes back into the body</note> if the patient lies on his back, in which dissolution of the tumor a gurgling and a certain rumbling is felt. In this case, the learned man seems to affirm two things from the accounts narrated above: one, the descent of some intestine; the other, a varicose <term>varicose: an enlargement of the veins</term> condition in the *didymus* <note>original: *didymo*; a term used historically for the spermatic cord or the protective membranes of the testicles</note>. 

Regarding the first, since it is on the left side, it is worthwhile to believe that a part of the colon intestine descends there. Nor can it be the *zirbus* <note>original: *zirbus*; an Arabic-derived term for the omentum, the fatty apron of the abdomen</note>, or omentum, since if the omentum has descended, it has no way to be raised back up as the intestines do, which, through contraction while one part moves, the remaining parts follow. Furthermore, if the ascent of the omentum after falling into the *oscheum* <note>the scrotum</note> were granted—which ascent all the illustrious ancients deny by its nature—I say even if it were granted, it certainly would not occur with gurgling and rumbling, since in the omentum neither wind nor water is contained within the matter, such that gurgling or rumbling would occur from its movement. 

It is otherwise in the intestines, as they are always filled with various moistures and also windiness. And lest there be any hesitation regarding the names, note that the Arabs call the *oscheum* the inner skin that covers the testicles, but they call the outer part the *scrotum* or *scortum*. The *didymus* indeed they call the suspensory of the testicles. 

Regarding the latter varicose condition: this is nothing other than the dilation and filling of the veins existing there, for there are many veins there nourishing and descending to neighboring parts, both inside and outside the *didymus*. Wherefore from these things it is clear that the second condition is a varicose dilation and filling of the veins existing both inside and outside the substance of the *didymus*; and since they are soft based on what was said, the filling itself is from blood that is not too thick or not particularly "earthy" <note>referring to the melancholic humor, which was thought to be thick and dry like earth</note>. For varices for the most part [contain] melancholic blood...

Nor was this the work of Nature shaping the body correctly, but rather of Nature erring. But if in that place there appears a cluster of swollen small veins or arteries, this should be attributed to a certain mild varicose condition.

Having thus declared these conditions, which the Latins call <term>ramices: an archaic term used for hernias or ruptured blood vessels</term> of the intestines or the groin, and "varicose," the cure is not easy, even though all the illustrious ancients teach how to treat them. For since the condition is not a single one, and the ailments are large and long-standing, they cannot be treated without danger; they possess great difficulty due to their complexity—namely, with which condition one should begin the treatment. Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire whose works dominated European medicine for 1,500 years</note> discussed this in the 10th and 11th books of his *Method of Healing*, and he mentions this same point in his commentary on the 16th [aphorism] of the first part of the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to Hippocrates’ Aphorisms</note>, and here and there in other books: that in complicated illnesses it is worthwhile to begin with the stronger or more dangerous one, or with the one which is the cause of the other, or that which, if not healed, prevents the remaining ones from being cured, and so forth. 

In this specific case, while the descent of the intestine <note>an inguinal hernia</note> seems to hold greater danger, and also by its descent hinders the treatment of the varicose condition, one might think the treatment should start with that descent. Nevertheless, in my opinion, a contrary order of proceeding will be necessary, and it is worthwhile to begin first with the varicose condition, since by beginning there we can heal both illnesses with a single operation. For the varicose condition cannot be healed in this man unless the skin is cut so that the swollen veins appear; these must be opened with an incising scalpel and all the blood contained in them must be extracted and emptied out. Then, one must most diligently cauterize the place and the cut veins with a "glowing iron" <note>original: *candenti ferro*; a traditional surgical tool used to seal vessels and prevent infection</note> (as they say), so that no opened vein is left behind.

There are some, however, who after the incision of the veins and the emptying of the blood, bind the vein with a thread <note>the surgical practice of ligation</note>, a device which pleases me immensely, since it undoubtedly protects against the flow of blood. For the flow of blood is often the cause of a notable evil, and sometimes it destroys a man. However, even after ligation, "cauterization" (as they call it) should not be omitted, since the healer achieves two goals from it. The first is the drying out of the varicose condition and the constriction of the blood:

The subsequent tightening of the *didymus* <term>didymus: in this context, the term refers to the "tunica vaginalis" or the protective sheath surrounding the spermatic cord and testicle</term> by cauterization is such that if the hernia arises from a loosened *didymus*, there is no doubt that through such burning and drying, the parts are united and the descent of the intestines is blocked. But before the varicose veins are cut, the site of the peritoneal rupture (the intestines having been pushed back first) must be carefully sutured. This method of suturing I have written about distinctly and clearly in my short book *On the Dissection of the Human Body*. Once the peritoneum is sewn, the operator should turn his attention to the varicose veins and open them; once they are cut and the blood drained, and the veins tied off (if he chooses), and the area cauterized with a glowing-hot iron (as I said above), the remaining upper skin should be sewn. Finally, let the final care of the site be pursued by applying medicines and waxes, first to stop [bleeding] and then for the remaining therapeutic intentions. This way, in my opinion, is indeed better and less dangerous, even though the Physician must proceed not without the greatest pain and risk in such cases.

And lest I should seem to have failed in a most necessary matter—namely, whether the testicle should be torn out in the aforementioned operation, as the empirics <note>unlicensed practitioners or "quacks" who relied on trial and error rather than formal medical education</note> do, or not—I respond to this doubt as follows: I say that it is always an evil thing to cut away the testicle, since, besides other significant disadvantages, masculine strength and sex are lost, according to the testimony of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine until the 17th century</note> in his *Short Treatise on Seed*. Therefore, if the testicles are healthy—which is to be believed, taking the evidence from his activities—[they should remain]. For I hear that he is not only potent in sexual matters, but has even procreated children of both sexes. This is also shown by the senses: since the testicle in the lowest part of the scrotum or "purse" feels healthy to the touch; indeed, by touching it, no diseased condition is detected. Therefore, in this operation, we must strive by no means to harm the testicle. But if some neighboring part should be corrupted, as seems possible from what has been written, whatever part that may be, let it be cut away, even if it were the testicle—since laboring on the other parts would then be in vain. # L E T T E R  IV

...in precisely the same method as is used for wounds of the belly involving an incision of the peritoneum <note>the thin, translucent membrane that lines the abdominal cavity</note>. For once the incision of the outer skin has first been made, one must suture the rupture. It is worthwhile to first make the inner edges bloody <note>This refers to "freshening" the edges of a wound—scraping them until they bleed to ensure they will knit back together during healing</note>, and then it must be sewn in the same manner as the wounds already mentioned: namely, by taking the *mirach* <term>mirach: an Arabic-derived term for the abdominal wall, including the muscles and fat</term> along with the peritoneum on one side, and leaving the peritoneum on the other. See this method of suturing in my aforementioned little book *On the Dissection of the Human Body* <note>Referring to Berengario da Carpi’s famous anatomical work, likely the "Isagogae breves"</note>. 

The protrusion of the navel and the groin can also be healed by cautery <note>burning the tissue with a hot iron to create scar tissue</note>, but in adults, neither of those cures is effective; and regardless of the age at which such an operation is performed, it will not be without the greatest danger. Let these things suffice, then, which pertain to the treatment of the proposed case. Now I shall proceed to the resolution of doubts and questions. 

First, in the descent of the intestines, or the *omentum* <term>omentum: a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines</term>, or fluid matter to the *oscheum* <term>oscheum: a Greek-derived term used here to refer to the inner layers or sac of the scrotum</term> or to the scrotum, one must notice whether only the peritoneum (or *sifach* <term>sifach: the Arabic term for the peritoneum</term>) is ruptured, or whether only the *didymus* <term>didymus: here referring to the vaginal process or the sheath of the spermatic cord</term> is dilated, or whether both the *didymus* is relaxed and the peritoneum ruptured at the same time. 

For if the peritoneum is torn, and the omentum, some intestine, or fluid matter has descended, it does not descend to the substance of the testicle itself in such a way that it touches it directly. Instead, it descends to the scrotum between the *oscheum*—which is made of the substance of the peritoneum covering the testicle—and the outer skin, which they call the scrotum. And thus, if someone were to cut the outer skin (that is, the pouch of the testicles), that which has descended immediately appears and is the cause of the swelling, whether it be the omentum, the intestine, or something else, so that it can be seen with the eyes and felt with the hand. But if it were fluid matter, it would continually flow out. 

Here you will note from the science of incision that, besides the skin where there is no fat, one must cut the *panniculum carnosum* <term>panniculum carnosum: a layer of tissue containing thin muscle, which Berengario identifies as a distinct layer beneath the skin</term> (or "shroud of the whole body") along with the skin. This is a part of the body unknown to the ancients, yet through my own diligence it is now very well known to all who are currently practiced in dissections. 

But if there were a relaxation of the *didymus* without a rupture of the peritoneum, those things which descend will reach the substance of the testicle and thus touch the testicle itself directly, without anything in between. Whether it be the omentum, the intestine, or other fluid matter, when the *didymus* is dilated, that which descends will go into the *oscheum*, which is said to be the covering of the testicle. It can happen, however, that a thin fluid, by way of "sweating out" (as they say), comes from the *oscheum* to the scrotum, so that once [the skin is] cut...

so that fluid may exit through the skin externally.
