The most learned man then asks whether, in ruptures where the scrotum has become hardened over the course of time, a physician striving to heal this condition through an incision should remove the testicle itself along with the hardened skin, or not. He also criticizes the treatment used by Alexander Benedictus <note>Alessandro Benedetti (c. 1450–1512), a famous Italian anatomist and surgeon</note>. I say (whatever Alexander, a man otherwise most learned, may have said—for it is not my place to find fault with the dead) that, as I said above, a physician ought not to act in such cases except insofar as he works to remove a thing that is against nature, without hope that it can be restored. Therefore, where there is an incurable *apostema* <term>apostema: an abscess or large inflammatory swelling</term>, or an ulcer, or corruption within the testicle itself along with skin that has been deprived of the governance of natural heat <note>the vital warmth believed in Galenic medicine to sustain living tissue; its absence implies gangrene or necrosis</note>, it is necessary to remove the testicle. But if none of these things are present, only the skin is to be removed.

Furthermore, as to the third point which the doctor raises as a doubt—namely, whether a *ramex* <term>ramex: a general term for a hernia or swelling in the groin; in this context, a hydrocele</term> which occurs from the descent of water into the scrotal sac can be referred to as a species of *hydrops* <term>hydrops: dropsy or edema; the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the body</term>—I say that this is true. This is evident from the name itself, as it can signify nothing else, and also from the material cause, or the "conjoined cause" (as physicians say). 

But if it be asked whether it arises from the same "efficient cause" <note>the primary force or organ responsible for creating the condition</note>, I respond that, although it is clear from what was said by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the foundational authority of medieval and Renaissance medicine</note> in the fourteenth book of *The Method of Healing*, there are nevertheless reasons to prove that watery matter can sometimes collect in the scrotum without any damage to the liver. This happens easily by way of sweating <note>resudatio: the seeping or exudation of fluid through membranes</note> through the passages from the intestines and other places, especially where moist foods have been eaten; the matter can descend and gradually collect there. Whatever the cause of its generation may be, this matter, seeping through the passages into the hollow part of the belly, can collect and finally descend to the scrotal sac itself.

But when it is asked: why did it cause more pain in a tumor of this kind when the swelling was much smaller than it is at present? (For he reports that while it was the size of an egg, the pains were greatest and most acute. Now, however, when it already exceeds the size of a human head, the pains are incomparably less and milder, so that it is almost without pain.) To this, setting aside questions of whether a "bad temperature" <note>an imbalance of the four humors (hot, cold, moist, dry)</note> alone, or only a "solution of continuity" <note>a physical break or stretching of the tissue</note>, or both together is the cause of pain—which is more consistent with the truth—whatever those causes may be, if we consider the causes of pain, no...

### FIFTH LETTER

...in another way they cause pains, except while they are active and (as they say) when they are "in the process of becoming" <note>original: *in fieri*; a philosophical and medical term meaning a state of change or development</note>. In the "completed state" <note>original: *in facto esse*</note>, however, there is no pain, according to the testimony of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> in his booklet *On Unequal Temperature*, and scattered throughout his other books. 

Therefore, when in those first days the matter that was descending changed the temperament <term>temperament: the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body part; also called "complexion"</term> of the limb—which was not similar to its own temperament—it caused pain. For an ill temperament has greater power in causing pain than a breach of continuity <term>breach of continuity: a physical tear or separation of tissue, such as a wound or rupture</term>, a fact which the illustrious ancients do not deny. 

Wherefore, once this kind of matter has entirely changed the temperature of the part, the painful quality that was caused by the ill temperament is diminished; what remains is only that pain which can be caused by the breach of continuity. Thus, if any matter continues to descend to the affected place (as is evident by the increase of the area), that matter is now similar in temperament to the affected place, or at least not far from it. Therefore, even if the swelling <term>tumor: used here in the classical sense of any swelling or localized enlargement, not necessarily cancer</term> becomes larger in the present moment, because there is no conflicting action from the descending matter due to this similarity, and because the physical tearing of the tissue is at its minimum during its development, the pain is less—even minimal.

Finally, he asks: why is it that in scrotal conditions of adults that began in their tender years, the diseased testicle is sometimes diminished, so that it reaches the size of a bean or a hazelnut, or even smaller, and is even pulled upward toward the belly, while the healthy one increases to the size of an egg? 

To this question, although many answers could be adapted, one in particular seems to satisfy me for the present: since the testicle, over the course of time, has been changed from its native temperament by the disease, it cannot attract nourishment according to its needs. Furthermore, certain constricting obstructions occur in the nearby passages due to the lack of nourishment. This results in a deficiency of nutrition, and consequently a drying out and shrinking of the limb. 

Because this drying occurs not only in the testicle but also in its suspensory <term>suspensorium: likely referring to the cremaster muscle or the spermatic cord which "suspends" the testicle</term>, the dried tissue contracts or shrivels into itself, thus pulling the testicle upward. In this way, because nourishment is not being drawn in, both the testicle and its suspensory are dried out. The other testicle, however, since it retains its proper temperament, attracts the nourishment prepared by nature for both of them; thus it increases to a larger size, so that it can sometimes reach the size of an egg. Indeed, there can be many other reasons why a limb might not be nourished, such as if the passages through which the nourishment...

Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Greek medical compiler</note> is also illustrious among the Greeks who wrote on this matter. For *Avicenna* said that enduring hunger fills the stomach with bad and putrid humors.

Sleeping a great deal is beneficial, since sleep strengthens the internal nature. For this reason, better and healthier bodily functions follow; but let it be done at the proper hours and in the proper quantity. For one should sleep at night, and that at least two hours after dinner; let the sleep be eight hours long and not exceed ten, yet it should not be less than six hours. Nor should it be during the day or at the noon hours, because it is very harmful and moistens the body, and thus will be **contrary to the ulcer** about which this discourse began.

To be sure, staying awake dries the body; however, because excessive wakefulness is greatly harmful, it is safer to abandon long vigils and sleep temperately. And since the greater part of health comes from temperate exercise, while rest makes the body sluggish, one must act cautiously here. For although exercise is beneficial by stirring up the heat, nevertheless movement is harmful and provokes the humors of the body to flow toward the downward and weak place <note>the site of the fistula</note>. Therefore, in place of exercise, let there be daily **rubbing** <term>fricationes: therapeutic massage or friction applied to the skin to stimulate the vital spirits without the strain of exercise</term> before food, first on the legs and arms, then on the other parts of the body. This would prevent such wastes from being sent by the intent of nature to the **ulcer** <note>the specific injury being treated</note>, where they might feed it and thus prolong its healing. This course of action would please me greatly, were it not that both reason and the authority of Galen in his book *On the Therapeutic Method* <note>original: *De arte curatiua*; one of Galen's most influential works on clinical practice</note> stood in the way.

For Galen said that one must turn toward the opposites and not draw [wastes] toward the site of the illness, because by such a method of evacuation, the malice of the ulcer will be increased. Therefore, as much as possible, medicines that draw out the body's wastes through the **lower channels** <note>original: *per inferiora*; referring to the bowels</note> must be avoided, as they harm the ulcer by pulling such wastes toward it. If any evacuation is necessary, let it be done through **vomiting** (if vomiting is easy for the patient). ## TO APOLLONIUS MASSA.
### Letter XXV. On Superfetation.

I shall now write to you about the matter I promised in those letters in which I replied to two of your letters received at the same time; although (as I judge) the matter cannot be explained without the greatest difficulty, since if I wish to look into the ancients, they wrote very few things, or things that were not clear in every part. Therefore, I have decided not only to explain those things which the most eminent Aristotle, and also Hippocrates, Galen, the Prince Avicenna, and other wise men wrote: but I also profess to add my own opinion on this matter, which is worthy of being known, as far as can be done by a very busy man. 

You wrote, therefore, that the most excellent doctor, Lord Giovanni Triandri, asked you by what means **superfetation** <term>superfœtatio: the rare occurrence of a second conception during an ongoing pregnancy, resulting in twins of different ages</term> can happen in a woman. This is a puzzle because, according to the opinion of Galen and other illustrious doctors, and from my own words in my booklet *On the Section of the Human Body* <note>original: "de sectione corporis humani," referring to an anatomical treatise</note>, the mouth of the uterus is closed after receiving the **prolific seed** <note>the male and female reproductive fluids as understood in 16th-century biology</note>, so tightly that not even the point of a needle could enter. Truly, the matter is not a marvel to a wise and studious man, if he is willing to hear what Aristotle wrote in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*. Moreover, man is a prolific animal for this reason: because there is some space in the uterus...

<meta>This page continues Letter XXV (identified as Epistola IV in this section's numbering) to Apollonius Massa regarding the medical phenomenon of superfetation. The author continues to explain why some species and certain women are capable of conceiving a second time while already pregnant.</meta>

<page-num>142</page-num>

->**LETTER IV**<-

it has the capacity so that, besides one, it can also carry other offspring, and even has nourishment present to sustain several. Since nature—wise and provident, and always intent on the preservation of the species as far as possible—recognizes this, she permits sexual intercourse in a woman even after impregnation. Although this is common to both horses and hares, they do not share the same underlying cause. In the case of the mare, she has acquired this through the firmness of the parts of the womb itself and the heat of her nature, which stimulates her toward desire because the burning blood is held back within the veins. For the mare does not have menstrual purgings of blood like a woman does.

In the hare, however, because it is a hairy animal and possesses much <term>waste product</term> <note>In the medical context of the time, "excrementum" or waste product refers to any leftover substance from the body's metabolic processes, including sweat, hair, and even reproductive fluids.</note>, it generates a great deal of seed along with those waste products. Thus, <term>superfetation</term> <note>The rare occurrence of a second conception during an ongoing pregnancy, resulting in a second fetus of a different age.</note> occurs, as the genitals are stimulated toward desire by the sheer quantity of seed. Since all hairy animals are stimulated to desire by heat, the hare undergoes superfetation for that reason—namely, the abundance of seed and heat—yet it cannot nourish the second fetus. Nor can anyone say that the hare is not a "hot" animal, since it is very fast and agile.

A woman, however, although she is a "hot" animal, has menstrual purgings of blood and a looser womb, which is far less firm if you were to look at the wombs of mares. Therefore, you will assign different causes for these various appetites of desire. From these points, it will be most excellent to conclude that superfetation in a woman arises from the suitability of the womb's location. Indeed, according to the opinion of **Porphyry** <note>A third-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the nature of the soul and the body.</note>, "place" is a necessary factor in generation, just as the father is; it also arises from the abundance of nourishment, so that she can nourish several offspring, since she is a hot animal.

For nature strives to move the woman toward desire for the sake of the preservation of the species through the procreation of individuals. Primarily because of this heat, you will say that those women are more prepared for superfetation who are hotter and firmer, such as those who have <term>choler</term> <note>Also known as yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors associated with a hot and dry temperament.</note> mixed with a sanguine temperament. These women have the exterior parts near the genitals hot, firm, and abundant with much hair, together with an abundance of seed—whether that seed be that menstrual blood, as **Aristotle** preferred, which I can hardly believe. I find it difficult to agree with him since the womb possesses manifest <term>internal testicles</term> <note>An early anatomical term for the ovaries.</note> and <term>seminal vessels</term> <note>Likely referring to the fallopian tubes.</note> originating from those same places, just as in a man. For menstrual blood is, for the most part, a waste product of the blood, and it does not [travel] through those vessels which are called "seminal" to the place...

...it is conveyed to them, but through other channels, as is known from the science of dissection: or whether it is <term>prolific seed</term> (as Galen said). Add also that those women undergo these superfetations more easily who have some space remaining in the womb even after conception; those [who lack this space or lack] the evacuation of blood are less suited to superfetation. <note>The author argues that physical space within the uterus and the body's management of "excess" blood are prerequisites for a second conception.</note> But the thing that keeps you more uncertain is the constriction of the womb, which (if I look at the beginning of the questions) hardly permits seed to be projected into it; yet even this does not bring us an unsolvable difficulty.

For, as Aristotle, Galen, Avicenna, and daily experience testify, very many robust pregnant women have an evacuation of menstrual blood. After this evacuation, they are better suited for superfetation because of the space [opened] in that location. This evacuation occurs in robust women because their nourishment is in surplus, so much so that the fetus does not need it all; for that very reason, they undergo superfetation and can even nourish a second fetus. The strength of the genital organ works together toward this intention through all its <term>natural powers</term>, namely: <term>attraction</term>, <term>retention</term>, <term>concoction</term>, and <term>expulsion</term>. <note>In the medical tradition of this era, these four "faculties" described how an organ pulled in what it needed, held onto it, "cooked" or processed it, and expelled waste.</note> Therefore, even if the overabundant nourishment is pushed out by the "expulsive power" of the veins acting at the proper time, it nonetheless cannot expel that which is in the womb but not yet ready for expulsion <note>i.e., the first fetus</note>.

Similarly (though it happens in a contrary manner), it is due to the strength of the womb and nature's inclination toward procreating offspring that the mouth of the womb may open during the time of intercourse even in a pregnant woman. While the womb descends during the friction [of coitus], it can receive the seed, and immediately afterward it is closed without any delay. Once the seed is received and the womb is wrinkled up—since the womb delights in the seed—this can easily occur.

As the "Prince" Avicenna said (in book three, chapter seventeen, section twenty-one), such women are fleshy, hot, and fat, as can be seen in the corrections by <term>Andrea of Belluno</term> <note>original: "Andrea Belunense." Referring to Andrea Alpago (c. 1450–1522), a famous physician and translator of Arabic medical texts who lived in Damascus and Venice.</note>. For these women have solid limbs that are not at all loose; they are of a sanguine temperament mixed with <term>yellow bile</term> <note>original: "cholera." One of the four humors, associated with heat and a fiery temperament.</note>. For this reason, they also have much hair (as I said) around the genitals, which is formed from the material of "smoky waste products" stimulated by heat. Sometimes, a longing for lust also happens because of the heat of the organ, a cause which is not foreign to what was said above.

But as to whether multiple fetuses require a greater number of <term>cells</term> <note>original: "cellulas." A reference to the medieval belief that the uterus was divided into several distinct chambers or "cells" (often seven) to hold different fetuses.</note>—as many moderns, ignorant in this matter, have written—this is a disgraceful and ridiculous question. The womb, always known through the sensory evidence of dissection...

# TO THE MOST LEARNED LORD
## Vincenzo Riccio, Secretary to the Most Illustrious Venetian Dominion. Letter XXVI. On the Calderian baths.

**Y**OU ASK, most learned Vincenzo—you who can by right and merit compel me—that I should write to you what I think about the **Calderian baths** <term>balneis calderianis</term> <note>The thermal springs of Caldiero, located near Verona, known since antiquity for their medicinal properties.</note>, from which you have very recently departed to travel to **Padua** <term>Patauiū</term>. You declare in your letters that you heard many things from the local inhabitants concerning their effects; because these accounts are not entirely consistent with reason, they keep you in no small state of suspense. Although you ask me to commit a difficult matter to writing—especially since the illustrious ancient Physicians left no record of them in their writings—I will nevertheless comply with your wish to satisfy you in some part. Hindered by many affairs, I shall begin the matter itself in a hurried style. 

The Gauderian baths, or as they are commonly called, the **Calderian baths**, gush forth in the village of Gauderio in the **Veronese territory** <term>agro Veronesi</term>, about ten miles from the city toward the east. They sit at the roots of certain small hills which are quite pleasant and delightful. As you have seen, there are two places where the waters that form the baths gush forth. One place is enclosed in the manner of a theater by a wall with steps; it is from this place that those drinking the water take their fill. The other, however, is open and protected by no fortification; it is here that those who require washing enter. These two spots are distant from one another by about as far as a man can throw a stone. The bottom of these pools is sandy, and the sand appears rusty <note>The "rusty" appearance likely refers to iron (ferruginous) deposits in the thermal water.</note>...

# TWENTY-SIXTH

...from which [the spring] does not gush continuously, nor in a single place, but in several; the water is cold or rather lukewarm, and it is very clear. In taste, it is not excessive, being neither sweet nor bitter, yet it seems to show a slight saltiness; if anything beyond what has been said is noted in it, it can be attributed to the odor and quality of **sulfur** <term>sulfuris</term>. This is, therefore, a clear mineral water (not obviously hot) springing from the sand. Its taste is neither sweet nor very salty, nor is it bitter, but rather a middle ground with some admixture of sulfur and a silty sensation on the palate. 

The **mineral vein** <term>minera</term>, however, from or over which it passes and flows, is undoubtedly for the most part **iron** <term>ferrea</term>, which is not without a small amount of sulfur and **nitre** <term>nitri</term> <note>In early modern science, "nitre" or "nitrum" did not just mean saltpeter, but referred to various alkaline salts believed to have cooling or cleansing properties.</note>. That the mineral and the places through which it passes and lingers are iron-bearing is attested by the **rust** <term>rubigo</term> in the sand itself and the mixed-in rusty pebbles, as well as by experiments performed by boiling. Indeed, after the boiling of the said water, a residue remains that is in all respects similar to **iron rust** <term>erugini ferri</term>. To confirm this, there is also what the inhabitants say: namely, that tiny fragments of iron are very frequently found mixed with the sand. 

We can also easily recognize that sulfurous and nitrous quality which I mentioned to be in the water through its smell and taste during vigorous boiling; for the steam shows a certain odor of sulfur, and if anyone tastes it, they perceive a slight flavor of salt. Since, therefore, it is water and passes over an iron mineral bed that is not devoid of sulfur and nitrous parts, no one who rightly understands the principles that constitute the nature of things could correctly say otherwise than that this water is, in the first place, cold. This is both because it is water and also because it has passed through iron-rich places and lingered there. 

Furthermore, this is not a pure elemental water, but an aqueous body which also contains something of the substance and power of the other elements. From this it follows that, besides being cold by its own nature in the first place, it has also acquired a notable **dryness** <term>siccitatem</term> from its lingering and passage through iron-bearing, sulfurous, and nitrous places. It also possesses from that same sulfurous and nitrous mineral part a sufficiently moderate heat, and moisture from the proper substance of the water. I would not want you to believe this impossible, since many other mixed bodies contain these diverse qualities, so that one and the same thing, through its different parts, is able to both heat and cool, and to moisten and dry—just as can be seen, for example, in the seed of **psyllium** <term>psilii</term> <note>Psyllium, or flea-wort, was often cited in medical texts because it was thought to possess paradoxical qualities, such as cooling the body despite its external "dry" appearance.</note>, which...

...seed is composed of different parts, namely hot and cold ones, which can be separated. For indeed, the part which exists as hot and dry in that **substance** <term>semine</term> <note>The author uses the Aristotelian concept of a "seed" or "generative substance" to explain how a single material can contain opposing qualities.</note> is the intrinsic, marrow-like substance. The exterior part, however—the husk, so to speak—is cold and moist. There are also many other things that possess a diversity in their parts, both in substance and in qualities (as can be seen in milk); nor are there lacking things which have different parts that can hardly be separated at all, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note> testified concerning vinegar and other substances. 

Therefore, since these things are clearly evident, I will not labor over them further. Nor should it be believed that this water possesses these diversities inherently, or by the very nature of its own substance, but (as has been said) they are acquired from its passage and stay in a hot and dry place, and from the mixture of another substance existing in the location of the **mineral vein** <term>minere</term>. And thus, by its primary nature, water is moist and cold, just as all natural waters are when they are without admixture. 

If they contract another quality, or multiple other qualities, these come to them **by accident** <term>ex accidenti</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature (like the heat in boiled water).</note> and from an external source (as **Aristotle** and **Averroes** <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" for his influential work on Aristotle.</note> stated in the second book of *Meteorology* <term>Metheorum</term>). For indeed, whatever water possesses besides moisture and coldness must necessarily happen to it by accident. 

That the **Calderian waters** <term>aquæ calderianæ</term> acquired their dryness by accident can be easily proven; for, as stated, the places through which they pass and linger display the nature of **iron** <term>ferri</term>, evidenced by the **rust** <term>rubigine</term> and fragments of iron found in them (as I have said). Furthermore, if you consider the odor of **sulfur** exhaling during boiling, and the taste of **nitre** <term>nitri</term>, there is no reason to doubt this matter, for both sulfur and nitre possess a remarkable dryness in addition to their heat. 

And since the portions of both sulfur and nitre in the mineral vein are not at all numerous, the water acquired a lesser degree of the "hot" quality from them. Nor do I believe you are ignorant of what Aristotle and Averroes said in the place cited above regarding the cause of the sea's saltiness—attributing it to the sun and celestial bodies. Since these factors do not apply to this water, I did not wish to recount them; for it is enough that it is likely that, from the aforementioned stay and passage, a great deal of dryness and a moderate heat have happened to it. 

Yet, the heat is less intense than it might be from the heavy mixture of iron, sulfur, and nitre in the mineral vein, even though water in the hollows of the earth can be heated by many other causes (besides the one mentioned): such as from the exhalation of some hot and dry vapor evaporating from the earth itself and mixed with the water, or from the movement of vapors and the shaking of winds in the hollows of the earth, or from the compression of some heat, or from the

But whatever the case may be regarding other methods of heating, I for my part would rather approve of the first: namely, that the water passing through an iron-rich place with a sulfurous and nitrous portion acquires an accidental dryness and heat through the mixing of vapors rising from the **mineral vein** <term>minera</term> and subsequently mixed with the water. This was the opinion of the most learned **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher and physician whose medical encyclopedia, the *Colliget*, was a standard textbook in European universities.</note>, and with him many illustrious modern authors. 

From what has been said, we hold that the **Calderian water** <term>aquam calderianam</term>—since it is water—is able primarily to cool, and all the more so because it has been strengthened by the mineral vein of iron; secondly, it can dry, yet not from its own power but through an accidental dryness acquired from the said iron mineral, and also from the sulfurous and nitrous portions. From these it also acquired the ability to heat moderately—that is, not beyond the human temperament—since there are not very many sulfurous or nitrous parts in such a mineral. 

And for this reason, it opens the passages of urine and sometimes induces sweat, and performs other effects of light heat, besides the fact that through its primary operation it moderately cools and exquisitely dries. With this diverse temperament, it possesses diverse powers and operations. For beyond the operations arising from the stated qualities, it is also of use for many morbid dispositions, with the exception of certain fevers; for it is beneficial for all long-standing diseases that arise from immoderate heat, and also those which come from excessive moisture not regulated by weak heat, or mixed with **bilious** <note>Related to yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with a hot and dry nature.</note> or salty humor. ...they call it **ringworm** <term>tineam</term> <note>original: "tineam"; literally "moth," used here to describe skin conditions that appear to eat away at the skin or scalp like moth larvae.</note>, as well as the loss of hair from the head and other limbs, and also **scabies** <term>scabies</term>, **leprosy** <term>lepræ</term>, and other infections of the skin of the body, such as early-stage **elephantiasis** <term>elephantiasis non confirmata</term> <note>A condition characterized by extreme thickening of the skin; "non-confirmed" suggests the early stages before the disease is fully established.</note>. For the aforementioned conditions, the said water provides relief, first when drunk, and then—if the ailment requires it—by washing the affected limbs in it, as I shall explain shortly. However, for those suffering from the **French disease** <term>morbus Gallicus</term> <note>original: "morbo Gallico"; a common historical name for syphilis, which was a widespread epidemic in Europe during this period.</note>, it is of no use at all, neither for drinking nor for bathing. For both drinking and bathing in this water have always been harmful to those patients. This is because the qualities of this water are not able to reduce the **matter** <term>materia</term> <note>original: "materiam"; in Galenic medicine, diseases were thought to be caused by physical "matter" or humors that needed to be balanced, thinned, or expelled.</note> of the French disease to a benign state, since they are too weak to resist the stubbornness of that matter; indeed, it is almost a contrary medicine if you choose to consider everything carefully. I could certainly enumerate many other similar illnesses and unnatural conditions for which both drinking and bathing in this water are beneficial, but since these can easily be understood from what has been said, I will deliberately pass over them, lest I trouble you with an excessively long discourse, and also because I believe I have sufficiently answered the first part of your letter.

As for what you say—that you feel either no benefit or an **excessive** benefit from drinking and bathing in these waters—this is no cause for wonder. Indeed, this usually happens in many cases, especially where skin defilements and leg ulcers have arisen which have troubled people for a long time. In such conditions, two things are primarily required for health. The first is that the internal and "sending" organs (if I may call them that, such as the **stomach** <term>uentriculus</term> and **liver** <term>iecur</term>) must be restored. The second is that the individual parts to which the **derived matter** <term>materia deriuata</term> <note>The waste products or diseased humors that have traveled from the core organs to the extremities.</note> has flowed—and which is not regulated by heat—must be strengthened, and the matter held within the limb must be consumed. These two operations in the external limbs cannot be completed except over many days, so that the restoration of the external limbs' defilements becomes visibly apparent.

I believe, for my part, that the internal cause has been removed, and that your stomach and liver have returned to their former health, since I hear that you have a better appetite for the food offered to you, and even that you have become **more potent in sexual matters** than you were before. But that matter which is in the limbs far from the **innate heat** <term>calor natiuus</term> <note>The vital heat believed to reside in the heart and blood, which powers digestion and healing; extremities like the feet were thought to be "colder" and thus harder to heal.</note> and weak (due to the delay and residence of that bad matter itself) cannot be dissolved in a short time, so that the limbs might be entirely freed from it and reach their former health and strength. For this operation requires the innate heat, nature’s internal instrument, which, coming gradually through the passages to those limbs, may resolve the matter—which it will undoubtedly do, now that the limbs no longer receive any more matter from the internal organs, which have been made healthy. Whence, or for whatever reason, the inhabitants say that the protection of the said water is often not perceived by the sick except after one or two months. Therefore, you should be of a mind to wait for nature’s fulfillment—which will occur without any doubt—nor do I see anything to the contrary when I choose to examine everything you write with care and accuracy. First, as I hear, you purged your bowels with **cassia fistula** <term>cassia fistulari</term> <note>original: "cassia fistulari"; a tropical plant whose pulp was widely used in this period as a mild, "cooling" laxative to clear the humors.</note>; soon after, you drank that water for several days, and then you bathed in it not once but many times. You also took both food and drink moderately and sparingly, and managed the **regimen** <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regimen"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to a holistic lifestyle plan—diet, exercise, sleep, and emotional state—tailored to balance the body's humors.</note> of other necessary things excellently. Thus, you might think that if any relief has occurred, it was from that moderate regimen. I, however, would say the relief was produced by both: certainly from the regimen, but even more from the power of the water you drank. It not only drew out many **irregular substances** <term>materias non regulatas</term> <note>original: "materias non regulatas"; refers to "unnatural" humors or waste products that the body's nature could not process or expel on its own.</note> through urine and stool, but it also tempered the internal organs by correcting them.

Furthermore, since you also used bathing in the said waters for several days, the external limbs were greatly strengthened; for this reason, I would say it is reasonable that you feel somewhat better more from the use of the water than from the regimen alone. Nor is this surprising in your case, since the same has been seen in many other diseases cured by this water: namely, that they could not be healed by drinking it just once. Instead, it was necessary to return to these **baths** <term>balnea</term> <note>original: "balnea"; refers to the therapeutic facilities or the act of immersion at mineral springs.</note> again and again. As they say, in major illnesses, taking it once provides some benefit but does not heal entirely; however, if they drink it again the following year, they acquire the very best health. There have even been some with similar long-standing conditions who used the drinking and bathing of that water for many years, and were finally restored to health in a miraculous and excellent way. 

Moreover, in this use of the water—both for drinking and bathing—you have observed everything that the power and unnatural states required. Indeed, thus do **illustrious Physicians** <term>illustres Medici</term> <note>original: "illustres Medici"; a respectful nod to the medical authorities and practitioners who followed the Galenic tradition of individualized treatment.</note> prescribe for other similar ailments, so that they order different things to be administered in different ways according to the diversity of the patient and the morbid condition. All these things—regarding the use of the waters as well as the conditions they cure—I shall write down for you individually in a certain order to satisfy you and reduce them to a rational practice. For if anyone desires to be cured by this water of any of the aforementioned unnatural conditions...

...cured, first of all before he drinks that water—if it should be necessary to drink it—or before entering the bath, if it is necessary to wash in that water, it is worthwhile to lower the belly with some light medicines and to evacuate the **common superfluities** <term>superfluitates communes</term> <note>In the medical theory of the time, "superfluities" were waste products or excess humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that needed to be cleared to prevent the mineral water from "trapping" them in the body.</note> (as the Physicians say). For example: if there should be an ailment in the chest, or the **liver** <term>iocinore</term>, or the kidneys, or the bladder, let an evacuation of the bowels be made with **cassia fistula** <term>cassia fistulari</term> <note>original: "cassia fistulari"; a mild, cooling laxative made from the pulp of the "pudding-pipe tree."</note>, or with a similar light medicine. But if the **spleen** <term>lien</term> suffers, let it be evacuated with a **lenitive electuary** <term>electuario lenitiuo</term> <note>A medicinal paste or syrup made by mixing powders with honey or sugar, designed to "soothe" or soften the bowels.</note>, or with **diasena** <term>diasena</term> <note>A compound medicine based on senna leaves, known for its laxative properties.</note>, or with another medicine suitable for it. Similarly, if the stomach suffers, let him use for evacuation **diacatholicon** <term>diacatolicone</term> <note>A "universal" or "general" purgative intended to cleanse all the humors of the body.</note> with the **hiera of Galen** <term>hiera Galeni</term> <note>A famous, ancient "holy" (hiera) bitter remedy used to purge the head and digestive system.</note> and light medicines of this kind.

If the person suffers from the **itch** <term>scabiosus</term> <note>likely referring to scabies or general skin eruptions</note>, or has some other defilement of the skin, let him be evacuated in the same way—namely with the lenitive electuary, or with cassia fistula, and the rest which serve to evacuate humors mixed from bile and phlegm, or from salty phlegm. To these, **rhubarb** <term>rabarbarum</term> can be added, especially if there is a flow of blood, either from the veins of the seat—which they call **hemorrhoids** <term>emorrhoidas</term>—or from the uterus in women. Once this purgation is done, let the sick person begin to drink the water of the aforementioned bath from the **spring enclosed by a wall**; for in the other spring, which is not surrounded by a wall, beasts drink, and those with the itch and those who have ulcers wash themselves. Because it is therefore unclean, I do not recommend drinking it. 

As I said above, this water is most beneficial to those in whom the **liver** <term>iecur</term> has become overheated, from which overheating a burning of the urine often occurs. Similarly, it benefits overheated kidneys and ulcers of the neck of the bladder, if they have arisen from the already mentioned overheating of both the liver and the kidneys. 

The suitable time for drinking this water and washing in it is summer—specifically after the middle of the month of June until the middle of the month of August, or even until the end, because in this time the days are hottest and driest; for the sky, due to the directness and stay of the sun above the earth, heats the air the most. In cold or tepid times, however, this drink is not in use, nor if there should be rains during the summer time. Furthermore, if the said water is drunk immediately when taken from the spring itself—if it can be done—it will work more strongly and better; and on the contrary, if it remains for any notable time after it has been taken from its own spring, its operation will be weaker and not so effective. For the **virtue and property** <term>uirtus, & proprietas</term> <note>The specific "healing power" believed to be inherent in the mineral composition (the "mineral vein") of the water.</note> which it holds from the **mineral vein** <term>minera</term> is greatly diminished after some time...

# LETTER

If it has been removed from its proper place, its **acquired virtue** <term>uirtus aquisita</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance science, "virtue" refers to the inherent power or medicinal property of a substance. An "acquired" virtue is one gained from its environment—in this case, the minerals it passes through.</note>—which consists of a manifest dryness and tempered heat—easily vanishes if it remains for a long time outside its own **source** <term>mineram</term>. For this reason, it will be less beneficial and will work more weakly if, for example, it is carried away to some distant place or to another region. I have said that it possesses a weaker power in such a case, yet I do not say that it does not work at all; for although outside its own place it loses a part of its **accidental virtue** <term>uirtus accidentalis</term> <note>According to Aristotelian philosophy, "accidental" qualities are those that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing, such as its temperature or specific mineral potency.</note>, it retains its **primary virtue** <term>primariam uirtutem</term> for its own preservation. This virtue (as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose theories on physics and the natural world formed the foundation of university education in the author's time.</note> says) preserves its subject through a specific power granted by the heavens.

If by chance you wish to know why I have said these things, I respond that I said them for this reason: it has often been seen that if this water is drunk, or used for washing after it has been carried away to other distant places (so that it has remained too long in vessels), or if it is not drawn from the spring at its proper hour and time, it truly works most weakly. In such a case, one ought not to blame the power of the water once you have understood the reason why it worked less effectively and more weakly.

Furthermore, the water should be taken, if possible, where it gushes forth, in the morning hour just after the sun has risen, and it should be drunk in that place. Similarly, if it is necessary to wash, one must wash at the spring itself; but if the patient, for some reason, is unable to go to the spring, let him drink it warm at home, and also wash himself with the warm water at home if he requires a bath. The proper hour for drinking is the first hour of the day, having first had a **bowel movement** <term>uentris beneficio</term> <note>Literally "the benefit of the belly." Medical authors stressed that the digestive tract should be clear before therapeutic drinking.</note> either naturally or by using a **clyster** <term>clistere</term> <note>An enema.</note> made from a **decoction** <term>decocto</term> <note>A medicinal tea made by boiling down plant material.</note> of common herbs mixed with the water of the said spring.

Moreover, it must be observed that the person taking it should not be suffering from a fever, nor should the body be naturally weak in every part such that its strength is feeble, or if he has a lack of power and weakness in the nerves; for such people can neither drink nor wash themselves without the greatest risk. 

The quantity of the drink of said water shall be according to the tolerance of the patient and also of the stomach. For those who have a weak stomach ought to take a smaller quantity; but those who are strong begin on the first days by drinking five, six, or seven cups, of a weight of eight or ten **ounces** <note>original: "unciarum"; 10 ounces is roughly 300 milliliters or about 1.25 cups in modern U.S. measurements. Drinking seven of these would be nearly 2 liters of mineral water.</note>. And while drinking, if possible, one ought to **stroll lightly** <term>deambulare</term> so that heat may be stirred up and the water may more easily descend from the stomach. Indeed, some people, not long after it has been drunk, either urinate a great deal or have many bowel movements; for some, both the urine and the **stool** <term>secessus</term> are moved at the same time; some...

If, after six or eight days have passed, the stomach feels an aversion <term>fastidium</term> <note>In a medical context, this refers to a physical loathing or nausea that prevents the patient from continuing the treatment.</note> or any other side effect from the drink, let him abstain from the water for one or two days; then, once the aversion is calmed, let him return to drinking again, and let that always be the quantity he can tolerate. 

He should continue drinking for at least twenty days because, since this water works weakly and gradually, it cannot complete its work in a few days—neither in evacuating superfluities nor in altering the afflicted organs so they return to their former health. In this method of curing, my advice—when the patient's strength tolerates it and the stomach does not shrink from it—is that it be drunk for a full month. ...the springs can be reached by very few for many reasons. It was said a little while ago that the virtues <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the medicinal power or "active ingredient" of the water.</note> of this water become weaker if it is kept in a vessel for any notable amount of time after it has been drawn from its own source <term>minera</term>. From this, a difficulty arises: if it is transported to other cities and drunk by someone, can it still benefit the aforementioned conditions? Furthermore, what rule must be followed by those who do not drink it at the site itself? 

To this doubt, the response must be as follows: namely, that although the strengths of the said water are diminished by the delay or the passage of time outside its proper place, they are not entirely lost; they still perform some action, more or less depending on the time since it was carried away from the source <term>minera</term> and the spring. And so I say that this water, transported to other cities, is able to work. 

However, it is not as powerful as if it were consumed in the place where it gushes forth. If anyone, therefore, wishes to drink it outside its proper place, let him observe the rule (as was stated): namely, that he should drink it in the morning, slightly warmed. I said "slightly" because through strong heating over a fire, the virtue acquired from the source <term>minera</term> is mostly dissipated. Nor is it safe to take it cold, especially if the stomach <term>ventriculus</term> is weak, or if the patient has become listless from the long duration of the illness. 

In other matters, let the order of walking, food, and drink be observed (as was stated regarding those who drink the said water taken immediately from the spring). However, it is always necessary to ensure that the patient does not drink it unless his bowels have moved that morning, either spontaneously or aided by a clyster <term>clisteri</term> <note>A medicinal enema used to clear the bowels.</note>. 

The time for taking food is five hours after drinking. The food should be bread made from the best wheat and well-leavened, along with the meat of small chickens, or kid, or suckling veal, or similar animals; these should be boiled in that very same water with little or no salt. One must not eat to the point of satiety. 

The wine should be a weak, watery white wine rather than a dark red; if it is strong, it should be diluted with the said water. If white wine cannot be obtained, let it at least be of a middle color—namely reddish—neither sweet nor sour. Other types of food are forbidden, such as fish, dairy products, and other viscous things or those that produce "bad juices" <note>Galenic medicine taught that certain foods produced "bad humors" or "juices" in the body that caused illness.</note>. 

However, soft-boiled eggs, or things mixed with broth, panatella <note>A traditional soup made of bread crumbs, eggs, and broth.</note>, and bread cooked in broth are the best foods. After lunch, one must rest; and as I also said above, it is in no way appropriate to sleep, because sleep causes inflammation and [prevents] urination and bowel movements if...

Similarly, in the evening, if dinner is moderate and sparse, let the patient lie down two hours afterward. Let him then sleep at will according to his own habit. 

It is, however, worth the effort to observe one thing in such drinking of the water: namely, that if on the first, second, third, and fourth day nothing or very little has passed through the urine or the bowels, the drinking must be stopped altogether. For example, in cases of difficulty breathing and asthma, the said water should be given warm and by sipping <note>original: "lambendo," literally "licking," referring to taking the liquid in very small, slow sips</note>. Likewise, in cases of weakness of the stomach, it is necessary to drink it warm, nor should the quantity be too great, lest it produce loathing and nausea. Furthermore, after the patient has drunk it for six or more days, he should pause for one or two days. 

Similarly, in "hepatic flux" <note>original: "fluxu hæpatico"; a historical term for a type of chronic diarrhea or discharge thought to originate in the liver</note>, a very large quantity should not be taken; rather, the quantity should be that which can strengthen the liver and stomach and restore them to their natural balance <term>temperies</term>. 

In the same way, one must act in cases of gout <term>podagra</term> <note>specifically gout of the foot</note> and other joint pains arising from "hot matter." But in such cases, the bowels must first be purged with a mild medicine, and then the patient may gradually drink the said water. After drinking, it is also beneficial to wash or bathe the affected limbs in the said water. This is helpful not only in this case, but also in other "preternatural" <note>conditions that are "outside of nature" or abnormal</note> ailments listed above, if they require washing. 

In the case of scabies <note>a contagious skin infestation</note> and other skin conditions, however, one must drink a very large quantity with the full strength of the water's power; yet it should not be excessive, since in all things a certain mode and measure must be observed. Let those with scabies drink it for many days, and let them wash the whole body by entering into the spring itself—not just once, but many times daily, or on alternating days. 

And since not all who come to these springs drink the water, but many come to wash themselves in them, where it is necessary to wash in the said waters, it will first be worth the effort to [clear] the belly...

...to cleanse the common superfluities of the stomach <term>ventriculus</term> and other neighboring organs, with some light medicine according to the necessity of the overflowing matter. Also, if blood should be overabundant, one should first perform a bloodletting <note>original: "venam incidere," the practice of opening a vein to balance the humors</note>, so that one does not enter the baths unless the body has first been cleansed. After this purification of the body, the patient should rest for one or two days; then, let him enter the bath to wash himself, washing either the whole body, or a part, or one limb and then another, according to the demands of the illness. The more suitable hour, indeed, is the morning hour, two hours after sunrise, on a clear day without clouds. One should not wash or drink during the conjunction or opposition of the moon <note>the New Moon or Full Moon, which were thought to affect the movement of bodily fluids</note>; rather, one must wait on that day.

Those who enter the baths for washing may also do so in the evening hours, provided it is eight hours after lunch, so that the food in the stomach is fully digested. Whether one washes in the morning or the evening, the bowels must first be evacuated; if this does not happen spontaneously, they should be moved by an enema <term>clyster</term>. The patient should stay in that water or wash for half an hour, or at most one hour.

But if nausea <note>original: "fastidium"</note> or any other symptom <note>original: "accidens"</note> should arise, let him exit or cease the washing, and the symptom should be treated according to the opportunity. For example, to strengthen the "mouth" of the stomach <note>the cardia or upper opening of the stomach</note>, let a morsel of bread soaked in aromatic wine be given, or some of the confections that strengthen the stomach, such as *aromaticum rosatum* <note>a rose-scented aromatic powder</note>, *diarodum abbatis* <note>the "Abbot’s rose-mixture," a cooling electuary</note>, *dia muscus* <note>a musk-based tonic</note>, *dia margaritum* <note>a restorative powder containing crushed pearls</note>, and similar things.

Similarly, if there should be nausea or fainting <term>lipothymia</term> caused by a bilious humor in the mouth of the stomach, let a morsel of bread soaked in pomegranate wine be given, or quince wine, or in the juice of unripe grapes. Or, let confections be given such as *diatriasandalon* <note>a cooling mixture made from three types of sandalwood</note>, or rose-sugar with corals and pearls, and similar things. But if there is constipation <note>original: "stypticitas"</note>, let a soothing enema <term>clyster</term> be used, made from a decoction of common herbs in the water of the said baths, or let a honey suppository be inserted, or let a bolus of *cassia fistula* <note>the purging cassia, used as a mild laxative</note> or another light medicine be given according to the patient’s needs.

If a headache should occur, let there be rubbing of the legs and arms, and let cupping glasses <term>cucurbitulae</term> <note>suction cups used to draw humors away from the head</note> be applied to the buttocks and shoulder blades. Similarly, in other symptoms, one must provide help according to the need of the matter. But since the whole body does not always require washing, and sometimes only one limb or part is poorly affected, in such a case—if the limb is not suited to be submerged in the said spring—let fomentations <note>warm, moist compresses</note> be made with sponges on the limb with wool...

# TWENTY-SIXTH

...fomentations <note>original: "fomenti" (reconstructed), referring to warm medicinal compresses</note> moistened in the said hot water. If indeed the uterus or vulva should suffer, for example from infertility, a discharge of blood, or a flow of white matter <note>original: "cursu materierum albarum," a historical term for leukorrhea or similar vaginal discharge</note>, let the area be washed with the said hot water, or let the patient sit in it, as it is wonderfully and greatly beneficial.

After the patient has washed their whole body or a specific part, they should wipe themselves dry and put on their clothes; they must also protect themselves from the outside air until they return home. Soon after, they should enter their bed and wipe and rub themselves again with linens and towels, so that all the humidity from the bath <term>balneum</term> is dried away. Let them rest in bed, well-covered, for at least an hour. 

If it happens that they fall asleep, let them sleep only a little. Then, after they have risen, a light walk is very beneficial. For in this way, the passages <note>original: "meatus," the pores or internal channels of the body</note> of the body are better opened, so that if any trapped hot vapors remain, they are able to escape. 

After the light walk—if it is morning—the patient may take lunch; if it is evening, let them take dinner. After dinner, they should rest in bed for two hours and sleep until the morning hours. 

The foods, indeed, should be as I have said above: those which are easy to digest <term>concoctionis</term> and provide the best nourishment, such as the meats mentioned in that section and fresh eggs. Fish, however, should not be eaten unless the intention is to provide less nourishment and generate a "cold" sustenance. In that case, scaly fish living in clear waters are better, such as:
- trout
- carp (not salted)
- barbel
- gilt-head bream <note>original: "auratæ"</note>
- and similar varieties. 

Likewise, all fruits, legumes, vegetables, dairy products, and salted foods are forbidden. One must also abstain from an immoderate quantity of any food or drink, lest harm be brought to the stomach <term>ventriculus</term>; in all things, however, custom and the patient's tolerance should be the rule.

Furthermore, whether drinking or washing in the said water, one must absolutely abstain from all sexual activity <note>original: "uenereis," literally "matters of Venus"</note>, as well as from anger and all immoderate exercise. For in all these things, there occurs a great alteration and dissolution of the spirits <note>the "spirits" were thought to be vital substances that fueled bodily functions</note>, and in sexual acts, a drying out of the radical moisture <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidi radicalis," the innate fluid believed to be the basis of life and longevity</note>. 

No one, however, who requires the drinking or bathing in said water should enter the bath unless they have first drunk the water for several days, so that they know the internal organs have been cleansed of superfluous waste and strengthened. The sign of this is when the water is returned—both through the stool and the urine—clear and unmixed, in the same quantity as was taken in. This does not always happen in a fixed period of time; sometimes this process is completed in fewer days, and sometimes more, but most often it is recognized after the fourteenth or twentieth day. # LETTER

As long as signs <note>These "signs" likely refer to the color or consistency of the urine and stool, which medieval doctors used to determine if the "humors" had been properly processed.</note> appear in the waste products, no one can safely enter the bath or wash themselves in any other way. Furthermore, this rule must be perpetually observed: namely, that on the day they drink the water, they must by no means enter the bath, neither in the morning nor the evening; and on the day they wash themselves, they should not drink the water at all. Instead, one single operation in one day will be sufficient—either drinking or washing. If it should be necessary to both wash and drink for some reason, let the patient drink on one day and wash on the other. Thus, one must proceed according to the needs of the case: for example, drinking for several days, and afterwards washing for several days, or washing continuously (as was said) and drinking for some or for consecutive days. However, this law is observed with an exception: where there are skin infections, such as scabies <note>A contagious skin disease caused by mites, characterized by intense itching.</note>, leprosy <term>lepra</term>, and other similar or even more severe conditions on the external limbs, it is better to wash very often, even twice a day. 

If, however, either rain or coldness of the air should occur for any reason, it will be in no way safe to wash (as was said regarding the conjunction and opposition of the moon with the sun <note>Medieval medicine closely linked bodily fluids to lunar cycles, advising against treatments during certain phases.</note>). Similarly, those who are exhausted from bodily labor, or those who languish from mental disturbance, or cares, or anger, or "burning" <note>original: "excandescentia," referring here to a state of heated passion or a feverish temper.</note>—unless their strength of both body and mind first returns to them, the baths are in no way suitable for them. 

And since those who suffer from a "distillation" <term>distilatio</term> from the head to the chest and other lower members often come to these springs—which distillation is a thin, hot matter arising from the mixing of some sharp humor <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health.</note> that is either produced in the head from some bad imbalance <term>temperie</term>, or if produced elsewhere, runs to the head and is not regulated there due to the weakness of that limb—for such patients, it is an excellent help to receive this water at a moderate warmth, placed in a bucket <term>situla</term> and dripping over the head through a small pipe <term>canula</term>. This should be done in the morning hours, at least two hours before lunch. It is most effective in strengthening the head and rectifying its temperature, so that it may be able to digest and assimilate its own nourishment, and also so that waste products and overflowing humors are not able to fall down to the lower members. This "distillation" of water over the head—specifically over the site of the coronal suture <note>The joint where the bones of the skull meet at the top of the head.</note> and over the site of the lambdoid suture near the origin of the <term>nuchæ</term> <note>The "nucha" historically referred to the spinal cord or the nape of the neck where it meets the skull.</note>—is beneficial. For this reason, it also helps those with asthma and other conditions contrary to nature caused by the drainage of matter from the head. This dripping of water through a pipe, which they call a douche <term>ducia</term>, ought to be continued for many days, say for fifteen or twenty days, for it is rarely...

Wherefore one must not depart immediately from the site of the springs, but it will be useful to rest for several days after drinking and bathing. 

Let them also beware of the heat of the air, and of cooling winds, and of excessive exercise, and of overfilling—both of food and drink—and of the rest of those things which can alter a sickly body. And when they wish to return home, let the rule be that the journey is performed without trouble or fatigue of the body; for example, by riding moderately, or in a carriage, or on foot—which I do not praise, since it is not entirely safe for those recovering and weakened by medicines <note>original: "medicinis inanitis"—referring to the state of a body whose "humors" have been emptied or purged by medical treatment.</note> to undertake a long journey on foot. 

But if walking should be necessary, let it be light, and divided over several days, so that a weak strength is not consumed by the causes already mentioned. And after they have arrived at their own home, they must rest from business and other things for certain days, but let them use light walking before lunch, and in the evening before dinner. And let them flee all overfilling and variety, both of food and drink; let them also flee midday sleep, and Venus’s embraces <note>A common euphemism for sexual intercourse, which was believed to deplete the body's vital spirits.</note>; finally, let them be joyful and cheerful with friends. These are, most learned Vincent, the things I wished to write to you at present in response to your letters concerning the **Baths of Caldiero** <term>balneis calderianis</term> <note>Thermal springs near Verona, Italy, renowned since Roman times for treating various ailments.</note>, so that I might satisfy you as far as possible; if I have satisfied you, it will be most pleasing to me; if less so, I certainly consider it enough that I have not neglected your requests. Farewell. Venice. August 27, 1523.

A young man suffering from the <term>French disease<gloss>morbus Gallicus: a common 16th-century name for syphilis, which was then a new and terrifying epidemic in Europe</gloss></term>. **W**ho had not long ago been infected, so that it was undoubtedly a new case of the disease, although very intense pains troubled him throughout his whole body, affecting all his joints and even his head, so that he slept very little at night. There was also a significant ulceration of the throat and the <note>original: "Vuluae" — while this usually means the womb/vulva, in the context of a male youth ("iuuenis") and throat ulcers, it is likely a printer's error for "uvulae" (the uvula)</note>. Upon this youth, a <term>tertian fever<gloss>tertiana febre: a fever that spikes every third day, often associated with malaria</gloss></term> occurred; following a light medicine which you administered to him, on the fourth day he was freed not only from the fever itself, but from all his pains and the ulceration of his throat, and was thus made as healthy as if he had never suffered any ill. **W**hich thing you write of with no small wonder. 

But you will cease to wonder if you remember those things which I wrote very concisely in my little book on the French disease, in the second tract, seventh chapter, near the beginning and after the middle, and in the chapter immediately following. There it is asked whether the opening of a vein or the letting of blood <note>original: "missio sanguinis"</note> is beneficial for the French disease. Those things which I touched upon there briefly for the sake of conciseness, I shall here (to gratify your wish) explain more broadly. I said, therefore, in the cited places, that a new sickness arising from a "less thick" matter <note>In Galenic medicine, diseases were caused by imbalances of "humors" or bodily fluids; "thick" humors were harder to clear than "thin" ones</note>, mixed with heat, where the patient’s strength is robust, can be cured by even a single evacuation—whether that be through administered medicine or by bloodletting, it matters little. 

But this depends on the sound judgment of the physician, which we do not see often, by the testimony of <term>Hippocrates<gloss>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</gloss></term> who says in the first of his *Aphorisms* that "judgment is difficult." However, I shall say by what means that youth of yours was healed. If I first describe the natural intrinsic and extrinsic disposition (as well as the <term>preternatural<gloss>praeternaturalem: referring to a state of disease or imbalance</gloss></term> state), once these are tasted, it will not be difficult to understand this wonderful operation of nature and art. 

That youth (as you write) was primarily of an excellent constitution and a well-balanced temperament, namely hot and moist. If he seemed to deviate in any part from the best temperament, it was toward dryness; so that in his active qualities his heat was equal, but in his passive qualities there was less moisture, declining toward a certain dryness. This is a temperament which young **German** men for the most part are accustomed to have—namely, a middle ground between the <term>sanguine<gloss>associated with blood: hopeful and energetic</gloss></term> and the <term>choleric<gloss>associated with yellow bile: ambitious and prone to heat</gloss></term>. You see, therefore, two things contributing to a speedy recovery: youth and an excellent temperament, with which strength prevails. But also the time of year, which was summer (which shortens all illnesses, according to the testimony of <term>Galen<gloss>A 2nd-century Roman physician whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years</gloss></term> in his second commentary on the *Aphorisms*, and by experience), helped not a little in this matter. This, with another cause added, was why he was quickly freed. Add to this that the sickness was from a matter...

...few, and those indeed mixed with thin, bilious blood from his own <term>temperament<gloss>In Renaissance medicine, "temperament" or "complexion" referred to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—unique to an individual.</gloss></term> and produced by the season of the year. This mixture is revealed by the vehement pains, which do not occur except through the admixture of a thin, stinging matter that thins the thick <term>humors<gloss>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance was thought to dictate health.</gloss></term>. Thus, such pains can be described as both "stinging" and "stretching." Galen best explained this type of pain in his booklet *On Unequal Intemperance* <note>original: "de inæquali intemperatura"</note>, in the second book of *On the Affected Parts* <note>original: "de locis affectis"</note>, and in *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "methodo curandi"</note>, as well as scattered throughout his other books. The onset of a **tertian fever** <note>a fever that spikes every third day</note> confirms this same mixture; for that tertian fever would not have occurred unless a great deal of bilious matter, predominating over the phlegmatic matter, had been mixed in. 

Therefore, if you examine everything that allows a physician to restore a patient to health quickly, there is no reason for you to wonder why he was restored to health so well and so fast by such a slight medicinal aid. This is especially true if you consider what the <term>Prince Avicenna<gloss>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in European universities for centuries.</gloss></term> said in the first part of the fourth book regarding the nourishment of feverish patients in general: namely, that the "virtue" <note>original: "uirtutem" — here meaning the body's innate healing power or vital force</note> is primarily responsible for healing. Therefore, this recovery happened because his "virtue" was strong due to his youthful age, combined with an optimal temperament during the summer season, with the fever assisting in the thinning of the matter in a fresh illness. This was aided by a significant mixture of thin, hot humors, which are easily moved through both sensible <note>visible, like sweat or urine</note> and insensible <note>invisible, like "vapors" through the skin</note> evacuation. 

In the beginning, the matter of the <term>French disease<gloss>morbus Gallicus: Syphilis</gloss></term> is not of such great viscosity in everyone that it cannot be carried through all the passages by the power of the body alone, or assisted by some medicine. In this way, it can be entirely evacuated, leaving no notable earthy or thick part behind in the limb. But it is different in an **ancient disease** <note>a chronic or long-standing infection</note>, in which the thin parts have already been dissolved. 

The things said above might set your mind at ease, were it not kept in suspense by the method of healing—whether through **liniments** applied to the joints, or through **fumigations** <note>The use of medicated vapors, often containing mercury, which was a standard but dangerous treatment for syphilis.</note> applied to a part or to the whole body. For by such liniments and fumigations, the matter in the limbs is thinned and evacuated through the mouth <note>A reference to "salivation," a common side effect of mercury treatment where the patient would drool excessively, which doctors then believed was the disease "leaving" the body.</note>, which very often happens over many days and even copiously. Sometimes the same matter is evacuated through the stool—matter which would otherwise be thick, but is here pure and refined—and sometimes it is even mixed with other good humors. Occasionally, it is evacuated through sweat. 

These latter two modes of evacuation do not happen frequently. But beyond what has been said, I see you asking by what reasoning this can happen, and even answering yourself by saying that the matter which is spread throughout the entire body cannot be led out through the mouth unless it passes back through the same veins by which it traveled to the limbs, returning to the **liver** and the **stomach**...

Nor is this mode of nature's operation, aided by medical art, unusual, since Galen said in the fourth book of *On Preserving Health* <note>original: "de tuenda valetudine"</note> that the matter causing <term>phlegmonic fatigue<gloss>A state of exhaustion caused by an inflammatory "phlegmon," or a buildup of blood and heat in the tissues.</gloss></term> can return again to the veins through repeated <term>venesection<gloss>Bloodletting; the practice of opening a vein to drain blood and associated humors.</gloss></term>.

From this matter are generated pustules, abscesses, pains, and other symptoms according to its variety. is thick, which is not changed into a watery substance, it passes not to the kidneys, but to other veins, which pass to the stomach. For the members do not draw just any matter to themselves, but a specific kind, as Galen learnedly said in the first and second books of *On Natural Faculties* <note>original: "de potentiis naturalibus"</note>, where he brings forward the example of the kidneys attracting watery matter to the urinary passages from the blood. Indeed, if anyone should swallow it in a small quantity, even though it is a poison, because it descends quickly by its own weight, it will be least of all deadly. For it is not received, for the reason already mentioned, by the <term>meseraic veins<gloss>The mesenteric veins, which carry absorbed material from the intestines to the liver.</gloss></term>, so that it might be carried to the principal members; how much less, then, standing on this hypothesis, will it be able to penetrate [from the outside]. And if penetration were granted, it would still not travel to the liver, the stomach, and ascend to the mouth; which is confirmed if someone considers the quantity of quicksilver used for a single day's anointing.

And unless I had written more in my own book, and were not now very busy, I would write more here; but since time is lacking, let these things suffice.

<meta>This page continues the medical and philosophical inquiry into the physical causes of pain, shifting from the specific treatment of the "French Disease" (syphilis) discussed on the previous page to a broader theoretical debate between the authorities of Avicenna and Galen regarding the nature of sensation and bodily injury.</meta>

->### TWENTY-EIGHTH<-

...itself, or from the <term>interruption of continuity<gloss>In Galenic medicine, 'solutio continui' refers to any physical break in the body's tissues, such as a cut, tear, or ulcer.</gloss></term>, as I have written, according to the testimony of **Avicenna** <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose 'Canon of Medicine' was a foundational text in Europe.</note> in the second book of the first volume. This statement can be corroborated by many arguments of the ancients, and especially by **Galen** in his short work *On Unequal Temperature* <note>original: "de inaequali temperatura"</note>. Galen says that pain occurs if nature is changed: it is changed, indeed, if it becomes cold, or grows hot, or is moistened, or dried out, or if its continuity is dissolved. Nor can anyone say that these two Princes of Medicine do not feel the same way about the causes of pain based on their writings, as Avicenna himself and many other writers have claimed.

For truly, if anyone reads the twelfth book of Galen’s *The Art of Healing* <note>original: "Methodus Medendi"</note> carefully, he seems to have said this very thing when he states: "Furthermore, natural knowledge teaches us that the vice of the body from which pain arises is either a division of continuity or some alteration." And a little later, concluding, he says that it is necessary that the affliction which excites pain be either a division or an alteration. Thus, through a long examination, it is clearly evident that Galen believed both sudden alteration and the <term>interruption of continuity</term> to be the causes of pain. 

He expressed this more clearly in the first commentary on the second book of *Regimen in Acute Diseases* <note>original: "de ratione victus in morbis acutis"</note>, where he says: "Sensible bodies feel pain as soon as they are suddenly changed; moreover, the change happens in two ways: sometimes by qualities being changed violently and suddenly, and sometimes by a break in continuity." These bodies are altered by these things immediately when they grow hot, are cooled, are moistened, or are dried. Galen repeats these sayings very frequently in his volumes, as is clear in the second book of *On the Affected Parts* <note>original: "de locis affectis"</note> and the fourth book of *On Simple Medicines* <note>original: "simplicium pharmacorum"</note>, and in other places in which he endeavors to reduce all things to the category of the interruption of continuity; yet he did not say because of this that pain occurs without a <term>bad temperament<gloss>Also called 'dystemper'; an imbalance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</gloss></term>.

However, there are arguments from wise men opposing these statements. For they say that the entire reason for pain occurs because of a bad temperament. If it has sometimes seemed that pain happened to someone from an interruption of continuity, that pain does not occur except because the <term>temperament</term> of the place was changed by the separation of the continuity, since the separation of continuity can by no means occur without a "bad movement" in that part—from which movement the <term>complexion</term> or temperament is changed. And they say that pain is not from both causes (namely from broken continuity and from bad temperament), since, as **Aristotle** testifies in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, the objects of the sense of touch are the four primary qualities in mixed bodies—namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—which, when they are in excess for any reason, cause a sorrowful sensation, which we call pain.

->**S 2**<-
