->### FOURTH LETTER<-

...they call it. Nor should one believe that pain occurs in living beings through the sense of touch alone, since we see that pain can be caused by all the senses, though not without the involvement of touch. For indeed, pain is a sorrowful sensation, or the perception of something contrary to nature. Nor does pain arise from only two active qualities—namely, heat and cold—since dryness and moisture, although they do not act primarily and by themselves, nevertheless cause a sorrowful sensation in the animal by means of natural heat or some other factor. 

It is clearly evident, therefore, how pain is caused by a diverse <term>bad temperature<gloss>A 'mala temperatura' (or dyscrasia) refers to an imbalance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</gloss></term>, whether it occurs with matter or without it, or whether it follows or precedes the <term>interruption of continuity<gloss>The physical separation of parts that should be joined, such as a wound, ulcer, or internal stretching of tissues.</gloss></term>. Indeed, what **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the 'Father of Medicine.'</note> said concerning the causes of pain in his little book *On Winds* <note>original: "de flatibus"</note> does not deviate from these things said above, if you weigh them correctly. 

Returning, then, to the causes of the **French Disease** <note>Syphilis, which was frequently called the 'morbus Gallicus' or 'French Disease' in Europe during this period.</note>, and presupposing those things which I have said in the same book—in the fourth and fifth chapters of the first treatise, and elsewhere—concerning the matter that produces the French Disease; for there I established that the matter of the disease itself is, for the most part, an unnatural <term>phlegm<gloss>One of the four humors; 'unnatural' phlegm was thought to be corrupted, thickened, or mixed with other humors.</gloss></term>, neither simple nor pure, but mixed in various ways with other humors. This matter passes through the veins throughout the entire body and to all its parts. Since it is phlegmatic and predominantly cold, when it reaches some member that is naturally cold and sensitive—such as the nerves, tendons, and membranes—and is not regulated by heat (either by being consumed or changed for the better so that it might be fit to be converted into nourishment), it acquires a further bad quality. This quality, along with a certain stretching caused by weak heat, is the cause of most intense pain. 

This happens more in the evening, when the body's strength is already dissolved or diminished from the day's labor, or because at such an hour the passages of the body are constricted due to the cooling of the air. Thus, the vaporous superfluities retained in the sensitive members—such as the muscles, nerves, and membranes—separate the parts that were once joined. Also, as the sun recedes, bodies have less resistance; therefore, in the evening hours, cold matters are set in motion and infest our bodies more, inasmuch as they descend to the sensitive places and, through their quality along with the interruption of continuity, cause pain. 

Therefore, you have answered them excellently: namely, that although the matters are cold, when they descend to the nerves, tendons, and membranes, they cause pain by their quality along with stretching. But if they still ask what kind of matter that phlegmatic or pituitary substance is, one must answer that it is phlegm...

# TWENTY-EIGHTH

...pituitous <note>original: "pituitosam," meaning phlegm-like</note> matter, whether raw or insufficiently "cooked" <note>In humoral medicine, "cooking" (coction) refers to the body's process of refining or neutralizing harmful fluids through heat.</note> in proportion to the phlegm, with an admixture of other humors, including hot ones. However, it is for the most part phlegmatic—or call it pituitous, it makes no difference. 

And when they say that cold matter is by its very nature immobile, this can be conceded if the matter is pure. But when they say the matter of the **French Disease** <note>Syphilis</note> is cold and not mixed with others, they poorly understand our writings; for I did not say it was pure matter, but mixed with other humors. This mixture, being drawn by the attractive power of a limb and also assisted by other hot humors acting as a "vehicle," passes to the limbs and is received into them, where it causes pain (as I have said). 

That there is a naturally attractive power in each and every limb to draw in nourishment is testified by **Galen** <note>A foundational Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> in his booklet *On Natural Faculties* <note>original: "de uirtutibus naturalibus"</note>. But when bad nourishment is drawn in and is not corrected by the power of the limb, pain or some other foul sickness is caused. For this reason, **Galen** himself said that in a time of hunger, the stomach (or ventricle) attracts "superfluities" from neighboring parts, and thus it becomes filled with bad humors. The Prince **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the highly influential Persian physician and author of the 'Canon of Medicine.'</note> mentions this opinion in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk.

With these things established, you can answer everyone that I never said these pains arise from pure phlegmatic matter, but from phlegm mixed with other humors—even though phlegmatic matter alone could, and in fact does, cause pain. Nor is it always necessary for cold matter to have a "vehicle" of hot matter, since it can be drawn by the power of a limb or descend from place to place by its own weight, provided the passages are wide enough. I believe that, given the shortage of time and the many obstacles posed by the sick, I have satisfied you and those doctors on these points. Please commend me most highly to all of them. And if they deign to read these words, do not be reluctant to show this to them.

Finally, you ask about the names of the **German** herbs that heal those with **empyema** <note>original: "Empycos," referring to patients with an accumulation of pus, here specifically from a penetrating chest wound.</note> resulting from a chest wound. I say that they call these herbs as follows:
* **Sendauch**, that is, **Lady's Mantle** <note>original: "Alchimilla"</note>
* **Senichel**, called **Sanicle** <note>original: "Diapensia"</note> in Latin
* **Vuintegrum**, named **Wintergreen** <note>original: "Pirola"</note>
* **Trinitas**, that is, **Wild Pansy** <note>original: "Yacea"</note>

These four herbs, therefore, are those which heal (as I mentioned above). They are found in the mountains of **Germany** which are near **Italy**. Whether they are found where you are, I do not know. But they are wonderful (believe me) when boiled down <note>original: "Decoctæ"</note> with sweet, white mountain wine, and at the end of the boiling...

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT LORD
## Michael Lippus. Epistle 29. On the cure of a creeping ulcer <note>original: "ulceris formicosi," a type of spreading or stinging ulcer named for the sensation of "ants" (formica) crawling on the skin.</note> on the hip, and a tumor on the back, resulting from the remnants of the French disease <note>Syphilis</note>.

**Y**OU ASK, most learned Michael, that I wish to signify to you by letter through the main points (as they say) how one should proceed in the case of the Magnificent Lord Count Bernard Tompich. He has suffered for many years from the **French disease**, and though he was treated before, it seems that from three years ago until today he has fallen back into this sickness. He now has a **creeping ulcer** on his hip and a **tumor** on his back near the loins. Although the Magnificent Count has tried many remedies, he has not been able to be cured until now. To this, I respond with how he should act, according to our judgment. 

First, it is necessary to purge the Magnificent man with certain <term>minorative evacuations</term> <note>Gentle or gradual treatments to clear the bowels and "bad humors."</note>; for example, with a <term>lenitive electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste or jam intended to soothe and loosen the bowels.</note>, <term>Diacatholicon</term> <note>A "universal" laxative made from various plant extracts.</note>, and some small portion of the <term>confection Amech</term> <note>A specific medicinal mixture often used to purge "black bile" or thick humors.</note>. This should be done according to his strength and the time of year <note>Medical treatments in the 16th century were strictly timed according to seasons and the patient's physical constitution.</note>. 

Then, the remaining matter itself must be "digested" <note>In humoral medicine, "digestion" (or coction) was the process of thinning or "ripening" harmful fluids so they could be removed from the body.</note> using appropriate <term>digestives</term>, such as syrup of <term>fumitory</term> <note>original: "fumoterre," a plant traditionally used for skin diseases and liver health.</note> and diluted endive, mixed with waters of hops and fumitory. However, water of <term>nightshade</term> <note>original: "solatri."</note> mixed with these would please me more, because of the "burning" of the humor. Let these syrups be given for several days after the aforementioned purging. 

Next, I would wish to cut the **liver vein** <note>original: "uenam iecorariam," usually referring to the basilic vein in the right arm, believed to be connected to liver health.</note> of the right arm and extract a quantity of blood, according to the patient's tolerance and the "malice" <note>The perceived toxicity or corruption.</note> of the blood itself. Indeed, in a confirmed case of the **French disease**, the fault lies in the mass of the blood, even though the resulting symptoms appear in the external limbs. After this **bloodletting** <note>original: "phlobotomia."</note> has been performed, I would proceed for several days with the aforementioned "digesting" medicines. Then, I would wish to purge him with a more specific medicine, namely, with the electuary...

The proposed regimen follows traditional humoral medicine, including gentle purging, bloodletting from the "liver vein," and various herbal syrups.</summary>

# TWENTY-EIGHTH

...with a laxative, made of <term>sebesten</term> <note>A type of plum-like fruit (Cordia myxa) used in pharmacy as a gentle expectorant or laxative.</note> and the <term>confection of Hamech</term> <note>original: "confectione Aniech" (Hamech); a famous, complex purgative electuary from the Arabic medical tradition, specifically attributed to Mesue, used to purge "burnt" or melancholic humors.</note>, dissolved in a decoction of <term>Dodder of Thyme by Mesue</term> <note>original: "Epithimi Mesuae"; a parasitic plant used to treat diseases of the liver and spleen.</note>, so that by your most expert judgment the body might be cleansed everywhere from common <term>superfluities</term> <note>Excess or waste humors that were believed to cause disease.</note>, evacuating twice or thrice, according to the necessity of the case. Once these evacuations are completed, I would wish that the most illustrious count take a <term>decoction of Indian wood</term> <note>original: "ligni indici"; this refers to Guaiacum wood, a remedy from the Americas that became the standard treatment for syphilis in the 16th century.</note> for a suitable time—namely forty days, or more if needed. 

Give, therefore, in the evening and morning one cup of the water from the first boiling. Of the water from the second boiling, however, give it both before lunch and throughout the whole day as desired, and even at night if he wishes to drink; for this is a universal rule, especially in a long-term illness, that the more the patient drinks—both of the first and the second decoction—the better and more quickly he will be freed. 

Therefore, after eight or ten days have passed, I would wish that he drink two cups of the first decoction in the morning and two in the evening, and during the day an even greater quantity of the second decoction. And this should continue until the end of forty days, with a diet suitable to his age, <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four humors in an individual's body.</note>, and other factors. 

Know this, however: **wine is in no way appropriate.** If it must be given, whether by reason of habit or for other reasons, let it be diluted and in a small quantity. Your excellence will note, however, that if after twenty-five days have passed you see neither the ulcers healed nor the tumor resolved, it will be necessary in the evening to anoint the groin, the area of the **sacrum** <note>original: "ossis sacri"; the large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note>, and the back down to the tailbone. This is so that through such an anointing, the breaking down of the matters contained in the limb might occur, and the descent of matters flowing to the sick areas might be prevented. It does not matter if you call this method of smearing—as the common people say—a **defensive** <note>original: "defensivum"; a medicinal application intended to protect a part of the body or stop the flow of harmful humors.</note>, provided the patient achieves the desired end from it. 

Indeed, let the anointing be done with our **glorious blessed ointment**, with an added quantity of <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>original: "boli armeni"; a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent and to "dry out" excess fluids.</note> as shall seem appropriate to your excellence. I believe, most learned man, that this is the true way to proceed, so that the most illustrious count may be led in an orderly fashion to his desired health, which may God, three and one, deign to grant him. 

As for those things which can strengthen the principal organs after the cure, or if any of the remaining humors require further evacuation, I have passed over them in silence, since I have known you to be both learned and experienced from your own writings. 

Farewell. Venice. The 20th day of August, 1535.

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT GIOVANNI
## Battista Pantino. Letter 30. Concerning the loss of hair, the erosion of the gums, the falling out of teeth, and certain other conditions that occur with the French Disease, and concerning their remedies.

<note>Giovanni Battista Pantino was a contemporary physician and colleague of the author. "The French Disease" (Morbus Gallicus) was the common 16th-century name for syphilis.</note>

A FEW days after I sent you the letters together with the prescription for the syrup of apples, which loosens the bowels, your letters were delivered to me again. In them, you ask of me things no less difficult than they are desired by me; and because I think these will be health-giving first of all to you—to whom I owe very much—and then to others whose illnesses you treat, I do not refuse to write these things to you, in almost the same order in which they were written by you. 

First, you ask whether the loss of hair which happens everywhere to men in these times of ours—a symptom of the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "morbi quem Gallicum uocant"; syphilis, which famously caused patchy hair loss in its secondary stage.</note>—is merely an incidental symptom, or rather the specific condition which the most excellent ancient Greek physicians call <term>Alopecia</term> <note>Greek for "fox-mange"; used to describe patchy baldness.</note> and <term>Ophiasis</term> <note>Greek for "snake-like"; a form of baldness that winds around the head like a serpent.</note>, and which the Arabs call <term>Tiria</term>. This is a question I can easily answer, if I first recall the final definition of the <term>French disease</term> written by me in my booklet on the subject. 

For in that booklet, I said that the <term>French disease</term> is a bad <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperiem"; in Galenic medicine, health depended on the "temperament" or balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> resulting from a certain <term>cooling of the liver</term> <note>original: "iocinoris... refrigerationem"; the author argues that the liver has become too cold, a controversial stance at the time as others believed the disease was "hot" or inflammatory.</note>, yet not without a certain effect of dryness and an immoderate complication of other qualities. Thus, besides the cooling that is manifest from its effects, there is also a certain hidden bad quality, like a form or "final difference," which is communicated to the whole body, as you will see clearly enough from my writings on fevers. 

Nor do those things stand in the way which have been said by some people—poorly and without experience—to the contrary of this description. They believe indeed that the liver is badly affected, but they stubbornly assert that this bad <term>temperament</term> is not that cold one (as I have said), but is instead hot and dry. They use certain frivolous reasons, such that I am ashamed (I call God to witness) to contradict such empty arguments. For they say (not to dwell too long on these matters) that this temperament is preternaturally hot for this reason: because sometimes, at the beginning of the disease, a slight fever arises, and because...

# THIRTY

...since ulceration is accustomed to occur in the genitals and other parts of the body, and these are not without redness, especially on the outer skin; and often corrosive ulcers of this kind are formed, which proceed for the worse by creeping or wandering; and also pains, which are mostly sharp, occur. In the same way, the pustules that appear often seem red, and even in tumors or <term>gummata</term> <note>Soft, non-cancerous growths or swellings characteristic of late-stage syphilis.</note>, some redness is sometimes seen. They say, moreover, that hair loss occurs from the same hot and dry temperament, and also any ulcers in the throat, jaws, or gums which cause the teeth to fall out, or in any other place of the body—namely in the genitals, the vulva, the penis, or in the anus—all these attest to this hot and dry temperament. Indeed, some go to such madness that they even say the matter or basis of the <term>French disease</term> <note>Syphilis.</note> is <term>burnt bile</term> <note>original: "choleram adustam"; in ancient medicine, bile was thought to become toxic and "burnt" if the body's heat was imbalanced.</note>, or bile converted into <term>melancholy</term> <note>Black bile.</note> through scorching, although nothing is more absurd than this position. For if what they say were true, one would have to say without any doubt that the French disease is <term>elephantiasis</term> (or as the Arabs say, <term>leonine leprosy</term> <note>A severe form of leprosy that causes the face to resemble a lion's.</note>) or some cancerous sickness (if I may call it that), if we consider any particular affliction in such a disease. 

But because, as you have seen in my already mentioned little book, all of those men were far from the mark of truth—as I shall soon reveal to you—let these things remain as they are for now so that I do not interrupt what I have already begun. I will therefore follow the proposed matter, namely the proof of the parts of our definition. For that the <term>French disease</term> is primarily in the category of a bad temperament of the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "iocineris"</note>, no one of sound mind among those writers I have seen denies; rather, all who think correctly affirm this constantly and without hesitation, which I will also show by reasoning in due course. But if some place this unnatural temperament primarily either in the heart or in the brain—and such people are certainly not lacking—they wander entirely from the path, since in the practice of physicians only the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "iecur"</note> generates or prepares the humors for the nourishment of the whole body. Nor are the materials causing the symptoms of the disease (such as pains, pustules, tumors, ulcerations, hair loss, and others) shed from any other part first than from the veins. These veins draw from the liver, namely through the attracting power of the organs, as <term>Galen</term> <note>A foundational Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> learnedly said in his book *On Natural Faculties*. That which is drawn, since it is not in every part healthy and suitable for the nourishment of the organs, the power itself which is always in health...

He cites Galen's physiological theories to support his claim that the symptoms of the disease are distributed through the veins from the liver.</summary>

->E P I S T O L A<-

...of blood purification is intent, it separates out the unhealthy matter which is in the blood and drives it first to the muscles, or to other places where the veins carry nourishment. If these matters are thick, they remain there and cause a heaviness of the muscles and other parts, as well as a certain impotence or difficulty of voluntary movement, so that the arms are lifted with effort, and the legs or other limbs are moved with difficulty. For indeed, this symptom <note>original: "accidens"; in medical terms of the time, this refers to a secondary symptom or clinical occurrence rather than a random accident.</note> is accustomed to appear from the first days of infection, since they become slower and duller in their senses, and—to speak more truly—in all **animal operations** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "animal" (from the Latin "anima," soul) refers to the functions of the brain and nervous system, such as thought, sensation, and voluntary movement.</note>, both external and internal, as the nourishment is surely affected in this way and drawn from the liver by the member that needs nourishment. 

Nor because of this, as some have said (and wrongly), was it necessary to say that the **source** <note>original: "minera," literally a mine or vein of ore; used here to mean the primary site of the disease.</note> is in the brain, and that the matter first falls from it to the other members. This is neither consistent with reason nor does it conform to the senses, as I will reveal to you a little below, where I shall describe what I have very often seen in the **dissections of the corpses** <note>The author emphasizes his empirical knowledge gained from performing autopsies, a practice that was becoming more common in the 16th century to understand disease.</note> of dead men who, while they lived, suffered from the <term>French disease</term> <note>Syphilis.</note>. 

I would not, however, deny that some matter descends from the brain which could not be regulated by the heat of the head, since it was first not properly prepared by the liver. For as I said, a chilled liver does not prepare the blood properly, and also because, by its already mentioned hidden quality, it infects the other members by **sympathy** <note>original: "per consensum"; the medical theory that organs can affect one another through shared connections or "consensus."</note>. Thus, the members infected by the liver itself are able to assimilate their nourishment less than their nature allows, since it did not receive perfect **concoction** <note>digestion or refinement.</note> during the **second concoction** <note>The second stage of digestion was believed to take place in the liver, where food was transformed into blood.</note>, which is in the liver. Thus, if any matters are sent from the brain or another member to increase some symptom of the French disease, the brain or that member is not for that reason the primary cause, but should be called a fostering cause or a "co-cause." 

Because if other members are affected, they are indeed affected by the liver; and as I said, a liver that is first chilled prepares bad nourishment for the others, which cannot be corrected by the other members and their powers. For neither is the **first digestion corrected by the second, nor the second by the third, nor the third by the fourth concoction.** <note>A fundamental rule in Galenic medicine: if the initial stage of digestion (in the stomach) failed, the subsequent stages (liver, veins, tissues) could not fix the "corrupted" material.</note> Therefore, if matter in other members is mixed with the prior matter, it will be a "co-cause," and not the primary cause (as they say). ...vitiated through **sympathy** <note>original: "consensum"; a medical theory where one organ suffers because it is physiologically "in sympathy" or connected with the primary site of disease.</note>, and for other causes (as you have seen); indeed, all the other members are vitiated if the disease has gained strength. Furthermore, the **French Disease** <note>original: "morbus Gallicus"; a common 16th-century name for syphilis.</note> is not rarely complicated with other illnesses, such as with **gout** <note>original: "podagra"</note> or with some fever, so that when these conditions are found to be so complicated, they are indeed very difficult to cure, as you will see in my "Great Book on Fevers." From these things, you see that this bad temperament, regarding its active qualities, is a certain **cooling**; this is surely attested by all the symptoms which proceed from the primary disease. Its heat is not at all sharp or biting, but is quite similar to the heat of a **quotidian fever** <note>A fever that recurs daily, traditionally associated with an excess of phlegm.</note>, without thirst, and very much conforming in its other symptoms to those following quotidian fevers. This is because it depends on matter that is for the most part **phlegmatic** <note>original: "pituitosa"; relating to the humor of phlegm, which was considered cold and moist.</note> and putrefying. <note>original: "E P I S T O L A"</note>

The hair loss that occurs everywhere among people in these times is (for the most part and in the majority of cases) a symptom of the often-mentioned **French Disease**. Nor do the things that the ancients wrote about <term>Alopecia</term> <note>A classic medical term for patchy hair loss, derived from the Greek word for "fox."</note> and <term>Tyria</term> <note>Also known as ophiasis; a form of hair loss that follows a winding, snake-like path.</note>—which are both types of baldness—stand in the way of this conclusion. For in those conditions, the cause is a clear, bad matter present in the skin itself, which prevents nourishment from reaching the hair and also rots the roots of the hair along with its nourishment. 

But in the hair loss of the <term>French Disease</term>, the cause is what I stated above: namely, an unnatural quality arising from a mixture and alteration that is not manifest, beyond the obvious mixing of the four qualities, which corrupts the nature of the nourishment; and this is the primary difference. For <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his theories on humors formed the backbone of European medicine for 1,500 years.</note> wrote in his first book *On Medicines According to Localities* that hair loss occurs from corrupted nourishment; he teaches us to recognize which humor is at fault by the color of the skin. 

Therefore, gather the signs that are seen everywhere in those who lose their hair from the **French Disease**, and you will see that the causes of the hair loss show a certain cold temperament and an abundance of slow humors of unnatural **phlegm**, even if other humors are also mixed in. That primary matter, with its hidden quality and its thickness, blocks the <term>passages</term> <note>original: "meatus"; referring to the pores or channels in the skin through which humors and "vapors" were thought to flow.</note> so that it prevents the proportionate vapors from being carried to the outermost parts of the body for the nourishment of the hair. This is the primary cause, and it is clearly seen in women and eunuchs, whose bodies, because they are cooled, lack hair, especially in the beard and certain other places. 

In men who are not mutilated, if this should happen—namely, that certain parts are deprived of hair, such as the beard and other areas—the cause is not merely cooling, but often a multitude of matter blocking the passages through which the smoky evaporation ought to pass. Or, the cause is an excessive moisture that dilates or relaxes the passages and thickens the vapors, converting them into another substance so that they are no longer the material for the generation and nourishment of hair. Consequently, the hair either does not grow, or if it is present, it falls out due to a lack of nourishment, aided by the widening of the passages. 

Nor shall I omit one thing that is most striking in the hair loss of the **French Disease**, which creates a distinction between it and the aforementioned "non-French" types of hair loss: in the French condition, we see not only the hair of the head and the beard fall out, but even the eyelids and the eyelashes, which are hairs fixed in...

For as has been said, this matter, spread through the entire body, cools, moistens, and obstructs, and by its hidden quality, it corrupts and infects all natural powers. For I have said that even if this matter is always, or often, phlegmatic <note>The author refers to "pituita," or phlegm, one of the four traditional humors. Through this mixing, a diversity arises both in the substance and in the qualities of that matter. For if the <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>The "black bile" humor, associated with coldness, dryness, and thickness.</note> is mixed in, this matter becomes thickened and hard. But if blood is mixed in, it becomes less hard and is rendered milder. However, if it is mixed with the <term>bilious humor</term> <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and sharpness.</note>, it is rendered corrosive, especially if the bile has been made <term>adust</term> <note>From the Latin *adustio*, meaning "burnt." A pathological form of phlegm believed to be sharp and stinging, causing skin irritations and ulcers.</note>. This humor corrodes, causes ulceration, and excites itching, according to the greater or lesser mixing and the "burning" of the bile. 

Add also that phlegm, even without mixing, can be made salty and corrosive if it is "burnt" by some cause. These things being so, if that humor is detained in any part of the body—which happens easily since it is sluggish and blocks the passages—and if by this obstruction it hinders the passage of nourishment to the limb, as well as the "spirits" <note>In Galenic medicine, "spirits" (pneuma) were subtle substances that traveled through the body to enable movement, sensation, and vital functions.</note> required for natural operations, all these consequences follow easily: first, corrosion and ulceration if it is in a soft member (such as the jaw/gums); then a lack of nourishment; and finally, the destruction of the member or part.

This latter heat, when communicated to the heart, is what we call a fever. I do not want you to wonder if I say that heat and cold can exist unnaturally in one and the same organ; for what I have said is possible given the diversity of the parts. For example, if we wish to assign the possibility of different temperatures in the liver, we shall say the liver has an upper part of its substance, which they call the **gibbous part** <note>The rounded, convex upper surface of the liver.</note> of the liver, and a lower part which they call the **hollow part**. It also has the substance of the veins, which is different from the flesh of the liver, and these veins are distinct according to their origin, even though they are joined within the organ itself. Therefore, since there are many distinct parts, one part can be heated either by the humor it contains or by neighboring parts and veins...

Nor is the drink of the decoction of Indian wood made with wine (with other things added) a healthy medicine in every part for a *new* case of the French Disease. This is because nature has not yet prepared the thick, **phlegmatic matter** <note>original: "materiam pituitosam," referring to the cold, moist humor that physicians believed slowed down the body's healing.</note> mixed with the blood in such a way that it can direct it toward the paths of the natural ducts and drive it out of the body through some suitable region. For as **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> wrote in the first of his **Aphorisms** <note>original: "primo aphorismorum"</note>, they err who attempt to move and lead out crude and unprepared matter, especially when it is not "unbridled" <note>That is, when the matter is not already in a state of flux or high activity.</note>. 

Now, since a decoction of the wood made with wine and other dissolving things moves nature and leads matter out through the bowels, and directs it to other regions (since it is hot and provokes both urine and sweat), it moves the crude matter along with that matter which is naturally at its best. Thus, a mixing of good and bad humors occurs, which are not led out except with labor and difficulty, and with the greatest harm to nature. This issue does not occur in the common decoction of Indian wood made from **spring water** alone. Rather, this decoction thus prepared is a suitable medicine, tempered enough to prepare the matter in the **liver** <note>original: "iocinore"</note> and the veins, in which the "ultimate malice" <note>The most advanced or toxic stage of the disease.</note> has not yet been reached. When the thinner parts are resolved—even if the matter is crude and cold—it undoubtedly requires tempered qualities that do not exceed in their active properties. 

And even if it is so (as I have said), the drink of the decoction of the wood made with water does not for that reason heal the new French Disease easily, quickly, or perfectly in the same way that **ointments** <term>illinitiones: medicinal rubs or inunctions, often containing mercury.</term> and other aids do, which do not provoke and open the body so much from the start. Therefore, in a new case of the disease, if anyone desires to be healed with the said decoction, it is worthwhile first to empty the body—namely, by opening a vein...

But the established time which may reasonably apply to everyone is the space of forty days, which duration and limit is the midpoint between acute and chronic illnesses; or, as <term>Galen</term> <note>Claudius Galenus, a 2nd-century physician whose medical theories based on the four humors dominated Western medicine until the 17th century.</note> said in his 22nd commentary on the second book of the <term>Aphorisms</term> <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, which Galen frequently annotated.</note>, it is the duration of acute diseases which are judged <note>reaches a "crisis" or turning point</note> in forty days.

Besides this distribution, it also possesses manifest heat and moisture, qualities which oppose the disease and [provide] much power...

# ON SKIN ERUPTIONS AND HAIR LOSS

->E T<-

[The properties of] the wood increase, so that they cause a greater dissolution where the slow-moving matter already adheres to the veins, muscles, and other parts of our body. Let these things suffice for the general cure through the decoction of the wood in wine. It remains for me to record those remedies which are conducive to baldness and the falling out of hair, as well as the erosion of the gums and the falling out of teeth.

First, the regimen of food and drink prevents the loss of hair—namely, by eating those things which provide good nourishment <note>original: "boni succi" (good juices); in humoral theory, food was transformed into "juices" or humors that sustained the body.</note>, and by cutting back on immoderate quantities and all excess of every kind. One must especially abstain from things prone to decay and those that are hard to digest, such as all viscous things and those of poor substance: such as old meats, cheese, and vegetables like cabbage, rocket, and similar herbs. This which I have said must also be understood regarding fruits and fish. Similarly, all sharp things should be forbidden, such as spices, salted foods, legumes, garlic, onions, and the like.

Then, after the regimen, the greatest caution and precaution in the case of hair loss is to purge the body of bad and superfluous humors. In this disease (as has often been said), these are slow, phlegmatic humors <note>original: "humores pituitosi lenti"</note> mixed with other humors against nature; but in those in whom the hair falls out, it is a "salty phlegm" resulting from a mixture of bile <note>original: "pituita salsa est ex permixtione bilis"</note>. Therefore, one should proceed as follows where there is a great abundance of humors—especially of "bad blood"—and if the age, strength, and time of year allow.

First, by opening the vein in the arm which they call the **liver vein** <note>original: "vena iecoria"; usually refers to the basilic vein in the right arm, which was historically believed to drain the liver.</note>, and the blood should be evacuated according to the requirements of the matter and the endurance of [the patient's] strength. For the letting of blood evacuates all humors. After the evacuation of blood, the other humors should be prepared for evacuation with these syrups (for the sake of example):

<term>Recipe</term> <note>original: "℞"</note>: One ounce of syrup of **fumitory** <note>original: "fumoterrae"; a plant used to treat skin diseases and cleanse the blood.</note>, either simple or compound depending on the requirement of the phlegmatic matter mixed with bile; half an ounce of **honey of roses**. One and a half ounces each of the waters of **hops** <note>original: "lupulorum"</note> and **scabious** <note>original: "scabiose"</note>. 

These syrups should be taken in the morning at dawn for several days. And when signs of "concoction" <note>A medical concept where the body "cooks" or matures the bad humors so they can be expelled; often judged by changes in urine.</note> appear in the urine, let the said humors be evacuated with appropriate [medicines]. For example:

<term>Recipe</term>: Seven drams each of **lenitive electuary** <note>A mild laxative paste.</note> and **hiera picra** <note>original: "hiera pichræ"; a famous "holy bitter" purgative made of aloes and spices.</note>. Mix with three ounces of a decoction of **dodder of thyme** <note>original: "epithimi mesue"</note>. Let it be made into a drink and taken in the morning five hours before lunch. 

And because the matter is thick and cannot be drawn out by a single evacuation, stronger syrups should be given again for preparation, such as syrup of **dodder** or of **stoechas** <note>original: "stœcados"; French lavender.</note> and similar things, and they should be evacuated again.

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT DOCTORS
## To the physicians Master Pietro Beroaldo and Master Paolo a’ Pargo. Letter XXXI. Concerning a deep, painful, and corrosive ulcer, with the greatest inflammation and pustules around it.

**I** confess that I owe much to you, most excellent Paolo, and indeed there is nothing I could deny you; and you also, most learned Pietro Beroaldo, I always cherish for your integrity. Now, since in your letters, my dear Paolo, you ask that I should signify to you what I think about the essence of the illness of a certain noble patient, and about the manner of curing it, I will gladly do so to satisfy you. 

And first, as you write, the noble man is 70 years of age, of a sanguine and choleric temperament <note>Based on the theory of the Four Humors; a "sanguine" person had a dominance of blood (warm and moist), while "choleric" indicated yellow bile (warm and dry). This balance determined health and character.</note> from a "sub-dominion," <note>An astrological or medical term referring to a secondary influence on the patient's constitution.</note> as some more modern writers say, and full of many bad humors. This man began to fall ill on the fourth day of February with a common and yet singular disease: specifically, a small abscess <note>original: "apostemate"; a localized collection of pus or a swelling.</note> on the neck near the nape <note>original: "nucam"; from the Arabic "nukha," referring to the spinal cord or the back of the neck.</note>, about the size of a chickpea <note>original: "ciceris"; medical authors frequently used seeds and nuts (lentils, chickpeas, walnuts) to describe the size of tumors or wounds.</note>, with a certain crust. This finally suppurated over the space of eight days so that pus was discharged. 

After six more days, it increased to the size of a nut, around which appeared very many pustules, which themselves were full of discharge (as I hear). Then, after many treatments were applied by both the most experienced surgeons and the most excellent physicians, it developed into a very large ulcer with a great quantity (I will not say of discharge) but of corrupt blood. Having carefully weighed all these things, I say the magnificent man...

...that he suffered a hot <term>aposteme</term> <note>original: "apostema"; an ancient term for an inflammatory swelling or abscess caused by an accumulation of humors.</note>, which is of the kind of evil abscesses that they call a <term>carbuncle</term> <note>original: "carbonem"; literally "coal," referring to the black, charred appearance of the necrotic tissue.</note>, by the testimony of **Galen** in the second book of *To Glaucon*, and **Avicenna** in the third book of the fourth volume. This carbuncle is indeed caused by bad, thick, and burnt blood. For **Galen** said in the place previously cited:

> when the flowing blood has become sufficiently hot and thick, whatever limb it suddenly occupies, it creates a crust by burning it. Whatever lies around it, it raises in inflammation, and brings on a burning and heavy pain. This kind of suffering is called a **carbuncle**. But when the flowing blood is black, thick, dreg-like, and boiling (of the kind we mentioned before), and at the same time contains some thin moisture, it excites certain pustules upon the surface of the skin similar to those caused by fire. When these are broken, a crusty ulcer is found beneath them; this too is a **carbuncle**, a certain species of inflammation.

These are the words of **Galen** which I wished to recite, so that your Excellencies may see how greatly they fit this magnificent patient; nor do I believe I need further witnesses regarding the essence of the previous illness. But if I wished to apply here those things which the most learned men, both ancient and modern, have written concerning <term>cancer</term> <note>original: "cancro"; in this period, "cancer" often referred to any spreading, malignant-looking ulcer, not necessarily a modern oncological diagnosis.</note> (as was doubted), they undoubtedly do not fit this case.

What molests the man at present, however, and makes your Excellencies fearful, is a painful ulcer with very many pustules and the greatest inflammation around it, such that it is neither matured nor benign, but rather spreading, deep, and not free from a certain hardness and the remains of bad, burnt blood, which was the material of the previous abscess. Since all these things require a medicinal regimen, you asked me in the second place for my opinion on what remedies are necessary to use for such a complicated and malignant ulcer. 

To comply with your wishes, although I believe everything is undoubtedly well known to you, I will endeavor to explain them very briefly, starting first with the regimen of air and other things—especially food and drink. These foods should entirely lean toward a temperate coldness and a certain dryness; even if a moist diet is appropriate by reason of the fever, nevertheless, since carbuncles are formed from poisonous and pestiferous matter and the ulcer requires some drying, this seems to be better (nor do I intend to "teach Minerva" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to teach someone who is already an expert.</note>). It is perfected by defining, dividing, and arguing; for the dialecticians say they are defining when...

<page-num>121</page-num>
<header>LETTERS</header>

...either they explain the essence of a thing, or they interpret the name by describing it. They "divide" <note>original: "Diuidunt"; referring to the logical process of division, breaking a whole into its parts.</note> when they enumerate members or parts, but they "argue" when another conclusion is derived from previously established reasons. Truly, those things which are usually first defined by the dialectician <note>A student or practitioner of dialectic, the art of logical discussion and reasoning.</note> are utterances, or **terms** <note>original: "termini"</note> (as they say), propositions, and the argument. They define a term in its primary sense thus: **Terms** are the simple parts of a proposition that signify something entirely; or a term is that into which a proposition is resolved; or terms are those things from which propositions or sentences are constructed. For example: **God**, **man**, **animal**, **blessed**, **happy**, **wretched**, **wisdom**, **prudence**, **avarice**. They even call verbs "terms," such as **I am**, **I read**, and the rest. They say such a term is twofold: namely, **common** and **discrete**. A **common** term is one that signifies, or can signify, several things under one word, such as **man**, **knowledge**, and the like. A **discrete** term is one that signifies, or can signify, only one thing under one word, such as **Peter**, **John**, **Mary**, and the like. There are also certain terms which are called **universal signs**, and some which are called **particular signs**. **Universal** signs are those like **all**, **anything**, **none**, **no one**, and the like. **Particular** signs are those like **someone**, **a certain one**, **another**, and the like. 

Furthermore, among the terms that constitute a proposition as its principal parts, one is called the **subject**, one the **predicate**, and one the **copula** <note>The "linking" word in a sentence.</note> or conjunction. For example, in this proposition: "**Antonius is a doctor**." In this proposition, the **subject** term is **Antonius**, and it stands before the copula; the **predicate** is **doctor**, and it stands after the copula; but the copula will be the verb **is**, because it joins one thing with the other. As the grammarians say, this is the first, second, or third part, or person—singular or plural—of the indicative mood of the verb: **I am**, **you are**, **he is**. 

Often, however, not all three parts are explicitly stated in a proposition, but they are understood. For instance, if I say "**Aristotle teaches**," here only the **subject** and the verb are expressed. The **predicate** is implicit in the verb, which you can recognize if you resolve the verb "**teaches**" through the verb "**is**" and a participle, saying: "**Aristotle is teaching**." But the terms called particular and universal signs—such as **all**, **none**, **someone**, **a certain one**, and similar terms—can be neither the primary subject nor the predicate. A **proposition**, moreover, is an indicative and complete sentence, composed of terms, signifying that something is...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of logic and dialectic, following the definitions of "terms" provided on the previous page. It transitions from discussing individual words to how those words are combined into complete statements.</meta>

<page-num>152</page-num>
<header>THIRTY-SECOND [LETTER]</header>

# THIRTY-SECOND [LETTER]

...to be, or not to be, signifying either what is true or what is false without ambiguity, such as: **"Man is an animal"** or **"A stone is a donkey."** Thus we say that a **proposition** <note>original: "propositionem"; a statement or assertion that expresses a judgment.</note> is either true or false. A true proposition is one that signifies a thing exactly as it is, as in the example: **"Man is an animal."** A false one is that which signifies a thing in a way other than it is, as in the example: **"A stone is a donkey."**

Among the aforementioned propositions, one kind is the **simple enunciative**—or as the logicians say, **categorical**—and another is the **joined** kind, which the Greeks call **hypothetical**.

A **categorical** <note>original: "Categorica"; a direct assertion about a subject.</note> or enunciative proposition is a single statement made of a **subject**, a **predicate**, and a **copula** <note>The "copula" is the linking verb, usually "is," that connects the subject to the description.</note>, such as: **"God is omnipotent."** Such a proposition is either **universal**, **particular**, **indefinite**, or **singular**.

*   A **universal proposition** is one (whether it be affirmative or negative) whose subject is a common term or word to which a **universal sign** has been added, such as: **"All men are animals"** or **"No man is an animal."**
*   A **particular proposition** is one that (whether affirming or denying) is only applied in a particular way; a common term is placed as the subject and restricted by a **particular sign**, such as: **"A certain man is a doctor"** and **"A certain man is not a doctor."**
*   An **indefinite proposition** is one uttered without any mark of universality or particularity, whether affirming or denying; it is one whose subject is taken without any sign at all, such as: **"Man is an animal"** or **"Man is not an animal."**
*   A **singular proposition** is one that picks out a specific individual, either by a proper name or by a common word with a **demonstrative pronoun** <note>Words like "this" or "that" which point to a specific object.</note> added to it, both in affirming and denying. For example: **"Anthony is a doctor"** and **"This man is a musician,"** or in the negative: **"Anthony is not a doctor"** and **"This man is not a musician."**

Furthermore, of categorical propositions, one kind is **affirmative** and the other is **negative**. An **affirmative** proposition is one that pronounces or establishes that something belongs to the subject and attributes it to them, such as: **"Man is rational."** A **negative** proposition is one that takes something away from the subject and properly removes the predicate, such as: **"Man is not rational."**

Regarding propositions, three things are usually asked—or rather, there are three standard questions: namely, **what** it is, **how great** it is, and **of what kind** the proposition is.
1. When it is asked **what** it is <note>original: "quæ sit"; referring to the structure or species of the statement.</note>, one asks whether it is categorical or hypothetical.
2. When it is asked **how great** it is <note>original: "quanta sit"; referring to the "quantity" or scope.</note>, one asks whether it is universal, particular, indefinite, or singular.
3. But when it is asked **of what kind** it is <note>original: "qualis sit"; referring to its logical "quality."</note>, one asks whether it is affirmative or negative.

Furthermore, certain propositions which are called categorical agree with others in certain ways, and...

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of logical propositions, moving from the definitions of universal and particular statements to how these statements relate to one another and how they can be logically rearranged through "conversion."</meta>

...certain propositions do not agree, but they do agree in three ways. First, if they are of the same <term>quantity</term> <note>Quantity refers to whether a statement is "universal" (applying to all) or "particular" (applying to some).</note>, for example if one is <term>universal</term> and the other is also universal; similarly, if one is affirmative, the other must be affirmative, and the same applies to negative statements. 

Second, <term>propositions</term> <note>In logic, a proposition is a complete statement that can be judged as either true or false.</note> agree when they have a similar <term>subject</term> or <term>predicate</term> <note>The "subject" is what the sentence is about; the "predicate" is the description or action attributed to that subject.</note>, such as: **Animal is substance**, **Man is substance**, and **Animal is living**, **Man is living**. 

Third, they agree when they are similar in both the subject and the predicate, such as: **Some animal is capable of laughter**, **Some animal is not capable of laughter**. 

Propositions do not agree when they are different in both subject and predicate, such as: **Man is an animal**, **A stone is a substance**, and the like. 

There are also certain changes in propositions which they call <term>conversions</term> <note>Conversion is a logical operation where the subject and predicate of a proposition are swapped to see if the statement remains true.</note>, and this occurs whenever we turn the subject into the predicate or the predicate into the subject. This happens in two ways: either <term>simply</term> or <term>by accident</term>. 

<term>Simple conversion</term> <note>original: "simplex conuersio"</note> is when the subject is changed into the predicate and the predicate into the subject while the same quantity and quality remain in both propositions. For example: **Every Man is capable of laughter** <note>original: "riſibilis"; in medieval logic, the ability to laugh was considered a unique property of human beings used to test definitions.</note>, which is converted in this way: **Everything capable of laughter is a Man**; and **A certain Man is capable of laughter** [becomes] **A certain thing capable of laughter is a Man**. 

But <term>accidental conversion</term> <note>original: "conuerſio per accidens"</note> does not happen in the same way in every respect. Propositions are converted "by accident" when the subject is changed into the predicate and the predicate into the subject while the same quality remains in both propositions, but the quantity is changed. This happens only in two types of propositions: namely, in the universal affirmative and the universal negative, which are converted into the particular of their own quality. 

For instance, in the affirmative, if you say **Every Man is capable of laughter**, it is converted "by accident" by saying: **A certain thing capable of laughter is a Man**. Similarly, the universal negative is converted, such as **No Man is a stone**, by saying: **A certain stone is not a Man**. By this same conversion, the <term>particular affirmative</term>, the <term>indefinite</term>, and the <term>singular</term> are converted. 

However, it should be noted that in the <term>particular negative</term>, conversion does not properly occur; this is because a true proposition could be converted into a false one. For example: **A certain animal is not a Man**; its conversion would be **A certain Man is not an animal**. Since the converted statement is false, such a proposition ought not be converted. Furthermore, those things which have been said regarding propositions...

It distinguishes between simple conversion and accidental conversion, noting that particular negative statements cannot be converted without losing their truth value.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of logical propositions, transitioning from the concept of conversion to the "oppositions"—how different types of statements (like "all" vs. "some") conflict with or support one another. It then introduces more complex proposition structures involving "either/or" and "and" logic.</meta>

<page-num>153</page-num>
<header>THIRTY-SECOND</header>

Regarding propositions which serve the knowledge of truth and falsehood, it is worthwhile to know how <term>propositions</term> <note>In logic, a proposition is a statement that can be proven true or false.</note> either conflict with or agree with one another. Thus, it should be known that among propositions agreeing in a similar <term>subject</term> and <term>predicate</term> <note>The subject is who/what the sentence is about; the predicate is what is being said about them.</note>, there are four <term>oppositions</term> <note>original: "oppoſitiones"; these are the standard ways statements can disagree in formal logic.</note>: namely, <term>contraries</term>, <term>sub-contraries</term>, <term>contradictories</term>, and <term>subalterns</term>.

**Contraries** are two universal statements, of which one is affirmative and the other is negative—for example, saying **Every man is an animal** and **No man is an animal**. These can never truly be true at the same time. However, they can both be false, especially if both are in <term>contingent matter</term> <note>original: "materia contingenti"; this refers to topics where the facts can change or vary, rather than being essential definitions.</note>, such as **Every man is a doctor** and **No man is a doctor**. These are contraries, and both are false.

**Sub-contraries** are two particular statements, one of which is affirmative and the other negative, which agree in subject and predicate—for example, **Some man is an animal** and **Some man is not an animal**. These can indeed be true at the same time in contingent matter; however, in <term>necessary matter</term> <note>original: "materia neceſſaria"; refers to essential, unchangeable truths.</note> (as in this example), if one is true, the other is false.

**Contradictories** are opposed as a universal affirmative and a particular negative, or a universal negative and a particular affirmative—for example, **Every man is an animal** and **Some man is not an animal**, or **No man is an animal** and **Some man is an animal**. These disagree with each other so completely that they can never be true or false at the same time. Also considered contradictories are a particular affirmative and negative <note>original: "particularis affirmatiua, & negatiua"; usually these are sub-contraries, but the author may be grouping them here by their capacity to conflict.</note>, or two singular statements, such as **Peter is a man** and **Peter is not a man**.

**Subalterns**, finally, are a universal affirmative paired with its own particular affirmative, and a universal negative paired with its own universal <insert>particular</insert> negative. These do not disagree, but are either true at the same time or false at the same time—for example, **Every man is an animal** and **Some man is an animal**, and in the negative, **No man is an animal** and **Some man is not an animal**.

Furthermore, it should be known that the two "extremes" in a categorical proposition are the subject and the predicate. From these, two-part names are given to propositions; we say that a categorical proposition is either of a **disjunct extreme** or of a **copulate extreme**.

A categorical proposition of a **disjunct extreme** <note>original: "extremo diiuncto"</note> is one in which a "disjunctive" term or mark (like "or") is placed in the subject or predicate—for example, **A man or a stone is an animal**, or likewise, **A man is an animal or a stone**.

A categorical proposition of a **copulate extreme** <note>original: "extremo copulato"; referring to a "conjunctive" or "and" statement.</note> is one in which they place in the subject or predicate...

...a term or a copulative sign <note>A word like "and" that joins two things together.</note>, such as **A man and a donkey are animals**, or by saying **He is a man and a doctor**. But take note that sometimes a <term>categorical proposition</term> <note>A simple statement with a subject and a predicate, like "The sky is blue."</note> involves both "extremes"—namely the disjoined and the joined—and sometimes one of the extremes is disjoined and the other joined (to use the language of the <term>dialecticians</term> <note>A term for scholars of logic.</note>). And so that this letter does not go on for too long, let this be enough said regarding the categorical.

Now I shall follow with the <term>hypothetical proposition</term> <note>A complex statement made by joining two or more simple statements together.</note>, which consists of several categoricals. Therefore, a hypothetical proposition is a statement which consists of two or more categoricals, or simple statements, as its main parts. These are united together by some conjunction or its equivalent, such as **A man is an animal and the earth is immovable**. The Latins call this kind "suppository" or "conditional." There are six species of these, namely: **Copulative, Disjunctive, Conditional, Rational, Temporal, and Local**.

However, these are reduced to three types in this way: they are formed either by connection, by disjunction, or again by connection or copulation. Furthermore, the **copulative** is formed when parts are joined by a "copulative" conjunction <note>Such as the word "and".</note>. And by "connection," we mean that which becomes a single statement through a certain conjunction of two or more parts. But so that you may understand better, I will list all of them according to the six modes mentioned before, the first of which is the copulative.

1.  **Copulative**: This is one in which two categorical statements are joined by a copulative particle, such as: **A man is an animal, and an animal is a substance.**
2.  **Disjunctive**: This is one in which two categoricals are united by a disjunctive conjunction <note>Such as the word "or".</note>, such as: **A man is an animal, or a substance is a being.**
3.  **Conditional**: This is one in which two categoricals are joined by a conditional sign or particle, such as: **If a man runs, an animal runs.**
4.  **Rational**: This is when two categorical propositions are joined by the particle "therefore" or "ergo," as in saying: **An animal runs, therefore it moves.**
5.  **Temporal**: This is one in which two categoricals are joined with a particle serving time, such as: **A man is healthy when all his functions appear unharmed.**
6.  **Local**: Finally, the local is that which has two categoricals joined with a particle describing place, such as: **Where there is pain, there is disease.**

And since <term>dialectics</term> <note>The study of logic and the art of reasoning.</note> teaches us to recognize truth and falsehood in speech, you will note—not without benefit—that for a **copulative** statement to be true, it is necessary for both categorical statements within it to be true. ### THIRTY-SECOND

<margin>V 2</margin>

A <term>hypothetical proposition</term> <note>A complex statement made of two or more simple statements joined together.</note> is called false whenever any of its <term>categorical</term> <note>Simple, direct statements like "The sky is blue."</note> parts is false. For example, if one says: **A human is an animal, and a human is a donkey.** Since the second statement is false, the entire <term>copulative proposition</term> <note>A statement using "and" to join its parts.</note> is said to be false, because it contains one false part. 

But for a <term>disjunctive proposition</term> <note>A statement using "or" to join its parts.</note> to be true, it is enough for just one of those statements to be true. For example: **A human is an animal, or a donkey is not a stone.** Thus, it is clear that if one part of a disjunctive statement is true, the whole proposition is called true. However, for it to be false, it is necessary that all its statements be false, such as if I were to say: **A human is irrational, or a stone is an animal.** 

Regarding the truth of a <term>conditional proposition</term> <note>An "if-then" statement.</note>, it is required that the "antecedent" <note>The "if" part of the statement.</note> cannot exist without the "consequent" <note>The "then" or "therefore" part of the statement.</note>. For example: **You are a human, therefore you are an animal.** This will be true if the opposite of the consequent is incompatible with the antecedent. You will recognize its falsehood if the opposite of the consequent can stand alongside the antecedent, or if the antecedent can exist without the consequent.

Furthermore, it should be known that every proposition is either <term>necessary</term>, <term>possible</term>, <term>impossible</term>, or <term>contingent</term>. 

A **necessary** proposition is one that is true in such a way that it cannot be false in any way. For example: **God is almighty**, **God is good**, **God is the cause of all causes**, or **A human is rational**, and similar statements. 

A **possible** proposition is one that could go either way; that is, it can be true or not true. For example: **A human will be a doctor**, or **A human will not be a musician.** But take note: that which "can be" refers to the present, and signifies that a thing in the present is not "possible" except in its "mode" <note>This refers to Modal Logic, where the author suggests that present facts are already fixed, whereas future events are truly "possible."</note>, because regarding actual existence, it is fixed; but if it denotes the future, it is possible. 

An **impossible** proposition is one that signifies a thing in a way that it cannot possibly exist, such as saying: **A human is a stone**, or **A human is not an animal.** 

A **contingent** proposition is one that can be true because it has been so at other times, yet it is not necessary. For example: **A student will be a teacher**, and **A boy will be a man.** 

And in the same way for the rest. Since propositions are made of words or terms that have certain "degrees" by which more common terms are distinguished from less common ones, it will be very useful to list those words and degrees after these things. Indeed, there are primarily five degrees, namely: <term>genus</term> <note>A general category, like "Animal."</note>, <term>species</term> <note>A specific category under a genus, like "Human."</note>, <term>difference</term> <note>The specific quality that distinguishes one species from another, like "Rationality."</note>, <term>property</term> <note>A quality belonging only to one species, like "the ability to laugh."</note>, and <term>accident</term> <note>A quality that can change without changing the thing's essence, like "being seated."</note>. 

A <term>genus</term> is that which is predicated <note>Stated or affirmed.</note> of many things that differ in their species. A <term>species</term> is that which is predicated of many things that differ only in number <note>Meaning individuals of the same kind, like Peter and Paul.</note>. A <term>difference</term> is that which is predicated of many things and is the defining characteristic of a certain species, making it differ from others.

<header>P R E F A T O R Y   L E T T E R</header>

# P R E F A T O R Y   L E T T E R

A <term>property</term> <note>original: "Proprium"; a characteristic that is not part of a thing's essence but belongs only to that species, like "laughter" for humans.</note> is that which belongs to only one thing and not to others, just as being capable of laughter is a property only of a human. An **accident**, finally, is that which is present or absent without the destruction of the subject, or it is that which cannot exist by itself, nor in itself <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "sitting." You can stop being tall or sitting without ceasing to be a human.</note>. There are, furthermore, ten **categories** <note>original: "praedicamenta"; the ten fundamental ways of classifying everything that can be said about a subject.</note> which exist as simple terms and name the principles of all things; they are namely: **substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, position, when, where, and state.**

Those who study <term>dialectics</term> <note>The art of logical discussion and investigation.</note> and express things through speech or propositions say that **substance** is self-subsisting and requires nothing else. For this reason, they say certain words signify "substance," in which the other nine categories reside—for example, "this Man," as well as species and genera. After the first and second substance, there is the word signifying **quantity**, which is that by which a substance is measured, such as a line, a surface, a physical body, and others which are called "continuous quantities"; there is also "discrete quantity," such as a number and similar things.

**Quality**, however, is that according to which a thing is said to be "of what kind," such as white, black, a musician, a doctor, and the like. **Relation** (or "towards something") is that whose very being refers to another, such as a Father to a son, or a Master to a servant. **Action** signifies the act of doing, such as heating, cooling, or the verbs "to heat" and "to cool"; whereas **Passion** <note>In this context, "passion" means "being acted upon" or "undergoing," rather than an emotion.</note> is the result or the effect of the action, such as "being heated" or "being cooled."

**Position** is named from the way something is placed, as one is said to "stand" from a certain stance, or to sit, to lie down, and the like. Furthermore, **When** signifies being in time, such as being in a day, a night, a month, a year, and the like. Similarly, **Where** signifies being in a place, such as in a house, in the forum, in the street, and the like. Finally, **State** <note>original: "habitus"; referring to something external that a person "has" or wears.</note> signifies that which comes from the outside and is not at all innate, but is something distinct from the one who has it, such as having a garment, being armed, and being shod, or similar things. Indeed, all the categories subsist in the first one (substance) as if in another, because the existence of an "accident" is found within "substantive" things.

Regarding these types of terms and their number, they give the primary praise to **Aristotle**; but whatever the case may be, this doctrine of categories is marvelous for investigating and understanding all sciences and arts. You will be able to experience this in your patients (since you are a physician), seeing how much utility it provides for perfect understanding. Furthermore, the order of the categories is wonderfully conducive to knowing diseases with precision; for when you approach...

If you proceed toward a patient through these categories, undoubtedly nothing further can be devised that contributes to a perfect understanding of the disease. In this way, you should first examine its **substance**; and although a disease is strictly an **accident** <note>In logic, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to the subject's being. While a person is a "substance," a disease is an "accident" because it happens to them.</note>, physicians very often speak of the "substance of the disease" in a proper sense. 

You will recognize this substance if you first investigate what the disease is—namely, whether it is a **bad temperament** <note>original: "mala temperies"; referring to an imbalance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note>, a bad composition of parts, or a breach of unity. 

Secondly, it will be worthwhile to investigate its **quantity**—that is, whether it is large or small. 

Thirdly, one must investigate its **quality**: for instance, if there is a bad temperament, is it a fever? And is it of a malignant nature <note>original: "malimoris"</note> or not, or something else? 

Fourth is **relation**: whether it is proportionate or disproportionate, or whether it is similar or dissimilar to something else. 

Fifth is **where** it is located first; for the bad temperament called a fever is first located in the heart. 

Sixth is **when**: namely, in what season of the year, at what hours it afflicts the patient, or at what age of life. 

Seventh is the **action** of the heat, and what it produces. 

Eighth is what follows in the patient <note>Representing the category of **passion**, or what the patient "undergoes" or "suffers."</note> and what their level of endurance is. 

Ninth is **position** <note>original: "situs"</note>; even if position does not strictly belong to the disease itself, the position of the patient often reveals the nature of the illness. 

Similarly, regarding **state** <note>original: "abitu" (habitus); the tenth category, referring to external equipment or condition.</note>, though the type of clothing—of the whole body or of a single limb, such as the head—may not lead to an understanding of the disease, it is nevertheless very useful in treatment. 

From these things, you can certainly gather how much utility the knowledge and enumeration of the **categories** <note>original: "praedicamentorum"</note> brings to the excellent investigation of things. 

But since wise men very often use one word for another, practitioners of **dialectic** <note>The art of logical reasoning and debate.</note> explain **suppositions** <note>original: "suppositiones"; a technical term in logic for how a word "stands in" for specific things in a sentence.</note> in this way: **Supposition** occurs when they place one word for another, or rather, "to suppose" is to substitute one word for another. 

There are many types: for one is called **material** and another **formal**. 
**Formal** is divided into **proper** and **improper**. 
**Proper** is then divided into **simple** and **personal**. 
**Personal** is divided into **discrete** and **common**. 
**Common** is then divided into **determinate** and **confused**. 
**Confused** is divided into **confused collective** and **confused non-collective**. 
**Collective** is then divided into **confused-only** and **confused distributive**. 
Finally, **confused distributive** is divided into **absolute** and **accommodated**. 

I wanted to list these types of suppositions because logicians and <term>sophists</term> <note>While often a negative term today, here it refers to those skilled in complex logical distinctions and academic disputation.</note> use them very often in their debates. 

Thus far, my Anthony, I have spoken of simple **propositions** <note>Complete statements that can be true or false.</note>, which exist as the elements of arguments. Now I shall write about the **argumentations** themselves, so that you may have a record of everything I spoke with you about when you were present. And first, I want you to know...

# ->E P I S T L E<-

An argument must be an ordered collection of propositions from which a settled or sought-after conclusion may be gathered, such as: "Man is an animal, therefore he is a sensible being" <note>original: "Homo est animal ergo est sensibile"</note>. There are, moreover, four species of <term>argumentation|The process of forming reasons and drawing conclusions.</term>, namely: **Syllogism**, **Enthymeme**, **Induction**, and **Example**. There are also proofs beyond these, and later, demonstrations, regarding which I shall note a few very brief points for you.

First, concerning the <term>Syllogism|A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises (the major and minor).</term>: A syllogism is a discourse in which, from two premises set forth in the proper **mode** and **figure**, a conclusion follows by necessity. For example: "Every man is an animal; every being capable of laughter is a man; therefore every being capable of laughter is an animal" <note>In traditional logic, "risibility" (the ability to laugh) was considered a unique property of human beings.</note>. The first two propositions are the "premises"; the third which follows is the "conclusion." The <term>Dialecticians|Logicians; those who study the art of investigating the truth of opinions.</term> call the first proposition the **major**, and the second the **minor**; the conclusion follows from these. This third part is not strictly a part of the syllogism itself, but rather follows from the syllogism.

Furthermore, in a syllogism there are three terms or words: namely, the **major extremity**, the **minor extremity**, and the **middle term**. The **major** is that which is placed only in the first proposition. The **minor** is that which is placed only in the second. The **middle term**, however, is that word which is spoken in both; or, it is that which is placed twice before the conclusion—namely, once in the major extremity and once in the minor extremity. Thus, there are two propositions when the middle term is expressed twice. 

If a syllogism should consist of more than three terms, it will undoubtedly be faulty. Moreover, the middle term never enters into the conclusion, since the conclusion is made from the major and minor extremities, as you can see in this syllogism: "Man is an animal; Francis is a man; therefore Francis is an animal." 

Regarding these matters, you will note that some conclusions are **direct** and some are **indirect**. A direct conclusion is one in which the major extremity is predicated of the minor. Furthermore, for a syllogism to be good, it is necessary that it be in **figure** and **mode**. **Figure** is the proper coordination of the terms from subject to predicate; there are three figures, and each of these figures has its own modes. **Mode**, within a figure, is the congruent order of terms, both in **quantity** <note>Whether the statement refers to "all" (universal) or "some" (particular).</note> and in **quality** <note>Whether the statement is "is" (affirmative) or "is not" (negative).</note>. 

Indeed, for the sake of a simpler order, the Dialecticians have established four vowel letters signifying the quantity of the propositions, which are: **A, E, I, O**. 
* **A** signifies a universal affirmative. 
* **E** signifies a universal negative. 
* **I** signifies a particular affirmative. 
* **O** signifies a particular negative.
