<header>THIRTY-SECOND 156</header>

In all these figures in general, it is necessary to observe these five laws. The **first** is that in any <term>syllogism|A logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two premises.</term>, at least one of the premises must be universal; this is because a true syllogism cannot be formed from two purely particular statements <note>For example, you cannot conclude anything certain from "Some men are tall" and "Some men are doctors."</note>. The **second** is that at least one of the premises must be affirmative, for a valid conclusion does not follow from two negative statements. The **third** is that if either of the premises is <term>particular|A statement referring to "some" rather than "all" of a group.</term>, the conclusion will also be particular; however, it does not follow that if one premise is universal, the conclusion must be universal. The **fourth** is that if the conclusion is negative, it is necessary that one of the premises be negative, and conversely, the same applies if it is affirmative. The **final** law is that in none of the figures does the <term>middle term|The term that links the two premises but disappears in the final conclusion.</term> enter into the conclusion.

There are, moreover, three figures of syllogisms and nineteen **modes**, which are contained in certain verses devised by <term>modern logicians|Referring to the "Logica Moderna" of the late Middle Ages/Renaissance.</term> for the purpose of memory and easier instruction; they are these: <term>Barbara</term>, <term>Celarent</term>, <term>Darii</term>, <term>Ferio</term>, <term>Baralipton</term>, <term>Celantes</term>, <term>Dabitis</term>, <term>Fapesmo</term>, <term>Frisesomorum</term>, <term>Cesare</term>, <term>Camestres</term>, <term>Festino</term>, <term>Baroco</term>, <term>Darapti</term>, <term>Felapton</term>, <term>Disamis</term>, <term>Datisi</term>, <term>Brocardo</term>, and <term>Ferison</term>. <note>These strange names are actually mnemonic codes. The vowels (A, E, I, O) tell the logician whether the statements in the argument are Universal Affirmative (A), Universal Negative (E), Particular Affirmative (I), or Particular Negative (O).</note> In each of these words, one of the four spoken vowels (which were mentioned a little earlier) is placed once, twice, or three times; or there are two, three, or all four. These denote the quantity of the propositions for each syllogism in every figure, as you will see shortly when I enumerate them all.

The **first figure** is that in which the subject in the major proposition is the predicate in the minor proposition. That word which is repeated twice and does not enter the conclusion will be the middle term. For example: *Every human is an animal; every being capable of laughter is a human; therefore, every being capable of laughter is an animal.* <note>original: "omnis Homo est animal, omne risibile est Homo, igitur omne risibile est animal"</note>

There are nine modes of this first figure, four of which conclude directly and the remaining five indirectly. The first four direct modes are contained in the first four words of the aforementioned verses: namely, **Barbara**, **Celarent**, **Darii**, and **Ferio**.

The first mode is contained in the word **Barbara**, in which the vowel **A** appears three times. This denotes that such a syllogism has two universal affirmative premises and a universal affirmative conclusion, which is recognized by the three vowels in this word. For example: *Every animal is a substance; every human is an animal; therefore, every human is a substance.* <note>original: "omne animal est substantia, omnis Homo est animal, ergo omnis Homo est substantia"</note> In this example, you see how the con—

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the first "figure" of syllogisms, completing the description of the mode Barbara (begun on the previous page) and detailing the other direct and indirect modes of reasoning using mnemonic names.</meta>

-> # ON THE EPISTLE <-

...the direct universal conclusion is concluded from universal premises. <note>This refers to the mode "Barbara," where two "All" statements lead to an "All" conclusion.</note> The **second mode**, which is contained in the word <term>Celarent|A mnemonic where E denotes a universal negative and A a universal affirmative.</term>, is a word that has the vowel **E** in the first syllable, **A** in the second, and **E** again in the third. This mode is formed from a universal negative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise, which conclude a universal negative; for example: "No animal is a stone; every human is an animal; therefore, no human is a stone." The **third mode** is contained in the word <term>Darii|A mnemonic for a syllogism with a universal affirmative and a particular affirmative premise.</term>, which word has **A** in the first syllable and **I** in the second and third. In this mode, a syllogism is made from a universal affirmative major premise and a particular affirmative minor premise, which conclude a particular affirmative; for example: "Every human is an animal; Francis is a human; therefore, Francis is an animal." <note>In traditional logic, a specific individual like "Francis" is treated as a "particular" instance.</note> The **fourth mode** is in the word <term>Ferio|A mnemonic for a syllogism concluding in a particular negative.</term>, in which **E** is in the first syllable, **I** in the second, and **O** in the third. From these, a syllogism is made from a universal negative major premise and a particular affirmative minor premise, concluding a particular negative; for example: "No animal is a stone; Francis is an animal; therefore, Francis is not a stone."

The five modes of the first figure that conclude **indirectly** are contained in the five following words, namely: <term>Baralipton</term>, <term>Celantes</term>, <term>Dabitis</term>, <term>Fapesmo</term>, and <term>Frisesomorum</term>. 

**Baralipton** has three initial vowels which form the premises of an indirectly concluding syllogism; from two universal affirmative premises, they produce a particular affirmative conclusion, such as: "Every animal is <term>sentient|Latin: 'sensibile,' referring to the ability to perceive with senses.</term>; every human is an animal; therefore, a certain sentient thing is a human." In the fourth and final syllable of this word <term>Baralipton</term>, there is the vowel **O**, which letter should not be weighed in any way for the purpose of forming the syllogism or reaching the conclusion, because it was added only for the rhythm of the verse. <note>Medieval students memorized these names in a rhyming poem; extra syllables were often added to make the poem scan correctly without adding logical meaning.</note> The same is to be said of other words that have more than the three vowels already mentioned, as you see in the word <term>Frisesomorum</term>, where only the first three vowels ought to be counted.

**Celantes** has three vowels: in the first syllable is **E**, in the second is **A**, and in the third is **E** again. In this word, a syllogism is made from a universal negative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise, which conclude a universal negative; for example: "No animal is a stone; every human is an animal; therefore, no stone is a human." 

**Dabitis** has the first vowel **A** and the two following as **I**; and therefore the syllogism in this word consists of a universal affirmative major premise and a particular affirmative minor premise, concluding a par- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; the intended word is "particular."</note>

From what has been said regarding this **first figure**, you see two conditions. The first is that within it all types of propositions are concluded: namely, the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative, and the particular negative. The second is that the <term>middle term|The term that appears in both premises but is absent from the conclusion, serving as the "bridge" between the other two terms.</term> is the subject in the major premise and the predicate in the minor premise.

However, these five modes that conclude indirectly are reduced to the first four that form a conclusion directly, if we wish to prove them and show them to be valid. Indeed, **Baralipton** is reduced to **Barbara** by the "conversion of the conclusion by accident" <note>original: "conuersionem conclufionis per accidens." But the **second figure** contains four modes that conclude directly and negatively. In this figure, a syllogism is formed in which the middle term—which is the predicate in the major premise—is also the predicate in the minor premise. In all its syllogisms, the major premise is universal; for example: "No stone is an animal; every human is an animal; therefore, no human is a stone." The four modes are explained in these four words: namely, **Cesare**, **Camestres**, **Festino**, and **Baroco**. 

The first mode indeed has three vowels, namely **E**, **A**, and **E**, which denote that the syllogism is made from a universal negative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise, forming a universal negative conclusion. Therefore, a syllogism is formed in this mode from a universal affirmative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise, resulting in a particular affirmative conclusion. For example: "Every Human is a substance, every Human is an animal; therefore, a certain animal is a substance."

->## LETTER<-

I shall list the various types of arguments according to the order set out above. An **Enthymeme** is therefore a mode of argumentation in which only one of the premises is expressed, from which the conclusion is gathered. Or, an <term>Enthymeme|A logical shorthand where the speaker leaves one of the premises unstated because it is assumed to be obvious.</term> is a "mutilated <term>Syllogism|A formal argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</term>" because it omits either the major or the minor proposition. For example: "Every Human is an animal, therefore Francis is an animal." In this case, the minor premise <note>The missing minor premise is "Francis is a human."</note> is missing, and the major premise is stated. The first proposition is called the **antecedent**, and the second is called the **consequent**.

**Induction**, however, is a mode of argumentation in which a universal proposition is gathered from many individual cases. For example: "Peter is rational, Francis is rational, Anthony is rational," and so on for other individuals of that species; "therefore, every human is rational."

The last mode of arguing is the **example**, by which one argues from one particular case to another similar one. For example: "If rhubarb cleared the bile in Francis, it will also clear the bile in Anthony," and "if Francis, who reads <term>Galen|A prominent Greek physician and philosopher (129–c. 216 AD) whose works dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</term>, became a physician, then Anthony, who reads him, will also become a physician."

And although what I said about the enthymeme a moment ago can be conveniently applied to the "consequences" used in the modern way of arguing, I will not fail you in any part of common modern **Logic** <note>original: "Dialecticis"</note>. You should note that the principles of a **consequence** are the antecedent propositions from which conclusions are inferred in this mode of arguing. A **consequence** is a certain way of arguing containing an antecedent and a consequent, along with an "illative particle" <note>A connecting word like "therefore" or "thus" that shows one thought follows from another.</note> of consequence, such as "therefore." For example: "A human is an animal, therefore a human is a living thing," or by saying "he is rational, therefore he is intellectual." The **antecedent** is "Human," and the **consequent** is "animal." The sign of inference is "therefore." It is the same in the second example.

However, all these types of Syllogisms mentioned above—as well as Enthymemes, inductions, examples, and consequences (if indeed a consequence differs from an Enthymeme)—likely explain things, but they do not produce certain knowledge unless certain specific properties and laws are added to the premises. When modified in this way, they become **scientific demonstrations**. Indeed, a **demonstration** is the manifestation of an unknown thing through something known. It is achieved through a Syllogism that produces knowledge. That Syllogism is "most scientific" which occurs in the first mode of the first figure <note>This refers to the most direct form of logic, often called "Barbara," where a general rule is applied to a specific case.</note>, but the other types of Syllogisms serve other demonstrations that are not as powerful. And thus, a proper demonstration...

...logicians (as they say), for indeed nothing can be demonstrated unless the demonstration arises from true things. This is because it is only possible to *know* that which is true; and although a conclusion may sometimes proceed from false premises, it will not be "known" <note>original: "scita." In medieval logic, "knowing" (scientia) required certain, true, and necessary foundations, not just a valid logical structure.</note> through them. For the things through which scientific knowledge is generated in us must be more true and better known to us—known in such a way that they are the causes of the conclusion, because causes are prior to and better known than their effects.

Likewise, regarding the causes which are taken up in a demonstration (since to "know" is to recognize through a cause), it is worthwhile for them to be the precise causes of the conclusion being sought. For a demonstrator must always proceed from his own immediate and necessary principles, and also from those which belong to the study of **Posterior Analytics** <note>original: "posterioristico." This refers to Aristotle’s *Posterior Analytics*, the foundational text on formal logic and scientific proof.</note>, to use the words of modern logicians. These logicians say that "to be of everything" <note>original: "de omni." A technical term in logic meaning a predicate applies to every instance of the subject.</note> is that which is predicated universally and always of another, in itself.

Furthermore, demonstrations either proceed through causes to an effect, and are called **demonstrations of the reason why** <note>original: "propter quid." This is a demonstration that explains the underlying cause of a fact.</note>, or they proceed through the effect to the cause, and are called **demonstrations of the fact** <note>original: "demonstrationes quia." This proves that something is true based on its effects, even if the cause isn't yet understood.</note>.

There is also a third way, or mode of proceeding, through **comparison**. This occurs when we declare some unknown (or less known) equal thing through a similar equal thing that is better known.

A phenomenon is demonstrated through its cause when, for example, a **Lunar Eclipse** is demonstrated through the earth’s diametrical interposition between the moon and the sun. This is the precise and immediate cause, and the knowledge thus acquired is called "scientific knowledge" in the simple and proper sense. Conversely, the cause is demonstrated through the effect when this same example is used but the middle term is changed—namely, by demonstrating the interposition of the earth through the Lunar Eclipse. This is a "demonstration of the fact," which can also be made through a remote or mediated cause.

However, a **demonstration of the reason why** is a process toward an effect through the immediate cause only. Those things which are shown through comparison are **topical** <note>original: "topice." These are arguments based on probability or similarity rather than absolute logical necessity.</note>. For example: if Peter, by keeping the commandments, was made a partaker of the kingdom of God through the promise of Christ, then we too, who keep the commandments, shall be partakers of that kingdom.

Beyond those mentioned, there is another useful way of arguing which the Greeks call **Topical** and the Latins call **Local** <note>original: "localem." This refers to the *Loci* or "Places" of argument, a system of categorized themes used to find persuasive points.</note>; indeed, Orators <note>original: "Rectores." Likely referring to teachers of rhetoric or public leaders.</note> use these "places" very often. Although philosophers occasionally make use of this mode of arguing, they do not do so frequently. I shall therefore proceed by enumerating the different types of "places," since they are of great benefit in the arts and sciences. The first shall be the "place from the greater to the less," for the greater...

Thus, if someone argues: "A frog can swim very well, therefore a donkey can swim very well," it does not follow. Even though the frog and the donkey agree in being animals, they do not agree in the act of swimming.

# THIRTY-SECOND

...whether an argument is derived from them or not; for if it deviates, one must reject the argument entirely. This will be done more easily and almost without effort by one who has been practiced in disputations. Whatever the case may be, I will list certain more common errors and fallacies so that through them you may avoid the rest. Since, as the <term>Dialecticians</term> <note>Dialecticians were scholars who studied the art of logical discussion and investigation of truth through debate.</note> say, a fallacy primarily occurs in two ways: namely **in the word** and **outside the word**. There are six types of deceptive arguments that occur "in the word," corresponding to six ways a word can be flawed and obscure a speech. These are: <term>Equivocation</term>, <term>Ambiguous speech</term> (or as the Greeks say, <term>amphiboly</term>), <term>Composition</term>, <term>Division</term>, <term>Accent</term>, and <term>Figures of speech</term>.

The fallacy of **equivocation** is an error occurring in a word that can signify multiple things. For example, in the word **dog**, which can mean a barking dog (a four-legged land animal), or it can mean a sea fish, or even a certain heavenly constellation <note>original: "canis". In the ancient world, "dog" could refer to a canine, a shark/dogfish, or the star Sirius (the Dog Star).</note>. Therefore, if an argument is made: "A dog barks; the dog is a heavenly constellation; therefore, the heavenly constellation barks," since the conclusion is false, there is a need for a distinction of this word "dog." Because in the first and "major" premise "dog" means one thing, and in the "minor" premise it means another, the conclusion does not follow.

But the fallacy of **amphiboly**, or ambiguous speech, occurs because a sentence can be constructed in different ways and thus signify different things. It differs from equivocation because in that case the ambiguity lies in a single word, but here it is in the whole sentence. This is seen in a very famous example taken from the poet **Ennius** by the grammarians, which is:

> I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, the Romans can defeat. <note>original: "Aio te Æacides Romanos uincere poffe." This is a famous double-meaning oracle. Because of Latin grammar, it can mean "I say you can defeat the Romans" or "I say the Romans can defeat you."</note>

This ambiguous meaning is very often found in other sentences as well, such as saying: "these writings are mine." This can be explained as "these writings were written by me," and also as "these writings are possessed by me." Therefore, in this type of trickery, one must affirm only one sense of the sentence.

Furthermore, an error or fallacy occurs in **composition** and **division** through the different grouping of words within them. This happens when a sentence has a certain small part that can be attached to different parts of the proposition; from this application, the meaning is changed to the opposite of the truth by either joining the speech together or dividing it. Take, for example, this proposition:

> Whatever lives will always be.

In this word, or rather in this small part which says "always," there is the force and power to change the sense. For if it is joined to "lives," it makes a "composite" sense and is true; but it is false in the "divided" sense if it is instead joined to "will be" <note>The ambiguity is whether the person lives forever, or whether the fact that they live will always be a truth.</note>...

...is true in the divided sense but false in the composite sense. For instance, by saying: "Whatever lives will always exist; but a donkey lives; therefore a donkey will always exist." Because the <term>composition</term> <note>The Fallacy of Composition arises when one infers that something is true of the whole because it is true of some part of the whole.</note> is false, it is called the fallacy of composition. On the other hand, the fallacy of **division** occurs in the opposite way. For if the division in a speech is false, it will be a fallacy of division. 

There is also a fifth fallacy which occurs through **accent**. This arises from the fact that a word is not pronounced with its proper accent, or the correct syllable length, or is pronounced with or without an "aspiration" <note>In linguistics, "aspiration" refers to the breathy 'h' sound.</note>. For **Ara** means one thing without the 'H' aspiration, and **Hara** means another with the 'H'. Specifically, the word **Hara** written with an 'H' signifies a pigsty, while without the 'H' it signifies an altar. 

The final linguistic trickery occurs in the **figure of speech**. This is where a word or a specific grammatical case has ambiguity. For example, when I say "man" <note>original: "hominem" (the accusative case for 'man')</note>, I can understand it as referring to the human species in general, or to a specific individual man. Likewise, if I say **manus**, I can understand this word as being in the nominative case <note>The subject of a sentence: "the hand".</note>, the genitive <note>Indicating possession: "of the hand".</note>, or the accusative plural <note>The object of a sentence: "the hands".</note>. Thus, when a word is taken in different ways, the meaning of the speech is changed.

Trickery and corrupted arguments also occur **outside the word** <note>These are "material fallacies," where the error is in the logic of the ideas rather than just the language used.</note> in seven ways. These are: **Accident**, **Relative to Absolute** <note>original: "secundum quid, & fimpliciter"</note>, **Ignorance of the Refutation**, **Begging the Question**, **The Consequent**, **Non-cause as Cause**, and **Many Questions as One**. To explain this part briefly, as is my custom, a deception or fallacy "outside the word" occurs when the error resides in the subject matter or the reality of things rather than in the phrasing.

**Accident** is the first fallacy. It occurs when attributes [accidents] are not correctly joined, so that some attribute is poorly assigned to something. For example, if I say: "Animal is a noun; a noun is a part of speech; therefore, animal is a part of speech." This conclusion is false because "animal" <note>The living creature.</note> and "noun" <note>The grammatical category.</note> belong to different categories.

Next is the fallacy of **Relative to Absolute**. This is a flaw that occurs if something that is only true in a particular way is assumed to be true simply and universally. For example, it is best to use a restricted diet during acute illnesses; therefore, [to say it is best] always and for everyone is not valid. Or, as the <term>dialecticians</term> say: "An Ethiopian is white in respect to his teeth; therefore, the Ethiopian is white entirely and absolutely." This is not valid.

The third is the fallacy of **Ignorance of the Refutation** <note>original: "Ignorantia elenchi"</note>. This occurs through a lack of skill in disproof, and happens when the methods of firm proof are not understood. For instance, if the requirements for a proper contradiction are not observed—as if someone were to say: "The prince is in the palace, and not in the suburbs; therefore the prince is and..."

# THIRTY-SECOND
X

->THIRTY-SECOND.<-

...is not the primary one. In this mode, various quibbles <note>original: "cauillationes"</note> arise which would require a long explanation, unsuitable for a letter. Therefore, having dismissed those according to my plan, I shall briefly write down the remaining ones. According to the prescribed order, the **fallacy of begging the question** <term>petition of the principle</term> follows. 

This occurs when we confirm that which is uncertain without any proof, or by using things that are equally uncertain, or by using a different word that means the same thing. Thus, when someone tries to prove something through something else that is not evident, this fallacy occurs. For example, if someone were to say the heavens are eternal because they are not made of the same matter from which the elements—which are subject to corruption—are composed, he proves nothing. For the claim that the heavens are not made of that same matter is itself uncertain, and thus the reasoning does not hold. 

Furthermore, the **fallacy of the consequent** <term>fallacia consequentis</term> arises from a deception where one believes a conclusion follows from a premise <note>original: "antecedenti"</note> when it actually does not. For instance: "If it is a human, it is an animal; therefore, if it is an animal, it is a human." This second inference is false because while an inference is valid from the specific <note>original: "inferiori," referring to the species</note> to the general <note>original: "superiori," referring to the genus</note>, it is not valid from the general to the specific.

The fallacy of **false cause** <term>non causa ut causa</term> <note>Literally: "non-cause as cause."</note> occurs when certain propositions are placed in the premises of a **syllogism** <term>syllogismus</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two shared premises.</note> that contribute nothing to the conclusion. Since they are not the actual causes of the conclusion, they are called "non-causes." This can be seen in arguments that lead to an impossible conclusion. It is very similar to the fallacy of the consequent. For example, if you say: "Drunkenness is bad, therefore wine is bad." In this case, wine is not the immediate cause of drunkenness; rather, the cause is its immoderate use or perhaps a weakness of the head. Therefore, it is a "non-cause" treated as a cause. It does not follow that wine is bad, since it is very beneficial to those who drink it moderately.

The final mode of fallacy or faulty argumentation is **multiple questions** <note>Also known as the Fallacy of the Complex Question.</note>, which involves treating many questions as one, so that only a single answer is given to several distinct inquiries. For example, if someone asks you: "Do you think that a human and a donkey are rational animals?" If you answer "yes," it follows that a donkey is a rational animal. If you answer "no," it follows that a human is not a rational animal. The same applies to many other cases.

Finally, since **dialectic** <term>dialectica</term> <note>The formal study of logical argument and dialogue.</note> is both a science and a method of teaching—and the method of teaching consists of defining, dividing, and arguing—it will be worthwhile to notice this: namely, that in obscure and unknown matters, there is a need for disputation. To "dispute" is to agitate a matter with words and the mind so that the [concept of the] sou<unclear>l</unclear> <note>The text cuts off at "ani-", likely "animus" (mind) or "anima" (soul).</note>

LETTER

...concepts formed with reason: against the other. And this must be noted for the knowledge of truth: that in any controversy, regardless of the obscurity or difficulty of the matter, the first step is to seek the truth and flee from falsehood, and to dispute about those things which can be known. This should be done through sensory perception <note>original: "sensata"</note> and things already well-understood—if we believe Aristotle, who said that **nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses.** Also, in disputing, one should always bring forward reasons, both affirmative and negative, proving the unknown from what has already been established <note>original: "praelibatis"</note> through some form of argumentation. These, dearest Antonius, are those concise precepts of **Dialectic** <term>The art of logical discussion and reasoning</term>, which, if anyone observes them, can easily bring back the doctrine of the Ancients to memory, since almost all the main points of the entire science of Dialectic are contained in them; and I send them to you, complying with your wishes and responding to your letters. **Farewell, Venice.**
**1527. January.**

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT HENRY
## Stromer of Auerbach, Letter XXXIII.
->On the creation of the world.<-

**W**ould that nature, most learned elder, had given us our inner senses clearly explained and visible, and had shown us the nature of higher things; for if she had done this, surely the judgments of discursive science would not be proven with such uncertainty. But since the matter is not so, but rather our senses are obscured and hidden in the innermost parts of the body, and the nature of higher things lies far from them, it happens that men often hunt for knowledge of an unknown thing through external means sought far from nature. Although this is the case, they are nonetheless not entirely removed from true and intellectual discourse, as you will see me do at present (in order to respond to your letters and reveal the truth of what you seek). For you ask that I be willing to write my opinion to you regarding the **creation of the world** or its **eternity**. In the first place, I constantly and perpetually affirm this with these words: without any doubt and without hesitation, I believe the world was thus created, since I have clearly received this from the Holy Scriptures. For Moses, the proclaimer of the divine laws who received them from the Lord, says in the first part of **Genesis**: "In the beginning, God created heaven and..."

# THIRTY-THIRD.

...that He created the earth, and all things that are with them; but as I seem to see, your letters do not only ask for this, but also what other wise men have said regarding the beginning or eternity of the world that is consistent with Christian truth. Furthermore, to be honest, some wise men, by not distinguishing between the acting creator and the created thing, have mixed many and almost inextricable disputes into this business. I, however, lest I perish with them, will approach the matter itself in this way. First, I will propose two modes of understanding. 

The first indeed is from the senses, such that men can understand nothing beyond sensible things, since it is necessary for the one understanding to gaze upon mental images <note>original: "phantasmata," referring to the Aristotelian idea that the mind requires sensory images to think</note>; Aristotle wrote this opinion in the third book of *On the Soul* <term>Latin: De Anima</term>, in the text of commentary 39. The second mode, however, proceeds not only from the senses but also through discourse upon things already understood; thus the intellect, through things previously understood, also understands those things which do not fall under the senses—just as the intellect, in its habitual state and while operating, understands itself. I set aside the discourse stemming from principles implanted in us by nature, or even those conceded by all, about which Aristotle and the commentator Averroes <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> have spoken abundantly in the second book of *Divine Philosophy* <term>The Metaphysics</term> and elsewhere.

With these things tasted beforehand <note>original: "praelibatis," meaning introductory remarks</note>, although you ask for a difficult thing which has exhausted many wise men, I will gladly approach it to the best of my ability. Indeed, nothing is more deeply implanted in the human soul than intelligence; the more someone excels in it, the more they involve themselves in the investigation of the most difficult matters, so that if it were possible—as Paul, the disciple of Christ and teacher of the nations, said—one might strive to know through their innate power of understanding those things which "neither eyes have seen, nor ears heard." Thus the Divine Plato, thus Aristotle, and Averroes his faithful interpreter, thus Avicenna and the most learned Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali, a Persian theologian and philosopher</note>, and not a few moderns have philosophized. These men, having laid down diverse principles and deduced their reasons, have disputed concerning the beginning and eternity of the world. 

I shall begin, therefore, from that principle which is approved by all: namely, that there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. Aristotle said this in the eighth book of *Natural Hearing* <term>The Physics</term> in the text of commentary 15, and in the first book of *On the Heavens*, and in other books. There is no one who does not approve this truth. If this is so, let it please me to reason with you thus: the operations of the Blessed God proceed from His eternal wisdom, which, since it is infinite, is equivocal <note>In this context, "equivocal" means the two things—divine and human wisdom—share a name but are fundamentally different in nature</note> to our own, as is written in the twelfth book of *Divine Philosophy*, text of commentary 51. Our intellect, however, as Averroes said in the second book of *On the Soul*...

Those who see that created nature in these lower realms produces all things through motion, and who then argue by analogy to the divine, wander far from the path. For the supreme agent <note>Referring to God as the ultimate cause</note> is distant far and infinitely from nature as it acts in these lower realms. Regarding this knowledge, as the most learned <term>Algazel</term> <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian and philosopher whose works on logic and metaphysics were influential in the Latin West</note> warns in his first disputation, we must not proceed from pre-existing sensory knowledge alone, but also from intellectual discourse after God's effects have been recognized. 

This mode is "mixed" (as I was saying a little while ago), and because it is not in every part conformed to the nature of lower things, nor does it always correspond to sensible things, it can be understood by many only with difficulty. Nevertheless, it is understood by the best intellects and by those who are called "children of nature"—that is, those who are of an excellent temperament <note>In Renaissance thought, a "balanced temperament" was believed to be necessary for high intellectual and moral capacity</note> and especially if they have been exercised in contemplations. Since I know you are by no means lacking in these gifts, I shall write boldly, affirming the beginning of the world with reasons: namely, that the world was made anew by God in the beginning out of His own will. 

This will is nothing other than Himself, for it is God Himself; all attributes in God are the very essence of God, and indeed, besides His essence, there is nothing in God. Those things that are said by us are said according to our limited human mode of understanding; they cannot, however, be perfectly conceived or understood by us in their exactitude.

But since my conversation is with a most learned philosopher, now that these things have been asserted and established concerning the **creation of the world**, it will not be unwelcome to write out the contrary reasons against certain objections of the philosophers. They say that for anything to be produced anew in actuality, it is necessary to posit some subject <note>In this context, "subject" refers to underlying matter or substance that receives a new form</note>, since "nothing can be generated from nothing" <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil generari possit." This was a fundamental axiom of ancient Greek physics that challenged the Christian doctrine of creation out of nothing</note>. 

To this objection, those who discourse from intellectual things beyond mere sensory data easily respond (based on what was said just before). For it is not repugnant to an intellect that reasons well that no subject preceded the making of a thing. Indeed, that **pure act** <term>Latin: actus purus</term> <note>A theological term for God, describing Him as complete and perfect reality without any mere "potential" or need for change</note> who is all things does not need any matter to be subjected to Him in the act of creation, since all things flow from Him abundantly and profusely as if from the "first being." 

This is just like the actual light that proceeds from virtual or spiritual light, coming from the very intelligence that illuminates the celestial sphere. Philosophers necessarily posit a process of this kind; otherwise, they would be forced to grant an infinite regress, which nature abhors. Furthermore, unless the intellect determined a single first point from which all things proceed, one would always have to search from one thing to the next forever. # THE SEVENTH TREATISE

...in the <note>original: "divino"; the text continues from the previous page's discussion of divine attributes</note> divine act, all things exist, even though many remain hidden from us because of the previously mentioned disproportion between the creature and the Creator. They <note>The "philosophers" or opponents who argue for an eternal universe</note> say, furthermore, that if God had created the world anew, surely an infinite time would have preceded its creation, since God is eternal. This crude imagination is without a doubt far from the truth, since with God, the Creator of all, there is no time; rather, all things are in Him eternally and proceed (so to speak) according to His eternal decrees, which (as the philosophers say) are firm and immutable. For indeed, time is the measure of motion, if we believe <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose works formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance science and logic</note> in the fourth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "Phisico auditu"</note>, commentary one hundred and one. Nor is time anything in itself; for it is constructed by the human intellect when it distinguishes between "before" and "after," as the same Aristotle said in the cited book, commentary fourteen. 

How, I ask, can the human intellect imagine that time preceded the world, if time is an effect of the world created anew? For indeed, there is no one who does not say that the world consists of celestial spheres and the lower elements; the spheres indeed move, and it is from their motion, according to our cognition, that time is caused. There is no reason for them to say, based on what has been said, that an infinite time preceded the world. Furthermore, they say that if the world were created anew, it would undoubtedly follow that in God there was a "power" or "possibility" <note>Aristotelian concepts of potentiality versus actuality</note> for that creation. But this too is discordant to an intellect that examines it well, since they have not distinguished created nature from the Creator. For where there is no subject <note>In philosophy, the "subject" is the underlying thing in which properties exist</note>, there can be no "possibility," since possibility is an <term>accident</term> <note>An "accident" is a quality that can change or be absent without the thing losing its essential nature</note>; and an accident cannot exist unless it is in a subject, as all wise men affirm. Still less can it exist in the Producer, since He is <term>pure act</term> <note>original: "actus purus"; a theological term meaning God is fully realized and has no unrealized potential or "possibility" to become something else</note>. Far be it from us to say that any "accident" exists in God; nor has any of the wise men—whether natural philosophers or "divines" (whom they call theologians)—dared to say this. 

They also say that if the world had been created anew, we would necessarily be positing a change in God. Since this is discordant, alien to all truth, and merely imaginary, this very line of reasoning carries no weight at all; for the choice of the Creator is eternal and immutable. Indeed, the effect of the Creator as the one acting and producing—acting out of His own eternal (as I have already said) will, and according to the aforementioned decrees of His simplicity which do not differ from His most simple being—is not at all exhausted by the act of producing. This is because production is performed by Him without any outward or inward effort, and there is no intrinsic or extrinsic resistance. And although in created nature at work...

# THIRTY-THIRD

...if there were to be some change, it is nonetheless not perpetual; rather, an agent is often perfected in the very act of operating. Nevertheless, no effect proceeding from Him can make Him more perfect, since He is the highest perfection, nor can anything external be granted that would have been either an object or an obstacle, since nothing existed before the world except Him. Nor does God reason through discourse <note>original: "discurrit"; referring to "discursive" reasoning where the mind moves from one premise to another</note>, but He understands through His own very being, and He understands causes according to an eternal choice, which exists alongside His inviolable wisdom. And just as what is done cannot be "un-done" in Him, so too can His eternal love produce what is ordained and chosen at the appointed limit. Nor do they take away this eternal choice, which is immutable and as powerful as His infinite nature, though it is minimally comprehensible to us through our senses; in this way, no one can perceive any change in God. For even if God is a cause, He is not an inferior or created cause, but is the first [cause], bestowing laws and powers upon other causes, which in His own essence are most eminent. These we know in no other way than through their effects, because our intellect relates to the innermost powers of God just as the eye of a bat <note>A famous metaphor from Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* used to describe how human reason is blinded by the "light" of supreme truths</note> relates to the light of the Sun.

They say, furthermore, that since God is an active agent, it is necessary that He acts, especially since He has no obstacle. To this position, the response is not difficult, for it has been said that the operations of the Creator are far distant from created nature. This is because a created nature, when acting, acts by changing the subject it is applied to until it has brought that subject back to its own nature—unless it is hindered—and once the subject is changed, the action ceases. But the Creator does not act by changing [pre-existing matter], but by producing from nothing <term>ex nihilo</term> <note>The doctrine that God created the universe out of nothing, rather than from pre-existing matter</note>. Therefore, it is not necessary for God (since He is the first agent) to act [continually in a way that requires a subject]; for He is not an agent applied to a subject, but is indeed an agent producing anew without being attached to any underlying matter. The cause of this error is that they do not distinguish between the first Creator agent and created nature.

Finally, regarding what they say about the infinite revolutions of the celestial spheres, and about the acceptance of "more" and "less" within the infinite itself—which would follow if we posited that the world is eternal—none of this stands as an obstacle, at least for the intellect that understands multiple motions just as it understands multiple times. For the motion of the spheres (as I have said) is nothing in reality <note>meaning motion has no independent existence outside of the moving body and the mind that measures it</note>, nor are past revolutions to be found [now], but those motions are known and remembered by the intellect; nor do they have any existence or plurality because of this, since motion is a single, continuous thing...

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT HEINRICH
## Stromer of Auerbach. Letter 34.
### On the immortality of the soul.

**I** know indeed, most learned Heinrich, that you will wonder why I have responded so late to the letters you sent to me, but you will cease to wonder if you look upon the magnitude and difficulty of the subject matter. It is a topic that has left the minds of all the ancients and the moderns <note>original: "neotericorum"</note> exhausted by the labor, so much so that unless the Gospel truth confirmed our opinion—which is fortified (as you shall see) by both reasons and the authorities of the ancients—I would truly fear to write to you about it as a philosopher. You ask, therefore, most learned elder, that I might be willing to indicate to you what I feel regarding the souls that have migrated from this life: namely, whether they remain even when separated from the body and exist by rushing toward the blessed God as the ultimate good and their final end; or whether they perish and fail together with the body, so that nothing more of them remains. 

Regarding this question, I can only write with the philosophers with a certain anxiety of mind, even though I am not at all anxious when guided by the light of the Gospel; for great is the power of Christian truth, which defends itself by its own merit against the cleverness of men. Furthermore, you are not unaware that certain illustrious philosophers have said the soul is mortal—such as Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who argued that the soul does not survive the death of the body</note> and others who devoted themselves to the Aristotelian interpretation, so that they posited its mortality (although some affirm that Alexander felt otherwise based on his writings). Not all of them used the same reasons precisely, but being diverse, they differed among themselves in some manner. Into their company, not a few moderns have entered while interpreting Aristotle, such as Pietro Pomponazzi of Mantua and Cardinal Thomas Cajetan, who have met their end in recent days (so to speak). I pass over <term>Duns Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian who argued that the soul's immortality could not be strictly proven by reason alone</note> and <term>Hervaeus Natalis</term> <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian who also grappled with the limits of philosophical proofs for immortality</note> and other noteworthy theologians who, while also interpreting Aristotle, did not fully clarify this question in every part. For they say that Aristotle [held] the soul to be not entirely immortal...

->A T E R P I S T I O I L E A D I R T<-

...to have confirmed with reasons. But [they say] he posed it simply without any proof. They say this was done because of the ambiguous knowledge of its being, so that it was necessary for Averroes and his followers to posit it as a unique, eternal entity, since it can by no means be multiplied <note>The "multiplication of souls" was a major debate: Averroists argued that if the soul is immaterial and separate from the body, there can only be one "Intellect" for all humanity, rather than individual souls for each person.</note> without a body. 

However, when I diligently examine Aristotle’s process—which is primarily learned and also admirable—I do not hesitate to affirm to you that the soul, even when separated from the body, remains for eternal time. Indeed, Aristotle could not have sought out the ambiguity of this soul's existence unless he had first revealed all its powers and acts. When he had proven these powers and acts by enumerating them, and by proving them had established the operations emanating from them, he immediately began to doubt: Are all of them common to the soul and the body, or are some for the soul only, and some for the body alone? 

He began to open this question first in the twelfth text of the commentary on *The Soul*, where he strives to hunt for this operation of the soul, which is "to understand," through a conditional proposition, reasoning in this way: "To understand this either is a kind of imagination, or it cannot exist without imagination; but imagination cannot exist without the body." Therefore, this reasoning (which establishes nothing here as existing, since it is conditional and part of an argument) they adapt to every mode of understanding, and they say <gloss>dicunt</gloss> that understanding is not the work of the soul alone, but an operation with <gloss>cum</gloss> the body. 

As I will explain to you later, you will recognize that this is not simply true, especially since Aristotle does not intend to end the question here, but to propose it and suspend his judgment <gloss>sententiam</gloss> until the end of his process. Wherefore, affirming what he said above: In the thirteenth text he proceeds thus, introducing another conditional proposition in this manner: "If, therefore, there is some operation or proper affection of the soul, it is possible for the soul to be separated." And these propositions (as I said) he left undiscussed in this first book, intending to examine them in the second and third. 

From this, he gave many a cause for doubting. Nevertheless, I will strive to resolve these for you naturally to the best of my ability, if first a distinction is made between the soul which is a form common to the vegetative <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>The level of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition, shared by plants and animals.</note>, sensitive <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The level of the soul responsible for perception and movement, shared by animals and humans.</note>, and finally the discursive. Whether you wish to call this soul also the "estimative" or "cogitative" <note>The "cogitative" or "estimative" faculty was believed to be the highest power of the animal soul, allowing for the evaluation of sensory data (like a sheep sensing the danger of a wolf).</note> does not matter; it is the most perfect of the forms educed <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "educed" forms are those that arise naturally from the potential of matter, rather than being "infused" by a divine act.</note> from the power of matter. And [then there is] the intellective soul or intellect <gloss>intellectum</gloss>...

# THIRTY-FOURTH

which arises from the perfection of all these virtues in man, and is immaterial, not depending on the body even if it is in the body. Nor is it the perfection of the body, but it is the perfection of the soul. You will see that Aristotle affirmed this division if you correctly understand him in the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*</note>, where he criticizes the ancients for not distinguishing the soul from the intellect. For the soul, because it is the "form" of the body <term>forma corporis: the organizing principle that makes a body a living thing</term>, gives being to it and cannot exist without the body. But the intellect, as intellect, does not result from the body nor from the soul itself, but is immaterial; it can exist without the body and remain incorruptible.

And since the soul is that which gives being to the living body, so that it has the existence of an animal through the soul, if the animal perishes, the form that gives it being—which is this soul—will also perish. But in man, besides the soul which gives individual existence and makes him a "discursive animal" <note>An animal capable of step-by-step logical reasoning</note>, there is also an intellective being. This intellect has nothing to do with the senses, but is the ultimate perfection of the human soul and a power separated from the body; that is, it does not depend on matter nor on bodily instruments for its operation, unlike the other bodily powers. 

For the discursive or "thinking" power uses the imagination, and the imagination itself receives its data from the senses, tied to material and specific conditions. But the intellect knows without these material conditions; that is, it knows universally and by category, and it does this through its own power. Since it understands the universal and the abstract without matter or material conditions, one must undoubtedly say that it understands "through itself" <term>per se</term>, and this is its own proper operation, which Aristotle was seeking. 

If anyone tries to attribute this operation to the discursive soul (which depends on matter), they will certainly be in error, since that soul is the "form" of a rational living being and is therefore corruptible <note>Subject to decay and death</note>. The intellect itself, however, is the perfection of the soul and is incorruptible. This perfection necessarily follows the human soul, even though the soul itself depends on matter. Theologians rightly say this intellect is "infused by God," and Aristotle believed it "comes from without" <note>original: "deforis venire"</note> in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter three. 

This perfection is eternal and incorruptible and can be separated from the body, just as we speak of a power detached from something else which nevertheless remains without the subject from which it flowed and performs the same operation. For example, if a magnet is placed together with some iron so that they touch for a time, or if they are rubbed together, that iron acquires the power of the magnet and attracts other...

...iron, and this is because a power is somehow communicated to another subject, and it remains and operates without its own proper subject, even though it may be currently residing in some subject; we experience this same thing in a severed seed <note>The author refers to the Aristotelian idea that the "form" or life-force of a plant or animal is present in the seed even after it is separated from the parent</note>. But if this is true regarding powers that depend on matter—powers which can operate even if they are not entirely stripped of material qualities—how much more can the intellect, which does not depend on matter, be separated from it? And once separated, it can have its own proper operation. 

If opponents insist that the intellect must have some underlying subject <term>subiectum: the physical or metaphysical "base" in which a quality exists</term>—just as the celestial Intelligences are granted the heavenly spheres to move—we may reasonably grant to this intellect either God or some other celestial entity hidden from the Philosophers. Our adversaries can hardly deny this if they believe Aristotle, who established a manifest order of forms. 

Indeed, the first and most imperfect of all forms is the **complexional** <term>forma complexionalis: the basic "mix" or temperament of the physical elements in a body</term>. The second, for example, is the **vegetative** form, which brings the first to perfection <note>The power of growth and nutrition found in plants</note>. The third is the **sensitive** form <note>The power of perception found in animals</note>. The fourth, which is the human mind, is the form that gives being and depends on matter; this form is called **discursive**, **estimative**, or **cogitative** <term>cogitatiua: the highest physical power of the human brain that prepares sensory data for the intellect</term>. This is the perfection of all the aforementioned powers. I say this so that you do not think I am positing multiple souls by assuming multiple powers; rather, the "form" is always the final power in the sequence, which grants a thing its specific, perfected existence. 

The intellect, however, does not depend on the body but on that ultimate power called the **cogitative**, which is the furthest removed from matter. Thus, we say the intellect is the ultimate perfection of man, which they call the "intellective soul." This established order is therefore an order of perfection. 

Yet (if you elevate your mind), the intellect is not the ultimate *material* perfection. For the discursive power, although it deals with the imaginations derived from the senses and thinks and reasons alongside them, nevertheless does not use entirely immaterial things. Instead, as the Philosophers say, it works with "abstracted conditions" which are not entirely stripped of the conditions of matter. The intellect itself, however, understands by its own nature without the sensitive powers. It does not use the imaginative or cogitative powers except insofar as it understands a "discourse" or a "thought" that is no longer material; this occurs because it is the cogitative power that prepares for the intellect objects of thought that are sufficiently proportioned to it. 

For if the intellect were separated, it would certainly understand other separated objects proportioned to itself. Indeed, this kind of "understanding" is the operation of the intellect simply, which exists through itself; nor is it a "form" in any other way than by understanding things that have been understood. Hence, when separated, the in- <margin>telli</margin> <note>The catchword "telli" suggests the next page continues with "intelligit" (understands) or "intellectus" (intellect)</note>

-># THIRTY-FOURTH<-

...it understands [in]telligible things, and primarily God and the Intelligences <note>original: *intelligentias*; in medieval philosophy, these are non-physical beings responsible for the movement of the stars and planets</note>, according to the nature of the intellect itself. Similarly, it understands everything else; but since the things understood are eternal, separated intellects will be eternal, because they have a means to preserve their own being through their operation—that is, through the act of understanding. You see, therefore, most learned Henry, that the operation of the **intellectual soul** <term>anima intellectiva: the highest part of the human soul, responsible for reason</term> does not depend on the "instruments" of the soul that are derived from matter <note>The "instruments" refer to physical organs like the eyes or ears</note>, but rather on its own proper power. 

Therefore, since the intellectual soul possesses its own operation—which is to understand without physical instruments and in a separated state—it can, according to Aristotle, be separated and remain for eternal time in the act of understanding. This is especially true since it has no cause within itself that would destroy its being, and it possesses a preserving cause, as I have said—namely, an eternal celestial body, or the blessed God himself and the Intelligences. 

That the intellect (and even the soul that depends on matter) are "perfections" following the **complexional**, **vegetative**, and **sensitive** forms <note>These represent the hierarchy of life: physical makeup, plant-like growth, and animal-like sensation</note>, can be confirmed from the words of Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university life</note> in his thirty-first commentary on the second book of the *Metaphysics* and his fifth commentary on the third book of *On the Soul*. 

However, the "soul" and the "intellect" differ from one another. The soul is that which is "drawn out" from the potentiality of matter and is the perfection of the animal; the intellect, however, is a non-material perfection that follows after the discursive or thinking power. Averroes affirms this opinion in the aforementioned commentary on the third book of *On the Soul*, where he rebukes Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisiensis, a 2nd-century commentator</note> for saying that the intellectual soul fails and dies along with the body. 

Alexander deceived himself by believing that the intellectual soul was produced merely from the mixture of elements into the subsequent **complexional form** <term>forma complexionalis: the basic physical temperament resulting from the balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</term> and other forms, as I wrote above. Yet, even though Averroes recognized Alexander’s error, he did not know how to protect himself from a massive error of his own: proposing that there is only one single intellect common to all human beings <note>This "huge error" is Monopsychism, the idea that humans don't have individual souls, but all share one "cloud" of intellect</note>. The cause of his error was that, proceeding only from things perceived by the senses, he wished to separate abstract and universal operations from material things without making the aforementioned distinction regarding the soul. Thus, along with the ancients before him, many modern followers have also been deceived. 

If these thinkers had placed a distinction between the soul (which comes from matter) and the intellect (which understands without material instruments), they would undoubtedly have known, along with Aristotle, that the intellectual soul has its own proper operation. Nor can anyone doubt whether the imagination is the same as the intellectual soul, since Aristotle clearly declared this in the second book of *On the Soul*, in the text of the 153rd commentary. Nor do the statements made above forbid a plurality of separated souls. Since the intellect is by its nature immaterial and has no matter that needs to be divided, it is nonetheless distinct within each individual so that it may understand. For (as I have said) the operations of the intellect are certainly to understand abstract things; it does not possess the condition of matter such that it must work upon matter itself, or that its preparation must happen through matter, but rather it depends upon itself. The **cogitative power** <term>cogitativa: the faculty that links sensory images to the abstract intellect</term> is like its perfection. Since this cogitative power is multiplied and numbered among many people, so too the intellect itself is multiplied and separated, and it remains with its own operation. This reasoning would only fail if the intellect depended on or had an affinity with material things.

As you write, you are nearing death—not doubting, but rather wishing through your writings to move me to contemplate the higher secrets of nature. Since this is manifest and apparent to the senses, I will not labor much to show that the present air is not corrupted in a way that would make it the cause of so great an evil; for if anyone wishes to weigh all the facts correctly, he will recognize that the air retains its proper condition and temperament. From this definition, one can see that the plague is a "passion" or "affection" of the air—something that corrupts the air itself—and is not an affection of the animal <note>In medical Latin, "animal" refers to the living patient or "breathing being"</note>. # LETTER TO THE STATE

...explained clearer than the midday sun in describing the various alterations of the air, when he said that **Pestilence is the putrefaction of the air**. Philo the Jew <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) who blended Greek philosophy with Jewish theology</note> confirmed this definition of the plague in the Greek language with these words: <term>plague is the death of the air</term> <note>original: "λοιμὸς ἐστὶ ἀέρος θάνατος"</note>. These words say nothing else, if translated into the Latin tongue, than that the plague is the "death of the air." This makes it the greatest of all diseases, and for that reason it was called <term>disease</term> <note>original: "vός", likely a transcription of "νόσος" (nosos)</note> by Homer by way of excellence. No other remedy was given for it by the ancients than to take to flight and go far away. This was said for no other reason than this: since it is a corruption of the air, the true remedy will be to flee far from it, lest we be infected by that corrupted air. Plutarch also, an ancient and learned man, seems to have confirmed the aforementioned definition. For by him, pestilences are called <term>corruptions of the air</term> <note>original: "ἀέρων φθοραί"</note>, which words signify the spoilage of the atmosphere. This air, once so corrupted and turned into the nature of poison, infects the greater part of the people living in it, and often kills them, so that it is the external cause of infection and death. 

This definition of the plague and those things said about its essence are also confirmed by the words of Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> in his book *On the Nature of Man*. He says that when one sickness seizes many people at the same time—namely, the young as well as the old; women as well as men; those who drink wine as well as those who drink water; those who eat non-wheat bread as well as those who eat wheat; those who labor little as well as those who labor much—the cause of this must be attributed to the **air**. 

Since, indeed, it is manifest from what has been said that the plague, or pestilence, is a corruption of the air from which contagious and destructive diseases common to all people arise, I say that the present ailments can in no way be called "the plague." Even though they are contagious and deadly, they do not depend on a corruption of the air, nor even from the influence of the super-celestial bodies and the stars. For there have been no preceding conjunctions or other aspects of, for example, Saturn, Mars, and the Moon, which are accustomed to prepare the air for a pestilential putrefaction or corruption. 

Therefore, let those who believe this pestilence arises from the malice of the air, or the influence of super-celestial bodies, see in how great an error they are engaged. For many things are accustomed to appear [during a true plague] which have not appeared at all in these times—namely, the generation of animals that multiply from rot, such as numerous worms, flies, gnats, locusts, frogs, mice, toads, snakes, and other things very similar to these. Furthermore, certain birds that live in the mountains flee from the mountains and betake themselves to the plains or other places, recognizing the pestilential air by instinct. And so that it may be more...

<summary>Massa argues that the current outbreak is not a "true" plague because it lacks the classical markers of atmospheric corruption, such as specific planetary alignments and the mass emergence of vermin.</summary>

## THIRTY-FOURTH.

...to prove that the present air is not corrupted, and consequently that the present diseases are not caused by the corruption of the air or by the influence of the superior bodies <note>The "superior bodies" refers to the stars and planets; Renaissance medicine often attributed epidemics to astrological alignments.</note>, I shall record a summary of what Thucydides committed to writing regarding the Athenian plague, as well as what Giovanni Boccaccio <note>The author of the *Decameron*, which famously describes the Black Death in Florence in 1348.</note> wrote about a certain plague of the Florentines, and after him what Marsilio Ficino <note>A celebrated Florentine philosopher and physician who wrote a famous treatise on the plague in 1481.</note> wrote regarding another of their plagues.

Thucydides, therefore, in the second book of his *Histories*, recorded the wretched plague by which he himself was afflicted. It had its origin in Ethiopia; soon moving into Egypt and Libya, it then seized the entire region of Attica, and finally encompassed the city of Athens with such violence and miserable severity that there were never more cruel or atrocious deaths. In this most savage plague <note>original: "sæuissima lue"</note>, no beneficial medicine was ever found; indeed, the greater part of the physicians perished, as medicines contributed nothing to so grave an evil, nor were prayers made to the Gods profitable in any way.

The nature of this most savage pestilence was as follows: the heat in the rest of the body was not excessive, yet the head was tormented by the greatest burning; the eyes were reddened, and the tongue was seen to be red and dripping with blood. There was a perpetual ringing in the ears, the face was fierce, sighs were frequent, and their breath appeared foul-smelling. There were also most troublesome bouts of sneezing and a hoarseness of the voice; they coughed and breathed with difficulty, and thus the chest, along with the internal organs, was racked by violent coughing; similarly, hiccups brought great distress.

The exterior of the body was reddish and livid, and affected by many ulcers. Inside, the heat was such that they could not endure even the thinnest coverings, and the languishing patients most gladly threw themselves into the coldest water or into wells. Perpetual wakefulness <note>i.e., total insomnia.</note> afflicted everyone; there were few who did not succumb before the seventh or ninth day. Some were even cruelly troubled in the genitals and in the extremities of the feet and hands; many of these escaped the rest of the pestilential malice, though with the loss of their limbs. Some also recovered having been blinded. Many also, from the extreme severity of the pestilence, fell into a forgetfulness of all things; some no longer recognized their friends, and remained alive yet unmindful and ignorant of even themselves. Of these, Lucretius <note>The Roman poet (c. 99–55 BCE) who adapted Thucydides' description of the plague into Latin verse in his work *On the Nature of Things*.</note> sang thus:

> And even upon some came forgetfulness of things
> Entirely, nor could they even know themselves:

->EPISTLE<-

Giovanni Boccaccio <note>The famous Italian author (1313–1375) whose masterpiece, the *Decameron*, opens with a harrowing eyewitness account of the Black Death in Florence.</note> himself, in the preface of the *Hundred Tales*, also recounts—as I have said—the wretched history of the plague which, in **1348**, invaded the Florentines along with many others. It caused a vast and cruel slaughter of people, in which no human remedies and no prayers made to Almighty God were of any help to them. In this outbreak, the greater part of both men and women perished; indeed, few were delivered who labored under such a most cruel pestilence. 

It was believed to attack without fever; furthermore, there was a flow of blood from the nostrils, by which many were deprived of life. There were also abscesses in the groin <term>apostemata in guinum</term> <note>These are "buboes," the characteristic swollen lymph nodes of the bubonic plague.</note>, and certain other destructive tumors in other parts of the body. These afterwards began to degenerate into certain black and livid spots, which arose indiscriminately on the arms and hips as well as on all other parts of the body. These spots varied in size and were the most manifest sign of swift death, from which very few escaped; the greater part, and nearly everyone, departed from this life within the third day of the spots appearing. 

These sicknesses were certainly contagious beyond measure, so that not only those who lived together, or even held conversation with an infected person, or touched anything handled by an infected man, but even animals of another species were not only infected but also killed if they touched anything handled by an infected man. For indeed these sicknesses were truly pestilential, since they had arisen from the corruption of the air; for it had come into Italy from eastern parts, and at last reached even the western ones.

**Marsilio Ficino** <note>A leading intellectual of the Italian Renaissance and a physician who wrote *Consilio contro la pestilenza* (Advice against the Plague).</note>, a man learned in every respect, at the end of a certain treatise concerning the Plague which occurred in Florence in his own time, in **1478**, said among other symptoms <note>original: "accidentia"</note> which he himself enumerates, that bloody and red spots appeared in certain infected persons. 

Therefore, I wished to pluck these details from historians and other trustworthy writers concerning the nature of ancient, wretched, and horrible pestilential sicknesses, and to recount them in as brief a speech as I could. I do this so that those who were saying that our present evils arise from the "superior bodies" <note>The celestial bodies or stars; a reference to the astrological theory that planetary alignments caused epidemics.</note> and the corruption of the air might see how far they distance themselves from the target of truth. It would be better if, besides the definitions of the plague's essence provided by the ancients, they would consider the behavior of past pestilential diseases that depended on the corruption of the air—which we have recently reviewed—and compare them with these diseases of our own time. To ensure these current diseases are more easily recognized and understood, I have decided to set down below the matters as they were debated in the Senate.

# THIRTY-FIFTH #

And so that all things may be understood clearly and openly, I shall propose that pestilential diseases be distinguished into two kinds. The first and principal kind is that which arises from the **corruption of the air** and the **influence of the celestial bodies**, as was said above. The second, however, is that which contains the other pestilential diseases caused by internal alteration or from contact; such are the present diseases which are depopulating the city. These have been noted according to three differences, and they cannot truly be called "pestilential" since they do not depend at all on that true plague which arises from the corruption of the air. 

But if anyone wishes to call them pestilential, this name will certainly be used improperly, spoken according to a certain metaphor and similarity which these destructive diseases have with those that usually happen from the corruption of the air. Or, the name will be used derivatively from "the plague," which is a corruption and affliction of the air, not of an animal. 

The present diseases, which are not truly pestilential, arise from various causes, from which three species of sickness are generated according to the three differences distinguished by their causes: 

The **first** of these is that which arises from an intrinsic alteration of the internal <term>humors</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) had to remain in balance for health.</note> produced within themselves, or from other internal excremental superfluities mixed with them, or from some other similar cause making them degenerate into the nature of **poison**. These humors, thus affected and poisonous, having become overheated or putrefied in the veins, arteries, or some other place—or even persisting in their poisonous nature—usually produce various kinds of putrid fevers if they first putrefy. 

If, however, they do not putrefy, but passing through the said vessels they reach the heart itself, they kill a person even without a manifest fever by corrupting the spirits of the heart and its temperament. From this follow **sudden, unforeseen, and unexpected deaths**, the cause of which doctors often hesitate to name. But if they are not so affected by malice as to cause death quickly, various conditions are caused by nature's attempt to expel them, such as abscesses in the <term>emunctories</term> <note>The "emunctories" were understood as the body's drainage points or sites where waste was expelled, specifically the lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, and groin.</note>, carbuncles, and cutaneous eruptions which the common people call *pestichias* <note>original: "pestichias." These are petechiae—small purple or red spots on the skin caused by minor bleeding, often seen in typhus or plague.</note>, as well as other contagious spots on various parts of the body. 

The **second** species is that which is brought about by contact and the commerce of men, or from the handling of infected things. These things retain within themselves a certain <term>seedbed</term> <note>original: "seminarium." This is a significant early concept of contagion, suggesting "seeds" of disease that can lie dormant in clothes or objects.</note> (so to speak) of a pestiferous quality, through which they infect spirits, or vapors, or humors, or other solid substances. These, if retained in the veins and inflamed, excite a bad fever. If the humors are thus infected because of their poisonous quality...

Indeed, these things of poor substance include many vegetables, rotting fruits, and certain stinking fish; among other foods which men eat and which generate poisonous and pestilential humors are certain bad, wicked, and rotting meats. There are also certain marshy and muddy waters of poor substance which, if drunk, generate poisonous humors. From these humors, bad and pestiferous illnesses arise, such as <term>putrid fevers</term> of various kinds, in which—just as in the others—abscesses of the emunctories (that is, in the groin, under the armpits, and behind the ears) as well as carbuncles, pimples, and various contagious spots usually appear. This occurs not without the greatest danger, and often even with the death of the sick person, as I shall say a little further below. 

These three latter species are those "improperly called pestilential" which are currently depopulating the city and striking terror into everyone. For besides a constant fever, the mentioned abscesses in the emunctory sites, and in other parts of the body carbuncles, <term>anthrax boils</term> <note>original: "antraces"</note>, and various pimples—as well as certain broad, large spots—appear in various locations on the body, from which the greater part of the sufferers perish. ...heavy breath, distress of the stomach, and a tension across the entire lower abdomen; the urine is thick and "undigested" <note>original: "indigestæ"; in Galenic medicine, this meant the body's internal "heat" had not yet successfully "cooked" or processed the diseased matter</note>, livid and cloudy; there is a heaviness and pain in the head and eyes; and a powerful thirst accompanied by a white coating on the tongue.
