Finally, if they are black, they arise from an overabundance of the natural melancholic humor or a "burnt," poisonous version of it; few escape when these black spots appear, as they show that the mass of the humors has already degenerated into the nature of poison. 

Let these remarks suffice concerning the signs of the three mentioned types of "evil" sicknesses. Along with these signs, I have chosen to include some of the causes for a clearer understanding of these diseases which, as I said, seize and kill very many poor men, women, and children. 

There are certainly other signs of the said sicknesses which contribute to a general understanding of them; however, since they have already been mentioned, I thought it better to leave them to be gathered by the reader and instead respond to the questions put forward by the **Senate** <note>The governing body of the city-state, likely Venice, requesting expert medical testimony during the outbreak</note> in this presence, setting them out in order. 

One thing, however, I shall note first: although it has been said that the present diseases do not arise from a "corruption of the air" <note>original: "aeris corruptione"; a common theory that disease was caused by "miasma" or poisoned atmosphere</note>, I did not mean to imply that the air of the present or past year had qualities perfectly proportional to the seasons, or appropriate to the times of the year, such that the air was excellent in every respect. Indeed, the four seasons of both the present and past years were unequal and did not follow the natural order in every part. Even if the air currently possesses some quality harmful to our bodies, it is not of such a nature that it could, by itself, cause these cruel sicknesses.

The first thing that was asked, therefore, was whether the large and broad spots that appear in many people are of the same nature and quality as those which mostly appear in "malignant fevers" and those called of "bad character" by **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose writings were the absolute authority on medicine in the Renaissance</note>, and whether those pimples or "efflorescences"...

# THIRTY-FIFTH:

...described by Hippocrates and the ancient physicians. To provide a clear answer to this inquiry, allow me to digress slightly, having first established this conclusion: that these **petechiae** <term>pestichias: small purple or red spots caused by bleeding under the skin, often called "flea-bites" at the time</term> are not the same as those usually seen in the "bad fevers" of our present and past times. First, this is because they do not possess a similar nature, substance, or behavior, nor any other quality like them. For if we first examine the matter of the **petechiae**, it has the nature of "bad bile," which does not possess an entirely ultimate, venomous malice. However, the matter of *these* [current] spots consists of burnt and corrupted blood, reduced to the nature of a poison; because of this poisonous quality, it quickly kills by attacking the heart.

And although the matter of the **petechiae** (which is a non-natural bile) is not without pestilential malice, it is nonetheless not so poisonous that it cannot be managed by the body’s "regulating power" <note>The "virtue" or natural healing force of the body in Galenic medicine</note>. Thus, even if not all patients are saved, the greater part of them are recovered, and few perish. Furthermore, those who do die do not perish in the first days, but resist until the eleventh or fourteenth day; many are even freed from the disease. Therefore, they are not similar in terms of their matter nor the malice of their poisonous quality. 

Nevertheless, both the **petechiae** and the aforementioned large spots share the fact that they are contagious and malignant. However, the malice of the **petechiae** can be better regulated by the air, food, drink, and medicinal aids. Among them, those spots that are black are worse and more destructive, though some people still escape death from them. But the large spots mentioned above are truly the worst, from which almost everyone dies quickly—most on the very day they appear. 

How can this be? It is due to nothing other than the extreme corruption and poisonous malice contracted in the **blood-mass** <term>massa-sanguinea: the total volume of blood in the body, viewed as a mixture of humors</term> and other humors. This matter first corrupts within the veins and arteries; then, when it is moved by the body's nature to be driven outward toward the **lesser limbs** <note>original: "ignobiliora membra"; the extremities or skin, considered "less noble" than vital organs like the heart</note>, it then evaporates toward the heart itself, infecting and corrupting its spirit, from which follows a swift and unexpected death. 

And although in cases of **petechiae**, bad symptoms sometimes occur during the movement of "nature" as it expels the matter—such as **fainting spells** <term>lypothymiæ: a sudden loss of strength or consciousness</term>, mental alienation, and others—their evaporation is not affected by such a wicked, poisonous quality that they could cause sudden death without any interval of time.

The second point of inquiry was whether the present wide and large spots—which appear in many of the weak before death, or after death as has been seen in some—differ in color...

# EPISTLE

...are indeed red, livid, black, and of other colors. The question is whether they can truly be called the **plague**, and whether they are as contagious as the pustules or scattered eruptions—those small ones called **petechiae** <term>pestichias: small red or purple spots on the skin caused by minor hemorrhaging, often compared to flea bites</term>. Furthermore, it is asked whether they possess that ultimate malice found in **apostemes** <term>apostemata: large inflammatory swellings or abscesses</term>, **carbuncles**, and **anthraxes** <note>original: "carbones & antraces"; in this period, these referred to necrotic, burning plague sores</note> which usually appear in other pestilences, and whether they ought to be named petechiae. 

To these questions, I first responded that these spots are not the plague itself, since the plague arises from the corruption of the air. Instead, they follow the **malignant fevers** of the second and third species already mentioned, which are caused by contact, a poor regimen of food, and other factors. To the second inquiry, I said that although the said spots are contagious, they are not as contagious as the pustules; this is because their matter is thicker than the matter of the pustules or petechiae. 

To the third, I replied that these spots do not have the same malice as truly pestilential fevers accompanied by abscesses, carbuncles, and anthraxes; nor do they spread contagion as quickly. Nevertheless, if the multitude of corrupted matter communicates a great deal of "evil evaporation" <note>The contemporary belief that diseases spread through toxic vapors or "miasmas" released by corrupt humors</note> to the heart, it causes death. 

To the fourth inquiry, I said that the wide, broad, livid, or otherwise colored spots are not abscesses, but rather **expulsions** <note>The body’s "expulsive virtue" attempting to drive toxins from the internal organs toward the skin</note> resulting from the sweating out of corrupted and poisonous blood contained in the veins. When this blood is moved—either by its substance, its quality, or its evaporation—it seeks the heart, and thus kills the living being. 

To the fifth, it was stated that these spots have not appeared except in those aforementioned diseases depending on the corruption of the air. Therefore, they are new to us, and were not seen in the fevers of other past years. However, these spots are evil and "taste" of the nature of poison, so much so that all the weak patients upon whom they appear perish. Yet, they do not have that subtle evaporation seen in petechiae. Thus, we can say that these broad spots have been a certain "new accident" <note>In Galenic medicine, an "accident" refers to a symptom or secondary condition arising from a disease</note> of our times. 

I would not want anyone to believe, simply because I called these large and broad spots a "new accident," that I meant they were so new as to be unnamed, or never seen by the ancients such as **Hippocrates** and after him **Galen**. Nor do I believe that in a similar plague many other symptoms cannot occur. Rather, it was said in this sense: namely, that these spots do not occur in all pestilential and malignant fevers, nor even in the majority of them, as **petechiae** do. Similarly...

<summary>The author classifies the current epidemic's large spots as "expulsions" of poisonous blood rather than the plague itself, noting they are more lethal but less contagious than common petechiae. He characterizes them as a "new symptom" of the current age, while acknowledging they were likely known to ancient physicians like Hippocrates.</summary>

# THIRTY-FIFTH [EPISTLE]

<margin>Furthermore</margin> it has not been many years since certain pestilential fevers first appeared in **Britain**, and then in some other provinces and cities of **Germany**, accompanied by other symptoms hardly written of or seen by the ancient physicians. These were **ephemeras** <term>ephemerae: fevers that last only a single day</term>, in which the suffering patients sweat with a constant and profuse perspiration; because of this sweat, they call this evil **The Sweat** <note>original: "Sudorinam"; this refers to the "English Sweat" (*Sudor Anglicus*), a mysterious and terrifying epidemic that struck Europe in several waves during the 15th and 16th centuries</note>. Those who are seized by such a plague perish without doubt unless they immediately go home, place themselves in bed, and cover themselves with suitable blankets so that they may sweat as moderately as possible. This is accompanied by many other symptoms of pestilential fevers, namely: a weak pulse, a total loss of strength, **fainting** <term>lypothymia: a medical term for a sudden loss of strength or a "sinking" feeling, often preceding a faint</term>, a general lethargy of the whole body, difficulty breathing, and even coldness of the extremities. 

From these examples, one can see that the same symptoms do not always appear in every pestilential constitution. Instead, they are diverse, sometimes never seen before, and not recorded by ancient writers. This variation occurs according to the different dispositions of the patients' bodies, the regions, and the climates. To clarify this final inquiry and the rest—and to confirm my response—I have briefly noted above the history of the most cruel pestilences of both the **Athenians** <note>referring to the Plague of Athens (430 BCE) described by the historian Thucydides</note> and the **Florentines** <note>referring to the Black Death in Florence (1348) famously described by Giovanni Boccaccio</note>, in which certain spots were also seen. 

Thus, let those who were wondering cease to marvel, knowing now that these pestilential diseases were far worse than reported and possessed even more severe symptoms that were not witnessed by everyone. Having said and explained these things, I shall bring an end to this part. I will now write down the second part, which will concern the **method of treatment** <note>original: "agendorum ratione"; literally "the reasoning of things to be done," referring to the practical medical response</note>. This next section, also divided into several parts, will explain everything as previously stated.

# ON THE MANNER OF FREEING THE CITY
## FROM THE PESTILENTIAL CONTAGION.
### THIRTY-SIXTH EPISTLE.

While many other very cruel and difficult-to-cure diseases may be found, the illustrious ancients first enumerated pestilential fevers among the most difficult. This is because they are diseases extremely hard to heal and are, for the most part, deadly. For this reason, this part of the work concerning remedies has always seemed difficult to me, and it remains so at present. Nevertheless, relying on the help of God, the best and greatest <note>original: "Dei optimi maximi"; a common Latin invocation, often abbreviated as D.O.M.</note>, I shall approach the matter itself and describe which remedies should be applied to this arduous evil; these I will distinguish into many sections.

The first and most important remedy that can resist the present disease (which for the most part snatches away the lives of poor and humble men, women, and children) <note>the author highlights that the plague disproportionately affected the lower classes, likely due to living conditions and nutrition</note> will be this: to look first to those causes mentioned above. These were diverse, one of which was the consumption of bad foodstuffs, such as bad fruit and rotting vegetables; foul-smelling meat, stinking fish, and other poor things that the poor eat. Therefore, with all possible diligence, some means must be found for the poor and wretched to avoid that excessive and gluttonous eating of bad and rotten things. This will be easily accomplished if it is prohibited by edict that bad and rotten edible items be brought into the city, and that they not be sold if they are already in the city, but rather burned. Care should also be taken that there is a plenty of wheat flour and other grains so that they can eat bread made from them. Let the wells of the city also be cleaned of all filth, lest the people drink rotten or foul-smelling water.

The second remedy will be that, with all care and diligence, the entire city and specific locations are cleaned of every kind of filth and rotting matter. Therefore, first, let the streets be kept clean, and especially those places where meat is sold, which they call the butcher's market <term>macellum: a market building for meat and provisions</term> and the slaughterhouse <term>carnarium: a place where meat is stored or hung</term>. For these places are always teeming with rotting things and smell horribly; nonetheless, people must necessarily frequent them when they go there to buy meat. Similarly, the fish markets should also be clean, for fish rot very easily and...

# THIRTY-FIFTH.

...[they] smell bad, and since a multitude of people gather there to buy things, they must ensure they do not prepare themselves for a worse evil by breathing in bad and putrid air. Both the meat markets and the fish markets should be washed daily, every morning and evening, so that they are cleansed of all filth and stench. This can be done very easily and with minimal labor in this most noble city <note>The author is referring to Venice, where the proximity to the sea and the canal system provided a natural means for waste removal</note>, as seawater is available everywhere in all parts of the city and is always at hand. 

Likewise, all the canals and streams, both large and small, which are filled with all kinds of filth, should be dug out and cleared with the greatest possible speed, so that putrid vapors do not rise up and, by lingering, corrupt the air itself. 

But since it is the poor who are seized by these evils and die—those who for the most part live in the cramped parts and places of the city where there are narrow alleys in which the houses are small, dirty, and full of the impoverished—special care must be taken. For in one small house, very often many people live together, so that sometimes there are twenty or even more people of different sorts (if I may say so): for there are men and women, and older and younger children, all working, eating, and relieving themselves <note>original: "egerentes"; the author uses a medical term for bodily evacuation</note> there. They have only one latrine <term>latrina</term> <note>a communal toilet or privy</note>, and sometimes they have none at all, in which they deposit all their uncleanness and bodily excrement, along with many other kinds of filth. 

Therefore, it is necessary that these narrow alleys, among others, as well as the houses and latrines, be cleaned and purged so that all places—alleys, small houses, and the latrines within them—are entirely clean of all uncleanness and stench, lest they be able to corrupt the neighboring air. This filth should be carried outside the city and burned.

The third appropriate remedy will be that the poor and the children living in those dirty little houses be led outside the city for several days, for instance to the shores or other open fields. But the shores will be more convenient since they have seawater with which they can clean everything, and they are also exposed to the winds. There, small houses or wooden huts <note>original: "capanæ"; likely referring to temporary shanties or cabins</note> should be constructed for them to live in for some time—namely, until the deadly contagion is removed. 

Alternatively, small or large boats should be provided according to the size of the family. For example, let them use the larger boats common in the city if the family is small, or larger ones like those that sail to Padua or Vicenza if the family is larger. Or, where there is a very large family, they should take large or medium-sized ships, such as those used to transport goods to Ferrara. They should remain either on the shores...

# EPISTLE

...or in the aforementioned skiffs and ships until all suspicion is removed. This method of precaution—boarding skiffs and ships—has been found better than all others. Indeed, almost all who boarded them for the sake of precaution have returned unharmed; if any died, they were very few in number. Therefore, it must be pursued and seen to that those suspected of illness who leave their own homes board these skiffs. Furthermore, to ensure the healthy do not mix with the infected, the Lords presiding over health <note>These were the *Provveditori alla Sanità*, the Venetian health magistrates</note> should appoint guards to prohibit contact between the infected and the suspected. Nor should they allow bad or putrid things, foul-smelling fish, or similar perishable goods to be brought to them.

The fourth health-giving aid for guarding against this evil plague and liberating the city (according to the opinion of all) was for the Lords of Health to find certain honest and faithful physicians to daily inspect those who have newly fallen ill or who are dying day by day. These physicians should be learned, skilled, and practiced so they can distinguish between the symptoms of pestilential fevers and other fevers caused by inflammation or putrefaction that lack a plague-like quality. They must also be able to distinguish between plague-related abscesses, carbuncles, and anthrax sores <note>The author uses "carbones" and "antraces," both referring to the dark, necrotic sores characteristic of the bubonic plague</note> and other unnatural abscesses and tumors that lack that malignant, plague-like quality. 

For those who are unskilled and practice without reason have very often been deceived during this bad state of affairs. They see the buboes <term>Buboes: painfully swollen lymph nodes in the groin or armpit</term> that usually occur in men from the French Disease <term>Morbus Gallicus: Syphilis, which was widespread in Europe at this time</term>, or similar tumors caused by physical labor, or others arising from causes other than the plague, and they declare them to be pestilential abscesses, even though it was later recognized they were from the French Disease. Similarly, because they did not know how to distinguish them, they have claimed that inguinal ruptures <note>hernias in the groin</note> were plague-related abscesses; and often they even said scrofulas <note>A form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</note> were plague tumors. This happened for no other reason than ignorance of the first principles of medicine; they did not know how to distinguish the symptoms of pestilential diseases from harmless symptoms, and so they deceived the suffering and placed them in the greatest danger, and thus threw the whole city into the greatest fear and terror. 

But when the suffering were later seen by learned and skilled men, the diseases were recognized—both which were plague-ridden and which were not—and the city was liberated by this help with the cooperation of God the Best and Greatest. And although other rational physicians arrived to see the sick and dead daily by the appointment of the Lords of Health, the same physicians did not go continuously, but were changed every day...

->### THIRTY-FIFTH<-

...and on the other hand, if there were many different "gods" <note>This likely refers to a variety of individual physicians acting independently, whose conflicting opinions the author likens to a pantheon of disagreeing deities.</note>, their judgment was rarely optimal, since they were always differing in age, doctrine, and experience. Thus, it was extremely difficult to have a true and firm opinion regarding both the suffering and the dead, or at least one close to the truth; indeed, they would arrive and be changed daily by turns. 

For this reason, it will be best to have two or more skilled physicians who daily visit or inspect both the suffering and the dead. From this assiduous, daily, and continuous inspection, they will acquire the habit and knowledge of recognizing those infected with the plague's evil quality, and of distinguishing them from those not suffering from this malignant pestilence <term>lue: an archaic term for a contagious disease or "slough"</term>. Thus, without error or hesitation, they will be able to know the infected from the non-infected. 

These physicians, therefore, may be chosen by the aforementioned prefects in this manner: namely, let a public edict be made that if any learned and skilled physicians wish to serve in such a case, for an honest and honorable public salary established for them, they should present themselves to the Lords of Health <note>The *Provveditori alla Sanità*, the Venetian health magistrates</note>. All their names should be written in their register. When, from the many noted down, many of them are believed to be equals in doctrine and experience, and in such a case they desire to choose the better ones from those best candidates, yet doubt they might err in the election: let the senior, more prudent, and upright physicians from the College be called. These shall say under oath which ones among the many listed seem better suited to them to fulfill this task. 

The duty of the said physicians will be to see all newly suffering or suspected persons, and also the dead, every day; however, they are to remain in the street, neither entering the house nor touching them in any way. And first, they should inspect the face and also diligently question them: whether they have shivered, or if a shuddering or cold has bothered them at any hour, and whether they suffer from an unusual heat, or sleep too much or stay awake, whether they crave or loathe food, or even have a dry tongue or head pain, or heaviness, and whether they experience delusions <note>original: *alienationes*, referring to mental wandering or delirium</note>, and also whether they have spontaneous bowel movements and of what kind they are. They should also inspect the urine and ask about stomach disturbance, anxiety, and vomiting. Furthermore, they should inquire whether any swelling has appeared in any part, or if any rashes <term>exanthemata: skin eruptions or rashes characteristic of infectious diseases</term>, pimples, or spots have broken out, and also what color they are. 

But if, as often happens in these suffering patients, they are unable to rise from bed due to the weakness and laxity of all their limbs <note>original: *membrorum*</note>, and because of a suffering head <note>meaning a clouded or pained mind</note> they are unable to respond to questions at all, or speak incoherently, those who are in the house with the sick should be questioned, and they should judge according to what is reported and seen, and also...

# EPISTOLA

...they should give advice to the household <note>original: "filiis" - literally "sons," but here referring to the family or dependents</note> regarding what must be done, as much for the daily regimen as for the preparation of medicines and other remedies. This is to be done not only for prevention but also to provide aid for the present illness if it should be there. This is necessary because many people are sick who are not infected with the pestilential and contagious infection, but are laboring under or held by another sickness or disease—for instance, a tertian fever <note>a form of malaria where the fever recurs every third day</note>, or gout, or some tumor resulting from the French disease <term>morbo gallico: a common 16th-century name for syphilis</term>, or some other abscess or ulcer. These ailments are entirely free of malignancy or suspicion of plague, and yet, because of the dread of the pestilence, physicians do not wish to enter the house. Therefore, the physicians standing outside the house should advise them on the remedies to be used; they should order the dietary plan, appropriate medicines, or the letting of blood through the incision of a vein, or by the application of cupping-glasses with scarification <term>scarification: the practice of making small superficial incisions in the skin before applying a suction cup to draw out blood</term>, or through the application of leeches to hemorrhoids or other locations. 

And lest Christian charity fail the poor and the sick, let there also be chosen by the Lords of Health <note>The *Provveditori alla Sanità*, the Venetian magistrates in charge of public health</note> certain surgeons <term>chirurgici: medical practitioners who specialized in manual procedures like surgery, bleeding, and wound care</term> or operators who know how to cut veins, apply cupping-glasses with scarification, and apply leeches. These operators should receive a salary from the public treasury during this time of suspicion, and they shall be required to serve those sick people who are not infected with the contagious pestilence, as much in bloodletting by opening a vein as in the application of cupping-glasses and leeches, and also, if there is a need, in the opening of non-pestilential abscesses <term>apostemate: a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term> and the care of those wounds, by the order of the said Lords of Health. I have said this because many people perish from other illnesses because they do not have physicians to advise them on what should be done. 

But if by some chance it should happen that such surgeons are called to someone in whom signs of the pestilential contagion appear after the surgeon has entered, that surgeon shall be prohibited <note>placed under quarantine</note> until all suspicion has been removed. The sick person, however, should be sent to the places designated for the suspected and infected sick, or should board one of the aforementioned boats <note>original: "cimbis" - small vessels or skiffs used in the Venetian lagoons to isolate the sick</note>. I praise this latter option more for various reasons and from observed experience, since the majority of those who boarded the said boats escaped death. In such a case, the surgeon who is suspected and prohibited should be given double pay for only that time he was prohibited, so that after his release he may more freely serve the sick and be able to nourish himself and his family during that time. It is also fitting that Christians study the health of the soul with no less care than that of the body; therefore, let the ancient institution of the Health Office be observed: namely, that there be two or more honest, elderly priests...

...let them have houses in different parts of the city, or in the six districts <note>original: "sexteriis" — referring to the *sestieri*, the six traditional administrative divisions of Venice</note> as they are called; let them receive a public salary and those things which are necessary for food. Let the healthy be separated from the sick, and let boats be given to them or let them be sent to designated places, so that the sick might (if God wills) be healed and the healthy preserved. Nor will it be useless to repeat some things which we said a little while ago: that with all diligence, whether they are in the Lazarettos, in monasteries, in houses, or in any other place, they should strive for cleanliness, so that the bedding, the linens for the beds, and the coverings are all bright and clean. To accomplish this, women should be present to wash everything with lye <term>lixivio: a potent cleaning solution made from wood ash, used as a precursor to modern bleach</term>, and men should also be there to serve, and to carry out and burn the filth. All of these, both men and women, should be upright, merciful, honest, and God-fearing. To say it in a word: let everything be governed as has already been begun. For from the past management of affairs, things succeed better and many more are set free from the disease.

This has already been seen. For those who were first seized by this plague in this city were seized for the reason that they possessed and handled infected things from **Justinopolis** <note>original: "Iustinopoli" — the Latin name for Koper/Capodistria, a Venetian territory in modern-day Slovenia</note>, a city of Illyria. -># LETTER<-

...if infected items are found in any houses, let them be burned, since they are tainted with the most foul contagion.

The sixth provision shall be that all houses in which those suffering from this **pestilential disease** <term>pestilentiali morbo</term> <note>A standard term for the bubonic plague, believed at the time to be spread by "corrupt air."</note> have stayed or died must be cleaned quickly and most diligently. This is especially necessary for the small houses of the poor, as they are always filthy and foul-smelling; let the filth found there be burned, as well as those items that are least able to be cleaned. After this cleaning, and before the healthy enter, let the walls be smeared with fresh lime <note>original: "calce" — whitewashing with lime was a common early modern disinfectant</note>, and let old wooden floors be renewed. Furthermore, **fumigations** <term>suffumigia</term> <note>The practice of burning aromatic substances to "purify" the air; people believed pleasant smells could counteract the "miasma" of the plague.</note> should be performed using fragrant things according to a person’s means and convenience. For the houses of the poor, use fragrant herbs, flowers, and fruits, such as citrus leaves, roses, and sweet-smelling apples, or sprinkle the area with vinegar and water. For the wealthy, however, use the aforementioned roses along with **aloeswood**, **benzoin** <note>original: "belzui" — a balsamic resin from trees in East Asia</note>, **amber**, **musk**, **cinnamon**, **mace**, and similar substances. These items should be boiled in rose or violet water to remove their "heat" <note>This refers to the Galenic medical theory of balancing "hot" and "cold" qualities in substances.</note>, or a mixture of vinegar and rose water and the like may be sprinkled. But among all other methods, a fire made of fragrant woods—such as laurel, myrtle, juniper, cypress, and the like—is one of the best for purifying the air.

However, since there are almost countless large houses that are exposed to the sun and winds and have every convenience of water, air, and fire, I say that if any nobles, citizens, or merchants have worked in these large houses and wish to take care of their own affairs so that they are cleaned with all diligence, let it be granted to them. Let them choose and pay whomever they wish to hire to cleanse their house. This is because if their belongings are handled by their own people, they will certainly apply greater diligence and there will be less damage to their property. For when infected items remain for a long time together without airing or other purification, their malignancy will increase, and thus the infection will be more difficult to remove. But to ensure that houses and all items are thoroughly cleaned, and to remove all suspicion of inadequate cleaning, since some men are poor or greedy—fearing the expense and unwilling to pay the proper wages for the labor—the hired laborers <note>original: "mercenarii" — here meaning laborers for hire rather than soldiers</note> often become less diligent for this reason. Therefore, so that such hired ministers may enter the infected houses with a cheerful countenance and perform their duty of cleaning...

<header>THIRTY-SIX</header>

# THIRTY-SIX

...so that they do not fail, the Lords of the Health Board <note>original: "Domini præsides salutis" — the officials in charge of public health and plague response</note> should determine fairly how much, at a minimum, they ought to earn for purging or cleaning this or that house. This stipend should be paid to them by the owners of the infected property without any delay. For **the laborer is worthy of his hire** <note>A reference to the New Testament (Luke 10:7), emphasizing that even those performing "unclean" work deserve fair pay.</note>. And those who serve in such a crisis are far more deserving. Indeed, the method of purging should be as we have said above, and as will be said hereafter; first, items of no value or small value shall be burned, both in large and small houses, lest they infect healthy men if handled by them, and this evil spread once again through the whole city.

The seventh provision or precaution for removing the present evil and avoiding it in the future will be instruction on the manner in which infected things can be purged and cleaned. Regarding this method of purification, there has been long and much doubt, especially since those who serve the infected and those languishing from such a **pestilential plague** <term>pestifera lue</term> are often poor and cruel, lacking Christian charity. They desire nothing other than the pay, whatever it may be, and therefore they have no intention toward anything else but themselves; such ministers should in no way be admitted. Instead, let upright, good, and merciful men who fear God be chosen, so that they may clean all things, acting faithfully in everything out of Christian love and charity.

But if those in large houses, or those who are wealthy, wish to clean their own infected things, I would not deny this to them, provided they show everything openly and take them out of chests or boxes and expose them to the air, or purge them by other methods of purification. To do this, they should call or hire men who know how to complete the business and can perform it perfectly and safely in said houses. Indeed, the methods for cleaning infected things are various: sometimes it is achieved by multiple washings, sometimes by frequent and vigorous wiping, and sometimes by long **airing out** <term>eventatione</term> by exposing them to the air and winds for many days, or by long and frequent **fumigations** <term>suffumigiis</term> <note>Purifying by smoke or aromatic vapors.</note> performed over several days.

Truly, in the case of those things which can be cleaned neither by washing, nor by wiping, nor by airing, nor even by fumigation, let all these be burned by fire. And since it was the ancient custom for infected and suspected things to be sent to the **Lazarettos** <term>Lazareta</term> <note>Quarantine hospitals, named after St. Lazarus; the first was established in Venice in 1423.</note> for cleaning, and this manner of cleaning is too difficult and long, and they are not cleaned perfectly or optimally—even though the Lazarettos or hospital sites have many spacious places—nevertheless, there are many reasons why they are not well purged...

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>EPISTLE</header>

...and upon the return of the said items, some of those who handled them were newly seized by the pestilential evil. The first and most powerful reason for this is that those places, or **Lazar-houses** <term>Lazareta — quarantine stations used to isolate people and goods suspected of carrying the plague</term>, and the people living in them, are undoubtedly infected. The second reason is that even if those places are spacious, as has been mentioned, they are nonetheless cramped in comparison to the vast and diverse number of items brought there daily. For more and more things are always being sent from the city to those locations, so that they cannot accommodate everything comfortably; instead, it becomes necessary to pile them into heaps, which is a matter of the greatest concern. For when these items remain packed together, they cannot be aired out, and thus they acquire a greater malignancy and a pestilential, contagious quality that is very difficult to remove.

Therefore, the best advice will be that in no way should infected or suspected items be brought to the said Lazar-houses. Instead, they should be taken to open-field locations with good air and exposure to the winds—namely, to the meadows of the mainland or nearby shores. In those places, let there be many sheds or roofs—whether you call them coverings or shelters does not matter—under which moveable goods may be placed (so they are protected from rain and other elements). This should be done as quickly as possible, and the items should be cleaned and aired out promptly so that they do not (as I said) acquire greater malignancy by sitting together in a heap, in small chests, or in bundles.

And since there are some things that cannot be cleaned by the aforementioned methods, or if the delay causes a danger of infection over time, let them be burned. Nor should those things that have been cleaned be kept there after their purification; rather, they should be moved to other locations exposed to the winds before they are carried back to the private homes of their owners, so that they are purged of every suspicion of a contagious, bad quality. And as I said, all these purifications of things should be done as quickly as possible, whether by washing, wiping, and airing out, or by fumigating, or as a last resort, by burning.

But indeed, since not everyone is suited for the aforementioned purification of goods, let wise, strong, courageous, and—as we said above—upright and God-fearing men be chosen, who can endure the labor of purging these things. And since it is very difficult to guard against thieves and avoid their wickedness, let there be upright supervisors and guards who are superior to and in command of the aforementioned workers. These supervisors should have all the items cataloged, designated, and numbered; they shall then hand these items over to the workers who must clean them. Until the items are purged, the supervisors shall keep them constantly in view from a distance and oversee the entire process. Let them be vigilant and take care with all diligence that the items are cleaned: the discourse <note>original: "discur" — catchword for the next page, likely continuing "discursus" (discourse) or "discurrendo" (discussing)</note>

<summary>This page argues that traditional quarantine houses (Lazarettos) are often too overcrowded and infected to be effective, recommending instead that goods be purified in open-air fields. It emphasizes the need for honest, God-fearing supervisors to prevent theft and ensure the rigorous cleaning of belongings.</summary>

<keywords>Lazar-houses, Lazaretto, quarantine logistics, purification of goods, plague prevention, contagion, public health officials, open-air aeration, fumigation</keywords>

### THIRTY-SIXTH

...assigning for this purpose meadows or shores, now in one area and now in another, where items are cleaned. Once the purification is complete, a full restoration should be made, ensuring that the items returned match both the type and the number of those received. Similarly, care must be taken that houses, both large and small, in which the infected or suspected individuals lived, are themselves cleaned of every kind of filth in all their parts before people return to inhabit them. This applies especially to the latrines and sewers <note>original: "cloacas"</note>, and this must be done with all diligence, lest perhaps they are infected again by the poor quality of decay <term>putredinis — the "putrefaction" or corrupt state of matter thought to generate and spread disease in the 16th century</term> left behind in them. Indeed, the waste and filth of the said houses should be carried outside the city and burned without any delay. In short, all suspected things that cannot be cleaned by washing, wiping, rubbing, airing out <note>original: "ventatione" — the practice of exposing items to the wind to "blow away" the plague miasma</note>, or any other similar kind of purification, should be burned as much as possible. For as we have often said, there is danger in delay, lest they conceive a greater decay, and having conceived a greater malice, they might be able to further infect the air and the people.

These are the things which I myself (as you know) had spoken before you and the Senate regarding this very matter. I have committed all these things to writing so that posterity may see that you have omitted nothing that might lead to the city's liberation and the cure of these ruinous diseases. This record will perhaps also have the benefit of showing a way to lighten the burden of a pestilential slaughter <note>original: "stragis pestiferæ" — referring to the massive loss of life during an epidemic</note> if, by some chance, the city should labor under such a calamity at some time—which may God avert.

But as for you, stay well and keep yourself safe for us; to you, I most highly commend myself and my Laurentius. 1557.
In the month of December.

->FINIS.<-

# OF BERNARDINO FELICIANO
## A Poem.

*Whoever you are who desires to heal serious*
  *Diseases, and to soothe the burning heat*
*Of fevers through medical arts, read now*
  *Massa alone: for here, in the briefest manner,*
*He explains everything that the old man of Kos,*
<note>original: "Cous". This refers to Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE), the "Father of Medicine," who was born on the Greek island of Kos.</note>
  *Or the man of Pergamon in his own*
<note>original: "Pergamenus". This refers to Galen (129–c. 216 CE), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, who was born in Pergamon (modern-day Turkey). Together, Hippocrates and Galen formed the backbone of medical knowledge in the 1500s.</note>
*Books once wrote, and he has added much besides;*
  *Just like a stream flowing from a great*
*Fountain, leaping here and there, it*
  *Irrigates the joyful pastures, so that the most*
*Abundant fruits may be gathered by whoever*
  *Tills the nearby fields. You will not find*
*Here words too select or ornate, but*
  *Rather each one common and familiar,*
<note>Renaissance scholars often debated between using "ornate" flowery language and "plain" technical language. Feliciano is praising Massa for choosing clarity and practical use over fancy rhetoric.</note>
*Yet expressing the matters he treats with gravity:*
  *So that with little labor—or rather*
*None—you may find whatever you have*
  *Decided to investigate in this field. Therefore, come,*
*Studious reader; putting all else aside, devote*
  *Yourself to this with your whole heart.*

# TO LORENZO PRIULI,
## MOST SERENE PRINCE
### OF THE VENETIAN REPUBLIC,
### Niccolò Massa sends his warmest greetings.
<note>original: "S. P. D." (Salutem Plurimam Dicit). A standard Latin epistolary greeting meaning "sends many greetings" or "gives greatest health." Lorenzo Priuli was the Doge of Venice from 1556 to 1559.</note>

**M**any are the reasons, Most Serene Prince, which urge me—as I wish to bring the second part of my small works into the light—to inscribe and dedicate it to your name. 
<note>original: "opusculorum meorum." *Opuscula* literally means "little works" or "treatises," a modest way for authors to refer to their intellectual output.</note>
For since you are the Prince of this city, in which I myself first drew breath and have lived until this age dear to all, it seems to me that you can demand of me by your own right that which I owe to my fatherland. But since there are also exceptional and very great reasons in you yourself why I should do this—the very same reasons, surely, that made you Prince of the Republic—I shall set aside the rest and speak of your virtues. These virtues could have impelled toward this very thing which you see me wishing at present, not only me—who more than all others have always striven to express my goodwill toward you—but anyone else, even one desiring or thinking of it not at all, if the name and reputation of virtue held any weight with him. For who is there who admires virtue, who does not likewise love him in whom virtue resides? Who has cultivated justice, fortitude, and temperance, and does not honor a just, brave, moderate, and temperate man? 
<note>These are three of the four "Cardinal Virtues" (the fourth being Prudence) which were considered the essential qualities of a successful and moral ruler in Renaissance political thought.</note>
But that you are he, who

<summary>Niccolò Massa begins his formal dedication to Lorenzo Priuli, the Doge of Venice, explaining that he owes this work to his prince both as a loyal citizen and as an admirer of the Doge’s personal virtues.</summary>

--- Page 379 ---
<meta>Continuity with previous page: This page continues the dedication of Niccolò Massa’s medical treatises to Doge Lorenzo Priuli. For this reason also, you can and ought to be honored and revered by all. The proof of this is that, although there are many in this city who are indeed famous men and endowed with every kind of virtue (as no one is unaware), nevertheless the fathers and the **flower of the senate** itself, from among so many and such great, clear, and illustrious men, wished to choose you alone to be declared the **Prince of the Venetian Empire**.
<note>original: "principem ueneti imperij." While we think of Venice as a Republic, the term "Empire" (imperium) here refers to its sovereign authority and its vast maritime and terrestrial territories. The Doge was often called the "Prince" in the classical sense of "Princeps" or "First Citizen."</note>
This matter is of such great and massive importance that it could not be greater. For by their own testimony, they have ensured that no one should doubt that you are most abundantly filled with all virtues, and that you stand as the most excellent of all in your city. 

Nor do I think I say small things when I call you the most excellent of all those who are in this city. First, because to surpass and excel all others in virtue who are in a single city has always been considered and judged a glorious thing. Second, because I consider it the same to triumph over your fellow citizens in this kind of praise as if you were to surpass all the nations that exist everywhere on earth with that same glory, leaving them in a long trail behind you. 
<note>original: "longo post te tramite relinqueres." A poetic way of saying he has left all others far behind in his wake.</note>
For if there is no nation or people more illustrious than the **Italian people**, and more admirable in every virtue; and if likewise the origin and beginning of the **Venetian city** was that which no one denies—that is, founded by men most excellent of all for their virtue who then flourished in **Italy**, who escaped the madness of those times in this corner of the **Adriatic Sea**—what reason is there why [you should] doubt...
<note>original: "rabiem eorum temporum." This refers to the "madness" of the barbarian invasions (such as those by Attila the Hun) which, according to tradition, forced the most noble and virtuous Romans to flee to the lagoons, leading to the founding of Venice.</note>

<summary>Massa argues that Priuli’s election as Doge by the Venetian Senate is ultimate proof of his superior virtue, comparing the nobility of Venice to the height of Italian excellence and its ancient refugee founders.</summary>

...[should we] hesitate to affirm that which we have just said? And should we not also establish that you so excel among other mortals that you have no equal? For if someone sees that the sun, by its own light, makes even the more noble and bright stars appear dark, and yet claims that the sun cannot do the same—and even greater things—to those stars that are weaker, he would be considered utterly foolish. In the same way, when we see you surpass and overcome your peers in every kind of virtue, we would be fools not to admit that you excel all others by far. 

Indeed, having known you for a long time—and because I am responsible for the care of your body and health, and thus interact with you intimately and familiarly—I never fail to observe your excellent <term>virtue<gloss>The Latin "virtus" implies not just moral goodness but also strength, excellence, and the qualities of a "great man."</gloss></term>; I never cease to admire your character, setting it before my eyes as a model to imitate, as I strive to attain that divine nature of yours. 

Moreover, it has always been the unique and characteristic trait of your ancestors to excel in virtue. They were placed in the highest magistracies and appointed to the rank of <term>procurator<gloss>The Procurators of Saint Mark were the highest-ranking life-long officials in the Venetian Republic, second only to the Doge.</gloss></term>—as many were, and as your brother is now—and they have never failed to prove the truth of the common saying:

->*Nor do fierce eagles*<-
->*Bring forth a timid dove.*<-
<note>original: "Neque imbellem feroces / Progenerant aquilæ columbam." This is a famous quote from the Roman poet Horace (Odes 4.4), suggesting that noble qualities are inherited.</note>

You, however, through the <term>study of literature<gloss>original: "studijs literarum," referring to the "Humanities" or liberal arts.</gloss></term> and philosophy itself—as if by a diligent cultivation added to a most fertile soil—have acquired the means to increase that happiness which the [liberality] of the Most High God...

...generosity was in you. There is no matter in <term>philosophy<gloss>In the 16th century, philosophy encompassed all systematic knowledge, including the natural sciences.</gloss></term> so abstruse or so hidden that it is not easy and clear to you. This is true partly because you possess a mastery of Greek literature and draw your philosophy from clear and pure sources—that which you call the "science of human affairs," joined and coupled with Christian Theology. It is also because whatever time and leisure is granted to you from your great responsibilities, you devote it entirely to the <term>liberal arts<gloss>The "liberaliores doctrinae" refers to the traditional curriculum of a gentleman, including rhetoric, logic, and classical literature.</gloss></term>, through which you both adorn your soul and govern the peoples subject to you with the utmost justice. 

Indeed, even before you were declared <term>Prince<gloss>In Venice, the Doge was often referred to as the "Serene Prince."</gloss></term>, amidst the weightiest business you conducted for the <term>Republic<gloss>Specifically the Republic of Venice, often abbreviated as "Rep." in Latin texts.</gloss></term> both at home and abroad, you never abandoned your literary studies. For this reason, those who obey you and live under your rule can truly be called happy; for even your <note>Massa refers to Plato as "yours" to highlight Priuli's deep familiarity with the philosopher's works.</note> Plato considered republics to be blessed if either learned and wise men began to rule them, or if those who rule devoted all their efforts to learning and wisdom. 

And since medicine is in no way inconsistent with the principles of philosophy, I believe this is why you have wished to make it familiar to you, taking pleasure in mastering the precepts of that discipline. This field is, in a sense, necessary for everyone—for each person ought to preserve himself from harmful things—and it is useful at times when one is afflicted, so that he might [be able to judge] medicines, the nature of his illness, and the opinions of his physicians...

...is able to make a judgment based on the art: thus it produces such great delight that nothing more pleasant for the mental refreshment of the soul can be found than the <term>study of medicine<gloss>In the 16th century, medicine was considered one of the highest forms of natural philosophy, combining practical healing with deep insights into the human condition.</gloss></term>. But I would not want you to think that I send my labors to you for the purpose of returning thanks for your <term>benevolence<gloss>original: "benevolentia"; a technical term in patronage referring to the favorable disposition of a superior toward a subordinate.</gloss></term> with this small gift; rather, I do so to leave it witnessed to everyone for all time that I am most deeply indebted to you. I also wish that my writings—which cannot achieve this by their own resources—might be commended to the opinions of readers by the glory and majesty of your name, so they may live longer among men. Supported by your most solemn <term>patronage<gloss>original: "patrocinio"; authors in the 1500s required a powerful sponsor to lend legitimacy to their work and protect them from legal or professional attacks.</gloss></term> and your highest authority, I hope they may avoid the hatred and withstand the envy of those who produce nothing themselves to benefit posterity, yet are always accusing and condemning the industry of others. Such critics will be all the more deterred when they see that you take up these works with eagerness and willingness. I ask you again and again to do this. *Farewell.*

# TO THE STUDENTS OF THE LIBERAL ARTS AND LOVERS OF TRUTH AND TRUE WISDOM

## NICOLAUS MASSA

When, as is customary, we were traveling in a boat to visit the sick <note>Nicolaus Massa lived and practiced in Venice; physicians there typically visited patients by gondola or small boat.</note> along with certain young men most studious of the liberal arts <term>liberal arts: the traditional curriculum of "good arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, etc.) that formed the foundation of Renaissance education</term> and medicine, and we were discussing among ourselves (as we usually do) philosophical and medical questions—they being in the habit of questioning me for the sake of their own mental improvement—and many things on both sides of the matters we were disputing had been said and examined by us, we at last happened upon a conversation concerning the elegant discourse of the mind and the perfect knowledge of things, as well as the ornament of words and polished, refined speech. Regarding these matters, we defended our opinion with arguments that were perhaps not weak. Since these views were approved by those young men, I wished to commit all of them, or at least the greater part, to writing. My goal was that those who excel most among the professors of literature, both in the goodness of their intellect and the ornament of their speech, might read these things and—having set aside the persuasion of certain bad authors—might better recognize, strive for, and emulate the perfect elegance and purity of the mind.

Our discourse, therefore, began thus (after some remarks which I do not write down, so that I do not seem to wish to waste time on things that appear less necessary to me):

"Professors of the liberal arts truly wonder and grieve deeply—especially those who apply themselves more diligently to the study of philosophy and medicine—that in recent years, certain men, through an incredible rebellion <note>original: "seditione"</note> against the most eminent writers in every kind of science, have so attacked them that it is not sufficiently clear which of the ancient writings of illustrious wise men one ought to study, or which are better ignored, both in every other field of study and in medicine itself. Wherefore, if no cause or duty was ever undertaken by learned men that is more necessary than for the sake of truth..."

<summary>In this preface, the Venetian physician Nicolaus Massa describes a scholarly discussion held on a boat with his students, leading him to defend the importance of classical wisdom and refined language against contemporary critics.</summary>

to speak, and to take up the defense of illustrious men against **talkative rivals**, certainly in this task everyone ought to be most engaged. For me, however, as I reflect on doing this, it will perhaps not be difficult to achieve what we strive for. Indeed, anyone can encounter these detractors of truth, since truth herself defends herself by her own power against human wit, craftiness, and **captious ingenuity**; and she possesses many open followers and enemies of deceit, whose authority and reasons will carry more weight with truth-telling men than with the malicious, those eager for conflict, and the contentious.

Furthermore, it seems to me that inquiry and the investigation of truth are the proper work of a wise man; indeed, I have always thought nothing so unworthy of the gravity of a wise man as either to hold a false opinion, or to defend without any hesitation that which has not been sufficiently explored, perceived, and understood. This is precisely what happens to those **slanderers** who spare no one and disparage everyone, a condition of our times which I am accustomed to deplore. In these days, we see so many famous talents standing out in every kind of science that men are quite stunned with admiration. Yet, I know not by what spirit so many are led that they strive to change and overturn everything against almost all the ancient wise men. 

These people not only petulantly attack grammarians, rhetoricians, and the authors of the other arts, but they also—rashly, insultingly, and insolently—insult the practitioners of **sacred and divine letters** <term>sacred and divine letters: theology and scripture</term>, of philosophy, and even of medicine (which pertains to our own faculty). They do this not without the greatest danger to the human race, and even with hatred, accusing those men, among other things, because they did not use a great abundance of words, or richness, elegance, and eloquence in their writings.

But those who agree with the opinion of these "ornate speakers" ought to consider among themselves that, when dealing with great and deep matters, a greater eloquence is not to be desired, since the greatest and most sublime things, which are produced by an elegant intellect, are sufficiently adorned and cultivated in themselves. Indeed, all wise men affirm that the elegance and beauty of the mind consist in excellent discourse and firm reasoning. If you add the <note>original: "fucum," meaning cosmetic dye or pretense</note> **rhetorical paint** of words to these, you will perhaps take away much of their majesty—just as usually happens to beautiful women: when they strive to paint their faces with colors, they do not increase their beauty at all, but rather defile it. For that reason, I am the one who, conquered by care...

# PART TWO.

I feel, along with our <term>Averroes</term><note>original: "Auerroe"; Averroes (1126–1198) was an influential Al-Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle. In the Renaissance, he was a standard authority in university curricula.</note>, that those people are barbarians who lack true elegance of the intellect and a genuine knowledge of things. I only wish that those who want to be considered wise in our own time possessed elegance and subtlety of mind and intellect alongside their decorative words; I wish they would study the truth of a matter rather than the ornament of words and the artificial "dye" of speech. For those who excel only in oratory and are not endowed with any deeper meaning seem to me, like the song of the sirens, merely to lure frivolous men and to accomplish nothing else. 

But the cause of this ignorance and error has been certain <term>grammarians</term><note>Massa is critiquing the Renaissance Humanists, who often dismissed medieval scientific texts because they were written in "clunky" Latin rather than the polished style of Cicero.</note> who have emerged in our time, attempting to change everything, and likewise others who claimed to be not grammarians, but <term>philosophers</term>; would that they truly had been, for then we would have no reason to grieve so greatly. For these people, teaching philosophy with artificial words—rather than being instructed by those truly wise men who handed down the principles of the arts and sciences (such as <term>Aristotle</term><note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose logic and natural philosophy were the bedrock of medical education.</note> and many other illustrious authors and commentators)—persuaded men to learn things adorned with the artificial coloring of words, metaphors, and the fictions of poems. They follow those who, having been given the opportunity to write on various subjects, narrate, dispute, warn, and persuade, such as the orators and rhetoricians who claim to speak on every proposed subject, and the Poets, from whose songs they want us to be able and obligated to learn every single science. 

I cannot but detest their counsel and rashness, seeing as they plant a most terrible evil and plague within students unless it is countered in some way. But who, I ask, is so sluggish and dull-witted as to believe they can learn better from outsiders who do not teach the principles of the sciences than from those who have professedly applied themselves to passing down a specific science? This is true even though they taught the method of knowing and the sciences through mental dexterity rather than through verbal elegance or beautiful phrasing. And although they are considered the most learned by everyone and are clearer than the midday sun, it would not be a burden to list some of them, so that you may see the depth of the error in which those who think otherwise are entangled. 

We shall begin with the wise men of divine matters, who wrote the divine laws with intellectual eloquence and elegance, laid the foundations of our religion, and illuminated the secrets of nature. Good gods! Who among theologians has written on divine matters and the tenets of our religion more clearly than <term>Thomas Aquinas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic theologian whose work synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>? And [he defended it] from all slanders and—

...defended [the truth] against sophistical quibbles and published a clearer exposition of the books of Aristotle? O, what admirable elegance of mind! O, seeker of all sciences without the <term>dye of words</term><note>original: "uerborum fuco"; Massa uses the metaphor of "fucus" (a red dye or makeup) to describe rhetorical flourishes that hide a lack of actual knowledge.</note>, and the fiercest enemy and warrior against heresies! He not only equaled the teaching of his teacher, <term>Albert the Great</term><note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a polymath and teacher of Thomas Aquinas. Massa is likely referring to Thomas Aquinas here as the "he" who surpassed Albert.</note>, but truly surpassed it by far, giving others (especially the <term>Most Subtle</term><note>original: "fubtiliffimo"; a reference to John Duns Scotus, known as the "Doctor Subtilis."</note> John Duns Scotus) material for emulation, so that this competitor, seized by the opportunity of such great elegance of genius, strove to surpass him if it were possible. 

Yet, he claimed the name of the "Most Subtle Doctor" for himself not through the harmony of words, but through the marvelous and unheard-of brilliance of his genius. By the sublimity of his intellect, he surpassed and conquered the subtleties of all the ancients. Finally, he won every dispute and cause through the truth and constancy of the matter—not (as I said) deceiving men with a song in the manner of the Sirens, blinding them so they cannot recognize the truth, but rather showing the whole matter clearly and lucidly with the most exquisite reasons.

And lest I weary you with a long speech by listing all the cultivators of divine literature who wrote of great matters with no affectation of words, I leave the many others who were famous for their genius to be recalled by your own memory. However, I will list a few of those truly illustrious men who were outstanding in their intellect and discourse in supernatural, natural, and rational philosophy, as well as in medicine and other sciences. 

This is despite the fact that some people call them <term>barbarians</term><note>Renaissance Humanists often used "barbarous" to describe medieval Scholastic writers because their Latin did not follow the strict classical standards of Cicero.</note> and despise them as if they were worthless, barking against them. Among the number of those most elegant geniuses, we have the most learned commentator, <term>Averroes</term><note>The 12th-century Cordoban philosopher Ibn Rushd, whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to European universities.</note>. He was certainly a man of great genius and incomparable learning, such that he is judged by learned men to be second to none. 

Would that we also, having cast aside the "dyes" of words, knew such worthy and such many things, and possessed that elegance of intellect found in this illustrious man; for then, those who could truly be called learned would not be so rare. May the gods grant that those who in our age profess philosophy and the rest of the liberal arts were endowed with that elegance of genius in assigning the causes of things and in asserting all true demonstrations, so that they might one day be compared, at least in some part, with the most learned Averroes. By God, he not only equaled all the wise men of our age, but also far surpassed the ancients, whoever they were. He showed himself to be a wonderful [student] of Divine, rational, and natural...

### PART TWO

...[subtle] philosophy, he shows himself in all his writings to be an incomparable commentator and a seeker into the causes of all things. He also clarified moral philosophy—which the Greeks call <term>Ethics</term><note>original: "Ethicam"; the study of right and wrong conduct.</note>—with an elegant intellect. But why do I labor? Is not the fame of <term>Averroes</term><note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Cordoban polymath known in the West as "The Commentator" for his work on Aristotle.</note> known above the stars? He is renowned not only in the subjects already listed, but in all the other highest sciences, and even in medical speculations. 

I could also enumerate other illustrious Arab philosophers and doctors, whom [the Humanists] scorn as barbarians, such as the marvelous and most learned <term>Algazel</term><note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian and jurist.</note>, a man indeed of divine genius and most subtle reasoning, and <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), perhaps the most influential physician-philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, whose teaching I cannot praise enough. This is especially true of that supernatural branch which the Greeks call <term>Metaphysics</term><note>original: "Metaphysicam"; the study of the fundamental nature of reality.</note>, and the rational branch they call <term>Logic</term><note>original: "logicam"; the study of reasoning.</note>, as well as his discourse on all parts of natural philosophy. Likewise, there is his work of medicine <note>The "Canon of Medicine" (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb), which served as the standard medical textbook in European universities until the 17th century.</note>, in which he taught both speculative and practical science so learnedly and fully that if anything could be added to it, it would indeed be beyond comprehension. 

Indeed, how much antiquity valued the physician <term>Rhazes</term><note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–925).</note>, <term>Avenzoar</term><note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162).</note>, <term>Haly Abbas</term><note>‘Ali ibn al-‘Abbas al-Majusi (d. 982).</note>, <term>Isaac</term><note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon (c. 832–932).</note>, <term>Serapion</term><note>Likely Yahya ibn Sarafyun (9th century).</note>, <term>John Mesue</term><note>Masawayh al-Marindi (10th/11th century).</note>, and many other most learned Arabs endowed with genius, is testified by very many ancient writers and volumes filled with the praises of these men. 

I could also enumerate many Latins <note>Medieval European scholars who wrote in Latin.</note> who were famous not for the ornament of their language, but for their genius and reasoning. Such are <term>Gentile da Foligno</term><note>d. 1348; a famous commentator on Avicenna.</note>, the most subtle expositor of Avicenna, as well as Jacques Despars, Matteo Ferrari da Gradi, Taddeo Alderotti of Florence, Tommaso del Garbo, Giacomo da Foligno, and the monk Torrigiano de' Torrigiani—who is surnamed "more than a commentator"—<term>Pietro d’Abano</term><note>c. 1257–1316; an Italian philosopher and professor of medicine known as "The Reconciler" (Conciliator).</note> the Reconciler, Niccolò Falcucci of Florence, Michele Savonarola, Guglielmo da Saliceto, Bernard de Gordon, and almost innumerable others, who all illuminated ancient medicine with their writings. 

But perhaps you will ask: why say so much about this excellence of genius and sublimity? It is so that we might warn those candidates for the <term>good arts</term><note>original: "bonarū artiū"; referring to the liberal arts and medicine.</note>, if there are any who, neglecting the actual causes of things, are accustomed to fall in love with this exquisite way of speaking, so that they may finally begin to come to their senses and prepare a health-giving medicine against this plague. For it is (as I believe) the greatest disease of minds to prefer empty words to truth and the solidity of things. This medicine will be easily prepared if, first and before all else, they resolve to investigate the truth through discourse and reason, [placing] those things which pertain to speaking well and correctly not entirely...

# THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICOLÒ MASSA

...omitting [them]. Therefore, I greatly exhort and beseech you and others—whoever they may be, whether professors or candidates of any science and discipline—who understand these complaints of ours and desire to know the truth: read all writers, whether Latin, Greek, Egyptian, Chaldean, Arab, Hebrew, and even Italian, or any others, provided they were learned and of an elegant intellect. Do not despise them, even if they are read in translations from various languages into one's own specific tongue or any other—even if that language itself is unrefined or lacks an abundance of ornate words—provided that while they disregard the words and decoration, they do not miss the elegance of the meanings. It is in these meanings that all wise men place the majesty and true elegance of writers.

Indeed, when the renowned <term>Cleanthes</term><note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 330–230 BCE) who succeeded Zeno as the head of the Stoic school in Athens.</note> (that philosopher who succeeded to the school of <term>Zeno of Citium</term><note>The founder of Stoicism.</note>) was asked what the reason was that, although few practiced philosophy among the ancients, more emerged as illustrious and famous than now, he replied: **"Because then the thing itself was practiced, but now only words."** 

O, what a wonderful sentiment from a truly philosophical man, consistent with nature and reason! By this we are warned that it is necessary to learn the truth of the matter—which I also advise you to do, as you are already doing—and to disregard mere words. For we are not wise because we speak ornately, but because we discourse by reasoning through causes, while the mind recognizes and distinguishes the true from the false, and the probable from the necessary. <term>Plato</term> also held this opinion; he did not wish men to be considered wise simply because they studied the decoration of words, but he thought those were wise who excelled in intellect and were strong in the best arts and singular learning. 

Since this is so, I advise you again; but why do I advise you? For I know your intellect. Let me rather advise those who labor under that delirium <note>Massa is likely referring to the "Humanist" obsession with pure Ciceronian Latin, which he views as a distraction from scientific truth.</note> to strive to prepare a healthy medicine: namely, that they first turn their minds to those things which pertain to reasoning or the "rational art," and prepare the instruments for doing this. This is called <term>Logic</term><note>original: "logica"; the formal study of reasoning.</note>, and it is the rational science that holds the path to the principles of all sciences. Without it, the other sciences cannot be acquired at all, whether they be divine or natural. If they were to associate this rational science with the method of speaking correctly and even with the art of poetry (which few in our time possess), these would be a great ornament to a wise mind; but if poetry and the art of speaking are absent, I do not greatly [crave them]...

<meta>catchword: [I] crave (exopto)</meta>

<summary>Nicolò Massa argues that scientific truth and logical reasoning are more important than eloquent language, citing Cleanthes and Plato to defend the study of "barbarian" authors. He defines Logic as the essential "rational science" and foundational tool for all other disciplines, including medicine.</summary>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>PART TWO</header>

# SECOND PART

...in a wise man. Truly, those who strive only to speak ornately, thinking nothing of the truth and omitting the divine science of reasoning and demonstration—or thinking they can learn it better from orators and poets than from its proper professors—are involved in the highest and greatest error (to put it in a single sentence). This is especially true when they despise and accuse <term>Aristotle</term> and his commentator <term>Averroes</term><note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to medieval medicine and philosophy, though often criticized by later Renaissance humanists for their "unpolished" Latin translations.</note>, as well as other most eminent expositors. They blame them for their brevity in writing or for their explanations of the obscure and hidden operations of nature, claiming that this doctrine is often found corrupted by the wordy entanglements and <term>sophisms</term><note>Fallacious arguments, usually used intentionally to deceive or show off rhetorical skill.</note> of its commentators. 

Indeed, I am persuaded that this accusation by famous men provides and continually supplies nourishment for a stronger and worse evil. For it dulls the minds of students and obstructs the lights of knowledge, so that afterward they are not ashamed to attack the doctrines and sciences that have been cultivated and venerated by everyone through so many centuries. This happens because they lack true knowledge and have formed a habit of speaking ill of everything and sparing no one. 

For knowledge (according to the opinion of all wise men) is nothing other than the use or function of those images which are in the mind, just as if in a mirror. Those who are ignorant of how this knowledge works cannot perceive the secrets of the wise; and thus, a long-standing habit is turned into almost a "second nature" <note>original: "alteram quasi naturam"</note>. 

I would consider enough to have been said on this matter, if I could first ask those who think poorly of ancient writers to set aside their zeal for accusing the ancient and modern authors of the liberal arts. I would also, again and again, most strongly and vehemently urge and exhort both students and all professors of the finest literature to strive to defend these wise and elegant minds against false reasonings and slanders. They should be willing to read all writers and teachers of good disciplines who possess an elegant intellect—not so that they may gain from them a wealth of words, a persuasive style, phrasing, or refined speech, but so that they may be able to learn and extract the truth and those things which lead to a correct knowledge of the subjects they desire to know. 

They should turn these things to their own use, adding to them where they are deficient and clarifying them where they have written obscurely. They should always extol with praise those who have uncovered the most subtle <term>secrets of nature</term><note>A common Renaissance term for the underlying laws of physics, biology, and the cosmos that are not immediately apparent to the senses.</note>, even if these were not written in ornate and refined speech. I would also wish them to be advised that I do not...

<summary>Massa defends Scholastic and Arabic authorities like Aristotle and Averroes against humanist critics, arguing that students should prioritize the "truth of things" over rhetorical polish. He defines knowledge as the mind's internal processing of reality and urges scholars to improve upon old texts rather than dismissing them for their style.</summary>
