<meta>This page continues Nicolò Massa’s argument against the intellectual rigidity of his contemporaries. He transitions from defending Aristotle and Averroes to a broader plea for intellectual independence, urging students to value reason over blind adherence to ancient authority.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>NICOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS</header>

...[that] I must instruct with no less zeal that those people should be avoided who persuade others that no one is to be believed except (for example) **Aristotle**, **Plato**, **Theophrastus**, **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and certain similar ancient and famous writers, unless their sayings are confirmed by the authority of said authors. This is despite the fact that it is permissible to grant faith to everyone speaking with reason, even without the authority of the ancients, and to read their own writings. It should also be permissible, in this abundance and plenty of authors, to choose certain proven individuals writing with reason and to adapt them for one’s own instruction and learning. 

Furthermore, one must beware of factions and deceptive sects, fleeing them as if from a poisonous contagion. And, if I were able to instruct them, I would warn them that in imitating ancient writers, they should not wish to imitate them in every word and saying, nor (as the saying goes) <term>to swear by the words of a master</term><note>original: "in uerba magistri iurare"—an expression originally from the Roman poet Horace, describing someone who follows a teacher’s doctrine blindly rather than thinking for themselves.</note>, but rather to place their foundations in the best reasons and discourse. Thus, let them draw only as much from those ancients as the mind is able to understand through its own rational discourse. Moreover, it is foolish and absurd to wish to draw from someone that which they either did not possess or which we ourselves cannot attain. 

If you take these things to heart, everything will be clear to you, as they are drawn from the healthy fountains of the good arts. If you wish to impart these things to others, you will have performed a truly divine work, since to benefit everyone is the gift of <term>God, the Best and Greatest</term><note>original: "dei optimi maximi"—a standard Renaissance honorific for God (often abbreviated as D.O.M.), originally used by the Romans for Jupiter.</note>. I could have told them—and now committed to writing—many other reasons and examples besides these to further confirm my words; but since I judged the matter to be self-evident and in the clearest light, I wished for what has been said to be sufficient. The learned will easily recognize, by reading, how much these things favor the truth. 

Farewell. 1556.

<summary>Nicolò Massa concludes his argument by advocating for intellectual freedom, urging scholars to prioritize logical reasoning over the blind worship of ancient authorities like Galen or Aristotle. He emphasizes that while the ancients are valuable, one should only accept what the mind can rationally confirm.</summary>

# THE UNIVERSAL METHOD OF HEALING
### for all specific diseases, according to the purpose of all il-
### lustrious physicians: namely Hippocrates, Galen,
### Avicenna, and others; in which the quantities and
### qualities of medicines, and their specific
### powers are taught. A short work
### dedicated to Laurentius Massa,
### his nephew.

<margin>The Intention.</margin>
**J**UST AS we must derive <term>curative intentions</term><note>The "intention" or *intentio* in Renaissance medicine refers to the physician's strategic plan or goal for treatment based on the patient's condition.</note> in diseases from ten pre-noted factors, my dear Laurentius—regarding things <term>natural</term>, <term>non-natural</term>, and <term>contrary to nature</term><note>This is a standard Galenic classification. "Natural" things are internal (like humors); "non-naturals" are external factors like diet, sleep, and air; and "contrary to nature" refers to the diseases themselves.</note>—I believe this was sufficiently explained in that Letter which I wrote to Apollonius Massa, my nephew and Doctor of Medicine, on the first of December, 1541. Now, however, so that I may satisfy you as much as I can, I shall pursue those matters which pertain to the specific care of men in various conditions <gloss>contrary to nature</gloss>; indeed, I shall write to you regarding specific medicines and regimens. I am truly attempting a great and arduous task, for it is extremely difficult for anyone to correctly find specific medicines for specific diseases and circumstances, and even for the unique conditions of individual men according to a person’s <term>temperament</term><note>The "complexio" or temperament was the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) unique to every individual.</note>, age, habits, and the rest, as I clearly wrote in those letters to Apollonius. 

But since I see from your letters that you desire these things with your whole heart—so that you might possess the ultimate goal and perfection of good literature, especially of medicine—I shall begin to speak of them, even though I know that what you ask me to write is both difficult and laborious. But I shall do this gladly, not only to rouse you to read these our instructions for curing the specific diseases of men, but also to urge your studies toward the reading of illustrious physicians. For indeed, our instructions (as you will see) do not differ from the opinions of Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and other most famous physicians—a matter on which I shall appoint you the judge. These instructions are taken from those who wrote the <term>method of healing</term><note>original: "curatiuum methodum"—the systematic approach to therapy developed by Galen.</note> using only the highest reason and art. Nevertheless, I say again, choosing specific medicines for each illness and for a specific person imposes no small difficulty on the task; since this method of correctly choosing and adminis...

<margin>
Source of the curative method.
</margin>
...administering medicines has not been distinctly written about in every part by all the ancients. Because of this, it has always been difficult to apply a specific method for curing diseases; Galen noted this difficulty in the eleventh commentary on the second book of *The Regimen in Acute Diseases*. Whatever the case may be, with this foundation established, I shall begin to explain the matter to you: namely, it is worthwhile to derive the <term>curative method</term><note>The systematic approach or logic used by a physician to determine the correct treatment for a specific patient.</note> primarily from the understanding of the disease itself.

<margin>
There are three kinds of diseases.
</margin>
But since all wise physicians affirm that there are three types of disease—namely **bad temperament**, **bad composition**, and **dissolved unity** <note>In Renaissance medicine, these three categories covered all ailments: "bad temperament" (imbalance of heat/cold/moisture), "bad composition" (structural or organ defects), and "dissolved unity" (physical breaks like wounds or fractures).</note>—I will begin by speaking about the cure for diseases of temperament. However, since a bad temperament is sometimes found alone, and sometimes found with "matter" <note>In this context, "matter" refers to the physical humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) being present in an unhealthy or excessive state.</note>, physicians do not proceed in the same way in both cases, but in different ways.

<margin>
When only altering remedies should be used.
</margin>
For if the disease consists of a temperament without matter, it will be sufficient if, in addition to the <term>regimen of necessary things</term><note>The management of lifestyle factors such as diet, sleep, and exercise.</note>, you administer **alteratives** <note>Medicines that "alter" the body's qualities (e.g., cooling a hot fever) without necessarily purging the humors.</note> contrary to the disease. For example, for a purely hot distemper, by providing cold things both internally and externally, according to the nature and location of the limbs; similarly by administering hot things for a cold distemper, and in the same way helping moist conditions with dry remedies and dry conditions with moist ones.

<margin>
A pure humor is rarely found.
</margin>
But if the disease is a bad temperament with matter—which you will see very often, as it can hardly happen that a disease exists without some "malice" of the humors, or something contrary to nature in both quantity and alteration—indeed, a pure and unmixed humor is only rarely found in us without being mixed with something else. This is testified by **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose works formed the backbone of medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> in the forty-ninth commentary of the fourth part of the *Aphorisms*, and by **Avicenna** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university textbook in Massa's time.</note> in the first book, first chapter on humors near the end, through a long examination; and also in the third part of the fourth book, in the chapter on abscesses.

<margin>
The source of knowledge regarding the quantity and quality of a disease.
</margin>
Therefore, if a disease is a temperament with matter, whether universal (like a fever) or particular (like inflammations of specific limbs), it will first be worthwhile to know the quantity and qualities of the humors with which the disease is associated. Indeed, this knowledge can be more easily obtained through the **accidents** <note>In medical terminology of this period, "accidents" refer to the symptoms or observable clinical signs of a disease.</note>, and also through those things that follow afterward, as Galen taught in the tenth book of *Medicines According to the Places*; and Avicenna in the second part of the third book, the third doctrine.

<margin>
The method of knowledge *a priori*.
</margin>
You will obtain this method of knowledge, which the wise call *a priori* <note>original: "à priori." In this medical context, it refers to reasoning from the cause (the patient's lifestyle/regimen) to the effect (the disease).</note>, from evident or primary causes. For example, if you know the past regimen of the **six necessary things** <note>Also known as the "six non-naturals": air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, evacuation and repletion, and passions of the mind.</note>. In this knowledge, one must study very hard so that the material cause may be correctly investi—

->B ii<-

<margin>...he teaches how to investigate through examples.</margin>
...you may be able to manage. For if a sick person has used foods that can generate <term>yellow bile</term><note>Latin: *cholera*. In the humoral system, this is the hot and dry humor. It is not the modern bacterial disease.</note> during a specific time of life, or in a hot region, or with other things that unnaturally increase heat, you would undoubtedly say the disease arose from bilious matter as its material cause. But if in winter they have eaten lettuce or other foods that generate cold and moist nourishment, and have led a sedentary life, you would say that <term>phlegm</term><note>Latin: *pituita*. The cold and moist humor.</note> is the material cause rather than a simple imbalance of temperament. But if their regimen has been mixed, so that it could produce both bile and <term>black bile</term><note>Latin: *melancholia*. The cold and dry humor.</note>, you would say the disease involves a diversity of matter. Thus, proceeding from causes to effects, you will recognize the nature of the disease in its temperament along with its matter and their qualities.

<margin>He teaches the method of knowing from the effect through examples.</margin>
We also recognize it <term>a posteriori</term><note>Reasoning that works backward from effects to discover their causes.</note>, namely by knowing the cause through the effect: and this occurs when we investigate the cause through the symptoms. For example, as Galen said near the end of his book *On Fullness*, we recognize a <term>repletion of blood</term><note>Latin: *repletio sanguinis* or plethora; an excess of blood in the system.</note> from the fullness and tension of the veins, and also from the symptoms that follow these occurrences. In the fourth book of *On the Preservation of Health*, he also teaches how to recognize this same thing.

<margin>Signs showing a repletion of blood.</margin>
Avicenna also, in the second part of the third book in the place cited a little above, said that an excess of blood is shown by a heaviness of the entire body, heat, a full and strong pulse, restlessness and yawning, heaviness of the head with redness of the face and eyes, a sweet taste in the mouth, redness of the tongue and palate, and red urine that is not thin, as well as the patient's own natural temperament and age.

<margin>Signs of phlegm.</margin>
The abundance of phlegm, however, is signified by a laziness of the entire body, heaviness, and looseness together with coldness, and a body color tending toward whiteness; likewise an abundance of spit which is nevertheless tasteless; and a lack of thirst, unless perhaps other humors happen to be abundant along with the phlegmatic matter itself:

<margin>Signs of phlegm mixed with another humor.</margin>
for example, blood—in which case the taste of the spit will be sweet; but if it is associated with yellow bile, the taste will be bitter; and if it is mixed with black bile, the taste will be sour. Furthermore, among the signs that show phlegm is multiplying are a weakness of the stomach, and the color and dominance of the excrement and the mixture of humors; such as whiteness of the urine and a watery substance, stools (or waste from the lower belly) that are colorless and mixed with much phlegmatic matter, a swollen face, heaviness of the head, and heavy dreams appearing in which rain, snow, rivers, cold, and a numbness of the limbs seem to be seen.

<margin>Signs indicating a superabundance of bile.</margin>
The superabundance of <term>yellow bile</term><note>Latin: *cholera*.</note>, however, is shown by the physical constitution and a yellow color of the body,

...and bitterness of the mouth, as well as thirst, and also a rapid and frequent pulse; furthermore, you will easily recognize the dominance of bile from the quality of the excrements of the lower belly: for in such patients, the urine is citrus-colored and fiery, and the feces are saffron-hued, or citrus-yellow, and stinging. Such people often vomit yellow and even red bile: their dreams are also restless <note>Latin: *læuia*. In this medical context, it suggests light, easily interrupted, or vivid dreams.</note>, in which they seem to see fires, outbursts of anger, quarrels, and similar things. 

<margin>Signs of melancholy.</margin>The dominance of black bile or melancholy is shown by a slender build and a dark or leaden color of the body, as well as weakness in all bodily functions, sad thoughts, and anxieties: furthermore, these people are wakeful, and while sleeping they see terrible dreams. If black bile should abound in the stomach, it is accustomed to excite a false hunger <note>Latin: *famem mendosam*. A craving for food that does not stem from a true nutritional need, often associated with melancholic imbalances.</note>: in these people, the spleen often swells, the urine is leaden or dark, and the feces appear blackish and like lead.

Having noted these things for the recognition of diseases—whether they are with matter <note>A "material" disease involves an excess of a physical humor, like phlegm or bile.</note> or without matter—and also for the diagnosis of the predominant humors, one must also include those ten medical considerations for curing specific diseases which I have written elsewhere to Apollonius: these are the knowledge of the disease itself, its causes, its symptoms <note>Latin: *accidentia*. These are the clinical manifestations or "accidents" of the illness.</note>, its temperament, the patient's vital strength, age, sex, habits, the air, and the season of the year. To all these, one must add the knowledge of all parts of the body, which is obtained through dissection <note>Niccolò Massa was a famous anatomist; here he emphasizes that a physician must know internal anatomy to treat patients effectively.</note>.

<margin>He teaches the treatment of a material disease.</margin>
Having established these points, you will first strive to remove the cause of the illness through a regimen of diet according to the needs of the disease and other symptoms, once you have recognized whether the cause is immaterial or involves matter. If it is a material disease, you will do this by evacuating the humors causing the illness. 

But since at present evacuation (as physicians say) is of two types—namely, "minorative" <note>A gentle reduction or thinning of humors.</note> and "elective" or "eradicative" <note>A stronger purging meant to completely remove a specific humor.</note>—the minorative type removes common superfluities by softening the belly to lead waste out of the stomach and intestines. 

<margin>Softening can always be performed.</margin>This can be done without hesitation and without any preceding "alteration" (which physicians call digestion or concoction) at any time. For instance, it can be done with a softening clyster <note>An enema.</note>, or through a softening medicine taken by mouth, such as **cassia fistula** <term>Cassia fistularis: The "purging cassia," a legume whose pulp was used as a mild, safe laxative.</term>: or another similar medicine depending on the variety of humors existing in the stomach and other nearby common passages. Indeed, such superfluities are always ready for removal, since they are located in the intestines and nearby passages: this is what Hippocrates advised in the second book of his *Aphorisms*, Aphorism 29, and Galen at the end of his commentary...

# PART TWO

...[to be moved], since he said: "When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to move, move it." One must certainly move the superfluities—whether they are faulty in quantity or in quality—that are in the nearby passages of the ducts, specifically by soothing them.

<margin>When eradication should occur.</margin>
Elective or eradicative evacuation <note>The complete removal of a specific harmful humor.</note> is not performed unless the offending matter has been digested, or prepared and cooked <note>Latin: *concocta*. In humoral medicine, "concoction" refers to the body's natural heat ripening or preparing a humor so it can be easily expelled.</note>, according to that saying of Hippocrates in the first part of the *Aphorisms*, aphorism 22, which says: "Medicines should be applied to cooked matter and should move what is cooked, not what is raw, nor in the beginning of the disease, unless it is swelling." In the commentary on this aphorism, Galen clearly warns that matter fixed in some part of the body should not be moved; however, those things which are in the common passages of the ducts can always be evacuated. For this reason, I will first come to those medicines which, by soothing and diminishing the matter in material diseases, evacuate it. 

For diseases which arise from a bad temperament <note>Latin: *malitia temperaturae*. A state where the body's qualities—hot, cold, wet, or dry—are imbalanced without an excess of fluid matter.</note> are cured through altering opposites without evacuation. And so that you may have everything at hand, so that you can desire nothing more, I will write for you in order the medicines—both the minorative <note>Mildly reducing or softening the humors.</note> and the concoctive, as well as those that evacuate each humor. The reduction or evacuation of blood, however, since it does not require preparation and is always ready for extraction (by the testimony of Galen in the eleventh book of *On the Method of Healing*), should be done by opening a vein. Where there is a necessity to evacuate blood, you will evacuate it safely, provided that the strength, age, disease, and time of year, etc., allow it. 

And since, in evacuating either by lessening or eradicating, it is necessary to extract not just one kind of matter or humor, but different ones according to the opportunity; therefore, I will begin with those that evacuate <term>bile: also called yellow bile or cholera; associated with heat and dryness</term>, or humor tasting of the nature of bile, according to the diversity of the bile. Next, I will proceed to those which evacuate <term>phlegm: or pituita; the cold, moist humor</term> or phlegmatic matter according to its variety. Finally, I will note those medicines which evacuate <term>melancholy: or black bile; the cold, dry humor</term> or the melancholic humor according to its diversity. 

First, therefore, I will begin with the minorative, concoctive, and elective treatments that draw out bile: since the choleric humor, or thin bilious humor, is more troublesome and more frequently leads to putrefaction, according to Galen and experience. When bile is at fault, therefore, you will prepare such a medicine:

<margin>Remedies for the evacuation of bile.</margin>
Take of cassia flowers, 1 ounce or 1 ½ ounces <note>Latin: *unc. i. s.* stands for *uncia una et semis*, one and a half ounces.</note>, more or less according to the patient's disposition. Let a bolus <note>A large pill or soft mass for swallowing.</note> be made from it with the best sugar, or let it be made into a drink with a decoction of hyssop and mastic <note>A resin from the mastic tree used as a digestive aid.</note>, or with chicory water, and let it be taken an hour before lunch or before dinner, according to the requirements of the case.

...opportunity: however, there are some who wait two or three hours after taking **cassia** <note>The pulp of the "pudding-pipe tree" (*Cassia fistula*), used as a mild, sweet laxative.</note>; they do this because they fear that eating might trigger vomiting. But I want it to be known that the medicine is better activated by the heat of the stomach <note>Latin: *ventriculi*. In this period, the "ventricle" usually refers to the stomach cavity.</note> if more time is allowed to pass before eating. However, because cassia—owing to the stickiness of its substance—often tends to stir up wind and gas, sometimes causing even severe intestinal pains to arise, doctors usually add certain things to remove this windiness.

<margin>
He teaches how to remove the gas caused by Cassia.
</margin>

They typically add one drachm of powdered **licorice**, if the patient’s temperament is very hot; or one drachm of powdered **hyssop**, when there is no suspicion of excess heat; or one drachm of **mastic** <note>A resin from the lentisk tree used to settle the stomach.</note>. Indeed, all of these moderate and remove the flatulence of the cassia. Nevertheless, if the patient takes food immediately after taking the cassia, they will be less troubled by its windiness. The reason is that after eating, heat retreats to the interior parts—especially to the stomach—where it is concentrated. Having been made stronger in this way, the heat breaks up and even dissipates the windiness. Experience bears witness that cassia purges both types of bile <note>original: *choleram*. In humoral medicine, "cholera" refers to yellow bile, one of the four bodily fluids, not the modern infectious disease.</note>—namely, the pure and the mixed—by soothing them. **Avicenna** <note>A foundational Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard textbook in Europe.</note> says the following about cassia in the second book of his *Canon*:

> It softens the belly, drawing out burnt bile <note>original: *choleram adustam*. Yellow bile that has become "overcooked" or charred by excess heat, making it toxic.</note> and phlegm without harm and without "biting" <note>original: *mordicatione*. A technical term for the sharp, stinging, or cramping sensation caused by harsher laxatives.</note>, so that it is suitable even for pregnant women.

Similarly, **Mesue** <note>Referencing "Mesue the Younger," a pseudo-author of influential Arabic pharmaceutical texts.</note> said that cassia is among those medicines in which one can trust for help; it is without harm, lacking in sharpness, biting, or any damaging excess, so that it can be administered at any age—to children and even to pregnant women. He says:

> It cleanses the stomach and draws out bile and phlegm without harm.

<margin>
He teaches what to use as a substitute for soothing medicines.
</margin>

In cases where cassia cannot be obtained, it was Avicenna’s advice to take half a portion of **manna** <note>A sweet, dried sap from the flowering ash tree, used as a gentle purge.</note>, three times the weight of **raisin pulp**, and an eighth part of **turbith** <note>A root used as a purgative for phlegm.</note>, with a portion of licorice added as well. There are, furthermore, not a few other medicines that diminish and draw out bile by soothing it without distress. For example: Take two ounces of **tamarind pulp**; let it boil in six ounces of **borage** and **chicory** water until a third of it has evaporated. Administer this as I described for the cassia. One can also give **solutive rose syrup** (made from a multiple infusion of roses) in doses up to four ounces; or **solutive violet syrup** (made from a multiple infusion of violets) at four or five ounces. Or, manna may be given, which evacuates pure and lemon-colored bile. The quantity should be as follows: Take two ounces of choice manna, more or le...

# PART TWO

...or according to the patient's condition, and dissolve it with a decoction of **raisins** <note>original: *passularum*</note> or **chicory water** and the like. But among the rest, **cassia** is a medicine that draws out all humors by softening them, so much so that it can be safely given in any case of **choleric matter** <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors</note>. There are also certain composite minorative medicines, such as the **non-laxative electuary of prunes** <note>An "electuary" is a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup; *diaprunis* refers to plums/prunes</note> according to the recipe of **Nicolaus** <note>Nicolaus Myrepsos, a famous 13th-century medical author</note>. Patients can take from one and a half up to two ounces of this in the form of a **bolus** <note>A soft, rounded mass of medicine to be swallowed, like a large pill</note> with sugar, or dissolved in borage or endive water. Similarly, the **lenitive electuary** and the **incomplete electuary of sebesten** <note>A fruit used as a mild laxative and cough remedy</note> can be given. These electuaries can be taken as a bolus or dissolved with some decoction—for instance, of raisins or tamarinds—or with the distilled waters of borage, chicory, and similar plants.

<margin>The error of those who give strong medicines at the beginning.</margin>

Those who, at the beginning of an illness when no sign of **concoction** <note>The process where the body's natural heat "ripens" or prepares diseased humors for expulsion</note> appears, add strong medicines to these aforementioned mild ones err most gravely and are worthy of every rebuke. This includes things like the **Electuary of Rose Juice**, the **Laxative Electuary of Prunes**, or **Mesue’s Rose Electuary**, and other strong medicines in which a great deal of **scammony** or **turbith** <note>Harsh vegetable purgatives used for "digging out" stubborn humors</note> is mixed. Such medicines do not work by softening, but by purging and dissolving selectively. However, these might be added at the beginning if the matter were **swelling** <note>original: *turgeret*; referring to humors that are so excessive or agitated they threaten a vital organ</note>, such that there was a risk of it reaching and harming one of the "princely" <note>primary</note> organs. This follows the rule of **Hippocrates** in the first book of his *Aphorisms* (in the passage cited above, comment 22): "Things that are concocted should be treated with medicine," etc., provided the matter is not swelling. Usually, it does not swell; however, that which is affected by a poisonous bad quality does swell, as happens in those fevers which **Galen** called "of a bad character" in the first book of his work *On the Differences of Fevers*.

And since there are many people who do not want to or cannot swallow the aforementioned medicines in the form of a bolus, or drink them dissolved—as they find them loathsome—in this case, when necessity compels and there is a great fullness of humors, **pills made of aloe** <margin>About pills.</margin> washed with endive juice may be administered. These should be taken along with some syrup consumed immediately after swallowing them. For the sake of example, here is a prescription:

Take one and a half drachms of **washed aloe pills**. Let five pills be made and **gilded** <note>Coated in gold leaf to hide the bitter taste and appeal to wealthy patients</note>. Immediately after swallowing them, the patient should drink this syrup: Take one ounce of **Endive syrup**, half an ounce of **Rose syrup**, and one and a half ounces each of **Chicory** and **Borage waters**. Mix them. Let him take lunch two or three hours later. For these pills are a light medicine, drawing out **stercoraceous matter** <note>Fecal waste</note> from the intestines and mixed bile found near the openings of the veins.

<summary>Massa warns against using harsh purgatives (like scammony) before the body has "ripened" the diseased humors, advocating instead for gentle electuaries and aloe-based pills. He provides a specific prescription for gilded pills and syrup for patients who cannot tolerate thicker medicinal pastes.</summary>

...of the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: *mesaraicarum*; these are the veins draining the intestines</note>: the common **"pills of three"** <note>A standard medicinal compound usually containing three main ingredients, such as aloes, scammony, and colocynth, though here used in a mild dose</note> can also be administered as a minorative, as can **simple hiera** <note>A bitter laxative powder, usually *hiera picra*</note> in the same quantity, and with the prescribed syrup immediately after swallowing them.

<margin>
Various types of bile.
</margin>
But since **cholera** <note>Yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors</note> is sometimes "exquisite" <note>Pure or unmixed</note>, and sometimes of greater or lesser "fame" <note>Likely referring to how clearly the humor manifests its specific symptoms</note>, and since it has been said in the examples of minorative medicines that those mentioned can evacuate exquisite choleric matter when mixed with other humors: therefore, I would have you advised that these same medicines, in the examples of the treatments written above, can also draw out the "lesser known" cholera found in common practice. For this reason, if you recognize that this lesser cholera is abundant, do not depart from the administration of **cassia**, with which you will mix some **lenitive electuary** or **diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" mild laxative paste</note>, more or less according to the greater quantity or malice of the humor and the patient's tolerance. Furthermore, **pituitous** or **phlegmatic** <note>Phlegm-based</note> matter also requires its own minoration if it should be abundant. Therefore, where it is necessary, you shall evacuate it thus:

**Recipe:**
One and a half ounces or 15 drachms of **lenitive electuary**.
Let a **bolus** <note>A large, soft pill</note> be made with sugar, or a potion with a decoction of **fennel** or **betony**, or with the distilled waters of fennel, betony, or **hyssop**.

You can also lessen phlegmatic matter where it predominates with the **incomplete electuary of sebesten** <note>A mild fruit-based remedy</note>; for example:

**Recipe:**
12 or 15 drachms of the **electuary of sebesten**.
Let a bolus be made with sugar, or a potion with the above-written decoction or distilled waters; it will be a light medicine that draws out humors by soothing them without distress.

Instructions on lenitives for lesser-known cholera.
</margin>

Note on laxative syrup of roses.

You will note, however, that **laxative syrup of roses** <note>original: *syrupus rosatus solutivus*</note> has the power to draw out matter where phlegm predominates in the stomach and intestines. A decoction of **senna** with **raisins** in distilled fennel or hyssop water also draws out predominant phlegmatic matter by soothing it. For example:

**Recipe:**
6 drachms of **senna leaves**.
2 ounces of **raisins**.
3 ounces each of **hyssop** and **fennel water**.
Let them boil until a third part is consumed, and let it be given with two ounces of **simple oxymel** <note>A medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>.

But if the patient recoils from taking medicines in the form of a bolus or a potion, **violet troches** <note>Medicinal lozenges</note> without **scammony** <note>A harsh, resinous plant-based purgative</note> may be given as a minorative, up to two or three drachms; you can dissolve these troches with fennel water and administer them. Also excellent are the **alephangine pills** <note>Aromatic pills, often containing aloes and spices</note>, **mastic pills**, and **pills of asaieret** <note>Pills based on the "Hiera Ayayeret" formula</note>, because they draw thick matter from the stomach and intestines without distress or agitation. Let them be given at the weight of one drachm or five scruples; for example:

**Recipe:**
**Alephangine pills**...

<header>P A R T   T W O</header>
<sig>C</sig>

# P A R T   T W O

...of **phangi** <note>original: *phanginarum*; referring to the "Pills of Phangi," a common stomachic and purgative compound</note> five scruples; let five pills be made and gilded <note>coated in gold leaf to mask the bitter taste and prevent premature dissolution</note>. All these medicines should be taken in the morning, and food should be delayed for at least four hours afterward. Let these things be said concerning **cholera** <note>yellow bile</note>.

Now it must be noted that **pituita** <note>phlegm</note>, or the phlegmatic humor, has many species within it—namely, natural and unnatural.
<margin>Differences between natural and unnatural phlegm.</margin>
Natural phlegm is that which is sometimes fit to be converted into blood, since it is blood that is insufficiently "cooked" <note>original: *decoctus*; the body's digestive processes were viewed as a form of metabolic cooking</note>; its flavor is sweet, and it is not excessively cold. Unnatural phlegm, however, is divided into many categories: raw, watery, thin, mucous-like, glassy, or gypsum-like <note>referring to its consistency and appearance</note>. To use the words of **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina, whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university text</note>, unnatural phlegm has a variety of essences according to the senses; thus phlegm may be tasteless, sweet, acidic, vinegary, or harsh <note>original: *pontica*; a sharp, puckering taste</note>. There is also an acrid or stinging phlegm, which is salty either through the mixing of a bilious humor or through some further boiling caused by a heat that "scorches" it beyond its natural state. But lest I delay you with these details, let enough be said so that you can, when the occasion arises, administer "minorative" medicines according to the variety of the abundant phlegm.

<margin>Lenitives for phlegm.</margin>
For example, you will diminish thin phlegm with a **lenitive electuary** <note>a mild, syrupy medicinal paste</note>; but for thick phlegm, use the same electuary, adding **violet troches** <note>medicinal lozenges</note> without **scammony** <note>a harsh purgative resin often excluded from "gentle" treatments</note>. This is because its base is **turpeth** <note>original: *turbit*; the root of the Indian jalap, known for purging thick humors</note>, which by its own property purges thick phlegmatic matter without distress. You will also note that **cassia fistula** <note>the "purging cassia," a mild legume-based laxative</note> successfully draws out thick matter existing in the stomach and intestines; to this, you can add one dram of the species of **hiera** <note>likely *hiera picra*, a classic bitter purgative</note> or violet troches without scammony in the amount of one dram, so that its evacuation is better suited to the specific humor.

Finally, we must consider the minoratives for **melancholic humors**. This **melancholia**, or melancholic humor, is itself manifold:
<margin>
The melancholic humor is manifold.
</margin>
namely, natural and unnatural. Natural melancholy is the "dregs" of the blood. Unnatural melancholy, however, is of another kind: it is produced either by the "burning" <note>original: *adustionem*; the "scorching" of humors through excessive bodily heat, which turned them dark, bitter, and toxic</note> of natural red bile, or by the burning of unnatural thin yellow bile. A certain type of melancholy is also formed by the burning of thick yellow bile; melancholy also arises from the burning of phlegm, if we believe Avicenna, and similarly from the burning of blood. Scorched melancholy also arises from the burning of natural melancholy itself. All these melancholic humors are harmful both in their quality and their quantity; therefore, when it is necessary to draw out the melancholic humor by minoration, it will be worthwhile to know its nature, as described...

# NIC. MASSAE EPIST. MED.

...to know what we intend to evacuate, so that if you wish to lessen an abundance of natural **melancholic humor** <note>black bile, the cold and dry humor</note>, you will do so by administering 
<margin>Gentle remedies for the melancholic humor.</margin>
the **lenitive electuary** <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or sugar</note> together with Nicolaus’s *diasena* <note>a classic senna-based laxative formula attributed to Nicolaus Salernitanus</note> according to the patient’s tolerance—for example: Take one ounce of lenitive electuary and half an ounce of Nicolaus’s *diasena*; mix them, and let a **bolus** <note>a large, soft pill</note> be made with sugar. 

But if you wish to lessen the melancholic humor arising from the **adustion** <note>the "burning" or scorched state of a humor caused by excessive heat, turning it into a toxic form of black bile</note> of both natural and yellow **cholera** <note>yellow bile</note>, the best thing will be the lenitive electuary along with **cassia fistula** <note>the pulp of the "purging cassia" tree</note>; for instance: Take six drams each of lenitive electuary and flowers of cassia—more or less according to necessity—and let a bolus be made from them with sugar, and let it be given an hour or two before the morning meal; or let a potion be made from them with **bugloss** or **borage** water. 

If, however, you wish to lessen the melancholic humor arising from the adustion of **pituita** <note>phlegm</note>, which is thick, you shall give the lenitive electuary with the aforementioned Nicolaus’s *diasena*, or **diacatholicon** <note>a "universal" laxative electuary</note> with *diasena*, made into a bolus with sugar, or dissolved with **fumitory** water. 

When you wish to lessen the melancholic humor arising from the adustion of **blood**, you shall do so by ordering the medicine thus: Take one ounce of lenitive electuary and half an ounce of **tamarind** pulp; mix them, and let a bolus be made with sugar, or let a potion be made with a decoction of borage or **hops**; or with the distilled waters of said herbs; or let the electuary *diacatholicon* be given at one and a half ounces in the form of a bolus, or dissolved as above. 

And although the best lessening of melancholy from the adustion of blood is achieved by **bloodletting** <note>phlebotomy</note> from the **black vein** <note>original: *vena nigra*; likely referring to the median cubital or basilic vein of the arm, traditionally associated with draining black bile</note>, or the common vein, or by applying leeches to the hemorrhoids;
<margin>Pharmacy is safer than bloodletting in the evacuation of melancholy.</margin>
nevertheless, it is safer to administer medicine by mouth. This is because often in such bloodletting, the thin and good blood exits, and thus the thick blood is rendered more "disobedient" <note>resistant to treatment</note>, since the natural heat—which digests and prepares the humor—has already been weakened in some way by the evacuation of the good blood. Nevertheless, melancholic blood can be safely evacuated, as **Hippocrates** says in the sixth part of the *Aphorisms*, aphorism 12. 

There are also other medicines that can be given when you wish to lessen the melancholic humor, such as a decoction of **senna** with raisins and "milk water" <note>whey</note>, or borage water; a decoction of **Epithymum** <note>dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant highly prized for treating melancholy</note> with raisins is also effective for the same purpose, using milk water or distilled waters such as borage, bugloss, and fumitory. There is, furthermore, the **Syrup of Apples of Sabor** <note>referring to a formula by the Persian physician Sahl ibn Sabur</note>, which draws out the melancholic humor without distress if four ounces of it are administered, which is prepared thus: Take two pounds each of the juice of domestic and wild bugloss, and the juice of sweet apples...

Massa also debates the merits of pharmacy versus bloodletting, cautioning that purging via the mouth is often safer than opening a vein.</summary>

...of fragrant ingredients. Take 3 pounds of [syrup], 4 ounces of senna pods, 2 drams of saffron, and 3 pounds of **Tabarzet sugar** <note>original: "sacchari tabarzet"; a high-quality, refined white sugar originally from Persia, prized in medieval pharmacy</note>. Let the saffron, however, be rubbed in a cloth during its decoction. There is also another **laxative syrup of apples** <note>original: "syrupus de pomis solutivus"</note> which evacuates all melancholic matter <note>black bile</note> without distinction, if it is administered in a dose of three to four ounces. Its description is as follows:

Take 15 ounces of sweet apple juice; 6 ounces each of the juices of **fumitory** <note>original: "fumiterrae"; a herb used to "cleanse" the blood and bile</note>, hops, and endive; 7 drams each of the flowers of **bugloss** and borage, their roots, and **maidenhair fern** <note>original: "capillorum Veneris"</note>; 1 ounce each of **Cretan epithyme** <note>original: "Epithymi cretensis"; dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant considered essential for purging black bile</note>, senna, polypody <note>a type of fern</note>, and fumitory; 3.5 drams each of germander, **stoechas** <note>original: "stoechados"; French or Arabian lavender</note>, and chamomile flowers; 6 drams each of the rinds of Indian, chebulic, and citrine **myrobalans** <note>original: "myrobalanorum"; astringent plum-like fruits from India used to purge different humors</note>. Let all these—except the epithyme—boil in 3 pounds of common water until a third remains. Then let the juices and the epithyme boil for a single boil; let it be strained with a good pressing, in which 3 pounds of sugar are added, and a syrup be made. To this, add 1 ounce of **black hellebore** <note>original: "ellebori nigri"; a powerful and potentially toxic purgative that required careful preparation</note> tied in a scrap of cloth, so that it boils together until the syrup is perfectly cooked. This hellebore should remain always with the said cloth and the syrup in its vessel. Use this syrup, for it is a medicine of unparalleled benefit in every evacuation of the melancholic humor.

All these things having been said, and others as well, **rational physicians** <note>doctors who rely on logic and theory rather than just experience</note> use these to lessen the matter of the humors that are contrary to nature in illnesses involving a "distemper with matter" <note>an imbalance caused by an actual physical accumulation of a humor</note>, according to their **estimative judgment** <note>the doctor's intuitive ability to judge a case based on signs</note> which comes close to the certain truth. Therefore, once the matter is lessened, the residue will need to be evacuated. But since, according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** in the first book of the *Aphorisms*: **"Matters must be medicated and moved when they are concocted, not when they are raw"** <note>original: "Concocta medicari, & mouere non cruda expediat"; a fundamental rule of ancient medicine: do not try to purge a "raw" or thin humor; it must first be "cooked" or "ripened" (concocted) into a state where the body can expel it</note>, I shall therefore write down for you the **concoctives** <note>original: "concoctiua"</note>, or digestives, or preparatives for the various humors described above. 

However, I must first advise you that the **digestion** <note>in this context, the metabolic "ripening" of a humor</note> or preparation of humors sometimes occurs in a humor that is not entirely contrary to nature; this is called a "helpful humor" by physicians, and I shall say nothing of its preparation, since it can be corrected by the [body's] natural power alone. Instead, my discourse will be concerning the preparation of those other humors which have already become contrary to nature, which are called harmful. But since humors become contrary to nature in more than just one way, we do not always proceed in one way for their preparation or concoction. For digestion in a "helpful" [humor], according to the opinion of **Aristotle** in the fourth book...

-># NICHOLAS MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS<-

<page-num>91</page-num>

->## THE RIPENING OF HUMORS<-

The **process of ripening** <note>original: "Meteorum"; referencing the Aristotelian idea that internal bodily "cooking" follows the same physical laws as atmospheric phenomena</note> always proceeds by thickening, whatever others may please to say. Nevertheless, when humors have already become unnatural, they are processed not only by thickening, but also by refining, thinning, and "cutting" <note>the process of breaking down thick or sticky fluids so they can flow</note>: indeed, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous 11th-century Persian physician</note> learnedly said in the first part of the fourth book regarding the preparation of humors for evacuation: **digestion** <term>digestion: in this period, "digestion" (concoctio) meant the "ripening" or "cooking" of bodily fluids by natural heat, not just the stomach's processing of food</term> is the thickening of thin substances, the thinning of thick ones, and the cutting of viscous ones, about which I shall write to you. But allow me to digress a little for your better understanding of the digestion or preparation of the humors.

<margin>
Note the different ways the humors are "cooked."
</margin>

I was saying just a little earlier that **humors** <note>the four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> are sometimes not entirely unnatural, even if they have undergone some alteration in their qualities, either to a lesser or greater degree, according to their own balanced nature. These humors, when disposed in this way, physicians call **beneficial matter**, which is always brought back to a healthy state by the body's internal power <note>original: "a virtute"; the "virtus" or natural healing force of the body</note> without the help of medicines—unless it is hindered by either internal or external causes. If I wished to write to you about those causes at present, this speech of ours would be far too long. I will therefore speak of that preparation which occurs in **harmful matter**. Regarding this, I want you to know first that sometimes the humor called harmful, although it is unnatural, is nevertheless changed in such a way that it is close to being good; because of its innate nature, it is still "good" enough that it can easily be led back to its original, natural, and benign state through digestion or preparation. In such a case, no condition of **putrefaction** <note>rot or decay within the fluids</note> remains. This is what **Galen** <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years</note> meant to signify in the third book of his *Small Art* <note>original: "Artis parvae"; also known as the *Tegni* or *Ars Medica*</note> when he said that **concoction** <note>ripening</note> causes putrefaction to cease, while the matter itself remains. This is one method of the concoction or preparation of the humors.

There is, however, another concoction or preparation of humors that cannot be led back to a benign state through digestion. This is because the humor has already reached a stage of putrefaction so close to total corruption that it cannot return, since the humor has lost its own **proper form**. These humors are so putrid that they cannot be brought back to a healthy state or to their natural consistency. Therefore, the "digestion" that occurs in them is not the kind that can make them benign again so that the rot ceases while the original matter remains in its own nature. 

<margin>
The two ways of preparing yellow bile.
</margin>

Instead, it is a certain method of preparation for **evacuation** <note>the removal of waste or harmful humors from the body, usually via purging or bloodletting</note> by nature or by medical art. This preparation, as I said a little while ago, is not always done by thickening. Having prefaced things in this way, I will list in order the digestive remedies for **cholera** <note>original: "cholerae seu bilis"; yellow bile, the hot and dry humor</note>, beginning with the **simple medicines** <note>medicines made from a single ingredient, usually a plant</note> that prepare yellow bile; and these are: **chicory**,

<vocab>humors, concoction, preparation, yellow bile, bile, Avicenna, Galen, digestion, putrefaction</vocab>

-># SECOND PART<-

endive, sorrel, borage, bugloss, lettuce, hops, and all species of chicory, from which are given distilled waters, or decoctions of them, from 6 to 10 ounces, with or without sugar. There are also compound syrups written about by authorities, such as simple vinegar syrup, **oxysaccharum** <note>original: "oxyzacchara"; a medicinal syrup made of vinegar and sugar</note> made of endive, of chicory, of sorrel juice, and syrups of violet, rose, citron, currant, pomegranate, **verjuice** <note>original: "agresta"; the tart juice of unripe grapes</note>, water-lily, poppy, bugloss, and other similar types. Take note, however, that even if the simple "digesting" medicines listed here, as well as the compound syrups, are able to prepare pure or thin **yellow bile** <term>cholera: in this context, "cholera" refers to yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness, not the modern bacterial disease</term>,

<margin>
Not all preparing medicines are suitable for every disease, even if the underlying matter is the same.
</margin>

they cannot always be safely administered to everyone in every disease. For when the yellow bile putrefies in some specific member, such as the chest, the head, or another sensitive part containing **nerves**, you cannot give vinegar syrup, oxysaccharum, pomegranate syrup, verjuice, or similar things without risk. 

<margin>
Vinegar and all acidic things harm the nerves, the chest, and the head.
</margin>

This is because vinegar and all acidic things harm the nerves, the chest, and the head. For that reason, when there is a fever accompanied by a cough, or with an abscess of the side <note>likely pleurisy</note>, or with headache, delirium, and insomnia, or with pains in the nerves, one must abstain from all acidic things. Furthermore, do not neglect to prescribe syrups according to the various locations in which the yellow bile often putrefies. Physicians indeed call this the **mine of the fever** <note>original: "febris mineram"; the localized source or "focal point" of the diseased humor</note>. For example, if the humors or the putrefaction are mostly around the region of the **liver**, syrups of chicory, endive, or simple vinegar syrup should be given with a decoction of endive, chicory, borage, bugloss, and the like; or with the distilled waters of those same plants. When there is a headache or an ailment of the stomach, **rose syrup** should be given along with the aforementioned syrups. If there is a cough or difficulty breathing, **violet syrup** or licorice syrup should be given, as these extinguish the feverish heat by their particular moisture. But so that you may have everything ready at hand, let us suppose a young man of a bilious temperament suffering from a **tertian fever** <note>a fever that spikes every third day, traditionally associated with yellow bile</note> caused by pure or orange-colored yellow bile. In such a case, you would prescribe a "digestive" syrup as follows:

<margin>
A case in which he teaches how to prepare yellow bile.
</margin>

**Take** 1 ounce of simple vinegar syrup, half an ounce of endive syrup, and 3 ounces of a decoction of chicory, endive, and borage. **Mix them.** Or let it be diluted with the distilled waters of the said herbs and given in the morning. Or let it be given by following this order: **Take** 1 ounce of simple chicory syrup, half an ounce of simple vinegar syrup, and 2 ounces each of bugloss and endive water. **Mix and let it be administered.** A decoction of endive, borage, sorrel, and similar herbs can also be administered.

<margin>
Bile of greater renown and of lesser pursuit.
</margin>

Since all these medicines can prepare "refined" and "citron-colored" bile—which is called **thin yellow bile of greater renown** <note>original: "cholera subtilis maioris famæ"; "of greater renown" refers to the standard, most well-known classifications in Galenic medicine</note> to distinguish it from **thick yellow bile of greater renown**—it is that which is formed by the mixing of red bile with thick **phlegm** <term>pituita: also called phlegm, the cold and moist humor</term>. Such bile resembles the yolks of eggs, and for that reason it is called **vitelline** <note>yolk-like</note> bile. In preparing this, physicians do not provide syrups that are as cold as they do for thin citron-colored bile, lest they thicken the matter even more through cooling. Instead, they give them syrups, for example, in this manner: Take one ounce of syrup of endive, half an ounce of vinegar syrup, and one ounce each of the waters of chicory, hops, and borage; mix them. Or let a decoction be given of chicory, endive, borage, and hops with syrup of chicory and simple vinegar syrup. Where a great deal of thick matter has been mixed with the bile, simple **oxymel** <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> should be used in place of the vinegar syrup, and fennel or parsley water should be added along with chicory or endive water, or in other syrups in this manner: Take one ounce of simple Byzantine syrup, half an ounce of endive syrup, and one and a half ounces each of chicory and hops water; mix them. Or if the matter is even thicker, give Byzantine syrup with vinegar up to one ounce, or oxymel of two, three, or five roots, according to the sluggishness of the offending matter.

<margin>
He teaches the preparations for bile mixed with phlegm and melancholy.
</margin>

But if the bilious matter has been mixed not only with thick phlegm, but also with the **melancholic humor** <term>melancholia: black bile, the cold and dry humor</term>, as often happens, then let syrups be given in this manner: Take half an ounce each of syrups of endive, bugloss, and simple vinegar; and one ounce each of the waters of chicory, borage, and **fumitory** <note>original: "fumiterræ"</note>; mix them. Or let a decoction be given of borage, bugloss, chicory, hops, and fumitory, with one and a half ounces of simple chicory syrup. But if a great deal of "burnt" bilious matter has been mixed in—which is what is called **bile of lesser renown** <note>original: "cholera minoris famæ"; referring to "adust" or burnt bile, which was considered a more complex or corrupted form of the humor</note>—then you shall give the syrup in this manner: Take half an ounce each of the syrups of bugloss, violet, and **water-lily** <note>original: "nenuphare"</note>; and one ounce each of the waters of endive, sorrel, and borage; mix and administer it. A decoction can also be given of bugloss, borage, water-lily, hops, and sorrel with syrups of bugloss and vinegar; for these and similar things can extinguish the burning heat of **adust** <term>adust: "burnt" by excessive bodily heat, making the humor more toxic and pungent</term> bile. And since, besides adust bile, there is also given **leek-green bile** <note>original: "cholera praxina"</note>, which is produced from the further burning of vitelline bile and is often generated in the stomach; physicians call this **eruginous** <note>resembling verdigris, the green rust of copper</note> bile, since it is similar to the rust of copper. It is poisonous, and if a fever should arise from its putrefaction—which rarely happens—no one survives. Nevertheless, since it is so sharp and hostile to nature, before its putrefaction...

## PART TWO

<margin>Remedies for preparing tasteless or sweet phlegm</margin>
...or acidic, or sour, or harsh: according to their diversity, it is necessary to arrange appropriate digestive medicines. If, therefore, you wish to prepare tasteless or sweet phlegm <term>pituita: the humor of phlegm, associated with cold and moisture</term> for concoction <note>the process of "ripening" or thinning a humor so it can be safely expelled</note>, you will arrange the syrups or decoction in this way: *Take one ounce of rose honey, half an ounce of simple oxymel <term>oxymel: a medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</term>, and three drachms of a decoction of betony and wormwood. Mix them; or let it be diluted with the distilled waters of betony, wormwood, and the like. You can also administer oxymel of two roots or of five roots <note>These were standard Renaissance pharmaceutical blends. The "five roots" usually consisted of smallage, asparagus, fennel, parsley, and butcher's broom</note> for such phlegm, with fennel and scabious water, or with a decoction of the aforementioned things.*

<margin>Instructions for preparing salty phlegm.</margin>
But if it should be salty, let these be given: *Take one ounce of simple vinegar syrup, half an ounce of rose honey, and one and a half ounces each of fennel and fumitory waters. Mix them, or let a decoction be made from these; and where the matter is exceedingly salty, vinegar-sugar syrup <term>oxysaccharum: a syrup made from vinegar and sugar</term> and even chicory syrup can be added.*

<margin>Instructions for preparing acidic and harsh phlegm.</margin>
Acidic and harsh <note>original: "pontica," a term for a puckering, astringent taste like that of unripe fruit or alum</note> phlegm is prepared in this way: *Take half an ounce each of simple oxymel, syrup of hops, and syrup of betony; and one and a half ounces each of maidenhair fern and calamint waters. Mix them, or let there be decoctions made from the stated things.*

<margin>Preparations for thick and mucilaginous phlegm.</margin>
But if the phlegm should be thick, mucilaginous, and raw, the syrups should be stronger, for example: *Take one ounce of oxymel of the two roots or of the five roots, half an ounce of betony syrup, and one and a half ounces each of sage and hyssop waters. Mix them, or let a decoction be made from honey, hyssop, fennel, and similar things, with which the aforementioned syrups are to be diluted.* And where the matter is thicker, you will be able to administer stronger syrups, such as *squill oxymel* <note>a medicine made from sea onions (squill), often used as an expectorant</note>, *syrup of stoechas* <note>French lavender</note>, and similar ones according to the pressing necessity, with your own judgment mediating; always, however, beginning from the milder ones.

<margin>Instructions for preparing thinner phlegm.</margin>
Similarly, if the matter is thinner in its substance, you will administer milder syrups. You must observe this same thing regarding the diversity of the phlegm's flavor: for if the phlegm is very salty, the syrups should be milder and less "hot" than those administered for non-salty phlegm. For example, in the case of salty phlegm: *Take one ounce of simple vinegar syrup, half an ounce of rose honey, and one ounce each of scabious, fennel, and bugloss waters. Mix them.*

I could have written many other preparatory medicines for phlegm which physicians use, but I leave them out so that I do not confuse you by writing a multitude of remedies rather than teaching you. These, therefore, will be sufficient for the present, and I shall come to writing those things which can prepare melancholic humors. This melancholic humor has various species: for one is natural, which is the dregs of the blood, and the other is non-natural...

# PART TWO.

<margin>He teaches how to prepare the phlegm.</margin>
...They moisten greatly with a moderate heat, such as decoctions <term>decoction: a concentrated substance made by boiling down medicinal plants in water</term> of borage, hops, lemon balm, bugloss, fumitory, and the like; or let them be syrups. Take half an ounce each of syrup of fumitory, bugloss, and dodder of thyme <note>original: "epithymo"</note>; and one and a half ounces each of the waters of borage, hops, and lemon balm; mix them. If, however, the melancholic humor <note>The "humors" were the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health. "Melancholic" refers to black bile.</note> resulted from the burning <margin>He teaches how to prepare the melancholic humor from the burning of melancholy.</margin> of the blood, then it will be worthwhile to administer those medicines that purify the blood, such as hops, fumitory, borage, chicory, asparagus, maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillus Veneris"</note>, or their decoctions. Or let the syrups be given in this manner: Take half an ounce each of the syrups of hops, fumitory, and simple chicory; and one and a half ounces each of the waters of bugloss and borage; mix them.

<margin>He teaches how to prepare the humor made from the burning of blood.</margin>
Lastly, you ought to know that humors are very often mixed together, such that yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> and phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> are mixed with the melancholic humor; and the blood is also very frequently infected by their admixture. Therefore, when such mixtures occur in the humors, in their digestion <term>digestion: the medical process of "ripening" a thick or diseased humor so that it can be easily purged from the body</term> one must always consider the mixed humor alongside the principal one. This allows you to include in the digestive remedies, whether syrups or other medicines, things that benefit the secondary humor as well as the primary one. And this applies not only to mixtures made with <margin>How we ought to prepare mixed humors.</margin> the melancholic humor, but in any other mixture of other humors whatsoever. For instance, if phlegm is mixed with another humor, let honey of roses be added, or oxymel, or Byzantine syrup with vinegar; if yellow bile is present, add syrup of chicory; if blood, add syrup of hops; if melancholy, add syrup of fumitory or bugloss. Thus, by considering the various mixtures of different natural or unnatural humors, you will prepare different digestive medicines. For example, in a mixture of burnt yellow bile, add also syrup of violets or water-lily <note>original: "nenupharinum"</note>; and so with others according to the nature of the humors.

<margin>The error of certain people regarding melancholy.</margin>
And since we have spoken of melancholy arising from the burning of blood, or mixed with blood, there are some who say that in such a case, only bloodletting <note>original: "missionem sanguinis"</note> is appropriate. These people—with all due respect to the teachings and the men of antiquity—are in error. This is because bloodletting is not a "concoction" or a preparation preceding evacuation (of which Hippocrates spoke), but is rather a reductive or eradicative evacuation. Galen feared this in his work *To Glaucon on the Treatment of Quartan Fever* <note>Quartan fever is a form of malaria where the fever peaks every four days; it was traditionally associated with an excess of black bile.</note>, since the melancholic humor is always resistant to evacuation unless it is first prepared. Indeed, since it is "earthy" <note>Melancholy/black bile was associated with the element of Earth, making it thick and heavy.</note> in nature, when a vein is opened, the thinner blood exits while the thick humor remains behind. For that reason, Galen taught in the cited passage to test in the treatment of quartan fever whether opening a vein...

-># LETTERS ON MEDICINE BY NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

...whether clear or black blood comes out: for if the blood is clear, he ordered the vein to be closed; if it is black, he ordered it to be left open so that it may flow out. However, letting blood in this way is not considered a type of concoction <term>concoction: the process of "ripening" or preparing a diseased humor for removal</term> or digestion. Nevertheless, those who apply leeches to hemorrhoids do not act entirely wrongly when there is a mixture of melancholic humor <note>black bile</note> with the blood, provided those hemorrhoids are innate and the patient is accustomed to evacuating blood through them.

<margin>He now proposes to deal with elective medicines.</margin>
Up to this point, I have spoken about the reduction, concoction, and preparation of various unnatural humors according to their diversity. Now we must come to those medicines which doctors call **elective** and **eradicative**, which draw out specific and partial humors. But first, I want to warn you that there is no medicine currently known, or at least not yet discovered, which draws out blood through the stool <note>original: "per secessum"</note> as its primary and direct effect. This is true even though Galen <note>A Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> stated in his book *On the Power of Purgative Medicines* that a certain man had found a herb that draws out blood; however, lest he perhaps show it to others, the magistrates—with their eyes blindfolded <note>original: "obturatis oculis"; this may imply the execution was done in secret or with a deliberate blindness to mercy</note>—condemned him to the punishment of death. 

<margin>How a medicine can evacuate blood secondarily.</margin>
Nevertheless, a medicine can occasionally draw out blood in a secondary way. This evacuation can happen in three modes: for example, if the medicine is so strong that it can strip or erode the lining of the vein—among these are **euphorbium** <note>a caustic plant resin</note>, **scammony**, **squirting cucumber** <note>original: "cucumerus asininus"</note>, **mezereon**, and similar substances. Second, a medicine can draw out blood by its specific property of opening the orifices of the veins, so that blood flows out from those openings, as written by the divine Mesue <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> and others regarding **Aloe**. For as he said in the chapter on Aloe, it harms hemorrhoids and opens the vein orifices, causing blood to flow out—let the most learned Manardi <note>Giovanni Manardi (1462–1536), a contemporary medical reformer</note> and other more recent doctors say whatever they please on this matter. The third mode of blood evacuation is when a medicine is unbridled and untamed in its operation, or if an excessive amount of it is taken, as is the case with all "hot" medicines like scammony and others. Since this is the case, a medicine specifically for drawing out blood via the bowels is not to be sought. 

<margin>On phlebotomy.</margin>
With these things noted, if the necessity of a "fullness" <note>plethora, or an excess of blood</note> or a corruption of the blood compels its evacuation, the vein should be opened according to the opportunity of the situation. Indeed, doctors commonly cut the vein they call the **liver-vein** <note>original: "iecorariam"; the basilic vein in the arm, then believed to be directly connected to the liver</note> in the crook of the arm during fevers and other diseases where the primary intention is to evacuate blood, such as in *synocha* <note>a continuous, non-intermittent fever</note> and pleuropneumonia. From this vein, and in such cases, one draws blood copiously, limited only by the endurance of the patient’s strength...

<summary>Massa explains that unlike other humors, blood cannot be safely purged through the bowels with medicine; instead, it must be removed through leeches or phlebotomy (bloodletting). He lists the risks of using strong drugs like scammony or aloe, which can cause bleeding by eroding or opening the veins.</summary>

<keywords>bloodletting, phlebotomy, elective medicines, humors, Galen, Mesue, scammony, aloe, liver-vein, hemorrhoids, fevers</keywords>

->## PART TWO<-

<margin>Personal opinion on bloodletting.</margin>
**And** some practitioners even dare to drain blood until the point of fainting <term>fainting: original Latin *animi defectum*, referring to syncope or loss of consciousness</term>. I, however, always praise moderation and safety, since I have often seen through my own experience that such excessive evacuation in young and strong men leads to the death of the patient. Sometimes it causes a shift to a "cold" state, leading to long-term illness, paralysis, and other cold dispositions <note>In Galenic medicine, health was a balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry; excessive bleeding was thought to deplete the body's "vital heat," leaving it dangerously "cold."</note>. I would wish for you to be cautious, learning from the dangers others have faced. Other veins are also opened for the evacuation of blood in the arm and in other parts of the body, such as the "black" or common vein in the arm, or the cephalic vein; or in the foot, the popliteal vein; or that which the Arabs call the **saphena** <note>The great saphenous vein of the leg.</note>, but which the Latins call the **malleolar vein** <note>The vein near the ankle bone.</note>; or they open the vein located between the pinky and the fourth finger. Many other veins in various parts of the body are opened according to which specific part is suffering. Whenever the blood is dominant <note>a condition called "plethora"</note> or its corruption is the cause of some disease, it is best to let blood fearlessly, provided the patient’s strength can tolerate it and there are no contraindications—such as a pestilential fever after the fourth day, or an unsuitable time of year or age. For example, in women, if the menstrual evacuations have been retained, you shall open the ankle vein (or saphena) according to the rules <note>original: "canonice"</note>; and for a surplus of melancholic <note>black bile-heavy</note> blood, you shall open the hemorrhoidal veins, especially if they are naturally swollen or become so by accident. By evacuating in this way, you will always remove the cause of the disease, which, according to the opinion of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>, is called the **true cure**.

<margin>What is called the true cure.</margin>
But beyond the evacuation of blood—where, as I said, it is necessary because blood exists in the veins throughout the entire body—a regimen must also be observed using those things which are known to make the blood clear. This is done by soothing or altering it with tamarinds, maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillo Veneris"</note>, hops, borage, bugloss <note>a plant often used to "cheer the heart" and temper humors</note>, and similar things. 

<margin>When the extraction of blood is done with cupping glasses.</margin>
Furthermore, you can perform this or a similar evacuation of blood through the application of cupping glasses <term>cupping glasses: *cucurbitulae*, heated vessels placed on the skin to draw blood to the surface</term> if the blood is abundant in the outer parts of the body, or if it is corrupt and being pushed from the veins toward the surface of the skin, as occurs in bad and pestilential fevers. 

<margin>Exemptions from bloodletting.</margin>
But, leaving aside the evacuation of blood, I shall turn my discourse to the evacuation of other humors, after first informing you that sometimes we can excuse ourselves from opening a vein by instead cleansing the blood through a softening of the belly or a light loosening with purgative medicines. The simple medicines which gently move the bowels and cleanse the blood are primarily: **cassia fistula** <note>a legume used as a mild laxative</note>, tamarinds, manna, hops, the juice of fumitory <note>original: "fumiterra"</note>, whey <note>original: "aqua casei"</note>, and the like. The compound medicines, however, are the syrups...

But first, and before I describe the medicines for evacuating various humors, I will briefly note the weight—or as physicians say, the <term>dose: original: *dosim*</term>—or the quantity that can safely be given of both the individuals (or "simples") and the compounds that loosen the belly and draw out different humors. I will focus especially on those said to be most in use among healers, beginning with the simples. **Cassia**, therefore, although it is a mild laxative, nevertheless draws out yellow bile and phlegm; its pulp is given in doses from one ounce up to 15 drams <note>One ounce (unc.) was roughly 28-30 grams; a dram (ʒ) was about 3.9 grams.</note>. **Tamarinds** also draw out yellow bile; they are given in doses from one ounce up to two, after removing the seeds, or as a decoction in water. **Manna** <note>A sweet, gummy sap from the flowering ash tree, used as a gentle laxative.</note> also draws out yellow bile by soothing the system; it is given from one ounce up to three. Of **Rhubarb**, it is given from one and a half drams up to three, often prepared as an infusion, and sometimes using the whole substance. Of **Agaric** <note>A fungus (*Laricifomes officinalis*) that grows on larch trees, then prized as a powerful purgative.</note>, it is given alone from one dram up to three drams. Of **Aloe**, it is given from one dram up to two, sometimes washed, sometimes unwashed. Of **Scammony** <note>A harsh purgative resin derived from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*.</note>, it is given from four grains up to thirteen. Of **Hermodactyls** <note>Likely the tubers of *Colchicum*, often used for joint pain and gout.</note>, it is given from one dram up to three. Of **Senna**, it is given from half an ounce to one and a half ounces, prepared as a decoction. **Turpeth** <note>The root of *Operculina turpethum*, an Ayurvedic and Mediterranean purgative.</note> is given from one dram up to three. Of **Polypody** <note>A type of fern root.</note>, from two drams up to half an ounce. An infusion of **Myrobalans**—whether yellow, chebulic, or Indian varieties—and also emblics <note>Astringent fruit from various species of *Terminalia* and *Phyllanthus*, staple ingredients in medieval and Renaissance pharmacy.</note>, is given; the dosage for the infusion is from two drams up to six drams of their substance, especially the yellow ones. But for the chebulic, from four drams up to ten; for the Indian, from two drams up to four; and for the emblics, from one and a half drams up to five or seven. Physicians also administer these myrobalans in their solid substance, according to the specific needs of the case.

The quantities or doses of common **compound medicines** will be as follows: of the **laxative electuary** <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note>, one dram up to one and a half or two is given; of **Diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" purgative compound containing cassia, senna, and rhubarb.</note>, from one ounce up to two is given; of **Diaprunum** <note>A plum-based electuary.</note> (the non-laxative kind), from half an ounce up to one ounce or one and a half ounces; of **Diasena**, half an ounce up to one; of the incomplete **Electuary of Sebesten**, from one ounce up to one and a half ounces; of **Simple Hiera** <note>From the Greek *hiera pikra* or "holy bitter," a very old medicine usually based on aloes.</note>, from half an ounce up to one; of the **Electuary Diaphoenicon** <note>A date-based purgative electuary.</note>, from three drams up...
