Of "fetid" pills <note>So-called because they contained pungent resins like asafoetida.</note>, 1 to 1.5 drams are given. Of pills made of hermodactyls <note>A type of colchicum used historically for joint pain and gout.</note>, both the larger and smaller varieties, 1 to 1.5 or 2 drams are administered. Of the "aggregative" pills <note>A broad-spectrum pill designed to purge multiple humors at once.</note>, 1 to 2 drams are given. Of "Arabic" pills, 1 to 2 drams. Of the pills of agaric <note>A type of mushroom (larch fungus) used as a laxative.</note> by Mesuë, 1 to 2 drams. There are also many other compound medicines in daily use, which I will not speak of at present, lest our discourse proceed at too great a length.

<margin>Medicines should be combined with certain things.</margin>
One thing, however, I will not pass over: namely, <term>that: original: *qp* (quia/quod)</term> medicines should always be combined or prepared with things that address the humors to be evacuated, or the specific body part from which the humors must be drawn. And to reach my intended goal: I shall turn my discourse toward medicines that selectively evacuate the humors. Among these, the first will be yellow bile <note>Original: *cholera*.</note>, which is either simple and natural, or compound and contrary to nature.

<margin>Selective medicines for natural yellow bile.</margin>
Natural yellow bile, when it is in excess, is drawn out by cassia, tamarinds, and rhubarb, if they are administered, for example, in this manner: **Recipe** 1 dram of choice rhubarb, 6 grains of spikenard <note>An aromatic plant used to improve the medicinal action and protect the stomach.</note>, 3 drams of Malmsey wine, and a decoction of tamarinds and raisins with 4 ounces of chicory water. Let it be infused for eight hours, and once strained, dissolve in it 12 drams of cassia pulp to make a drink; let it be given five hours before a meal. Cassia can also be taken with rhubarb in the form of a bolus <note>A large, soft pill, often the size of a grape.</note> in this way: **Recipe** 13 drams of cassia flowers and 1.5 drams of choice mature rhubarb. Form a bolus from these and administer five hours before a meal. But if necessity requires administration in pill form, let them be given this way: **Recipe** 5 scruples <note>A scruple was roughly 1.3 grams.</note> of choice mature rhubarb. Form five pills from these with chicory water or pure rose juice; let them be taken five or six hours before a meal with some apozeme <note>A medicinal decoction or tea.</note>; for example: **Recipe** syrup...

Correctives for tamarinds.
</margin>
It should also be noted that since tamarinds may in some way harm a "cold" stomach <note>In the Galenic medical tradition, a "cold" stomach lacked the necessary "heat" to digest food properly; tamarinds were considered cooling and could exacerbate this.</note>, they must be corrected <note>In pharmacy, to "correct" an ingredient meant adding another substance to balance its temperature or mitigate unwanted side effects.</note> with mastic, or camel grass <term>schoenanthus</term>, and mace. There are also pills that thoroughly draw out the aforementioned yellow bile, such as "golden pills," "aggregative pills," "pills of three," pills of washed aloes from an infusion of rhubarb, and similar ones. From these, when the occasion for evacuation arises, you shall prepare them as follows.

Take of non-laxative *diaprunum* 1.5 ounces, or of *diacatholicon* <note>A "universal" purge intended to cleanse all the humors of the body.</note>; let a bolus <note>A large, soft pill intended to be swallowed.</note> be made with sugar, or let a potion be made with water of chicory and endive, or with a common decoction of fruits, which you shall arrange thus: Take of raisins, licorice, barley, and common seeds <note>Usually referring to the "four greater cold seeds": cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon.</note>, half an ounce of each; 10 jujubes, 6 plums, and 10 ounces of borage water. Let them boil until a third part is consumed, then strain it. With this liquid you can dissolve other medicines, or infuse rhubarb in it.

But if you desire to give a stronger medicine, add up to 2 drams of the rose electuary of Mesuë, since it draws out lemon-yellow bile without causing distress. You can also add an infusion of rhubarb, preparing it in this way: Take of selected ripe rhubarb 1.5 drams, of spikenard or camel grass 6 grains, of aromatic wine 3 drams, of chicory and bugloss waters 2 ounces of each, or 3 ounces of the common decoction. # SECOND PART.

...and by compounding other stated things according to the occasion and the need of the matter. If it should be worthwhile to give pills, you shall arrange them thus: Take <term>1.5 drams</term> <note>Original: *drach.i.s.*</note> of <term>aggregative pills</term> <note>A standard multi-ingredient laxative pill intended to "aggregate" or collect various humors for expulsion.</note>; let five pills be made and gilded <note>Pills were often coated in gold leaf to mask bitter tastes or as a luxury treatment.</note>. They should be administered six hours before food, and immediately after taking them, the patient should drink this syrup: Take <term>1 ounce</term> of <term>syrup of endive</term>, <term>half an ounce</term> of <term>rose syrup</term>, and <term>1.5 ounces each</term> of <term>chicory and borage waters</term>. Mix them. You can also arrange the pills in this way: Take <term>1 dram</term> of <term>golden pills</term> <note>*Pilulae aureae*, a popular purgative recipe often containing aloe, diaprunum, and other herbs.</note> and <term>1 scruple</term> of <term>choice ripe rhubarb</term>. Other pills already mentioned may also be taken, as well as others, by adding and subtracting the quantity of one or the other as necessity demands—always considering the age, strength, the disease, and other factors.

<margin>Medicines choice for unnatural yellow bile</margin>
It follows that I should speak concerning the evacuation of <term>unnatural yellow bile</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "natural" bile was a healthy humor; "unnatural" bile was humor that had become corrupted, burnt, or mixed with other fluids.</note>. First, since there are diverse species of it—some being unnatural through the mixing of other humors, such as <term>vitelline bile</term> <note>Named for its resemblance to egg yolk (*vitellus*).</note>, which is more well-known and caused by the mixing of <term>phlegm</term> with <term>yellow bile</term>; and some through <term>adustion</term> <note>A process where humors were thought to be "burnt" by excessive bodily heat, making them dark and toxic.</note> and also through mixing, such as the less-renowned bile mentioned before—it will therefore be worthwhile to exhibit different medicines according to their differences. These are of two kinds: simple and compound. Simple medicines include <term>purging cassia</term> <note>*Cassia fistularis*, a legume used as a mild laxative.</note>, <term>pure juice of roses</term>, <term>washed aloe</term>, <term>rhubarb</term>, <term>agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus used as a purgative.</note>, <term>scammony</term> <note>A harsh purgative resin from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*.</note>, and the like. Compound medicines, however, are such as <term>lenitive electuary</term> <note>A sweet, paste-like medicinal preparation designed to soothe while purging.</note>, <term>electuary of sebesten</term>, <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>A "universal" or general purge.</note>, <term>diaphoenicon</term> <note>An electuary based on dates.</note>, <term>diafenae</term>, <term>diaprunum</term> <note>An electuary based on prunes.</note>, <term>simple and compound hiera</term> <note>*Hiera picra*, one of the oldest known purgative formulas, usually containing aloe and spices.</note>, <term>Mesue’s electuary of rose juice</term> <note>Referring to recipes attributed to the famous 9th-century physician Mesue the Younger.</note>, <term>confection hamech</term>, and <term>purgative rose syrup</term>, and similar things, from which you shall give according to the need of the matter. For example, if the matter is vitelline bile from a mixture of phlegm and not from adustion, you shall arrange it thus: Take <term>1.5 ounces</term> of <term>flowers of cassia</term> newly extracted; let a <term>bolus</term> <note>A large, soft pill, often the size of a grape.</note> be made with sugar, or let a drink be made with <term>fennel</term> or <term>hops</term> water, or with a decoction of fennel or <term>anise</term>. Or, let <term>purgative rose syrup</term> be given up to <term>4 ounces</term>, diluted with water of hops and borage. For this purpose, the <term>lenitive electuary of sebesten</term> is useful, as was said, given in the form of a bolus or diluted with the said waters or decoction in this way: Take <term>1 ounce</term> of <term>lenitive electuary</term>, <term>half an ounce</term> of <term>sebesten electuary</term>, or <term>3 drams</term> of <term>diaphoenicon</term>. Let a bolus or a drink be made from them, and after five or six hours, let the patient eat.

# NICOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

<margin>On Rhubarb.</margin>
...since, beyond the fact that it evacuates both types of bile <note>In the humoral system, "both types" usually refers to natural yellow bile and "unnatural" or "burnt" bile.</note>, it is also a medicine that corrects the harmfulness of other medicines and is a strengthener of the stomach and liver; you shall prepare it thus. Take 1.5 <term>drams</term> <note>A dram is approximately 3.9 grams.</note> of choice rhubarb, 6 grains of spikenard, 4 drams of Malmsey wine, and 3 ounces of the common decoction written above. Let them be infused according to the art [of pharmacy], and once the straining is done, dissolve in it 1 ounce of lenitive <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note> and 3 drams of <term>sebesten</term> <note>A fruit from the Cordia myxa tree, used in Galenic medicine as a mild laxative and for chest ailments.</note>. Mix and let a potion be made, to which add half an ounce of pure rose juice; let it be given as [described] above, five hours before food. If, however, the bile should be "vitelline" <note>Yellow bile that has become thick and bright yellow, resembling the color of egg yolks (*vitellus*).</note> from <term>adustion</term> <note>The "burning" or overheating of humors, which was thought to make them toxic or morbid.</note>, cassia is excellent, as is the electuary of <term>diaprunum</term> <note>A purgative compound made primarily from plums (*pruna*).</note> with an infusion of rhubarb, as we said above.

<margin>What violet troches are useful for.</margin>
Indeed, you shall evacuate "burnt" bile, or bile mixed with another humor—which is said to be of lesser repute <note>Original: *minoris famae*. This may refer to a less common or less significant secondary humor.</note>—in this way: Take 10 drams of <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>A "universal" or "general" purgative electuary containing many ingredients.</note> and 5 drams of psyllium electuary. Mix, and let a <term>bolus</term> <note>A large, soft medicinal pill, often the size of a grape.</note> be made with sugar, or a drink with the common decoction, or with distilled waters of chicory, borage, endive, hops, and the like; to which, as said above, you can add 1 or 1.5 drams of infused rhubarb. In this way, you will purge better and more successfully. <term>Troches</term> <note>Small medicinal lozenges or tablets.</note> of violets, both without <term>scammony</term> <note>A harsh, resinous purgative derived from the root of Convolvulus scammonia.</note> and with scammony, are very effective in evacuating thick vitelline matter; therefore, they should be added to strengthen the operation of the medicine in doses of 1 to 2 drams along with cassia and the other mentioned medicines. You can also give pills, such as "aggregative" pills <note>So called because they were thought to "aggregate" or collect various humors for expulsion.</note>, "pills of three" with rhubarb, "golden" pills, and the like, if the patient can tolerate a potion or a medicine in the form of a bolus. You shall arrange them thus: Take 1 or 1.5 drams of aggregative pills; let five pills be made and let them be gilded <note>Coated in gold leaf to mask the taste or signify a high-quality preparation.</note>, and let them be taken six hours before food. Or, where you wish to evacuate thicker matter, you shall arrange it thus: Take 2 drams each of golden pills and aggregative pills; let five pills be made and gilded, and let them be taken as said with the <term>apozeme</term> <note>A medicinal decoction or concentrated herbal tea.</note> or syrup mentioned above, or with 4 ounces of chicory water, or with small-chicken broth. And when you recognize a greater burning [adustion], or a mixture of burnt humors, you shall administer stronger medicines; however, they should not be stripped of the virtue of soothing. For example: Take 1 ounce of lenitive electuary, or diacatholicon, or "incomplete" sebesten <note>Original: *sebesten non completi*, likely referring to a specific stage of preparation.</note>; 4 drams of laxative diaprunum; 1 ounce of pure rose juice; and a sufficient amount of a decoction of raisins, barley, sebesten, and <term>senna</term> <note>A powerful herbal laxative.</note> with milk-water or hops. Mix, and let a potion be made from them, in which [you may use this] in place of the diaprunum electuary if the matter is mixed with melancholic humor...

# PART TWO

...it was there, you can put 2 <term>drams</term> <note>A unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams.</note> or 2.5 drams of the <term>confection Hamech</term> <note>A famous, complex purgative electuary containing many ingredients, used to purge "thick" humors.</note> and in the decoction add chebulic myrobalans, and flowers of borage and bugloss. If indeed it is accompanied by phlegm, let <term>diaturbith</term> <note>A medicinal powder made from the root of the *Ipomoea turpethum* plant.</note> or violet <term>troches</term> <note>Small medicinal lozenges.</note> be added; however, you can always safely mix in infused rhubarb, either by itself or with <term>agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus, the Larch polypore, known for its strong purgative effects.</note> as well. For example, if the bile be of "lesser fame" <note>Meaning a less malignant or common variety of bile.</note> and mixed with thick phlegm: Take 1 dram of choice mature rhubarb, 1.5 drams of the best crumbly white agaric, 4 grains of spikenard, 10 grains of ginger, half a dram of rose honey, 3 drams of aromatic wine, and 3 drams of a decoction of raisins, barley, senna, and polypody, with the waters of hops and borage. Let them be infused according to the art [of pharmacy], and once the liquid is pressed out, add 6 drams of lenitive <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note> and 3 drams of the [electuary] of dates. Let a potion be made, to be taken six hours before lunch.

<margin>Note on how to avoid vomiting when the medicine is taken as a whole.</margin>
And because agaric often causes vomiting, if the patient sleeps for two hours after the administration of the medicine, its operation will be less troublesome. If you wish to give it in the form of a <term>bolus</term> <note>A large, soft medicinal pill, often the size of a grape.</note>, let it be given in this way: Take 6 drams of lenitive electuary, 3 drams of [electuary] of dates, 2 <term>scruples</term> <note>A unit of weight equal to 1/3 of a dram, or about 1.3 grams.</note> of choice powdered rhubarb, and 1.5 drams of prepared or troched agaric. Mix, and with sugar let a bolus be made; let him sleep for two hours afterward and eat five or six hours after taking it. But if you wish to give pills, the best are the "pills of three" with rhubarb, pills of <term>hiera</term> <note>A "holy" bitter medicine, usually containing aloes and spices.</note> with agaric, or the agaric pills of <term>Mesue</term> <note>Referring to the 9th-century physician Masawayh, whose pharmaceutical formulas were standard in the Renaissance.</note>. For instance: Take 1 dram of "pills of three" with rhubarb, and 2 scruples of Mesue's agaric pills; let five pills be made and gilded <note>Pills were often coated in gold leaf to hide their bitter taste and increase their prestige.</note>. Or let "aggregative" pills be given alone, or with troched agaric, along with some syrup suited to the substance and nature of the humors to be evacuated. For example: Take 1 dram of wood betony syrup, half a dram of rose honey, and 1.5 drams each of chicory and hop water. Mix and let it be given. For all these listed medicines draw out both types of "lesser fame" bile—namely, both that made by <term>adustion</term> <note>The "burning" or overheating of humors, thought to make them toxic.</note> and that made by the unnatural mixing of other humors.

If, however, you see that "aeruginous" <note>Literally "verdigris-colored," a deep metallic green bile thought to be extremely toxic.</note> or "leek-green" bile abounds, 

<margin>Those laboring under leek-green and aeruginous bile very rarely survive.</margin>
know this: those who produce this humor rarely escape death. Indeed, since it is a most troublesome humor, it usually tends to provoke vomiting; and either without it or with it, it kills the man. Therefore, medicines that evacuate and move the humors are not safely administered. Nevertheless, as physicians can rarely help him with their aids—whatever the case may be, since I myself have sometimes seen some who were troubled by aeruginous bile escape [death]—therefore, if time and opportunity are given...

...convenience, some mild evacuant should be administered, such as <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>A "universal" purgative electuary, so named because it was intended to purge all humors safely.</note>, which is effective in acute and very acute diseases; or let those medicines be used which draw out from the stomach without distress, such as the <term>lenitive</term> <note>A mild laxative electuary often containing senna and tamarind.</note>, laxative rose syrup, or <term>manna</term> <note>The dried sap of the flowering ash tree, used as a gentle sweetener and laxative.</note> dissolved with a decoction of senna can be of use <margin>Note on administering medications.</margin> according to common practice. However, whatever the case may be, you should always add to the medicines themselves something to strengthen the stomach and the rest of the internal organs, such as pure rose juice, or <term>geleniabin</term> <note>A conserve of roses and sugar, from the Arabic *julanjabin*.</note> made with sugar, or syrup of citron peels, and similar items that draw out different types of <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note>. 

It follows that we should speak of those things which evacuate <term>pituitous matter</term> <note>Matter pertaining to pituita, or phlegm.</note>. Since this phlegm consists of various species, I shall begin with one, proceeding in order, and that is "sweet and tasteless phlegm." This can be evacuated by various medicines, both simple and compound. <margin>Things that selectively draw out sweet phlegm.</margin> The **simples** are <term>turbith</term> <note>The root of *Ipomoea turpethum*, used as a purgative.</note>, rock salt, <term>agaric</term> <note>The Larch polypore fungus.</note>, <term>hermodactyl</term> <note>Likely the root of the meadow saffron (*Colchicum*), used for joint pain and purging.</note>, safflower, and <term>myrobalans</term> <note>A'stringent plum-like fruits used in medieval pharmacy; types include chebulic, belleric, and emblic.</note>—including the chebulic, belleric, and emblic varieties—and others like them. 

The **compounds**, however, are <term>hiera diacolocynthidos</term> <note>A "sacred" bitter medicine made with colocynth, or "bitter apple."</note>, <term>diaphœnicon</term> <note>A purgative electuary primarily made of dates.</note>, lenitive electuary, electuary of <term>sebesten</term> <note>A fruit also known as the Assyrian plum.</note>, <term>benedicta</term> <note>Literally "the blessed," a common laxative compound.</note>, prepared or <term>trochiscated</term> <note>Formed into small medicinal lozenges or "troches."</note> agaric, violet troches without <term>scammony</term> <note>A harsh, resinous purgative root.</note>, <term>alephangine pills</term> <note>Highly aromatic pills meant to cleanse the head and stomach.</note>, <term>cochia pills</term> <note>A classic purgative pill formula.</note>, mastic pills, pills of benedicta, "fetid" pills, pills of the agaric of <term>Mesue</term> <note>A reference to the pharmaceutical formulas of the influential Persian/Arab physician Mesue.</note>, pills of hermodactyls, pills of <term>euphorbium</term> <note>A very strong purgative resin from the spurge plant.</note>, and many other similar ones, both simple and compound, from which you shall choose according to the needs of the disease or the unnatural disposition. 

For example: Take 1 <term>dram</term> <note>A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of lenitive electuary, half a dram of the electuary of sebesten, and 2 drams of the electuary of dates. Let a <term>bolus</term> <note>A large, soft pill intended to be swallowed.</note> be made from them with sugar, or a potion with fennel water, or with a decoction of raisins, senna, and <term>polypody</term> <note>A type of fern whose root was used as a laxative.</note> in fennel water, and let it be administered five hours before a meal. Or let 1 dram of the lenitive be given with 2 drams of prepared agaric, or with 2 drams of the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, a powdered mixture of ingredients.</note> of simple <term>hiera</term> <note>A bitter medicinal powder.</note> in the form of a bolus, or dissolved in fennel water or the aforementioned decoction. Or let the electuary of dates be given in a dose up to 6 drams, either in solid form—specifically in <term>lozenges</term> <note>original: "rotulis"</note> made of sugar—from half a dram up to 6 drams. 

Similarly, you can give other electuaries alone or mixed with others: when the phlegmatic matter is thicker, for instance, by giving the *benedicta* or the *hiera* of Pacchius, either with the decoction already mentioned or another regarding the thick matter. If you wish to evacuate with pills, these will be of use: Take 1 dram of *cochia* pills and 2 <term>scruples</term> <note>A unit of weight, roughly 1.3 grams.</note> of trochiscated agaric. Let five pills be made, and let them be given five or six hours before a meal, or let others be given according to various intentions; and consider the weakness of the stomach, which is most often present in those who abound in phlegmatic humor: therefore, be mindful...

Of this broth, up to 6 ounces or more is given in the morning six hours before food. It is also effective for those having thick matter in the chest, and for asthmatics, or those breathing with difficulty due to a material, cold cause; it digests and evacuates, as I said, all thick and pituitous matter. 

The broth of an old cock is also given alone when the matter is not so thick, nor the disease so severe; or when the symptoms are of the least malice, such as in light <term>colic</term> <note>Severe abdominal pain often attributed to gas or blockages.</note> from windiness or the retention of feces. # MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

<margin>
If he teaches you to evacuate your phlegm.
</margin>
If you wish to evacuate your **phlegm** <note>original: *pituita*; one of the four bodily humors, traditionally thought to be cold and moist.</note>, first observe that it is generated in two ways: namely, through the **adustion** <note>The "scorching" or overheating of a humor, which changes its physical properties.</note> of phlegm, or through the mixing of a **biliary humor** <note>Yellow bile, the humor associated with heat and choler.</note> with thin phlegm. Therefore, since both conditions possess heat, let the medicine for its evacuation be given in this manner. **Take** 7 drachms each of **flowers of cassia** <note>A mild laxative derived from the pods of the *Cassia fistula* tree.</note> and **lenitive electuary** <note>A standard medicinal paste used as a gentle laxative.</note>. Mix them, and let a **bolus** <note>A large, soft medicinal pill.</note> be made with sugar, or let a **potion** be made with the waters of **chicory** and **fennel**; it should be taken six hours before a meal. Alternatively, let **aloe pills** and **golden pills** <note>original: *pilulae aureae*; a common purgative formula often containing aloe, diapenidion, and other herbs, named for their "golden" value in healing.</note> be given. **Take** 2.5 scruples each of washed aloes and golden pills. Let five pills be made, and let them be administered five or six hours before food. In this case, you can also administer lenitive electuary, as well as electuary of **sebesten** <note>A fruit similar to a plum used to soothe the chest and bowels.</note>, and also of **dates**, and **aggregative pills** <note>original: *pilulae aggregatiuae*; a compound pill designed to purge multiple humors at once.</note> according to the necessity of the matter and the convenience of the patient.

Finally, I shall write down those things that dissolve or evacuate the **melancholic humor** <note>Black bile; the humor associated with the earth element, coldness, and dryness.</note>, after I have first warned you (as I have concerning the other humors) that the melancholic humor is manifold beyond its natural state. That is to say, it may be mixed with other humors, or it may exist alone, or it may be created from different humors through adustion. You will be able to evacuate this with both simple and compound medicines.

<margin>
Selective medicines for evacuating the melancholic humor.
</margin>
The **simples** <note>Individual medicinal ingredients, not yet mixed into a compound.</note> are **hellebore**, **senna**, **epithymum** <note>Dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant highly valued for purging black bile.</note>, black and chebulic **myrobalans** <note>Astringent fruit from India used in various stages of ripeness to treat different humors.</note>, **lapis lazuli** <note>The blue stone, powdered and used as a potent purgative for melancholy.</note>, **Armenian stone**, and similar things. The **compounds**, however, are lenitive electuary, **diasena** <note>A compound primarily made of senna.</note>, **confection of hamech** <note>A famous, complex bitter purgative used specifically for stubborn melancholic diseases.</note>, **Indian electuary**, **Mesue’s decoction of epithymum**, **solutive syrup of apples**, pills of lapis lazuli, **Indian pills**, and pills of **fumitory**, **Arabic pills**, and others similar to these.

If, therefore, the melancholic humor is an overabundance of the **dregs of the blood** <note>A common historical description of natural black bile, which was seen as the thick, sediment-like portion of the blood.</note> which must be evacuated, the medicine is made thus, for example: **Take** 1 drachm of lenitive electuary and 1/2 drachm of diasena. Let a bolus be made from them with sugar, or a drink with **fumitory water** or with a decoction of senna and raisins in water of **borage** or fumitory. Or let such a decoction be made: **Take** 3 drachms of senna pods, 2.5 drachms of raisins, 1.5 drachms of epithymum, 2 drachms each of black and chebulic myrobalans, 10 ounces of whey or distilled water of borage and fumitory. Let them boil until a third part is consumed, and let it be given six hours before food. Or let 2 drachms of fumitory pills or Indian pills be given at least six hours before food.

<margin>
From the adustion of choler.
</margin>
But if the melancholic humor has arisen from the **adustion of choler** <note>The "burning" of yellow bile, which creates a particularly toxic and "burnt" form of black bile.</note>, it must be purged in this way. **Take** 1 drachm of lenitive electuary, 1/2 drachm of diasena, and 4 ounces of the decoction written below. Let a potion be made from them, and let it be administered five hours before food. The decoction shall be as follows: **Take** raisins...

# PART TWO.

[...raisins] <note>The beginning of the word "passularum" (raisins) is on the previous page.</note> 2 ounces, **senna** pods 2 drachms, **Damascus prunes** 6 in number, **yellow myrobalans** <note>A dried plum-like fruit from India, used as a purgative.</note> 2 drachms; **flowers of fumitory**, **borage**, and **bugloss** 1.5 drachms of each; **waters of fumitory** and **chicory** 5 ounces of each. Let them boil until a third part is consumed, and let it be strained. With this liquid, you can dissolve the aforementioned **electuaries** <note>Medicinal pastes made with honey or syrup.</note> up to 4 ounces, as I have said, and you may even take it in a larger quantity, such as 6 ounces; it will be an excellent medicine and a gentle purgative. There are also other medicines that draw out the said **melancholy** <note>The "black bile" humor, thought here to be produced by the "burning" or overheating of other humors.</note>: for example, **Take flowers of cassia** and **lenitive electuary**, 5 ounces of each; **solutive diaprunum** <note>A laxative compound made primarily from prunes.</note> 3 drachms. Let a **bolus** <note>A large pill.</note> be made from them, or let a **potion** be made with the waters of borage and **endive**, either with the above-mentioned decoction made in distilled waters, or with **whey** <note>original: "aqua lactis"; literally "water of milk."</note>. In this decoction you can also infuse 1 drachm of **rhubarb**, since it has the power to draw out **burnt choler** <note>Yellow bile that has become thickened and "scorched" by heat, turning into a form of melancholy.</note> and the melancholy made from it. Or, let the complete decoction of **dodder of thyme** <note>original: "epithymum"; a parasitic vine used to purge black bile.</note> by **Mesuë** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a famous 9th-century Persian physician whose formulas were standard in the Renaissance.</note> be given, up to 6 ounces. Pills are also given for the melancholic humor caused by the burning of choler in this manner: **Take aggregative pills** 1 drachm, **pills of fumitory** half a drachm. Let five pills be made and let them be **gilded** <note>original: "aurentur"; pills were often coated in gold leaf to prevent the patient from tasting the bitter ingredients and to signify high quality.</note>. With them, let a syrup be given as follows: **Take syrup of endive, bugloss, and fumitory**, half an ounce of each; **waters of chicory and borage**, 1.5 ounces of each. Mix them. Or let other pills be given, such as **Indian pills** <note>original: "pilulae Indae"; a specific formula containing myrobalans and other Eastern spices used for melancholy.</note> and the like.

phlegm.
</margin>
If, however, the **melancholic** matter to be evacuated was caused by the **burning of phlegm**, it will be best to provide a medicine that targets the **pituitous humor** <note>Phlegm; the cold and moist humor.</note> along with those things that draw out melancholy, in this manner: **Take raisins** 1 ounce, **senna** and **polypody** <note>A type of fern root used as a mild laxative.</note> 3 drachms of each, **dodder of thyme** 1.5 drachms, **black and chebulic myrobalans** 1 drachm of each; **waters of fumitory and bugloss** 5 ounces of each. Let them boil until a third part is consumed, and let it be given alone, or let **lenitive electuary**, or **electuary of sebesten** or **dates** be dissolved in it. You can also arrange the medicine thus: **Take lenitive electuary** 1 ounce, **Indian electuary** 3 drachms, and a sufficient quantity of the above-written decoction. Mix them and let a **potion** be made. The **confection Hamech** <note>A complex, strong purgative specifically used for stubborn melancholic diseases.</note> and the **Indian electuary** are also effective. **Rooster broth** <note>original: "ius galli"; a common base for medicinal drinks, thought to be highly nutritious and easy to digest.</note> boiled with dodder of thyme, senna, and polypody, etc., also purges melancholy caused by the burning of phlegm. There are also **golden pills**, which are called **pills of turpeth** <note>A root related to the morning glory, used as a powerful purgative.</note>; these, together with **Indian pills** or **pills of lapis lazuli** <note>The gemstone was ground and used in pills specifically to treat deep melancholy and depression.</note>, can purge this matter. **Indian pills** given alone or with others also draw out this matter, which can be prepared thus: **Take Indian pills** 1 drachm, **golden pills** half a drachm; let pills be made...

# LETTERS ON MEDICINE BY NICOLÒ MASSA

...five, and let them be administered as has been said. Melancholy caused by the **scorching** <note>original: "adustionem." In medieval medicine, "burning" or "scorching" occurred when a humor was overheated, causing it to thicken and become toxic.</note> of fecal melancholy <note>Refers to the thick, sediment-like part of the black bile humor.</note> can be purged in this way: **Take 1 drachm of Nicolò’s senna-confection, half a drachm of lenitive electuary** <note>A medicinal paste used as a mild laxative.</note>. Mix them, and let a **bolus** <note>A large medicinal pill.</note> be made with sugar, or let a **potion** be made with a decoction of **fumitory, borage, bugloss**, and **dodder of thyme** in **whey** <note>original: "aqua casei"; literally "cheese water."</note>. Let the potion be made and taken five hours before food; or let a decoction of **senna** and **dodder of thyme** with raisins be given in borage water. The **Indian pills** are also suitable, as well as the others mentioned above made from **lapis lazuli** and **Armenian stone**, and similar ones.

<margin>From the burning of blood.</margin>
Furthermore, the melancholic humor which is produced by the **burning of the blood** should be purged with light medicines that cleanse the blood; for instance, with this or another similar medicine. **Take 1 drachm of flowers of cassia, half a drachm of senna-confection**; mix them, and let a bolus be made with sugar, or let a potion be made with this decoction: **Take 1 drachm of raisins; 2 drachms each of tamarinds and licorice; 1 drachm each of the flowers of fumitory, borage, bugloss, and hops; 4 drachms each of the waters of maidenhair fern and spleenwort**. Let them boil until a third part has evaporated, with which the aforementioned potion should be made, to be taken five hours before food. Or, let **diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" laxative electuary used to purge all humors.</note> be given with a common decoction; and to sum everything up in a single word, all light medicines that cleanse the blood are excellent in this case, whether they are simple or compound.

<margin>On evacuating the melancholic humor when mixed with others.</margin>
When, however, the melancholic matter is mixed with other humors, the cure is to evacuate both matters using permitted medicines that are effective for purging one and the other. For example, if the melancholic humor is mixed with **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita." One of the four primary bodily fluids.</note>, let there be given along with the medicine that purges melancholy: **electuary of dates**, or **diaturbith** <note>A purgative made from the root of the Turpeth plant.</note>, or **violet lozenges** without **scammony** <note>A harsh purgative resin; omitting it makes the medicine gentler.</note>, or **agaric** <note>A type of mushroom used as a laxative.</note>, and similar things. If it is mixed with **bilious humor** <note>Yellow bile.</note>, let there be added **cassia, tamarinds, rhubarb, manna, Mesuë’s rose-scented prune electuary** <note>referring to a popular recipe by the physician known as Pseudo-Mesuë.</note>, and the like. If it is mixed with blood, let medicines that cleanse the blood be added (as I said a little above), such as **fumitory, borage, hops, maidenhair fern, manna, cassia, tamarinds**, and similar ones, etc. But the best cleansing and evacuation of the blood—if there is a mixture with the melancholic humor—is to **open a vein** <note>Phlebotomy or bloodletting.</note> and let blood. I say this is the reasoning in a case where you have cut the **liver vein** <note>original: "uena iecoraria"; specifically the basilic vein of the arm, traditionally associated with the liver.</note> of the right or left arm and drawn blood. However, while the vein is cut, if the blood comes out clear and thin, it is better to stop that evacuation and draw very little blood; and thus in this case it is best...

# PART SECOND.

...you will work best: indeed, you will do even better if such patients have innate **hemorrhoids**, to open them and draw blood from them to the extent that the patient can tolerate. This opening is performed through the application of **leeches**, or by opening them with a cutting instrument <note>In Galenic medicine, hemorrhoids were seen as a natural safety valve for "melancholic blood." If they were natural to the patient, doctors often reopened them to relieve pressure.</note>. And these instructions regarding medicines that prepare, alter, and evacuate each humor through substances taken by mouth shall be sufficient for you. But so that other modes of evacuation do not fail you when the situation requires them, I will also write the method for **evacuations** which physicians are accustomed to perform through **clysters** <term>clyster: a liquid injected into the rectum; an enema</term> inserted through the anus to draw out the waste of the intestines. You will find this operation praiseworthy; it is useful and, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university text.</note> used to say, it is highly favored. <margin>He teaches how to prepare clysters for various purposes.</margin> Therefore, different clysters are administered according to the variety of conditions that are "against nature," and according to the causes of the humors that are offending or in excess within them.

Therefore, if you wish to soothe the intestines and draw out their waste, use a **common clyster**, which you shall prepare in this manner: **Take a handful each of the leaves of mallow, violets, blite, and mercury herb** <note>original: "mercurialis"; refers to the herb *Mercurialis annua*, used as a laxative.</note>. Let them boil in fresh water; then take **one pound** (or one and a half pounds) of this decoction; **4 ounces of common oil; 3 ounces of red sugar; 2 drachms of common salt; and the yolk of one egg.** Mix them, and let it be administered warm.

But if, in addition to common feces, you wish to draw out **phlegmatic** <note>original: "pituitosam." In the four humors system, pituita (phlegm) was cold and moist.</note> matter existing in the intestines, you shall arrange the clyster thus: **Take a handful each of the leaves of mallow, blite, cabbage, betony, centaury, chamomile flowers, and dill.** Let them boil in common water. From this decoction take **one pound** (or one and a half pounds); **4 ounces of chamomile oil; 3 ounces of honey of roses; 2 drachms of common salt; and the yolk of one egg.** Mix them and let it be administered.

And if you desire a greater power for softening the bowels and drawing out matter, you can add these **electuaries** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term>: **Take 6 drachms each of lenitive electuary and electuary of dates.** Mix them and add them to the aforementioned clyster. Many other electuaries are also effective for this if added; primarily **cassia**, which is prepared for clysters; **hiera picra** <note>original: "hiera picra," literally "holy bitter." A famous ancient purgative made of aloes and other herbs.</note>, which also evacuates very well; and **electuary of sebesten** <note>A fruit-based laxative using the *Cordia myxa* fruit.</note>, and others.

Truly, if you wish to evacuate **bilious matter** <note>Yellow bile.</note> from the intestines in addition to common feces by means of a clyster, you shall do it thus: **Take a handful each of the leaves of mallow, violets, blite, and barley.** Let them boil in fresh water. Then take **one pound** (or one and a half pounds) of this decoction; **4 ounces of violet oil; 3 ounces of red sugar; 2 drachms of common salt; and the yolk of one egg.** Mix them and let it be inserted. If you desire a greater effect...

...[scour] the intestines, add one **dram** <note>A dram (ʒ) is a unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce.</note> of **cassia** <note>original: cassiæ; the pulp of the "pudding-pipe tree," used as a mild laxative.</note> prepared for a clyster. However, when you wish to evacuate the **melancholic humor** <note>In the Galenic system, "melancholy" or black bile was a cold, dry humor that needed to be softened before purging.</note> existing in the intestines in addition to the feces, let a clyster be made in this way:

**Take a handful each of the leaves of mallow, violets, borage, fumitory, and blite**; let them boil in common water. Then, **take one pound, or one and a half pounds, of the said decoction, four ounces of sweet almond oil, three drams of red sugar, one and a half drams of common salt, and one ounce of lenitive electuary** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term>. Mix these together and let it be administered. But if you desire stronger clysters, add also half a dram of the **Diaphoenicon of Nicolaus** <note>original: diaphenæ Nicolai; a standard purgative made from dates, from the influential "Antidotarium" of Nicolaus Salernitanus.</note> or the **sebesten** <note>A fruit similar to a plum, used for its mucilaginous properties.</note> of **Montagnana** <note>Referring to Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. 1460), a famous professor of medicine at Padua.</note>; in which case, the prepared cassia for clysters is also effective.

<margin>A noteworthy instruction.</margin>
Be mindful, however, when drawing out melancholic wastes, to abstain from **drying agents** and those that are excessively **heating**. Indeed, substances that are soft and moderately warm are suitable. However, if there should be a troublesome **windiness** <note>original: uentositas; gas or flatulence, which was believed to be a "spirit" or vapor that caused pain if trapped.</note> in the intestines that causes pain, let a clyster be made in this way: 

**Take a handful each of the flowers of chamomile and dill, and the leaves of mallow, mercury herb, pellitory-of-the-wall, hyssop, and betony; half a dram each of the seeds of fennel, anise, and cumin; and one small handful of bran.** Let them boil together. Then, **take one or one and a half pounds of the said decoction, two drams each of chamomile oil and dill oil, one dram of "the blessed laxative"** <note>original: benedictæ; likely "Benedicta Laxativa," a famous compound medicine named for its "blessed" effectiveness.</note>, **two drams of common salt, and one egg yolk.** Mix these and let it be applied. 

Nevertheless, if sharp humors are present along with the windiness, one must beware of excessively heating substances. Therefore, in place of the "blessed laxative," the **lenitive electuary** can be used; and in place of dill oil, **sweet almond oil**; and in the decoction, use a larger quantity of **violet leaves**. You shall do similarly for other humors in the intestines when accompanied by windiness. For instance, when there is **glassy phlegm** <note>original: phlegma uitreum; a specific type of thick, cold, and clear mucus thought to resemble molten glass.</note>, add **rue** to the decoction and remove the violets, and in place of chamomile oil, use **rue oil**. Or, in place of the above-written decoction, use **rooster broth** with the ingredients mentioned above, boiling the rue in the broth of the intestines. 

In this manner—by changing the medicines or adding to them according to the diversity of the humor—you shall proceed. Thus, up to this point, you have the method for applying medicines that are **minorative** <note>mildly laxative</note>, **digestive** <note>preparing the humors</note>, and **eradicatively purging**, whether taken from above [by mouth] or administered from below [as a clyster], which can be sufficient for you in general for the partial purging of the humors. But because many diseases and conditions arise from the aforementioned material causes—both in the body as a whole and in the particular parts that constitute the body—we must now discuss how the humors in each individual organ causing a disease are to be regulated, prepared, and purged.

...someone, or those things altering the body **contrary to nature**, and which members ought to be strengthened, I shall subsequently write down for you in order, beginning from the head. <margin>Case study.</margin> And so that I may correctly demonstrate to you the treatment of particular ailments **contrary to nature**; let us imagine a young man, or one in the prime of life, of a **hot and dry temperament**, who indiscriminately consumes everything (as often happens) and errs in the use of other necessary things, so that he suffers in various parts of the body, and at various times, from various diseases or dispositions **contrary to nature**. I shall begin, therefore, by enumerating the ailments and treatments starting from the head. Let this patient, then, call a physician and say that he suffers from a **headache**, and let him indicate that the causes of his illness are **fullness** <note>original: repletionem; a state where the body is overfilled with humors, often blood or digestive waste.</note>, and <margin>On headache and its method of treatment.</margin> let him say the pain is heavy, with heat and tension in the area, from which you will immediately judge that an **ill temperament** <term>ill temperament: an imbalance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that disrupts health</term> along with [excess] matter is the cause of this evil. Therefore, you must think about its removal; so that once the cause is removed, the disease—which is the **ill temperament** in the head—and the symptom—which is the pain—may be removed.

Therefore, beginning first with abstinence from drinking wine and moderation in food, you will begin to evacuate the matter, surely by first administering a **clyster** <note>an enema</note> and then evacuating blood by cutting the **black vein** <note>original: uena nigra; likely referring to the basilic vein in the arm, which was traditionally bled to treat ailments of the head and upper body</note>, unless there should be some contraindication: such as <margin>Soften the belly.</margin> weakness of strength, the time of year (such as the **Dog Days** <note>The hottest days of summer, associated with the rising of the star Sirius, during which physicians were often cautious about invasive procedures</note> and their opposites), or some bodily disposition prohibiting the evacuation of blood. In which case, when it is necessary to evacuate, you will evacuate to the amount of six ounces, <margin>Bloodletting.</margin> more or less, according to your rational and estimative judgment. 

Then the remaining humors should be prepared for easier evacuation with medicines that address the offending matter and the nature of the organs where they reside and from which you wish to draw them away. Since not all things can act upon everything, but a specific thing upon a specific thing, according to the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>A reference to the Aristotelian principle of "proportionality," suggesting that a specific medicine must correspond directly to the nature of the disease</note>. Truly, the medicines that moderate hot and mixed <margin>Preparations regarding matter in the head.</margin> matter and prepare it for evacuation, as we said above, are **chicory, endive, borage, bugloss, water lily, hops**, and the like. While those that specifically concern the head and draw matter from it are **roses, coriander, chicory, betony**, and the like. Those addressing **cold matter** are, for example, **topped lavender** <note>original: stœchas; a species of Mediterranean lavender</note>, **peony, sage, and betony** (which addresses both types of matter), and many others. First, therefore, if the patient has an abundance of other humors in addition to an abundance of blood, especially **choleric** <note>humors related to yellow bile, associated with heat and irritability</note> humors, then...

NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

<margin>When "lessening" medicines should be used at the beginning.</margin>
When you fear a sudden rush of humors to the head, you should take care to draw them away with some mild "lessening" medicine <term>minorative: a gentle laxative intended to reduce the volume of humors without causing a violent reaction</term>, for example: Take 12 drams of flowers of cassia <note>cassia: a tropical plant pulp used as a mild laxative</note>. Let a bolus <note>bolus: a soft, round medicinal mass, like a large pill</note> be made from it with sugar, or a drink with chicory and betony waters. Give this an hour before eating, as I said: because when medicines are mild—such as cassia, manna, or laxative syrup of roses—they can easily be overcome by the heat of the stomach, so that they might be altered and fail to work. Also, because they are not among those medicines that draw humors from distant parts of the body, they do not require a long time to pull matter from afar; therefore, when food is taken shortly after, they purge the matter of the intestines and nearby parts.

<margin>He teaches about syrups that prepare the matter.</margin>
After this "lessening" <note>original: minorationem</note>, it will be worthwhile to prepare the rest of the matter for a "root-clearing" evacuation <term>eradicative evacuation: a stronger purge meant to completely remove the cause of an illness</term>. You will do this by giving syrups in this way: Take 1 ounce of syrup of endive, half an ounce of syrup of roses, 2 ounces of chicory water, and 1 ounce of betony water. Mix them, and let them be given in the morning until signs of the "digestion" of the matter appear in the urine <term>concoction: the process where the body's internal heat "ripens" or prepares an excess humor so it can be expelled</term>. When these signs appear, you shall evacuate the rest of the matter in this way:

<margin>Remedies for drawing out choleric matter.</margin>
Take 1 ounce of flowers of cassia and 2 drams of the rose electuary <note>electuary: a medicinal paste made of powders mixed with honey or syrup</note> of Mesuë <note>Johannes Mesuë: a widely cited medieval Arabic medical authority</note>. Mix, and let a bolus be made with sugar, or a drink with chicory and betony waters. You can also give pills in this way: Take 1 and a half drams of "Golden Pills" <note>pilularum aurearum: a famous recipe for purgative pills, often containing aloes</note>. Let five pills be made and gilded <note>original: aurentur; pills were often coated in gold leaf to hide the taste or signify luxury</note>, and let them be given five hours before food. Or let "Aggregative Pills" be given, or "Pills Without Which" <note>original: sine quibus; a common name for a general-purpose laxative pill</note>, or "Pills of Three" with rhubarb.

<margin>Soothing remedies for cold humors.</margin>
But if there is an abundance or "malice" of **cold humors** <note>phlegm or black bile</note> alongside the headache or injury, the matter should be lessened with a soothing electuary or one made of sebesten <note>sebesten: a plum-like fruit used to soothe the chest and move the bowels</note>, for example: Take 1 ounce of soothing electuary and 3 drams of sebesten. Mix, and let a bolus be made with sugar, or a drink with betony water.

<margin>A syrup to prepare cold matter.</margin>
Then, let the rest of the matter be prepared in this way: Take 1 ounce of honey of roses, half an ounce of syrup of betony, and one and a half ounces each of hop water and scabious water. Mix and give them warm in the morning. Or give syrups of bugloss and fumitory if the matter is **melancholic** <note>black bile</note>, and do this until signs of concoction appear in the urine.

<margin>Medicines to evacuate cold matter.</margin>
When these signs appear, let evacuating medicines be given in this way: Take 1 ounce of soothing electuary, half an ounce of electuary of dates <note>original: de dactylis</note>, 1 ounce of laxative syrup of roses, and enough betony water. Mix, and let a drink be made; it should be taken five hours before food. But if you wish to evacuate mixed melancholic matter, let it be given in this way: Take 1 ounce of soothing electuary and half an ounce of "diaphoenicon" <note>original: diaphēnæ; a purging paste made primarily from dates</note>. Mix and let a bolus be made with sugar; or let a drink be made with a decoction of senna and raisins; or let pills be given, in this way:

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Massa’s instructions for purging humors. ## SECOND PART

Take of golden pills <note>original: "pilularum aurearum"; a standard purgative of the era, so named for its value or perhaps its color</note>, aggregative pills, and Indian pills, half a dram of each; let five pills be made and given. Or let *cochiae* pills <note>pills specifically formulated to purge the head</note> be given, as well as others, even for other remaining parts of the head and for conditions of the throat or jaws. These may be given alone or with the appropriate decoction <term>apozem: a medicinal decoction or concentrated infusion</term> or syrup written above, so that you always have a medicine that addresses the humors to be evacuated and the locations or members from which it is necessary to evacuate. Indeed, in medicines (according to Galen in his book *On Simple Medicine*), there are powers <note>original: "uirtutes"</note> derived from the forms of their component elements, through which they are called hot, cold, moist, or dry; these are called the primary powers.

<margin>The powers in medicines are threefold.</margin>
There is also a second power in them, which depends on those primary ones mentioned, through which they work by thinning, resolving, drawing, drying, relaxing, and performing similar operations. And there is a third power which regards the specific humor, so that it purges that humor first. An example is found in rhubarb <note>original: "rhabarbaro"</note>, which by its second power opens obstructions of the liver and purges bile <note>original: "cholera": yellow bile, one of the four humors</note>. But by its third power, it draws bile out from the liver more than from other parts. Rose, however, purges bile specifically from the head; and thus these powers appear in many other simple and compound medicines. For hermodactyl <note>likely a species of Colchicum, used for joint pain</note>, besides the fact that it leads out phlegm <gloss>original: "pituita"</gloss>, also has the faculty of evacuating it from the joints, as you will see in the progression of the disease, both in the middle belly <note>the chest or thorax</note> as well as the lower belly and other extremity parts. Having seen, therefore, the way of proceeding in conditions contrary to nature—both hot and cold—in the head or upper belly, and their parts, let us move to the manner of curing conditions contrary to nature in the middle belly, or the chest, whether hot or cold, where matter descends.

<margin>Concerning medicines regarding the chest.</margin>
And first, I want you to know that the medicines which regard the chest are some simple and some compound. The simples are such as: violets, coltsfoot or *farfara*, licorice, raisins, maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillus Veneris"</note>, hyssop, scabious, pine nuts, almonds, fox lung <note>a traditional remedy for breathing, based on the belief that the fox's long-windedness could be transferred to the patient</note>, and the like; also manna, agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, cassia, iris <note>original: "ireos"</note>, colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>, and similar things. The compounds, however, are: syrup of violets (both simple and compound), syrup of licorice, of maidenhair fern, of lungwort, of hyssop, of horehound <note>original: "prassio"</note>, and the like. The dissolving medicines <note>purgatives</note> are: *diacassia*, electuary of sebesten <note>a plum-like fruit</note>, *diasenna*, prepared or trochisced agaric, *hiera pacchii* <note>a holy bitter medicine</note>, pills of agaric of Mesue <note>referring to the influential physician Masawaih al-Mardini</note>, and others of that kind.

<margin>A case in which the chest is diseased and cured.</margin>
Let us suppose again that the aforementioned young man has fallen into a condition contrary to nature—specifically a hot condition of the chest involving matter. He must be helped with its contraries. First, a dietary regimen should be established.

# NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

<margin>
Dietary regimen.
</margin>
The dietary regimen involves abstinence from meat and wine. If there are signs showing a dominance of blood, and there are no contraindications, you should not hesitate to let blood <note>original: "sanguinem mittere"; a common practice to balance the humors</note>. Then, you shall reduce the <margin>Phlebotomy.</margin> matter with a soothing <term>lenitive: a mild laxative or soothing medicine</term> medicine, ordering it in this way: Take one and a half ounces <note>original: "℥.i.s."</note> of cassia <term>cassia: the pulp of the purging cassia pod, used as a gentle laxative</term> flowers, newly extracted through a sieve, or less as the situation requires. Let a bolus be made with sugar, or a drink be made with a pectoral <note>chest-related</note> decoction, ordering it thus: Take raisins, licorice, and barley, half an ounce of each; two drams <note>original: "ʒ. ii."</note> of violet flowers; twelve jujubes <note>a date-like fruit used for coughs</note>; ten sebestens <note>a plum-like fruit from the Middle East used as an expectorant</note>; four ounces each of violet and coltsfoot <note>original: "farfaræ"</note> waters. Let them boil and be strained; with <margin>Lenitives for hot matter given in various ways.</margin> this strained liquid, you shall dissolve the above-written cassia. Or let it be dissolved with the waters of violets and maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillorum Veneris"</note> and be made into a drink, to be taken one or two hours before food. Then, syrups should be given to prepare the rest of the matter in this way: Take one ounce of violet syrup, half a dram of licorice, and one dram each of the waters of coltsfoot, scabious <note>a plant often used for skin and chest ailments</note>, and maidenhair <margin>Syrups preparing hot matter.</margin> fern. Mix them, and let it be given in the morning five hours before food for several days—specifically until signs of concoction <note>the "ripening" or processing of humors by the body’s heat</note> appear in the urine. When these signs appear, medicines should be given to evacuate the rest of the matter, thus: Take one ounce of cassia flowers, two drams of prepared agaric <note>original: "agarici"; a wood-rotting fungus used as a potent purgative</note>, <margin>An evacuative.</margin> half an ounce of simple oxymel <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>, and a sufficient amount of the pectoral decoction described above. Let a potion be made from these, to be taken five or six hours before food. And since agaric, by its lightness, often evaporates toward the upper parts and provokes vomiting, if the patient <margin>He prescribes sleep after taking agaric.</margin> sleeps for one or two hours after taking it, it will descend to the bottom of the stomach, and that desire to vomit or that nausea will cease. If, however, the matter in the chest or its parts is thick, as often happens, let this be given as a reducing medicine: Take one ounce of cassia flowers, four drams of electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note> of sebesten (not fully prepared), more or <margin>For thick hot matter.</margin> less according to the strength of the sick person and the responsiveness of the bowels. Mix them and let a bolus be made with sugar, or a potion with this decoction: Take half an ounce each of raisins, barley, and licorice; ten sebestens; three drams of marshmallow seeds; half a handful of hyssop; and four drams each of the waters of maidenhair fern and scabious. Let a decoction be made, in which the cassia and the electuary are dissolved, and let it be taken in the morning five hours before food. Then, for several days after, syrups should be given in this way: Take half a dram of licorice syrup, one dram of compound violet syrup, and one and a half drams each of the waters of maidenhair fern and scabious. Or, if the matter is very thick, let such a syrup be given: <margin>For thicker matter.</margin> Take one dram of compound violet syrup, half a dram of hyssop syrup, and where you wish to "cut" <note>to break down or thin thick humors</note> the matter, add half a dram of oxymel and scabious water...

# SECOND PART.

<margin>
In conditions / of the / chest.
</margin>
...scabious and hyssop, one and a half ounces <note>original: "℥. i. s."</note> of each, and let it be given. However, in conditions of the chest, beware of vinegar and compounds made with vinegar, because by its coldness and dryness it causes harm, and sometimes does not allow one to cough up phlegm. Once the preparation is complete—which you will recognize by the improved quality of the sputum <note>phlegm coughed up from the lungs</note> and also by the "concoction" <note>the process of the body "ripening" or processing a diseased humor</note> of the urine—you shall purge again with this medicine: *Take* five drams <note>original: "ʒ. v."</note> each of cassia flowers and incomplete electuary of sebesten <note>a fruit-based medicinal paste</note>; two drams of prepared agaric <term>agaric: a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</term>; half a dram of simple <term>oxymel: a mixture of honey and vinegar, used here to cut through thick phlegm despite the general warning against vinegar</term>; and as much of the above-written decoction as is sufficient. Let a potion be made from these, and let it be taken five or six hours before a meal.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>
*Note, however,* that according to the opinion of Galen, Avicenna, and all the illustrious doctors, in diseases stemming from thick matter <note>original: "materia crassa"; viscous or heavy humors like thick phlegm</note>, or those mixed with it, we can rarely eradicate that matter with a single evacuation. Therefore, the <margin>A rule / for diseases / stemming / from / thick / matter.</margin> rule in such cases is to prepare it gradually, and to draw it out gradually and in several stages. Reason also dictates this, since thick matter can only be prepared for evacuation with difficulty and over a period of time. Therefore, the preparing medicines—such as syrups and decoctions—must be repeated, as must the evacuating <note>purgative</note> medicines; in this way, you will be able to evacuate the whole of the matter.

Finally, we must speak of the conditions of the lower belly, its matter, and its parts; I shall begin with the stomach and the intestines. Medicines that benefit the stomach (just as has been said for other organs) <margin>On medicines / benefiting / the / stomach.</margin> are both simple and compound, and also hot, cold, or dominant in other qualities.

**Simple medicines** are such as roses, chicory, sorrel, wild grape, coriander, coral, mint, wormwood, fennel, mastic, cinnamon, clove, ginger, myrobalans <note>dried plum-like fruits used as a tonic or laxative</note>, rhubarb, aloes, and the like.

**Compound medicines** include <term>diacatholicon: a "universal" mild purgative</term>, <term>hiera tryphera: a "holy" delicate herbal electuary</term>, <term>diaphoenicon: a purgative made from dates</term>, aloe pills infused with rhubarb, "of three" with rhubarb <note>a specific compound pill</note>, mastic pills, pills of *hiera*, <term>alephangine: fragrant "aloe-refined" pills for the stomach</term>, and the like.

For example, if there is some bad condition in the stomach with "hot" matter, let an evacuative be given thus: <margin>Evacuative / for hot / matter.</margin> *Take* one dram of diacatholicon and one and a half drams of the species <note>powdered ingredients</note> of *hiera*; mix them, and let a bolus be made with sugar, or let a potion be made with chicory water, to be taken four hours before a meal. Then, let syrups be given in this manner: *Take* one ounce of rose syrup, half an ounce of chicory syrup, and one and a half drams each of hop and sorrel waters. Mix and administer in the morning, five hours before a meal, until signs of concoction appear. Afterward, you shall evacuate the remaining matter thus: <margin>Evacuation / of the / same.</margin> *Take* one ounce of diacatholicon, two drams of dates <note>referring to the diaphoenicon electuary</note>, and one and a half drams of the species of *hiera*. <margin>Concerning those things applied to the body from the outside.</margin>
It remains for me to turn my discourse to that category of medicines applied externally to various limbs and for various conditions contrary to nature, beginning from the head. Therefore, if there is a "hot" illness <note>in humoral medicine, illnesses were classified as hot, cold, moist, or dry</note> in the head, and it has not been removed after the aforementioned evacuation [of humors], let local remedies be applied, first shaving the hair down to the skin; command that the head be anointed with oil of roses

<margin>Applications for the head in a hot condition.</margin>
several times: but if it does not help, let an *oxyrrhodinum* <note>original: "oxyrhodinum"; a traditional cooling mixture of vinegar and rose oil</note> be made in this way. Take three ounces <term>℥.iii.</term> of rose oil, two ounces <term>℥.ii.</term> of rose water, and one ounce <term>℥.i.</term> of white vinegar; mix them, and let them be shaken together in a flask until they are incorporated as well as possible, and let it be applied to the head with a fine linen cloth frequently moistened:

<margin>An Ointment.</margin>
or let an anointing be done with this liniment: Take one ounce <term>℥.i.</term> of Mesue’s rose ointment <note>referring to a standard formula by the influential physician Mesue the Younger</note>, half an ounce <term>℥.s.</term> of violet or water-lily oil <note>original: "nenupharinum"</note>; mix, and let the head be frequently anointed with it, or take equal parts <note>original: "an. partes æquales"</note> of lettuce juice and violet juice with rose oil, and let a fine linen cloth be frequently moistened and applied to the head.

<margin>To induce sleep.</margin>
But if the patient does not sleep, let the temples and nostrils be anointed with *populeon* ointment <note>an ointment made from poplar buds used as a sedative</note> and water-lily oil, and let washes be made for the legs and arms, especially in cases of extreme pain, in this manner.

<margin>Washes. Rubs. Cupping. Enemas. For delirium.</margin>
Take two handfuls <term>m. ii.</term> each <term>an.</term> of violet flowers, mallow, lettuce, willow, water-lily leaves, white poppy bark, and mandrake roots. Let them boil in spring or well water; with this decoction, while moderately warm, let the legs and arms be washed: because this diverts [the humors] from the head, and also lessens the scorching heat, and induces sleep. Let rubs <note>original: "frictiones"</note> be performed on the legs, arms, and other parts: let cupping glasses <note>original: "curbitulæ"</note> be applied both with and without scarification <note>the practice of scratching the skin before cupping to draw blood</note> to divert or draw the matter elsewhere. Let enemas <note>original: "clysteria"</note> or suppositories be made to draw out the matter through the stool. If there are indeed alienations of mind or delirium, let leeches <note>original: "sanguisugæ"</note> be applied behind the ears, or let a vein in the forehead or nostrils be opened: so that the blood may flow out according to what the patient’s strength can tolerate; in such cases, this is the ultimate and proven remedy.

<margin>In a cold condition. Evacuations.</margin>
But if the disease is "cold," and arises from a cold cause with [excessive] matter, once the evacuations have been performed, let local medicines be applied to the head thus: Take chamomile oil...

# PART TWO

<margin>Anointing</margin>
Take ointment of lilies, nard, of each half a drachm <term>ʒ.s.</term>, powdered lavender <note>original: "stœchados"</note>, marjoram, of each half a drachm <term>ʒ.s.</term>, and a little wax; mix them. Anoint the head with this, the hair having first been shaven, or let a rose-vinegar mixture <note>original: "oxyrhodinū"</note> be made in this way: Take one ounce <term>unc. i.</term> of chamomile oil, and half an ounce <term>unc. s.</term> each of nard and rose oil, and two ounces <term>unc. ii.</term> of vinegar. Mix and let them be shaken together until the best possible mixture is formed, with which you should anoint the head; or let a linen cloth soaked in it be placed frequently upon the warm head. Or let a warm compress <note>original: "fomentum"</note> be made thus: Take flowers of betony, lavender, chamomile, calamint, and marjoram, one and a half handfuls <term>m. i. s.</term> of each. Let them boil in common water; with this decoction, and a linen cloth soaked in it, let the head be bathed. In all of these, something stronger and "warmer" can be added to invigorate their power, such as labdanum <note>a resin from rockrose</note>, castoreum <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, or euphorbium <note>a potent plant resin</note>; however, I do not recommend this last one except in the most desperate cases.

<margin>Note. Blistering agents.</margin>
Blistering agents <note>original: "vesicatoria"; substances used to intentionally cause blisters to draw out "corrupt" humors</note> can also be applied over the coronal suture <note>the joint between the frontal and parietal bones of the skull</note>, using Spanish flies <note>original: "cantharidibus"; toxic beetles used as a skin irritant</note> and leaven in this way: Take four drachms <term>drach. iiii.</term> of Spanish flies (with the wings and heads removed), one ounce <term>unc. i.</term> of leaven, and as much vinegar as is sufficient. Let a soft ointment be made and placed upon the site.

<margin>Cauteries.</margin>
Furthermore, for long-standing pains, cauteries <note>the application of hot irons or caustic chemicals to the skin</note> are performed over the coronal suture, which is the final remedy. But before these stronger remedies are applied, let cupping glasses be used without scarification <note>suctioning the skin without cutting it</note> on the shoulder blades, after first performing rubbing treatments on the legs, arms, and back.

<margin>Compresses.</margin>
There are some, however, who by frequently applying compresses to the aching head, dissolve the matter causing the pain and change the "bad temperature" <note>an imbalance of the four humors</note> in this way: Take two handfuls <term>m. ii.</term> each of millet and common salt, and one pound <term>l. i.</term> each of fragrant white wine and brandy <note>original: "aqua uitæ"; literally "water of life," referring to distilled spirits</note>. Let them boil together, and with a linen cloth soaked in it, let the area be bathed many times a day. They also make a small bag filled with salt, millet, chamomile flowers, and mint, and place it warm over the site of the pain. Also, the juice of mint alone, if a linen cloth is frequently soaked in it and applied, heals headaches caused by "cold" matter.

<margin>Cure for deep sleep through scents.</margin>
In cases of deep sleep <note>lethargy or loss of consciousness</note>, let scents be made and applied to the nostrils in this way: Take half a handful <term>m. s.</term> each of wild thyme and spikenard; let them boil in vinegar and be applied to the nostrils. <insert>Take half a handful each of wild thyme and spikenard; let them boil in vinegar and let it be applied warm to the nostrils</insert>, into which you may add a portion of castoreum.

<margin>Chewing remedies.</margin>
Head-purgatives <note>original: "caputpurgia"</note> and chewing remedies <note>original: "masticatoria"</note> are also prepared. Indeed, it is good to chew mastic <note>a resin from the pistachio tree</note> in the morning, for they cleanse the brain of phlegmatic superfluities. You can also make a chewing remedy from the seeds of stavesacre <note>original: "staphisagriæ"; a type of larkspur</note>, mastic, and wax mixed together; or it may be drawn up through the nostrils as a head-purgative.

<margin>Head-purgatives.</margin>
Take equal parts of the juice of beet and marjoram. Also the use of theriac <note>a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all"</note> and Mithri- <note>referring to Mithridatium, another complex medicinal paste</note>

<margin>Lye made from decocted medicines.</margin>
which these simple herbs have been boiled is most effective. <margin>Beneficial for vertigo and blurred vision.</margin>
The aforementioned medicines are also effective for dizziness <term>vertiginem</term> or blurred vision <term>scotomiam</term> if the condition is long-standing.

<margin>Remedies for the throat and gullet in hot conditions.</margin>
Local medicines for the throat and gullet are appropriate for "hot" discharges <note>the theory of "humors" classified illnesses as hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>, such as houseleek <note>original: "semper uiua"</note> with butter heated by the fire and applied externally. The juice of nightshade <note>original: "solatri"</note> is also effective, and if the area is anointed with violet oil, it is useful for both hot and cold matter. Purging cassia <term>cassia fistularis</term> dissolved with rose oil is used for hot conditions, and with chamomile oil for cold conditions if applied externally in the manner of a plaster. For hot conditions, they make gargles from barley water and mulberry syrup <term>diamorone</term>, or pomegranate wine, or the juice of unripe grapes. Egg whites mixed with rose water are wonderfully effective. In cold conditions, let a wash or gargle be made with a decoction of barley with its husk, raisins, and licorice, into which a portion of oxymel <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note> should be placed.

<margin>Local remedies to be applied to the chest.</margin>
Local medicines that assist with conditions of the chest should be applied according to the diversity of the condition, whether in hot or cold qualities.

<margin>Electuaries <note>medicines meant to be licked or dissolved in the mouth</note>.</margin>
In a hot condition, let syrup of violets be given to be licked with coltsfoot water <note>original: "aqua farfaræ"</note>, or let a decoction be made from jujubes, barley, coltsfoot, and white sugar candy, from which the patient should lick frequently.

<margin>Saponea <note>a thick, syrupy lozenge</note>.</margin>
Or let a *saponea* be made with water of violet flowers.

<margin>Ointments.</margin>
And let the chest be anointed with this ointment: Take one ounce <term>unc. i.</term> of violet oil, and half an ounce <term>unc. s.</term> each of sweet almond oil, fresh chicken fat, and fresh butter. Mix them, and with this, anoint the external parts of the chest; or let it be anointed with the pectoral ointment that is usually prepared by the apothecaries.

<margin>In a cold cause.</margin>
If, however, the condition arises from a cold cause, let a compound syrup of violets be given to be licked, made with maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillis Veneris"</note>. And where the matter is very thick, let syrup of hyssop, syrup of horehound <note>original: "prassio"</note>, and the like be given, such as a healthy and proven *loch* <note>an electuary</note> or syrup of pine. Let an external anointing be done in this way: Take one ounce <term>unc. i.</term> each of sweet almond oil, oil of white lilies, and chicken fat, and half an ounce <term>unc. s.</term> each of marshmallow mucilage and linseed. Mix them.

<margin>Compresses.</margin>
But if the heart should suffer, whether with fever or without fever, let local remedies be prepared thus. And first, a compress <term>epithema</term> for a hot cause: Take four ounces <term>unc. iiii.</term> each of rose water, sorrel water, and borage water; half an ounce <term>unc. s.</term> each of aromatic wine and white vinegar; one and a half drachms <term>ʒ. i. s.</term> of tempered cordial spices; and red coral and sandalwood...
