If the stomach suffers from a bad hot disposition, and the evacuations of the materials causing or fueling it have already taken place, let this inunction <note>an ointment or oil rubbed into the skin</note> be made.
<margin>Ointments for the stomach.</margin>
Take one ounce of finished rose oil, half an ounce of myrtle oil, three drams <note>original: "drach.iii."</note> of rose juice, and one dram each <note>original: "an.drach.i."; "an." or "ana" means equal parts of each</note> of prepared red corals, sandalwood, roses, flowers of wild vine <note>original: "labruscae"</note>, and prepared coriander. Mix with a little wax and let an ointment be made, with which the region of the stomach should be anointed before eating. Or, use the customary stomach ointment, or let an epithem <term>epithema</term> <note>a topical liquid medicine or poultice applied with a cloth</note> be made in this manner.
<margin>Epithems.</margin>
Take one handful <note>original: "m.i."; "m." stands for "manipulus"</note> each of red roses, sandalwood, chicory, wild vine, and coriander; let them boil in water, and in that decoction let a linen cloth be soaked and applied over the region of the stomach. Let an epithem also be made thus: Take five ounces each of pure rose juice and chicory juice, one dram of the species of "Abbot’s Rose" <note>original: "diarrhodonis Abbatis"; a famous rose-based medicinal powder</note>, half a dram of the three sandalwoods, and two scruples <note>original: "℈.ii."</note> of red corals.
<margin>Sachet.</margin>
Mix these, and apply with a linen cloth as has been said; or let a sachet <note>original: "sacculus"; a small bag filled with dry medicinal herbs</note> be made thus: Take two drams each of red roses, all the sandalwoods, flowers of wild vine, and prepared coriander. Let them be powdered and placed in a linen sachet and applied to the stomach, having first warmed it by sprinkling it with warm rose water. Let confections <term>confectiones</term> <note>medicinal sweets or electuaries</note> also be given, such as "Abbot’s Rose," quince honey <note>original: "diacytoniton"</note>, rose sugar, and similar things.
<margin>Confections for hot matter.</margin>
If, however, the stomach should suffer from a cold cause, let it be anointed with mastic oil and oil of wormwood <note>original: "absinthio"</note> mixed together, or let an oil be prepared in this way: Take four ounces of bitter almond oil, three ounces of aromatic wine, one handful of finely cut wormwood, and half a handful of chicory. Let them boil until the wine is consumed, and once the infusion is strained, let the region of the stomach be anointed. Or use this liniment: Take half a dram each of oils of wormwood, mastic, mint, and spikenard <note>original: "de spica"</note>; one dram of the species of "rose aromatics" <note>original: "aromatici rosati"</note>; and one scruple each of cloves, cinnamon, and mace. Or let a fomentation <term>fomentum</term> <note>a warm, moist medicinal application</note> be made in this manner: Take half a handful each of wormwood, mint, and pennyroyal <note>original: "pulegii"</note>; one dram each of spikenard, camel grass <note>original: "schœnanthi"</note>, galangal, and aromatic sweet flag <note>original: "calami aromatici"</note>; half a dram of cloves; and three drams of coriander. Let them boil in spring water with a fourth part of astringent mountain wine, and with a cloth or a sponge soaked in the warm liquid, let it be applied to the stomach; or place the warm decoction in a bladder and hold it over the stomach. Or let a sachet be made in this manner: Take half an ounce each of mint, wormwood, betony, and pennyroyal; and one and a half drams each of the species of galangal <note>original: "diagalangæ"</note>, cloves, and nutmeg. Mix and crush them all, and place them in a linen sachet, and [apply] to the stomach, with a sprinkling of aromatic wine...

<margin>On the care of conditions of the spleen.</margin>
Know, however, that the frequent use of chicory syrup with rhubarb and wormwood mixed together is of great use in **conditions of the spleen**, since for the most part these are cold, and rarely hot. You shall proceed thus: if the spleen suffers some inflammation from any cause, after universal purgings have been performed and blood has been let from the same left side, let the place be anointed with this liniment.

<margin>Liniment.</margin>

<margin>Confections.</margin>

In a **cold condition**, however, proceed with local applications as follows: *Take one ounce each of caper oil and white lily oil; half an ounce each of spikenard oil and chicken fat; two scruples each of tamarisk flowers and hart’s-tongue fern; one dram each of agnus-castus seeds, fennel, bdellium <note>a fragrant resin</note>, and gum ammoniac. Let them be pulverized and dissolved in vinegar, and from these let a liniment be made.*

Or let **enemas** <term>clysteria</term> be made from a decoction of the leaves of **mallow** <term>maluæ</term>, **water lily** <term>nenupharis</term>, **endive**, **chicory** <term>cichorii</term>, and **mugwort**. From this decoction, take one pound: add **oil of violets** <term>olei uiolati</term> and **sweet almonds** <term>amygdalarum dulcium</term>, one and a half ounces <note>original: "℥. i. s."</note> of each; and for the enema, one drachm <note>original: "ʒ. i."</note> of **cassia** <note>a mild laxative pulp</note> and one egg yolk; mix and apply. This is done because while it remains in the intestines, it works to reduce the heat of the **womb** <term>matrix</term> and to open the mouths of the veins by softening them.

<margin>
On the cure for excessive menstrual flow.
</margin>
But if there should be an excessive flow of blood caused by a "thinning" heat <note>a condition where the blood was thought to become too thin and hot to be contained</note>, besides a cooling and thickening regimen, **cupping glasses** <term>uentosæ</term> should be applied under the breasts without **scarification** <note>cutting the skin</note>. Let bandages or tight bindings be placed on the arms, and anoint the back with an ointment made of **chestnut bark** <term>corticibus castanearum</term> and **unripe rose oil** <term>oleo rosato omphacino</term>. Give confections made from **sandalwood**; and if the flow is too great, let **bdellium** pills <note>original: "pilulæ de bdellio"; a bitter, resinous gum similar to myrrh</note> be given as follows: Take one drachm of bdellium pills; let three pills be made and given five hours before food. ...let this be done. Take of the aromatic compounds **musk gallia** <term>galliæ muscatæ</term> and **musk alipta** <term>aliptæ muscatæ</term> <note>These were complex medieval perfumes used as medicine, often containing musk, ambergris, and aloe wood</note>, one drachm each; of **ladanum** <term>ladani</term> <note>a resin from the rockrose plant</note>, three drachms. Let **suppositories** <term>suppositoria</term> be made from these; let them be attached to a thread and inserted into the **vulva** <term>uuluam</term>. Also, let there be frequent anointing with **oil of white lilies**, **elderberry oil** <term>sambacino</term>, or **oil of rue** <term>rutaceo</term>. This is done because it not only serves to correct an unhealthy cold temperament of the womb, but it also opens its obstructions and encourages the menstrual flow. 

Local remedies can also be prepared in this way: namely, by taking cotton and making from it an oblong shape like an acorn <note>original: "glandem oblongam"; here referring to a pessary or tampon</note>, which you shall then soak in this liniment: Take of elderberry oil, **oil of nard** <term>nardini</term>, and oil of white lilies, one ounce each; a little wax; mix them, and let the coated suppository be placed into the vulva. You may also do the same with this other liniment: Take one drachm of **mercury-herb juice** <note>original: "succus mercurialis"; the herb Mercury, not the metal</note>, half a drachm of **squirting cucumber** <term>cucumeris asinini</term>, three drachms of crushed fat figs, two drachms of **gentian roots**, and two drachms of **dyer’s madder** <term>rubeæ tinctorum</term>. Mix these, and with the mixture anoint the suppository as described above. Or let this liniment be made: Take one and a half drachms of musk gallia and one drachm of elderberry oil; mix, and let a liniment be made with which the **mouth of the womb** <term>os uteri</term> <note>the cervix</note> may be anointed.

<margin>
Scented things must be avoided for the nostrils.
</margin>
Yet take care not to bring these scented medicines near the nostrils, for they are very harmful <note>In early medicine, it was believed the "suffocated" or displaced womb was attracted to sweet smells and repelled by foul ones; sweet smells at the nose were thought to pull the womb upward, causing choking</note>. Instead, let foul and ill-smelling substances be applied to the nose, such as **castor** <term>castoreum</term> <note>a pungent secretion from beavers</note> and **Asafoetida** <term>Asa fœtida</term> <note>a strong-smelling resin sometimes called "devil's dung"</note>. By mouth, let **diagalanga** <note>a warming tonic made of galangal root</note> be given, or pills of Asafoetida, or one or more pills of **galbanum** <term>galbano</term> <note>a bitter resin</note>, in this manner: Take one drachm of galbanum; let one pill be made and given to the woman suffering from **suffocation** <note>original: "præfocatæ"; referring to "suffocation of the womb," a historical term for hysterical symptoms</note>. Or thus: Take one drachm of Asafoetida; let one pill be made and given. Or let pills be made in this way: Take of Asafoetida, castor, and **peony seeds**, one drachm each; let pills be made from these with **motherwort water** <term>aqua matricariæ</term>. Or let these be made: Take of galbanum and castor, one drachm each; peony seeds, half a drachm; let pills be made with motherwort water, and let it be given for harmful "suffocations," and even to those already suffering a seizure.

It now remains for me to turn my discourse toward local remedies for the extremities; and I shall write of the remedies by which you may assist suffering joints. 

<margin>
On local remedies for the joints.
</margin>
And since the joints are sometimes afflicted by an unhealthy hot temperament and sometimes a cold one, if it is by a hot one—which is recognized by redness of the area and sharp pain—the remedies are arranged as follows: Take of **oil of roses** and **oil of violets**, one drachm each; one egg yolk; mix, and with a linen cloth soaked in it, let it be applied often to the painful spot. Or let this liniment be made: Take of oil of roses, oil of violets, and **psyllium mucilage**, half a drachm each; one drachm of fresh butter; mix and anoint the place of pain. Take care, however, that you do not open the **passages** <term>meatus</term> <note>the pores or channels of the body</note> by applying hot things, which might cause more of the harmful matter to descend, or perhaps you might dissolve the thin matter while the thick remains, making the disease more persistent. Nevertheless, in cases of intense pain, you may make a **plaster** <term>emplastrum</term> from barley flour with a decoction of roses and mallow, or a plaster made of breadcrumbs and milk with rose oil, and apply it to the painful place.

In both types of matter, whether hot or cold, at the beginning an anointing of the area with **weasel oil** <term>oleo muſtellino</term> is very useful and greatly mitigates the pain. It is prepared as follows: Take a living weasel and put it in common oil; let it boil until it is thoroughly cooked, then use this to anoint the painful areas.

# MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLO MASSA

...of violets, liverwort, sorrel, scabious, and **fumitory** <term>fumi terræ</term> <note>literally "smoke of the earth," a plant traditionally used for skin disorders and liver health</note>, one handful <term>m. i.</term> of each. Let them boil in fresh water, with which the scabious areas should be washed; then, let them be anointed with this **liniment** <term>linimento</term> <note>a medicated liquid or semi-liquid preparation for rubbing on the skin</note>. 

**Take** <term>Recipe</term> of turpentine and butter (both washed in a decoction of mallow leaves), three ounces <term>℥</term> each; of refined rose oil, one and a half ounces; of the roots of dock, **acutus** <note>likely *Rumex acutus*, a species of dock</note>, black hellebore, and celandine, one ounce each. Once the items that need powdering are pulverized, place them all in a mortar and subdue them with a pestle until they are perfectly blended. At the end, while mixing, add five ounces of **litharge** <term>lithargyri</term> <note>lead monoxide, used in historical medicine to dry and heal wounds</note>, two ounces of **ceruse** <term>cerussæ</term> <note>white lead, often used as a pigment or in medicinal ointments</note>, and one ounce of liquid storax <note>a fragrant, medicinal resin</note>, and let a liniment be made.

This liniment is also effective: Take four ounces of butter washed in a decoction of mallow; of ceruse and of the best powdered sulfur, one ounce each; and one and a half ounces of lemon juice. Mix until all are perfectly incorporated, and anoint the scabious areas. A liniment made of sulfur and rose oil is also effective and is a safe application.

If, however, the **scabies** <note>at this time, "scabies" referred generally to scaly, itchy, or contagious skin eruptions, not just the specific mite-based infection we recognize today</note> is long-standing, first apply **cupping glasses** <term>cucurbitulis</term> <note>glass jars used for bloodletting or suction therapy</note> after a general purging of the body. Then let the limbs be washed with this decoction: 

Take of fumitory, scabious, **wild sage** <term>gallithrici</term>, **maidenhair fern** <term>polithryci</term> or <term>capillorum Veneris</term>, mallow, barley with its husk, and **epithyme** <term>epithymi</term> <note>dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant used as a purgative</note>, one handful of each. Let them boil in spring water, with which the scabious limbs are to be washed. Then, let the areas be anointed with this liniment:

Take of lard, butter, turpentine, and oil of bitter almonds, two ounces each. Let them boil together in water so that they all melt; then allow them to cool and solidify. Take that solidified fat and add to it: half an ounce of golden litharge, three drachms of ceruse, one ounce of liquid storax, and one and a half ounces of common salt. Mix all these together, having placed them in a mortar, and work them with a pestle until they reach a perfect mixture and are reduced to the form of a liniment, with which you may anoint the scabious areas. 

However, a miraculous remedy, suitable for all types of itching and scabies, is an application of rose oil and sulfur mixed together.

Thus far, my dear Lawrence, I believe our discourse has proceeded correctly regarding the method of administering medicines that diminish, **digest** <term>digerentium</term> <note>ripening or preparing the humors for removal</note>, and eradicatively purge various **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Galenic medicine sought to balance</note>, as well as regarding local remedies suitable for specific limbs and diseases. I hope that through my labors you may now be introduced to the method of curing particular illnesses. 

Farewell, and again, farewell.

-># TO LORENZO PRIULI, THE MOST<-
->## Serene Prince of the Venetians,<-

->### LETTER III.<-

**E**VEN IF many things have been written brilliantly and with great talent by the most learned men regarding endives or chicory plants <term>cichoraceis</term>, Most Serene Prince <note>a formal title for the Doge of Venice, the chief magistrate of the Republic</note>, I would not wish to have it attributed to rashness or impudence if I write to your Serenity about these same things. Truly, I have seen many writing different things about this vegetable, as various authors express various views according to their own taste; let me also be permitted, among so many wise men, to comment on these same vegetables more briefly and precisely, so that I might do something pleasing for your Serenity. Nor could I ever be persuaded by any reasons that a brief method is not more to be approved (provided it is not affected by any obscurity of speech) than a longer one, which requires many labors for reading that are less necessary for its understanding—especially since your Serenity is constantly intent on the highest matters of the Republic and devotes effort without any intermission of time. 

Indeed, Lorenzo Massa, my nephew, invited me to this most pleasant labor while I was lying in bed these past days with an afflicted body. He told me that you had indicated to him a great desire to know the powers and use of chicories <term>cichoreorum</term>, so that this food might serve as a help and medicine for the ailments of both the stomach <term>ventriculi</term> and the liver <term>iecinoris</term> through its use. This is because you have otherwise always been averse to the medicines and drugs of the apothecaries <term>seplasiariorum</term> <note>original: "seplasiariorum"; historically, sellers of perfumes and ointments who also prepared complex medicinal mixtures</note> due to the mixture of diverse things within them, and also because you are not at all accustomed to them. 

Therefore, for all these reasons, and so that all the labor of reading might be removed along with the trouble of administering medicine, I wanted to write these things to you, most illustrious Prince. I am leaving aside the superfluous and touching only on the necessary, so that with less effort from a brief and well-organized <term>dearticulata</term> reading, you might better care for the health of your body more safely and easily by administering or using this food—putting aside medicated medicines—and so that you may happily preside over us as leader, protector, and Prince for a long time. 

But so that the matter can be settled briefly, I have decided first to declare what and how many species of chicory there are; next, to enumerate their actions, powers, and properties; and finally, by what preparations they ought to be made ready for use as food (so that they may benefit the aforementioned ailments). Starting with Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical manual for centuries</note> as if from the prince...

-># NICCOLÒ MASSA'S MEDICAL EPISTLES<-

...certainly, and I shall begin from him whom all the posterity of wise men has trusted: who, primarily in the second book of *On Medical Matters* <note>The famous botanical work *De Materia Medica* by the Greek physician Dioscorides</note>, where he treats endives <term>intybis</term> and chicories <term>cichoreis</term>, first describes the sow-thistle <term>cicerbitam</term>, or **prickly sow-thistle** <note>original: *sonchon asperam*</note>, saying: "Of the **prickly sow-thistle**, which some call **chicory** <note>original: *cichoreum*</note>, there are two kinds. The wild kind is more bristly with thorns; the other is softened by a certain thinness and is more pleasing in foods." He also described a third species, which is tree-like, which all the most experienced herbalists and writers of our time are ignorant of. Also in the following chapter where he describes **endive** <note>original: *intubum*</note> and **seris** <note>a Greek name for chicory or endive</note>, he declares: "**Seris**, which the Romans call **endive** <note>original: *intybum*</note>, has two kinds: one is wild, which is called **bitter-herb** <note>original: *picris*</note> and **chicory**; the other is the cultivated kind with broader leaves, which is more useful for the stomach than the garden variety. This is again divided into two species: one comes forth with a broader leaf very similar to lettuce—and that is the one (in my opinion) which they commonly call **endive** <note>original: *endiuiam*</note>; the other has a narrower leaf and is quite bitter." Also in the same book, in the chapter on **Chondrilla** <note>a genus of plants in the dandelion tribe, often called gum succory</note>, he says: "**Chondrilla**, which some call **chicory**, has a stem, flower, and leaves similar to chicory; for which reason some say it is a species of wild endive, but the whole plant is thinner, and in its branches a gum very similar to mastic <note>a resin obtained from the mastic tree</note> is usually found in a small tubercle the size of a bean." And a little later he writes: "There is another kind of **Chondrilla** bearing an oblong leaf, jagged <note>original: *circumrosum*</note>, spread on the ground, and so forth; it grows in rich and cultivated places." Furthermore, in the third book in the chapter on **Hawkweed** <note>original: *Hieracio*</note>, he described it in these words: "**Great Hawkweed** <note>original: *Hieracium magnum*</note>, others call it **Sonchites**, the Romans call it **stray lettuce** <note>original: *lactucam erraticam*</note>." And in the following chapter, which is titled **Small Hawkweed** <note>original: *Hieracio paruo*</note>, he declares it thus: "**Small Hawkweed**, the Romans call **wild endive** <note>original: *intybum sylvestre*</note>, it has leaves divided by intervals," etc. These are the species of endives and what has been described by Dioscorides concerning endives and chicories, which are ten in number. Their temperature <term>temperatura</term> <note>the balance of "humors" or qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a substance</note>, virtues, and specific operations are described by him as not dissimilar; for indeed they all have a cold and dry temperament, so that in some way they moderately cool and moderately bind <note>original: *adstringant*</note>, since their substance (according to the testimony of Galen in the eighth book of *On Simple Medicines*) consists predominately of watery and earthy parts. However, it does not lack some slight heat; which temperament he also confirms in the eighth book of *On Medicines According to Localities*, and in other places as well. And although so many species of endive and chicory vegetables were described by the ancient writers, nevertheless all...

I ii

# PART TWO

...as I said, they moderately cool and dry in the first degree, not reaching the second <note>In the medical system of the time, qualities like "cold" or "dry" were measured in four degrees; the first degree was the mildest and safest</note>; however, the wild varieties cool less but are more astringent <note>having a tightening or contracting effect on body tissues</note>, while the cultivated ones are more pleasant to the taste, as they possess less bitterness. For a burning stomach and those suffering from gnawing pains, all these are an exceptional food and medicine. They are also beneficial for heart conditions <term>cardiac passions</term>, whether drunk or applied externally as a plaster, or if the affected parts are rubbed with them. They help those suffering from gout <term>podagra</term>; and when drunk with honey, they provoke urine, as they also do when mixed with wine. They also help with inflammations of the eyes. Furthermore, they are a singular medicine for the stings of scorpions and vipers if they are drunk, or even if the affected area is rubbed with them externally. Their juice by itself, or the herb itself boiled in wine, stops an excessive flow of the bowels <note>original: "aluum nimium fluentem," referring to diarrhea</note>. They mitigate the heat of bilious fevers, especially the domestic varieties; they also open obstructions, strengthen the internal organs, and cleanse the openings of the veins. Nor does their cooling effect cause too much harm to those with "cold" ailments, unlike other plants that are cold and moist without being astringent.

These endives <term>intybi</term> and chicories <term>cichoracei</term> already mentioned grow everywhere in the flat fields and even in cultivated and domestic gardens. Therefore, some have rightly made a division, saying that of endives and chicories, some are wild and some are cultivated; the cultivated ones are more pleasing to the taste than the wild ones, since they are less bitter, as I was saying a little while ago. I could certainly add many other things written by the most eminent Greek physicians to these remarks, but since they would add nothing in the way of clarity or utility to what has been said, I shall omit them. Instead, I will examine what certain learned Arabs, such as **Serapio** <note>likely Ibn Sarabi, or 'Serapio the Younger,' a 12-century author of a highly influential book on medicinal plants</note>, have said about chicory.

**Serapio**, therefore, in the book he wrote on simple medicines and plants, chapter 143—which is titled "On Endive and its Species"—wrote as follows: "**Dundube** <note>an Arabic-derived name for endive</note>, that is endive; of this there are two species, domestic and wild. The domestic is **Escarole** <term>Scariola</term>, while the wild is called **Dandelion** <term>taraxacon</term>. There is also a third species, which is called **Candarel** <note>possibly a type of gum-succory or Chondrilla</note>, which is **Amiron**." And again, dividing the domestic kind, he says: "But of escarole there are two species: one of which resembles lettuce, having broad leaves; the other has narrower leaves. And the dandelion has leaves broader than the domestic kind. **Candarel**, truly, resembles wild endive, and for that reason it is said to be a species of it; and upon its branches is found a gum similar to mastic, about the size of a bean." There is also another species of the aforementioned **Candarel** having leaves that are, as it were, incised, and so forth. And a little later he says all these species...

...species, both wild and domestic, are astringent and cooling, and good for the stomach; for when they are cooked, they assist its weakness. And when a porridge <term>polenta</term> <note>at this time, a thick mush made from grains like barley or wheat, rather than the modern cornmeal version</note> is made from any of them alone, or with honeycombs <note>original: "fauis"</note>, or with barley or wheat flour, it soothes inflammation of the stomach. It also benefits those with heart conditions, those suffering from gout <term>podagra</term>, and hot swellings <term>apostemes</term> of the eyes, as well as scorpion stings, St. Anthony's fire <term>erysipelas</term> <note>a skin infection characterized by a bright red rash</note>, and other such things. From these facts, it can be gathered that there are many species of endive <term>intybus</term>, chicory, or escarole <term>scariola</term>, and that they have the same temperaments, virtues, and specific actions that <term>Dioscorides</term> and <term>Galen</term> <note>the fundamental authorities of ancient Greek medicine</note> attribute to them, and what <term>Serapio</term> <note>an Arabic medical author, likely Serapion the Younger</note> wrote in the chapter on endive and its species concerning endives and chicories. These can be confirmed from the first sayings of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian 'Prince of Physicians'</note> in the second book of his *Canon* in the chapter on dandelion <term>taraxacon</term>, and also from <term>Isaac</term> <note>Isaac Judaeus, an influential 10th-century North African physician</note>, who, in his book on particular diets, listed the virtues of endive, especially the wild kind—which I affirm, beyond any doubt, is a species of chicory. He also enumerated these virtues and specific actions in the second book of his *Practica*, which are consistent with what has been said. The most learned <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd, the great 12th-century philosopher and physician from Al-Andalus</note> listed the same virtues in the fifth book of his *Colliget* concerning wild endive, which, as I have said, is certainly a species of chicory or endive. It possesses the aforementioned virtues, for it heals hot conditions of both the stomach and the liver by its "whole substance" <note>original: "a tota substantia"; a medical concept meaning the plant acts through its inherent nature rather than just its primary qualities of heat or moisture</note>, as physicians say; and because of its moderate temperament, it does not harm the "cold" conditions of these organs. Not a few illustrious Latin authors were of this same opinion, such as <term>Pliny</term> and <term>Cornelius Celsus</term> in his second book, in the chapter on those things that are suitable for the stomach.

Having thus seen the species of chicory according to the opinion of the Greeks, Arabs, and Latins, and having seen their virtues and specific actions, it remains to describe the method of preparing them both as food and as medicine made from chicory plants, after I first take note of certain things: namely, that the chicories commonly sold are species of endive, both cultivated and wild, as all learned men, all herbalists, and likewise the common people affirm. Among these, I believe that the one everyone calls "endive" should be included; however, everyone affirms that the medicinal powers are stronger in the wild variety, as we mentioned above. Therefore, both the leaves and the roots of chicories are eaten at different times; for in the spring and summer, the majority of common people eat the raw herb, and many also eat it cooked. In the autumn and winter, they eat the cooked roots prepared with salt, oil, and vinegar; there are also those who eat the leaves cooked at these times, according to the variety of their palate, and...

# PART TWO

...of cities or the customs of places. I always praise them when they are cooked, whether they be the cultivated or wild variety, and whether they be leaves or roots. The best method of preparation in the springtime, before they grow large and while they are still tender, is that they first be washed and sprinkled with salt; then, having poured sweet oil over them, let them be mixed thoroughly. Soon after, vinegar should be poured in, and they should be eaten as a first course. However, if they are boiled and then sprinkled with salt and oil and mixed together, and then moistened with vinegar, they will be easier to digest. In winter, however, the roots are of greater use and more pleasing to the taste. They are prepared first by washing and by the removal of the woody and hard core <note>literally "wooden marrow"</note>; once washed and cut, let them boil in water until they are rendered soft, then mix them with salt, oil, and vinegar, with a portion of powdered sugar sprinkled on top according to the taste of the eater. Prepared for eating in one way or the other, they benefit an overheated stomach and strengthen its very opening with their light astringency, and they even benefit the entire intestinal tract. From this it follows that for those suffering from the difficulty of the intestines which the Greeks call <term>dysentery</term> <note>a severe inflammation of the intestines resulting in bloody diarrhea</note>, its use is of great help. It is also beneficial, as I said, to an overheated liver and to the kidneys as well—especially if they are boiled with raisins and eaten together, for this stimulates urine. However, in place of raisins, a portion of <term>defrutum</term> (which they call <term>sapa</term> <note>grape juice boiled down to a thick, sweet syrup</note> and boiled wine) can be mixed with vinegar; and where there is fear that excessive cooling might cause harm, a portion of cinnamon powder should be sprinkled over it. For in this way it will be of the greatest benefit by opening obstructions of both the liver and the spleen and other internal organs, and by cleansing them excellently. For since <term>chicory</term> partakes in a certain bitterness, it possesses the power of cleansing and opening the orifices of the <term>meseraic</term> <note>the mesenteric veins, which carry nutrients from the digestive tract to the liver</note> veins when eaten. It also counteracts poisons, both of scorpions and of the viper; and it is also a singular medicine for burning and pestilential fevers. There are those who even prepare chicory with <term>liquamen</term> <note>here referring to rendered fat or broth</note> or pork fat, which I do not praise at all, since all fats harm the stomach. There are also those who put vinegar boiled with honey along with oil and salt over the boiled chicory, which method of preparation is very pleasing; especially if there is a sluggish <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily humors, associated here with slow digestion or mucus</note> in the stomach, for it cleanses and cuts through the phlegm. But even if it is boiled in its own broth and eaten as a side dish without the aforementioned preparation of salt, oil, and vinegar, it will be of no small use in the aforementioned conditions. One thing, however, I think should be noted: it should not be eaten when it is too old and has already grown into a large, grassy mass, since it fatigues the stomach too much and...

## EPISTLE IV

I had promised you, when you were setting out for Padua <note>Padua was the site of one of the most prestigious medical universities in Renaissance Europe</note>, that I would write for you a certain brief exposition of the first <term>fen</term> <note>original: "fen"; a term derived from the Arabic "fann," meaning a branch or section of a science, used to divide the books in Avicenna's Canon</note> of the fourth canon of Avicenna. He was a man most learned in every faculty, and until this very day has been held and esteemed as the prince of all medicine after Galen <note>Galen (2nd century CE) and Avicenna (11th century CE) were the two primary authorities in European medicine until the early modern period</note>. This task, my dear Lorenzo, I willingly undertake at present for your sake, though at this time it seems quite difficult to me. For I am distracted by continuous business which, as you well know, is far from my desire and foreign to the study of literature. Added to this difficulty is the authority of the most grave man whom I intend to explain, who in past centuries has exhausted a vast number of most learned interpreters. 

But what of it? Although I am deprived of that peace of mind and body which I have often desired so that I might eventually apply myself to my studies—and which I greatly need at present—nevertheless, the paternal affection I have always felt for you makes this labor of mine seem not only easy, but even most pleasant. Receive, then, these writings of ours, which I have written to satisfy you, so that you may emerge more learned through my labors (for I desire nothing more in this life, nor do I hope for anything more). You shall join these to the interpretations of those most excellent men whom you hear daily teaching this part of medicine publicly...

### SECOND PART

...of those teaching at Padua. As far as my duty is concerned, I will clearly explain the author’s intent to you, setting aside superfluous and unnecessary questions, while treating the necessary ones as diligently as the matter demands.

I think it best to omit at this point some of those eight elements which interpreters—especially the best ones—are accustomed to note in the prefaces of books. This is because there are some things which (as it seems to me) contribute little or nothing to this discussion; however, we shall discuss certain others, because they are not only helpful but in a certain way necessary. These are: the title of the book, the subject, and the intention. To these I would also add something about the author’s life, in order to encourage you to take up these disciplines. But there is no need, since you encourage yourself enough, and you have also very diligently read and re-read that *Life of Avicenna* <note>Massa published a Latin translation of the "Life of Avicenna" (the *Sira*) in 1544, based on Arabic sources</note> which I translated, the copy of which you still have with you. Therefore, leaving aside those things that do not pertain to our purpose, we shall begin with the title.

The title is this: **The fourth book of the Canon, on particular diseases which, when they occur, do not occur in a single member.** From this title, you will gather that a fever is a particular disease and does not happen to only one member—that is, it is not an affliction of only one specific, designated organ. But you might say that fever is not contained under this title, because it is a "universal" disease, which is evident from the fact that it is a "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to a state of being acted upon or suffering, i.e., an ailment</note> of the whole body, since fever tortures and afflicts the entire body. 

To this objection, I reply as follows: Fever is, in the first place, a **particular** disease, because it is primarily a suffering and affliction of the heart; for the febrile heat first afflicts the heart. Then, it is also called **universal** because the heat, proceeding from the heart itself, travels through the veins and arteries to the entire body and warms it. You, however, should understand fever in the first sense and place it under this title; I believe Avicenna understood fever according to this interpretation, although others think differently. It "does not happen to one member" because when the febrile heat is in the heart, it proceeds from the heart itself through the veins and arteries to other members unless it is hindered. And it harms not only the functions of the heart, but also the operations of the other members, so that not only the **vital virtues** <note>In Galenic medicine, the "vital virtue" or faculty was centered in the heart and distributed through the arteries</note> are rendered weak, but also the **natural** <note>The "natural virtue" was centered in the liver and governed nutrition and growth</note> and **animal** <note>The "animal virtue" was centered in the brain and governed sensation and movement</note> virtues, and those of the other members. For in fevers, sometimes this member and sometimes that one is hindered from its duty—and sometimes all of them. Therefore, fever is an affliction of one member...

...happening first [in the heart]; which is then shared with the remaining parts so that it clearly harms them and their operations. From this, the damage is said not to be assigned to a single member. And this is enough regarding the title. Next follows the intention of the writer, which is solely about fevers. Take what a fever truly is from Avicenna himself: **"Fever is an extraneous heat kindled in the heart and proceeding from it by means of the spirit and the blood through the arteries and veins to the whole body,"** and so on.

Almost all interpreters, while expounding upon this definition, bring forward many arguments in favor of Avicenna and many against him. Furthermore, they compare this definition to those left to us by the ancients who wrote about fevers. Likewise, they inquire whether this one is better or worse. However, even if I do not review everything they pass down—for that would be a great inconvenience to me (being hindered by business, as I said) and would also bring you the greatest boredom—nevertheless, I shall write as much as the shortage of time permits and as much as seems appropriate for clarification. 

First, therefore, so that understanding may be easier, you will note that Avicenna presupposes that fever exists, and does not prove it, because fever is the subject and intention of this book. For no practitioner <note>original: *artifex*, referring to one who practices a specific art or science</note> proves his own subject, as you saw from Aristotle while I was reading to you. For this reason, he rightly does not prove it but declares it; he declares it, moreover, when he defines it with an **essential definition**. That this is an essential definition of fever is easy to persuade anyone of. For the best and essential definition consists of a **genus** and a **difference** <term>difference: in logic, the specific characteristic (differentia) that distinguishes a species within its broader category or genus</term> or differences; since this definition is of such a kind, there is no doubting whether it is essential. 

See how this is so. Galen used to say, in that book titled *On the Differences of Fevers*, that fever belongs to the genus of "heat contrary to nature." Therefore, the **genus** in this definition is [**heat**], which is the substance of fever—though in a loose and improper sense <note>original: *abusiue*, meaning the term is used outside its strict technical application</note>—and this is as far as the genus goes. Avicenna then adds in the definition [**extraneous**], which is the **difference**. For this makes fever differ from any other innate heat—from vital heat, from animal heat <note>refers to the heat associated with the "animal spirits" or nervous system</note>, and from natural heat—which differ in degree according to the various operations of the members. 

Then he adds [**kindled in the heart**], since even if there were extraneous heat in any other part of the body and not in the heart, it would not be a fever. For fever is a suffering <note>original: *passio*, meaning an affliction or a state of being acted upon by an external force</note> first of the heart and then, through communication (as we said), of the entire body. There are, therefore, two essential differences in this definition; those other parts, as if Avicenna...

# PART TWO.

...he adds, namely <note>Massa is quoting Avicenna's definition of fever here.</note> [proceeding from it by means of the spirit and blood through the arteries and veins into the whole body] following from these. For since the vein and artery proceed from the heart to the entire body, the vein indeed first ascends from the "hump" <note>original: *gibbo*, referring to the convex part of the liver</note> of the liver to the heart, from which it afterwards receives heat, both native and extraneous. It receives native heat when the heart is not feverish, and this is for the purpose of carrying out its functions. It receives extraneous heat when the heart is in a state of fever, and this is contrary to nature. And in this way, when extraneous heat is in the heart, it proceeds through the veins to the other parts of the body unless it is hindered, as will be discussed more fully in what follows. The artery, however, proceeds first from the heart and it carries the <term>spirits: *spiritus*, the vital refined substances believed to animate the body</term> to the parts of the body; through the artery, extraneous heat passes—if not hindered—to those parts to which the spirits are carried. Therefore, febrile heat is carried to the entire body through the veins and arteries. [And they are inflamed in it by an inflammation that harms natural operations.] He said this so that the essence of fever might become better known through the effect of the acting extraneous heat.

For this distinction also separates extraneous heat from any other kind of heat, whether extraneous or natural, that does not harm natural operations. For as he himself says, [the heat of anger, and of labor when it is not brought to its ultimate end]—that is, when it does not proceed so far that, by continuing in the heart, it impresses a heat that hinders natural operations—is not to be called a fever. But if anger harms natural operations in some way, it does not do so primarily, since that heat does not first proceed from the heart’s own extraneous heat, but from an external cause. For in order for it to truly harm, it is necessary that while the "kindling" <note>original: *accensione*, the metaphorical "firing up" of the heart</note> remains in the heart, the heat which is fever is ignited, from which follows the injury of operations; this does not happen, however, from the heat of the sun or a <term>sweat-bath: *hypocausti*, originally a Roman underfloor heating system, here used to mean a dry-heat bath</term> alone.

Furthermore, those last words [it hinders the operation so that it is held back] are placed there so that he may distinguish febrile heat from any heat whatsoever that does not only hinder, but corrupts the operation of the heart, if any such thing is found. It is found, indeed, because those poisons which kill by their heat completely corrupt the operation of the heart and destroy it so that they immediately kill the man; other heats of this kind do the same thing. Febrile heat, however, hinders and injures the operation in some way, but the operation nevertheless remains and is not "flattened" <note>original: *sternitur*, meaning completely suppressed or struck down</note>. We said above that fever hinders natural operations; I shall now explain how I understand this. Fever can hinder operations, not only those which physicians call "natural," which proceed from the liver itself. There are...

...however, these [operations] are to attract, retain, digest, and expel; but also every operation that can proceed from all the <term>virtues: the innate biological powers or faculties of the body</term>. Not all of these are always harmed at the same time, but sometimes one, sometimes another, sometimes these and those, and sometimes truly all of them at once, as can be seen in the most violent fevers. For in those cases, you will see the damaged operation of the heart clearly from the frequency, difficulty, magnitude, and irregularity of <term>inspiration and respiration: inhaling and exhaling</term>, and from other symptoms. 

In the same way, the operations of the brain [are harmed], as shown by the same signs when patients either sleep or stay awake excessively, or when they struggle to reason, remember, or move. Likewise, you will perceive the powers and operations of the liver and of the members serving the liver itself. For they are harmed either when they have no appetite, or when they thirst excessively, and when they either spoil the consumed food or prepare it poorly; and they do not clear out the <term>excrement: the waste products of digestion</term> through the urine or through <note>original: *secessum*, referring to stool or bowel movements</note>, nor through the other parts through which those members are accustomed to be purged. Or, if they are purged, they emit either more than is right, or substances different from their natural quality, or corrupted matter. 

From this, it appears how great an error those have fallen into who believed that Avicenna, when he speaks of "natural operations," understood nothing other than "accustomed duties"—such as walking and performing other exercises that any healthy person can do. They fail to understand those things which we, as I was just saying, understand. From all these things we have said, you can easily gather that fever, among all other ailments, distresses a person the most, since it can sometimes hinder all operations. For every other disease affects only a certain specific member, such as <term>dropsy: *aqua intercutem*, literally "water between the skin," a swelling often linked to liver failure</term>, which is a suffering of the liver; and colic, which is of the intestine; and <term>apostemes: internal abscesses or swellings</term>, which harm a single member (though they sometimes harm other members as well). But that does not happen instantly. 

Fever, however, immediately harms all the members, provided it is not hindered within or without them. Note, furthermore, that febrile heat does not always warm the whole body, because it can be hindered. Yet, that extraneous heat is not so hindered that it cannot be perceived either in many parts or in the <term>noble members: the vital organs like the heart, brain, and liver</term>. For Galen said in the sixth book of *On Popular Diseases* <note>original: *de morbis vulgaribus*, commonly known as the *Epidemics*</note> that febrile heat is sometimes so hindered that the exterior skin is not affected; in such cases, neither the attending physicians can feel the fever by touching the patient, nor can the patient himself recognize that he has a fever, because the heat is trapped in the deepest parts of the body, from which it does not [escape]...

This can be seen primarily in the elderly, for the fevers of the elderly, as our <note>The author uses "our" as a term of professional respect common in the Renaissance.</note> Avicenna maintained, are "buried" and latent. In them, the febrile heat does not pass to the skin because their veins are filled with much <term>pituita: phlegm, one of the four bodily humors, considered cold and moist</term>. Therefore, before the division, I will bring forward those matters that fall into doubt, and once those are dissolved, I will apply myself to the division of fevers. 

It is asked first by those who explain this definition whether the essence of fever is contained within some matter of the heart, which is approved by everyone to be the case, nor can the matter be otherwise. Since in a <term>putrid fever: a fever caused by the corruption of the humors</term>, either the <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term> of the heart putrefy—which happens rarely and would be a very great evil—or at least they are positioned in a <note>original: "calefacto esse," a Scholastic term referring to the state of having been heated as a fixed quality</note> heated state. This is what mostly happens in putrid fevers, as those say who are favored by the words of Galen in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*. For Galen says that febrile heat occupies either the solid body of the heart, or the humors contained in its ventricles, or finally the <term>aereal substance: the "vital spirit" or pneuma believed to circulate through the heart</term>. From these words of Galen, they hold that every fever has a "heated state" in that matter from which it arises. 

In the first kind, in which the febrile heat heats the solid substance of the heart, they say that extraneous heat is fixed in that substance, and for that reason it is also permanent. But since when that heat is ignited in the substance, it also ignites the humors and vapors, they say these vapors and humors have their existence in <note>original: "in calefieri," the process of being heated</note> being heated, and depend upon the "heated state." 

In the second kind, they say the "heated state" exists in the humors that are in the heart, such that they have already received some degree of putrefaction, and are consequently hot with a heat beyond nature—or at least, even without putrefaction, they possess a heat beyond nature from inflammation. They think this heat is fixed and confirmed in the humors themselves; and so they say the humors of the heart possess the "heated state," while the heart itself "is being heated," as are the vapors and <term>spirits: the subtle substances that carry life and sensation through the body</term> from that heated state of the humors. <meta>This page continues Niccolò Massa's investigation into whether fever is essentially an affection of the heart's substance or its contents. He is refuting the contemporary view held by Matteo Corti, arguing instead that hectic fevers are secondary developments rather than the primary state of all fevers.</meta>

->Page 81<-

[...unnatural heat] kindled in the vapors and spirits originates from the state of being heated and from the heating of the vapors and spirits, and that the heat of the humors and even of the solid substance of the heart depends upon them. **Matteo Corti**, an otherwise most learned man, held this opinion and stubbornness, as did other not unlearned men before and after him. For they have **Galen**, in that same first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, saying that fever is primarily an affliction of the heart, which he said depends either on the solid substance of the heart itself, or on the humors themselves, or on the vapors and spirits contained within the body or ventricles of the heart.

But you, take note that this opinion is not at all true, and that the passages cited from Galen do not favor this view. For if it were as they assert, it would follow that every fever is either pestilential or ruinous and mortal, which is by no means true. I demonstrate that this conclusion necessarily follows in this way: Galen, in the first book of *Differences of Fevers*, where he openly shows the differences of fevers based on the parts of our body to which unnatural heat occurs, maintained that heat is not primarily and of itself in the solid parts, humors, or vapors, but proceeds from other organs.

Indeed, if we run through all types of fevers (as the same Galen said), a habitual or <term>hectic fever: a persistent fever that has settled into the solid tissues or "habit" of the body</term> does not occur primarily and of itself when it begins, but follows either a humoral or <term>ephemeral fever: a "one-day" fever usually caused by transitory factors like heat, exhaustion, or emotion affecting the spirits</term>. Therefore, from this it appears that hectic fever does not have its primary existence in the solid substance of the heart, but follows from other fevers. 

But once the moisture or vapors are consumed, heat can be kindled in the solid substance; and that is the kind of fever that receives a cure either not at all or only with the greatest labor. This is because the heat kindled is such that it no longer has an underlying cause in the humor or spirit communicating heat to the solid parts; rather, it remains fixed and established in the organ itself. And for this reason it is called "fixed" and "independent," and <note>original: "hectica"</note> **hectic** by the Greeks, and by our people <note>original: "habituata"</note> **habituated**. 

The same is to be said of that heat which has its existence in the humors; since the humors are not permanent but are always flowing. For they are always being generated, dissolved, changed, and converted into something else: either when they nourish the body, or are consumed in some other way. Indeed, the humors of the heart are kindled from that place where the source <note>original: "minera," literally a mine or ore-bed</note> of <term>putrefaction: the corruption of bodily fluids thought to generate unnatural heat</term> and boiling is found, and it is communicated to the inflamed heart; the humors within it. Who, I ask, is so ignorant and...

### PART TWO ###

...who is experienced in medical matters, who does not know that febrile heat kindled in the <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health</term>—which are continuously generated, changed into something else, or evacuated from the body—cannot have a <term>state of having been heated: original: "calefactum esse"; a philosophical term for a completed state of heat versus the process of heating</term> since one humor always replaces another, or is changed, or dissolved, or evacuated, while taking on unnatural heat. Furthermore, in every fever, the causes are distinct from the fever itself, except in a "completed" and independent <term>hectic fever: a persistent fever that has settled into the solid tissues or "habit" of the body</term>. I say "independent" because there is both a dependent and an independent hectic fever; I want to briefly show you now how these differ, for they will be of great use to you later. 

The **dependent** hectic fever is that which arises from an ulcer of the lung, or from suppurated matter in the <note>original: "clibano pectoris"</note> furnace of the chest <note>Massa uses the word "clibanus" (an oven or pot) to describe the ribcage as a vessel containing heat and fluid</note>. This fever can be cured by removing the cause—namely, if the ulcer in the lung is healed, or if the <term>pus: original: "sanies"; infected or corrupt fluid</term> held in the cavity of the chest is cleansed. Although this is difficult, it is not impossible, for I have cured many others of this fever. 

The **independent** hectic fever is that which has no remaining cause to nourish it, as the moisture has already been consumed—those fluids which were first seized by the putrid matter of the humors or by the foreign quality of vapors and spirits. When this fever has become habitual over a long time and has dried up all moisture, it becomes fixed in the solid substance of the organs and is said not to depend on anything else; rather, it is a "completed" fever, and when it reaches this final stage, it does not admit a cure. 

The <term>ephemeral fever: a short-lived fever, often lasting only a day, caused by environmental or emotional factors</term> behaves in the same way. For the vapors and spirits are kindled by external or internal causes, such as labor, eating, drinking hot things, staying in hot places, sleeplessness, and "accidents of the soul" <note>This refers to sudden emotional states like stress or grief</note>, which are sometimes to be placed among the intrinsic causes. 

Moreover, the intrinsic cause of ephemeral fevers is that heat which comes from anger, and from vapors and spirits inflamed by other things. Since these are not permanent, they cannot have a "state of having been heated," but are <note>original: "in fieri"</note> in the process of becoming, for they are continually kindled and dissolved. 

I concede and do not deny that it is true to say this about pestilential and deadly fevers. But to say that every fever has a "state of having been heated" in the heart seems to me most absurd and false. Therefore, you see that all kinds of fevers have primary causes from which they arise, and even the hectic fever arises from its own cause; while it exists, it does not have a static state of heat, but depends on its cause, whatever that may be. Concerning these things, then, enough has been said; farewell, and devote yourself to your studies.

->Venice, November 15, 1552.<-

# SECOND LETTER TO HIS NEPHEW LAURENTIUS MASSA.

## LETTER V.

**E**VEN IF many of these things which I am now writing to you have been treated and explained by us previously, nevertheless, since things repeated ten times over are beneficial again and again, I will take this liberty of repeating those things which have been said when it seems appropriate; especially since necessity sometimes draws me to do so, and utility sometimes leads me. Therefore, if you happen upon any points that have been explained to you by me until now, and even if we are treating these matters about which we previously discussed, and the material is one and the same, take care not to despise them as if they were superfluous and redundant. Rather, read with a calm mind and patiently, because here you will see many things explained more clearly, and not a few things added, which will later be of great use and maximum benefit to you. 

But to the matter at hand: besides those things which we said in the first letter, the most serious <note>The author refers to "interpreters" or commentators on medical authorities like Galen or Avicenna</note> ask whether a fever is a <term>passion of the heart: original: "cordis passio"; in this context, "passion" refers to a suffering, condition, or affliction affecting an organ</term>. And they argue it is not, since a fever which comes from an <term>abscess: original: "apostemate"; a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term> is not an essential injury to the heart but happens <term>by consent: original: "per consensum"; the medical theory of "sympathy," where one organ is affected because of a disease in another</term>; therefore, they say, it is not a passion of the heart. 

But you will note first, before I dilute <note>In this context, "diluam" means to weaken or refute the opposing argument</note> the argument, that the "passion" of a thing is spoken of in many ways. First, when it signifies a "proper" passion, which arises from essential principles—such as the capacity for laughter, or the turning gray of hair in old age in a human being. Considering it in this way, a fever is not a passion of the heart since it does not depend on essential principles, but is an <term>accident: a non-essential quality or property that can change without the subject losing its identity</term> which rarely happens, and in some people, even never occurs. Because if fever were a passion of the heart in this way, it would never leave a person, or at least they would necessarily have a fever at some time during the course of their life, which is against daily experience. Therefore, a fever is not a passion of the heart flowing from essential principles. 

Furthermore, a fever is considered as an accident of the heart only, and not primarily of another member. This is the same consideration by which we say it is an accident of a human to be a musician or a geometer; for a fever happens to the heart alone, although it does not always happen. Or, a fever can be considered in that manner by which we say <term>substance: the underlying reality or essence of a thing</term> is the subject of all accidents, and an accident is the subject of another accident. To explain the matter with an example...

# PART TWO

Let us posit some clear substance which, besides having its own <term>temperament: original: "temperamentum"; the specific balance of qualities like heat and moisture inherent to an organ</term> by which it is preserved, can also be altered and heated by an external agent. Let this substance be wood, which can be altered and changed by fire, by the sun, by water, and by many other external things; and thus, besides its own temperament, it will also possess an external heat, by which it is called "hot." It can also be changed by internal factors, such as by some rot, by which it grows warm with a <term>putrid heat: original: "putredinali caliditate"</term>.

In this same way, a fever can be a proper <term>passion: original: "passio"; here meaning a state of being acted upon or a suffering</term> of the heart and an accident happening to the heart itself, while the natural temperament of the heart remains—except in a <term>habitual fever: original: "febre habitudinali"; a fever that has become a settled "habit" or state in the body's tissues</term> of the third kind. In that specific case, the <term>innate moisture: original: "natiua humiditas"; the vital fluid believed to fuel the body's life-force</term> and, consequently, the heat contracted from the seed <note>The "heat contracted from the seed" refers to the Galenic belief that vital heat is inherited from the parents at conception</note> have already been consumed for the most part. In this final stage of fever, the innate moisture—which fed the innate heat—is greatly changed. It is true that in the place of the lost heat and consumed moisture, another heat and another moisture are generated; however, whether this new moisture and heat are as good as the previous ones is a major question. I would have you know, however, that they are not good, since the operations and virtues arising from them are not sound and strong, but weak and diminished.

But let us return to where we left off. I say, therefore, from these things which we noted above, that fever is not a passion arising from the natural and essential principles of the heart itself. Instead, it is both an "accident" and a "passion" in this sense: namely, that it can in no way happen that someone has a fever unless the heart itself first grows warm with a heat <term>against nature: original: "præter naturam"</term>. This may occur in the heart's solid substance, or in the <term>humors: original: "humoribus"; the four primary fluids of the body</term> held within the heart which heat the organ, or in the spirits and vapors heating the heart's humors and its solid substance.

That these things are true can be seen from the definition of fever provided by both the ancients and the moderns. It is also confirmed by what I said: that if fever were a passion flowing from essential principles, the heart would always be in a state of fever. Nor is it valid to say that even if it does not currently have a fever, it is "by nature suited" to fever. For "aptitude" presupposes a foundation once an impediment is removed, or a prepared matter from which an action can be born and proceed. We say this about infants, who do not yet reason, because they do not yet have a brain <term>fit: original: "aptum"</term> and prepared for contemplating <term>phantasms: original: "phantasmata"; the mental images required for thought in Aristotelian psychology</term>. Similarly, this can be seen in those whose minds are seized by some condition; for if the bad <term>disposition: original: "dispositio"</term> of the organ were removed in them, they would without any...

It specifically discusses the depletion of "innate moisture" in chronic fevers and argues that fever is not an inherent part of the heart's nature but a condition that arises when the heart is heated "against nature."</summary>

...without doubt they would understand, and thus these organs are suited and born for understanding. In the heart, however, there are no natural aptitudes for fevers, since to have a fever is not a property of the heart; rather, its property is to preserve life and the operations of life. Therefore, it must be said that fever is a proper and primary <term>passion: original: "passionem"; in a medical context, an affliction or state where the body is being acted upon by disease</term> of the heart. 

And when people say that a fever arising from <term>abscesses: original: "apostematum"; a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term> is not an essential injury to the heart but occurs merely through <term>sympathy: original: "consensum"; the medical theory that one organ can suffer because of a disease in another connected organ</term>, it is necessary to deny that premise. For if an unnatural heat in an abscess becomes the cause of a fever, it is the cause only because it first heats the heart—mediated by vapors or a warm, putrid evaporation. This is because for a fever to truly exist, it is necessary for heat to be ignited in the heart, whether that fever exists by its own nature or by accident. 

Nor would I wish you to believe those who have judged that fever can happen not only to the heart but also to other members; for although they were otherwise most learned men, they were deceived in this. And although some among the ancients affirmed that fever is a non-natural heat of the whole body, they do not for that reason deny that the heat is first ignited in the heart, and spreads from there to other parts unless something stands in the way. 

Nor do the arguments regarding a heated <term>liver: original: "iecinore"</term> oppose this opinion of mine—even though an injury to the body's operations and <term>virtues: original: "uirtutum"; the natural powers or faculties of an organ, such as the power to digest or filter</term> follows that heat. For it to be a fever, it is not enough for there to be external heat and a loss of function; it is necessary for that heat to be ignited in the heart. 

But if they should say that in a <term>fainting fit: original: "syncopi"</term> caused by heat, the heart is inflamed and ignited without any fever, we respond that if that unnatural heat remains for a longer time, it will undoubtedly produce a fever by heating either the <term>spirits: original: "spiritus"; the subtle substances believed to flow through the body to enable movement and sensation</term> and vapors, or the humors, or the very substance of the heart. But before the heart itself, or the spirits and humors contained in the heart, are actually set aflame, it is not to be called a fever. Indeed, a fever often arises from a strong, hot cause heating the heart itself; but notice that in a "failure of the soul" <note>original: "defectu animi"; a severe collapse or deep faint</note>, which is caused by a powerful force, the patient very often dies before the fever can even take hold. 

Therefore, from these points, you have the solutions for this argument and for others that can be made in this matter.

### Whether Natural Heat Can Become Fever

Furthermore, they ask whether a fever can be natural heat that has been converted into a fiery state. They confirm and prove that this can happen both by the authority of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> and **Galen** <note>The 2nd-century Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note>, and by their own reasoning. They argue this because the fever that comes from anger is of this kind, since anger is nothing other than blood ignited in the heart. Although many most learned men have followed this opinion, I however cannot be led...

## PART TWO

...I cannot bring myself to believe that this is true; for they are greatly deceived and wander far from the truth. They understand neither Galen nor Hippocrates <note>Galen and Hippocrates were the two most authoritative figures in ancient medicine; Massa is asserting his superior understanding of their foundational texts</note>, whom I shall now explain, and I will show the manner in which they ought to be understood. For the words of Hippocrates and Galen are not to be interpreted in the way those people interpret them. 

In the human body, there flourishes a **heat** drawn from the beginning of generation, which is called natural and **innate heat** <term>innate heat; original: "innata caliditas"; the vital spark or internal energy that ancient doctors believed drove all biological processes from birth</term>, by which the soul of the fetus is formed with reason. There is also a heat that arises from the mixing of the simple parts; this differs from the innate heat because the former is necessary for a human's being and for the introduction of the soul. This second heat, however, is that by which this specific body exists and is preserved through the mixture and composition of the elements. 

Furthermore, there is a third heat, which is called accidental and sickly; this does not always exist in the body, but is present at that time when the body is unwell and suffering. It can be present or absent according to the various changes of the body and the dispositions of its parts, its **humors** <term>humors; original: "humorum"; the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health</term>, its spirits, and its vapors, when these are in a state contrary to nature. Indeed, the body is frequently altered by external things and affected by internal conditions from which an unnatural heat follows, giving birth to various ailments—for example, when bad **superfluities** <term>superfluities; original: "superfluitates"; excess waste or undigested matter from food that the body has failed to expel</term> accumulate from food and disturb the body, or when the pathways are blocked, causing the humors to then heat up and putrefy. 

Such a condition is a disease that is "hot" in its temperament; but if this heat is communicated to the heart, it shall be called a **fever**. This heat is foreign, since it harms the natural operations—specifically those that belong to a human according to the justice of nature. 

Of these heats, the first one, which we called "innate," is always in the body and is present as long as we live; it is never changed into another type of heat. This is because, since it is the source from which the **rational soul** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition used by Massa, the "rational soul" is the highest level of the soul, unique to humans, responsible for thought and reason</note> proceeds, if the heat were changed, the soul within us would necessarily have to change as well. The second heat, which provides "being" to the body and which we said arises from the mixture of the component elements, is also not changed as long as we live; rather, it remains even when the soul has been separated from the body, until the parts decay and it is changed into something else. This is because it provides the body with its existence (as we said), and does not desert it until it is no longer the body of a human, but some other thing. Therefore, from these points, one can see that these heats can be made neither greater nor lesser, since they can in no way be changed. It remains...

<header>THE MEDICAL EPISTLES OF NICCOLÒ MASSA</header>

Therefore, this third heat is adventitious <note>original: "aduentitia"; meaning coming from the outside or not part of the body's essential nature</note> and accidental; it is a heat that can be increased, diminished, or separated from the body, and indeed it must be separated, for it hinders our natural operations. However, not every unnatural heat is called a fever unless it is ignited in the heart. If such heat were to occupy all parts of the body and every limb without occupying the heart, it would indeed be a disease, or the cause of a disease, but it would not be a fever. For if it were present in the whole body, or in one or several limbs, it would be considered a type of disease of temperament <note>original: "morbis in temperatura"; a condition where the qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry are out of balance</note>, but certainly not a fever.

Now, if you ask how this third heat causes a fever, I answer that it happens in two ways. Either this heat is ignited in some limb, or in the humors and waste products where there are nearby arteries, through which the heat can be carried to the heart. Or, it occurs when the putrid heat is so close to the heart that it does not need arteries to carry it, as happens frequently in pestilential diseases, in cases of suppuration <note>original: "suppuratis"; the formation of pus or abscesses</note>, and in ulcers. 

But take notice <term>that</term> <note>original: "q̄" (abbreviation for "quod")</note> in every single particle of our body there is a certain proper heat that preserves it. Since this heat is an "accident" <note>In the philosophy of the time, an "accident" is a property that belongs to a thing but is not part of its essential definition; it exists within a "subject" like a limb or a fluid</note>, it remains with its own specific particle, whether that be a limb or a humor; for it could by no means exist without a subject. If that third heat we mentioned—which is foreign to our natural heat—comes upon these particles, it mixes with them. A composite is formed from the natural heat and the heat that is contrary to nature. It is because of this that the particles are corrupted, especially in **hectic fevers** <term>hectic fever; original: "febribus hecticis"; a chronic, wasting fever that ancient doctors believed gradually "dried out" the body's solid parts</term>. 

In these cases, not only are the humors putrefied or changed in their substance and qualities, but the spirits, the vapors, and even the solid parts of the body are altered. This is seen in the third stage of a hectic fever, in which all the natural moisture has already been consumed by the foreign febrile heat.

From everything we have discussed, it is now clear how we can defend the views of **Hippocrates** and **Galen**. We can do so by stating that this third, non-natural heat (which we call fever) does not mix with the first or second heats, which we have shown to be natural. Instead, it mixes with the heat of the specific parts and the humors. If it were otherwise, a person suffering from a fever could not continue to live or preserve their body, as is clear from the reasons I stated above. 

The example of a fever arising from anger does not contradict our argument. In that case, neither the first nor the second heat is ignited for the reasons we have given; rather, a particle of blood located in the heart is ignited. This blood possesses its own heat that preserves it (as I explained a moment ago), and from that inflammation...
