# PART TWO

...spirits and vapors are ignited, and they themselves possess the heat by which they are preserved.
&emsp;&emsp;There is also another question: whether in every fever there is a state of <term>having been heated</term> <note>original: "calefactum esse"; a technical term in Scholastic medicine referring to the primary substance that has already reached a state of feverish heat</note> as they call it. That is, whether the very thing from which a particular fever takes its name is what grows hot; for example, in an <term>ephemeral fever</term> <note>original: "febre ephemera"; a fever lasting only a day, believed to be caused by overheated spirits or "pneuma"</note> it would be the spirits and vapors; in a putrid fever, the humors; and in a <term>hectic fever</term> <note>original: "hectica"; a chronic fever that has "dried out" the solid tissues of the body</note>, the solid substance. The majority of commentators believe this to be the case, and they strive to confirm it with many arguments, asserting that <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential physician of antiquity (2nd century AD), whose theories on humors and heat formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance medicine</note> intended this in the first book of his work *On the Differences of Fevers*. There, it makes no small difference whether we say a thing "is growing hot" or "has been heated." For they believe Galen intended in that passage to mean that the part which first heats the rest of the parts is "already heated," while the others are "growing hot." Here, so that the matter may be more clearly revealed, I must again take up and repeat the greater part of those things we discussed above; but I would wish you to read these things with a good and patient spirit, and to trust that you will derive the greatest benefit from these very matters.
&emsp;&emsp;Let us suppose, then, first that someone suffers from an ephemeral fever. In a person so affected, these thinkers hold that the spirits and vapors in the heart possess a "produced heat," and through this heat the humors of the heart are ignited, as is its solid substance. Thus, the substance of the heart and the humors are, as they say, <term>growing hot</term> <note>original: "in calefieri"; referring to the process of receiving heat from another source</note>, while the spirits and vapors which heat the heart are in a state of <term>having been heated</term> <note>original: "in calefacto esse"</note>. They say the same regarding a humoral fever; for when the humors of the heart are inflamed, they are said to be "heated" first, and from there they subsequently heat the spirits, the vapors, and even the substance of the heart. Nor do they speak differently regarding the ignited substance of the heart itself than they did regarding the spirits and humors. For when the substance of the heart has been heated, they assert that the humors and spirits are ignited by it. Thus, they say that in any fever, the state of "having been heated" exists in the matter that first receives the <term>extraneous heat</term> <note>heat coming from outside the body's natural constitution</note>, while the state of "growing hot" exists in the other two parts. Afterwards, that heat is extended to the entire body—unless it is hindered—through the arteries and veins by means of the blood and spirit. This is because heat is an <term>accident</term> <note>in Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a quality (like color or heat) that cannot exist on its own; it must have a "subject" or physical substance to inhabit</note>, and it cannot exist without a subject, nor can it be carried from place to place on its own. Therefore, the blood and spirit are the "subjects" that carry the extraneous heat to the whole body after it has been ignited in the heart. The arteries and veins, meanwhile, are the locations and spaces through which the heat moves within its subject from the point of origin to its destination. How ephemeral, humoral, and hectic fevers arise from their respective causes will not be difficult to teach through examples, since I may demonstrate them more easily...

...perceived through those things which first offer themselves to the senses, and which are called "sensible things." Therefore, let us imagine a man of a hot and dry temperament <note>The four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were associated with qualities like hot, cold, moist, and dry. A "hot and dry" temperament was considered more prone to inflammatory fevers.</note>, in the prime of his youth, and accustomed to much food and drink. <margin>|</margin> Let him walk about in the summertime, under the sun, when the peasants are gathering the harvest; let us suppose further that from these very causes the vapors of the body become overheated in such a way that he is seized by an **ephemeral fever**. I say that this fever has arisen from external causes in this manner: For the heat of the surrounding air, acting upon a body prepared to be inflamed by labor, its own temperament, and its age, will first ignite the vapors and spirits <note>In Galenic medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle, air-like substances that carried vital heat and functions through the body.</note> that are in the vicinity of the outer layers of the skin. These, once ignited, will heat other neighboring spirits and vapors and other parts, bit by bit, until this heat reaches the arteries themselves; by heating them, it simultaneously heats the spirits contained within them. Next, it will ignite the spirits of the heart and its vapors through the continuous transmission of heat from the spirits and vapors existing in the arteries. 

This heat, thus kindled in the vapors and spirits of the heart, will be a fever—specifically an **ephemeral fever**, which does not last beyond the space of a single day. If it should sometimes last until the fourth day, this is not due to the "thickness of the spirits" as some claim, but from a cause nurturing the foreign heat, as happens in the ephemeral fevers that occur alongside buboes <note>A "bubo" is a painful swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the groin or armpit, frequently associated with the plague.</note> in the groin or other areas. For when the heat kindled in the vapors is nurtured by the heat of the buboes, it is prolonged until the fourth and even the fifth day; and if it proceeds further, it inflames the humors and sets them on a path toward putrefaction or corruption. Therefore, when they have already begun to rot, the putrid vapors are carried to the heart, giving rise to the fever called a <term>putrid humoral fever</term> <note>A fever caused by "rotting" or "corrupting" bodily fluids (humors).</note>, to distinguish it from humoral fevers that are not putrid, such as a <term>synocha</term> <note>original: "finocha"; a continuous, non-putrid fever caused by an excess of blood.</note> without putrefaction. 

Let what has been said thus far suffice regarding how foreign heat passes to the whole body. From this you see that an ephemeral fever possesses no heat created by internal causes, nor by preceding and conjoined external causes. For the heat of the external air, which ignited the vapors in the outermost skin, is certainly not permanent, as it does not continually affect the body. Likewise, those spirits which were first heated by the external air are not permanent, since they are continually dispersed through the passages of the body and replaced by others. Similarly, those in the arteries that are inflamed are not permanent, since they are continually dis[persed]...

He also explains how a simple one-day fever can transition into a more dangerous "putrid" fever if it is sustained by localized infections like buboes.</summary>

# PART TWO

...are [dissipated], and because of natural heat as well as long-lasting labors, wakefulness, and the location, the dissolved spirits are replaced as the heart supplies more and more of them. Nor are those spirits that reside in the heart permanent, since they are continually generated and regenerated from that blood which comes from the liver to the **right auricle of the heart** <note>The right atrium, where blood enters from the body</note>, and are always distributed to the entire body.

This same process can be seen in a **humoral fever** <note>A fever caused by an imbalance or "putrefaction" of the body's four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, whether it occurs with putrefaction or without it. Indeed, so that this may become clearer to you through an example, I shall proceed in the same way I did above. I will present to you a young man, as before, of a hot and dry temperament, accustomed to much and varied food and drink, and having a **cacochymous** <note>original: "cacochymum" - a body filled with "bad juices" or corrupted humors</note> body. Suppose that during the very hot harvest time, after staying a long time in the sun and being exhausted by much labor, he exposes himself to a cold wind and is seized by an incipient **bastard tertian fever** <note>original: "tertiana notha" - a malaria-like fever that recurs every three days but lacks the clear, classic progression of a "true" tertian fever</note> starting with a chill. This chill is not very intense and lasts for an hour; afterward, a biting heat follows, though not very sharp. To these symptoms are added thirst and a headache, though not a violent one, and the fever ends with a sweat after the sixteenth hour, finally reaching a period without fever. Without any doubt, if someone correctly examines both the internal and external causes, they cannot say that an external heat has been produced within the humors of the heart. For the heat of the external air and the labors of the body, which first changed the external parts, do not remain, since we have said above that after the sweat, the patient is free from that external heat. Nor does that heat which is caused by the cold air remain. For <term>enim</term> <note>Latin "enim," meaning "for" or "indeed," abbreviated as ".n." in the original</note> it is possible that the external cooling has blocked the passages and, through **antiparistasis** <term>antiparistasis: a philosophical and medical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as internal heat becoming trapped and concentrated by external cold</term>, caused a concentration of heat that produces and feeds the fever for the same reason. For if this concentration of heat is to cause a fever, it must heat the heart by means of the spirits and humors which, as we said above, cannot be permanent. 

Much less can a repletion or a multitude of humors cause this, since those things should rather be categorized under the "material cause." And although the labors of the body, such as running and walking, heat our body greatly, one must not say that the heat produced by labor is fixed in the humors of the heart, nor that the **hot soot** <note>original: "fuliginem calidam" - metabolic waste products or "smoky" vapors produced by the body's internal heat</note> which rises from the mineral fibers <note>The "source material" or tissues of the body</note> and is received in the heart—from which the humors then grow hot—remains there. This is because physicians do not believe that the vital spirits, nor the blood itself, as we have said, stay in place. For if they were fixed and remained for a continuous time...

...otherwise there would be no need for new blood, which is continually regenerated from those things we eat and drink, as is known to all. Therefore, you see that since these substances are not permanent, it follows that they do not possess an inherent "heatedness" in the heart, unless one is able to attribute the entire cause of the putrefaction to the humors already existing in the heart. In that case, they would rot within the heart, and thus the substance of the heart would be heated by its own putrefaction, rather than being made hot by a putrid vapor coming from elsewhere. If this were to happen, it would be a pestilential and ruinous fever, of which Galen <note>A Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium</note> speaks in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*. 

Even if this were the case, as often happens, it should not therefore be said that the heart's humors have an inherent state of being heated. However, to bring this to a close, you can easily respond to all arguments that can be made on this subject once you hold as your foundation the fact that neither humors nor spirits are permanent. If any other doubts are raised regarding this matter, they are easy to solve, and you shall shatter them yourself. Therefore, I purposely omit writing them to you. Farewell, and apply yourself to your studies. 

Venice, November 20, 1552.

That abscesses—especially "hot" ones—can excite a fever is a fact no physician doubts. I specified "hot" ones, because even from "cold" abscesses, a fever arises if they begin to <term>suppurate<note>To form or discharge pus.</note></term>, according to that saying of Hippocrates: "While pus is being formed, fevers and pains occur" <note>original: "Dum pus conficitur febres & dolores fiunt"</note>. An example is a fever of putrefaction; for the rotting is its immediate cause, and the rotting is not a disease in itself, but rather the cause of a disease. However, a fever of an abscess is an accident existing in the abscess; while the abscess is present, the fever follows it, and the abscess is a disease in itself. 

The meaning of this text is as follows: it is called a "fever of disease" when it does not depend on any other illness. It is called an "accidental fever" when it arises from some other cause or an unnatural state (which is not a disease). Indeed, the causes that can excite a fever—which are not themselves diseases—are numerous and listed by physicians, especially by Avicenna. Lest I trouble you with a long speech, I will list some and not all; you may find the rest in Avicenna himself and in Galen.

*   A "constipation" or blockage of the outer skin
*   Burning from the sun
*   Condensing cold
*   Anger and outbursts of temper
*   Sadness, fear, grief, and other <term>passions of the soul<note>In this period, "passions of the soul" referred to what we now call emotions or psychological states, believed to have a direct physical impact on the body's heat and humors.</note></term>
*   Lack of sleep, hunger, or drunkenness
*   Any other type of "fullness" or over-satiation
*   Indigestion or hard labor
*   Physical pains
*   Foods that produce "bad juice" <note>Referring to poor-quality humors produced during digestion.</note>
*   Poisons
*   Abscesses, ulcers, and an abundance or retention of <term>pus<note>The original "saniei" refers to a thin, blood-stained discharge from a wound or ulcer.</note></term>
*   An excess of blood or other humors, or from their rotting or "burning."

++ <term>abscess<note>original: "apostema"; a localized collection of pus or a swelling.</note></term> and ulcer are not, however, the immediate causes of fever. This is because a fever is not excited by the tumor itself, nor by the <term>dissolution of continuity<note>A medical term for a break in the body’s tissues, such as a wound or tear.</note></term>, nor by an imbalance of temperament existing in some limb. Rather, it is excited by hot vapors that are stirred up from the site of the abscess, which then heat the heart and the spirits contained within it; and this is the immediate cause of fever. 

An abscess, from which these vapors are raised, is not the immediate cause but a "remote" one. Similarly, <term>obstructions<note>Blockages in the "vessels" or pathways of the body, thought to trap humors and cause them to rot.</note></term> are not the immediate cause of fever, but are the immediate cause of <term>putrefaction<note>The decomposition of bodily humors, which was believed to generate the "unnatural heat" of a fever.</note></term>. From this putrefaction, hot vapors are raised to the heart, causing the fever. Thus, if obstruction and hindered <term>transpiration<note>The body's ability to "breathe" through the skin or release waste vapors; modern medicine might compare this to perspiration or gas exchange.</note></term> are causes in any way, they are not first and immediate causes, but remote ones. This interpretation is made clear by the following words of the text, namely: that between the cause (which is not a disease) and the fever, there is no other disease. 

But so that you may more clearly understand the mind of <term>Avicenna<note>The influential Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037).</note></term>, take note that there are certain difficulties in his words. As it pleases some to argue, the matter may stand differently; for instance, a <term>tertian fever<note>A fever that spikes every third day (counting the day of the spike), traditionally associated with an excess of yellow bile.</note></term> depends on the putrefaction of bilious humors. Even though this putrefaction and its <term>putrid soot<note>original: "putrida fuligo"; in Galenic medicine, metabolic waste was often described as a smoky or sooty vapor that needed to be expelled.</note></term> are not themselves diseases, the site or "source" in which the humors rot is nevertheless made hotter and is changed from its natural temperament. Thus, there exists a "bad hot temperament" there, which is called a <term>complexional disease<note>A disease caused by an imbalance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note></term>. 

For this reason, they say the heat of the heart in that fever—which <term>Rhazes<note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925), a celebrated Persian physician and scholar.</note></term> and other physicians believe does not depend on another disease—actually depends on the heat of the limb contracted from the putrefaction. You will easily respond to this objection using Avicenna’s own words in the text, which are as follows: 
> A sickness-fever is that which has no intermediary between itself and a cause that is not a sickness. <note>original: "febris ægritudinalis eſt illa, inter quam & cauſam, quæ non eſt ægritudo non eſt medium"</note>
Indeed, these words are so clear they need no further declaration. Therefore, the objection is null, since you see that the immediate cause creating the fever is not the limb's unnaturally hot temperament, but the hot or putrid exhalation (or soot) raised from the limb that heats the heart; neither of which are diseases in themselves. 

And if they should object again, saying that the site of the abscess has a bad imbalance which *is* a disease, say as I said before: that bad temperament is certainly a disease and is a cause of the fever, but it is not an *immediate* cause. This is because it does not cause the fever primarily and by itself, but through the mediation of putrefaction and the hot evaporation heating the heart. You can also respond to the objection in another way, by saying that such a bad temperament is not a disease if it does not sensibly hinder or corrupt the <term>operations<note>The natural functions or "workings" of an organ or body part.</note></term>...

They also object, saying that an **accidental fever** <note>In this context, an "accident" (accidens) refers to a secondary condition or symptom that arises from a primary disease, rather than being the disease itself.</note> is therefore a **disease in itself**, because between the accidental fever and its cause there is no middle ground that is a disease. To these objections, it must be said that an "accidental" fever is one that follows another disease or an unnatural disposition, whether it occurs mediated by something else or immediately. Furthermore, in contradiction, they say that **pain is not a disease**, and consequently, fevers caused by pain are not accidents but diseases in their own right. Responding to this objection, you will say that pain does not cause fever simply as pain, but because it has as its cause a bad <term>temperament<note>The specific mix of qualities—hot, cold, dry, moist—within a body part.</note></term> or a <term>dissolution of continuity<note>A physical break or wound in the body's tissue.</note></term>, or both. Both of these are diseases, and according to the consensus of all illustrious physicians, they can cause an accidental fever. 

To those who still contradict, one must respond according to the opinion of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for over 1,500 years.</note> in the third book of *On the Difference of Symptoms* as follows: namely, that it can sometimes happen that a disease or another unnatural disposition precedes, and in this case, one must call this disease or unnatural disposition the non-immediate cause of another disease—especially if vapors, spirits, or humors are ignited from that cause and reach the heart. Thus, pain will not be the immediate cause of the fever, but rather that hot evaporation. This is especially true if the prior condition does not primarily impair the <term>functions<note>original: "operationes"; the natural actions or "work" of the organs.</note></term> of the body on its own. However, if both the first disease and the one that follows it impair or hinder functions, they are called **complicated diseases** that depend on one another. The same cannot be said of pain, because it is in no way a disease, but an accident of a disease following a bad temperament, or a dissolution of unity, or both; but since **inflammation** often arises from pain, which is the cause of fever, physicians heal the fever by relieving the pain. ...repeated objections, yet all are solved with a single response; which I wanted to note for you, and Avicenna also seems to have solved by responding to his own arguments with the following words; the arguments, the response, and the words of Avicenna are these: **AND TO THE ONE CONTRADICTING**, it is possible for him to say that if the fever of an abscess follows its heat, and follows or accompanies its own heat, it appears to be a fever that is an accident <note>original: "febris accidens"; in medieval medicine, an "accident" is a symptom or secondary effect rather than the primary disease.</note>, then it must be that most ephemeral fevers are accidents; and if it follows the putrefaction <note>The process of decay or "rotting" within the body, which was thought to produce heat and vapors.</note> which is in the abscess, then the abscess is not its first cause insofar as it is an abscess, but rather regarding the putrefaction which is in it; therefore its essential cause is putrefaction, and the abscess is not its cause except by accident. 

From these you have two reasons by which he dissolves the position of the aforementioned division. The first of these is: if the fever of an abscess follows either the heat or the pain of the abscess, a certain falsehood would follow—namely, that very many <term>ephemeral fevers<note>original: "febres ephemeras"; fevers lasting only a day, often caused by emotional or physical exertion like anger or exhaustion rather than infection.</note></term> are a symptom and not a disease. Since ephemeral fevers that arise from heat or pain are all symptoms—add to this that not only those mentioned, but many others, such as those arising from labor, from anger, and similar causes—and since this is hardly true, he rightly refutes them with these reasons. He says it was not correctly stated that accidental fevers are caused by a hot abscess, such as from a <term>bubo<note>original: "bubone"; a visible swelling of a lymph node, famously associated with the plague, but here used as a general example of a hot abscess.</note></term>. 

The second reason refuting them is this: if anyone understands the fever of an abscess to be an accident because it follows the putrefaction of the abscess, he wanders too far from the truth. This is because putrefaction is neither the abscess itself nor a part of the abscess, since it is neither a "bad temperament," nor a "bad composition," nor a "loss of unity" <note>These were the three formal categories of disease in Galenic medicine: an imbalance of qualities (hot/cold), a structural defect, or a physical break like a wound.</note>. If someone says that putrefaction is contained within the abscess, it must be said that this is true, but we do not therefore say that putrefaction belongs to the essence of the abscess, since an abscess can exist without putrefaction. Furthermore, putrefaction follows after the abscess and is its accident. 

From this it is gathered that the abscess does not cause the fever directly; instead, the fever that follows the abscess is created from elevated vapors from the putrefaction, which follow the abscess. Therefore, the putrefaction—or that hot, putrid evaporation seeking the heart—excites the fever and is the essential cause. But if they further object and say that the putrefaction is in the abscess, and therefore causes the fever, Avicenna responds that if it is considered according to this second view, it is necessary to say the abscess is the cause of the fever, not...

primarily and in itself, but by accident. The third reason refuting the aforementioned position is written subsequently, and it is:

> **AND WE SAY** that if they did not mean this by "fever"—rather, they only understood by it that the fever follows an existing abscess <note>original: "apostema"; a localized collection of pus or a swelling caused by humors.</note> simply because the abscess exists—then the condition of putrid fevers <note>Fevers thought to be caused by the "rotting" or corruption of the bodily humors.</note> is similar in relation to putrefaction.

This part of the text is read differently in various manuscripts, but I have noted it here based on the correction by <term>Andrea Alpago of Belluno<note>A famous 15th-century physician and scholar known for his updated translations of Avicenna from Arabic into Latin.</note></term>. The meaning of the text is this: in this section, Avicenna argues for the third time against the stated division of fevers. He does this by considering that division in another sense—namely, that a fever is a symptom because we recognize the existence of an abscess through that fever (since symptoms contribute greatly to the knowledge of diseases). Avicenna says this argument is invalid, since it would be just as worthwhile to say the same about other putrid fevers that occur without an abscess. For certainly, putrefaction is recognized through the fever itself; and not only is putrefaction known, but even the putrefaction of a specific <term>humor<note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note></term> is identified. 

Furthermore, from the intensity of the heat and the pattern of the onset—occurring from every third day to every third day—we learn not only that the fever is putrid, but specifically that there is a putrefaction of the <term>bilious humor<note>Yellow bile; a "tertian" fever occurring every other day was traditionally linked to an excess or corruption of this humor.</note></term>. Note the phrase "the condition in comparison to putrefaction"; he means to signify that the abscess is the path leading to the fever. You will also note that in the same way, the type of internal abscess can often be recognized from the heat and the pattern of that heat, which afflicts the patient more on one day than another. However, because he believed these questions were less necessary for physicians, once he satisfied these objections, he continues his intended explanation of fevers, though only after offering an excuse; he says:

> **BUT** to be occupied with contradictions of this sort is something that contributes nothing to the science of medicine; it causes the physician to stray from his art into inquiries that might perhaps hinder him from his craft.

In this part, I would also like you to be warned that almost all commentators do not correctly explain Avicenna’s mind. They say that these divisions of fever into "fever as a disease in itself" and "fever as a symptom" cannot offer much utility to physicians, and consequently, it is better to set them aside. However, the matter is otherwise. For you know—and it is the common opinion of physicians—that the goal of medicine is the preservation of health and the removal of disease, so that...

-> LETTERS ON MEDICINE BY NICCOLÒ MASSA <-
<meta>Digitized by Google watermark in bottom right corner</meta>

The duty of a physician is this: that health in the body is either preserved or, if it has been lost, restored. This preservation or restoration of health happens through the management of necessary things <note>Referring to the "six non-naturals" in Renaissance medicine: air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, evacuation, and emotions.</note>, the administration of medicines, or some manual operation <note>Surgery or physical manipulation.</note>. Since this is so, how shall we treat a patient suffering from a fever stirred up by pain, inflammation, or an abscess <note>original: *apostema*; a localized swelling or collection of pus.</note>, unless we first understand the nature and causes of the disease? Indeed, we will treat such a person with a different regimen than one who suffers from a fever that is a disease in itself <note>original: *per se*; a primary condition.</note> and is not merely a symptom <note>original: *accidens*</note> of another condition.

Furthermore, because a symptomatic fever depends on another "unnatural" <term>disposition<note>A physical state or condition of the body.</note></term> or disease, the treatment and primary goal will be to remove that initial unnatural condition as the cause of the fever. For according to the opinion of Galen and all illustrious physicians, true healing can by no means occur unless the cause of the disease is removed. Therefore, in a fever caused by an abscess, it will be worthwhile to treat the abscess first. In a fever that is a disease in itself, however, this is not the case; for although we are also intent on removing the cause, the first intention is to extinguish the febrile heat. 

For that reason, since febrile heat is unnatural and is followed by dryness, cooling and moistening remedies must be applied first. Then the cause must be removed, whatever that cause may be—whether it is the <term>conjoined cause<note>The immediate cause currently maintaining the disease.</note></term> or the <term>antecedent cause<note>The prior factor that triggered the condition.</note></term>. Truly, causes in putrid fevers are either material or efficient, both of which require removal. The material cause demands evacuation <note>The removal of excess or corrupt humors through methods like bloodletting or purging.</note>, while the efficient cause—since it involves a blockage—requires the opening of the passages. If the cause should be immaterial, as happens in a habitual fever <note>original: *febris habitudinalis*; often referring to a 'hectic' fever that has settled into the solid parts of the body.</note>, it requires only cooling and moistening. 

Thus you see that the division of fevers into "fever as a disease in itself" and "fever as a symptom" is not only useful to the physician but necessary. Say, therefore, that Avicenna wished to warn physicians to abstain from those questions which can distract a physician from his duty. Those [useless questions] are the ones that do not clarify the essence of diseases and their differences—essences from which the curative intentions are derived—since a diligent physician must always seek the intended end, which is health. 

Having noted these things for you, I shall return to another part of the text, in which he [Avicenna] sets down the essential division based on the matter in which the febrile heat is grounded, having first confirmed the aforementioned division of fever into "in itself" and "by accident." And he says: 

**LET US PROCEED** therefore according to what is customary; let us say, then...

<summary>Massa defines the physician's duty as the restoration of health and argues that distinguishing between primary and symptomatic fevers is vital for treatment. He emphasizes that while symptomatic fevers require treating the underlying cause (like an abscess) first, primary fevers require immediate cooling of the heat itself.</summary>

-> ## PART TWO <-

Because fevers arising from <term>abscesses<note>original: *apostematum*; localized swellings or collections of pus.</note></term> and <term>obstructions<note>original: *oppilationum*; blockages in the body's vessels or passages.</note></term> are "accidental" fevers <note>Meaning they are symptoms of another condition rather than the primary disease.</note>, and other fevers are diseases in their own right, it is fitting for us to speak of the three categories that make up the human body. These are: the members which contain the fluids and spirits; the fluids contained within them; and the animal, vital, and natural spirits along with dispersed vapors.

To understand how heat affects these, we can compare the body to a **bathhouse**:
1. The **members** (organs and tissues) are like the **walls** of the bathhouse.
2. The **moisture** (humors/fluids) is like the **water** in the bath.
3. The **spirits** and vapors are like the **air** within the bathhouse.

When a fire is lit, the primary inflammation creates an external heat. If that primary heat is extinguished, the things nearby will cool down. However, even if a neighboring part cools, the original source might not be extinguished; it can persist and return to reheat the surrounding area. This occurs within these three physical categories that constitute the human body.

Thus, <term>Avicenna<note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note></term> proceeds by declaring the essence of fever through a fundamental division. He identifies the specific material in which this "unnatural heat" is first generated and nourished. Accordingly, he designates three different types of fevers based on the three types of parts that make up our body, each of which receives this unnatural heat differently. These three constituent parts are, of course, the **members**, the **humors** (fluids), and the **spirits** (or vapors). Nothing else can be found in the composition of a human being in which a febrile heat could be rooted.

Avicenna adopted this division from <term>Galen<note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note></term> in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, and from <term>Hippocrates<note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–c. 370 BC).</note></term> in the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>original: *Morbis vulgaribus*.</note>. Since the text is quite clear on this, we need not labor too much over the explanation of the words.

The first part of the text confirms the opinion of those who say that fevers from abscesses, obstructions, or other unnatural conditions are "accidental" fevers, as the ancients called them. However, it must be noted that even though they are called "accidental," they should not be thought of as mere accidents in the simple sense. They are called so because they arise from some other disease or unnatural affection. Indeed, every fever is a disease of the <term>complexion<note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in an individual.</note></term>. Thus, you see that <term>Avicenna</term> confirms the view that a fever is sometimes a disease in itself, and sometimes a symptom of another disease or unnatural state. Having confirmed this, he then explains how this unnatural heat operates.

He categorizes fevers based on which of these three "materials" the heat first takes root in, citing the authority of Galen and Hippocrates.</summary>

...for it can ignite the three mentioned parts of our body. Indeed, according to the opinion of <term>Hippocrates</term> in the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>original: *de Morbis uulgaribus*; a foundational Greek medical text containing case studies.</note>, eighth part—which <term>Galen</term> praised as being better and truer—the words of <term>Hippocrates</term> are these: our body is composed of **the containers, the contents, and the driving forces** <note>original: *continentia, contenta, & impetum facientia*.</note>. Here, <term>Avicenna</term> calls those parts "members" <note>Meaning the solid organs and tissues.</note> which <term>Hippocrates</term> called "containers." But the parts he calls "contents" are the moistures or humors existing both in the vessels and in other parts of the body; <term>Avicenna</term> called these the "moisture contained in the members." Finally, he said the "driving forces" are the **animal, vital, and natural spirits** <note>In pre-modern medicine, these were subtle substances that governed the brain (animal), heart (vital), and liver (natural).</note> and scattered vapors. Indeed, winds, vapors, and spirits create an impulse, since wind is nothing other than "driven vapors" according to the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term>. 

It is established, therefore, that the body is composed of these three mentioned parts. Everyone accepts this division and everyone praises it, since it concerns the very subject of sickness and health. Furthermore, the first thing necessary for a physician to know is the understanding of the human body and its parts; the second things are the diseases, causes, and accidents. For if these are ignored, he will be able neither to predict nor to cure correctly. 

Next, <term>Avicenna</term> continues and compares these three parts separately to the three parts found in a bathhouse. First, he compares the solid members of our body to the **walls** of the bathhouse. Second, he compares the contained moistures or humors to the **water** present in the bathhouse. Third, he compares the animal, vital, and natural spirits and scattered vapors to the **air** of the bathhouse. Specifically, when the bathhouse is heated by an external heat—a primary inflammation—this is what happens: if its heat is extinguished, it will certainly grow cold, as will that which is near it—that is, the neighboring parts. Following his explanation, he says:

> **AND WHEN** that which is near it is cooled, it is not necessary for the bathhouse itself to be extinguished; rather, it is possible for it to remain, and to return and heat that which is near it, being one of these three types;

He means to say that the bathhouse does not only heat the internal parts and those things contained within it, but also the nearby exterior parts. This is perceived by the senses, because if someone approaches the exterior parts of a bathhouse that have been heated by the interior heat of the bath, he will recognize that they are warm. If, however, the internal heat of the bath is removed, not only will the bath itself grow cold, but also the exterior par[ts]...

->SECOND PART<-

...parts; but if for some reason the outer parts are cooled, the heat of the bath will not be extinguished for that reason. On the contrary, it is possible for the heat of the bath to remain, and even to warm the outer parts that had been cooled—especially if those parts are one or more of the three mentioned parts that constitute the bath. These parts were compared to the human body: they are the **members**, **moistures**, **spirits**, and **vapors**. Beyond these, there is no other kind of physical substance in a human being that contributes to their material composition. He <note>Referring to Avicenna.</note> said this because of the "form," which is an essential part of the composite whole. Having explained these things, let us look at the following part of the text, in which he provides examples of this division, saying:

> **AND IF** a fever is ignited in the **radical members** <note>original: *membris radicalibus*; the solid, fundamental parts of the body like bones and organs.</note> by a primary ignition—just as a burning is ignited, for example, in the walls of a bath, or in a blacksmith’s bellows, or in a cook's pot—then that genus of fever is named **hectic fever** <note>From the Greek *hektikos*, meaning "habitual" or "settled."</note>. And if a fever is ignited by a primary ignition in the humors <note>The body's fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, and then is ignited from them into the members—just as it happens when hot water is poured into a bath and the bricks are heated because of it, or hot broth is put in a pot and the pot is heated because of it—then that genus of fever is named **humoral fever**. And if a fever is ignited by its own primary ignition in the spirits and vapors, and then is ignited from them into the members and humors—just as it happens when hot air reaches a bath, or a fire is lit in it, whereby its air is warmed and reaches the water and the walls—then that genus of fever is named **ephemeral fever** <note>original: *febris ephemera*.</note>, which means "of one day." This is because it is ignited in a subtle substance <note>The spirits/vapors.</note> which is dispersed with speed; it rarely lasts beyond a day and its night, unless it is converted into another genus of fever.

In this series and progression of words, <term>Avicenna</term> confirms and declares his division—which was taken from <term>Hippocrates</term> and <term>Galen</term>—through various examples according to the variety of the underlying matter in which the "heat against nature" is ignited. He says that if a fever is ignited in the radical members by a primary ignition, it is like a burning. He means to say that if the solid members (which contain the other two parts constituting our body) are ignited first, these solid members relate to the previous comparison just like the walls of a bath, or the bellows of a smith, or the pot of a cook relate to the water existing in the bath. Such an inflammation in the solid members is called by the Greeks **hectic fever**, but by the Latins **habitual** <note>original: *habitudinalis*.</note>, since the heat does not depend on something else but exists in the member itself, possessing a "habit" <note>In this context, a "habit" refers to a deeply ingrained or permanent physical state.</note> and permanence...

...acquired. But if a heat contrary to nature, which is called a fever, is ignited first in the humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, and afterwards the solid members are ignited by that heat—so that one might understand this through sensory perception—the comparison is of bath-water to the walls of the bath. For example, if one pours hot water into a cold bath, and by means of the heat of the boiling water, the sides or parts and walls of the bath are set on fire; or if someone puts hot broth in a cold pot, and the pot which was cold is ignited by the boiling broth, then that kind is called **humoral fever**. You will note, however, that humoral fevers are of two kinds: namely, **putrid** and **non-putrid**. The putrid ones are *synocha* <note>original: *synocha*; a continuous fever believed to be caused by the fermentation of blood.</note> with putrefaction, tertian, quartan, and quotidian fevers <note>These refer to fevers that recur on the third, fourth, or every day, respectively.</note>. The non-putrid humoral fevers are *synochus* and "burning" tertian; but in order to include everything under one category, he <note>Avicenna.</note> called them all "humoral."

Next, he said: and if a fever—that is, a heat that is foreign and contrary to nature—is ignited first in the **spirits and vapors** <note>In Galenic medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle substances that carried life and sensation through the body.</note>, and then the spirits so heated by that foreign heat warm the members and humors (as happens when hot air reaches a bathhouse and warms it for that reason), this kind of fever is called **ephemeral** or "one-day" fever. And giving the reason why this fever is most often of one day’s duration, he says this is because the foreign heat is ignited in a subtle, spiritual, or vaporous substance, which is resolved <note>Dissipated or evaporated.</note> quickly and without difficulty. He says it is rare to see this fever last through a full day and night, unless it converts into another kind of fever, namely into the humoral or "habitual" <note>Related to the "hectic" fever mentioned on the previous page, which settles into the body's constitution.</note> kinds. Both of these fevers—the humoral and the habitual—are often long-lasting or protracted, and not without danger. 

Having said these things, Avicenna concludes his essential division with a note of inference and says: **THIS**, therefore, is the division of fevers by a method close to a division occurring through "differences" <note>original: *differentias*; a logical term referring to the specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within a genus.</note>. You will also note here that Avicenna said the division of fevers into three material subjective parts (in which the febrile heat is ignited) is a method close to a division by differences—you may add "essential" differences. And this is because fever does not have essential differences, but rather certain things similar to essential differences. This is sufficient for a physician to recognize a fever—which falls under the genus of "heat"—through certain alterations that distinguish febrile heat according to the various modes of that heat. These alterations are nothing other than the modes of various "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature.</note> in a heat contrary to nature, such that the heat remains the same contrary to na—

->PART TWO<-

...as for the other according to kind, which is called "altered" or "another" according to its name, just as we say of a sick man that he differs from his healthy self, or of a sleeping man that he differs from one who is awake. These differences are useful in the study of fevers, just as essential differences are, because they distinguish one fever from another—for instance, a **hectic fever** from a **humoral** or **ephemeral** one. They also help us recognize that the essence of each is different. Furthermore, according to the opinion of *Aristotle* in his *Topics*, and *Porphyry* in the *Predicables* <note>original: *in Praedicabilibus*; a standard textbook on logic used by medical students to learn how to classify things.</note>, essential differences are what constitute a species.

Thus, in this division based on the three underlying substances that take on the feverish heat, doctors establish three primary kinds of fevers, as was mentioned above. This division is more clearly defined than the previous one and is called an "essential" division by doctors. Indeed, the primary essential differences in a fever—which falls under the general category of heat—must be taken from the variety of the **heat contrary to nature** <note>original: *caloris praeter naturam*; a fundamental medical concept meaning heat that disrupts the body's healthy balance.</note>. This variety comes from a greater or lesser sharpness <note>original: *acredine*; referring to the "sting" or intensity of the heat.</note>, whether the heat afflicts the patient continuously and uniformly (as in a "habitual" fever <note>Refers to a fever that has become settled in the body's constitution, like a hectic fever.</note>), or with variation and relief (as in humoral fevers), or because the heat is mild and simple (as in ephemeral fevers).

Next, after this first division, he <note>Avicenna.</note> sets down another and says: AND fevers ARE DIVIDED in another way. For it is said that among fevers, some are **acute** and others are **non-acute**; some are **chronic** and some are **non-chronic**; some are **nocturnal** and some are **diurnal**; some are **rightly healthy** <note>Meaning they follow a predictable, non-lethal course.</note> and others have **horrible accidents** <note>In this context, "accidents" means symptoms or complications.</note>; some are **remitting** <note>Fevers that go away and come back.</note> and some are **inseparable** <note>Continuous fevers.</note>. Among the inseparable ones, some have intensifications and lulls <note>original: *remissiones*.</note>, or tepid periods, or strengthening surges; some are similar to one another; some are hot, and some are cold (having rigors or shivering); and some are simple while others are composite.

In this final part of the chapter, *Avicenna* provides these other divisions. These are not as "essential" as the ones he set down above, but they are nevertheless useful and follow from the ones already mentioned. Because the substance in which the feverish heat is ignited varies, the types and modes of fevers also vary, as I shall explain in each part of this final division.

Beginning with the first: some fevers are **acute**, which means they end quickly. As *Hippocrates* said in the second section of his *Aphorisms* <note>A famous collection of medical principles.</note>, these are the ones that end within fourteen days. Or, as *Galen* said in his commentary on that same work, acute diseases are those that are severe and move rapidly toward their **peak** <note>original: *statum*; the "status" or crisis of the disease when it is at its most intense.</note>, such as...

...the **exquisite tertian** <note>original: *tertiana exquisita*; a "perfect" or classic form of a fever that recurs every third day.</note> and the **burning fever** <term>causon</term> <note>From the Greek *kausos*, describing a high, inflammatory fever with intense thirst.</note>, as well as those that have severe **symptoms** <note>original: *accidentia*; literally "accidents," referring to the complications or signs that accompany the fever.</note>. And even if sometimes in acute cases the crisis or termination is delayed until the twentieth day, they still do not lose the name of "acute," because it is also inherent to the nature of acute fevers that they are accompanied by fear <note>Meaning they are inherently dangerous or life-threatening.</note>. 

On the other hand, fevers which are said to be not acute are mild, such as the **ephemeral fever**, which, even though it usually lasts only one day, does not for that reason have intense heat or severe symptoms. Or they are those that are neither severe nor malignant, even if they do not end quickly but are sometimes long, such as **quartan fevers** <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day.</note> and certain **false tertian fevers** <note>original: *tertianae nothae*; "bastard" or atypical tertian fevers that do not follow the standard cycle.</note> that lack bad symptoms. 

The second division is: some fevers are **chronic**, and some are **not chronic**. Those are called **chronic** which are long-lasting, passing the fortieth day and beyond; such are quartans, quotidians <note>Fevers that recur every day.</note>, and certain false tertians, or those in which the **humors** <note>The body's vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to cause disease if they became too thick or "corrupted."</note> are seized by a heat that is much thicker than is natural. And as you know, among the Greeks, the word **chronic** <term>χρονίος</term> <note>transliterated: *chronios*</note> signifies an "ancient man," and **time** <term>χρόνος</term> <note>transliterated: *chronos*</note> signifies that which the Latins call "long" or "long-lasting." Therefore, some are long, as has been said. 

**Non-chronic** fevers, however, are all those which end quickly and are brief—for instance, those that end on the fourteenth, the twentieth, or at least before the fortieth day. Among these are exquisite tertians, the burning fever, continuous fevers <note>original: *sinochae*; fevers that persist without intervals of relief.</note>, and also certain false tertians in which not much thick matter is mixed in.

Immediately following, he sets down the third division, which is as follows: among these fevers, some are **diurnal** and some are **nocturnal**. 
*   **Diurnal** fevers are those which either afflict the patient more during the daylight hours, or those which leave the sick man in the evening hours, as is the case with many tertian fevers. 
*   **Nocturnal** fevers, however, are those which trouble a person more at night. Such are those that are either quotidians, quartans, or false tertians mixed with a great deal of **phlegmatic** <note>original: *pituitoſa*; relating to phlegm, one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note> or **melancholic** <note>Relating to "black bile," associated with cold and dryness.</note> matter. 

You will note here that both the diurnal and nocturnal types are bad, because they are usually long-lasting due to the mixing of thick humors, or due to the weakness of the "virtue" <note>The body's natural healing power or vitality.</note> which is not strong enough to process the cold matter that has been mixed with the heat.

The fourth division follows: among these, some are **salutary and regular**, and some have **horrible symptoms**. 
*   **Salutary and regular** fevers are ephemerals and intermittent ones, such as tertians and quartans, which kill no one—especially if the patient uses a proper regimen of both the "six non-natural things" <note>The six factors health depends on: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind.</note> and medicinal treatments. 
*   They are called **regular** <note>original: *rectae*; literally "straight" or "right."</note> if they do not have fearful symptoms, such as **fainting** <term>lipothymia</term>...

-># PART TWO<-

...mixed, **mental disturbances** <note>original: *alienationes*; a term used in Renaissance medicine for delirium or a loss of mental clarity.</note> and similar **symptoms** <note>original: *accidentia*; literally "accidents," referring to the complications or secondary signs that accompany a disease.</note> which dull the vital force. However, those fevers having horrible symptoms are all fearsome, such as **syncopal fever** <note>A fever accompanied by sudden fainting or loss of strength.</note> and other non-intermittent fevers, because as **Hippocrates** said in the fourth section of the *Aphorisms*, Aphorism 43: "Fevers which do not intermit on the third day are not without danger," <note>original: *febres, quæ non intermittunt tertia die non carent periculo*</note> because from the continuous decay in the veins, a poisonous bad quality is contracted in the **humors** <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which doctors believed must stay in balance for health.</note>, from which follow often terrible symptoms, such as weakness of the pulse, sleeplessness, and mental disturbances. 

The **fifth division** is: some fevers are **intermittent** <note>original: *dimittentes*; fevers that pause or "leave off" between attacks.</note>, and some are **inseparable** <note>original: *inseparabiles*; meaning continuous or constant without a break.</note>. Intermittent fevers are those which place some time between one onset and the next, such as **tertian** and **quartan** fevers; these are mostly the ones that begin with a specific **pattern** <note>original: *typo*; the "type" or predictable cycle of a fever's return.</note> of shivering, cold, or rigors, and end with sweating. **Inseparable** fevers, however, are those which afflict the patient continuously; these are **synochas** <note>A type of continuous fever thought to be caused by the putrefaction of blood.</note>, **burning fevers**, and those that are continuous in a proportional or habitual way. 

You should also note that **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university text.</note> applied these five divisions to both **simple** and **complicated** fevers. The reason is that when fevers are combined with one another, one changes the condition of the other; for example, if an **ephemeral fever** <note>A short-lived fever lasting usually one day.</note> is combined with a **putrid** or **habitual** fever, it will be called either long or acute—not because of its own nature, but because of the complication of the other fever. 

Note also that **Avicenna** subdivides the second part of the division, saying: "And among the inseparable fevers, there are some which have **intensifications** and **remissions**." Indeed, in three kinds of continuous **synocha** fevers, these variations were noted by the ancient doctors. In an **augmastic** fever—which is called **increasing** by the Latins because it always proceeds by increasing—this is clearly apparent. The opposite is seen in a **paragmastic** fever, which is called **decreasing** by the Latins, for this fever always proceeds by decreasing until it reaches the state of no fever. 

When Avicenna says in his subdivision, "and of these some are similar," this refers to the third type of **synocha**, which is called **homotona** <note>From the Greek for "same tone," referring to a fever that stays at the same intensity.</note> by the Greeks, and **equal vigor** by the Latins, because from the beginning to the end the unnatural heat is uniform and equal. Furthermore, continuous tertians and quartans have a reduction in heat at certain hours, and continuous **quotidians** <note>Fevers that recur daily.</note> have a period of mildness <note>original: *teporem*; literally "lukewarmness."</note> at certain times. 

**Sixth**, he divides fever into **hot** and **cold**, and those accompanied by **rigors** and **shivering**. In my opinion, this section can be explained differently than many commentators explain it, and thus we will have a better understanding; for there are those which...

->## MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

...some **mixed fevers** <note>original: *febres compositæ*</note> in which the external parts of the body are hot, while the internal parts are cold; conversely, there are others in which the external parts are cold and the internal parts are hot, as seen in **empiala** <note>A type of fever where the patient feels internal cold and external heat simultaneously.</note> and **liparia** <note>A fever where the patient feels internal burning heat while the surface of the body remains cold.</note> fevers. Indeed, in an **empiala** fever, the cold is hidden within, while the external parts are mostly hot; for this reason, these are considered similar to "hot" fevers. Even though other fevers are also hot, this one might be called hot specifically in comparison to **liparia**, in which the external parts are cold and the internal parts are hot.

This passage can also be explained by saying that certain fevers are hot and are **continuous** <note>original: *continentes*; fevers that do not break or remit.</note> without any coldness, specific **cycle** <note>original: *typo*; the predictable period of a fever's return.</note>, or shivering—such as **synocha** <note>A continuous inflammatory fever often attributed to an excess of blood.</note>, **burning fevers** <note>original: *causonides*</note>, and **hectic fevers** <note>original: *habitudinales*; fevers that have settled into the "habit" or solid tissues of the body.</note>. However, because **liparia** has cold external parts, in this sense it can be called a "cold" fever. Alternatively, it may be explained as "cold" as many do by adding the words of **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard text in the Renaissance.</note> which follow: those having **shivering** <note>original: *rigorem*</note> and **goosebumps** <note>original: *horripilationem*</note>. Thus, the shivering and goosebumps serve as the clarifying part to explain what he means by a "cold fever"—that is, a fever in which cold, shivering, or goosebumps appear at the start of the **onset** <note>original: *accessionis*; the "attack" or period when the fever's symptoms are most acute.</note>. By this method of the onset's beginning, it is distinguished from other fevers that lack shivering, cold, or goosebumps.

The **last division** is: some fevers are **simple** and some are **composite**. A "simple" fever is defined in many ways. A **pure tertian** <note>original: *tertiana exquisita*; a fever caused by yellow bile that peaks every third day (a 48-hour cycle).</note> is called simple when only the **yellow bile** <note>original: *cholera*</note> decays without the mixture of another **humor** <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>. Similarly, a **quartan** <note>A fever that peaks every fourth day (a 72-hour cycle).</note> is called simple if the **black bile** <note>original: *humor melancholicus*</note> alone decays; and the same must be said for others. A fever is also called "simple" when it is not associated or complicated with another fever. It is also called simple if it is not composed of other types of fevers—such as a **one-day fever** <note>original: *ephemera*</note> by itself, or a purely **putrid fever**, or a **hectic fever**.

**Composite fevers**, on the other hand, are the opposite. Fevers can be called composite if they are not caused by the decay of a single humor, but by a mixture of one with other humors. This occurs in the more famous **spurious tertian** <note>original: *tertiana notha*; an "illegitimate" or irregular version of the 48-hour fever.</note>, in which the **black bile** is mixed with **yellow bile** and **phlegm** <note>original: *pituita*</note>. Fevers are also called composite if they are complicated by other fevers or another disease; for example, if a tertian fever is complicated by a **hectic fever** or another fever, or if the fever occurs alongside an **abscess** <note>original: *apostemate*; a localized collection of pus or a swelling.</note> or another specific disease. Also called "composite" are two tertian fevers afflicting the patient every single day, or two quartans, or even three afflicting them daily or with one day skipped. You should note, however, that although these last divisions are not as essential as those taken from the **heat** and the **matter** in which the heat is ignited...

<summary>Massa describes the differences between fevers with inverted internal/external temperatures (empiala and liparia) and defines the "last division" of fevers: simple (caused by one humor) versus composite (caused by mixed humors or multiple overlapping cycles).</summary>

# TO LORENZO MASSA, HIS NEPHEW,
## A Letter on the place where the humors putrefy in intermittent fevers.

## LETTER VII.

Lorenzo, you ask of me a thing that is in every respect arduous and difficult, which would require more rest for both mind and body than I currently have, and which cannot be explained so clearly and lucidly in the hurried style of a letter. Nevertheless, whatever it is that greatly hinders me, I will strive to satisfy you and our friends to the best of my ability, and I will begin the explanation of the question thus. The question, therefore, as you say, has long been debated among physicians concerning the location where the matter—which causes a **putrid intermittent fever** <note>A fever that comes and goes, believed to be caused by the "rotting" or decomposition of bodily fluids.</note> with periodic **attacks** <note>original: *accessiones*; the recurring episodes of fever and chills.</note>—actually putrefies: whether it is within the veins, or rather outside the veins, as the majority of physicians claim. And so that we may proceed with a **leaden foot** <note>original: *plumbeo pede*; a Latin idiom meaning to move slowly and with great caution.</note> in a difficult matter, while maintaining due respect for the ancients, I will reveal the matter to you better than they left it to us; for it is easy for anyone to add something of their own to things already discovered. Therefore, setting aside a longer prelude so the discourse is not overextended, I will begin to speak with you on this matter, starting from the weaker points.

Furthermore, the causes of the attacks are some disordered **breath** <note>original: *halitus*; a fine, vaporous substance thought to circulate in the body.</note>, or vapors, or the finer parts of a **humor** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined health in Renaissance medicine.</note> altered by a non-natural change, not without **bitterness** <note>original: *acredine*; a sharp or pungent quality believed to irritate the tissues.</note>. These very often exit the veins, driven by the stimulated **expulsive faculty** <note>original: *expultrice virtute*; the biological power responsible for ridding the body of waste or harmful substances.</note> sending them to neighboring sensitive limbs. Sometimes also those vapors raised outside the veins are driven to those same sensitive parts, such as the nerves or things mixed with nerves, like muscles and membranes; which indeed...

when vapors reach the sensitive parts of the body, they cause a distressing sensation and pain. For this reason, once those parts have perceived the harm, they are moved by the **motive power** <note>original: *uirtute motrice*; the vital force believed to govern involuntary movement and bodily functions.</note> to expel that harm, sometimes through a contracting motion and sometimes through a shaking motion. In this way, **attacks** <note>original: *accessiones*; the periodic episodes of chills and fever.</note> occur—or rather, certain movements intended to expel the substance that is harmful first by its quality and also by its quantity in those fevers which they call "intermittent." These movements or attacks do not always happen in the same way when the quality or quantity of the matter is stimulating them, as they are frequently observed to differ.

Indeed, a **trembling** <note>original: *tremor*</note> arises if the outer skin is so compressed that the vapors are barely able to escape freely. There are also, as I have said, often certain thin and sharp **humors** <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health.</note> which, for the reason already mentioned, are driven out of the veins toward the sensitive parts. When the passages in the circuit of the body or the veins are closed off by some obstructing cause, the humors contained within them cannot "breathe" <note>meaning to ventilate or release pressure</note> but can easily **putrefy** <note>rot or decompose</note>. These humors, by their quality and quantity, weigh upon and stimulate the motive power, causing not only a trembling motion, but—since they are more substantial than vapors—they cause greater harm to the sensitive parts than the vapors themselves do. 

From this follows a greater movement, which is not merely a trembling but a violent shaking; this they call **rigor** <note>A medical term for sudden coldness with shivering, typical of the start of a fever.</note>. After this, if the passages have been closed so that "respiration" <note>The skin's ability to "breathe" or release internal heat and vapors.</note> is prohibited, a fever is very often ignited, as I said. However, where both the said vapors and the humors are not so potent in their quantity or quality (either in the whole body or in parts), none of these accidents we have just mentioned will follow. That is to say, there will be neither **horripilation** <note>Goosebumps or the sensation of hair standing on end.</note> nor rigor, but a certain uneven sensation will be perceived, which is called "ulcerous." 

But when the vapors or thin humors driven from the veins are harmful, they create no small difficulty regarding the manner of their expulsion, whether by their quality or quantity. <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated medicine for over a thousand years.</note> says in the sixteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts* that veins and arteries do not feel or suffer pain if they are cut. Since the matter stands such that they entirely lack sensation, someone might ask: how can the veins be stimulated by either the quality or the quantity of a humor? At first glance, this question appears difficult; nevertheless, I can easily resolve it, provided I first touch upon certain things that are very well known even to common men and to those who have not yet greeted the first lights of medicine—for I shall not speak to those who have already grown old in the craft. The first point is that an impulse toward expulsion is created by the power of the parts...

## SECOND PART

limbs <note>original: *membri*; completing the word from the previous page.</note> innate, if some matter or vapor residing unnaturally in the members themselves should harm them. But since my business is with **rational physicians** <note>Those who practiced "rational medicine," a tradition following Galen that used logic and theory to understand the causes of disease, rather than relying solely on experience.</note>, who readily yield to both reason and experience, I shall therefore explain the matter again in this way. 

Since four **powers** <note>original: *uirtutes*; the vital faculties or functional abilities believed to be inherent in every part of the living body.</note> have been given by nature to each individual member for its own guardianship and preservation—as everyone experiences daily within themselves—namely the **attractive power**, the **retentive power**, the **concoctive power**, and the **expulsive power** of excrement and harmful things. All wise men affirm this opinion, and **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity (2nd century CE), whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> proved it most beautifully with both experience and reason in his book *On Natural Faculties* <note>original: *De Potentiis Naturalibus*.</note>. 

For since **natural heat** <note>The innate warmth of a living body, often compared to a lamp's flame.</note> continually feeds upon and is nourished by **radical moisture** <note>The vital fluid or "oil" that sustains the body’s natural heat; its exhaustion was thought to cause aging and death.</note>, it is consistent that this heat consumes and dries it out. For that reason, Nature—which neither fails in what is necessary nor abounds in what is superfluous—gave to each member and its parts (even if they lack sensation) these other powers: 

*   The **attractive power** <note>original: *uirtutem attractricem*</note>, so that they might draw in nourishment to replace the moisture lost and dried up by the native heat. 
*   And so that it might be applied according to opportunity, she also gave the **retentive power** <note>original: *retentricem*</note>, so that it might hold the attracted nourishment for the required time. 
*   She also gave the **concoctive power** <note>original: *uirtutem concoctricem*; "concoction" refers to the process of "ripening" or digesting food and humors to make them useful to the body.</note>, so that by cooking the retained nourishment, it might transform it and make it similar to the member being nourished, converting it into its own substance. 

But because in every concoction, wastes are always separated out—which are also sometimes affected by some evil quality—Nature therefore also gave the members an **expulsive power** <note>original: *uirtutem expultricem*</note>, so that they might expel every kind of waste and harmful thing. 

Since the matter stands thus, anyone will be able to easily solve the proposed question and recognize the truth of Nature's operation. By explaining the matter in this way, we will not say that the expulsion occurring in the **attacks of intermittent fevers** <note>original: *accessionibus febrium intermittentium*; fevers like malaria that come and go in cycles.</note>, or in any other way, happens because the veins or arteries or other members (in which the matter from which the sharp vapor rises has already collected) "feel" the harm through the sense of touch—as if they perceive the quality or quantity of the vapor through a sensory organ. 

Instead, we shall say that by the intention of Nature, the **expulsive power** of the troubled member—which recoils from such a thing—performs a **sequestration** <note>A separation or sorting out.</note> of the bad from the good. This is done so that the part which is harmful and least able to provide nourishment is expelled, while those parts which contribute to nourishment are attracted. For if that which is driven out by the nature of the member as harmful were to remain with the good, it would certainly hinder good nutrition, as can be seen in bodies filled with **evil juices** <note>original: *malis succis*; referring to corrupt or unbalanced humors.</note>.

<summary>Massa explains the four natural faculties (attractive, retentive, concoctive, and expulsive) that govern how every part of the body feeds itself and stays healthy. He argues that fever attacks are not "felt" like a touch, but are the result of the body's expulsive power trying to separate harmful waste from good nourishment.</summary>

which are called <term>cacochymia</term> <note>original: *cacochima*; from the Greek *kakochymia*, meaning "bad juices" or an imbalance of unhealthy humors.</note> by the Greeks. But when these bad humors do not have an external cause to make them rot, they instead <term>putrefy</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "putrefaction" (rotting) was the process by which humors broke down, often generating the heat that caused fevers.</note> either of their own accord due to their substance, their quantity, or their quality. If they are drawn to the limbs, they do indeed nourish them, but not properly; since the nourishment is <term>excrementous</term> <note>Waste-filled or full of impurities.</note> and is not regulated by the power of the limb, there follows from it <term>scabies</term> <note>A general term for itchy skin eruptions, rashes, or mange.</note> or other skin infections, or pains in the joints—specifically when the matter is driven toward the joints.

This power does not act because it "feels" or thinks, but through its own nature, so that it may purge waste and drive out whatever is harmful. 

This can be seen in spontaneous sweating, in the "descent" and <term>distillations</term> <note>Catarrh or the dripping of fluids (phlegm) from the head into the throat.</note> from the head to the throat, and in very many transfers of matter from one limb to another. This matter is not felt while it is moving, yet it is felt if it settles in some sensitive limb. 

But let the discourse return to where it digressed. As was said at the beginning of the speech, that which is expelled is either a certain sharp vapor or some subtle, sharp matter which is driven out from the **humoral mass** within the veins. It does not matter whether this vapor or subtle humor is raised from **bile**, or is a part of a more subtle **bilious**, **melancholic**, or **phlegmatic humor**. It is enough—if we believe **Galen** in the tenth book of his *Method of Healing* <note>original: *Methodus Medendi*; one of Galen's major therapeutic works.</note>, where he gives the cause of the shivering, cold, and rigor that happens in <term>intermittent fevers</term> <note>Fevers that come and go at regular intervals, such as malaria.</note>—who says the cause of all these things is a "stinging breath," or some subtle humor or juice, carried through the sensitive limbs. When it arrives there, it causes a shuddering and an unequal shaking of the whole body. In those who have tight skin, when those <term>sooty</term> vapors <note>original: *fuliginofa*; waste gases or "smoke" produced by the body's internal heat which were supposed to be exhaled through the skin.</note> (which were previously breathed out) are retained, they produce a fever as they seek the heart. 

From this it appears that shivering, coldness, and shudders in intermittent fevers are caused by a vapor or a rotting humor driven to the sensitive limbs. When these limbs feel the harm, they are moved by a natural and not a voluntary motion, so that they may expel what is harmful to them—either because of its quality or its quantity—whether that harm comes from vapors or...
