# PART TWO

to the humors: and for that reason <term>rigors</term> <note>original: *rigores*; severe shivering or shaking chills often associated with the onset of fever.</note> occur, because the vapor or humor that is driven to the sensitive limbs is sharp and biting, so much so that this quality cannot be tolerated by the limbs. But if the vapor or humor is less sharp, a type of coldness will follow from its expulsion; and if the sharpness is only very slight, <term>horripilation</term> <note>original: *horripilatio*; the sensation of hair standing on end or "goosebumps."</note> will follow. Nor is it necessary to seek any other explanation in the case of other humors or vapors arising from the <term>melancholic</term> <note>The humor associated with black bile, considered cold and dry.</note> or the putrefying <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>original: *pituitoso*; relating to phlegm (pituita), the cold and moist humor.</note> humor. For in the onset of [fever] attacks, the cause of such symptoms must be taken from the matter which has been stirred up by the sharp, putrid quality within them or from them (even if they are naturally cold). According to what has been said, the vapors and moisture which are driven from the veins by the <term>expulsive power</term> <note>The natural faculty of the body to rid itself of waste.</note> are from the more <term>subtle</term> <note>Thin, refined, or volatile parts of a substance.</note> parts that were beginning to rot in the veins. When these are separated and driven out by the expulsive power, it is reasonable to say that in this manner of expulsion—if only vapors are expelled—no matter has actually exited the veins, and consequently, no rotting occurs outside them.

But if a more subtle part of the humor [exits], as <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential physician of antiquity (2nd century AD) whose system of medicine focused on the four humors.</note> also believed in the tenth book of the *Method of Healing* <note>original: *Methodi* (referring to *Methodus Medendi*), one of Galen's major works on therapeutics.</note>, that portion will indeed be small and thin, and it would rot after exiting. Those who believe that the matter in <term>intermittent fevers</term> <note>Fevers that come and go at regular intervals, such as malaria.</note> rots for the most part within the veins do not deny this, since such matter can be consumed by heat quickly—even very quickly—because it is both small in quantity and thin. Therefore, since the opposite appears to be true in intermittent fevers—which, if they are not from pure <term>bile</term> <note>original: *bile/cholera*; yellow bile, the hot and dry humor.</note> but are mixed, they afflict a person for many hours—it is found that <term>tertian fevers</term> <note>A fever where the paroxysm (attack) occurs every third day (every 48 hours).</note> sometimes continue with an external heat for thirty or forty hours, and often right up until the next new attack. This happens for no other reason than because the remaining matter was not expelled, either due to its thickness, the narrowness of the passages, or some weakness of the expulsive power. Thus, while it rots even within the veins, there is a continuous evaporation toward the heart and a heating of the heart itself; this heat differs according to the underlying matter of the thing.

For if the bile has not been mixed with a great deal of phlegm, the febrile heat will be sharp; but if much phlegmatic matter has been mixed with the bile, as happens in the more famous <term>spurious bile</term> <note>original: *cholera notha*; a "false" biliary fever caused by a mixture of yellow bile and phlegm.</note>, the febrile heat will not be sharp. Similarly, if pure phlegmatic humor rots, so that the putrid vapors are raised to the heart, the febrile heat will be very mild. The same must be said of natural melancholic humor when it rots, relative to the biliary humor. [f]ever. This notion is not at all consistent with the senses, and let us see how it is so: <term>horripilation</term> <note>original: *horripilatio*; the sensation of "goosebumps" or hair standing on end.</note>, cold, and <term>rigor</term> <note>shaking chills.</note> occur because, as has been said, a vapor or some subtle, sharp humor—when it reaches the sensitive limbs, such as the muscles or membranes, driven by the power of the pulse—irritates those very limbs with its biting quality. For then the muscles, and not the membranes, are altered and stimulated by the sharp quality of the humor or vapor; they cease, however, after they have already changed their <term>temperament</term> <note>The internal balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> back into their own nature. 

Indeed, if the [opposing] notion were true, since the expelled matter continuously acquires a greater degree of putrefaction and consequently greater heat, there would follow a continuous increase in horripilation, cold, or rigor, up to the peak of the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>original: *paroxysmi*; the point at which a fever or fit is at its highest intensity.</note> (that is, the fever attack), since putrefaction always increases until that hour. For if putrefaction increases continuously, the matter becomes hotter and stimulates the sensitive limbs even more. 

Furthermore, if this expelled matter were plentiful and descended to the muscles, it would certainly raise some part into a swelling; and if it were too thick, it would cause some hard abscess—or a soft one if the matter were not thick. This abscess, once the matter has <term>suppurated</term> <note>formed pus.</note> and turned into pus, would eventually cause a rupture or ulcerations in the limbs. This happens sometimes if matter is pushed down from the head to the throat, causing <term>synanches</term> <note>original: *synanchæ*; an ancient term for severe throat inflammation, such as quinsy or tonsillitis, that threatens suffocation.</note>. 

And in the expulsion of <term>smallpox</term> <note>original: *variolarum*.</note> in children, while nature attempts to purify the blood, there is first a heating of the blood and a great fever, and soon an expulsion of the matter throughout the entire body, which matter is also converted into pus. This is evident in certain pestilential diseases, when nature, in a final effort arising from the <term>malignancy</term> <note>The harmful or infectious quality of the disease.</note> contracted in the humoral mass, rises up to purify the blood and expel the harmful substance. From this, pestilential tumors, <term>carbuncles</term> <note>original: *carbones*; painful, pus-filled boils.</note>, and other types of <term>tubercles</term> <note>Small lumps or swellings.</note> often follow, for no other reason than that, besides vapors, a great deal of matter is also driven out of the veins. 

Therefore, since in mild fevers not much matter is expelled, nor is it thick, but rather vapors and more subtle moistures (which cannot transmit a long-lasting "smoking out" to the heart nor be prolonged for many hours), it follows that the matter causing the fever is partly outside the veins (and that is subtle and small in amount) and partly inside the veins (and this is thicker and rots for the most part). This is confirmed by the red color of the urine resulting from the thickness and the mixing of various humors. Different kinds of sediments also appear in them; such sediment or "little clouds" usually attest to the good...

## PART SECOND

[maligni]ty, or the malice, and the manner, and the time of the putrefaction of the putrefying humors. For indeed, if all the matter were to putrefy (as some say) outside the veins, how, I ask, could we recognize through the <term>urine</term> <note>original: *lotium*; used here interchangeably with *urina*.</note> the thickness and the preparation of the humor that is putrefying and causing the fever? This is because urine is the waste of the blood separated from the <term>liver</term> <note>original: *iecinore*.</note> and the veins. 

If there appears in the urine a white, smooth, and uniform <term>little cloud</term> <note>original: *nubecula*; a suspension of sediment in the urine which medieval doctors used to judge the progress of a disease.</note>, it is an indubitable sign of the preparation and the "goodness" <note>Meaning the ripeness or readiness of the harmful humor to be expelled.</note> of the matter causing the fever. Galen wrote of this in his books *On Crises* <note>original: *de Crisibus*; a fundamental text by the Greek physician Galen regarding the "turning point" of a disease.</note>, and he compared this cloud in the urine of feverish patients to the discharge and pus found in the ulcers of internal and external limbs. He further expanded on this in his cited example concerning <term>Pleurisy</term> <note>original: *Pleuritide*; an inflammation of the lungs and chest cavity.</note>. 

Furthermore, just as when matter in an ulcer is plentiful and is not quickly regulated in every part by the <term>natural heat</term> <note>original: *calore naturali*; the internal warmth of the body responsible for digestion and healing.</note> while the heat begins to prepare it, but as the action of the heat continues, it begins to turn white and be converted into a better substance; in the same way, if the matter putrefies within the veins and the natural heat begins to prepare that humor, there also appears a cloud in the urine, along with a change in substance, color, and other qualities. 

Nor can the humor contained in the veins be evacuated through the urine in any other way, except because the watery waste is attracted by the nature of the kidneys and descends to the bladder; and that which was putrid in the veins is led out through the urine—either driven out by natural heat through <term>imperceptible evaporation</term> <note>original: *insensibilem euaporationem*; the belief that the body expels waste through invisible pores in the skin.</note> after being converted, or reduced to a benign state by that same heat. This aligns with Galen’s belief in his handbook *The Art of Medicine* <note>original: *libello artis paruae* (Ars Parva); a standard medical textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, where he says that <term>concoction</term> <note>The "ripening" or "cooking" of raw humors by body heat.</note> removes putrefaction while the matter itself nevertheless remains. 

Thus we examine diverse urines—in substance, heat, and quantity—and the clouds contained within them, which are signs of the victory that the body’s <term>vital power</term> <note>original: *uirtus*.</note> reports over the overcome matter. On the contrary, if the urines are disturbed and not regulated by heat, they show cause for fear, danger, and sometimes certain destruction.

But (to come to the point), if the matter were putrefying outside the veins, how could that ash-colored substance between the muscles or between other limbs and places enter the veins and be led to the pathways of the liver, kidneys, and bladder? How could it show us the victory of either the regulating heat or the matter causing the disease? 

It remains, therefore, for us to say—as has been proven—that the matter causing an <term>intermittent fever</term> <note>original: *febrem intermittentem*; a fever that comes and goes, such as malaria.</note> putrefies partly inside the veins and partly outside the veins, and in greater quantity [outside], especially when the <term>paroxysms</term> <note>The fits or spikes of a fever.</note> become longer. And lest the matter should in any part, as far as possible, leave ambiguity from the words of the ancients...

<summary>Massa argues that since urine (a byproduct of the blood and liver) reflects the state of a fever, the putrefying humors must exist inside the veins, not just in the muscles. He uses Galen’s theories of "concoction" and "clouds" in urine to prove that natural body heat works to ripen and expel these diseased humors.</summary>

...this I leave to you, it will be worthwhile for me to declare certain things that may seem to contradict the writings of the ancient physicians. For they say that **intermittent fevers** <note>Fevers that come and go at regular intervals, such as those associated with malaria.</note> begin with shivering, cold, or rigor, and end with sweat. This occurs for no other reason than this: the matter which was driven outside the veins is converted into vapors; these, reaching the outermost part of the skin, are thickened, changed into the nature of water, and expelled from the body. 

But if this is so, how, I ask, can the **urine** <note>original: *lotium*</note> reveal the "rawness" or the **concoction** <note>original: *coctionem*; the process by which the body's internal heat "cooks" or ripens a harmful humor to prepare it for expulsion.</note> of the humor that causes the fever and has been driven outside the veins? Nor, as I have stated, can it be argued that the matter driven outside the veins enters them again once it has already been evacuated through sweat. 

If anyone wishes to know the manner in which these vapors are changed into sweat, I can easily explain it. For since the matter driven outside the veins is continuously refined until the peak of the fever, and as the heat lessens during the decline, the skin is cooled somewhat. The vapors are then united and thickened; thus they change into a watery substance and exit the body perceptibly, whereas before they were exiting imperceptibly <note>Massa is describing the transition from "insensible perspiration" (evaporation you can't feel) to visible sweat.</note>. 

And even though natural sweat is the waste product of the **third concoction** <note>In Galenic medicine, the "third concoction" is the final stage of nutrition where food is fully transformed into the body's actual tissues.</note>, which is completed in the small veins that carry and prepare nourishment for the limbs, this does not contradict what has been proven regarding the location where the humor putrefies during an intermittent fever. 

If anyone should happen to say that the **ash-like residue** <note>original: *cineritium*; a term for the dry, burnt-looking sediment left over after a fever has "burned" through a humor.</note> which remained outside the veins from the putrefying matter enters the veins again and travels to the urinary passages, he would certainly be in error. He would be considered ignorant of the operations of nature rather than a diligent seeker of truth. It is extremely difficult for waste products to return once they have been expelled by a revolted nature, for they can no longer provide nourishment or any other growth. 

Therefore, it must be said that the ash-like residue does not enter the veins at all. Instead, it is gradually consumed by nature—either converted into vapors or into that excremental filth familiar to the skin—and it exits along with the sweat. However, that ash-like residue which remains in the veins (as doctors call it)—which is not dry like actual ash, but is simply drier in relation to the fluid humor—is that very matter which was putrefying. It is for this reason that it is called **ash-like**, and it is the portion of the matter that was putrefying within the veins themselves. When this matter is regulated and "cooked" by the body's heat, it is set aside by nature and separated from the mass of the humors. A certain part of it passes with the filtered blood to the urinary tracts, drawn there by the kidneys. Thus, there appears in the urine a sediment or...

<summary>Massa explains that while some fever-causing matter is expelled as sweat, the diagnostic signs found in urine come from "ash-like" residues processed within the veins. He argues that once waste is expelled from the veins, it cannot return to them.</summary>

## PART TWO

...the cloud-like sediment <note>original: *nubecula*; a floating sediment in the urine used by Renaissance doctors to judge the state of a disease.</note> is altered in various ways according to the progression of the disease and the passage of time by **natural heat** <note>The body's innate warmth, which was believed to drive digestion and healing.</note>. This heat is the instrument nature uses for all its operations. The remaining matter is either returned to a healthy state, or it is dissolved by the heat, consumed into vapors, and evacuated imperceptibly. 

However, if it were true that all the matter in **intermittent fevers** <note>Fevers that cycle between peaks and periods of apparent health.</note> was pushed outside the veins and rotted between the muscles or other parts of the body, how could those muscles and other parts protect themselves from the obvious rot caused by direct contact? For that which touches something putrid can easily rot itself; at the very least, by absorbing the temperature of the area and breaking its "unity" <note>An "interruption of unity" was a classical medical term for a wound, lesion, or internal tear.</note>, it would cause pain or some other very great injury that would persist for several days after the patient was free from the fever. Furthermore (as we said above), the area would be raised up in a swelling by the thinned matter. 

If they should ask again: "If the matter in intermittent fevers putrefies not only outside, but also inside the veins, how can these patients reach a period where they are free from fever?" For the consensus of all physicians is that in continuous putrid fevers, the matter rots inside the veins. 

The answer to this question is not difficult, provided that the matters can resist more or less based on their quantity. Each **humor** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health.</note> has its own substance, differing in thickness and thinness, through which it can be dissolved, consumed, or **incinerated** <note>original: *incinerari*; a term used by physicians to describe the process of a humor being "burned up" or completely resolved by internal heat.</note> by heat, either quickly or slowly. 

Since **bilious humor** <term>Yellow bile; one of the four humors, associated with a hot and dry temperament.</term> is thin and subtle in its substance, it is easily seized by "non-natural" heat and easily consumed. We can take an example from **tow** <note>Waste fibers from flax or hemp, used here as an example of highly flammable tinder.</note> and wood. If they are caught by fire, the tow is quickly ignited and quickly consumed wherever it may be; wood, however, is neither quickly lit nor quickly consumed. 

From this, it appears that the reason for the continuity and the length of the heat in putrid fevers is not always because the matter rots in the veins, but rather because the matter which putrefies and was seized by unnatural heat is abundant and thick—either by its own nature, or because it is mixed with another humor, or altered in some other way. For example, it might be scorched by heat or have its finer parts dissolved. Sometimes the cause lies with the **virtue** <note>original: *uirtutis*; the body's innate vital power or strength.</note>, if it is too weak and unable to regulate the matter. Thus, a continuous fever is not necessarily produced because the matter is ignited specifically in the veins, but because its quantity and thickness allow it to remain longer before being "incinerated" by the putrid heat, or because the weak virtue cannot...

<summary>Massa argues that the duration of a fever depends on the consistency and quantity of the "putrid matter" (humors) rather than just its location in the body. He uses the analogy of tow versus wood to explain why some fevers are brief and intermittent while others are long and continuous.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Massa’s technical explanation of how "matter" (the humors causing disease) interacts with the body's internal heat to produce different types of fevers. He is concluding his argument that the location of this matter—whether inside or outside the veins—determines the fever's pattern.</meta>

-># THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

...to consume it quickly; for a fever will persist for as long as the matter, wherever it may be, serves as fuel for **unnatural heat** <note>Heat produced by disease or putrefaction, as opposed to the body's healthy "innate heat."</note>. Thus, an **intermittent fever** <note>A fever that comes and goes, like malaria.</note> can be caused by thick matter rotting in the veins, provided there is only a small amount of it. Conversely, a **continuous fever** could be produced by thick and abundant matter rotting outside the veins—retaining its heat for a long time—due to its sheer density and quantity. Indeed, when the matter is thick and plentiful, it cannot be consumed by the heat until other rotting matter, having been pushed to that spot, is driven out.

Because of these facts, it will not be difficult to believe that an **intermittent tertian fever** <note>original: *tertianam intermittentem*; a fever that peaks every third day (counting the day of the peak), typically associated with malaria.</note> is sometimes caused by a small amount of matter rotting within the veins. It will be even easier to believe that in cases of intermittent fevers where cold, shivering, or **rigor** <note>original: *rigor*; a clinical term for violent shivering accompanied by a sense of cold.</note> has preceded the fever, these sensations have in some way drawn out some part of the matter from the veins; what then remained in the veins could be more effectively and quickly finished, consumed, or **incinerated** <note>original: *incinerari*; the process of the body's heat burning off the "sooty" byproducts of disease.</note> by the heat. This occurs so that vapors can no longer be raised from that ashy residue remaining in the veins to heat the heart.

Furthermore, humors sometimes rot in veins far from the heart—for example, in some extremity of the body—and vapors are raised which cause no fever unless they actually reach the heart itself. Instead, one observes dryness and a **withered appearance** <note>original: *squalor*; a dry, rough, or unhealthy condition of the skin and flesh.</note> in those extreme parts, especially those near the site of the rot. Once that putrefaction is finished, the limbs are no longer withered but are restored to a balanced state. 

From this, you can also gather how that maxim which is always in the mouths of some doctors—namely, that it is characteristic of continuous fevers not to involve shivering—is not always true. For it very often happens, for the reasons stated, that sometimes a small, thin matter rots in the veins and is consumed so quickly that the patient reaches a fever-free state before new matter can gather at the site of the rot; thus, it will be an intermittent fever without shivering. Because that small quantity does not weigh upon the veins nor is it even perceived by them, it is not set apart by the **innate power** <note>The body’s natural defensive faculty or "virtue" that recognizes and expels harmful substances.</note>. 

On the contrary, it also happens sometimes that matter rots outside the veins and nonetheless causes a continuous fever, as occurs in **pleurisy** <note>An inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs.</note>. For even if the rotting matter is outside the veins, because it is located so near the heart, it ignites not just a fever, but a continuous one.

I shall put an end to this curious question, my Lorenzo, which I wanted to write to you so that I might eventually excite you toward greater contemplations, rather than merely stimulating you to diligence. 

Farewell. 

Venice, 
January 16, 1552.

## LETTER VIII.

**I** was wishing, most learned Vincent, and also my dearest friend, that an opportunity might finally be given to me to write to you about some arduous matter, so that I might at last testify to you how much I value your judgment. Now chance has brought about that which I have long desired. For when certain most learned young men were with me in a boat <note>Likely a gondola, as Massa practiced in Venice.</note>, visiting patients as is the custom, they began to debate among themselves concerning the essence or substance of **febrile heat** <note>original: *caloris febrilis*; the specific type of heat that constitutes a fever.</note>. They were attempting to demonstrate that febrile heat is a substance and a certain body. They argued this because, on the authority of **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated medicine for over a thousand years.</note> following the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient "Father of Medicine."</note>, a **fever** <note>original: *Febris*</note> is **innate heat** <note>original: *nativus calor*; the natural, life-sustaining warmth found within a living body.</note> converted into a fiery state. And since—on the authority of the same Hippocrates and Galen likewise—innate heat is a **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*; in ancient medicine, a subtle, vaporous substance that carries life through the body.</note> and a subtle body, and a body is said to be a substance, it follows that fever is a corporeal substance. 

They said this conclusion, thus derived, was rare and solid, because they had heard it debated and approved in the **University of Padua** <note>original: *Gymnasio Patavino*; one of the most prestigious medical schools in Renaissance Europe.</note> among the most famous professors of medicine teaching publicly. These young men also, in order to defend the decrees of their teacher, in addition to many arguments brought forth here and there, showed certain writings. Having read these (in my judgment, at least), these things seemed very difficult to resolve—especially since other most famous commentators on **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> have not fully clarified it from every perspective, among whom were **Gentilis, Ugo, Arculanus** <note>Gentile da Foligno, Ugo Benzi, and Giovanni Arcolani—all major scholastic medical authorities.</note>, and others. 

The speech or question began thus with the authority of **Aristotle**: that which reason shows is a definition; but the name itself is that which confusedly, in some way, judges the definition. With these things thus established, the weight of the name "fever" was proposed for consideration. Thus, "fever" has the same meaning in both the Greek and Latin name, and signifies the same nature. For as Galen said in the eighth commentary on the third book of *On Fractures*: in Greek, it is called **Pyretos** <note>original: *Piretos*; from the Greek *pyr*, meaning fire.</note> from fire, namely, having its name from it. From this, it is inferred that fever is nothing other than a certain fiery heat. In Latin, it also signifies the same, since "fever" signifies a burning...

This he also confirms by the testimony of **Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor and a pioneer in botany and physics.</note>, who say that a word of this kind signifies first "fire," and then "heat." From this, he infers that this distinction is necessary so that we might be able to know whether fever is **heat-ness** <note>original: *caliditas*; refers to the abstract quality of being hot.</note>, which is a quality, or a **substance** <note>original: *substantia*; here meaning a physical matter or "body".</note> which is affected by heat. And it is called a substance as Galen says in the cited book *On Temperature*, saying <insert>that</insert> <note>Common abbreviation for 'quod'</note> the first principles and elements of the body are the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry. 

Since this is so, the aforementioned distinction concerning heat was necessary, so that when it is said "fever is heat," we may see whether it is "heat-ness" or a hot body. Immediately following these words, other words of Galen followed—taken from the book which was to be explained by the teacher—serving as contradictory foundations; for there he said that fever is a **heat contrary to nature** <note>original: *calorem præter naturam*; heat that disrupts the body's natural balance.</note>, which heat, according to Galen, is a quality. 

And for confirmation, he says Galen wrote in the book *On Temperaments* that there was no one who refers the term <term>thermodes</term> <note>original: *chermodis*, a Latinization of the Greek word for "hot" or "warm".</note> to the subject alone: therefore, it signifies a quality when we say fever is heat—that is, "heat-ness." He leaves aside many other passages of Galen which confirm the first hypothesis—namely, that febrile heat is "heat-ness"—since there are also other authorities contrary to these sayings, such as in the first [book of] *Aphorisms*, commentary 14; and in the fourth commentary of the sixth [book] of *Epidemics*, commentary 25; as well as in the second [book] of *On the Composition of Medicaments according to Genera*, chapter 22. 

In all of these places, he says that "the hot contrary to nature" can be referred to a quality and to a hot body, nor should it be believed otherwise: because if anyone were to say that he speaks of "the hot" as a quality, Galen would contradict himself. From these, he says again that Galen is wavering and doubtful in this matter; wherefore...

->## PART TWO.<-

P

To reconcile his words so that he might not contradict himself, [the author] says—following the opinion of **Hippocrates**—that things can be considered in different ways and according to different meanings. For that reason, they can be named differently by **Galen**. In confirmation of this, he says that in the bodies of living creatures there is found a certain hot substance in which fire dominates, which is mixed with airy and watery parts and is necessary for every living thing. This substance, according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, is either the soul of the living creature itself, or the immediate instrument that the soul uses for its operations. This substance has a temperament <note>The "temperament" or "complexion" was the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determined a person's health.</note> which results from the mixing of the aforementioned parts—namely fire, air, and water.

**Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and **the Philosopher** <note>A standard honorific for **Aristotle**, whose physical theories underpinned Renaissance medicine.</note> call this substance **innate heat** <term>calidum natiuum</term>. It is generated from the thinner and more refined part of the blood, and it is nourished and preserved by it. But if this substance is changed and exceeds the limits of its proper temperament, becoming hotter, then that heat—insofar as it exceeds its proper limits—surpasses its nature because of its excessive hotness. This is because the proper definition of innate heat is its balanced temperature. Thus, to the extent that the innate heat exceeds its own nature, it is changed into the nature of **extraneous heat** <term>calor extraneus</term>. 

However, if it should incline or be changed toward the cold, it is a different matter. By the same logic, if it has been turned toward a hotter quality, **fever** or other hot diseases arise. But if it is changed toward the cold, cold diseases occur, such as **dropsy** <note>original: *aqua intercutem*, literally "water between the skin," a condition of swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>, **apoplexy** <note>A sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke.</note>, **epilepsy**, and other similar conditions. Therefore, just as natural heat consists in its proper temperament, diseases are created through an excess of heat beyond its proper limits. 

From these points, he draws an inference and says: therefore, this is the same nature and the same body which, under different temperaments, is at one time **natural heat** and at another time **extraneous heat**. He says that **Galen** affirmed this conclusion in the eighth book of the *Therapeutic Method* and in the book *On Natural Faculties*. He also repeats what I said a little while ago: namely, that according to this reasoning, when we say a fever is an extraneous, fiery heat, we are saying it is that same substance and that same body which was called "natural heat" when it was balanced; but when it exceeded [that balance], it is called "fever," as **Hippocrates** intended in his book of *Epidemics*. 

He confirms this deduction and says it is true based on the progression of the sixth book of the *Epidemics*, commentary 5, when he speaks of the **innate heat** <term>innatum calidum</term>. And he exclaims, saying: "Behold, therefore, that this heat which previously used to rule the body and rendered all its operations whole—"

<summary>Nicolò Massa explains the physiological transition from health to disease, arguing that fever is actually the body's "innate heat" that has exceeded its natural balance and become "extraneous." He cites Hippocrates, Galen, and Aristotle to prove that the same physical substance can be either life-sustaining or pathological depending on its temperament.</summary>

...to [nourish] and sustain the body, it turns into something fiery and corrupts its functions. Moving forward, he notes that **Galen** said in the third book of *On the Causes of Pulses*, chapter six—while explaining **Hippocrates**, who said in the *Aphorisms*: "those who are growing," etc., and "bellies are [hotter] in winter"—that he did not call them "hot" in an absolute sense. Instead, he was comparing natural heat to **adventitious heat** <note>Adventitious heat is heat introduced from the outside or produced unnaturally by disease, as opposed to the "innate" heat a person is born with.</note>. 

He affirms this opinion in the thirteenth aphorism of the first book, when he said the substance of native heat is mild, soothing, and gentle <note>original: "mitem, mulcebrem, & lenem"</note>, while adventitious heat is sharp and biting. As he proceeds further to confirm this explanation, he says: there are different degrees of adventitious heat. 

A little later, he affirms that a substance, as a substance, has no power to act in any way; rather, it is necessary for it to have some faculty through which it acts, just as the elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> act through their own qualities. Since elements and things composed of elements act as substances through their own qualities—whether these qualities are "forms" or not does not matter—therefore, mixtures act through their own temperament or form. It is a constant rule that a thing does not act of itself, but through its own form or instrument. 

He notes that a mixture <note>In this context, a "mixture" or "compound" refers to the human body or its parts, composed of the four elements.</note> does not act by form alone, nor by temperament alone; rather, the mixture acts, and the instrument by which it acts is its own quality and its own temperature. Concluding from these points, he says that the whole compound acts. To support this with the authority of **Galen**, he says that heat is the first instrument of the soul by which it acts—a point also made in the books *On the Affected Parts*, *On Temperaments*, the treatise *That the Habits of the Soul Follow the Temperament of the Body*, and the first book of *On Prognosis from the Pulse*. 

In these places, he said that just as health consists in a good temperament, so diseases arise from an imbalance <term>intemperie</term> <note>An "intemperie" or dyscrasia is a disruption of the healthy balance of the four humors or qualities.</note>. Hence, fever is categorized among those diseases which cause harm by reason of a bad temperament. He affirms that fever, according to its formal definition, consists in heat. 

To defend himself against the common truth—which everyone affirms—he confirms that **Galen** said all diseases are "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not part of the essential nature of a thing. Here, it means disease is a state the body falls into, not the body itself.</note>. Therefore, he says it does not follow that if fever were a substance (since it is natural heat turned fiery, which heat is "spirit" and a bodily substance), it would be counted as a new thing in number. He says it does not follow because nothing is added to the total count of things; rather, that very body which was natural heat has been changed and made "contrary to nature." 

In conclusion, he says that the nature of fever has been explained by these words. Thus far, I believe it is enough to have indicated through these summary conclusions what was written so extensively in the paper, so that...

<meta>catchword: so that</meta>

For since I have decided to write about the truth of the matter without rivalry, I want you to be advised that I have not sworn an oath to the words of any master <note>original: "me in uerba magiſtri non iuraſſe." Also in the first book of *On the Differences of Diseases*: "Fever is when immoderate heat attacks the body of the whole animal," or: "Fever is heat contrary to nature diffused through the entire body, and..."

The result is that if the fourth element—fire—were added in equal portions to both, an equal or similar substance would not be produced in both, since the subjects receiving the heat or fiery quality are different. # PART SECOND.

...taken from the eighth book of the *Method of Healing* <note>original: "Methodi medendi"; a foundational work by Galen on medical therapeutics.</note>, and from *On Natural Faculties* <note>original: "de potentiis naturalibus"; Galen's work on how the body functions.</note>, and also from the sixth book of *On Common Diseases* <note>original: "de morbis uulgaribus"; this refers to Galen’s commentaries on the *Epidemics* of Hippocrates.</note>, since they unhesitatingly <term>beg the question</term> <note>original: "petant principium"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note> and prove nothing. But so that this truth may shine more brightly, I will set forth—according to the opinion of illustrious authors and my own—the manner in which extraneous heat, or heat "beyond nature," is generated in fevers.

For since febrile heat is most often kindled in an animal's body either in the <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> from inflammation, or from their putrefaction due to the blocked breathing of the passages—and also from contact with a putrid thing, or in the <term>spirits</term> <note>Subtle substances believed to circulate in the blood and nerves to facilitate life and thought.</note> and vapors, and also in the solid members—I will speak first of that which is kindled in the humors. For Aristotle said that the actions of agents occur in subjects [already] disposed to receive them. Wherefore, if the humors of our body are changed from their natural temperament and qualities by some occasion, so that they cannot resist other causes that produce illness, or if the heat of the members itself has become either weak or too strong for some reason, unnatural alterations easily occur in them, such that they are changed either toward putrefaction, or inflammation, or some other quality beyond nature.

Indeed, the primary duty of natural heat is to preserve all parts of the body, to convert nourishment into the substance of the members, and to expel waste products, so that there may be an excellent purging of the blood, which should be suitable both for the spirits required for bodily functions and for proper nourishment. But when [the natural heat] either fails or exceeds in these duties, heat that is "beyond nature" or "extraneous" is generated in them.

Furthermore, when there is a deficiency, the humors rot; but since things that rot necessarily grow warm (even if they were cold by their own nature), because they are no longer regulated by their natural temperament, the same thing happens in the bodies of animals. When they cannot be regulated by their natural warmth, another warmth beyond nature is introduced, especially in the humors and other bodily fluids. This introduced warmth is called "extraneous heat," since it did not arise from the natural heat one is born with, but from putrefaction or some other mode of overheating. The causes can be both external and internal. Indeed, if the humors should be drier, and the members grow warm for some reason—whether that cause be external or internal, such as the heat of the **dog days** <note>original: "dies caniculares"; the hottest days of summer, historically associated with the rising of the dog star Sirius and the onset of fever.</note>, or the eating and drinking of hot things such as spices, potent wines, and the like—inflammations often occur without putrefaction, and thus [heat] is introduced, or ge- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "generatur" (generated), which will begin the next page.</note>

<summary>Massa explains that febrile heat arises when the body's natural heat fails to regulate its humors, leading to putrefaction or inflammation. He identifies both internal causes, like diet, and external causes, like summer heat, as triggers for this "extraneous" heat.</summary>

...[is ge]nerated an extraneous heat in the humors, which in no way has a likeness to natural heat, neither in its essence nor in its operations. This heat, having been introduced into the humors <term>beyond nature</term> <note>original: "praeter naturam"; a standard medical term for a pathological state that disrupts the body's natural balance.</note>, subsequently communicates its hot quality to the heart by means of rising warm vapors, and it alters the <term>spirits</term> <note>Subtle substances believed to circulate in the blood and nerves to facilitate life and thought.</note> and humors within the heart itself. From these, the other parts—both the contained [fluids] and the containing [tissues]—become hot by a heating beyond nature. Doctors call this kindled heat "fever," and they say it is an extraneous heat kindled in the heart, which, proceeding from there through the arteries and veins, is diffused to the whole body, unless it is hindered.

An <term>ephemeral fever</term> <note>original: "ephemera febris"; literally a "one-day fever," a short-lived fever often attributed to spirits or emotions rather than corruption of the humors.</note> occurs in almost the same way; namely, through the inflammation of vapors and spirits, which, being kindled in one or more members or in the whole body, communicate their heat to the heart. This happens both from the inflammation of the solid parts and of the "radical members" (as doctors say) through the <term>secondary humidities</term> <note>original: "secundas humiditates"; these were fluids within the tissues, distinct from the primary humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) found in the veins.</note>. Even if the process is not exactly that, it is nevertheless very similar to what has been described. For indeed, the said secondary humidities are kindled and become hot; these then heat the solid parts and the nearby humors. This heat is then communicated to the spirits and vapors, and then at one and the same time is extended through the arteries and veins to the whole body.

There is also another way (as I said above) of introducing extraneous heat into the heart, which happens either from the inhalation of air and putrid vapors, or through contact with bodies infected with a poisonous, hot quality. This occurs to those staying in air corrupted by a pestilential corruption, or to those touching or staying with people infected with a <term>pestilential quality</term> <note>Massa is describing the mechanism of contagion, which he believes carries a specific "quality" that disrupts the body's heat.</note>, which is hot beyond nature. In this manner, contact—whether through the inhalation of pestilential air or through contact with the external members—infects the heart and the humidities first contained within it. This quality, combined with an extraneous poisonous heat, if it is strong, brings about sudden death because it corrupts the heart's <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities necessary for an organ's health.</note> and the vital spirit.

However, contact with bodies in a pestilential infection, or with other infected things, does not always infect the heart itself first, but rather the parts touched. These then infect the neighboring parts, and then others, until the infection reaches the heart. Thus, swift death often occurs without a <term>manifest fever</term> <note>A fever with symptoms obvious enough for a physician to diagnose through pulse or touch.</note>. I say "manifest," because I can scarcely conceive in my mind how the spirits of the heart could be infected by an alien, extraneous heat without a fever following; but sometimes the time is so brief that neither the sick person, nor the doctor, nor those present can

they could perceive; especially that infection which occurs from the breathing in of pestilential air. In those, however, who are infected through the contact of the remaining parts of the body, a manifest fever often—and for the most part—appears, which is quiet on the outside but greatly disturbs the internal organs before death. Since, before the extraneous heat (acquired through the contact of body parts) with its poisonous quality reaches the heart, it first infects and alters the humors, <term>spirits</term> <note>Subtle substances believed to circulate in the blood to facilitate vital functions.</note>, and vapors in the passages and vessels. These then proceed part by part until they reach the heart itself, until, as we have said, the heat also infects the moisture of the heart with its poisonous heat <term>beyond nature</term> <note>original: "praeter naturam"; a state where the body's natural balance is disrupted by disease.</note>. Although this heat is poisonous, since it does not seek out the heart immediately at first, it is not of such swift activity that it can destroy the <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities unique to an individual's healthy state.</note> of the heart instantly. 

Indeed, the heat of the spirit and the temperament resist for as long as possible; nevertheless, they succumb if they are conquered by that poisonous heat. But if the natural spirit of the heart is robust and abundant enough to resist the malignancy of the extraneous heat, health follows, though only gradually. To corroborate what has been said, I could cite the mode of the generation of <term>pus</term> <note>original: "puris"; the fluid produced during inflammation.</note> in abscesses and ulcers according to the opinion of **Galen** <note>A highly influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> in the final commentary of the first book of the *Prognostics*, and in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*, chapter six. This mode differs from the way semen is generated: because pus is produced neither by natural heat alone, nor by heat beyond nature alone, but by both heats together. Neither heat is the sole total acting cause, but both; whereas semen is produced by natural heat alone. 

From these points, I would say that the natural heat, hindered by that which is beyond nature, fails in its duty. For natural heat does not intend <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putredinem"; the breakdown of matter, viewed here as the opposite of the body's self-preservation.</note> (which is the path to corruption), but rather preservation and permanence. Galen proposed this comparison in his book *On Crises*, when he compared the "clouds" seen in the urine of feverish patients to the pus in ulcers. He argued that nature works in the same way—namely, through both natural heat and heat beyond nature—both of which are present in the limb where the "mine" or source of the fever exists. 

Then, the heat is communicated to the heart if a warm evaporation reaches it, such that the heat beyond nature in the heart is distinct from the natural heat. Therefore, since the two are separate, the position of **Averroes** <note>An influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher and physician known for his commentaries on Aristotle and Galen.</note>—who says that febrile heat consists of both natural and beyond-natural heat—is not pleasing, because they are distinct and fight against each other. This is confirmed by all illustrious physicians, who say that innate heat is nature's instrument, which it uses to resist the substance or harm of the arriving heat.

...expels it by fighting. For indeed, the decline of a fever after it has reached its peak is nothing other than the victory of **natural heat** over the **heat beyond nature** <note>original: "calorem praeter naturam"; heat that exists outside the body’s healthy, balanced state.</note>, and conversely: destruction or death follows when the heat beyond nature overcomes the innate heat. But, whatever the case may be, feverish heat is not mixed in the heart with the natural heat contracted from the beginning of generation <note>referring to the heat an individual is born with</note>; nor does it change that natural heat into a fiery nature. Rather, what the heat beyond nature has managed to do is change the **complexional heat** of the members, which is the <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities that defines a person's health.</note> of the human body derived from the elements. 

And this complexional heat is distinct from the complexional heat contracted from the seed <note>the "primordial" heat from conception</note> at the beginning of generation, which remains until death; for while the substance of the seed consists of elements, the temperament of the body remains after death until the body decays and is converted into something else. And let these things be sufficient for the present concerning the order and modes of the generation of fever. If these matters are examined without the passions of those teachers who merely defend their own opinions, they destroy all the arguments of the commentator who says that feverish heat is a corporeal substance, and also that natural heat is converted into fire, so that one might place it directly in the category of substance.

But I shall return to the point from which I diverted: for I was saying that fever is heat beyond nature kindled in the heart, continuously heating both the heart and the <term>humors</term> <note>The internal fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note> and <term>spirits</term> <note>Subtle, vaporous substances thought to carry life and sensation through the body.</note> contained within it. This heat beyond nature—or extraneous heat—arises from either external or internal causes. 

Indeed, the internal causes are humors, putrefying either within the veins or outside the veins, and consequently becoming overheated, or inflamed by their own kindling, or by kindled spirits and vapors, or by secondary humors being kindled in the solid parts, and finally even in the solid parts themselves. This last stage of kindling is called "fixed" and "habituated" by physicians, and it is not dependent <note>meaning the fever has become self-sustaining in the tissues themselves, rather than just being a reaction to bad fluids</note>. And this, as all physicians affirm, happens almost never or very rarely at the beginning [of an illness], so much so that they are scarcely willing to concede that it can occur at the start. 

I say, adding to what has been said, that the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humiditatem radicalem"; the innate fluid that acts as the "fuel" for the body's natural heat.</note> and innate moisture, in which the innate heat is grounded and on which it feeds, is not the fever, as we have proved by many authorities and reasons. Rather, fever is an extraneous heat, or the effect of an extraneous heat, in one or all three of the substances constituting our body, heating the heart and the parts contained within it; <term>that</term> <note>original: "qd" (quod)</note> if on this occasion the natural heat is altered in some way, it nonetheless does not change its own specific temperament...

->Q ii<-

...temperament, for most eminent physicians demonstrate with many arguments that human <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's health and personality.</note> does not exist as a fixed, exact point in all individuals. Indeed, the individual temperament of the bilious Socrates is one thing, that of the sanguine Plato another, that of the phlegmatic Nicomachus another, and that of the melancholic Democritus yet another. By the same reasoning, this must be said regarding the sexes, ages, regions, exercises, and other factors. Although these individuals may have a different temperament when compared in detail, they nevertheless agree in the **specific temperament of man**, which is warm and moist, mild, and pleasant, within the aforementioned range. If it were not so mild, but instead sharp and acrid, it could not perform natural operations, as Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> said; indeed, it could not even preserve life. Furthermore, if the native heat were changed and made extraneous, the animal would certainly be changed into something else, <gloss>so that</gloss> <note>original: "q", an abbreviation for "quod".</note> a healthy man and a feverish man would not be the same being, since they would possess neither the same heat nor the same temperament—which the <term>expositor</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific commentator on medical texts, such as Averroes or a contemporary academic.</note> said was the "form" of the body by the authority of Hippocrates and Galen. This heat was said to be generated from the subtle parts of the blood. And since the opinion of Galen and Hippocrates cannot save this position (unless one says Galen is contrary to himself), the expositor offers excuses for him, yet he does not teach the truth on that account, nor the method by which we might investigate it. Therefore, according to my own opinion for the discovery of the truth and its inquiry, I shall set down certain necessary points. You know indeed that according to Aristotle's opinion, no action can proceed except from a **form**. We read this position confirmed in the writings of the expositor. To clarify the matter with an example: suppose any man performs a natural action; this action will certainly be produced by his own form with a determined quality and quantity. Since this is so—namely, that the action of an agent occurs through its own form—the agent, by acting, will certainly change the subject <note>original: "passum"; the thing being acted upon.</note> and make it similar to itself, since an agent acts for the purpose of making the subject similar to itself according to Aristotle's opinion. Therefore, since this is true, why should we not posit a separate changing agent that moves the natural heat toward an **extraneous heat** (as they call it)? This will be an extraneous heat which, having first been kindled in the vapors, or the moistures, or the solid parts of the members, changes the proper quality of the natural heat. Therefore, whether we wish it or not, we must grant that there is some hot agent which acts and sets on fire the spirits, vapors, humors, and even the solid parts. And this kindling, or heat, produced in the said parts, is called **extraneous heat**.

...wherever it may be: when it reaches the heart, it is called a **fever** by physicians, because it heats the heart and the moistures, spirits, and vapors contained within it. From these, the spirit and natural heat are subsequently altered. However, as long as the person lives and maintains the functions of life, this heat is not changed into some other fiery nature, but remains within the aforementioned **specific range**. And although not all bodily functions remain unharmed, they do not for that reason fail entirely, nor are they mostly alienated from their natural essence. 

This is explained even more clearly from what I wrote to my nephew, **Lorenzo Massa**, while he was a student of the liberal arts at Padua and was hearing the first part of the fourth book of **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook in European universities for centuries.</note>. For I clearly demonstrated to him that in every body there is a heat contracted from the seed at the beginning of generation; also a heat resulting from the composition of simple parts; and a heat which is proper to each individual particle, preserving it. It is this last one which can be changed into a foreign and extraneous heat. If a fourth heat—which is extraneous and <term>contrary to nature</term> <note>Medical terms for states that oppose the body's healthy, "natural" function.</note>—arrives and is mixed with it, then a composite is formed from the natural and the unnatural heat. Thus, that part in which the extraneous heat is mixed is corrupted. 

From that lesson, it is clear to see that a fever is either an effect following a heat distinct from the natural and innate heat. Indeed, from what has been said, there are three natural heats that differ among themselves. The fourth, however, is **contrary to nature**. According to the opinion of **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity, whose system of medicine focused on the balance of humors.</note> in the fourth book of *On Simple Medicine*, chapter 3, this unnatural heat corrupts by separating the heat of the thing it destroys; and this happens because coldness overcomes it. Galen also said in the eleventh book of the *Method of Medicine* that **putrefaction** <note>In the medical theory of the time, putrefaction was a process of decay or "rotting" of the bodily humors, which was thought to generate the unnatural heat felt during a fever.</note> occurs from extreme heat, since nothing is corrupted by its own proper heat; rather, a thing is especially strengthened and increased by its own heat. From these and other things written by me, everyone can see that a fever (or that which causes a fever) is an extraneous heat distinct from natural heat, and is not a corporeal substance, as the <term>expositor</term> asserts on the authority of Hippocrates, Galen, and other philosophers. 

This truth was learnedly declared by the most learned **Averroes** <note>The Latin name for Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle and medical works were highly respected by Renaissance scholars like Massa.</note> in his first commentary on the fourth book of the *Meteorologica* <note>Aristotle's treatise on natural phenomena, including the transformation of elements.</note>, following this sense of the words: <note>original: "forma transmutans materiam ad aliquam aliam recipiendam formam, & facies primam separare , necessario calida erit, sed nihilominus respectu corrupti subiecti calor extraneus & putrefactus est, respectu uero generati ex ipso naturalis est"</note> "A form transforming matter to receive some other form, and which acts to separate the first form, will necessarily be hot; but nonetheless, in respect to the corrupted subject, it is an **extraneous and putrefied heat**, while in respect to that which is generated from it, it is natural." ...it implies that it has been shown that heat is twofold: one is **natural**, the other is **extraneous** <note>Also referred to as "foreign" or "unnatural" heat.</note>. The cause of the progression of this extraneous heat within a substance is one of two things: the first is "through itself" <note>original: *per se*</note>, which is external heat that is not compatible with the natural heat. Indeed, it cools the natural heat and dissolves it; for this reason, we see **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term> <note>In ancient medicine, this referred to the breakdown of bodily fluids (humors) caused by an imbalance of heat and moisture.</note> multiply during the summer.

However, the other efficient cause—or what we might call the secondary cause—is the coldness and freezing of the natural heat itself. For when the natural heat is weak and lacks the power to gather matter and dominate it, that matter putrefies. This can be seen in the bodies of the dead, in the elderly, and even in all inanimate things that have been chilled. Often this also happens to matter because of **humidity**, as moist matter is easily affected by external forces and is weak at retaining its proper form. 

Therefore, **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – 370 BCE) often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> and other physicians stated that the cause of putrefaction is heat and humidity. They did not distinguish between what causes it "through itself" <note>original: *per se*</note> and what is said to cause it "by accident" <note>original: *per accidens*; meaning a secondary or indirect cause.</note>. 

In the progression of the commentary, he adds: once it has been declared that generation <note>The creation or maintenance of life and tissue.</note> occurs through natural heat, while corruption occurs through extraneous heat and coldness—and once it has been explained how extraneous heat is produced—he defines extraneous heat with these words: 

> The primary and essential operation of extraneous heat, in things where it dominates, is **indecoction** <term>indecoction</term> <note>From the Latin *indecoctio*, meaning a failure of the body to "cook" or process food and humors properly; essentially, indigestion or lack of metabolic ripening.</note> or **combustion** <note>Burning or scorching.</note>. 

For since the process and property of extraneous heat is to extinguish the natural heat and resolve the underlying humidities, those substances are ignited and burned. This is visible in the fevers they call "combustive" <note>original: *febribus combustiuis*; high-intensity, burning fevers.</note>. Sometimes, however, when extraneous heat is weak, it causes "indecoction" and corruption, as happens in fevers caused by putrid phlegm, and often at the end of burning fevers. 

This happens "by accident" due to the feebleness of the natural heat and the dominion of coldness. For coldness—essentially and primarily because it is cold—is the deprivation of natural heat, leading to "indecoction" and the corruption of food. "Indecoction" is the opposite of ripening <note>The Latin text here reads *corrugationi*, likely a printer's error for *concoctioni* (digestion/ripening).</note>, and the corruption of food is the contrary of digestion; when this operation dominates, the generation of life ceases. 

Many very beautiful things are read in that commentary, from which it appears most clearly and without hesitation that extraneous and feverish heat is truly distinct from natural heat. This feverish heat is an "accident" <note>In philosophical terms, a quality that exists in a subject but is not part of its essential nature.</note> and is in no way a "body" <note>Meaning it is a quality or state, not a physical substance.</note>, as the commentator has tried to prove by the authority of Hippocrates and **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher (129 – c. 216 CE) whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note>. ...is generated by humidity, which is not natural, along with the already mentioned weakness of the natural or intrinsic heat. Therefore, it should not always be said that a fever exists because of an **excess** of natural or intrinsic heat—as many very serious physicians have claimed—since febrile heat is often actually lower than natural heat, as can be seen in some patients. Rather, the true cause is that the humidity is in a state where it can quickly succumb to **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term> <note>In the medical tradition of the time, this refers to the "rotting" or breakdown of the body's humors (fluids) due to trapped heat and moisture.</note>. Indeed, things that are prone to rotting do so precisely because of a **weak heat**. 

In confirmation of this, **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose works on natural history were foundational to medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note>, in the first section of his *Problems* (problem 6), describing the essence of febrile heat, declared it thus: "When certain places in the body become moist, a burning inflammation arises. Since this is nothing other than an overabundance of heat, it can certainly ignite a fever." 

These are the words of Aristotle, who intended to convey nothing else but this: when heat "beyond nature" is generated in any moist body, vapors are raised—or as physicians call it, a **putrid soot** <note>original: *putrida fuligo*. This refers to the smoky, waste-like vapors believed to be produced by "burning" humors.</note> which is hot because of the rotting process. If this heat reaches the heart, it excites a fever by heating the heart and the substances contained within it.

**Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle who lived around 200 CE; his works were highly influential in Renaissance medical schools.</note> also, in the second book of his *Problems* (problem 7), asks why a severe inflammation of the lungs is triggered by a high fever. He responds that the burning heat arises from **yellow bile** <note>One of the four "humors" or bodily fluids; it was associated with fire, heat, and dryness.</note>, which is accustomed to flow back toward the stomach and the lungs from its usual reservoirs. From this, it clearly appears that the extraneous heat that excites a fever is distinct from our natural heat.

To confirm this further, in his first book (problem 77), Alexander investigated why it is that **Ethiopians** <note>In early medical texts, this term was often used generally for people from hot, dry climates or those with very dark complexions.</note> for the most part die when they suffer from fevers. He responds that because they are already excessively hot and dry, the fever causes the entire balance of their elements to be destroyed. For the moisture hidden within them is very scarce, and so on. These words clearly show that febrile heat does not simply turn our native heat into fire, but rather **consumes the moisture** of the body.

**Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) and successor to Aristotle, famous for his works on botany and natural causes.</note>—a most learned man who can never be praised enough regarding natural matters—describes two modes of "corruption" (decay) in the fifth book of his *On the Causes of Plants* (chapter 9). He says: "Some corruptions happen according to nature, and some are contrary to nature. Disease appears to be partly contrary to nature, because it is a departure and a disturbance of the natural state." 

This most wise man meant nothing else but that there are two ways in which things perish. One is through the **natural course**, where the continuous action of natural heat consumes the **substantial or radical moisture** <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The "innate" fluid that acts as the primary fuel for the body's life-force; its exhaustion was thought to cause old age and natural death.</note>. The other way...

## PART TWO

...heat, which corrupts the other humors by tainting them; and in this second mode of corruption, in my own opinion, we must place **heat beyond nature** <note>original: *calor præter naturam*. This is a central concept in Renaissance medicine, referring to an unnatural, pathogenic heat distinct from the "natural heat" that sustains life.</note>, as well as other causes. But why do we still need witnesses? Does not **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), the most influential physician of antiquity whose system dominated medical thought for over 1,500 years.</note> himself, in the first book of *On the Differences of Diseases*, contend to prove that disease in general is either a defect of action or of constitution? If this is true—as he attempts to prove—and if fever is a "hot disease," and since disease is an **accident** <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property or quality (like color or temperature) that cannot exist on its own but must exist within a "substance" (like a body or a humor).</note> and cannot be categorized under the heading of **Substance**, it must necessarily be placed in one of the nine categories of the accidents of substances. 

Fever, therefore, based on what has been said, is heat beyond nature, since it is caused by an **imbalance of heat** <term>imbalance</term> <note>original: *intemperie*. A disruption of the "temperament" or the ideal proportions of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in the body.</note>. This conclusion of mine is confirmed by what Galen left written on this opinion in the eighth and ninth books of his *Method of Healing*, where he says that fever is an excess and abundance of heat beyond nature. 

If anyone should doubt whether a "substance" can sometimes be a disease, it is a ridiculous question and unworthy of a wise man, since no wise man denies that disease is a **constitution beyond nature**. The definition of fever in the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers* also favors our conclusion, where Galen declared it to consist solely of heat beyond nature. Therefore, most learned **Vincent** <note>Likely the recipient of this medical letter, possibly a fellow physician or student.</note>, I intended these things written to you regarding the **Essence of Fever** to be sufficient for the present; if opportunity is given in the future, we shall speak of these things further.

It remains for us to debate whether the **soul** <term>soul</term> <note>original: *anima*. In this context, it refers to the animating principle or "life force" of a biological body, rather than purely a theological concept.</note> is the aforementioned natural heat, or a **temperament** <note>A specific "blend" or balance of the four qualities/humors.</note>, as many affirm that **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BCE).</note> and Galen believed. We should first state what the most learned Galen, the interpreter of Hippocrates, said: he never dared to affirm that he had fully grasped the essence of the soul, since he described the soul’s essence ambiguously in different places. Indeed, at times he affirms it to be the temperament or the substance of the brain; at other times he calls it the **spirit** <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*. A refined, vaporous substance (pneuma) believed to flow through the nerves and arteries to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>; or he describes it as that which uses the spirit as an instrument for its operations; and sometimes he says it is that which results from the four primary qualities of the elements. Thus, Hippocrates did not clearly declare his own opinion in the same way every time.

In order that we may understand this truth and restore the opinion of the most wise Hippocrates and Galen to its true sense, I will discuss the matter as follows. For since there are two modes of cognition, just as there are two objects of cognition: one is **sensory**, which occurs without **discourse** <term>discourse</term> <note>original: *discursu*. This refers to "discursive reasoning," or the step-by-step logical process of the intellect, as opposed to direct, intuitive perception.</note>; the other is **intellectual**, which occurs with discourse. Similarly, regarding the objects of knowledge: one is corporeal and material, along with its accidents; the other is incorporeal and spiritual. The first, the sensory...

...[By sensory] cognition we know material objects and their **accidents** <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or temperature that can change without the object becoming a different thing.</note>, while by intellectual cognition we understand spiritual and incorporeal substances—though never without some preceding knowledge obtained through the senses. 

But since the **soul** <note>original: *anima*. In this context, it refers to the "vital principle" that makes a body alive.</note> or **form** <term>form</term> <note>The "form" is the organizing principle of a thing; for humans, the soul is the "substantial form" that gives the body life and structure.</note>, according to the opinion of all who philosophize correctly, is a substance that is not matter (even if it always exists with matter and stands as a part of the composite human being), the wise say it is a "spiritual substance." 

Therefore, since **Hippocrates** and **Galen** were the wisest of men, their words are not to be understood "nakedly" and without interpretation; rather, they must be explained and brought back to their true sense. To do this, I will first form arguments based on the intentions of Hippocrates and Galen. 

If **innate heat** <note>original: *calor innatus*. A foundational concept in pre-modern medicine; a vital, life-sustaining warmth present in the body from birth.</note> is a certain mixture of the elements, as has been said—and elements in a mixture are neither in **act** nor in **potentiality** <note>Aristotelian terms: "act" is the fully realized state, "potentiality" is the capacity to become something else.</note>, but in a certain middle state that exists between potentiality and physical act—how can it be the "form"? Furthermore, since the form or soul is a spiritual and immaterial substance, the "complexional innate heat" cannot be the form of any composite being. 

Next, since it is a property of **substance**, as **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), the Greek philosopher whose logic and physics provided the framework for Renaissance science.</note> said, not to admit "more or less," whereas the **spirit** <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*. A subtle, vaporous substance believed to circulate in the blood and nerves to perform bodily functions.</note> or the **temperament** <note>original: *temperies*. The specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> do in fact admit "more or less" (since they increase daily in their substance, quantity, and quality), then they cannot be the soul. Aristotle also said that substance does not receive **contrariety** <note>That is, a substance cannot be "opposite" to another substance, but qualities (accidents) can be opposites, like hot and cold.</note>, yet the spirit does receive its contrary. This is apparent in fevers and in **hectic fever of the third kind** <note>original: *hectica tertiæ fpeciei*. A severe, chronic fever believed to "dry out" the fundamental moisture of the body's organs.</note>, in which the spirit and the hot temperament are changed and made colder. 

Furthermore, Galen said that innate heat and spirit are a "subtle spirituous body" which is nourished by the subtlest blood. How, I ask, can this be the soul or form? For a form is not nourished, nor does it increase or decrease—especially a **substantial form**. 

And so, by explaining more correctly, I would say that Hippocrates and Galen meant that natural heat or temperament cannot possibly be the soul. It is, however, that without which the soul cannot "inform" <note>To "inform" here means to give life and functional structure to the physical body.</note> the subject; it is the soul's **instrument** for perfecting all its operations. Indeed, all philosophers and physicians alike affirm that natural heat is the instrument of nature. If it is an instrument, it certainly is not the soul, nor can it be. 

Galen affirms this truth in the place cited by the commentator on the fifth book of *On Simple Medicines*, when he says that the spirit innate in every animal, although some may call it the "essence of the soul," is nonetheless at least its instrument. And adding to this, he said: "But I, concerning the essence of the soul..."
