->## PART SECOND.<-

...[of its es]sence I do not dare to say anything. There are also other nearly similar authorities confirming that the **soul** is neither **heat** nor **temperament** <term>temperament</term> <note>original: *temperatura*. In Galenic medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's health and personality.</note>, as is evident in the book *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato*, in the second book of *On the Causes of Symptoms*, and in *On the Natural Faculties*. It is also found in the book *On Respiration*, as well as in the book *That the Character of the Soul Follows the Temperament of the Body*, and *On the Formation of the Fetus*. In all these places, **Galen** said that he did not know the essence of the soul; indeed, in the second book of *On the Causes of Symptoms*, he used to say it was the mark of a bold man to define what the soul is. For if the soul "follows" the temperament of the body (as he believed in the cited book), how can you claim that the temperament *is* the soul?

I say, therefore, that assuming a twofold way of knowing, **Hippocrates** and **Galen** did not know the soul by primary **sensory cognition**, but by **intellectual cognition** through reasoning. This intellectual reasoning does not exist without a "phantasm" <note>original: *phantafmate*. In medieval psychology, a 'phantasm' is a mental image or sensory impression stored in the imagination upon which the intellect works.</note> derived from the external senses. Furthermore, the external senses best apprehend the *operations* of the soul and place them in the imagination; then, the intellect—through its capacity for combining and dividing ideas—reasons its way to understanding the essence of the soul. Hippocrates and Galen do not deny having this intellectual cognition; they only deny that the soul is something "sensed" or, if I may put it this way, "sensory."

They knew through the senses the soul's operations and the **instrument** by which it works—including the operations of life, the "animal" <note>Refers to 'anima' (soul); these are functions like movement and perception.</note> operations, and the natural ones. This instrument is the aforementioned subtle, spiritual body <note>The 'spiritus' or pneuma.</note> resulting from the mixing of the elements. Therefore, the soul is neither heat, nor spirit, nor temperament, but the **form** <term>form</term> <note>The organizing principle that gives a thing its identity and 'being'.</note> that gives being to a subject that has been prepared or disposed, and qualified with certain determined qualities. For heat or temperament, since they admit of **"more and less"** <note>A logical term: accidents like temperature can vary in intensity, but a substance—like a human soul—cannot be 'more or less' a soul without the being ceasing to exist.</note>, are increased and decreased; they are affected by corporeal qualities and are changed into another nature or subject. 

But the soul and the **form**, which is called **substantial** <term>substantial form</term>, do not change in this way. I will write down below not all, but some of the inconsistencies and absurdities that would follow if the spirit, heat, or temperament were the form of the body. First, if the soul were heat or spirit or a natural temperament, it would follow that the soul is either an **accident** <term>accident</term> or some sort of composite mixture, and that it could be affected by bodily causes—being nourished, increased, decreased, heated, and many other things from which those who philosophize correctly recoil. It would also follow that a **substance** could admit of "more and less."

Indeed, most learned **Vincent**, I could have added many other reasons—and powerful ones at that—to these words while writing to you: reasons which affirm that **febrile heat** is an extraneous heat, and not the natural heat turned into fire...

<summary>Massa argues that the soul is a "substantial form" rather than a physical substance like heat or temperament, citing Galen's admissions of ignorance regarding the soul's essence to support his philosophical distinction between the soul and its biological instruments.</summary>

### LETTER IX.

A certain physician sent me a lecture by Giovanni Battista Monti <note>original: *Joannis Baptistae Montani*. Monti (1498–1551) was a famous professor of medicine at Padua who popularized clinical bedside instruction.</note> concerning pestilential fever, its essence, and its cure, most learned Agostino. I read it with great eagerness and examined it as diligently as my strength allowed, as much as can be done by a very busy man. Since I noted numerous difficulties in every part of it—which, in my opinion, are read by medical candidates and new initiates not without the greatest risk to the human race—and since his method of teaching is far removed (as you will see here) from the approach of both modern and distinguished ancient physicians in the <term>diagnosis</term> <note>original: *dignotione*. A technical term referring to the identification of a disease through its signs and symptoms.</note> and treatment of pestilential fever, I wished to write these observations to you to defend the truth and for the benefit of mankind (at your urging). 

To begin "from the egg" <note>original: *ab ouo*. A Latin idiom meaning to start from the very beginning.</note>, as the saying goes, the matter is introduced by this otherwise most learned man as follows: "When dealing with pestilential fevers, it will first be worthwhile to account for the name." In this explanation, he brought forward many points that offer the readers an obscure rather than a clear definition of the name. It would have been enough if he had said that "plague" and "pestilence" (if he wished to use synonyms) are primarily a <term>corruption of the air</term> <note>original: *aeris corruptionem*. In the 16th century, it was believed that diseases like the plague were caused by "miasma" or poisoned air.</note>, and from this contagion, pestilential fevers usually arise among the multitude, which are ruinous; this would have been sufficient for him. 

However, since in Homer only that sickness—original: *νόσος* <note>original: *nosos*. Greek for "disease" or "sickness." Massa is referencing the plague at the beginning of the Iliad.</note>—is called "pestilence" for which no help was assigned by the ancients except flight and withdrawal, from which it appears...

## SECOND PART

It is evident that pestilence is an infection of the air, while plague is a destructive disease communicated to a multitude. But since long-winded speeches bring no benefit to the declaration of truth—and indeed, very often make it more obscure—you have already read the interpretation of this name in my work *On Pestilential Fever*, which I advise you to look at again. 

He <note>Referring to Giovanni Battista Monti, whose lectures Massa is critiquing.</note> then proceeds to teach by laying a foundation in this way: "Pestilential fever is divided into two types. It either possesses all the properties of a plague and is a destructive epidemic disease, or it is particular—arising not from an external cause but from an internal one—and is so malignant that it kills or can kill a person." For this reason, it is called a pestilential fever. This seems to be the logic of his division, although the words are written in a convoluted way and are not entirely clear in every part; perhaps it was a failure of the scribe who, while listening to the learned man lecture, did not record every word. But whatever the case may be, this opinion is not clear in all respects; however, so that the rest may be understood, I leave the division as it is and turn my discourse to the remaining part of his process.

He says, therefore: "Since this fever is not only malignant but the very worst—as it depends on the putrefaction of the heart—it is fearful and almost without hope." From this position, he draws the following conclusion: namely, that pestilential fever depends on the putrefaction of the heart, and consequently, not all such fevers are entirely incurable, but only those that have a confirmed putrefaction <note>original: *putredinem*. In the medical theory of the time, "putrefaction" referred to the rotting or decomposition of bodily fluids (humors), which was thought to generate the heat of a fever.</note> in the heart itself. But if the putrefaction is only in the "contents" of the heart <note>This likely refers to the blood or the "vital spirits" contained within the chambers of the heart, rather than the heart muscle itself.</note>, then even though the condition is very grave, those suffering may nevertheless be restored to health. 

Indeed, most learned Agostino, to be frank with you, I cannot help but be astonished at the man when he posits—without any proof—that a pestilential fever always involves a putrefaction in the heart or in its contents. From this unproven position, he then infers a consequence regarding the treatment of such fevers. He ought to have proven this with reasons or through sensory experience, since the reality of the matter is quite different. This can be seen in my already-cited booklet *On Pestilential Fever*, where I have explained this not only with logical reasons but also with many authorities from the ancients. For if you take note, this point contributes greatly to the correct path of treatment, which is why he sent those writings to me. 

From these points, thus posed but not proven by Montano <note>The Latinized name for Giovanni Battista Monti.</note>, he himself attempts to draw out an essential definition or description of pestilential fever, which seems to be as follows: "Pestilential fever is a hot and dry <term>distemper</term>" <note>original: *intemperies*. In Galenic medicine, this refers to an imbalance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within the body.</note>. And adding the difference between this and a "putrid" fever that is not pestilential, he affirms that pestilential fever differs...

...[distinguished] from other putrid fevers because a pestilential fever involves putrefaction in the humors of the heart—a point which (as I have said) was yet to be proven. While he confirms this opinion of his with words, he reproaches certain modern physicians (who certainly deserve reproach) for saying that in other putrid fevers, the putrefaction is in the humors of the heart. This is false according to the judgment of all illustrious ancients who thought correctly. For even if the suffering of a fever is primarily a heat of the heart, it does not follow that the cause of its heat must reside within the heart itself—except in a <term>hectic fever</term><note>A "hectic" fever (from the Greek *hektikos*, meaning "habitual") was one that had become "deep-seated" in the solid tissues of the body, rather than just the fluids or spirits.</note> or a "settled" fever, where the cause is already in the substance of the heart and does not depend on any other of the <term>three constituents</term><note>In Galenic medicine, the body was composed of three parts: the solids (members), the fluids (humors), and the vapors (spirits).</note> of our body. 

And because he tentatively questions whether one might call this pestilential fever a fourth genus of fevers, and concludes it is not; furthermore, it would have been enough for him to say that the name "pestilential" applies to all three genera of fevers, since a plague is a certain <term>accident</term><note>In philosophy and medicine, an "accident" is a property or quality that happens to a thing but is not part of its essential nature.</note> occurring to the aforementioned fevers. But enough on this.

He continues by declaring his definition and division, saying: "a pestilential hectic fever is separated from other simple hectic fevers because a pestilential hectic fever depends on putrefaction." This statement, however, cannot stand with any of the ancients, nor with reason itself. For a hectic fever, of whatever kind it may be, does not depend on some other heat—whether of the humors, the spirits, or the vapors—since the "settled" foreign heat is already in the solid substance. Nevertheless, a settled febrific heat can be nourished and increased by some other heat, for example, by the putrefactive heat of the humors, as happens in those with abscesses or those with ulcers in their lungs. But such a fever, after the heat has become settled in the substance of the heart, is a <note>original: *complicata*</note> "complicated" fever, consisting of an accidental fever depending on putrid matter and an independent hectic fever. Such a hectic fever is not, for that reason, called a "dependent" fever; if we wished to add some distinction to it, we might call it a "hectic fever increased by the heat of putrefying humors."

From these points, you see what must be said regarding his unproven position: namely, that all pestilential fevers have putrefaction in the heart or in its contents. But since I have already proved the contrary in my little book *On Pestilential Fever*, this unproven foundation will amount to nothing. Indeed, in that book, I stated that <term>putrid soot</term><note>original: *putrida fuligo*. In medieval medicine, "soot" referred to the waste vapors produced by the body's internal "cooking" or metabolism that needed to be exhaled.</note> in its pestilential quality—which is not without heat—reaches the heart and causes a putrid pestilential fever, even without putrefaction of the heart or of the things contained within it. This source of putrefaction...

## PART TWO.

[putrefactio]n is very often found in the <term>natural parts</term><note>In Galenic medicine, "natural" parts or faculties refer to the liver and the digestive system, responsible for nutrition and growth.</note>, and frequently in the <term>animal members</term><note>The "animal" members (from the Latin *anima*, meaning soul or breath) refer to the brain and nervous system, responsible for sensation and movement.</note>, and within the whole circumference of the body, and sometimes in the heart and its contents. These latter fevers—those involving putrefaction in the heart—are always the most destructive. He <note>Referring to Monti (Montanus).</note> further asserts that pestilential fevers arise from various <term>efficient causes</term><note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the primary agent that produces an effect; in this case, what actually triggers the fever.</note>. For while some causes are extrinsic—those which happen from the outside—they are the ones that arise from the consumption of something poisonous, from bad food, or from inspired air. But those which arise from intrinsic causes happen in this way: namely, when some <term>humor</term><note>The four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were the fundamental fluids of the body; their balance determined health.</note> in our body has become so putrid that it is converted into the nature of a poison, and thus the pestilential fever arises from this extreme putrefaction.

Immediately after this division, he said that this humor which causes the pestilential fever—whether it be from an intrinsic or extrinsic cause—possesses something poisonous and contrary to our nature, and does not differ from other poisons that are consumed. In these statements, you can see a contradiction. For when he later rebukes more modern physicians who claimed that in pestiferous fevers there is a poisonous quality beyond the <term>manifest quality</term><note>A "manifest quality" is one that can be perceived by the senses, such as heat or moisture. "Occult" or "poisonous" qualities were thought to be hidden and beyond simple sensory detection.</note>, I ask: if (as he says) a pestilential fever is nothing other than that "extreme putrefaction in the heart contrary to life" (which he calls manifest), why then did he say here—and repeat throughout the entire lecture—that this fever possesses a "poisonousness"? 

Furthermore, he neither explained the quality which he wants to be "manifest," nor did he declare the degrees of its quantity. He certainly ought to have declared this if he wished to prove it was manifest. But it is an eternal condition for men, and shall be forever, that they remain ignorant of the specific quantities of the elemental qualities in mixtures. But if we know anything, we say we know it not precisely and truly, but by a certain estimated judgment that is close to the truth. This is what wise men do when they see a complex mixture and alteration that cannot be perfectly known by the senses or by reasoning. Indeed, all mixtures act through the dominant quality within them; but besides that, there is a quality composed from the refraction and mixture of the qualities and substances of the elements, which will always be hidden from us. This can be seen in the **stomach of an Ostrich**<note>It was a common medieval and Renaissance belief that ostriches could digest iron and other hard metals due to an incredibly "hot" or powerful stomach quality.</note> which dissolves iron and other very hard things that fire cannot dissolve at all. Thus, wise men speak of a "pestiferous quality" which results from the putrefying alteration of the humors, or even of more solid things. And when they strive to assign appropriate names, they either hide the quality or call it a "temperament"; nevertheless, they are not ignorant that it results from a predominance...

of any of the <term>primary qualities</term><note>In the medical tradition of this time, the four primary qualities were heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; all health and disease resulted from their balance.</note>, such as heat, cold, and the rest; even if these qualities are not the primary cause of the disease’s action, they later assist in its operation. He <note>Giambattista da Monte (Montanus)</note> follows this by distinguishing that **pestilential fevers** arise and terminate sometimes in the <term>humors</term><note>The humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were the bodily fluids thought to govern health.</note> of the heart, and sometimes in its actual substance. It would have been better said that the heat of putrefaction is mixed with the natural heat. 

He then proceeds to the other part of his division and says that the fever which terminates in the substance of the heart is called a **hectic pestilential fever**. He then compares these to other fevers, but since these things are known to everyone and do not serve our current purpose, let it be enough to have reminded you of what was said, so that you may see how much they can actually teach students, since he repeats almost the same things he said before without any proof. 

But since he was unable to prove his position, he fled to the authorities of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the supreme authority in medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> as if to a <term>sacred anchor</term><note>A common Latin idiom (*sacra ancora*) for a last resort or final refuge in an argument.</note>. I know you have read these authorities in the third book of *On Prognosis from Pulses*, but as you see, they have nothing to do with the matter at hand, since they do not speak of putrefaction in the heart or its contents, but rather of an extreme "foreign heat" ignited either in the humors or in the substance of the heart. 

These ignited humors or the substance of the heart are not always putrid, even though they are ignited; for indeed, an acting foreign heat does not always cause putrefaction, even if it is raised from putrid matter. This can be seen in stables, where the vapors rising from the <term>manure</term><note>original: "sterquilinio"</note> heat and dry out the stable or the walls, yet they do not cause them to rot. 

Nor does Galen assert in that passage that the substance of the heart or the humored contained within it always produce a pestilential fever in cases of deadly disease, since (as I have said) a putrid evaporation with a "pestilential quality" is sufficient to generate a pestilential fever. Furthermore, if this heat with its pestilential quality should seize the substance of the heart or the moisture soaked into it, it will produce a **hectic pestilential fever**; but it cannot cause that without the presence of the pestilential quality itself. 

Thus you see the nature of the authorities of Galen brought forward by Montanus. I would not deny that sometimes—and indeed very often—in pestilential fevers there is putrefaction in the contents of the heart, as I have seen this many times in practice; but it is not a perpetual rule for everyone. The same must be said regarding the hectic pestilential fever, since it can be imprinted...

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Massa’s critique of the physician Giovanni Battista da Monte (known as Montanus). Here, he specifically addresses whether blood can putrefy within the heart or veins and challenges Montanus's interpretation of the ancient authority Galen.</meta>

## SECOND PART

the pestilential quality in the substance of the heart [comes] from the external heat of the humors contained within it, even if the source <term>minera</term><note>original: "minera"—literally a "mine" or "ore," used here to mean the primary site or breeding ground of the disease.</note> of the putrefaction is not in the contents of the heart itself. I can easily convince you of this by the following reasoning. For if, through the breathing in of pestilential air, both the spirit and the humors can be ignited—so that a fever is kindled from their hot evaporation—and if that ignited heat in the spirits can inflame the contents of the heart, how much more so can it place the substance of the heart and its fluids into a heated state, if the moisture contained in the heart is ignited by the pestilential heat of putrefaction? 

Now you see from what has been said that putrefaction is not always in the heart, nor in the heart's contents; but as *Montanus* says in the third chapter, it can be in all the humors and begin from them. These humors are neither created in the heart nor do they reside there; for we know that the heart draws blood from the liver to convert it into the <term>vital spirit</term><note>The vital spirit was thought to be a refined substance produced in the heart that carried life and heat throughout the body via the arteries.</note>, which it preserves as much as it can. It should not be said that it putrefies there, because if it were to putrefy for any reason, a swift death would undoubtedly follow. For in those where putrefaction is already in the heart, the pulse undoubtedly fails, as *Montanus* himself asserts. 

Furthermore, he said in this third part, without any proof, that no other fever arises from the putrefaction of blood than the **pestilential fever**. Good gods! Look, and let those who have read all the books of the illustrious physicians, both ancient and modern, look at this. I am indeed amazed, my dear *Augustinus*, that a man otherwise so learned should say that blood cannot putrefy in the veins except in a pestilential fever. 

As for how consistent the explanation is which he brings from the authority of *Galen* <note>Galen of Pergamon was the most influential physician of antiquity; his works remained the standard medical curriculum in the 16th century.</note> (in the second book of *On Crises* and the first book of *On the Differences of Fevers*), saying that blood putrefies where there is an inflammation of the blood—let the physicians consider this, for they experience the matter so often. Since blood, by its own <term>temperament</term><note>The "temperament" or "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, is both hot and moist, it is the humor most ready to putrefy. If you look at the other three humors, I do not see any reason why blood should be less able to putrefy. But those who seek a reason for contradiction in some apparent rather than true reason are easily deceived, as you see here how *Montanus* was deceived by this authority of *Galen*. 

In fact, if someone wanted to turn his own words back on him, he would certainly convict the man. For nowhere in our body is blood found outside the veins, except in the ventricles of the heart and, according to some, in that passage of the brain called the <term>torcular</term><note>The *torcular Herophili*, a confluence of sinuses in the brain where several blood vessels meet.</note>.

<summary>Niccolò Massa critiques Montanus's claim that blood only putrefies during pestilential fevers, arguing instead that blood's naturally hot and moist temperament makes it highly susceptible to putrefaction in many conditions. He further notes that the heart's primary role is to create vital spirit from blood, and that any actual putrefaction within the heart leads to immediate death and pulse failure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Niccolò Massa’s rebuttal of Giovanni Battista da Monte (Montanus). The previous page ended with a discussion on where putrefaction begins in the body. Massa here clarifies his anatomical observations regarding the heart and veins before moving into a critique of Montanus's practical treatment of the "pestilential fever" (the plague).</meta>

### THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...they call [it], which is not at all true in the <term>torcular</term><note>original: "torculari"—literally a "winepress." In anatomy, this refers to the *torcular Herophili*, the drainage point where the brain's major veins meet. Massa is arguing that blood is still contained within vessels here.</note>, since extremely fine veins holding the blood are located there, as can be clearly seen in my book on the dissection of the human body. Therefore, in the heart alone is blood found outside the veins, and it does not putrefy there first, as Montanus also asserts.

But, lest I trouble you with a long speech, these words shall suffice, since all illustrious ancient and modern physicians confirm my reasoning in their writings: namely, that blood putrefies in the veins, and that fevers arise from its putrefaction. These fevers differ in this manner: some proceed by increasing, some by declining, and a third type remains in the same state until the decline. These are called "sanguineous fevers," specifically because they arise from the putrefaction of the blood, and they are in no way <term>pestilential</term><note>Massa is distinguishing between common "blood fevers" caused by internal corruption and the "pestilential fever" (the plague), which was seen as a distinct, more dangerous category.</note>.

You have also read that all fevers have as their subject the three substances that constitute our body, which are very well known to you. I have therefore seen fit to set forth this discourse on the nature of pestilential fever, so that you might see the manner in which a physician ought to proceed in the cure of pestilential fevers. And although I have noted many things in the rest of the process, I do not intend to contradict them at present. 

My only intention is to discuss whether modern physicians behave correctly in the cure of this pestilential fever, both in the management of necessary things <note>This refers to the "six non-naturals" of Galenic medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind.</note>, as well as in medicines administered by mouth, those applied externally, and even those which require manual operation, such as <term>Enemas</term>, <term>rubbing</term>, <term>anointing</term>, <term>the application of cupping glasses</term>, <term>the opening of veins</term><note>original: "uenae apertiones"—phlebotomy or bloodletting.</note>, and other aids of this kind which are enjoined upon the sick by physicians. 

I wish to examine whether these things were correctly established and examined by Montanus, or whether he says many things without reason, based on his own unproven foundations. Therefore, setting aside what he said regarding the signs and predictions of the disease—since those do not contribute in every part to what you say you desire with your whole mind—I shall examine only those things which concern the curing of fevers, in the same order in which Montanus examined them. And so that the order is not confused, I will omit the intentions for preventing a future pestilential fever; however, I will follow the rest by declaring the truth. 

Montanus proposes certain doubts pertaining to evacuation, the first of which is whether in a pestilential fever the letting of blood by the opening of a vein is useful. To this doubt, he responds that this question is absurd, and not worthy of being put into doubt by a physician for that reason. Furthermore, he adds the reasons of those who, in such a case, fear to open a vein and let blood, which are namely:

# SECOND PART

...namely, so that the matter is not agitated, and by this agitation, the putrefaction is increased; with these reasons he accuses inexperienced physicians. Indeed, for the clarification of this doubt, I would write more to you, which—since I know you have read them in my little book on <term>pestilential fever</term><note>Massa is referring to his work *Liber de febre pestilentiali*, a famous 16th-century treatise on the plague.</note>—I have judged it superfluous to repeat here. For the discourse would be drawn out at too great a length; you will therefore be able to read those things again, since all of them are so clear that they do not require clarification. And since every man persuades himself that he knows, I cannot praise a man who chose to reproach the "inexperience of physicians" rather than the men who are unskilled in the medical art and the professors of other businesses; for I have followed up on all necessary things in that little book.

The second question is whether, after the fourth day has passed, it is safe to send away blood by the opening of a vein <gloss>bloodletting</gloss>. In this inquiry, he cites <term>Avicenna</term><note>original: "Auicennam" — a 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> in his own favor. But whatever may be the case regarding Avicenna's authority, I know you have seen this question resolved by many reasons in my already-cited little book. In the present case, however, I will add this: namely, that putrefaction is not always in the heart, or in the humors contained within the heart, as I said above—unless one wishes to assert that putrefaction has been made in the humors contained in the heart only near the moment of death, which, when it happens, the sick can be freed by no medicinal aid. 

And since I have already proved in my said book, by very powerful reasons, that this fever depends upon a <term>poisonous bad quality</term><note>original: "mala qualitate uenenosa" — In the medical theory of the time, the plague was thought to be caused by a specific "venomous" corruption of the body's fluids or the air.</note> (whether you call it "pestiferous" or not makes no difference), I shall not labor in further proof. Therefore, let what has been said be enough for you, if I also add one thing to those which follow: that is, that the fourth day is a <term>critical day</term><note>original: "dies critica" — In ancient and Renaissance medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a "crisis" was expected to occur, determining if the patient would live or die.</note>, even if it is seen rarely, as <term>Galen</term><note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity, whose theories dominated medical practice during the Renaissance.</note> said in the third book of *On Crises*, chapter 4, and in the second book of *On Decretory Days*. He also said that the fourth day has two indications: the first of which is that it may be a critical day, though a weak one; the second is that it may be indicative of the seventh day (although, according to Galen's opinion, crises occur very rarely in pestilential fevers). 

But if the fourth day is <term>decretory</term><note>original: "decretorius" — a day that "decides" the course of the disease.</note>, even if it is weak, Nature undoubtedly moves something on that day, especially in an acute disease. But since Nature in such fevers moves toward the parts of the skin—so much so that spots, which they call <term>pestichias</term><note>original: "pestichias" — modern "petechiae," the small purple or red spots on the skin characteristic of the plague and other fevers.</note>, appear on the skin—Nature pushes toward this part especially, as if to a member which, besides the other uses it has, also receives the <term>excrements</term><note>original: "excrementa" — in this context, metabolic waste or "corrupt humors" that the body is trying to expel.</note> of the entire body, if we believe Galen in the second book of *On the Causes of Diseases*. If it is so that Nature works on the fourth day, especially in a most acute disease, in which [the matter moves] very often and for the most part to the skin...

...drives it out, as experience witnesses; it is not without the greatest danger that physicians are able to cut a vein and evacuate blood after the fourth day. For we must in no way recall the <term>matter</term><note>The "matter" (materia) refers to the corrupted humors or poisonous substances thought to cause the disease.</note> which nature drives from the more noble members to the less noble ones, especially if it should be poisonous—as is matter affected by an evil <term>pestilential quality</term><note>In the 16th century, "pestilential quality" described the specific, often airborne essence of the plague that corrupted the body.</note>—but rather we should assist nature with frictions <gloss>massages</gloss> and other aids taken by mouth, which can prepare the matter so that it may exit more easily. And to ensure it does not return inside, one must abstain from the sending away of blood through the opening of a vein; but if the blood should be in excess, it ought to be drawn out by applying <term>scarified cupping glasses</term><note>A procedure where small cuts were made on the skin and a glass with a vacuum was applied to pull "bad" fluids to the surface without opening a main vein.</note>.

However, if the body is so <term>plethoric</term><note>An old medical term for having an unhealthy excess of blood or bodily fluids.</note> that it abounds with a great deal of bad blood while the patient's strength remains steady, the physician can send away blood by opening a vein, but this must not be done except with caution. For where there are <term>choleric fevers</term><note>Fevers believed to be caused by an excess of yellow bile, which was associated with heat and dryness.</note>, we do not evacuate blood by opening a vein without risk, since blood acts as the "bridle" of yellow bile; once the bridle of the bile is removed, the bile truly runs wild. From this, more violent fevers follow, as well as hotter and drier vapors rising to the head; thus, headaches occur, along with wakefulness and <term>alienation</term><note>A historical term for delirium or a state of mental confusion.</note>, and very often patients fall into inflammation or an <term>abscess of the brain</term><note>original: "apostema cerebri"</note>, or of its membranes.

But it is even worse when, after the fourth day, nature already begins to somehow purify the blood from a humor infected by some evil quality and attempts to drive it toward the skin; if the vein is cut and the blood is evacuated, there is a fear that the part which was pushed out by nature might enter the vein again. And since blood outside the veins putrefies easily—as it acquires a greater malice outside its proper place—it will communicate that malice to the blood within the veins. Thus, part by part, it will change the entire mass of blood into a greater evil and, seeking the heart, will kill the man.

That this is true, experience witnesses: indeed, many have died—and almost all on the day after the bloodletting—to whom a vein was opened after the fourth day. However, if (as I said) blood is so abundant that from its excessive quantity symptoms of suffocation appear, it is appropriate to open a vein and send away blood on any day or hour, provided the patient’s strength remains steady.

The third question was concerning the quantity of blood: namely, whether it is conducive to evacuate blood until <term>the point of fainting</term><note>original: "ad animi defectum" — Some physicians believed that bleeding a patient until they fainted (syncope) could "reset" the body's systems, a practice Massa is beginning to scrutinize here.</note>. In favor of this opinion, he brings forward <term>Hippocrates</term><note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine," whose writings remained the gold standard for physicians in Massa's time.</note> in the first part of his *Aphorisms*, Aphorism 6, in favor of those who dare to bleed to the point of...

# PART TWO

...to draw off the infected blood, because from such a large quantity of evacuated blood, patients are greatly cooled and dried out, and their bodies become more porous, and thus <term>putrefaction</term><note>The "rotting" or decomposition of humors (bodily fluids) that was believed to cause the symptoms of the plague.</note> is prevented. On the contrary, the opposite happens if the evacuation of blood is small, because the boiling of the blood hinders the evacuation of the <term>matter</term><note>The "matter" (materia) refers to the corrupted humors or poisonous substances causing the disease.</note>, by which putrefaction is increased. From these points, they draw such a conclusion: namely, that either blood must not be drawn at all, or it will be worthwhile to evacuate it copiously. 

And although they may answer this doubt, the response nonetheless does not satisfy in every respect. I say, therefore, that since it is characteristic of <term>pestilential fevers</term><note>A term for the plague or other deadly infectious diseases accompanied by high fever.</note> to make all the virtues weak, and especially the <term>vital virtue</term><note>The "vital virtue" or "vital spirit" was the energy source believed to reside in the heart and sustain life; weakening it was considered fatal.</note>, it will in no way be safe to evacuate thoroughly and copiously. Instead, it should be done gradually, moderately, and without violence, whatever the evacuation may be—whether of blood or of other humors. 

Add also that in a pestilential fever, one should not first seek a reduction of heat, but rather to prevent the increase of <term>venomosity</term><note>The poisonous quality of the plague that corrupted the body's natural humors.</note> and to strengthen the heart so that it can defend itself against it. This should be done with those things which can cool moderately without disturbing the humoral mass, as happens through the cutting of a vein, especially if the evacuation is copious. 

What he says about repeating the evacuation of blood several times is not rational for the reasons stated, since it draws the bad matter back into the great veins—except in cases where there is a very great abundance of blood that is suffocating the patient. However, whether the evacuation of blood is small or copious, it is always pernicious <gloss>harmful</gloss>, or at least not without the greatest danger, as has been clearly demonstrated in the frequently cited booklet.

The fourth question asked by him is from which vein the blood should be drawn. In that section, please see what things, and by what reasons and authorities, he proves the things said and cited, and how much he teaches. Furthermore, concerning the location or the vein from which the blood should be drawn, no one can teach definitively without making a distinction about the <term>source</term><note>Massa uses the word "minera" (literally "mine" or "source") to describe the specific area where the rotting humors have gathered.</note> of the putrefying humors. In that case, according to the different members in which the humors—affected by the evil pestilential quality—are putrefying, it is worthwhile to choose the specific vein to be opened. 

Yet he, forgetful of his own unproven position, hesitates about the place from which the blood is to be drawn. If his position were always true—namely, that in any pestilential fever, the putrefaction and pestilential quality were located in the heart or in the humors contained in the heart—then no other vein should be cut except the right <term>basilic vein</term><note>A major vein in the arm; early modern doctors believed specific veins connected directly to specific organs, with the basilic vein linked to the heart and liver.</note>. This is because (as appears from the sensory dissection of the limbs) it evacuates immediately and primarily from the right ventricle of the heart, secondarily...

...from the liver, so that it might evacuate the <term>peccant matter</term><note>The "sinning" or harmful fluid believed to cause the disease.</note>. One should also see if there is a retention of any accustomed evacuation—such as <term>hemorrhoids</term> or, in women, the menstrual blood—or however else a customary evacuation may have been held back. In such cases, blood should be drawn from those veins corresponding to the source of the retained evacuation, whether or not <term>rectitude</term><note>The practice of "linear" bloodletting, drawing blood from the same side of the body as the affected organ to ensure a direct flow.</note> is preserved. If we were able to preserve this rectitude, we would deal better with our patients. Even if the Greeks did not see this at all (as <term>Montanus</term><note>Giovanni Battista Monte (1498–1551), a celebrated Italian physician and contemporary of Massa.</note> said), that does not mean that the Arabs and Latins cannot find better remedies and add them to ancient discoveries.

Whatever the case may be, it is not safe to draw blood by opening a vein after the fourth day, unless a "multitude" <note>An excessive volume of blood (plethora) that threatens to overwhelm the patient’s system.</note> of blood is suffocating the person, as I have said. Regarding the fifth question—whether <term>concoction</term><note>The process by which the body "cooks" or matures the harmful humors so they can be expelled.</note> should be waited for in pestilential fevers—this seems superfluous to me. In acute diseases, it is worthwhile to evacuate on the very same day and hour; to delay is dangerous. Similarly, when the matter is "swelling" <note>Latin: *turgente materia*. A state where the humors are active and ready to be moved.</note>, it is expedient to evacuate immediately, as <term>Hippocrates</term><note>The ancient Greek physician often cited as the ultimate medical authority.</note> testifies.

Since a pestilential fever is acute and its matter is swelling, the physician should evacuate at whatever hour he arrives, if it can be done safely. I say "safely" because after the fourth day—unless there is a suffocating volume of blood, or if the blood is "thin" <note>Latin: *subtilis*. Thin or watery blood was thought to be easily agitated into yellow bile if drawn at the wrong time.</note> such that its evacuation might cause bile to rage unchecked—and especially if spots or <term>petechiae</term><note>Small purple or red spots on the skin caused by broken capillaries, a common and dreaded symptom of the plague.</note> have already appeared, a vein is not to be cut without the greatest risk, for the reasons and experience already mentioned.

Similarly, we should not evacuate using strong medicine taken by mouth without the greatest risk. Instead, it is beneficial first to draw out excrement from the bowels with mild <term>clysters</term><note>Enemas used to clear the lower digestive tract before more systemic treatments.</note>, and then to draw out the remaining waste and superfluities from the stomach and other common nearby paths without distress using some mild medicine. This can be done conveniently with a decoction of <term>tamarinds</term>, <term>manna</term><note>A sweet, gummy sap from the ash tree used as a gentle laxative.</note>, <term>cassia</term>, <term>rose syrup</term> made from multiple infusions of roses, or a similar gentle medicine.

And although bloodletting cools the body, it does not always cool it; rather, it very often causes bile to become unrestrained, or it may allow the poisonous matter, affected by a pestilential quality, to reach the <unclear>maritum</unclear><note>This may be an OCR error for "mucronem" (the tip or apex) of the heart.</note> of the heart; or if the blood is very copious, it might cool so much as to make the <term>virtue</term><note>The "virtue" or "spirit" was the patient's innate strength and life force.</note> far too weak. From these things, you see what is to be done, and when, and how, and from what place the evacuation should be made. And since the matter is twofold in many illnesses, the matter...

...causes <note>original: *libus*, the suffix of a word like *causalibus* ("causes") likely ending the previous page</note> (namely the antecedent and the conjoined causes), and if not all the matter has been emptied out by the aforementioned evacuations, then a regimen is appropriate that can prepare the remaining matter. Whether you wish to call this preparation "concoction" <note>The process where the body's internal heat "ripens" or matures harmful fluids so they can be expelled.</note>, or "rectification," or "balancing," or by any other name, it does not matter. This one thing remains constant in pestilential fevers: one must always and by every skill strive to rectify and balance the **humoral mass** <note>The total collection of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—in the body.</note>. This is done either through the management of air, food, and drink, and other necessary things, or through administered potions, all of which I have written about clearly in my previously cited book on pestilential fever.

From what has been said, conclude that <term>digestion</term><note>In this context, "digestion" refers to the metaphorical "cooking" or preparation of diseased humors, not just the processing of food.</note> is beneficial in this fever, which is nothing other than the preparation and correction of the humors, which is always necessary; and you will easily answer the sixth question posed by **Montanus**. For there is one intention that regards the matter, another that regards the <term>pestiferous quality</term><note>The specific "poisonous" nature of the plague that distinguishes it from a normal fever.</note>, and another that regards the cause—both the "agent" cause and the "patient" <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "agent" is the force acting (the plague), and the "patient" is the substance being acted upon (the body's moisture).</note> cause, which is the moisture ready to receive putrefaction alongside the poisonous quality. Whatever the case may be, when the pestiferous quality is present, it is worth the effort to dry it out, though it is not always necessary to use the same degree of drying.

In a similar way, the doubt as to whether it is permissible to use strong and dissolving medicines is answered by what was said above: first, because they agitate the poisonous matter, and second, because they exterminate the **vital virtue** <note>The "spirit" or life force that allows the organs to function.</note> and weaken the natural members, such as the stomach, intestines, and liver. The sayings of **Montanus** affirm this. However, if he had weighed his own words more subtly, he would not have been so bold in the "mission of blood" by the opening of a vein <note>Bloodletting or phlebotomy.</note>, since there is a far greater "resolution" <note>The weakening or dissipation of the body's strength and substance.</note> in the evacuation of blood than there is in purging through the bowels. Nevertheless, sometimes in those who are very <term>plethoric</term><note>Having an excessive volume of blood.</note> and robust, it is very helpful; but in an evacuation of this kind, the physician must act cautiously, consulting both the patient’s utility and his own honor. 

And although **Montanus** said that **cassia** <note>A mild laxative derived from the *Cassia fistula* tree, common in Renaissance medicine.</note> increases <term>putrefaction</term><note>The "rotting" or decay of humors believed to cause fever.</note>, I can hardly believe him. Perhaps it was an error of the scribe who did not understand, for I have given cassia countless times to those suffering from pestilential fever, and the putrefaction was not increased; rather, the matter was lessened, the "accidents" <note>The symptoms or secondary effects of the disease.</note> became milder, and finally, they were restored to health. I also know other physicians who have given it, and it turned out well for both them and their patients. 

But what should be said to the question regarding the **Medicine of Rufus** <note>A famous ancient pill or compound attributed to Rufus of Ephesus (c. 80–150 AD), often used as a preventative or purge during plagues.</note>, a most excellent physician, and one followed by all others after him...

## THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...confirmed, that the medicine made from **aloe, myrrh, and saffron** <note>This specific combination is known as the "Pill of Rufus," a famous ancient remedy for the plague attributed to Rufus of Ephesus.</note> can be of use. I will say, alongside Aristotle in his *Topics* <note>original: *Topicis*; Aristotle’s treatise on the art of reaching conclusions from probable premises.</note>, that those things which are confirmed by everyone in their own profession are like axioms, principles, and foundations, which students ought to receive without hesitation. Therefore, to question this seems to me the mark of an ignorant man. It should have been enough for him to confirm it with others, since beyond the authority of all the ancients and moderns, reason itself affirms it. 

Indeed, this medicine primarily evacuates **putrid matter** <note>Humors that have "rotted" or become corrupted, causing fever.</note> without agitation and very gently; it strengthens the stomach, liver, heart, and brain, and preserves the humors from putrefaction. Nor, as he says, is it only effective for preservation <note>Prevention.</note>, but also in treatment if it is mixed with other soothing medicines—such as **cassia, manna, rose syrup**, and others that blunt its heat, should the heat within the medicine be excessive. And just as he teaches how to correct the drying effect of **rhubarb** <note>rhabarbarum; used as a potent laxative in the Renaissance.</note> through infusion, so we can temper the heat of Rufus's medicine with something cooling or modestly moistening. I say "modestly" moistening because while the heat is easily blunted this way, the dryness is not entirely removed.

The eighth doubt was whether, when <term>petechiae</term> <note>pestichiae; small purple or red spots on the skin caused by broken capillaries, a common symptom of the plague or typhus.</note> or abscesses of another kind appear, evacuations by bloodletting or by medicine taken by mouth are appropriate; he brings forward reasons for both sides. However, lest I be tedious to him with a long speech, I will declare the matter itself (besides what I said above) in this way: when petechiae or other swellings appear, the matter having been pushed out by nature working well—which occurs if the said spots appear on an **indicative day** (which rarely happens) or a **critical day** <note>In Galenic medicine, the "critical days" (decretoria) were specific days in the course of a disease, like the 7th or 14th, when the body's "nature" fought the crisis and the patient either improved or died.</note>, and from which appearance follows an alleviation of the fever—it is not necessary to perform any treatment by bloodletting, nor even by an internal medicine that moves the bowels. This is because when nature is operating correctly, nothing should be done, as **Galen** said in his *On the Treatment of Fevers, to Glaucon*. 

But if such petechiae or tumors appear on a day that is neither indicative nor critical, and no alleviation follows, and the body is <term>plethoric</term> <note>Having an excess of blood.</note> or even <term>cacochymic</term> <note>cacochymum; a state where the body is filled with "bad humors" or corrupted fluids.</note>, and the patient's strength is steady, and their age and other factors agree, we can safely evacuate both by opening a vein and by medicine given by mouth. This allows the body's strength to better regulate the remaining matter. 

But that which seems to displease **Montanus** the most is the application of **scarified cupping glasses** <note>cucurbitularum scarificatarum; a procedure where the skin is scratched (scarified) and a heated glass cup is applied to create a vacuum and draw out "poisoned" blood or humors.</note>; for he says...

<summary>Massa defends the "Pill of Rufus" (aloe, myrrh, and saffron) as a standard treatment and argues that bloodletting or purging should only be avoided during a "critical day" when the body is successfully expelling the disease on its own.</summary>

SECOND PART.

# SECOND PART.

...the expulsion or appearance of spots and tumors does not come from the strength of the body’s **operating power** <note>original: *uirtutis operantis*; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the body's innate ability to perform biological functions and heal itself.</note>, but from the sheer abundance and malice of the matter, and also because of a weakness in the **retentive power** <note>original: *retentricis uirtutis*; the faculty believed to keep nourishment and humors inside the body until they are properly processed.</note> which leads to this expulsion. It is not because the **expulsive power** <note>original: *expultrix [uirtus]*; the faculty responsible for driving out waste.</note> is strong, but rather, when the retentive power fails to hold, the expulsive power casts out the matter easily. The patient is not relieved by this; indeed, [Montanus] teaches that in such a case, one must either evacuate the patient or predict their death. Having made the distinction as to whether the power is weak through **dissipation** <note>original: *resolutionem*; the "thinning out" or loss of vital energy.</note> or because it is weighed down, he provides a sign by which one may know if the power is weak through dissipation: this occurs when those things which can dissipate the power have not previously happened. These things that dissipate the power are, namely, excessive evacuation and the long duration of the disease. 

In this assignment of the causes of dissipation or weakness of the power, he has failed greatly, since he did not list the most potent cause of dissipation: the pestilential, poisonous malignancy infecting the **spirits of the heart** <note>original: *spiritus cordis*; the "vital spirits" believed to be generated in the heart and distributed through the arteries to sustain life.</note> and of the other principal organs. He then follows up on the case and orders evacuation so that the power may be made stronger against the remaining matter, even if spots or **small tumors** <note>original: *tubercula*; likely referring to buboes or plague sores.</note> have appeared. He cries out against those who apply <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>cucurbitulas; glass vessels used to create suction on the skin to draw out "corrupt" blood.</note> with scarification <note>The practice of making small cuts in the skin before applying a suction cup.</note>, and they teach when <term>cupping glasses</term> can be applied, saying it is when the matter is scarce; but if there is much matter, it is not at all suitable. This is because we would draw out the thin part of the blood while the thick part remains, which would cause the heat to diminish and the rot to increase. He concludes from these statements that it is necessary to evacuate the patient either by opening a vein or with medicine. 

You see, my dear Augustine, what sort of position this is. Who, I ask, is so unrefined as not to know that in a continuous **putrid fever** <note>A fever caused by the corruption or "rotting" of the bodily humors.</note> the matter rots within the veins? As <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Renaissance medicine.</note> said regarding tertian fever, this happens not only in the large veins near the **liver**, but even in the veins located in the periphery of the whole body. This is recognized by the weariness of the limbs during attacks. What way, therefore, could be better than that through which nature intentionally purges the waste of the entire body? This is the skin, the outermost part of the body, as <term>Galen</term> said in the second book of *On the Causes of Diseases*. 

Nor is the reasoning of <term>Montanus</term> <note>Giovanni Battista Monte, a prominent physician and Massa's contemporary rival.</note> valid, which claims that with the application of cupping glasses the thin part is drawn out while the thick remains—the supposed cause for the heat being rendered weak. He argues that what has been pushed to the edge of the skin is no longer regulated by nature, whether that expulsion came from a power operating well and rightly, or "symptomatically" from an overwhelming quantity or a stimulating malice. I cannot...

->NICCOLÒ MASSA, MEDICAL LETTERS<-

...[one should] not wonder at the sayings of Montanus, who said that the application of **cupping glasses** <note>original: *cucurbitularum*; glass vessels used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out humors.</note> with **scarification** <note>original: *scarificatione*; the practice of making small incisions in the skin to allow blood to be drawn out by a cupping glass.</note> simply cools the skin, in such a way that it prevents the body’s perspiration; this statement, however, if understood simply, is false. This is because the drawing of blood through scarification returns the skin to its proper **temperament** <note>The healthy balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) and qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> by removing that part of the bad blood that was inflaming the skin and by opening the **pores** <note>original: *meatibus*; literally "passages" or "channels" in the skin.</note> at the surface. Thus, the skin is not merely cooled but restored to balance, and therefore no obstructions occur, nor do those other things imagined by Montanus happen; rather, nature is relieved by such scarification. 

For if the matter remains there, it will certainly become worse, since, as I have said, when it is deprived of natural heat and is outside its proper place, it is rendered worse. From this new "malice" <note>Malignancy or harmful quality.</note> acquired from the stated causes, it could increase the malice of the remaining humor existing in the nearby veins. Once increased, it passes part by part to the remaining larger veins, all the way to the **source** <note>original: *mineram*; literally "the mine," referring here to the central reservoir of humors or the liver/heart.</note> and even to the heart. 

And therefore, those who apply scarified cupping glasses work most excellently. If he [Montanus] rebukes the abuse of these cupping glasses—both with and without scarification—that is granted to you, since those who work without reason are always to be rebuked and condemned; it is otherwise if they work correctly. Now, the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity (c. 460 – c. 370 BC).</note> is very well known: that where nature begins to work, there the physician ought to assist it through the appropriate place. Montanus affirms this proposition, but if spots already appear, why should we not imitate nature and assist it if it works weakly, hindered by the sheer quantity or malignancy of the humors? 

Therefore, given these facts, lightly scarified cupping glasses are to be praised, since they can always draw the matter back to a **less noble limb** <note>original: *ignobilius membrum*; in the medical hierarchy of the time, "noble" organs were the heart, brain, and liver. Drawing disease to the skin or legs was seen as a way to save these vital organs.</note>, and because they cool, divert, and evacuate. 

As for his claim that those suffering from **pestilential fever** <note>The plague.</note> have a weak innate heat and a great or strong febrile heat, this is contrary to his own exposition. He previously explained **Galen** <note>A Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> by saying that fever is "natural or native heat converted into a fiery state." According to his own explanation placed there, there is only one native heat, which, when converted into a fiery state, is called fever. Nevertheless, forgetful of his own position (which is not approved by everyone), he now lists two heats: namely, one natural and weak, and the other febrile and strong. Therefore, there is not some heat "besides nature" in the heart of those with fever, since there is only one heat; thus, his reasoning does not follow. Moreover, his claim that the application of cupping glasses cools the extremities is absurd, be-

...[since] from these the heat is drawn outward, and the paths and **passages** <note>original: *meatus*; the pores or channels in the skin and tissues through which humors and vapors move.</note> are opened, so that the **pestilential vapors** <note>In the 16th century, plague was believed to be carried by "miasma" or corrupt air that turned into poisonous vapors within the body.</note> can better escape. Indeed, any kind of drawing toward the external limbs—provided it is done without violence—is always useful, whether it is done through rubbing, or with substances that open the pores in some way, or with the aforementioned **cupping glasses** <note>original: *cucurbitulis*; glass vessels used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out humors.</note>. As long as they do not move the matter too forcefully, they help greatly; they do not cause inflammation but, as I said, they balance the heat by making the body "breathable."

If the application of cupping glasses "cools" the body, it does not do so in a simple sense. Rather, it cools by removing the **unnatural heat** <note>original: *caliditatem... praeter naturam*; heat caused by disease or corruption of the humors rather than the body's healthy biological fire.</note> produced by the matter that is sent to the skin with a pestilential malice. Therefore, it is wrong for him to say that drawing blood through cupping glasses "cools the skin" [in a harmful way]; he ought to have said that from such drawing and evacuation of blood, the skin returns to its proper **temperament** <note>The healthy balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. In this way, no obstructions are formed, and consequently, no further rot occurs.

Similarly, when he speaks of evacuation through **opening a vein** <note>Bloodletting or phlebotomy.</note> or medicine taken by mouth, it is a very great error and a statement against reason. For both the opening of a vein and evacuation by medicine lead the humors—which nature has already pushed toward the skin—back to the internal parts, regardless of how those evacuations are performed. For if blood is drawn by opening a vein, that bad part which nature had already begun to push to the skin will surely retreat, hindered by the contrary action. Similarly, regarding medicine taken by mouth: while it invites waste to the intestines, other matters in the neighboring limbs follow it, and so, part by part, they return to the interior.

Therefore, those who apply cupping glasses and lightly **scarify** <note>original: *scarificant*; the practice of making small, shallow incisions in the skin so that the cupping glass can draw out blood.</note> them work more safely and effectively. From this, you can see that it is better and more rational to work with scarified cupping. For a physician who works with reason inspects the disease, the patient's strength, and the way the disease operates; then, by imitating nature, he draws the matter out through the appropriate place.

If someone were to say in his defense that **Montanus** <note>Giovanni Battista Monte (1498–1551), a prominent medical authority and contemporary of Massa. The two often disagreed on clinical practice.</note> only accuses **empirics** <note>Practitioners who relied on experience and trial-and-error rather than formal university education and Greek medical theory.</note> and the ignorant, and not the learned who provide healing through reason, he at least erred in this: he should have stated that clearly and not accused everyone.

Montanus also continues and accuses physicians who use **enemas** <term>clysters: liquid medications injected into the rectum to clear the bowels or deliver medicine.</term> to soften the belly, asserting that nothing is more destructive in a pestilential fever than the use of enemas, because it prepares the way for a flux of the belly <note>Diarrhea, which was considered potentially fatal in plague victims due to dehydration and loss of "vital spirits."</note>. Indeed, I saw six hundred (so to speak) restored to health in those most unhappy years of **1527 and 1528** <note>Years of devastating plague outbreaks in Italy, particularly following the Sack of Rome.</note>, in which there were pestilential fevers with...

He specifically refutes Montanus's opposition to these methods and his rejection of enemas, citing his own success treating hundreds of patients during the outbreaks of 1527–1528.</summary>

# NICCOLO MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

...[cupping] glasses and tumors, according to my advice and that of other physicians; and this was a rational course of action because the bowels were constricted and spots <note>likely referring to petechiae or "tokens," the red or purple spots associated with the plague.</note> broke out across the whole body. Since they took food twice a day and the waste from the belly did not exit spontaneously, **enemas** <note>original: *clysteribus*; a liquid injection into the rectum used to clear the bowels of "corrupt humors."</note> were necessary. This was because the patients fell into greater distress, restlessness, and headaches, as well as other similar symptoms, both from the malice of the putrid matter causing the fevers and from the vapors rising from the retained waste. It was necessary to work in this way.

Therefore, **Montanus** <note>Giovanni Battista Monte (1498–1551), a prominent Italian physician often criticized by Massa for his theoretical approach.</note> is wrong on this point; for when a flow from the belly appeared, even the bystanders—to say nothing of the doctors—did not dare suggest that enemas be administered.

Afterward, he asks whether a **flow from the belly** <note>original: *fluxus ventris*; diarrhea or dysentery.</note> in a pestilential fever should be restrained. This is a beautiful question, worthy of a physician. To settle the matter briefly: I say that if the belly flows and the fever becomes lighter, the symptoms subside, and the patient's strength remains steady, it should be allowed to continue and not be restrained in any way. Instead, it is worthwhile to assist the **natural virtues** <note>The body's innate power to heal and maintain life according to Galenic medicine.</note> with altered foods and things that settle the stomach, as well as medicines with this same intention.

There are many **confections** <note>Medicinal preparations made by mixing various ingredients, often with sugar or honey to make them palatable.</note> that strengthen the natural organs and the heart, and refresh the **spirits** <note>In the 16th century, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle substances that carried life-force and sensation through the body.</note>. Furthermore, there are many "altering" medicines that do not constrict the bowels but strengthen the substance of the stomach, clarify the blood and spirits, and resist the pestilential putridity. These include **coral**, **pearls** <note>original: *Margaritae*; ground pearls were often used in expensive medieval and Renaissance cardiac tonics.</note>, **Lemnian earth** <note>original: *terra Lemnia*; a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, used since antiquity as an antidote to poison.</note>, **currants**, **barberries**, and the like.

There are also many compound confections well known to you as a physician, which learned doctors use either alone or mixed according to the needs of the case. Thus, they refresh the stomach's **concoction** <note>original: *concoctionem*; the process of digestion, which was viewed as a "cooking" of food within the body to create blood and humors.</note>, partly by tightening the linings or its substance, partly by preventing corruption, and also by resisting the pestilential malice. In this way, the virtue of the stomach is made stronger, so that if any bad matter remains within it, it is expelled more easily and quickly. Once evacuated, the nutrition taken in is better prepared by the body's heat.

Many other things were said by that most learned man [Montanus] in his lectures, which require greater care and examination. I would have finished speaking here, had I not declared certain things out of order; it was for this reason I wanted to write to you, to speak summarily in the manner of an epilogue and in an orderly way, so that you might have my opinion more clearly on the primary matter—the one that (so it seems to me) weighed heavily on the mind. First among these was the question regarding evacuation through **bloodletting** <note>original: *sanguinis missione*; the surgical removal of blood to balance the humors, a cornerstone of medical practice at the time.</note>...

# PART TWO

...namely [the opening of] a vein, and also concerning the application of cupping glasses, as well as medicines administered by mouth and enemas. Having collected these points, I shall conclude this process, and I will add one question which physicians use very frequently: whether applying leeches (or bloodsuckers) to hemorrhoids is useful in pestilential fevers. 

First, I will begin with the opening of a vein, which, as I have said, is least appropriate after the fourth day <note>The "fourth day" was considered a critical turning point in medieval and Renaissance crisis theory for diseases.</note>, especially when spots and tumors appear throughout the entire body, unless there is an extreme fullness of suffocating blood. In such a case, it will be beneficial to open a vein not just once, but twice or three times, and to apply leeches to the hemorrhoids, as was extensively proven in my booklet on pestilential fever. 

It is also beneficial to perform an evacuation in cases of **bad humors** <term>cacochymia: a condition where the bodily fluids are disordered or "corrupt."</term> and in the greatest fullness of humors, both from the beginning and after the fourth day, even if spots and **abscesses** <term>apostemata: inflammatory swellings or boils, often associated with the buboes of the plague.</term> have appeared, provided that the patient’s vital strength remains steady. However, if neither the aforementioned fullness of blood nor the fullness of humors is present, and spots have appeared, there is no way that bloodletting or evacuation can be useful. Instead, it is safer to draw out the waste of the intestines with enemas and to apply scarified cupping glasses <note>Cupping glasses where the skin was lightly cut (scarified) before the vacuum was applied to draw out "toxins."</note>; for the reasons, causes, and benefits of these, see the previously cited booklet. 

Once these things are done, it will always be worthwhile to provide the sick with things that strengthen the heart and refresh and clarify the spirits, such as **Lemnian earth** <term>terra lemnia: a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, used since antiquity as an antidote to poison.</term>, **Armenian bole** <term>bolus armenicus: a red clay used as an astringent and to treat plague symptoms.</term>, coral, pearls, fragments of gems, and other noble medicinal mixtures. These are useful because, besides their ability to strengthen the heart by their very substance, they also have the power to clarify spirits infected by the putrid vapors raised from the source of the fever. 

Nor would I wish you to believe that position of **Montanus** <note>Giovanni Battista Monte, a contemporary medical authority whom Massa frequently debates.</note>, namely that in every pestilential fever the rot is in the heart or in its contents, since he contradicts himself. Indeed, when he deals with the signs of pestilential fevers, he teaches how to recognize when the rot is in the heart primarily by this sign: the failure of the pulse. For he says that if the rot is in the heart, the pulse will surely fail. Since he also attempts to teach other signs of the heart’s decay there, it appears from his own words that the rot is not always in the heart, but also in other parts of the body. Thus, those who use astringent aids that strengthen the heart, such as those mentioned above, act very well; they drive nothing into the heart when the source of the disease is not located there. Rather, by strengthening the heart, they defend it from the pestilential malice.

You have now, most learned Augustine, my opinion on evacuation in pestilential fevers.

### DISCOURSE ON TERTIAN FEVER
### and on the signs of all fevers, addressed to certain disciples.

### L E T T E R X.

SINCE you have often asked me to write down for you, amidst so many consultations on fevers, some example for diagnosing fevers; which indeed I would have done more gladly if I could accommodate the entire subject of fevers in a single example, since it is very difficult to describe something that can be adapted to all fevers, all ages, all sexes, and **temperaments** <term>temperatura: the specific balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—determined at birth.</term>, and even the seasons of the year. 

But since in those past autumnal days I was called, together with those most famous physicians, to a consultation for a noble and well-born young man, Master N., thirty years of age, who has had a hot and dry temperament from the beginning of his life, and who was suffering from a fever with headache, dryness of the tongue, and burning thirst, along with the greatest restlessness; and since many things were said in your presence and that of many very learned men regarding the diagnosis of the disease and the prediction of its outcome, and finally the removal of the disease—nevertheless, after we returned to the boat <note>In Venice, where Massa practiced, physicians often traveled to patients' homes via gondola. These journeys through the canals served as informal mobile classrooms where masters discussed cases with their students.</note>, you began to ask me if I would be willing to explain something for diagnosing and curing other fevers as well, beyond those things said in the consultation by the most serious men and by myself. 

In this matter, because the day was already waning, I could not satisfy you at that time; however, I promised to write something about this same case for the benefit of all and for your own, which I shall begin thus: The noble young man was of a slender bodily habit and not filled with much flesh, with the color of the external parts of his body tending toward a certain **yellowness** <term>citrinitas: a yellowish or lemon-colored skin tone, which Renaissance doctors often interpreted as a sign of excess yellow bile or "choler."</term> mixed with darkness, along with a prominence of the veins, as you saw; but so that all things may proceed according to method and the custom of illustrious rational physicians...
