# SECOND PART

observed by the physicians; those things which were previously noted by us regarding the knowledge of the disease and the rest, I shall write in order. First, following the authority of Galen in the first book of *On the Constitution of the Medical Art* <note>original: "de Constitutione artis Medicae"; a foundational text by Galen (2nd century AD) regarding the theoretical basis of medicine.</note> and according to the reasoning which dictates the knowledge of the quantity and quality of a "bad hot **temperament**" <term>temperamentum: the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). A "bad temperament" (dyskrasia) signifies an imbalance causing disease.</term>, which is a fever, we first weighed his natural temperament. For it is hardly possible for anyone to rightly know the quantity and quality of a disposition and affection that is "contrary to nature" <note>This refers to a state of disease or injury.</note> unless he first knows the natural dispositions. Indeed, the natural things or dispositions are namely age, temperament, sex, and those things annexed to them, such as the **strengths** <term>vires: the innate functional powers of the body.</term>, the operations of the body, the **humors** <term>humores: the four vital fluids.</term>, the **spirits** <term>spiritus: the subtle vapors that carry life and sensation through the body.</term>, the seasons of the year, and what follows them, as well as habits and places, or regions. And since those things which are known to the senses do not require explanation, having set the rest aside, they arrived at the diagnosis of his temperament based on Galen's precepts in the booklet of the *Small Art* <note>original: "Ars Parva"; also known as the *Tegni*, this was a standard textbook for medical students in the Renaissance.</note> and they endeavored to establish it as such, as I have said, beginning their reasoning primarily from the inherent substantial signs.

By weighing the principal members, and first the temperament of the head and its parts and operations, [they observed] that because the head has an excellent shape and size, it shows a dominance of heat. The citrine <note>A yellowish-brown color, often associated with an excess of yellow bile.</note> color of the skin along with a certain duskiness testifies to the same. The blackness and curliness of the hair and beard prove a dominance of heat and dryness. Furthermore, since according to the opinion of all illustrious men the "interior virtues" are known through their operations, they examined the operations proceeding from the **brain** <term>cerebro: regarded as the seat of the "animal spirits" and cognitive functions.</term>, both interior and exterior. Since they understood his imaginative, discursive, and memorative faculties to be unimpaired, together with his exterior senses and the movement of his parts with agility and promptness while he was healthy, they affirmed a dominance of heat with a modest dryness. 

One could add to their findings the shape, size, and blackness of the eyes, and if I may say so, their vivacity, along with a scarcity of sputum and nasal mucus. Add also the promptness of his speech; all of which confirm that the temperament of the head is the same. They examined the second of the principal members, or rather its temperament, in this way: that it was hot and dry from the beginning of its generation, contracted with these essential primary signs, and they confirmed this from the "accidents" <note>In medical philosophy, "accidents" are observable symptoms or characteristics that are not part of the essential nature of a thing but result from it.</note> by first listing the breadth of the breast or **thorax** <term>thorax: the chest area, housing the heart, which was considered the source of "vital heat."</term>, which was not of excessive fleshiness or fatness; and also, since he breathes excellently, this occurs only because of an extending heat that lacks a superfluity of moisture...

->LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA ON MEDICINE<-

...occurred in that region, <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the chest/heart region.</note> as these parts are shaggy and covered with many hairs; furthermore, the patient is prompt, high-spirited, and prone to anger and outbursts, with fierce manners and a large, strong pulse—all of which signs the physicians affirmed to attest to a **hot** quality.

The third principal member weighed was the **liver** <term>hepar: the liver, considered in Galenic medicine to be the source of the veins and the site of "haematosis" or blood-making.</term>, which they proved to have possessed a hot and dry **temperament** <gloss>natural balance of humors</gloss> from the very beginning of his life. They deduced this from the thinness of his fleshy limbs and the large size of his veins, especially around the parts of the lower belly, where they noted a significant amount of hair.

We also noted among the natural organs the **stomach** <term>ventriculus: literally "the little belly," referring to the stomach as the organ that "serves" the liver by preparing food.</term>, which we judged to be **cold and dry**. This was because the exterior parts corresponding to the region of the stomach are quite thin, and similarly, its internal powers and operations—both in preparing and expelling food—labor over a great span of time. This can only happen because the layers of its membranes have been chilled, partly by the excessive heat of the liver consuming its moist substance, and partly because its own innate heat dissipates through drying out, so that its substance, having become thinner, is unable to retain heat. This is also seen in the "crudities" <note>original: "cruditatibus"; undigested or poorly "cooked" food matter in the stomach, thought to cause various ailments.</note> which are continually generated within it; for a chilled stomach cannot properly transform the food that has been taken in.

The knowledge of the temperament of the genitals also contributes to the understanding of the whole constitution. By weighing their operations, the physicians determined them to be **hot and moist**, since the patient was always inclined to sexual matters and fathered male children; furthermore, he has hairy genitals covered in much hair, which can only arise from an abundance of heat, though properly tempered.

Therefore, when all these things were collected together, Galen said in the second book of *The Art of Medicine* <note>original: "Artis paruae"; also known as the *Microtegni*, this was the most common introductory textbook for medical students in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> that the whole body is **very hot and dry**, declining from its proper balance. Having thus seen the natural temperament, along with the patient’s youthful age, the autumn season, and his habits, it remains to write what was said concerning the **essence of the disease**.

They declared this essence by first setting down the foundation of Galen in the first book of *On Diseases* <note>original: "de Morbis"</note>, where he says that things which exist in the body "contrary to nature" are either diseases, or causes, or the symptoms following diseases. The **disease**, therefore, as you have seen, is a **fever**. This was proven by a sign taken from its essential nature: an unnatural heat in the heart that is common to the entire body. But since there are three types of fevers—namely the **ephemeral**, the **putrid**, and the **habitual** <note>original: "ephemerarum, putridarum & habitudinalium"; ephemeral fevers lasted a day and involved the spirits; putrid fevers involved the humors; habitual (or hectic) fevers were settled into the solid tissues of the body.</note>—to recognize the type of this fever...

## SECOND PART.

This was discovered through a comprehensive classification of fevers. For the physicians stated that it was not a **hectic** <term>hectica: from the Greek 'hektikos' (habitual); a fever believed to be deeply rooted in the "solid parts" or tissues of the body rather than the fluids.</term> fever, since that type rarely or never occurs at the beginning of an illness, but instead follows two other types of fever. In a hectic fever, neither shivering nor "gooseflesh" nor chills precede the heat; rather, it afflicts the patient with a constant intensity of heat. Without any relief or increase, they burn uniformly, and their pulses are small, weak, hard, frequent, and without variation. Furthermore, patients have this permanent and inseparable sign: that after taking food, they grow hotter for one or two hours or more. But since the fever of this noble gentleman is not of this kind, it cannot be a hectic fever.

Nor is it an **ephemeral** or "one-day" fever <gloss>diaria</gloss>, because the heat of ephemeral fevers is mild and has no "biting" quality <note>In Galenic medicine, "biting" heat (calor mordax) felt sharp or stinging to the physician's touch, indicating putrefying humors.</note>. In such cases, the pulse does not change much from its natural state, whether in size, frequency, or other characteristics. Furthermore, an ephemeral fever rarely lasts until the third day without changing into another type of fever; but since it is now the sixth day since he began to suffer from the fever, and as it possesses sharp heat and lacks the characteristics of those other fevers, it can in no way be a type of ephemeral fever.

It remains, therefore, that it belongs to the **humoral** <term>humoralis: a fever caused by the corruption or "putrefaction" of one of the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, or black bile.</term> category. And since there are as many types of humoral fevers as there are humors that either putrefy or possess an unnatural heat, it was sought through diligent examination which humor was involved, so that the specific type of fever could be identified by its inflammation and putrefaction. For this diagnosis, according to the authority of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose 'Canon of Medicine' was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> in the fourth section of the first book, it was stated that:

*   The putrefaction of **yellow bile** <term>cholera: also called yellow bile; associated with fire, heat, and bitterness.</term> causes **tertian** fever <note>A fever that spikes every third day (i.e., every other day).</note>.
*   The putrefaction of **blood** causes a **continual** or constant fever.
*   The putrefaction of **melancholy** <term>melancholia: also called black bile; associated with earth, cold, and dryness.</term> causes **quartan** fever <note>A fever that spikes every fourth day (i.e., every two days).</note>.
*   The putrefaction of **phlegm** creates a **quotidian** <gloss>daily</gloss> fever.

This putrefaction in different humors creates a variety of unnatural heat—namely greater or lesser, sharp or mild. Thus, we first recognize the species of a "putrid" fever more easily by this essential, inherent sign. Indeed, the putrefaction of yellow bile creates an acute and biting heat. The putrefaction of blood, however, because there is so much moisture in it, causes a milder and non-sharp heat compared to the putrefaction of yellow bile. The heat of putrefying melancholy is not as biting and sharp as that of yellow bile. Finally, the putrefaction of phlegm does not cause much heat, but rather a dull and quite gentle warmth.

Therefore, by taking the signs from these fundamental qualities, it was stated that the fever of this noble gentleman is, and depends upon, the putrefaction of **yellow bile**; for the unnatural heat is very sharp and biting to the touch. The pulse further attests to this, being large...

...magnitude, frequency; speed with variation. Indeed, a **fast pulse** <term>pulsus uelox: refers to the speed of a single arterial expansion.</term> differs from a **frequent pulse** <term>pulsus frequens: refers to the shortness of the interval between beats.</term>, since that pulse is called "fast" which strikes quickly, but "frequent" is that which strikes very often and with almost no pause between one pulsation and the next. In this way, there are many numerous strikes within a single period of time. In this case, such frequency and speed can only arise from the heart's great need for cooling. Similarly, there are **chills** which feel like the pricking of needles <note>original: "rigores qui acuū pūcturarum similes sunt"</note>, which testify to the sharpness of the rotting humors. This is also confirmed by the bilious stools and the saffron-colored or red urine, which can only be caused by the mixing and abundance of **bile** <note>Yellow bile (choler) was one of the four humors; it was associated with fire, heat, and dryness.</note>. There is also restlessness, thirst, dryness of the tongue, and a sharp headache—all of which are symptoms caused by the "boiling" and evaporation of the choleric humor. Indeed, bile is the hottest of all humors, especially when it has putrefied. Sometimes it putrefies while pure and unmixed, but most often it is mixed with other humors; however, whether alone or mixed, when it putrefies, it excites a **tertian fever** <note>A fever that spikes every third day (by inclusive counting), typical of malaria.</note>.

But since a tertian fever is not of just one kind but is manifold—namely, **continual** and **intermittent**—let us distinguish them. Among the continual types, one is the *causon* <term>causon: from the Greek 'kausos,' meaning a burning heat; an acute, inflammatory fever.</term>, and the other is a "proportional" continual fever <note>Equivalent to two overlapping tertian cycles.</note>. Among the intermittent types, one is "exquisite" and pure, while the other is not exquisite, but rather "spurious" or "bastard" <note>original: "spuria, & notha"</note>. Both of these usually have manifest attacks accompanied by a regular cycle, coldness, shivering, or rigors.

Because this particular fever intermits, has manifest attacks, and ends with a fairly heavy sweat, it is not a "continual" or "unremitting" fever. However, since I have mentioned different kinds of fevers in general, I will explain something to you that you may find useful: the *causon* fever is the most burning of all the continual tertians, in which no manifest increase [of symptoms] appears, or if it does, it is almost imperceptible. The "proportional" continual fever is that in which the heat proceeds without a break, yet every third day some remissions and corresponding intensifications appear from one third day to the next. Because of this correspondence, they are called proportional to two tertians. 

Furthermore, according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, considered the father of medicine.</note>, it is characteristic of continual fevers not to involve shivering. But since in this Magnificent Man the shivering and chills are manifest, his fever is **intermittent** and periodic, not continual. This indicates that the putrefying matter is located for the most part outside the veins. Thus, this will be a **putrid intermittent fever**, depending on putrefying bilious matter. But since one type of bile is pure and "exquisite," and another...

...others are not pure, but either mixed in themselves or corrupted by something else; it has been said, and it is clear, that this does not arise from the putrefaction of **pure yellow bile** <note>original: "exquisitæ choleræ"</note>, since its heat passes through and lasts for a duration of sometimes twenty hours. Indeed, pure yellow bile is consumed within twelve hours and then leaves the sick man; since pure bile does not exceed a twelve-hour span, the putrefying humor is therefore, as I said, a **spurious yellow bile** <note>original: "cholera notha." A "bastard" or atypical fever that does not follow the standard 12-hour cycle of a true tertian fever.</note>, which is mixed and not pure.

This spurious bile is called by some physicians "of the greater renown" and by others "of the lesser renown." That which is called "**of the lesser renown**" <note>original: "minoris famæ." This refers to a specific classification system in Renaissance medicine used to categorize types of atypical fevers.</note> is that which is created by the mixing of the **melancholic humor** <note>Black bile, the humor associated with earth, cold, and dryness.</note> (whether pure or impurely mixed). Its signs are difficult fever attacks and "accidents" following melancholy, which are not present in this patient. 

Alternatively, it may be produced by **combustion** <term>adustio: the "burning" or "overheating" of a humor, which changed its medical properties, often making it more toxic.</term>, especially in choleric people, so much so that sometimes such great burning occurs in it that it is reduced to the nature of a poison. This can be seen in that bile which is called **leek-green** <note>original: "porrina"</note> or **verdigris** <note>original: "æruginosa," referring to the bright green color of oxidized copper.</note>, and it often kills men because its malice cannot be regulated by physicians or by natural heat. Instead, as I said, it most often leads the sick to their destruction. 

In such a fever, the most savage symptoms appear, such as **cardiac distress** <note>original: "cardiaca passio," likely referring to severe heart palpitations or fainting.</note>, a pounding of the heart, and other accidents such as great thirst, dryness of the tongue, headache, sleeplessness, cold resolving sweats, and perpetual restlessness. The lower or turbid urines also appear in such cases, and even corrupted feces appear, which show a green or black color according to the diversity of the burning. 

However, since these symptoms are not present in this noble man, this bile cannot be that which is called "of the lesser renown." Therefore, since the signs of that type are not in this noble patient, it will not be a fever from the putrefaction of the "lesser renown" bile, but will be from a putrefaction of the "**greater renown**." This type is also said to be not just one kind, as some are caused by a thin **phlegmatic humor** <note>original: "humoris pituitoši." Phlegm was the cold, moist humor.</note> and some by the mixing of thick phlegm, or by the burning of bile, as pleased Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire whose theories dominated medicine for over a thousand religion.</note>. 

And <term>that</term> <note>Abbreviation for 'quod'</note> it was not from a mixing of thin phlegm, they attempted to prove by this argument: because in such a mode of putrefaction, headache, mental alienation, anguish, and bad restlessness follow, along with "raw" urine and bowel excrement with very little color—things which have not yet been seen in this case. 

Wherefore, it remained to be said that this fever depends on the putrefaction of bile of the "lesser renown" resulting from a mixture of **thick phlegm**, or has been caused by the burning of bile, which is called **xantha** <note>original: "xantha," from the Greek for "yellow."</note> by physicians. And they confirmed this because the excrement that was seen resembled both the substance and the color of mixed egg yolks...

From these signs, therefore, you can conclude that the noble man's fever is a **tertian fever** arising from the putrefaction of bile mixed with thick, phlegmatic matter, which doctors call **spurious** <note>original: "notham." A "bastard" or atypical fever.</note> and **yolk-like** <note>original: "uitellinam." This refers to bile that has the thick, yellow consistency of an egg yolk, suggesting a specific type of humoral imbalance.</note>.

But since we have moved into a discussion of different fevers, for your greater understanding and benefit, let me digress a little regarding the signs of other fevers. By setting these out, you may recognize other species of fevers as well. I shall begin, therefore, with the **ephemeral fever** <note>A "one-day" fever, usually non-lethal and caused by environmental factors rather than internal rot.</note>: the signs of an ephemeral fever in general are these: namely, a heat that is not sharp but mild, little different from natural body heat. The pulse is also perceived as not very different from the natural state in its size, frequency, and rhythm. Similarly, the urine does not change much from its natural consistency in color or substance. Furthermore, this fever for the most part does not last past the third day, but very often ends on the first. It declines with a certain dewy evaporation or a very light sweat, and it lacks the "accidents" <note>In Renaissance medicine, "accidents" are secondary symptoms or complications like delirium or extreme vomiting.</note> of putrid fevers. Moreover, every ephemeral fever arises from a **triggering cause** <note>original: "causa procatarctica." An external factor like exhaustion, anger, or too much sun.</note>, except for some that arise from an antecedent cause, such as from inflammation or from a surplus of hot humors that are not yet rotting. These are the signs of ephemeral fevers; I shall now move down to the signs of the **burning fever** <term>causon: an "ardent" or "burning" fever (Greek: kausos) traditionally associated with the overheating of yellow bile.</term> and other humoral fevers.

The signs of a **burning fever** are, first of all, a vehement, sharp heat of strong inflammation, which seems to afflict the patient without pause and uniformly at all hours of the day—though it always has a slight remission every third day that is barely perceptible, and recognized only by a highly skilled physician. The pulse is large, full, swift, frequent, irregular, and hard. There is restlessness; the exterior parts of the body are dry and parched; there is great thirst and a blackness of the tongue, together with dryness and even roughness. One also sees bilious vomiting and a corrosive pain in the stomach, as well as headache, sleeplessness, and mental wandering. The urine is a reddish-yellow, almost fiery color. Similarly, the waste from the bowels is bilious, tinged with a saffron color, and sometimes, due to internal **combustion** <note>original: "adustione." The "burning" of humors which makes them toxic and dark.</note>, tending toward blackness.

The signs of the **continuous fevers** <note>original: "Synocharum." These are fevers that do not have distinct breaks or cycles.</note>, however, are these: first, the heat is vehement but not sharp, afflicting the patient continuously without any remission until the disease begins to decline. However, according to their different species, they have different levels of heat and progression. For instance, that fever which depends solely on the inflammation of the blood without putrefaction—and is a middle ground between an ephemeral and a putrid fever—has a heat that is not sharp, nor [does it feel sharp] to the touch...

# SECOND PART.

...bitingly; the pulse, though it may be large, is nevertheless not very frequent. The heat, however, is consumed with a dewy sweat before the fourth day, unless the fever turns into a putrid one. In the case of putrid **Synochis** <term>Synochis: a type of continuous fever where the heat remains constant or follows a specific progression without breaks</term>, of which there are three species, the heat is also continuous, though it afflicts the patient in different ways. For one of them maintains the same degree of heat from the beginning until its decline, and this is called **continuous of equal vigor** or heat; the second, however, has a heat that always proceeds by increasing until the decline, and this is called **increasing continuous**; the third has a heat that always proceeds by diminishing, and it is called **decreasing continuous**. In these three species of fevers, the heat is intense but not sharp or biting. The pulse, although it may be large, intense, and frequent, does not for that reason have much irregularity or hardness; rather, it is soft. The **urines** <note>The study of urine (uroscopy) was a primary diagnostic tool for determining the state of the humors.</note> are red and thick, reflecting the color of blood; similarly, the excrements of the bowels appear with some redness. The eyes are reddish and heavy; there is some thirst, but it is not very troublesome.

The signs or markers of a **continuous choleric fever**—which is said to be proportional to two tertian fevers—are these: a sharp, varying heat that afflicts continuously so that it never reaches a state of being fever-free, yet it has some manifest remission, with a correspondence in both its remissions and its flare-ups from every third day to the next. It has, however, different degrees of heat in different subjects according to the difference of whether more or less **cholera** <term>cholera: in this context, yellow bile, the hot and dry humor</term> is mixed with other humors. Furthermore, where a great deal of **phlegmatic** <note>original: "pituitosæ"</note> matter is mixed in, the heat is not so sharp and intense; but when the matter is for the most part "burnt" <note>Adust or "burnt" humors were thought to be charred by excessive bodily heat, becoming much more toxic and irritating to the system.</note>, then the heat is sharp, biting, and acute. The pulse is also large, frequent, intense, and varied, more or less according to the variety of the putrefying humors mixed with the bile itself. There are, moreover, restlessness, thirst, dryness of the tongue, headache, persistent sleeplessness, stomach pain, nausea, and bilious vomiting, along with back pain and heat. The urines are indeed saffron-colored, red, or lemon-yellow; the bowel movements are also similar in color.

The signs of an **intermittent tertian fever**—which most often occurs in bilious young men, during the summer, in hot regions, and in those who follow a heating and drying lifestyle—are these: it begins with cold or shivering, in which they feel as if they are being pricked by needles in the back, and it begins suddenly and ends quickly.

...follows a sharp heat throughout the whole body; difficulty breathing, the pulse is large, frequent, fast, and varied. Along with a general dryness of the skin, the parts of the body are hot; there is also intense thirst, dryness of the tongue, headache, sleeplessness, and mental distractions <note>original: "alienationes" — referring to delirium or a wandering mind</note> and especially afflictions. When the fever is **pure** <note>A "pure" tertian fever was considered a straightforward case caused by simple yellow bile, typically following a predictable cycle.</note>, it intermits <note>stops temporarily</note> before twelve hours have passed and ends with a sweat. However, when the **paroxysms** <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase in the intensity of a disease</term> become longer and exceed a duration of twelve hours, they are no longer considered simple or pure; they are considered "impure" in proportion to how much they exceed that twelve-hour window.

The signs of **impure tertian fevers** are that they begin with cold or shivering, which does not strike suddenly but creeps in gradually and is not of the highest intensity. This shivering is often prolonged for several hours, especially if a great deal of thick, phlegmatic matter is mixed in. Then follows an intense heat, though not of the ultimate sharpness found in the "exquisite" or pure variety. The pulse is large, frequent, and varied; there is great thirst and some dryness of the tongue. There is also pain and heaviness of the head, sleeplessness, and a tendency to fall into a heavy sleep, especially at the time the fever comes on. There is also pain in the stomach and nausea, and sometimes the vomiting of **vitelline bile** <term>vitelline bile: bile that resembles the yolk of an egg (Latin: vitellus), considered thicker and more "cooked" than standard bile</term>; combined with stomach anxiety, these restlessnesses are difficult for the patient. The urines appear thick and red, and the excrements of the bowels resemble mixed-up egg yolks.

If there is an admixture of thin phlegm (which is called **citrine bile** <note>original: "cholera citrina" — a lighter, lemon-colored bile</note>), then in addition to the symptoms mentioned, there is primarily a vehement headache, sleeplessness, along with mental distraction, thirst, and dryness of the tongue; however, the urines are not so thick, nor are the feces so saffron-colored.

But if the **melancholic humor** <note>Melancholy, or black bile, was the heaviest and coldest of the four humors; its presence indicated a more serious, lingering illness.</note> has been mixed with the bile, or if the bile itself has been **scorched** <term>scorched: "adusta" bile was thought to be "burnt" by excess heat, making it dark, acrid, and highly toxic to the body</term> and turned toward the nature of melancholy—which they call "bile of lesser fame" <note>original: "minoris famae" — likely a reference to a specific classification in the Galenic medical tradition for degraded bile</note>—the signs of its putrefaction are these: namely, intense and sharp heat. The pulse is large, frequent, and swift, and it sometimes skips a beat if the matter is particularly malignant. There is restlessness without relief, headache, mental distractions, dryness of the tongue, and a powerful thirst. There is also stomach pain, anxieties, nausea, foul vomiting, and a pounding of the heart. The urines are thick, red, and livid; similarly, the excrements of the bowels are bad—either corrupted or held back, and extremely foul-smelling. All these species of impure fevers, if they are intermittent, have paroxysms that last for the most part the spa...

## SECOND PART

...of twelve hours, so that sometimes the attacks <note>original: "accessiones"</note> are prolonged until one begins before the previous one has ended, and they become continuous through this overlapping of paroxysms. From this, you will note that the more the twelve-hour interval is exceeded in these attacks, the more "impure" the fever will be—either through the mixing in of **phlegm** <term>pituita: one of the four humors, characterized as cold and moist</term>, or the **melancholic humor** <term>black bile: the humor associated with the earth, coldness, and dryness</term>, whether natural or "burnt" <note>original: "adusti" — referring to bile that has become overheated and toxic through "combustion"</note>, as I have told you.

The signs of **quartan fever** <note>A fever that typically peaks every fourth day, such as Monday then Thursday</note>—which rarely starts on its own but usually follows other fevers—is rarely seen as continuous, but is mostly intermittent. However, since it sometimes happens as a continuous fever in some people, I will declare the signs of the continuous type to you. First, the heat is not particularly sharp, yet it is in some way sweltering and difficult; it afflicts the person more every fourth day and has a corresponding major worsening <note>original: "exacerbationem"</note>. It has some remission <note>a lessening of symptoms</note>, after which the patient grows hot again, and that heat proceeds by increasing gradually. Along with this sweltering restlessness, there is an increase in pain in all the muscles, feeling as if they are being broken; there are also feelings of anxiety, restlessness, and sadness. The **pulse** in these cases is large, infrequent, varied, and often hard. The **spleen** usually swells; the **urine** and its contents are of a leaden <note>original: "liuidi coloris" — a bluish-gray or leaden hue associated with black bile</note> color, and similarly, the excrement from the lower belly is somewhat blackish. This fever is always long-lasting and difficult to cure.

The signs of **intermittent quartan fever** are these: specifically, this fever begins sometimes with a certain pattern <note>original: "typo"</note>, sometimes with cold, and sometimes with shivering <note>original: "rigore"</note>. The onset at the beginning is not difficult or overly bothersome, but it increases as it proceeds and soon becomes painful and difficult. Usually, the start of the attack lasts for several hours, more or less according to the thickness of the decaying matter. Unlike in tertian fevers, this cold does not immediately spread to the outer parts of the body, but is delayed as it proceeds and seems to feel cold internally—as happens to those walking through northern winds and snow. After this long cold, they begin to grow warm gradually, and the heat, progressing bit by bit, increases; it is not sharp or piercing, but sweltering and difficult, bothering the person deep inside so that it feels like the bones are being crushed. The **pulse** is large, slow, and infrequent, and often hard. The attacks, moreover, are long and come to their decline very slowly; this decline is sometimes accompanied by sweat, but not always. Furthermore, stomach pain often tends to bother these patients.

...and they sometimes, and often, vomit various substances, including acidic ones; the urines are thick, **leaden-colored** <note>original: "lividae" — a bluish-gray or bruised color associated with poor circulation or cold humors</note>, and reddish, yet often they are seen to be discolored and watery; similarly, the stools of the belly are leaden and dark; these fevers often end with sweating, which is sometimes copious and sometimes slight and dewy; they are always long-lasting and difficult to cure.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Quotidian fevers** <note>A fever that returns every single day, usually attributed by Renaissance physicians to an excess of phlegm</note>, although they are rarely seen among us <note>Massa practiced in Venice; this may refer to the local climate or his specific patient population</note>, I have nevertheless sometimes seen and treated them; and they happen especially to the elderly, women, children, and those who lead a sedentary life and live in cold regions. The signs of these are as follows: First, the heat of the **continuous type** <note>original: "continentis" — a fever that stays present without a break, though it may fluctuate in intensity</note> is quite hidden and latent, and this is for no other reason than because the putrefying matter is cold and has much moisture, so that the febrile heat is dulled by both its coldness and moisture. Thus, the heat appears very little biting or sharp on the outside, yet internally it is indeed troublesome, for these patients are anxious, listless, and restless;

Furthermore, the pulse is small, soft, irregular, and weak without notable speed; there is a painful heaviness of the stomach or **the region of the belly** <note>original: "ventriculi regio"</note>, and sometimes **phlegmatic vomiting** <term>pituitoſus uomitus: the vomiting of "pituita" or phlegm, the cold and moist humor</term> occurs; there is no thirst, and no or little difficulty in breathing is present; the heat increases and grows stronger every day and uniformly during the evening hours, yet it is not sharp (as was said); they sleep or are inclined toward sleep, and are sluggish; the urines are white, thin, and watery, but sometimes they appear thick and turbid, without sediment or with sediment appearing at the bottom of the **flask** <note>original: "matulae" — the glass vessel used by doctors for uroscopy, the visual inspection of urine</note>; similarly, the excrements of the belly are discolored, mucous, and smooth. 

Now, the notes or signs of the **intermittent quotidian** <note>A daily fever that completely leaves the patient for a few hours before returning</note> are these: namely, from the first day there is a **pattern** <note>original: "typus" — the specific cycle or schedule of the fever</note> with which a long chill is felt throughout the whole body; then a heat follows, which is neither violent nor sharp, but latent, so that it hardly offends the touch clearly; with this heat, the whole body is soft; then, after the long chill, an almost hidden heat proceeds, troubling for no less than a ten-hour period, but it proceeds further and is prolonged, so that they rarely reach [a break in] the **feverishness** <note>original: "febricitationem"</note>; the pulse is rare, soft, small, and irregular; the **attacks** <note>original: "accessiones" — the paroxysms or fits of the fever</note> are seen daily with the pattern, after which follows a chill throughout the whole body similar to the chill of those who are stiff with cold walking in the coldest places; they feel pain around the region of the stomach, a heavy or stretching pain, and often vomit phlegmatic matter, which for the most part is tasteless; they do not sweat nor feel thirsty, nor do they breathe with labor; they are sluggish and inclined toward sleep; the urines, however, are white, watery, and fi... <note>The text breaks off and continues on the next page</note>

->## PART TWO ##<-

...without sediment; however, sometimes they are passed cloudy, in which a thick sediment settles; the excrements of the intestines are passed discolored, viscous, sluggish, and filled with much **phlegm** <term>pituita|one of the four bodily humors, characterized as cold and moist</term>. 

**Hectic fevers** <note>original: "Hecticæ febres" — a slow, persistent fever that gradually wastes the body, historically associated with consumption or tuberculosis</note> either never or rarely occur at the very beginning of an illness. There are three types in order:

The first type is difficult to recognize at the start, since the heat is not perceived as sharp when first felt; but when the hand remains in contact, it recognizes that the febrile heat is impressed upon it more deeply, such that it clearly causes discomfort. Furthermore, this febrile heat always bothers the patient more for an hour or two, or more, after they have taken food. The pulse is weak, hard, frequent, small, fixed, and remains in the same condition. The face is haggard and exhausted, the eyes are hollow, and similarly, a certain **wasting** <term>macies|an extreme leanness or thinning of the body</term> begins to appear throughout the whole body. These marks or signs in this first stage are not known to everyone, but only to those who are well-practiced in visiting the sick.

The signs of the second type, however, are not hidden but are manifest; for those who have entered the second stage of hectic fever have, in the first place, limbs that are dry and wrinkled, so that the eyes are somewhat sunken, the temples are depressed, and the face is haggard and discolored. The heat is sharp enough, especially in the area of the arteries and the pulse. There are also other signs which I mentioned in the first type, but they are stronger here.

The third kind of wasting (which they call **hectic of old age** <note>original: "hecticam senectutis"</note>) is that in which no heat is perceived, but rather a certain ultimate consumption of the flesh and other fluids. Therefore, it can hardly be called a fever, but rather **consumption** <term>tabes|a progressive wasting away of the body</term> and extreme leanness caused by a settled heat in the **radical members** <note>The "radical" parts were the fundamental solid structures—like bones and vital organs—that held the body's "innate heat"</note> consuming all the moisture, so that all the limbs remain chilled. 

In these fevers—since they are "immaterial," that is, not dependent on humors or inflamed vapors—signs are not usually taken from changes in the excreted wastes. Nevertheless, in the first and second types, some change may appear in the excrements; for instance, a certain fatty and floating **liquefaction** <term>colliquatio|the melting or breaking down of body fats and tissues into fluid form</term> may appear in the urine. An oily substance and the like may be seen both in the intestinal waste and in the urine, which indicates the melting away of the secondary humors and the fat of the limbs.

But I have digressed further with you in describing the signs of the remaining fevers in general than I had intended; yet I do not believe this is unwelcome to you, since much of what has been said leads to the care of individual patients—namely, so that once the fever is recognized through its signs, the right remedies may be...

-># NICOLAS MASSA'S MEDICAL LETTERS #<-

...you may be able to enjoin his care. I will return, therefore, to the explanation of that fever which I had proposed in the young man; and after the signs have been enumerated, it remains for me to set out for you the causes producing the said fever. Truly, the causes which excited this fever are of three kinds: namely **primitive** <term>primitiuae|also called 'evident' causes; these are external factors like heat or diet that trigger an illness</term>, **antecedent** <term>antecedentes|internal predisposing factors, such as a buildup of excess humors in the body</term>, and **conjunct** <term>coniunctae|the immediate or 'joined' cause that is actively maintaining the disease state</term>.

The evident causes were the abuse of the regimen of the **six necessary things** <note>In Renaissance medicine, these were the "six non-naturals": air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, excretion and retention, and the passions of the mind. Health depended on balancing these.</note>; for, as you heard, this past summer—during which there were very hot, sweltering, and burning days—he exposed himself to that air for common business during the afternoon hours. Furthermore, he consumed many things of bad substance, such as vegetables, fruit, dairy products, fish, and the like, and he drank excessively without observing any order of time or the quality of the food. This regimen gathered together many **superfluities** <note>Waste products or excess humors that the body failed to expel through natural processes.</note>, which are the material of the antecedent cause. 

Now, the primitive agents leading to **inflammation** <term>inflammationem|a condition of heat and redness in the body's tissues</term> and **putrefaction** <term>putredinem|the "rotting" or breakdown of humors, believed to be the primary source of many fevers</term> were those hotter times and immoderate exercise; after which he exposed himself to cold air, so that many **obstructions** <term>obstructiones|blockages in the vessels or pores that prevent the flow of humors or the release of internal heat</term> were created, both internal and external. 

The internal ones were made more easily because the body was **ill-humored** <term>cacochymum|a state where the body is filled with "bad juices" or corrupt humors resulting from poor digestion</term> and very full. From these obstructions, a **putrefaction** <term>putredo|decay or corruption</term> of the humors arose, certainly from the prevention of internal and external ventilation; since indeed hindered respiration is one of the most powerful causes of putrefaction. From this putrid matter, hot vapors or smokes are raised up, which ignited the heart, or the humors, **spirits** <term>spiritus|vital forces or subtle fluids thought to circulate in the body and carry life-force</term>, and **vapors** <term>uapores|gaseous substances produced by heat acting on humors</term> contained within it. This ignition is called a **fever** <term>febris|defined here as an unnatural heat kindled in the heart</term>. 

It has as its conjunct cause the hot smokes or vapors inflaming the heart and its contents; and so you have seen the causes, both the primitive or evident ones and the antecedent or internal ones, from which internal parts the hot vapors are raised, which are said by physicians to be the conjunct cause in the heart. 

But if any of you should ask in what part of the body the said humors putrefy, he will easily understand it from what has been said, especially since the body has gathered many superfluities from the preceding bad regimen; and since the urine is red and thick, and also bilious excrements are discharged from the belly, and there is tension in the **hypochondria** <term>hypocondriis|the upper lateral regions of the abdomen, just below the ribs</term>, these things attest that the source of the putrefaction is in the natural parts, namely in the **liver** <term>iecinore|the Latin term for liver, then considered the center of nutrition and blood production</term>, the stomach, and the neighboring veins. 

But if I should also say, with **Galen** <note>original: "Galeno" — Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated European medicine for over a thousand years.</note> in his work *On the Differences of Fevers*, that the matter is also putrefying in the circuit of the whole body, it will not be said without reason; for certainly, besides the other symptoms enumerated, the weariness of the whole body and the heaviness of the limbs trouble him greatly. Whatever...

->## PART TWO ##<-

...nevertheless, for the most part, the material putrefies in the **natural members** <note>The vital organs responsible for nutrition and metabolism, such as the liver and stomach.</note>, from which vapors are raised. These vapors heat the heart (as has been said) and the fluids contained within it, communicating that same heat to the whole body through the arteries and veins. Furthermore, all the **symptoms** <term>accidentia|Literally "accidents"; in Renaissance medicine, these are the observable signs or effects that accompany a disease rather than the disease itself.</term> that have been mentioned follow this material or hot evaporation. These include a headache, which occurs from the hot evaporation seeking out the membranes of the brain and causing a poor **temperament** <term>malam temperiem|An imbalance of the four qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) within an organ.</term> there. 

Similarly, the dryness of the tongue is caused by that same hot evaporation parching the tongue; restlessness also occurs because vapors are raised from the source of the putrefaction. These vapors, being sharp, irritate the muscles so much that they make the patient restless. It remains for me to tell you about the **stages of the disease** <note>Galenic medicine divided every "salubrious" or curable illness into four distinct phases to help the physician determine the timing of treatments.</note>, since every curable illness has four stages: namely, the **beginning**, the **increase**, the **peak**, and the **decline**. 

Knowledge of these stages was taught by **Galen** <term>Galenus|The 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories of humors and disease stages dominated European medicine for centuries.</term> in his book *On Crises* <note>original: "de Crisibus"</note>, determined both through the **digestion** <term>coctionem|The process where the body's internal heat "cooks" or matures harmful humors so they can be safely expelled.</term> of the disease's matter and through symptoms that are either increased or diminished; therefore, in this same way, we can investigate the stage of the disease in this noble gentleman.

And first, the **beginning** of a fever is said to be that period in which no sign of digestion appears in the urine and other excretions, and the disease or the symptoms following it do not increase. The **increase** of the disease is the time in which some sign of digestion begins to appear in the urine and other excretions, and the symptoms become stronger. The **peak** <term>status|Also known as the "acme," the point where the disease is at its most intense before either resolving or worsening.</term> of the disease, however, is when perfect digestion appears in the urine and other excretions, such that the urine is moderate in color, substance, and content; that is, it is of moderate consistency and color, and there is a **cloud** <note>original: "nebula"; a suspension in the urine sample used by physicians to judge the progress of the "coction" or digestion of the illness.</note> in it that is white, smooth, and even. 

Finally, the time of **decline** is after all the things mentioned; then the urine is at its best in all its parts—namely in substance, color, and the cloud contained within. Similarly, one must take note of other excretions at all times, since in the decline, the fever becomes milder and the symptoms are fewer, accompanied by good sleep, an appetite for food, and the easy expulsion of waste. Let these things be said regarding the signs taken from the digestion of the matter; now I shall speak of those which signify the stages of the disease through the symptoms following the illness. For when the symptoms that began with the disease do not increase, they show the **beginning** of the disease regarding symptoms; but when the symptoms intensify, they indicate the **increase** of the disease according to them.

### MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICOLAUS MASSA ###

When, however, the **symptoms** <term>accidentia|Literally "accidents"; the outward signs and clinical symptoms of a disease.</term> trouble the patient most and remain strong, they denote the **peak** <note>original: "consistentiam"; the middle stage where the disease is at its strongest.</note> of the disease; but if they are relieved and made milder, they signify the **decline** <note>original: "inclinationem"</note> of the fever or the disease. Having noted these things according to the opinion of Galen, in this case it must be said: first, the disease is in that stage which is the **increase** <note>original: "incrementum"</note> as far as the **concoction** <term>concoctionem|The process by which the body's heat "cooks" or processes harmful humors to prepare them for expulsion.</term> of the matter is concerned. This is because the urine seen by us was **crude** <note>In Galenic medicine, "crude" urine is thin and watery, indicating that the body has not yet "cooked" or processed the diseased humors.</note> and colored with a red color verging toward yellow, although there appears in it a bit of a reddish, scattered "little cloud" <note>original: "nubeculæ"; a floating sediment in urine used for diagnosis</note>, which shows not the completion of concoction, but the path toward it. 

If we wish to judge the stage of the disease by the symptoms, they show not the increase but the **decline** <note>original: "inclinationem"</note> of those symptoms; for indeed all of them have now been made milder. Specifically, the headache, dryness of the tongue, thirst, and restlessness have for the most part been relieved. It is not a contradiction to say the fever is in the "increase" regarding the concoction of the matter, but in the "decline" regarding the symptoms. This is because often—whether by the physician's art or stimulated by nature—through some reduction of the offending matter, or the cooling of its quality through a regulated diet, or by some other alteration, diversion, or derivation, the symptoms become milder or are completely relieved. 

This is exactly what happened in the case of this Magnificent patient, who four days ago <note>original: "nudius quartus"</note> took **Cassia fistula** <term>Cassia fistula|The "Golden Shower tree"; a common mild laxative used in the Renaissance to purge "burnt" or excess humors.</term>. This medicine led out through the bowels many corrupt materials existing in the stomach and intestines which, while they remained there, caused symptoms through their rising vapors. He also took syrups that extinguish the febrile heat, and thus the symptoms were reduced with good reason, so that regarding them, a "decline" can be said to have occurred.

Having seen these things, it follows that I wish to predict the future outcome. The method of making a **prognosis** <note>original: "praedicendi"</note> (according to Hippocrates, Galen, and reason) is taken for the most part from the **strength** <term>uirtute|The patient's inherent "virtue" or life force, which resists the disease.</term> of the patient, the nature of the disease, and the quantity of the humor. I said it is taken *for the most part* from these, because there are certain other secondary factors that matter much—such as age, the time of year, habits, and others. 

Furthermore (to begin with the patient's strength), if the "virtues" are strong and the disease is small or moderate, without any doubt the prognosis will be good. If, on the contrary, the strength is weak and the disease is great, the prediction will be bad. But if the disease and the strengths are equal, the opinion will be uncertain and doubtful. But in this noble patient, let us see and examine first how the primary **virtues** <note>In traditional medicine, the body was governed by three "virtues" or faculties: the Animal (brain/nerves), Vital (heart/pulse), and Natural (liver/digestion).</note> are faring, which are three in kind: namely, the **animal**, the **vital**, and the **natural**. The Animal—

->## PART TWO<-

The internal as well as the external faculties are certainly unharmed. Internally, the **common sense** <term>sensus communis|In Renaissance medicine, the internal faculty that gathers and processes data from the five external senses.</term>, the imagination, the reasoning, and the memory are all excellent and intact. Similarly, the external senses are healthy, as sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch do not fail in their operations. Likewise, the **motive power** <term>motiua uirtus|The faculty responsible for voluntary movement, believed to originate in the brain.</term> which proceeds from the brain—although it is not vigorous—is nonetheless not greatly weakened, since the patient moves himself through the bed quite easily. In the same way, the **vital power** <term>uitalis uirtus|The faculty centered in the heart that governs the pulse, breathing, and the "vital spirits."</term> appears to remain stable, as the pulse is strong, large, and resistant; and although it appears varied and fast, this strength nevertheless demonstrates its great resistance to the disease. It is not surprising that he breathes frequently, since that happens not from a failure of the vital power being dissolved, but from the continuous hot evaporation rising from the **putrid matter** <note>original: "materia putrida"; refers to the decaying humors causing the fever.</note>.

In the third place, the **natural powers** <term>naturales uirtutes|The faculties centered in the liver and gut responsible for nutrition, growth, and digestion.</term> must be examined. Although these labor greatly, hindered by the quantity and malice of the rotting humors, they are not so weak or oppressed that they do not perform their operations in some way. Indeed, I said a little while ago that in the urine some slight sign of a certain **concoction** <term>concoctionis|The process of "cooking" or ripening the humors so the body can expel them.</term> appeared, and similarly in the excrement of the lower belly; this is a sign of the strength of the natural power, which is capable of regulating the matter of the disease. Furthermore, there is an appetite for food and even some preparation of what is taken into the stomach. From these things, I gather that the natural powers do not lack strength.

Consequently, given the goodness of the animal and vital powers, and according to the rational opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) considered the father of medicine.</note>, we must say that this fever will be survivable. This is confirmed by the opinion of the same Hippocrates, who says that **intermittent fevers** <note>original: "febres intermittentes"; fevers that fade and return at regular intervals.</note> are free from all danger if the necessary things are properly administered. Furthermore, physicians number the **tertian fever** <term>tertiana|A fever where the paroxysm or "spike" occurs every third day (by inclusive counting), typically associated with yellow bile.</term> among the acute illnesses, which, if it is intermittent, lacks any danger. He will, therefore, be healed.

But if anyone should ask whether this will happen in a short or long space of time? I respond that he will not be healed in a short time, because the matter is thick and abundant, and it cannot be quickly prepared in a short time by either medical art or by nature. Furthermore, the season of the year is one that prolongs all diseases, as Hippocrates testifies when he says that autumn and winter prolong all diseases, while spring and summer shorten them. Therefore, this fever will be survivable, yet he will not be healed quickly. It remains for me to declare the curative methods, after I have first recounted what has been done up to the present day. Therefore, having been summoned, as you know, I explained all the things related above to you...

->### THE MEDICAL EPISTLES OF NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

I have previously noted those things which constitute the knowledge, causes, and symptoms of the disease; for since I recognized the disease was primarily material <note>original: "materialem"; meaning the fever was caused by an actual physical accumulation of humors rather than just heat.</note> and caused by a great fullness of the humors, I judged it necessary to reduce this matter with some gentle medicine, so that by removing part of the matter, the symptoms—namely headache and thirst—might be diminished. Therefore, I gave **cassia** <note>A mild laxative derived from the pulp of the *Cassia fistula* tree, very common in Renaissance medicine.</note> in this way:

**<term>Recipe|Take</term>** 1.5 drams of the flower of cassia; let a **bolus** <note>A large, soft pill, often sweetened to make it palatable.</note> be made with sugar.

This cassia drew out the viscous matter that was in the stomach and the common passages of the ducts, mixed together with **bilious humor**. Furthermore, as you know, I enjoined a regimen of food and drink in this manner: namely, that he should take **barley broth** made from chicken broth, in which I ordered **endive** and **borage** to be boiled. His drink was barley water with **rose julep** <note>A sweet syrup made from rosewater and sugar, used to cool the body.</note> up until this day; for this drink, besides the fact that it opens [the passages] and cools, also cleanses if any matter is sticking in the said passages. Moreover, I kept him from meat and wine. The time for eating was five hours before the **onset** <note>original: "accessionem"; the "paroxysm" or the periodic return of the fever chills and heat.</note> of the fever; likewise, during the decline and after the sweating, he took barley broth for his second meal. 

Then, since the matter—based on the signs from the urine and others—was **raw** <note>original: "cruda"; in Galenic medicine, this meant the humors had not yet been "cooked" or processed by the body's natural heat to a state where they could be easily expelled.</note>, it was ordered that he should take these syrups every morning and evening before dinner:

**<term>Recipe|Take</term>** 1 ounce of simple vinegar syrup, half an ounce of rose syrup, 1.5 drams each of chicory and bugloss waters; mix them.

This was done according to the rational advice of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity (c. 460–370 BCE).</note> in that Aphorism: *Treat and move things that are digested, not raw.* On the days, however, when his bowels did not move, he used a common enema with violet oil. These things have been ordered and done by me up to this hour, which is the sixth day; and although the sixth day has passed since the first day of the fever's onset, nevertheless, if you wish to measure the time by the **tertian fits** <note>Fever fits that occur every third day (counting the day of the fit itself), characteristic of certain types of malaria.</note>—as **Galen** <note>The influential Greek physician (129–c. 216 CE) whose works dominated medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> enumerated in his commentary on the 59th Aphorism of the second book of Aphorisms—an **exquisite tertian** <note>original: "tertiana exquisita"; a pure, textbook case of tertian fever.</note> is judged by seven cycles. Yesterday was the third day of the fit, and tomorrow will be the fourth fit.

It now remains for me to tell you in order about the future regimen for regaining health, as **Avicenna** <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of the "Canon of Medicine," the standard medical textbook of the era.</note> advised in the fourth [book] of the first [Canon] when he said the cure of a disease is accomplished in one of three ways: namely, by the regimen of diet, by the use of medicines, or by the work of the hands <note>original: "manuum operatione"; referring to surgery.</note>. And although he said "one of the three things," yet one alone is not always sufficient, since sometimes physicians must necessarily use two, and sometimes all three. I shall begin, therefore, with the plan of diet and other necessary things in the regimen, which I would wish to be such as...

->## PART TWO<-

# PART TWO

As I previously enjoined upon him: namely, that he should take **barley broth** <note>original: "iusculum hordeaceum"; a thin, nutritious soup thought to be easy on the digestive system during fever.</note> made from chicken broth, and his drink should be the so-called **barley water** with **rose julep**, or it may be **distilled waters** of **borage** and **endive**. One should proceed in this way until the **status** <note>original: "statum morbi"; the peak stage of a disease when symptoms are at their most intense before they begin to decline.</note> of the disease, adding nothing unless some **accident** <note>In Galenic medicine, an "accident" refers to a sudden complication or secondary symptom.</note> occurs that might change this intention of a **subtle diet** <note>A restricted, "light" diet intended to avoid fueling the feverish heat.</note>. Indeed, when the disease already tends toward its peak, I would rather decrease the food somewhat; however, if we feared that the peak would not occur soon, then I would provide some meat so that the **virtue** <note>The body's innate vital strength or "power" to heal.</note> might be able to fight against the disease. He must, however, abstain from wine in every way until the **inclination** <note>The "decline" or fading stage of the illness.</note> of the disease.

And since we have spoken of the **status**, that stage is recognized by the better and optimal **coction** <note>original: "coctione"; the process by which the body "cooks" or matures the raw, diseased humors so they can be expelled.</note> in the **urine** and from the intensity of the symptoms, according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** and **Galen**. In the meantime, let light **frictions** <note>Therapeutic rubbing of the skin to stimulate circulation and open the pores.</note> be performed on the legs, arms, and remaining parts of the body before food, since this assists in the opening of the passages and the **ventilation** of the feverish heat. Similarly, let common **clysters** <note>Enemas used to clear the bowels and cool the internal organs.</note> be administered, as they are called, made with **violet oil** from a decoction of **mallow**, **violets**, and **beets**, in which **red sugar**, **egg**, and **salt** are also placed—specifically, two **drams** <note>A unit of weight; ʒ.ii indicates two drams.</note> of each. 

He should avoid sleep during the hours of the **accession** <note>The "onset" or periodic return of the fever's intensity.</note>, and even before the decline of the fever. In the state of the **paroxysm** <note>The point of greatest severity in a fever fit.</note> and in the decline, sleep is very beneficial, since it brings about the flow of **sweat** by concentrating the heat within. I have said nothing about the cooling of the air, since at present we have a sufficiently temperate sky. Let him also beware of **anger** and **mental perturbation**, since these set the **spirits of the heart** <note>In this period, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried life and emotion through the body; anger was thought to literally "inflame" these vapors.</note> on fire and increase the fever.

The second instrument of treatment is the administration of medicines. But since—according to the opinion of **Galen** and **Avicenna** in the first [book] of the fourth [fen]—the intention or goal in healing fevers sometimes turns toward the fever itself, and sometimes toward the **cause**. First, if the intention is only toward the fever, it will be worthwhile to administer those medicines which can extinguish the feverish heat, such as **syrup of endive**, of **bugloss**, of **chicory**, and similar ones diluted with distilled waters of bugloss, chicory, borage, **sorrel**, and the like, or with a decoction of any of the said simple herbs. 

But if we look toward the **cause**, let syrups be given both to **prepare the matter** <note>To thin or "ripen" the humors so they are ready to be purged.</note> and to remove the cause, which open **obstructions** and prevent **putrefaction**—such as **vinegar syrup** <note>original: "syrupus acetosus"; a mixture of sugar or honey with vinegar, valued for its "cutting" and cooling properties.</note> or **oxymel** <note>A traditional medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note>, and syrup of endive diluted with distilled waters of borage, bugloss, **hops**, and the like, so that the obstructions may be opened and the putrid matter can be evacuated either by nature or by art. Therefore, we have ordained, as you have seen, the syrup in this manner:

...having both intentions, namely to extinguish the heat and to open obstructions: **Take** <note>original: "Recipe"; the standard opening for a medical prescription.</note> one dram of **syrup of vinegar** <note>original: "syrupi acetosi"; used to cool the body and cut through thick humors.</note>, half a dram of **rose syrup**, and two drams each of the waters of **chicory** and **borage**; mix them, or let a **decoction** <note>A medicinal preparation made by boiling down herbs.</note> be made from the herbs to dilute the syrups, which we said he should take twice a day. Then, when a better **concoction** <note>The "ripening" of humors, indicated here by changes in the urine.</note> appears in the urine, if nature has not moved or evacuated the matter by some other discharge, let this medicine be given on a day of rest in the morning hour: **Take** two drams of **raisins**, one dram of **barley**, three drams of **tamarinds**, ten **sebestens** <note>A plum-like fruit from the Assyrian plum tree, used as a laxative.</note>, five **plums**, and one dram each of the flowers of **borage**, **bugloss**, and **violets**; as much as suffices of the waters of **chicory** and **bugloss**; let a decoction be made from them. Then, let the following be infused: **Take** one and a half drams of **choice mature rhubarb**, six grains of **spikenard**, and three drams of **aromatic wine**; let these sit together for ten hours to infuse, and after pressing them out thoroughly, let there be added: **Take** six drams of **flower of cassia** and **diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" electuary or purgative paste made of various plants like senna and rhubarb.</note>, and one and a half drams of **laxative rose syrup**; mix and let a drink be made, and let it be given as I described; and let him eat five hours later. This medicine will be excellent for evacuating the various matters of the disease, as we can judge by the ingredients. For **rhubarb**, besides the fact that it evacuates **bilious matter** <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with heat and dryness.</note> whether thick or thin, also opens obstructions and strengthens the natural organs; **cassia** soothes and draws out bile, both thin and thick; likewise **diacatholicon**—which is interpreted as "the universal [remedy]"—is very effective in acute and very acute diseases. Furthermore, **laxative rose syrup** draws out thin and thick matter by its soothing action, and it strengthens the stomach and liver.

Having said these things regarding the correction of the **accidents** <note>Secondary symptoms or complications arising during the main illness.</note>, finally it was stated in this way: when the head aches, the pain must be relieved by anointing the forehead with **Galen’s cooling ointment** <note>original: "unguento infrigidante Galeni"; a traditional formula usually containing wax, oil, and water or rosewater.</note>, which is very helpful for pain caused by **hot evaporations** <note>Medical theory suggested that "vapors" rose from the stomach or humors to the head, causing pain.</note>; it is also helpful to anoint with **Mesue’s rose ointment** <note>A recipe attributed to the famous Persian or Arab physician Mesue.</note>, or with **violet oil**. Or, let a linen cloth be placed on the forehead, soaked in three parts **rose water** and one part **white vinegar**. To this end, it also helps greatly to rub the arms and legs before eating, and also to wash before meals in fresh, moderately warm water in which have been boiled **roses**, **violets**, **water lily**, **mallow**, and some **chamomile**. One may even apply **cupping glasses** <note>original: "cucurbitulas"; heated glass jars used to create suction on the skin to draw out "bad" humors.</note> to the buttocks and shoulder blades. We stated that thirst should be extinguished by constant rinsing every hour with **barley water**, or spring water mixed with **rose or violet julep** <note>A sweet medicinal syrup.</note>; or let **oranges** or **pomegranate seeds** and similar things be given to relieve the dryness of the tongue and palate. As for the fact that not even a word was spoken by me about **bloodletting**...

# PART TWO.

<meta>Significant ink bleed-through from the verso page makes some areas look cluttered, though the primary text remains legible.</meta>

I do not want you to be surprised. Indeed, I did not see how I could have safely opened a vein <note>A reference to phlebotomy or bloodletting, a common but risky treatment in the 16th century.</note> since the body of this noble youth is quite slender, and also his stomach is filled with many raw humors <note>original: "cruditatibus"; in Galenic medicine, these are undigested or improperly processed fluids that cause illness.</note> due to his natural weakness. Furthermore, as you have heard, that fever is of the kind that does not arise from a mixing of blood with other humors, but from phlegm <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note>, and it putrefies for the most part outside the veins; therefore, not without reason did I dismiss the consideration of opening a vein. I feared that if the natural heat were diminished by the letting of blood, the body would be less able to process the thick, putrefying matter. 

It remains, after the discussion of evacuations, for the vital powers and the natural organs to be restored. This shall be done once the fever has subsided by the presentation and increase of food—namely, by offering soft-boiled eggs, or eggs mixed with a broth in which it is beneficial to boil roots of parsley <note>original: "petroselini"; used as a diuretic to help clear the system.</note> and similar herbs (during the decline of the illness). Let the best meats for eating be offered, such as chickens, and the meat of kid, calf, and similar animals. Let him also drink diluted white wine, since it provokes urine and sweat, distributes food throughout the body, and restores the vital powers. 

However, due to the disease and the medicines, it can hardly be otherwise than that the natural organs—which we showed were greatly damaged from the beginning—have been made even weaker; therefore, it will be useful and appropriate to aid them. First, therefore, let him take every morning one lozenge <note>original: "rotulam"; a small round tablet or medicinal candy.</note> of **Abbot's Diarhodon** <note>original: "diarhodonis abbatis"; a famous rose-based tonic used to strengthen the heart and stomach.</note> some hours before food, because it will open any remaining obstructions and strengthen all the natural organs. 

Then, you shall take care to anoint the region of the stomach with this liniment before food: 

**Take** <note>original: "Recipe"; the traditional start of a medical prescription.</note> half an ounce <note>original: "℥.s."; the symbol ℥ denotes an ounce, and "s" stands for "semis" or half.</note> each of **oils of wormwood**, **mastic**, **mint**, and **roses**; one and a half drams <note>original: "ʒ.i.s."; the symbol ʒ denotes a dram.</note> of the **species of Abbot's Diarhodon**; one dram of **red coral**; with a little wax, mix them and let an ointment be made to be used as I have said. 

Indeed, I could have told you many other things, but the discourse would be too long, and therefore let these suffice for you at present regarding these matters. If the occasion is given, I will also have a discussion with you about other diseases. Farewell.

## E P I S T L E  XI.

**N**OT without wonder, most learned Pasinus, will you read these our writings which concern the work and the operations of the hands <note>Massa is referring to surgery, which in the 16th century was often considered a manual "trade" distinct from the more "philosophical" practice of internal medicine.</note>: since I know you are always occupied among the most subtle speculations of the greatest philosophers and famous physicians—Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and other illustrious writers. Thus I have always judged you a most outstanding philosopher and an excellent physician, who can understand every part of philosophy and medicine and teach others. In these best of sciences, I know indeed that you have devoted your efforts with long labors and vigils. Add to this that since Medicine is a gift of God (as all wise men say), those who perfectly understand the whole of medicine (in my opinion, at least), even if they have never practiced it, can truly be called the offspring and propagation of the Divine Will. 

Since I have always known you to be such as I have described, and there exists with me a copy of what was once dictated by me—not without subtle discourse and strong philosophical speculations—to Pedro Domitio Meloni, a Spaniard and student of medicine, concerning the wounds of the three <term>noble parts</term> <note>In Renaissance anatomy, the "noble parts" (head, chest, and abdomen) were the three main cavities of the body that housed the vital organs: the brain, heart, and liver/intestines.</note> constituting the living body—namely the head, the chest, and the lower belly <note>original: "uentris inferioris"; referring to the abdominal and pelvic cavity.</note>—and written by him while we were being carried in a boat to visit patients along with other learned young men: I decided to send it to you as to a man learned in every respect. And so that men may recognize in you the perfect virtues among philosophers and the best physicians, I wished to dedicate these my labors to you, a philosopher and distinguished physician. And so as not to detain you with a longer preface, beginning from the wound of the head, I shall write the matter as set forth, to which I will add those things which seem to me to have been omitted at that time, such as <note>The text cuts off here with the catchword "of nerves" (neruorum) intended for the following page.</note>
