## SECOND PART

...of nerves, and wounds of the face, which will be most useful and necessary for the perfection of the work. But since wounds that occur in the head and other limbs do not exist in one and the same quality, but are diverse, therefore I will first say what a wound is as to its name, and also as to its being; furthermore, from what causes it may arise, and what differences are both common and proper, and how they differ among themselves, which are harmful and lethal; and finally, by what aids it is necessary to heal them canonically <note>In a "canonical" way refers to following the established, authoritative rules of medical practice.</note>. 

<margin>Definition of a wound</margin>
The name "wound" is not described in only one way: for some have said a wound is a "stroke" <note>original: "plagam"</note>; others indeed a "manifest opening." But those who define it by its essence say that a wound is a <term>disruption of continuity</term> <note>original: "diuisionem continui". In Galenic medicine, health was defined by the "continuity" of tissues; any break in that physical unity—whether by a cut or a break—was a disease state.</note> in the flesh and other limbs, made by a thin cutting thing. They also say a wound is a recent disruption of continuity with an outflow of blood without putrefaction <note>The absence of rotting or infection (putrefaction) distinguishes a fresh "wound" from an "ulcer."</note> in the skin, flesh, nerves, veins, and other limbs, whether simple or composite. Almost everyone accepts this definition or description as the better one, since it has both genus and difference <note>Massa is using Aristotelian logic here to define the "category" (genus) and "specific characteristics" (difference) of a wound.</note>, through which it can be distinguished from every other disruption of continuity. 

<margin>External causes</margin>
The causes of wounds in general are incident things, such as a sword, a rapier, a spear, a staff, and other incident instruments that break, pierce, and in any other way cause a disruption of continuity. Among these causes are listed the bites of animals, tearing made by claws, horns, and thorns, or by any other art disrupting the continuous; all of which are external causes. 

<margin>Internal causes</margin>
There are also internal causes that sometimes cause wounding, often causing an intrinsic wound, and sometimes an extrinsic one, such as when blood, either by its quantity or its <term>acridity</term> <note>original: "acredine". This refers to the chemical or "sharp" quality of humors that might corrode tissues from the inside.</note>, either cuts, tears, or erodes the veins and neighboring parts; so that it disrupts continuity from the beginning without the putrefaction of humors or the limb; but only blood emanates, either from the skin broken on the outside, or from the intrinsic and interior parts. 

<margin>Simple wound</margin>
In the present case, these are the differences of wounds: because one is simple and another composite. A simple wound is that which exists in a simple part, for example, in the skin. 

<margin>Composite wound</margin>
A composite wound is said to be that which is not only in the skin, but in the flesh, nerve, veins, arteries, membranes, bones, and others. Furthermore, of the simple wound, one is large, another small—whether you call it long does not matter. Similarly, of the composite, one is small and narrow, another large and long; but that which is small can harm either more limbs or fewer; that which harms more is that which wounds not only the skin and flesh, but also...

<summary>Niccolò Massa defines a wound as a "disruption of continuity" and classifies wounds based on their external or internal causes, as well as their complexity (simple vs. composite).</summary>

...nerve, vein, artery, membrane, bones, and the rest; all these differences are recognized through their symptoms. For from the piercing or cutting of a nerve and nerve-like parts, there follow pains and <term>convulsions</term> <note>original: "conuulsio"; in 16th-century medicine, this referred to involuntary muscle contractions or spasms often associated with nerve damage.</note>; from a vein, a flow or discharge of thicker, dark blood—not bright; from the cutting of an artery, there follows a flow of thin, bright, <term>spirited blood</term> <note>original: "spirituosi"; based on Galenic theory that arteries carried "vital spirits" along with blood, making arterial blood appear frothy or "spirit-filled" compared to venous blood.</note>. The cutting of bones, however, is recognized by the senses, or by a <term>probe</term> <note>original: "radium"; a thin instrument used by surgeons to explore the depth or state of a wound.</note> inserted into the wound. Furthermore, all wounds in a <term>vital part</term> <note>original: "principe parte"; also called "principal parts," these were the organs deemed essential for life: the brain, heart, and liver.</note>, even if they are small, are not without danger. The vital parts are the chest, containing the heart; the head, containing the brain; and the lower belly, containing the liver and the remaining natural organs. When these organs are wounded, a certain and swift death follows in some cases—as when the heart is wounded. Similarly, if the brain is wounded, death follows from its wound for the most part; yet death is not certain or swift, regardless of what the divine Hippocrates and other most eminent physicians have been pleased to say. Indeed, I have cured many whose brain substance had been wounded by very large wounds. I do not say this because I believe that the majority of those wounded in the brain do not trade life for death. Those wounded in the liver, stomach, spleen, kidneys, intestines, and bladder are in the same danger of death, as Hippocrates also testifies; for even if they do not die quickly, they die nonetheless when the wound is significant. I will not attempt to list the causes of this danger here, lest our discourse appear too long-winded; let these things said in general suffice. The rest I shall state in the specific treatment of wounds, according to the requirements of the case, for the sake of its explanation. I shall begin, therefore, with the cure of wounds of the head.

<margin>A wound in a simple <unclear>part</unclear></margin>
**Therefore, if a wound of this member, involving a disruption** of the continuity of the skin only, has been inflicted by a thing or a cutting instrument—since it is simple—it lacks all danger and is healed by the union of the parts alone. If it is long, it is healed by suturing and bandaging which brings the parts together, along with the application of an adhesive and "gluing" medicine. Such a medicine is, for example, egg white with crushed <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>A medicinal red clay used in antiquity and the Renaissance as an astringent to stop bleeding.</note> and frankincense; or let it be a decoction of "gluing" things with <term>austere wine</term> <note>A dry, harsh, or astringent wine used for its perceived cleansing properties.</note>, such as, primarily, horsetail, comfrey, myrtle, roses,

<margin>A composite <unclear>wound</unclear></margin>
centaury, and similar things. But if the wound is composite, such that it reaches as far as the bone of the skull, it is not without danger, even if it be small—as Hippocrates testifies in *On Fractures of the Skull* and as daily experience shows. Therefore, for that reason, it is worthwhile for the physician providing the cure to foresee everything. For from the incision of the membrane covering the skull, which the Greeks call the <term>pericraneum</term> <note>The periosteum or outer membrane of the skull.</note>, to the internal membranes...

-># SECOND PART<-

...harm is brought to the membranes covering the brain. For the <term>pericranium</term> <note>original: "pericraneum"; the dense, fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of the skull.</note> is bound through the sutures of the cranial bones to the internal membranes wrapping the brain. Because of this, it happens that they suffer together not only through <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "consensum"; the medical theory that one part of the body can be affected by an injury to a related part due to their physical connections.</note> from the pain, but also if—due to the air or another substance present or placed in the wound (such as blood, pus, or medication)—not only is the bone altered, but also the inner membranes and even the substance of the brain itself. From this, terrible symptoms follow, and often the death of the wounded person.

Therefore, in <term>compound head wounds</term> <note>original: "uulneribus capitis compositis"; wounds involving complications like bone fractures or exposed tissue, as opposed to "simple" flesh wounds.</note>, the care is far different from the cases previously mentioned. For this reason, surgeons and those who provide healing in such matters, if they recognize a compound wound that reaches all the way to the bone, they do not seek any joining of the parts (even though a <term>break in continuity</term> <note>original: "solutio continui"; the standard medical term for any injury, like a cut or break, that interrupts the natural wholeness of tissue</note> requires the joining of parts as its primary goal). Instead, by dilating the wound if it is narrow, they make it larger, so that they can see with their own eyes the extent of the internal damage through the widened wound and apply medicines according to the needs of the situation. 

They do this with <term>pledgets</term> <note>original: "lychniis"; small plugs of lint or wool used to keep a wound open or absorb fluid.</note>, or <term>pencils</term> <note>original: "penicillis"; small rolls of lint or fabric.</note>, or <term>tents</term> <note>original: "tentis"; absorbent material inserted into a wound to keep it open for drainage.</note> made from well-combed <term>tow</term> <note>original: "stupa"; the coarse, fibrous part of flax or hemp.</note>, or filaments of old linen cloth cut into pieces and shaped according to the needs of the wound, or even made from cotton. But first, it will be worth the effort to notice if there is any fragment of bone in the wound from the cut or the crushing, and that must first be removed from the wound without causing pain. If the wound is narrow, it must be enlarged and dilated as the situation requires. Then, medicines should be placed in the wound that can soothe the pain and stop the flow of blood. 

These two goals are in common use among healers, sometimes using only egg white, and sometimes even with the yolk mixed in well together, which I praise more. For they take the white or the whole beaten egg, soak the aforementioned pledgets or "pencils" in it, and fill the wound. They apply this both to dilate the wound, to calm the pain, and to stop the bleeding. On top of this, they place a broad piece of combed tow or a linen cloth soaked in the said egg white or whole egg. However, they first shave the hair and smear the surrounding parts with <term>rose oil</term> <note>original: "oleo rosaceo"; a cooling and soothing oil often used in Renaissance medicine to prevent inflammation.</note> and protect it with dry tow. They bind it with bandages, not with the intention of joining the "break in continuity," but so that the medicines are held perfectly in place and the area is protected from the cold. And since the flow of blood is often abundant in wounds, wound-doctors or surgeons...

<margin>
Where there is doubt about the flow of blood, astringent powders should be mixed in along with the egg white.
</margin>

->NIC. MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS<-

To restrain the flow of blood, they apply along with egg white both <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>original: "bolum armenicum"; a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent to dry wounds and stop bleeding.</note> and a blood-constricting powder from the fifth book of Galen’s *Method of Healing*: which is prepared thus:
<margin>for stopping blood</margin>
Take one part <term>frankincense</term> <note>original: "thuris"</note>, one and a half parts aloe, and together with the softest hairs of a hare, from which wicks or small pads are made; let them be soaked in the said mixture and placed into the wound, packed tightly so that they might glue and constrict the mouths of the cut veins, or the blood should be stopped with this other remedy. Take <term>dragon's blood</term> <note>original: "sanguinis draconis"; a bright red resin from certain plants, highly valued as a styptic.</note>, frankincense, and aloe, equal parts of each; mix with the said egg white, and let the wound be filled with the wicks. Once the blood is suppressed, if the patient's strength is robust and their age also permits, they are accustomed to let blood <note>Perform phlebotomy or bloodletting.</note> by opening the <term>cephalic vein</term> <note>original: "uena cephalica"; a prominent vein in the arm. In medieval medicine, it was believed to have a direct connection to the head.</note> of the arm on the same side; for in this way, a <term>revulsion</term> <note>original: "reuulsio"; a medical strategy of drawing blood or harmful "humors" away from a wound by bleeding the patient at a different point in the body.</note> of the humors flowing to the wounded limb is achieved. Some of those who heal open the vein of the arm opposite to the wound, and in my opinion, they do so wrongly and with less benefit to the wounded person. Since the cephalic vein, proceeding from the head to the arms, goes from the right to the right arm and from the left to the left arm. 

But if the flow of blood is not restrained by these actions, they strive to stop the blood by applying stronger medications to the wounded place; for example, if a vein or artery (from which the blood issues) is visible, they <term>cauterize</term> <note>original: "cauterizant"; the practice of using heat or chemicals to burn and seal a blood vessel.</note> and sear it by placing ignited cotton upon it, and this device is often repeated at the orifice of the vein. But if even by this device they cannot restrain the blood, they are accustomed to place burnt <term>calcanthum</term> <note>original: "calcanthum"; likely copper or iron sulfate, used here as a caustic chemical to stop bleeding.</note> over the cut vein or artery. Then they place the wicks or small pads soaked in the aforementioned egg white mixed with the above-written crushed powders: and they fill and pack the whole wound, then cover it with <term>tow</term> <note>original: "stupa"; coarse, unrefined fibers of flax or hemp used for surgical dressing.</note> soaked in the same egg white and powders. 

If indeed the flow of blood is stubborn (as often happens) and cannot be stopped by the said medications and aids, they order that the medicine not be removed from the wounds at all; rather, let it remain over the spot for four days without any change. For indeed, the blood held and clotted there blocks, glues, and closes the mouths of the veins. They also use another powder for the flow of blood, which they prepare thus: Take Armenian bole, dragon's blood, <term>sealed earth</term> <note>original: "terrae sigillatae"; a medicinal clay, often from the island of Lemnos, stamped with a seal to guarantee its purity.</note>, gypsum, washed <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: "calcis ui- uae lotae"</note>, and hare's hair, equal parts of each; and they turn it into a very fine powder and mix it with the said egg white for use. Often they also make wicks or pads out of spiderwebs, and with them...

## SECOND PART

...they use the aforementioned powders. But if they cannot restrain the blood with all the mentioned remedies, then, according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BCE).</note> who says that for extreme diseases, extreme remedies are appropriate—and also according to experience—they sear the vein or artery with a **cautery** <note>original: "cauterio"; a surgical tool used to burn tissue to stop bleeding or prevent infection.</note>, that is, a glowing hot iron. Furthermore, they enjoin a <term>regimen of the six necessary things</term> <note>original: "regimen sex rerum necessariarum"; in Galenic medicine, these were the six factors external to the body that governed health: air, food and drink, sleep and wakefulness, motion and rest, evacuation and repletion, and the "passions of the soul" (emotions).</note>: first, they protect the wounded person from cold and excessively damp air; in winter, they light a fire in the bedchamber and close all the windows; even in summer time, they do so so that winds or any evil vapors cannot enter. They order the sick person to lie in a small bed and to abstain from meat and wine. Twice a day, they provide <term>panatella</term> <note>original: "panatellam"; a simple, thin soup or porridge made of bread crumbs boiled in water, often given to the infirm.</note> in water with sugar for food. For drink, they prepare water from a decoction of prepared coriander along with <term>rose julep</term> <note>original: "iuleb rosaceo"; a sweet, medicinal syrup made from rose water and sugar.</note> or barley water. They proceed in this way until they are safe from a "warm <term>aposteme</term>" <note>original: "apostemate"; a swelling or abscess. In this period, "warm" indicated an inflammation caused by an excess of the humor blood.</note>, which is usually a space of fourteen days; however, this is not a permanent rule, because often in the case of large wounds, they maintain this abstinence until the twentieth or even the twenty-seventh day. Furthermore, every morning before lunch, they order a common <term>clyster</term> <note>original: "clysterem"; an enema used to purge the bowels.</note> (as they call it) to be administered. Both morning and evening before eating, they perform frictions <note>therapeutic rubbing or massage</note> on the legs, arms, and back; sometimes they apply <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>original: "cucurbitulas"; the practice of "cupping" to create suction on the skin.</note> without <term>scarification</term> <note>original: "scarificatione"; cutting the skin. "Dry cupping" used only suction to move humors without drawing blood.</note> to the buttocks and shoulder blades, so that vapors ascending to the head might be diverted. They also warn the patient to beware of all noise, excessive talking, and disturbances of the mind.

<margin>Purging in a wound</margin>
Once this regimen is established after the opening of the vein <note>bloodletting</note>, on the following morning they administer a bolus or a potion made sometimes of simple **cassia** <note>A mild herbal laxative derived from the seed pods of the *Cassia fistula* tree.</note>, and sometimes mixed with a laxative syrup of roses, so that the excrements of the stomach and intestines may be evacuated, lest they damage the head with their vapors. Every morning they also give a syrup to strengthen the stomach and the head and to prevent the said evaporation; the syrup is usually as follows: Take 1 <term>dram</term> <note>original: "ʒ.i."; a unit of weight equal to 1/8th of an ounce.</note> of rose syrup, 1/2 dram of endive, and 1.5 drams each of chicory and betony water. 

<margin>The method of healing once the packing is removed</margin>
While they are administering these things, and once the flow of blood is restrained, twice a day (namely morning and evening) they fill the wound with <term>wicks</term> <note>original: "lychniis" or "penicillis"; small rolls of lint or gauze (tents) used to keep a wound open so it can heal from the bottom up.</note> soaked in simple rose oil, or omphacine rose oil <note>oil made from unripe olives</note>, or "complete" rose oil, warmed moderately. They pack the wicks into the wound so that it may be dilated as much as possible; this must be done without pain or tearing of the parts, so that humors are not drawn to the weakened site. Indeed, they pour the oil into the wound to soothe the pain, extinguish the heat of the blood, and also to produce **good pus** <note>original: "saniem bonam"; 16th-century surgeons believed that "laudable pus" was a sign of a healthy, healing wound.</note>. And the wound...

...sufficiently to the bone of the skull.

<margin>Care in a skull fracture</margin>
If, however, the wound is complicated by an incision or fracture of the skull bone: then those who follow the teaching of Hippocrates, Avicenna, Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician known for his surgical compendium.</note>, and other illustrious ancients and moderns, first diligently inquire into the cause of the blow: namely, whether it happened by falling from a high place, and whether the surface upon which the patient fell was a hard thing, such as a stone; similarly, if the patient was struck, whether it was by a sword, or a club, or a heavy, weighty object, and also whether by a strong man, so that from the examination of these stated causes they may understand the ultimate force of the wounding object. In those wounds where a fracture or incision of the bone is not obvious, they can reach a conjecture about the harm based on what has been said; so that if, either by the senses or by evaluative judgment, they judge or see the bone to be broken—even if the site of the blow or the outer part has been minimally wounded but rather bruised or raised in a swelling—then they cut the site of the blow until the skull bone is clearly visible. Or, if the wound is narrow, they dilate it to such a size that they can reach the full extent of the incision or fracture of the cut or broken bone; and this is done by stripping the membrane covering the skull away from the skull bone <note>original: "excoriando membranam craneum tegentem"; referring to the pericranium.</note>. It is worthwhile to perform this without violence and with as little pain as possible; in which manual operation, where the <term>sutures</term> <note>original: "commissurae"; the fibrous joints where the plates of the skull meet.</note> are located, stripping should be avoided if possible. 

Having gained a perfect understanding of the broken or cut bone from the stated operation, both as to its quality <gloss>and</gloss> its quantity: first, if any part of the bone has been separated, they remove it entirely and gently, in the easiest way possible. If, however, the bone has not been completely separated, they take care to soften it with the aforementioned oils, and then with <term>forceps</term> <note>original: "tenaculis"</note> or another lifting instrument, they extract it from the wound, so that by its removal they may recognize if any harm has reached the internal membranes or the substance of the brain. In such a case, they often use <term>scrapers</term> <note>original: "fricatoriis"</note>, or <term>rasps</term> <note>original: "raspatoriis"</note>, and the <term>trepan</term> <note>original: "tripano"; a cylindrical saw or drill used to remove a section of the skull.</note>; which operation, however it is performed, the sooner it is done, the better it will be.

<margin>
In summer on the 4th day; in winter before the 7th.

Once the bone is elevated and the unripe oil has been poured into the wound for several days, they add a fourth part of **honey of roses** to the said oil and pour it into the wound, and they moisten the <term>lint-plugs</term> <note>original: "lychinia"; strips of linen or lint used to pack the wound.</note>; and they also smear the area around the wound with unripe rose oil, or oil...

<margin>Flesh-generating powder.</margin>
Take of frankincense, sarcocolla <note>A Persian gum resin traditionally used for healing wounds and "gluing" flesh together.</note>, mastic, myrrh, and roses, one dram of each. Let a powder be made from these, which you shall place in the bottom of the wound, and above it the said wicks with the said ointments; they often mix this powder with the honeysuckle ointment, or another of the aforementioned ones, and use it thus mixed, so that the flesh may be generated more quickly. But if they see the ulcer abounding in excessive moisture, they take care to strengthen and dry the limb with such a decoction.

<margin>Where the knitting together of the wound is hindered by excessive moisture.</margin>
Take of roses, myrtles, betony, stoechas <note>French lavender.</note>, and marjoram, one handful <note>original: "m. i." for "manipulus unus".</note> of each; as much slightly styptic <note>A substance that causes tissue to contract to stop bleeding or secretions.</note> red wine as is sufficient. Let them boil with an excellent boiling: in which decoction they dip carded wool <note>original: "stupam carminatam"</note>, and they place it warm over the other said medicines to strengthen the limb and dry out the excessive moisture. And when the generation of flesh is complete and the <term>wound</term> <note>original: "uulnereq;"</note> is filled up, they manage the sealing of the wound with a cerate <note>A waxy ointment.</note> of betony or another drying agent.

And since often in penetrating and non-penetrating wounds, not a few accidents are accustomed to occur—and often frightening and lethal ones—which accidents sometimes happen to the wound alone, and sometimes to other limbs.

<margin>How to remove soft flesh growing on the membranes.</margin>

### SECOND PART

<margin>How to treat swollen membranes or a "fungus"</margin>
There are even some who dare to remove that soft flesh with the <term>ointment of the apostles</term> <note>A famous detergent ointment made of twelve ingredients, including resins and litharge, used to clean wounds.</note> or something similar. However, if the little membranes of the brain should swell without inflammation—an affliction called <term>fungus</term> <note>In this context, a "fungus" refers to a spongy, mushroom-like protrusion of brain tissue or the dura mater through a skull fracture.</note> by modern doctors, but called <term>Alfuturati</term> <note>A Latinization of the Arabic term used by Avicenna for this type of growth.</note> by <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook.</note>—it happens most often from coldness, and sometimes from an excessive overgrowth of the soft flesh, so much so that it occasionally protrudes outward through the hole in the bone like a small mushroom. According to the opinion of <term>Avicenna</term>, they treat this kind of tumor as quickly as possible by widening the opening of the bone before the third day. This operation is performed with the iron instruments already mentioned, namely <term>rasps</term> <note>original: "raspatoriis"</note> and <term>forceps</term> <note>original: "forficibus"</note> that cut without needing grippers. Once this is done, they apply things that moderately warm and dissolve the swelling with a certain astringency, such as a decoction of <term>betony</term>, <term>stoechas</term> <note>French lavender (*Lavandula stoechas*).</note>, <term>marjoram</term>, <term>roses</term>, and <term>myrtle berries</term> in red wine. They bathe the wound with warm linen cloths and place a fire nearby or a heated pot lid. I, however, have very often ordered this ailment to be remedied with the application of <term>distilled water</term> made from wine, which they call <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aquam vitae"; an early term for distilled alcohol or brandy.</note>. It is an extraordinary aid, to which there is no equal; for it moderately dissolves and warms, and it strengthens and gives life to the power of the limb.

<margin>When the pus does not exit freely, a drawing plaster must be used.</margin>
A wound with penetration also often inspires fear if the <term>sanies</term> <note>A thin, greenish-yellow or bloody discharge from a wound.</note> held inside the <term>skull</term> <note>original: "craneum"</note> does not flow out freely. This sometimes happens because of the thickness of the bone or the smallness of the opening. In this case, they proceed by widening the hole or the fracture of the bone with the aforementioned instruments so that the pus can flow out freely. Once the bone is widened, they apply those ointments and plasters that have the power to draw out fluids, among which the <term>ointment or wax-salve of gum elemi</term> and of <term>betony</term> is praised, or a <term>plaster of leaven</term> <note>Yeast or fermented dough used as a base for medicinal poultices.</note>, or some other prepared from one’s own reasoned intention. For example: Take two ounces each of <term>bitter vetch</term> <note>original: "orobi"</note> flour and bean flour; half an ounce each of roses, myrtle berries, betony, and stoechas. Let them be powdered, and from them let a plaster be made with astringent wine; at the end of the cooking, add the leaven dissolved in the said wine, and cook until it is perfectly done, so that it is reduced to a moderate consistency. They also use fomentations made with the same things boiled in wine.

<margin>Where inflammation is either present, or absent, or imminent.</margin>
Furthermore, in wounds of this kind, symptoms are likely to appear that threaten a future inflammation of the membranes or the brain, such as a headache reaching the hollow of the eye, a fever preceded by coldness and often by shivering, accompanied by restlessness and thirst. But if the inflammation follows, there is also...

<header>NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS</header>

...dryness of the tongue, sleeplessness, redness of the eyes, delirium, and incoherent chatter—especially if the inflammation arises from a predominant **bilious humor** <note>In the theory of the four humors, "bile" or "yellow bile" was associated with heat and dryness; an excess was thought to cause fever and acute inflammation.</note>—and if the edges of the wound become parched, withered, and sunken, with little or no **sanie** <note>A thin, greenish, or bloody discharge from a wound, often considered a sign of poor healing.</note> appearing. This is an infallible sign of internal damage, and when all or most of these symptoms appear, the patients usually perish. 

In such a case, if the patient’s **vital strength** <note>original: "uirtus"; the patient's underlying physical energy or ability to withstand treatment.</note> permits, one of the best remedies (both for preventing future inflammation and treating that which has already begun) is to **let blood** from the **cephalic vein** <note>The large vein running along the outer side of the arm, traditionally bled to treat ailments of the head.</note> on the arm of the same side. After this bloodletting, according to the teaching of the prince **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the most influential physician of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, you must purge the bowels once or twice with **cassia** <note>A mild laxative derived from the pulp of the *Cassia fistula* pod.</note> or some other light medicine. 

The site of the wound and the fracture should be treated with the constant pouring on of **omphacine rose oil** <note>Oil made from roses and unripe olives, used for its cooling and astringent properties.</note>; if necessary, let the oil be poured on three or four times a day. During this time, all warm ointments and plasters are forbidden. They also perform massages of the legs, arms, and shoulder blades every morning and evening, and they apply **cupping glasses** <note>A therapy using glass cups to create suction on the skin to "divert" harmful humors away from the head.</note> to the buttocks and shoulder blades—both with and without **scarification** <note>The practice of making light incisions in the skin before applying a suction cup to draw out blood.</note>—to divert the humors. Furthermore, they thin the diet, forbidding meat and wine until the patient is safe or free from the inflammation or **aposteme** <note>A swelling, tumor, or abscess caused by an accumulation of humors.</note>. Afterward, they treat the wound with the **cleansing** and **flesh-generating** medicines mentioned above.

<margin>
And the cold aposteme.
</margin>

Often, a **cold aposteme** <note>Unlike a "hot" inflammation caused by bile or blood, a "cold" swelling was thought to be caused by phlegm or melancholy, presenting with less redness and heat.</note> also occurs in these membranes or the brain itself. This is recognized by symptoms opposite to those mentioned above: there is no sharp pain, but rather a heaviness in both the head and the eyes, which appear watery without fever. There is a great inclination toward sleep, and if the condition is confirmed, a very deep sleep is present. The tongue is moist without thirst, the patient speaks with difficulty, and he does not remember. Because of the matter retained inside, the wound dries up, and the edges are seen to be sunken without discharge, or with very little, and they move with difficulty. If any fever is present, it is "buried" or hidden. 

These are signs of impending death. For this, as was said regarding inflammation, the best and final remedy is to let blood from the cephalic vein on the same side to divert and evacuate the matter, whether it is localized or flowing toward the site. Even if the matter is "cold" by nature, it is nonetheless mixed with the blood; since the letting of blood evacuates this mixed matter and the overall excess, it is the best and most immediate help for both hot and cold swellings of the brain and its membranes. They refine the diet or nutritional plan, abstaining from meat and wine; instead, they provide **panatella** <note>A thin, easily digestible bread soup or gruel.</note> with sugar and a drink of **coriander water**, setting aside all other medications.

<header>PART TWO</header>

# PART TWO.

Into the wound, they pour one part of finished rose oil and two parts of chamomile oil, and they apply this constantly. They also add a woodbine <note>original: "matrisylva", likely honeysuckle</note> ointment and a betony <note>a common medicinal herb used for many ailments in the Renaissance</note> ointment. Next, they prepare **fomentations** <note>warm, medicinal compresses</note> made from a decoction of betony, stoechas <note>a type of wild lavender</note>, chamomile, and roses boiled in red wine. They proceed in this manner until the patient is out of danger or the **abscess** <note>original: "apostematis", a term used for any inflammatory swelling or gathering of pus</note> has resolved. After this, they return to the previously mentioned **cleansing agents** <note>original: "mundificantia"</note> and medicines that **generate flesh** <note>known as "sarcotics," these were intended to help the wound fill with new tissue</note. They perform constant massages <note>original: "frictiones"</note> on the legs, arms, and the entire body, in the morning before lunch and in the evening before dinner. They also apply **cupping glasses** <note>heated glass vessels used to draw blood or "humors" toward the surface</note> to the buttocks and shoulder blades without incision, and occasionally—though not always—with an incision to draw out blood as the clinical opportunity arises. They also administer **enemas** <note>original: "clysteria"</note>, both to divert the humors away from the head and to clear waste from the intestines. All these remedies are suitable for diverting the harmful matter in both "hot" and "cold" cases <note>referring to the qualities of the humors causing the illness</note>.

<margin>On Vomiting.</margin>
There are also other complications <note>original: "accidentia"</note> that frequently occur in head wounds. These are not strictly part of the wound itself but happen through **consent** <note>a medical concept where one organ suffers because of its connection to another via nerves or humors</note>, such as **vomiting**, which often happens in head wounds because of the stomach's shared connection with the brain. This is because the nerves known as the **recurrent nerves** <note>the vagus nerves</note>, which originate in the brain, descend to the mouth of the stomach as well as to other organs. Therefore, when a sign appears indicating harm to the brain or its membranes, the stomach should be supported, even though the cause is not essentially within the stomach itself. This is done by anointing the stomach region externally with a mixture of mastic oil, wormwood oil, and rose oil. To strengthen the "mouth" of the stomach internally, **rose sugar** <note>sugar infused with rose petals, used as a tonic</note> should be given before meals, along with prepared coral or a powder made from the **three types of sandalwood** <note>red, yellow, and white sandalwood were highly prized in pharmacy for their cooling and strengthening properties</note>. 

**Fever**, which is an affliction of the heart, also often <margin>On fever.</margin> happens to the wounded. Although this fever is a secondary symptom, it must nevertheless be treated so that the head does not become further inflamed by rising heat and vapors. Therefore, **barley water** should be given as a drink, and syrups should be administered morning and evening before dinner to extinguish the feverish heat. This can be conveniently done with syrups of **endive** and **rose**, diluted with **chicory** and **betony** waters. But if, in addition to the fever from the wound, there is also a **fullness of the body** <note>an excess of blood or fluids, known as "plethora"</note> or **bad humors** <note>original: "cacochymia", a general corruption of the bodily fluids</note>—which is easily detected by the patient's physical state and their urine—the best help is to evacuate the body according to the dominant humor. For instance, if blood is in excess, a vein should be opened; if other humors are in excess, they should be purged with medicines like **cassia**, **manna**, or **solutive rose syrup**...

And although Hippocrates, Galen, and other most eminent ancient and modern physicians following the ancients have said that wounds to the brain involving the cutting of the membranes <note>original: "velaminum," referring to the meninges, the protective layers around the brain</note> and the brain's substance cannot possibly be healed by medicinal skill; and that if any such wounded persons were restored to health, it was not done by the power of medicines or the medical art, but rather by divine power (from which nothing is impossible) acting in such a way: I bear witness before God—and many men still living are witnesses—that I have cured many wounded in the head involving incisions of the bone, the membranes, and the very substance of the brain through art and medicinal remedies. These were not only those wounded by a sword, but those with fractures caused by blunt objects or from a fall from a height, such that there was not only a wound in the meninges <note>original: "myningis," the membranes of the brain</note> but a laceration in the substance of the brain with the loss and crushing of a significant amount of brain matter.

<margin>Case 1.</margin>
Among these men, the most distinguished Paolo Raimondo, a noble Venetian man, still lives. He was struck by a sword in the head in the back part near the lambdoid suture <note>original: "suturam landæ," the joint at the back of the skull shaped like the Greek letter Lambda</note>, resulting in a cut through the bone, the membranes, and the brain substance. The wound was two fingers long and three fingers deep, and a part of the bone was entirely separated from the rest of the skull. All the symptoms forecasting impending death followed, yet at last, with the help of Almighty God illuminating my mind, and through art and medicinal remedies, he was restored to health. The primary witnesses are not a few physicians of this city, as well as the entire multitude of nobles and citizens. Also restored to health by my work was

<margin>Case 2.</margin>
the magnificent youth Marco Goro, who was wounded by the sharp end of a certain polearm—one side of which bears an axe and the other a point or dagger-shape, which they call a **halberd**. A fracture was made not only of the skull, but of the membranes and the brain substance all the way to the basal bone <note>the bone at the base of the skull</note>. This was attested by a silver probe <note>original: "radius argenteus"</note> placed in the wound, which descended all the way to the basal bone so that the strike of the probe against the bone could be felt. This man, besides other complications, was mute for eighteen days. Having been requested by many most distinguished senators...

# PART TWO

I approached, and when I had seen a quite significant fracture of the bone, about the length of half a little finger <note>original: "digiti auricularis," the pinky finger, used here as a unit of measurement</note> and as wide as the thickness of that same finger, I asked those doctors who had provided the treatment about that part of the bone where the fracture was. When they asserted that no bone had been seen by them, I realized that the cause of his lost voice was that part of the bone lodged in the brain. Taking an instrument from a certain surgeon who was serving him in his treatment, I extracted the bone from the wound. Immediately, he began to speak and said, "To the praise of God, I am healed," which did not happen without the greatest applause and admiration of all the doctors who were present, as well as the noble senators and bystanders. 

Later, however, due to a poor dietary regime—for he was an insolent and unrestrained youth—on one day he wanted to eat "ovatarica," which the common people call caviar <note>original: "ouataricam, quam cauiarum uulgares uocant," referring to salted fish roe, which was considered a "heavy" or dangerous food for a recovering patient</note>. He fell into all those symptoms that signaled certain and impending death. Yet, finally, by the help of blessed God and the medical art and aids, he was restored to health, and he still lives today. This nobleman later suffered epileptic fits from the retention of pus <note>original: "sanies," an old medical term for an infected discharge or pus</note> upon the basal bone of the skull. This fistulous ulcer <note>a "fistula" is a narrow, tunnel-like wound that refuses to heal</note> could not be cured by any other ingenuity except by making a silver tube <note>original: "canula argentea"</note> the length of one finger, so that the ulcer would remain continuously open. And so, twice or even three times a day, it was purged of pus. Specifically, by taking the lower part of the nose with the hands and squeezing it tight, and by holding the breath and making an effort <note>this describes the Valvsalva maneuver, used here to create internal pressure to force fluid out of the head wound</note>, the pus would exit the ulcer at the top of the head in a quantity very often half the size of a chicken eggshell, or even more. 

Once this had exited, I ordered rose honey diluted with two parts of "burning water" made from the distillation of wine—which they call "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitæ," or brandy/concentrated alcohol, used here as an antiseptic</note>—to be applied. Over that silver tube, I ordered a plaster of betony <note>a common medicinal herb used for head wounds</note> to be placed. He kept that tube in the wound for a year and more. Thus, as the ulcer was gradually cleansed, the parts grew back together, <margin>Case 3.</margin> and with a scar having formed, he escaped death.

There was also Alfonso of Bologna, who was struck with a sword on the left side of the head between the sagittal and the false sutures <note>original: "suturam sagittalem, & mendosam." The sagittal suture runs down the middle of the skull; the "mendosa" or squamous suture is on the side</note>, with an incision not only of the bone and the membranes, but also of a significant quantity of the brain's substance. Indeed, the wound was the length of one and a half fingers, so that the substance of the brain was most clearly seen to be cut and could be touched with a finger. All the bad symptoms followed him, testifying to death and destruction: such as fever, shivering fits, paralysis of the opposite side <note>a classic observation of how a left-brain injury causes right-side paralysis</note>, and continuous delirium. He finally escaped, with the Lord's help, through our rational administration of a regime and medicinal remedies...

For even the pus (of which there was little) was foul-smelling. When I began to consider that all other remedies would be vain and ineffectual unless the rot and the cause of the rot were first removed, I ordered that rose honey be taken, with an equal amount of rose oil and two parts of "water of life" <note>original: "aqua uitae," a term for distilled alcohol or brandy, here used as an early antiseptic</note> made from wine. This medicament was combined into one; then, with small lint pledgets <note>original: "penicillis," small swabs or rolls of lint used to pack a wound</note> moistened in this same medicine, the wound was filled, and the entire head was anointed with rose oil. This process continued until the perfect correction and cleansing of the ulcer; then, I used an ointment of honeysuckle <note>original: "matrissylua," also known as woodbine</note> applied upon the lint pledgets moistened in the same. By the grace of Almighty God, he escaped death (though not without the greatest labor) within the space of three months. He did later suffer epileptic fits, from which he was also freed through the frequent administration of agaric <note>original: "agarici," a medicinal fungus used to purge the body of "bad humors"</note> and a regimen of necessary things.

# SECOND PART.

From those first days, there followed severe chills which invaded the man not once, but many times in a single day; there was a burning fever, dryness of the tongue, a sinking of the lips of the wound, a nearly universal collapse of strength, and a blue discoloration of the brain substance itself. The discharge emanating from the wound was poisonous and foul-smelling. In response, besides opening the cephalic vein <note>a major vein in the arm often used for bloodletting</note> of the right (healthy) arm, and emptying the bowels with cassia <note>a mild herbal laxative</note>, and also following the regimen of the six things necessary for health <note>original: "sex rerum necessariarum," a standard medical concept involving air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, evacuation, and emotions</note>, many remedies were applied to the head. 

When these did not help, we judged that the only health-giving remedy would be if someone could remove the rot that had already begun and its underlying causes. For since the cause of rot is moisture not regulated by natural heat, that which has already become putrid cannot be corrected and removed except by drying remedies that provide moderate warmth. Our plan was to mix rose honey and rose oil with a double portion of <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>original: "aqua uitæ," literally "water of life," a term for distilled wine or brandy used for its antiseptic properties</note> made from distilled wine; this medicine was placed into the wound for several days. But when more laudable pus <note>original: "sanies laudabilior," a medical term for white, odorless discharge seen as a sign of healing</note> appeared, the rose oil was removed, and they poured into the wound a mixture of rose honey and <term>aqua vitae</term> in equal portions. Over this was placed a dressing of honeysuckle ointment <note>original: "unguentum de matrissylua"</note> spread on a cloth, and the entire head was anointed with a finished rose oil. 

And because he suffered for many months, troubled by various symptoms and especially by epilepsy <note>seizures</note>, it was decided by every skill to keep the wound open. Therefore, the ulcer was continually filled with <term>lychniis</term> <note>lint wicks or pledgets used to keep a wound from closing too early</note> or small plugs with the honeysuckle ointment, and a large betony <note>a common medicinal herb</note> wax-plaster was placed over it. He did not stop this until the perfect closing of the ulcer. He also used agaric <note>a medicinal mushroom used as a purgative</note> and cochia pills <note>standard herbal laxative pills</note> mixed together, so that the thick matter held around the membranes of the lower part of the brain might be evacuated; and finally, he escaped from all these evils, <margin>Case 5</margin> not without the greatest amazement of the entire city. 

Furthermore, in the neighborhood of Santa Maria Formosa <note>a district in Venice</note>, a young man of twenty-two years escaped a similar fate. He suffered a massive contusion of the skull from a heavy gold rod wielded by a strong man, which caused a rupture not only of the skull but of the <term>meninges</term> <note>original: "myningarum," the protective membranes of the brain</note> and a contusion of the brain substance itself. He recovered with nearly the same regimen and the same medicines applied, although he did not suffer from such bad symptoms, except for a fever in those early days; <margin>Case 6</margin> he was healthy within the space of two months.

[The wou]nd could not be healed by any applied medicines, but discharge always leaked from it, especially if, with his nostrils closed and his breath held, he made an effort to blow. This discharge persisted for many months, even though he went out of the house to perform all his duties. Finally, after many months, a fragment of bone the length of half a finger came out; after its departure, the wound was restored to health. I could list very many <gloss>original: quam</gloss> other miraculous cases healed despite the incision and tearing of the substance of the brain; but let these be enough so that you may know that wounds involving deep incision and loss of brain substance have often been healed by me. Let the ancient and modern physicians say whatever they please. A diligent young man also wrote down, while we were being carried in a boat, what I dictated regarding **wounds of the face**; since I know I will do something very pleasing to you if I also share these things with you in addition to what has been said, I have sent them to you. Now that these matters regarding head wounds have been declared, read then, as I promised you, concerning wounds of the face.

<margin>On Facial Wounds.</margin>

Although wounds of the face are not of such great danger as wounds of the head and brain, they must nonetheless be treated with no less diligence for this reason: if they are not treated carefully, they leave the face disfigured. First, therefore, whether the wound be small or large, whether it be simple or compound. For a simple wound, for the present purpose, is one involving an incision of the skin without much depth in the fleshy part; and I call that a compound wound which involves not only an incision of the skin, but a significant incision of other parts, namely the flesh, veins, membranes <note>original: "panniculorum," likely referring to the fascia or layers of tissue</note>, and bone, as we have also declared above. Whatever the wound may be, the physician's first intention must be that the **lips of the wound be joined**, so that they may knit together perfectly. Doctors perform this conveniently through **suturing**. The method of sewing should be such that it not only joins the cut parts, but restores them to the natural composition and shape of the limb, and does so evenly, so that the lips of the wound are joined together at the same time, neither clinging too tightly nor standing even the slightest bit apart. The eye itself recognizes this perfect union without any debate or instruction. Surgeons also <gloss>original: etiam</gloss> do this with a long needle, the point of which is triangular and cutting so that it can pierce more easily. Different men put different threads in this needle: some use a soft silk thread and sew with it; others use a silk thread, but doubled and twisted; and still others use a linen thread.

...and this last option pleases me more since it is softer than silk; because of this softness, you cannot cut through the stitched flesh as easily. <margin>Method of stitching wounds</margin> The method of stitching is as follows: first, they bring the edges <note>literally "lips" (labia)</note> together according to their natural position. Then, an assistant helps by holding the joined edges together with his fingers. The <term>surgeon</term> <note>original: "chirurgus"</note> then pierces both one edge and the other of the wound with a needle, taking up not only the skin but also a portion of the flesh at the same time; for they would quickly tear if only the skin were stitched. They take the thread and tie a knot. Afterward, they cut off a portion of the thread, and proceed again with the same needle to pierce the remaining part of the wound at a distance of one finger's thickness, tie a knot, and cut the thread. They continue in this way along the length of the wound, stitching and leaving a space of one finger's thickness—and sometimes more—between one stitch and the next. Then, let the white of an egg, very well beaten, be taken, and a linen cloth soaked in it be placed over the wound. If they fear a flow of blood, the blood-restricting powder described above should be mixed with the egg white, and this should be continued until the bleeding is stopped. And since motor and sensory nerves proceed to certain parts of the face, the physician should be careful not to pierce them or injure them in any other way; similarly, one must be careful of the piercing and injury of the <term>tendons</term> <note>original: "chordarum"</note>. For from their injury, pains and other accidents are provoked, which cause the **humors** <note>the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Galenic medicine believed must be balanced for health</note> to flow to the site. After this joining of the edges and the stopping of the blood, if it is necessary to use it, <margin>Bloodletting</margin> the second intention is to divert the flow of humors away from the wounded site. Therefore, let the **cephalic vein** <note>original: "uena cephalica," a prominent vein in the arm; in the humoral system, bleeding this vein was thought to relieve the head and face</note> of the same side as the wound be opened, and let blood be drawn according to the requirements of the case, after first administering a <term>clyster</term> <note>an enema used to clear the bowels</note>. <margin>Softening the belly</margin> On the following morning, let a **bolus** <note>a large, soft medicinal pill</note> of **cassia** <note>a pulp from the "purging cassia" tree, used as a mild laxative</note> be given to soften the belly and evacuate the common superfluities; this evacuation also serves to divert harmful fluids from the wound. The regimen of food and drink should involve abstinence from both meat and wine; let the patient beware of cold air, and also of hot air, but let the environment be temperate. Since wounds of the face bring about disfigurement rather than a danger to life—unless they are large and not correctly treated—the physician seeks to heal them with all his skill, if possible, by way of the **first intention** <note>original: "primæ intentionis," a surgical term for healing where the edges are joined directly and heal without the formation of granulating "proud flesh" or significant scarring</note>. This is completed with those aids that can make the edges stick together or glue them. Therefore, he shall proceed with the same beaten egg white until the perfect "gluing" of the wound is achieved, unless he is hindered by some intervening accident. If something should happen that makes it necessary to...

<meta>This page continues the surgical discourse on facial wounds. ### THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICOLÒ MASSA

...to apply another medicine, the **palm ointment** <note>original: "unguentum de palma"; a traditional multi-purpose ointment</note> is very effective in this case: for it binds, strengthens, dissolves, cleanses, and forms a scar. 
<margin>Glues.</margin> 
And since sometimes, before the wound is perfectly healed, the points of the stitches often loosen because the skin and flesh holding the thread have torn—from which rupture an ulceration and unsightly scarring occurs—in this case, before the edges break apart, they use a glue or adhesive spread on a linen cloth. This glue, or adhesive spread upon the cloth, is placed near the edges of the wound on both sides. These cloths should be separated by the thickness of half a finger, so that between one glued cloth and the other, they can apply medicines. Once these cloths are applied and dried, the original stitches or prior suture should be cut and the thread removed.

Then, the pieces of cloth glued to the flesh are to be stitched in the manner previously described, so that through this kind of stitching, the edges of the wound are brought together into their natural position. The method of stitching and applying the aforementioned glue is done this way: they take a linen cloth smeared with the glue described below, cut to the length of the wound; the width depends on the size of the limb, so that it can stay comfortably in place for enough time for the wound to heal perfectly. After the glue has dried, the cloths are to be stitched, but the skin must not be stitched at all; a space is left between the cloths, and also between the individual stitches, as I said above. 

The adhesive or glue with which they smear the cloth is composed in various ways. Some prepare it thus: **Take** <term>tragacanth</term> <note>a natural gum obtained from dried sap</note>, <term>mastic</term> <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>, <term>frankincense</term>, fine mill-dust flour, and <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent</note> in equal parts, and two parts of <term>slaked quicklime</term>; mix and make into a very fine powder. When you wish to use it, take the white of an egg, long beaten and shaken; put the said powder into the egg white, and by mixing very well, let them be incorporated together, and use it. 

Others take mastic, tragacanth, frankincense, and slaked quicklime in equal portions, mix them with beaten egg white, and use this mixture. There are also those who use "carpenter's glue" made from cheese soaked in water and kneaded for a long time on wood or with some instrument until it acquires the form or substance of birdlime <note>original: "visci"; a sticky, viscous paste</note>; with this, they add powdered slaked quicklime and incorporate it by mixing thoroughly. 
<margin><unclear>They prevent flesh from forming</unclear></margin>
But when wounds are not joined by glue but by the suture mentioned above, it is best to use some powder that prevents the growth <note>referring to "proud flesh" or excessive granulation tissue</note>—

...cleansing the pus, and also preventing corrosion, and which might be able to glue the wound in some way. Since pus is often the cause of the separation of stitches and makes a wound difficult to heal, such a powder shall be as follows:

Take equal parts each of <term>dragon's blood</term> <note>original: "sanguinis draconis"; a bright red resin obtained from several different plant genera, used historically for wound healing</note>, frankincense, and aloes; mix them and let a powder be made from them, and let it be placed upon the lips of the wound twice a day. However, it is always better, if possible, to unite the lips of the wound with the aforementioned glue by applying and sewing a linen cloth, rather than sewing the wound itself; for in this way, the scar is made less unsightly. Therefore, if anyone called to treat the patient on that first day proceeds with the glue or adhesive, and joins the lips of the wound by this ingenious method, he will achieve a better and more successful result. There are those, however, who sew on the first day, and on the second day apply the linen cloth with the glue and let it dry; afterwards, they sew the cloths that have been glued to the flesh and cut the previous stitches before any <term>discharge</term> <note>original: "sanies"; a thin, greenish-red discharge from a wound or ulcer</note> is produced.

<margin>Hard scars.</margin>
And because where the lips of the wound have been joined, the site very often remains hard and even red, in this case, an **ointment of citron apple** <note>original: "unguentum de pomo citri"</note> is most beneficial if the scar is smeared with it two or three times. For the same purpose, the fat of a certain river fish is effective, which they call a **grayling** <note>original: "Temolum"; the Thymallus thymallus fish, prized for its scent</note>; many are caught in the **Sile river** <note>original: "Sili flumine"; a river in the Veneto region of Italy</note> passing through the **Trevisan territory** <note>original: "agrum Taruisinum"; the area surrounding Treviso, Italy</note>, and they are also caught in many other rivers. There are also those who, to refine the scars on the face, take the fat found around the body of a newborn infant and smear the scar. There are also other ingenious methods described by the ancients where they discuss **aesthetics** <note>original: "decoratione"; the art of beautifying the body or repairing its form</note>, which they can use according to the necessity of the case; but let these suffice.

He also wrote (while I was away), in addition to the treatment of head wounds, about wounds of the chest, which I wished to write to you about.

<margin>On Wounds of the Chest.</margin>
Chest wounds, if they penetrate to the internal organs, are lethal, or at least cannot be treated without the greatest risk of death. Those, however, which only injure the external parts, besides the fact that they are not healed without difficulty, sometimes bring with them bad complications such as pain, cough, and fever; these complications often arise from the size of the wound, or frequently from the error of the patient, the physician, or those standing by. And so that they may better provide a cure for those wounded in this way, it is worthwhile for healers to distinguish between penetrating wounds by certain specific notes and signs; for if a wound penetrates to the hollow part of the chest, a breath and a sound come out of the wound, sometimes so strong that it can extinguish a lit candle. 

<margin>Signs of penetrating wounds.</margin>
Sometimes, however, breaths like small intestinal rumbles come out, especially if the patient coughs. If a <term>probe</term> <note>original: "radium"; a surgical instrument used to explore the depth and direction of a wound</note> [is placed] in the wound without obstacle and not...

For if frothy and clear blood comes out, it denotes that the wound penetrates to the substance of the lung; if, however, it comes out without froth, it declares the lungs are not wounded. But if the wound has penetrated as far as the capsule <note>original: "capsulam"; referring here to the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart</note> or the substance of the heart, not long after, with the face changed, all the limbs grow cold, and the wounded person dies. Therefore, every penetrating wound is lethal; yet not everyone so wounded perishes, although they are healed with the greatest difficulty. For many have been restored to health through my efforts and those of other doctors, who, from putrefied blood held in the hollow of the chest for a very long space of time, came to a perpetual cough together with a continuous fever and a wasting of the entire body, so that all illustrious and senior doctors asserted they were suffering from the final stage of <term>hectic fever</term> <note>original: "hecticae febris"; a chronic, wasting fever often associated with consumption or deep-seated infection like tuberculosis or empyema</note>. I, however, besides local aids, healed them with a decoction or potion made from <term>diuretic</term> <note>substances that encourage the production of urine</note> and chest-cleansing things administered for forty days, as I shall tell you immediately after. Nor can I help but wonder that neither the Divine **Hippocrates**, nor **Galen**, nor **Avicenna**, nor any of the ancients taught a particular and distinct way—so to speak—of proceeding in the curing of wounds of this kind, even though they wrote many things worthy of all praise concerning wounds and even ulcers. Because of this, among modern doctors there is no lack of difficulties concerning the method of curing wounds and ulcers penetrating within the chest. Whatever they may say, I shall nevertheless describe the common and rational way of proceeding in treating the said penetrating wounds and ulcers, where much <term>discharge</term> <note>original: "sanies"; a thin, foul-smelling or greenish-red discharge from a wound</note> is contained in the hollow of the chest.

<margin>Cure of the aforementioned wound, namely the non-penetrating one.</margin>
First, therefore, whether the wound be penetrating or non-penetrating, one must move to stop the flow of blood and the course of the humors running to the place. This is done through the wound with a beaten egg together with powder of <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>original: "boli armenici"; a medicinal red clay traditionally used as an astringent to stop bleeding</note>; let hemp-tow be soaked in it, and let <term>pledgets</term> <note>original: "penicilla sive lychnia"; small wads or tents of lint or cloth used to dress wounds or absorb fluids</note> or lint-plugs be placed over the wound. But if the wound does not penetrate to the cavity, and yet is large, they stitch it in the manner said above, and (if it can be done) they seek the bonding of the lips <note>the edges of the wound</note> without healing of the wounded place <note>likely meaning without internal closure</note>, namely by changing the said tow every day, soaked in the said beaten egg with powder of Armenian bole. But if the wound remains "raw" <note>unprocessed or inflamed</note>, for its <term>digestion</term> <note>the process of promoting healthy suppuration or "ripening" of a wound</note> they make an ointment from equal parts of turpentine and egg yolk, which they call a "digestive." Then, when the digestion appears, they compose an ointment by adding rose honey and barley flour, with which they cleanse the wound; and finally, they apply a "triapharmacum" ointment <note>a "triple-medicine" ointment</note> or "palm ointment" until the perfect sealing of the ulcer is achieved. This is done after first performing a general evacuation of the intestines by a <term>clyster</term> <note>an enema</note> or with <term>cassia</term> <note>a mild fruit-based laxative</note>. In the case of large wounds, they proceed by drawing blood from the right arm and instituting a strict regimen of food and drink, with abstinence from wine and meat for at least seven days—and even longer if a fever should come on. Similarly, having established a regimen for the air and the rest of the <term>non-naturals</term> <note>original: "rerum non naturalium"; a Galenic medical concept referring to environmental and lifestyle factors like air, sleep, and diet that affect health</note>, which one must always observe in the management of penetrating wounds, they proceed as follows.

<margin>Treatment of a penetrating wound</margin> For if the wound is a penetrating one, they do not sew it up by any means, for this reason: so that if any part of the blood has descended from the wound into the cavity of the chest, it can be extracted from the wound on that first day, or after it has been turned into <term>pus</term> <note>original: "saniem"</note>. And so that this may be more easily achieved, they place into the wound a soft <term>tent</term> <note>original: "tenta"; a small plug of lint or absorbent material</note> that penetrates to the chest cavity, which they moisten with warm turpentine, and over it a linen cloth moistened in the said turpentine. Around the parts of the ribs, they smear <term>rose oil</term> and warm sweet almond oil to mitigate the pain; then they proceed with the "digestive" ointment, without stopping the turpentine. On the first day, however, after the clyster has been administered, they open a vein in the arm opposite the wound and evacuate blood to divert the course of the humors so they do not flow to the injured place. Afterward, on the second day, they cleanse the stomach and intestines of common superfluities. 

Indeed, following the intention of the divine <term>Mesue</term> <note>original: "Mesuæ"; referring to the influential, likely legendary, Arabic physician Pseudo-Mesue, whose texts were standard in European medical schools</note> in the chapter on rhubarb, they take the pulp of cassia together with rhubarb, <term>mumia</term> <note>original: "mumia"; a substance derived from embalmed bodies, believed to have profound healing and blood-clotting properties</note>, and <term>madder</term> <note>original: "rubea tinctorum"; a plant root used both as a red dye and a medicine to treat internal bruising</note>. They add these things with the cassia itself so that, after the evacuation, the power of these substances remains for the restoration and strength of both the stomach and the chest. Once these things have been performed (as I said), they place on the wound and over the wound turpentine, or "albotim" glue <note>original: "glutinum albotim"; "albotim" is an Arabic-derived term for a type of resin or turpentine</note>—it matters not which we call it. This method of healing was taught by <term>Albuchasis</term> <note>original: "Albuchasis"; also known as al-Zahrawi, a famous medieval Islamic surgeon</note> in his writings on penetrating wounds of the chest. He taught how to provide a prognosis in such cases, saying: if bad complications do not occur—such as delirium, sleeplessness, seizures, <term>fainting</term> <note>original: "lipothymia"</note>, or <term>suffocation</term> <note>original: "praefocatio"</note>—before the seventh day, the patient will be saved. If, however, they do occur, it will be fatal; so he says. Therefore, healers proceed with <term>turpentine</term> <note>original: "terebinthina"; a resin from the terebinth tree used as an antiseptic</note>, in which they soak <term>tents</term> <note>original: "tentas"; small wicks or plugs of lint used to keep a wound open for drainage</note> and place them inside the wound. These tents they tie with a thread, lest they accidentally remain inside the wound in the chest cavity. They also place over the wound a linen cloth soaked in the said turpentine, and, as I said, they anoint the chest and the parts of the ribs near the wound during the first days with warm rose oil and almond oil mixed together. Afterward, when the <term>pus</term> <note>original: "sanies"; a thin, often foul-smelling discharge from a healing wound</note> has been generated and the patient begins to cough, they smear the nearby parts with a pectoral ointment according to the description of Lord <term>Mesue</term> <note>original: "Mesuae"; referring to a celebrated medical authority, likely Mesue the Younger</note>.

<margin>Dietary regimen.</margin>
The food for these patients is <term>panatella</term> <note>original: "panatella"; a simple, easily digested bread-soup</note> made from water and breadcrumbs with sugar, or a barley <term>tisane</term> <note>original: "prissana" (ptisan)</note>. Their drink is barley water with its husk during those first days, with sugar or a violet julep. But as the case progresses, when the matter is <term>suppurating</term> <note>ripening into pus</note>, they give honey-water, and then move up to a syrup of <term>liquorice</term> <note>original: "liquiritia"</note>, especially if the cough is troublesome. Furthermore, they see to it that they empty the body again, in addition to the bloodletting mentioned shortly before. But first, they prepare the body for evacuation with syrups suitable for the chest in this manner; for example: Take 1 oz. of syrup of liquorice, 1/2 oz. of syrup of Maidenhair fern, and 1 1/2 oz. each of scabious water and Maidenhair fern water. Mix them. For this syrup, or another similar in its properties, besides the fact that it <term>digests</term> <note>processes or breaks down</note> the humors, also provokes urine. Thus, the matter that has collected in the chest, once prepared in this way, can be more easily drawn out through the urinary tract. This was the belief of <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Galenus"; the most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> in the sixth book of *On Affected Parts*. After the administration of these syrups, they give a light medicine made from <term>cassia</term> <note>a mild, fruit-based laxative</note> and <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: "rhabarbaro"</note>, as I said shortly before, and sometimes they add <term>agaric</term> <note>original: "agaricum"; a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note>, because it draws humors from the chest. The wounds, however, are treated with the aforementioned turpentine until the perfect preparation of the pus, and for cleansing, they mix it with half a part of rose honey and a little barley flour. They also order him to lie upon the side of the wound. However, if the wound is in the lower ribs, which are near...

## PART TWO

...[relative] to the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "diaphragmati"; the muscular partition separating the chest from the abdomen</note>, for example around the fourth or fifth rib, starting from the lower parts, the exit of <term>pus</term> <note>original: "saniei"; a discharge of fluid and blood from a wound</note> or blood is easy. But if the wound should be between the upper ribs toward the <term>collarbone</term> <note>original: "furculam"; literally "the little fork," referring here to the hollow of the throat or the clavicle area</note>, it is difficult to evacuate the pus or blood contained in the chest through the wound. In this difficulty, a violent cough and constant fever follow from the retention of the matter in the chest. Since this is caused by the aforementioned retention, the most expert doctors are accustomed to evacuate it by cutting the wounded with a razor, or another instrument fit for this purpose, between the fourth and fifth rib, starting to count from the first of the <term>false ribs</term> <note>original: "spuriis costis"; the lower ribs that do not attach directly to the breastbone</note> below. This aid is a prompt remedy, although it may seem horrific to some. Indeed, I cannot help but praise it greatly; however, there are those who do this with a glowing hot iron. There are also those who place caustic medicine between the already mentioned fourth and fifth ribs; afterward, they procure the falling away of the <term>scab</term> <note>original: "escharae"; a piece of dead tissue or slough produced by a burn or caustic</note> or burnt flesh by applying butter two or three times a day, and so they cleanse the chest of the pus contained within it through the hole made, as I have said. And since, for the most part, penetrating wounds within the chest are long-lasting and can only be restored to health with the greatest labor, it is therefore necessary to apply all diligence and study so that by various medical contrivances the pus may exit either through <term>sputum</term> <note>original: "sputum"; matter coughed up from the respiratory tract</note> by coughing, or by another path.
