### THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...[this is a] wonderful decoction by which I have healed very many people who were believed by all physicians to be suffering from an ulcer of the lung <note>In the 16th century, a lung ulcer often referred to "phthisis" or tuberculosis.</note> because they coughed continually and their sputum was putrid, along with a continuous fever and a wasting away of the entire body. 

<margin>First potion</margin> **Take** wood avens <note>original: "garyophillatæ"; an herb often used for its astringent properties</note>, mugwort root, burnet, chamomile, cinquefoil, violets, red cabbage, self-heal <note>original: "consolidæ minoris"; a common wound-healing herb</note>, hemp, blackberry shoots, centaury, mouse-ear hawkweed, strawberry, comfrey <note>original: "consolidæ maioris"</note>, olive leaves, vervain, tormentil, and yarrow. Take one handful of each. Take madder <note>original: "rubeæ tinctorum"; a plant whose root was used for red dye and believed to "consolidate" or knit together wounds</note> in double the amount of the other ingredients—namely, thirty-six handfuls. Take sixty pounds by weight of mountain wine. Let all these things boil until half the liquid is consumed, and let them be strained; then add two pounds of honey, and let them boil again thoroughly. Afterward, let it be clarified skillfully by adding the whites of three eggs well beaten; then let it be strained through a cloth and saved. From this decoction thus prepared, let it be given as described above, morning and evening, warm, in the quantity written above—more or less according to the severity of the disease and the needs of the patient. And on top [of the wound] let our ointment for penetrating wounds be placed, which is made in this way:

<margin>The ointment written below is approved.</margin> **Take** red lead <note>original: "minii"; lead tetroxide, historically used in plasters to dry and heal wounds despite its toxicity</note>, 24 ounces; naval pitch <note>original: "picis navalis"; a resinous substance used for caulking ships, used here for its drawing properties</note>, 4 drachms; rose oil, 20 drachms. Mix them, and let them all boil together until through cooking they are reduced to the form of a <term>wax-salve</term> <note>original: "ceroti"; a medicinal preparation consisting of wax, oil, and medicinal substances, stiffer than an ointment</note>. Then add 2 drachms of turpentine and mix. Afterward, while it is still hot, throw it into a bucket of cold water and let it cool. Later, let it be worked with the hands to ensure the best mixing, and keep it for use. 

This wax-salve is not only effective in penetrating wounds of the chest, but also in many old ulcers that are difficult to heal. Certain surgeons indeed in such a case finally apply an ointment or salve which they call the "Grace of God" <note>original: "gratia Dei"; a very popular medieval and Renaissance healing plaster recipe</note>; others use other things, such as the <term>triple-medicine ointment</term> <note>original: "unguentum triapharmacum"; a simple Greco-Roman ointment typically made of lead, oil, and vinegar</note>. But whether this or that wax-salve is placed on top to manage the ulcer does not matter, because almost the whole power of the cure consists in the administration of the said potions, or some other equivalent medicine. Therefore, I shall provide another potion by writing it here, which is as follows:

<margin>Another potion.</margin> **Take** burnet, mugwort, red cabbage, chamomile, cinquefoil, blackberry shoots, wood avens, hemp seeds, and centaury; take one handful of each. Take madder in an amount equal to the weight of all the other ingredients. Let them boil in white mountain wine until half is consumed, then strain it, and to the strained liquid add a fourth part of honey, and let them boil again thoroughly. Give it as described above, morning and evening, warm.

# SECOND PART

...penetrating. **Take** seeds of red cabbage, tansy, or <note>original: "danetæ," likely a variant of wild tansy</note> wild tansy, hemp seeds, madder <note>original: "rubeæ tinctorum," a plant used for red dye and believed to "consolidate" or knit wounds</note>, and comfrey <note>original: "consolidæ maioris"</note> in equal parts. Let them boil in white mountain wine and strain it; in the strained liquid, add a fourth part of honey and boil them again thoroughly. 
<margin>Troches.</margin>
Give this to the patient as described above. One can also make <term>troches</term> <note>small medicinal lozenges or cakes</note> from the ingredients written above, which heal those who have developed pus from the aforementioned cause. **Take** seeds of red cabbage, hemp seeds, tansy (or wild tansy), madder, and comfrey in equal parts. Let them all be ground, and make troches from them with aromatic wine in the month of August. Administer these in the morning and evening, in doses of one to two <term>drachms</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note>, or even more, ground into a powder and mixed with mountain wine. Alternatively, let them be made into pills, to be administered in the stated quantity with mountain wine. 

Indeed, I have healed many people with these potions and remedies administered internally; in such cases, they are so effective that some practitioners, working fearlessly and with every skill, strive for the consolidation of the wound as quickly as possible from the very beginning, giving these types of potions morning and evening. For since these medicines are powerful in the provocation of urine, they hope to evacuate the matter in the chest through it, leading it to the urinary passages by those veins which Galen mentions in his work *On the Affected Parts* <note>original: "de locis affectis"; a fundamental medical text by the 2nd-century physician Galen</note>. However, this closing of the wound from the start is not entirely safe in every part. While these things are being done, one must not cease using those things which make spitting easier and provoke a cough, 
<margin>Note.</margin>
such as a <term>saponea</term> <note>a thick, syrupy linctus</note> made of sugar with water of maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillorum Veneris"</note> or scabious, nor should one abstain from a linctus of pine, nor from compound violet syrup, nor from maidenhair fern and other things that facilitate spitting through coughing. 

And because very often, in those wounded with a penetration into the chest cavity, bad symptoms occur from the beginning—which even lead to suffocation and death—or, as has been said, the blood in the chest cavity turns to pus as the case progresses so that a continuous fever comes on, along with a perpetual cough and foul, purulent spitting. Although such patients are treated by physicians only with things to facilitate spitting, they still cannot be freed [from the illness]. Therefore, it is necessary to find another way or other remedies for cleansing the chest. Rational modern surgeons have left certain records of these in their writings, with which I have healed very many people—adolescents, young men, and even the elderly. Among these was Demetrius Draco (nicknamed "the Dragon"), a ship's captain fifty-six years of age, who was wounded in the chest with a penetration into the cavity...

->aa<-

...after twenty-five days, he came to Venice, suffering from a persistent fever. His cough was violent and constant, and he was spitting up pus. Although other senior physicians had been called in, they were unable to heal the man. I, however, being a young man at the time, saw that the other remedies they provided had not helped. I proposed to them the method of **modern physicians** for <term>suppurated</term> <note>original: "suppuratis"; refers to internal areas filled with pus</note> conditions. This method involves using substances that provoke urine to digest the matter contained in the chest, thinning it, reducing it to the best possible state of pus, and directing it toward the urinary tracts. Because the fever was so intense, the other doctors were unwilling to administer these types of potions. I, however, insisted. I argued that the fever did not arise from an inflammation of the internal organs, nor from matter rotting due to obstructions within them, but rather from <term>suppurated blood</term> mixed with other humors and a certain amount of matter "distilling" from the head. This matter was putrefying in such a way that the fever could be called an **accidental symptom** <note>original: "febris accidens"; a fever caused by an underlying condition rather than being a primary disease of the spirits or organs</note> rather than a disease in itself, since it depended on that putrid matter existing in the chest cavity. I argued that if this matter were not removed, it would eventually lead to the man’s death. 

When they finally grew weary of the many medicines they had tried, and being without hope, they relented and were content to let the potion be administered to him. Thus, it was given twice a day according to the first description noted above—namely, morning and evening—in the quantity of **seven ounces**. In this way, he was restored to health before forty days had passed, contrary to the opinion of those other physicians. Indeed, from such a drink, his cough became milder, and he spat up more "concocted" <note>original: "concoctam"; in Galenic medicine, this means matter that has been "cooked" or matured by the body's heat, making it easier to expel</note> matter. He also began to pass a very large quantity of urine, which led to a continuous decrease in the fever; he coughed less and spat with less effort. Finally, when he was relieved of the fever, he passed a great quantity of thick urine, and once the matter was entirely consumed, his urine became excellent in substance, color, and content.

He suffered from a severe cough, pain under the <term>false ribs</term> <note>original: "costis mendosis"; the lower ribs that do not attach directly to the sternum</note> on the wounded side, a constant fever, and a wasting away of his entire body. He struggled greatly to cough up a large amount of <term>foul fluid</term> <note>original: "saniosam"; a thin, protein-rich discharge mixed with blood and pus</note>. Because of the constant coughing, he could neither sleep nor rest. When the other physicians who had been treating him abandoned hope and left him to nature, I was asked by his relatives and dear friends to visit him. First, I ordered...

Take one ounce each of:
*   Scabious water

*   Pimpernel water

I also applied the <term>wax salve</term> <note>original: "cerotarium"</note> for penetrating wounds described above. Indeed, I could have used some other medicine, but this one pleases me more than others because its effect is wonderful in similar cases. Then I ordered him to proceed fearlessly with the drinking. ...within the space of two months he was restored to health, to the great wonder of all those doctors and the joy of the patient and his kinsmen. Therefore, to God, the Best and Greatest, be praise and honor always. I have also healed many others suffering from suppurations <note>original: "suppuratos"; patients with internal collections of pus, usually in the chest</note> who could not be cured by other doctors using their own methods.

<margin>Case 3</margin>
Indeed, among others, I treated two noble youths from the Morosini family <note>original: "familia Maurocena"; one of the most influential noble families in Venice</note>. One of them could take no medicine by mouth, for he would fall into a fainting fit <note>original: "animi deliquium"</note> and a massive fever after taking them; as a result, his parents despaired of his health, even though he was under the care of the senior physicians of this most illustrious city. The regimen I used in this cure is as follows:

First, his food consisted of the best meats of birds—specifically, young chickens. Their broth was used to prepare a **bread-mash** <note>original: "panatellam"; a medicinal bread soup</note>, or spelt, or a beaten egg as a dish. He also ate the meat of the chickens or small birds, as well as **soft-boiled eggs**. He drank a small amount of white wine of medium flavor, diluted with **maidenhair fern water** <note>original: "aqua capillorum Veneris"; a common herbal preparation for respiratory issues</note>. 

Upon the ulcer, I applied the ointment previously mentioned for penetrating wounds. In place of a **tent** <note>original: "tenta"; a plug of lint or linen used to keep a wound open</note>, I inserted a **silver cannula** <term>cannula: a small metal tube used by early surgeons to allow continuous drainage from a cavity</term> wrapped in fine, old linen cloth and greased with the said ointment softened with **mastic oil** <note>an oil derived from the resin of the mastic tree, used for its binding and healing properties</note>. In this way, he was restored to health with little effort, even though the other doctors did not believe he could be cured by these means since he could not take medicines by mouth. 

The reason he fell into this **empyemic condition** <note>original: "Empicam dispositionem"; a collection of pus in the space between the lungs and the chest wall</note>—or as the Latins say, became "suppurated"—was that he had suffered from **pleurisy** <note>inflammation of the lung lining</note>. He had been unable to use any medicinal help; the doctors could not relieve him through **bloodletting** <note>original: "venae sectionem"</note> or through purging medicine. Consequently, the abscess ruptured inside the chest cavity. The rot <note>original: "sanies"</note> remained there for a long time and caused ulceration; it eroded the **intercostal muscles** <note>the muscles between the ribs</note> near the sixth rib (counting from the **false ribs** <note>original: "mendoris"; the lower ribs not attached to the breastbone</note>). An external abscess also formed and broke through. From this ulcer, a great quantity of pus, which was contained inside above the **diaphragm** <note>original: "septum transversum"</note>, would flow out. Even though the other doctors had used ointments and linen tents, he could not be healed until the silver cannula was applied. Through this tube, the pus flowed out continuously; previously, the wound had been blocked for many hours by those linen tents, preventing the ulcer from drying out due to the constant presence of pus.

The other noble youth was also suffering from suppuration. He had reached this condition because of the same inflammation of the membrane lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note>, which had ruptured. There were both...

...in the one patient, just as in the other, there was wasting and a fearful loss of flesh <note>original: "excarnatio"; a literal thinning or "un-fleshing" of the body</note>, a continuous fever, and a frequent dry cough. I used no other skill in this case than the previously mentioned regimen of food and drink, and a **silver cannula** <note>a small, hollow tube used to drain fluids</note> placed in the ulcer, except that sometimes I administered **prepared agaric** <note>original: "agaricum"; a type of larch fungus used as a laxative and to purge phlegm</note> at the weight of one **drachma** <note>approximately 3.5 grams</note> in pill form once a week, and sometimes every ten days. Thus, this second patient was also restored to health, for no other reason than that the silver cannula placed in the ulcer did not allow pus to accumulate and collect in the chest cavity, but ensured it was all evacuated.

I could write to you, most learned man, of many patients with **suppurations** <note>original: "suppuratos"; patients with internal collections of pus, usually in the chest cavity</note> who were restored to health by my efforts. For example, there were those who, from a wound near the **upper notch of the chest** <note>original: "furculam superiorem pectoris"; likely referring to the suprasternal notch or the area near the collarbone</note> that penetrated the body, became **empyemic** <note>original: "Empici"; those suffering from empyema, a condition where pus gathers in the area between the lungs and the inner chest wall</note>, or arrived at a state of internal suppuration. These were cured without any other medicinal potion by an **incision** made between the fourth and fifth ribs of the same wounded side, counting upward from the **false or spurious ribs** <note>original: "mendosis seu spuriis costis"; the lower ribs that do not attach directly to the breastbone</note>. However, these patients also used both **digestive** <note>ointments intended to "ripen" or mature a wound</note> and **cleansing** ointments, and even washings injected through the wound into the chest cavity using a **syringe**. But these accounts shall be enough so that you may know well that those suffering from suppurations can be freed by various aids arising from different causes.

Therefore, all these things regarding wounds of the chest were spoken by me and written by him. To these I also wanted to add something concerning **wounds of the nerves** in different parts of the body, so that everything might be clear to you; these often follow penetrating wounds of the chest. Indeed, in the chest, there are many outer muscles and **intercostal muscles** <note>the muscles between the ribs</note>, besides the membrane lining the ribs internally <note>the pleura</note>, all of which are wounded in such cases. And since wounds of the nerves share similarities with wounds of the chest, I will therefore speak of them; afterward, I will continue our discourse on wounds.

## ON WOUNDS OF THE NERVES.

**W**ounds of the nerves can undoubtedly occur in various parts and members of our body, and also from different **efficient causes** <note>in Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary source of the change or rest; here, the immediate physical cause of the injury</note>. For the present, I will review some and not all of them. Indeed, it will be enough to enumerate those that occur from manifest efficient causes; these can then reveal the rest regarding other distinct causes as far as the method of cure is concerned. They occur...

->LETTERS ON MEDICINE BY NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

[1]

Therefore, wounds of the nerves <note>original: "neruorum uulnera"</note> occur from a falling, piercing, or bruising object, as is customary in other wounds. But since wounds of the nerves are not always manifest to the senses—as very often the skin and the flesh are wounded while the nerve remains uninjured—physicians require specific signs so that they may proceed cautiously in a doubtful matter. First, so that we may recognize a wound involving an injured nerve <margin>Signs of a wounded nerve</margin> by its proper signs: among these signs are immense pain, and sometimes the loss of sensation in the limb, or at least its impairment, and likewise difficulty of movement. 

When, indeed, the wounding of the nerves is manifest, or at least conjectured from the signs, first, drying medicines <term>medicamina exiccantia: substances used to "dry out" a wound to prevent rot or excess fluid</term> that are not lacking in heat <note>meaning medicines that have a warming quality in the humoral system</note> must be applied over the fresh wound, unless a flow of blood prevents it. If blood should flow, it must be stopped <margin>To stop the blood</margin> with the powders mentioned above, which consist of one and a half **drachmas** <note>a unit of weight, approximately 3.5 to 4 grams</note> of **aloes** and one **drachma** of **frankincense**. These should not be mixed with egg white as the **barber-surgeons** <note>original: "tonsores"; at this time, barbers performed many minor surgeries and wound treatments</note> do, but with a small amount of styptic <note>an agent that constricts tissues to stop bleeding</note> red wine, reduced to the thickness of honey, with hare’s fur smeared into it. This is placed in the wound and most diligently bound with bandages. 

After the blood has been stopped, <margin>Local treatments</margin> there are those who place washed **turpentine** <note>original: "terebinthinam"; a resinous balsam used for its antiseptic properties</note> into the wound; then they smear the neighboring parts of the wound with warm **rose oil**. To prevent "matter" and humors <note>fluids like phlegm or bile believed to cause inflammation</note> from rushing to the injured limb, they protect the limb for four fingers' breadth above the wound with an ointment they call a **defensive** <note>original: "defensiuum"; a barrier cream intended to "defend" the area from harmful fluids</note>. This is made from **Armenian bole** <note>a medicinal red clay</note>, **dragon's blood** <note>a bright red plant resin</note>, vinegar, rose oil, and wax melted with it, all mixed together and reduced to the form of an ointment. 

Furthermore, lest the body’s "superfluities" <note>excess waste fluids</note> run to the injured place, the belly must be softened by administering **cassia** <note>a mild fruit-based laxative</note> or by applying a common enema. Then, it is necessary to open the vein on the opposite side of the wounded limb <note>a practice called "revulsion," intended to pull blood away from the site of injury</note> to divert the flow, unless the excessive flow of blood from the wound itself has already prevented the need for it. 

These things must be performed first at the beginning; then one should proceed to local treatments. As was said, some apply turpentine first; however, there are those who do not dare to administer it to the wounds on the first day. Instead, they apply carded **tow** <note>original: "stupam"; coarse flax or hemp fibers used as a dressing</note> soaked in a small amount of styptic red wine. On the second day, they then apply the turpentine or some other equivalent medicine. This is the doctrine of **Galen** <note>the most influential Greek physician of antiquity</note>, both in his books *On the Composition of Medicines according to Kind* <note>original: "Catageni"; referring to Galen's work *De Compositione Medicamentorum per Genera*</note> and in others. 

This doctrine was followed by the "Prince," **Avicenna** <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, in the fourth book of his *Canon*, in the fourth section on the cure of nerve wounds, when he said that **albotim glue** <note>original: "glutinum albotim"; likely a resin or pitch, possibly terebinth</note> is among the best treatments for nerve wounds. But note from the teaching of illustrious physicians that turpentine and other "biting" <note>mordicantia: substances that cause a stinging or sharp sensation</note> medicines are not at all suitable if the nerves are exposed, or if the flesh...

## SECOND PART.

...unless they have been exposed; in which case it is necessary to wash the **turpentine** <term>terebinthina: a resinous liquid from trees, used here as a base for ointments</term> with distilled betony water, or a decoction of it. Alternatively, one may mix the turpentine with some **mastic oil** <note>oil infused with resin from the mastic tree, used for its binding and soothing properties</note> to remove its sharpness and stinging quality, and apply it warm to the wound upon **lint** <note>original: "lichynia"; soft material made from scraped linen</note> or **tents** <term>tenta: a small plug or wick made of twisted linen threads used to keep a wound open for drainage</term> made from clean linen. Then, the areas surrounding the wound should be anointed with a mixture of rose oil and mastic oil.

One must proceed in this way until the wound is "regulated"—that is, until it generates the best kind of **pus** <note>Early modern doctors believed "laudable pus" was a sign of healthy healing</note> and some flesh grows over the exposed nerve. This is so that the nerve may be protected by the flesh itself from the harm of more stinging medicines. When this appears, cleansing ointments that generate pus and flesh may be freely applied to the wound with filaments or tents. Such remedies include an ointment made of turpentine, rose honey, barley flour, myrrh, and **sarcocolla** <term>sarcocolla: a Persian tree resin, its name literally means "flesh-gluer," used to heal wounds</term>, or the **basilicon** ointment <note>a famous "royal" ointment made of yellow wax, pitch, resin, and olive oil</note>.

While they administer these local remedies, they also establish a regimen of air, food, drink, and other necessary things. For they protect the patients from cold air, order them to rest in bed, and have them abstain from meat and wine. For wine is harmful to the nerves in itself, as **Mesuë** <term>Mesuë: referring to Masawaih al-Mardini, a famous medieval Arabic medical authority widely cited in the Renaissance</term> said. Therefore, they provide **panatella** <note>a simple bread soup or gruel</note> with sugar, and for drink, a decoction of coriander along with a rose **julep** <term>iuleb: a sweet medicinal drink, originally from Persian "gulab" (rose water)</term> until the seventh, or even the fourteenth day. As the healing progresses, they give panatella made with the broth of a small chicken. If the bowels do not move on their own, they administer common **clysters** <note>enemas</note>. 

If a fever should come on, as often happens around the time pus is generated, they give syrups in the morning to extinguish the febrile heat, such as syrup of endive or rose syrup diluted with distilled waters of chicory and betony. In all wounds of the nerves, one must always beware of all acidic things; therefore, **oxymel** <note>original: "syrupus acetosus"; a syrup made of vinegar and honey</note> is not appropriate, for vinegar always harms the nerves with its coldness. Since other accidents besides fever often happen with nerve wounds—such as intense pain, convulsions, delirium, and **abscesses** <note>original: "apostemata"</note>—these events do not occur without the greatest risk to life.

<margin>To soothe pain</margin> Wherefore, if pain should come on, it must be relieved with those things that soothe pain; for instance, with rose oil, if the pain arises from a flow of hot humors. <term>q</term> <note>a shorthand for "but" or "if"</note> if it arises from a mixture of hot and cold humors, the limb can be anointed with chamomile oil alone, as it is tempered in its qualities. They also apply **plasters** made of barley flour, fenugreek, and linseed, prepared with **sapa** <note>must or grape juice boiled down to a thick syrup</note> and a decoction of marshmallow roots in the said chamomile oil, or similar things.

# NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS
<page-num>60</page-num>

...with similar things applied externally, doctors are accustomed to soothing the pain. However, when the pain is extremely intense, bloodletting from the opposite side is the greatest remedy. But if a convulsion <note>In this context, "convulsion" likely refers to muscle spasms associated with tetanus</note> should supervene, or if those signs appear which threaten a future convulsion:

<margin>The cure for convulsions.</margin>
And these signs are: difficult movement of the injured limb, difficulty swallowing, difficulty opening the mouth, a change in facial appearance, and contraction along with the retention of pus <note>original: "saniei"</note> and the drying out of the wound. In that case, first, the regimen of food and drink should be lightened, and it is beneficial to evacuate the whole body, and also—provided the patient's strength <note>original: "uirtus"; the vital power or constitution of the patient</note> remains—to permit bloodletting from the injured part. Next, use those things that can draw out the other mixed humors, such as a **lenitive electuary** <term>electuarium: a medicinal paste made of powders mixed with honey or syrup, designed here to be "lenitive" or soothing/laxative</term> or something similar, according to the abundance and diversity of the humors.

Then, let the limb be smeared with chamomile oil or white lily oil, and in the ulcer itself, apply a medicine made of turpentine and **euphorbium** <term>euphorbium: the caustic resinous sap of a succulent plant, used here to create "attraction" or irritation to draw out fluids</term>. To remove the sharpness of the euphorbium, some rose oil or mastic oil should be added, so that through this kind of attraction produced by the power of the euphorbium, the retained moisture may be purged. This is the teaching of **Galen** <note>The famous Roman-era physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose works dominated medieval medicine</note> in his book *On the Composition of Medicines according to the Types of Wounds* <note>original: "libello catageni"; referring to Galen's 'De compositione medicamentorum per genera'</note>.

But if, despite these actions, the patient falls into worse conditions—namely, a manifest convulsion of the wounded limb, tension of the neck, and contraction of the mouth and jaws, such that they can barely open the mouth, or can only do so with the greatest difficulty so that nothing can enter between the teeth—one must say the convulsion is established and confirmed. Therefore, one must strive with all ingenuity to dilate the wound as much as possible. This can be done by opening the wound with a razor or another cutting instrument, or by placing thicker **tents** <term>tenta: a small plug or wick made of twisted linen threads used to keep a wound open for drainage</term> into the wound. These should be smeared with the aforementioned medicine made of euphorbium and other ingredients. However, care must be taken that the substance of the euphorbium is not placed directly upon an exposed nerve, as it can cause the greatest pain.

Furthermore, let the injured limb be anointed with chamomile oil or white lily oil combined with chicken fat. Also anoint the spine and the hip areas if the wound is in the hip or leg. But if the wound is in the arm, it will be necessary to anoint the **nucha** <term>nucha: the nape or back of the neck/upper spinal cord</term>, the spine, the area between the shoulder blades, and under the armpits with the said medicine. These anointed places should be protected with **raw wool** <term>lana succida: greasy, unwashed wool, prized in ancient medicine for its natural oils and warmth</term>. Where such a remedy does not help, one must proceed to stronger ones, such as oil of **costus** <note>an aromatic root from India used in expensive ancient ointments</note>. You should also note that the wonderful **Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a renowned physician from Islamic Spain</note> highly commends anointing said places with simple olive oil in such cases; and all the said medicines are

It will be worthwhile to administer warm treatments. Nor should the evacuations mentioned above be neglected—whether through bloodletting or the administration of medicine to loosen the bowels—according to the patient's ability to tolerate them and the necessity of the case. When, however, the patient seems to find very little relief from the aforementioned aids, the **ultimate remedy** <note>original: "remedium"; this word is circled in red in the manuscript</note> established by the most eminent physicians, and especially by the prince **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note>, is to place the patient in a tub of oil made from linseeds or olives (which is more pleasing to me).

<margin>Puncture of a nerve.</margin>
But if the cause of the convulsion is a puncture of a **nerve** <note>original: "nervus"; in the 16th century, this term was used for both nerves and tendons</note> or a cord, in which some retained matter has caused an **abscess** <term>apostema: a swelling or internal collection of pus</term>; or even because the nerve or cord was not entirely cut through (such that the limb is convulsed by this incomplete incision), the final and certain aid—when other mentioned treatments do not help—is to cut the nerve or cord completely. This is according to the doctrine of all the ancients and experience backed by reason: even though the function depending on that nerve or cord will fail and be lost on all sides. For when a case is entirely without hope, it is better to save a life and lose the use of one limb than to surely die. If, therefore, a convulsion occurs because of an abscess on a wounded nerve—which is generally "hot" due to the predominating humor—one must help the patient first by diverting the flow of humors. This is done by opening a vein on the opposite side, if strength allows, and also (if there are many superfluities in the body) with gentle evacuants to move the bowels without distress. As I said a little earlier, let the injured limb be smeared with rose oil, and as it progresses, let chamomile oil be added, so that while the flow of humors is prohibited, there is also some degree of "resolution" <note>the breaking up or dispersal of a swelling</note>. But if the abscess still proceeds after these things are done, it will be necessary to use plasters that have the power to resolve and to soothe pain. The plaster is made as follows:

After this plaster has been made, let it be enriched with chamomile oil. When the sign of pus generated within appears, let the abscess be opened with a **lancet** <term>sagitella: a small, sharp surgical knife or lancet, named for its arrow-like shape</term> or another cutting instrument. ## On wounds of the lower belly.

**S**ince wounds of the lower belly <note>the abdomen</note> do not occur without injury to the nerves if they penetrate to the internal parts, it is fitting that I should also write to you here at the end, following what has already been said, in much the same order that he had written them down from my words. For the anterior part of the lower belly consists, among other parts, of eight muscles, which are not lacking in "cords" <note>original: "chordis"; likely referring to tendons or aponeuroses</note> that surround almost the entire belly. If, therefore, a wound is made in the lower belly that does not penetrate to the area of the intestines, but wounds only one of the aforementioned muscles, or several muscles, or the cords, the first care—after universal measures such as a regimen of food and drink and other necessary things—will be bloodletting (if needed to divert the flow of humors) and also the evacuation of common superfluities. ...protection from complications: First, however, if the wound is large, it should be joined by common stitching <note>original: "fuitione communi"; likely a transcription of 'sutione,' referring to suturing or sewing</note>; the flow of blood should also be restrained with powders, or other medications mentioned above: then the remaining ointments should be applied, which can both cleanse and achieve a perfect healing.

<margin>
A penetrating wound.
</margin>

But if the wounds are penetrating into the abdominal cavity <note>original: "uentris concauitatem"</note>; since they involve the highest risk, one must strive with all diligence in their cure, lest an error occur. Indeed, almost all the natural internal organs are healed with the greatest difficulty or only rarely (if they have been wounded), and according to the opinion of **Hippocrates** <note>the famous Greek physician of antiquity</note>, wounds to them are for the most part lethal. For this reason, the wounded person must be diligently questioned, or those standing by, regarding the manner and the instrument with which he was wounded: since it helps greatly in recognizing the quality of the wound to know whether it was caused by a cutting instrument, or a forceful stabbing, or by a strong hand, arm, or similar things.

Furthermore, in wounds of the lower belly, many organs can be harmed, such as the **stomach** <note>original: "uentriculus"</note>, **liver** <note>original: "iecur"</note>, **spleen** <note>original: "lien"</note>, **omentum** <term>omentum: a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron to protect them</term>, **intestines**, **mesentery** <term>mesentery: a fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and holds them in place</term>, **kidneys** <note>original: "rhenes"</note>, **urinary vessels**, **bladder** <note>original: "uesica"</note>, and in women the **uterus** and other parts; it must be diligently investigated whether any of these mentioned have been wounded or have sustained an injury in any way.

If, for example, because of a wound, the omentum should protrude outside, one must see whether it has changed in substance or color, or if it has received any alteration from the external air: especially if it has been outside the wound for some time, so that its natural temperature has been altered by the cold external air. Indeed, if any lividness appears to the sight, or coldness to the touch from the delay outside, or anything of that sort, then the part that protrudes and is altered outside the wound must be cut off in this manner: first, let it be tied with a thread <note>original: "filo"</note> as close as possible to the skin of the belly; then let it be cut off with a razor <note>original: "nouacula"</note>; and after the cutting, let it be cauterized with a red-hot iron <note>original: "candenti ferro"</note>. Then, let it be gently put back inside, leaving a part of the thread with which you tied the omentum outside the wound, so that after nature has separated the burnt part, you can pull out the thread so tied by tugging it—lest, of course, by remaining inside, it should rot.

Now, why do they cauterize with a glowing iron after the cutting of the omentum or another of the mentioned parts? It is so that after the cutting, the blood flowing from the cut veins does not remain there in the belly and putrefy. For in the omentum, there are many veins and arteries, as well as in the mesentery, which contains many veins. But if there has been no alteration of the protruding omentum, nor has it been outside the wound for a notable time...

...[penetrat]ing it was, you can safely insert it <note>Massa is likely referring to a probe or a finger to test the depth of the wound</note> without any further incision. Soon, if the wound is small, you must proceed with the medications for wounds of the nerves <note>original: "neruorū"; in this period, "nerves" often referred to any white, fibrous tissue, including tendons and membranes</note> mentioned above, such as turpentine and others. But if the wound is large and requires a suture, the rule of all illustrious physicians—and especially of **Galen** <note>the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> in the sixth book of his *Method of Healing*, and **Avicenna** <note>the famous 11th-century Persian physician</note> in the fourth tract of the fourth book on the management of wounds to the internal organs—is that the wound should be sewn with a suture according to the craft passed down by the science of anatomy, so that the lips and the parts that have been cut and separated can be consolidated and united together. 

For this reason, one must first know from a sensible understanding of anatomy that beneath the eight muscles of the lower belly there is a membrane, which the Greeks call the *peritoneum* and the Arabs call the *siphac* <term>siphac: the medieval Latin term derived from Arabic for the peritoneum</term>. This membrane is fibrous and bloodless; for this reason, if someone does not catch this membrane between the lips of the wound while sewing, but leaves it cut as it is, it cannot unite by its own substance. This would result in a descent or 
<margin>Regarding a wound of the omentum</margin> 
protrusion of the **omentum** <term>omentum: a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines</term> or some of the intestines between the peritoneum and the eight muscles, which the Greeks call the **epigastrium** <note>original: "epigastrion"; here referring to the abdominal wall muscles</note>. This is a most troublesome condition. 

However, if the surgeon catches the entire membrane between the lips of the wound, it does not allow the lips of the wound to be perfectly united. Therefore, one must proceed according to the stated art, as skilled practitioners do: first, they take the muscular flesh on one side of the wound together with the part of the peritoneum directly adjacent to it, and pierce it with a needle while sewing. On the other side opposite that part—namely, in the other lip of the wound—they leave the peritoneum alone and pierce only the muscular part with the skin. In this way, they have their first stitch. 

Then they proceed with the sewing, and in the second stitch, they take the skin and the muscular flesh without the peritoneum. This is done so that in that part where the peritoneum was left out, a better union and consolidation of the parts can occur. Thus, according to the size of the wound, they proceed with the sewing in this manner: always catching one part of the peritoneum between the lips of the wound and leaving the other, so that they catch the peritoneum alternately as they sew. They never sew both parts of the peritoneum together at once. They proceed in this way, stitch by stitch, catching one part of the peritoneum and leaving the other until the stitching is perfectly completed, as we have said in our book on anatomy. 

These stitches should be close together so that they may better unite the parts and contain the weight of the internal members. Finally, once the stitching is done, turpentine should be applied, along with those things that are able to gently glue the wound together, as was said regarding wounds of the nerves. One must always strive to sedate the pain across the entire belly...

By doing these things, a wonderful and indeed rational effect followed. For the said syrups and regimen contribute to the consolidation of internal wounds and the strengthening of the principal organs.

# PART SECOND.

I was present with other physicians: the wound was on the left side under the **false ribs** <note>original: "costis mendosis"; the lower ribs that do not connect directly to the breastbone</note>, from which wound a certain white, fatty substance full of many veins was protruding. Among those physicians, it was a matter of doubt which of the internal members that part might be. For some of them asserted that it was a part of the **omentum** <note>a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines</note>; the others did not dare to affirm that, since they could be sure neither from the substance nor from the location of the wound. But I, both from the location of the wound and from the substance of the member filled with very obvious veins, said that it was a part of the **mesentery** <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and carries blood vessels to them</note>, and specifically that part to which the section of the **colon** <note>original: "intestini coli"</note> is tied, which "rides above" the stomach. Therefore, I ordered that the protruding part be bound with a thread, cut away with a razor, and **cauterized** <note>burned with a hot iron to stop bleeding and prevent infection</note> with a glowing or fiery iron, and then placed back inside the wound—though with the thread remaining outside, as we said above regarding the omentum. With the application of **turpentine** <note>original: "terebinthina"; used as a topical antiseptic and sealant</note> and other medicines along with a regulated diet, he was restored to health in a short time.

If, however, there is a wound with an incision in one of the **thicker intestines** <note>the large intestine</note> and yet it does not protrude outside, this is recognized because feces exit from the wound, or through the administration of an **enema** <note>original: "enematis"</note>, if something exits through the wound. Whatever the case, even if the matter is doubtful, a **clyster** <note>another term for an enema</note> is prepared without any stinging quality, such as with a **broth of intestines** <note>original: "iure intestinorum"; animal-based broths were often used as a base for medicinal injections</note> in which have been boiled **horsetail** <note>original: "cauda equina"</note>, **lesser centaury** <note>original: "centaurea minor"</note>, **St. John’s wort** <note>original: "hypericon"</note>, **chamomile** <note>original: "chamaemilla"</note>, and the roots of both **comfreys** <note>original: "consolidae"; plants used to "consolidate" or knit wounds together</note>, namely the greater and the lesser.

Which intestine is wounded can be easily discovered from the site of the wound; for if it is one of the **higher and slender ones** <note>the small intestines</note>, the cure is in vain and useless, as I have said according to the opinion of all illustrious physicians, especially **Hippocrates**, and from experience itself. Therefore, the wound should be stitched, as was said, and turpentine applied externally, and care taken that it is healed as quickly as possible. Internally, those things should be administered which help the healing of the internal wound, such as decoctions of horsetail, **maidenhair fern** <note>original: "capillorum ueneris"</note>, **marshmallow** <note>original: "altheae"</note>, **cinquefoil** <note>original: "pentaphyllonis"</note>, and both greater and lesser comfrey, made in distilled water of horsetail. And if it is necessary to administer enemas both to draw out the feces of the intestines and to heal the wound, let it be from the aforementioned decoction, in which **Armenian bole** <note>original: "bolus armenius"; a medicinal red clay</note>, **frankincense** <note>original: "olibanum"</note>, and **sarcocolla** <note>a Persian tree resin used to "glue" flesh</note> should be added, along with other things that lead to quick binding. Indeed, I saw a poor young man wounded in the lower belly with an incision of the intestine; for some part of the feces was always exiting the wound, who nevertheless was healed, not by the help of medicines, but by nature, which—

## MEDICAL EPISTLES OF NICCOLO MASSA

...since a certain ignorant barber provided a remedy only for the external wound. But if there is a wound, and the intestine protrudes from the thicker parts being wounded: experienced surgeons are accustomed to sew such a wound in various ways. The majority of them sew with silk thread using a strong stitch, just as **furriers** <note>original: "pelliparii"; craftsmen who make or repair fur garments</note> do when sewing skins. Some even write that a suture—or rather a joining of the parts—can be conveniently achieved in this way: if the wounded intestine protrudes outside the wound, they take large ants and offer them to the wound of the intestine so that they may seize it with a bite, and after they have gripped it, they cut the body of the ant away from the head. Thus, by continuing this, they teach how to unite the parts of the wound with the heads of said ants. Then they order the intestine to be placed back into the belly. Let those who are experienced in medical discourse and frequent practice, and in the curing of diseases, judge how much difficulty such an operation contains. But leaving these things aside as if they were fables—since we do not always have these living ants at hand—I have therefore used another device, which I described very distinctly in my **Anatomy** <note>Massa is referring to his work *Liber Introductorius Anatomiae* (1536)</note>. 

I take a membrane from a goat skin and, with scissors, I cut a thin part in the manner of a thread, so that it can enter the oblong eye of a needle. I moisten the skin cut in this way like a thread, and I order the joining of the intestine to be done by sewing the wound with it in place of thread. This is a new invention not described by the ancients. Once the suture is made, let the intestine be put back inside, but first let it be well washed with warm wine in which **horsetail** <note>original: "cauda equina"; a plant rich in silica, traditionally used to stop bleeding and heal tissue</note> has been boiled. After this insertion, let the outer wound be sewn with the suture mentioned above, using powders that preserve the suture. 

Then let **pledgets** <note>original: "penicilla, siue lychnia"; small plugs of lint or wool used to apply medication or keep a wound open</note> be applied, soaked in **turpentine** <note>a resin used as an antiseptic and sealant</note> as was said above concerning the treatment of a belly wound involving the cutting of muscles alone without penetration. Then, let it be anointed on the outside all around with a complete rose oil, and finally, adding **mastic oil** <note>oil derived from the resin of the mastic tree, used for its binding and anti-inflammatory properties</note>, let it be anointed further. Let the **viscous or "gluing" enemas** <note>original: "enemata inuiscantia seu glutinantia"</note> described above also be administered, and let every other device be used that might more quickly achieve the consolidation of the parts. To achieve this, some use an enema made from a decoction of **centaury** <note>a bitter medicinal herb</note> and horsetail in a **styptic** <note>astringent; having a contracting or drying effect</note> red wine; I highly praise this medicament, especially at the end of treatment. 

The diet in such cases should be light, having the power to bind and to dry. For instance, in those first days, one must abstain from meat and wine; the food should be **panatella** <note>a simple bread soup or gruel</note> made in **chalybeate water** <note>original: "aqua chalybeata"; water infused with iron, thought to have strengthening properties</note>...

Farewell. Venice, 1555. In the month of December.

## ADVICE CONCERNING A HEADACHE TO
## Lord Priest Vincentius Maurus.

### E P I S T L E  X I I.

**T**he Reverend Father, Lord Priest Vincentius—as I was informed by a most learned man regarding a certain long-standing headache—complains that it afflicts him in the front part of the head, which the Greeks call the **bregma** <note>The top of the skull where the frontal and parietal bones meet</note> and the Latins call the **synciput**. This pain (as it was reported to me) followed an acute illness. This pain does not trouble him constantly or uniformly; rather, sometimes more and sometimes less. Nor (as I have been able to gather) is it a stinging pain, or one depending on "hot" causes, since there is no heat or biting sensation to testify to this. Instead, it is a certain heaviness, and this heaviness arises from the thickness and the abundance of matter. This matter can be nothing other than "cold," judging by the type of pain. And since cold matter is of two different kinds—namely, **melancholic** <note>original: "melancholica"; associated with black bile, considered cold and dry</note> and **phlegmatic** <note>original: "phlegmatica"; associated with phlegm, considered cold and moist</note>—I must necessarily say that this arises from a predominance of **phlegmatic** matter, though with a mixture of other **humors** <note>original: "humoribus"; the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that Renaissance doctors believed governed health</note> that lead it to the head and increase the pain. For no long-lasting effect can arise from hot causes in any way, unless in...

...be converted into cold humors. Nor should we believe that the pain itself is present only "by consent" <note>original: "per consensum"; a medical term for sympathetic pain, where one part of the body hurts because of a problem in another part</note> (as they say). For when pain persists for a long time, those diseases which afflict through a shared connection usually, with the passage of time, begin to afflict the part by itself and by its own essence without controversy. In my judgment, one cannot say otherwise than that the pain—which first grew strong through a connection with the lower organs—now afflicts and disturbs essentially, both because of the weakness of the organ receiving the distress and because of the long-standing action of the preceding cause. Nevertheless, it is still fed by the lower organs, as can easily be detected from the way the pain sometimes pauses and sometimes increases. Truly, we should not believe that only the material cause of this pain is present, since (as is **Aristotle's** opinion) matter also alters a limb by the action of its own quality and by changing the thing that receives it, thus altering its temperament <note>The "temperament" or "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within a specific organ</note>. Having touched upon these few causes and the essence of the disease; since every cure of diseases proceeds from contraries according to the principles of physicians, if we now have the essence of the disease and its causes discovered, it will be very easy to find their opposites.

In the regimen of health and the cure of illnesses, it is of great benefit to consider age, the season of the year, and the other "non-natural things" <note>The "six non-naturals" were the pillars of Galenic medicine: air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, excretion and retention, and passions of the soul</note>. Having considered these, your Reverend Lordship shall conduct yourself regarding these six things in the following manner:

And first, let him beware of cold and excessively humid air; let him flee from that which is misty, foggy, rainy, and the night air. In winter, let there be a fire continually lit in the bedchamber; and let the head be so protected that it cannot easily be harmed by winds or external air; and let the remaining parts of the body also be covered with skins and garments suitable for repelling the cold.

Furthermore, he must abstain from drinking too much, and from eating sweets and many humid things, such as the meat of young lambs, pigs, geese, and others following the same nature, as well as the feet, heads, and intestines of animals—all of which can benefit you very little, but will rather be of the greatest detriment to you. He must also abstain from those fish that live in fresh and marshy waters, such as those which in common speech are called **Tench**, **Carp** <note>original: "Rainas"; likely the Venetian term *reina* for carp</note>, and **eels**. Similarly, some of the sea fish, such as mullet, cuttlefish, and shellfish, are considered harmful. All dairy products are considered bad; fruits that are cold and full of humidity are not good, such as apples, cherries, and **apricots** <note>original: "chrysomala"; literally "golden apples" in Greek</note>. All cabbages, whether green or white, are entirely bad among the vegetables. Furthermore, among the legumes, he must give up be—

### PART TWO. ###

...kidney beans, fava beans, chickling vetch, and peas; among prepared dishes, however, avoid all those made from kneaded flour. To summarize everything in a single word: all things that are viscous, flatulent, tough, prone to decay, and difficult to digest must be set aside and shunned.

Therefore, let there be first of all bread made from the best wheat, well-leavened, moderately salted, and thoroughly baked; after it has been baked, it should rest for at least a full day. The wine should not be new, nor sweet, nor sharp, but if possible a middle ground between sweet and sharp, of good flavor and scent, and of a medium color; it should be a moderate balance between being "winey" <note>Strong or high in alcohol</note> and watery. Meats such as veal, kid, mutton, and young ox are good. Also good are hens, capons, chickens, partridges, pheasants, thrushes, blackbirds, forest birds caught with <term>birdlime</term> <note>A sticky substance used to trap small birds on branches</note>, and all those that nourish themselves on good seeds and by no means live in waters or marshes. Also good are young hares, rabbits, and similar animals; their meat may be eaten either roasted or boiled, though roasted meat is of more difficult digestion. 

Dishes should be made of <term>spelt</term> <note>original: "farre"</note> cooked in the broth of the aforementioned meats, or prepared with almond milk; or made from washed bread, or <term>panatella</term> <note>A traditional bread soup made from breadcrumbs, broth, and sometimes eggs</note>, either cooked in broth or similarly prepared with almond milk. One might also have a dish of egg beaten into the broth of the said meats; the vernacular language calls this kind of dish *brodeto*. Spinach, borage, and bugloss are occasionally good for such dishes. Sauces made from parsley, almonds, and a small quantity of ginger, with cinnamon and cloves, or made from almonds and sugar, may be eaten with the specified meats. The flavor of quinces with spices should also not be neglected in this case. You may also eat a salad of capers, or borage, bugloss, or lemon balm prepared with raisin vinegar <note>original: "aceto passulato"; vinegar made from dried grapes</note>. 

However, lettuce and other things that are cold must be set aside, as they are considered harmful. Fish are rarely to be eaten; but if they are eaten, let them be the scaly kind that live in good, clear waters, and roasted rather than boiled. If you wish to eat them boiled, they should be prepared with spices—such as gilthead seabreams or <term>red mullets</term> <note>original: "barbones," which the Latins call "trigulas"</note>. Also praised are scorpion fish, picarels, sardines, and those of the same genus, such as the fish the Latins call <term>fragolini</term> <note>Common Pandora fish</note>. Of those that live in fresh waters and can be eaten, there are pike, trout, and grayling; others are certainly not good, nor are prawns or crabs. Oysters can be eaten occasionally; even if they are not good by way of nutrition, nevertheless, since according to the testimony of **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician (c. 980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe</note>, when eaten after food they [benefit] the stomach...

Or, if it pleases you more, candied coriander may be eaten after the meal, because it comforts the stomach and the head. Cheese should be excluded from the meal; but if a desire to eat it should occasionally arise, let it be salted so that it may be more easily digested. 

Your Lordship might sometimes in the morning, before food, use a root of candied <term>ginger</term> <gloss>ginger</gloss>, because it comforts the stomach and assists it by warming it moderately, so that it can better digest cold superfluities. 

The order of foods is highly praised by all physicians; therefore, foods that are more easily digested ought to precede those which are more difficult to digest. For example, if several meats are served at one table, such as kid and veal, the kid should be eaten first, and then the veal. And because meat that is roasted remains in the stomach longer than boiled meat, the boiled meat should also be eaten first. The same order must be observed in other foods: those that are sippable should precede those that are thick and hard. 

However, it will be better to avoid a great variety of foods, because since they are of different "complexions" <note>The specific balance of hot, cold, moist, or dry qualities in a substance</note>, they fight amongst themselves and corrupt the digestion. It will also be necessary to observe the hour of taking food according to the different seasons of the year. Dinner, however, should take place after the <term>third hour</term> <note>Around 9:00 AM in the traditional Roman timekeeping used by the Church, though here likely referring to three hours after sunrise</note>, and one must not eat before an appetite arises. Between dinner and supper, there should be a space of at least eight hours. Also, supper should be smaller than dinner; in this, one should not believe the words of certain poorly-informed people. Indeed, sometimes, especially in the summer time, the supper...

...it will be better to omit them, since when the <term>internal heat</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, 'innate heat' was the energy in the stomach responsible for 'cooking' or digesting food.</note> is not strong, one must eat less, and especially of those things which are difficult to digest. And since overfilling the stomach is harmful at any time, you should therefore eat sparingly. Your drink, moreover, should be in proportion to the quantity of food; it is proper to drink not before the meal, but during the meal. It is not beneficial to endure hunger, because, as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A Persian polymath (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university textbook in the Renaissance.</note> used to say, enduring hunger fills the stomach with <term>putrid humors</term> <note>Waste products of digestion that were believed to rot if the stomach remained empty too long.</note>. These are proven in cases of long-standing headache arising from various <term>cold matter</term> <note>In humoral theory, 'cold' substances were sluggish and required warming, drying medicines.</note>. The ancients praised the practice of inducing vomiting once a week so that the humor of the stomach might be evacuated if it should cause any sickness. I also praise this, if it can be done without distress, since there should be no doubt that it preserves one from many illnesses. Indeed, it is superfluous to write how much exercise is praised by all physicians; yet I do not want you to be ignorant of the fact that there are two things among others which both preserve health and cause sickness: namely, moderate or immoderate food and drink, and likewise bodily labor. ...that the entire body may be exercised. However, one must abstain from excessive exercise, since it dissipates the <term>innate heat</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, 'innate heat' was the vital energy responsible for digestion and life; over-exertion was thought to "evaporate" this heat.</note> and overheats the body; nevertheless, in all things, one’s habit must be observed. Rest is always harmful, because (as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A Persian physician (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a primary authority in the Renaissance.</note> says) the abandonment of exercise weakens the body's strength; for just as heat is stirred by motion, so sluggishness and the cooling of the <term>spirits</term> <note>In this period, 'spirits' were considered subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> are produced by rest. But if (as sometimes happens) the body becomes inflamed by excessive walking or other labor, or if exhaustion comes upon it, <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> said that resting immediately is the remedy. And since we have said that not only a material cause, but also an immaterial one causes pain, it will therefore be good once or twice a week to wash the head with a <term>lye</term> <note>A liquid cleaning solution, here used as a base for a medicinal hair and scalp wash.</note> in which the following have been boiled: <term>Take Melilot flowers, chamomile, mallow, and betony, one handful of each.</term> <note>original: "Recipe florum meliloti, chamæmeli, maluæ betonicæ, ana. manip. i."</note> These will prepare the matter for <term>resolution</term> <note>The process of breaking down and dispersing harmful humors or fluids.</note> and resist contrary qualities. 

**Sleep and wakefulness** are of no small importance, and therefore moderate sleep contributes much, provided it is not stretched beyond eight hours, nor brought on in less than six. It should take place at least two hours after dinner. Nor should it be during the day or at midday, as both are harmful to the head and multiply cold and <term>catarrhal</term> <note>Referring to "catarrh," an excess of phlegm believed to flow from the brain and cause illness.</note> matters. Excessive wakefulness is also harmful, because it dissipates the <term>virtues</term> <note>The internal powers or energies of the organs.</note> and multiplies superfluities. You should begin to sleep on your right side, then turn yourself onto the left; physicians praise sleeping longer upon the left than the right <note>Renaissance doctors believed sleeping on the left aided digestion by allowing the stomach to sit properly under the liver.</note>. Furthermore, it is appropriate to sleep covered according to the requirements of the season. 

**Regarding sexual intercourse,** I shall say nothing other than what <term>Galen</term> <note>A foundational Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note> says in the third book of the *Medical Art*, where he states that, according to the opinion of <term>Epicurus</term>, there is no healthy use of sexual matters. However, for those who are accustomed to it, its abandonment is harmful, and it is also harmful to those unaccustomed if they should suddenly take it up. 

**The passions of the soul**—Galen used to say in the same place that since they are bad, they change the body from its natural disposition. For this reason, anger, strife, bad thoughts, mourning, and similar things must be fled. It is beneficial to be joyful, to be in good company with fellow men, to have conversation about pleasant things, and to play delightful games; to hear songs and hymns, sounds and melodies, and such things that gladden the soul. 

**And since, according to the opinion of Hippocrates, alterations occur according to the change of seasons,** it will therefore be good twice a year to evacuate the body of certain thick <term>superfluities</term> <note>Excess or waste humors that the body has not properly processed.</note>, namely in the Spring and at the beginning of Autumn—for example, at the end of April and September. PART TWO.

**Take** half an ounce each of <term>rose syrup</term> <note>original: "syrupi rosati"</note>, <term>quince syrup</term> <note>original: "melini"</note>, syrup of <term>Arabian lavender</term> <note>original: "stœchade"</note>, and syrup of <term>fumitory</term>.
Take one and a half drachms each of <term>betony</term> and <term>bugloss</term> waters. Mix them, and let it be taken warm at dawn; then let him sleep, and four hours having passed, let him take his midday meal. Let him proceed in this way for four or five days; afterward, let him take this <term>evacuative medicine</term> <note>A purgative designed to "evacuate" harmful humors from the body.</note>. **Take** one drachm of <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>A "universal" laxative electuary used in medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note>, two drachms each of the electuary of dates and prepared <term>agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus often used as a purgative.</note>, and one drachm of simple <term>oxymel</term> <note>A medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note>. Add a sufficient quantity of betony and bugloss waters. Mix them, and let a small potion be made to be taken at dawn, and let the hour of the midday meal be five hours later. But if the pain should at any time be more troublesome, or if the belly should increase at other times, it will be most useful to purge in the manner we described above. But if Your Reverence should wish, besides the said evacuations to be performed twice a year, to take some pills once a week or twice a month to evacuate the <term>matter</term> <note>The physical substance (humors) believed to cause disease.</note>—both that which is collected in the stomach and that which exists in the head through continuous <term>evaporation</term>—the following pills will be the best aid. **Take** one <term>scruple</term> <note>A unit of weight equal to about 1.3 grams.</note> each of <term>mastic pills</term>, <term>alefangine pills</term> <note>Aromatic purgative pills common in the pharmacopeia of the time.</note>, and <term>aggregative pills</term>. Let three pills be made, and let them be taken six hours after dinner, and afterward let him sleep at his pleasure. These few things I have wished to write in stolen time <note>A common Renaissance idiom meaning "in my spare moments."</note>, hindered as I am by very many visits to the sick, so that I might inform you of my respect for you regarding those things you sought from me by letter. Farewell, Reverend Lord, and love me (as you do). It will not be a burden for you to pray to God, the giver of true health, that He might deign to keep me safe along with you. Farewell.

->August 10, 1542.<-

...of the jaw hinders you, so that you are neither able to open it nor chew properly. Therefore, you requested that I send you through letters those aids which might dissolve the tumor and restore the natural function and use of the jaw. But since, as Galen <note>A second-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> used to say, the method of healing is taken from the essence of the disease—which is achieved through the removal of the cause, or causes, if there be several—I shall first write what this disease is and its causes, and then its method of healing. 

Since it is a swelling <note>original: "tumor"</note> contrary to nature, which shows itself clearly to the senses as a cause, it is called an **aposteme** <note>A general term for an inflammatory swelling or internal abscess.</note> by the Greeks. And even though there are many other swellings that are not apostemes—such as ruptures of the groin <note>hernias</note>, protrusions of the navel, or swelling of the throat and other places caused by the retention of breath or wind—there is no doubt about this case. For in this [case], there are those three types of disease: namely, a corrupted **temperament** <note>The balance of the four bodily "humors": blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, a corrupted composition, and a **solution of continuity** <note>A medical term for a break or separation in the body's tissues, such as a wound or a internal rupture.</note>, which necessarily occur in the formation of all apostemes. 

Indeed, even if in those other swellings mentioned, a break in the tissue and a bad composition occur, they do not remain constantly, nor do they always bring a bad temperament with them. If they ever do combine, they are then called apostemes. For apostemes are not made by only one or two causes of swelling, but when the three aforementioned types of illness are joined together. 

But putting these aside, for the sake of clearer teaching, I will distinguish the apostemes themselves, which according to the variety of their **matter** <note>The physical substance, usually one of the four humors, that makes up the swelling.</note> are of six types: namely, the **sanguineous** <note>caused by blood</note> and the **choleric** <note>caused by yellow bile</note>, and these two are "hot." The remaining four types are the **phlegmatic**, **melancholic** <note>caused by black bile</note>, **watery**, and **windy**, which are "cold." 

And lest I delay longer than is fitting in listing the signs of the other apostemes, since there are no signs of "heat" in your case, it cannot be called a hot aposteme. It must therefore be from the "cold" category. Since it is neither watery nor windy, it remains that it is either phlegmatic or melancholic. But it is not melancholic, because that would be a **cancer** <note>In the Renaissance, a "cancer" was specifically a hard, painful tumor attributed to "burnt" black bile.</note>, which arises from choleric matter turned into black bile through **combustion** <note>The medical belief that humors could be "scorched" or "burnt" by excessive heat, making them toxic.</note>, or when there is burnt choleric matter present. The signs of which are a stony hardness with a bluish color in the area, pain, and sometimes a throbbing in the spot, with swollen veins appearing around it. Since these symptoms do not appear at all in this hard tumor, it can by no means be called a cancer. And since it is not cancer, nor that which physicians call a "pure **scirrhus**" <note>A hard, painless swelling, usually considered a stage of tumor development before becoming malignant.</note>—because a pure scirrhus has a leaden and dark color in addition to hardness and tension—it remains, therefore, that it is a scir—

## PART TWO

...[scir]rhus <note>original: "rhus" - likely the end of "scirrhus," a hard, non-cancerous tumor.</note> that is not pure, but not that type which is usually generated very often from the four **humors** <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health.</note> with a predominance of **melancholy** <note>The humor associated with black bile, often resulting in hard, dark, or painful tumors.</note>, which is said to be all the worse when it involves greater sensation and pain, and has a color tending toward leaden. Rather, it is the type formed from **phlegmatic matter** <note>Matter related to phlegm, the cold and moist humor.</note>, from which the thin, subtle parts have been dissolved, while the thick parts remain. In this type, there is neither pain, nor any sensation, nor a change in color, nor any other sensibly altered quality. Since all these signs are present in the extreme hardness that has grown in your Excellency’s jaw, I say that this hardness should be named a **non-pure scirrhus** arising from the aforementioned phlegmatic humor, from which the subtle parts have been dissolved; for it is without sensation, pain, or tension. No other quality appears in it except for the hardness, which is not excessive.

I say that this phlegmatic matter is not so pure that some small portion of other humors is not also mixed in, because **apostemes** <note>A general term for an inflammatory swelling or abscess.</note> are rarely entirely pure in every part, as is the opinion of all physicians regarding the humors. Even though **Galen** <note>A second-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for centuries.</note> said in the second book of *On Crises* that an aposteme can be formed from a single and simple humor, since this one lacks the signs of simple and purest phlegm, it has (as I said) something of the other humors mixed in. However, it is in such a small quantity that it does not change the nature of the simple phlegm. 

Indeed, if the humor causing this tumor were pure phlegm, beyond all doubt the area would first be whiter than the neighboring parts, and there would be a numbness in that spot. Nor could one doubt or ask without apparent reason whether this tumor could be called a **Node**, or **scrofula** <note>A swelling of the lymph nodes, typically in the neck.</note>, or **fugillae** <note>A historical term for glandular swellings, specifically those near the ears or jaw.</note>; for these mentioned tumors are usually formed from phlegmatic matter. But since all those mentioned tumors have a **cyst** <note>original: "cystim"</note> or a bladder containing the humor, and this hardness shows no signs of having a bladder containing the humor, it is therefore not of that kind. 

Let these words suffice for now regarding the essence of the said aposteme. Next, I shall write of the **efficient causes**, which are either external (which they call **primitive**) or internal (which they name **antecedent**), since I have already written abundantly regarding the **conjoined cause** <note>The immediate, active cause of the disease currently present in the body.</note> as the matter required. Since your Excellency related to me that this tumor arose two years ago from a certain long journey on horseback under the rays of the sun, it was from this that the cold phlegmatic matter congested in the head was set in motion. Thus, descending gradually, it caused this tumor; and although for the most part watery phlegmatic matter is in excess in the head, nevertheless since your Excellency has...

These things having been previously discussed regarding the nature and causes of the tumor, something must now be said about the stage of the disease, so that the tumor can be treated with the correct cure through that knowledge.

There are, in general, four stages of a disease, namely: the beginning, the increase, the peak, and the decline. I say that this <term>apostema</term> <note>A general term for any swelling, abscess, or tumor.</note> is at the beginning of its peak, or full vigor. From this, I can hope for the best recovery, especially given this youthful age and this time of year—namely the beginning of spring—if the right care and diligence are applied. I say this because benign swellings often change into <term>cancers</term> <note>In this period, "cancer" referred to malignant, spreading tumors, often compared to the legs of a crab.</note> due to poor management; how much more so might this one, if not well treated, be transformed into some kind of malignancy, since it is of the kind that can be converted into malignant things.

And so that we may proceed according to the rules for its cure, the first instrument will be a <term>regimen of the six necessary things</term> <note>Also known as the "six non-naturals," these were environmental and lifestyle factors—air, food, sleep, exercise, evacuation, and emotions—that physicians believed were the primary tools for maintaining health.</note>, which physicians call "non-natural"; however, these must be applied by the principle of opposites to both the antecedent and the joined causes. Since the primary cause is not our concern here, we must first beware of air that is both cold and damp, such as rain, mists, or fog, and air altered in some way—for example, by a swamp—since it multiplies <term>phlegma</term> <note>Phlegm, the cold and moist humor.</note>, fills the head, and causes the matter to flow. Too much hot air is also harmful, such as staying in the sun or remaining in a closed place where a large fire is lit, because it melts the moisture of the head. Let the air therefore be tempered, not very hot nor cold, but rather leaning toward a certain dryness.

Foods should also lean toward dryness. First, let the bread be well-baked, well-leavened, and salted; and it should not be entirely cleaned of all its bran. Likewise, meats should provide good nourishment and produce few waste products, such as the flesh of woodland birds—namely partridge, thrush, and blackbird—as well as chickens and young capons that are not fat. The meat of kids <note>young goats</note> is also excellent, as is veal; but pork and lamb are not good, because they are too moist. Therefore, all meats that are too moist should be avoided, as well as those that are too dry, such as old beef, venison, and other wild animals; for they generate many <term>melancholic</term> <note>Related to "black bile," the humor associated with hardness, dryness, and dark colors.</note> waste products and also generate <term>melancholic blood</term>.
