## PART TWO

...therefore, they <note>Referring to heavy or "slimy" foods mentioned on the preceding page.</note> must not be eaten; soft-boiled eggs are good, either beaten into a **broth** of good meats, or in water with a little sugar and cinnamon. All fish should be avoided, for they are **moist**: dishes should be made of grain, or of eggs beaten as described above, or **panatella** <note>A traditional bread soup made from breadcrumbs, broth, eggs, and cheese.</note>; or bread soaked in meat broth. **Borage**, **bugloss**, **hops**, **lemon balm**, and **fennel** are good, because they produce the best blood; and to speak briefly, one must abstain from all cold and excessively moist foods.

Wine should be of good aroma and flavor, not sweet, nor overly potent, nor even sour, but moderate and white. If it is watered down for any reason, let it be with water that has been boiled with fennel root. It should not be drunk after a meal, but rather a little and often during the meal, so that a proper mixing of food and drink occurs, and the wine does not harm the stomach or cause vapors to rise to the head.

Furthermore, dinner should be smaller than lunch, and one should not eat to the point of satiety at either dinner or lunch, lest undigested matter multiply and the underlying cause of the disease increase; yet, some allowance must be made for habit. And since abstinence purges the whole body equally, it is always good to eat sparingly, and also to drink sparingly. 

Furthermore, there should be a daily purging of the bowels and other superfluities. If the belly is not "obedient" <note>A common Renaissance medical euphemism for regular bowel movements.</note>, use a **clyster** <note>An enema.</note>, or certain **pills** that move the bowels and are intended to evacuate thick matter from the head. These include the *pills of agaric* described by **Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue, a major authority in medieval Islamic and Renaissance pharmacology.</note>; or, if stronger ones are needed, use *foetid pills* or *cochiae pills* <note>Two standard types of purgative pills; "cochiae" were specifically formulated to draw humors away from the head.</note>. However, allow four or five days between uses, depending on how the bowels respond—for example, once or twice a week.

Moderate **exercise** also helps, which should be taken in the morning before lunch, and also in the evening before dinner. Let it be a light walk or horse riding, and not in the sun. Excessive exercise dissolves one's strength and should therefore be avoided. 

**Sexual intercourse** also—since it does not occur without a depletion of strength and physical labor—should be avoided as much as possible, for it chills the body and weakens the brain. Nevertheless, when **seminal matter** <note>original: "materia feminis"; likely a typesetter's error for "materia seminis" (matter of the seed), as the context refers to Galenic theories of retention.</note> abounds, if it is expelled through intercourse, it relieves the body; and as **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity whose theories dominated medical practice until the 17th century.</note> used to say, the man finds rest and sleeps better. Therefore, if it is an accustomed habit, it may be practiced, but not frequently. 

Furthermore, it is appropriate to sleep at the accustomed hours, namely in the evening two hours after dinner. Sleep should not be longer than seven hours, nor shorter than six, because long sleep chills the body, and wakefulness weakens the strength. Nor should one sleep during the day, because it multiplies...

### THE TREATMENT CONTINUED

...take care. Finally, it is fitting to hope for future health based on what has been said, and to rejoice with friends, and to listen to cheerful conversation, songs, and music, and to flee every cause of sadness: because the **accidents of the soul** <note>A technical term in Galenic medicine referring to emotions or psychological states like anger, joy, or sadness, which were believed to physically alter the body's humors.</note> change the body toward a state that is contrary to nature, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> used to say. 

I intended these brief remarks on lifestyle <note>original: *regimine*; referring to the "six non-naturals" which include diet, exercise, and emotional state.</note> to be sufficient. I now transition to the second instrument of healing, which is the **medicinal regimen**. 

According to the opinion of the Prince <note>Referring to **Avicenna** (980–1037 AD), the Persian physician-philosopher whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook in Europe; he was often titled the "Prince of Physicians."</note>, the medicinal regimen must be proportional to the regimen of food and drink and other non-natural things. Therefore, in this case, the goal is to cut off and remove the cause of the disease. Since the illness is material—involving a physical buildup or "repletion"—and material illnesses are not cured except by **evacuation** <note>The medical practice of removing excess or corrupted humors from the body through various means.</note>, it is necessary first to evacuate, without neglecting the goal of drying out the affected area. 

Since some evacuation is performed through bloodletting <note>original: *missionem sanguinis*.</note> and some through the evacuation of other humors, I will first speak of bloodletting itself. Although the material causing this tumor is something other than blood (as previously stated), it might seem that evacuation by bloodletting is inappropriate. However, since the evacuation of blood is considered by both Avicenna and Galen to be a general evacuation of **all humors**, blood can be appropriately drained for this reason. 

Furthermore, we do not only intend evacuation, but also **diversion** <note>A common practice in humoral medicine where blood was drawn from a distant site to "pull" harmful fluids away from the diseased organ or area.</note> and the reduction of the matter mixed with the blood, which is **phlegmatic** <note>Relating to phlegm, the cold and moist humor. The patient’s tumor was identified as a buildup of thick phlegm.</note> and nourishes this specific illness. For when the humoral mass mixed with phlegm rises through the veins to the head—to the site of the illness, which is weak—it feeds the sickness. Therefore, if the blood is reduced, the body's natural power will be better able to regulate and correct it, as Avicenna testifies in his chapter on phlebotomy <note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood.</note>.

Furthermore, by the authority of all ancient physicians, phlebotomy is appropriate for any **abscess** <note>original: *apostemate*; used here broadly to mean any morbid swelling or tumor.</note>, even if it is "cold," as is clear in the cure for a **scirrhus** <note>A hard, painless swelling, often a precursor to cancer in early modern medical thought.</note>. This is especially true if the blood that comes out is bad in color; if it is of good color, it should by no means be evacuated. 

I am persuaded to this course not only by the time of year—which is **Spring**, the season when **Hippocrates** <note>Ancient Greek physician (c. 460–370 BC) known as the "Father of Medicine."</note> and Galen command the opening of veins—but also by the patient's age and his **complexion** <note>The individual's unique balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note>, which is dominated by blood. But what persuades me most is the authority of Galen, who says in his booklet *On Bloodletting*, that phlebotomy not only frees one from a very severe present illness, but even from a future one if we fear it. But since the present illness is great, preventing the opening of the mouth, and we must fear (as Galen said) lest the scirrhus should become a can- <note>The text cuts off here at the word "cancer" (Latin: *cancer*).</note>

<summary>Massa argues for the use of bloodletting to treat the patient's tumor, justifying the practice through the authority of Galen and Avicenna. He explains that even though the tumor is phlegmatic, reducing the overall blood volume helps divert harmful humors and prevents the swelling from turning into a malignant cancer.</summary>

# PART TWO

...scrofula <note>A swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, often associated with tuberculosis, historically known as the "King's Evil."</note>, which is a very great and cruel sickness. Therefore, after your Lordship is settled at home, you shall take a <term>minorative</term> <note>A mild laxative intended to gently reduce (minorate) the volume of harmful humors in the body without causing physical distress.</note> to loosen the bowels slightly, which shall be as follows:

> Take 12 drams of lenitive electuary <note>A medicinal paste made of herbs, honey, and sugar designed to have a soothing, mildly laxative effect.</note>
> 4 drams of dates

Mix these, and with sugar make it well, and let it be taken five hours before lunch; then rest for the day after taking the said minorative. Then, on the third day, let a vein be opened in the right arm—the <term>common vein</term> <note>Likely the median cubital vein or the cephalic vein, commonly used for bloodletting.</note>, or the "black vein" as it is sometimes called, it matters not—and let blood be drawn to the quantity of five or six ounces if it appears bad and black; but if it is red and clear, the procedure should be stopped. On the following day, it will be best to take a <term>digestive</term> <note>A medicine intended to "cook" or "ripen" the raw, cold humors so they can be more easily expelled from the body.</note>, for as **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460–370 BC) often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> said, one must treat and move those humors that are digested, not those that are crude <note>original: "digesta medicari, & mouere non cruda"; a fundamental principle of Galenic medicine where "raw" humors had to be matured before purging.</note>. The digestive should be as follows:

> Take 1 ounce of syrup of fumitory <note>A herb traditionally used to "purify" the blood and treat skin conditions.</note>
> Half an ounce of composite oxymel <note>A mixture of honey, vinegar, and various herbs used to cut through thick phlegm.</note>
> 2 ounces each of betony and fennel waters

Mix these, and let it be taken in the morning five hours before lunch, and do this every day until signs of <term>digestion</term> appear in the urine <note>In pre-modern medicine, physicians examined the color, consistency, and sediment of urine to determine if the "concoction" or ripening of humors was successful.</note>. Afterward, let the matter be reduced again with this "blessed" evacuative, which is stronger and more specifically targeted. I say "reduced," because in the case of thick matter we do not attempt a radical, total evacuation all at once, but rather a gradual lessening. The minorative is as follows:

> Take 1 ounce of lenitive electuary
> 3 drams of sebesten <note>A plum-like fruit used as a gentle laxative.</note>
> 2 drams of prepared agaric <note>A medicinal fungus (*Laricifomes officinalis*) used as a potent purgative.</note>
> 1 ounce of simple oxymel
> A sufficient quantity of fennel and betony waters

Mix these and make a potion, and let it be taken at dawn. It will be good if you sleep for an hour afterward, because agaric—due to its light substance—seeks the upper parts of the body, whereas sleep causes it to descend to the bottom of the stomach. However, once that hour has passed, you must not sleep. You shall eat lunch five hours after taking the medicine. On the following day, early in the morning, drink one cup of broth with sugar, and again take the syrups to digest the remaining parts of the matter. These syrups can be prepared according to the previous instructions, or by making them stronger as follows...

After the two aforementioned evacuations, I would be pleased to use pills, as they are more effective at drawing humors down from the head; therefore, let them be as follows:

This constitutes the "third instrument" of treatment, which is necessary for the perfection of the cure through medicines applied over the swollen spot. Therefore, the medicines placed upon the site should not deviate from the previously stated intention of "drying" the humor, even though it is necessary to soften the area beforehand. Indeed, this kind of softening is done so that the conjoined matter can more easily be both resolved and evacuated; for unless it is softened, it cannot be resolved. Therefore, the rule for applying these medicines shall be: first, the place must be anointed several times a day with the above-written liniment, then ap- <note>The text continues on the next page: "apply..."</note>

# TO LORD GIOVANNI DALM
## A Nobleman of Brescia, regarding a swelling on the lip and also on the right foot.

### L E T T E R  X I V.

YOUR Excellency showed me in Venice two locations on the body affected externally, namely the lip and the right foot. Because these locations are manifest to the senses, they do not require speculation as to their existence, since they are [plainly] affected. However, one might ask whether some other organ is suffering in sympathy with them, and whether these are merely symptoms of that diseased organ <note>In Galenic medicine, a "sympathetic" condition occurred when one body part suffered because of a primary disease in another, such as the liver or stomach.</note>. To clarify this doubt, let me digress thus: For Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the chief authority for Renaissance physicians.</note> said in the first book of *On the Affected Parts* <note>original: "de locis affectis"</note> that the knowledge of internal sufferings is a sort of middle ground between ignorance and certain knowledge; but those things which are open to the senses possess the most certain knowledge. Therefore, no physician could doubt the existence of these swellings, but he might be ignorant of the "antecedent" and "fostering" causes, since those are internal matters. 

I heard from your Lordship that you suffered certain pains of the joints, from which you were released, and there followed a long-lasting and powerful fever. Once that fever was cured, these swellings appeared. Since they are somewhat hard, and red in color tending toward duskiness, a physician cannot judge them to be anything other than a "mixed matter" <note>A combination of different bodily humors, such as blood and black bile.</note> that is nevertheless predominantly "cold" <note>In the humoral system, "cold" diseases were characterized by thick, sluggish fluids that were difficult for the body to expel.</note>. The prior material illnesses—namely the pains and the aforementioned fever—agree with this assessment. For it is in the nature of "subtle" [thin] matter, whether it rots or infests our body in another way, to reach its end quickly, either for good or for ill. But thick and cold matter, since it is resistant to <term>digestion</term> <note>The internal process by which the body "cooks" or prepares harmful humors so they can be expelled.</note> and is slow-moving, causes long-lasting illnesses, as were those prior general ailments of yours. 

And even these most recent specific swellings, which, speaking medically, I can only call <term>apostemes</term> <note>A general term for a swelling, tumor, or abscess where "bad humors" have gathered.</note>, were formed by way of "permutation," so to speak. This occurred because the entire <term>matter of the disease</term> <note>original: "materiam morbi"</note> that preceded them was not fully evacuated by medical art, nor rectified by nature, nor drawn out. Those remnants that remained, by the power of the body prevailing over the matter of the disease, were shifted to these external parts, as if to the "less noble" and weaker parts of the body <note>Physicians believed the body's "vital force" would push toxins away from vital organs like the heart toward the skin or extremities to protect the patient's life.</note>. Nature certainly should not have transmitted these remnants to these parts...

<summary>This page contains a medical consultation for Giovanni de Ulmo regarding swellings on his lip and foot. Massa explains that these are "apostemes" caused by leftover "cold matter" from a previous fever that the body has pushed to the extremities.</summary>

<sig>FF ii</sig>

...by acting rightly, but since nature is weak from the long duration of the disease, it did the best it could among the possibilities, not being strong enough to expel the matter entirely. Instead, it shifted it at least to the less noble members <note>In Galenic medicine, "noble members" are the vital organs like the heart, brain, and liver; "ignoble members" are the extremities or less vital parts where nature sends harmful waste to protect the life of the patient.</note>, as is the opinion of Galen in many places. And so, through the gradual release of nature, the matter was collected in the said members, and two tumors were caused. 

Now, since sometimes a certain part of the body can swell up and yet not be an <term>aposteme: an inflammatory swelling or abscess</term>—as can be seen in a rupture of the groin [a hernia], where those locations sometimes swell because the <term>omentum: a fold of fatty tissue in the abdomen</term> descends to that spot, or a part of the intestine, or wind, or an inflating spirit <note>Renaissance medicine often attributed swelling to "pneuma" or "spiritus," types of air-like substances in the body.</note>—these and similar tumors are not called apostemes. 

For a tumor to be called an aposteme, according to the opinion of the Prince <note>The "Prince" refers to Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980–1037 AD), whose *Canon of Medicine* was the primary textbook for doctors in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, three types of ailments are required to cause a single disease: bad composition <note>original: "mala compositio"; a structural or mechanical deformity</note>, bad complexion <note>original: "mala complexio"; an imbalance of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—or the humors</note>, and a breach of continuity <note>original: "solutio continui"; a physical separation or disruption of the tissue's wholeness</note>. 

It is good to see whether these three are present in these tumors. First, there is a manifest tumor both on the lip and on the foot, which takes away the proper composition [structure]. Next, a change appears in the qualities of both sight and touch: for the locations are red with a duskiness tending toward blackness, and the affected areas are also harder than what is required for a natural disposition. Since this only occurs because bad matter is soaked into the pores of the members, causing them to swell, and since bad matter does not maintain its proper "complexion," it must be said without a doubt that the complexion of the member has been changed by it. It is also clear that there is a breach of continuity there. Since these three factors are joined as one, it must be called an aposteme.

But since an aposteme, according to a twofold division, is divided into "hot" and "cold" based on the opinion of the Prince [Avicenna], it is necessary to know which kind these are: are they hot or cold? If anyone wished to establish these as hot apostemes, it would not be rational. Hot apostemes come in two species: namely, sanguine [bloody] and choleric. 

The signs of a sanguine aposteme are a sudden red swelling occurring with some softness, a pulsing sensation, and the accompaniment of fever. The signs of a choleric aposteme are a bright redness tending toward lemon-yellow, a tumor that is almost imperceptible [to the touch], and an accompanying fever; the redness is such that if someone applies a finger, it disappears, yet quickly returns. Nor can anyone say these are "composite" tumors [made of both], since the signs of such things are not present. Therefore, by applying these rules, it is necessary—as was said above—that these belong to the category of "cold" apostemes. Since there are many species of these, I shall assign them to their proper species while setting aside the others, so that excessive speculation does not become tedious to the readers. I presuppose...

<meta>This page continues the diagnostic analysis for Lord Giovanni Dalm's condition. Niccolò Massa is moving from the general observation of the tumors on the lip and foot to a specific humoral classification, determining that while the swellings involve melancholy, they are not "true" melancholic tumors but rather a complex mixture of "burnt" humors. ->## THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

The antecedent cause is situated as stated above, which was the remains of the matter from previous illnesses; these have been called "cold" by many due to their predominance. <note>In Galenic medicine, diseases were classified by primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry. A "cold" cause suggests a lack of vital heat or an excess of phlegm or melancholy.</note> The matter that has joined them also testifies to this, since it is hard and not red with the brightness of blood, but a livid red. This is ascribed to the conditions of <term>unnatural melancholy: a toxic form of the melancholic humor created when other humors are "burnt" or overheated</term>, which is not derived from blood, but created by way of <term>adustion: the "scorching" or cooking of humors through excessive internal heat</term> from phlegmatic and <term>choleric: related to yellow bile</term> matter that has been let in. 

Nor should these <term>apostemes: inflammatory swellings</term> be called purely "melancholic" for this reason, since they lack the conditions of such swellings: these are typically dark, black, earthy, and obscure in color, and have a stony hardness to the touch (which is a diagnostic sign alongside dryness and roughness) and lack pain. Since these [the patient's tumors] are not of that kind, etc., let us instead enumerate what *is* present in them, so we may more easily recognize their essence. 

First, the swelling is not stony, nor is it entirely soft, but occupies a middle state between extreme hardness and softness. Nor is it entirely deprived of pain and sensation. The redness is not bright but dark and somewhat livid, and there is no pulsation. These are signs of admitted phlegmatic and melancholic matter—not of "fecal" melancholy <note>original: "melancholiæ fæcalis"; referring to the thick, sediment-like dregs of the blood</note>, but matter made from the adustion of thick <term>cholera: yellow bile</term> with some mixing of blood. 

Once these things are known, such apostemes may be named whatever one likes, for Galen said everywhere that once an illness is known through its essential nature, it is foolish to dispute over names. They are, as has been said, "compound" apostemes. 

But someone might ask: why were so many and such great things said? Galen responds that it is impossible to cure an illness unless it has first been understood, and the reasoning for the cure is taken from the very essence of the disease. This will also help us in predicting the future outcome (the prognosis). Above all, all these things will be better accomplished if the doctor knows the natural <term>complexion: the unique humoral temperament or "constitution" of an individual</term> of the sick man. In my judgment, his complexion is hot and dry by predominance, with a sub-dominance of melancholy, as I have been able to gather from the present circumstances. 

This can easily be shown according to the rule of Galen in the second book of the *Techni* <note>original: "Techni"; refers to Galen's *Ars Medica*, often called the *Tegni* in the Middle Ages</note> and the rule of Avicenna. But lest I be too long-winded, I leave these as very well-known facts. From what has been said, therefore, you have the essence of the illness through its causes and signs.

But before I arrive at the cure, it will not be useless to know whether the illness is curable or not. And if it is curable, can health be restored quickly, or will the doctor be able to do this only over a certain period of time? (I will not say a very long time, but certainly not a brief one). However, since according to the opinion of Hippocrates and all illustrious doctors, the <term>prognosis: the forecast of the disease's likely course</term> is taken from the patient's <term>virtue: the vital strength or "living power" of the body</term>, and since the virtue of your Lordship is sufficient...

<summary>Massa identifies the patient's swellings as "compound apostemes" caused by a mixture of "burnt" humors (adust bile and melancholy) rather than a single source. He emphasizes that a correct diagnosis of the patient's natural "hot and dry" temperament is essential before a prognosis or cure can be attempted.</summary>

->## PART TWO<-

...good, both by reason of <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person’s temperament</term>, and by reason of age, which is that of youth; according to the opinion of **Aristotle** in the last part of his *Problems*, youth is full of hope. Therefore, it is to be entirely believed that with the canonical application of the proper and necessary instruments, **your lordship** will undoubtedly be healed. Nor does the essence of the sickness, in any way known to the wise, contradict this judgment of ours—specifically regarding the nature of humors that are rebellious to digestion and cure, such as melancholy—since for the most part it is a thick, <term>phlegmatic: relating to the humor phlegm, associated with coldness and moisture</term> humor that is at fault. Neither does the time from the beginning of this disease until this day terrify me at all, since spring—the healthiest season according to the opinion of **Hippocrates**—is now present. Wherefore I say that your lordship shall be healed, but this requires some time. 

How this is to be accomplished you shall hear from what follows. We say that the business of healing is completed by one of three things: one of them is the <term>regimen: a prescribed way of life, including diet, exercise, and environment</term> and nutrition; another is the administration of medicines; the third is manual operation <note>This refers to surgery or the external application of remedies by hand</note>. These are the words of **The Prince** <note>original: "Principis". This refers to Avicenna (Ibn Sina), known in the Middle Ages and Renaissance as the "Prince of Physicians."</note> teaching the method of procedure in the cure of ailments. Since these things are highly necessary, I wished to bring his words here, and I will detail them according to the needs of your lordship.

Regarding the first, the regimen must be the opposite of the sickness; for a sickness is medicated by its contrary, and health is preserved by its like, as the same **Avicenna** said. And since it has been said that these <term>apostemes: inflammatory swellings or abscesses</term> are composed [of multiple humors], yet a cold matter dominates them, let us not confuse the order of the cure. Let us say that the ailment is in its "state" <note>The "state" (status) refers to the plateau phase of a disease where symptoms are neither increasing nor decreasing</note>; for the beginning was when those parts perceptibly began to swell, and they increased up until a certain time; now they neither increase nor decrease. And if it seemed to some that the swelling of the foot was dissolved in some part by the medicines applied, since that was but a small amount and no further resolution followed, I would say that those were rather concomitant matters and not the "true" aposteme, but were of another kind transmitted there from the weakness of the site, causing a greater tumor on the surface, yet not reaching the place of the true aposteme. If they were the true matter, once nature was unburdened, the rest surely would have either resolved or <term>suppurated: formed pus</term>. 

And since in the "state" of a disease all things are at their strongest, therefore your lordship ought boldly to choose a contrary regimen—not a weak one, but according to what is possible—which should be both contrary [to the disease] and similar [to your nature], so that the natural disposition of the limb may be preserved, as well as the natural temperament of the whole and of the suffering members. First, therefore, cold and damp air must be avoided, as well as places having such qualities...

# THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICOLÒ MASSA

...[avoiding such] air as is found in marshy, windy, foggy, earthy, and damp places, such as valleys and shady spots; however, dryness should not be excessive. It is suitable to live in a part of the house positioned toward the east. And after the sun has consumed the vapors of the bad air, which is around the <term>third hour: approximately 9:00 AM, the third hour after sunrise</term>, let the windows then be opened, so that such air may enter. But if the weather, as often happens, becomes rainy, or foggy, or misty, the windows should not be opened; instead, let a fire be lit in the bedroom, so that in any case the air may be warmed; and this with a small or large fire according to the requirement of the season. And since excessive heat is harmful, therefore in the summer season, and during times of maximum excessive heat, it is not bad to cool the air, especially since the composition of the <term>apostemata: swellings or abscesses</term> themselves also requires this. 

Foods should be of the same quality, tending toward warmth and temperate dryness, not generating many <term>superfluities: waste products or excess humors that the body cannot process</term>, and being well-nourishing, such as well-leavened bread, moderately salted and baked. The meat of kids <note>young goats</note> is most highly praised, as is veal that is not too fatty, and similarly wethers <note>castrated rams</note> of two years; young capons, small chickens, partridges, pheasants, thrushes, and blackbirds; and among other birds, those caught with <term>birdlime: a sticky substance used to trap birds on branches</term> are the best, etc. 

Bad are the meats of pork, lamb, and similar ones, such as goose, duck, etc. Soft-boiled eggs are good, and also whisked into meat broth; fried and hard-boiled eggs are bad. Cheese and all dairy products are bad, such as butter, etc. All fish are bad, and therefore to be avoided; but if they are occasionally eaten, they should be scaly fish caught in running waters, such as pike and trout, seasoned with some temperate spices such as cinnamon, mace, and the like. Marine fish are better, especially those found in rocky areas, such as the <term>scorpion fish: also known as scarpena</term>, but it is better to roast them than to cook them by boiling. 

Excellent dishes are things like <term>far: an ancient grain similar to spelt</term> and <term>panatella: a traditional bread soup or gruel</term> well-cooked in meat broth, borage, fennel, bugloss <note>an herb often used to "comfort the heart"</note>, and similar herbs; hops are highly praised if eaten in place of salad or as a side dish. Capers are also pleasing, and this at supper. If any sauces are to be eaten, they should be made from mint, parsley, almonds, and sugar with a little cinnamon and rose water, or other equivalent things. 

After the meal, your Lordship may eat pistachios, pine nuts, fresh almonds, raisins, and coriander; and whether these are with sugar or not matters little, since they are not taken as a meal but, as they say, for the "sealing of the stomach" <note>the medieval belief that certain foods could "close" the stomach to ensure proper digestion</note>. Other fruits are bad, such as cherries, apples, and <term>apricots: literally "golden apples" (*chrysomela*)</term>. The wine should be good, not too strong, nor...

->## SECOND PART<-

[The wine should be] small, not sharp, of a good scent and good taste, and of a middling color, and rather tending toward a full-bodied one <gloss>than</gloss> toward a thin or acidic one. And since the cause of all these statements is known to learned physicians, for the sake of brevity let it be omitted; <gloss>that</gloss> if it is necessary to dilute the wine with water, either because of <gloss>habit</gloss> or some other necessity, let it be water in which coriander has been boiled—specifically coriander which has not been soaked in vinegar—as is commonly prepared for those with fever. And let the drink be according to the quantity and quality of the food; nor should one drink after eating, but during the meal. Dinner should be smaller than lunch, because those who eat much at dinner abound in many <term>superfluities: waste products or excess humors that the body cannot process</term>, whatever others may say on this matter as they please. Nor is it necessary to always eat until full, but as <term>Galen: a prominent Greek physician of the 2nd century whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium</term> said, the sick person must be fed in such a way that strength is preserved and the disease is not nourished. And since the aforementioned illness is material <note>meaning it is caused by a physical buildup of humors</note> and arises from <term>repletion: a state of being overfilled with food or humors</term>, repletion must be avoided above all else; and the true measure of food is taught by <term>Hippocrates: the ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</term>. Therefore, food should be diminished from one's usual habit in every way, little by little. What I say about food should be understood the same way regarding drink, and thus repletion will be avoided, etc. Furthermore, one must strive to expel the customary superfluities, namely the stool, urine, spit, and others. If nature purges these by itself, it is enough; if not, it should be aided by old clysters <note>enemas</note> and suppositories, or with a mild, blessed medicine, such as <term>mastic pills: digestive aids made from the resin of the mastic tree, used to strengthen the stomach and aid excretion</term>, which can be taken twice a week in the morning, five hours before lunch, when the bowels do not flow on their own. The quantity should be according to the responsiveness of the body; for example: Take one <term>drachm: a unit of apothecary weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> <note>original: "ʒ.i."</note> of <term>mastic pills</term> and let three pills be made. If these do not move [the bowels], let the dose be one and a half <term>drachms</term> <note>original: "ʒ.i.s."</note> and let five pills be made. To retain urine is bad, and therefore one should urinate, spit, and the spit should be encouraged especially in the morning. Above all else, which benefits both the healthy and the sick, is that the <term>spirits: vital forces believed to circulate through the body to sustain life and function</term> be vivified and superfluities be purged, as <term>Avicenna: a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard medieval textbook</term> testifies in the chapter on exercise. And therefore, since Your Lordship suffers in the foot, and the limbs we intend to heal (as <term>Galen</term> said) require rest, it is not inappropriate to wonder whether exercise is <gloss>suitable</gloss> for Your Lordship. I briefly respond <gloss>that</gloss> it is; but not the exercise of walking, <gloss>since</gloss> there are <gloss>very</gloss> many types of exercise. Therefore, let Your Lordship be exercised not with the exercise of walking, but according to the other limbs: by stretching the arms upward and downward in the morning, moving them from side to side; let the hands and palms be rubbed with a swift motion. Drawing a bow is extremely beneficial, as is combing the head with a long combing toward the back part...

# THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICOLÒ MASSA
<meta>catchword: Recipe</meta>

[The body] should be rubbed, almost as if scratching it, even with rough linen cloths, so that the <term>superfluities: waste products or excess humors that the body cannot process</term> can evaporate. Let it be washed with <term>lye: an alkaline solution used for cleaning and medicinal washes</term> once a week. Practice some indoor game while sitting, such as throwing a staff or a javelin, so that heat may be excited by the movement of the body. There are also many other modes of exercise which Your Lordship will be able to use, which are well known and which I will omit, such as playing with a wooden ball. 

The convenient hour for this is at least one hour before taking food. Let the game not be excessive so as to provoke sweat, but—as they say—exclusively up to the point of sweat. I praise rubbings, which take the place of exercise, over the whole body except in the leg where the <term>aposteme: an inflammatory swelling or abscess</term> is located. And so, let no day pass without some kind of exercise; because too much rest cools the body and makes it moist. 

And since sexual intercourse does not happen without a dissipating exercise, it must be set aside, because it cools the body by dissipating the <term>spirits: the subtle fluids believed to flow through the nerves to animate the body</term>, which are the instruments of the <term>Soul: the vital principle of life</term>. 

Sleep is likened to rest, as <term>Aristotle: the Greek philosopher whose works formed the basis of medieval science</term> said in *On Sleep and Vigilance*. Therefore, it should not be excessive, nor should it occur during the day or immediately after food. Let it be taken at night, and let it not be more than eight hours, nor less than five hours. For <term>Hippocrates: the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</term> says that sleep and wakefulness, if they exceed moderation, are bad and very harmful. Nor is it proper to stay awake for long periods, because it dissolves all the <term>virtues: the natural powers or faculties of the body</term>; whereas moderate sleep provides strength to the body by restoring the spirits. 

The <term>accidents of the soul: emotional states or passions, such as anger or joy, that were believed to physically alter the body</term> change the body from its natural consistency and are therefore extremely harmful. Therefore, one must beware of sadness, anger, and evil or worrying thoughts. It is beneficial to hear songs and sweet sounds, to occupy oneself with humorous things, to be with dear friends, and to dance and leap with honorable matrons. One should flee from those who are mournful or weeping, and avoid the burials of the dead and similar things; for these sadden the soul and make the vital power drowsy. 

Let these things suffice concerning the lifestyle and nutrition. The medicinal regimen must be arranged as follows when the illness is <term>material: caused by a physical buildup of humors rather than just a change in temperature or quality</term> and has a cause that fosters it. First, it is necessary, as <term>Galen: the 2nd-century Roman physician whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years</term> pleased, to remove each cause, and then to arrive at the treatment of the illness itself. Hippocrates said that a material disease, or one arising from <term>plenitude: an overabundance of blood or other humors</term>, is cured by evacuation. 

However, he advised us to treat things that are <term>digested: humors that have been "cooked" or processed by the body's heat</term> and to move those that are not <term>raw: unprocessed or "cold" humors</term>. This intention is the true cure. Therefore, let the bad materials that reside in other members due to the preceding cause be digested by their contrary, beginning first with this syrup.

<summary>Massa provides instructions on physical activity, sleep, and emotional health, emphasizing that "accidents of the soul" like sadness can harm the body. He concludes by transitioning from lifestyle advice to a medicinal regimen focused on digesting and evacuating excess humors.</summary>

Mix: let it be taken warm at dawn, and let him wait for five hours before he eats. Let this be done every single morning for five or six days, so that the physician may recognize from the urine and other signs that the <term>matter: the "bad" or excess humors causing the illness</term> has been prepared for <term>evacuation: the removal of excess humors from the body, usually through purging</term>. Once this is done, it is necessary to evacuate with a mild "blessed medicine," as <note>original: "Princeps." In this era, "the Prince" refers to the 11th-century Persian physician Avicenna.</note> the Prince taught regarding thick matter. Let the medicine be as follows:

Take <term>lenitive electuary: a mild, paste-like laxative meant to soften the bowels</term>, }
<term>diasenna: a medicinal compound based on senna, used as a purgative</term>, } 5 drachms of each.
Prepared <term>agaric: a type of fungus (Larch Agaric) used to purge phlegm</term>, 1 drachm.

Mix, and let a <term>bolus: a large, soft pill</term> be made with sugar. If you would rather drink it, you can prepare a potion with waters of fumitory and wormwood. Take it in the morning, and wait five hours before lunch is taken. On the following day, let him use the regimen for one who has been purged: namely, let one cup of <term>broth: a light meat stock used to restore strength after a purge</term> with a little sugar be given at dawn. And again, let him take the above-written syrups for some days—say, six—as was said above. Let the same medicine be repeated if it previously moved the bowels moderately; but if it moved them very thoroughly, let only the lenitive and the diasenna be given, omitting the agaric. If by chance it moved them too little, let the dose of agaric be added this second time—say, a half-drachm, or one at most—and on the following morning let him use the stated regimen for one who has been purged: namely, let him take one cup of broth, etc. Afterward, one must proceed with a stronger <term>digestion: the process of "ripening" or breaking down humors so they can be purged</term> for several days, which should be as follows:

Take syrup of fumitory, }
Syrup of <term>dodder of thyme: a parasitic plant used to purge "melancholic" humors</term>, } 1/2 ounce of each.
Sugared julep, }
Decoction of dodder of thyme by <note>original: "Mesuae." Refers to Mesue the Younger, a famous (though perhaps legendary) author of Arabic pharmaceutical texts.</note> Mesue, 3 ounces. 

Mix, and let it be taken warm at dawn, and let him eat five hours later, as has been said. It is necessary to continue this for many days. Then return to the medicine, which should have the same power but with greater <term>confortation: the strengthening of the internal organs</term>; therefore, let this be given: 

Take choice <term>rhubarb: a potent purgative root</term>,
Best agaric, 1 drachm of each.
<term>Schoenanthus: an aromatic grass, also known as camel grass</term>, 4 grains.
Ginger, 1/2 scruple.
<term>Oxymel: a medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</term>, 1/2 ounce.
Decoction of dodder of thyme by Mesue, 3 ounces. 

Let them be infused for eight hours, and after a diligent straining, let 5 drachms each of lenitive electuary and diasenna be dissolved in it.

Firstly, because it was mentioned that some blood was also mixed in, which is shown by that dark redness in the tumors themselves. Some letting of blood is necessary in any <term>aposteme: an inflammatory swelling or abscess</term>, even a "cold" one, for the sake of <term>diversion: a medical strategy of drawing harmful humors away from an affected area by bleeding a distant vein</term>. Therefore, for all these reasons, I highly recommend it in the spring, as it is now.

And let this be done from the "black" or <term>common vein: the median cubital vein of the arm</term> of the right arm, two hours before he takes lunch. Later, when the intention is to resolve the swelling (which occurs after the softening), let the aforementioned ingredients boil in three parts white wine and one part vinegar; for in this way, the resolution will become stronger. One must not, however, boldly administer vinegar to members that are full of <term>chords: sinews or tendons</term> and ligaments, since sometimes the harm is greater than the help, as <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD), the primary authority on medicine in the Renaissance.</note> Galen teaches in the 14th book of his *Method of Medicine*. 

We ought to note, however, that one must proceed more by softening than by resolving, as the same Galen learnedly said in the 14th book of his *Therapeutics* and in his work *To Glaucon*. Although he himself says in *To Glaucon* that we ought to mix both intentions together, you might—if these treatments do not help—proceed to further and stronger remedies. **Take:** 
Hen fat, half a dram; 
Duck fat, 1 dram; 
Deer marrow, 2 drams;

Let it be covered by some device so that the concentrated steam can better act upon the hardness itself. However, if the site begins to harden again, stop the suffumigation and return to...

# NICOLAUS MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

...the spitting of blood <note>original: "sputus sanguinis"</note>; for which reason you requested through the aforementioned letters that I send you life-saving remedies in writing. Indeed, I, who for a long time have greatly loved and respected your lordship, cannot fail to obey your requests. However, because all rational physicians derive their curative intentions from the essence of the disease, I will first write about what kind of illness I judge you to be suffering from; next, what I hope for the future; and finally, by what aids you may be set free.

The disease, therefore, according to what has been written and reported, is a **rupture of a vein** in the anterior part of the chest on the left side. As I shall declare shortly, this disease is a <term>break in continuity: a physical injury where naturally connected tissues are separated</term> <note>original: "solutio continui"</note>. That it is true that you suffer from a rupture of a vein is shown first of all by the blood which is cast out through spitting; for blood is not found in a living creature except in the veins, aside from that which is held in the ventricles of the heart. That heart-blood cannot be drawn out by a cough or any other way, but is processed there and converted into a **spirituous substance** (so to speak), passing through the arteries to the entire body as the instrument for all operations.

That this rupture of a vein is in the parts of the chest and not in the lungs can be easily demonstrated. First, from the pain around the ribs of the left side; for <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – 370 BC)</note> said: *where there is pain, there is the disease.* Next, from the violent cough; for when the matter which is in the chest is brought out by coughing, nature labors more by coughing than if it were in the lungs, since the ribs and the membrane covering them are a more distant place from the windpipe—or the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: "aspera arteria," a historical term for the trachea</note>—than the lungs are. 

Furthermore, the blood which comes from the lungs is thin, bright, and frothy; but this blood (as I hear) is spat out neither frothy, nor thin, nor bright, but with a certain stickiness and darkness, and without foam. And because the blood is spat out with a cough, and since it was not of a significant quantity, it is necessary to say that it was not severed from a large vein, but from a quite small one, such as those that nourish the ribs, which are narrow and small enough. 

But if I wish to proceed further by reasoning as physicians are accustomed to do, and attempt to assign the causes of this rupture—which could indeed be many—I shall begin by enumerating natural factors. I have known your lordship for a long time, and from the habit of the whole, you are of tall stature, not fat, but possessing a certain medium fleshiness with a breadth of veins and a body color rather dark, tending toward yellow. These conditions are possessed by those who have contracted a **hot and dry** <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperiem," referring to the balance of the four humors</note> from the beginning of their generation, which all your bodily operations prove, such as...

He applies Hippocratic principles to locate the source of the bleeding near the ribs.</summary>

## PART TWO

...readiness for movement, and the agility of the rest of your limbs: for even if you have always been lame from the moment of your birth, I nevertheless saw a wonderful readiness and agility in all your limbs, especially when I had very often seen you play the game of both the small and <gloss>and</gloss> the large ball; I pass over the goodness of your natural talent and many excellent natural operations. Indeed, this temperament <note>In historical medicine, "temperament" or "complexion" referred to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in an individual.</note> encourages the production of much thinner blood, which is not without a certain sharpness. 

However, when a slender habit of body and an abundance of warmer and thinner blood was joined together with a poor regime of air, food, and drink, as well as movement and labors, and with the season of the year contributing to the **boiling of the blood**; for at that time, in which your lordship first began to spit blood, there was the greatest heat, and it was around the end of the month of May. At that time, as I hear, your lordship labored greatly both by riding under the sun’s rays and by walking on foot. 

When, however, you were exhausted at your church on that day when they celebrate the church festival, and you wished to sing the divine offices with the other clerics, it happened that on the following day you began to spit blood with a cough. All these, therefore, were the causes of this spitting of blood: for a hot and dry temperature generates a thinner blood, especially when joined with a similar diet. For you have often used both spices and salted foods and other hotter edibles, and you have drunk powerful and **undiluted wines** <note>original: "meracia"</note>, all of which can render the blood thinner and hotter. 

Furthermore, riding and walking can greatly heat the body, agitate the **humors**, and thin them out, since movement contributes much toward the over-heating of the whole body. The sun’s rays, moreover, could inflame the head with the excessive heat of the air, so that as sharp and corrosive matter descended and dripped from the head to the organs below, they prepared them for this rupture. The final cause was the singing in the sacred building, which is not done without labor of the chest, and thus one vein was ruptured in that part, or several from among the small ones nourishing the ribs or the intercostal muscles. 

These things having been discussed beforehand, the consideration arises whether this ailment contains anything of a crisis within itself, and whether it can be healed quickly or slowly. To this question I can easily respond that the disease, in the first place—since it is a <term>break in continuity</term> <note>original: "solutio continui" — a medical term for a wound or physical separation of tissues that should be joined</note> in a noble member, namely in the chest—is not without danger, especially since it has a cause fostering the matter dripping from the head; but when I later consider the strength of all your physical powers...

...and considering your age, your <term>temperament</term> <note>In the 1500s, health was seen as a balance of the four "humors." A person's "temperament" was their unique natural balance of these fluids.</note>, and the strength of your entire body, I truly hope that your lordship will, without any doubt, recover your former health. This is especially likely since, based on what has been said and observed, the vein that broke is judged to be one of those small ones that nourish the muscles of the ribs; for I do not believe it to be in the lung itself, for the reasons already stated. Therefore, I will set down the remedies that are appropriate for this condition. 

And since the underlying cause of this ailment is a <term>flux</term> <note>A "flux" or "distillation" referred to a pathological flow of fluids (humors) from one part of the body to another—in this case, from the head down to the chest.</note>, or a distillation of sharp and thin matter from the head, and the disease itself is a rupture of continuity in the chest, our efforts must be focused on: 
1. Preventing the flux by cooling it. 
2. Thickening the <term>humors</term>. 
3. Aiding the healing of the broken vein's connection. 

Beginning, therefore, with the regulation of the things necessary for our life, and first regarding the **air**: I say that you must stay in a place where the air is temperate, so that it does in no way exceed into excessive heat. You must avoid the <term>hypocaust</term> <note>original: "hypocaustum"; a room heated from below. In this context, it refers to any overly heated room or sauna-like environment.</note>, or a steam room, or a closed chamber where a fire is kept so hot that it warms the room excessively. Such heat "melts" the matters in the head, which then descend to the chest and nourish the primary disease. 

Furthermore, the coldness of the air is harmful, as is air chilled by northern winds or snow, because it increases the distillation by constricting the body; besides that, it also harms the head by chilling it and diminishing its natural heat. Similarly, the night air is very harmful, as is foggy or misty air. Therefore, let the location be one that is neither too hot nor too cold, nor windy, nor misty, nor closed off, but moderate and temperate.

Next, the **food** should be of the kind that can, in some way, reduce the heat and thinness of the blood. It should not be "vaporous" <note>Foods thought to produce "vapors" that rise to the head and cause congestion or headaches.</note>, lest it fill the head and assist the distillation. Recommended foods include:
*   The meat of suckling veal or boiled kid goat.
*   In the broth of these meats, dishes should be made of <term>spelt</term>, rice, or crushed eggs.
*   *Panatella* <note>A traditional bread soup or pap.</note> made from ground bread, or washed bread.
*   Above all, I highly recommend barley broth made in the aforementioned meat broth, especially for dinner.

Eggs crushed into the broth are also excellent, as is the meat of boiled chickens. However, let them be boiled with <term>purslane</term> <note>original: "portulaca"; a succulent herb used in salads and soups for its cooling properties.</note> if it can be found fresh, or its seeds if the green plant is unavailable. It will also be useful if <term>sorrel</term> <note>original: "acetosa"; a perennial herb with a sour, lemony flavor, used here to "cool" the blood.</note> or its seeds are boiled with the said meats. Occasionally, your lordship might also eat the boiled meat of two-year-old wethers <note>Castrated rams, considered a more digestible meat in historical dietetics.</note>, and prepare the same dishes with their broth, boiling the herbs and seeds within it. Soft-boiled eggs <note>original: "oua sorbilia"; literally "sipping eggs," cooked just enough to be liquid.</note> are also excellent, or eggs cooked in an open pan—not hardened, but "trembling" (as they say) with **sugar**.

...among dairy products, that secondary cheese which is commonly called *puina* <note>original: "puina"; a Venetian term for ricotta cheese.</note> and fresh, soft, unsalted cheese may sometimes be eaten. Salads and all salted things, as well as every kind of legume, are harmful. Let the hour for eating be the second or third hour of the morning, and let there be a space of eight or ten hours between lunch and dinner. Dinner should be lighter than lunch, nor is it helpful to drink between lunch and dinner, especially wine, because it evaporates to the head and increases the <term>distillation</term> <note>A "distillation" or "flux" was the downward flow of harmful fluids from the head to the chest.</note>. Since your lordship writes that your lower belly empties its excrement spontaneously every day, that is excellent; however, if the bowels should happen to be suppressed, they must occasionally be moved with a common <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema.</note>. 

One must avoid daytime sleep as it fills the head; it is beneficial, therefore, to sleep at night two hours after dinner, with the head slightly raised. The pillow should be made of a material that does not cause heat but is somewhat drying, such as finely cut straw. It is not appropriate to sleep on one's back, as this contributes greatly to the rising of vapors; rather, one should sleep now on one side, now on the other. Excessive wakefulness will be harmful, because it sharpens and thins the blood, and inflames and dries the body. In the morning, when your lordship rises from bed and has dressed, I advise you to walk gently—I say *gently*...

Take one <term>drachm</term> <note>A unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams.</note> of **amber troches** <note>original: "trochiscorum de Karabe"; "Karabe" is the Arabic-derived term for amber, used here as an astringent.</note>; let three or five pills be made with **plantain water**, and let them be taken at dawn, after the taking of which it will be best to sleep. There are also many other simple medicines which physicians use; and I have experienced them, and among others, if it should be necessary, let this powder be made here. Take the **shells of chicken eggs**, cleaned of their skins and membranes, in whatever quantity and number you wish, and put them in a new pot; let it be covered with some membranous lid so that it can breathe as little as possible. Let the pot be placed in an **oven** <note>original: "clibano"; specifically a bread oven.</note> overnight after the bread has been removed from it, so that all the moisture of the said shells is dried out. Then let them be pounded in a mortar so that they are turned into a very fine powder. Of this powder, let one drachm’s weight be administered in the morning with a decoction of plantain or **sumac seeds** four or five hours before lunch. It will also be useful to continuously keep **red diadraganth** <note>A medicinal lozenge made from gum tragacanth.</note> made from **Eastern Armenian bole** <note>original: "bolo armenio orientali"; a high-quality medicinal red clay used to stop bleeding.</note> in the mouth. These are the things, Reverend Lord, which I wished to advise you at present in response to your letters regarding this your **unnatural condition** <note>original: "præter naturali dispositione"; a Galenic term for a state of disease or illness.</note>. I truly hope that with these things done, all will proceed for the better, so that you may have excellent health in the future; which may the Greatest God deign to grant you. Farewell.

...whether you are at home, or riding on a journey, you must not expose yourself to the winds or the burning sun unless you are dressed in suitable clothing and your head is covered with a hat or some other thing. Or let a dish be made of **almonds** and **pine nuts** with **rose water** and **verjuice** <note>original: "succo uuae acerbae"; the acidic juice of unripened grapes, used as a culinary acid before lemons were widely available.</note>. Use preserves which strengthen the stomach, such as **citrons** or **spiced quinces**, both before food and after food. # ADVICE FOR THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## Lord Valerian regarding an ulcer of the rectum, following liver
## flux, and very ancient pains of the joints.

### LETTER XVII.

You were most earnestly requesting, Most Illustrious Valerian, that we strive to the best of our ability to write clearly and thoroughly all those things which might benefit your now long-standing illness in the future: specifically so that, if possible, you might be restored to health, aided by my help and effort. To accomplish this, since at present enough leisure has been granted to us from public business, we shall not omit those things which seem necessary.

The condition, therefore, for which you set out for Italy (leaving aside the older pains of the joints) is a flux of the belly, and that indeed which doctors call **liver flux** <note>original: "fluxus iecorarius"; in Galenic medicine, this was a form of diarrhea where the stool resembled the washings of raw meat, believed to be caused by a weakness of the liver's ability to process nutrients.</note> together with a significant enough ulceration of the rectum. This poor condition of the liver <note>original: "iecinoris mala dispositio"</note> has reached a nearly excellent state and health (due to the remedies performed by us), so that now the greatest part of our curative intention focuses on the ulcer of the rectum. Because this ulcer is still nourished by the weakness of the old liver condition, liver-strengthening medicines must not be entirely omitted.

And although the method of curing intestinal ulcers has always been difficult for all doctors, both ancient and modern, for many reasons—which, lest this discourse of ours be too long-winded, we shall omit—I would not, for that reason, want you, my Lord, to abandon hope of its cure.

Therefore, I come to the care of the stated conditions, beginning with the regimen of the **six necessary things** <term>regimen sex rerum non-naturalium</term> <note>In the Renaissance, health was managed through six "non-natural" factors: air, food and drink, sleep and waking, motion and rest, evacuation and repletion, and the passions of the mind.</note>. First, therefore, one must beware of every excess in the qualities of the air, so that, if possible, the air is always temperate, especially in heat and cold. However, there should not be excessive dryness or humidity; for the one, namely dryness, sharpens heat, while the other <note>humidity</note> prepares the humors for putrefaction, besides the fact that very often, if humidity is excessive, it can chill the body. 

Therefore, all rainy, dark, and cloud-shadowed air is to be avoided; we also believe that the night air can be very harmful in this case. In the same way, one must beware of sweltering and dry air mixed with great heat, especially during the **dog days** <note>original: "diebus canicularibus"; the hottest days of summer (July/August), traditionally associated with the rising of the star Sirius, which were thought to be dangerous for the sick.</note> and times of maximum heat, since all strengths at that time are weak—

## PART TWO

...minced meat is the best food; but whatever meats are boiled, let them be boiled in **chalybeate water** <term>iron-fortified water</term>, that is, water in which glowing steel has been quenched. Among fruits, he may use raisins, fresh almonds, and even pistachios; moreover, **quinces** <note>original: "citonia"</note> cooked under hot ashes and eaten both before and after a meal are beneficial for strengthening the stomach. You shall set aside other fruits, as they are difficult to digest, such as **medlars** <note>original: "mespila"; a fruit related to apples that is only edible when it begins to decay or "blet."</note>, which very easily rot in a weak stomach and turn into gas, as well as most apples and others of that kind.

The hour for eating should be in the morning, three or four hours after sunrise. Dinner, however, should not be taken until eight or ten hours have passed since lunch, and the quantity of both food and drink should be less than at lunch. Whatever the case, always eat sparingly and drink sparingly; nothing will be more helpful.

The drink should be a moderate wine of medium flavor and warmth, neither sweet nor sour. If it must be diluted, let it be diluted with the aforementioned **chalybeate water**. As I said, it is not beneficial to drink a great deal, but only as much as serves to distribute the ingested food. Similarly, I judge that one should drink very little between lunch and dinner, or during the night.

And since (as I hear) an abundance of the best wines—or even those of moderate quality—is not always available in **Poland** <note>original: "Polonia"</note>, as such wines are rarely imported to you, for this reason you asked whether **beer** <note>original: "ceruisia"</note> could be safely drunk. I told you during the time you were in **Venice** <note>original: "Venetiis"</note> that beer is not of use, for it greatly harms the stomach and the internal organs. Therefore, if by chance you lack the aforementioned wine, we have devised a way to compose a drink in this manner:

Take:
*   Eight ounces of **barberry** fruit
*   Three drams of the best cinnamon
*   Two pounds of chalybeate spring water

Let them boil until a quarter part is consumed, then strain it. In this strained liquid, add:
*   Two ounces each of syrup of citrus peel (without musk) and **sugared rose-honey syrup** <note>original: "syrupi geleniabini saccharini"; a specific medicinal syrup often made from honey, sugar, and rose water.</note>.

Mix these and use this drink at both lunch and dinner; for first, it will be pleasing to the palate, and second, it will greatly strengthen the stomach, the intestines, and the liver. Likewise, all surfeit <note>excess</note> of both food and drink must be avoided, as it generates many "superfluities" <note>waste products or bad humors</note> and harms the stomach and intestines.

Before eating, let the stomach be rubbed with this **liniment** <term>a medicinal liquid or salve</term>:

Take:
*   One dram each of oil of wormwood, oil of mastic, and oil of roses
*   One and a half drams of the powder of **Abbot’s Diarhodon** <note>original: "diarhodonis abbatis"; a classical rose-based medicinal powder used to cool and strengthen the internal organs.</note>
*   One dram each of the "three sandals" powder <note>sandalwood</note> and red coral
*   A little wax

Mix these to make an ointment. Care must also be taken that sleep occurs at a suitable time, namely at night, two hours after dinner has passed.

### THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...nor during the day, unless perhaps there is a long-standing habit of sleeping during the day. If that should happen, let it be two hours after lunch. At night, however, he should sleep at will, for up to ten hours more or less, according to the necessity of the time. I say this because at certain times sleeping is especially beneficial, such as in winter and spring, and also when either some pain or another specific symptom demands it. In such a case, sleep is always profitable. Indeed, it is better to sleep than to stay awake too much, since through sleep all the faculties <term>virtutes</term> <note>In the medical theory of the time, "virtues" were the natural powers or faculties (like digestion or growth) that governed the body.</note> acquire strength.

And since wakefulness is the opposite of sleep, one must guard against excessive wakefulness; for through long wakefulness the spirits <term>spiritus</term> <note>Refers to the "vital spirits," a subtle substance believed to circulate through the body to facilitate life and sensation.</note> are dissolved, the body is inflamed, and it is prepared for "putrid fevers" resulting from poor digestion <note>original: "concoctione"</note> of food. 

Finally, according to the opinion of all the ancient physicians, disturbances of the mind <term>perturbationes animi</term> <note>These are what we would call "passions" or "emotions," which were believed to have a direct physical impact on health.</note> change our bodies greatly from their natural state. Therefore, one must guard against all mental disturbances, such as anger, fear, worry, sudden impulses, and grief, as well as other sad and fearful thoughts. 

This will be easily achieved if there is conversation with dear friends about pleasant things. Thus, one should live in pleasant places where there are gardens and other things that can induce joy, such as singing and the playing of musical instruments; for harmonic proportion is greatly able to make the mind cheerful and pleasant. Similarly, the sight of beautiful things cheers the mind significantly, since the outer senses are the mind's servants and messengers. In this regard, the sight of beautiful and honorable noblewomen <note>original: "matronarum"</note> provides the greatest delight to the mind. 

We shall not overlook sexual intercourse <note>original: "venereos complexus"</note>, which, although it might make the mind cheerful and even lighten the body, does not seem beneficial in this case. It drains the strength, dries out and cools the body, and leads toward a state of "senile wasting" <note>original: "senilem tabem"; a physical decline resembling premature aging.</note>, especially in those recovering from illness. 

But since **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, regarded as the "Father of Medicine."</note> said that consideration must be given to age, habit, time, and other factors: because you are a young man, even if a long-standing illness does not favor it, it sometimes happens (when the seminal matter demands it) that a sexual embrace occurs. However, it should not be provoked by flirtations, nor should it be frequent. For all physicians, both ancient and modern, have judged that such an embrace—if it is not moderate—is most destructive. 

Having touched upon these matters, I shall turn my discourse toward medicinal remedies. And since, as I said above, the unnatural conditions which presently trouble you most...

->**PART TWO.**<-

...remain, the affections of the intestines and of the natural organs are such that the first affection was a liver flux <term>fluxus iecorarius</term> <note>original: "fluxus iecorarius"; a type of diarrhea thought to originate from a weakness or "cooling" of the liver.</note>, which is clearly evident through the excrements of the belly, which were like the washings of meat <note>A classic medical description of bloody or serous discharge that looks like the water used to rinse raw flesh.</note> and sometimes like the dregs of wine. Thus, in my opinion, it needs no other testimony. Therefore, I shall begin with that affection from which this ulceration followed, which has not yet been entirely restored to health, although both the liver <term>hepar</term> and the ulcer are doing better. This second affection, then, or disease, is an old, foul ulcer of the rectum <term>intestini recti</term>, and a quite significant one at that, since a great deal of pus <term>saniei</term> has descended from it, and even now some descends. But it is not as bad as before, nor in such quantity, nor with such sensation or painful urge to evacuate. All these things clearly show that you are doing better and are tending toward health, and they promise a total recovery in the future; even though **Hippocrates** said that ulcers of the intestines are very difficult to cure.

I will begin, therefore, with the remedies that can remove the bad and contrary temperament <note>In medieval medicine, "temperament" refers to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of the liver and the stomach. Since weakness of the stomach produces many raw superfluities <note>Undigested materials that the body cannot use.</note>, and the hot temperament of the liver was the cause of burnt humors <note>Humors, such as bile, that have become "overheated" and caustic, leading to tissue damage.</note> and of the ulceration of the rectum, it produces many burnt humors which nourish the aforementioned ulceration. First, therefore, besides the regimen mentioned above, let us proceed with the medicinal regimen by taking syrups effective for all the things mentioned before, which shall be these:

**Recipe:**
*   **Syrup of simple chicory** — 1 ounce
*   **Rose syrup** — 1/2 ounce
*   **Decoction of chicory, five-leaf <note>Also known as cinquefoil.</note>, and plantain** — 3 ounces

Mix these, and let it be taken in the morning at dawn. And since the disease is long-standing, it requires stronger measures. Therefore, after you have taken the above-described syrup in the morning for several days, you shall purge the burnt materials, prepared by the syrups, with a light medicine that evacuates once or twice. This will be easily done with this mild remedy:

**Recipe:**
*   **Diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" mild purgative electuary used to cleanse the system of all humors.</note> — 1 ounce
*   **Choice mature rhubarb, powdered** — 1 dram

Mix these, and let a drink be made with white sugar or with the aforementioned decoction of chicory, five-leaf, and plantain. Let it be taken in the morning five hours before lunch. Or, if another method of evacuation is more pleasing, let 1 dram of choice mature rhubarb be infused in the aforementioned syrup and administered in the morning as I said. After this first light evacuation, it is my advice that the treatment be carried out in the latter part of summer, when the air has become milder, and after the dog days <term>caniculares dies</term> <note>The hottest days of the year (roughly July to August), when heavy medical treatments were often avoided due to the extreme heat.</note> when the winds are calm and the breeze is gentle...

## NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

...as soon as you begin to breathe more easily. I say again, for the greater restoration and strength of the stomach and liver, it will be best to take more effective syrups in this manner: **Take one drachm of syrup of chicory with rhubarb** <note>original: "syrupi de cichorea cum rhabarbaro"</note> according to the description of **Nicolò of Florence** <note>Nicolò Falcucci (d. 1412), a famous Florentine physician whose massive medical encyclopedia was a standard reference.</note>; **half a drachm each of barberry and currant syrups**; and **three drachms of a decoction of plantain, chicory, cinquefoil, and parsley**. Mix these, and let them be taken in the morning, at dawn, for several days, so that both the stomach and liver may be strengthened and the heat of the liver may be tempered, lest it burn the humors. 

After these syrups, I would again recommend—for the final evacuation of those matters that are produced daily—that the aforementioned light medicine of **universal purgative** <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>original: "diacatholicon"; a "catch-all" laxative electuary used to purge all four humors.</note> and ripe rhubarb be taken in the form of a pill <term>bolus</term> or a drink. The drink would please me more, since its virtue and substance can be more easily distributed to the neighboring veins if it is swallowed. Or at the very least, the last-described syrup should be taken with one drachm of the best ripe rhubarb infused in it. 

After this light evacuation has been administered twice, it will be best finally to take things that can strengthen the stomach, liver, and intestines, lest you fall into a relapse. For where a disease, or long-lasting diseases, have taken hold, the limbs grow weak and easily incline back toward their old morbid disposition—which is very often worse than the first and harder to cure due to the already mentioned weakness of the limbs. 

Those things which can strengthen the said limbs are these: the **confection of the three sandals** <term>diatrium sandalorum</term> <note>original: "diatrium sandalorum"; a cooling preparation made from red, white, and yellow sandalwood.</note>, of which it will be best to take one or two lozenges every morning, four hours before lunch. Likewise, **two-year-old rose sugar** in the quantity of half an ounce, with half a drachm of the aromatic powder **rose of the Abbot** <term>diarrhodon Abbatis</term> <note>original: "diarrhodon Abbatis"; a famous cooling digestive powder containing roses, sandalwood, and spices.</note>, can excellently strengthen the stomach and liver in this case, if taken in the morning four hours before lunch. 

Likewise, I highly praise the eating of **raisins**, both before food, with food, and after food, according to the opinion of all physicians and especially **Galen** in the eighth book of *On Medicines According to Location*, where he placed the description of the **raisin electuary** <term>electuarii cyphi</term> <note>original: "electuarii cyphi"; a medicinal paste made primarily from raisins (Greek: "kyphi").</note> on the authority of **Andromachus**. **Avicenna** also approves of this description in the third book of the *Canon*, in the chapter on the weakness of the liver. I myself would also praise this confection in the winter time, since it can preserve the patient from that future extreme weakness of the liver, from which patients very often fall into **dropsy** <term>aqua intercutem</term> <note>original: "aqua intercutem"; literally "water between the skin," referring to edema or fluid buildup caused by liver failure.</note>. But if I feared any heat from its ingredients, I would mix into the said raisin electuary an equal amount of rose sugar to temper the heat, and I would administer it thus mixed every single [morning]...
