...in the morning. There are also other common confections described by **Master Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue (the Elder or Younger), influential medieval Arabic medical authorities whose pharmaceutical works were standard in the Renaissance.</note> which are extremely effective and time-tested for treating and preventing future **dropsy** <term>aqua intercutem</term> <note>Literally "water between the skin," referring to anasarca or edema associated with liver failure.</note>. These include **confection of lac** <note>original: "confectio dialacæ"; a resin-based preparation used for liver and spleen disorders.</note> and **confection of turmeric** <note>original: "confectio diacurcumæ".</note>. If I were to fear the excessive heat of these medicines, I would mix them with the aforementioned **rose sugar** <note>original: "saccharum rosaceum"; sugar infused with rose petals, used to cool the temperament of other drugs.</note> and take them in the morning, four or five hours before lunch. There are also preserves that can be taken after food, such as **quince preserve** <term>diacytonitem</term> <note>A medicinal marmalade made from quinces, used to settle the stomach.</note>, either with or without spices; even plain quince preserved with sugar can be taken after a meal. This should be sufficient regarding the primary disease, both for its prevention and for the complications that might follow it.

It remains for me to write concerning the care of the **foul ulcer in the rectum** <note>original: "ulceris sordidi in intestino recto"</note>. However, since many things have already been done by us when I was attending to your specific care—which contributed a great deal—it can be said without hesitation, judging by the signs of the quantity and quality of the **pus** <gloss>saniei</gloss>, that the condition is in decline. Therefore, setting aside the recollection of past remedies, I shall write of the future life-giving remedies that should be administered for the ulcer. These remedies will consist of **enemas** <term>clysteria</term> that partly cleanse the ulcer, partly dry it, and partly strengthen the intestines. The first goal to be intended by the enema is to cleanse the pus, ease the pain, and preserve the strength of the intestine. All these things you shall do with the enemas described below.

An enema that possesses the power of cleansing and easing pain while leaving the intestines strengthened is as follows: **Take a quantity of the intestines of a goat, or a wether <note>A castrated ram.</note>, or a calf**, as much as you wish. Let them be boiled thoroughly. Then, **take four pounds of said broth; three ounces of barley with its husk; two handfuls of the roots and leaves of cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphyllonis"; a common astringent herb.</note>; one handful of chamomile flowers; and four ounces of the best honey.** Let them boil until a quarter part is consumed, then strain it. Of this strained liquid, let eight ounces be administered by enema twice a day, before lunch and dinner, for several days—provided the judgment of those most distinguished physicians requires it based on the pus; specifically, if the substance of the discharge is not uniform and smooth. 

Once uniformity and smoothness are observed, the intention should be changed toward greater drying, though without abandoning the goal of cleansing the ulcer. This shall be done with this enema described by **Galen** in the ninth book of *On Medicines According to the Places Affected*, which I have tested in similar cases: **Take three ounces of the ash of burnt paper; one drachm each of orpiment <note>original: "auri pigmenti"; an arsenic sulfide mineral used in small amounts in traditional medicine for its caustic/cleansing properties.</note> and gallnut; and one and a half drachms each of sandarac <note>A resin from the North African cypress tree.</note>, quicklime, bitumen, and sulfur.** Let lozenges be made from these with juice...

## TO THE MOST EXCELLENT DOCTOR OF LAWS,
## Lord Girolamo Cesana. On the weakness of the

### EPISTLE XVIII.

I HAVE read, most excellent man, what you wrote to the magnificent and most illustrious knight Bollanus <note>Likely Domenico Bollani (1514–1579), a Venetian diplomat and later Bishop of Brescia.</note>, to whom I confess I owe a great deal; I have also spoken about these matters with the most excellent and learned Girolamo Amalteo <note>A famous physician and Latin poet from the prominent Amalteo family.</note>, who explained everything said and done with the greatest diligence. Having been asked by the most illustrious knight, I shall write to you about these things in order. 

First, I consider this long-standing weakness of the nerves and muscles <term>lacertorum</term> <note>Literally "lizards," a common anatomical term for muscles due to their shape under the skin.</note>, the tremor, and the inability to perform the functions of the limbs throughout the whole body. This arises from an abundance of phlegmatic <term>pituitoſa</term> matter <note>One of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with coldness and moisture.</note> first generated in the stomach, and then transmitted from the head to the nervous members. It does this in such a way that it first blocks the passage of the "spirits" <note>In Galenic medicine, "vital spirits" carried through the nerves were thought to enable movement and sensation.</note> to the nerves originating from the spinal cord <term>nuca</term> <note>A Medieval Latin term derived from Arabic, referring to the spinal cord or the nape of the neck.</note>; then, by its great quantity, it moistens them, which results in the arms, legs, and the entire body being moved only with great difficulty. 

Furthermore, I hear that your excellence fell upon your right side, from which a contusion <term>cõtuſio</term> <note>A bruise or internal injury from impact.</note> occurred in that part and place which the Latins call the hip-bone <term>coxendicem</term> and the Greeks call the ischium <term>iſchiam</term>. In that very place, a huge pain immediately followed, which still remains; the tremor and the inability or weakness of voluntary motion also remain. If I wished to trace all these things back to their causes, the progress of this discourse would be long; however, I will not pass over this one point: namely, that all conditions contrary to nature have contracted their first origin from a certain chilling of the stomach, which generates many (as the Physicians say) crudities <term>cruditates</term> <note>Undigested or "raw" humors that have not been properly processed by the body's heat.</note>, or phlegmatic superfluities...

...humors, which, because they could not be corrected by the heat of the liver <term>iecinoris</term>, have occupied the entire body, and the brain especially—not only through the nourishing veins, but also through continuous evaporation. From this, a cold and moist temperament was produced and communicated to the whole, along with the presence of much phlegmatic <term>pituitoſarum</term> <note>Phlegm was one of the four humors of ancient medicine, considered cold and moist; an excess was thought to cause sluggishness or tremors.</note> matter mixed with the blood and other humors. As for the pre-disposing causes <term>causæ procatarcticæ</term> <note>These are the external or triggering causes, such as environmental factors or lifestyle choices, that lead to the onset of a disease.</note> of the said condition—since they are no longer present, and we cannot reach a correct method of administering aid by their removal—I will pass over them in silence for now. I will say only this: the case is extremely difficult to cure, not only for an absent physician but even for one who is present, visiting daily, seeing everything, and examining it with reason. Nevertheless, whatever the case may be, I shall write briefly what I believe should be done.

The first intention, and that from which we must begin, will be the alteration of the air by its contrary—namely, that it should lean toward hot and dry. Since it is winter and the place of residence is cold, a fire should always be lit in the bedroom, so that the chill of the air is lessened and the place is kept dry. It cannot be beneficial to heat the room through the evaporation of a hypocaust <term>hypocausti</term> <note>An ancient system of heating where hot air from a furnace circulated under the floor. Massa warns against it here, likely because he believes the "heavy" or steamy heat would aggravate the humors in the head.</note>, since such heat fills the head and also liquefies the matter contained within it, which then descends to the nervous members. Therefore, let the air of the room be moderately warm and dry from the lighting of a fire. Exercise would indeed be most helpful, but since the capacity for it is not granted due to the weakness and tremor of the limbs, it is enough to have said that it could be beneficial if the condition of the limbs allowed it; I shall now move on to the dietary regimen.

Galen <note>A Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years.</note> testified in his book *On the Thinning Diet* <note>original: "Victu attenuante"</note> how much the scarcity or thinning of food can achieve in cold and long-lasting diseases. For as he said—and reason and daily experience confirm—not a few chronic diseases have been removed solely by the administration of a thinning diet without the exhibition of any medicines. Indeed, it dissolves and dissipates thick, cold humors. Therefore, first, let bread be made from the flour of the best wheat, not entirely cleared of bran, and in it let crushed seeds of anise or fennel be placed; let it be well-salted, leavened, and baked. The meats should be from birds, such as pheasants, partridges, and those birds which the common people call quails, turtledoves, blackbirds, thrushes, sparrows, and other birds of this kind. Furthermore, those that are not fat should be chosen; they generally follow the same course; but those that live in water or marshy places, such as geese, ducks, and similar...

...similar things should be forbidden, as they produce thick nourishment. Among the four-legged animals, the meat of kids <note>Young goats.</note> is praised, followed by the meat of young hares. If veal is eaten, let it be boiled with the roots of parsley, fennel, celery, and the like, or their seeds. In the broth of these meats, boiled with the roots or seeds, a dish should be made of grated bread—which they call <term>panatellam</term> <note>A restorative bread-based soup or pap.</note>—or let bread be soaked in the said broth, or let an egg be beaten into it. Also, emmer <note>A type of hulled wheat common in ancient and medieval diets.</note> boiled in the same broth will be an excellent dish. These meats may also be roasted and sprinkled with spices reduced to a powder, such as cinnamon, mace, cloves, and the seeds of fennel and anise.

Before lunch, it will be excellent to chew a portion of candied ginger root (they call it "green" <note>Fresh or preserved ginger was often referred to as 'green' to distinguish it from the dried powder.</note>), or half of a candied nutmeg <term>nucis muscatæ</term>, or galangal root <term>galangæ</term>, or candied aromatic calamus <term>calami aromatici</term> <note>Also known as sweet flag, used as a digestive aid.</note>. If you wish to swallow a soft-boiled egg, it will be beneficial to mix in a portion of powdered pepper. After lunch, you should eat the seeds of fennel or anise candied with white sugar, or pine nuts, or pistachios.

Let the time for dinner <term>cœnæ</term> be at least eight hours after lunch, and let it be light. For example, before the meal, one might eat capers <term>cappares</term> preserved with <term>oxymelite</term> <note>A medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar.</note>, and soon after, the *panatella* made from the broth boiled with the aforementioned roots or seeds. If you eat a portion of roasted partridge or another roasted bird in a small quantity, you will do very well. After dinner, let the seeds of fennel and anise, or pine nuts or pistachios, be taken again.

All fish and other moistening foods that fill the head—such as most legumes, dairy products, fruits, and greens—should be given up. For drink, let there be honey-water <note>Mead or hydromel.</note> boiled with ten crushed peppercorns; or let it be betony <term>betonicæ</term> water boiled with honey. Indeed, wine is harmful because it fills the head and causes cold matter to penetrate the nervous members; it is also harmful because, in a stomach filled with many phlegmatic <term>pituitoſis</term> humors, it easily turns into vinegar. Vinegar, moreover, harms the brain and nerves primarily and by its own nature. However, during the true decline of the illness—which is recognized by the lessening of the tremor and better vigor of the limbs in motion—an old wine that is neither sour nor sweet, but somewhat potent, should be drunk in moderation; nor should one eat too much, especially in the evening hours at dinner.

Care must also be taken to soften the belly if the feces are not expelled naturally, by administering enemas <term>clyſteria</term> and a decoction of mallow leaves, beets, betony, and chamomile <term>chamæmillæ</term>, which should be boiled in common water. From this decoction, take one pound...

### THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICOLÒ MASSA
<note>original: "NIC. MASSAE EPIST. MED."</note>

...of oil of white lilies, or of bitter almonds, and of rose honey <note>Honey infused with rose petals, used for its soothing properties.</note>, 3 drachms <note>A drachm, represented by the symbol ʒ, is a measurement of weight roughly equal to 3.9 grams.</note> each; half a drachm of <term>hiera picra</term> <note>A traditional bitter purgative medicine, literally "holy bitter."</note>; 3 drachms of <term>hiera logodium</term> <note>A complex medicinal compound used to purge the head and nerves.</note>; and 1 drachm of common salt. Mix these, and let it be applied in the morning before lunch, every fourth day, or even on alternate days.

One must be careful of excessive and long sleep, which should not exceed the space of seven hours; nor should you begin to sleep until two hours after dinner. But if sleep is prolonged beyond what is prescribed, the patient must be woken up, because long periods of sleep fill the head and cool the entire body. Wakefulness, however, does the opposite, for it dries and heats the body; therefore, one must strive to avoid sleep as much as possible, especially during the day. Finally, since the passions of the soul <note>In the Renaissance, "passions of the soul" referred to emotions or psychological states, which were believed to directly impact physical health.</note> greatly change the body from its natural constitution, one must flee from sadness, grief, worry, and all bad thoughts, by meditating on happy things, hoping well for one’s health, and occupying oneself with words and deeds that move one toward joy, and by rejoicing with dear friends. Having touched upon these matters regarding the "six unnatural things" <note>The "six non-naturals" (air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, evacuation/repletion, and passions) were the foundation of Galenic preventative medicine.</note> necessary for health, I shall now subjoin the remaining medical methods to be performed.

Indeed, our first intention is to correct the bad temperament <note>The "bad temperament" or dyscrasia referred to an imbalance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which in this case is described as "cold and moist."</note> which is cold and moist. We shall first evacuate the matter that resides in the stomach and the common vessels, which is generated daily and can act as an obstacle to the altering medicines, in this manner: Take one ounce of a <term>lenitive electuary</term> <note>A mild, honey-based laxative paste.</note> with 2.5 drachms of the species of <term>hiera</term>; take this in the morning four hours before lunch. Then, on the following morning, to prepare the remaining matter and to alter that unnaturally cold temperament, you shall take this syrup: Take syrup of <term>stoechas</term> <note>French lavender (Lavandula stoechas), believed to strengthen the brain and nerves.</note> and rose honey, 1 drachm of each; let it be diluted with a decoction of betony, ground pine <note>original: "iua"</note>, and sage, 2 drachms of each, or let it be taken with the distilled waters of said herbs twice a day—namely, in the morning before daybreak and in the evening several hours before dinner. You shall take this similarly for several days until some "preparation" of the raw humors <note>In humoral theory, "preparing" or "cooking" humors meant making them thin enough to be purged from the body.</note> appears in the urine. When this appears, the belly must be purged again with the medication written below; for example:

Take 1 drachm of lenitive electuary, 3 drachms of <term>Hiera Pachii</term> as described by Scribonius <note>Scribonius Largus, a Roman physician; his "Hiera" was a famous purgative recipe.</note>, or 3 drachms of <term>Hiera Logodion</term> of Nicholas <note>Referring to the "Antidotarium Nicolai," a famous medieval medical text.</note>. Let them be diluted with the aforementioned decoction and taken in the morning five hours before lunch. On the following morning, however, sip half a bowl, so to speak, of capon broth <note>original: "iuris capi"</note> in which betony and ground pine have been boiled, to which add 2 drachms of rose honey. Then, after the said evacuation, one must pause from the evacuations of loosening medicines for several days; but...

## PART TWO

Every morning before lunch, for at least two hours, you should take two spoonfuls of this syrup made of wormwood <note>original: "absinthio"</note> and stoechas <note>French lavender (Lavandula stoechas), often used for neurological disorders.</note>, 2 drachms <note>The symbol ʒ represents a drachm, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of each; and 1 drachm of oxymel of squill <note>original: "oxymellis scillitici"; a medicinal syrup made of honey, vinegar, and sea onions (squill), used as an expectorant and digestive aid.</note>. Mix and use these. Meanwhile, you shall stimulate the bowels twice a week with the previously mentioned clyster <note>An enema.</note>; and before eating, you shall soothe the region of the stomach with this liniment: Take oil of spike <note>Lavender oil.</note>, of wormwood, and of mastic, half a drachm <note>The "s." stands for "semis," meaning half.</note> of each; 1 drachm of the species of galangal <note>original: "diagalangae"; a warming spice blend based on the galangal root.</note>; half a drachm each of cloves and cinnamon; and a little wax. Mix these and let a liniment be made. However, once the week has passed, six hours after dinner following the second evacuation <note>The second scheduled bowel cleansing.</note>, you shall take these pills: Take 2 scruples <note>The symbol ℈ represents a scruple, about 1.3 grams.</note> of cochia pills <note>original: "pilularum cochiarum"; highly effective purgative pills usually containing aloes and colocynth.</note> and 1 scruple of euphorbium <note>A potent, irritating resin from the spurge plant used as a drastic purgative.</note>; let three pills be made from them to be taken as described above. If you drink the syrup noted above along with these pills, you may expect a more successful operation.

Once these things are done, certain local remedies must be administered to the origins of the nerves. First, beginning with the milder ones, the entire spine should be anointed with warm oil of white lilies for several days. Then, to this oil, add oil of costus <note>An aromatic root from India used in ancient and Renaissance medicine.</note>, or of peppers, or of fox <note>original: "vulpinum"; oil in which a fox had been boiled, traditionally believed to cure joint and nerve pains.</note>, of juniper, of iris, or something similar. Let the site of the bruising be anointed with this liniment: Take 1 drachm each of marshmallow ointment <note>original: "dialtheae"</note>, oil of laurel, and oil of earthworms <note>original: "de lumbricis"; thought to soothe nerves and reduce inflammation.</note>; mix and use while warm, anointing the site and surrounding parts well. Or, let this plaster be made: Take flowers of chamomile, betony, stoechas, laurel berries, costus, and sage; let them be powdered, and with <term>defrutum</term> <note>Grape juice boiled down to half or a third of its volume, also called sapa.</note>, which they call *sapa*, let a plaster be made. Let it be applied warm over the site of the pain after the anointing with the aforementioned liniment; if this plaster is placed over the spine of the back after the anointing, it will be of the greatest help.

Furthermore, we must not cease from those things which strengthen the stomach and the head and correct a bad "cold and moist" temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, tremors were often attributed to an excess of phlegm (cold and moist), which needed to be countered by warming and drying remedies.</note>. This is done by taking every single morning some confection from those to be mentioned, among which *pleres archonticon* <note>original: "pliris arcoticum"; a restorative powder or "confection of the masters" used to strengthen the heart and brain.</note> will be very beneficial if you take one or two tablets <note>original: "rotulas"</note> in the morning before food, and even after. For this purpose, the "confection of the three peppers" <note>original: "confectione trium pipereum"</note> is also wonderful, as it strengthens the stomach and thins the phlegmatic matter in the head. I also praise the confection of galangal, of musk <note>original: "diamusci"</note>, and of ambergris <note>original: "diaambrae"</note>. But among the rest, the confection of <term>Mithridate</term> and of <term>Theriac</term> <note>Two of the most famous polypharmaceutical "cure-alls" of the era, containing dozens of ingredients including opium and viper flesh.</note> holds the leadership in strengthening the stomach, head, nerves, and the entire body. Therefore, once the aforementioned evacuations of the overabundant humors have been administered, and the remaining altering treatments both internal and external have been performed, use either the Mithridatic or Theriac confection indifferently, for several hours in the morning before food...

I do not wish for you to wonder why, in writing about evacuation <note>The clearing of humors from the body.</note>, I have passed over the evacuation of blood <note>Bloodletting.</note> in silence. For although many believe that the opening of the veins of the anus (which they call hemorrhoids) <note>original: "mariscas"</note> can be beneficial in such a case and unnatural condition, I myself would never recommend it for your Excellence. This judgment is based on the essence of the disease, the multitude of crude humors <note>In the medical theory of the time, "crude" humors were fluids that had not been properly "cooked" or processed by the body’s internal heat, leading to blockages or illness.</note> with which you abound, and also the long duration of the illness.

Finally, I shall not omit that which perhaps your Excellence greatly desires to know: whether a decoction of Indian wood (which they call *guaiacum*, after the island from which it is brought to us) <note>Guaiac, or "Holy Wood," was a famous New World remedy imported from the Caribbean, primarily used to treat syphilis.</note>—whether, I say, prepared in some way with water or with wine, using a significant quantity of its bark—might be of use to you and could help your unnatural disposition. Furthermore, you asked whether drinking sulfurous, nitrous, or aluminous thermal waters, or bathing in them, or dousing <note>original: "gucia"; likely referring to *gutta*, a therapy where medicinal water is poured or dripped steadily over the head.</note> (as they call it) the head, might be beneficial in the future.

To these questions, lest I weary you, I respond briefly as follows: Indian wood, by a certain marvelous virtue—both in its manifest temperament <note>The physical qualities of the wood (e.g., its heat or dryness).</note> and its hidden substance <note>The "occult" or chemical properties that are not immediately apparent.</note>—cures the "French disease" <note>original: "morbum gallicum"; a common name for syphilis in the 16th century.</note> and certain other diseases related to it. However, it does not cure all "cold" diseases. This is according to Aristotle’s opinion: "not just anything acts on anything," but rather a specific thing acts on a specific thing, according to certain modes, laws, and determined conditions regarding the patient's matter or quality. 

Now, your unnatural temperament, acquired over many years, as well as the cause, the matter, the tremor and weakness of your limbs, the part in which the disease is generated, and the subsequent symptoms and other afflictions—these do not allow for a comparison with the temperament, cause, and matter of the French disease. Therefore, the virtue and use of the wood cannot serve as a common medicine for them. Furthermore, the method of preparation, especially with wine, seems to harm the part which most contributes to the tremor and impotence of the limbs; for wine harms the brain, the spinal cord <note>original: "nucæ"; derived from Arabic, this term was used by medieval and Renaissance physicians to refer to the spinal marrow.</note>, the nerves, and the origin of the nerves themselves—not to mention what I have said about its tendency to cool the stomach...

...easily converted into vinegar, so that it may later act as a vehicle carrying the medicinal material to the innermost parts of the nervous members. Nor can wood boiled in water <note>A reference to the decoction of Guaiac wood mentioned on the previous page.</note> be of benefit, since it does not possess that heating, thinning, and drying power necessary to transform the phlegm <term>pituita: one of the four humors, characterized as cold and moist; here describing a viscous or watery buildup</term>—which varies in substance, being watery and viscous and having no heat of its own—or to restore it to a healthy state. Only once that humor is changed can the cold and moist temperament, which has become habitual, be converted back to a balanced state. Therefore, all thought of administering a decoction of Indian wood in the future should be set aside. 

Enough would have been said, had I not heard that your Excellence drank the waters of the Abano baths <note>The thermal springs of Abano Terme, near Padua, famous for their medicinal properties since antiquity.</note> and washed your entire body in them, and even received a douching <note>original: "guciam"; likely a Latinization of the Italian "doccia," a treatment where thermal water is poured or dropped onto a specific body part, in this case the head.</note> upon your head. However, this was done so out of order that I am ashamed a famous physician allowed it to happen; but whatever the case, even "good Homer sometimes nods" <note>A famous Latin proverb (*quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus*) meaning that even the most skilled experts can make mistakes.</note>. I would say, indeed, that the Abano waters can be very beneficial if administered in the proper order and at the right time; but since at present neither the season nor many other circumstances permit their use, these words shall suffice. May God, the Best and Greatest, who alone heals sickness, deign to lead you to your desired health. 

From Venice, November 23, 1556. Written in haste while suffering from illness, Nicolaus Massa.

## Lord Joannes Laimiger, Archpriest of Villach, 
## concerning the French Disease. <note>The "French Disease" (morbus Gallicus) was the common 16th-century term for syphilis.</note>

But the matter <note>The infectious or morbid substance according to humor theory.</note> flowed down from the head to other members and, as he himself reports, the disease was stirred up anew; in place of the pustules, certain hard tumors and malignant, filthy ulcers appeared.

But if anyone should ask: if there is diminished digestion in the liver, how can choleric humors—which are made by the final decoction <note>The "cooking" or processing of nutrients in the body to create blood and other humors.</note> of blood—be generated? To this I think the answer must be that digestion is not therefore removed, but diminished and corrupted, or affected by some malignancy; and therefore many choleric humors can be generated, albeit in a diminished state, which are not good for the body, but evil and contrary to health. I could resolve this in another way, but let these briefly spoken things suffice. For it does not escape me that there are many opinions about the efficient causes in this disease, which it is not our purpose to review at present—and especially that opinion which, assigning no natural sensory cause, pronounces it to be an affection of a higher faculty <note>Perhaps referring to astrological or divine causes rather than physical ones.</note>. ...be removed by the aforementioned temperate qualities of certain medicines. But since I do not intend to dispute the opinions of others here, but only to investigate diseases through their accidents <note>In Galenic medicine, an "accident" is a symptom or secondary condition resulting from a primary disease.</note> and causes, I shall set those opinions aside for the present. Having understood the cause of the pustules and the generation of tumors—or hard abscesses <note>original: "apostematum"</note>, which appear in the second place after the pustules—let us proceed to the explanation. 

These symptoms are formed from thick matter when the expulsive power <note>The "virtus expulsiva" was the body's natural ability to push harmful substances or waste from the internal organs out toward the skin.</note> of the body is strong. These tumors, when heat supervenes or when some hotter matter is mixed in and retained, begin to putrefy and, as we see through our senses, they turn into ulcers. There are, moreover, pains of the joints, nerves, and muscles, which arise from thick matter when the expulsive power is weaker; for nature always does (when it can) that which is better <note>A common medieval medical maxim: nature attempts to push toxins to the surface (the skin) to save the vital organs, but if the body is weak, the toxins settle in the joints and muscles instead.</note>. 

These mentioned pustules, tumors, pains, and ulcerations are the signs, or accidents, that declare this sickness and distinguish it from all others. This sickness is a single entity because it proceeds from a single origin. Pustules, abscesses, ulcers, and pains are indeed the accidents accompanying this disease. This does not mean that all of them must be present; it suffices, for example, that when a small amount of matter is mixed with a thin [subtle] substance, pustules appear. The symptoms vary according to the diversity of the mixture and the strength of the body’s power: thus, sometimes pains appear, sometimes tumors, and sometimes all appear together according to the said diversity of the mixture and the strength of the power. 

Whether the sickness be old or new <note>Massa is likely addressing the contemporary debate over whether syphilis was a "new" disease brought from the Americas or an "old" disease described by the ancients under different names.</note>, it does not matter to know; let those things which have been said about its essence suffice for the present. Namely, it is a bad disposition of the liver toward coldness and humidity <note>In the humoral system, the liver was the seat of blood production; a "cold and moist" liver failed to "cook" the blood properly, leading to raw, phlegmatic humors.</note>, communicated to the whole body. From this arise bad pustules, hard abscesses, malignant ulcers, and pains of the joints, nerves, and muscles. Sometimes all these are present; sometimes only pains or tumors appear without the others, and sometimes others appear without these. 

No one doubts that the humors causing such accidents are predominantly cold and undigested. This is known both by their whiteness and their hardness, by the long duration of the illness, and also by the time of the movement of the painful affliction, which usually torments the patient at sunset <note>Night pains (nocturnal dolors) were a hallmark symptom of syphilis, which Massa attributes here to the cooling of the body at night.</note>. It is also known by the rare and slight presence of fever, for such a disease is never, or rarely, accompanied by fever. Finally, to speak in a word, if we may argue from the things that help and those that harm: the symptoms are helped by hot treatments. Yet we do not say that this matter is so purely cold that it has no hotter humor mixed in; it contains enough heat to sometimes cause it to evaporate. This evaporation is the reason why the disease is contagious. Man-

...tules are, as I said, the difficulties in this matter, which I leave aside as I hurry to more important things. Having noted the essence of the disease, I proceed to declare the particular **complexion** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual's body.</note> of this Most Reverend man, which will be highly necessary. 

I say that his complexion is **choleric** <note>Associated with yellow bile; typically characterized by a hot and dry nature.</note> with a certain sub-dominion of accidental coldness. This appears clearly by considering his principal organs. For since his head is large enough in respect to his body, it denotes a dominion of heat. And since in practical affairs and intellectual discourse he is very skillful, gifted with talent, and of good judgment, it is certain that this also arises from a warm temperament. The beauty and proportion in the parts of his head show the same temperament. The color of the hair of both the head and beard, tending toward blackness with some redness, leads to the same judgment. 

Furthermore, the most principal organ, which is the heart, is (as it appears) of a hot and dry complexion. This is declared by a fairly broad chest, greatness of spirit, generosity, agility in movement, promptness, and speed; because he is almost always in motion, this can only proceed from thin blood that is not very fatty. The hair on his chest, which is not very extensive, also bears witness to this. Truly he has a liver of a hot and dry complexion, for all the limbs being well-extended and not fatty declare this; and similarly the veins of the whole body, which are large. 

The stomach, however, is quite temperate, because it is fleshy enough and digests well, and he feels neither belching nor fumes. Therefore, it must be concluded that he deviates from a balanced temperament <note>original: "temperamento iustitiali"</note> through heat and dryness. The sub-dominion of accidental coldness, however, arises from a superfluous accidental humidity of the head, which blunts the heat. 

Whence, in applying this, I say: since we know the quantity of the sickness through the measure of the natural temperament, as <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD) was the foundational authority on medicine in the Renaissance.</note> taught, by reason of his complexion—since the sickness is not proportional to his native temperament—it is to be feared and is more difficult to cure. ...of its proportion is to be feared, yet by reason of his age and good vital strength <term>virtue (virtutis): the innate life-force or energy that drives bodily functions in Galenic medicine</term>, we must say that the condition is easier to cure. Let these words suffice for the consideration of the sickness, its causes, symptoms, and prognosis; there would be many problems and many difficulties to be solved, all of which I omit in my pursuit of brevity.

To transfer myself, therefore, to the particular regimen: in the first place, since air is so necessary to us—as Haly Abbas <note>original: "Aliabbas"; a famous 10th-century Persian physician whose works were central to European medical education</note> said in the fifth book of his *Theory*, the air must be considered above all else, because whether we wish it or not, we must grant it to the sick, and it contributes greatly to the transformation of our bodies. Therefore, I say that air that is tempered in heat and dryness is very suitable, such as that part of spring which is close to summer. As Avicenna <note>A foundational Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037)</note> testifies in the chapter on Air, saying: <note>original: "& aer quidem dum eſt temperatus & clarus, nec ſubſtantia extranea, complexi ſpiritibus contraria et admiſcetur, eſt ſanitatis effectrix atque conſeruatrix."</note> "And indeed, air, while it is temperate and clear, and no foreign substance contrary to the spirits <term>spirits (spiritibus): subtle substances that were believed to circulate through the body to facilitate life and movement</term> is mixed into it, is the producer and preserver of health." 

In other seasons, however, the air should be altered: in winter with fire, and in summer with those things which in some way counteract excessive heat. In autumn, which sometimes tastes of the nature of summer and sometimes of winter, the air of the bedchamber should be altered in the same way we described above for summer and winter. In no way, however, should it decline toward coldness, which is an enemy to life and the operations of the body, and favors disease. 

He should stay (if it can be done) in a free-standing house, exposed to the sun and facing the eastern side. Or, if such a place cannot be had, let it at least be far from marshes and stagnant waters. Furthermore, when leaving the house or the city, he should be dressed in clothing appropriate to the season—such as fox skins in winter, or their equivalents—and thus proceed according to the necessity of the times, provided that cold is kept far away with all care and diligence. 

Furthermore, it is not good to leave the house until the sun has been above the earth for at least an hour, so that the purification of the air by the solar rays has taken place. Similarly, staying out in the night air is ruinous; therefore, it is good to return home an hour before sunset. For as the sun declines, the air "thickens" and becomes heavy, filling the head with many thick vapors which, later descending from the head to other limbs, cause many evil symptoms. Therefore, the air must always lean toward the warm and dry. If a stove <term>stufa: a heated room or room containing a stove, common in Renaissance medical treatment for regulating humors</term> is chosen, let it not be intensely fired, but possess a gentle warmth. This can be achieved by adding a moderate amount of fire, so that the cure happens "through contraries," as Avicenna wished, saying...

->## PART TWO<-

->LL ii<-

...we treat the illness by its opposite, and we preserve health by its like. <note>This refers to the fundamental Galenic principle that a disease caused by "heat" must be treated with "cold" remedies, while a healthy state is maintained by things that match the body's natural temperament.</note>

One must also take food and drink according to the proper quality, quantity, and timing. For as Damascenus <note>original: "Damaſcenus"; likely referring to the influential 9th-century physician John Mesue the Elder, often called "Damascenus" in Latin texts</note> said in his *Aphorisms*: "Diet is the primary instrument of care, without which other instruments are in vain." Therefore, in the first place, let bread be moderately baked and well-leavened, which has rested for at least a day after it was baked. Meat, indeed, should be from calves or kids of at least one year old, or from castrated animals. Also good are hens, capons, young chickens, partridges, pheasants, thrushes, blackbirds, and similar forest birds that are caught with birdlime. Beef, although not entirely bad, is not praiseworthy because it is thick and generates <term>melancholic (melancholici) blood: in humoral theory, a heavy, cold, and dry blood that could lead to depression or "black bile" disorders</term>. Similarly, the meat of hares, deer, goats, and similar animals caught by hunting are bad. Pork, whether fresh or salted, is always bad because its humidity harms the stomach. Likewise, all salted meats and foods must be abandoned because they harm the liver. All birds, whether domestic or wild, that live in water and marshes should be avoided, such as geese, ducks, and the like, because they have bad flesh that is <term>melancholic</term> and hard to digest. Pigeons, too, must be avoided because they cause <term>ebullition (ebullitionem): a "boiling" or agitation</term> in the blood. And if at any time one desires to eat meat caught during hunting, let it be from rabbits or very young deer; however, because they generate melancholic humors, they should be set aside in my judgment. I also praise soft-boiled eggs sprinkled with <term>verjuice (ſucco uuæ acerbæ): the sour juice of unripened grapes</term>, because this preserves them from putrefaction. Or, if they are eaten in another way, let them be "trembling" <note>soft-set or poached</note> and not hardened, and sprinkled with verjuice or orange juice. Cheese, however, is not pleasing, because it is hard to digest and generates <term>viscid (uiſcidos) humors: thick, sticky fluids that were thought to clog the body’s internal channels</term>; therefore, let it be set aside. Similarly, all dairy products are bad on account of their viscidity, so they should be omitted. <gloss>but</gloss> if one wishes to eat cheese at some time, let it be old and only slightly salted. All fish are bad and therefore to be avoided; but if one wishes to eat them occasionally, let them be of the kind that live in clear waters, such as pike and the like. It is fitting to note, however, that in this case, those that live in fresh water are better than those in salt water; and they are better roasted than boiled, because during roasting the moist part, which is difficult to digest, is consumed. If sea fish are eaten, let them be scaly and without viscidity, such as sea bream, barbel, and the like; nevertheless, it will be better to abandon their use.

Dishes should be made of spelt with almonds and meat broth. I also highly praise broth made from red chickpeas and the aforementioned meats, whether simple or mixed with egg yolks and crushed with verjuice <term>verjuice: the sour juice of unripened grapes, used as a common acidic seasoning in medieval and Renaissance cooking</term>. You may also eat rice occasionally (but rarely); however, let it be very well cooked so that its "windiness" <note>original: "uentositas"; in humoral medicine, this refers to the tendency of food to produce gas or "flatulence" in the body</note> is removed, for all the most skilled physicians have said it is flatulent. Among vegetables, spinach, beets with endive, bugloss, borage, and fennel are good. Almost all other dishes of vegetables and legumes are bad, such as kidney beans, broad beans, and cabbages—whether white, green, or red. Capers are also good. Condiments or sauces made from quinces <term>cytoniis: quinces (Cydonia oblonga)</term>, almonds, sour cherries, and parsley, sprinkled with a small amount of cinnamon, are good. However, others made from mustard, garlic <note>original: "aliis," likely a variant or error for "allis" (garlic)</note>, nuts, pepper, and ginger are all bad and therefore to be abandoned. Indeed, the use of spices like ginger, pepper, and the like is not good; but if needed, use simple cinnamon, because it strengthens the stomach and the liver, increases the digestive power, and opens obstructions <note>original: "opilationes"; blockages in the vessels or organs that were believed to impede the flow of humors</note>. Confections, however, should be such as almonds, coriander, pine nuts, anise, and marzipan. Preserves should be made from pine nuts, citrons, chebulic myrobalans <term>myrobalanis chebulis: a type of astringent medicinal fruit from India, highly prized in the Renaissance pharmacopeia</term>, and the like.

Fruits are not good by any means because they easily rot in the stomach. However, those among them that are better are roasted pears, damson plums, almonds, sour cherries, roasted quinces, sweet and mild pomegranates, pistachios <term>fistici: pistachios</term>, and raisins. Hazelnuts, however, are not pleasing—along with peaches, apricots <term>crissomalis: literally "gold-apples," a common term for apricots</term>, and figs—because they are hard to digest and because they fill the head with "bad vapors." The use of lemons harms the stomach because of their coldness; sour oranges taken in large quantities do the same. Other preparations made from eggs, cheese, milk, and butter should rarely be eaten, because they are digested with great difficulty due to their viscosity. <note>unclear abbreviation mark, possibly "quod" (that) or "sed" (but)</note> But if they are eaten, let them be in a small quantity.

You shall note, moreover, that <term>nothing</term> <note>original: "qd," abbreviation for "quod"</note>—according to the witness <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a 10th-century Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the most influential medical textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk—harms digestion, the stomach, and one’s strength so much as foods of different qualities taken at a single meal; for they fight among themselves and tire the stomach. Therefore, the simpler the meals, the better they are, and you should be content with a single food (if you can). Furthermore, all foods must be chewed thoroughly, because chewing is a kind of preparation for the "first digestion" which takes place in the stomach. The hour of the midday meal should be the third hour of the day, when...

# PART TWO

When the desire to eat arises, the midday meal <term>prandium: the first substantial meal of the day, similar to a modern lunch but often the main meal</term> can even be more substantial than dinner <term>coena: the evening meal</term>, since in the morning the stomach is better prepared. This is because heat is concentrated during the night and completes digestion, and since this heat has not yet been dispersed, the stomach will digest better; for as it is Aristotle's opinion, "united virtue is stronger than itself when dispersed." <note>Aristotle's *Physics* and *Meteorology* were often cited by physicians to explain how "innate heat" concentrated in the body's core during sleep to aid digestion.</note> Let dinner be at least eight hours after the midday meal; and because habit is a "second nature," you may increase or decrease food according to your own domestic and national customs. For Hippocrates said, "something must be granted to custom." <note>Hippocrates, the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine," emphasized that sudden changes in diet—even to a "healthier" one—could be harmful if they broke long-standing habits.</note> Note, however, that enduring hunger (if it is natural hunger) is very harmful; therefore, Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in European universities during Massa's time.</note> said in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk that enduring hunger fills the stomach with putrid humors.

Drink, however, must be offered with the greatest care, for if it is moderate, it will be very beneficial; on the contrary, it will be very harmful. Strong, wine-heavy wine <note>original: "Vinum uinofum"; referring to wine with high alcohol content or "body" that overwhelms the system</note> is harmful, as is sweet wine; and very old wines provide little nourishment, as Avicenna said in his writing on the regimen of water and wine, and they are like medicine rather than food. New wine is also harmful because, due to its "inflammation," it predisposes the liver to hepatic dysentery. <note>In Galenic medicine, "new" or unfermented wine was thought to be too hot and turbulent, irritating the liver and causing digestive flux.</note> 

Therefore, let the wine be neither too fresh nor too old, but as Avicenna teaches in the place mentioned above, a middle ground between old and new. It should be clear, and not overly white (since that draws humors to the joints), nor very thick, because thick wine is digested with difficulty and "fills the head" <note>This refers to the belief that heavy vapors from thick wine rose to the brain, causing headaches or lethargy.</note>. Let it be of good smell and good taste, not overly sweet nor astringent <term>ponticum: a sharp, tart, or puckering flavor</term>. It should not be a "great" wine or (as I said) too wine-heavy, but moderate. If it should sometimes have too much potency, let that be quenched by mixing it with sweet, clear water—not water that is putrid or lingering on marshy ground. Instead, let the water be (if possible) from a cistern or from those sources that flow over stones; and if such water cannot be found, let it be boiled over a fire, for by boiling, the bad, putrid, or "putrefying" quality will be removed. 

Furthermore, one must drink temperately. Since we live by heat and are nourished by moisture, we cannot be well-nourished without drink. To ensure that food nourishes well and can "penetrate" the body better, it is necessary to drink temperately so that the moistened food may be digested more easily. For this reason, during a meal, it is better to drink a little and often rather than a lot and rarely. Drinking after the midday meal, however, is bad, because the drink "floats" above the food and seeks the head. Therefore, if possible, let him drink nothing after he has finished eating; but chewing coriander seeds <note>original: "coriandri grana"</note> is very beneficial, for they both strengthen the head and invigorate digestion.

<meta>This page continues Nicolò Massa’s medical advice regarding the "six non-naturals"—the environmental and behavioral factors that govern health. ->### LETTERS ON MEDICINE BY NICOLÒ MASSA<-

Furthermore, one must avoid excessive fullness from food and drink, for the <term>virtue: the innate vital power or energy of the body</term> becomes exhausted, and nature becomes so preoccupied with the food that it cannot act against illness. As Hippocrates said, "the more you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them." <note>This famous Hippocratic aphorism suggests that feeding a sick person—whose "humors" are out of balance—only provides "fuel" for the disease rather than strengthening the patient.</note> **Averroes** also stated in the first book of the *Colliget* <note>The *Kulliyat* or *Colliget* was a major medical encyclopedia by the Andalusian philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd).</note> that abstinence from food is a kind of <term>evacuation: the medical process of removing excess or harmful humors from the body</term>. **Galen** similarly asserted that abstinence from food purges the entire body equally.

In the same way, <term>inanition: exhaustion caused by lack of nourishment</term> is considered harmful because when the stomach is empty, it fills with superfluous bad humors, and the body's heat, acting upon its own <term>radical moisture: the innate fluid believed to be the fuel of life</term>, weakens it. Since the stomach is the principle source of nourishment, an error occurring there is not easily corrected by other organs. Therefore, with the greatest diligence and study, one must take care that neither necessary food is skipped, nor is an excess taken in.

**Sleep and Wakefulness**, if either exceeds moderation, are harmful according to the opinion of Hippocrates. Therefore, one must guard against sleep that exceeds the space of eight hours; for long sleep is a cause of "moist" illnesses, which are followed by a chilling of the body, and it fills the head with many vapors. Nor should sleep occur immediately after food, as this increases <term>catarrh: a buildup of mucus or "downflow" from the head</term>, which descends to the principal organs and weakens them. Daytime sleep is also to be avoided, especially that which is sought during the noon hours, for it generates "rheumatisms" <note>In Renaissance medicine, "rheumatism" referred generally to the flow of harmful fluids (rheum) from the brain to other parts of the body.</note> and corrupts the healthy heat of the body. For this reason, sleep should be sought at least two hours after dinner. One should first sleep upon the right side for at least two hours, because in this position food descends quickly to the bottom of the stomach; afterward, one should lie upon the left side, as in this position the heat will be invigorated and aid digestion. But (as **Avicenna** teaches in the third *fen* of the first *Canon*) lying upon the stomach is far better.

Excessive **wakefulness** (as has been said) is very harmful, destroying the heat and all the vital powers; hence it is better to fail on the side of too much sleep than in prolonged wakefulness. For Averroes says in his book *On Sleep and Wakefulness* that the powers of the body acquire strength through sleep; yet all extremes are always faulty. As the poet sang, ***You will go most safely in the middle***. <note>original: "Medio tutissimus ibis" — a famous line from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* often used to advocate for the "Golden Mean" or moderation in all things.</note> Therefore, all things must be undertaken with the greatest modesty and moderation.

Concerning **movement and rest**, let this be the rule: I would say first of all that exercise for an hour specifically before lunch and dinner is very suitable. However, let it be temperate, and continued until the point of sweat, in lo... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing with a discussion of the "place" (loco) or "type" of exercise on the following page.</note>

->## PART TWO<-

...on flat ground, not mountainous, by walking moderately; for labor with sweat greatly inflames the body, dissolves the <term>spirits: the subtle substances that carry life and sensation through the body</term>, and weakens the <term>virtue: the innate vital power</term> and the innate heat of the stomach. But moderate exercise invigorates the heat, dissolves the <term>superfluities: excess waste fluids or humors</term> which are in the stomach, rouses the spirits, dilates the pores, and finally prepares the stomach to embrace food more readily. I would even dare to say that exercise is the most noble cause of preserving health. After taking food, it is very beneficial to rest for two hours, so that the heat is not scattered by movement and abandons the digestion; therefore, one must diligently observe the rules of exercise. It should also be noted <gloss>that</gloss> exercise done much before digestion is complete causes undigested food to descend to the intestines, for perfect digestion is only completed through rest. Literary exercise <note>original: "Exercitium literarum"; referring to intense study, reading, or writing.</note>, especially immediately after food, is to be set aside, but it should be done in the morning, since it does not cause as much harm, and the reason for this is self-evident. This is not the place for <term>frictions: therapeutic massages or the rubbing of the skin</term>, because even if they could take the place of exercise, since he is able to exercise himself, he does not need frictions. Nevertheless, it would please me greatly if twice a week he washed his head with warm <term>lye: a solution of alkaline salts (often from wood ash) used for cleaning</term> poured from above, because it resolves moisture, comforts the head, and warms it; therefore, I highly praise that practice.

**The accidents of the soul** <note>In the medical tradition of the "six non-naturals," the "accidents of the soul" refer to emotions or psychological states.</note>, if they are good, increase the innate heat, which is nature’s primary instrument against the harms of our body. And therefore **Hippocrates** said that in every sickness, for the mind to be comforted and to be well-disposed toward offerings is good, but the contrary is bad. And by the "contrary," we mean sadness, about which **Galen** said in the second book of the *Art of Medicine* <note>original: "artis paruae," referring to the *Ars medica*, a foundational textbook by Galen.</note> that bad accidents of the soul destroy the body and change its consistency from that which is according to nature. Therefore, it is good to be joyful and to be with friends, relatives, and others with whom there is goodwill. To tell jokes to honorable women and, in turn, to hear their natural wit, and to listen to songs, and to play the lute and other instruments, because these things clarify the blood; they expand the soul, or rather the spirits, from which all operations proceed. Furthermore, sadness is to be avoided, as are lawsuits, controversies, long stays among those who weep, the laments of the dead, and other things of this sort, because they chill the blood, disturb it, and prevent digestion, as **Avicenna** said in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk.

I place **sexual intercourse** among the labors of the soul at present, which in no way...

...[intercourse] is not good, and it is to be avoided like poison, especially that which is excited by force, or by the sight of some beauty, or by charms whether external or internal; and because the memory of these things is troublesome, and to think of them is harmful, therefore let these things be avoided. So much for the <term>non-natural things: the six factors within human control—such as diet, exercise, and emotions—that determine health</term>.

And since healing is not always achieved through a <term>regimen: a prescribed way of life or diet</term> in the aforementioned things alone, it is necessary to turn to other medicines. As **Galen** said in the first book of *The Regimen in Acute Diseases*, if it becomes necessary to use them, the practice will always be praised by all physicians. Since healing occurs sometimes through medicines taken internally and sometimes through those applied externally or through surgery, I will first speak of those taken internally. If by the taking of the <term>bath water: thermal or mineral waters used for drinking or bathing</term> which you have with you and have decided to drink, you are not freed from the remains of this disease (which may the gods avert)—which you will be able to recognize very well by the pains, tumors, or ulcers that have not healed—it will be best to purge the body very often with a <term>minorative evacuation: a gentle or gradual cleansing of the bowels</term> appropriate for the <term>sinning matter: "materia peccans," the excess or corrupt humors causing the disease</term>. And although in "boiling" <note>original: "feruantibus"; referring to acute, high-fever diseases</note> illnesses medicines that bring the matter for the most part to a single <term>critical evacuation: a sudden, decisive discharge of humors marking the turning point of a disease</term> are useful, in this case, let that "lessening" <note>the minorative evacuation</note> be done generally and through the common channels. However, in <term>chronic: long-lasting</term> diseases in which the matter is newly regenerated, one must not attempt a radical, "rooting-out" evacuation; rather, we ought to evacuate as often as the signs of the said regeneration of matter appear. Even if the matter were not entirely <term>digested: "concocted" or processed by the body's heat so it is ready to be expelled</term>, lessening it often relieves nature and prevents the multiplication of these matters, especially the <term>cold: humors characterized by coldness, like phlegm or black bile</term> ones. Therefore, let such a minorative evacuation be first performed by a selective purging, to be carried out three hours before lunch.

Six <term>drachms: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> of pulp of cassia, 
two drachms each of <term>confection of hamech: a purgative electuary used to treat melancholy and skin diseases</term> and prepared agaric.

This minorative evacuation can also be done with pills—for example:

**Recipe** <note>Take</note>: 
Half a drachm each of <term>fetid pills: pills made from strong-smelling resins like asafoetida</term>, Indian pills, and <term>aggregative pills: a complex pill designed to purge multiple humors at once</term>. 
Let five pills be made, to be taken four hours before lunch. Indeed, it will be very beneficial to repeat these evacuations if necessary, and it will diminish the disease. But since **Hippocrates** said that one should medicate and move things that are <term>concocted: "cooked" or matured by the body's heat</term>, and not those that are raw, etc., therefore, between one and another taking of the aforementioned drugs (which shall be done with an interval of four, five, or even more days), one should take this <term>digestive: a medicine that aids the "cooking" or preparation of humors for evacuation</term>...

...you ought to measure out. Take half an ounce each of <term>syrup of fumitory: a plant traditionally used to "cleanse the blood" and treat skin ailments</term>, of <term>stoechas: French lavender</term>, and of violets. Take one ounce each of the waters of endive, bugloss, and <term>iva: ground pine, used for joint pain and strengthening the nerves</term>. Mix these, and let it be taken warm at dawn; four hours later, lunch may be taken. Also very beneficial for this kind of illness—acting both as a <term>minorative: a gentle laxative that gradually reduces excess humors</term> and as a <term>digestive: a medicine that "ripens" or prepares humors for evacuation</term>—is the decoction of <term>epithyme: dodder of thyme, a parasitic vine considered powerful for purging black bile</term> described by **Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue (the Younger), a major medieval authority on pharmacy</note> in the seventh distinction of his *Antidotary*. For beyond the virtues mentioned there by Mesue, it has many others which I omit for the sake of brevity. I will add only this: it purges cold, melancholic, and phlegmatic matter contained in all parts of the body by "digesting" and thinning it. Thus, if the said decoction is taken in a proper quantity, it draws out the matter by loosening and digesting it; but if taken in a small quantity, it merely digests the aforementioned humors and prepares them for evacuation. The dose for digesting is four <term>drams: a unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</term>, while for evacuating it is six drams. In my judgment, this is more noble than the others. It can be made sweet by adding one ounce or more of <term>sugar of seleneabini: likely a specific sugar-based syrup or confection</term>, and one can safely take this decoction daily or every third day. If someone wished to provide a dose that was twice as strong, it would not please me. If there is a need to vary the treatment, this can be done with the "Indus electuary," the "electuary of dates," and similar medicines that evacuate thick matter from remote places near the joints and nerves.

And since among practitioners there are many opinions as to whether <term>phlebotomy: bloodletting</term> is appropriate in this illness, I will set those opinions aside for now. I would say that it is not suitable, both because of the "accidents" <note>in this context, "accidents" refers to symptoms or side effects like fainting or weakness</note> which your Lordship is accustomed to suffering, and (if you also ask this) because there are no signs present attesting to the necessity of it.

But note that if your nature can tolerate vomiting, and if you could use it without great distress, it would be of great benefit in this condition, especially in the morning, and when provoked by easy means—such as by putting a finger into the mouth, or a chicken feather smeared in oil, or with a fairly common <term>emetic: a substance that induces vomiting</term>. Take two ounces of simple <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> and three drams of the water from a decoction of <term>radish</term>. Mix and take it warm. Or: Take three drams of vinegar and four drams of the water from a decoction of <term>acorus: sweet flag or calamus</term> and radish. Mix and let it be drunk warm. These are emetics that are sufficiently mild and without danger. Note, however, that in this case vomiting is a suitable and convenient remedy; it evacuates the proper matter from both near and remote parts. Therefore, if it can be provoked with little difficulty, it will be a very noble aid. After the evacuation, it benefits the stomach...

<header>MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA</header>

# MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...and to strengthen the liver. Therefore, on the days in which he does not take <term>solutive medicines: laxatives or treatments intended to "loosen" and expel humors</term>, it is a wonderful restorative to take, one hour before lunch and dinner, one <term>lozenge: a small, round medicinal tablet (Latin: rotula)</term> of <term>aromatic rose: a preparation of rose petals and spices</term> and another of <term>diarhodon of the Abbot: a famous rose-based tonic used to cool the organs</term> according to the description by **Nicolaus** <note>Nicolaus Praepositus, a 12th-century medical authority whose "Antidotarium" was a standard pharmaceutical text</note>. For this strengthens the stomach, the liver, the heart, and the brain; it invigorates digestion, strengthens the <term>innate heat: the vital warmth believed to be the source of life and metabolism</term>, and expels the residue of <term>superfluities: excess waste products or humors</term> caused by indigestion. Let these words suffice concerning internal medicines, and so I come to those applied externally.

In the last place, we must provide relief for the <term>accidents: symptoms or secondary complications of a disease</term>. For sometimes these are so severe that they demand the entire focus of the treatment. But in this case—since pains of the nerves, tumors, and ulcers follow the primary <term>dyscrasia: an imbalance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term>—I say that if pains are present, no remedy can be more excellent than using the aforementioned evacuations, either by loosening the bowels or by vomiting, which I praise more highly. 

Tumors, however, should be dissolved with a <term>cerate: a stiff ointment made of wax and oil</term> made from <term>diachylon ointment: a traditional plaster originally made of plant juices and lead litharge</term> with gums, a softening ointment, and a cerate of hyssop. Take equal parts of these and dissolve them in a bronze vessel over a fire; then, this cerate should be spread upon leather to the size of the tumor. This wonderfully dissolves hardened matter. Alternatively, use an ointment with oil of chamomile or lilies, or with an equal amount of chicken fat. But if these hard masses tend more toward <term>maturation: the process of "ripening" a tumor or abscess so it can be drained</term>, let them be ripened with this maturing plaster:

Take <term>mucilages: thick, gluey substances extracted from plants</term> of marshmallow, fenugreek, and linseed—four handfuls of each; barley flour, two <term>drams: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term>; and <term>leaven: yeast or fermented dough</term>, one dram. Let these be mixed over a fire, and afterward add three drams of pig fat and four boiled white lily roots. Let them be pounded together in a mortar and incorporated with the aforementioned ingredients, and placed upon the tumor; this will be the best ripening agent.

As for the ulcers that occur, which are caused by such tumors—leaving aside many things that could be said of them—let them be cleansed with **Damascene ointment** or with **red powder** <note>likely "pulvis rubeus," a mercuric or herbal caustic used to clean wounds</note>, always maintaining this order: Specifically, first by inserting a <term>tent: a small plug or wick of lint used to keep a wound open for drainage</term> made of threads soaked in Damascene ointment, or by applying the powder over it. Afterward, let the softening ointment be applied, spread upon a linen cloth, as has often been done by me. 

But if the sickness should descend into some malignancy, increasing the pains and other symptoms (which may the Gods in their piety avert), it would be a long task to write out all the final remedies. Since these are powerful, they should not be attempted except in the presence of a prudent physician experienced in this matter. But if, among other things, something...

## Vincenzo Negusanti, Bishop, etc. Advice regarding the French Disease.

### LETTER XX.

**H**IC <note>This "H" refers to a decorative woodcut initial in the original manuscript depicting a figurative scene</note> disease (Most Reverend Lord), since it is savage and situated in the highest degree (so to speak) of malignancy, has deceived many most learned physicians, both in the understanding of it and in its cure. For which reason, I shall speak or write about it not without the greatest reverence, especially since I understand myself to be a man who can easily be deceived in such an arduous matter. Nevertheless, trusting in divine mercy and having first implored His help, lest I seem to make a delay in words, I will endeavor to briefly declare some things (as much as shall be in my power) concerning its essence; afterward, I will recount its complete cure in a more lengthy discourse, while always omitting superfluous details.

I say, therefore, that <gloss>that</gloss> this sickness (to adhere to the truer opinion) is rooted fundamentally in the liver and is communicated to the whole body. Through this poor disposition of the liver—which declines toward coldness and dryness with a great deal of moisture, and that moisture indeed being crude <note>unprocessed or "undigested" by the body's internal heat</note>—it infects the whole body, chiefly through the veins and arteries. This occurs so that, through poor digestion, many bad humors are generated, which are afterward scorched <term>adust: humors that have been "burnt" by internal heat, becoming toxic, dark, and difficult to treat</term> by the heat of other organs and become malignant through the mixing of bile <note>original: "cholerae"; yellow bile</note> and other humors. Consequently, a body affected by such a disease cannot be cured without the greatest difficulty and the strongest remedies. I certainly confess this, Most Reverend Lord, that <gloss>that</gloss> in curing other ailments I feel little or no labor, but when I am in the stormy sea of this sickness, I always...

...I fear a shipwreck; for so great is the darkness and the mixing of other humors, from which various accidents <term>accidents: the secondary symptoms or complications of a disease, such as pain or sores</term> arise, such as pustules, pains, hard abscesses <term>abscesses: also called apostemes; localized collections of inflammatory matter or hard swellings</term>, and malignant ulcers. All of these occur according to a greater or lesser adustion <note>original: "adustionem"; the "burning" or overheating of humors, which was thought to make them toxic and dark</note>, or the mixing of humors, or the greater strength or weakness of the transforming or expelling power <note>the "virtues" or internal biological forces believed to manage the body's health and waste</note>.

Thus, it is possible that sometimes in this sickness only pustules appear, even in small quantity; this happens when the matter is thinner and scarce, and the strength of the expelling power is able to drive it out to the skin. Sometimes, however, the matter is thick and the power is weak; at that time, pains are caused by the matter soaked into the nerves, where it has already been pushed. Or, the matter is not expelled by the weak power to the parts of the skin—both because of its thickness and the weakness of the power—and the readiness of the receiving members, such as the joints. Furthermore, there is no doubt that abscesses are formed from thick matter when the power is strong. 

Ulceration, however, sometimes comes from these hard abscesses, and sometimes from small but malignant pustules. From this malignancy, there often appears a corruption not only of the flesh and nerves, but even of the bones, as can be seen in many suffering from such a malignant sickness. But let this suffice regarding the essence of the sickness, taken from its symptoms and causes. 

I come now to the disease from which your lordship currently suffers, and for whose cure you have shown us you have need. You suffer, therefore, at present a quite malignant and fearsome ulcer on the thumb <note>original: "pollice digito"</note>, but by divine mercy it seems the malignancy has just now been removed by our medicines, so that only the cleansing and closing of the ulcer remains, which (God willing) will be completed in a few days. 

You suffer, moreover, a burdensome heaviness or pain of the arms and shoulder blades, so that the arms are moved in all directions not freely, but with difficulty. I assert that this arises from the aforementioned matter soaked into the nerves and ligaments. This matter not only prohibits free movement by its thickness and weight, but also blocks the pores so that the animal spirits <term>animal spirits: in Galenic medicine, these were subtle fluids or "breaths" that traveled through the nerves to enable movement and sensation</term> cannot freely perform their office, which provide movement by passing through the pores. There would be many problems to solve here, which I omit for the sake of brevity, and I come to the more necessary part, which consists in the appropriate application of remedies.

...now to diligently graduate <term>graduate: to measure the intensity of qualities—heat, cold, moisture, or dryness—on a scale of four degrees, as used in medieval and Renaissance medicine</term> as Avicenna <note>original: "Auic."; referring to the Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose *Canon of Medicine* was the primary medical textbook of the era</note> teaches in the first book, fourth part, first chapter, so that through the state of health we may be able to recognize how far the sickness has strayed from its natural constitution. The beauty and proportionality in the parts of the head itself testify to a balanced state. The color and growth of the hair and the hair of the beard, which tend toward redness with a certain blackness, seem to indicate this same thing. Furthermore, the heart, which is the most principal member, appears to be of a hot and dry temperature, which we can also gather from the width and breadth of the chest. It is certain that greatness of soul, as well as practical ability, promptness, and a cheerful face, proceed from very hot, non-fatty blood. The liver, however, is of a hot and not very dry temperament, which appears through the length and straightness of all the limbs; for it is the nature of heat to ascend and expand. And since no width of the veins or fatness in the limbs appears, no one should doubt that dryness is the cause of this. The stomach is quite tempered, as it is sufficiently fleshy and conducts its operations well; for it digests optimally and expels waste optimally without bad accidents <term>accidents: secondary symptoms or complications arising from a disease</term>. Therefore, in concluding, I say that the temperament declines from a perfectly balanced state <note>original: "temperamento iustitiali"; the ideal, theoretical point of balance between the four qualities</note> toward heat and dryness. The secondary dominance of accidental moisture, however, arises from the moistures of the head and from an acquired coldness of the liver, which is the cause of many generated moistures being scattered throughout the entire body, rendering it accidentally moist. And so that we do not seem to speak superfluously, I say in application (as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> taught) that the measure of the distemper is known through the healthy temperament; so that when a sickness is not proportional to the temperament itself, it is most to be feared, as it is more difficult to cure. Although, to speak truly, by reason of age, the scarcity of the humor, and the duration of the disease, it should be of lesser fear, as Galen himself testifies in the books of the *Aphorisms* <note>Referring to Galen's commentaries on the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates</note>. However, we consider age itself not only for the application of remedies, but also...

And let these words suffice so far concerning the knowledge of the sickness, its causes, its symptoms, and the prognosis; I come now to the specific regimen. 

The air, first of all, must be corrected, because it does the most both for the preservation of health and for the cure of diseases, since we must remain in it whether we wish to or not. Therefore, air tempered in heat and dryness is very necessary, like that part of spring which approaches summer; for when it is tempered and clear, and nothing of foreign substance is mixed into it that might be contrary to the complexion of the spirit, it creates health and preserves it. For this reason, it should be altered in other seasons: as in winter with fire, and in summer by the sprinkling of cold things, so that it may be reduced to a tempered state, leaning toward the warm and dry. In Autumn, however, since it is changeable, if it is cold, it must be altered with heat; if it is too hot, with tempering influences. We ought to endure an excess of heat rather than of cold, for besides the fact that coldness is an enemy to life, it also fosters the disease itself and its cause. 

The house, therefore, if it can be managed, should be open, exposed to the sun, and far from swamps and stagnant waters. Furthermore, it is appropriate to dress oneself in clothing suitable for the weather, whether one chooses to be at home or outdoors; such as being lined with fox skins <note>fox skins: "uulpinis pellibus"; a common recommendation in Renaissance medicine for providing "temperate" warmth without being overly heavy or stifling</note> or other equivalent furs in winter, less so in spring and autumn, but according to the needs of the season, provided that the cold itself is kept far away. 

Indeed, the time at which you may leave the house should be after the Sun has been above the earth for at least an hour, so that the resolution <note>resolution: the process of dispersing or "melting away" harmful substances through heat</note> of evil vapors has been achieved by the solar rays.
