## ->SECOND PART<-

...one must return home; the reason is that after sunset the air thickens and is made gross, and fills the head with evil vapors, which afterward descend to the nerves and the joints of the shoulder blades, increasing heaviness and pains. Therefore, so that the cure might be done through contraries <note>original: "per contraria"; a fundamental principle of Galenic medicine where a "cold" disease is treated with "hot" remedies</note> (as Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), the "Father of Medicine"</note> said), the air must always be altered toward heat and dryness.

In the second place after air, the administration of food and drink according to the proper quality, quantity, and time is necessary; for <term>diet: in the Renaissance, this referred to a whole lifestyle regimen—food, drink, sleep, and exercise—rather than just weight loss</term> is the first instrument of healing among the three <note>The three traditional pillars of medical treatment were Diet, Pharmacy, and Surgery</note>, without which the other instruments are useless. Therefore, bread should first of all be made from wheat purged of foreign matter, well-fermented, and moderately baked, having sat for at least a day. Suitable meats are such as veal, kid-goat, and the meat of a castrated sheep of at least one year is considered good; also hens, capons, pheasants, partridges, turtledoves, thrushes, blackbirds, forest birds caught with <term>birdlime: a sticky substance spread on branches to trap small birds</term>, and the like. However, beef must be avoided, because it generates <term>melancholic: associated with black bile, which was thought to be cold, dry, and heavy</term> blood; for the same reason, meat from hares, deer, goats, and similar animals caught by hunting should be avoided. Pork is always bad and must be left aside; the reason is that by its humidity it always harms the stomach and generates <term>viscid: thick, sticky, or "gluey" fluids in the body</term> humors, whether it is fresh or salted. Similarly, all salted foods are bad, whether they be meat or fish, because they harm the liver. Furthermore, all birds that live in the water, whether domestic or wild—such as geese, ducks, and the like—are in no way good, because they have hard flesh that is melancholic and difficult to digest. Pigeons are also to be avoided, because they cause a boiling in the blood. If, however, one occasionally wishes to eat meat caught while hunting, let it be from rabbits or very young deer, though it is better to avoid them since they generate melancholic blood. It should be noted, however, that it is better to eat a greater quantity of meat than bread, because in those who have a <term>symbolum: a shared quality or "fittingness" between the food and the body's humors</term> the transit is easier. And <term>Avicenna: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe</term> says in the previously cited place that the hindrance of bread when it is not well digested is great, while that of meat is less. Soft eggs (especially in the morning) are also good; if they are eaten in another way, they should be "trembling" <note>original: "tremula"; what we would call soft-poached or soft-boiled</note> and not hardened, and sprinkled with <term>verjuice: the acidic juice of unripened grapes</term> with boiled fennel, or orange juice. Cheese, however, [should be avoided] both on account of its viscidity, and because the humors...

# NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

...things that generate melancholic and viscous humors <note>original: "res melancholicos uiscidos generat"; in humoral theory, "viscous" humors were thick and sticky, potentially blocking the flow of vital spirits and leading to illness</note>, I do not praise. All dairy products are also bad, because they generate viscous humors. But if they are sometimes eaten, such as cheese, let it be aged and only lightly salted. 

All fish should be avoided because they are cold; but if it is pleasing to eat some of them occasionally, let it be in a small quantity. They should be from those that live in clear waters, and should not be slimy but scaly, such as gilthead bream, red mullet, and scorpion fish. These should be roasted rather than boiled, because during roasting, that moisture which is difficult to digest is consumed; however, it would be better to avoid fish altogether. 

Dishes should be made from spelt with almond milk [the juice of almonds], or from meat broth. I also highly praise bread soup <note>original: "panatellam"; a simple soup made of breadcrumbs, broth, and often eggs</note>, especially in the evening, as well as red chickpea broth and the broth of the aforementioned meats—sometimes plain, sometimes mixed with egg yolks and a small amount of <term>verjuice: the tart, acidic juice of unripe grapes, used to balance "heat" in cooking</term>. 

Rice you may eat sometimes, though rarely; it must be very well cooked, and to remove its "windiness" <note>original: "uentofitas"; referring to the tendency of certain foods to cause gas or flatulence</note>, let it be sprinkled with plain cinnamon, which benefits the stomach—though use only a small amount. 

The vegetables that are considered good are: beets with endive, bugloss, borage, and fennel. You may also sometimes eat dishes sprinkled with cinnamon to temper the coldness of these foods. Almost all other legumes and vegetables are bad, such as beans, kidney beans, and cabbages, whether white, red, or green. Capers preserved with verjuice and sugar are good. 

The condiments or sauces that are suitable are: the flavor of quinces with cinnamon and almonds, sprinkled with the juice of parsley and mint, or grapes and similar things—provided that ginger, pepper, and other such spices are not included. All other sauces made from mustard, garlic, nuts, pepper, and ginger are considered bad and should therefore be avoided. The use of spices like ginger and pepper is also bad; but if needed, you may use plain cinnamon, because it strengthens the stomach and the liver, aids the digestive power, and opens all <term>oppilations: a historical medical term for obstructions or blockages in the body's internal passages or organs</term>. 

Confections such as almonds, coriander, pine nuts, anise, and cakes made of sugar and almonds may be eaten. Let the preserves be such as quinces, citrons, <term>myrobalan: a dried, plum-like fruit from the East, highly valued in the Renaissance for its supposed ability to purge specific humors</term>, chebulic myrobalans, and the like.

Fruits, however, are not good, because for the most part they are cold. As Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose "Canon of Medicine" was the most influential medical textbook in Europe for centuries</note> said in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk: fruits are not good except for those who labor and exercise. ## SECOND PART

...however, sweet and mild pomegranates <note>original: "mala granata"</note>. Ripe grapes, almonds, pistachios, raisins, and such are sometimes to be chosen; but hazelnuts are bad because they are difficult to digest and fill the head with many vapors <note>in humoral theory, "vapors" rising from the stomach to the head were thought to cause headaches and mental confusion</note>. Other fruits are similar, such as apricots <note>original: "chrysomala," literally "golden apples"</note>, peaches, and sweet cherries. Figs, whether fresh or dry, are to be avoided because they cause a boiling in the blood and generate <term>viscous humors: thick, sticky fluids believed to cause blockages in the body</term>; however, fresh ones are less harmful. The use of lemons, citrons, and cucumbers greatly harms the stomach because of their coldness, and they even nourish sickness.

I will also add this regarding the dishes themselves, so that nothing seems to be missing: other dishes made from eggs, cheese, milk, and butter are rarely to be eaten. Because of their stickiness, they are digested with the greatest difficulty; if they are eaten, let it be at least in a small quantity. It is also proper to note that, according to the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook for centuries</note>, nothing is so contrary to digestion as taking in foods of different qualities at the same table. For besides the fact that they tire the stomach, they harm it for a twofold reason: first, because of their different rates of digestion, that which is already digested is mixed with that which is undigested; and the second is because one can eat more of these than of a single food. 

**Avicenna** praises dishes of a single kind, both in the morning and in the evening, so that you are content with only a single food. All food should be well chewed, for <term>mastication: the act of chewing</term> is a useful and necessary preparation for the first digestion, which takes place in the stomach. 

The hour for eating in the morning should be the third hour of the day <note>roughly 9:00 AM, following the canonical hours</note>, when the desire to eat arises. This is because the stomach is then better prepared, aided by the heat concentrated during the night's sleep; therefore, it better consumes superfluities <note>waste products or excess humors</note> and completes digestion. Thus, in the morning the stomach is empty, and the heat, not yet dispersed, better embraces and digests the food. Supper, however, should be smaller than the midday meal, and should occur at least eight hours after that meal. Night is truly the mother of moistures, and the heat cannot perfectly digest—especially in the first part of the night—or expel and consume the superfluities. 

But because **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> said in the first book of *Physics* that "custom is a second nature," the amount can be increased or decreased according to the custom of one's country and domestic habit. For **Hippocrates** said that something must be granted to custom, and this matters a great deal.

The drink should be wine that is neither fresh nor too old, but should be as **Avicenna** teaches in the chapter on the regimen...

...of water and wine, a middle ground between new and old, clear but not too white, because that draws humors to the nerves; nor should it be very thick, because it is digested with difficulty and fills the head with many vapors <note>in humoral medicine, "vapors" were gases produced by digestion that were thought to rise to the brain, potentially causing headaches or confusion</note>. Let it therefore be of a medium color and good odor and taste, not very sweet, not tart <note>original: "ponticum," referring to a harsh or astringent taste</note>, nor too strong or heavy, for sweet wine harms the liver, while strong wine generates <term>obstructions: blockages in the vessels or organs that prevent the flow of humors</term>.

If a light wine cannot be had, it should be diluted with fresh water that is clear—not stagnant or from a marsh, but from a well or a clear river that runs over stones, or from clear springs. If such water cannot be found, let whatever water is available be boiled over a fire, so that the bad, decaying quality may be removed by boiling and it may be purified.

Furthermore, one must drink in moderation; those should not be listened to who dare to claim that heavy drinking and strong wines are beneficial for this sickness, for these are the words of foolish and shameless men. But since we cannot be well nourished without drink—as it allows food to easily penetrate and provide nourishment—one must drink moderately so that the moistened food may be more easily digested and distributed. It is better to drink sparingly and more often than to drink a lot and rarely.

Drinking after dinner is always bad, and for this reason **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a primary medical text in Europe</note> said that wine after food causes obstructions because it makes undigested food penetrate the system too quickly. Therefore, after food, coriander seeds should be eaten, which strengthen both the stomach and the head and favor digestion.

Overfilling with both food and drink is bad, for it harms the stomach, the liver, and all the bodily powers <note>original: "virtutibus," the natural faculties or spirits believed to govern the body's functions</note>, so that the power thus oppressed succumbs to the disease. As **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (c. 129–216 AD), the influential Greek physician whose theories of the four humors dominated Western medicine</note> said, the body's power is the opposite of disease, as I shall say in the section on medicinal regimen. This damage is even greater in an unhealthy body; for **Hippocrates** <note>the ancient Greek "father of medicine" (c. 460–370 BC)</note> said: "The more you nourish impure bodies, the more you harm them."

Great emptiness <note>excessive fasting or starvation</note> also harms, since it makes all the bodily powers weak. In hunger, the body's heat acts upon the <term>radical moisture: the fundamental fluid believed to be the fuel for life and innate heat</term> of the stomach itself and weakens it. Since the stomach is the source of nourishment, a failure there is not easily corrected by other organs. Therefore, the greatest diligence must be shown in this: that food is not omitted, nor is an excessive amount taken.

### On Sleep and Waking

Since, in the opinion of all physicians, all bodily powers are strengthened through sleep and dispersed through waking, it is proper to sleep especially during the night hours; but let it not be longer than the space of eight hours. For long-lasting sleep harms much, as it generates foreign humors, by which the stomach and...

# PART TWO

...cooling of the liver follows; indeed, during long sleep the head is filled with many of these evil <note>original: "uaporibus." In humoral medicine, "vapors" were gases produced by digestion that rose to the brain, potentially causing lethargy or illness.</note> vapors. Furthermore, sleeping immediately after food is extremely harmful because <term>catarrhal: related to the buildup of excess mucus or phlegm</term> illnesses are generated; it causes undigested food to penetrate the system and ruins a good complexion. Therefore, you should go to sleep at least two hours after eating. It is first proper to sleep on your right side, then on the left for a few hours, because this aids digestion; finally, return to the right side so that the stomach may better complete the digestive process. However, it is far better to begin by lying on your stomach. It has also been said that excessive wakefulness is very harmful, for it destroys the <term>natural heat: the internal "fire" believed to drive life and digestion</term> and all the body's powers. For this reason, it is better to err on the side of too much sleep than too much wakefulness, as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> said, since the body's powers acquire strength through sleep. Yet, all extremes are always flawed, and therefore everything should be managed in a middle way and with temperance.

Exercise is very suitable, especially for an hour before lunch and dinner. Let it be moderate, however, and continued up to the point of sweating, such as a short walk on level—not mountainous—ground. For labor that leads to heavy sweating inflames the body and dissolves it, weakening the innate heat of the stomach; but moderate exercise strengthens the heat and dissolves the <term>superfluities: excess waste or humors</term> which are in the stomach. It rouses the <term>spirits: the subtle substances believed to flow through the body to provide life and sensation</term>, opens <term>obstructions: blockages in the vessels or organs</term>, and finally prepares the stomach to receive food. Thus, among the causes for preserving health and preventing illness, exercise is the most noble and worthy cause. Rest after food is also much praised in this manner: one should rest for two hours after taking food, lest the heat be scattered through the body by movement and abandon the work of digestion. Since perfect digestion is completed through rest, it is not good to engage in much exercise before digestion is finished, as this causes undigested food to descend to the intestines. Literary exercise <note>studying, reading, or writing</note> should be set aside immediately after lunch; the hour for studying should be in the morning, because at that time the spirits are purified, and with digestion already completed, study is performed better and without harm. Frictions <note>massages or vigorous rubbing of the skin</note>, which take the place of exercise, should be set aside, for when one can walk and be active, one does not need frictions. However, I highly praise washing the head every single week, specifically with warm <term>lye: a cleansing solution made from wood ashes and water</term>, as it strengthens the head and dissolves humid superfluities. I will say nothing of the exercise of the small ball <note>likely a game similar to tennis or handball</note>, since everyone knows how much it helps in the preservation of health, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD), the preeminent medical authority of the Roman world</note> testifies in his booklet on exercise with the small ball.

### MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...by the virtue of their ingredients and through daily experience itself, we know these medicines to possess such power, for they digest cold matter—both phlegmatic and melancholic—that has been absorbed into the nerves, the joints, or any other part of the body, and they do so without causing distress. Afterward, the evacuation should be repeated with the lenitive <note>mild</note> electuary and the confection of Hamech mentioned above. By proceeding in this way for many months through the benefit of medicines, you will be able to be freed from such a sickness.

But if anyone—whether a learned physician or an experienced empiric <note>an unlicensed practitioner who relies on trial and error rather than theory</note>—should persuade you that this must be done using strong medicines, their advice is to be completely avoided. For although the nature of these humors might require a strong medicine, the body's strength could not tolerate it, and the harm would be greater than the benefit. Indeed, it has happened that many, after taking strong medicines, have fallen into a worse state, because the limb having been made weak, the superfluities <note>excess or waste fluids</note> are neither corrected, nor separated, nor expelled, but remain and become the cause of a worse sickness.

Among practitioners, I am not unaware that many opinions exist regarding whether bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia."</note> is appropriate, which I omit for the sake of brevity. This is because it first evacuates all the matter which is scattered through the large veins, and thus it will be more useful—indeed, more noble—than the other treatments. For <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose works were the backbone of European medical education.</note> says that bloodletting is a universal evacuation of the entire mass of humors, both those generated in the liver <note>original: "hepate."</note> and those contained in other places; and as he himself testifies in his own chapter, it contributes greatly to melancholic illnesses.

## SECOND PART

**Bloodletting** <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> may be performed multiple times, such as twice in three months, or four times in five, if the sole intention is to eradicate the matter using drugs and other evacuants. A third method of eradication was devised through the **anointing of the joints** <note>original: "illinitiones iuncturarum"</note> with an ointment or liniment appropriate to the disease. Therefore, in my opinion, a better, safer, and more certain curative medicine for this disease cannot be devised, nor has it been discovered by anyone else. # MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...if] Your Lordship should decide to take the <term>decoction</term> <note>A medicinal liquid produced by boiling plant material in water to extract its active ingredients.</note> of <term>Indian wood</term> <note>original: "lignum indicum." Also known as Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," imported from the Americas and famously used to treat syphilis.</note>, and if after taking it (which may God in His mercy avert) you should suffer a relapse, I urge you to use no other medicine than this ointment, or these <term>anointings</term>. But since one must always begin with the milder treatments, I shall first speak of the intake and the regimen of the decoction of this wood, which is a milder medicine, and afterward, in the final place, I shall speak of the regimen of anointings.

In the first place, all who use this wood, or this decoction of wood, choose that wood (which is large) which has the most pith and black part, and is close to the roots. The ideal conditions for this wood are: its great size, having a wide and black pith, and that the part of the wood we use in the decoction be close to the roots. 

The virtues of this wood—as is apparent from its effects, and can be gathered from its color and taste (according to the teachings of the "Prince" <note>Referring to Avicenna (980–1037), whose "Canon of Medicine" was the foundational textbook for medieval and Renaissance physicians.</note> in the second book of the <term>Canon</term> and of <term>Galen</term> in his work *On Simple Medicine*)—are hot, opening, and provocative of urine and sweat. They also resolve other superfluities <note>In Galenic medicine, "superfluities" are excess humors or waste products that cause disease.</note>, and the substance of this wood, when taken in a broth or in the form of an <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powder with honey or syrup.</note> (as we shall describe), loosens the bowels. 

A quantity of at least six pounds of this wood is necessary. I say this because even if the illness were mild, recent, and of little consequence, it is nonetheless necessary to take the said decoction twice a day for a full month; therefore, a smaller quantity than this cannot be used. For your condition, Most Reverend Lordship, it is necessary to take ten "large" pounds. I specify this because the sellers do not weigh it by the apothecary's weight used for spices, but by the <term>common scale</term> <note>original: "statera grossa." The heavy commercial scale used for bulk goods rather than the precise troy or medicinal weights.</note>, as it is popularly called. 

This wood shall be reduced to a very fine powder by means of a file or a rasp. One pound of this powder shall be taken with fourteen pounds of spring water—or a greater quantity if necessary—and after it has been infused in an <term>earthen pot</term> for a day and a night, let it be placed on the fire to boil until a third part is consumed. The fire should be clear, pure without smoke, and with little flame. The decoction must be constantly skimmed of froth with a wooden instrument, not one of brass or iron. One must save this scum, for if you anoint painful tumors, pustules, and ulcers with it at the same time you are drinking the decoction, it will be very beneficial. 

Once the boiling has consumed a third part, the decoction should rest for a day, and afterward, it shall be carefully preserved after being very well strained. This water, which they call the "first water," thus purified, <insert>shall be kept</insert> in a <term>glass vessel</term> or a glazed jar, well-sealed...

## PART TWO

...shall be kept. And this is the **first decoction**, which should be drunk twice a day, both in the morning and in the evening. The **wood** which has boiled once should have as much water added to it as was used the first time; let it sit in infusion as before, and then placed over a slow fire, let it boil until a third part is consumed (just as before). Once strained, it should be kept in a glass or glazed earthenware vessel. And this is the **second decoction**, which it is useful to drink at lunch and dinner, and throughout the day and night whenever thirst arises. 

And while this water is being drunk, another pound of wood powder should be prepared. After it has remained in infusion for the required time, let it boil as the first decoction did, so that when the other decoction is finished, this new batch is ready. In this way, there is no day on which this drinking regimen is omitted. It is worth noting, however, that the more the water is boiled, the more excellent its action will be, and it will possess greater virtue and efficacy. Nevertheless, all things must be managed moderately and in a balanced manner. 

Let these words suffice regarding the preparation of the wood; now I shall speak of the **preparation of the body**. For it is necessary, before the decoction is taken, that the body be purged so that it is cleared of "superfluities" <note>In Galenic medicine, 'superfluities' were excess humors (fluids) that caused disease.</note>. This prevents the "bad humors" from being carried through the veins and pores to the nerves and joints by the penetrating power of the water, which would cause greater blockages and prevent the medicinal virtue of the water from reaching its destination. 

Therefore, for fifteen days before starting the decoction of <term>guaiac wood</term>, let the body be purged with these medicines. The first recipe is: 
One ounce of <term>lenitive electuary</term> <note>A mild, sweet laxative paste.</note>, and two drams each of <term>Confection of Hamech</term> <note>A stronger purgative intended to expel "black bile" or melancholic humors.</note> and <term>prepared agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus (Laricifomes officinalis) used as a purgative.</note>. Mix these and make a bolus with sugar, to be taken three hours before lunch. 

And since—according to the opinion of <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>—one must treat the humors once they are "cooked" <note>The medical theory that humors must be "digested" or ripened by heat before they can be safely purged from the body.</note>, a warm <term>digestive</term> should be taken at dawn the following day. 
**Recipe:** half an ounce each of <term>syrup of endive</term>, <term>fumitory</term>, <term>dodder of thyme</term>, and <term>stoechas</term> <note>A type of wild lavender.</note>; and one ounce each of the **distilled waters** of endive, fumitory, and <term>ground-pine</term> <note>original: "iuae." A medicinal plant used for joint pain.</note>. Mix these and let it be taken at least four hours before lunch. This procedure should be followed for four days. 

On the fifth day, let the middle vein (or the "common vein") of the right arm be cut, and let six ounces of blood be drawn. Lunch should be taken two hours later. Then, on the seventh, eighth, and ninth days, you shall take the "digestive" mentioned above. 

On the tenth day, take this evacuating medicine: 
**Recipe:** six drams of <term>lenitive electuary</term>, three drams of <term>Confection of Hamech</term>, and one and a half drams of <term>prepared agaric</term>. Mix these and make a bolus with sugar, or a potion with the waters of endive, fumitory, and ground-pine, to be taken six hours before lunch.

# THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...be taken. On the **eleventh day**, you shall take a cup <note>original: "cyathum," a standard medical measure similar to a small glass or cup</note> of broth with sugar, which will serve as a laxative. On the **twelfth day** and the following days (up to the **fifteenth day**), the aforementioned digestive syrups should be taken at dawn. On the **sixteenth day**, the bolus <note>a large pill or medicinal morsel</note> previously described should be taken four hours before lunch; it is then good to rest for the next two days. 

And on the **eighteenth day**, you shall begin to drink the water from the decoction of the wood <note>The "wood" refers to Guaiacum, also known as "Holy Wood," imported from the Americas to treat syphilis.</note>. But it must be noted that one ought to be in a very well-closed chamber; if there is any cold in it, let it be altered to a warm temperature with a fire or with a stove, so that in no way is coldness felt. Similarly, if there is excessive heat, the room should be altered somewhat with cooling agents. One must not leave this room until the sickness is entirely consumed. It is even better and safer to be overheated than to be chilled, because we live by heat; and **Aristotle** said that whatever the soul performs, it performs by fire <note>Aristotle's *De Anima* and other works posited that "natural heat" was the instrument of the soul's vital functions.</note>, that is, by natural heat, the extinction or excessive cooling of which is followed by death.

Therefore, once the aforementioned evacuation is completed and the closed chamber prepared so that no wind may enter (but with the fire kept at a distance to ward off the cold), you shall take a cup of the warm **first decoction** at dawn. Afterward, you shall remain in bed, very well covered with cloths, and if possible, you shall sweat. Six hours after taking the decoction, you shall have lunch. This shall consist of small chickens, boiled hens, and well-leavened bread weighing four or five ounces. You may also eat roasted chicken; if small chickens cannot be found, something similar should be eaten, such as partridges, thrushes, and veal or kid meat, weighing four or five ounces.

At least seven hours after lunch, you shall take another cup of the said warm **first decoction** in the evening, and remain covered in bed to sweat. It will be better if you eat nothing in the evening. But if the stomach cannot tolerate being without food, you may take two morsels of bread and nothing else. 

As for drink (if thirst is present), both during lunch and at other times, day or night, let it be the water of the **second decoction** of the said wood, which you may drink as you please. It is necessary to do this for at least **twenty days**. Once these have passed, you should not increase the food, but you may divide it in this way: taking two parts of the said food in the morning and one part in the evening. In my counsel, it is necessary to proceed in this manner until the **fiftieth day**, taking the said **first water** in the morning and evening; let no day pass without drinking it. For drink, when thirst is present, use the **second water**. Under no circumstances should one drink wine; rather, these things must be observed with the greatest diligence, as I have said...

# SECOND PART

...must be observed, because otherwise you might perhaps fall into a worse condition. Nor should one fail in the middle of the journey, because all those who have done so were not cured. However, there are some deceptive doubts which someone might bring against us; therefore, I shall resolve them. 

First, Hippocrates says in his <term>Aphorisms</term> <note>original: "Aph." - This refers to the *Aphorismata*, a collection of medical maxims by the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates.</note> that in long-lasting and acute illnesses, a <term>thin diet</term> <note>original: "tenuis diæta" - a restrictive diet often consisting of little more than broths or light liquids, intended to prevent the body from being "distracted" by digestion.</note> is difficult to endure. Since this [syphilis] is a long illness, it would appear that the aforementioned thin diet is not suitable. To this objection, one must respond that in this illness—which arises from a repletion of bad, cold <term>humors</term> <note>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed in pre-modern medicine to control health and temperament.</note> caused by indigestion—a thin diet takes the place of evacuation [purging]. This is supported by Galen in his second commentary on the fourth Aphorism, where he says that abstinence from food purges the whole body equally, and thus it is appropriate. 

Furthermore, the words of Hippocrates do not contradict what we have said, because he is speaking of long illnesses that cast down one's strength, such as a fever. Additionally, I say that this diet is suitable because it is "strength" <note>Galen's concept of "virtus" or "faculty," the body's natural power to heal itself.</note> that heals the disease; and since a large amount of food hinders that strength (as Galen said) by keeping it busy with digestion, it cannot act against the illness. Therefore, abstinence from food is very appropriate, because strength, when unhindered, resists the sickness with every effort and expels the bad humors with the help of some <term>medicine</term>, such as "this water" <note>The primary decoction of Guaiac wood.</note>. 

For Galen says in his commentary on the first Aphorism that the sick person should be dieted in such a way that their strength is nourished, not the disease; food is an enemy to nature when it acts as a friend to the disease. Furthermore, the "second water" <note>A weaker, second boiling of the same Guaiac wood chips, used for general hydration during the treatment.</note>—which should be drunk while eating and whenever thirst is present—is thick, substantial, and nourishing. Therefore, even if it has some bitterness, you ought to drink it when you are thirsty, both because it nourishes and because it acts against the disease by expelling the [corrupt] matter and strengthening the limbs.

But because the feces are often retained in those who sweat and urinate excessively (due to the dryness created in the intestines), if the belly becomes dried out and you lack "the benefit of the body" <note>A common euphemism for regular bowel movements.</note>, you must occasionally use a common <term>clyster</term> <note>clyster: an enema used to clear the bowels.</note>, which shall be made as follows:

| Ingredient | Quantity |
| :--- | :--- |
| Waters of a decoction of mallow, violets, and beets | 1 <term>pound</term> <note>original: "lib. i." - roughly 12 ounces in the apothecary system.</note> |
| Common oil | 4 <term>ounces</term> <note>original: "℥. iiii."</note> |
| Cane honey | 2 <term>ounces</term> |
| Common salt | 2 <term>ounces</term> |

Mix these and let it be administered in the morning before lunch. Or, you may also take one pill of washed aloes an hour before lunch. Or, you may take the powder of this wood [Guaiac] to the weight of two <term>drams</term> <note>original: "drachmarum" - a small unit of weight.</note> with chicken broth and sugar, as this will loosen the belly. Note one other thing: you may walk about the bedchamber, but by no means go outside of it...

...Finally, it should be known that wakefulness is more beneficial than sleep; therefore, I do not praise sleeping during the day unless you wish to provoke a sweat, which is more easily achieved during sleep. However, it is good to be with friends and to be cheerful. At night you shall sleep well so that your strength may be restored. If pains, swellings, pustules, or ulcers are present, let them be anointed with that foam which you saved from the first boiling <note>The "foam" refers to the scum skimmed off the top of the Guaiac wood decoction mentioned in the previous sections of the treatment.</note>. After fifty days have passed, one must return gradually to the original habit of health, since nature does not tolerate sudden changes. Therefore, one should not return immediately to the usual quantity of food, but rather increase the amount of meat and bread step-by-step. The wine should first be well diluted with water, and later less so, so that the body is returned to its former habit with a certain moderation. If all these things are done according to the rules, there is no doubt that you will be restored to your former health, which may Christ the Son of God deign to grant you through His mercy.

It remains for us to look at the treatment by ointments, which I set aside earlier, and which I indeed praise highly as being the more effective method. Once the aforementioned evacuations have been performed, along with <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "phlebotomia" - the surgical opening of a vein to balance the humors.</note> and the preparation of the matter through syrups as has been described, and all other things by which the body ought to be purged before taking the water of the <term>Indian wood</term> <note>original: "ligni indici" - Guaiacum, a dense wood from the Americas believed to be a "miracle cure" for syphilis.</note>, all the joints of the arms and feet must be anointed with this ointment. Add a little <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "aquæ ardentis" - literally "burning water," referring to distilled alcohol.</note>, mix them, and let an <term>ointment</term> be made in a mortar, stirring it well with a pestle. With this, let all the joints be anointed in the evening, three hours after dinner; place hemp tow over them and let them be well bound. Afterward, go to bed, and being well covered, you shall sweat for an hour if possible, and sleep at your pleasure. And so it is necessary to anoint every evening until an alteration of the gums appears in the mouth—but not rot—or a foul smell from the mouth. This is a sign that the matter is flowing toward the stomach through paths that are secret and hidden to us, but known to nature. Therefore, when the body is così altered, the bad <term>humors</term>—having been digested and prepared for expulsion by the quality of such an ointment—are driven out by the body's strength so that (if no error occurs) a perfect cure of this disease is achieved, as has already been seen in many cases. And since mouth ulcers usually follow such an anointing, as well as spitting—which is the matter from which the pains are caused, and...

It will also be useful and necessary to do this same thing at the beginning of Spring and Autumn; for in this way, you will preserve the health you have acquired, which may God, blessed in His goodness, deign to grant your Lordship.

You have here, then, Most Reverend Lord (if you examine it carefully), all these things: first, the preventive care; second, the eradicative treatment; and after the eradication, the preservation of health. All of these you can achieve through these means: namely, the regimen of life, the taking of drugs and other medicines that evacuate cold matters, and those things which strengthen and fortify the liver—the primary root of this sickness.

->PART ONE<-

## TO THE MOST REVEREND
### Master of Theology, Lord Bartholomew, concerning the French disease. <note>original: "morbo Gallico"; the common Renaissance term for syphilis.</note>

### EPISTLE XXI.

**A**LTHOUGH, Reverend Master, this sickness of yours is simply to be dreaded, nevertheless, when I look at all things from a medical perspective—things which promise the most certain and swift health—they are so abundant and clear that they invite me, contrary to the usual custom of physicians, to promise you a complete recovery. Therefore, lest I seem to use a longer preface than is fitting, I will approach the matter as briefly as I can. First, I say that this sickness is "confirmed," and no sensible physician can doubt this, since many <term>symptoms</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; in Galenic medicine, these are the outward signs or "accidents" that manifest from an internal disease.</note> are present which make this clear.

And since in the French disease the <term>Liver</term> <note>original: "Iecur" or "hepar"; Renaissance doctors believed the liver was the primary organ for creating blood and humors, and thus the source of systemic diseases.</note> is the primary source, in which—due to a certain "cooling"—a <term>phlegmatic humor</term> <note>original: "pituitosus humor"; one of the four bodily fluids. An excess of cold, moist phlegm was thought to cause various sluggish or chronic diseases.</note> predominates (one that is unnatural and not lacking in dryness, possessing a certain hidden quality), it is established that this humor is the foundation of this evil disposition. From this location and from this matter—because of the connection the rest of the body has with the liver—the entire body becomes infected. Thus, the sickness is called "universal," even if the entire body does not appear universally infected; it is, however (as I said), affected through its connection to the liver.

By this, I solve a frequently asked problem: namely, why is it that those who suffer either pain, or an ulcer, or any other symptom in one particular limb are not healed unless there is a rectification or a <term>cleansing</term> <note>original: "mundificatio"; the process of purging the body of "corrupt" humors.</note> of the whole body, and primarily of the liver and the blood? From what has been said, the answer is clear: namely, because the sickness is primarily in the liver, which multiplies that unnatural humor with its evil quality.

And this is why Your Reverend Paternity <note>A formal honorific for a high-ranking member of the clergy.</note> cannot be healed of that ulcer on your leg, or rather the <term>back of the knee</term>, <note>original: "poplitis".</note> even if the most suitable remedies are applied [locally]. This is because the limb contains the matter that nourishes the disease existing within, which must be dealt with first. Thus, through the "removal of the cause" (according to the doctrine of <term>Galen</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note>), the limb must be restored to its former health.

Therefore, so that I may turn my full attention to the matter itself: since I am aware of the duration of the previous sickness, its quality, your age, the strength of your <term>constitution</term>, <note>original: "complexionis"; the specific balance of the four humors (hot, cold, moist, dry) unique to an individual.</note> your habits, and all other things which physicians consider before they come to the practical act...

<summary>In this letter, the physician explains that syphilis is a systemic disease rooted in the liver, which is why local symptoms like leg ulcers cannot be cured without treating the whole body. He uses Galenic theory to justify a "universal" treatment plan for his patient, a Master of Theology.</summary>

**Take:** one pound (which consists of eighteen ounces) of Indian wood, very finely pulverized with a file. Then remove it from the fire, and when this decoction has cooled, let it be strained through a clean linen cloth. Keep it in a glass or glazed stone vessel; this will be the **First Decoction**, to be taken morning and evening.

...has been taken, let it be strained and kept in a glass vessel. This will be the **second decoction**, which should be taken at lunch, at dinner, and during the day as desired. Therefore, once the water is taken at the warm hour already mentioned, cover yourself with blankets, and sweat, and sleep—if you are able to sweat and sleep. If not, let whatever is possible be done without causing harm. You must delay lunch until noon. Two hours before lunch, take a cup of the second decoction. Along with the raisins, you should also eat bread that is well-leavened and moderately baked, the quantity of which should be four ounces in weight, or five at most. You may also have three ounces of meat: either veal or kid, either roasted or boiled.

## PART TWO

<margin>PP</margin>

...you may drink the water of the **second decoction** as much as you like. And since this water—both the first and the second boiling—leaves a burning sensation and roughness in the throat, you may therefore always take one or two spoonfuls of well-washed **raisins** <note>original: "passularum"; raisins were frequently used in early modern medicine as a "lenitive" to soothe the throat and soften the bowels.</note> in the morning, during the day, and at lunch after drinking the water. These are very beneficial, not only for removing the burning and sweetening the mouth, but also for softening the bowels and even for correcting a bad <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperiem"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an organ.</note> of the **liver**.

Two or three hours after lunch, you should drink one cup of the second decoction and also eat the aforementioned raisins. Then, once another three hours have passed, drink another cup of the same decoction, even if you are not thirsty. Afterward, before you go to sleep or wish to sleep, drink one cup of the **first decoction** while it is warm, eat the raisins, and cover yourself with blankets so that you may sweat, if you are able. If you cannot sweat, at least cover yourself so that by retaining the warm air, the <term>potency</term> <note>original: "uirtus"; the specific medicinal power or "virtue" of the wood.</note> of the medicine is made stronger; then sleep. If you become thirsty during the night, drink the water of the second decoction as much as you like, whether it be cold or warm. During the day, at lunch, and at night, you should drink the second decoction.

Because it often happens—especially to **choleric** <note>Those with a "hot and dry" constitution, thought to be easily irritated or prone to hunger.</note> individuals who cannot tolerate hunger—that a looseness of the stomach, pain, or sometimes **fainting** <note>original: "syncope".</note> may come upon them, if any of these symptoms appear, you may take a small portion of bread and meat or raisins two hours before the evening dose of the first decoction. For instance, take two ounces of bread and a little meat or raisins, so that the medicinal potency is not frightened away by these bad accidents and ceases its proper operation—which is to direct the medicine against the disease and its cause, if the cause is <term>material</term>. <note>Referring to the "matter" or corrupt humors causing the illness.</note>

One must proceed in this way for eight or ten days. When these have passed, it is good to take two cups of the warm first decoction in the morning at the stated hour; and do the same in the evening, while drinking a larger quantity of the second decoction during the day. If, as I said, the belly becomes "dried up" so that it does not discharge anything, it is best to use a common **clyster** <note>An enema used to clear the bowels.</note> every other day in the morning before lunch. Or, if necessary, take **pills of fumitory**. <note>original: "fumoterræ"; a plant used to treat skin conditions and "purify" the blood.</note> For example:

->**Take 1 dram of pills of fumitory.**<-

Let three pills be made and taken in the morning at the time you take the water of the first decoction. After taking them, drink the water, cover yourself, and sleep; then take lunch at the usual hour. The necessity for taking these pills arises if any tension of the stomach or belly occurs; and note that it is enough to take them once a week.

->**THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA**<-

...take these pills, if there is a need, and proceed in drinking the said water, from both the **first** and **second boiling**, always increasing the quantity and never decreasing it, and continuing this for a period of forty days. But if, after twenty-five days have passed or even before then, a looseness <note>Referring here to diarrhea or loose bowels, a common side effect of the intensive liquid treatment.</note> or a loss of strength appears, you may increase the amount of bread and even meat—namely, by eating six ounces of bread and four of meat, or even more if it is necessary. However, for no reason is it appropriate to drink wine during the time you are drinking the water, nor should you eat a variety of different foods.

But since there is an ulcer with hardness behind the knee <note>original: "in poplite"; the popliteal region.</note>, and because this ulcer is not particularly deep nor is the hardness very stone-like, it will be sufficient for the dissolving of the hardness and the healing of the ulcer to apply the **scum** <note>original: "spumam"; the frothy residue skimmed off the top of the Guaiacum wood while it boils, which was believed to have concentrated healing properties for skin lesions.</note> which you have saved on top of it. Change this morning and evening; the ulcer will be healed and the hardness dissolved by the power of this scum. This, then, shall be the order of time and the quantity for drinking the said waters. Therefore, once forty days have passed, begin to return yourself gradually to your former habits of both food and drink; specifically, by eating a larger quantity of meat and **soft-boiled eggs**, and begin to drink watered-down wine, and afterward even pure wine, provided it is in small amounts. For at least two months, however, you must not eat "moist" meats such as pork or lamb, and similarly you must avoid all fish, legumes, vinegar, and sharp things, as onions are harmful.

Furthermore, once those forty days have ended, it will be good to drink one cup of the **first boiling** at dawn, and also in the evening when you go to sleep, for at least fifteen days. When these have passed, it is best to purge the body or the bowels once more with this "blessed medicine":

**A Purgative Draught**
| Ingredient | Amount |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Universal Purge** <note>original: "diacatholicon"; a standard Renaissance laxative paste made from cassia, tamarind, and senna.</note> | 7 drams |
| **Soothing Electuary** <note>original: "electuarii lenitiui"; a sweet medicinal paste used to ease the passage of stool.</note> | 7 drams |

Mix these, and let a bolus be made with sugar, or let a potion be made with **borage** and **fumitory** waters to be taken in the morning, four hours before lunch. Afterward, to comfort the stomach and liver, take for several days in the morning one **Abbot’s rose-lozenge** <note>original: "diarhodonis Abbatis"; a famous compound of red roses, sandalwood, and spices used to "cool" a liver overstimulated by medicine.</note>, two hours before lunch, and likewise in the evening before dinner. These are the things, Reverend Master, which I wished to write briefly for the health of your Fatherhood. May God himself, the giver of all good things, deign to restore your health. Farewell.

->**THE LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA**<-

# NICCOLÒ MASSA to the most excellent Physician, Master Giovanni Romano, sends many greetings.

## On the French disease <note>original: "morbo Gallico"; the 16th-century term for syphilis, which was then a relatively new and terrifying epidemic in Europe.</note>.

## LETTER XXII.

I have read the letter which you, most learned and dear friend, sent to me, and it brought me both great joy and much distress. I say joy, because I learned from it how much you value me—for I have always considered it no small matter to be loved and esteemed by a man of such great learning and integrity. But I felt distress when I heard that you are greatly pained and troubled by the long-standing illness of your most beloved wife. At your request, I visited her together with the illustrious doctor Donato de' Mutis <note>A contemporary physician and author who wrote on the "French disease."</note>, who is also very dear to me, and Master Giovanni Battista of Reggio, a man truly excellent and most learned. We held a lengthy consultation with them, and we came unanimously and without hesitation to this conclusion: that she is suffering from that epidemic condition which they call the **French disease**.

Of this fact, many symptoms <note>original: "accidentia"; in Renaissance medicine, these were the observable signs or "accidents" of a disease.</note> which preceded the illness, and those which are present even now, provide indubitable proof, which it will not be troublesome for me to list. Indeed, we heard your Excellence say that you yourself had long struggled with the French disease, contracted from an infected woman, such that you had **ulcers** on the penis that were difficult to heal, and **buboes** <term>buboes</term> <note>Swollen, painful lymph nodes in the groin, a characteristic sign of primary syphilis.</note> in the groin that were hard to treat. After these were cured, **pustules** <note>Small, inflamed skin elevations or sores.</note> appeared over your entire body, and especially on the head and chin. These could not be healed at all until many <term>evacuations</term> <note>The process of "clearing out" the body's fluids (humors) to restore balance, usually via laxatives or bloodletting.</note> were performed, both through bloodletting and through medicines taken by mouth to draw out the corrupt humors. After these evacuations, you used <term>unctions</term> <note>The application of medicinal ointments, often containing mercury, rubbed into the skin at the joints.</note> on your joints and other parts of your body. 

And since your wife did not refrain from your embrace <note>A 16th-century euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note>, she also developed ulcers of the vulva, tumors around the groin, and some pustules, especially on the head. She could not be cured, even though your Excellence purged her through both bloodletting and medicines taken by mouth; on the contrary, the matter always seemed to progress for the worse. Thus, at present, she suffers from pain in her head and in almost all the joints of both her arms and legs. But among other things, that which seems to trouble her the most is a tumor around the jaw...

[mand]ibles, which even prevents the voluntary movement of the jaws themselves. Nor is it difficult to assign a cause for this hindrance in opening the mouth, since tumors are manifest around both the one and the other jaw joint. These tumors arise from a material cause with a predominance of phlegm <note>original: "pituitosa"; in the theory of the four humors, phlegm was considered cold and moist. Its buildup was thought to cause sluggishness or blockages.</note>, from which material the subtle parts have been gradually dissolved. This is because, as I hear, when the matter first began to descend, the area was softer. For you know, most learned man, from the science of dissection <note>Massa was a renowned anatomist; here he refers to "scientia dissectionis" to explain the physical connection between muscles and bone.</note> that the muscles terminate at the jaw joints by means of cords <term>tendons</term>, which have the power both of opening and closing the mouth, whether in eating, shouting, speaking, or yawning. But since I am writing to a most learned Physician, I will not recount everything that seems to pertain to an exact knowledge of the disease, but I shall come to the primary site affected.

The organ, therefore, which was first affected (as is not hidden from you) is the **liver**. Its affliction, regarding its own temperament, is a **cooling** <note>original: "refrigeratio." Galenic medicine taught that the liver should be naturally warm to "cook" food into blood. A "cooled" liver failed to process humors correctly, leading to the production of excess phlegm.</note>, from which a great deal of phlegmatic matter is generated. This matter later passes with the blood and other humors through the veins and typically affects the entire body. Thus, in the beginning, besides ulcers of the private parts <note>original: "pudendorum ulcera"; a primary symptom of syphilis.</note> or changes in other members, a heaviness of the entire body appeared, especially in the head, shoulders, and legs, so that she could hardly lift her arms to her head and walked with difficulty. 

This long-standing heaviness is something that must be helped quickly and with appropriate remedies. I say "appropriately," because often **empirical physicians** <note>original: "medici empirici"; these were practitioners who learned by trade rather than university study. Massa, as a university-trained physician, often criticizes them for acting without theoretical "reason."</note> are accustomed to treating these ailing people with certain experiments of theirs without reason, which in the end usually lead the patients into a worse condition. Indeed, they either administer "loosening" medicines <term>laxatives or purgatives</term> before the thick matter (which requires the most diligent digestion and preparation) has been "ripened," and thus they draw out other fluids instead of the offending humor. Or, they exhaust every body without any distinction using the most violent medicines, which harm the primary organs such as the stomach, the liver, and the intestines. Thus, they cause—as the saying goes—an "outpouring"; that is, through immoderate and untimely evacuation, those humors and fluids which were already prepared in the veins for excellent nourishment are drained away. This leaves behind or impresses the "bad quality" of the medicines upon the stomach, liver, and intestines. Frequently, by their purgings, they lead patients to **fainting** <note>original: "lipothymiam"; a sudden loss of strength or consciousness.</note> and mental failings due to the harm inflicted on the opening of the stomach. Often, they are not only the cause of a "looseness" <term>diarrhea</term> of the intestines, but even lead to the end of life with the most severe ulceration of the bowels...

reason. I add also that you have seen many, and I have seen very many, and all physicians everywhere have seen those who—from such untimely and irrational healing with the medicines already mentioned, or with ointments wrongly applied to the body, and certain fumigations, and the drink of **Indian wood** <note>original: "ligni indici"; likely Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," often used to treat the "French Disease" (syphilis), but here Massa warns against its improper use.</note> administered without reason—have fallen not only into that bad condition which the Greeks call <term>cachexia</term> <note>original: "cachexiam"; a state of severe physical wasting and malnutrition.</note>, but even into **water under the skin** <note>edema or dropsy</note> caused by the aforementioned cases and that final cooling of the liver. I wanted to note these things to your excellence, not so that I might "instruct Minerva" <note>a Latin proverb meaning to teach someone who is already an expert; Massa is showing professional humility to his colleague.</note> (as they say), but to remind you, lest perhaps being weary from the long duration of the illness and the many remedies already tried, you might wish to consult such quacks <note>original: "empiricos"; practitioners who relied on experience alone without theoretical medical training.</note>. We have seen your wife, in her suffering, come to the aforementioned major cooling of the limbs; so much so that not only is her face swollen and discolored, but even the legs themselves and the hips begin to swell. 

Therefore, my most learned and beloved <term>John</term> <note>original: "Ioannes," referring to the recipient, Giovanni Romano.</note>, having touched upon these matters, I shall write down those things which were praised by us for a regular cure (in a case indeed very difficult to cure, but easy to recognize). And since it is impossible for the pains throughout the entire body and the swelling of the jaws to be removed unless the cold matter generated by the bad temperament of the liver is first moved, for that reason it is worthwhile that necessary things be regulated in this manner. 

First, therefore, since the disease is now long-standing and all the limbs together with the liver show a manifest cooling, let those foods be such as can best nourish and modestly warm, not deprived of even some slight drying effect; and since I am writing to a most learned physician, I will not labor over a detailed list of foods. Let her also drink the best wine, neither sweet nor acidic, and to complete everything in a single word (as they say), let the regimen in other necessary things be that which can modestly warm and in some way dry out. 

With the regimen thus established, there follows the second part or instrument: the cure of the illnesses, and the preparation and evacuation of the matter from the said bad temperament. And since, from what has been said, the matter is predominantly phlegmatic <term>pituitous</term> <note>original: "pituitosa"; relating to the humor of phlegm, characterized as cold and moist.</note> and cold—yet not pure but mixed with other humors, namely **melancholy** and to some extent even **bile** <note>original: "bilioso"; referring to yellow bile or choler.</note> (if the urine can testify to the mixture of humors, for if they are at first crude and livid <note>bluish or grayish in color, indicating poor "digestion" of the humors.</note>, they nevertheless do not lack a yellowish tint)—this preparation of the humors in the common channels will be easily done. If your excellence, every single morning at dawn and also in the evening hours for four [days...]

...hours before dinner, she should be given syrups made from a mixture of **rose honey** <note>original: "mellis rosacei"; a common medical base in this period combining honey and rose petals</note> and **syrup of fumitory** <note>original: "syrupo de fumoterrae"; fumitory was used to "purify" the blood and treat skin ailments</note> and of **stoechas** <note>original: "stoechade"; French lavender, used for its warming properties</note>, diluted with water of **chicory**, **wormwood**, and **ground pine** <note>original: "ivae"; Ajuga iva, often used for gout and stomach issues</note>. When, indeed, some evidence of the preparation of the aforementioned humors appears in the urine, they must be drawn out by "diminishing" means (as they say); this should be done with substances that can reduce the matter by evacuating it lightly and without violence. Examples include a **lenitive electuary** <note>a medicinal paste or conserve with mild laxative properties</note> or **diacatholicon** <note>a "universal" purgative paste used to cleanse all humors</note> together with the electuary **diaphinicon** <note>a purgative made primarily of dates</note>. Nor would I omit a small portion of **rhubarb**, since her liver has already been greatly weakened. If it should happen that she must be evacuated again, as one might do for the veins, there should undoubtedly be in the said medicine some **agaric** <note>original: "agarici"; a medicinal fungus used as a purge</note>, and I would also mix in the **confection of hamech** <note>a complex, bitter purgative used to treat "melancholic" or thick humors</note> more than once (as I said), according to the needs of the situation. This is so that the body may be cleansed of superfluous wastes, and the limbs—which are currently in a state contrary to nature—can return to a better temperament once these wastes are evacuated.

One must not consider the evacuation of blood by opening a vein <note>bloodletting</note>, since a cold **ill-temperament** <note>original: "mala temperies"; an imbalance of the four bodily humors</note> has already been contracted not only in the liver, but throughout the entire body. However, we shall all reach the consensus that it is worthwhile to proceed with what has proven health-giving for many: namely, that she should drink a **decoction of Indian wood** <note>original: "decoctum ligni indici"; Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," imported from the Americas and famous for treating syphilis and chronic "cold" obstructions</note> not only for forty days, but even for fifty, or two months if necessary. For in a long-standing disease and in a weak body, medicines are not so easily activated by [internal] heat.

Physicians commonly prepare the decoction in this way: they take one pound of the best **Indian wood** reduced to powder, over which they pour fifteen or sixteen pounds of the best spring or well water. They put everything together in a stone vessel for a day and a night, and then they allow it to boil over a slow fire until a third part is consumed. Once this is done, they remove the decoction from the fire to cool. After it has cooled, they order it to be strained through a very clean linen or hemp cloth. This decoction must afterwards be kept in a glass, stone, or glazed earthenware vessel. A quantity of eight or ten ounces should be taken hot early in the morning—more or less according to the tolerance of her stomach. This mentioned liquid is called the "first decoction" by physicians. The wood that has boiled once should be put back into the pot after straining, and the same amount of water poured over it; let it boil again until a third is consumed, and be strained as before. This second strained liquid is kept in another glass or glazed stone vessel...

## PART TWO.

...is served. And this is called by doctors the **second decoction** <note>A weaker medicinal tea made by boiling the same ingredients a second time, used for general hydration during the day.</note>, which the sick drink both while they eat and when they are thirsty during the day, or on any other occasion. For this is an eternal truth: that the more the sick drink of both the first and second decoctions, the more quickly and better they are cured. One thing, however, must be observed: while the wood is boiling, the foam should be collected and kept, so that if necessary, swollen and painful areas may be anointed with it; for it makes them soft and in some way dulls the pain. This foam also heals long-standing ulcers. 

And let these things be sufficient, most learned man, concerning the preparation of the decoction of <term>Indian wood</term> <note>original: "ligni indici"; likely Guaiac wood from the Americas, which was famously used in the 16th century to treat the "French Disease" (syphilis) and other chronic conditions by inducing sweating.</note>, as it is commonly prepared.

Therefore, once the purgings have been performed as stated above, first your excellence should prepare a **chamber** <note>original: "thalamum"; a private room or bedroom</note> in which cold air can by no means enter. In it, the sick Lady should remain and drink both the first and second decoctions in roughly this order: 

->**The Morning Routine**<-

In the morning, specifically at dawn, she should drink one <term>cup</term> <note>original: "cyathum"; a vessel used for measuring, here roughly 8 ounces in weight as specified by the text.</note> of the first decoction while hot, which should weigh at least eight <term>ounces</term> <note>original: "unciarum"; a unit of weight.</note>. After this, she should eat two spoonfuls of <term>raisins</term> <note>original: "passularum"; dried grapes were a standard part of this diet, thought to provide gentle nourishment without interfering with the medicine.</note>, and stay in bed well-covered, and sweat if she can; if she cannot, she should remain thus for five hours. 

Once these hours have passed, she should take <term>lunch</term> <note>original: "prandium"</note> consisting of four or five ounces of well-leavened and well-baked bread, with an equal amount of meat—either chicken, partridge, pheasant, kid, or veal—and let them be either boiled or roasted, along with raisins. She should drink the water of the second decoction as she pleases, and remain thus after lunch for six or seven hours; she should not sleep during this time if she slept during the night. 

If she becomes thirsty, she may drink one cup or a half-cup of the second decoction at will. When those seven hours have passed, she should drink again from the first decoction, eight or ten ounces. She should also eat raisins afterward, and staying in bed, cover herself modestly with blankets, and sweat if she can; if not, it does not matter, let her at least rest. 

If she can go without <term>supper</term> <note>original: "cœna"</note>, it would be best; if not, let her sup sparingly four hours after drinking the decoction. She should eat two ounces of bread and two of the mentioned meats with raisins. She should abstain from wine if possible. Regarding this abstinence from wine, there was a discussion among us, and we finally arrived at this opinion: that she could not eat lunch without wine, since there is a fear that, by changing her habits in every respect, her <term>stomach</term> <note>original: "stomachus"; in this period, the "stomach" often referred to the entire digestive system and the "seat" of appetite.</note> might be further weakened. For this reason, let wine diluted with the second decoction be given at lunch. It will be worthwhile to proceed in this way for at least forty days, and even more if necessary, as [was stated] above...

...I have mentioned, for a period of up to two months. We say this because this method of drinking this decoction, which I have described, is the easiest and gentlest of all those used by physicians. We also desired that after she has begun for several days—let us say eight—to drink one <term>cup</term> <note>original: "cyathum"; a vessel used for measuring, here roughly 8 ounces.</note> as mentioned, she should become accustomed (if it can be done without distress) to drinking two cups in the morning hours, and similarly in the evening hours. Let her also become accustomed to drinking a larger quantity of the **second decoction** <note>The weaker, secondary boiling of the wood used for general hydration.</note> at lunch and during the day, because, as I said, the more of the said decoctions the sick drink, the more quickly and easily they are set free from illness. Also, the less they eat—and if the foods are simple—the better and safer we find the operations of the decoctions <gloss>of them</gloss> to be. And all these things we leave to your excellence to manage. 

And since <gloss>because</gloss> this decoction has a diuretic power and the power to provoke sweat, for which reason the bowels often remain constricted, it is necessary for this reason to use common <term>clysters</term> <note>original: "clysteribus"; an enema used to clear the bowels when the main treatment causes constipation.</note>. But in this case, I would recommend a clyster prepared in this manner:

¶ Take one pound of the second decoction of the said wood, 3 <term>ounces</term> <note>represented by the symbol ℥</note> of common oil, 2 ounces of honey of roses, 1 ounce of common salt, together with an egg yolk; let all be mixed, and let it be administered as the opportunity arises. 

Furthermore, your excellence should order that in the morning before lunch, and in the evening hours before <gloss>that</gloss> she begins to sleep, all painful places, and all tumors—and especially the jaw—should be smeared with the warm **foam** of the said decoction. But since this foam adheres with difficulty to the limb, it should therefore be placed upon a linen cloth and bound with a bandage or some other device. 

And so that these letters of ours do not lack advice in any part, if the Lady does not show herself compliant with the clysters and the bowels are constricted, let him order that she sometimes take one of the lighter medicines having the power to move the belly at the morning hours, such as a <term>lenitive electuary</term> <note>original: "electuarium lenitiuum"; a mild, sweet medicinal paste used as a laxative.</note>. Or if she would rather take <term>pills</term>, let them be made from the **"aggregative pills of the Indies"** and from **fumitory** <note>original: "fumoterræ"; a herb used to "purify" the blood and treat skin conditions.</note> mixed together, which I have always used successfully in similar conditions. 

And lest I seem reckless in writing to a most learned physician (as if I wished to <term>teach Minerva</term> <note>A classical idiom meaning to teach someone who is already an expert, as Minerva was the goddess of wisdom.</note>), let these things be said enough; all of which we submit to your most sharp judgment, for you will most diligently administer everything to your dearest wife. When all these things are done, if she can be set free (as we hope), we will give thanks to Almighty God. But if she has not returned to her former health in every respect, it is agreed between us that after some days have passed since the <gloss>drinking</gloss>...

Since the patient is elderly, and because the very state of her health (which is one of neutral convalescence) demands it, and since the heat of the elderly cannot easily process sluggish matter or expel it entirely—especially matter that is in the limbs far from the source of heat, such as the legs and arms—that matter should be prepared for some method of evacuation by the natural heat of the limbs, aided by the aforementioned ointments. Mix them, and let an ointment be made in a mortar, first processing the mercury with the fats, then adding the oil, then adding the other ingredients which have been very well powdered, and finally the distilled spirits. 

With this ointment, let the joints of the collarbones, knees, hands, and elbows be anointed. If the joints of the groin and shoulder blades are also anointed, it will be best; for the power to prepare and expel the harmful matter residing in the extremities of the limbs will be more quickly aroused. This anointing should be done after dinner, for two or three hours, on alternating days; so that sometimes one day, and sometimes two days are allowed to pass without anointing. Indeed, let the joints be protected with <term>hemp tow</term> <note>original: "stupa cannapina"; coarse, unrefined fibers of hemp used here as a dressing or padding.</note> that has been very well combed. Let her remain in bed and cover herself with cloths so that she may sweat modestly, if possible. I could indeed, most learned man, add many other ointments and remedies to those mentioned, which I have deliberately left out so that I do not (as I said) appear superstitious to you. One...

However, I will not overlook the fact that when much matter <note>In humoral medicine, "matter" refers to the excess or corrupted fluids—like phlegm or bile—believed to cause disease.</note> is sent to the mouth, which has already reached a stage of putrefaction, or through the mixing of a sharper humor, and with that substance continually flowing, ulcerations of the gums and other parts of the throat occur. If this complication should arise, you will assist her with frequent washing with a decoction of barley water (boiled with its husk), in which some <term>diamoronis</term> <note>original: "diamoronis"; a medicinal syrup made from mulberries and honey used to treat mouth sores.</note> should also be mixed to extinguish the heat of the ulcerated area. Externally, the cheeks and jaws should also be anointed with <term>rose oil</term> <note>original: "oleo rosaceo"</note>. Then, as the spit <note>Refers to the saliva or phlegm being expelled during treatment.</note> proceeds and is made somewhat better, a portion of <term>rose honey</term> <note>original: "mellis rosati"</note> should be mixed in for greater cleansing. Finally, let olive and myrtle leaves boil together with the barley, or something else that aids in the drying and consolidation <note>The closing and healing of an open wound.</note> of the ulcers. But if too much matter flows to the mouth, it must be diverted by cupping glasses applied to the buttocks and the shoulder blades. It must also be evacuated by the administration of <term>cochia pills</term> <note>original: "pilularum cochiarum"; a common purgative pill containing aloes, used to "draw" humors away from the head.</note>; and this is because much matter, which fills the head by evaporating, fosters the ulceration of the mouth. Your excellence will be able to correct other complications if they arise, for in these cases the bowels sometimes tend to flow too much, and sometimes they are constipated. Fainting and a loss of spirit <note>original: "animique defectus"; a feeling of profound weakness or depression.</note> also occur at times, along with many other things which would be long to list. Finally, both of those most distinguished doctors believe without any doubt that if these things are done, she will emerge unharmed. I easily subscribed to this opinion, since I know how much, besides your other virtues, you excel most fortunately in the art of healing. But if, besides those things I have written above, you desire to know anything further, do not be reluctant to read my little book on the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "morbo Gallico"; a common 16th-century term for syphilis.</note>; for from reading it you will gather many things, both regarding the disease itself and its complications, so that nothing will be lacking to you. Farewell, most learned man in every respect, and do not cease to love me (as you do). Venice, the seventh day before the Ides of June <note>June 7th</note>, 1532.
