# FOR THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE AND LORD
## Vladislaus Orza, a Pole, a treatment for long-standing French disease, along with ulcers and varicose veins in the leg, addressed to the most excellent physician, Master Johannes Raister.

### LETTER XXIII.

**YOU ASK**, most learned Johannes, that I might write down for you those things which were examined during the consultation for your most illustrious Prince. And although you have heard many things brought forward by the other physicians consulting together, you nevertheless desire to hear my opinion on this matter. Indeed (to satisfy you), although very many things were said, it will not be troublesome for me to write them as briefly as I can, given the narrowness of time.

In previous years, the distinguished and most illustrious Prince, while he was still a young man, suffered from <term>phlegmonous erysipelas</term> <note>original: "erisipelate phlegmonode"; a severe, painful inflammation of the skin and underlying tissues, often accompanied by fever.</note> in the hip, with a swelling in the knee that later descended to the shin, and pain in the leg. Once these were healed, he fell into certain pustules of the face and head, along with pains of the whole body—especially the chest, the muscles of the arms, the legs, and most of all the shoulder blades. All of these symptoms testified that his lordship was suffering from that evil disposition which they call the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "morbum Gallicum"; the common 16th-century term for syphilis.</note>. 

And since he desired to be healed from these unnatural affections, certain medicines that smacked of the nature of poison were administered without any correction of their harshness; such as <term>fumigations of cinnabar</term> <note>original: "suffumigia ex cinnabrio"; cinnabar is mercury sulfide. Patients were placed in a closed tent or box and exposed to the vapors of heated mercury.</note> and ointments prepared with no small portion of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento uiuo"; liquid mercury.</note>. Certain waters made of quicksilver, <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "uitriolo"; metal sulfates used for their drying and caustic properties.</note>, and other <term>sublimates</term> <note>original: "sublimatis"; chemical compounds produced through sublimation, often highly toxic mercuric salts.</note>, prepared in the manner of the <term>Alchemists</term> <note>original: "Alchimistarum"; refers here to non-academic practitioners or chemists who used aggressive metallic preparations.</note>, were applied to the shins and knees. 

These medicines were so far from being of any benefit that they instead led his lordship into so foul an ulceration of the mouth that almost all his teeth were loosened, accompanied by the greatest weakening of all his vital powers. Although those strong medicines were applied three times at different intervals, the sickness—which is foul by its very nature—did not depart for all that. Rather, by the poor administration of those stronger medicines, it has come to the point that his lordship still suffers from the same disease at present, not only with those earlier pustules and pains, but with a certain hard tumor near the collarbone, in...

...where a red color appears, mixed with a certain dusky darkness. There are, furthermore, certain superficial ulcers present, which do not proceed much beyond the surface of the skin. Along with these ulcers, swollen and soft veins filled with black, melancholic blood appear at the extremities of the shins. I cannot, at present, name this swelling of the veins in any other way than a <term>varicose disposition</term> <note>original: "varicosam dispositionem"; what we would today call varicose veins, though here associated with a buildup of "black bile."</note>, as the Arabs do. From this naming neither the Greeks nor the Latins seem to deviate, as evidenced even by **Cicero** in his *Tusculan Disputations*; I omit what both **Hippocrates** and **Galen** said about it. 

When a discussion regarding all these conditions was held among us in the presence of the Most Illustrious Lord, we said many things while investigating the essence and cause of the disease. In investigating the persistence and severity of the illness, some wished to attribute the cause to the poorly managed <term>six non-natural things</term> <note>original: "sex rebus non naturalibus"; the six external factors physicians believed governed health: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, exercise/rest, excretion/retention, and mental passions.</note> and to the bad administration of medicines. 

Then the curative intentions were investigated, by which the Most Illustrious Lord might be restored to health. His healing seemed most difficult to everyone, since—due to both a disordered way of life and the improper administration of drugs—a certain "bad habit" <note>An unhealthy physiological state or "disposition" of the organs.</note> has been left behind in the liver as well as in other parts of the body, and in the whole body generally. This is especially true of the leg which is currently suffering, so that these conditions, which are long-standing and depend on very powerful causes, cannot be healed without the greatest effort. 

Nevertheless, the Most Illustrious Lord is of an excellent <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionis"; the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) unique to an individual.</note> and in the prime of youth, a time when all vital powers appear strong. For **Hippocrates** used to say that those illnesses acquired over a long period cannot be cured in a short time. Yet I would not say he is in the ultimate stage of difficulty, since youth is full of hope. 

And let these things said about the essence and causes of the disease suffice for the sake of brevity, since our intention is more to deal with the cure and the regimen. But I wish to approach that which his Lordship requested above all else. His Most Illustrious Lordship asked first by what aids he might pass through the coming winter, so that a condition of this kind might not increase, but if possible, be diminished. Next, he asked by what remedies applied in the spring he might be healed and freed from the evils already mentioned so often. 

These things having been asked, when the most excellent junior doctor proposed certain things regarding a preventative regimen, they were all highly praised by us, with some additions that pertain more to the customs, fatherly manners, and the pleasures of the Most Illustrious Lord rather than to the actual method of curing. Therefore, first...

->PART TWO<-

The question was raised whether a light diet would be beneficial and necessary, given that the Hungarian Lord is accustomed to consuming many various foods and drinks without keeping to regular hours. To this petition, following the teachings of **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>, it was answered that a habit can only be changed with difficulty and not without danger. Therefore, we stated that his Illustrious Lordship may safely eat veal, kid, pheasant, partridge, thrush, turtledove, and other birds that live in the woods—the sort typically enjoyed by Princes and the wealthy—along with well-leavened bread and dishes not entirely foreign to the tastes of his homeland. He should, however, beware of poor-quality and moist meats, such as pork, goose, and the like. He should also avoid "bad" fish, such as eels. He must abstain from cheese, butter, and similar things which produce bad <term>chyme</term> <note>original: "mali chymi"; the semi-liquid mass of partially digested food in the stomach.</note>. Let him also drink a moderate wine in moderate quantities; the measure of all these things should be determined by his own tolerance and habit.

Furthermore, it was stated that rest will be very beneficial for him, since the specific affliction is in his leg, and the <term>procatarctic</term> <note>original: "procatarctica"; the external or immediate triggering cause of a disease.</note> or primary cause of this <term>varicose</term> disposition is disordered and constant riding or walking. Because rest is the opposite of motion, he will be greatly helped by it. However, light riding or walking performed at the proper time would not displease me, since, in the opinion of **Hippocrates**, some concession must be made to habit; those who are accustomed to specific labors do not suffer as much from them.

And since the afflictions appearing in the leg testify to a <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>original: "humorem melancholicum"; Black Bile, one of the four humors, associated here with the dark color and heaviness of the leg.</note>, it is therefore good for him to be joyful and to hope for the best; for worry increases the melancholic humor. Sexual intercourse, however, as a harmful thing that weakens the "spirits" and vital powers, must be entirely avoided. 

Nor should it be believed (as one of our colleagues suggested) that this affliction arises from "vitiated" or corrupted semen. For the Most Illustrious Lord appears healthy in all other parts of his body—excepting the leg—as can be seen from his physical functions, his readiness for action, his good complexion, and the strength of his entire frame. For those who have corrupted semen suffer a heaviness of the entire body, become chilled, and are rendered sluggish and powerless in movement; they also experience headaches, feelings of suffocation, insomnia, melancholic thoughts, and even manias. 

Nor should it be believed (as that colleague was saying) on the authority of **Hippocrates**, that semen for the most part descends from the brain through two veins. **Hippocrates** did not intend to say this, nor do anatomical observation or reason show it, although **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> followed this opinion...

# THE MEDICAL EPISTLES OF NICCOLÒ MASSA

...it appeared to have reached his opinion. For the most learned **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> never said that the matter of semen comes from the brain, except by a certain reflux; since it is secreted from all parts of the body as a superfluity of the <term>fourth digestion</term> <note>original: "quarta digestione"; in medieval medicine, this was the final stage of nutrition where food is transformed into the actual substance of the organs.</note>, and is shaped by the power of all the members, and especially the principal ones. It is from these that it receives the power to generate another like itself. Thus, it receives only the "animal virtue" <note>The "animal virtue" or spirit was thought to be centered in the brain, governing sensation and movement.</note> from the brain, and the matter is secreted together with virtue from the liver and the heart (as is apparent from sensory <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: "sensata anatomia"; knowledge of the body gained through direct observation and dissection.</note>) through the veins themselves and the arteries that form the seminal vessels—the veins descending from the liver and the arteries from the heart to the testes.

Nor should anything else be said than what I have stated in my own book, *Introduction to the Dissection of the Human Body* <note>original: "libello de introductione sectionis corporis humani"; Massa's famous anatomical text published in 1536.</note>. Namely, that the matter of semen is secreted from all the members and is prepared by them in such a way that, through reflux in the heart and liver, it receives a certain perfection before it is transmitted to the testes, where it attains its final power.

But if the semen were corrupted, not only would the symptoms mentioned above appear, but many others besides. Since these were not present in this Most Illustrious Lord in the past, nor are they present now, it should not be said that corrupted semen is the cause. Rather, the cause is the liver first, and from it, the whole body; since the <term>humoral mass</term> <note>The total collection of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in the body.</note> causes this due to the aforementioned reasons, as well as the harmful administration of <term>fumigations</term>, <term>unctions</term> <note>original: "suffumigii... unctionum"; these refer to the common, often dangerous treatments for the "French Disease" (syphilis) involving mercury vapors and ointments.</note>, and those medicinal waters. 

For even if many are infected by such a disease through intercourse, the signs that appear in them are not of a poorly affected semen, but of the humoral mass and the liver. This clearly shows the defect of a poorly affected liver, as do <term>cachexia</term> <note>original: "cachexia"; a state of severe physical wasting and malnutrition.</note> (or the bad habit of the whole body) and <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydrops"; an accumulation of fluid in the body, now called edema.</note>, which conditions often appear in the final stages of the disease's malice. But let it suffice to have said these things for the essence of the disease and the declaration of the truth. It is from the essence of the disease that one must take the primary intentions for curing, as **Galen** learnedly taught in many places, particularly in his book *On the Method of Healing* <note>original: "libro de sanitatis ingenio"; referring to Galen's "Methodus Medendi."</note>. Therefore, I shall follow his method of curing and preserving, setting aside other necessary things as they are very well known, which are called the <term>non-naturals</term> <note>The six factors external to the body that doctors believed could be regulated to maintain health: air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, evacuations, and emotions.</note> by physicians.

The most excellent Doctor had also proposed a medicinal regimen in which, for the preservation of the Most Illustrious Lord, it was asked whether it might sometimes be good to move the bowels with certain light medicines appropriate for the disease and its causes—medicines that would not be troublesome, but rather (as they say) "without supervision" <note>original: "sine custodia"; medicines so mild they do not require the patient to stay indoors or follow a strict regimen during their use.</note>. And first, he proposed pills made of washed aloe, which were praised by us if they were prepared in this manner:

Take two ounces of aloe washed with endive juice, prepared according to the art. Take of choice rhubarb...

...[extrac]ts <term>two drams</term> <note>original: "z.ii."; in 16th-century pharmacy, the "z" symbol typically denoted a dram (approx. 3.9 grams).</note> of <term>yellow myrobalans</term> <note>The dried fruit of the *Terminalia citrina* tree, valued as a gentle laxative.</note>, <term>best agaric</term> <note>A fungus found on larch trees, used in medicine as a powerful purge.</note>, and <term>dodder of thyme</term> <note>A parasitic plant believed to purge melancholy from the body.</note>, <term>one and a half drams each</term> <note>original: "an. z.i.s."</note>, and <term>prepared black hellebore</term> <note>A potent root used to purge "black bile," often carefully prepared to reduce its toxicity.</note> <term>one dram</term>. All these shall be infused in this manner in this decoction: Take <term>two drams</term> of <term>tamarinds</term>, and <term>five drams each</term> of the waters of <term>endive</term> and <term>bugloss</term>. Let them boil according to the art <note>A standard phrase in early modern medicine meaning to prepare a remedy according to established pharmaceutical rules.</note>, and after a careful pressing, let them be placed with <term>aloe</term> and left until they are dried. From this mass, let <term>pills</term> be made, and let <term>one to two drams</term> be given in the morning. For these will be marvelous for the <term>rectification of the liver</term> <note>Restoring the liver to its natural, healthy balance of humors.</note>, in which the source of the <term>Gallick disease</term> <note>original: "morbi Gallici"; a common 16th-century name for syphilis.</note> resides. They will also lead out the matter that descends to the leg itself, which causes the hard swelling and inflammation of the veins, along with that bad color and the ulcers—matter which exists as the "antecedent cause."

Another method of prevention is also proposed: certain decoctions to be taken on alternating days, which have the power both to rectify the liver and to purify the blood, as well as to prepare those "burnt" superfluities <note>In humoral theory, "burnt" or "adust" humors were those that had become overheated and toxic.</note> generated daily from bad humors, and to gently move the bowels. Take <term>one dram</term> of <term>senna pods</term> <note>A classic herbal laxative.</note>, <term>half a dram each</term> of <term>dodder of thyme</term> and <term>dodder</term>, <term>one and a half drams each</term> of <term>liverwort</term> and <term>hart's-tongue fern</term> <note>original: "scolopendriae"; a fern traditionally used for spleen and liver ailments.</note>, and <term>half a dram each</term> of the flowers of <term>borage</term>, <term>bugloss</term>, and <term>fumitory</term>. Let them be boiled according to the art in the waters of <term>endive</term>, <term>bugloss</term>, and <term>chicory</term>, or in <term>cow's milk</term> or <term>goat's milk</term>. From this, the patient may take <term>six drams</term> in the morning with <term>two drams</term> of <term>syrup of roses</term> made from rose juice, which they call <term>geleniabinum</term> <note>A medicinal preserve of roses and sugar, often used as a carrier for other drugs.</note> made with sugar. 

But if anyone wishes to make a preventive decoction that is even more specifically targeted, the best and most praiseworthy will be a decoction of <term>India wood</term> <note>original: "ligni indici"; commonly known as Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," imported from the Americas and famously used to treat syphilis.</note> prepared with spring water, or water of <term>endive</term> or <term>borage</term>. It will be best if you place one pound of honey in this decoction with twelve measures of the waters and one measure of <term>India wood</term> powder; this should boil until a third part is consumed, and from this, one <term>cup</term> <note>original: "cyathus"; a small drinking measure.</note> should be taken in the morning. And this, in my opinion, is more effective than the others for prevention. Many other decoctions could be established, but this decoction of <term>India wood</term> is more favored and truer than the others. 

Furthermore, <term>sweating treatments</term> <note>original: "sudationes"; induced sweating was a primary treatment for syphilis, intended to expel the poison through the skin.</note> have been proposed, both because they purge the waste products of the <term>fourth digestion</term> <note>The final stage of the digestive process where nutrients are converted into body tissue.</note> and because the patient is accustomed to them by the custom of his country. Therefore, if they are performed at intervals, they will be an excellent aid for prevention; thus, the Most Illustrious Lord may sweat. But since it was asked whether it would be good to apply <term>leeches</term> to the leg where that redness is, in order to remove the bad blood, this was also praised by everyone—provided it is done after some other evacuations. Therefore, he must proceed with these and similar aids throughout the winter; and if the Most Illustrious Lord wishes to be entirely freed...

<header>NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS</header>

# NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

The treatment that the Lord desires will be necessary. In the spring, therefore, if he desires to be freed from the already often-mentioned dispositions—and first from that which we, for the reasons stated, called universal, ancient, and malignant, which is communicated first to the liver and then to the whole body—and if the leg near the ankle is more infested, since there is redness, and hard swelling, and fullness of the veins with bad pain, and those evils from ulcers of corrupted blood, it is necessary to proceed as follows.

First, therefore, it will be worth the effort to empty the body through several <term>evacuations</term> <note>The process of purging the body of "excess" or "corrupt" humors, such as blood, bile, or phlegm.</note>, both through <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>Bloodletting, a standard practice to balance the humors.</note> and also through many evacuations that draw out the remaining humors. Therefore, His Most Illustrious Lordship shall purge himself with this light <term>minorative</term> <note>A mild laxative intended to gently clear the bowels.</note> which empties the stomach and the common passages.

**Recipe:** Take <term>flowers of cassia</term> and <term>lenitive electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste, usually sweet, used as a mild laxative.</note>, <term>six drams</term> <note>original: "ʒ.vi."</note> each. <term>Confection of Hamech</term> <note>A famous, complex purgative used specifically to purge "black bile" or melancholy.</note> <term>two drams</term>. Mix, and let a <term>bolus</term> <note>A large, soft pill, often coated in sugar or honey.</note> be made with sugar, or a potion with a decoction of fruits, to be taken four hours before lunch. After taking the minorative, it is necessary to rest for an entire day.

Afterward, truly, let the <term>basilic vein</term> <note>A prominent vein in the arm; in humoral medicine, the right basilic vein was specifically associated with treating the liver.</note> of the right arm be opened, and at least six ounces of blood should be extracted—or even a larger quantity, such as ten ounces, if the blood is bad and black. For this is a very useful thing, and the cutting of a vein is praised by all, not only by reason of the liver, which is badly affected by the <term>French infection</term> <note>original: "Gallica infectione"; a 16th-century term for syphilis.</note>, but also by reason of the particular <term>varicose</term> sickness, for which (according to the opinion of <term>Galen</term> and <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The two most authoritative medical writers of the Middle Ages and Renaissance; Galen was Greek, Avicenna was Persian.</note>) phlebotomy is a necessary and singular defense.

Once the blood has been sent out, in order to prepare the matter for evacuation, let syrups prepared in this manner be given.

**Recipe:** Take <term>syrup of fumitory</term> <note>original: "syrupi de fumoterrae"; a plant used to treat skin conditions and liver blockages.</note> <term>one ounce</term> <note>original: "ʒ.i." but here likely referring to a larger measure or dram depending on the volume of water; however, "ʒ" usually signifies a dram in this context.</note>, <term>syrup of roses</term> <term>half an ounce</term>, and the waters of <term>endive</term> and <term>hops</term>, <term>one and a half ounces</term> each. Mix them, and let the syrups be administered warm in the morning for several days, until <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctio"; the stage in the digestive process where humors are properly "cooked" or matured by the body's heat, indicated by changes in the urine.</note> appears in the urine. When the signs of digestion appear, he must again be purged by the similar evacuating medicine mentioned above, five hours before lunch. Add to it <term>rhubarb</term> and <term>agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus used as a potent purgative.</note>, <term>one dram each</term>, infused in a decoction of fruits.

If His Lordship should sometimes wish to use pills to facilitate the bowels, those which were placed in the preservation regimen will be best. However, because the fault is in the liver, and consequently in the mass of humors, such that the blood is mixed with other humors, and especially <term>burnt melancholy</term> <note>original: "melancholicis adustis"; humors that have become overheated and toxic, believed to cause chronic diseases and skin ulcers.</note>, it would be an excellent defense if His Lordship wished to apply <term>leeches</term> to the <term>hemorrhoids</term> <note>Referring to the veins around the anus; bleeding these was thought to relieve the liver and lower body of "melancholy" blood.</note> and extract eight ounces of blood. And this remedy will be profitable for all. Nor, while these things are being performed...

# PART TWO

...should [not] be omitted; rather, the syrups preparing the <term>matter</term> <note>The "matter" refers to the excess or corrupted humors—the bodily fluids—that the physician aims to expel.</note> for <term>evacuation</term> are to be taken every single morning. But after this kind of evacuation by <term>leeches</term> <note>Leeches were applied to specific parts of the body to draw out "corrupt" blood, particularly when localized swelling or pain was present.</note>, I would wish to dilute the aforementioned syrups with a decoction of <term>epithymum</term> <note>Also known as Dodder of Thyme, a parasitic plant highly valued by ancient and Renaissance doctors for its ability to purge "black bile" or melancholy.</note> according to **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a famous 9th-century physician whose medical recipes remained authoritative for centuries.</note>; for they will wonderfully cleanse the blood of the residue of **melancholic humors**. And in the final stage, let him take a laxative made from the already mentioned <term>electuaries</term> <note>Medicinal pastes made with honey or sugar.</note>, along with <term>rhubarb</term> and <term>agaric</term> <note>A type of mushroom (Larix europaea) used as a potent purgative.</note>, with the said decoction of **Mesue’s** epithymum.

Once the body has been purged by these evacuations, His Lordship may then begin taking a decoction of **Indian wood** <note>original: "ligni indici". This is Guaiacum, or "Holy Wood," imported from the Americas and considered a miracle cure for the French Disease (syphilis) in the 1500s.</note>, prepared in spring water, or water of <term>endive</term> or <term>borage</term>. It should be prepared so that upon one pound of the wood, very finely pulverized, are poured twelve pounds of the aforementioned water; let them remain in infusion for a day and a night. Afterward, let them boil until a third part, or half if preferred, is consumed. When this decoction has been strained, let just as much water be poured again over the same wood that has boiled once, and let it boil until a third part is consumed. This should be strained and kept in a glass vessel, or at least a glazed one, separately from the first batch.

The first of these decoctions is to be taken warm two hours before daybreak, in the quantity of ten ounces or even one pound; after taking it, he may sleep if he wishes. Then, after four hours have passed, let him take another cup of the **second decoction**. Afterward, when two or three hours have passed, he may take his midday meal. Nor should he fear taking it before the decoction is fully digested, since it works better afterward when it is received into the veins along with nourishment to rectify the <term>humoral mass</term> <note>The total balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within the body.</note>.

The midday meal should consist of well-leavened bread, and of veal or kid, or the meat of chickens or the forest birds mentioned above; these meats may be roasted or boiled, as he prefers to eat them. Let him also eat some dish such as <term>emmer</term> <note>original: "far", an ancient grain similar to spelt.</note>, or an egg beaten in broth, or bread soaked in broth, or borage, or <term>bugloss</term>, or hops, and similar things. Let him also drink wine of good aroma and flavor, which is neither sweet nor sharp, but of middle flavor and color. Let him also beware of excessive eating and of eating many different things, and also of excessive drinking; let him eat sparingly and drink sparingly.

Five hours after the midday meal, let him take again one cup of the **second decoction** of the same quantity; afterward, three hours before the evening meal, let him drink one cup of the **first decoction**. The evening meal should be smaller than the midday meal. Then, two hours after the evening meal, let him sleep, being covered according to the necessity of the season. But if in the night...

And because the affected limb, namely the leg, [requires] some preserv[ing]...

### LETTER XXIV.

In these recent days, letters from a certain distinguished and excellent physician were brought to me, written in your name. From these, I understood that your excellence previously suffered from the common disease called **the French disease** <note>original: "morbo Gallico." This was the standard 16th-century name for Syphilis.</note>, from which you were healed and remained healthy for many years, with all natural functions intact and without any incident of this disease. Now, however, for some months, two hard tumors have appeared in the groins <note>original: "inguinibus." These are likely "buboes," a common symptom of syphilis.</note>, which for a long time have caused no small amount of distress. And although many remedies were administered by that excellent physician, both through internal purgings and through various medicines applied externally to the tumors themselves, they have nonetheless neither been resolved nor changed in any part. Having seen this, that most excellent man decided that your excellence [needed] stronger remedies...

to aid with these means: and first, after the body was purged, four times this year he wished to smear you with the ointment with which those suffering from the **French disease** <note>original: "morbum Gallicum." This was the standard 16th-century name for syphilis.</note> are anointed, allowing many days to pass between one anointing and the next. Nor, for that reason, were those hard tumors entirely resolved; indeed, after the aforementioned anointing, a tumor of no small size appeared on the head, which generated pus from the applied medicines: and at last, when opened with a cutting instrument, the bone of the skull was found to be blackened <note>The "denigratum" or blackened bone indicates necrosis or decay of the skull, a common and painful complication of advanced syphilis (tertiary stage) or sometimes a side effect of aggressive mercury treatments.</note>. Yet in the groins, the remnants of the former tumors still remain with some ulceration: there is also pain in one of the shoulder blades and the arm, together with a certain blockage of the nostrils, so that he cannot draw in air or purge mucosal wastes without difficulty. 

Given that these symptoms are persisting in this way, I cannot believe otherwise in such a difficult case than that—even if many things were done which have cured most people suffering from the French disease—they were nonetheless unable to cure you. This is because that **bad French disposition** still persists in the **liver** <note>original: "iecinore." In the medical theory of the time, the liver was the primary organ for creating blood and humors; a "disposition" there meant the disease was rooted at the very source of the body's nutrition.</note> from which many phlegmatic matters are generated, mixed in various ways with other humors, and especially with the **melancholic humor** <note>One of the four "humors" or bodily fluids; an excess of melancholy (black bile) was thought to cause heavy, persistent, and "cold" diseases.</note>. Since this disposition is old and already communicated to the whole body, it is no wonder if it has not been cured even by the strongest medicines. Indeed, the French disease can always be restored to health only with the greatest difficulty; how much more so when it has already become chronic? 

But if anyone should ask whether this new invasion is from the remnants of the old disease already cured some years before, or if it is new: I say that it can be both. For since the matter of this disease is thick, it is possible that it was not totally dissolved or led out of the body when your Lordship was freed from those symptoms—but only that portion which was able to harm the natural operations was removed, and not regulated by the bodily virtue <note>The "virtue" or "force" refers to the body's innate power to heal itself and manage its functions.</note>. The residue which remained within the body and members was not able to impede the operations; and even if it was not consumed or driven out by the virtue, while it did not increase, it was no hindrance to the body's functions. However, from some new alteration—either external or internal—which hindered or altered that virtue, whether it be food, or labors, or **venereal embraces with an infected woman**, or some other alteration in the humors, it was able to increase the first bad quality of the liver. From this, the aforementioned matter, mixed in various ways, was able to renew the prior disease and the matter primarily in the groins.

...to drive [it] out, then to the other limbs, which already held the **bad French quality** <note>original: "malam qualitatem Gallicam." **Decoction of epithymum** <note>A preparation of "Dodder of Thyme," a parasitic plant believed to purge melancholy and phlegm.</note> according to **Mesue** <note>A reference to Joannes Mesue, an influential (though likely legendary) Arabic medical authority whose formulas were standard in Renaissance pharmacies.</note>, as much as suffices; mix and let a potion be made to be taken at dawn five hours before lunch. If after taking it you wish to sleep for an hour, you may; but once that hour has passed, it is not at all appropriate to sleep. 

The food should be, as I said above, bread washed in the broth of the best meats—namely chicken, veal, and kid [goat] and the like. After the aforementioned "minor" evacuation has been performed alongside an excellent regimen of food and drink, one must rest for several days under the following diet: 

First, the food must be of this sort: the bread should be very well-fermented and baked in an oven. The meats should be light and easy to **concoct** <note>Digest</note> in the stomach, such as those already mentioned, and also the meat of blackbirds and other small woodland birds. Furthermore, partridges, quails, turtledoves, pheasants, and the like are good. Soft-boiled eggs are also excellent dishes. Meals should consist of bread washed in the broth of the said meats, or an egg beaten into broth, or well-cooked farro, or **borage and bugloss** <note>Two flowering herbs (Borago officinalis and Anchusa officinalis) highly valued in Renaissance medicine for "cheering the heart" and purifying the blood.</note> and similar things. 

Abstain from all fish, from cheese, and from all dairy products. Furthermore, all legumes and vegetables are bad, especially lettuce and its like; salads are similarly bad, as are all salted things. However, if borage and bugloss are cooked in broth and eaten, they produce an excellent **juice** <note>Nutritive fluid or "chyle" produced during digestion.</note>. The wine to be drunk should be moderate—neither sweet nor sour—of good flavor and medium color. 

It is very helpful to eat twice a day, namely in the morning and evening. It is not useful to drink after food, and even less so between lunch and dinner; it will be useful to govern oneself in this way until the body is perfectly purged. Let these remarks suffice regarding the regimen to be followed before the consumption of the **water of Indian wood** <term>Guaiacum (Lignum vitae), a resinous wood imported from the Americas. It was considered a "sacred" cure for syphilis because it induced heavy sweating, which was thought to expel the "French" toxins.</term>.

Once the said evacuation has been performed, one must rest for at least two days; then, drink the decoction of **Indian wood** according to the following order: namely, with a bed prepared facing the east—though it should not be exposed to cold winds, nor situated near marshes or sewers—and with the windows closed and a fire lit in the room so that the air is altered toward...

-># ## PART TWO<-

...domestic warmth with some degree of dryness, let the bed be prepared, and let there be covers, so that both after taking the decoction and at night when you wish to sleep, the body is so protected that it suffers from the cold in no way, but is best covered and defended from the cold of the exterior air.

The decoction of the wood <note>Referring to Guaiacum, also known as "Holy Wood" or "Lignum Vitae," imported from the Americas as a cure for syphilis.</note> is to be prepared in this manner: Take one pound of **Indian wood** reduced to a powder by a rasp; take fourteen pounds of spring or well water, and place them in a **stone pot** <term>original: "cacabo lapideo," a heavy earthenware or stone vessel used for slow cooking.</term>. Let it sit for twenty-four hours so the wood is thoroughly soaked by the water. Afterward, let them boil over a slow fire until a third part is consumed, and strain it through a strainer or linen cloth. Keep the strained liquid in a glass or glazed stone vessel; and this will be called the **first decoction**.

Then, take the wood that you boiled once and put it back in the pot, and pour over it the same quantity of water. Let it boil again until a third part is consumed. Afterward, let it be strained as said before, and let the strained liquid be kept in another glass vessel; this liquid is called the **second decoction**. And since those who take this decoction often become accustomed to drinking a larger quantity of the second decoction, it is necessary to boil the twice-boiled wood again—as was said above—placing it once more in the pot, though with a smaller quantity of water. Therefore, if necessary, let the said wood be placed a third time to boil with ten pounds of water until a third part is consumed. This **third decoction** can be mixed with the second, so that the second drink does not run out before the first decoction is finished by drinking. 

But since it is quite difficult to ensure exactly a third part is consumed by boiling, I want you to be advised of this: the more this decoction boils, the better its action is, especially in a **long-standing disease** <note>original: "morbo antiquo," referring here to chronic or advanced syphilis.</note>. 

Furthermore, in the first as well as the second and third decoctions, it will be best to collect the **foam** <note>The "spuma" or scum that rises to the top during boiling was believed to contain concentrated medicinal properties.</note> and save it; for it is useful for the old ulcers of this disease, and for dissolving the hardnesses or tumors of said disease, and also for mitigating pains, if it is placed warm over the ulcers, tumors, and painful areas. 

Therefore, once the decoction is prepared as stated above, and two days have passed since the aforementioned purgings, one must begin to drink this decoction in this order: in the morning, two hours before dawn, let one **cup** <term>original: "cyathus," a measure here defined as ten ounces.</term> of the said first decoction be taken warm, and after the drink let two spoonfuls of **raisins** <note>original: "passularum," often given to patients to provide a small amount of nourishment and cut the bitterness of the wood.</note> be eaten. Let the patient be covered in bed with cloths; and even if he sleeps, it will be best, and if he sweats...

[...so that] sweat may be provoked: nor in any way let him suffer cold, or let the body be allowed to be chilled. Five hours after lunch, let a ten-ounce cup of the said first decoction be drunk again, and raisins eaten. Three hours after this drink, let dinner be taken. Yet let it be light, namely three ounces of bread and two of meat with a small amount of raisins; and let the drink of the second decoction be taken. Two or three hours after dinner, let a cup of the second decoction be drunk again, and let raisins be chewed afterward. Let him sleep then as much as he likes, and in the morning, two hours before sunrise, let the said decoction be taken warm with raisins. And so let him follow the said order, as much regarding quantity and time as for food and drink, for up to forty days—and even longer if the swellings <note>Massa refers to "tumores," likely the skin lesions or "gummata" characteristic of advanced syphilis.</note> have not been completely resolved.

If thirst should come upon him during the day, he can drink the second decoction as he likes, nor is it fitting to sleep during the day; unless perhaps for some reason he was recently restless and without sleep, then he may sleep, though in the morning hours before lunch. One must proceed with this drinking regimen for a period of fifteen or twenty days. If the stomach is able to tolerate it, it will be best to increase the quantity of the first decoction in the morning hours up to twelve ounces. It will be necessary to follow this order for up to forty days, and even more as I said. But since this potion, while being drunk, sometimes provokes sweat and sometimes also—as in most cases—a very large quantity of urine, the dried excrements of the intestines are for this reason not evacuated daily. In such a case, it is necessary to soften the bowels with common enemas <term>original: "clysteribus," a liquid medicinal injection used to clear the bowels.</term>. If half of the first decoction of the wood is mixed with a decoction of herbs for the enema, the evacuation will be better, and the [strengthening] <meta>continuity with catchword "roboratio"</meta> of the intestines [will be achieved]...

## PART TWO

->ss<-

...strengthening: these enemas <term>original: "clysteria," liquids injected into the rectum to clear the bowels or deliver medicine.</term> should not be administered daily, but on every fourth day during the morning hours before lunch. Certain pills can also be taken to move the bowels and to draw out the materials that are ready to flow to the limbs; let those pills be of this sort:

> Take two scruples <note>A scruple (℈) is an apothecary weight equal to about 1.3 grams.</note> of pills of fumitory <note>original: "fumoterræ," a herb traditionally used to treat skin diseases and "purify" the blood.</note>.
> Take one scruple of <unclear>fetid</unclear> pills <note>original: "pilularum foetidarum," a standard medical preparation often containing strong-smelling resins like asafetida, used to balance the body's humors.</note>.

Let three pills be made, to be taken in the morning when the first decoction is drunk before dawn. But since the tumors in the groin are ulcerated <note>This refers to buboes—swollen lymph nodes common in syphilis—that have broken open into sores.</note>, one must not neglect their particular care: therefore, if the foam of the said decoction is applied warm in the morning and evening, and wiped twice a day, it will be the best aid. Both the tumors and the ulcers can also be treated with ointments praised for such a disease; among others, our mastic ointment <term>original: "unguentum mastichinum," a resin-based ointment used for its drying and healing properties.</term> is very effective when spread upon lint <note>original: "lychinia," fibers or linen used as a wick to keep a wound open or to apply medicine.</note> and placed into the ulcers. Truly, place over them the diachylon ointment with gums <note>A common plaster made of plant mucilage and lead, used to soften and heal swellings.</note> or an emollient ointment, so as to cleanse and heal the ulcers. 

And while these things are being carried out, it is necessary to rest, to be joyful with friends, and to abstain from winds, the open air, and even from sexual acts <note>original: "venereis," referring to Venus; sexual activity was thought to heat the body and deplete the patient's strength.</note>. It will also be necessary to observe this regimen of exercise, air, and embrace for several months after drinking the said decoction. Similarly, one must abstain from bad foods, such as the meat of pigs, lambs, geese, ducks, and the like. 

Once the days have passed in which the decoction was drunk, your Excellence will be able to eat (modestly, however) a larger quantity of meat, and also bread that is not twice-baked, and to swallow soft-boiled eggs in the morning. And you may drink the best wine, but not "winey" so to speak, or undiluted; thus, successively and gradually, one must arrive at the accustomed way of living. However, it will always be worthwhile to abstain from sour, cold, and moist foods, such as fish, cheese, and the like. You will also gain much benefit—both in preserving yourself from a relapse <term>original: "recidiva," the return of a disease after a period of improvement.</term> and in consuming the remains of the matter of the disease, if any were left behind—if, after the entire time of drinking the said decoction, even when you have returned to your usual duties, you drink a cup <term>original: "cyathum," a small measure or ladle.</term> of the said decoction every single morning for ten or fifteen days. Similarly, to prevent a relapse over time—as happened from the residual matter left behind and not evacuated, which by creeping again changed the whole body—it will be useful to take medication in this way to lead it out of the body.

### TO THE MOST EXCELLENT PHYSICIAN
Master Valentin Podlodosius: A consultation concerning the French disease <note>Syphilis.</note> accompanied by pain in the head, chest, vertebrae of the neck, and the rest of the joints, as well as ulcers.

### LETTER XXV.

<margin>

</margin>
**N**O ONE, indeed, most illustrious and excellent Master, can doubt from the reports of the most distinguished Master Valentin Podlodosius that the affliction which his lordship has suffered for two years now was that French disease. This is clear because, besides other symptoms which occurred at that time, very many pustules <note>Small, fluid or pus-filled bumps on the skin.</note>—though dry ones—appeared scattered throughout the body. These vanished through the application of mercurial ointments <term>original: "unguentorum mercurialium," the standard but highly toxic 16th-century treatment for syphilis.</term> performed twice, and through very many evacuations. However, he was not restored to health in every part, since even now the head, the whole chest, and the joints of the shoulder blades, along with the vertebrae of the neck, [are in pain], in addition to an ulcer that appeared two months ago in the seat <note>original: "in sede," referring to the anus or rectum.</note>, which...

## ->PART TWO<-

...seems to be increasing daily. When, therefore, this most noble lord, suffering from such painful afflictions, arrived in Italy and wished to discover whether drinking the Paduan thermal waters, the "douche" <note>original: "ducia," a medical treatment where a stream of water is poured over a specific body part</note>, and baths in the waters of Abano <note>Abano Terme, a famous spa town near Padua</note> could offer him any help, he wished to both drink the water and try the douche, as well as bathe in said waters multiple times. Since, having tried all these things, he recognizes they have been of no benefit to him, and he desires to return to his homeland—and there, if possible, be freed from this painful disposition and these ulcers—he summoned me, requesting that I write a plan for what must be done after he reaches his country. 

I have indeed complied with him. First, since the pains and the ulcer are symptoms which depend upon a cold, unhealthy temperament of the liver—both manifest and containing an "occult quality" which physicians call the French disease <term>original: "Gallicam," referring to syphilis</term>—and since an unhealthy temperament is, according to the teaching of Galen in the first book of *On Diseases* and elsewhere, a disease in itself, I shall therefore first direct the curative method toward that temperament. 

First, therefore, while his lordship is on the journey seeking his homeland, let him beware of excessive heat of the air and the sun; let him beware even more of the cold, especially at night. Let him also beware of excessive physical labor and exhausting horse-riding. Let him eat the best meats and drink the best wines, which should not be potent, but medium—of medium flavor and color. Let him sleep at appropriate hours, so that his strength, which was made not a little weak by taking the thermal waters, may be restored. 

Therefore, after he has returned home and rested for several days from the labors of the journey, let the following evacuations <note>referring to medicinal purging of the bowels</note> be performed first, after the aforementioned regimen of air, food, drink, and other things is established, as I shall write in the course of this discourse. Let him first take a medicinal ball <term>original: "bolum," a soft, chewable mass of medicine</term> in this manner:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Take of lenitive electuary <note>A mild, sweet medicinal paste used as a laxative.</note> } | |
| and of diacatholicon <term>original: "diacatholiconis," a "universal" purgative containing senna and rhubarb.</term> } | 6 ounces of each |
| of confection of Hamech <note>A famous, complex purgative used specifically to "purge melancholy" and treat chronic skin conditions.</note> | 2 ounces |

Mix them, and with sugar let a medicinal ball be made. Let it be taken in the morning, and let food be delayed for five hours. This food should consist of the best bread, perhaps soaked in the broth of the best meats, such as chicken, hen, young capon, veal, and similar things. Let him drink a thin wine that is neither sour nor very sweet, or a beer made from barley, hops, wormwood, and sage. Let him also rest at home, and not sleep except at night. On the following day at dawn, let him take this warm syrup; let him also sleep as much as he likes, and after taking it, let lunch be delayed for five hours.

Once it has been carefully strained, let the decoction be kept in a glass vessel or a glazed stone jar; this is called the **first decoction**.

Then, once again, pour twenty pounds of water over the same powder that has been boiled once, as was done before. Let it boil again until half is consumed. Once strained as above, let it be kept in another glass vessel or glazed stone jar; this will be the **second decoction**.

...by staying at home. First, let his lordship take at dawn one small cup <term>original: "cyathium," a measure of volume</term> of the first hot decoction <note>A decoction is a concentrated liquid made by boiling medicinal herbs or wood in water to extract their properties</note> weighing ten ounces, and immediately afterward let him eat a handful of the best black raisins. Then let him sleep moderately covered with blankets so that, if possible, a light sweat is induced, and thus let him rest for five hours afterward; then let him drink again one cup of the second decoction weighing ten ounces as above: and let him eat raisins, and rest for three hours after the second drink. 

Then let him eat his lunch, which shall consist of the best bread, well-leavened and excellently baked, soaked if he wishes in the broth of chicken, or veal, or a young capon; let him also eat a portion of meat, either of a small chicken, or a young capon, or partridge, or thrushes, and other forest birds, which whether they be boiled or roasted, should be eaten together with raisins. Indeed, let the quantity of both bread and meat be, say, half or a third—if he can tolerate it—of his usual amount of eating when he is accustomed to eat alone without companions. Let him drink the third decoction <note>The "third decoction" was usually the weakest, used as a daily beverage to replace wine or water</note> made with honey and cinnamon as much as he likes. 

After lunch, let him rest or walk lightly through the bedchamber, and after five hours have passed, let him again take the first hot decoction and eat raisins. Then after two hours let him eat dinner of half the quantity of his lunch, with raisins; let him drink the third decoction as much as he likes. Then two hours after dinner let him drink again a cup of the second decoction and eat raisins; let him enter his bed and sleep covered, and again in the morning let him drink the first decoction as above while covered, and let him sweat if possible. 

And so, as was said, after five hours let him drink the second; and take lunch; and let all things be done according to the prescribed order both in the drinking of the decoctions and in lunch and dinner, and this for fifteen continuous days. 

After fifteen days have passed, if things proceed for the better so that the pains are relieved, let him follow this order of drinking the said decoction until the forty-fifth day. But if he has not been relieved of these pains, after fifteen days have passed, let six ounces of the bark of the said wood be added to the said decoction. Namely:

Take two pounds of powdered Indian wood <term>Guaiacum, a dense wood from the Americas used as a primary syphilis treatment in the 16th century</term>, six ounces of the bark of the same also powdered, and twenty pounds of spring or well water. Let them be infused and boiled as was said above, and let three decoctions be made. Let the third indeed boil with cinnamon and one and a half pounds of honey. It is to be drunk at lunch and dinner, and from these decoctions let it be taken according to the above-written [order]...

...namely in this manner: in the morning at the first light of dawn before lunch; a second dose before dinner. Again, the first dose after dinner; the second with raisins, so that he follows the procedure described above by drinking for another fifteen continuous days, while eating as previously instructed. If matters proceed well so that the pains are diminished, nothing should be changed, but he should continue drinking in this way until the forty-fifth day. 

But if the pains remain stubborn even by the thirtieth day, add one and a half pounds of the best honey to the wood and bark; and let it boil until the liquid is reduced by half. Similarly, let honey be added in the second decoction, and also in the third, and let them all boil until reduced by half. Let the drinking continue until the forty-fifth day, as was said. 

As for the ulcer which is in the seat <note>The "seat" refers to the anus or rectum, a common location for lesions caused by the "French Disease" (syphilis)</note>, it should be treated first with astringent and cleansing ointments, such as the <term>unguentum damascenum</term> <note>Damascene ointment: a traditional cleansing preparation often containing roses and oils</note>, or with <term>ceraseos Mesuæ</term> <note>Mesue’s Cherry Ointment: a cooling salve attributed to the Persian physician Mesue the Younger</note>. Once the cleansing is complete, the final stage of care must be sought, which is the "sealing" <note>Closing or scarring over the wound</note> of the area with <term>unguentum de palma</term> <note>Palm ointment: a healing salve containing litharge and oils</note>, or with our own <term>masticino</term> <note>Mastic ointment: a resinous salve used to dry wounds and strengthen tissue</note>, since it dries the area and strengthens the limb. 

When all these things have been administered and the forty-five days have passed, one must gradually return to the accustomed way of eating and drinking, and also to performing other duties. And because residues of the diseased matter remain, and also because the natural organs—especially the stomach and the liver—are weakened by the fasting, it is necessary even after the forty-five days to take those things which strengthen the stomach and liver, such as <term>aromaticum rosatum</term> <note>Rose-scented aromatic: a powdered spice blend used to aid digestion</note>, and <term>diarhodon Abbatis</term> <note>The Abbot's Rose Tonic: a famous compound medicine made of roses, sandalwood, and spices to cool the liver</note> in this manner:

> Take *Rose-scented aromatic powder* 1 dram <note>original: "ʒ. i."</note>
> *The Abbot's Rose Tonic* 2 drams <note>original: "ʒ. ii."</note>
> *Fine sugar* as much as needed.

Mix these and let a confection be made with rose water into tablets <note>original: "rotulis," small circular lozenges</note>: of which one or two should be taken in the morning, four hours before lunch. 

It is also important to note that after drinking the aforementioned water, it is worthwhile to abstain from all vinegary salads, from pork, from cheese and butter, from legumes, from fish, and from bad vegetables such as cabbage and arugula; also avoid salted foods and excessive eating of spices; avoid the strongest wines, sexual intercourse, and other harmful foods. After ten or fifteen days, once the strength has been restored, the remaining residues of the humors are to be purged. Therefore, let them first be prepared for evacuation with these syrups.

<header>GIOVANNI MATTEO</header>

# CONSULTATION ON EPILEPSY OR
the "falling sickness," and cold swellings <term>apostematibus frigidis: swellings or abscesses caused by an accumulation of cold, phlegmatic humors</term> in the temples, as well as obstruction of the right ear and nostril, dimness of the eyes, and heaviness of the entire right side.

## LETTER XXVI.

Everything that has been written by you, excellent doctors, concerning the most noble sick man, we praise and most strongly approve. We do so because you have followed everything that could be desired for the knowledge of the disease in such a difficult case both learnedly and diligently, and because you have employed method and reason in treating it. These things indicate that you are not only most experienced, but also most learned physicians. Nor has the progression of the disease deceived this opinion of ours; neither has the difficultly of his relief diminished our judgment of your skill. For it is clear and well-known to us that this same disease, by its very nature and for many other reasons, could by no means be easily diminished or cured, as we shall declare more fully in the proper place; therefore, we shall proceed to the matter itself.

That distinguished man is established in the age of "first old age" <note>senium: in early modern medicine, the mid-forties were considered the threshold of the body's decline toward old age</note>, for he is passing the forty-sixth year of his life. This stage is said to be of a temperament which significantly declines from a perfectly balanced temperament <term>iustitiali temperamento: the ideal Galenic balance of the four humors</term> toward heat and moisture. According to your writings, all three principal organs <note>the brain, heart, and liver</note> and their subordinate parts clearly demonstrate this in their formation, size, color, and function—against which (as you say) the coldness and moisture of the stomach <note>uentriculi: referring here to the stomach as the site of initial digestion</note> act with no small opposition. This noble man, I say, has fallen into a poor, cold temperament of the entire body, and especially of the brain, due to various discomforts and the improper use of the "six necessary things" <term>sex rerum necessariarum: the "six non-naturals"—air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions—which were the pillars of health in Renaissance medicine</term>. Indeed, when he was a young man, he traveled through many cold regions and remained in them. Furthermore, beyond that cooling of the whole body which he contracted from the cold air, he also made use of foods without discrimination in their substance, quantity, quality, or order, which generated many bad superfluities <note>waste products from improper digestion</note>. Indeed, he ingested and devoured a very large quantity of diverse edibles at a single table without order or proper chewing; nor did he stick to one or even three kinds of food...

...was satisfied with [excessive] food. But he also drank various potent wines in significant quantities without discrimination or order; and to sum everything up in a single word, he abused all other necessary things—namely, by engaging in untimely, immoderate, and vigorous exercise, or even very often remaining entirely without any exercise at all. He slept a great deal, yet often stayed awake far too long due to the pressures of great business affairs. Nor did he take care that the excrements of the lower belly were purged daily, whether naturally or stimulated by art; nor were they ejected through the upper parts by attempting to induce vomiting. Furthermore, he least of all abstained from sexual acts and sorrowful thoughts.

From these <term>procatarctic causes: external or triggering factors, such as lifestyle and environment</term>, it is easy to find the internal or antecedent causes: namely, an abundance of crude humors. These, together with a cooling of the entire body, were and are the material and efficient causes of all the unnatural dispositions troubling this most noble Lord. The first and older of these (as you write) are two tumors in the temples which appeared ten years ago, though the one located on the right temple appears larger. There was also an obstruction of the right nostril for many years, as well as deafness in the ear on that same side, from which he was freed after the discharge of a great deal of viscous matter. Furthermore, there was (as we have heard) and still is at present a darkness of the eyes, or <term>scotomia: a dizzying darkness or "spots" in the vision</term>, especially after taking food. Along with all these symptoms, there exists a certain heaviness of the entire right side without trembling—all of which symptoms attest to a multitude of cold humors.

Lastly, indeed (as your excellencies write), it has now been ten years since this Magnificent man, in addition to the things already mentioned, fell into a light epilepsy or <term>morbus comitialis: "the assembly sickness," a traditional name for epilepsy because meetings of the Roman assembly were cancelled if someone had a seizure</term>. He was seized by this occurrence twice in one year, during which he suddenly fell down without sensation; and even if there was some convulsion of the limbs, he was not troubled by it for some time afterward. In the meantime, however, he was dizzy, and not without some light stupor. Finally, after some time, worse and stronger obstructions of the ventricles of the brain returned, from which a worse epilepsy returned. For I hear that this most excellent man was troubled three times this past year with worsening symptoms: namely, the loss of all senses, a very great convulsion of all the limbs, and foaming at the mouth. These symptoms did not exist previously.

From these facts, without any hesitation, we reach the same opinion as you...

...namely, that besides all other unnatural affections, this Magnificent man suffers from an unnatural disposition which the Greeks call <term>epilepsy: a neurological disorder characterized by seizures</term> <note>original: "epilepsiam"</note>, the Latins call the "comitial disease" <note>original: "comitialem morbum"; so called because meetings of the Roman assembly (*comitia*) were abandoned if someone had a seizure</note>, and is commonly called the "falling sickness" <note>original: "morbus caducus"</note>. This arises from a cooling and fullness of the entire body, and especially of the brain. We also believe through rational discourse that other symptoms—such as the tumors of the temples, the obstruction of the right ear and nostril, and the dimness of vision, or <term>scotomia: a condition where the patient sees spots or dark patches</term> <note>original: "scotomia"</note>, along with the heaviness of the entire right side—arise from these same causes.

Having understood these things, as physicians are accustomed to inquire about the future, we must see what end the primary disposition and the others will have: whether they are curable, or entirely without any hope, and whether the outcome will be quick or slow. We have gathered all these things briefly from the patient's strength, his unnatural dispositions, their causes, his habits, and other factors.

And although we might have judged the stability of the <term>virtues: in Galenic medicine, the three fundamental biological forces (natural, vital, and animal) that sustain life</term> <note>original: "uirtutum"</note> based on his age and temperament; nevertheless, since the long duration of the disease makes it impossible for all the virtues not to have been weakened—especially the <term>natural virtue: the power of nutrition and growth, centered in the liver</term> and the <term>animal virtue: the power of sensation and movement, centered in the brain</term>—we can only provide a poor prognosis based on these impaired functions.

For since the natural virtue also serves the heart by preparing blood for the generation and restoration of <term>spirits: subtle substances thought to circulate in the body and enable life and thought</term>, and that very virtue is greatly weakened, the spirits made from the blood prepared by the liver are not entirely healthy. Therefore, it is worthwhile to say that the <term>vital virtue: the power of life and heat, centered in the heart</term> is also weak. Thus, because of this languor of all the bodily powers, a great part of the hope for healing is taken away.

Furthermore, to proceed in the proposed order, these diseases or unnatural dispositions are of the highest magnitude, since they are diametrically opposed to optimal health and the cause of health. For health consists in the best <term>temperament: the balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry)</term> of the whole, and indeed one that is moderately warm. But this primary disease is a bad temperament—a material coldness of the natural parts and the entire body, and especially of the brain. Therefore, the disease is rendered more severe and difficult to cure the further it stands from natural health. Let us add that it also has causes that are already habitual, and as I hear, he can hardly be regulated in the <term>six non-natural things: the six external factors (air, food/drink, sleep, exercise, excretion, and passions) that physicians used to manage health</term> since he is poorly disciplined.

And to omit other natural matters, as you write, this most noble man, devoted to delights, even now swallows all foods without discrimination, and indeed copiously, without order, and without chewing, so that he eats with a wolfish voracity; he also drinks diverse and stronger wines most copiously...

...by drinking very [excessively], from which it has happened that the accumulated <term>pituitous</term> <note>original: "pituitosæ"; relating to phlegm, one of the four bodily humors thought to cause sluggishness</note> materials are not only thick but also mixed with a <term>melancholic</term> <note>original: "melancholico"; referring to "black bile," a humor associated here with "adustion" or the metaphorical burning/overheating of humors</note> humor caused by internal heat. For they are always accumulating new matter." Since this Gentleman is of such a sort, I do not see how he can recover his health through medicinal aid. 

Add also the opinion of Galen and Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC)</note> in the seventh commentary on the fifth section of the *Aphorisms*: that those who have already passed their thirty-fifth year and are seized by the <term>comitial disease</term> <note>original: "comitiali morbo"; epilepsy</note> can very rarely be cured; rather, for the most part, they die with this condition. We could indeed, most distinguished men, include many other authorities and reasons, but since we judge them to be very well known to you, we will set them aside and turn our discourse toward the intended goal; for as we have said, the long-standing nature of the disease demonstrates a difficulty that border on impossibility.

It remains to write down what pertains to the curative rule, so that if he cannot be cured, he might at least not fall into a worse state. Beginning with an account of the necessary things, he must first—as stated above—beware of cold, cloudy, and rainy air, as well as cold winds that fill the head. He should especially avoid the night and morning air. Nevertheless, his dwelling place should not be too hot, and therefore a long stay in <term>hypocausis</term> <note>original: "hypocausis"; rooms heated from below, like sweat baths or stove-heated rooms</note> is to be avoided. A light exercise should precede both the morning and evening meal. ->## PART TWO<-

...of unnatural conditions, and their maintenance: therefore, he should be content with a single type of food, both at lunch and at dinner, and in a smaller quantity. These foods should be of the best meats, easy to digest, and of the kind that thin the <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health</note>, such as wild forest birds. Likewise, his drink should be honey-water along with grains of pepper, a little *ginger*, and *peony* root, as well as its seeds. If possible, he should either abstain from wine or drink it diluted with a great deal of the aforementioned decoction; it should also be in a small quantity and neither strong nor sweet. Before eating, he should eat a root of preserved *ginger*, and after food, *peony* root preserved in honey. It is not appropriate to drink in any way after lunch or dinner; but if he is accustomed to drinking after food, let him drink a decoction of *peony* seeds and roots along with a syrup made from a decoction of *ginger* and honey. After this, let him eat one <term>rotula</term> <note>A small, round lozenge or medicinal tablet</note> of the medicinal confection *pliris arcoticum* <note>A traditional compound medicine used to strengthen the heart and brain</note>. To speak briefly, the diet should be "thinning" and one that produces very little vapor rising to the head. There should be a suitable amount of time between lunch and dinner, so that he does not dine at all unless he has first thoroughly digested his lunch.

He should have the benefit of a daily movement of the lower bowels; if the bowels are not moved spontaneously, a <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema used to clear the intestines</note> should be administered made from a decoction of mallow, betony, centaury, safflower seeds, and chamomile, to which should be added rose-honey and a <term>hiera</term> <note>original: "hiera composita"; a "sacred" purgative compound often containing aloes</note>.

Before food, he should exercise moderately, and he should rest at night. He must avoid <term>sexual intimacy</term> <note>original: "amplexu venereo"</note> because it resembles a "semi-epilepsy" <note>Early modern doctors believed the physical exertion and "loss of spirit" during sex could trigger seizures in those prone to epilepsy</note>. He should also flee from the "accidents of the soul," such as sadness, anger, and fear.

And since, in addition to the poor <term>temperament</term> <note>The balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note> arising from the causes mentioned above, many raw, phlegmatic "superfluities" mixed with <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>Black bile, associated with heaviness and cooling of the brain</note> abound in all the limbs of this Most Noble Man—but especially in the natural organs and common pathways—therefore, one must strive for their evacuation with all skill and diligence. For this reason, since these humors are "raw" <note>unprocessed or undigested by the body's internal heat</note>, it is necessary to treat and move them only after they have been "cooked" or prepared. They should be prepared with syrup of <term>stoechas</term> <note>A type of lavender used to "cleanse" the head</note>, of betony, and of <term>squill honey</term> <note>Honey infused with sea onion, used as an expectorant and purgative</note>. These syrups should be diluted with a decoction of *peony* roots and their seeds, betony, rue, mint, wormwood, and similar herbs.

These aforementioned superfluities should be evacuated with a soothing <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>, along with the "thick sacred medicine" <note>original: "hiera pachi"</note> described by Scribonius Largo <note>A Roman physician from the 1st century AD</note>; for in this case, it is said to be a singular medicine without equal. Nor should one hope that the matter can be diminished by a single evacuation when there is such a great quantity of it, so that the body's strength might be able to regulate the remainder; and therefore, with repeated syrups, again...

## NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

...the matter should be prepared for evacuation. In this second evacuation, alongside a mild laxative, let half an ounce of <term>hiera pachi</term> <note>A variation of "Hiera Picra," a traditional bitter purgative powder usually containing aloes</note> and a portion of prepared (or what they call "trochisced" <note>formed into small lozenges or tablets</note>) <term>agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus from the larch tree used as a laxative</note> be added, in a quantity of one or two drachms. This agaric is itself particularly suited for cases of <term>epilepsy</term> <note>The "falling sickness," which Massa is treating here</note> (besides its other manifest virtues). Pills of *hiera* with *agaric* may also be given; and since these are sometimes mild, <term>cochia pills</term> <note>Highly effective purgative pills, often containing aloes and colocynth</note> may occasionally be added, or even "fetid" pills <note>So called because they contained strong-smelling ingredients like asafetida, used for "hysterical" or neurological complaints</note> to invigorate their operation. But if we intend to use even stronger measures to aid a long-standing condition of the head, <term>Arabian pills</term> <note>A complex purgative formula from the Islamic medical tradition preserved in Latin texts</note> are most highly praised. We could have written many other things, but we have deliberately passed over them in silence, lest we seem to wish to **instruct Minerva** <note>original: "minervas instruere"—a Latin proverb meaning to teach an expert or "carry coals to Newcastle"</note>.

After the evacuations, and even while the aforementioned things are being administered in succession, it is customary to strengthen the limbs and organs that have been made weaker, both by the unnatural conditions and by the medicines themselves. This goal will be easily achieved if, in the morning before food, the patient takes green *rue*, or *Cretan dittany*, *hyssop*, or *juniper* berries. Alternatively, let him take one <term>rotula</term> <note>A small, round medicinal lozenge</note> of the confection *diagalanga* <note>A preparation based on galangal root, used for digestion</note>, *diatrium piperium* <note>A digestive formula made of three types of pepper</note>, or the bitter confection of *musk*, or of *ambergris*, or the confection *pliris arcoticum*, which is more approved by me. Or, he may take a spoonful of <term>oxymel of squill</term> <note>A mixture of honey, vinegar, and sea onion (squill) used for respiratory and digestive clearing</note>, and finally use a <term>Mithridatic confection</term> or <term>theriac</term> <note>Two of the most famous "universal antidotes" and restoratives in pre-modern medicine, containing dozens of ingredients</note> itself. There are also many other confections which this most noble man will be able to use with the greatest benefit, such as the "human confection" described by **Lord Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century physician influential in the West; his works often covered eye diseases and general pharmacy</note> in his book on the diseases of the eyes. There are also confections of rosemary flowers, *sage*, *betony*, *stoechas* <note>French lavender</note>, and similar ones made with honey; therefore, let these be chosen and administered according to the preference of your Excellencies. It is also helpful to strengthen the stomach externally; therefore, before food, let it be anointed with oil of *mastic*, *mint*, *wormwood*, and *nard*, with the species of *diagalanga* and a little wax added. Similarly, after food, to strengthen the brain and to prevent the evaporation of foods and other superfluities existing in the stomach and nearby passages, let him take (as said above) *peony* root preserved in honey, or one lozenge of *pliris arcoticum*.

And since it sometimes happens that worse symptoms occur together, as happened last year, we say that in such a case, fragrances should be offered to the nostrils made from *rue*, or its juice, or from a decoction of *rue*, *marjoram*, and *spikenard* in vinegar, or with <term>castoreum</term> <note>A pungent secretion from the beaver, highly valued for treating "vapors" and nervous disorders</note> in vinegar...

<summary>Massa prescribes a series of specialized purgative pills and restorative confections to clear the patient's system and strengthen the organs. He emphasizes preventing "vapors" from rising to the brain, which was believed to trigger epileptic seizures.</summary>
