...is dissolved: for they will work in a wonderful manner toward a swift awakening. And after the patient has revived, it is necessary that he rest until the vapors that were causing the obstruction are entirely dissolved. Let a lozenge of <term>diamusci</term> <note>A musk-based aromatic compound used to strengthen the heart and brain</note> or the confection <term>pliris arcoticum</term> <note>A restorative medicine made of many aromatics, often used for neurological or "cold" ailments</note> be given for this purpose, so that its vapors may be dissolved, and the brain may be strengthened, as well as the stomach after the medicine has descended into it.

As for the other **unnatural conditions** previously described: since they arise from the same material and efficient causes and remain sustained by them, we have written no specific remedy for them, as our entire intention has been to remove the aforementioned causes. By their removal (if it can be achieved), we hope beyond any doubt for the resolution of those afflictions.

But since we have understood from you that many things have been done according to reason which have not at all freed His Lordship, your excellencies have therefore requested and desired to know certain things from us. And first: whether any **bloodletting** <note>original: "sanguinis missio"</note> could be useful, not only for the cure but for prevention. For there are many things that suggest the opening of a vein; yet the rational opinion of **<term>Galen</term>** <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> denies this in the fourth book of *On Preserving Health*. He fears and warns us to abstain from bloodletting in bodies in which "good blood" is scarce. This is also stated in the booklet *On Bloodletting* cited a little earlier: in other "bad juices" <note>humors</note> that are mostly crude and foreign to the blood, he prohibits opening a vein. There is also a fear because all these unnatural conditions are **cold**, and are sustained by a material cold cause, as I have said.

Therefore, we respond to the question that drawing blood by the cutting of a vein is in no way appropriate—especially if one wishes to open a vein in the arm. We believe the better and purer blood is near the heart and nearby organs, even if the entire blood mass is infected in its surroundings and in those places where nature is accustomed to deposit excrement-like blood, such as the <term>mariscae</term> <note>Hemorrhoidal swellings or "piles"</note> or the so-called hemorrhoidal veins in the seat. For since so much matter is infected and mixed with bad and crude superfluities, we can rationally believe—indeed, we can assert with certainty—that they are there. Therefore, the best remedy and immediate help will be to apply bloodsuckers, or **<term>leeches</term>** <note>original: "hirudines"</note>, to those hemorrhoidal veins in the seat and to evacuate a significant quantity of blood, especially if it is thick and black. For the prince **<term>Avicenna</term>** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook</note> said in the chapter on <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>The practice of bloodletting</note>...

...**bloodletting** <note>The OCR begins mid-word: "phlebotomiam"</note> is a universal evacuation of the humors, clearing out an abundance and variety of them. In this state, you will not be draining away good blood through this site, but rather the bad, thick, and waste-filled blood.

The second point requested by you was whether **cauteries** <note>The practice of burning the skin with a hot iron or caustic chemicals to create a permanent sore, intended to "drain" morbid humors from the body</note> applied to any limb might be useful to this noble man. However, you fear the man’s own dread, especially since he is not at all accustomed to them. To this second question, we respond that, according to the opinion of all the most excellent physicians, the cautery—being a truly noble remedy—can only be of the highest benefit, both by diverting and deriving humors, and by evacuating them from the affected area. Therefore, the common consensus was that they should first be applied to both legs on the **outer side** <note>original: "parte syluestri," literally the "wild" or lateral side of the limb</note>, specifically below the knee. Then, after several days have passed, they should be applied to the upper part of both arms. Finally, after many more days, they should be applied to the head in the region of the joint, or what is called the **coronal suture** <note>The seam across the top of the skull where the forehead meets the top of the head</note>. No more noble aid could be found in such a difficult and bad case.

The third question concerned the great hope you have for the drinking of **thermal waters**. Since, besides being able to evacuate raw matter and humors, they can also strengthen chilled limbs, we affirm this and strongly advise it to you. Indeed, from drinking the aforementioned **Paduan waters** <note>Thermal springs near Padua, Italy, famous for their healing properties</note>, you will evacuate many diverse materials over several days without interruption. This will do much to prevent new matter from gathering; then, it will leave a trace of warmth and dryness in the primary natural organs and throughout the entire body. However, let it be given cautiously according to the patient's strength and endurance, along with a moderate abstinence from food and drink, but without daytime sleep. Nor should the distance of the location be feared, since in this season, the water can be transported to other regions and still be very effective. However, the **shower** <term>ducia</term> <note>From the Italian "doccia," a treatment where water is poured or directed onto a specific body part</note> is suspect to us, both because of the "fullness" of the head and the weakness of the entire body due to the long duration of the illness and poor diet; therefore, its consideration and administration should be entirely omitted.

Finally, you ask whether perhaps the use of a decoction of **Indian wood** <note>original: "ligni Indici"</note>, or **guaiacum** <note>A resinous wood from the Caribbean/Americas, which was a 16th-century "wonder drug" for chronic illnesses</note>, could be of use to him. To this final question, we respond in agreement with your own opinion: it will not be very profitable, as he has already drunk it three times and has not received much benefit from it. Instead, your excellencies believed that if there was any improvement, it came from a meager **regimen** <term>diaeta</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "diet" or "diaeta" referred to the entire lifestyle, including food, exercise, and sleep</note> rather than from the medicinal drink. ## PART TWO

...[we believe] that a potion of **guaiac wood** <note>original: "ligni guaiaci." A medicinal wood from the Americas, highly prized in the 16th century for its warming properties and as a treatment for the "French Disease" (syphilis), though here used for its drying effects on the stomach</note> can be beneficial in some way due to its warming quality and its ability to dry out the stomach. However, it will contribute very little to the **primary affliction** <note>The main neurological or humoral imbalance discussed earlier in the letter</note>, even though the medicine is hot and dry. Furthermore, according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, "not just anything acts on anything, but a specific thing acts on a specific thing" <note>original: "non quodlibet agit in quod libet sed determinatum in determinatum." A philosophical principle meaning that a remedy must be specific to the nature of the disease, not just a general stimulant</note>.

Nevertheless, the Magnificent man could use a potion of **Indian wood** <note>Another name for guaiac</note>, or guaiac, in place of a drink at both lunch and dinner, which should be prepared in this manner:

| Ingredient | Amount |
| :--- | :--- |
| Powdered Indian wood | 6 ounces |
| **Peony root** <note>Often used in this period to treat "falling sickness" (epilepsy) and nervous disorders</note> | 2 drams each |
| **Ginger** | |
| Best clarified honey | 4 ounces |
| **Betony water** <note>A distilled herbal water from Wood Betony, believed to strengthen the head and nerves</note> | 5 pounds each |
| **Peony water** | |

Mix these, and let them sit together for twenty-four hours. Then boil them until a third of the liquid has evaporated. After performing a careful straining, the **decoction** <note>A concentrated liquor resulting from heating or boiling plant substances</note> should be kept in a glass vessel. You may drink from this at lunch and dinner as you please.

These, most illustrious and learned men, are the things we wished to write to you on behalf of this distinguished and most noble patient, though we are hindered by many obligations in visiting the sick without any pause in time. May God, the Greatest and Best, who alone heals all ailments, direct your minds so that by your help this Magnificent man may (if it be possible) be restored to health; if not, at least may he be preserved from a worse evil, so that he may be able to lead his life with less distress in the future. Farewell, and greetings, most learned men, and please look kindly upon these writings of ours, produced in haste.

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND LEARNED
Physicians of Padua <note>original: "Patavinos." Padua was home to one of the most prestigious medical schools in Renaissance Europe</note> on behalf of the most Noble and illustrious Matron, Lady Helena Centani, concerning an afflicted leg with a tumor in the knee and loss of movement.

## LETTER XXVII.

THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS Matron has earnestly requested that I write to you regarding what I have observed of her afflicted leg, and what I have gathered from others (for I was not present for everything that was done, especially in the beginning); because of the constraints of time, I am doing this as best I can, briefly and in haste. They report, therefore, that the sick woman fell while descending a stone staircase in the month of February, while there was still ice. As her body is quite heavy <note>original: "obesi." In Renaissance medicine, a patient's "constitution" or body type (such as being stout) was a critical factor in diagnosing the severity of an injury</note>, she suffered greater harm from the fall, and she felt herself to be seriously injured upon the right knee where the **kneecap** <term>rotula: the patella or kneecap</term> is located. A **bonesetter** <term>instaurator: a practitioner specializing in setting broken bones or "restoring" joints, often distinct from university-trained physicians</term> was called to provide her with a remedy; after carefully touching the knee, he firmly asserted that he believed the kneecap was broken.

When I was asked to visit a few days later and inspected the site, I realized that the bonesetter had strayed far from the truth and had been greatly deceived. For although I saw a fairly obvious swelling around the knee and the thigh itself, I could not find any irregularity in the kneecap when I moved it back and forth. Instead, everything seemed to be whole and without any fracture. However, not content with these signs, I ordered the patient to contract her leg; she did so, though not without pain. From this contraction, the kneecap did not appear to be separated in any way, but appeared continuous on all sides, united, even, and situated in its proper place. 

I arrived on the seventh day after the fall, and the bonesetter said that up until that day he had applied medicines that were able to thicken and cool, such as **egg whites**, **Armenian bole** <note>original: "bolus armenus." A medicinal earth or clay from Armenia, used in the Renaissance for its drying and astringent properties to reduce swelling</note>, and similar things. These treatments—along with the pain occurring from the fall, the new and necessary intervention of the bonesetter, the **frictions** <note>massaging or rubbing the area</note>, and the very tight bandages—caused a great quantity of matter to descend to the site. Thus the limb swelled up; because these matters are for the most part **pituitous** <note>original: "pituitoſae." Referring to phlegm, one of the four bodily humors, which was thought to be cold and moist</note> and have been thickened by the medicines, they still reside deep within the limb around the kneecap and the muscles of the leg...

<summary>Nicolò Massa describes a knee injury suffered by Lady Helena Centani after a fall on ice, debunking a previous diagnosis of a fractured kneecap. He argues that the swelling was exacerbated by the bonesetter’s tight bandaging and cooling remedies, which caused phlegmatic fluids to settle in the joint.</summary>

# PART TWO

...and those muscles moving the joint, as well as around the outer parts and hollow spaces. For on the lateral side <note>original: "syluestri parte." In Renaissance anatomy, this term often referred to the outer or "wild" side of a limb, away from the midline</note> above the knee, there is a quite significant swelling, and below the knee there is also a broad swelling due to non-uniform matter. These swellings and the absorbed matter have resisted treatments so much that, by no skill, have they been able to be resolved up to this day. I purged the body of common superfluities <note>excess humors believed to cause disease</note>, and did so rather frequently. Then, on my advice, the **bonesetter** <term>instaurator: a practitioner specializing in setting bones and "restoring" joints</term> applied ointments made of chamomile oil and dill oil; sometimes costus oil <note>an aromatic oil from the root of the Saussurea lappa plant</note> was added, and occasionally chicken fat when we desired to soften the affected area. However, these were not of much benefit; rather, we found greater utility, with less irritation to the limb, from the application of chamomile oil alone, without any other mixture. 

There were also compresses applied, made of chamomile, dill, sage, betony, and seeds of flax and fenugreek, boiled in common water with a little white wine; some plasters of similar properties were also used. Yet all of these brought little or no help. On the contrary, the patient is doing worse regarding the contraction of her leg; at present, she suffers more. For previously she could lift the leg in some way, albeit not without difficulty, and could contract and extend it; now she is able neither to lift it in any way, nor to contract or extend it. 

This inability was increased by a second fall. A month having already passed, just as she had begun to walk, she fell toward her healthy side and onto her left side or leg twice, with some days in between. And although she felt no pain, she nevertheless called the bonesetter, fearing that on account of the fall the weak limb might again be badly affected. The bonesetter said he found no dislocation or other unnatural alteration, whether in position or in shape, besides that previous swelling; he bound the limb with bandages again. The patient, however, affirmed that she felt a certain kind of numbness <note>original: "stuporis." A medical term for a loss of sensation or a heavy, "dead" feeling in a limb</note>, not only in the leg but in the entire hip. 

So much for the history. Now, if I assign some causes for these incidents to you, perhaps it will not be unwelcome. The material cause (in my judgment) is none other than cold, **phlegmatic matter** <term>materia pituitosa: matter dominated by phlegm, one of the four humors, characterized as cold and moist</term>, predominantly absorbed both around the knee joint and around the muscles and **tendons** <note>original: "chordas." Literally 'strings,' used in this period to describe tendons, ligaments, or nerves</note> moving the joints and the leg. If anyone should ask me why it does not hurt so much, even if there is a great deal of matter in the place—which, even if it is cold, nevertheless changes the **temperament** <term>temperamentum: the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body part</term> of the limb by its quality and in some way **ruptures the continuity** <note>original: "soluit continuum." A standard medical phrase for tissue damage or the separation of parts that should be joined</note> by its quantity—they ought not to be ignorant that...

...in those first days, while much matter was still flowing, the patient used to be affected by the greatest pain for this reason: namely, because of the change in temperament <note>The "temperament" refers to the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a specific body part.</note>. Now, because such a great amount [of matter] no longer flows, but only a little, and the temperament has already been changed, she no longer hurts so much. 

But if someone should say that the "continuity is broken" <term>soluta continuitas: a standard medical phrase for any injury where tissues that should be joined are separated, such as a wound or fracture</term>, and therefore it is impossible for her not to suffer greatly, we reply to this: pain is caused *while* the continuity is being broken; however, once the continuity is broken, it is no longer necessary for it to hurt. For the temperament in the limb has become accustomed to its state, and the "continuum" <note>the healthy, unbroken connection of tissue</note> is no longer being broken, since it has already been broken. 

Perhaps someone will persist and say that new matters descend to the limb every day, altering it and causing a painful sensation. I reply that there is indeed some sensation, and it is possible that matters still descend to the limb, but they are cold, being of the same quality as the injured limb itself. Thus, since they are similar, no change occurs, and no new break is made. I would therefore affirm that there is no significant pain; and if there is any further breaking of continuity, it does not happen all at once, but so gradually that the pain caused is not perceptible.

Therefore, that significant swelling contributes to the limb’s "impotence" <note>The inability to move or use the leg</note>. This swelling is on the lateral side <note>original: "latere syluestri" — the outer side of the leg</note> above the large muscle, as are the absorbed moist matters and the other parts below and around the knee which are swollen. These moisten and hinder all the muscles so that they cannot move the limb freely. 

I judge these to be the causes of the inability to move the leg and knee. If we wish to look even more closely, there is also the weakness of the limb caused by the fall during a very cold time, and the fact that the woman herself is full of much phlegmatic humor <term>humore pituitoso: "pituita" or phlegm was one of the four humors, characterized as cold and moist</term>, as well as the application of cooling and astringent <note>original: "inspectantium" — medications intended to draw tissues together or cool them</note> medications, as was mentioned above. 

If anyone truly wishes to heal this woman and free her from this swelling—which, due to the length of time, has become like an abscess <note>original: "apostemoso"</note>—it is necessary to remove this matter, strengthen the area, and restore its balance. Since it was by no means possible to achieve this with the lighter remedies we mentioned, I turned my mind to the mud of Saint Bartholomew, in the Paduan countryside <note>The thermal springs and mud baths near Padua, famous since antiquity for their healing properties</note>, and I placed no small hope of recovery in it. 

For there is in this mud a heating and moderately dissolving power, along with a clear faculty for spreading and anointing. This allows it to dissolve [the stuck humors] without drying the area out too much. Furthermore, it lacks sulfur, which might dry it out excessively; for this mud is soft and fatty, as is apparent to the senses. This also suggests a great mixture of (so to speak) "airiness" <note>original: "aereitatis" — in Galenic medicine, the element of Air was hot and moist; this quality would help soften the hard swelling without the harshness of Fire or the dryness of Earth.</note>, and therefore, beyond the parts which con...

# PART SECOND

...contains many terrestrial parts; there are also manifest airy parts, which easily vanish and dissolve if left alone in warmer air. I add softness with a certain ease of dissolution, which signify moisture and heat. Its moisture is spreadable and dissolvable, which can be proven both by logic and by experiments. For its power is undoubtedly softening, dispersive, and resolving <note>In Renaissance medicine, a "resolving" agent is one that breaks down and disperses "bad humors" or hardened blockages in the body.</note>, yet moderate and not greatly exceeding the [human] temperament. It is able to dissolve all hardnesses and nodules arisen in the joints and other parts of the limbs—whether caused by dislocation, or by fractures, wounds, gout <note>original: podagris — specifically gout of the feet</note>, or hand-gout <note>original: chiragris — specifically gout of the hands</note>—as has very often been experienced. 

It achieves this through its mild heat, raised just a little above the human temperament, by which it can open the passages <term>meatus: the pores or internal channels of the body through which waste and vapors are expelled</term> and convert cold matter into vapors, so that the matter may easily exit from there, aided by the heat of the limb itself. For the mud would indeed soften and warm it, if the limb were weak in every part; yet it would not for that reason dissolve tumors unless it were aided and helped by the natural heat of the limb. 

From this, everyone can see how greatly those who believed this mud to be of such great heat and dryness as to reach the third degree <note>Physicians categorized medicines on a scale of 1 to 4. A "third degree" substance would be very intense and potentially damaging or caustic.</note> have been deceived. For if it were so, it would not only fail to dissolve hardnesses and nodules, but would instead make them harder by dissolving the thin parts and drying out the thick parts. I do not deny that there is some dryness in it (for it does not lack earthy parts), but it is of such a kind that it is better able to strengthen the limb after the resolution [of the blockage], and then [strengthen] what was altered by the moist humor, rather than drying it out before the resolution. For the dryness in it is quite small and light, and not at the third degree as some have thought.

I believe that not only this mud, but also washings of the leg in the water of the spring itself that rests above the mud, would benefit this woman, since the same power is found in them. For they are born together and proceed from one and the same mineral <note>In this context, the "mineral" refers to the geological source or "vein" of the thermal spring.</note>, and they differ from one another only by the diversity of their substance. For since mud is of a thick substance, it can retain its warm virtue longer and better than water, which is of a thinner and more subtle body. 

But someone might ask me: in what way will this woman be able to receive help from this mud and these waters, when she was not helped by medications of the same virtue as the mud (of which, as we said above, many were applied)? For the same power that is in those medications is also in this mud and these waters—though perhaps not exactly. But even if the virtues in them were exactly similar...

...we are not unaware of those qualities; for though we are ignorant—and will eternally remain ignorant—of the exact proportions of the elements within mixtures, we nevertheless recognize them to some degree through estimative judgment <note>In Renaissance science, "estimative judgment" refers to the ability to perceive the nature or utility of a substance through observation and experience, even if its internal makeup remains a mystery.</note> and from their effects. One might object that if previous medicines offered no help, then neither the waters nor the mud will be able to contribute anything. We can answer this objection by stating that those former treatments failed to work either because of some resistance in the patient, the coarseness or weakness of the medicinal agent itself, or because the natural heat of the limb was not strong enough to bring the medicine into action. Add also that, according to the opinion of Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotelis" — Massa refers to the Aristotelian principle that for a change to occur, the "agent" and "patient" must be properly matched and disposed to one another.</note>, not just any thing acts upon any other thing; rather, action is limited to specific things with certain shared conditions. Furthermore, if we wish to suggest that within the mud—beyond its obvious qualities—there is a specific power derived from its own unique temperament, we shall perhaps not be in error.

Therefore, moved by these reasons, I advised the lady to travel to these baths after first purging her body of common wastes <note>original: "excrementis" — In Galenic medicine, this refers to excess humors or metabolic byproducts that must be cleared to prevent them from interfering with the treatment.</note>. She should begin by coating the limb with hot mud. If the mud is not naturally hot, it must be heated using the boiling water from the same spring. Once the limb—namely the hip, the knee, and the leg—has been carefully coated on all sides, she should dry the mud in the sun. When it has dried and fallen off, it is appropriate to coat the limb with mud again: twice in the morning before lunch, and twice in the evening before dinner, staying in the sun for an hour or two until it dries. This should be continued for as long as it takes for the movement of the limb to appear free and for the swelling to be cured—a result that will occur in a space of days that cannot be exactly predicted.

However, the practitioners who work there sometimes manage the mud differently, a method of administration which I praise most highly. They take the mud and place it in wooden boxes <note>original: "capsulas ligneas"</note>, into which they put the limb and surround it with mud. They allow the limb to stay there for the space of one hour, and sometimes more, so that the affected limb can comfortably sustain the power of the mud. Thus aided and supported, the heat more easily dissolves the humors <term>humors: the various fluids in the body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to cause swelling or disease if they became stagnant or "stuck" in a limb</term> trapped within the limb. Furthermore, it will be useful to wash the entire leg daily with the spring water; this same spring water should be used especially when it is time to wipe the dried mud from the limb.

Regarding the dietary regimen, I advised that in the morning—before the mud is applied to the limb—if the lower bowels have not moved spontaneously, she should use a clyster <note>A "clyster" is an enema, here made of a common decoction of oil, sugar, and salt to ensure the body is "clean" before the heat of the mud treatment begins.</note>. After the coating, washing, and wiping, she should rest for at least an hour in bed. Then she should take a meal consisting of bread soaked in the broth of the finest meats; the meats should be veal, kid, or chicken, or...

# TO THE MOST EXCELLENT PHYSICIAN
## of Cividale regarding a fistulous ulcer of the leg.
### LETTER XXVIII.

**From** your letters which you sent to me, I have understood that Master James of Cividale has suffered for a long time from a fistulous and deep ulcer <term>fistulous ulcer: a chronic, pipe-like sore that penetrates deep into the flesh, often difficult to heal because it forms a hardened internal channel</term> in his left leg, specifically in that part which they call the popliteal <note>the hollow at the back of the knee</note>. This is accompanied by a shell-like hardness <note>original: "duricie ostracosa" — a medical description for skin that has become as hard and callous as an oyster shell</note> and a discharge of poor quality <term>sanies: a thin, foul-smelling, or greenish fluid tinged with blood, seen as a sign of unhealthy humors in a wound</term> in which there are three narrow enough openings from which the aforementioned bad discharge flows out. Two symptoms follow this, which are very troublesome beyond all others: one is pain through the entire leg, and the other is the greatest difficulty in voluntary movement, with significant tension in all the remaining muscles. The cause of this, as you write, was an abscess <term>apostema: a localized collection of pus or a swelling caused by an accumulation of "corrupt" humors</term> from a preceding internal cause in that place where it reached suppuration <note>the formation of pus</note> and burst spontaneously—that is, without the help of any medicine. Nor after it burst did he wish to apply anything to the ulcer, but left the whole matter to nature. Since nature was strong, he seemed to be healed from the ulcer; at length, after some days, the place swelled up again, and suppuration and a rupture occurred from which he could not be healed by the benefit of nature. This, most learned man, is the history of the case, concerning which you ask that I first declare to you the essence of the disease, its causes, and its symptoms, and also signify whether it can be healed or not; and if it can be healed, by what remedies...

...remedies you ought to use, so that he may be able to have perfect health of the limb. Regarding your first question, I say the cause of the previous <term>abscess: an "apostema" or localized collection of pus</term> was a flow of matter from a great fullness of bad humors. Since this was not caused by any external factor, and because it was not fully cleared away during the first treatment, it became the cause for the return of the second swelling. This happened more easily because the limb, already made weak by the preceding ailment, received the matter again and could not regulate it. Once this abscess ruptured, an ulcer was formed; it is indeed a deep one because the <term>discharge: "sanies," a thin, greenish, or bloody fluid from a wound</term> was held for a long time in that cavity, making it very large and causing the "lips" or walls of the wound to harden.

From these facts you have, most learned man, the diagnosis that the disease is a <term>break in continuity: "solutio continui," a standard medical term for any injury that breaks the skin or flesh</term>, along with a diverse <term>bad temperament: "mala temperies," an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term>. For it is a deep break in continuity with discharge from the stated causes, combined with a bad temperament that causes the variety of the discharge; there is also pain, which arises both from the broken flesh and from the humoral imbalance. 

The hardness attached to the ulcer is caused by thick matter soaked into the parts of the body. Furthermore, the difficulty of voluntary movement and the inability to extend the limb have their cause in that same thick matter soaked into the passages of the muscles and nerves. This not only weighs down the limb but even prevents the <term>motive spirits: "spiritus mouentes," the invisible vapors believed to travel through the nerves to trigger muscle movement</term> from descending to the limb. 

And since, as you write, many local remedies were applied by a most expert surgeon and the openings of the ulcer were widened, I can only praise those actions as well done. I shall now direct my discourse to the rest of the remaining cure. There is a huge hardness in the said muscle and a depth to the ulcer which passes through the entire fleshy part as far as the beginning of the <note>original: "chorda" — here referring to a tendon or ligament</note> itself, though in the lower part. This results in a loss of power or difficulty of movement, as well as a lack of perfect extension and difficulty planting the foot when he wishes to walk. 

First, I will investigate the causes of these things. As we know from the <term>science of anatomy: "incisionis scientia," literally the knowledge gained through dissection</term>, many muscles descend from the knee which contain nerves originating from the spine; these provide both natural and voluntary sense and motion. For muscles, besides voluntary motion, also have a natural motion. Therefore, we must say that the cause of the difficulty of motion and planting the foot—beyond the reasons already stated—is the injury in the great muscle where the large ulcer and great hardness are located. For in order for any part to be movable and flexible in every direction, it must necessarily be soft. Therefore, we must conclude that the primary impediment is that hardness which prevents extension, affecting not only voluntary motion

...but also natural, since the hardness is communicated to the nerves passing through the muscle. We have already stated that the cause of the pain is a bad temperament <note>an imbalance of the four humors</note> and the dissolution of unity <note>a "break in continuity" or physical wound</note>. Having noted these things, I say also that the ulcer can be healed, but not in a short time nor without great labor; therefore, I will strive to provide the causes of this difficulty, so that once they are removed, health may be restored. I said above, based on the written report, that a flow of *new matter* was the cause of the recurring <term>abscess: "apostema," a localized collection of pus</term> and ulcer. Therefore, the first thing that comes into consideration as an antecedent cause—which feeds the disease—is the depraved humoral mass, unregulated by natural heat. Thus, the first intention in this case will be to evacuate this offending matter, in both its quantity and quality, as it is the cause that sustains the ailment. I will write the method of evacuating it after the general regimen. 

There are also other causes hindering the healing of the ulcer, among which hardness must first be considered and removed, since it prevents the joining or conglutination of the parts, as hard things can only be joined together with difficulty. Hardness also prevents suitable nourishment from reaching the limbs and even blocks the passage of the <term>spirits: "spiritus," the vital vapors believed to carry life and movement through the body</term> required for natural operations. 

The second cause to be considered and removed is the shape of the ulcer, which is <term>fistulous: "fistularis," meaning it has formed a deep, pipe-like passage</term>; namely, the depth of the ulcer combined with the said hardness and the narrowness of the openings, which prevents medicines from being properly applied. The third hindering cause to consider is pain, which greatly opposes the consolidation of the ulcer because it attracts—or is the cause for attracting—moisture to the ulcer, which works against its healing. The fourth cause is the "malice" or bad quality of the <term>discharge: "sanies," a thin, often foul-smelling or acrid fluid from a wound</term>, which I hear is virulent, thin, sharp, and corrosive, whether this is its inherent nature or caused by external factors. And although there may be many other causes hindering consolidation, these—as was indicated to me—are the ones clearly obstructing the healing in the aforementioned ulcer, and we will speak of removing them later so that a perfect cure can be reached.

And first, setting aside the consideration of the hot and dry temperament, and setting aside his youthful age and the evidence of the strength of all his faculties—all of which promise a certain hope of future health, especially since the time of the cure is Spring, which shortens even the most difficult diseases—even if the long duration of the disease and the "malice" of the remaining symptoms may stand in the way. Therefore, the cure contains several chapters within it; I have, however, divided it into the three instruments mentioned by physicians...

...to accomplish these things, I shall propose a plan in three parts: namely, the regimen and diet, medicinal potions, and the work of hands <note>this refers to "chirurgia" or manual surgical intervention</note>. And since the air at present is suitable enough, and will become even better for the ulcer with the coming of summer, I will say nothing further of it and turn my discourse to the manner of nourishment.

First, therefore, let the food be of good <term>chyme: "chymi," the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food, which was believed to be converted into blood and humors</term> and easy digestion, such as can generate a "drying" nourishment. For this reason, bread should primarily be leavened, salted, and very well baked. Meats should be from birds, such as chickens, partridges, quails, and thrushes; or also goat kids, young hares, and similar animals. These should be roasted or cooked in a pan with certain spices, such as cinnamon and the like. However, if they are eaten boiled, let them be boiled with fennel seeds or roots and similar things. In their broth, a dish may be made from <term>spelt: "far," an ancient grain</term> or a beaten egg.

All heavy and moist foods are forbidden, as are legumes—except for spelt with almonds or cooked in broth—and likewise those things which generate sharp juices, such as onions, garlic, radishes, and all salted things. These are harmful, some by making the body too moist and others by causing corrosion <note>irritation or "eating away" of the tissues</note>. Furthermore, soft-boiled eggs <note>literally "sipping eggs"</note> are excellent, as are eggs cracked and cooked in water or meat broth, sprinkled with the juice of sour grapes <note>verjuice</note> or oranges, and a portion of cinnamon. Other spices and salted things should be omitted. All fruits and vegetables are also harmful. 

Furthermore, wine that is too "winey" <note>original: "vinosum," meaning very strong or high in alcohol</note> and undiluted is harmful. Let it therefore be a small amount, of good smell and taste, not sweet, nor dark, but of a medium color and clear. If it is strong, it should be diluted with water in which coriander seeds have been boiled. But if, for any reason, inflammation should arise alongside the said ulcer, one must abstain from wine entirely. In place of wine, a drink should be made from the water of boiled coriander with <term>rose julep: "iuleb rosaceo," a sweet, medicinal syrup made of rosewater and sugar</term> and pomegranate wine. 

Moreover, all overfilling of the stomach is to be avoided, especially in the evening hours, because during the night the natural power is more occupied with the <term>concoction: "concoctione," the metaphorical "cooking" or ripening of the humors by the body's internal heat</term> of the remaining humors; therefore, it is bad to weigh it down with too much food. A variety of different foods is also to be avoided, as it greatly hinders good digestion. 

Furthermore, care must be taken to ensure a daily evacuation of the lower belly; if this does not occur, a common <term>clyster: an enema</term> must be used. And since sleep restores all the body's powers, let the patient sleep as much as he likes at night; but during the day, he should beware of sleep unless it is a long-standing habit, or if he has not slept at all during the night.

And because it is necessary for limbs that are sick to rest if they are to be cured, since movement agitates the humors, which [flow] to the location...

Let him also abandon Venusian embraces <note>sexual activity</note>, since they harm ulcers greatly by their agitation; and let him be cheerful and pleasant.

And since, from what was said above, among the other causes maintaining this ulcer and preventing consolidation was a certain malice <note>a bad or corrupt quality</note> and fullness of humor generated in the stomach and liver, therefore, so that every cause may be removed, the first thing that comes to the curative intention is this: one of the days after these initial steps have been taken, in the morning hour, having first administered a soothing <term>clyster: a medicinal enema</term>, the liver vein <note>original: "uena iecoraria"; the basilic vein of the right arm, which Galenic medicine associated with the liver</note> of the right arm should be opened, and the blood should be allowed to exit up to six or eight ounces, and more if his strength permits. 

The sign indeed that blood is abundant is the size of the veins and a heaviness of the entire body, considering his temperament and age. On the following morning, the remaining humors must be prepared <note>in humoral medicine, humors were "cooked" or "prepared" with syrups before they could be purged</note> by taking these following syrups: 

Take: syrup of endive, syrup of roses, and syrup of hops, half an ounce of each. Waters of borage and chicory, one ounce of each. Mix them, and let them be given four or five hours before food, and for several days—say six or seven—so that some preparation of the humors appears in the urine. 

Then let this medicine be administered: Take: lenitive electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or sugar</note> and <term>diacatholicon: a "universal" purgative made of various herbs and fruits</term>, six ounces <note>original: "℥. vi."; while this is a large amount for a single dose, it may represent a multi-day supply</note> of each; prepared <term>agaric: a medicinal fungus used as a laxative</term>, one ounce; pure juice of roses, one ounce; waters of chicory and hops, as much as is sufficient. Mix and let a potion be made. After taking this, let him wait five hours before he eats. On the following morning, let him take half a bowl of chicken broth with a portion of sugar, and let him rest from the administration of medicine for several days. 

Then let him again take the above-written syrups for five or six days; after these syrups, let him also take the above-written medicine with the aforementioned regimen. In this way, the material cause of the disease will be removed. If indeed there should be need for further evacuation, it will be best to add one dram of <term>rhubarb: a root highly valued as a gentle purgative and for its "cleansing" properties</term> infused in chicory and borage water; and this because rhubarb is effective for both external and internal ulcers, especially those of the stomach and liver.

The second cause which prevents consolidation, and which is worthwhile to remove, is hardness; for hard things cannot come together, wherefore one must strive for the softening of this hardness...

# NICOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

...even if soft things are contrary to an ulcer insofar as it is an ulcer <note>In Galenic medicine, ulcers were considered "wet" diseases that required "drying" agents; however, if the edges were hard, they first required softening agents, creating a therapeutic paradox</note>; therefore, let softening be procured first with this **fomentation** <term>fomentation: a warm, moist medicinal application</term>: 

Take six ounces of **marshmallow root** <note>original: "radicis altheæ"</note> cut into small pieces, two handfuls <note>original: "m.ii," a maniple or handful</note> of **mallow leaves**, five ounces each of **linseed** and **fenugreek**, and one handful each of **chamomile flowers** and **melilot**. Let these be boiled in common water, and let the area be bathed with a sponge soaked in said decoction. 

After the fomentation, rub the hardness with this **liniment**: 

Take half an ounce each of **hog’s lard**, **bear’s grease**, **hen’s fat**, and **goose fat**; one ounce of **marrow from cow shanks**; half an ounce of **moist hyssop** <note>original: "hyssopi humidæ," likely referring to lanolin or a specific oily extract</note>; and two ounces of **oil of lilies**. Mix these and let a liniment be made, and rub it on morning and evening. 

You will note, however, that when the fomentation is applied with the sponge, the ulcerated place ought to be protected with some ointment, lest the ulcer be harmed by that moisture. Let an ointment be made—for instance, **palm ointment** alone or mixed with **diachylon** <term>diachylon: a common lead-based plaster used to soothe and protect</term>. Truly, while the hardness is being prepared so that it is rendered soft, let the treatment of the ulcer proceed in this manner: 

Take two ounces of the **cherry ointment of Master Mesue** <note>original: "unguenti ceraseos domini Mesuæ"; Mesue was a legendary Arabic medical authority whose recipes were standard in the Renaissance</note>, and one ounce each of **bdellium** and **mastic**. Mix these and place them upon **tents** <term>tents: small plugs of lint or linen used to keep a wound open and deliver medicine</term> made of threads, to be placed into the openings of the ulcers; then let it be spread over a linen cloth and over the entire hardness. 

But if, after these things are done, the hardness cannot be removed, I would ascend to stronger remedies. That is to say, I would wish to remove the entire hardness with a cutting instrument—namely, a **razor**—or with some medication that eats away that hard flesh. For example, by dissolving **Egyptian ointment** <note>original: "unguentum ægyptiacum," a sharp, corrosive ointment made of verdigris, honey, and vinegar</note> with wine and injecting it inside with a syringe, and dilating the holes or openings of the ulcer by inserting a tent made from **gentian root**, or **elder pith**, or the **pith of a reed**. Or, by placing upon a linen tent a **corrosive ointment** made from **quicklime** and **Saracenic soap**. 

Or let this ointment be made: 

Take half an ounce of **populeon ointment** <note>an ointment made from poplar buds, often used for cooling and pain relief</note>, two ounces each of **hematite stone** and **sublimated litharge** <note>lead monoxide</note>, and **Thebaic opium**. Mix these and let an ointment be made. 

The method of administering said ointments is this: place one of the said ointments upon carded linen threads in a quantity sufficient to remove the flesh, and let it remain for eight hours. 

But if, after these things are done, the hard flesh cannot be removed, the final, certain, and singular remedy is to remove it with a **glowing actual cautery**—that is, a heated iron. 

After the application of the ointments, or after the cooking performed with the heated cautery, place **butter** upon the spot two, three, or four times a day so that the **eschar** <term>eschar: a dry slough or crust of dead tissue</term> or crust made by the ointments or the cautery may soften and fall off. Then, after the falling of the eschar, those medicines must be applied which cleanse the ulcer of filth or other corrupted matter <note>original: "sanie"</note> and help to generate new flesh.

Mix these and let an ointment be made; use this on **lint plugs** <note>original: "penicilla," small pieces of lint or sponge used to clean or pack wounds</note> and also apply it externally. Afterward, use **basilicon ointment** <note>a classic "royal" ointment made of resin, wax, and oil to promote healing</note>. If you desire greater drying action, use **Damascene ointment**, which is made in this way: Take two ounces of **yellow ointment** <note>original: "unguenti citrini"</note> and two drachms <term>ʒ: the symbol for a drachm, about 1/8th of an ounce</term> of **verdigris** <note>original: "uiridis æris," a green pigment made from weathered copper with antibacterial properties</note>; mix these over a fire and use it. The previously mentioned **cherry ointment** <note>original: "unguentum ceraseum"</note> is also very effective in this case. 

And because the ulcer is in a place where **veins**, **arteries**, and **nerves** are scattered about, one must be extremely careful when removing hardened flesh—whether that is done with a **razor** <note>original: "nouacula"</note>, with **corrosive ointments**, or with **fire** <note>cautery</note>—lest any vein, artery, or nerve be cut or burned with the cautery. If a nerve is harmed, the function and movement of that limb would be lost due to the damage to its "instrument."

The **third cause** that makes consolidation <note>the closing and healing of the wound</note> difficult and slow is the **fistulous shape** of the ulcer itself. According to the report of the most excellent surgeon, it has a hole in the lower part; therefore, this hole should always be kept open with **tents** <term>tents: small plugs of lint or absorbent material used to keep a wound open so it heals from the bottom up</term> so that the **discharge** <term>sanies: a thin, greenish or bloody fluid discharged from a wound or ulcer</term> may flow out freely and so that medicines can be placed inside.

The **fourth cause** which prevents and delays the healing of ulcers is **pain**, which must be removed by anointing the area with **oil of roses**. This is done if a redness is visible to the eye or if heat is felt by the touch. If, however, no change in color or inflammation appears in the limb, the place should be anointed with **oil of chamomile**, or a **plaster** should be made in this way: 

Take one ounce each of **chamomile flowers**, **fenugreek flour**, **linseed**, and **barley**. Take as much as needed of **sapa** <note>a syrup of grape juice boiled down to a third of its volume</note> or **sweet wine**. Mix these and let a plaster be made in good form; let it be enriched with **oils of chamomile and roses**, and place it over the site. If the pain is accompanied by extreme inflammation, let the anointing be done with a high-quality rose oil, and let a plaster be made from barley flour and a water made from a decoction of **rose leaves**, **violets**, and **mallow**, with a little sweet wine. Finally, add oil of roses and place it over the site of the pain.

The **fifth cause** hindering healing is the **diversity and corruption of the discharge**. This will require the best judgment of the excellent surgeon—namely, if the discharge is too thin, it must be thickened; if it is too thick, it must be reduced to an optimal consistency. Thin discharge is thickened with ointments and plasters in this manner: if the discharge is thin and **virulent** <note>infectious or foul-smelling</note>, take two and a half ounces each of **tutty ointment** <note>original: "thucia," an ointment made from zinc oxide</note> and **yellow ointment**, and one drachm of **powdered litharge** <note>lead monoxide</note>. Mix these...

Once the discharge of the ulcer has been corrected, you must proceed with those agents that generate flesh (which were written about above) and those that heal old and "fraudulent" <note>Massa uses "fraudulenta" to describe ulcers that seem to heal but repeatedly break open or resist standard treatment</note> ulcers. This includes the **cherry ointment of Mesue** <note>Mesue the Younger was a major authority in medieval pharmacology</note> applied on **tents** <note>original: "tentas," absorbent plugs used to keep a wound open so it heals from the bottom up</note>, and also with **palm ointment** used alone or mixed with **diachylon** <note>a lead-based plaster used to soften and heal</note> spread upon a linen cloth so that all the hardened tissue is covered. Continue this until the perfect regeneration of new skin occurs. 

If, while these flesh-growing agents are being applied, the flesh increases too much due to humidity—raising it into a large swelling <note>this refers to "proud flesh" or hypergranulation, which prevents proper healing</note>—it should be dried or removed with **burnt rock alum** <note>original: "alumine rochino combusto," a mineral salt used as an astringent to "eat away" excess tissue</note> powdered over it. 

After consolidation has been achieved, it is necessary to provide for the strengthening of the limb, which has been made weak by the long-standing illness. This should be done first through moderate rest, and then by applying aids in this manner: Take one handful <term>m.i.: "manipulus," the amount a hand can hold</term> each of **sage**, **stoechas** <note>a type of lavender</note>, **ground-pine** <note>original: "iuae"</note>, **betony**, **wormwood**, and **chamomile**. Let them boil in equal parts water and red wine. Wash the leg with this decoction for several days, morning and evening, then anoint it with this liniment: 

Take two ounces <term>℥.ii.</term> each of **oils of chamomile**, **white lilies**, **earthworms**, and **costus**; one ounce <term>℥.i.</term> each of **calf leg marrow** and **duck fat**. Mix and let a liniment be made, with which you should anoint the leg as described. Furthermore, the limb should be comforted with this **cerotary** <note>a wax-based plaster, firmer than an ointment but softer than a plaster</note>: Take half an ounce <term>℥.s.</term> of **diachylon with gums** and three ounces <term>℥.iii.</term> of **oxycroceum** <note>a complex plaster containing saffron and vinegar, used for aches and strengthening joints</note>. Mix and spread this upon leather to cover the leg. This should be worn for at least a month, though the aforementioned washings and anointings should still be performed morning and evening. 

These are the things I wished to write reasonably for this most difficult case. If all these instructions are diligently administered, they will lead to the cure of the sickness by removing the causes—both those that preceded the illness and those joined to it—and by correcting and removing the symptoms. May God the Best and Greatest, who truly heals all languors, be the one who disposes all things happily so that you may recover your former health. 

Farewell, most learned man.

# ON THE GENERATION OF MAN, AND HIS
### nobility, addressed to Bernardino Feliciano.
## LETTER XXIX AND THE LAST.

**WHEN**, for so many years previously, I was learning Greek letters from that most learned man Giovanni Bernardo Feliciano, your uncle (Bernardino), our constant association and the similarity of our studies brought about such a great love between us that there was no day in which either I did not come to your house, or he to mine, where very often we had much conversation together about philosophy and other most excellent arts. Therefore, not so long before he died, while we were together and talking amongst ourselves, he proposed a question to me in a doubting manner: Why Aristotle (in the eighth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physico auditu," the standard title for Aristotle's *Physics* in this period</note>) called man a **little world** <term>microcosm: from the Greek 'mikros kosmos', the idea that the human body reflects the structure of the universe</term>, comparing him to the **greater world** <term>macrocosm: the universe as a whole</term>. He asked me again and again to explain this to him. 

But I said, "This belongs to you, Feliciano, and this is your province <note>meaning his area of expertise</note>, since for many years now I have had you as my teacher." But he, who was always most modest and kind, said, "I seek this from you by right, since you are older than I and have professed philosophy for a long time." 

I replied, "Indeed, since this subject is obscure, understanding it will be very difficult for me, as I—who, as you know, have for the most part withdrawn myself from reading the books of Aristotle while applying myself to medical studies and practice—have been busy elsewhere. And although I have often read these same books of Aristotle before and interpreted them for others, I do not for that reason profess to have all his opinions and arguments at hand in the present. But even though I might grant that to your modesty, allowing you the role of a listener, and would not altogether refuse to speak on this matter myself: since it seems so to you, I would wish you not to be unaware that if you wish to compel me to speak, I can do so only through great leisure <note>original: "magnum ocium," meaning significant free time or dedicated study time</note>. Therefore I ask of you that you would rather be willing to state your own opinion to me, and that my mind might be delighted by your words: For I will gladly subscribe to your opinion (as becomes a student), and for this I will owe you immortal thanks." 

"Come now," he said, "since you call me your teacher, and hold me as such, see to it that your teacher can obtain this from you." I indeed, who always respected Feliciano and to obey him as...

# NICCOLÒ MASSA’S MEDICAL LETTERS

—I have studied as much as I was able, and thus I began the explanation of what was asked. I have set forth a certain long preface, having first asked for permission to digress for a little while from that most learned man <note>referring back to Giovanni Bernardo Feliciano, the recipient's uncle</note>. Almost all wise men, both ancient and modern (especially Aristotle in the eighth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physico auditu," the standard title for Aristotle's Physics in the Renaissance</note>), have seen fit to call man a **small world** <term>microcosm: the idea that the human body is a miniature reflection of the universe</term>, and an imitator of the celestial order in his entire essential structure, and especially in the arrangement of his limbs and their operations. I will try to explain to you in the course of this discourse the reasoning that moved them to say this.

And so that the explanation of the inquiry may proceed in an orderly fashion, it is worthwhile (it seems to me) to draw our beginning from the ideas of that same book, and first to briefly explain the sense or intent of the progression of the eighth book of the *Physics*: doing so, however, without causing offense to our Catholic faith <note>Massa is navigating a common Renaissance challenge: discussing Aristotle's theory that the universe is eternal while upholding the Christian belief that God created the world at a specific point in time</note>. 

Aristotle’s opinion or mind in said book, based on natural light <note>reasoning based on observation rather than divine revelation</note> and reasoning derived from the senses, was to prove that the **Mover** and **motion** are eternal. He also intended to prove certain conditions of this eternal mover: namely, its perpetuity, unity, indivisibility (or lack of parts), and infinity. To explain these things, he first proposes this question and asks whether motion is perpetual; finally, he strives to prove that it is perpetual through many arguments. This is so even though, in the first book of the *Topics* <note>original: "Topicorum," Aristotle's work on logic and debate</note>, he asserts that this is a **neutral problem** <term>a dialectical problem where arguments for and against are equally balanced, allowing for debate on either side</term>, so that a debater, by arguing through logic, could maintain that either the negative or the affirmative side is true. 

To prove this first intention, Aristotle relies on the authority of all the illustrious wise men of old who disputed concerning the beginning and eternity of the world. He assumes and affirms as a truth—one that no wise man doubts—that **Motion** exists. Next, concerning the question of the mover and the moved, he lists four opinions of the ancients: 

The first is the opinion of those who affirmed that infinite worlds are generated and destroyed, which cannot happen without motion; of these, some were being continually generated, and some were successively perishing, for generation and corruption <term>the Aristotelian terms for the process of things coming into being and passing away</term> cannot exist without motion. 

The second opinion belonged to those who asserted there is only one world, and that it is indeed perpetual. 

The third was the opinion of those who said the world was created, confirming that motion began at a certain time; yet they claimed that neither the world nor motion could end in the future, but would endure forever. For they said that all things lay hidden in chaos, which were later separated by God, and from this, the world and motion had their beginning.

## PART TWO

...stated. The fourth and final opinion was that of those who say the world is repeatedly restored and repeatedly destroyed, assigning two most powerful causes, namely: **strife** and **friendship** <note>original: "lite, & amicitia." These are the two cosmic forces proposed by the philosopher Empedocles</note>. For strife dissolves unity by separating things, while friendship constitutes one whole from many by bringing them together. But when neither friendship nor strife is at work, all things rest, and the processes of coming-into-being and passing-away <term>generation and corruption: the philosophical terms for birth/creation and death/destruction</term> cease. Aristotle intends to destroy and annihilate these four enumerated opinions in the first part of the book. 

To do this, he sets forth the definition of motion proven in other books, which is this: **Motion is the actuality of a movable thing insofar as it is movable.** <note>This is the classic definition found in Book III of Aristotle's Physics</note>. I omit the arguments destroying the opinions of the ancients, so that the discourse is not too drawn out, for indeed they are many. From these, he posits two conclusions: the first of these is, **Motion did not begin in such a way that there was no motion before it.** The second is: **Since motion was not created and does not begin, it will therefore never end.** 

For neither Anaxagoras nor Empedocles, who believed the world was created, proved it was created through reasoning. Indeed, since in the explanation of nature it is worthwhile to reveal everything through reason and also to adopt causes that are true causes—and since Anaxagoras did this not at all, nor Empedocles—they both certainly erred. For Anaxagoras posited certain fictions and assigned no cause at last for the delay in the world's creation <note>Aristotle's critique of Anaxagoras often centered on why Mind/Nous would wait an infinite time before suddenly starting to move the universe</note>. 

Likewise, Empedocles—who asserts that strife and friendship are the causes of the world's generation and corruption (without giving any reason)—was deceived, doubtless because he did not know that in the whole of nature there is nothing that lacks reason or order. Therefore, he concludes and says that when Anaxagoras believed things had rested for an infinite time and then began to move, he destroyed the order of infinite rest in relation to the infinite motion to come. In the same way, he rejects the outlandish words of Empedocles, although they were not uttered entirely without reason, since he posits that the world is generated and then destroyed, and rests in the intervening spaces of time. For such a process does not lack order, although he assigned no reason for his position. 

Having examined all these, Aristotle deletes and removes three arguments asserting that motion is not perpetual. I will relate these as briefly as I can, lest I become a burden to you, who understand all these things better than I. The first of the stated arguments was this: **Motion which is from one thing to its opposite can by no means be infinite.** The second is this: things which were never moved, either as a whole or in part (whatever they may be, whether animate or inanimate)...

...can at some point begin to be moved; in the same way, it could have happened in the universe—namely, that after the universe was at rest, motion began. Indeed, the third reason is that in which the title of our inquiry is contained, which I will strive to explain in a longer discourse so that it may be more clearly understood.

For Anaxagoras said—as reported by Aristotle, in order to persuade others that his opinion was true—that if animals move themselves after a long rest without any external mover pushing them (since they do not require an outside mover, but in fact move themselves), what prevents the universe from being able to begin its motion after a long rest, if we believe this occurs in the **tiny world** or the **minor world**? By the "smaller" or "tiny world," he meant man, since, according to the opinion of all illustrious wise men, other animals are inferior to humans. For man is the perfection and completion of animals.

And although this reasoning is rhetorical and seems plausible, and is very persuasive, nonetheless Aristotle most beautifully dilutes and rejects it. He argues that an animal is never truly without natural or voluntary motion; indeed, we know that even when an animal is sleeping, there are many internal motions within it. This could easily be proven if anyone wished to enumerate all the powers, virtues, and operations in an animal. 

Since an animal has within itself the power and motion of the **vegetative soul** <note>The "vegetative soul" was believed to be the part of the soul responsible for basic biological functions like growth and nutrition</note>, through which it first draws in nourishment and then converts it into the substance of the one nourished; and it also has the power and virtue through which the heart is agitated steadily and continually, so that while the animal lives, it moves without any intermission or notable rest; and it has other external and internal natural and voluntary motions. From this, we can easily recognize that an animal has within itself that which can move without an external mover. 

And although these virtues and operations are common to other living beings, they exist more nobly in man, so that man rests by himself and also moves by himself without any external mover. For that reason, the illustrious ancient sages and Aristotle in this book have called man a **small world** <term>microcosm: the ancient philosophical idea that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe, containing all its elements and principles</term>. Nor do the arguments of Empedocles—who said the world was newly made, and could be dissolved and made again—prove anything in this matter, if one correctly understands Aristotle's reasoning. 

But since I have strayed enough in explaining the intent of the first part of the eighth book of the **Physics** <note>original: "de physico auditu," a standard Latin title for Aristotle's work on nature</note>, these words will suffice. I say the "first part" because the intention of the whole book was to prove that there is one **first mover** <term>Prime Mover: the original, eternal source of all motion in the universe that is itself unmoved</term>, eternal and immovable, and also to prove the eternity of the first motion and the movable thing, but since (as I said)...

# PART TWO

Now that our discourse has wandered enough, let me return to my first purpose. We were asking, therefore, for what reason man was called a **tiny world** <note>original: "exiguus mundus," often referred to as the "microcosm," the idea that the human body reflects the structure of the entire universe</note> by the ancients; and from what was said a little earlier, it was decided to name him so because they compared the essential parts, operations, and movements of man with the parts and motion of the heavens, as I will show more clearly both at the conclusion of this speech and as we proceed. But to confirm this, let us discuss it more deeply, so that we too may see how we ought to compare man to the **greater world** <note>original: "maior mundus," the "macrocosm" or the universe at large</note>. For man possesses a certain divine nature given by the **supreme Craftsman** <note>A reference to God as the architect of the universe</note>—especially evident in the marvelous composition of his parts and the excellence of his powers and functions—by which he understands universal things. But before I declare this divine nature of man itself, it seems worth my while to describe the manner and order of his **generation** <term>generation: the process of conception and biological development</term>.

For the conception or generation of man proceeds in a certain admirable order. First, the male seed, fit for conception, is greedily drawn into the womb during the embrace. After this attraction, the womb gathers itself entirely around the seed, and the mouth of the womb is closed with a final constriction, so tight that not even the point of the finest needle could enter. There, it is mixed with the female seed, and they act upon one another with their own heats—either through the spirit born with them and the heat directed in both seeds by the **informative power** <term>informative power: the "uirtus informatiua," a biological force believed to shape the developing embryo</term>, with the heat or temperament of the womb also assisting, nourishing, and preserving the balance of both seeds. This power is more excellent and primary in the male seed. 

These seeds, thus mixed and acting upon each other through the aforementioned spirits and their heats (which are the instrument of the informative power for the generation of a living being), in the space of about six days, more or less, change the matter of the seeds into a consistency resembling milk or—as some prefer—**egg white** <note>original: "albuminis oui"</note>. From this change, the substance which physicians call the **fetus** is produced; and it is covered by a very thin membrane. During this same time, from the said mixing and action, there are generated and separated the **three spirits** necessary for the essence, growth, and preservation of the future animal: these are the **vital spirit**, the **animal spirit**, and the **natural spirit** <note>In Galenic medicine, "natural spirits" (from the liver) governed nutrition; "vital spirits" (from the heart) governed heat and life; and "animal spirits" (from the brain) governed sensation and movement</note>. 

Then, after the six days already counted, because the heat clearly acts upon the matter of the seed or fetus for the three following days and begins to dry it out in some way, the **attractive power** within the innate heat and the matter of the fetus begins to draw the purer parts of the **menstrual blood** from the neighboring veins. Thus, during these three days, the matter of the fetus changes in color toward redness...

[...constricts so tightly that it appears to have a] certain [shining], and three locations of the **principal organs** <note>The heart, liver, and brain, which Renaissance medicine considered the three pillars of the body</note> begin to appear, as if they were three points, or three bubbles, or small flasks displaying a certain brilliance. And there are (as I said) three locations of the said organs in which the **spirit** <term>spirit: or "pneuma," a subtle substance believed to carry life and function through the body</term> and the first **innate heat** <term>innate heat: "calor congenitus," the vital warmth present from birth that powers biological processes</term> in the seed—which is also called "implanted"—is founded, and remains always until death. The subject and foundation of this heat is the aforementioned spirit, which, being thus founded and positioned, gives life and functions to all parts; but the heart is the first to possess them. This priority is not one of time (in my opinion) but of nature.

Therefore, the matter of the fetus and the locations of the three principal organs having been thus prepared in nine completed days; in the next six days, that which had taken on a certain redness is changed and altered, so that it takes on the color of blood in every way. At this time the **umbilical vein** clearly appears formed, through which the attractive power of the fetus draws the purer blood from the **menstrual blood** <note>Early medical theory held that the fetus was nourished by the mother's retained menstrual blood</note>, so that around the fifteenth day, the matter of the fetus shows the color and substance of blood. 

As the action of heat and the informative power proceeds in the following twelve days, the matter changes and takes on the substance and likeness of unformed flesh; and even in the spine or vertebrae, the outlines clearly appear, and the locations of the three primary organs are clearly recognized. And all these changes through various times or spaces of days, by counting the days, occur over twenty-seven days; at which limit the fetus thus prepared is called an **embryo** <note>original: "embrio"</note> by physicians, and it lives the **life of a plant** <note>The "vegetative soul," the most basic level of life responsible for growth and nutrition</note>.

Then, in the next nine or ten days, distinct parts are seen, namely, the head, arms, shoulders, legs, and the remaining parts, all of which are jointed and extended. And thus the embryo, after it has reached this point (as I was saying before), lives not only the life of a plant, but also the **sensitive life** <note>The "animal soul," which grants the ability to feel and move</note>. This sense is not refined and clear, but dull, and this is because the excessive moisture with which the animal is generated dulls the sense and also makes the movement of the limbs difficult and sluggish. However, some of the ancient wise men say that the embryo, after another four days have passed following the said nine days, clearly feels and clearly moves; which time is a space of forty days. At this limit, the **rational soul** <note>original: "anima rationalis," the immortal and intellectual soul unique to humans</note> created by God, the glorious and blessed, is infused, as all theologians affirm together with philosophers and physicians. Truly, even if the embryo very often and for the most part in forty and for[ty-five days...]

<header>PART SECOND</header>

[...within] forty-five days it feels and moves; nevertheless, sometimes it feels and moves in thirty-five days, although this is rare, because (as I said) for the most part and in the majority of cases, it begins to feel and move in forty days, at which time it is also **formed by the rational soul** <note>original: "anima rationalis informatur." In Renaissance philosophy, the "rational soul" was the uniquely human part of the soul, believed to be infused by God after the physical body was sufficiently developed</note>. Therefore, the embryo, having been formed by the rational soul, is ruled and governed by the already mentioned infused soul. 

However, someone might ask me a doubting question: in what part does the rational soul reside, and what is the first underlying member or part that it occupies? I respond and say, along with **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose biological works were foundational for 16th-century medicine</note>: first in the **heart** and in the part contained within its own implanted or innate **spirit** <term>spirit: "spiritus," a subtle, vaporous substance believed to be the intermediary between the soul and the physical body</term>. This part is called "spirit" and is generated from the most noble and subtle part of the nourishing blood and is contained within the seed. Therefore, it is in this underlying spirit that the soul first resides, and the whole of it is diffused through the entire body along with the aforementioned spirit. 

Nor would I wish you to believe that the rational soul is not "entirely in the whole, and entirely in every part" <note>This was a standard theological and philosophical definition: the soul is not spread out like a liquid, but is fully present at every point in the body</note>, since it does not depend on matter but comes from outside; and yet, it is first in the heart, giving life and other operations. Nor is this contrary to the opinion of those who say the seat of the soul is the **brain**. Since I have already said that the soul is in the whole and in every part, it nonetheless has the spirit as its underlying subject within a certain determined range and power of the temperament of that spirit. This can be easily proven: for if the spirit of the heart is removed, or if it is somehow infected or corrupted so that it departs from the range of its own proper temperament, the soul will leave the human being, since its primary subject—through which it first gives form—is failing. 

But if someone, especially following the physicians like **Galen** <note>The most influential Roman physician, who argued that the brain was the center of sensation and movement</note> and others, wishes to affirm that the soul has its seat in the brain, I do not deny it, lest I seem argumentative. Although I know that all the senses are first manifested in the brain as if in an organ serving the soul, I cannot therefore affirm that the brain itself is the *primary* seat of the soul. For this reason, Aristotle’s opinion is more pleasing to me. 

Let these points mark the limit of our discussion on the subject of the soul; but let us speak of the rest, which pertains to the already-formed embryo as it comes toward the light of day. The embryo thus formed proceeds continuously in the growth of its members, taking nourishment through the **umbilical vein**, until the ninetieth day (if it was formed on the forty-fifth day), at which time it feels and moves most clearly. But if it is formed on the thirty-fifth day, it feels and moves clearly on the seventieth day. If, however, it is formed on the fortieth (as many believe)...
