...[they say] it is formed; in the eightieth day it manifestly feels and moves. But if anyone should ask why the embryo moves sluggishly on the thirty-fifth, fortieth, and forty-fifth day, I answered a little earlier that this is because all the members are more humid—especially the nerves, which are the instruments of sensation and motion. This humidity prevents the nerves from being able to feel and move properly. There is also much humidity in which we are born <note>This refers to the amniotic fluid and the "moist" nature of the womb in Galenic medicine</note> which in some way blunts the heat of the innate and sensitive **spirit** <term>spirit: "spiritus," a subtle, vaporous substance believed to be the intermediary between the soul and the physical body, carrying life-force and sensory information</term>, whereby their operation is rendered sluggish and weak. 

But as the embryo grows in the process—namely, after the first period of the formation by the **rational soul** <note>The "anima rationalis," the uniquely human soul that confers intellect, believed to be infused by God during pregnancy</note>, when it reaches a span of time double that of the said formation—during which earlier time and the remaining process, some have said the embryo rests, since it does not move in an altogether manifest way. This inability or sluggishness of movement can be called neither sleep nor wakefulness. For sleep is nothing other than a contraction of the sensitive faculty toward the interior parts of the body in an animal that actually exercises sensation while waking; whereby, once the natural heat is withdrawn and gathered inward, there follows a rest of the senses and a restoration of the **spirits** that were exhausted from labor. This is not necessary in the embryo existing in the womb, since there is no labor there, and no cause for the dissolution of heat or spirit. 

Furthermore, in the embryo, there is perpetual rest and no exhaustion, but a continuous drawing of nourishment through the umbilical vein, the generation of spirit, and the nutrition of the whole body. Therefore the embryo rests, and from what has been said, such rest can by no means be called sleep: for heat is not scattered for any reason (while the embryo is healthy) so as to be diminished and require a return of heat inward to restore and increase what was lost. Nor indeed is it wakefulness, since wakefulness is the release and outward exercise of sensation, as **Aristotle** <note>The 4th-century BCE philosopher whose works on biology and the soul were the standard university textbooks in Massa's time</note> said in his book *On Sensation and the Sensible* <note>original: "De Sensu et sensibili," one of Aristotle's "Short Physical Treatises" (Parva Naturalia)</note>. 

Indeed, in wakefulness, the soul commands the senses and their external powers. Thus the embryo rests, and neither sleeps nor wakes, according to the prescribed senses and reasons. There are also those who deny that the rational soul forms the embryo before manifest sensation and motion, which they say do not appear in a span of less than seventy days, and often beyond ninety. This opinion, however, is rejected by almost everyone, especially since many perceptive women recognize and feel the embryo moving in the womb on the thirty-fifth and fortieth day—which is most frequent—and even very often on the forty-fifth. But I wish enough to have been said of these things, and toward the embry[o]—

...so that the discourse may return to its completion. I was saying indeed that the embryo, after that first weak sense and motion—specifically in the span of seventy to ninety days—proceeds by increasing in size, mediated by nourishment drawn through the **umbilical vein** <term>umbilical vein: "vena umbilicalis," the vessel through which the fetus receives nutrient-rich blood from the mother</term>. This is a maximum span of three solar months, and a minimum of seventy days, during which time (as I said) it most clearly feels and moves. 

But in truth, a fact approved by all the wise and confirmed by pregnant and healthy women is that the male is formed in a shorter span of time, and the female in a longer one. Even though the female's exit from the womb may be hurried <note>Massa refers to the common belief that female infants might be born sooner but take longer to develop their "form" in utero</note>, it is because nature does not labor for so long a time toward her perfect completion, but a little less; hence it is that the female is called a **defective male** <note>original: "mas occasionatus"; an Aristotelian concept suggesting the female is a "misbegotten" version of the male, caused by a lack of generative heat</note> by the wise. 

Therefore, the embryo is sometimes formed on the thirty-fifth day if the strength of the seed is robust, and if the temperament, age, and a helpful warm region are favorable; and the female similarly in forty days, although this happens rarely and not frequently. These claims are proven by frequently observed **abortions** <note>The text uses "abortus" to mean any premature expulsion of the fetus</note>, both of males and females, if the aborted embryos are placed and washed in cold water. For in such immersion in water, all the members appear distinct, as do the remaining parts of the body; sense and motion also appear, for they certainly move when they feel the coldness of the water. At this sad sensation of cold, the embryo contracts into itself to flee from the thing contrary to its nature. 

Although all these things have been seen by the ancients and by ourselves, the time of preparation varies, so that it receives its form sometimes sooner and sometimes later. But after the initial shaping of the embryo, all the limbs, parts, and the entire body proceed by growing in the womb toward the perfection of the features and the figure or formation, up until the limit of three months. This time of formation is diverse and is not precisely the same in all cases, occurring sometimes on the thirtieth, and sometimes the thirty-fifth, or thirty-sixth, or fortieth, or forty-second, or forty-fifth, or forty-sixth, or even the fiftieth day, as some affirm regarding the formation of the female—which formation is without any doubt slower. Within this three-month period, the embryo moves most clearly, since it possesses a better shape and strength of the limbs. 

And to deal honestly with you, in my opinion, there is no one who can affirm the **precise time** <note>original: "punctuale tempus"; literally "point-like time"</note> of the perfection of preparation or formation, since in every conception there is a **latitude** <term>latitude: "latitudo," a medical and philosophical term referring to a range of acceptable variation rather than a fixed point</term>...

At that time, its nourishment was in some way withdrawn, since nature was striving to bring it forth into the light. And therefore, if it is born in the eighth month, since it is weak, it can rarely or never live long in our climate, but dies.

For often the <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which was believed to determine health and development</note> or the quality of the seeds is the cause of both brevity and slowness. ...semen of diminished heat and less (so to speak) spirited quality. On the contrary, in a person of warm temperament—such as those who are **sanguine** and **bilious** <note>In the medical theory of the four humors, sanguine (blood-dominant) and bilious/choleric (yellow bile-dominant) types were considered naturally warmer and more active</note> in whom the spirit abounds and whose actions are more vigorous—the time of conception and the perfection of the embryo’s formation will be accelerated. Furthermore, the previously mentioned humidity in some way dulls the heat of the sensitive and motive spirit, from which a sluggish and weak power is produced, and thus the shaping of the embryo will be delayed.

The same must be said regarding the various ages of life. For the semen of the elderly—who through the natural course of age have become cooled and dried out—is colder, and thus it is sluggish in performing the work of generation or conception. For this reason, the conceptions and formations of the elderly are slower, while those of the young are indeed shorter, since they are warmer. Indeed, those who are still growing possess a great deal of **innate heat** <note>term: calor innatus; the vital, life-giving heat that ancient physicians believed was central to metabolism and growth</note>, and consequently their semen possesses greater power, so that they can complete the development of a conception in a shorter time.

Geography also contributes much to this; for in warm regions (such as in Egypt and other hotter provinces), infants born in the eighth month survive, and many born in the seventh month are healthy and robust, which does not happen in cold regions. Moreover, the sky and the warm surrounding air strengthen all powers, especially the **natural powers** <note>The "natural virtues" were the biological forces responsible for nutrition, growth, and reproduction</note>. This ensures that the spirit—which is the instrument of the formative power—is warmer because of the surrounding and inhaled air, and is thus able to complete the conception better and faster according to its own temperament.

In colder regions, however, the opposite usually happens. Since the bodies living there have colder spirits, they are not able to prepare the matter of the fetus as quickly or complete the conception so that it may receive its form. Instead, the time of labor is sometimes extended to the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and even the fourteenth month.

When I was a young man in this most noble City <note>Massa refers to Venice, where he spent his career</note>, I saw a most noble Matron, nearly sixty years old, who had conceived with her most illustrious husband, who was himself an old man of nearly seventy years. I myself provided medical care to this distinguished woman, and I had judged that she was suffering from **water under the skin** <note>Edema</note>, or **ascites dropsy** <note>An accumulation of fluid in the abdomen (hydrops ascites). In an era before ultrasound, pregnancy in older women was frequently mistaken for this condition</note>.

She lay in her bed with a very swollen belly, suffering from loss of appetite, thirst, and other stomach ailments. Since she was thus in her "second old age," neither her relatives nor I suspected that she had conceived. At last, in the fifteenth month, she gave birth to a girl, deprived of eyes and with truncated hands, who lived for five months. And because this was such a miraculous event, an inquiry was made regarding the time when they [the couple] were together...

Thus the child, having been so increased and formed, once the space of seven months is complete, if he is strong and robust, he attempts to exit and come forth into the light. Secondly, because the air passing through the arteries of the embryo in the womb cannot properly vent the heart; for a pregnant mother cannot breathe in such a quantity of cold air that it would be suitable for tempering the heat of the embryo’s heart.

Add also another reason, which is that since the embryo has become larger, it needs a larger place or space, wherefore it seeks a larger space; and then, if it is robust, it exits. But if it is weak, remaining in the womb until the ninth month, it is regulated by the **formative power** <note>term: virtus informativa; the biological force believed to shape the physical body according to its specific form</note> along with the other powers serving it—such as the **nutritive power** <note>term: virtus nutritiva; the power responsible for the assimilation of food and growth</note> and the rest—as it awaits its exit. This power proceeds by providing nourishment, growth, and strength until the said ninth month, in which (as I have often said) women give birth successfully. Nevertheless, birth often proceeds to the tenth month and beyond (as you have heard) for the reasons stated.

Therefore, the child—complete and robust from the causes narrated and by the command of Blessed God—is moved naturally, and according to its own power given by the **unerring intelligence** <note>A Scholastic concept suggesting that nature, guided by God, possesses an innate "instinct" or "intelligence" to perform biological functions correctly</note> from the same Most High Blessed God. The **sacrum bone** <note>term: os sacrum; the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> at the back is also relaxed and yields to the embryo so that it may exit more easily. Thus far I have compared the formation and origin of the human body in the briefest way I could, and even compared it to the heaven or the "great world" through its form and certain operations; and I have said that man is the fulfillment and the end of divine operations. After the creation of man—which is truly a divine work—the glorious God ceased from the creation of the world and of all things that are in it, as the lawgiver Moses said in the first part of Genesis, when He had already perfected the ultimate intended purpose. Indeed, first He created heaven and earth and also light. <header>PART TWO</header>

## PART TWO

...made by the eternal creator himself and shaped by a <term>rational soul</term> <note>original: *anima rationalis*; the highest level of the soul, unique to humans, responsible for intellect and reason</note>, he exists as a counterpart to the world. This soul is the primary cause of all human movements and operations. For just as in the universe and the <term>great world</term> <note>original: *magno mundo* or macrocosm</note> there are diverse parts, and diverse operations and effects: so also in man, who is called the <term>small world</term> <note>original: *exiguus mundus* or microcosm</note>, there are parts proportional and similar to the parts of the greater world. And as I said a little while ago, there is in him first the rational soul, giving being and operations, which is similar to the <term>intelligence</term> <note>original: *intelligentia*; celestial beings or forces believed to move the stars and planets</note> that gives being and motion to the heavens. Furthermore, both the intelligence shaping the heaven and the soul shaping the man are directed and regulated by the first artisan <note>God</note> through his primary self, or through another medium. And just as the remaining parts of the greater world are the instruments of its operations, so also the parts of man are the instruments of human operations; therefore, it is most fitting that man, composed of a rational soul, be compared with the greater world or the heaven shaped by its own intelligence. For those things which are less noble are always said to exist for the sake of the more noble in the order of nature: for just as the lower intelligences of the heavens exist for the sake of the first and are subject to it, so the other forms of living things exist as inferior to the rational soul, and even (if I may say so) must naturally serve it and be subject to it. Moreover, the greater world has essential parts of which it consists, and these are the heavens shaped by their own intelligences with their powers and operations, which are the seats and tabernacles of the glorious God and the intelligences. Accordingly, there also exist in man more noble parts in which the rational soul first, then the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>responsible for perception and movement</note>, and lastly the <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>responsible for growth and nutrition</note> exist, serving the rational soul, and in which powers and operations are established. And the said soul has as its subject the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; subtle substances that acted as intermediaries between the soul and the physical body</note>, which are the natural, the animal, and also the vital: which spirits are shaped by an innate heat, or a natural heat contracted from the action and mixing of seeds, as I said before, in which spirits each soul resides with its powers. Furthermore, the figure of the greater world is round, as perceived by our senses: likewise, man is most conveniently contained within a circle. Indeed, if we wish to test this, we can easily adapt this round figure to a man; if we place one part of a compass on the site of the <term>pubic bone</term> <note>original: *ossis suminis*; likely referring to the pubic region or lower abdomen as the geometric center of the body</note> as if at a point or center, and we lead the other part of the compass around with the arms somewhat extended: you will see indeed that he can be very beautifully contained by a circular figure. Next, just as in the greater world there is nothing that is not, from every side, most beautifully...

<summary>Massa explains the "microcosm" theory, arguing that the human rational soul governs the body just as celestial intelligences govern the heavens. He further demonstrates this cosmic symmetry through the "Vitruvian" concept of the human body fitting perfectly within a circle.</summary>

<keywords>microcosm, macrocosm, rational soul, celestial intelligence, spirits, anatomy, Vitruvian man, geometry of the body, Niccolò Massa</keywords>

--- Page 757 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from page 183 of Niccolò Massa's *Epistolae Medicinales*. Massa is deepening his comparison between the "macrocosm" (the universe) and the "microcosm" (the human body). In the previous section, he established that both are governed by a rational force (God/Intelligence for the world, the Soul for the man). Here, he moves into the functional and elemental similarities between the two.</meta>

->THE MEDICAL LETTERS OF NICCOLÒ MASSA<-

...is placed, and even if it did not provide benefit, utility, and ornament, so also in man no part is so vile, nor so ignoble, that it is not for the utility, benefit, and ornament of the whole body. You will be able to prove this easily if you wish to call to memory those things which you have read in the book *On the Use of the Parts* written by <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician in Roman and medieval medicine; his work *De usu partium* explained how every part of the body was perfectly designed by nature for a specific function.</note>. Furthermore, all the members and parts have proportions and qualities for movement which are very similar to the movements of the celestial bodies, along with their benefits and utilities. For just as the <term>inferior spheres</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the "lower" planets like the Moon received power or influence from the "higher" spheres like the Sun or the fixed stars.</note> receive <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *uirtutem*; in this context, it refers to a specific power, vital force, or influence.</note> from the superior ones, so also in the <term>small world</term> <note>original: *pusillo mundo*; the microcosm, or the human being.</note>, the more ignoble parts receive virtue from the more noble ones; for example, they receive life from the heart, nutrition from the liver, and sense and motion from the brain. Therefore, if we weigh all that has been said, we will recognize the greatest similarity and <term>homogeneous nature</term> <note>meaning "of the same kind" or "sharing the same essence."</note> of man with the heaven or the <term>greater world</term> <note>the macrocosm, or the entire universe.</note>. Thus, if through moral art he purges himself of vices and those things which exist unlike the heaven, he will easily escape as a celestial being; for when he is thus removed from vices and reaches that brightness and purity of soul, he may even be able to understand supra-mundane and celestial things, and (as <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Spanish-Muslim philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> wrote in his preface to the <term>Physics</term> <note>original: *physico auditu*; Aristotle’s lectures on nature.</note>) be joined and united with the glorious God, and even understand Him. And by this reasoning, he may enjoy celestial beatitude and happiness in this life, and so be compared without controversy to the heaven or the greater world.

Furthermore, there are many other things in the heaven very similar to those which are in man, which we observe—such as the Sun and the remaining stars. And just as the Sun indeed bestows light upon all the rest and even provides the knowledge of things, so also the eyes of man perform the duty of the Sun in the small world. For they are placed in the upper part, namely so that they may provide us light for the knowledge of things; so that through them we may discern what is necessary to follow or what to flee. And just as in the greater world there are <term>four elements</term> <note>The classic building blocks of the universe: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>—namely fire, air, water, and earth—from which all things in the inferior part consist (since nature generates all other composite things from them as from underlying matter), so also in the small world there are <term>four humors</term> <note>original: *humores*; the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note>, namely: <term>bile</term> <note>original: *bilis*; specifically yellow bile or choler.</note>, blood, <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *pituita*.</note>, and <term>black bile</term> <note>original: *atra bilis*; also known as melancholy.</note>, from which all parts of our body consist. Indeed, these humors are proportioned to the four said elements. Furthermore, <term>choler</term> <note>original: *cholera*; yellow bile.</note> or yellow bile exists as most similar to fire, since it is subtle, light, hot, and dry; <term>blood</term>, however, is proportioned to air, since it has a substance midway between the remaining humors, and is indeed hot and moist; while <term>phlegm</term> is truly like water...

<summary>Massa explains the functional correspondence between the human body (microcosm) and the universe (macrocosm), comparing organs to celestial spheres and bodily humors to the four elements.</summary>
<keywords>microcosm, macrocosm, Galen, Averroes, four humors, four elements, yellow bile, blood, phlegm, celestial spheres</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Niccolò Massa's letter, rounding off his discussion of the "microcosm" (the human body) versus the "macrocosm" (the universe). The text transitions from discussing the primary organs to describing the humors—the bodily fluids—and how they correspond to the physical elements of the world. It then concludes with a personal address to the recipient, Bernardino, regarding his uncle.</meta>

### P A R T  T W O .

...exists, for its substance is remarkably soft, as well as cold and humid, containing a certain whiteness. Finally, black bile, or <term>melancholy</term> <note>One of the four humors in ancient medicine, associated with the element of earth and a temperament that is serious or somber.</note>, corresponds in its substance and qualities to the nature of the earth, since it is more material, heavier, colder, and drier than the other <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which Renaissance physicians believed governed health and personality.</note>. Furthermore, the lower belly and the other cavities bear a resemblance to the sea and other lakes and ponds, doubtless because the excremental humidities of the entire body, and others as well, are for the most part contained there; and indeed these have an entrance into them and an exit from them, toward which all <term>superfluities</term> <note>Waste products or excess fluids that the body must expel to maintain health.</note> are pushed, such as evacuations, sputum, <term>catarrhs</term> <note>original: *destillationes*; the downward flow of fluids, often from the head or brain, thought to cause various illnesses.</note>, and other similar excrements. These can be compared with the rains, meteorological phenomena, and other "imperfect mixtures" <note>In Aristotelian science, "imperfect mixtures" were transient phenomena like clouds, rainbows, or snow, as opposed to "perfect" lasting substances like minerals.</note> of the greater world. 

Why say more? Just as in the heavens, or in the greater world, there exists a marvelous order of parts and a composition of all things which show the admirable omnipotence and wisdom of God—so that nothing further or better could be adapted or put to work—this is surely the ultimate and most perfect comparison of man to the <term>machine of the world</term> <note>original: *mundi machinam*; a common Renaissance metaphor describing the universe as a beautifully designed and complex mechanism created by God.</note>. Ancient <term>architects</term> <note>A reference to the tradition, famously noted by Vitruvius, that the proportions of sacred temples should be modeled after the proportions of the human body.</note> very much followed this observation and measurement, especially in the construction of divine temples. For just as the eternal and blessed God exists as the prince and ruler of all things that are in the world, so too the intellect exists as the prince within us; it gives being and commands all parts. 

However, since the hour is now late, I will not delay you any longer; at another time, if the occasion is given, we shall have a longer conversation about these matters. These are the things, Bernardino, that I discussed that day with your most learned and not sufficiently praised uncle; and lest such a praiseworthy conversation remain dormant, I wished to write to you at present what was said during it. This shall be as a certain testimony for posterity of the singular love of so dear a friend toward me, and of my respect for him. Enough, therefore, has been said for the present. It will be your part to imitate his most holy character, life, and doctrine. Farewell, and love me as you do. **1556.** In the month of January.
